consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when all goods are given in dowry, the right of patronage, which was held by the woman giving all her goods in dowry, is also deemed to have been given.
2. The right of patronage passes with the universality [of the estate]; it is transmissible and assignable. And number 5.
3. A dowry is a universal thing.
4. The universality contained in the donation of all goods is included.
5. Whether a pact, by which the bishop does not present due to the lapse of time, is valid.
6. A monk has no will, neither to will nor to refuse, without the license of the Abbot; hence he cannot execute what is entrusted to him without his license.
7. The right of patronage, as regards the power of presentation, descends gradually in successive order to descendants.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.
Whether a woman, by giving all her goods and rights which she has in dowry, appears to grant the right of patronage together with such a universality, may be doubted. And it seems that she does.

First, because the right of patronage passes with the universitas. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis; D. de acquisitione rei donatae, l. quaedam. Second: because the right of patronage of a church or hospital passes even to an extraneous heir. 16 q. 7, c. Considerandum, and the glosses there noted. Therefore, if it is transmissible, it is also cessible. D. de administratione tutorum, l. ex pluribus. Third: because a woman who gives a dowry still remains, in terms of legal understanding, the owner. C. de iure dotis, l. in rebus; D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. sciendum, namely, by name. Hence, the title of dowry is not expropriative of ownership, but rather commissive. And it seems that this commission could be made more easily than expropriation, so to speak. See also Extravagantes de re iudicata, c. Cum Bertoldus; D. de iure patronatus, c. Ex litteris.
† For dowry is also a universal thing, as is noted in the law "quod dicitur" on expenses.

† Moreover, the term “all goods” includes universitates. D. ad Trebellianum, l. cogi. To the contrary, it appears that the term “goods,” when used by a person, does not properly signify a universitas. D. de iure dotis, l. mulier bona; nor do rights inseparable from the person pass by title of dowry. D. de iure dotis, l. si mulier. To the same effect are l. si pronomen and l. quia perinde. Also to the same effect is what Innocentius notes in the cited c. ex literis, for he states that spiritual rights, which are abstracted from temporal things, are never included under the term “rights,” unless there is a special mention of them and the efficient cause is capable, which is noteworthy according to him.

But mixed rights, such as the right of patronage, Innocentius says do not pass with a certain thing, for example, with the Botrian estate; but with a universality, he distinguishes. Either it is something universal by reason of a universal sign, or by reason of a universal thing. In the first case, as when I say, I sell all the possessions of such a village, and the rights which are there from him: the right of patronage does not pass. In the second case it passes: as in the case of an heir, according to Innocentius. The reason for the difference is that a genus is resolved into singularities. And therefore a genus does not import more than an enumeration of species. L. si chorus, de leg. 3. But a universality is not resolved into singularities, as C. de euic. l. 1, according to Innocentius. But certainly in our case mention was made of an inheritance, and thus it is a universal grant. And therefore it seems that the right of patronage passed, as the dotal right with the universality of the inheritance. It is said, however, that it returned to the woman, sol. ma. The truer view is that this right of patronage, according to the form of the agreements, is restricted to the children. And therefore it cannot be ceded to outsiders. L. 1, de bon. lib. de ritu nup. L. non solum, §. si puellae.

But if he neglects to present, can the bishop freely appoint a rector there? It seems not, on account of the agreement, since it states "notwithstanding the lapse of time." For this law could be said to apply to one's own right. Argument: Digest, On the Edict of the Aediles, law *Quod si nolit*, section *Si*. To the contrary: because the time for presentation is established for the public good, so that sacred places may not remain vacant. Hence, one cannot renounce it. Digest, On Agreements, law *Ius publicum*; nor can the form established from ancient times be changed. Digest, On the Administration of Guardianships, law *Quidam decedens*, which I believe to be true. Argument: Code, On Bishops and Clerics, *Autem*; although the testator. And in this case, the agreement that it could not be revoked at the will of the patron has no place. Argument: from that which is noted in question 17, question 3, chapter *Frater*.

† On another point, it must be said that a cloistered monk does not have the will to do or not to do without the permission of the abbot; nor can he carry out what has been entrusted to him. 12. q. 1. c. non dicatis. c. vlti. de test. lib. 6. cum sim. On another point, it must be said,

† that the right of patronage, insofar as it concerns the power of presentation, descends to the descendants in a successive order; and the son and the grandson from him do not concur. 16. q. ult. c. filiis. arg. de leg. 2. l. peto. §. fratre. and ff. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus. §. quidam recte. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A dowry advanced by the father returns to the father by virtue of the father’s stipulation.
2. A statute feigning that a dowry was given from the woman’s property does not hinder the father of the woman from stipulating that the dowry be returned to him.
3. A filiafamilias has an heir in the dowry.
4. The words of the notary are the words of the parties.
5. Against a presumption of law, and as a matter of law, proof to the contrary is admitted by the confession of a party.
6. In oaths, the light of truth, and not the dream of fiction, must be examined.
body:
The facts are as follows. John of Vanni of the Castle of Cortiano, constituted before the judge of civil causes of the City of Camerino, in the presence and with the consent of his nearest blood relatives in the degree, with the authority of the said judge, and having solemnly taken an oath, confessed and declared himself well satisfied that he had held and received from Jordan Corradi of the Burg of Saint Venantius, as dowry and in the name of Saint, daughter of the said Jordan and wife of the said John, 400 pounds of denarii of the currency now current, with renunciations and other stipulations. Moreover, the said John, before the said judge and in the presence of the said blood relatives, promised to the said Jordan, stipulating and receiving for himself and his heirs: if the marriage which was to be between the said John and Saint should be dissolved by divorce, death, or in any other manner without legitimate children, or with legitimate children not reaching the age of 25 years, according to the form and custom of the said city, immediately upon the dissolution of the said marriage, without awaiting the legal year, in every case of restitution of the dowry, to give, render, and restore the said dowry in full and effectively; for which dowry to be rendered in the case of restitution, he bound his goods and so forth.

Now it has happened that the said marriage was consummated by carnal copulation, and afterwards was dissolved by the death of the said Saint, with Marino, their common son, surviving. And afterwards, the said Marino died at the age of 8 years, with the said Jordan, his grandfather and the one who provided the dowry for the said Saint, his daughter, from his own proper goods, surviving, since this Saint had not, nor did she have, any goods of her own, and with the said John, father of the said Marino, surviving. Now the said Jordan, by virtue of the said stipulation, and of the dotal instrument and agreements, demands the said dowry in full from the said John. It is asked first, whether the said John is bound to make the full payment of the said dowries to the said Jordan, having regard to the dotal instrument and the state of affairs, and so forth.

† In law, it is certain that the tenor of a paternal stipulation provides that a dowry originating from the father shall revert to the father. C. de rei uxoriis actione, l. rem in praesenti; §. accidit, C. de communi utriusque iudicii, l. si; so. ma. l. dos a patre, C. de pactis conventis, l. ex morte; ff. so. ma. l. quotiens. And therefore, according to the common law, he who gave the dowry may recover it.

But let us see whether the statute, which fakes a dowry given from the wife's property, hinders the father of the wife, and it seems that it does. For when a daughter is dowered from her own property, the father cannot stipulate for himself. Rather, he is bound to remit the rights of stipulation to the heirs of the daughter. D. 35.1.15 § pater naturalis.

† Since, therefore, the daughter has an heir in the dowry, ff. de iure dotis, whose father must be repelled by her sons, per Auth. de haereditate ab intestato § 1, and again, when the children are dead, their father, not the grandfather, succeeds, as in Auth. de funere and in l. si infanti cum si. To the contrary it seems: because even he who counts another’s money can sue on the stipulation. C. si certum petatur l. si and l. non unde originem. Also, because the instrument states that it is customary to stipulate in this way, whence the instrument and the custom are upheld. arg. si certum petatur l. certi condictio § si nummos. And the custom is proved by the assertion of the parties: because they so confessed in the instrument. C. de contrahenda stipulatione l. optimam. C. de iure deliberandi l. cum aliquis.

† For the words of the notary are the words of the parties. As is noted in the Digest, under the title "De verborum obligationibus," in the law "Sciendum." Solution. I believe the agreement must be observed.

For although the statute, under that word, is understood to introduce a presumption of law, and a legal presumption in favor of the woman, nevertheless, to the prejudice of the promisor, his confession and agreement are upheld, as in § Aliud, in the Authentica De aequali dote, and in the Codex De dote antenuptiali, Authentica Sed iam necesse, according to Cynus. The objection from § Pater naturalis does not hold, because there the truth appeared, which cannot be overturned by confession, as is known in law and fact, L. Cum falsa. Although a presumption may be rebutted by a contrary confession made, yet the confession is not said to be erroneous by reason of a legal presumption, which is noteworthy. The conclusion, therefore, is that the instrument must be upheld, Extra, De pace, C. 1, and especially on account of the oath appended.

† For in oaths the light of truth is examined, not the dream of fiction. C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si; C. de nuptiis, auth. quod eius, with similar authorities. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The clause, that if the thing is worth more, from now on the seller donates it to the buyer: what effect it produces.
2. In the forum of conscience we stand by the truth, in the judicial forum by the written documents.
3. A confession made in the absence of the party creates an indication, which, when joined with other supporting evidence, proves the case.
4. A strong supporting evidence completes half-proof.
body: The case is as follows. Sidam Petrutius, by his own right and in perpetuity, sold and delivered to Petrutius, son of Peter of Alexandrinis of Viterbo, a certain vineyard of his situated in the territory of the City of Viterbo near its boundaries, for the price of four hundred and fifty pounds of good small denarii. The entire price, the said seller confessed to having received from the said buyer. And knowing that the thing sold was worth more and of greater value than the aforementioned price, he, the seller, freely, purely, and simply donated, among the living, that which was worth more and of greater value than the said price, for many favors, merits, and services which the said seller confessed to having received from the buyer. Concerning the possession of the thing sold, the same seller promised to give and deliver it, etc., and in the meantime constituted himself as holding it precariously for him, etc., and granted him license to enter, etc., and made Stephen Iuci Morelli, present there, his procurator to decide and deliver possession of the thing sold, etc. And on the same thousandth year and day, the same Petrutius, son of Peter, by himself, his heirs, and successors, out of certain knowledge and not by error, promised and agreed upon the price with Petrutius, late of Iucius Lauren., the aforementioned seller, present and legitimately stipulating for himself, his heirs, and successors, that the said vineyard situated within the aforementioned boundaries, sold to Petrutius, son of Peter, by the said Petrutius, son of Iucius, for the price and in the name of the price of four hundred pounds of small denarii, according to which it was openly asserted that there existed a public instrument in the hand of Peter Macharonis, public notary of Viterbo. Hence, within the next seven months, to sell to the said Petrutius, son of Iucius, or his heirs and successors, by his own right and in perpetuity, for the price and in the name of the price of four hundred and fifty small pounds; and to release to him freely and absolutely; and to make a care, or else a suitable charter of caution, to the sense of the wise man Petrucius Iucius, with all opportune clauses. And therefore, for all and each of the aforementioned matters to be attended to and firmly observed, the said Petrutius, son of Peter, obligated himself personally to the same Petrutius, son of Iucius, present and legitimately stipulating, in Viterbo and Rome, wherever of places and lands, and wherever he should find him to be sued and wish to sue and demand from him there, that the aforementioned vineyard at the time of the aforementioned sale was of the value and estimation of one thousand pounds and more, and that for so much it was truly sold at that time, and that it is also worth so much today.

† Now it is asked, what is the law, whether the said sale was valid or not. The sale made to Petrutius by the lord Peter is highly suspect: on account of the smallness of the price, and on account of the promise of repurchase. And although there is a clause of donation, nevertheless the interpretation of prudent men has broken down this captious liberality. D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana. It is proved: because this clause does not apply, except to a small sum: but not where there was deception beyond half of the just price. As D. de verbis significandis, l. hæc venditio; D. de legatis 2, l. cum filius, §. pater. Nor does it accord with good men that such enormous enrichment should occur to the loss of another. As noted in D. de regulis iuris, l. semper. Nor is it likely that there was an intention to donate, where a pact of restitution was appended. Arg. D. de solutionibus, l. qui sic solvit.

On the contrary, it seems. For since the seller knows the value of the thing, the aid of the law 2, C. de rescindenda venditione, does not avail him; rather, the sale is valid, and he cannot revoke it. As noted in l. 2 and l. quisquis, C. de rescindenda venditione. The pact of repurchase is not an obstacle: because it was for a time, and the time has ended; hence the sale remained free, and the donation free. C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. 2.

Solution, according to Bartolus, may be brought forward. D. l. 2, to rescind or to supplement: because that clause of donation seems to have been appended in great lesion by error: because no one is presumed to squander his own property. L. cum de indebito, de probationibus.

On the contrary, it seems: because the said clause must have some effect. But in a small sum, this clause is not necessary. D. de minoribus, l. in causa. Therefore, it must be extended to a large sum, so that it may have some effect. Moreover, in the instrument mention is made of knowledge. But if he knew, let the seller impute it to himself. D. si quis cautio, l. sed et si quis, §. si. Which I believe to be true. Nor do we have sufficient indications to the contrary, which are set forth in Extravagantes de contrahenda emptione, c. ad nostram; and de pignoribus, c. illo vos. And according to Cynus, C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione. Therefore, as a matter of law, this buyer cannot be compelled to restore. Arg. D. de verbis obligatorum, l. si ita quis, §. Seya.

But in the forum of conscience, one must adhere to the truth. In the forum of judgment, however, it is necessary that we observe the written documents, as stated in the Code, On Proof, in the law *Cum precibus*, together with the law *Cum si*. Nevertheless, if other evidence were proven, or if the confession of the aforementioned colorable purchaser that it was a pledge were established, this would suffice.
† for a confession, even if made in the absence of a party, creates an indication, and, when joined with other indications, fully proves or strongly corroborates:

† and a strong supporting argument completes half-proof. D. de edict. edict. l. quæro. §. si. and Extr. de succ. ab intest. c. dilectus. where there is a notable text. And if it is proved that the receiver was accustomed to receiving similar instruments in fraud of usury, that too would weigh heavily against him: because in the same kind of fault, a person who is often wicked is always presumed to be wicked. In the legal rule: semel malus, etc. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A son bringing an action for his mother’s unpaid dowry is met with the defense of the thirty-year prescription and beyond; yet restitution is granted if the party against whom the prescription runs was a minor.
2. A personal action under the ius commune is prescribed by thirty years.
3. A hypothec is prescribed by forty years.
4. A bona fide possession, under canon law, never prescribes.
5. The longest time that is to be called.
body: The facts are as follows. Lucius Pidam promised a dowry for his daughter Francisca. Both Lucius and Francisca have since died. First, it is said that Francisca left behind a son; afterwards, Lucius, her father, also died. Now, the aforementioned son of the said Francisca seeks execution of the said instrument, alleging that the said dowry was never paid. The exception of prescription of thirty-five years, or more, is raised against him.
† It is asked whether it should be an obstacle or not: having seen the said dowry instrument, and having seen the statutes of the city of Orvieto.

† Under the common law, the period of prescription for a personal action is thirty years. C. de praescrip. 30. anno. l. sicut. However, this person, who was injured while in minority and is now under the age of 28, may seek restitution in integrum, as noted in l. si. C. qui. cau. in inte. resti. non est ne.

† But if he were bringing a hypothecary action, the prescription would not have run: because forty years are required when the debtor possesses the hypothecated things. C. de praescri. 30. an. l. cum notissimi. And this is true according to civil law. But according to canon law.
† A possessor in bad faith never acquires by prescription. c. 2. de reg. iu. li. 6. But under municipal law, it appears that a very long period of time is required,

† And the law speaks variously of a very long time. For sometimes it will say "very long," i.e., 100 years; sometimes "longer," i.e., 40 years; sometimes "long," i.e., 30 years. C. de sac. san. eccle. l. fi. and note Azo in Summa C. de praescri. 30. anno. But I say that this statute does not apply to our case: because here the son is acting on the basis of a promise made by his father, not by his dowered mother. And thus we have decided in the ius commune, which provided as I said above. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, l. V. D.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The bishop cannot appoint rectors of the hospital without the consent and license of the said hospital, which has existed for one hundred years and more; nor is a fourth part of the property left to such hospital due to him.
body: Certain citizens of Amelia, for one hundred years and more, established in the said city of Amelia, in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a certain fraternity of laymen, which was called and is called the Fraternity of St. Mary. The members of the said fraternity established a certain hospital in the said city without the consent or authority of the bishop. And in the said hospital they appointed a rector and elders to govern and administer the said hospital, and to receive the said poor and pilgrims into the said hospital. And they have done all these things for one hundred years and more, without the license of the said bishop. Nor was there, nor is there, any altar in the said hospital. The said hospital, however, has been augmented by reason of bequests and legacies made to it. Now the said bishop wishes to appoint and install the said rectors in the said hospital. And he commands, under pain of excommunication, those who elect or accept, that they shall not elect or accept the said office without the express consent or license of the said bishop. Furthermore, the said bishop claims the fourth part of the bequests made to the said hospital. It is asked

† Question of law: whether the said bishop ought to have the said fourth part, and whether he can claim by right the right of appointing a rector in the said hospital, or any other right. I say that the fourth part is not due to the bishop from the aforementioned bequests according to the common law. For, by reason of persons, the fourth part is not due to the bishop according to the common law, as states Ala. and the gloss in Extra, De sepultura, c. 2. Nor by reason of place: because the place is profane, and not under the institution or visitation of the bishop; because it is not of public law, but of private persons. D. Si servi venditi, l. Testatrix, § Plures. And thus I said in l. Si quis ad declinandam, C. De episcopis et clericis. Also Extra, De relictis domibus, c. Ad hoc. And note in Inst. in c. Inter dilectos, De donationibus, since the fourth part is not due from bequests made to exempt places, as Innocentius notes in Extra, De testamento, c. Officium. And because such a college, which is established for the sake of piety, is lawful and approved by law, as in l. 1, De collegiis illicitis. I do not deny, however, that, as it seems, the bishop may in general repel the receivers and compel them to distribute to the poor, and on account of dilapidation alone may order that they be removed and other administrators appointed by those to whom, according to the statutes of their confraternity, the election pertains. Not that the bishop himself institutes, or has the power of institution. Argument to this effect: D. Ad Trebellianum, l. 1, § Imperator; D. Si solutum, l. Si cum dotem, § Si autem in severissimo. And thus I say and advise, I, Balde of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An agreement concerning the inheritance of a living person is invalid, for the parties to the agreement lose the right which they have.
2. To whom the inheritance, concerning which an agreement was made during the lifetime of the person whose estate is in question, should be assigned.
3. Add the opinion in the fifth part beginning "in the case above mentioned."
body: The point is as follows: A certain Fra. Herculant of Cortouio was instituted as a vulgar and pupillary substitute for Bonaventure John of Cortonio in the testament of the said John. After the inheritance of the said John had been accepted by the said Bonaventure, and while the said Bonaventure was still living, unaware, and without any necessity of a preliminary contract, he made an agreement with Matthew, son of Lady Metalda, together with the said Fra. (who was the substitute for the said Bonaventure) concerning the inheritance of the said Bonaventure, who was then living: namely, to share it among themselves and to divide it equally, whichever of them should come into possession of the said inheritance. Subsequently, the said Bonaventure died. It is asked whether the parties to the agreement lost their rights, if any, which they could have claimed in the inheritance of Bonaventure by virtue of the aforementioned substitution or any other cause; and if they did lose them, to whom do they devolve? Do they go to the fisc, or to those who would succeed the said Bonaventure intestate? It is asked what the law is. And so forth.

† Assuming the invalidity of the said agreement, since it is disapproved by law to contract regarding the inheritance of a living person, whether pupillary or obligatory, and not by necessity of some preceding contract, without the consent of the owner, by whatever species of contract. C. de pac. l. si. de dona. ff. quidam in iure. with the following law. Nor can there be any doubt about the loss of the hereditary right pertaining to those making the agreement: because they lose it, as stated in the aforementioned law quidam. with the following law, and l. 2. §. si. ff. de his quibus vt indi. and notably in the aforementioned law si. C. de pac. on the word "observe."

† There remains only the doubt as to whom the inheritance, which is brought into such an agreement, should be applied: whether to the fisc or to the legitimate heir of the said Bonaventura, who is a legitimate heir outside the persons of the said parties to the agreement. And it seems that it should be applied to the fisc: because it is taken away from the aforementioned substitute as unworthy; therefore, according to the rule, it seems it should be applied to the fisc, as in *l. Papinianus*, § *meminisse*, *de inofficioso testamento*, joined with *d. l. quidam*, § *si*, with the following law, *de donis*. And this is what the gloss there holds, as the text seems to indicate in *d. l. 2*, in the end, *de his quibus ut indignis*, by continuing the last response of the said law to the response before the penultimate one. For that connective term "idem" [the same] imports that it cannot be continued to the nearest, therefore it must be continued to the remote ones to which the continuation can be adapted. *C. de libris praeteritis*, *l. 1*; *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, *l. si idem cum eodem*, § *si*.

On the other hand, it seems to be inferred by reasons that the aforementioned inheritance is due to the legitimate heir of the said Bonaventura, and not to the fisc, in the terms of the proposed question, in which it is proposed that the pupillary substitute entered into an agreement regarding the receiving and dividing of the pupil's inheritance with an outsider, from which results an offense to a certain person, namely the pupil, whose life is considered to be endangered by the said agreement, as in *d. l. si*, *C. de pace*. And it can be said to have been inflicted on the testator and on the heir in various respects, just as pupillary tablets can be called the testament of the father and of the son, as in *d. l. Papinianus*, § *sed nec impuberes*, and *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, *l. patris et filii*. From which it is inferred that the said inheritance should be applied to the legitimate heir, for several reasons.

And first, with respect to the fact that pupillary tablets are considered the testament of the son, as induced by *l. 3*, § *finalis*, *de aditione legis*, and *de his qui ut indigni*, *l. si inimicitiae*, because from the loss of the legacy resulting from the offense done to the testator after the testament, nothing is acquired by the fisc, but by the heir of the one who left it, as if from presumed enmity, as in *d. l. 3*, § *fin.*, and *d. l. si inimicitiae*. And in the case at hand, there is such a loss of the said legacy, since it results from an offense done against the testator himself while living, with respect to the fact that pupillary tablets are the testament of the son, as has been said above, arguing from *ff. de vulgari et pupillari*, *l. ex facto*. For it would be unjust that the power attributed to the father to make a testament for the son should prejudice him in future events, and that the disposition should not be varied by a supervening cause, by which the son himself would presumably vary it, if he could, as in *d. l. ex facto*, and arguing from *C. de inofficioso testamento*, *l. 2*; *ff. de pace*, *l. tale pactum*, § *finali*.

Secondly, the same is proven, whatever law considers the pupillary tablets, *l. ab hostibus*, § *finalis*, *ff. solutione matrimonii*, because when a profit comes to be received from the disposition of a man, then an offense committed against him, from whose disposition or from whom it comes to be received, results in the loss of the profit to be applied rather to the offended party and his heir than to the fisc, as in the said *l. si ab hostibus*, § *finalis*.

Thirdly, the same is concluded, with respect to the fact that pupillary tablets are the testament of the father, from the fact that the said offense appears to have been inflicted on a certain person, namely, on the pupil himself, to whom the substitution was made. And consequently, just as that which is lost from an offense inflicted on the person of the heir is not applied to the fisc, but remains with the offended party himself or his heir, the aforementioned substitution is evacuated with effect, just as a legacy is evacuated in the terms of the aforementioned laws, from the same parity of reason, that it remains with him, it is shown, rather than being transferred to another.

From all of which it is concluded that the said inheritance is undoubtedly to be taken away from the aforementioned substitute and applied either to the fisc by the first aforementioned reasons, or to the legitimate heir of the said pupil, the aforementioned substitution being evacuated, by the second reasons, which seems more equitable and reasonable, and more in the interest of the offended pupil. And holding the second part, it can be answered to the laws induced for the first part that it is not determined to whom the inheritance is sought or from whose cause it is lost, but only of the loss itself, and the glosses determining the contrary are to be understood so that they do not contradict the said rules, namely, in the case where the inheritance does not differ from the disposition of a man, but of the law. In which case, that which is lost from an offense done to the deceased is applied to the fisc, *ff. de bonis damnatorum*, *l. cum ideo*, in the end, which does not happen when it is taken from the disposition of a man, as in *d. l. si ab hostibus*, § *fin.*, and the others alleged above. And according to the said mode, he distinguishes the said matter, in which the laws are varied and of difficult solution. Bartolus de Saxo Ferrato. Thus he wrote in *l. si*, *ff. de his quibus ut indigni*. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a daughter under the paternal power can sue her mother for the adventitious dowry without the father's consent: and the said matter is in court.
body: The point is as follows. Lady A., a daughter and under the power of her father, a woman of full age, after the death of her husband, one year later, through her procurator in court, demanded the dowry constituted for her by a stranger, which the stranger had stipulated, or had been stipulated, to be restored to the said Lady A. and to her heirs in the case of the restitution of the dowries. It is objected against her that she could not be in court, nor can she be without the consent of her father; whose father's absence in court, nor that the said attempt was made nor approved, was not proven. And that the judgment was null from the beginning. It is asked from the premises, what the law is, whether the said daughter could demand the said dowries by herself, or through a procurator, without the consent of her father: and whether the judgment was null from the beginning, or should be annulled. This question is doubtful due to contrary opinions concerning it.

For some say that in the recovery of an adventitious dowry, the father’s consent is not said to be necessary; and this is a special rule in favor of the dowry, as I note in ff. sol. ma. l. 2. §. si in patris. C. de calum. auth. quod locum. and Auth. de aequa. do. §. pe. Others say that the father’s true consent is required if the father is present, or absent in a nearby place, whose presence can be obtained quickly, and without delay or procrastination. But if he is absent from afar, then he is either to be interpreted as consenting tacitly, or the daughter’s license by law suffices. Hence Dy. holds that in court, if the father is present, his consent is required, as he himself notes in l. non solum. so. ma. and the same there by Ray. de For. The same is held by Iac. de Are. in auth. quod locum. They say that in adventitious property the father’s consent is always required in bringing an action, although not in receiving payment. I, however, consider two times and two cases in the dowry. The first case is during the subsistence of the marriage: at this time the father has no usufruct in the adventitious dowry, because it is not burdened by the obligations of marriage. The second time is after the dissolution of the marriage. At this time, as long as the dowry is not burdened by any obligations, I see that the father ought to have usufruct, according to the general rule, l. 1. de bonis maternis. and C. de bonis quae lib. l. 1. and 2. donec. n. non seruit alijs onerib. Why, then, would the father be excluded from the right of usufruct? Certainly he does not seem to be excluded, as long as the reason for exclusion ceases, where it is said that, since the dowry is destined by number, it seems to contradict the effect of the giver that the father should be denied usufruct. Argument: C. de bonis quae lib. auth. excipitur. There are also two cases. First, when the husband began to misuse his property; certainly at this time the father has no usufruct, because it is still burdened by the obligations of marriage. Hence, because the father has neither right nor exercise, and the action and exercise belong fully to the daughter, the judgment is valid, even though the father’s consent has not been given. But our question asks about an adventitious dowry after the marriage has already been dissolved. Hence, if the father is entitled to the usufruct, the action brought by the daughter is improperly instituted by an incompetent person. Hence the judgment is null by operation of law, as in l. non solum. §. necessitatem. de bonis quam lib. For I do not find that in the dowry there is always a special rule. And in auth. quod locum., which speaks when the dowry is recovered during the subsistence of the marriage, in which case and time the father has no right in it, outside those cases, that auth. also seems to remain under the general rule of that §. necessitatem only. Because the glossators commonly say that in an adventitious dowry it is special, so that the father’s consent is not required. I dare not depart from the glossators, and this is held by Iaco. de Belui. in Authen. de equa. do. §. pe., who says that in an adventitious dowry the father is not entitled to usufruct, although regularly it is otherwise in other adventitious properties. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the sentence of two arbitrators is valid notwithstanding the absence of the third who maliciously absents himself: and of the difference between civil law and canon law.
2. The parties in a compromise may waive citation.
3. Whether the third arbitrator, acting jointly with one of the two elected, may make an award without citation or the presence of the parties.
4. Whether a statute may confirm an award or arbitral sentence after the expiration of the peremptory time limits.
5. Whether citation of a party is required in an arbitral proceeding.
6. An arbitrator’s award is presumed to have been rendered properly and correctly.
body: The point of the question is as follows. A certain D. Par, on one side, and a certain D. Flora, on the other, compromised their lawsuit and the dispute which they had together into two arbitrators and arbiters, as is contained in the compromise. Then the judge chose a third arbitrator and arbiter according to the form of the statute. This third, together with one of the said arbitrators, for example, elected, gave his award and passed sentence, as is contained in the award. The compromise, the election of the third, and the awards are transmitted to you, together with the statutes bearing on the aforesaid matter.

† The matter is now in doubt, because the party of the aforementioned Flora says that the award was, and is, null on the ground that the other arbitrator was not present when the two rendered their award. But the party of the aforementioned Peace said that the award remained in the firmness of its validity, especially because the question of recourse, which was made on behalf of the aforementioned lady Flora to one of the judges appointed, according to the form of the aforementioned statute, was not decided, and that the award was, and is, something, and valid. Now it is asked whether the said award remained in the firmness of its validity according to the form of the aforementioned statute, assuming the passage of 30 days, or whether the said award was null for the aforementioned reason. And it pleases the consultant to pay attention to the circumstances in the aforementioned matters. The malicious or voluntary absence of one of the arbitrators notwithstanding, the award of two is valid according to canon law, as in c. ult. de arb. lib. 6. Although another answer is given according to civil law, ff. de arb. l. sicuti. But civil law has place according to strictness, canon law according to equity. Since therefore this arbitrator, who did not appear, was requested at his home, and was absent, according to canonical equity, the award is valid. But this seems false: because in the lands of the empire civil law must be observed, not canon law. I answer that canon law can distinguish civil law, and prevails everywhere by reason of equity. But it is still objected that the award is not valid: because the election of the third did not take place. For it ought to have been made with the parties present or cited: since their prejudice was at issue, as in l. de unoquoque de re iud.

† Solution. From the form of the compromise it appears that the presence of the parties is not necessary. D. de arbitris, l. diem proferre, § si quis litigatorum. Because full power was granted to them, even with both parties present and absent. Moreover, the said third party was duly elected, because just as one can be elected by the arbitrators when a judge is imminent, so too by the judge with both arbitrators consenting: because he who consents is deemed to elect. arg. not. in d. l. sicuti, and in l. si unus, § principaliter, cum si. Furthermore, because this statute expressly provides that the third party elected by the judge or by the parties, indeed by statute the sentence of the sole third party suffices, because it says, or the third party. And thus disjunctively. And some also hold this from civil law. as not. in d. § principaliter, in the small gloss. But another later statute seems to require the majority. Nevertheless, both statutes have been satisfied. And therefore the compromise, and the election of the third party, and the aforementioned award undoubtedly appear to be valid. But it seems to be an objection that at the time of the award the parties were not present, nor cited: nor is power found to have been given to the third arbitrator in this, but only to the first arbitrators. I answer, this third party, who was associated with them, appears to have been associated with the same power. And thus their power is extended to him, with whom he is joined. And this extension is made by law, which gives him authority. arg. D. de iudicibus, l. si iudex. This, however, is quite doubtful to me: because a personal concession, and relaxation of common law made to the first arbitrators, seems to be restricted to them alone. But not to the third, who has power from law, not extended by the parties. D. de arbitris, l. In compromissis; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multum in principio.

But in the case of the third arbitrator acting jointly with one of the first two, it seems that no citation or presence of the parties is required, as noted by Guillaume in *de episcopali audientia*, *l. episcopalem*, at the end, although Peter and Bartolus note the contrary in *de verbis obligatis*, *l. si quis arbitratu*, and in *pro quibus*, *l. quod si nolit*, § final, *de aedilicio edicto*, which Bartolus cites there: “Or he was not present to whom it should be returned, etc.” But there, it speaks concerning the restitution of the thing, not concerning the declaration of mind and of the arbitrator’s decision. Likewise, where the arbitration requires a redhibition, it is not sufficient to say, “It displeases me,” if one wishes to possess it, that is, to retain it and not return it; since, therefore, by its very nature, such an arbitration must begin with execution, the presence of the parties is required. This does not contradict *l. si quis arbitratu*, because if the arbitrator desires the presence of the parties and does not wish to arbitrate otherwise than after hearing the parties, he acts rightly; and the party who absents itself incurs a penalty, because it obstructs the arbitration. Therefore, the power of the arbitrator and his intention must be considered: he may, if he wishes, but if he does not wish, he may also abstain. Hence, absence cannot obstruct the power of the arbitrator. But it can probably obstruct his will, because of the merits of the causes, etc., *l. final*, *si per vim*, or in some other way. This is a very significant question. And I come to the next point, assuming that,

† If an arbitration award were invalid, whether it is confirmed by a statute due to the lapse of peremptory time, which provides that if the party did not pursue the cause of nullity within the certain time specified in the statute, the award shall remain in full force. It seems that it is not. On appeals, l. si expressim. I answer: when the award can be aided by extrinsic proofs, then the statute seems to confirm it. Certainly, this is doubtful, whether the statute remains in the firmness of its validity. And this word "remains" signifies that it was so from the beginning, according to its proper and strict meaning, as noted in C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si cum ante. But if it were an error that cannot be remedied by extrinsic proof, then without doubt it is not confirmed, as in the aforementioned l. si expressim. In our case, however, no error is expressly stated; rather, it is said that citation or presence was lacking. But this could be proven to have been present. And thus it could be aided extrinsically, hence there is no expressly stated error. And thus it seems to be confirmed, because the intent of the statute excludes all contradiction and precludes recourse. Argument from de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, § consequens.

† Whatever has been said, it seems necessary to conclude that, when an arbitrator is appointed to decide a dispute, which occurs where the parties were present during the discussion and the examination of the merits of the case, the presence of the parties at the time of the arbitral award is not required; because the arbitrator is not bound by the procedural order of courts, as noted by Innocentius in *de iureiurando*, chapter *Quintavallis*. And such citation is made in judicial proceedings so that the formal structure of the trial may be preserved. And because it would not be valid unless the party were present or deemed present, according to the rule on confessions, *l. certum*; since the arbitrator, in the absence of a party, is not required to imitate the rules of judicial procedure.

† Furthermore, it seems that one should say that the award of the arbitrator is presumed to be something that has been rendered correctly and duly, and that all matters are presumed to have been examined and acted upon properly and solemnly. As is expressly stated by Dino in the counsel beginning "Tholomeus Manentis," and thus Dino counseled there. And if it is said that the election of a third party has no place among arbitrators, it is answered: this is true according to the common law, because no law says this. But it is otherwise by statute, which disposes equally of both, as in the statute "How arbitrators, etc." From which it can be argued with probability that the award, in the form of an arbitration agreement, can be defended as valid, more so than in the true and proper form, as if of a judicial arbitrator. And thus I say and counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who kills a banned person who holds a safe-conduct for residence, of which the killer is unaware, cannot be punished: because the ban, having the form of a ban, even though the obligation is extinguished by payment or absolution, of which there is no proof, excuses the offender from punishment. And number 4.
1. A statute that those who kill banned persons are to be considered unpunished circumscribes the offense: so much so that the judge cannot proceed against it by inquisition.
2. Just or unjust ignorance excuses from corporal punishment.
body: To the evidence

Certain statutes must be premised for the discussion. First, there is the statute and edict of the Magnificent Lords of the House of Scala, which provides that whoever is banned for homicide or another crime punishable by death from the City of Verona is to be understood as banned from the City of Vicenza, and vice versa. Furthermore, a statute of the said City of Verona provides that those banned for rebellion, homicide, or another crime punishable by death may be attacked and killed with impunity by anyone, provided, however, that a condemnatory sentence has first been pronounced by virtue of the ban, and not before. Additionally, another statute of the City of Vicenza provides that those banned for homicide, rebellion, or another crime where the penalty is death may be killed with impunity, and those who kill them are to be considered immune from punishment, provided that a condemnatory sentence has first been pronounced against the said banned individuals by virtue of the ban, and not before. Moreover, another statute of the City of Vicenza provides that no one is to be considered banned unless he is written in the book of the commune by name and surname, together with the sign and name of the notary; nor is anyone to be considered removed from the ban unless he has been recorded as deceased in the Book of the Banned, with the sign and name of the notary and the ordinary official of the Books of the Banned. Finally, another statute of Vicenza provides that whoever causes another to be killed for money shall be punished with the ultimate penalty.

From the aforementioned statutes, the following case arises. A certain John negotiated in the district of Vicenza with Bartholomew and Anthony that they should kill a certain Henrichetus in the district of Vicenza. He promised them one hundred pounds upon the commission of the said homicide against the person of the said Henrichetus, who was banned and condemned by the commune of Verona for two homicides and two robberies. Bartholomew and Anthony, executing the said agreement, killed the said Henrichetus in the district of Vicenza. The said John was captured and confessed that he had negotiated with the said Bartholomew and Anthony that they should kill the said Henrichetus, and that he would give them one hundred pounds for the said homicide, and that by virtue of the said agreement ordered by the said John, the aforementioned Bartholomew and Anthony killed the said Henrichetus. Now, the Podestà of Vicenza is proceeding against the said John by inquisition for the said homicide, stating that he ought to die by virtue of the last-mentioned statute, which provides that whoever causes another to be killed for money shall be punished with the ultimate penalty. In defense of the said John, several arguments are advanced. First, that the said Henrichetus was banned and condemned for homicides and two robberies by the commune of Verona; and thus, by virtue of the Statute of Verona, he could be attacked and killed with impunity. Furthermore, by virtue of the edict of the said Magnificent Lords of the House of Scala, he is understood to be banned from the City of Vicenza; and by virtue of the edict joined with the statute of the commune of the City of Vicenza, which provides that those banned for rebellion, homicide, etc., may be killed with impunity, no action ought to be taken in any way against the said John. Thus, by inquisition, by virtue of the statutes of the commune of Vicenza, which are transmitted to you.

And especially because the aforementioned statute, which declares that those who kill banished persons are to be considered immune from punishment, circumscribes the offense to such an extent that the judge cannot proceed against it by way of inquisition. See the note by Jacobus de Arena and Raymond in l. 1 and §. quod vero, D. de aleatoribus; and it supports what we note in l. si seruus, C. de his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt. But it is objected against this that the said Richetus had a promise, or safe-conduct, from a certain Magni, Lord Consignorio della Scala, that he could remain secure in the Vicentine district, notwithstanding the bans and condemnations he had incurred in the commune of Verona. And thus stand the words of the said promise or safe-conduct, which are produced against the said John and against the said Ioan. And for the said Ioan, many arguments are alleged and produced on both sides, which are directed and transmitted to you for examination. Now the question arises whether the said judge can proceed against the said John, and whether the said Ioan ought to be punished by the penalty of the statute punishing those who cause others to be killed for money. That the said homicide could be committed and ordered with impunity is proven by these reasons. First, from the appearance of the ban, which remains and which seems to excuse those who act upon it. D. de interdictis et reliquis actionibus, l. de aetate, §. ex causa. Second, because since he is in the book of the banished, he is found to be in such a quasi-possession, and therefore he ought to be regarded as such. C. de testamento, l. 1; D. de servis exponendis, l. moueor. Third, from justifiable ignorance. For the purpose of excusing ignorance, having the appearance of existence operates in the same way as true existence; but this ban has the appearance of existence; therefore it will operate in the same way as if it had true existence. Just as a revoked mandate, which has the appearance of existence, operates in the same way to excuse the ignorant person as an unrevoked mandate having true existence. D. si certum petatur, l. cum qui in provincia; D. de solutionibus, l. cum quis, §. iuste enim ignorat, quid mutatum esse, quod olim fuit. Nor is it presumed to have been changed unless it is proven. D. de institutionibus, l. si pupillus, §. si praescribere. Fourth: because concerning another’s act, and especially a hidden one, ignorance is presumed unless it is proven that the person was informed. D. de mandatis, l. si fideiussor; and l. ultima, D. pro socio.

Fifth: Because ignorance excuses one from corporal punishment, whether such ignorance is just or unjust. D. de abigeis, l. 1, in fine; C. de plagio, l. Plagii; D. de liberali causa. Therefore, this ignorance is presumed. D. de probat., l. Verius. Sixth: Regarding this question, the case appears to be as follows. D. de adulteriis, l. Pen.; and this is noted by Cynus in C. de repudiis, l. Uxor. Seventh: Because a ban that is apparent is prima facie presumed to be something. C. de edicto divi Adriani tolerato, l. 2 and l. Edicto. And even if it is said to be null, the offender is excused, as noted by Decius in D. de acquirendo possidendo, l. 2, § Si servus. Eighth: Because the license granted to oneself appears to have expired upon the death of the grantor. Arg. l. Ultima, D. de poenis; and what is noted in I. 1, C. de postulando. Hence, before the successor in office, such license does not appear to be valid; because permission and prohibition made without cause appear to expire with the termination of the jurisdiction and office of the one promising or prohibiting. Arg. the aforementioned laws. Ninth: Because that which is lawful to do is lawful to command to be done, as noted in D. de vi et de vi armata, l. Cum fundum. And he who cannot be held liable principally cannot be held liable secondarily either, as in D. de furtis, l. Fullo, § Nemo. Tenth: Because this determination is general, namely that it is lawful to kill a banned person. It does not distinguish how, whether by having him killed for money, or in what manner. Hence, we cannot distinguish against the general determination of the law. D. de aleatoribus, l. 1, § Quod autem; D. de militum testamento, l. In fraudem, § Si. For since this banned person is an enemy, fraud is not said to be committed. D. de dolo, l. 1, § Non fuit. Moreover, one statute must be understood with the determination of another. Hence, a statute that prohibits and imposes a penalty should not be referred to cases in which a special permissive reason is found, as in D. de legibus, l. Quod ergo, § Haeres; and D. de verbis oblig., l. Qui servum mihi ex stipulatu.

† Finally, I say that both Jacobus Butrigarius and Jacobus Belvederius advised in fact in Florence that a ban having the form of a ban, although the obligation is extinguished by payment or absolution, of which there is no evidence to the one who sees and reads the ban, excuses the offender from the penalty. And so I hold, with both Jacobs. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How it is proved that someone is a manifest usurer: and who, and how many witnesses suffice in this matter.
2. If a witness says that someone is a usurer because he lent to him at usury, he is said to be competent: and he proves it.
3. Whether a witness to whom the benefit accrues secondarily is competent.
4. All witnesses are regularly said to be competent, even if they are blood relatives or domestics of the party producing them, to whom command cannot be given by reason of paternal or master’s authority.
5. Reputation is not established by slight evidence, even if it is proved by two competent witnesses.
body: I, Angelo of Castiglione, Arezzo, Doctor of Both Laws, Archpriest, and Canon of Padua, and Canon of Arezzo, having been requested to write the truth on the article, the tenor of which is as follows: In the litigation, the jurist is consulted between Vincentius, late of Master Azo of Malado, or Huguzone the notary, or Master Bartholomew the tanner: against Daniel, his procurator, and in his procuratorial name on behalf of him on one side; and Peace, son of Michael, or Ser John of Malado, notary, his procurator, and in his procuratorial name on behalf of him on the other side, whether the said Peace ought to be and come to be pronounced a public and manifest usurer, notwithstanding the oppositions and objections made by the party of the said Peace; or whether he ought not to be pronounced as such. And this, having seen the proofs of both parties, and all the acts and things done between the said parties, etc.

I state and advise, always reserving the right to a sounder opinion, that it is to be declared and ought to be declared that the said Pace is a manifest and public usurer, notwithstanding the objections and arguments raised by the party of the said Pace. And I say this having examined the depositions of the witnesses, both admitted and rejected, produced by both sides. This is especially so by virtue of a certain synodal constitution, which begins: “We declare a manifest usurer,” in that part where it states that the same should be said if it is proven by two suitable witnesses, even if they are singular in their testimonies, that he is a usurer, provided that public reputation is also adverse to him. Now it remains to respond to certain doubts arising from the proceedings, which at first sight seem to contradict my opinion. The first is whether that witness is considered suitable who says that Pace is a usurer, and as the reason and basis for his statement, says that the said Pace lent to him at usury. The second is whether a witness is considered suitable who is related by blood to the party producing him. The third is whether reputation can be legally proven by two witnesses. Regarding these doubts, although they could be discussed at greater length, I will, having rejected all superfluity, state what appears to me to be the simple truth, and conclude briefly.

† I therefore say in response to the first point, that the witness in question ought to be considered competent: because the advantage or disadvantage of the case in which he testifies does not principally concern him:

† Nor for this reason alone, that if the said Pax were declared a usurer in this case, some benefit would accrue to the said witness, or some restitution of usury ought to be made: for the principles that a transaction between others is no bar and other common law maxims apply. For it is not sufficient to prove that someone is a usurer and that one borrowed from him at usury, unless the payment of the usury is also proved. And other points are found in the authorities cited in the Decretals, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Ex litteris*. This opinion is supported by Innocentius in the Decretals, *De testibus*, chapter 3. The text proves this in the same title, chapter *Insuper*, together with chapter *Cum nuntius*, where it is clear that prelates and clerics may be witnesses in the cause of their church. And the reason is that the cause of the church is not properly that of the prelate or clerics, even though a secondary benefit may accrue to them. To the same effect is what is stated in the Institutes, *De testamentis*, § *Legatariis*, and what is noted in the Speculum, *De instrumentorum editione*, § *Postremo*, otherwise beginning *Instrumentum*, under the words *quod delegatario*. Nor does it avail what the doctors and glossators note in the aforementioned § *Legatariis* of the Institutes, *De testamentis*: for that rule applies when the legacy is such that it would not be due unless the will were valid, and once the will is approved, the legacy is necessarily due. But in our case it is otherwise: for even if Pax is proved to be a usurer, nevertheless nothing is due to Benevenuto, the witness, unless a new interpellation and proof have intervened, as has been said above.

† To the second point, I say that, as a general rule, all witnesses are considered competent, even if they are blood relatives or household members of the party producing them, provided that no authority can be exercised over them by virtue of paternal or master’s power. This is the text of 4 q. 3, at the words “Item idonei.” And note the doctors in C. de testibus, in l. 3. I concede, however, that there could be such strong affection between the witness and the party producing him, even without kinship, that the witness’s testimony would be weakened and he would not be fully regarded as competent. This is fully noted by Hugo, 3 quaestio, in the Summa, and by the Speculum in the title De testibus, § 1, at the words “Item excipitur, quod est domesticus,” and the following words. But in our case, no such affection has been established, nor has any such affection been presented to me.

† To the third point, I say briefly that although reputation is not established by slight indications, it is nevertheless proven by two competent witnesses. Extra, De testibus, Cum litteris. It accords with Codex, De bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas, l. 2; Codex, De fideicommissis, l. Si. To the same effect, what we teach in Extra, De iureiurando, cap. Ad nostram. And this is the ordinary gloss, 2 q. 1, § Finis. The same is noted by Archidiaconus and Dynus in their lectures on cap. Omnibus, 2 quest. 5. And most fully by the modern authors in Extra, De accusatione, cap. Inquisitionis. These are my words, and I advise accordingly. Angelus, the aforesaid, in whose true testimony I have affixed my seal. And so I say and advise, I, Argen. dom. Rayne., Doctor.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the children of the first marriage ought to receive more than the children of the second marriage, by reason of the pact which the husband interposed in the name of the children of the second marriage.
2. Whether a pact made in favor of the children of the second marriage, to the prejudice of the children of the first marriage, is valid.
body:
The case is as follows, and a certain minor point once arose before the Lord Judge of Cortone. A certain Minutia, having two sons from her first marriage, namely Angelo and John, entered into a second marriage and wed a certain Ristoro Benucci. From this Minutia, Benuccio, formerly of Vanni Ristoro of Cortone, father of the aforementioned Ristoro, her second husband, had acknowledged that he had received, given and paid and delivered for herself, as dowry and in the name of dowry, the goods, possessions, and assets estimated and contained in the said dowry instrument. This Lady Minutia bore and had six children from the said Ristoro, her second husband, namely: Roberto, Matteo, Lady Joanna, Clara, Antonia, and Luigia. Then the said John died before the said Lady Minutia, his mother, with his brother Angelo surviving. Then the said Roberto died before the death of the said Lady Minutia, one of the sons of the second marriage, with his daughter Liota, and the granddaughter of the said Lady Minutia, surviving. After the passage of time, the said Lady Minutia died intestate, surviving her were the said Angelo, the only son from the first marriage; the Lord Matteo, Lady Jacoba, Clara, Antonia, and Luigia, children of the said Minutia and Ristoro, born from the said second marriage; and Liota, granddaughter, and the said Ristoro, second husband of the said Lady Minutia, surviving.

This Angelo claims that he ought to have one-half of the aforementioned dowry of Lady Minutia, because he relies on *l. hac edictali* in the beginning, and on the following sections in the said law, and on the glosses there, which begin "sed pone" or otherwise "primi matrimonii." This law, with the notes there, and also *§. optime* in the *Authentica de nuptiis*, Collatio 2, seems to create doubt in this matter and to favor the part of the said Angelo, son of the first marriage.

On the other hand, for the part of the children of the second marriage, numbering six, including the aforementioned granddaughter named Liota, and for the part of the said Ristoro, second husband, in his own name and as father and administrator of his said children and granddaughter, it is objected and said that the said Angelo ought not to have from the said dowry more than the legitime portion according to the number of children of the first and second marriage, notwithstanding the pact made by the said Lady Minutia in the said dowry instrument in favor of the children of the second marriage. By which it was provided that, if it should happen that the said Lady Minutia should predecease her husband Ristoro, with a son or sons descending from both of them together and existing, or one existing, she shall not be bound to the restitution of the said dowry; but it shall be and ought to be of the aforementioned children to be born, or daughter, or son.

Furthermore, it is objected that to the said dowry and goods of the said Lady Minutia, succession is had at least equally and according to the number of children of both the second and the first marriage, notwithstanding the said *l. hac edictali* and the notes there, and notwithstanding the said *§. optime*, as is the case expressly stated in *Auth. de nuptiis*, *§. nec illud quoque*, there "ex qua et simili divisi," etc. Furthermore, that the said Angelo ought to have only the legitime and not more, notwithstanding the said pact, seems to be the text in *Auth. de nuptiis* near the end, *§. illud*, Collatio 4, although custom there says otherwise.

Now it is asked and brought into doubt, having seen the said point and what is contained therein, and having seen the said dowry instrument of the said Lady Minutia and the pact of convention contained therein, and the instrument itself diligently inspected in every part of itself, and considering the number of children of the first and second marriage: Whether the said Angelo, son of the said Minutia and of the first marriage, succeeds in the said dowry in a seventh part, or in a half, or whether he ought to have only the legitime in the said dowry, considering the number of children of the second and first marriage. Furthermore, whether in the fourth part the six children of the second marriage succeed in the said dowry. And whether the said Ristoro, second husband, can, against the will of the said Angelo, have the usufruct in his lifetime, with the right of removal, if any portion of the said dowry should fall to the said Angelo.

And it is responded to *l. hac edictali* and in *Auth. ad eos*, C. eo., and in the concordances whence it is derived, and to the notes there, where it seems to be said that to the sons of the first marriage alone pertains what was given beyond what was given to the sons of the second marriage, and by them it is revoked as if not written, and as if not given nor granted. Which seems strange, if this were true. And consequently, the sons of the second marriage would not succeed in the said dowry, at least equally according to the number of children together with the said Angelo; since the said Lady Minutia had granted to the said Ristoro all that she had in dowry at the time of the second marriage. It pleases to see and consult, as you otherwise consulted in this point. Which will be of three.

First, whether the children of the first marriage ought to have more than the children of the second marriage by reason of the pact which the second husband interposed in the name of the children of the second marriage; so that the pact appended for the second children might be turned against them. To this, certain persons, not understanding the matter, rely on the gloss to *l. hac edictali*, in the gloss beginning *Sed pone*, and wish to say that two children of the first marriage, or even only one, should have as much as ten from the second marriage; because that gloss says that the children of the second marriage revoke half of the gifts. But certainly that gloss is irrelevant to our question; because it speaks of a case where the pact of acquisition was granted to the second husband for himself, and not under the mention of the children of the second marriage. Hence, if there are surviving children of the first marriage, and no children survive from the second marriage, but only the second husband survives the wife, then rightly the children of the first marriage revoke [the gifts], so that they may be equal with the second husband. This is to be understood thus: that each of the children ought to have as much as the second husband. It is not, however, to be understood that the husband alone ought to have one half, and all the children the other half; because then it would be expressly contrary to the understanding of the law *hac edictali*. If, therefore, that gloss were understood in our case, it would follow that a single child of the first marriage would nevertheless have as much as all the children of the second marriage, which is not true; because the law speaks of the second marriage, not of its children. Nor does it speak of the acquisitions of the children; similarly, the gloss says in *ff. sol. ma. l. Si vero. §. de viro*. And that it does not speak of the children of the second marriage, namely, that the children of the first marriage would be in a better position than the children of the second marriage, is clearly shown in *Auth. de nu. §. nec illud quoque nobis relinquendum est etc.*, and there in the gloss, and *c. nisi dicatur*, that the woman’s own property and dowry, left to the children from either marriage, are divided equally among all intestate, where the dowry is given. To say simply that the case of the children of the second marriage is worse on the ground that otherwise the father and mother provided more for them is absurd; because the pact, which was ordered in their favor, ought not to be turned to their detriment. See *C. de secundis nup. l. generaliter. §. in his in ratione literae*.

Secondly, it is asked in the aforementioned point, whether the said dowry, notwithstanding the aforementioned pact concerning the acquisition and retention for the children of the second marriage, ought to be divided among all the children of both the first and the second marriage of the woman. And on this point, certain persons advised that a division per stirpes (or by male portions) should be made, and thus the pact would have no effect; but this opinion does not seem true to me, because in the law *Hac edictali*, the pact has some effect. For either we must say that it is a pact effective for the husband, and the husband is reduced to his male portion, and thus the division of the residue will be made among all the children, both of the first and the second marriage. This is ridiculous, because no law provides for it. Or it would have to be said that the children of the second marriage would have nothing of the mother’s dowry in their own person, nor as heirs of the mother. But the division would be made only between the husband and the children of the first marriage. And this is most false, because the pact appended for the retention in favor of the children of the second marriage ought not to operate to the contrary, as has been said.

If, however, we say that this is not a pact of the husband in effect, but is interpreted to be a pact of the children of the second marriage themselves, just as a father can stipulate for children born, so too can he for those yet to be born, then no law prohibits such a pact from being valid, because the law *Hac edictali* speaks of a pact of the husband, not of a pact of the children, for whom the mother herself can fully provide, if she wishes, as in Aurelianus, *De nuptiis*, § *Pe*. And therefore, the conclusion remains regarding the third pact, namely, whether the children of the first marriage ought to have only their legitime. Which I believe to be true, and so I advised, and I advise. For the aforementioned donation does not truly descend from the wife to the husband, but from the mother to the children, albeit through the ministry of the husband, at least as regards ownership, which cannot be sought by the husband in adventitious property. The husband therefore has retention not for himself, but for the children; because the donation is valid, just as if any other outsider had stipulated for the children, and I see no reason why the father could not stipulate in consideration of which an outsider could. Indeed, it ought to be permitted to the father all the more than to an outsider, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Quodcunque*, § *Si quis ita*.

Since, therefore, the donation made to the husband is valid, the children of the first marriage ought not to have more than their sole legitime. Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, Authentic *Unde et si parens*. The law *Hac edictali* does not obstruct this, insofar as it speaks of an interposed person; because it speaks where the husband interposes another person for himself. But here, when he interposes himself for another, not figuratively, but effectively. Likewise, it does not obstruct the Authentic *De nuptiis*, § *Optime*, because there the husband received for another, whereas here he did not receive for another. Likewise, it does not obstruct the fact that it seems to be profectitious property; because it is ridiculous to say that the dowry which the children acquire by the father’s pact is profectitious; because they do not take it as from the hands of the father, nor in consideration of the father, but with his ministry intervening only. As in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, law *Mulier*. Thus the pact ought to be interpreted, so that it may be sought for him to whom it can be sought by law. But it ought not to be interpreted with a defect. Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si ita stipulatus*, § *Grisogonus*.

Likewise, it does not obstruct the Digest, *De falsis*, law *De eo*, because there, if they are valid with effect, the act would be acquired with effect by a prohibited person; but here it is not acquired by any prohibited person, but by a permitted one. And so I hold notably, notwithstanding that a certain doctor of Bologna, like a fool, said that this opinion was contrary to the law *Hac edictali*, and answered by usage like a jester. And the aforementioned are true, unless this pact were understood for the children, as for the heirs of the woman; because all the children of the first and second marriage would succeed per stirpes. As in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Continuus*, § *Praeterea*. And this opinion would be quite more tolerable than the other opinion, which refers to the law *Hac edictali*, because that one cannot be sustained in any way. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "uncle" includes the great-uncle in the statutes.
2. Who are called paternal cousins.
3. Whether a ward is said to die intestate in a matter contrary to common law.
4. It is one thing to be such, and another to be considered as such.
5. In statutes, common usage of speech is established.
body: The case is as follows. The statute of the City of Castello provides that the mother shall not succeed to a son dying intestate, if there are surviving children of the deceased, brothers, or a brother, a nephew, or nephews through a brother, an uncle, or uncles, etc. Now, a certain Stephen, son of Arducio Bonasio, died intestate, survived by two children, one male and one female, both infants. Thereafter, the said children died in infancy without having accepted their father’s inheritance, survived by the relatives listed below, namely: Omdedeo, son of the aforementioned Bonasio; Vuando, son of Vannis Bonasio; and Sabatino, son of Martin Bonasio. The question is whether the inheritance of the said Stephen devolves by law. If the mother does not exist, or exists but is barred because she did not seek a guardian for the said wards, the aforementioned Omdedeo succeeds by common law as the nearest relative. But if the mother exists and is capable of succeeding, there is no doubt that the mother succeeds according to common law, as in Auth. de haeredibus ab intestato § 1 and § ex his, and in Auth. defuncto, with similar authorities. However, a doubt remains in the present case due to the statute. This doubt has two aspects. First, whether this great-uncle is included under the term “uncle” in the context of this statute. Second, whether a ward is said to die intestate in this matter contrary to common law.

† As to the first point, it seems that one should say that, although the fleshly brother of these wards is their great-uncle—because the text states thus: “a great-uncle is the brother of a grandfather” (Digest, *De gradibus*, *Iurisconsultus*, § *Quarto gradu*; and Institutes, *De gradibus*)—nevertheless, the term, when used simply, encompasses him; for what is said indefinitely ought to be understood generally, as in *L. In fraudem*, § *Si* (Digest, *De militum testamento*); and *L. Generaliter* (Digest, *De legatis praestandis*), together with similar authorities. And I hear that certain persons have consulted and reported a decision from Bologna. I hold, however, that the word, when used without any addition, signifies the nearest degree of unclehood, namely, that uncle who is in the third degree. For we properly and simply call these persons uncles. But an uncle who is in the fourth degree we do not call an uncle unless with an addition, because we call him a great-uncle, as stated in the aforementioned *L. Iurisconsultus*, § *Tertio gradu*. And therefore, interpreting the term primarily and simply, my opinion is correct. And those who say the contrary extend the statute beyond justice according to their own ingenuity. For to add is to extend. And therefore this Omdedeus does not exclude the aforementioned mother, because he is not a first uncle, but a great-uncle. Moreover, what the statute says, “uncle, or paternal *zius*,” means the brother of the father, not the *zius* of the father. Thus speaks the aforementioned §. For if *zius paternus* were explained as meaning the *zius* of the father, he would indeed be included in the number. But just as “paternal grandfather” means the father of the father, and not the grandfather of the father, so “paternal *zius*” means the brother of the father, not the uncle of the father, as stated in the aforementioned § *Tertio gradu*. Nor are the paternal cousins here included.

† because those who are properly called paternal cousins are those born of two full brothers, and thus they are in the fourth degree. But these Brandus and Sabatinus are in the fifth degree, because their fathers were in the fourth degree according to the laws. Therefore, the mother appears to me to favor justice on this ground. But even assuming that this were not so,

I say that the statute which excludes the mother from her right in intestate succession is as if irrational; and for this reason it is also considered odious; and it has no place when the son dies intestabilis, that is, as a minor (pupillus) or as a madman (furiosus); because intestatus and intestabilis differ. For no one who is intestabilis is properly speaking intestatus. But the law interprets even a minor as intestatus, because he produces the result of intestacy. L. 1, § 1, de suis et legitimis heredibus. But that is true where it is a matter of introducing a reasonable favor. But where it is a matter of an irrational and harsh exclusion, and especially in a statute, one should not depart from the proper meaning. According to Petrus Gulielmus de Cunio and Raynerius, alone, Bartolus says the contrary, based on common usage of speech. But as to this common usage, it is a matter of fact, and one should not believe it. For even the most expert are deceived by facts. But he says that there is a text about this common usage of speech. But with all due respect, this is not said there. And the said illustrious doctors, who say that there is a case for themselves there, would have been very foolish.
