Which is foolish to say about such great men. And although he says there that it is the reason why such is the common usage of speech in the said § 1, in the words "pro intestatis" and in the word "creditur," nevertheless this is not true; because that § neither in the text nor in the gloss speaks of the interpretation of the common people, but speaks of the interpretation of the jurist, which proceeds there for so much: because there it is a matter of reasonable favor; here, however, of irrational hatred. For to exclude the mother from the due succession, where the debt of nature is paid, rather than gain is sought, as C. de codicillis, l. fin., § pe., and C. de imponendis lucris descriptionibus ultra medium, this is said to be hatred. And even if it were not hatred principally and simply, it is hatred in a certain respect. And therefore it should be restricted, as in the said l. cum quidam, de liberis et posthumis, and l. maximum vitium, de liberis praeteritis. Nor does the text obstruct, when it says that these are held as intestate.

For it is one thing to be such, another to be considered as such, as noted in the gloss on the significance of words, *l. mercis*, and in the gloss on *statu*. It is not sufficient to be considered as such unless one actually is such as the statute requires, as in *D. de negotiorum gestione*, *l. 3*, § *haec verba*. Moreover, the ablative *ab intestato* placed in the conclusion signifies the true existence of the terms, not a fictitious one, at least in statutes and odious matters, in which conditions are required to be fulfilled formally, as in *D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, *l. meus*. Hence, concluding from the first point to the last: since an improper case has no place in statutes, and since this person is called an intestate only improperly, the mother’s exclusive statute does not claim application here, but we adhere to the common law.

† Nevertheless, I readily concede that if it were proven by custom, or by common usage of speech, namely, that an intestate is commonly referred to as such, even one who is incapable of making a will. On the meaning of words, l. auiculus; and l. ut Alphenus; and l. tuguri, D. de sup. leg.; l. 1, in fine, D. de fund. inst.; l. cum de lanionis, §. asinam, and D. de leg. 3; l. liberorum, §. quod tamen Cassius: yet it is difficult to prove that the common people interpret these terms, the distinction and understanding of which do not fall within the grasp of the unlearned. And thus I advised, adhering to the opinion of many, but not of just one: because those who held this view were more numerous. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The term "children born from one's own body" includes grandchildren born to a son or daughter.
2. This condictio, "if he should die without children," is to be interpreted as follows.
3. A son of a daughter is said to be born from the body of the grandfather.
body: Point

† Such is the case. A certain testator, having a brother, made his will, in which, after the institution of an heir and several other legacies, he bequeathed to this his brother certain possessions, and ordered, wished, and commanded by way of fideicommissum that whenever the said brother should die without legitimate sons born of his own body, the aforementioned goods should be restored to certain persons. Now it happens that this testator died, his legatee brother surviving him, and this legatee brother subsequently died, leaving two nephews through a daughter. Now the question arises whether the said possessions ought to devolve to the said persons under the fideicommissum, or whether they ought to remain with the aforementioned nephews of the said legatee brother, etc.

† This condition, if he should die without sons, inserted in favor of a brother or another legitimate heir, is explained by Scaevola, that is, if he should die without children. And this is based on the broad meaning of the term and the intent of the deceased. D. de haered. inst. l. Lucius. And therefore the son of a daughter excludes the substitute: because he is included under the name of children. C. de condi. inser. l. 1. D. de excusa. tuto. l. 2. §. auxiliantur. Auth. de verb. signi. l. liberorum. And there Bartolus holds this view and says that it is the case in the aforementioned l. Lucius. Nor do those words "born from his own body" constitute an objection.

† For since the daughter is born from his own body, by consequence the son of the daughter is also part of his own body, although he is not in his power. Nevertheless, in substitutions, we consider not so much power as natural affection. D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, § si quis rogatus. But in an affirmative disposition, if I bequeath to the sons of my brother, whether nephews are included if the sons do not survive, is treated in l. Gallus, § instituens, by Ancharanus, de Pisis, Cynus, and Bartolus. And the reason lies in the condition: because there it concerns some preference of persons, which is according to the order of natural charity. But where it is simply disposed, there no comparison of persons arises. C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The term "posthumous" or "future child," when used in the singular, encompasses any child subsequently born, so that the will may not be invalidated.
2. What effect the codicillary clause has when the will is void due to the omission of an heir.
body: The point is this: A certain man named Jacobus Putii deassisio, having his son Stephen and a pregnant wife named Fina, made a will, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows. In all his other movable and immovable goods, etc., he instituted as his universal heir Stephen, his legitimate and natural son, and the future offspring to be born from the said testator and his said wife, if it be male and come to light, in equal shares. But if the said offspring be female, he left for her dowries, according to law, 200 pounds of denarii. And if all his said sons, the universal heirs, should die within the age of pupillage, or afterwards at any time, without legitimate children born from them, he willed and commanded that all the goods of the said inheritance remain and devolve by full right to Cicheli Simonis. And thus, in the event of the said case occurring, he substituted as universal heir to all his goods. After this will, a certain daughter was born from the said Fina, his wife. Likewise, after some time, his said wife bore another daughter. After some time, while the said testator was still living, the aforementioned Stephen, the male son, and the said first-born daughter died within the age of pupillage. After the aforementioned events, the said testator died, with the said last daughter and his said wife Fina surviving. It is now asked whether the said will is broken by the birth of the second daughter, who now lives, as if she had otherwise been passed over, since the said disposition concerning the unborn offspring speaks in the singular; or whether it comprehends any offspring to be born after the said will was made, assuming as certain that the said Fina was pregnant at the time of the said will. Furthermore, it is asked to whom the said inheritance is due: to his last-born daughter or to the heir substituted in the will.

† This passage is doubtful, in speaking of a posthumous heir. For sometimes the testator speaks indefinitely, saying “I institute,” and then it is understood to refer to every posthumous child. D. 28.5.1 (Placet). It is not an obstacle that he speaks in the singular number; because the appellative of a singular name, when general, comprehends the plural. D. 50.16.1 (In usu iuris). This is well supported by D. 26.1.1 (Si quis ita), § Si quis filio. Sometimes the testator speaks determinately, restricting himself to the posthumous child who is then in the womb, for example by saying, “I institute as heir the posthumous child who is in the womb”; then no other is included, except that one. Therefore, the others would be passed over. D. 28.5.1 (Titius), § 1. Sometimes there is doubt; and then either the disposition concerning the posthumous child can be referred by reasonable interpretation to any one, as when I simply say, “I institute the posthumous child as heir,” then all are comprehended, as in the aforementioned § Si quis filio; or it cannot be referred to all without injury, or deduction, and diminution of a certain and fixed legacy, as is the case in our situation; because it would have been said to the twenty daughters born that they should have 200 livres among them all, D. 16.1.1 (Reos), § Si, which was not the intention of the testator. And therefore it seems rather to be said that this second posthumous child was passed over; because 200 livres were left to the first posthumous children by a fixed and determinate amount, and nothing to this second one. To this effect, see D. 36.1.1 (Iulius Phebus), where it is said: “For the word comprehends one, because it is in the singular number. But the word ‘n.’ comprehends more, because it is in the plural number,” as is stated there. And see D. 35.1.1 (Qui filiabus), in the beginning and § 1, with similar authorities.

From which it is concluded that the said will is invalid by reason of the omission. Nevertheless, on account of the codicillary clause, the estate ought to be restored to the posthumous heirs, after deducting the legitimate portion and the Trebellianic share. Cf. c. Ray. and c. Ray. For this codicillary clause has force even in the omission of a posthumous child, if the testator inserted this clause, that is, included it for his children. Otherwise, if for a stranger: because the testator had no children. D. de fideicommissis, l. generaliter, § ex testamento. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How many witnesses are required for the repudiation of a will, how many for its declaration, how many for a disposition, or for the limitation of a disposition.
body: C2sISalis is. Andreas made a will, in which, among other things, he purely and simply prelegated certain things to his wife, and made her heir to one-third of his goods. In the other two parts, he instituted two other blood relatives of the testator as heirs. After the death of the said Andreas, the testator, the said wife demanded from her coheirs the said things prelegated to her, and certain other paraphernal goods which had come to the said Andreas, her late husband. The coheirs oppose this and say that the said testator prelegated the said things to himself in compensation for the said paraphernal goods. And to prove this, they produced Master Jacob, the notary who wrote the said will, who, testifying, says that before the witnesses were called and before the said will was drawn up, in the presence of the said witnesses, for well over two hours, the said testator, in the presence of the said notary and his wife, said that he was leaving her the said things in recompense for the paraphernal goods. Furthermore, they produced one of the witnesses written in the will, named Vannes, who says that he was not present at that will. Furthermore, they produce another witness, not among the number of witnesses written in the will, named Laudum, who, testifying, said that he heard the said testator say, after the will was made, that he was leaving the said things to his wife and wanted her to be content with the said things. Now it is asked whether these witnesses render the said will suspect, or have anything to prove, or induce any suspicion against the said will, and what is the law, having seen the said will and the attestations of the said witnesses.

† Sometimes witnesses wish to prove against the testimony of other witnesses in order to weaken it; sometimes to induce suspicion. And these cases are determined in l. 1, in the end, *quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur*. Sometimes witnesses wish to prove beyond the written instrument of the will: and then sometimes they wish to prove for the purpose of clarification, and then two witnesses are sufficient. D. *de testamentis*, l. *heredes palam*, § *sed si novam*. Sometimes [they wish to prove] for a new disposition, or a new limitation of a disposition. Then, if they testify concerning the will, seven rogated witnesses are required. If concerning codicils, five are required, even if not rogated. l. *cum proponentur*, D. *de legatis* 2. Since, therefore, the witnesses in question are not the legitimate number, and also Vannis, described in the will, says that he was not present, and in truth he attended the will, he is rightly not believed. Moreover, the singular point is praised in the aforementioned reasoning of time: because he says that after the making of the will. And Master Jacobus says that before, by two hours. And they are thus singular and contrary. And therefore neither is believed regarding the testimony. Extr. c. *cum tu filii*. To the other question, I answer that those words, and this whole, refer to all the foregoing. l. *talis scriptura*, D. *de legatis* 1, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute providing that adultery, rape, or incest may not be adjudicated is extended also to an attempted offense.
body: The point is as follows: The statute provides that adultery, rape, or incest may not be cognized or investigated unless an accusation is brought by certain persons related to the parties, enumerated in the said statute. Now, the syndic of the village, a third party not among those contained and enumerated in the said statute, has denounced to the court a certain Titius for an attempt, with the purpose of carnally knowing a certain nun.

† It is asked whether one ought or may proceed regarding the aforementioned denunciation. If one cannot inquire about incest or consummated rape, much less can one inquire about an attempted act, since an attempt is deemed consummated with respect to the imposition of punishment, as stated in the law *Si quis non dicam rapere*, Codex, *De episcopis et clericis*. Rightly, that which is not permitted in true terms is not permitted in fictitious ones; for a fiction or similarity ought not to operate more than the truth does, as in the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Filius*. It is no objection that here sacrilege seems to have been committed by violating and assaulting, as in the law *Si quis in hoc genus*; for this entry is confused with the attempt itself, as in the Digest, *De furtis*, law *Verum*, and in the Codex, *De accusationibus*, law *Qui de crimine*. And if one cannot inquire about the principal offense, one cannot inquire about that which is confused with the principal; for from which the principal is removed, the accessory is also removed, as in the Digest, *De iniuriis*, law *Non solum*, section *Ego autem*. Whether with a nun it be called rape, incest, or adultery, it makes no difference nor matters; for the statute expressly enumerates all these. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The acceptance of an inheritance is not brought about by an assertion whereby someone affirms that a thing pertains to him by a just title, or by a legitimate cause.
2. A doubtful and general act receives its interpretation from the preceding and subsequent acts.
body: In the year of our Lord, in the second indiction, and so forth. A certain lady Isa, formerly of Bernardelli, and wife of Iaconello, lord of Niccolò of Perugia, of the gate of Saint Susanna, and of the parish of Saint Severus, in every way, manner, right, and form by which she could best do so, made, constituted, and appointed the said Iaconello her true and legitimate procurator, actor, and special messenger, to protest and to make a protestation by hand of a public notary to the lady Nesuscia, formerly of Bernardelli, of the gate of Ebur and of the parish of Saint Bartholomew, that she make no novelties, nor cause any to be made, in the underwritten plots of land which remained in the inheritance of John Bernardelli, the fleshly brother of the said lady Isa; and that she neither devastate nor cause to be devastated any thing or trees existing therein; since the said plots of land pertain to the said lady Isa by just title and legitimate cause, as she asserted. First, in one plot of land situated, etc. Then the said lady Isa declared, said, and protested that she did not wish to be the heir of the said John, but rather repudiated the said inheritance, etc. Now it is asked whether, by the words contained in the said power of attorney, when it is said that the underwritten plots of land pertain to the said lady Isa by just title and legitimate cause, as she asserted, the inheritance appears to be accepted or not; and whether the subsequent protestation of repudiation operates in any way.

† It is sufficiently doubtful whether those words spoken in the power of attorney induce acceptance of the inheritance, and it seems that they do: because by asserting from a just and legitimate title and cause, from which no other title appears, it is presumed from the preceding title, namely, from the title as heir. For such was the one protesting, who could also be the heir of the said John C. On acquiring possession, l. *minus instructus*. On the sale of a thing, l. *quaedam mulier* and l. *si a te*, if slaves are sold, with similar cases. For it is certain that from the protestation the intent is presumed, such as can be gathered from the protestation. On acquiring an inheritance, l. *pro haerede*, § 1. On legacies, l. *at si quis*, § *plerique*. And it does not seem that this protestation can be justified without the name and right of the heir. Therefore, and also, D. On acquiring an inheritance, l. *pro haerede*, § *Papinianus*. To the contrary, it seems that where no cause is specified, the protestation is uncertain, and the one protesting may declare it, but not his heir. D. On the sale of a thing, l. *Idem Pomponius scribit*, if wheat, § last. Because this antiquity is referred to the judgment, and thus it does not obstruct D. On the law, l. 1, l. *si quis a filio*, § 1, and what Bartolus notes D. On acquiring an inheritance, l. *gerit*, by reason. Therefore, due to uncertainty, acceptance of the inheritance is not induced, because it is not established that it was with the intent of accepting the inheritance. The objection from l. *minus instructus* does not hold, because there the intent and will preceded in the title of acquiring, and therefore it is also presumed in possessing. Here neither did the intent precede, nor is possession established.

† Moreover, as I have said, a doubtful and general act receives its interpretation from the preceding and subsequent acts. *De legibus 1*, l. *Si servus plurium*, § *ult.*, ff. *De testamento*; l. *Heredes palam*, § *Sed si notam*. But this woman later said and declared that she did not wish to be an heir. This declaration is extended even to the procuratory and the protestation, so that they were not made with the intention of being an heir. For later specific matters detract from general ones, as in c. *Generi*. Likewise, if effect is given to the protestation and repudiation, C. *De repudiatio hereditatis*, l. *Suus*; and ff. *De interpretatione actorum*, l. *Si filius* and l. *Quapropter*. Therefore, from a doubtful mind, declared at the beginning and later negatively, we must say that it is not presumed that there was an intention to accept at the beginning, and that those words, "by just title and cause," were not uttered with respect to the title of heir, but of another, for which proof does not lie, because it suffices that it is possible. For excluding the acceptance, it suffices that it is not established before us with what mind she uttered the words at the beginning, since she later asserted and declared that she was not an heir, when her declaration must be followed. L. *Pro herede*, § 1, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, according to Jacobus de Arena and according to Bartolus in the said l. *Gerit*. For the will, which is the declaration of the mind to embrace or reject something, does not appear at the beginning, because the words were uncertain; but from the repudiation itself, the mind is clearly established. Therefore, and c. *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Continuus*, § *Cum ita*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a renunciation or refusal made mutually between two brothers in the division of property causes the fideicommissum to be considered remitted.
2. Liberation is a certain kind of deprivation: and it does not refer to that which is in potentiality, but to that which is in actuality.
3. On the understanding of the law *Qui Romae*, § *Duo fratres*, in the Digest, under the title *De verbis obligatorum*.
body: The nobleman Vannes Procardi of Gubbio made a will, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows: in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they are and may be found, he instituted Petrutius and Conrad, his sons, as universal heirs for two parts, and Jacob and John, sons of his son Paul, as universal heirs for the third part. And if any of the said heirs should die without children born to him from a lawful marriage, that the entire said inheritance should devolve upon the survivors. And that nothing from the inheritance of the said Jacob and John could come into the hands of Nesola, the former wife of Paul and mother of the said Jacob and John. And if the aforementioned heirs all should die without children, as stated, that the entire inheritance should devolve upon certain other persons. Now, after the testator died, Petrutius died without children. Now Conrad, Vannes, and the said Jacob and John came to the division of the said goods and inheritance, and each made a settlement, renunciation, and release with the other, and the other with each, regarding the part or portion coming to the other in part; moreover, they promised each other reciprocally, with solemn stipulation on both sides, that they would not bring any suit or controversy at any time concerning the things coming to the other in part, nor consent to any such suit being brought. But that all and each of the aforementioned things should be held firm and valid, observed and kept, and not violated or contravened under any occasion or cause, under the penalty of double the value of the said things, with solemn stipulation on both sides previously made, and with restitution of damages, etc. All the aforementioned contracting parties, and each of them, swore on the holy Gospels, touching the scriptures, to hold and keep all the aforementioned things firm and valid, etc. Now it is asked: whether by this division and by this mutual renunciation made, the future right of the fideicommissum appears to have been removed and remitted, or not; and whether these promises made in the said division prejudice in any way the said fideicommissum in the future, etc.

Whether, because they mutually rejected one another, the future right of the fideicommissum is thereby removed and remitted. And it seems that it is: because the matter did not remain within the limits of a simple division, but proceeded further to a rejection, which is valid and applies even to a future right, as in l. 1, C. de pactis. Therefore, assuming knowledge of the will, the hope of the fideicommissum appears to have been remitted, C. de transact., in l. de fideicommiss. iuxta, no. per Dy. in § duo fratres. To this also seem to extend those rules that “at no time” do not imply what is conferred for the future, de verb. oblig., l. cum stipulamur; l. si a colono, de verb. sign.; l. verbum oportebit. The contrary is true: because a division does not prejudice a fideicommissum left after death, de leg. 2, l. cum pater, § haereditatem. Nor does the objection hold regarding the promise not to act against the division: because neither does this promise exclude a fideicommissum left after death. For it does not appear that any thought was given to the remission of the fideicommissum, de transact., l. qui cum tutoribus; de pact., l. tres fratres. And this is held by Pe. Ray. and Bar. in the said § duo fratres. Likewise, the objection based on rejection does not hold, because a simple rejection is understood to apply to present right, and not to a right that arises subsequently; for it is not presumed to be repudiated before it has arisen.

† Moreover, release is a certain kind of deprivation. And therefore it must be referred to that which was in act, not to that which was not even in habit. On conditions and demonstrations, l. Titio usufru.; and on exceptions of res judicata, l. cum mater, § eandem; and on conditions of the undue, l. si, § idem quaesivit. Furthermore, these clauses are clauses adjacent to the division. Hence they come more to express the effect of the division than to increase it itself, and to make the division exceed its proper and mere nature. Argument from ff. loca., l. si uno; on damage inflicted, l. damni, § et quod in stipulatione. The objection from l. 1, C. de pac. does not hold, because there an express and special pact was made not to claim a future fideicommissum, i.e., one left after death. And thus the objection does not hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman who marries a second time and claims a dowry from the children of her first marriage is bound to give security to those children for the restitution of the dowry in the cases ordained by law.
body: The fact is as follows: A husband, who was bound to provide a dowry for his wife, died, leaving his wife surviving and children born of both. After some time, the wife married another man, and for the purpose of the dowry, she assigned to her second husband the rights competent to the said woman to demand the dowry from the said sons and from the sons of the said first husband, as heirs of their father, who were bound to the said mother for the restitution of the said dowry. The second husband, possessing suitable assets and being an inhabitant of the same city as the aforementioned parties, demanded from the said sons and heirs of the first husband that the said dowries be paid to him by virtue of the assignment made to him by the said lady, their mother. The sons, however, demand security from the said husband, or from one of them, for the restitution of the said dowries in the cases ordered by law, in whole or in part, as shall be due to the said sons by right and according to the form of the statute of the commune of Siena. It is asked from the foregoing whether the said husband and wife, the mother of the said defendants, or either of them, is bound or can be compelled by the said sons to give security or provide some caution for the restitution of the dowries, as stated above. This is premised on a certain statute, the tenor of which is as follows: "If any woman having legitimate sons or daughters, one or more of either sex, makes a will, or codicils, or a donation, she cannot leave, donate, sell, or alienate in such a way that her children who remain afterwards may be deprived of their goods; unless for the cause of the necessity of her own sustenance, provided that she may dispose of one-fourth part of her goods at her own discretion, and dispose of it, notwithstanding the disposition which she first made. In the aforementioned chapter, this was added by the statute-makers: namely, nephews and nieces, and descendants from her. And they removed, namely, 'makes a will, codicils, or donation,' and added at the end: namely, the remaining three parts shall be divided equally among the sons pro rata."

† While the mother is alive, the children of the first or second marriage have no right to the dowry. And therefore they cannot demand any security from the mother or her assignee. Nor is the husband compelled to bind himself to anyone else for the restitution of the dowry other than to the wife, even if the wife does not wish it. These points are proven by: D. de lib. agn. l. si; Auth. de haer. et falc. § si vero; D. si a pat. quis fuer. man. l. usque adeo; C. ne fidei. dot. den. l. 1 and 2; D. sol. mat. l. 2 post princ. Nor ought they to be concerned about the inheritance of a living mother, nor can an agreement be interposed. C. de pact. l. si; cum si non ob. l. hac edictali § his illud; C. de sec. nup. because it speaks of the gains of the first marriage, not of the woman's dowry. It is therefore concluded that, without the burden of providing security, the said dowry can be demanded. D. sol. mat. l. si prior maritus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. That substitution is the one which most broadly excludes the mother.
2. Pupillary substitution includes the exemplary substitution made in favor of a person who is mute and deaf at the time of the will.
3. A tacit substitution excludes [the heir], where the testator's intent is apparent.
4. Since a usurer cannot make a will, he cannot make a pupillary substitution in favor of his underage son.
body: A certain Petus Atnardi, having Leoneta as his lawful wife, and a sole son in the age of pupillarity, and also mute and deaf from birth, made a will: in which he instituted his said pupil, named Blasius, as his universal heir. And if it should happen that Leoneta, the wife of the testator, is pregnant, and it should happen in the future that she becomes pregnant by the said testator, and bears one son, or more: then together with the said Blasius he instituted them as his universal heirs in equal portions. And he substituted them for one another, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum. But if daughters, etc., and it should happen that the said daughters die in the age of pupillarity, or afterwards at any time, he substituted the said Blasius vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum. All these failing, he substituted the said Brother James, his brother, excluding the mother, and all those coming intestate, as above. But if it should happen that the said Blasius dies, as above, then, and in that case so arising, he substituted the said Brother James Arnard of the Order of the Carthusians, his brother, in all his goods, in his own name, as well as in the name of the order: in such and such a manner, that the said Brother James is bound, and ought, from the goods of the said testator, to fulfill [pious obligations] for the soul of the said testator, etc., always excluding the mother, and all others coming intestate. And the said goods the said Brother James may take and hold by himself, at his own will, without contradiction of any person. Then the said testator died, the said Blasius then a pupil, and mute, and deaf from birth, surviving. Then the said Blasius died in adult age, the said Leoneta, mother of the said Blasius, aforesaid, surviving. Between whom, Leoneta on the one part, and the said Brother James, the substitute, on the other, a matter of question arose concerning the inheritance of the said testator. For the said Leoneta says that the inheritance of her said son pertains to her intestate. And on the contrary, the said Brother James says that the said inheritance pertains to him by the will.

† Now it is asked, to whom the said inheritance pertains, and by what right. And it seems that the said inheritance pertains to the said mother as an intestate heir, and this for several reasons.

The first reason is the time limit imposed by the pupillary substitution. And this is proven thus: whenever a substitution is limited by time, the passage of time causes it to vanish and not to endure further, as in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Ex facto, §. Item quaero. But it is certain that a pupillary substitution is limited by time; for it does not endure unless the testator dies while still an impubes in his pupillary age, even if the testator had added a more distant time, as in D. de pupillari substitutione, l. In pupillari. Since, therefore, this Blasius did not die in his pupillary age, but in adult age, it rightly seems that not only is the pupillary substitution extinguished, but also all its effects, to which it could be drawn in any way, as in D. de legatis primo, l. Quod fideicommissum, and noted by Cynus in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Ex tribus.

The second reason is as follows: a distinction and an express enumeration of substitutions restricts the substitutions, and the species and cases enumerated; for the enumeration of species is accustomed to restrict the genus, and especially the enumeration of times, according to that general rule which is laid down, that the species derogates to the genus, as in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Cohaeredi, §. Qui patrem; as in D. de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. Alimenta, §. Basilicæ, and l. Stichus in principio; and D. de legatis tertio, l. Heres meus, §. Duæ statuæ. But here the testator enumerated three species of substitutions, namely, vulgar, pupillary, and fideicommissary; and he said nothing about a substitutio exemplaris, and consequently he did not think of it; therefore, we are not in the case of a substitutio exemplaris, but in the case of a fideicommissary substitution. This fideicommissary substitution does not exclude the mother, although it burdens her with the charge of a fideicommissum, the Falcidian portion being saved, as in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. Precibus, and in c. Si pater, de testibus, lib. 6.

The third reason is as follows: the express makes the tacit cease, especially the subsidiary, which is introduced in default of an express provision, as in the aforementioned §. Item quaero. But after the pupillary age there was an express fideicommissary substitution; therefore, the substitutio exemplaris ceases.

The fourth reason is as follows: a testator who makes a substitution wishes the cause of that substitution to be able to exist; for he who appends a condition wishes it to subsist, as noted in C. de conditionibus insertis, l. Cum patrem. Therefore, I argue thus: The testator wishes the condition of the fideicommissary substitution to exist; therefore, not that of the direct substitution. For it is superfluous to substitute by fideicommissum if the direct substitution were to claim its place. And there is a kind of repugnance between the direct and the oblique, as is clear to one considering their natures; for the direct induces the acceptance of the inheritance in the person of the substitute; but the fideicommissum by no means does so; but it requires the acceptance of the inheritance to be made by another, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. Eam quam, and D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. Apud Iulium, §. Item Iulius.

The fifth reason is as follows: the pupillary substitution and the substitutio exemplaris are not of the same form and nature; therefore, one is not contained in the other; for different things have different reasons and conditions, as in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. Naturaliter, §. Nihil commune, and C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si maritus.

The sixth and last reason is as follows: This substitutio exemplaris was not expressed; therefore, it ought not to be tacitly understood, since the mother is in the middle, as in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. Precibus, and noted in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. Finis. Hence, in favor of the mother, the direct [substitution], being doubtful, is turned into an oblique one, as noted in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Verbis civilibus, according to one exposition of the gloss. Nor let anyone say that here the substitute was the brother of the testator, who, by the presumed will of the deceased, excludes the wife according to the note in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Lucius; for this brother was substituted as a minister, not as one feeling the benefit; nor in his own favor under fraternal charity, but as a minister of the poor, who are strangers, and do not exclude debts by the law of nature, as noted in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papiæ, §. Si Imperator.

From which reasons it seems to be concluded in favor of the mother. On the contrary, it seems for several reasons.

The first reason is as follows: an expressly stated pupillary substitution contains by implication a substitution made in favor of a person who was deaf and mute at the time of the will and who was subsequently not freed from this condition. As noted by Guillaume de Cuyac in the matter of pupillary substitution, and by Bartolus in the same matter, who discusses this same substitution in the law *Ex facto*, and it is proven by reason, in those having a greater symbol, i.e., a greater similarity, the transition is easier. As stated in the Digest, under the title *De actione empti*, in the law *An inutilis*, § *Si*: although the implied substitution has a greater similarity with the pupillary substitution than the pupillary substitution has with the vulgar substitution, yet one is expressly contained, the other arises from legal interpretation. As stated in the Digest, under the title *De vulgari substitutione*, in the law *Iam hoc iure*.

† The second reason is as follows: whenever the testator’s intent appears to be that he wished to exclude the mother of the ward by direct substitution, even a tacit substitution excludes the mother, as noted in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. Precibus, in the gloss beginning “immo,” which is a very notable gloss and commonly noted by the doctors. But here the deceased’s will is explicit, because in the will he repeatedly states “the mother being excluded.” The third reason is as follows: for if the substitutions made in the will are rightly considered, we find therein a fourfold substitution, namely, vulgar, pupillary, fideicommissary, and compendious. The first three are expressed, but the fourth is understood where he says, “all these failing, my lord Jacob, his brother, as below, the mother being excluded.” And also afterwards he adds, “if it should happen that my lord Blasius, his son, dies a second time, as above, then he substitutes my lord Jacob in all his goods.” What else is he saying above but “in pupillary age, or afterwards whenever, and even if he did not survive the time”? This substitution is called compendious according to all, as noted in the said l. Precibus. But it is so that a compendious substitution excludes her whom the mother excludes; therefore, the mother is excluded. Moreover, this compendious substitution, considering that other species are enumerated, cannot operate except by way of example; therefore, it operates in her, as in D. de legibus 1, l. Si quando, and D. de usu, Si stipulatus, and l. 1, D. ad municipalia. The fourth reason is: the testator said “in all his goods.” But only direct substitution conveys all the goods; therefore, this substitution is interpreted as direct. Bartolus approves this reason in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Centurio. The fifth reason is: because the testator wished that the said lord Jacob could take all the goods by his own proper authority, by which words he signifies the direct mode of taking, and not from the hand of another, as in D. de legibus 2, l. Titia cum testamento, § 1. The sixth and last reason is: because from the narration of the substitutions, the father made such a substitution after the children as he placed between the children and the poor in the place of children. But the children among themselves would exclude the mother; therefore, the poor also exclude her. This reason is proved by the text in the said C. Si pater. From which it appears that if the said will is otherwise valid, the said Leoneta, having a husband, is altogether excluded.

But it is doubted whether the said testament is valid or not. For it is alleged that the said testator was a manifest usurer, and that many usurious contracts appear, although he did not keep an altar prepared, and although citation was not made according to the form of the chapter *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, lib. 6. And it seems at first sight to be said that the said testament is valid, first on account of the favor of the soul, as in the argument of the Digest, *De usu*, l. *Si bene*, in the beginning; and *De religione*, l. *Sunt personae*. Secondly, because the exemplary substitution is the testament of the son, but the son was not a usurer; therefore the testament was valid, as in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Papius*, § *Sed nec impuberis*. To the contrary is the truth itself: for a manifest usurer, without having given security, is incapable of making a will, and can order nothing by disposition of last will. Hence both legacies made in any manner and substitutions are void and null by operation of law, according to the form of the chapter *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, lib. 6.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute that totally excludes daughters from their father's goods is inequitable and contrary to natural law; hence it is most odious.
2. A statute may well reduce a daughter's dowry, although it cannot exclude her from maintenance.
3. A statute excluding women from succession is understood to apply to those who are dowered, or to be dowered, from the goods of the person whose succession is in question; but what if the statute excludes on account of males, and all males are dead while a female survives, and no. 4.
4. Under the term "children," women are not included, nor are descendants through women.
body: Let them be satisfied if they cannot have recourse to the paternal goods. Heading. Whether daughters, or a daughter, given a dowry by their father, or by a full brother, grandfather, or grandmother, are satisfied, and whether they can, or cannot, from the deceased father, or mother, grandfather, or grandmother, brother, or brothers, or their living descending children, have recourse to the paternal or maternal goods, or of the grandfather or grandmother, said daughters, or their successors, to claim something on the occasion of the inheritance of any of the said persons, or for any other cause, whether they have renounced or not. But if anyone should die leaving several daughters, or granddaughters, nevertheless let each succeed in equal male share. But if any of them should have been married only, let them receive less from the succession, by as much as was the amount, or dowry. Furthermore, if the father, or mother, grandfather, or grandmother left anything to said married daughters, or granddaughters beyond the dowry, they cannot claim anything beyond that on the occasion of the legitime, or for any other cause, while male brothers, or uncles, or their children are living. On sons and daughters remaining together when the father dies intestate. Heading. The father dying intestate. Without disposing in any way of his goods, and leaving sons and daughters together, the brothers are bound to provide the sisters with a suitable dowry, having regard to the quality of the persons, and the condition of the patrimony established. The declaration of what constitutes a suitable dowry shall be made, and let it stand according to the declaration of two of the nearest blood relatives of said sister, or girl, within 25 years from the time of her birth. But if the father left something for their dowry, and they have declared themselves satisfied with what was left, let them be satisfied; let them not aspire further to the paternal or maternal goods as successors of the deceased, and in both cases aforementioned they cannot have recourse; but the male sons shall be universal heirs in the paternal or maternal goods. But if it should happen that any of the said brothers is absent and not ratifying the dowry established by the other brothers, he is not bound to adhere to the establishment of the dowry made by the brothers. But the woman shall have recourse against the absent brother for the portion of the dowry touching her. But if any of the daughters at the time of the father's death was under the age of 18 years by two or three years, the brothers are bound to marry her off; otherwise she may marry herself, even if the brothers are ignorant or unwilling, to whom the necessity of providing them with dowries is imminent, as is expressed above. The point of the question is this. A certain man named Gregory died intestate, leaving two children, namely, a male named Jacob, and a female named Aluanista. This latter married, having been given 300 livres in dowry by her mother, without any renunciation of the paternal goods. Afterwards, this daughter Aluanista dies, leaving a single son named Carbous, and with her said brother Jacob surviving. After this, the said Jacob dies, leaving his three children, namely, Christopher, and John, male sons, whom he instituted as his heirs, and another named Allumella, a female daughter. Then the said Christopher and John, male sons of the said Jacob, sons of the late said Lord Gregory, die, leaving, namely, Nicholas, son of one of them, whom Nicholas the said Christopher and John instituted as their heir, and to Nicholas they substituted the said Allumella, sister of the said Christopher and John, aunt of the said Nicholas. Finally, the said Nicholas, nephew of the said Allumella, dies. And Allumella says that she ought to succeed by virtue of the said substitution made to her by the said Christopher and by the said John, her brothers, in all the goods and the entire patrimony of the late said Lord Gregory, saying that she ought to be admitted in the person of her mother the said Allumella, and to the goods of the said Gregory, her grandfather, who died intestate, etc. It is asked what is the law. Having seen the statutes named above.

† A statute that totally excludes a daughter from her father’s goods: because if it is unjust and contrary to the common natural law, it is considered most odious, as noted by Dy. in c. indultum. Nor ought it properly to be called a favor, but an unjust favor: because it ought to be restricted, not extended. As in c. odia. But if a woman is not excluded simply, but in consideration of a dowry given or to be given, this statute is not called unjust: because a dowry takes the place of maintenance.

† Hence she has her legitime fixed for herself in the dowry: because the legitime could be diminished for her by statute. C. de nuptiis, l. patrem, according to Cynus. But she cannot be excluded by statute from alimony, so that she ought to have alimony from paternal property, or its equivalent, namely, a dowry. Moreover, the interpretation of a statute ought not to be referred to an impossible interpretation. ff. de verb. oblig., l. continuus; §. cum quis sub hac; ff. de legat. 1, l. apud Iul., §. si.

And therefore the statute is to be understood as applying to one who was endowed, or obtained something, or was to be endowed from the goods of the person whose succession is in question: this being the sound interpretation of the intellect, which is declared by another statute concerning sons and daughters, etc. Since, therefore, this Aluanista, wife of Gregory, was never endowed from her father’s goods, the cause of exclusion ceased in her case; and consequently, the exclusion itself. D. de inoff. test. l. si instituta. Therefore, by the common law, she transmitted her portion. C. de stipul. serv. l. liber hon. §. si hoc non. Cy. C. de bon. quae lib. l. non si.

† But if she had been endowed from her father’s patrimony, Carbous would have no right: because the succession having been transferred to the male line, and the female being entirely dead, it perpetually endures in the successions of males. C. de do. l. si auia. and noted in ff. de adult. l. pup. But if the daughter had survived all the males, with only one female remaining from her, the consideration of the statute, according to the consideration of the prudent, held that the female in the last degree was not of better succession than the daughter. C. de bo. ma. l. si viua matre cederet res ad suam naturam. de pac. l. si vnus. §. pactus. ver. quod et in spe dotis, ff. de pac. And although in the name of children are included grandchildren and great-grandchildren, even through a daughter. C. de condi. inser. l. 1.

† Nevertheless, I say that the term "children" does not include females, nor descendants through females: because the text says, "or children." For by the nature of conjunction, it is to join equals in reason. C. de ser. fu. l. si fugitivi. and l. 1. de re. du. But males and females are not similar in an exclusive favor. And the law speaks of the male where the female is excluded. The male person who perfectly, and not suspensively, excluded the female, and thus it should be understood, as no. Bar. in l. aequissimum. ff. ad Tert.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the hirer of a beast for carriage is liable for the death of the said beast.
body: Vannutius

† hired a certain beast for carriage, which fell sick on the journey and was left with an innkeeper, and was diligently looked after by the innkeeper; finally it died. It is asked whether Vannutius is bound to make compensation for it. I respond that he is not, because he is not liable for a natural defect; likewise nor for an accidental event (casus fortuitus); indeed, he is not even liable for slight fault (levissima culpa). If, however, it had not been diligently looked after, he would be liable. And so I have advised on another occasion. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether Greek clerics, who may have wives, enjoy the privilege with respect to their goods, so that they are not liable for taxes or levies; and what is the case regarding other non-married clerics.
2. The Authentica *de privilegio dotium* also includes Eastern clerics.
body: It is permitted to Orientals whether they contracted marriage before receiving sacred orders. Extra, De clericis coniugatis, c. Cum olim; and it is read at length, and noted, 28. Dist., c. Diaconi, and clerics lawfully married have themselves, and their wives, and their children, privileges of immunity. C., De episcopis et clericis, l. 2. For the Church protects such clerics, De poenis et remissione, c. Quaesitum. Therefore, they have the privileges of Westerners, just as others who do not have wives: so that they do not bear extraordinary offices, nor pay assessments, but only tribute is demanded from them. As noted, C., De episcopis et clericis, l. 1, and Auth., Item nulla communitas, De immunitate ecclesiarum, c. Nominatim. They themselves are true clerics: although they profess continence, and have the expressed sacred character just as Westerners do; because the order is conferred in the same form as for us, and the characters are imprinted even by women. Although we are bound more strictly than they, nevertheless the priesthood is common. And briefly, the case seems to apply literally for them, in l. 2, C., De episcopis et clericis, Soli tributa soluunt. Eo. tit., De his a quibus nemo excusatur, C., Sine censu vel reliquis, l. Omnes, because the thing rather than the person is more fitting. And the thing itself has been made perpetual, and has a perpetual cause of attachment. De muneribus et honoribus, l. Rescripto, §. Si; and l. Munera, ff., De censibus, l. Forma; 18. q. 2, c. Sed vitium; 11. q. 1, c. Si tribuatur.

† To the contrary it seems, on account of the general rule, that clerics, even those lawfully married, do not have immunities of their own property, as in c. 1, de clericis conjugatis, lib. 6, and no. 23, dist. c. clerici. It makes, that no. 54, dist. c. nulli, 11 q. 1, c. clericum, and 1, where this no. expressly and without distinction in any married person 31, dist. c. quoniam, and c. aliter 81, dist. c. Maximianus filius. And those who are schismatics do not seem to have the privileges of clerics, except in the lands of the Greeks, which are ruled by lay Greeks. In Auth. de privilegiis donandis haereticis mulieribus non praestandis: because those who live badly in the faith do not deserve the privileges of the faithful. C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. si sub praetextu, and no. in d. Auth. de privilegiis donandis, Guido, in d. l. 2, C. de episcopis et clericis, holds expressly, that Eastern clerics who are married have all the immunities of that l. s., that they are not bound to sordid or extraordinary duties, but only to the tribute. Nor are their estates subject to tribute, nor are they even bound to superindictiones. But the Emperor did not see this. c. unicum, de clericis conjugatis, in 6, which was not in existence at the time mentioned. And therefore it seems to be said, that either Eastern clerics are not married, and have privileges, but those who have wives do not enjoy the privilege of immunity. And thus that law is today corrected as regards married clerics in the West, East, North, and South. For the Vicar of Jesus Christ has been given power over all the earth, which he sees ascending, and the West of the Sun, and the North and the South. As in Auth. ut omnes obediant, in prov. §. haec considerantes, col. 5, Senioris, n. Rome, Pope first, and prince of priests. As in Auth. de ecclesiis, tit. in princ., col. 9, and 22, dist. c. de Constantinopolitana, and 21, dist. c. de certis, and c. clerici, and c. in novo, and 18, dist. in memoriam, and c. nullitas, and c. ita dominus, with infinite similar ones.

And that Authentica de privilegiis doctorum, which states that he is a heretic who is not a member of the Church, understands under the members of the Church also the Eastern clerics. Therefore, if they are married, they have the immunity of clerics, as in the Authentica de ecclesiis titulis, § 2, col. 9, and Codex de sacrosanctis ecclesiis. It pleases, and rather by tolerance than by Justinian law it is permitted to them to take wives. It supports what we note in the Authentica de sanctis titulis, § presbyteris aut diaconibus, and Distinction 31, chapter Maximianus, and Distinction 32, quasi per totum. And although one inconvenience is tolerated, that they retain wives in sacred orders, two inconveniences are not to be tolerated, namely, that they have wives and privileges. Codex de donationibus promissis, law 1, holding one foot in one state and the other in another, namely, in the sacred and the profane, living in act and habit. Codex de in dicta libertate, law unica; Codex de latronibus et latrociniis, law 1, § cum igitur; Digestum de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, law Titiae si non nupserit; Digestum pro suo, law si ancillam; Distinction 83, chapter si nihil.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To possess in bad faith, whether and when the defendant is said to do so.
2. Bad faith in the cause before the court is always presumed against the condemned defendant.
body: Title.

† of possession is given to the subsequent possessor who has a just cause for litigating; for he is not bound rashly to leave his right undiscussed, ff. de peti. hære. l. illud; and this avails up to the time at which the plaintiff's right is made clear, and not after it is established that the defendant himself does not have it. For then he begins to litigate in bad faith, and from that point on he begins to be held liable for the expenses of the suit, ff. de iudic. l. destitisse, C. de iudic. l. rem non nouam. §. fi., and this is in the principal case.

† But in the case of an appeal, bad faith is always presumed against the condemned defendant, because it is presumed by the sentence, C. de admi. tu. l. si bonam. And therefore, when the condemnatory sentence is confirmed afterward by the judge of the appeal, the defendant must be condemned in the expenses of the entire second suit; this is fully noted in c. ignorantia facti. de re iu. lib. 6. Therefore, the judge of the appeal ought to confirm the sentence in expenses just as in the principal case, with that modification of time, namely, that he is not held liable except from the day on which the right of the plaintiff was fully clarified; and in this manner also he ought to tax them, namely from the opening of the record of the first suit.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a natural loan is alleged in the libel, and a civil loan is proved in the course of the proceedings, whether the plaintiff’s claim is deemed proved.
2. Whether a difference of place disqualifies a witness.
3. Whether witnesses testifying to a smaller loan than that claimed provide proof.
body: The point of the foregoing opinion is apparent from the opinion itself, because three matters are inquired into, as will appear below. From the above-mentioned theme, three doubts are clearly elicited. The first is whether, if a natural loan is alleged in the libel and only a civil loan is proved, the plaintiff’s claim is proved. The second doubt is whether witnesses testifying concerning the loan, if they differ as to the place, provide proof. The third is whether, if they testify concerning a smaller amount than that alleged in the libel of the loan, they provide proof as to that amount concerning which they testify.

† And regarding the first point, I say that the plaintiff’s claim has not been proven: for if I sue on a loan (mutuum), and the witnesses do not prove the actual payment (numeration) of the loan, but only the confession thereof, the witnesses do not prove the case. So holds Speculum in the title De testibus, under the words “sed pone egi.” And therefore, in the libel, one should not allege only the payment, but both the payment and the confession, according to Guillaume; and this is true in the case of a loan, because confession is a species, i.e., a mode and form, of the contract itself. But in other cases, it is a species of proof: for in other contracts, the action does not arise from confession, but from proof. Otherwise it would be futile, and the species of proof would not be necessary, because the species of the contract is expressed in the libel. And thus, the law Publia at the end of the Digest, De deposito, is not to the contrary. Hence, either only the payment is alleged in the libel, as in the case proposed, and it is not sufficient to prove a civil loan, i.e., the confession. For where the proof is not conformable to the petition, an absolution from that action must follow. Digest, De his qui non infamantur, law Ob hæc verba. Or both the confession and the natural loan are alleged, and thus both are pleaded. And then, from the laws cited above, and from the number by Bartolus in the Digest, De verborum obligatione, law Si ita stipulatus, section Grisogonus, it is clear that a condemnation may follow. And this concludes the first point.

† As to the second point, whether diversity of place disqualifies a witness, I say that sometimes, when the fact about which the witnesses testify is not repeatable, if they differ as to the place, that diversity of place introduces a condition of impossibility; because when one fact is alleged, and testimony is given to prove another fact from a different place, it is necessary that they testify falsely. But if the fact about which the witnesses testify were repeatable, such as a confession, as is the case in our matter: then diversity of place among the witnesses, if it does not render them contradictory, renders them singular. And the singularity of witnesses divides and tears apart the testimonies; because every divided thing is torn apart, and therefore they do not prove, as in C. de test. l. testium, through the gloss and Cynus; and l. ob carmen, §. si, de test.; and through Innocentius in c. qualiter et quoniam, de accus. and de elect., c. bonae memoriae, Maguntino.

And from the foregoing it is clear, and the third doubt is also resolved, namely, that they do not prove the amount about which they testify, for the reasons stated above, namely, because they are inconsistent regarding the place, and because only a natural loan was deducted, whereas they testify about a civil one; otherwise, however, they would well prove the amount about which they testify, even if a greater sum was claimed in the petition. As stated in the law *Quidam aestimauerant*, Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, and it is expressly stated in the Digest, title *De libellis*, law 1.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A will made by a person in prison, when free disposition of the testator is required, is invalid; nor is such an heir admitted to the inheritance, who held the testator in prison. And no. 3.
2. Fear is proved by indications and causes.
3. One who kills the testator, or who does not provide necessities to him when he is ill, is deprived of succession by sentence: not, however, by operation of law itself, but to whom such inheritance shall be applied. And no. 5. OPINION XXVII.
1. Whether a church holding some property in emphyteutic lease from another church incurs forfeiture, either on account of improper alienation or non-payment of the canon.
body: The legal issue of the consilium written below appears from the consilium already written, for three things are required, as is clear below. In effect, the case is such: A certain man took a certain woman as his wife, who was not yet twelve years of age. At length, when she reached the legitimate age, since the husband was suspicious of her because she was beautiful—though nothing sinister appeared—he detained her in a private prison for several days; at length he drew her out of the prison, and while she was outside the prison, she made a testament in which, after some legacies, she instituted her husband as her heir. Eventually that instituted husband placed her back into prison and detained her there for several days; thereafter he killed her. The question is asked concerning her goods, whether they belong to the instituted husband or to her mother. From the aforementioned point, several doubts seem to be drawn. And first, whether a testament is valid when made at a time when someone was outside prison, yet both before the testament and after was kept surrendered in prison. Second, whether the instituted heir in a testament, if he killed the testator, is deprived of the inheritance. Third, if the inheritance is taken away from him who killed the testator as from an unworthy person, whether it is applied to the treasury, or to those coming intestate; because for the validity of a testament we look to the time the testament was made. But at that time this woman seemed free, because she was outside prison; therefore, it is permitted for a husband to induce his wife with flattering words to institute him, as in l. fina. C. si quis aliquem testa. prohibuerit. The truth seems to be to the contrary: because a testator's disposition ought to be free, as in l. 1. de sacrosan. eccle. But here it was not free; that it was not free is clear, for he is said to be compelled who vehemently fears lest he be compelled, as noted by Cyn. in l. nouissime. §. fi. ff. fal. tuto. an. and by Inno. in c. bonae. el 2. de elec., where he says that a just fear of pressure suffices, even though pressure has not followed; but here there was a just fear, namely, preceding fear of prison, as in l. qui in carcerem. ff. quod metus causa, which fear is deemed to endure while the indications continue, as noted by Cy. in l. carcerem. C. quod metus causa, and Inn. in c. 1. extra eo. and Bart. ff. de condi. ob tur. causam. l. si ob turpem. Furthermore, fear is presumed to have been caused where fear or blows had preceded, as noted by Inno. de offic. de lega. c. causam matrimonii, and the doctors in l. 1. §. quae honorandae. ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. And what was committed in the past is presumed to persevere, C. de nup. l. et si contra. through the gloss and Cyn. Furthermore, in our case the pressure of prison not only preceded the testament, but followed the testament; and thus from perseverance an indicative cause appears, ff. de regulis iur. l. quod calore. And the middle is to be judged from the two extremes; to this effect at the end is what is noted by Iac. de Are. in prooemio. C. and by Dyn. in l. 1. solu. mat., and there is the gloss in 16. q. 4. c. volumus. The aforesaid things do not stand in the way—namely, what is said that the time of the testament must be looked to—because I concede this, unless something precedes that renders it incapable and infers into the present from the past. Likewise, l. fin. quod si quis aliquem testa. prohibuerit does not stand in the way, because I concede that it is lawful to induce a wife with flattering speeches to institute oneself, provided that fear or fraud ceases, which is rarely presumed to cease, as noted by Cyn. in said l. fi.; and [the inheritance is] to be taken away from this husband as from an unworthy person, as in l. 1. C. si quis aliquem testa. prohibuerit. Nor does what the gloss noted in said l. si quis in carcerem stand in the way, namely that one staying in prison can make a testament, because I understand this not to be for the benefit of the detainer; the same if she is outside prison, since she does not have a free will, because she is still detained by guards, as noted there by the doctors.

† As to the second doubt, I say that, presupposing that no fear had intervened here, nevertheless, since this husband instituted by the wife killed the wife, he is repelled from the succession, as noted by Bar. in l. fin. ff. si quis aliquem testa. prohibuerit. For one who kills the testator—or even, what is less, neglects him when he is sick—is stripped of all benefit of the succession as an unworthy person, as in l. si ab hostibus. §. si vir uxorem. ff. sol. mat. Yet likewise the husband is unworthy by judicial sentence, not by operation of law: de adimen. leg. l. ex parte. and ff. de vulga. et pup. sub. l. ex facto Iul. and as noted by the gloss in ff. fa. her. l. primo consequenter. §. in familiae.

† As to the third matter indeed, whether this inheritance ought to be taken away from this husband as from an unworthy person and applied to the treasury, through what is noted in l. Pap. §. meminisse. and l. Lucius. ff. de iure fisci, it must be said that it should not, since a statutory heir survives here, such as the mother, and as noted by Bar. in l. cum ratio. §. praeterea. ff. de bonis dam. From all of which I conclude that the inheritance of her said daughter belongs to the mother as the legitimate heir on intestacy, and not to the instituted husband. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a church holding some property under emphyteusis from another church incurs forfeiture, either on account of undue alienation or unpaid ground-rent.
body: Most reverend and most singular father and lord,

† It is asked whether a church holding a property under emphyteusis from another church incurs forfeiture (commissum), as your aforementioned Lordship knows. There are diverse opinions; for Pe. and Abb. hold that it does incur forfeiture. In support of whose opinion the reason works: that ecclesiastical property cannot be alienated without solemnity, 10. q. 2. c. hoc ius, 12. q. 2. c. sine exceptione, even if it receives a price; therefore much less if it receives no price. Likewise, the prince granted that privilege, therefore it cannot be revoked, de re. iur. c. decet. lib. 6. Likewise, an occasion would be given for defrauding ecclesiastical rights. This is proved in the customs of feuds: where if a prelate commits felony against the king from whom the church holds a feud, while he is living he is deprived of the emolument of the feud, but after his death it reverts to the church, because a delict [binds] the person, etc., as in the rule delictum, de reg. iur. lib. 6. This opinion—namely, that the property does not incur forfeiture, but that an action should be brought for the ground-rent (canon) of the past time—is held by Gof. in the summa de immu. eccle., and this through l. placet, C. de sac. san. ec., which is canonized in 16. q. 1. c. placet. And Ioan. holds the same, 11. q. 1. c. si tributum; Ioan. And. holds the same in c. constitut., de reli. dona., and Ioan. de Lig. there, whose are the aforesaid reasons. But to the contrary works what the gloss, Innocen., and Hostien. note in the said c. constitut., where they expressly hold the contrary, namely, that it does incur forfeiture. On this there is the gloss in the said Auth. qui rem huiusmodi, where it expressly determines this; on this see Spec. in tit. de loca. §. nunc aliqua verse 14. And if the opinion of Ioan. And. were true, emphyteusis would not preserve its nature, nor would it ever return to ownership, which is absurd. And I believe that this side is more true, because in doubtful matters one must adhere, as I believe the gloss does, and I also hold this side. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the revocation or withdrawal of a legacy can be proven by two witnesses
body: Siper

† As to the question raised, whether the revocation of a legacy can be proved by two witnesses, there are differing opinions. For some say that a solemn legacy is not revoked by a less solemn expression of will, and they rely on a general rule and a special rule. The general rule is that as each thing is produced, so it is dissolved; and thus the principle of corruption is the same as that of generation. D. 45.1. pr. (De solutionibus). The special rule, regarding last wills, is that a less solemn act does not invalidate a solemn one. D. 35.1.3. (De legatis tertio); C. 6.23. (De testibus). In support of this view also stands this reasoning: namely, the solemnity of the number of witnesses is required so that nothing false may be committed by perjury concerning the last will. C. 6.42. (De fideicommissis). But falsehood can be committed just as easily in proving an ademption as in proving a legacy. To this reasoning also contributes natural reason. Suppose that in a solemn will I left to someone a very large quantity, or a major part of my goods; it would be unjust and not credible to believe two witnesses regarding the ademption. D. 49.17. (De testamento militis). For there would be no one who could impeach them; and thus true judgments could easily be nullified, which is absurd. Moreover, if a legacy is favorable, it is not proved by two witnesses; therefore, much less should the revocation of a legacy, which is in a manner odious, be so proved. Moreover, revocation is a last will; therefore, the rule stated must be observed. C. 6.33. (De codicillis). And at least five witnesses are required, unless this revocation had a cause inherent in it, such as enmity. D. 33.1. (De adimendis legatis). And since those causes come from outside and not from the will itself, they can be proved by two witnesses, such as capital enmity, as is said.

On the contrary, it is proved thus: from a non-solemn legacy made before two witnesses, a natural obligation arises, as is noted. C. 8.40. (De iure et facti ignorantia); through the gloss and the Ultramontane jurists. Therefore, conversely, by ademption the natural obligation is removed; because the opposing argument is removed: for written equity is against the actor. And to this point contribute laws sufficiently noted. C. 6.42. (De fideicommissis); D. 35.1.1. (De legatis primo); D. 49.17. (De testamento militis); D. 33.1.3. (De adimendis legatis). And the presumption is that, although there are only two witnesses, they nevertheless speak the truth. C. 7.62. (De rebus eorum). And this latter part is true if the witnesses are of known good faith and above all exception. Hence even a slight blemish, or a slight suspicion of bias, would weaken them in this case, so that they would not be believed. Argument from C. 4.15. (De contrahenda stipulatione); and in Auth. De testibus. And if the legacy were very large, and a universal fideicommissum, which in some respects is equivalent to the institution of an heir, perhaps two witnesses should not be believed in a matter so prejudicial and clandestine. It is suspicious. It is noted that what is done secretly is called clandestine; and it is said to be done secretly that which is accustomed to be done openly; and it is the duty of a good praetor to intercept such witnesses as much as he can, as is noted by Azo in his Summa De testibus. And therefore they must be questioned very subtly about each circumstance, unless, as I said, the witnesses were very trustworthy.

In canon law, I do not doubt that this ademption is valid. Extravagantes De testibus, cap. Cum esses; and cap. Relatum. The credibility of the witnesses being approved, which is left to the discretion of the judge, as in D. 22.5. (De testibus), in the verse Tutela maioris; and C. 4.20. (De testibus). If therefore the judge believed the persons, he ought to have believed their statements, as in D. 49.16. (De re militari). And therefore, according to what is proposed, he judged justly in absolving. However, let the records speak: for this consists in the facts, and the records are so numerous that I, being entangled in many other matters, cannot chew them over individually. But in law, this is what I myself have written. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a second will, lacking an institution of an heir, revokes the first: and whether at least this second will is valid as a last will.
body: Secondly

The will does not appear valid at first sight, because it lacks an institution of an heir. L. proxime, De his quae in testamento delentur. And if this is so, the first will is valid. Nevertheless, the time does not run for the Hospital of Scala until the will is known to them, because a potestative condition requires knowledge. D. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, L. 2. But if it were repudiated, assuming that the first will is valid, the other substitutes would succeed according to the order of the will. I have seen the document of the second will now shown to me, and it does not appear that the testator made anyone heir except from certain things: saving that to his wife, under a certain veil of words, he seems to have left everything; whether this was the mind of the testator or not, I do not know. Nevertheless, because the words say "denarii" and other things, and then it appears that the words are general; the intention, however, does not seem to have been so, by what follows, "and insofar as," etc. I cannot, with a clear conscience, condemn the second will, because the testator wished it to prevail over all others. At least, let the second will be valid as the last will. I, Baldus,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How property and fruits ought to be divided among brothers, from whom there remained one son from one and several from another; and what if two were captives and ransomed themselves, whether the others are bound; and what concerning dowries paid out of common money, and whether they are presumed to be partners; and if not, how this is to be proved.
body: How the property and fruits of the property are to be divided among brothers, from whom sons remained, namely: one from one, and two or more from the other. And what concerning the ransom, when two were captured and paid it, whether they are bound [to contribute]. And what concerning dowries paid from common funds.

† On the first petition for division, John has a right: because the goods of the deceased belonged to any of the sons, for half of this from the intestate heirs. §. cum filius. On the second petition, the said John has a right, namely, that the dowries paid from common money must be returned to Joan for half: because it did not pertain to John to provide those dowries. However, it must be seen from which common things they were endowed. For if they were from the price of sold things, it suffices that the said John be restored half of the price derived from the said things. C. de rei ven. l. mater. And thus it is answered, even to the fourth and fifth petitions. On the third petition, I say that what has been paid from common things to the heir must be returned to the said John for half, but what has been paid from the profit of persons and labor must be returned to him only for his proportional share, which is a fourth part: because there are four profiting. On the sixth petition, I say that the hereditary household goods must be divided in half: but the household goods acquired from labor must be divided proportionally, i.e., per capita. On the seventh petition concerning fruits, I say that the fruits collected from hereditary things must be divided in two ways. For half of the fruits must be divided into two parts, the other half into four parts, as the shares are to be assigned. But the fruits gathered elsewhere from the labor of alien things must all be divided proportionally, i.e., according to the number of persons. And John must have a fourth part from these. Profits and losses, businesses come into partnership: but those which are not business-related do not come into partnership. And from common paternal things, partnership is not proven. But from promiscuous acts and gains, and from the communication of losses, and from the quality of dividing one with another. As l. si socius. ff. si cer. pet. Those who trade separately are not partners. As l. itaque. ff. pro socio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In the restitution of the dowry, whether the statute or custom of the place of contract or of the husband’s domicile is to be observed.
2. Upon the death of the wife, the dowry ceases to be a dowry; nor do newly enacted statutes concerning dowries apply.
3. A statute must be interpreted so as not to abrogate natural rights.
body:
The statute of the city of Asti provides that if a wife dies before her husband without issue, the husband shall acquire the entire dowry. In this statute, it is asserted that, according to the custom of the place, the same rule had hitherto been observed. Thus, the said statute asserts an unwritten custom, reduced according to the form of written law.

Now it has happened that a certain Jacobus Mutius gave in dowry to a certain Gregory, residing in the village of Maxii, who is alleged to have been a citizen of Asti, in the said place of Maxii, which is not subject to the jurisdiction of the city of Asti, certain dowries consisting both in immovable property and in money; and accordingly an instrument was drawn up for the restitution of the dowry in this form, namely, because the said Gregory, the husband, promised to restore and pay the dowry, and especially according to the form of the statute, the order, and the customs of the city of Asti, whereby the husband bound himself, so that he might be more effectively held to the payment and restitution of the said dowry.

It is presupposed, furthermore, that the said statute was issued after the celebration of the said contracts, and also after the dissolution of the marriage. Nevertheless, in the said statute it is expressly provided that the statute itself extends to present, past, and future cases.

It is also presupposed that in the said village of Maxii the common law was observed; and that the said husband, at the time of the contract and the dissolution of the said marriage, was an inhabitant of the said village and had his domicile there.

And given all these circumstances, it is asked whether the said dowry ought to be restored in full to the heirs of the said woman; or whether, on the pretext of the said statute, it is not to be restored to the husband in any manner.
