† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that the heirs of the woman, in recovering the dowry, must follow the statutes and customs of the husband’s domicile, not only with regard to the forum but also with regard to the profit of the dowry itself; as that well-known law states: *tamen nobilis*, D. de iudic. l. *exigere dotem*; and there also by the doctors; and D. de cond. indebit. l. *qui certo loco*; and noted by Archidamus, distinction 12, chapter *illud*; and by Bartolus, in l. *cunctos populos*, in the third column, where he says: “it fails in the case of dowry,” D. de iudic. l. *exigere*, for the reason set forth in the text. And this is true, unless something else has been agreed upon between the parties, for example, because another place was inserted for the restitution of the dowry. For agreements that favor the restitution of the dowry are to be observed, especially those by which the action for the dowry is restored to its natural character, as in D. de pactis, l. *si unus*, § *pactus ne peteret*, verse *quod et in specie dantis*. Since, therefore, in the case proposed, it is alleged that the common law is observed in the husband’s domicile, the said dowry is, in the case of restitution, subject to that law. Here it should be noted that, with regard to the law of the forum, the custom of the domicile is to be considered more than the custom of origin; to this effect it is noted in c. *statutum*, § *nullus tamen*, on the word *unam dictam*, de rescriptis, book 6. And this is confirmed by another reason, because, upon the death of the woman, the heirs of the woman are not subject to the law of the marriage, because no remnants of the marriage remain, as in Auth. de nuptiis, § *deinceps*, column 4.

And this dowry is not a dowry, nor do the newly enacted statutes concerning dowries apply to it, after it has ceased to be a dowry. Although the action for dowry is available, regard is had to that which was formerly a dowry, but is not one now. Cf. D. 24.2.1 (Quod ait lex). Moreover, in the aforementioned instrument there are these words: "which he shall have given," which words properly signify the common law, as in D. 1.1.1 (Omnes populi) and Inst. 1.2.1–2. Furthermore, in the aforementioned instrument, although a place was added, the word "especially" is used there, which is an augmentative and not a diminutive term. It also appears that the said words were added in favor of the woman, even to enlarge her rights. Hence they should not operate to the contrary, as in D. 18.6.1 (Si vina emerim) and D. 19.5.2 with the following law, and C. 8.53.1 (Quod favore) with its subject matter. Moreover, those words, "according to the form of the statutes," refer to the statutes then in force at the time of the contract, as in C. 22.15.1 (Clericus) extr. de iureiurando. Nor can a new statute, or at least one newly disposing, contravene agreed pacts.

† because in case of doubt a statute ought to be interpreted so as not to deprive one of natural rights perfectly acquired. For such a statute would be unjust, as stated in the Institutiones, de iure naturali, §. sed naturalia quidem; and see the notes of Petrus de Bellapertica in l. si, Codex, si contra ius, vel uti, pu., ad hoc; Digestum, de pollutione, l. totiens; and Digestum, de exceptione doli, l. 1, in fine. From all of which it is sufficiently and clearly concluded that the said dowry must be restored in the case at hand, notwithstanding the said statute; and notwithstanding the prudently alleged arguments to the contrary; and notwithstanding the custom mentioned in the said statute. And especially because there is no proof that the said custom existed in the past. To this effect serves the case si Papa, de privilegiis, Liber Sextus. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Ubaldis, Doctor of Both Laws; and especially when two laws make one favor the dowry with respect to one law, and the other generally with respect to origin, preference should be given to the dowry rather than to a lucrative title. l. in ambiguis pro dotibus, de regulis iuris. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person fleeing from prison is to be considered as having confessed.
2. How the authority who has a prisoner under his custody is to be punished if the prisoner escapes.
3. Whether the flight of a prisoner induces proof against the accused.
body: First.

The first point of the question is whether one who flees from prison is to be considered as having confessed. The glossa states that this is so, in the law *Eos*, under the title *De custodia rei*. However, as a general rule, if someone flees, the flight renders him suspect, but does not convict him, according to the Authentica *De exhibendis reis*, section *Si vero*. And note this through Cynus in the law *1*, Code, *De raptu virginis*. Nevertheless, the aforementioned glossa to the law *Eos* must be limited in this way. For either a person is detained for a general inquiry, and he is not considered to have confessed, because a fictitious confession, just like a true one, must pertain to something certain, and therefore the specific crime must be proven, as stated in the law *1*, Code, *Ut omnes tam civiles quam criminales*, and in the Authentica *Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, section *Necessitas*. Or he is detained for an inquiry into a specific crime. And then either he flees with a breaking of bonds or conspiracy, and this is the case addressed by the law *Eos*; or he flees otherwise, and then he is not considered to have confessed, but he is nevertheless punished at the discretion of the judge, as noted by Guillaume de Cagnolo in the law *Succurritur*, under the title *Quibus ex causis maiores*. The second point is

† Concerning the power of him who has prisoners under his custody, and thus acts in the capacity of a *commentarius*, how he is to be punished if they escape, and indeed that he is subject to the same penalty as that which was due to be inflicted upon the prisoner himself, as stated in the law *Ad commentariensem*, Codex, *De custodia reorum*. For, by reason of his office, fraud (*dolus*) is presumed in him, which is equivalent to gross negligence (*lata culpa*), for which, in this special case, a capital penalty may be imposed, as noted by Cynus in the aforementioned law *Ad commentariensem*. It must be said that if he guarded them in the manner in which it is customary to guard, he is excused from gross negligence. Argument: commonly noted, Codex, *Communi*, law *Si ut certo*; § *Sed an etiam hominis*, Digest, *De negotiorum gestis*; law *Si negotia*. Nevertheless, he is punished by an arbitrary penalty. Law *Finis*, Digest, *De custodia rei*. The third article is,

Whether his flight induces proof against the magistrate. And it is said thus: as in the Digest, *ad Sillanum*, law *In conditione*. On the contrary, it seems that flight and contumacy of one do not harm another, unless perhaps the magistrate was acting in bad faith or with gross negligence. Code, *de examinationibus et testibus*, law *Quotiens*; and what is noted by Dynus in the law *Si*, Digest, *quando ex facto tutorum*. Moreover, fictitious proof is not extended to another in whom equal fault is not found, to this effect: Digest, *in litibus iudicatis*, law *Videamus*; and Digest, *de iure fisci*, law *Qui delatorem*; *de inofficioso testamento*, law *Qui repudiavit*, § *Ultimo*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who writes, or causes to be written, in an instrument that certain persons were present, when in fact they were absent, commits falsification.
2. Falsification is not committed without intent.
3. By what penalty is one punished who makes a public or private writing false.
body: Although

† he who writes, or causes it to be written, that certain persons were present who were in fact absent, commits forgery, as in C. de falsis, l. qui veluti, and C. de contrahen. et commi. sti., l. optimam, in fine, and extra de test., c. tam literis; nevertheless, one must prove this absence by witnesses who are not singular, extra de his quae fiunt a praela., c. 5, and as noted by the glossa ordinaria on the said c. tam literis; and it is expressly clear in de elec., c. bonae memoriae, in the case of the Bishop of Mainz; and what is noted in C. de testi., l. testium, and ff. de testi., l. ob carmen, §. finali, supports this. And therefore, in our case, singular witnesses do not suffice, even against a magistrate's notary who had drafted the letters, not the names of the witnesses,

† there is no doubt that he is not held liable, because forgery is not committed without dolus, as noted in C. de fal., l. nec exemplum; and what is noted in the same title, l. si quis decurio, by Cynus, and ff. quemadmodum te. ape., l. 1, in fine, and de fide inst., c. cum Io. haere., supports this.

† Likewise, these letters prejudice no one, nor indeed were they solemn, because there was no name of the Lord nor an indiction, as in Authentica ut praeponatur nomen Imperatoris, as noted in ff. de eden., l. j, §. editiones; and therefore the penalty of the lex Cornelia does not apply; but if the crime were established, it would be the crime of stellionate, as noted by Cynus on l. 1, C. de sepul. vio.; and it is clear in ff. de fal., l. si quis legatis, and ff. de penis, l. si quis aliquid, §. testamentum; and ff. de dolo, l. quaedam, supports this. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a dowried daughter, who by the form of the statute does not succeed to her father intestate, but to whom the father left something in his will, yet not by way of institution as heir, may declare the will null as having passed her over.
2. Whether a father, who, having instituted his son under puberty, left executors to inventory or distribute his goods after the death of said son, if he should die in pupillary age, appears thereby to have substituted them to his son by pupillary substitution.
body: The question is

† Whether a daughter, who is provided with a dowry and does not succeed intestate, but to whom her father left something in his will, not by way of institution of heir, can claim the will to be void as having been passed over. I answer: No; because one who does not succeed intestate does not break the will. As noted by Bartolus in the chapter *De liberis et posthumis*, in the law *Gallus*, § *quid si tamen*; and I have examined this most fully in the law *Maximum vitium*, in the final section, where you ought to look, under the title *De liberis praeteritis*.

Secondly, it is asked whether, if a father has appointed executors to distribute his property after the death of his son, and the son dies without issue, it should be understood that he made a pupillary substitution for him during his minority. I answer: No; because these executors are distributors, and not heirs. As stated in the Codex, *De episcopis et clericis*, in the law *Nulli vero*; and in the same title, in the law *Si quis ad declinandam*. For there, no prior institution of a universal heir had taken place, whereas here it has, according to the note in the Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in the law *His verbis*. Furthermore, the poor are not directly substituted heirs; because they must receive from the hand of the substitutor. And thus I, Baldus, have often advised.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an agreement that a wife, upon dissolution of the marriage, may enter into possession of the dotal property by her own authority, even if the property is possessed by someone other than the husband, can be enforced by a judge without summoning the possessor.
1. The present possessor need not be summoned.
2. Defense and summons are matters of natural law.
3. Dissolution of marriage retroactively restores ownership, although not possession.
4. Whether an agreement that a person may enter into possession by his own authority can be enforced against a third-party possessor, and whether it excuses the judge.
body: The question is

Whether a pact, by which a wife upon the dissolution of the marriage may enter into possession of the dotal property by her own authority after the death of her husband, even in things possessed by another, allows the authority of the judge to be exercised without the possessor being cited. And it seems that this is so. For by such a pact the woman appears to have retained possession for herself in the event of the dissolution of the marriage; therefore she could enter by her own authority: because this is not acquiring new possession, but continuing the old one. As in C. quod cum eo, l. si seruus. Also, because upon the dissolution of the marriage, dominion retroactively passes to the woman by operation of law. Therefore, possession also passes. For I do not see how dominion can pass without possession. As in C. de iure dotis, l. in rebus, which is noted in l. 1, § 1; and ff. de usucapione pro dote; and ff. de rei vindicatione, l. si ager. Also, in this case the judge is a mere executor of the agreed pact. Hence I do not see that he has need to cite the possessor: because a mere executor can execute without citation, as noted by Innocentius de appellationibus, ca. ex ratione. Also, this pact affects the thing and any possessor, when it is attached to her own thing and endures with it, because dominion never precisely departed from the woman, since the husband bears her image, as in the aforementioned l. in rebus; ad haec; ff. de servis exportandis, l. Titius. Also, that which is permitted without a judge is permitted through a judge. As in Inst. de libertis, § multis. Also contributing to this is what is noted in C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. 2. To the same effect is what is read and noted in C. de pignoribus, l. creditoris. Also, if this third-party possessor was present, no other citation is required: since he is present, and it is clear that he has no right. Argument from those things noted by Innocentius extra de filiis presbyterorum, cap. constitutus. Also, there must be some special favor for the dowry, by which dotal property is prohibited from being transferred to another to the prejudice of the woman. As in C. de iure dotis, l. si praedium. Also, it cannot be said that the judge was in bad faith by not citing: because although he omitted the order, he did without order what was not necessary to be done with order, as in ff. quod metus causa, l. si, § si. To this effect is what is noted in Speculum de locatione, § nunc aliqua, ver. 47. To the contrary, it seems that no one is to be deprived of his possession by a judge unless he is cited. As in C. unde vi, l. meminisse; and noted in the same title, si quis in tantam; and C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. si.

† for the possessor could have a defense, which is of natural law. Hence, when he does not cite, fraud is presumed: because he acts against natural law. As in c. Pastoralis, de re iudicata, in the Clementine.

† Moreover, the dominion reverts to the owner by operation of law, but not the possession, as stated in C. sol. ma. l. dotis. Furthermore, the judge cannot be excused from dolus (fraud), because what he did under violence contains fraud within itself. To this effect: C. de iure fis. l. facultas, lib. 10; and C. de bo. vacan. l. si, eo. lib. Moreover, the judge acts contrary to the sacred constitutions, which command that the possessor be always cited, as in C. si ob publicas pensitationes, l. si deserta; and see the note in l. quod miles, § 1, ff. qui ex causa maioris. But in one who transgresses the law, dolus and scientia (knowledge) are presumed, as in C. de legibus, l. leges sacratissimae. Also supporting this is Extra de praebendis, c. licet episcopi, lib. 6. Solution: if not

† if that pact existed, the magistrate would not be excused from fraud. As stated in l. 2, ff. quod quisque iuris, and in the aforementioned l. meminerint. Nevertheless, on account of that pact, he is undoubtedly excused from fraud, due to the various opinions of illustrious doctors, who held that such a pact could be enforced even against an unjust third-party possessor, as the glossator opines in the aforementioned l. 3, and Cynus and Petrus de Ancharano upheld this opinion there, although Jacobus de Belvis, in his disputation there, holds the contrary view, as do Jacobus Butrigarius and Bartolus. However, even if the negative opinion were true, since we have no text on this question and there are contrary opinions, nor are there demonstrative reasons for or against it, the judge is excused from fraud. As noted in Inst. de obligationibus quae ex quasi delictis nascuntur, in the principal part, on the word "videbitur" (shall see). By means of this gloss, this magistrate ought to be absolved: for when he has been accused of fraud, and fraud has not been proven, as in ff. de libellis, l. illud. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a dowried daughter, prohibited from succeeding by the form of the statute, can declare the will null as having been passed over.
2. Whether the share of one of the instituted heirs, lacking during the lifetime of the testator, accrues to the other coheirs.
1. Whether a codicillary clause is of any avail when the will is null due to the cause of passing over.
2. Whether those succeeding intestate, when sued, can deduct the two fourths.
body: It is alleged that the said Ant. Caracosam gave his daughter in marriage and assigned to her a certain sum as dowry; however, this is not proven by witnesses, but only by the confession of the said Caracosam and her voice, etc. It is also presupposed that there is a custom whereby a dowried daughter does not succeed the donor nor any other members of the donor’s lineage, nor does she inherit intestate. This learned man Ant. made a will and instituted certain collateral nephews as heirs, namely the sons of his brother, in which will he left nothing to his said daughter Caracosam by way of institution, but only by way of legacy. Now this Caracosam wishes to argue that the will is null on account of preterition.

† It is asked whether she can. I fully address this question. C. de lib. praet. l. maximum vitium. And there, under correction, I hold the better opinion that such a passed-over daughter cannot claim nullity on the ground by which she is excluded from intestate succession. First: because this daughter is not properly owed a legitime. Therefore, she does not break the will. Or because the dowry succeeds in place of the legitime, as noted by Cynus, C. de nupt. l. sancimus. For even under the law of the Codex, it was sufficient that anything be left to her under any title, and the dowry was imputed; hence, although she might be considered passed-over, having regard to the fact that no dowry had been constituted, nevertheless she could not declare the will null, nor could she come by way of contradiction. Moreover, she was excluded from the complaint of inofficiousness on account of the right of supplement, which was introduced by the new law, as C. de inoffic. testa. l. omnimodo and l. sancimus in the beginning, §. cum autem. Furthermore, since this daughter does not succeed intestate, it does not concern her to reduce the will to the case of intestacy. Hence, it is not permitted for her to act against the will, since she will have nothing from intestacy, as ff. de contrab. l. si post mortem, §. liberi. Moreover, Bartolus bases himself on this reason in l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum, de lib. et posth., where he says that today a grandson in the power of his grandfather, whom the father emancipated by the grandfather precedes, does not declare the will null, because he does not succeed intestate when the father precedes and accepts. Hence, he who does not succeed intestate does not break [the will]. And the reason is that he who is removed from the effect is equally removed from that by which the effect is introduced, or by which the effect is attained, l. oratione, de sponsalibus. Moreover, this daughter is in a manner dowered, and by the statute itself she is disinherited, and the act of the law succeeds in place of the act of man, as ff. de manumis. l. causam, §. 1. Sed si homo. If the father had formally disinherited her, the will would undoubtedly be formal, and such a daughter could not come by the right of declaring it null, as ff. de haere. insti. l. qui volebat. It is therefore concluded that the said will is valid. Hence, it must be observed that if the custom spoke only in the case of a testator, namely, that a dowered daughter does not succeed when a will is made, unless it excluded her from intestacy, then one might doubt whether the passed-over daughter could break [the will]. For a will is properly not a will when it is not formal, as appears from those things which are read and noted in l. 2, C. de edicto diui Adr. tol. and l. 2 in the beginning, ff. quemad. test. ape. and ff. de pęnis. l. si quis aliquid testamentum. Hence, it is not said that the testator died testate, since the will itself lacks formality by law, as C. de test. l. si vnus and ff. de lib. et posthu. l. Gallus, §. in omnibus and l. inter cętera, and ff. de iniu. test. l. 1 and l. posthumorum and l. cum in secundo. But since it is not expedient to dispute this at present, because we are not at this point, but at the first point, in which I hold against the dowered daughter. That which is noted by Cynus, C. de adul. l. publico, supports this. From this supposition that the will is valid, it follows to consider another point,

† namely, if one of the aforementioned nephews died during the lifetime of the testator, whether the share accrues to the other. And there is no doubt about this, that it does. As in C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, § pro secundo; and l. 1, C. quando non petuntur partes; and ff. de legibus primis, l. ciuitatibus, § Lucius; and what is noted in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si seruus eius ab extero. Now the third doubt is asked.

Let us assume that the said testament were null; would the codicillary clause “if it does not hold” and the like have any effect? The glossa briefly says no, in Auth. Ex causa, C. de lib. praet. and Guillaume de Coucy holds the same in l. ult., C. de codic. The reason is that, if the clause were valid, it would follow that this omitted heir was burdened by that clause; but this is impossible, since an omitted heir cannot be burdened, as l. 2, ff. de leg. 3, and C. de fideicomm., l. plura. The reason is that only he can be burdened who does not succeed against the testator’s will, as we see in l. 1, § vel maxime, ff. de coll. bon. But the omitted heir, being instituted by another, comes in against the testator’s will; therefore he cannot be burdened, as C. de fideicomm., l. ab eo. Moreover, he comes by the benefit of the law, and not of the testator; and the testator could not deprive himself of the benefit of the law, nor therefore of its effect, as ff. de adopt., l. si arrogator, § sed nec imputari. Furthermore, there is an express law for this, ff. de inoff. testam., l. Titia. And according to this opinion, the glossa was formerly practiced. But afterwards the Lord Dynus, Cynus, Bartolus, and many other doctors appeared, and they say that the said clause operates in this case of omission, just as it operates otherwise when the testament fails due to some other formality, as ff. de in ius test., l. posth., § si Paganus; ff. de leg. 2, l. Lucius, § filiam; de manum. testam., l. si iure; C. de fideicomm., l. ex testam.; ff. de testam., l. ex scriptura; ff. de leg. 2, l. codicil., § ult.; and we, ff. si quis omissa causa testamenti, l. qui autem, § quid ergo. And thus Cynus holds in Auth. Ex causa, and it seems expressly stated better than elsewhere, ff. de fideicomm. lib., l. generaliter, § ex testamento. And this opinion is commonly held by modern authors, and according to it, always saving the substance of the truth, I have often advised. Now follows another point,

Whether intestate successors, who are sued and to whom a fourth is due by natural right in their own person, may deduct two fourths from the fideicommissum. It seems that they may: because the person coming in intestate is requested under the condition that the testament should not be valid. But if a son requested under a condition deducts two fourths, namely a third of the whole as and a quarter of the half, that is, eight unciae, from the residue, as stated in Extra, De testibus, chapter Raynu. and chapter Raynal. Although this opinion, because it has been canonized by those chapters, cannot be denied against the true opinion of civil law, as in chapter Si pater, De testibus, Book 6. Nevertheless, I say that in this case only the legitima is deducted. And the reason is: because that condition "if it is not valid, etc." is true as to the present time of the testament. Hence it does not have the force of a condition. And thus the son succeeding in intestacy is purely requested, as in Digest, Si certum petatur, law Cum ad praesens, and Digest, De inofficioso testamento, law Cum in secundo. Hence, if two fourths were deducted, they would contradict each other, which is impossible. The objection from chapter Si pater does not hold, which speaks of successive conditions that coincide with each other and consequently do not conclude each other. And according to this opinion, I have often given counsel. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The cause on account of which the Prince is moved must be considered.
2. The intention of the Prince is always understood to carry the condition that the petitions are founded on truth.
3. Whether a Prince, who has interdicted a certain person alleged to live prodigally and luxuriously from any alienation without the consent of certain good men, appears to have intended to interdict him from making a will, especially since in the will he instituted his sons as heirs.
4. If, having instituted his sons, the testator appointed his executors to distribute, etc., and if the said instituted sons died without male issue, whether such substitution is considered direct to those dying in pupillary age, so that they exclude the mother: something has been said above.
5. Substitution for the poor is threefold, namely, institutive, distributive, and indefinite.
body: I decree that, by the rescript of the illustrious Prince Mas., of eminent virtue, at the instance of certain blood relatives of a certain Jac., who was said to live prodigally and through negligence, it was established that the said Jac. could not sell, donate, or exchange, or in any other way alienate, without the consent and will of certain good men expressed in the said decree. Who, Jacob, later coming to death, instituted in his testament, which he made without the will of the aforementioned named persons, John, his son already born, and the child existing in the womb of his wife, etc. He also appointed certain fideicommissaries and executors, distributors of all his goods, with full authority and power of selling, dispensing, and alienating, and of executing against debtors and delivering them, and this, in the case that his male heirs should die without children, and afterwards the said Jac. died at the age of 25 years, and afterwards the said John, his son, died in pupillary age, the mother surviving, and a certain sister of the said pupil, who was born after the death of the said Jac., and afterwards the said sister died in pupillary age. Now the mother claims that the inheritance pertains to her, asserting that the said testament was null on account of the interdict of the lord. In which testament, as I said, the sons were instituted: and if they should die without children, it was disposed as I said above. The question is what is the law.

And it must be considered, first, what cause moved the Prince; second, what was the disposition of the Prince. And regarding the first, it must be said that the motion of the Prince was founded upon the matters narrated to him. For it was narrated to him that, on account of seduction and his own fragility, he was alienating his goods and verging toward poverty. Hence it was alleged to the Prince that this person was suspect of dissipating his patrimony; which cause most strongly moved the Prince. From this cause, as from a foundation, one must not depart. As is stated in the Digest, *De legibus*, Title 2, Law *Cum pater*, Section *Dulcissimis*.

† Regarding the second point, it is that the intention of the Prince is always understood to carry this condition, namely, if the prayers are based on truth: as in C. de diuersis rescriptis, l. universa. Hence, elsewhere it is said that in the petition you have presented, you must prove the facts: as in C. novellae, l. 1. And even assuming that it were presumed that the prayers are based on truth, from the fact that the Prince grounds his disposition with an assertion of the cause: as in c. literas, de probationibus, in the Clementines. Nevertheless, we are in the third case, which is,

Whether the Prince appears to have forbidden the making of a will by a person who is not proven to have been alienated from his mind. And certainly it must be said that he did not. First: because the words of the decree of our lord do not imply necessity, nor any reason. For it is not presumed that he interposed a decree so that a father might not be able to institute his children as heirs: as in D. de vulgari et exercitatoria substitutione, l. Ex facto. Moreover, even if he wished to do so, the rescript or decree of the lord would not be valid unless he stated "notwithstanding such a law": as noted in C. de testibus, Auth. Hoc inter liberos. Furthermore, the Prince does not appear to have considered this case. As noted in D. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, §. Si. Moreover, alienation to sons is a necessary alienation: as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. In suis. Nor is it properly called alienation: as in C. de impositione lucrativae donationis, l. 1, §. Ita, n. lib. 10. And necessary alienation does not appear to be prohibited: as in D. familiae erciscundae, l. Alienationes; and as noted in C. de secundis nuptiis, Si quis prioris, §. Si quis certum. Moreover, he who confers a legacy or last disposition upon a closely related person is not said to alienate: as in C. de fideicommissis, l. Voluntas patris. To this effect it is noted in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissorum, §. Manifestum; and in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. In suis; and in C. de usucapione pro herede, l. Nihil. And from this it immediately follows that if he can constitute an heir, therefore he can also perform the other acts of a will: as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quando, in principio. Moreover, the decree of the lord does not regard last wills: as in D. de legatis tertio, l. Pater filium, §. Fundum. For, considering the tenor of the decree, the Prince is moved by this cause, namely, lest he become poorer. But this reason ceases in a last will. As is evident in donations between husband and wife, which, although prohibited lest one become poorer, are nevertheless confirmed by death: as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si cum uxore, §. Si. Moreover, by another reason it is not probable that the Prince wished to prohibit the making of a will: because he did not base himself on prodigality, but on age. For if he had considered the defect of mind, he would have prohibited it in perpetuity. But because he considered age, he prohibited it for a time. But such a prohibition does not extend to last wills: as in D. de libellis et legatis, l. Aurelio, §. 1. Moreover, when our lord gave, in a manner, curators, he is not understood to have given them for the purpose of making a will, because the authority of a curator is not required in a will, which ought to be made by itself: as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. Illa constitutio. And it ought not to depend on the will of another: as in D. communia praediorum, l. Receptis. From which I conclude that the will is valid: because the making of a will does not admit a curator by law. And the Prince is not said to infringe the rules of civil law in doubt: as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quando. From these, therefore, I conclude that the will is valid. Now it follows to consider
† whether the substitution is pupillary or fideicommissary.

† And it must be known for this purpose that there are three kinds of substitution for the poor: namely, institutive, distributive, and indefinite. Regarding the distributive, Bartolus says that it presupposes, albeit intellectually, an executory institution for the poor. I say the contrary: because we should not stretch distributive words against their proper mode of speaking, which is oblique. Regarding the institutive, i.e., when the testator says, “I institute executors to distribute,” then the substitution is direct on account of the word “institute,” which is a direct civil term. See D. 36.1.16 (Recusare), § Titius. And thus Lord Bartolus and I have often advised. Hence, in pupillary age, when the words “institute” and “substitute pupillarily” are appended. In the third case, however, where there is no difference in the discrete times of age, since the doctors commonly teach that at all times the substitution is fideicommissary. See D. 36.2.1 (Precibus) with its material. And thus I have always advised on account of the indifference of the modes of signifying this indistinct speech. Now it must be observed: because the testator instituted the lord, and constituted his fideicommissaries, and distributors, etc. For if the word “instituted” refers to the office, it is not therefore a direct substitution; otherwise, if it refers to the inheritance, then it can refer to both, saving the reason of correct speech. And in doubt, I hold that it refers to both: because when one determination regards several determinable things, it determines all equally. See C. 6.28.1 (Quamvis haereditatem). And because a doubtful substitution falling between direct words, as noted in D. 36.1.1 (Verbis civilibus), I say that the aforementioned substitution is to be considered direct, and excludes the mother of the pupils. See D. 28.2.18 (Papinianus), § Sed nec impuberes. Saving the substance of the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An agreement to restore the purchased thing upon repayment of the price is transmissible to heirs.
2. A personal action does not follow the land.
3. The promise and the instrument must be upheld.
body: Todeschina was bound to her same mother for the sale of the half-share of the paternal inheritance that had devolved upon Rafain, the male heir, to whom the entire paternal inheritance had previously devolved. But afterwards, by a certain arbitration award, it was thus divided between the said Rafain and Ruffineta, who were brother and sister. It is also proposed that a certain Ianinus Azo paid the said sum of money to the said Ruffineta on this condition, that the said Ianinus should succeed in place of the said Ruffineta in the said half-share of the inheritance, with this burden, that if the said Todeschina should repay the said Ianinus the entire sum, the said Ianinus is bound to return the said goods to the said Todeschina. It is also proposed that the said Ianinus redeemed certain goods alienated by the brother named Rafain before the aforementioned promise. It is also proposed that the said Todeschina died, and the said Ruffineta succeeded to her for a part, because they were two sisters; now the said Blasius brings an action against the said Ianinus, possessor of the said things. And first, because he purchased all the rights, or had them by donation from the said Ruffineta pertaining to the said Todeschina, and consequently to the said Ruffineta and her heir for one-half. He also claims the goods alienated by the said Rafain. Now the question is, what is the law? And first, let us consider the goods alienated by Rafain, which the said Ianinus redeemed.

Whether the aforementioned Ianinus can be sued for the release of the said goods. And it seems that he can: because the said Ianinus purchased universally one-half of the paternal inheritance of the said Rafainus, subject to the burden that, if 200 pounds were restored to the said Ianinus, he would be bound to restore the said half-share of the inheritance of the said Todesca. This right was indeed transmissible to the heirs of the said Todesca, as stated in the Codex, On actions against heirs and by heirs, law 1. Therefore, it was transmitted to the said Ruffineta. Moreover, the said Ruffineta, as heir of her mother, could cede this right, as stated in the Codex, On heirs or on the sale of actions, last law. She could also transfer the ownership of the said goods to him, because Todesca had not yet obtained the quantity according to the form of the laudemium. Therefore, concluding from the first point to the last, this Blasius can bring an action.

On the contrary, it seems otherwise, and here we must consider two rights. For we must consider the dominion of Ruffineta. Furthermore, we must consider the personal action which Todeschina has against Ruffineta. Now, if we consider the dominion of Ruffineta, certainly no right is found in her regarding the things previously alienated by Rafainus; because she could not, by compromising, remove or diminish the rights of prior possessors, as stated in the Codex, On the sale of property, law *Quotiens*; Digest, On the tutorship of pupils, law *Sive autem*, section *Si duobus*; Digest, On pledges, law *Si superatus*; Codex, On donations before marriage, law *Si ante*. And this is most certainly true.

† But if we consider the personal action available to Todeschina, from this she cannot sue Iani, because a personal action does not follow the possessor. Moreover, one who possesses his own property as if it were pledged to himself cannot be sued, as stated in C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. cum; and C. si certum petatur, l. 1; and D. ad Trebellianam, l. 1, § si haeres; and D. de iure, l. fideicommissum, § tractatum. Certainly, Ruffineta herself could not have assigned this action on behalf of her mother, since it is consumed by the acceptance of the inheritance, as stated in D. de servitutibus, l. Papinianus; D. de solutionibus, l. Stichum, § aliquam; D. de solutionibus matrimonii, l. si socer, in principio; D. ad Sillanianam, l. per verba, § neptis; C. de pactis, l. debitori tuo; C. de iure delictorum, l. si. Therefore, concluding from the first point to the last, it is clear that no ownership or any action is available to the said Blasino regarding the goods previously alienated by Rafainus. It is no obstacle if it is said that Rafainus has already paid the said quantity to the said Ruffineta with the burden of restoring the goods to the said Todeschina; and therefore it does not seem surprising if he can be sued, since he is bound by his own promise and his own contract. For to this it is answered that this agreement must be understood as applying only to the goods that could have belonged to the said Todeschina by virtue of the arbitration award, for this promise refers to the arbitration award. But by virtue of the arbitration award, Ruffineta was not bound to restore to her mother goods that did not belong to Ruffineta herself, nor could they have come to her through the arbitration award; rather, they came to Iani himself through his own expense, labor, and diligence, and not as hereditary goods of the late Richard, father of the aforementioned brothers, as stated in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. si haeres; and D. ad Trebellianam, l. debes, in § final.

† As to the second point, namely concerning the goods that came into the said arbitration award, which were possessed and held by the said Ianinus, it must be said that the promise and the instrument are to be upheld, as in C. de probat. l. cum precibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Three presumptions arise from the instrument.
2. How the simulation of an instrument in which an oath intervenes is to be proved.
3. An oath not to contravene has two effects.
4. When witnesses are said to be singular.
5. Whether an agreement to resell gives rise to a presumption of a simulated contract.
6. Usury is an ecclesiastical crime, and it is not presumed.
body: It is proposed that a certain contract was celebrated in the form of a sale, and it was sworn that the contents of the contract were true. However, upon the death of the buyer, the seller brings an action for the recovery of the property, claiming that the thing is his and that the contract was simulated. To prove this, the buyer’s will is introduced, in which he left the said property to a certain chapel with the burden that whenever the chaplain would have from the said seller such a quantity of money, he ought to make a resale to him. Furthermore, two witnesses are produced, one of whom in effect says that the buyer, in the presence of the said seller, stated that he ought to have so many pounds on the said property, and that if he gave him that amount, he would make an instrument of resale. The other witness says that he heard that the said person, who in the said instrument is said to have purchased, told Lady A. that he was prepared to make a resale of all those lands which he had from the said P. And thus the same person promised to the stipulator that whenever the said A. gave so many florins, as he had resold those properties, and made to him a confession and release of everything which he ought to have from him. Now it is asked whether the aforementioned contract has been proven to be simulated and whether it is presumed to be a pledge.

† It must be premised for the sake of clarity that three presumptions arise from the instrument: namely, that it is true, that it is formal, and that it is a contract concluded by mandate of the contracting parties. The first is proved by C. de probat. l. Cum precibus. The second is proved in l. Sciendum, together with its subject matter, de verborum obligationibus. The third is proved by the authorities noted in Auth. de tabellis, §. Nos vero, which begins alternatively “Nos autem.”

Now, these three presumptions admit contrary presumptions. For against the first presumption, rebutting witnesses are admitted directly, insofar as the described witnesses declare that the writing was not true; and indirectly, insofar as they prove something incompatible with that instrument, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. Optimam. Moreover, proof of simulation suffices as indirect proof against the instrument, yet it is not properly proof against the instrument itself; for there is one truth of the instrument, which pertains to the notary and the rogation, and another truth, which pertains to the intent of the contracting parties, who had agreed upon something else apart from the instrument. For the notary cannot write except in the manner in which he is requested to write. Hence, it is not correctly said that this instrument is simulated, nor is it correctly said that this contract is simulated; but it ought to be said that this alleged contract is simulated or fictitious, as in C. plus valere quod agitur, l. Emptione. Sometimes the force of the instrument is not entirely broken, but merely weakened; and then the contract is not properly called simulated, but rather less operative; for example, when it is proved that the whole matter between the parties was such that the question and answer had the force of a bare pact, as in ff. de pactis, l. Iuris gentium, §. Quod fere. Against the third presumption, when it is proved that the instrument was not drawn up by mandate of the parties.

† Now let us come to the point, and I say that he who wishes to prove simulation, if indeed an oath has been appended, namely because an oath was sworn, cannot prove the contrary unless he is first absolved from the oath. And perhaps according to the legists, since this oath is conventional, it must be upheld, unless it was appended in fraud of the law, or leads to detriment to eternal salvation: for example, if in fraud of usury, as in D. de iureiurando, l. iusiurandum, §. quod ex conventione. Hence, he who seeks absolution from this instrument ought not to make his petition in a vague manner; but he must allege a cause that pertains to the ecclesiastical forum, such as the crime of usury; otherwise, by reason of the pact, one would have to proceed by way of denunciation, as in X. de iudicibus, cap. novit, with its material. And it supports this: Auth. de iureiurando, a moriente præsto, in the red and black; and what is noted: D. 3, l. cum quidam dicens, §. codicis, and §. Titia.

There is also another oath of non-contravention, and this oath has two effects. For if it is indeed opposed to impede the proceedings, it impedes them. But if it is raised in the manner of a peremptory defense, it induces an absolute dismissal, as noted by Innocentius in the title *De institutione capituli*, in the chapter *Cum venisset*, where he states that an extrajudicial oath impedes the proceedings. It also produces a peremptory exception. As for the judicial oath, there is no doubt, as in the chapter *Si obligato*, *De lite contestata*, Book 6, and in the Digest, *De conditionibus indebiti*, law *Eleganter*, § *Si quis post*. Therefore, if the judge interposed a decree concerning the contract, and the oath was taken with his approval, this oath can be called both conventional and judicial. Moreover, the presence of the judge induces a strong presumption that the matter was not done in simulation, but truly, as in law 1, Code, *De praescriptione curiae*, Book 10, and by argument from the Code, *De donationibus*, law *In donationibus*. For where a decree has been appended, everything is presumed to have been done legitimately, as noted by Speculum in the title *De emptione et venditione*, and as noted in law 1, Code, *De fideiussoribus et iure hastae fiscalis*, Book 10. Now it remains to be seen regarding the singularity of witnesses.

And it must be known that witnesses are singular when they disagree in the matters testified, not when they converge on the same end of the matter: as in C. de pe. l. qui sententiam, and noted in ff. de arbi. l. diem proferre, §. si plures. Likewise, they are singular when they vary in place and time, as noted in C. de testi. l. testium, and noted in ff. de testi. l. ob carmen, §. fi. Likewise, they are singular when the fact upon which they testify is such that each knows it of himself and does not know it of another, because the nature of such a fact is that each testifies that he was not summoned, as in extra de elec. cap. bonae memoriae maguntino. Now let us see in our case whether the witnesses are singular. For one testifies with respect to the resale, and thus with respect to a new contract.

For from such a pact of repurchase, a pledge is not presumed, as in C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. 2. And it may be that at the time of the contract it was promised to resell, and yet it was not a pledge. Likewise, it may be that this occurred long afterwards: as in ff. de pactis, l. ab emptione. And neither of these implies a pledge, because the witnesses do not state this, nor is anyone presumed to be a usurer, since one is not presumed to commit a delict.

† To lend at interest is, however, an ecclesiastical crime; therefore, it should not be presumed. See the argument in D. pro socio, l. merito; and D. de probat., l. quotiens, § qui dolo; and Extravagant de pignore capiendo, c. illo nos.; and what is noted by Cynus in C. de probat., l. 1; and C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione. Therefore, concluding from the first point to the last, having considered what ought to be considered, although the contract is somewhat suspect when speaking according to conscience, nevertheless in law and according to the approved acts, the said contract ought not to be judged as a pledge. It must be considered that a pledge contract leading to sale stands as a species specifically added; see D. de regulis iuris, l. neque pignus. But a resale to a sale are not contracts specifically added, but subordinate, first and then later; hence, if the resale contract is proven, the first contract is verified. And therefore, witnesses proving the pact to resell prove in favor of the instrument of sale; because if a sale did not precede, a resale would have no place; but they do not prove the resale, or any obstacle. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a testator, having instituted his daughters as heirs in certain specified amounts, institutes his brother as his universal heir, and if he should die without male issue, substitutes his aforementioned daughters and their sons: and if he dies leaving a grandson through a daughter, whether this grandson excludes the substituted daughters, or vice versa.
2. The understanding of l. 1, C. de cond. ins.
3. In case of doubt, interpretation should be made in favor of the children.
body: A certain nobleman, having in his patrimony many castles and also three daughters, instituted them as heirs in certain shares, but instituted his brother as universal heir; to whom he substituted the daughters of the testator, and the sons of the daughters, if it should happen that his brother should die without male issue. The brother died, leaving a male son by his daughter. It is now asked whether this collateral grandson excludes the daughters of the testator, or the sons of the daughter:

† And briefly, in this question, it is alleged against the daughter of the testator and her daughters. For the decision of the question, the case in I. 1, C. de cond. ins. is cited, where it is expressly stated that he is not considered to have died without children who left a grandson through a daughter. But this brother left a male grandson through a daughter; therefore, he did not die without male children. And this is confirmed by such reasoning: because under the name of children are contained all descendants, as ff. de verb. sign. l. liberorum; and ff. de excus. tutor. l. 2, § non solum; and ff. de in ius voc. l. sed si hac, § liberos. Moreover, in conditions we do not examine the mere fact, but the mere truth, as ff. de cond. et demonstr. l. Mevius. But there is no doubt that according to the truth of the matter, the son of a daughter is male and among the children; therefore, although his mother would not exclude the substitute, he, because he is of the children and male, ought to exclude.

On the contrary, it seems that in wills and doubtful substitutions we must examine ordered charity, so that he is to be preferred in whom stronger charity is found, all other things being equal, as ff. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, § quidam recte. But according to ordered charity, the testator is more attached to his own daughters and their grandchildren than to collaterals; therefore, in doubt, his daughters and their sons are to be preferred. Moreover, if the daughter of the brother does not exclude the substitute, because the testator loved his own daughter more than the daughter of his brother; therefore, neither would the son of this daughter exclude, argumentum ff. de cond. et demonstr. l. Publius, § final. Moreover, this testator spoke of male sons on account of the favor of agnation and in honor of his family, as ff. de ventre insp. l. 1, § quamvis, where it says, the dignity of the orders of families, which is thus preserved. To this effect is what Cyn. notes in l. 1, C. de adul. Moreover, the son of a daughter ought not to have more right than the daughter of the brother herself, as C. de collat. l. illam; and Inst. de haered. ab intest. § Item vetustas. Moreover, it is not probable that the testator wished to prefer foreign lines, which are not of his own stock, to his own lines. C. de fideic. l. cum acutissimi. Moreover, if the testator had been questioned about this, it is probable that he would have declared himself in this direction, as ff. de pact. l. tale pactum, § final. Moreover, this subtlety of words, which rests in this word, without children, does not apply to every testator, as noted Inst. qui dat. tut. poss. § final. Therefore, the testator did not wish to say, without children and without male descendants. But these grandsons, who descend through a female, are more properly said to descend from their paternal line than maternal. And so it is also according to the usage of speech: because denomination is made from the male sex as from the more dignified. Hence, in the Twelve Tables, those who descend through a female were not considered descendants, as ff. unde cogn. l. 1, in princ.

Moreover, in the matter of substitutions, the law says that the prudent counsel of the testator must be considered; hence, that is understood which the testator meant, which a prudent man ought to mean. These are the notable words of d. l. Lucius, ff. de haer. inst., where it says, for the prudent counsel of the testator is observed: for he preferred not only the brother as heir to the substitutes, but also his children. I ask therefore, whether that testator is prudent who prefers the grandsons of his brother to his own grandsons through his daughter and of his own body. Certainly, I would not commend this man for prudence, who excludes his own born and in a manner neglects his own like a madman. Therefore, he is presumed to have loved his children and placed charity first. Hence, I do not presume him to have tested as one insane in mind, but as a diligent man, preferring his agnation to others, as C. de instit. l. generaliter; ff. de cond. et demonstr. l. cum auus.

Moreover, this substitution is doubtful: because we do not know whether he understood male children of the first degree, and also of further degrees, provided through the male line; and whether also males born through females. And a doubtful substitution ought to be interpreted in favor of the children of one’s own body, as appears from the laws cited above. Moreover, the daughter is a female intermediate person, whose degree her son enters; but the daughter does not exclude, therefore neither does the one following from her, as in the said § hoc autem notandum, de his qui feudum dare poss., collat. 10, which § is very material to our question. Moreover, the testator preferred his daughter to the daughter of his brother; therefore, he preferred the grandson through his own daughter to the grandson through the daughter of his brother. Moreover, the question of will is in the discretion of the judge: as C. de fideic. l. voluntatis. But a good man ought to judge that the will of the testator was due and ordered according to charity, and not contrary to charity: because a father takes counsel for his children: as ff. unde lib. l. scripto; and we prepare all things for our children according to our wish: as l. nihil, § facilior, ff. de bon. lib. Wherefore, it seems to be concluded that the son of the testator’s daughter excludes the son of the heir’s daughter.

† The law 1, Codex, de conditionibus insertis, does not stand in the way, because it is stated there that this is true, unless such a substitute is appointed who, by the presumed will of the testator, excludes the sons and daughters of the instituted heir. But here the substitutes are such as, by the presumed will of the deceased, exclude the collateral nephews. Moreover, in law 1, de conditionibus insertis, the daughter, through whom the nephew excluded the substitute, is present; but here she does not exclude. Since, therefore, the nephew does not come to represent his grandfather except through his mother: and the mother, whose image he is, does not exclude the substitute, therefore he himself cannot exclude: because this line of descent brings him nothing. And although the words of the testator, which are for common deliberation, have a broad scope, nevertheless the mind of the testator, and the reason of the law, ought rather to be considered, argumentum, Digestum, ad Trebellianum, law, Heredes mei, § Cum ita; and law, Lucius, § Gayo. To this is added, because the nephew is of the feminine gender, i.e., the generation of a female, but the feminine gender was not added for the exclusion of the children of the testator. And I argue thus: the nephew ought not to be in a better condition than the daughter, as in Codex, de bonis matri assignandis, law, Si viva matre. Moreover, when the intermediate party, through whom one arrives at another, is excluded, that other is also excluded, to whom it was necessary to arrive through such an intermediate: because it does not have an ordered and legally founded consequence, as in Codex, de captivis et postliminio reversis, law 1. Moreover, the mother and son are considered as one person, as in chapter, ultimo, de conjugio infidelium. Moreover, a more distant agnate ought not to be preferred to his own parent. Moreover, the nature of the mother cannot be separated from the son: as in Digestum, de regulis iuris, law, Iuris sanguineis. Moreover, the relationship of the nephew to his maternal grandfather is through the maternal blood. And if the degree of the mother is removed from the middle, it cannot be understood that this person is a nephew. Moreover, when something is derived or deduced from someone, it partakes of the nature and quality of that person from whom it is deduced: to this effect, Codex, de naturalibus liberis, law, final, in the reason thereof. Moreover, the nephew cannot fail to follow the innate quality, and that which is such, argumentum, Digestum, de interdictis et relegationibus, law 2. Considering, therefore, the presumed mind of the testator: and because testaments are said to be interpreted soundly, and according to the judgment of a good and discreet man. And because we ought to follow nature, which directs us to the true understanding: and because the prudent counsel of the testator ought not to prefer nephews from the daughter of a brother to his own proper nephews, it seems to be said, that this substitution, both by the person and by the tacit will of the deceased, excludes, or rather does not exclude, a male born of a female, whom the female testator did not wish to exclude in the substitution: but he considered his own proper descendants to be to be preferred in every way. And certainly we say in another matter, that those more closely related, but not those least closely related, exclude the substitute from a doubtful substitution: as in Codex, de institutionibus et substitutionibus, law, final; and de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, law, Precibus; and note, Digestum, de vulgaribus substitutionibus, law, Lucius. Furthermore, it matters little whether the substitution is doubtful because it is tacit, or whether it is doubtful because the mind of the testator is not established: as noted, Digestum, de vulgaribus substitutionibus, law, Verbis civilibus.

† For in case of doubt, interpretation must always be made in favor of children: whom natural hope, civil reason, and the wish of parents are accustomed to call to the succession, as in D. de adopt. l. nec ei. §. praeterea. From which, moved by natural reason, I hold that in this case the testator did not wish to exclude his own descendants. Notwithstanding that, according to the aforementioned l. 1. C. de cond. inser., if one looks at the mere surface of the words, much may be argued to the contrary: since that law must be understood, saving the intention of the testator. This rule governs conditions, as in D. de condi. et demon. l. in conditionibus primum locum. and l. pater Seuerinam. §. conditionem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone has confessed that he received one hundred from my debtor, whom, although he was not my procurator, he released as if he were, and which release I later ratified, can I bring an action against his heirs for those one hundred?
2. In case of doubt, the instrument must be upheld.
body: The case is as follows: Francesco and Pietro de Asinetiis had a debtor bound to them by an instrument for a certain quantity of money. Now it happened that Rainono of Monte Calveto, asserting himself to be the procurator of the said Francesco and Pietro—which Rainono is not proven to have had either a general or a special mandate from the aforesaid for the matters written below—confessed that he had had and received from the aforesaid debtor the said quantity of money in the name and for the use of the aforesaid persons, and made to the same debtor in the said procuratorial name a peace, discharge, and acquittance concerning the aforesaid debt, with the appropriate renunciation in such matters, and a public instrument is said to appear concerning the said acquittance. Afterwards, however, the aforesaid Pietro and Francesco, ratifying the said confession made by the said Rainono in their name, demand in court from the heirs of the said late Rainono the said money which the said Rainono confessed that he had had and received from the aforesaid debtor. Against them, on the part of the heir of the said Rainono, it is objected that the said Francesco and Pietro can demand nothing from them, even though they have ratified the said confession, because the said Rainono received nothing from the said debtor, although he confessed that he had received it; and that the said brothers may ratify the said confession to their own detriment and release the debtor if they wish, but not to the prejudice of the said Rainono, who had no mandate to make the said confession; and thus they cannot demand from the said heirs that which the said Rainono did not receive, and because he had neither a general nor a special mandate from them; and especially because the said debtor was not released from his creditors by such a confession. On the contrary, it is said that one must indeed stand by the said confession. Now it is asked what the law is. Standum

† One must stand by the said confession to the prejudice of the confessing party, because it is taken as the truth, as in ff. de admi. tu. l. Lucius. §. tutelae. Thus the confessing party is bound to the restitution of that which he is deemed in truth to have received, ff. depositi. l. pub. §. fi., ff. de ver. ob. l. si ita stip. §. Grisogonus, C. arbitrium tutelae. l. fi. Likewise, either he truly received it, and it is not equitable that he should not return it, as in ff. si cer. pe. l. si me, et Titium; or he did not receive it, and thus in so confessing he was in fault, which fault is brought under the action of negotiorum gestorum, ff. de ne. ges. l. Pompo. The presumption is also strengthened that a true counting of money took place, because the exception of non-numbered money was renounced, as is noted in ff. de dote cauta. l. 1. and C. de non nume. pe. l. si ex cautione.
† Likewise, in doubt one must stand by the instrument, C. de proba. l. cum precibus, C. de non nume. pe. l. generaliter, extra de proba. c. per tuas. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The testator may derogate from all penalties of secondary marriages, which are imposed by the law *secundo nubenti*.
2. What a wife who marries a second time ought to have from the goods of her first husband, if she relies on the will of her husband, or of her son, or on intestate succession.
3. Pupillary substitution is truly the will of both the father and the son.
body: For the sake of clarity,

† it must first be premised that if the testator wished, he could derogate from all the penalties of second marriages that are imposed by law upon a woman remarrying after the year of mourning, as in Authen. de nup. §. disponat. col. 4. But if the testator does not make this provision, the disposition of the law takes effect, which seems to dictate

† that either the mother claims by virtue of her husband's testament, or by virtue of her son's testament, or on intestacy. In the first case, she retains the usufruct and loses the ownership, which belongs to the other surviving children, C. de secund. nupt. l. feminae. in fi. C. ad tertu. l. mater. In the second case, she loses nothing, C. de secun. nup. authen. ex testamento. j. responso. In the third case, with respect to the property that belonged to the husband, she loses the ownership, which is assigned to the surviving children, while she herself has only the usufruct, said auth. ex testamento. and the notes to C. ad tertul. l. omnem. Now, doubt remains concerning pupillary substitution,

† for it is truly the testament of the father, and more truly that of the son, as noted in ff. de inoffi. testamento. l. Papi. §. sed nec impuberis. The gloss on auth. ex testamento understands the first response of that Authentica to apply when the mother had no other son than the one who made the testament, and it speaks incorrectly according to Bartolus, because the same applies if she has several. Therefore, I say that in this case the more favorable path must be chosen, namely, that she succeed as if by testament. Said l. omnem does not stand in the way, because there she offended in multiple ways, not merely in the passing to a second marriage. And this accords sufficiently with the words and intent of the above-mentioned statute. And thus I, Baldus, advise in favor of the mother.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who will be the competent judge, where jurisdiction is contested as a matter of property, or as a matter of office.
2. Acts performed by an incompetent judge are null.
body: For the sake of clarity,

† it must first be stated that sometimes a matter concerning jurisdiction is treated as concerning property, or as concerning territory: then neither party can be a judge, as if in his own cause, but the superior must be approached, as is read and noted in l. de iure, ff. ad muni., and C. ne quis in sua causa, l. j. Sometimes the question is concerning jurisdiction as an office: and then a distinction is made, as noted in ff. si quis in ius uo. non ierit, l. ex quacumq., namely that it is either certain, or the jurisdiction is doubtful; and then the one summoned is not bound to appear. From these points it appears that the proceeding of the podestà of Villanova, to whom the jurisdiction of this village was committed by the superior, is null by operation of law.

† Likewise because outside the territory, according to the well-known l. extra territorium, de iuris. om. iu. For that municipal magistrate belongs to that village, and cannot take cognizance of the rights of the village, but must act as a party against one not subject to him, as noted in ff. quod cuiusque vniuersi. nomine, l. nulli. It would proceed from a special commission and delegation made to him by the superior; which was not the case here, according to what I have seen; rather, according to what is set forth, the superior began to take cognizance by himself, and thus seems to have revoked the cause to himself. Wherefore the witness depositions were also null, as was that which followed from them, C. ne de statu defun., l. si pater. Even through the order to the governor, nothing was validly conducted by which a definitive sentence could have been rendered; and therefore his duty is to pronounce as void whatever was done by the said podestà, and to proceed in an orderly manner from the beginning upon the things sought and to be sought, and not to entangle the proceedings, extra de iudi., c. exhibita, and in the meantime not to eject the possessor from his possession until his sentence. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether fruits derived from tithes may be sold or granted for a term at an annual rent.
2. And whether, against such a buyer or lessee, if he is a layman, the secular judge is the competent judge.
3. If the buyer denies that the seller is a cleric or a tithe-collector, whether this [denial]
4. The lessee cannot allege. q. dominii.
5. Whether an appeal issued from a lay judge to a lay judge in spiritual matters proceeds.
6. When an appeal is taken from an interlocutory judgment rendered on the competence of the judge or jurisdiction, whether the form of c. cordi must be observed.
7. Whether an interlocutory appeal, in which the cause is not specially expressed but reference is made to the records, is valid.
8. The appeal having been rejected, the judge from whom is not said to neglect to issue letters of appeal, even when demanded by instance.
body: For the sake of clarity, it must be premised: First, whether the fruits derived from tithes can be sold for a certain period or granted for an annual rent. Second, whether the secular judge is the competent judge for a layperson who purchases or leases confraternal property. Third, if the buyer or lessee denies that he is a cleric or a tithe-collector, and requests that this case be remitted to him, whether this case ought to be remitted to the forum of the bishop. Fourth, if the lay judge has pronounced himself the competent judge in this case, and an appeal has been made to the superior lay authority, whether the appeal proceeds in spiritual matters from a layperson to a layperson, assuming that this is a spiritual case. Fifth, whether the cause of appeal must be expressed in writing, and how. Sixth, if the cause is not specially expressed, but refers to the records, and in the records all the causes are frivolous, whether this appeal holds. Seventh, and finally, whether, if the appeal does not hold, yet the Apostolic Letters, which have been requested, were not issued within 30 days, it is understood that the matter has been referred to the appeal, and whether the judge to whom it is referred is to obey the inhibition.

† Regarding the first point, it must be said that the revenues and profits of a benefice may be sold and leased to the prejudice of the person of the buyer and the seller, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *Ne prelati*, under the title *Vices suas*, in the chapter *Querelam*, and there fully noted.
† Regarding the second point, it must be said that the secular judge is the competent judge against a layman. 11. q. c. experientiae.

† Regarding the third point, it must be said that, once this question has been colored by law, lay jurisdiction cannot be impeded; and it is also said that pacts are to be observed even with a robber, as in D. de condictione indebiti, l. si urbana, and D. de deposito, l. bona fides; and see the note in c. nihil, Extr. de electione.

† Hence, he who has accepted the lessor cannot decline the agent, nor raise a question concerning the title, as in C. si certum petatur, l. non unde originem; C. de petitione hereditatis, l. cogi; ff. de deposito, l. quod servus; C. de agris et censibus, l. si coloni and l. litibus; C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam; C. de locato, l. si quis conductis; C. unde vi, l. non ab re; and as noted by Dynus in c. qui ad agendum, de regulis iuris, lib. 6.

† Regarding the fourth point, it must be said that to appeal in spiritual matters from a secular judge to a secular judge is to multiply inconveniences; therefore, the appeal does not proceed, but a complaint ought to be brought concerning this matter before the bishop. For he who appeals in this manner is acting contrary to himself, since he submits his adversary to the true examination in the same manner at the time when he himself claims to be such, as is stated in the Codex, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, law *In criminali*. Regarding the fifth point, it must be said

† It is, that the sentence passed on the law is merely interlocutory: because it is rendered on an emerging matter, from which an appeal must be made in writing, and the cause of grievance must be alleged, as in c. Cordi, de appellationibus, lib. 6, and Codex, de minoribus, l. Ait praetor, §. Permittitur. And the causes must be expressed specifically. For it is not sufficient to say, “I appeal, as aggrieved,” as appears in the records; because from the appeal itself the judge to whom the appeal is made is not made certain, as in Digestum, de iure fisci, l. Ita fidei, and note, Inn., de non operis novi nuntiando, c. Si. On the sixth point, I say,

† But if frivolous grounds are contained in the records, these evasions do not avail the appellant: because they are not probable grounds, as in the extrajudicial collection on appeals, c. Ut debitus; and in the Decretum, note 2, question 6, c. Ad Romanam. It is pertinent to what is noted in the Digest, on the exception of fraud, l. 2, §. Circa. On the seventh point, I say,

† But if the appeal is rejected by law on account of impossibility or defect of form, and the judge from whom it is alleged that he does not neglect to grant the Apostolic letters, even when demanded with insistence: and therefore the reason must be considered why he who does not grant the Apostolic letters is understood to defer to the appeal. For Bartolus says the reason is that, by not granting the Apostolic letters, he burdens the appealing party, insofar as it lies within him, with a justified appeal, as noted by Bartolus in l. eius, qui, de appellatione recipienda. And therefore the text in c. ab eo, de appellationibus, lib. 6, left negligence aside. It is certain, however, that he does not neglect to grant the Apostolic letters who is not bound to grant them on account of the nullity of the appeal; because the appellant was in a state of legal constitution, as is commonly held in l. si, ff. de appellationibus recipiendis. From these things it appears that either the inhibition does not hold, or at least it must be revoked as unjust. And even if it were not to be revoked, it must be pronounced that the appeal is unjust: and the appellant ought to be condemned in costs as one who appealed temerarily. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a layman can be the legitimate guardian of a cleric, and vice versa.
2. Clerics who are citizens enjoy the privileges and favors of citizens.
3. In this question, it must be seen whether a layman can be legi
body: We consider the tutor of a cleric. And it seems that he cannot be one: because the cleric is exempt from secular laws both in person and in property; for he has ceased to be within the forum of Justinian, and has begun to be within the forum of blessed Peter, that is, of the Church. Dist. 96, c. Bene quidem. And all the more would he not be subject to the ministers of secular laws, as in Extra, De foro competenti, c. Si diligenti. To the contrary: because I see that a cleric can be the legitimate tutor of a layman. Dist. 86, c. Peruenit. Therefore, the same applies conversely. Indeed, even more strongly, for guardianship was introduced by the privilege of the ward; and if the cleric did not have a legitimate tutor, the clerical status, which ought to obey the privilege, would incur odium to the contrary. L. Nulla, D. De legibus; and C. eod., L. Quod fauore. Moreover, neither law nor decretal distinguishes between a ward who is a cleric and one who is a layman; therefore, we ought not to distinguish either: saving that I do not speak concerning ecclesiastical benefices, as in C. Ult., De iudicibus, lib. 6. Otherwise, if we were to say the contrary, even the father would not be the legitimate administrator, nor would he claim the usufruct of adventitious property brought to a minor constituted in the lower orders, as if this cleric henceforth did not live under Roman law, which is absurd. Furthermore, those things which are established by the common law in favor of clerics are extended to clerics. Dist. 10, c. Si ad introitum. Otherwise it would follow that, if a lay tutor were appointed to a cleric, the cleric would not have the tacit hypothec, which is introduced by the authority of Roman law: which is false. And therefore I conclude that a cleric can have a layman as legitimate tutor, and a layman a cleric, whose goods are bound, if he administered the guardianship in any ecclesiastical manner, even without making an inventory, as in C. De administratione tutorum, L. Pro officio; and D. De administratione tutorum, L. Tutor, qui repertorium, in principio. And it is true that, if he had common goods, he is not liable for the undivided share. On this point, the glosses are contrary, as in Auth. Minoris debitor, C. Qui dari tutores possunt. And this would require some distinction according to Bartolus there; nevertheless, at least the actio tutelaris would have place there, as noted in C. Qui dari tutores possunt, L. Militiae armatae. Because there is no impediment on the part of the person of the ward, but there is an impediment of a certain accident, according to the note in L. 3, §. Hac actione, D. De negotiis gestis.

But it is doubted whether the decree of the lord benefits the lord. And it seems to be said that it does, as in Extra, De foro competenti, c. De clericis; and in the same chapter, Si in adiutorium; and in Digestum, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Falsa, § 1; and as is not stated in c. Hac constitutione, De officio delegati, Liber Sextus; and according to Bartolus in l. 1, Digestum, Ad municipalia; and therefore clerics who are citizens enjoy privileges and favors. And to this effect, Distinctio 12, c. Duo sunt. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A surety who is not bound to pay, if he pays voluntarily, is bound, both he himself and the surety.
2. A guarantee for the payment of the judge is said to be made regarding the preliminary stages of the proceedings: and it must be made before the judge.
3. A surety is not to be summoned in the assessment of expenses.
body: It must be noted,

† that even he who is not bound to provide a surety, if he provides one voluntarily, both he and the surety are bound. ff. de fideius. l. grece. §. a tutore. ff. si quis cau. l. sed et si quis. §. fi.

† Likewise, this security ought to be furnished before the defendant is compelled to receive the libel. C. de epis. et cle. auth. generaliter. Likewise, this security is said to pertain to the preliminaries and the introductions of the process, as noted in the Auth. in me. litis non fieri sacras iussiones. §. fi.; on that account, I declare it already valid. But attention must be paid to what is stated in ff. iu. sol. l. cum apud Sempronium; for it must be so conceived that it embraces new judges. Likewise, it is necessary that the taxation of expenses be made by a competent judge upon whom the entire jurisdiction has devolved; for if it has not been made by a competent judge, it does not hold. C. si a non coniu. throughout; de sta. de. l. si pater. Let us see therefore: as to the first, the words of the security say, "if it should happen that he succumbs," but they do not state before which judge; and therefore it is doubtful concerning which judge it is to be understood, since the name of the judge is not expressed. For the words speak directly to the matter and state, "as in the present case to succumb"; and it seems that, because the law uses the word of commission, the commissary judge seems to be the same with the one commissioning, and in the same way the stipulation is committed, as if before the one acting in his stead; and l. cum apud Sempronium speaks of an appellate judge, not of a commissary. The same concerning the taxations of expenses is not in doubt, on account of the words of the instrument of security and because, as I have said, I do not see a diverse forum in effect.
