To the contrary makes the argument that those having jurisdiction from diverse laws never have one and the same intellectual tribunal; and makes for this C. de iu. l. pen. circa fi. Furthermore, those three of whom the constitution speaks are arbitrators of law, because they pursue the same instance with its appendages, and therefore with the securities; to this makes what is noted in ff. de procu. l. qui proprio. §. item quaeritur. Nevertheless, it must be established concerning their election, and concerning the form observed in electing them, de offi. deleg. c. cum in iure.

† Now the question is, whether in the taxation of expenses the surety of iudicatum solvi ought to be cited; and it seems that yes, as in l. de vnoquoque. de re iudi. To the contrary makes the argument that the judgment rendered with the principal affects him secondarily, not principally. Therefore, since he was not cited in the principal matter, neither was he in its necessary appendages; otherwise, instead of one adversary, one would be compelled to have several. Hence this is the nature of this suretyship, that it affects sureties even when not cited. C. de vsu. rei iudi. l. fi. in fi. ff. iud. sol. l. 1. de verbo. obl. l. cum similibus. §. in hac. sol. ma. l. si filio. Although it would be more cautious if they were cited. C. si propter pu. pen. l. 2. ff. qui. ex cau. ma. l. cum miles. §. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a contracting university can bind individual persons as individuals, and at no. 3.
2. Who are called principals, and who are sureties.
3. Whether the syndic of a university can bind those who, at the time of the contract, are not members of that university.
4. The obligation of the individuals belonging to the university is one thing, and that of the university another. And for the obligation of the university, a tax (collecta) is imposed, which ought to be imposed having regard to property, although sometimes to persons.
5. A tax is imposed on citizens and inhabitants, who are inhabitants at the time of the imposition.
6. A tax can always be imposed on native-born citizens.
body: To the evidence

It must be noted that when a university contracts, such a contract does not bind individual persons as individuals, but binds only the university itself and the property of the university, as noted in l. 2, in the great gloss, C. quae sit longa consuetudo. And the reason is: because they have a mandate from the individuals, not as individuals, but as from the whole body. And the business being conducted does not regard the utility of the individuals, but that of the university itself. And if the individuals were bound, they would appear more as guarantors of the university than as principal debtors:

†because those are called principals to whom the benefit principally pertains; others are called intercessors, as noted in D. ad Velleianum, l. vir uxori, §. si. But no one would appoint a procurator to intercede for another, as in D. quod cum eo, l. Titianus, and D. de pactis, l. in personam.

† However, the aforementioned points do not apply if the municipal law provides that, for a contract of the city, the syndic may bind individual persons, as noted in Bar. ff. de re iud. l. 4. §. actor. Furthermore, it does not apply with respect to those who are specifically named in the syndicate or contract, and who have bound themselves in their own name and primarily, or have pledged their faith: as ff. de mag. conueni. l. 1. in prin. and what is noted in ff. si cer. pet. l. ciuitas.

Secondly, it must be premised for clarity that the syndic of a corporation cannot bind those who were not members of said corporation at the time of the contract: as provided in C. de decimis, l. providendum, lib. 10. And this is true in that he cannot bind them as individual persons for the aforementioned reason: because the time of the contract is considered: as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. si filius; and since at the time of the contract these individuals were not part of the corporation, they could not be bound as individual persons: as in ff. de pactis, l. si unus, § ante omnia. Thirdly, it must be premised for clarity,

† that one obligation is that of the individuals, another that of the universitas: and for the obligation of the universitas a tax (collecta) is imposed: as in D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. Rescripto, §. Si; and noted in D. quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, l. 1, §. Quibus. This tax, according to Innocentius, ought to be imposed having regard to property, as noted by Innocentius in X. de sententia excommunicationis, c. Gravem. Although sometimes regard is had to persons, or to those swearing, when such a tax takes the place of head-taxes. For from the beginning of the cause, that which is caused subsequently must be shaped, as in D. de donationibus, l. Quicquid, §. 1; and D. de fideiussoribus, l. Tutor; and D. ad Trebellianum, l. Nonnumquam; and C. de impositione lucrativae descriptionis, l. 1, lib. 10; and D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si donatae, §. Si sponsus. Fourthly, for the sake of clarity, it must be premised,
† that the tax is imposed on citizens and inhabitants, who are inhabitants at the time of the imposition.

† However, original citizens do not admit of a division of time: because they were always citizens and a tax could always be imposed upon them: as in D. 50.4.1 (ad municipalia), l. Assumptio; and see the note by Cynus in l. 2, C. 7.41.2 (de iurisdictione omnium iudicum). From these premises, the following conclusion follows, namely: since taxes could be imposed upon original citizens, even if they are not named in the contract, and may be imposed upon them for all time. But for those newly settled or incorporated, a tax may be imposed upon them for the future time, not for the past. And this applies with regard to bearing a universal tax; but as individual persons, these new and accidental citizens, who became citizens after the contract, cannot be compelled to pay. And by this the question in dispute is determined. And let the allegations made for and against be resolved with subtlety. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When theft is said to be united and continuous.
2. Whether a receiver of stolen goods is properly called a thief, so as to be included under the statute.
3. One must adhere to custom interpreting statutes. OPINION XLIX.
1. Whether, when alienation is prohibited by statute, it can be alienated otherwise, as if on grounds of necessity.
2. Penalties for delicts do not begin with the heir.
body: Regarding the unity of thefts, I say,

† that when multiple things are stolen at the same time, it is one theft, and it is noted in ff. de fur. l. eum, qui. §. idem dicit. in the gloss, indeed there where it says: 'But this is at the same time, whence it is one theft.' Concerning the truth of the reception, I say,

† that it is a single defense: as is noted in ff. de act. et ob. l. pe. in the gloss where it says, diverse acts are counted as one by reason of continuation; on which note that when it is questioned concerning the receiving of a stolen thing, whether speaking properly and without the interposition of law, thus a thief is gathered from the definition of theft, C. de fur. l. eos, and this if the statute does not distinguish, for the definition, which is general, is distinguished into its species. And therefore if the statute sets down receiving as a species separate from theft, the general laws concerning theft have no place in that specific species, even if there were multiple thefts, ff. de poe. l. sanctio legum; for from the kind of term and the diversity of the penalty, differences are granted, and a diversity of offenses is understood, as noted in C. qui ac. non pos. l. 1. in the gloss, and so also below, where it says, 'they are equal because an equal penalty is imposed'; whence the description taken from the kind of punishment is regarded more than the natural quality of the offense. And therefore, as far as pertains to municipal law, theft and receiving are not set down as the same thing, even if they coincide in the same thing, arg. l. 1. C. qui numero tut. where it is said that diverse imperfect species do not make one perfect species. I have regard to the statute; for it also seems reasonable enough to me that someone should not be hanged for a single receiving, unless it were exceedingly enormous according to Petrus; and certainly the statute requires plurality, arg. ff. ad Tre. l. fi., as in C. de epi. aud. l. 3., C. de ser. fu. auth. sed nouo iure, and what is noted in ff. de pę. l. capitalium. §. famosos; always saving the custom that interprets statutes, ff. de extraord. criminib. l. sacularii. §. sunt quidam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When alienation is prohibited by statute, whether it can be alienated otherwise, as if from a cause of necessity.
2. Penalties of delicts do not begin against an heir.
body: The Lord

† In favor of l. quaedam. de acqui. re. do., following the gloss, he says that that which is prohibited by law from being alienated can pass universally, as if it were a necessary alienation, because one cannot have an heir in certain things and not in certain others. ff. de haere. insti. l. si quis ita fuerit haeres insti. excepto fundo. l. 1. ff. de fund. do. de secun. nu. l. si quis prioris. noted in l. 1. C. non licere habitatorem metro. li. 11. The lord Bartolus says the contrary, when the alienation is prohibited to a certain quality of persons, de leg. 2. l. codicil. §. fi. and he himself notes eo. tit. l. peto. §. fratre. and de verb. obl. l. si ita quis. §. ea lege. In favor of the first part makes the lex in modicis. de contrah. emp. with its like, and it seems the more equitable side in a legal provision. But because the text says, "to alienate in any manner," it speaks very generally. ff. de mil. testa. l. in fraudem. §. fi. Likewise it says, "nor any right." Regarding that, it cannot be said that one is partly testate and partly intestate; it can rather be said that the fiscus takes it away from the heir, the statute not being revoked in doubt. The notary, however, seems to be excused if he was ignorant that it was in the inheritance: because the statute seems to speak of immovable things, or certainly indeed also of rights. But it must be seen whether the statute speaks of last wills, and a doubt is created by the fact that a penalty is imposed as if from a delict, which does not pass against the heir; and therefore from the comparison of the penalty, the act, and the person, it does not seem to speak of a last will, because

† the penalties of delicts do not begin against an heir. To this makes ff. de le. 3. l. pater filium. §. fundus. ff. de alie. iu. l. ex hoc edicto. §. sed haeredi. The lord who enacted the statute has to interpret it, since it is ambiguous; otherwise I incline toward the more benign part, namely the permissive one. ar. ff. de inoffi. test. l. posthu. in prin. On the reasoning of the letter, however, I say nothing assertively, because that article ought to be declared by the lord whom it concerns. But I incline, as I have said, because the whole and complete wording of the statute cannot be consonant with a last will, especially with universal successions. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who wishes to raise the exception of uncounted money must give security for the payment of the judgment and name the principal in court.
2. How the general clause that one may be sued in any place is to be understood.
body: These Jews have a firm foundation for their case, because the debt appears to be due.

And if anyone wishes to raise the peremptory exception of money not paid, when he comes to full defense, he must give security for the judgment to be satisfied, as in C. de satis. l. 1. Moreover, he is bound to name the principal in court, and to order him to appear, since he knows the truth better, as in C. de procu. l. si. And if he does not come, satisfaction is made from his property, as in C. ubi de crimine agi oportet. auth. qua in provincia. Certainly these Jews have a basis for jurisdiction: because although three places were simply designated for payment, or in one of them, yet if the debtors did not appear in any place except at their own domicile.

And let a general clause be appended, that from any place they may, if they have a defender who defends them, be sued, so that a remission of the forum may be made, as in the compilation on the forum, c. Romana, §. contrahentes, book 6. But if there is no defender, it seems that a curator may be appointed for those goods which the debtors have, and there they may receive actions and finally pay the creditors, as in l. ab hostib., quibus ex caus. mai. From which, in that place, if they were present, they would choose the forum. ff. depositi, l. Lucius. It seems, however, that the citation of the debtors is necessary, insti. de poena temer. litig., §. si. ff. qui sat. cog., l. fideiussor, §. si. But against this opinion, because the defendant is not found in that place where he was sued: therefore they cannot be sued there in another place. l. 1, ff. de eo quod cert. loc. Also, a personal action does not follow those things. ff. ad Treb., l. 1, §. si haeres, cum sim. Considering, however, that our lord wishes faith to be kept, and that these Hebrews are not defrauded: where, according to the truth, they ought to be paid in the place of judgment. And the truth is, that he himself would be debtor, or his procurator ought to pay the said Hebrews there, which they do not say is impeded by equity of the rescript on account of the fraud of the debtors, but they say that they are to be cited according to custom and statutes of the place where the judgment is held. l. 2, C. quemad. testa. aper. But that is certain, that the chirograph, which is valid in the place of contract, is valid in the place of judgment, as fully noted by the doctors in l. cunctos populos, and ff. de evict., l. fundus. Also, it is certain that if the said things were hypothecated, a hypothecary action could be brought there against the holders. C. ubi in rem actio, l. si. ff. de rei vend., l. officium. However, the instrument was made very simply. But if this place were not included under general words, it could not be said, "where I find your things, there I will judge you," unless it had letters of a competent judge. l. cum unus, §. is qui, de bonis Auth. iudic. poss., unless it were obtained from the prince. C. de iur. dominii impetrando, l. si. Nevertheless, this place is closed under the general clause: and therefore the place of the forum is competent. And there is no doubt in another, except in the absence of the debtors, it seems in founding judgment against them, and thus against the holders of these things.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a testamentary guardian mother is excluded from the inheritance and the substitution if she did not accept the guardianship, or if she entered into a second marriage, and thus whether she loses all that was left to her in the will. num. 2.
body: † This question is doubtful under the common law. It is also doubtful under municipal law. And I premise that this statute does three things: first, it provides for those who marry a second time; second, it provides against those who marry a second time; third, it exempts from the odium of those who marry a second time. The second point is found at “by the same equity.” The third point is found at “provided that if.” I come to the first point, and it seems,

† That this mother is excluded from succession, and the reason is that either she began to administer the guardianship of her son, and then there is no doubt that she is deprived, because she passed to second marriage without having requested a guardian: as C. ad Tert. l. omnem. and in Auth. de nup. §. si autem tutela. Or she never administered as guardian, nor ever accepted the guardianship: and then because she did not comply with the judgment of the testator, she appears to be excluded: as ff. de excu. tut. l. Nesennius. and what is noted, C. de leg. l. ab administratione. To the contrary it seems: because although she is deprived of legacies, she is not deprived of the pupillary substitution: as ff. de excu. tu. l. amicissimos. and l. tutor petitus. §. quę tutoribus. where there are many singular glosses. Consider, that if the mother administered anything as guardian, without doubt she is repelled from the pupillary substitution: because she did not request another guardian, and because she does not render an account of the administration. But if she administered nothing as guardian, then even by passing to second marriage she renders herself suspect, and by her own fault she appears to be repelled from the substitution: because she behaved immodestly and inordinately towards her children, and towards the will of her first husband, who had presumed better of her, arg. ff. de leg. 2. l. vnum ex familia. §. item Imperator Marcus. Moreover, if this were not according to law, nevertheless it seems that on account of second marriage she has lost at least the ownership, as in Auth. de non eligendo secundo nub. §. Gregoria. and what is noted, C. de secun. nu. l. fęminae. Moreover, according to municipal law the question is very doubtful, because the testator did not truly direct his judgment to this wife, who did not preserve marital honor. But this is not a sufficient reason according to some, since the statute preserves the widow. Therefore also the pupillary substitution, and the guardianship, since they are connected. But I answer, because the statute does not say this: and because the statute appears to repel her, unless this were truly and properly expressed by the will of the testator knowing that she had married, which knowledge does not fall upon the husband, who could not divine the future marriage bed: as noted by the doctors at the end of C. qui dari tut. pos. auth. minoris debitor. Hence the statute, which says, provided that if she were instituted etc., seems to be understood when the son himself instituted the mother as heir with certain knowledge, after she had passed to second marriage: as C. de secun. nu. Auth. ex testameto. In this matter it must be carefully considered, that this mother was left testamentary guardian, and as suspect she resigned even the testamentary guardianship, as noted by Cy. C. ad Tertu. l. omnem in addi.

† And in case of doubt, it seems that one should presume that the husband did not wish to grant her a privilege in his goods, since his memory is offended by her transition to a second marriage, although the rule would be different in the case of other blood relatives than in the case of a wife, and of a pupil substituted in a pupillary substitution, by argument from ff. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, §. Lucius Titius Damma. But if she had not been appointed guardian, I would not think that the statute would exclude her, as I have otherwise advised. I hold a contrary opinion regarding the mother, by §. si autem tutelam in the Authentica de nuptiis, because she who has previously accepted and administered the guardianship of her children, and then passes to a second marriage without rendering an account of the guardianship and administration, is deprived of the succession. The statute is not an obstacle: because it speaks of the case when she has committed a fault in one respect, namely by passing to a second marriage. Here, however, she has also committed a fault in another respect: because she is removed from guardianship and testamentary execution as suspect by law, according to the truth, as is noted by the doctors after the gloss in l. omnem, C. ad Tertullianum; and because she has spurned the guardianship of her children and has not rendered an account of the administration; and thus this is a case omitted by the statute. And so we are in the common law, in the Authentica de nuptiis, §. si autem tutelam. And thus Cynus confirms this in his additions there, unless the testator had granted her permission to pass to a second marriage, as in the Authentica de nuptiis, §. disponat. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who previously holds an express mortgage is preferred to the second, etc.
2. A nun is not excluded from her mother's dowry.
3. The author is bound to provide copies of the instruments to the person to whom he sold.
body: The first obligation made against Dominic and his brothers was with

† express hypothecation of goods: and therefore those having this express hypothecation, or rights, are preferred over a subsequently given dowry: as is noted in C. qui potior in pignore habent, l. assiduis. And therefore the possessor of the said house, by virtue of that hypothecation, can defend himself against the heirs of the woman up to that old sum. ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. ex sextante, §. Latinus. However, if new debts were contracted after the dowry was given, I say that the dowry is preferred, because these are preferred credits, or creditors: as in ff. qui potiores in pignore habent, l. si prior. If, however, those having the rights of this dowry have renounced them, they have lost their rights: provided that the renunciation is formal, and is not invalidated by any statute of the place in force at the time of the agreement, or renunciation. For if any statute were in force at that time, it would have to be observed: as in l. omnes populi, and de legibus, l. si quis inquilinos, §. ultimo. Statutes, however, enacted later do not derogate from prior contracts. C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. leges et constitutiones; C. de fidei instrumentis, l. comparationes. And therefore, if indeed there is no statute in the place, the renunciation in question was valid: as noted in l. 3, §. quid ergo, de contrario iudicio tutelae. But if there is some statute there, if indeed it is one that challenges the renunciation, and was in force at that time, then the renunciation is not valid; otherwise it is: because statutes prescribing form never have retroactive effect.

† Regarding the point raised about the nun, I do not see why or how she should be excluded from her mother’s dowry. Extra, De episcopis et clericis, c. Deo nobis; Codex, De iure dotium, l. In rebus, §. Finis. For the fact that she is a bride of God does not prejudice her. The conclusion is this: up to the amount of the old debt, neither Dominicus nor the nun has any right, according to the facts narrated in the case, except for one-half. But in the new debt contracted after the marriage and the dowry, the dowry claim is preferred, provided that if the other party renounced, he must impute it to himself alone, if the statute does not assist her. And therefore, according to the aforementioned case, Dominicus is entirely excluded, whereas the nun is called to one-half of the maternal dowry. I advised on this matter the day before, according to a differently formulated point. And I confirm the same, if that statute mentioned in the opinion were in force, and had been in force at the time of Dominicus’s renunciation. But since he has now asserted to me that the said statute was not then in force, it is necessary to advise with the case altered, just as the case is altered, as in l. Si ex plagio, §. In clivo, Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, cum similibus.

† Moreover, the author must provide copies of his instruments to the person to whom he sold. D. de actionibus emptoris, l. totius. And for this purpose, Johannes Ysnardus is bound in defense of possession and cession of rights: for every right of his pertains to the possessors according to the sense of the contracts. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How the words “I institute my brother as my heir, and if he should die, I institute his sons as my heirs” are to be understood.
body: I institute my brother as my heir, adding that if he should die, I institute his sons as my heirs, and I say nothing more.

† It is asked how these words are to be understood: “and if he should die, I institute his sons.” And it seems that they are to be understood in this way: “and if he should die,” that is, while I am alive, as stated in the Digest, *De libris et posthumis*, l. *Gallus*, and in the Digest, *De testamento tutorum*, l. *penultima*. But this seems inequitable, since the testator felt equally about the brother’s sons, and simply so, as in the Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, l. *Lucius*. Hence those words, “should die,” are sometimes understood even after the death of the testator. But it is doubtful what kind of substitution this is. For it is doubtful whether, after the death of the testator, he can die before having accepted the inheritance left to him, and then his sons come in by regular succession, as in the Digest, *De fideicommissis liberis*, l. *Thais*, § *splendeforus*. And then the civil and direct words stand in their proper meaning, as in the Digest, *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, l. *verbis civilibus*. And the case seems to be that in the Code, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, l. *ultima*. In another way it can be understood more broadly, so that “I institute” means “I substitute precariously,” as in the Digest, *De militum testamento*, l. *quaerebatur*. Therefore, if the brother were alive, he would not have these goods free: because they are subject to restitution in the person of his sons, which does not seem to have been the intention of the testator. Moreover, it would follow that this would be a double substitution, vulgar and fideicommissary. Of the vulgar there is no doubt, because it is the case in the aforementioned l. *ultima*. Of the fideicommissary there is not much doubt, according to what is found in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, l. *si frater tuus*. Nevertheless, the words are so direct and civil that they do not seem to imply a fideicommissum. Moreover, ordered charity seems rather to embrace this interpretation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person related on both sides is preferred in the succession to a paternal fief over a person related through only one parent.
2. A donation inter vivos is not revoked by a will.
body: It is proposed that a certain nobleman, holding a noble fief and having an uncle, died leaving four sons, one of whom was born of one wife, and three were born of another wife. Finally, the first son, who was from the first wife, died, leaving behind and surviving a certain legitimate and natural son of his. Then two of the sons from the second marriage died without issue.

† It is now asked whether the said nephew, on his father’s side only, succeeds to the said uncles, who are related on both sides, when the said two uncles die together with the brother of the said deceased, who is related on both sides. And there is no doubt that in non-feudal goods those related on both sides are preferred: because two reasons overcome one, in the Authentica *De consanguineis et uterinis fratribus*, in the rubric and the black text, and in the Authentica *Defuncto*, and in the Authentica *Cessante*, Codex, *Ad senatusconsultum Orphitianum*, and *De legitimis haeredibus*. But it is not so in the paternal fief: because a woman is not considered in a fief, nor is a closer relationship understood to exist on account of the nature of the fief itself, which regards consanguineous relatives, and not uterine ones, as in column 10 of *Qui feudum dare possunt*, chapter 1, § *Cum vero Conradus*.

Secondly, it is asked whether a donation made between living persons can be revoked by will. And it must be said that it cannot, as is stated in C. de testamento, l. verba, and in C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si ante. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an award made beyond the parties who compromised and beyond the matters compromised is valid.
2. When absolution from an oath given in a compromise may be sought.
3. Absolution from an oath cannot be granted unless the opposing party is cited.
4. A prohibition by an arbitrator against alienation does not impede the transfer of ownership.
5. What is the nature of a substitution made by these words: "I substitute you mutually, if any of you should die without children."
6. Wherever there is gross injury, fraud is presumed.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that an arbitrator, outside the persons between whom he was appointed, can award nothing. D. de arbitris, l. Arbitrator intra; and l. Sed interpellatur, § Si ex altera; and D. de evictionibus, l. Si dictis; C. si compromisero. Nor does it expedite to seek reduction or reformation of the award on this account; because this point is one of written law, which is evident from the law itself. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Quae sub conditione, § De hoc iure; unless it were such a point as to which there is dispute among the learned. D. de re iudicata, l. Cum prolatis; D. de minoribus, l. Aemilius. Secondly, it must be premised that there are three cases. For the award either contains in itself the good faith of the arbitrator; or it contains in itself express fraud, upon inspection of the award; or it contains in itself concealed fraud. In the first case, the power granted to the arbitrator is to be observed as to its extent and quality.

† Nor can absolution from the oath be sought. C. de transa si quis maior. In the second case, the award is invalid, and absolution from the oath is not necessary: since evident fraud and vexatious litigation appear. ff. de ope. lib. l. si libertus ita. and in c. quintauallis. de iureiu. and ff. man. l. creditor. §. Lucius. in fi. In the third case, it is presumed in favor of the award, until the contrary is established. C. de admini. tut. l. si bonam. de euictione. l. herennius. §. 1. But the contrary cannot be established except in court, to which one cannot proceed unless first absolved from the oath, extra de iureiur. c. 1. Thirdly, it must be premised that whenever some preliminary step is required in court, it must be taken after a summary cognizance of the cause, with tacit regard to what may be injured, as ff. ad exhiben. l. thesaurus.

† and therefore a release from an oath cannot be granted without the other party being cited. C. de transa. l. cum hi. §. si praetor. de re iu. l. de vnoquoque even if it is assimilated to an interlocutory judgment. de adop. l. nam ita diuus. cum si.

Fourthly, it must be premised that the arbitrator’s prohibition against alienating does not impede the transfer of ownership. Extra de testibus, c. Ray. However, if it is to the contrary, and this power had been granted to the arbitrator, a penalty would be incurred; otherwise, not. Because this chapter is outside the intent [of the law], and concerns the passage of future time, and is also contrary to rights, as in D. de pactis, l. nemo. Hence, if one has renounced the damage, one may also renounce the contingent event itself, as in § illud nulla, in l. iurisgentium, D. de pactis. Nevertheless, this precept is not encompassed within the granted power. Argumentum: D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, § haereditatis; and in § duo fratres, l. qui Romae, D. de verbis obligatis; and D. de transactionibus, l. qui cum tutoribus; and D. de pactis, l. 1.

Fifth and finally, it must be premised that such substitution, “I substitute you in each other’s stead: if any of you should die without children,” on account of the condition inserted regarding children, would be judged fideicommissary after the inheritance has been entered upon. C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; according to the notes in l. precibus, in the penultimate section, the major gloss. C. de impuberibus and C. de testamento militis, l. in testamento. From these it appears that the substitution made by Lord Alberic was fideicommissary. Furthermore, it appears that an award rendered beyond the compromittors was null. Furthermore, it appears that an award on matters not compromised was null: and in these cases absolution is not necessary, where no obligation has been incurred. D. de pactis, l. si unus, § ante omnia.

† Moreover, it must not be omitted that wherever an award contains in itself an enormity, it is also presumed to contain fraud, as noted by Bartolus in the last paragraph of the Digest title *De praetoria stipulatione*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If someone sold a thing to another so that he might hold it as a noble fief, and be able to sell and alienate it, etc., may he make a testament concerning that fief? And shall the Trebellian or Falcidian portion be deducted from it? And number 2.
body: The Commune of Asti, through its legitimately appointed syndic, sold and transferred to the noble man, Lord Antonio Turco de Turchis, the castle, village, and inhabitants of the place of Mons Magnus, holding the same, however, as a noble, ancient, and paternal fief from the said Commune of Asti. Among other stipulations, it was agreed that the said buyer and his heirs might sell, donate for the sake of the soul, adjudicate, or otherwise alienate in part or in whole the said castle and village with their appurtenances, as above stated, to whomever they wished, provided that such person be a citizen of Asti and obedient to the Commune of Asti, etc. It is presupposed that the Commune of Asti then had the power to sell and to grant jurisdictions, just as other communes have, such as Tuscany and similar ones, which possess full jurisdiction within their territory. Finally, the said buyer, or his successors, obtained from the Emperor the said castle and village of Mons Magnus with high and low justice and all manner of jurisdiction, under the title of a noble, ancient, and paternal fief. Thereafter, the said Lord Antonio made a will concerning the said fief. The question is whether he could make a will concerning the said fief and bind his sons according to the form of the will.

I answer that, according to the proper nature of a fief, no testamentary disposition is valid, as stated in the title *De successione feudorum*, chapter 1, column 10. However, this does not apply to an improper and alternative fief arising from a pact, as in column 10 of the title *De feudo non habente propriam feudi naturam*, chapter *Si quis ea lege*. And therefore, the disposition of the said paternal fief was valid, and he could grant the said fief on whatever terms he wished.

But it is doubtful whether the said fief could be granted more freely than his own property, that is, so that it should not be subject to the Falcidian or Trebellian fractions, just as it would not be subject to them if it were alienated by way of contract. And it seems that the fief is regarded in the same manner as the other goods in this case, so that it is considered part of the patrimony, as stated in the Digest, On the Separation of Goods, Law 1, Section "Sciendum"; for it is considered part of the patrimony, as stated in the Digest, On Vulgar Substitution, Law "Sed si plures," Section "Filio." To the contrary, it seems that the alienation is permitted rather by the favor of the lord than by the nature of the things to be acquired. The solution seems to be that it should be understood that the said fief is incorporated into other incorporeal rights. And it is not true that the favor of the lord is considered here, because this fief was sold. Hence, it is not properly called a fief, which by its nature ought to be gratuitous or quasi-gratuitous. And therefore it seems that it should be said that, like a military service purchased from the testator's goods, it is imputed to the legitime and the Trebellian fraction, as stated in the Code, On Inofficious Wills, Law "Omni modo," Section "Imputari." And that one cannot dispose by will of another's property more than one can dispose of one's own. But if the grant had been made by way of donation and under the nature of a fief, then the permission to alienate would be said to have been made by the permission of the lord; and it could be made in the entire fief, because there are two patrimonies, the hereditary and the feudal, and one does not partake of the nature of the other. Argument from the Digest, On Adoption, Law "Arrogator," Section "Sed impuberis." And it supports this: Digest, On the Petition of Inheritance, Law "Item videndum," Section 1; and in Chapter 1, "Whether the agnate or the son of the deceased," Collation 10. From these it appears that if in the other goods this son of him who disposed of the fief has a legitime and a Trebellian fraction, he can freely dispose by will of the entire fief, the pacts being considered. And the petition obtained from the Emperor is not an obstacle, because it was made so that the petitioner might be granted a double right, not so that a greater right might be taken away by a lesser right. Digest, On the Interrogatory Action, Law "Si quis usumfructum"; and Digest, On Acquiring Possession, Law "Si quis ante." I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How heirs instituted in specific things, and heirs instituted simply, are bound to pay legacies.
body: § father

† He instituted his sons as heirs, first in certain things, then as universal heirs; each is bound to pay the debts according to their hereditary portions, without regard to the legacies, as C. de haeredi. institu. l. quotiens. ff. eod. l. ex facto. C. si cett. petatur. l. 1. If a dowry was given to the father-in-law, and upon his death the wife remains with the husband, the dowry must be assigned to her for the shares of the coheirs, as ff. fami. erciscun. l. si maritus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an incompetent judge is bound to make a remittal in civil cases.
2. Whether a verbal remittal to a competent judge, or a warning, must be made when all exceptions and privileges have been renounced by agreement.
3. Whether a chirograph with the acts made upon it suffices for the interposition of the first decree.
4. For the interposition of the second decree, it must be established that two things are present.
5. The sentence of the prince is not valid without citation.
body: The fact upon which the law is to be determined, as follows below, is that a petition was presented on behalf of Jacobus Cerratus before the judge of the commune of Asti against the brothers Brachius and Petrus de Baragiis, on the one hand and the other. Security for the restitution of expenses incurred before their judge was requested and given. Then Antonius Bellonus acted as surety, who promised the restitution of expenses, etc. And afterwards, by virtue of the decree of three good men, the said petition was committed to three good men, who rendered their sentence in favor of the aforementioned brothers de Botagiis and condemned the opposing party in expenses. Furthermore, a legitimate taxation of the said expenses was made by the judge of the commune; nevertheless, the said surety having been cited, the opposing party raised multiple objections, as appears from the records. From these matters, the question of law arises. And among other things, four points are to be considered. First, whether the said suretyship is valid in law, notwithstanding the said decree. Second, whether that taxation of expenses is valid so as to merit execution against the said surety. Third, whether execution of the said expenses can be carried out according to the form of the chapters concerning things to be given in satisfaction. Fourth, whether the proceedings conducted by the officials and liberators, whom the opposing party denied were officials, are valid, and the rest. It must be considered whether this proceeding can be upheld.

† And the first doubt arises with respect to the judge: for the judge of the city of Cumae does not appear to be the competent judge of this German, since he is not within his jurisdiction, nor is he found there, nor is his procurator. Hence it would seem that at least a letter should be written to the judge of his domicile, so that he might order him to appear in the place where the litigation was initiated and the payment was made. For in this manner is remission effected in civil causes, as in c. Romana, § contrahentes, de foro competenti, lib. 6.

And a pact was appended, and there was a renunciation of privilege and of all exceptions. In this case, namely when there has been a renunciation, the glossa says that a verbal remission or admonition ought to be made, as I said; thus says the glossa singularis on l. 1, Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit. And the same is noted in c. Si, De foro competenti, on the word “contractus.” And this is also held by Bartolus, and it is noteworthy. Nevertheless, in our case this method cannot be upheld, because the judge of the place would not issue a citation. I say, therefore, that another course must be followed, namely, that the said debtors be cited according to the statutes of the place where the goods are, as is noted in C. De Iudaeis, l. Nullus. And Bartolus touches upon this in the matter of reprisals. For in the event of justice denied, or to be denied altogether, one may proceed contrary to the ordinary order, as I said. I think, however, that if it could be safely notified how the proceedings would be conducted, this should be notified, so that it would be an intimation, not a citation. C. Causam, De electionibus, in the Clementinae; Si per vim vel alio modo; l. Si, C. De his qui ad ecclesias consugiunt; l. Praesenti, § Sane.

The second doubt concerns the imperial rescript: but I care little for this, since there has been a renunciation. L. 2, C. De iure dominii impetrando.

The third doubt arises on account of usury. I answer that I am speaking of the principal and of just and proven interest, as is noted in l. Cunctos populos and Extra, De usuris, c. Post miserabilem.

† The fourth doubt is whether the aforementioned chirograph, together with the acts performed upon it, suffices. And I say that it does, at least as regards the first decree, as in the Authentica de exhibendis reis, §. si vero etiam, whereby, once this has been interposed, movable property ought to be kept in the custody of the commissioner before the second decree. L. 2, C. de praetorio pignore; L. a divo Pio, §. 2, de re iudicata. In the remainder, proceedings shall follow the statutes of the place, as noted in L. 3, C. de iure dominii impetrando. And if there were no statute, one would proceed to sale, and in the last resort to adjudication. C. de exceptione rei iudicatae; L. si longe, de peculio; L. aedium additio.

† Therefore, I consider that two things must be established: namely, the debt and the contumacy. Indeed, in the second decree, fraud or a security deposit is required. How, then, can those who are ignorant and not cited be considered litigants, as stated in the law *Haec autem*, under the heading *Quibus ex causis possideatur*?

† Moreover, the sentence of the prince is invalid without citation. On the matter of judgment, c. Pastoralis in the Clementines. Furthermore, who knows whether the Jews, who do not possess immovables, would dissipate these goods or depart with them? For an equitable arbiter must consider all things. But the answer to this is as follows: the debtor is suspect because he does not possess immovables in the place of the city of the galleys; therefore, the goods must be seized. L. Si fideiussor, §. Finis, D. Qui satisdare coguntur. Moreover, because he has obtained an unjust right. How then will he satisfy the creditors, who ought to recover what is theirs? It is difficult, for if the goods were encumbered by a mortgage, the legal process could be founded against the holders. L. 2, C. Ubi in rem actio; D. De rei vindicatione, L. Officium. And they would name the owner in court, if they wished, and notify the owner. But in these cases I do not find a mortgage on the goods: personal actions do not follow the land. I say that our illustrious and magnificent Lord may decree that the action is one in rem, and if this is so, the possessor may be cited, and his citation suffices. And if the decree of the lord or the statute of the place so dictates, a writ of sequestration may be issued due to the contumacy of the holder. And if it is said that the Jews could depart, this is not presumed; therefore, the holder, who holds in the name of those Germans, since he does not defend, the said Jews are to be put in possession, those Germans not being cited as to the first decree. However, the words of the statute or decree must be considered, which, having been seen, I would write precisely: for if the decree or statute says that justice is to be rendered where the goods are, there is no doubt that proceedings must be taken, arg. D. Ubi in rem actio, L. Finis; and D. Ad exhibendum, L. Tignum, §. Ultimo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when an outsider who gives or promises a dowry for a woman is deemed to give it with the intention of making a gift or of recovering it.
2. If a curator appointed over the estate repudiates the inheritance, or if the acceptance is suspended, whether he may nevertheless provide a dowry for the testator’s daughter from those assets.
3. Whether a daughter who repudiates her father’s inheritance must nevertheless be provided with a dowry from her father’s assets.
body: Three persons are to be considered here, namely the person of the promisor, who was the son of a curator appointed to certain assets, and bound to the vacant inheritance for the restitution of the remainder, that is, two hundred and four florins, which his father, the former curator, had received and is collecting from the hereditary debtors. Secondly, the person to whom the promise of five hundred florins in the name of a dowry was made must be considered; for he is the husband. Thirdly, the person of the girl herself, for whom the dowry was promised, must be considered. Furthermore, the cause of the promise, which pertains to all three aforementioned persons, must be considered, namely, the cause of the dowry. Therefore, first let us consider the person of the promisor insofar as he concerns the woman; secondly, the person of the promisor insofar as he concerns the husband. I return to the first point, and I say,

† that there are three cases. For sometimes an outsider promises a dowry with the intention of making a gift, and this is certain. And then there is no doubt that he must pay the entire promised amount, and he recovers nothing from the woman: as in *l. donatiuis*, D. de conditione ob causam; and *l. si*, C. de dotis promissis. Sometimes it is certain that he did not act with the intention of making a gift, but with the intention of managing the woman’s affairs; and then he has against the woman an action for management of affairs (*negotiorum gestorum*), as in *l. cum post*, § 1, D. de administratione tutorum. If he usefully managed the woman’s affairs, otherwise if he did not manage them usefully, for example because he promised beyond the woman’s patrimonial capacity, and she does not ratify it. Sometimes it is doubtful with what intention he promised, whether with the intention of managing or of giving; and then either some presumptions precede which indicate management, and it appears to have been done with the intention of managing; or some presumptions of a gift, and it appears to have been done with the intention of giving; or no presumptions appear, and then the law presumes a gift in the case of an outsider, as in C. de rei uxoriae actione, *l. rem in praesenti*, § *extraneum*.

Now therefore I say that here presumptions of management of affairs appear, and not of a gift, namely on account of the remaining paternal duty. Also on account of the legacy, as in *l. qui negotiationem*, in the beginning, D. de administratione tutorum. But what if this girl says that she has nothing in her assets, because she does not wish to accept the paternal legacy, fearing the hereditary creditors, as in C. de iure deliberandi, *l. fin.*, § *et si praefatam*? Also, because if the hereditary debts absorbed the assets of the inheritance, the legacies are not said to be due, as in C. de legatis, *l. si universae*. But this I will explain below.

Furthermore, I said that the promise itself must be considered insofar as it regards the husband; and then, since the promise was made to him simply, the husband can sue on the promise itself, as in the aforementioned *l. cum post*, § 1. For whether the promisor voluntarily managed the woman’s affairs or acted with the intention of giving, it is of no consequence regarding the husband, who ought not to have an undowered wife, as in the aforementioned *l. si donatarius*, and D. de actionibus et obligationibus, *l. si ex promissione*. Thus it must be concluded that the husband will demand the dowry promised to him; and this demand will be at the woman’s expense, therefore she becomes richer, because she has a claim for her dowry to be brought at that time, and from this her affairs are usefully managed. Hence she is bound either to keep the promisor indemnified, or at least to yield the hope of the dowry, which can be assigned during the subsistence of the marriage, since there is a just cause. Also, a stipulation of dowry can be named: as in *l. 2*, in the beginning, D. solutione matrimonii; and what is noted in *l. si*, C. de donationibus ante nuptias.

It is therefore concluded that the said Mich. is bound to the payment of the dowry; nevertheless, he has recourse against the woman herself, who, if she has present means from which to pay, is bound to pay. But if she does not have means from which she can pay, she is bound to assign the hope of the dowry, or that the husband obligates himself with the intention of novation according to the form of the aforementioned *l. 2*, D. sol. mat.

Now there remain other points which are touched upon, and it is not necessary to treat here of legacies: for even if the woman wished to acknowledge them, she could not; for legacies are not due without the inheritance having been entered upon, even if the inheritance is solvent: as in *l. si nemo* and *l. eam, quam*. But here it is proposed that the inheritance is not solvent on account of debt. Hence, even if the inheritance is not solvent on account of debt, even if the inheritance had been entered upon, the legacies would not be due. Also, this is established: that the husband is not compelled to do that by which the said payer is released from administration; for such release does not pertain to the husband’s concern, nor did the husband in any way obligate himself to this, and therefore he can demand the dowry promised to him with effect, as is clear from the laws cited above. A question arises here,

Whether a curator appointed for the goods of a repudiated inheritance, or one suspended as to whether it should be accepted, may provide a dowry for the testator’s daughter from those very goods: and it seems that he may, provided that it is not to the prejudice of the creditors. For the dowry itself is considered as a debt, and the obligation is inherent in the inheritance itself, as stated in the Digest, On the Rites of Marriage, in the law *Qui liberis*; and in the Digest, On Actions and Obligations, in the law *Obligamur*, section *Legi*. Another question arises in connection with this one,

Whether, if a daughter repudiates her father’s inheritance, she is nevertheless to be dowered from her father’s goods. And it seems that yes, this right pertains to her, not as to an heir, but as to a daughter. To the contrary it seems: because this dowry succeeds in place of the legitime portion, which is not owed to one who repudiates. On these two points, perhaps we do not have any express law for a daughter. Nevertheless, it is made out, because if the father was bound to give it during his lifetime, therefore this dowry is not acquired mortis causa, but separately: just as if she had been dowered by the father during his lifetime, she would have the dowry even after repudiating the inheritance: as in D. de collatione dotium, l. Pater nubenti. So also if it was not delivered, but was due. Argument from l. ultima, C. ad legem Falcidiam. But this similarity is not entirely good: because the dowry has already gone out of the father’s patrimony. And the same could be said regarding a promised dowry, but otherwise regarding one neither paid nor promised. As in D. de collatione bonorum, l. Dedit dotem; and l. 3, §. Sed utrum denuo; and l. Si, C. de coniunctis utriusque iudicii. Regarding the curator of the adult herself, there would be no doubt that he could dower her suitably: as in D. de iure dotium, l. Sive generalis, cum si. Finally, as to those matters about which inquiry is made, I say as I answered above. And add, that this husband would wish to bring a frivolous action, because he would wish first for the dowry, and afterwards he would wish that his wife have a legacy: because the sister’s goods would succeed, which are now suppressed: nor does it appear that he should have the fruit of his greed, nor could the said promisor be so damaged, that the said woman is bound to keep the said promisor indemnified, and under obligation of all present and future goods: as in D. de iudiciis, l. In omnibus; and C. quae res pignori obligari possunt, l. Nomen. Also, as to the inheritance, if the inheritance were solvent, he is released from the administration of 204 florins: because, as I touched upon, the goods themselves are bound to dower the daughter, just as to support her, as in l. 1, de venditionibus in possessione missis, §. Quotiens, where it is said that the curator of the womb and the curator of the goods are equivalent, therefore what pertains to the inheritance and the goods he can perform, under the same title, l. Curator. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether arbitrators, who do not possess absolute power and authority, but rather a free and unrestricted discretion according to their own will, may render a judgment on matters not yet submitted after the term has been extended.
2. A case omitted in the sentence remains subject to the disposition of general custom.
body: As is alleged, the arbitrators and arbiters had power and bailiffship with full liberty and at their entire discretion. And therefore it would seem to be said at first sight that they could also render judgment after the extended term on matters not yet adjudicated: as in the Digest, On the Interpretation of Obligations, the law *Qui Romae*, section *Calimacus*, in the Institutes.

But the truth is to the contrary: because such a reservation does not pertain to extending the time, which has certain limits: as in D. loc. cond. l. si in lege, in principio, and there Bartolus says that although the judge has discretion over any offense, he nevertheless cannot extend the term beyond the form of the statute, unless it is specially granted to him. To this effect is what our doctor teaches in C. de fruct. et lit. expens. l. terminato. And this concludes the first point. As to the second point, it must be said

It appears at first sight that the *talea* and other burdens to be imposed in the future by the said communities ought not to be borne without the declaration of the said arbitrators: as in D. de verb. oblig. l. triticum, understanding the declaration to be one that is valid in law. Therefore, if no declaration valid in law has been made by the said arbitrators, it seems, by contrary reasoning, that it is not valid and that they ought not to be paid: as in D. de off. eius, cuius man. est iurisdictio, l. 1, §. huius rei; and D. de testam. l. qui testamento, §. mulier. But I say the contrary: because, the sentence being absent, the custom of the places remains in common or generally, according to which the said *taleae* and other burdens may be imposed: as in D. de mun. et hon. l. rescripta, §. si. Therefore, the case omitted in the sentence remains under the disposition of general custom, arg. D. sol. mat. l. si cum dotem, in princ. And it is to be noted that the words speak, according to the declaration to be made by them from the power attributed by the parties. Where I note the word "from the power," which cannot be verified after the expiration of the term of the compromise. Hence it follows that, the declaration being held as not made, that which was made after the term of the *talea* is valid, and the other burdens remain under the disposition of the law. To this effect is C. de inst. et subst. l. plus; and D. de leg. 2, l. cum pater, §. vicos. And thus I hold, saving the substance of the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How a person is said to be suspected with reasonable probability.
2. The opportunity for defense must be afforded to the defendant, justice being preserved.
body: The letters of our Lord the Pope state, compelling each one who is culpable and reasonably suspected of transgressing such villages, enclosures, and fences, to provide strict and sure securities, etc. If these letters are indeed most just, they grant no discretion unless the case has been examined, namely, that he is reasonably suspected:

† which indeed must be proved by evident and clear indications: as in D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. si creditores; and what is noted in D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si constante, in the beginning. For, as appears from the force of the words, what is probable is that which is similar and close to the truth, and almost immediate: as in C. de quaestionibus, l. milites, § oportet.

† And on this point, proofs given on both sides ought to be received by him who is sued, for the means of defense, which cannot be denied to anyone, justice being preserved: as in C. de iu. fis. l. defensionis facultas, lib. 10; and ff. de re mili. l. 3, § si ad diem; extra de rescri. c. 2; de re iudi. c. pastoralis; in cle.; and quod no. Inn. extra de constit. c. quae in ecclesiarum. From which it is concluded that the duty of the noble and respectable official to whom it is written is, having ascertained the truth by faith and having heard proofs from both sides, if indeed there is evidence of probability, to compel the provision of security; if it does not appear beforehand, either to acquit the defendant, or at least to write magnificently, so that no charge of negligence can be imputed to him. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mill on private or public water can be built to the prejudice of the first owner, and when.
2. By what signs it is known that a river is public.
body: In the question

The matters stated above concerning the mill are further discussed by Cynus and others, to the effect that either the river was private, belonging to him who first held it and to him who secondly made or wishes to make [a mill], and then the second party may make [a mill] in his own portion, doing so principally for his own benefit, not to harm another: as in *l. Paulus*, *de damno infecto*; and thus it is understood, as noted by the gloss in *C. de servitute et aqua*, *l. manifeste*. Or the river was public, and then either the first party made the mill lawfully, and the second cannot make [one] nor deprive him of the profit which he lawfully derives from the public domain: as in *ff. ne quid in loco publico*, *l. 1*, § *merito*. But if the first party does not hold [the mill] lawfully, then the second may impede him: as in the aforementioned *l. 3*, *versic. idem ait*. From these it follows that, since in our case the first party holds the mill lawfully, as appears from public documents, the second cannot divert the public water from him. On this point, see fully the notes of Bartolus and the modern commentators in *ff. de flumine*, *l. quominus*.

† A river is recognized as public on two grounds, namely that it is navigable. And also on a third, that is, that it does not flow through the private estates of individuals, but through a public bed. The conclusion, therefore, is that the said new mill cannot be constructed to the prejudice of the old one. The same opinion is held by Andreas de Isernia in chapter 1, *Quae sint regaliae*, Collatio 10. And although many words could be said, I do not delight in a multitude of words, but in the truth of the law; and the truth is as I have said. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an inventory made, although it lacks certain subtle formalities of law, benefits the heirs.
body: In the making

† We can consider the common law and the customary or municipal law. If we have regard to the subtlety of the common law, the inventory in question is not legally valid and is considered null; hence, under the common law, the heir is liable in solidum. C. de iure deliberandi, l. si; §. et si praefatam; in Auth. de hereditatibus et falcidia, §. scimus; §. si vero absunt. However, because there is no subscription, as wisely alleged on behalf of the plaintiff: since three witnesses were not summoned in place of the absent creditors and legatees, especially such as are required by law; yet because they were not specifically cited; and also because it does not appear that those cited were contumacious, and for many other subtleties of civil law. But if we have regard to the simplicity of truth and what is observed by custom, a certain rudimentary and simple method of making an inventory. And certainly in many places the snares of the laws that entangle heirs through imprudence are not observed, as says the Speculum, and they are found in the formularies of notaries, and the notary himself asserts, and the two aforementioned witnesses concur. Nor is it said that any fraud was committed in the inventory: I hold that the benefit of the said inventory made according to the custom of the country should avail the heirs, so that they are not liable beyond the assets of the inheritance, argument from l. secunda, C. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, with similar cases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an arbiter, or arbitrator, may render an arbitral award without a party having requested it.
2. Whether an arbitrator may render an arbitral award after the lapse of one year.
body: Whether an arbitrator

† Whether he may render an award without the parties having been requested: Bartolus disputes this most fully and elegantly in *l. si quis ex arbitratu*, *de verbis obligatis*, and holds that he may not, by the text of that law and other well-known reasons. By what reasoning, then, is he bound to cite, to request, since this is not properly a citation? By the same reasoning, he is bound to hear, to inquire, to examine, to grant delays: because the principle of all these things is citation, as in *Inst. de poena temere litigantium*, § *fin.*, and in *Auth. de medio litis non fieri sacras iussiones*, § *fina*. This is contrary to Innocentius and all the doctors, for he differs little from a true arbitrator. Hence, regarding the truth, he ought to resort to his award being heard; yet this is not of the necessity of order, because that is not a judgment, as in § *recepisse*, as noted by Innocentius, *de iureiurando*, *ca. Quintavallis*. And I hold this when the compromise is regarding that which the arbitrator can form without information from the parties, for example, only how much a thing is worth, or what ought to be agreed upon as a dowry, and similar matters which are handled summarily, in which the presence [of the parties] would presumably not draw the arbitrator to anything other than what seems right to himself alone, *arg.* C. *de administratione tutorum*, *l. lex quae tu.*, and what Innocentius notes in *c. Raynaldus*, *de testamentis*. But if the compromise were made regarding a doubtful matter and an uncertain lawsuit, or controversy: then the arbitrator ought to hear the parties, and thus inform himself, *arg.* in *l. fin.*, C. *si per vim, vel alio modo*. And this having been done, it is not necessary, according to some, that the party be cited to his award. Therefore, when it is such a matter that the arbitrator cannot fully know without hearing the parties, then he ought to hear the parties: because when it is not discussed, it is not considered just. Otherwise, if the matter is not placed in controversy, nor requires the disagreement and disputation of the parties: because an award pertains more to contract than to judgment, as I said in *l. 1.*, ff. *de arbitris*.

Secondly, whether an arbitrator may render an arbitral award after the lapse of one year. Bartolus says that he may not; I hold the contrary, because no law states this, as is shown by the argument in the Codex, On Various Rescripts, in the law *Falso*, and it is expressly stated in the Codex, On the Time for Appeals, in the authentic *Item si*, and in the chapter *Quandiu*, On Appeals, in the Clementines. It is not objected by the law *Si*, § 1, *Communia de legibus*, because that section contains a singular rule in favor of the last will. Suppose that on the first day of the first year a compromise is made; the law says that the appeal is pending, and for infinite years, until the arbitrator renders his award. Hence, neither the year nor the biennium runs against the appellant. Thus says the third text there, when it says, “and even if a hundred thousand times the time has passed.” Likewise, in the case of dowry there is no doubt: because a dowry is a tacit judgment formed by law, not a certain declaration. On the law of dowry, in the law *Cum post*, § *Generale*, in the same way, the arbitrator, although he is not bound to follow the strict rigor of the law to the letter, is not objected to by the law *Theopompus*, On the Dowry Action, in the word *iuratus*, joined with the law *Si quando*, Codex, On Wills. Because the glossators understand that there he was produced as a witness concerning the amount of the dowry destined by the father for the daughter, the observance of which will the daughter sought; and thus the matter was reduced there to a judicial determination. Therefore, the arbitral power lasts as long as the delay for rendering the award has not lapsed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The assignee cannot sue against a person against whom the assignor could not have sued.
body: It must be premised

†? [He who has] the debt, acting by virtue of a cession in law, cannot sue him against whom exceptions based on a pact or consent stand, and against whom the cedent could not have sued, as is stated in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *In his*, section *Non debeo*; and in the Decretals, chapter *Si quis iuravit*, *De re iudicata*, Book 6, with its glosses. But the woman who made the cession could not have sued regarding the properties in whose alienation she had consented, if certain assets were sufficient for the satisfaction of the dowry. Codex, *Ad Velleianam*, law *Etiam*; and law *Iubemus*; and in the Authenticum *Sive a me*. Therefore, neither can he who holds the ceded rights from her, or from one deriving title from her, do so. However, concerning other properties which are subject to the hypothec, the second cessionary may sue even against the first; because he acts in the person of the woman, not in the person of the second cedent. Digest, *Qui potiores in pignore habeantur*, law *Miles*; Digest, *De rei venditione*, law *Si culpa*; and according to Durandus in chapter *Pro possessore*. And therefore, just as Margaret could have sued, so can the last cessionary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an instrument false in part is rendered false in its entirety. And item 4.
2. Whether a sale made at a much lower price is void, and whether it is sworn to.
3. Who ought to prove, whether the one claiming to be a minor, or conversely the adversary claiming him to be of age: and whether an oath creates a presumption that the swearing party is of age: and whether, where a decree has been appended concerning age, it must be adhered to, and there.
4. Whether one swearing upon a contract is presumed to be an adult or a ward.
5. One seeking restitution in integrum must prove his age: since it pertains to the substance of his claim.
body: The facts are as follows: there is a certain instrument stating that two castles were sold for a price of two thousand florins, although they are worth ten thousand. The seller is a minor (pupillus) and has sworn not to bring an action for rescission. It subsequently appears that the said instrument is false, because only one castle was sold. From the foregoing, several questions arise: First, whether an instrument that is false in part becomes entirely invalid. Second, whether a sale made at so low a price is valid. Third, whether the said instrument is valid. Fourth, whether the person who took the oath should be presumed to be of age, such that if he claims to have been a minor, he must prove his minority. As to the first point

I answer that when the falsity in part pertains to the whole matter, or to the entire contract, for example because it is stated in the instrument that several things were sold for one price, then the whole is vitiated. But if the individual things had been sold for individual prices, then only that which is false is vitiated: because there are as many writings and as many contracts as there are things in the presence of a distributive division; as is read and noted in C. de transactionibus, l. ex falsis. And it is clear from those which are read and noted in ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. Scire debemus; and ff. de evictionibus, l. si plura; and ff. de falsis, l. si filius.

The following question: Others say, and this is held by Bartolus in l. si ex falsis, through l. si aliquid, de susceptoribus et archariis, and by Lauro de Ravenna also in the same l. si ex falsis, that falsity vitiates the whole: because it condemns the author of the writing. Hence, since the writing derives its full faith from the act, unless faith is imposed, the entire writing is rendered void: as in ff. de edendo, l. si quis ex argento, § 2; and noted in C. de probationibus, l. iubemus.

But the first opinion is truer, namely that of Accursius and Oldradus. And it is supported by what Innocentius notes in Extra, de haereticis, fraternitatis. For although the notary makes one false writing, nevertheless, until he is removed from office, other writings are valid, as noted by the doctors in l. 1, ff. de infamibus, § miles; unless at the time when he wrote the instrument he was suspect and defamed for many other falsities. And thus the gloss is understood in the aforementioned l. iubemus. For guilt and infamy exclude all honor, as in l. 1, C. ubi senatores vel clarissimi.
† As to the second and third points, I say that the contract of a ward is invalid, nor is the instrument valid, as in the Authentica *Sacramenta puberum*.

† As to the last point, I say that if the judge’s decree has been appended, it is presumed in favor of the judge’s decree, as noted in the Speculum, De emptione et venditione. But if the judge’s decree has not been appended, the judge must decide and impose or transfer the burden of proof, as noted in the Digest, De minoribus, Law De aetate. But if the minor is absent, so that he cannot be judged by appearance, or the judge is unwilling or doubtful, then the one who wishes to rescind the contract must prove it from the age, because he bases his case on that, as noted in Law 3, Digest, De arbitris, and Digest, De in integrum restitutione, Law Minor, Law Si minorem te, with its glosses; and this is the truth. As to the first point,

Whether an instrument that is false in part is considered false in its entirety. The glossa says that it is not. C. de veteri iure enucleato, l. 2, in the last column; and C. de transactionibus, l. Si ex falsis. But Jacobus de Ravennate and Cynus, in the same place, say that if the instrument is false due to the fraud of the notary writing otherwise than what was said, it is not properly called false unless fraud intervenes, as we note in C. de falsis, l. Nec exemplum. Then the entire writing is vitiated, for that which is false is rejected because it is false; the remainder, because it is suspect, is tainted: indeed, it annihilates the faith of the writer, as we note in Dist. 9, c. Si ad sacras; and De edendo, c. Si quis ex Argentariis, § 2; and De his qui notantur infamia, l. 2, § Miles; and C. de suscepto et archa, l. Si aliquid, unless faith was placed in other parts of the instrument, either by assertion, or by impugning the instrument in one part and not in the others, or by witnesses, as in C. de probationibus, l. Iubemus. And we say the same regarding a witness, as in Extra, De testibus, c. In nostra.

But Lord Innocentius, in c. Fraternitatis, Extra, De haereticis, distinguishes: either the instrument is false in its solemnity, and then the whole is vitiated, as if the day is false or the consular dating is false; because that defect affects the instrument in every part of itself, as in C. de falsis, l. Si creditor colludens; and D. de fidei instrumentis, l. Repetita; and D. ad Velleiam, l. Seia mancipia; and C. de testamentis, l. Si unus; and D. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, l. 1; and what we note in D. de edendo, l. 1, § Editiones; and Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § Item verborum. Or it is false against the truth of the transaction, and then it matters whether it concerns substantial matters or certain accidental ones. In the first case, the whole is vitiated; in the second, it is not. In support of this is what is noted in C. de falsis, l. Satis aperte.

Others say that either the falsity in part affects the entire contract or disposition: for example, because several things are said to have been sold for one price, when no mention was made in the contract except of one thing. And then the entire instrument is false; because it is one instrument, and concerns one indivisible act, as in D. de aedilicio edicto, l. Cum eiusdem; because in correlatives, and also in confused matters, where one thing is false, necessarily the other is false. Or the falsity does not affect the entire act, for example, because in the same document there is contained the sale of individual items with a price distributed to each, as 10 for an ox and 20 for a horse. Now that in which falsity is not found is not considered false, as in D. de falsis, l. Filius, § Sequens quaestio. For this does not seem to be one instrument, but several instruments, as in D. de minoribus, l. Etiam, § Ex causa; D. de aedilicio edicto, l. Si plura; and D. de verborum obligatione, l. Scire debemus. And although the notary makes one instrument false, nevertheless other instruments are not invalidated until he is removed from office, as in Quando, where the rule is stated concerning all things done by public office: because that which he does in truth is valid until he is deposed from authority. To this contributes what we note in C. de dignitatibus, l. Iudices, lib. 12.

I conclude from all these that either the instrument, by reason of falsity, lacks solemnity, or lacks the truth of the fact, or is suspect, or is false by legal fiction and not by truth contrary to which proof has been made. In the first case, it is vitiated in its entirety; because solemnity is absent, which affects the entire instrument in every part of itself, as in C. de tabulis, l. Generali. In the second case, either the instruments are separated by place and time: and then only that which is proven false is vitiated, until the notary is deposed from office. Or it is one instrument made in one continuous context concerning the same matter: and then it is vitiated. Or concerning several matters differing in substance: and then there are opinions. It seems to me that the negative opinion can sufficiently be defended, i.e., that it is valid in no part. The new reason regarding the solemnity of the entire instrument is that the notary was requested, as we note in Auth. de tabellis, § Nos vero. If therefore he lies in this solemnity in any part: because he writes something false about which he was not requested, it seems that by the rule given above, the whole is vitiated. Others say the contrary: because this request is divisible, but the day and the consuls cannot be divided, as in D. de edendo, l. Si quis ex Argentariis, § Si initium tabularum. In the third case, only that which is suspect is invalidated, if it can be separated from the others without injury to the contracting parties, as we note in C. de edicto divi Adriani et divi Marci, l. Edicto. In the fourth case, only that in which the legal fiction is found is vitiated, as in the aforementioned l. Filius, § Sequens quaestio. Secondly

† It is asked, assuming the truth of the premise: namely, that the oaths of minors do not give firmness to their contracts, but that one capable of deceit and perjury may incur liability, as in the Authentica *Sacramentum*, C. *De pubertate*. Whether one who swears is presumed to be a pupil or an adult. And it must be said that if such a contract has solemnity, he is presumed to be an adult because of the presence of the judge and the decree; for where the judge’s decree is found appended, it is presumed that things were done rightly, as noted in l. 1, C. *De fidei instrumentis* and *Iure hastae fiscalis*, lib. 10; and l. 1, C. *De praediis curatorum*, in the same book; and l. *Actor rem rationem habet*; and in the Speculum, *De emptione et venditione*, § *Videndum*. Or, the judge’s decree is not appended; and then, if indeed the judge pronounced something based on the appearance of the body, we adhere to that pronouncement until the contrary is proved, because that pronouncement operates only regarding the shifting of the burden of proof, when pronounced solely on the basis of appearance, as in D. *De minoribus*, l. *Minor viginti quinque annis ex aspectu*; and as noted in the same title, l. *De aetate*. But if the judge pronounced nothing based on appearance, in case of doubt it is presumed in the direction that more favors the contract, as noted in D. *De arbitris*, l. *Labeo*, near the beginning. Others say that he who relies on age must prove the age, as noted in C. *De in integrum restitutione minorum*, l. *Si minorem te*. That opinion has this consequence: either the minor can [be held liable] and is guilty, and then the author [of the claim] must prove it, since age is of the substance of an effective contract, as noted in D. *De petitione hereditatis*, l. *Cogi et iusti*; and D. *Quibus alienare licet*, in the beginning. Or the adversary possesses, and the minor acts for the rescission of the contract, and then the minor must prove [his minority], as in Inst. *De interdictis*, § *Commodum*; and D. *De probationibus*, l. *Cum de aetate*.

† It is certain that wherever a minor seeks restitution in integrum, he himself must prove his age: because it is of the substance of his claim; and because he acts against the common law, as in D. de minoribus, l. intra utile; and D. de iureiurando, l. nam et postea, § si minor. I always presume age against the contracting party: because it is a solemnity, or intrinsic substantiality. But I do not presume another extrinsic solemnity, as is fully noted in l. sciendum, de verbis obligatis; and D. de publiciana, l. quaecunque, § fin., with its subject matter.
