And yet this is consistent with the fact that, from the appearance of the body, a pronouncement by the judge regarding the appearance, with the parties present, or one absent in contumacy, the judge may remit the burden of proof, as stated above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the execution of an arbitral sentence is impeded because someone alleges that he has the right to seek reduction, etc.
2. Within what time such reduction may be sought.
3. The rescissory remedy may be raised by way of exception.
1. Whether the exception of spoliation may be raised against the party seeking execution.
2. Whether the petitory action concurs with every possessory action.
3. The petition is admitted according to the form of law and statutes.
4. The terms for proof are peremptory.
5. The term fixed for producing evidence has the force of an interlocutory judgment.
6. The consultation has the force of a conclusion.
body:
I proceed, as in no. Inno. in d. c. fraternitatis. and de accu. c. qualiter, and Quia et facto oritur ius. l. ex plagiis. § inclinatio. ff. ad l. Aquil. Therefore, in the case of Ioannes Rotarius, I first set forth the facts themselves, as is required by law, so that the brief allegations to be described below may be properly understood, according to l. vt responsum. C. de transac. with similar authorities.

Behold, certain arbitrators, commonly elected and appointed by Ioannes Rotarius on one part, and Rosinetus Garretus in his own name and on behalf of Robertus Garretus on the other part, on account of the Castle, rights, and appurtenances of Bellengerii: among other things, they said, pronounced, and adjudged that the said Castle of Bellengerii, with all its rights, etc., as contained in the sentence. And they condemned the said Rosinetus, in the names mentioned above, to surrender and release to the said Ioannes the said Castle of Bellengerii, etc. Furthermore, they condemned the said Ioannes to pay and satisfy to the said Rosinetus, in the names mentioned above, up to a certain term now elapsed, 500 gold florins, on account of all rights competent to the aforementioned parties in the said castle, as contained in the said sentence.

After this sentence, as stated above, was rendered, within the term, the said Ioannes offered, consigned, and lawfully deposited in the presence of the Lord Judge the said 500 florins, which, by his order, are still in deposit with Ioannes Pellata. Hence, on the part of Ioannes, nothing remains to be performed before the Magnificent and Spectable Knight, Lord Franciscus Casseriaticus, governor of this city. Moreover, Ioannes offered a certain notification and exposition, fully narrating the aforesaid. And in conclusion, he petitioned and requested the aforementioned Lord Governor that, by pronouncing, he declare the said arbitral sentence, or award, to be committed to execution on the part and in favor of the said Ioannes, by every right, way, mode, and office by which he may do so better and more validly, and especially by virtue of a certain chapter of the City of Asti, placed under the rubric de sententiis ratis habendis, etc. To prove which, laws and instruments were produced, as appears in his production.

On the other side appeared Ugoninus de Gorzano, in the procuratorial name of the aforementioned Garretus, who, among other things, said that against the aforementioned arbitral sentence a reduction to the arbitration of a good man had been made before the Lord Judge, who, considering the form of the decree, committed it to three good men, who indeed said, pronounced, adjudged, and declared by the said sentence that the judgment contested between the said parties before them was null, reserving, however, every right which the said parties have from the proofs and attestations made and produced in the said judgment before them: so and in such a way that by the said sentence no prejudice be done to the rights and proofs made and produced by each party; reserving to the said Ugoninus, in the said names, the right to say again that the said arbitral sentence and award is null and inequitable, and that it ought to be reduced to the arbitration of a good man whenever. On account of which, the said Ugoninus said that what is requested by the said Ioannes cannot be done.

Furthermore, other exceptions and replies were made on both sides, as appears in the records, to which reference must be had, as in l. iudices. C. de iudiciis. and c. licet causam. extra de prob. and l. illicitas. § veritas. ff. de offi. prae. with similar authorities. Now, from the premises, it remains to see what is the law. And principally here it must be examined whether the request of Ioannes can be done according to law, notwithstanding the said reservation of reduction to the arbitration of a good man.

† And omitting the premises alleged, it must undoubtedly be said that so it is, since there is nothing impugnable or obstructive that would provide an impediment to the requisition sought. For although the right of reducing again and so forth was reserved to them regarding the garrets, because this is considered to have been in their power, they ought to have reduced that power to act by again reducing the said sentence to the arbitration of a good man. This power indeed has a limited term, within which the said reduction must be made, and according to Speculum, infra, ten days, as the same notes in the title de arbitris, § sequitur. Just as we say in appeal: because such reduction is a species of appeal, as l. non distinguimus, § cum quidam, ff. de arbitris. Since therefore this reduction was not made within ten days, it remains to conclude that there is nothing obstructive in the aforesaid. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that in the sentence of the three good men this word was appended, whenever: because it is limited and restricted according to the nature of the act to which it is attributed, arg. l. si uno, ff. locati et conducti, and l. damni, ff. de damno infecto, and that not, per Innocentius, in c. ex literis, extra de iure patronatus, and l. si stipulatus, ff. de usufructu. Therefore, etc.

Furthermore, following the opinion of Bartolus, who states, inquiring below regarding the time within which a reduction is to be made, that this question would require a decision by the Prince, nevertheless he says that if someone remains silent for a year, so that he does not reduce it to the arbitration of a good man, which seems to approve the award, as in the law *Qui segrauatos*, Code, On Censuses, Book 11. Thus he holds. Law *Si societatem*, section *Arbitrorum*, Digest, On Partnership. Now, to the point below: within a year from the day of the said sentence, it was not reduced to the arbitration of a good man; therefore, etc. Moreover, assuming that the right of reduction has not been brought into action, meanwhile the petition for the declaration of nullity is not impeded; because one thing is to be in act, and another in potentiality, as in the law *Labeo*, Digest, On the Status of Free Persons; and note in the law 1, Digest, On Rainwater to be Collected.

And in this case, the rescissory remedy, namely reduction, is reducible by way of exception, where otherwise it could have been deduced by way of principal action. Nor is this absurd: for thus we see in l. Papinianus, §. si filius, D. de inofficioso testamento, and in l. si praeteritus, D. de bonis possessoribus contra tabulas, and in l. nam et postea, §. si minor, D. de iureiurando, in which laws it is proved that rescissory remedies are examined by way of exception, which nevertheless could have been principally asserted. Thus therefore in the case at hand, since the said John requested the aforementioned things, the opposing party had the right to oppose on the grounds of inequity and lesion, and to prove them. Moreover, to the same effect: Let us see that the right of speaking is not a formed right, and lasts for a period of 30 years, and yet this can be examined incidentally. For example: because when execution is sought, nevertheless he against whom it is sought: excepts on the ground of nullity, as in l. 1, in principio, D. quae sententiae sine appellatione rescinduntur, and l. si praetor, §. Marcellus, D. de iudiciis. And nevertheless it could be principally asserted, as noted in the said l. 1, D. quae sententiae sine appellatione rescinduntur, and in l. 1, §. 1, D. de feriis. Thus also says the said Bartolus in l. si expressum, D. de appellationibus, in the question how nullity is cognized. Well therefore he concludes that the requisition made by John proceeds in law notwithstanding the reservation given to the said de Gerretis. Otherwise it would follow that if anyone could not seek execution of a sentence until one is in the faculty of speaking, or of reducing a sentence as null or inequitable, that the execution of the sentence would be proposed late, i.e., tardily: because the right of reducing, as is said, lasts 30 years, and the right of executing ends in 30 years, l. sicut, C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, which would be ridiculous to say. I therefore say that the petition proceeds in law: and by way of exception is examined on equity, as has been proved above regarding nullity, which is objected against execution, as in l. 4, §. condemnatum, D. de re iudicata, and what is read there. It makes l. iudicati, C. si ex falso instrumento, and l. si praetor, §. Marcellus, D. de iudiciis, and l. 2, C. de falsis, and c. suscitata, Extra de restitutione in integrum. And therefore since nothing was proved for the part of the said de Garretis, who doubts that it must be declared by sentence that the said sentence is to be committed to execution? For two things were to be proved for the part of the said de Garretis, so that what was requested by John should not be done. First, that the arbitrators themselves arbitrated fraudulently and out of spite. Second, that their arbitration contains great inequity and lesion in fact. But certainly the first is not truly proved: namely because nothing was produced to this effect. Nor even presumptively: because fraud is not presumed, as in l. merito, D. pro socio. The second is also not proved, which is evident from the fact that the contrary is not proved from the acts, as in l. super, C. qui militare non possunt, lib. 12. And still the mode of proving the aforementioned in reduction is very difficult: because it is not to be proved that the arbitrator arbitrated against justice in whole or in part: because for this they are not taken, but according to justice they arbitrate, as in l. si de meis, §. recepisse, and what is noted there, D. de arbitris. But it must be proved and estimated according to the doubtful event of the litigation, inspecting also the quality of the persons, as proves the gloss in l. Lucius, §. finalis, D. ad Trebellianum. Otherwise certain things are estimated one way, and uncertain things another. And uncertain things are sometimes reduced to the minimum estimate, as noted in D. de pactis, l. contra iuris, §. finalis, D. de verborum obligationibus, and in l. si societatem, §. arbitrorum, D. pro socio, and in l. 1, C. de rescindenda venditione, and by Raymond in l. si liber, D. de operis libertatis. And because they were not proved, it is concluded that he is considered to lack right, as in D. de edendo, l. argentarius, §. cum autem. For although in the truth of essence the right does not fail, nevertheless it fails in the truth of proof, as in D. de furtis, l. quidam tabularum, and l. duo sunt tituli, D. de testamento tutelis. It makes what is noted in D. de dolo, l. servus tuus, §. si persuaseris. And thus, as has often been said, it is to be concluded for the part of John, and from the foregoing the first exception of the opposing party is disposed of.

† Furthermore, I yield to the exception of spoliation: because it is objected on their behalf regarding the garrets that the said requisition does not proceed while the said case of spoliation is pending,

† For it is answered in the first place that, according to Petrus and Cynus in the law *Ordinarii*, Codex, *De rei venditione*, the petitory action concurs with every possessory action; and thus the said exception would not stand in the way. Moreover, the petitory and possessory interdicts for recovery are proposed in different respects: for example, because you bring a possessory action on account of civil possession in a sale of a thing, since you claim to have been dispossessed, at least of natural possession. In such cases, these actions proceed, as is argued from the law *Naturaliter*, § *Nihil*, according to the fifth reading, Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*; and this is held there by the aforementioned Bartolus in the fourth combination. And in this case, the privileged cause of dispossession ceases. Now, as to the point at hand, the parties invoke the matter as dispossessed persons; whereas John merely asks that the sentence be declared enforceable, and does not expressly claim the thing. Therefore, these differ, as is apparent to the observer’s sense: for these actions are incompatible. It would be otherwise if they were proposed in the same respect: for instance, if you claim to have been dispossessed, and thus bring a possessory action for recovery; while I, for my part, claim the same thing from you by way of sale. And then, because these are incompatible, you cannot say that you do not possess, nor can I claim possession from you, as in the last law, Digest, *De rei venditione*; consequently, they do not proceed simultaneously to that extent. For the possessory action is not impeded in this case, because I do not claim to be the owner in order to exclude you from the possessory action. Hence, since John has asked only for the aforementioned declaration, and by virtue of that declaration there is still room for real and military execution, it is clear that these actions are proposed in different respects; therefore, they proceed according to law. It would be otherwise if the aforementioned actions were proposed in one and the same respect. And thus are the words of the said chapter, *Sententiae arbitrales exequutioni mandentur* [Arbitral sentences shall be committed to execution], limited; it was submitted principally according to the form of the said chapter. Nor is this disapproved,

† because something may be demanded according to the form of law and statutes, as noted by Master Bartolus in *l. quidam*, D. rerum amotarum; and this is proven in *c. cum accessissent*, X. de eo qui mittitur in possessionem causa rei servandae. And then it is accepted according to the mode more advantageous to the plaintiff, as in *l. si quis intentione*, D. de iure. And it is relevant that what Innocentius notes in a certain new addition, which few possess, in *c. certificari*, X. de sepultura; and what I, Baldus de Perusio, note in *l. 2*, supra, de probationibus. From all and each of these, it is uniformly concluded that the petition and request of John proceeds in law, notwithstanding the said reservation made by those good men. And also notwithstanding the cause of alleged spoliation, with all due reverence and correction of your lordships and mine. Finally, a certain production of rights made by Ugoninus from the acts and proceedings before three good men, etc., does not obstruct, because the terms of the statute were peremptory for both parties to produce, etc., as appears from the acts.

† And also because all probatory terms are peremptory, as stated by Bartolus in l. finita, § Iul., ff. de damno infecto. Without doubt, he is not admitted to produce evidence any further. And first I prove this in a similar case through the chapter Pastoralis, extra de exceptionibus, [which holds that if an exception arises from an ancient matter or comes to his knowledge anew, as stated in the said chapter Pastoralis, and is noted in] 13. quaest. 2, in principio; therefore, and furthermore, I prove this through l. quae per aliquos, which is alleged to the contrary, namely through l. mancipiorum, ff. de optione legatorum, where, if a term is set for someone to choose, and after the term the opposing party does something and disposes of some of his goods, he is not admitted to choose. So in the present case, through the said term, it was literally acted upon in court by the said John, and also by Ugo, as appears from the records; therefore, after the term, he is not admitted to produce evidence. Thus holds Bartolus in the said l. mancipiorum, ff. de optione legatorum.

† Moreover, the aforementioned statutory terms for producing [evidence] and so forth have the force of an interlocutory judgment, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *Coram* in the title *De in integrum restitutione*; this is also proven in the law *Diffamari*, Codex, *De in integrum restitutione*, and in the law *Titia*, Digest, *De accusationibus*. Therefore, since rights are thereby acquired by the parties, such terms ought not to be revoked without a hearing on the merits of the case. And that no admission is allowed after the expiration of the term is notably held by Paulus de Castrensis in the chapter *Constitutionem*, Extrajudicial, *De electione*, in the gloss *Vbi plene de hoc*. For it would also follow that there would be no end to litigation, contrary to the law *Fratris tui*, Codex, *De transactionibus*. Furthermore, it would mean that the commands of judges could be evaded, contrary to the law *Si praetor*, Digest, *De iudicibus*. Moreover, the aforementioned case was referred by the Lord Vice-Governor for consultation to the Lord Bonominus Ariminensis and Antulus, and their fees were paid by both parties, as is known to you; therefore, they are not admitted subsequently.

†because such consultation has the force of a conclusion in the case. And therefore, from now on, nothing can be objected to or proven, as stated in l. quamuis indubitati, C. de adulteriis et perjurio, and by Innocentius in c. pastoralis, extra de causa possessionis et proprietatis, extra de procuratoribus, c. auditis, and de testibus, and fi. instr., c. cum dilectus. From which I conclude that such production is not valid in law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How is expulsive force, whether exercised by the person himself or through another, to be proved.
2. Whether one who commits an offense against a person against whom it does not appear that he intended to commit an offense is said to have committed a delict.
3. One who acts, binding himself to a day, must prove that day.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that expulsive violence, which is the subject of our discussion, is sometimes inflicted directly, and sometimes through another. For it is inflicted directly when the present person inflicts violence upon the present person, or upon his ministers, or upon a near relative, friend, or servant who are holding possession for another, as in C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. 1. For when those are expelled by force, it is understood that he is expelled in whose name they were holding, as in ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. peregre, §. quibus. But when those holding possession are themselves expelled, the owner is not said to have been expelled by force, as in ff. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, §. non autem alii. It makes to the point what is noted in C. de acquirenda possessione, l. si. If, therefore, anyone claims to have been expelled because those holding for him were expelled, he must necessarily prove that at the time of the expulsion they were holding for him, as in ff. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, §. interdictum autem hoc. And conversely, if anyone says he was expelled, and that the expeller acted in the name or consideration of another absent person, and therefore intends to bring the interdict unde vi against that absent person, he must prove that at the time of the ejection the expellers had a mandate to this effect, or that they later ratified the act done in his name, as in ff. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, §. deiecisse, and §. quotiens, and ff. de regulis iuris, l. hoc iure, §. deiecit. Nor is it sufficient to prove that the expeller was a familiar of his; for by this the mandate is not proved. For a special mandate is required for relinquishing. And this is determined by the text in extra de restitutione spoliorum, c. cum ad sedem, and is proved in its own reason in ff. quod quisque iuris, l. 3, §. si procurator. Likewise, it is not sufficient with regard to the interdict unde vi to prove that some knowledge later came to the master of that household, but that the master himself knew that violence was inflicted in his name. For if this is not established, since ignorance is presumed, it is established that the ignorant person could not have certified or ratified, as in ff. de regulis iuris, l. in totum. Therefore, sometimes the proofs for the interdict unde vi are easy, when they can directly be brought against the present violence. For the act of these men is proved by sight, as noted by Dy. in l. 1, in fine, and ff. de aqua pluviali arcenda. Sometimes the proofs are not so easy, as when they consist in a fiction, i.e., in ratification: then it is not proved unless the means are proved. From which the delict is inferred. Similarly, we distinguish in disproofs. For some disproofs are proved directly, some through a medium, as in C. de falsis instrumentis, l. scribentium. Hence, when the present person inflicts violence on the absent, or the absent on the present, which cannot happen except through intervening instrumentalities, or through certain intervening persons, it is necessary to prove the means, from which the nature of the action itself is inferred as proved. Having premised these things, I come to the point: for here it is alleged that the present person inflicted violence on the absent, i.e., through some medium; because he expelled those holding for that absent person. Therefore, it is necessary to prove the true possession at the time, i.e., of the violence inflicted. Likewise, that they were holding for him according to the assissentes in the Castle. Likewise, that the defendant, summoned by the interdict unde vi, expelled them. But one may doubt about a fourth point, whether it must be proved, namely, that the expeller knew that those holders were holding for that absent person. And this stands on a certain brocardic path, namely

Whether he commits a delict in a person in whom it does not appear that he intended to commit a delict. For there are certain real delicts, such as theft, and in these the intention to take is sufficient. It is not necessary that the thief had knowledge of the certain owner. He who is truly the owner of the stolen thing acts, notwithstanding ignorance or even error, as stated in D. de furtis, l. falsis, § qui alienum. There are certain delicts personal with respect to the thing, such as violence, as noted in the same title, l. Itaque fullo, and D. de iniuriis, l. lex Cornelia in principio. And in these it seems the same as in purely personal delicts, such as insult and battery upon a person: in which a distinction is made, either there is ignorance or error concerning the very body that is offended, and this does not excuse; or concerning the quality of the body, by which the insult is transferred to another person, and then it excuses with respect to this, so that an action is given to that other person, as this distinction is proven in D. de iniuriis, l. qui nocentem, § qui si iniuria, and § cum aliquis. Therefore, although someone offends the household member of another, whether he knows him to be a household member or not, he does not commit an insult against the master, unless we say that in expulsive violence the insult should not be considered according to the will, but according to the effect. For considering the effect, possession is taken away, and violence is consummated, as C. unde vi, l. cum quaerebatur. It must therefore be seen first, whether it is proven that those two nobles, namely Io. Ro. and Gul. aforementioned, by themselves, as alleged in the libel, approached the castle and invaded the castle. For this approach and this invasion must be proven by witnesses who saw them invade, according to the doctrine of the said Dyonisius, because it is a matter of proving a certain act of persons present inflicting violence against a present person. Furthermore, it is required that it be proven that those standing in the castle were standing there for the nobleman who is bringing the action. Also, it must be proven that they were detained or held captive in the castle, which is similar to ejection, as l. 1, § plures, D. de vi et vi armata, where it is noted that one who imprisons a prudent man seems also to deprive him of possession. Namely, because he deprives him of the use of possession and the discretion of possessing. And these things, above all, as it seems, must be proven: nor is rumor sufficient, but these do not appear to be proven, nor are they; because there is no witness who saw the persons and the act.
† And it should be noted that when the plaintiff binds himself to a specific day, he must prove it, as stated in l. 1, C. qui accus. non poss. and c. Ego Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A certain man instituted as heirs his two daughters and all children to be born of his wife; but he wished that the daughters should be content with 100 pounds if they married, or with 100 pounds if they entered religion; and he substituted to them a male son to be born; and if none should be born, he substituted A. and B., their uncles; and if a male should be born, he instituted him as universal heir; now, no male having been born, what is to be done regarding this inheritance?
body: A certain person instituted his two daughters and all children to be born of his wife as heirs; but he willed that the daughters should be content with one hundred pounds if they entered into a carnal marriage, and with fifty pounds if they entered into a spiritual marriage. In the meantime, they are to be maintained. He substituted a son to be born as male heir. And if no son existed, he substituted A and B, their uncles, namely A for two-thirds and B for one-third. And if any male child were born, he willed that he should be the universal heir. And if any of them should die in pupillary age, he substituted the said A and B. And if no male son were born, then, and in that case, he instituted the said A and B as heirs for three parts. Now, since no male son was born, it is asked what is the effect of the institution and substitution both of the daughters and of the substitutes.

And it seems that one should say that the testator in this case clearly passed to the dipondium, for he instituted his son as heir in all his goods. Moreover, he instituted substitutes in all his goods; therefore, he instituted the daughters in one *as*, and the substitutes in another *as*, and thus of necessity he made a transition to two *asses*, and thus to 24 *unciae*, and thus to the *dipondium*, or he divided the *as* into two *semisses*.

To the contrary, it seems that the testator spoke adversatively, for when in the first part of the will he had instituted the daughters, he appended a double adversative: one is there, "but he wished that they should be content," etc. Then he appended another, when he said that he instituted a male son as universal heir. But this cannot be, unless the universal institution of the daughters is reduced to a particular institution. And afterwards he instituted A. and B. if a male were not born. And thus, so to speak, the universal heir detracts from another universal heir, that is, from the daughters, the name and right of universal heir, and reduces them to particular heirs, e.g., in one hundred *librae*, or fifty, or for alimony; for the later writing reforms the earlier, as in C. de leg. l. *conquestio*; and ff. de haere. instit. l. *interdictum*, §. *pater*; and l. *item quod sabinus*, §. *sed si asse*; and ff. de condi. et dem. l. *nam ad ea*. And I think this part accords with the will and knowledge of the testator.

And by this, the said daughters ought to have legacies with the supplementation of the *legitima*. For a son or daughter instituted, even in one coin, has everything left to them under whatever title imputed, even to the *legitima*, as noted in ff. ad Treb. l. *si quis priore*. And if there is anything above the *legitima*, of that legacy beyond the limit of the Falcidian law, the heir instituted universally may detract a quarter from what is left above the *legitima*. Moreover, even if the daughters were heirs for a share, from the prelegacies for the share of the coheir the Falcidian deduction would be made, if they exceeded the *dodrans* portion of the coheir, as in C. fam. haer. l. *familia cuius*; and ff. ad leg. Falc. l. *Nesennius*. From which it appears what is the law regarding the other legacies and prelegacies made to the said daughters. And it is supported by ff. ad leg. Falc. l. 1, §. *si cohaereditis*; and C. fam. haer. l. *filium, quem habentem*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Heirs directly instituted do not suffer the Falcidian deduction in that which they acquire by hereditary right.
2. When there is more in legacies than in the legitime, whether that excess could be deducted by the coheir burdened, whose portion is exhausted beyond the quarter.
3. Whether the residue is computed in the Falcidian deduction, or in the legitime of the coheirs who are children.
4. Whether a son burdened under a condition deducts two quarters.
5. Whether a factitious condition is regarded as a condition.
6. Whether heirs burdened to restore are called mere executors, or heirs.
body: It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† that heirs instituted directly do not suffer the Falcidian deduction in that which they take by hereditary right. And the reason is: because they take by direct right and from themselves, and not from any heir. But for the share which they take to hold by right of a pre-legacy, when the portion of the co-heir from whom they take is exhausted because the charges exceed three-quarters of his portion, there is no doubt that the Falcidian portion can be deducted; because with respect to the co-heir's share, these pre-legacies are regarded as held by the right of a simple legacy, as in C. ad l. Fal. l. si cohaeredibus and l. si ut allegatis; unless he receives as much from the co-heirs as he wishes to deduct, as in ff. ad leg. Fal. l. Nesennius.

† Having premised this, in the aforesaid case I consider three things. First, the institution of the females together with the posthumous child to be born in the whole inheritance. Second, the encumbrance placed upon the daughters themselves, namely that in place of the said universal institution they ought to be content with a certain institution or particular bequest, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. in princ. Third, I consider the institution of the posthumous children made by direct civil word, because he said, 'institutes.' Fourth, I also consider to what extent these institutions are related to one another, namely whether the institutions of the daughters are reduced to two institutions through those adversative words 'but he willed that the daughters, etc.', so that the testator passed from the universal institution of the daughters to a particular bequest, or to a particular institution of them; or whether those words rather express the force that the daughters themselves are asked to restore to the said substitutes the remainder beyond what is allocated to them of the said amount above. And this second view seems truer through the case of the said l. cum pater. in prin. and l. peto. in prin. and de leg. 3. l. Paulo Callimacho. §. Pomponius. But it is certain that these daughters thus encumbered can deduct the legitime, as in ff. de inoff. testa. l. Papinianus. §. quarta and §. si conditioni; which legitime they will deduct in one of two ways: either by restoring that much less of what they receive by hereditary right, or by claiming legacies from the co-heir out of what is left to the daughters themselves. For from the moment a child is instituted, even in a single coin, he counts toward his legitime whatever he receives under whatever title of bequest, as in C. de inoff. test. l. omnimodo. For it is not necessary that he have the title of institution in the entire legitime; it suffices that the title of institution is left to him in a single coin, as is noted in ff. ad Treb. l. si quis priore, ff. de minor. l. denique. §. sed utrum.

† But suppose that there is more in the legacies than in the legitime: can that surplus be deducted by the encumbered co-heir whose portion is exhausted beyond three-quarters? I answer: undoubtedly yes. But whether

† that which is received by the encumbered daughters through those words 'that they are content, etc.' is computed toward the fourth for the said persons, that is, the co-heirs of the daughters? It seems not, as in ff. ad l. Fal. l. in quartam [l. in quod] and l. in quartam. But the text in the said l. Nesennius. ad l. Fal. seems to the contrary. Now another doubt remains: whether the universal institution of the said daughters was revoked by the universal institution of the said posthumous children and substitutes. And it seems that it was, as in C. de leg. l. conquestus. The contrary seems true: because when the whole inheritance is given to the first and the whole to the second, it either seems to expand to a double as (dispondium), or if it does not seem to do so, it is the same in effect: because each takes a half, that is, an equal division is made by concurrence, as in ff. de haere. instit. l. interdum. §. sed si in duos and l. Item quod Sabinus. §. sed si asse; and this view is more probable. It remains therefore to conclude thus: that if, after compensating for the charges, anything remains above the legitime of the daughters that was left to them by the co-heir, the Falcidian portion is deducted from such bequest, so that those co-heirs may have a fourth part of their share by right of the Falcidian law. For this is not deducted from the daughters as heirs, because direct successions are not subject to the Falcidian deduction, but it is deducted as from singular legatees.

† One matter, however, ought to be considered: whether the daughters ought to have both the legitime and the Trebellianic portion, because they were requested regarding the universal estate, and under a condition, as in c. Raynaldus and c. Raynutius de test. and in c. si pater. de test. in Sexto, presupposing as true the opinion of the canonists. And it seems that they should, by the said laws. The contrary seems true: because that condition—'if a posthumous child shall be born, let it be restored to the posthumous child; and if it shall not be born, let it be restored to the substitute appointed in place of the one to be born'—does not seem properly called a condition, because in every event the daughters are encumbered under contradictory expressions, whether the posthumous child is born or not; whence one of the said conditions must necessarily occur, as in ff. de condit. indeb. l. Iulianus. §. 1. The contrary seems true, for such an encumbrance is conditional, and in the meantime does not pass to the heir, because the person to whom it is owed is in the meantime uncertain, as in ff. quando dies leg. ced. l. cum homo; and thus, according to the common observance of the said chapters Raynutius and Raynaldus, and also according to the gloss of the civil law, it seems that the daughters can deduct two fourths as having been requested under a condition, and not more, as is noted in C. ad l. Fal. l. quisquis and de inoff. test. l. Papinianus and in Auth. de haered. et Falcid. §. si quis autem non in plures, on the word 'quartam.' But to this a twofold answer can be given: first, because the Falcidian portion was expressly prohibited, as in C. ad l. Fal. auth. sed cum testator. Likewise, because the condition of the birth of the posthumous child, or the condition itself, was not expressed in this encumbrance of the daughters; and although by implication it must be understood of the posthumous children or the substitutes, and a certain tacit condition seems to be present with respect to the persons to whom it is left, as in ff. de lib. et posthu. l. commodissime and l. cum postuma, ff. de vent. inspic. l. qui ventrem,

† nevertheless, that tacit condition is not regarded entirely as a condition, as in ff. de cond. et demon. l. conditiones quae extrinsecus and ff. quando dies leg. ced. l. quod pure, and what is noted in l. quae sub conditione. §. ult. de cond. instit., and ff. de contrah. empt. l. illud. §. fin. supports this, as well as ff. ad Silan. l. si quis in gravibus. §. ult. and ff. de legat. 1. l. haec verba, and what is noted in ff. de pact. l. item. Yet it is not necessary to dispute through this, because it suffices that the Falcidian deduction was prohibited. To the same point: It must be considered that these persons are not mere executors, but heirs, as well as executors, ff. de alim. et cib. leg. l. alio haerede, according to one reading. But I say this to the extent that we may see whether the election which they made of the Carthusian Order, and the grant and delivery made to the said Order, was a restitution under the Trebellian senatusconsultum, or not.

† For he who is requested as heir can restore under the Trebellianum; but the said executor cannot do this, unless he is reduced to the understanding of an heir in favor of the soul and the poor, as in l. si quis ad declinandam, C. de episc. et cler., and ff. ad Treb. l. mulier. §. ut Trebelliano. For if through the restitution made under the Trebellianum rights and actions have been transferred, so that the heirs can no longer sue the hereditary debtors, as in ff. ad Treb. l. ex lege. §. quamquam and fully noted in ff. de pact. l. si cum emptore, nor does a protestation of the heir made contrary to the Senatusconsultum avail when he is compelled against his will, as in ff. ad Treb. l. qui poterat. But let us see whether the words of the testator have this flavor. And it seems not, because the testator seems to have spoken of a particular distribution, not of a universal restitution, ff. ad Treb. l. cogere. §. et generaliter; because the words of the testament say there, where the testator says, 'and if anything shall remain, etc.'; for how can he be said to be requested regarding the universality, if he did not want anyone other than the heir to be liable to pay debts and legacies, and willed that the poor be chosen out of the clear assets after all debts were paid? But because authority was given to them universally and generally, he could have given and restored the inheritance to the aforesaid Order quasi under the Trebellianum with the hereditary rights and actions. And granting that it were not a restitution under the Trebellianum, but only a certain assignment: nonetheless, when an assignment is made pursuant to a last will, without the distinction of the lex Titia, C. de novat., the assignee sues and not the assignor, which is general in every necessary assignment, ff. de leg. 1. l. non quibuscumque. §. qui Caium, ff. ad Treb. l. facto. in prin. and §. si haeres, ff. de transact. l. fin., and in necessary matters a contrary protestation is of no effect. And through this the entire question is resolved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a term given by a statute or by a judge is considered continuous or useful.
body: When

A time period is established by law without the intervention of a judge, or by the praetor, or by civil law. In the first case, it is a useful period. In the second, it is a continuous period, as stated by the gloss in the Institutes, *De perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus*, in the beginning. Hence, Bartolus says that a time period established by an episcopal constitution is understood to be useful; but if it is established by the law of the people or by a decree of the prince, it is understood to be continuous. For a time period established by an episcopal constitution is established by praetorian law, because it is established by the law of a magistrate. But a time period established by the people is not established by the law of a magistrate, because a magistrate is one thing and the people another; in whom, according to Innocentius, jurisdiction never resides. Indeed, no civil law ever made the multitude and the people the arbiters of cases. For the prudence required in the determination and decision of cases is found in a few learned and solemn men, and nothing is honorable in what the multitude handles, as in the Authenticum *De referendariis sacri palatii*.

Consider that the gloss speaks of time periods established by praetorian constitutions, which are contained in the body of the law; but regarding extraneous constitutions, which are established daily, this distinction is not firm. For the judge is the praetor, and in his discretionary extensions he is understood to count continuous days. Codex, *De dilationibus*, law *Siue pars*. And therefore it must be considered that either the time is established for something that can be done while the judge is not sitting on the bench, such as filing a libel or appealing. Here there are no holidays, because all days are equal. Digest, *De feriis*, law *Miles*, § *Ultimo*; Codex, *De feriis*, law 1. Or it is established for something that requires a decree of the judge, not merely the simple hearing of the praetor; and the time is useful. Law 2, § *Dies*, *Quis ordo in bonorum possessione seruetur*. And because the statute says "shall have petitioned the cognizor," since by its nature this can be done at any time, it seems that the time is continuous, especially in its final course, as in the Codex, *De temporibus appellationum*, law 2, at the end.

I would hold this view, were it not for the preceding statute, which speaks in the manner of a rule, that no time periods run on non-session days. Hence, this determination is general, in the manner of a transmitted rule, and the reason and condition of our case are the same as those of others, as in the Digest, *Quando appellatio sit recipienda*, law 1, § *Dies*. Therefore, the same law applies to this matter. Digest, *De militum testamento*, law *In fraudem*, § *Ultimo*. And therefore, non-session days are not counted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To whom the instruments of the estates ought to be assigned.
2. To what extent the obligor is bound to assign the names of the debtors.
body: If it is asked

† Dowers and instruments of estates ought to be assigned to him to whom the estates remain, as they are furnished. C. ad l. Falcid. l. praediorum; C. de incest. nupt. l. cum ancillis; §. si non; C. de ver. sig. l. 1. But if the question concerns the assignment of the names of debtors, one must not depart from the words of the instrument. C. de probat. l. cum precibus; ff. de usufr. leg. l. si alij vero; ff. de verb. oblig. l. quicquid astringendae; extra de priv. c. porro; ff. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio and l. si colono.

† He who is bound to consign the names of debtors is bound to consign true debtors, but he is not compelled to consign such as are solvent, unless he can do so, or unless after the delay of the debtor to be consigned they have become insolvent. D. si cert. pet. l. periculum; C. de probat. l. ex persona; D. de haereditate vend. l. si nomen. And there it appears that he is not bound to accept those who, after the delay, have become unsuitable. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an heir is excused, by reason of the preparation of an inventory, from being deemed to have litigated rashly, and from condemnation in costs.
2. Whether the oath against calumny excuses one from costs.
3. Whether useful and necessary expenses are to be computed in the inventory.
4. Whether just and necessary expenses diminish the inheritance.
body: Loisius Parolius was condemned according to the petition presented on behalf of Lo. and the Cardinals, brothers of the Poleti family, as an heir with the benefit of inventory, and beyond the aforementioned matters, in costs. These costs were indeed taxed by the judge of the commune; now, their execution is sought. It is objected by the opposing party that he is not bound to pay them with the benefit of inventory, and thus from the goods of the aforementioned inheritance. To the contrary, on behalf of the Poleti family. From these matters, it is asked: what is the law?

And it must be said, omitting preambles and pompous allegations, that Loysius himself is bound to pay the costs, within the limits of the benefit of inventory, especially because, upon examination of the records and acts exhibited and produced in the aforementioned case, the said Loysius litigated temerously and maliciously; for, having been given the opportunity to produce the forged instrument, he litigated until the end of the trial, although it was clear to him that the Poletis could demand the aforementioned forgery. Yet this temerarious litigant denied that he was an heir and that the right did not belong to the Poletis, so that he was at fault, as is proven in *l. si quis inficiatus*, D. de deposito; and as is noted there by Bartolus in *l. qui alterius*, D. de regulis iuris, by the same author; and it is proven in *l. 2, §. item quaeritur*, D. de exceptione doli; *l. eum, quem temere*, D. de iure iurando; and *de poena temere litigantis, §. 1*.

† Moreover, in the case set forth above, the oath against calumny would not excuse, as Bartolus writes at length in l. 2, ff. ad Turpil., and more fully in a certain opinion of his, which begins, Andriolus. Therefore, having premised these things, that Loisius litigated temerarily, it must be said that Loisius is bound without the defense of the inventory; since in it must be computed

† Useful and necessary expenses, as stated in l. scimus, §. in computatione, C. de iure deliberandi. For the aforementioned expenses are deducted as if they were a debt, according to Bartolus in the said §. in computatione, to such an extent that if the heir, in order to satisfy the legatees, sells any property and incurs certain expenses for that sale—for example, in the public auction of the property, or because he paid a toll—such an expense will be deducted as if it were a debt. To the same effect is l. quo circa, ff. ad leg. Falcidiam. Therefore, by contrary reasoning, if expenses are not made usefully, they will not be included in the inventory; thus, the case is one of contrary reasoning in the said §. in computatione. This argument is indeed valid in law, as seen in l. 1, §. huius rei, ff. de officio eius, cuius manet iurisdictio, with the notes there. And for this side, the following are alleged: l. qui solutum, §. etiam, ff. de legatis 2; l. non est ignotum, C. de administratione tutorum; and l. quotiens, §. sicut, ff. de administratione tutorum. And what is noted in a similar case in l. 1, §. si procurator, by Bartolus, ff. si quis ius dicenti non obtemperaverit, and by the same author in l. si se non obtulit, ff. de re iudicata, where he fully addresses the point. For it would be absurd and ridiculous that, under the protection of the inventory, one should litigate recklessly, so that afterwards he would not be held liable from his own funds. Truth and all equity therefore suggest that they should be held liable from their own funds. And especially because, by virtue of that shield, namely the inventory, we have thus far conducted lawsuits and have not yet been able to obtain execution on the principal claim. Otherwise, it would follow that one could litigate recklessly in perpetuity and dissipate the hereditary assets, which would be to the greatest detriment of the creditors. The aforementioned requirements are also necessary because the estate will not be solvent regarding the principal claim. Let the discretion of the lord, who knows justice, deign to supply the rest. Francis de Ramponibus. To the same effect, see Baldus.

Whether, on account of just expenses, it appears that a smaller inheritance has come to the heir, and thus the benefit of inventory is of advantage. And it seems that this is so, as noted in the Digest, *De manumis*, l. *Per diversas*, in the great gloss; and in l. 1, *De impensis in rebus dotalibus factis*, according to Bartolus. For necessary expense is not for diminishing the inheritance, but for preserving it, by argument from the Code, *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Fina*, § *In computo*; and by argument from the Digest, *De iudicato solvendo*, l. *Iam tamen*, § *In hac*. For indeed the heir ought not to have rashly left the hereditary right undiscussed, Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, l. *Illud*.

On the contrary, it seems: because he incurred the expenses through his own folly, Digest, *De legatis 2*, l. *Qui solidum*, § *Etiam*. Moreover, if the deceased had been living, and this person, as a defender, had undertaken and succumbed, he would not recover these expenses; therefore, neither does he recover them from the inheritance, so to speak, d. § *In hac*. It supports this what is noted in the Code, *De evictione*, l. 1. Moreover, either this person succumbed justly, and let him impute it to his own temerity, or unjustly, and then the injury done to him ought not to harm the creditor, Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, l. *Exceptione*. Moreover, the benefit of inventory applies with regard to the creditors of the testator, not with regard to debts which the heir contracts: for which he is not bound as heir, Digest, *De separatione*, l. 1. Moreover, this supports it, Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, l. *Venditores*: the solution in these expenses does not have the benefit of inventory. And this specially by l. *Totiens*, Digest, *De re iudicata*, i. by the rule of that law. And because this debt begins not from the act of the deceased, but from the act of the heir. And it supports what is noted in the solution, *Matrimonial causes*, l. *Quae dotis*, by the doctors. But the benefit of inventory is understood to be reserved in those things which concern the inventory, and which can be placed in the inventory, not in others. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A petition concluding in this form: I request that such goods be shared, which he purchased during the partnership; and that all goods, both those already shared and those to be shared, be divided: whether the division of all goods proceeds among the partners.
body: The case in question is as follows: John Losetus contracted a partnership of all his present and future goods with James de Marco. During the partnership between the aforementioned John and James, the said John purchased certain estates in his own name alone. The aforementioned James, unwilling to remain any longer in the said partnership, filed a bill against the aforementioned John; and the conclusion in the bill was as follows.

† Wherefore I, the aforementioned Jacob, demand that the aforementioned properties, which the said John purchased during the partnership, be communicated, and that all goods, both common and those to be made common, be divided. The question now arises whether such a libel proceeds. That this libel proceeds appears to be proven by the authorities cited in the Digest, *de inofficiosa testatione*, in the law *Qui de inofficiosa*; in the Code, *de locato conducto*, in the law *Conductores*; and in the Code, *unde vi*, in the law *Non ab re*. On the contrary, that the cumulation does not proceed is proven by the laws *Fundi* and *Fundum* in the title *de exceptionibus*. The doctors state that it does not proceed if the action is brought simply. But if it is brought successively, thus: for example, I demand that the property be communicated, and after the communication has been made, I demand that it be divided, and they are not treated simultaneously, nor terminated by one sentence, but successively, yet as it were executively, according to the note by Dyonisius in the Institutes, *de actionibus*, § *Rursus*. In the gloss, it is stated: “And thus one must proceed first to communication; and after communication has been made, one proceeds to division. They cannot proceed simultaneously, but the order of judgments must be observed; because the action for dividing common property cannot be brought simply before the thing becomes common. For it would be acting out of order, and an action not yet born would be proposed. And therefore the said libel is not well conceived with regard to the chapter concerning the division of things to be communicated, because the action was brought simply. But with regard to the other chapters, the libel proceeds well.” Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a great-uncle and paternal cousins shall succeed.
body: Parruus

The nephew is in the fourth degree: as stated in the Institutes, *De gradibus*, § *Quarto gradu*: therefore, they succeed equally on intestacy: as if there are several from one side, who are from the paternal grandfather, they succeed per capita, as in the Code, *De legitimis haeredibus*, authority *Post fratribus*, the sons of brothers. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute excluding ascendants through the female line, when agnates are present, also excludes descendants through the same line.
body: A statute,

† That which excludes ascendants through a female line when agnates are extant, excludes descendants from the same female line. And it seems that it does not, because a case omitted by the statute appears to be left to the disposition of the common law. D. Divortio 24,2, Si vero, § De viro; D. De acquisitione hereditatis 29,2, Si servum, § Non dixit; C. De praediis 10,52, Fin. li. 10. Since therefore the statute does not exclude descendants, neither should we exclude them. To the contrary: because this would be true, unless the descent were from an incapacitated person: for then, the mother being excluded as incapacitated to succeed when males are extant, the descendants from her are also excluded, as being descendants from an incapacitated person, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. Quae sit longa consuetudo, and in c. 1, Qui feuda dare possunt, col. 10. But in our case there is no doubt: since the rubric is clear, which is held as text, as noted in C. De chirographaria pecunia, and in the Proemium, lib. 6. Moreover, it says this in black and white, if it is well understood, for after having spoken of ascendants, it adds generally, or from the same line as collateral, etc. Hence it is clear here that it speaks of the succession of collaterals, and thus the question is decided, that the son of a sister in no way succeeds. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether mere rumor suffices for torture: and what kind of rumor it ought to be. nu. 6.
2. A confession of a wrongfully inflicted torture, although persistent, is not valid.
3. What a judge is bound to do when a dead person is found.
4. Arson can arise in three ways.
5. Nocturnal sorcery is difficult to prove.
6. A judge proceeding by inquisition must interrogate the witness regarding the cause of his knowledge.
7. Torture is threefold.
8. Add the following opinion.
body: To make this evident, I premise,

† The reputation of the people, from which infamy arises, brings infamy; and unless it derives its origin from presumptions or indications, it is not sufficient for torture. Thus says Bartolus, ff. de quaestionibus, l. de minore, § tormenta. Beroldus says that solemn reputation is that which arises from arguments, extra, de usu, c. cum in dioecesi. But these do not say anything else concerning the quality of the judgments or arguments. However, the text says, C. de quaestionibus, l. milites, § oportet, that the arguments and indications from which someone comes to be tortured...

And by the term "arguments" I also understand "fame" in a broad sense, if it is plausible and probable, to such an extent that the judge is almost certain, which is left to his discretion, as stated in the Digest, *De testibus*, law 3, section *Tu magis*. Therefore, one must proceed to investigate the causes from which the fame originated. Likewise, the quality of the persons against whom the proceedings are directed, whether they are of good reputation or infamous, as stated in the Digest, *De re militari*, law *Nomen omnes*, section *Barbaris*, and in the glosses on the Decretals, *Ex quibus causis*, chapter *Obertus de Orto*. And if no enmity preceded, fame alone is not sufficient for torture. The same applies if the enmity is slight, as stated in the Code, *De testibus*, constitution *Si testis*, in the words *Si vero*. Nor do boasts suffice, as stated in the Code, *Quod metus causa*, law *Metum*, for often those who make great threats do less. For what is said in the heat of anger should not be drawn into punishment. This is supported by the Code, *Si quis Imperatori maledixerit*, law 1, for we judge words by the persons, and it depends on certain circumstances, as stated in the Digest, *Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*, law *Famosi*.

† Moreover, it could even be said that if the reputation is so negligible that it has no arguments in itself, and someone is tortured on the basis of reputation, and so that he may not be tortured again: he persists in his confession: such a confession would not be valid. ff. de quaestio. l. maritus. and l. non tamen. de app. To this effect are the things noted by Dy. in l. 2. §. 1. ff. de excu. tu.

But I premise that certain things can only happen in one way: for example, if someone is found killed by a sword. Others can happen in multiple ways: for example, if someone is found suffocated in a marsh. For it may be that he perished while swimming, or that he was thrown there by his enemies. And then one must resort to the considerations of a reasonable man, and proceed through the paths and circumstances, whether he was accustomed to bathe there or not, and whether he had enemies, and what kind, and whether there are robbers there or not, and such like. For facts are presumed according to the character of the persons involved. D. de acquisitione et obligatione, l. si. Secondly, I premise,

† That a fire may arise in three ways. First, by divine power and lightning. D. de damno infecto, l. si sinita. Secondly, by human malice. L. fi. de officio praefecti vigilum. And by the negligence of the inhabitant. D. de periculis et commodis rei venditae, l. si vendita insula. D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si servus servum, § si fornicarius. And by things happening commonly in a place, which induce a legal presumption from negligence. Having therefore premised these things, let us come to the question.

And it must be known that nocturnal maleficium is difficult to prove, as is stated in the Digest, title *Quod metus causa*, in the fragment numbered; in the Digest, title *Si cum exceptione*, section *Hæc autem actio*; in the Code, title *De furtis*, law *Furan*. And therefore, where there is an atrocious maleficium, the investigation should be most rigorous. See the argument from the Code, title *De falsis*, law *Ubi*. However, not to such an extent as to exacerbate matters so that the severity of torture compels an innocent person to suffer punishment. And therefore, consideration must be given to whether anything has been proven against this person who is sought to be tortured. Secondly, whether the infamy of the act has been purged or not. For the purification does not strike down nor absorb the reputation of the people, which is like smoke among the people, when it does not exist. See the Code, title *De poena iudiciaria*, authentic *Novo iure*; in the Extravagantes, title *De purgatione canonica*, chapter *Ex tuarum*.

For indeed reputation must be solid, unshaken, growing, not vague, not slight, not contradictory; because a later reputation, and especially a better one, which has in its favor the presumption of nature, defames or overcomes another which is contrary to it. C. ne de statu de fun. l. si mater. And I premise that it is one thing to prove reputation and cause, another thing to prove cause and not reputation. That is, it is one thing to prove reputation and cause of suspicion; another thing to prove reputation without any cause of suspicion; another thing to prove suspicion alone without reputation. And the hostile witness, who is called Guerinus, testifies against Antonius concerning a certain suspicion, that is, concerning threats. But he does not say that the people have a reputation against him. Lord Isntardus testifies nothing, according to my view, against the said Antonius. Perinus testifies against Antonius that he is of bad reputation. But this proof is obscure and avails nothing for the purpose; because here a special reputation is required, not one in the most general genus. Bernardus Suederus says nothing. Paulus testifies of enmity, not of a felony, nor of the reputation of a felony. Master Bassanus Ricardus says nothing. Mandrinus testifies against Antonius concerning reputation, but not concerning the root from which the arson should have originated. Moreover, he was examined again; because he was not asked how he knows.

† because when a judge proceeds by way of inquisition, he must interrogate the witness as to the cause of his knowledge; otherwise, the witness’s statement does not prove. For, since he assumes the office of inquiring into the full truth, he must himself formulate the questions from his own initiative, D. de quaest. l. unus § cogiturum.

And although there are three degrees of torture, namely the lighter, as stated in the Code, *ad leg. Silanianam*, in the final law, in the gloss; the heavier, when the body is afflicted and injured; and the most severe, when it would be just not to proceed without the skill of physicians, lest a fatal outcome follow from the tortures themselves. For some were hard of flesh when tortured, others soft, who could more easily release their breath during the tortures; which physicians also recognize through the judge of nature, which is called the pulse. Nevertheless, in our case, one should not even proceed to the preliminaries of torture, especially purgations, and considering the contrary testimonies that remove the cloud of crime from the court. And therefore, I say and advise that the aforementioned Antonio, weighed by both equity and reason, should be released, if it is expedient to do so first. And of this my opinion, along with its series, I transmit to the Most Serene and Most Illustrious Prince, the Lord Count of Virtues, Lord of Milan, whom God preserve. I, Bal,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The torture which ought to precede.
2. Whether public fame is said to be certain and probable evidence for torture.
3. An arson may arise in many ways.
4. Whether torture duly administered may be repeated, even if the matter is more evidently proven.
5. After the testimony of witnesses has been taken, new witnesses may not be produced, although the judge may receive them at any time, provided that he does so on his own motion, and when the inquiry is conducted purely ex officio.
6. With regard to the decision of the case, the statute of the place where the crime was committed must be considered.
body: Text. It is upon this, he says, that we ought to base ourselves,

† It is necessary, however, that judges, even in those crimes which fall under public trials, should not begin the investigation of the truth with torture. But the first argument should be based on probable and reasonable grounds. And if, guided by these as certain indications, they deem it necessary to resort to torture, then they should do so only if the condition of the persons permits, etc. This is the text, no. ff. de quaestionibus, l. milites, §. oportet. In these words, first, the judge is instructed not to proceed to torture without cause, there, "but by arguments." Second, the causes for resorting to torture are expressed. These causes are arguments and indications. Arguments must be probable and reasonable, which appear to all, or at least to the wise, or are considered as equivalent to probable and reasonable: or it is meant to say that these probable matters should be established by proof, not by divination. C. fam. haer. l. si. and in Auth. de test. imperfectis, post princi. and this until there. And if these, there, which and what kind of things move the judge, are left to the discretion of the judge. In the word, "deemed." On this matter, however, the judge must rule, and no appeal should be allowed from such an interlocutory decision. ff. de app. reci. l. an te. For this is not permitted by mere judgment, but by equitable judgment without the discretion of the judge, just as everything that requires knowledge of the case. ff. ad Treb. l. seruo invito, §. cum praetor. Fourth, he excepts certain persons there, "if the condition of the persons permits," etc. Finally, he praises his statute as full of humanity and benevolence. Now, since the text says that the indications must be certain and probable.

† It is doubted whether public reputation is said to be a certain and probable judgment. And it seems that it is so. See C. de rei vend. l. indicia. To the contrary it seems: because the text requires acute indications. An argument is a reason of a doubtful matter making faith, or something very close to faith, as noted C. de probat. in rub. gl. ad leg. Iul. maiest. l. si quis. says, by one witness of the truth, or another indication. s. valid, as ff. de probat. l. cum probatio. Dy. says that reputation does not suffice. ff. de exc. tut. l. 2. Cy. and C. de quaest. l. fi. says that reputation, enmities, threats, flight make an indication. Suppose therefore someone having many enemies, or many who have threatened someone with death, will they all be tortured? Suppose the lower ones are tortured, and by torture are purified, as in our case. Bar. says, that unless infamy draws its origin from presumptions, or indications, it does not suffice for torture. ff. de quaest. l. de ini. §. tormenta. near fi. Bernardus says, that solemn reputation is that which has support, extra de usur. c. cum in dioece. glo. decreti says, that reputation, which daily increases, and is more formed in the minds of discreet persons, makes a valid indication. However, I think that such reputation should be proven by prudent and discreet persons, for it should arise from them according to Inno. I think much of this matter is committed to the mind of the judge, which we call discretion, however with an even balance. It should be judged. n. to that extent he should be exasperated, so that severity of tortures forces an innocent person to punishment, nor yet should it be passed over with conniving eyes. But according to the quality of persons we weigh words, and presume facts, or non-facts, as C. si quis Imperatori male. l. 1. ff. de act. et obl. l. fi. ff. ad leg. Iul. maiest. l. famosi. §. nec lubricum. Having explained the text of the law, let us come to our case.

And I premise that we are in a case of fire, which can be attributed to negligence if it originated within the house. D. 9,2,27, § si fornicarius; D. 18,6,1, § in sola. Also, the maleficium of an arsonist if from outside. L. ult. C. 9,5,1. Also, due to the night, knowledge of the truth is difficult. D. 4,2,1, § haec actio. Also, there is uncertainty due to the multitude of those defamed, one of whom fled, namely the most vile of all, who alone could have set the fire, if it were true that someone set it with dolus. Given so many uncertainties, I do not think the said Antonio should be tortured. And this for several reasons. First, because he is a man of good, or at least moderate, reputation. D. 49,16,1, § a barbaris. And setting a fire is the act of the most vile and treacherous men. Second, because those who purified themselves under torture, who were more defamed, show that the reputation was false; therefore, it arose from malice and is presumed entirely false. C. 2,4,1. Third, because the witnesses testifying about the reputation are inconsistent on this point: some speak of this Antonio, others do not. For if the reputation concerning this Antonio were general among the people, all would have spoken of him; for all witnesses testifying swear to tell the full truth. D. 22,1,1. Fourth, because the testimony regarding the infamous reputation of this Antonio is very weak: for Geminus testifies only to a slight suspicion arising from general threats, which is insufficient. C. 4,2,1. As for boasts, Perinus says that Antonio is of bad reputation, but does not specify in this particular kind of malice. D. 35,1,1; D. 47,10,1. He who says more seems to me to be a certain Mandrinus. This one does not testify to any root of the reputation, nor was he questioned about the cause of his knowledge, as he should be by the inquisitor. Others prove nothing from the nine or ten witnesses whose statements I have seen, and I refer to the enclosed documents. Hence, my opinion is, without prejudice to the substance of the truth, that Antonio should in no way be tortured according to law. For even if there were any cloud against him, it is resolved by the maxim: truth weighed in the balance. A worse witness than reputation is found, because the people do not know the truth through bodily sense. Yet clamor arises, and therefore, chiefly to avoid scandal among the people, inquisitions were introduced. C. 3,11,1. But when the truth of innocence appears simply because the contrary does not appear, the accused should be dismissed after the case is examined, as in L. 2, C. 7,62, in fine. After this, a doubt was raised to me by one of the delegated judges.

† For he says that the enmity was subsequently proved more strongly, and therefore even those who had been tortured ought to be subjected to torture again, and it seemed that they should be tortured anew. For the law states that a defendant, when overwhelmed by more evident arguments, may be brought back into questioning. D. de quaest. l. vnus. §. reus. But weigh what it says, “more evident.” Understand, “than before.” D. Also note “more evident,” i.e., clearer, and more closely approaching the offense, because it contains an act proximate to the commission. For example, if it were later made clear that that night he was seen there nearby with fire, brooms, straw, or similar instrument, or material prepared for burning. D. de leg. 3. l. ligni. And enmities, which do not have a causal connection to the arson, are very doubtful supports, unless they were among those infamous in the same kind of crimes, because craftsmen deal with craftsmen’s work. In evil, and in good. Hence one must examine the glory or infamy of the preceding life. D. de re mili. l. non omnis. §. a barbaris. And in which it is, as noted, in the rule “once bad.” And C. de inoff. test. l. omnimodo. per Iac. de Belu. And therefore the ordinary torture ought not to be repeated.

† Moreover, it must be observed that once the designated witnesses have testified, new witnesses cannot be produced for the prior examination. And although, according to Innocentius in c. Cum clamor, de testibus, the judge may receive them at any time, this is true only on his own motion, and when the inquiry has been conducted purely ex officio; otherwise, where there is a prosecutor of the inquiry who offers the witnesses, for there is fear of subornation. To this effect is what is noted by Dynus, de quaestionibus, l. Repetita. If we were to say the contrary, there would be no end or limit to torture, which is false, as ff. de quaestionibus, l. Quaestionis modum. And therefore, I say that a solemnly administered torture cannot be repeated under the common law, even if another enmity has been more evidently proven. In the statute of Pavia, however, I do not base my argument,

† because torture pertains to the decision of the case in the absence of proof, and therefore the law in force at the place of the offense is examined, not the law at the place where the judges delegated by the prince hear the case. For they are regarded as if they were hearing the case at the place of the offense. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is bound to construct or restore a bank, and whether [this applies] at no. 4.
2. What a bectale is.
3. What a bank is.
body: To some

† However, it must be said, based on reasons, that the statement concerning the auctioneer is that he is not bound when the bank is carried away by an unusual accident. And first, by reason of the unusual accident, about which it does not appear that there was an agreement. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Fistulas, §. Frumenta, and there by Bartolus. Second, by the express pact in chapter 12, where it is said that if the false broke the weir, the auctioneer is not bound; but here the weir was broken, the bank being broken and shattered, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Si servus servum, §. Inquit lex, which makes a better case. C. de molibus aggeribus non rumpendis, in the rubric and the black letter. Third, by reduction to absurdity. D. de negotiorum gestis, l. Pomponius, at the end. Suppose, for instance, that the force of the river carried away the entire bank along its whole length: would this person be bound? Certainly not, because the form has changed outside the weir. D. de acquisitione rerum dominii, l. Adeo, §. Insula, at the words "however." Moreover, the same law applies to a part with respect to a part as to the whole with respect to the whole. D. de rei venditione, l. Quae de tota.

Fourthly, because I understand the term *bectale* to mean the channel through which water flows; that is, that concave bed having banks on either side, namely raised earth, like embankments, which are likewise raised earth, between which banks, as I have said, is the concave space and a certain watercourse. Since it is now the case that these banks have their slope towards the water they contain, and towards that slope they must be cleared and prepared by the said contractor. But from that side of the bank, i.e., from the outer side not facing the opposite bank, it ought not to be fortified; because such external clearing is not part of the concave bed itself, which is called the *bectale*. Therefore, if the bank is destroyed along its entire side, the said contractor or lessee ought not to be held liable to rebuild the bank, and it does not pertain to him if the bank is destroyed. But if it remains standing, he is well bound to prepare the bank, so that the usual flow of water is not impeded by the filling of that bed or concavity.

They are. The banks enclosing the water are like the container, and the water is like the contained thing, and there are two places. Namely, the place of the riverbed, and this ought to be cleaned. And the place of the banks, and this ought not to be newly constructed: but ought to be preserved as far as possible. It is one thing to promise to rebuild, another to cleanse, as in the Digest, On Rivers, Law 1, in the beginning. But it must not be omitted that custom also ought to be observed, as in the Code, On Places, Law "Although." Considering therefore, and that no thought seems to have been given to the unusual case, and the unusual and heavy expense, and the other reasons stated above.

I say that the aforementioned sorcerer is not bound to construct or repair the bank, notwithstanding the prudently alleged arguments to the contrary, to which it sufficiently appears from the foregoing that a response has been given. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Commentariensis is bound to keep safe the public records entrusted to his custody.
2. Interest is proved by oath, where a delict is established.
3. Witnesses are not singular if they agree on the same end of the matter: and when they are said to be singular.
4. When an oath should be tendered in default of proof.
body: Of the Prince

The duty of the *commentariensis* is to keep the accounts and public records entrusted to his custody, as stated in the Digest, title *De edendo*, law *Praetor*, in the gloss there: “But the curator, etc.”; and see the Digest, title *De legatis* 2, law *Cum ita legatum*, section *Species*, in the gloss: “Who therefore commits fraud.” Also, the Code, title *De custodiendo reo*, law *Ad commentarienses*. For it is established that these accounts were sometimes in the possession of the official who is now being sued. And therefore, if he does not produce them, fraud is presumed on his part, in that he conceals such accounts. He is held liable as if he had stolen them from the archive; for there is little difference between these cases as regards the effect, as stated in the Digest, title *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Haeredes*, section *Si*. For the writing produced by him is presumed to have been entrusted to his custody, just as we say in the case of a tutor, Code, title *Arbitrium tutelae*, law *Si*. He does not allege any just cause; but he denies it altogether, whence it is presumed that he stole it, since such writing concerns the fisc, Digest, title *De iure fisci*, law 2. For this reason also he commits falsification, Code, title *De falsis*, law *Cum*; Digest, same title, law *Paulus*.

And because the offense is established, the damage is proven by oath. C. unde vi, l. si quando; and see Inst. de verb. oblig., §. pen.; l. tutor, qui repertorium, in princ., de admin. tut.; ff. de off. praef. urb., l. 1, §. item solent. Nevertheless, in the case of this Magnificent and Spectable knight, Lord Antonio de Porris, the damage is sufficiently liquidated. What more? Even fraud is evidently proven, since he ordered the documents to be produced from the archive. For if they were true, he ought to have produced them; if false, knowledge and fraud are presumed from the fact that he ordered them to be produced: because he did not simply order the accounts to be produced, but this particular item specifically and expressly. Hence, in such a great crime and so detestable an act, fraud is presumed from the quality of the act, as is fully known. Cyn., C. de falsis, l. exemplum. Also, ad ostensorem, ff. de edendo, l. 1, §. edere, in the word "ad alium communicato." If I am not mistaken, fraud is proven from the effect and deceit. l. damno. For the ancients understood deceit as damage, and the moderns presume counsel of deceit from illicit acts, as is fully noted. C. de iniur., l. si non convicii.

And if it is said that the witnesses are singular, I answer that, in the production of books, including fraud as directed toward the same end of the matter, they are not altogether singular; although they are singular in a certain respect, as in C. de poenis, l. qui sententiam. Likewise, in having written instruments to prove a debt, they are not singular; because when something is presumed from the past in the present in a successive act, and one witness speaks of the first period, which can be joined with the period about which another witness testifies, they do not appear, as far as the understanding of the law is concerned, to be singular according to some authorities with regard to the matter to be proved; although they are singular in the mode of proving. D. de testibus, l. causam, §. finalis.
