Moreover, in such a great crime, I ought not to proceed by the subtleties of the law, where, if the criminal path were open, there would be place for torture as a matter of fact, as in C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. si quis, and D. de quaestionibus, l. maritus. And because by means of a rescript obtained, this defendant has deprived the plaintiff of this method of conviction, a stronger presumption arises against him, as in C. de probationibus, l. si de possessione. Likewise, even in crimes brought civilly, a supplementary oath is administered for goods taken away by the act of the adversary, as noted in l. 3, D. de iniuriis. And even if they were not sufficient, that is, sufficient proofs according to legal subtlety, nevertheless they are strongly corroborative, Extravagantes de successionibus ab intestato, caput Cum dilectus.

And therefore the arbiter of truth ought to believe strongly, that is, firmly, in suitable witnesses as making a strong indication, and at least to administer an oath, as in l. si duo patroni, in principio, de iureiurando, according to Guido de Columna; and what is noted in l. 2, § aetas, ff. de excusationibus tutorum, according to the gloss and Bartolus. And it supports the aforesaid what is noted in c. 1, de usu, in the Clementines. I therefore advise that the judge, having only God, the truth, and his own conscience before his eyes, should not suffer such a man to be defrauded by so unheard-of a fraud, provided that otherwise the proceedings are well and duly founded, at least according to the rescript of the illustrious Duke of Genoa. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It treats of certain depositions of witnesses.
2. A witness is excused from fraud on account of the rendering of a bad cause.
body: In the case

These are certain diversities, for in the case of Belso it is narrated how Beltramo pledged to Stephen a measure of one meadow for 9 gold florins. But afterwards in the said first argument it is said that he pledged to Stephen, or to John; another diversity is between the witnesses and the petition: because Bernard says that he was present when the pact was made between Stephen, and John, and Peter, brothers, that it should be a pledge. And that this also tends to what the witness deposes in the 2nd chapter. Moreover, the petition speaks of 10 florins, but the said witness speaks of 9 florins or gold pieces, whence it does not entirely accord with the petition. Another difference between the petition and the instrument of sale: because the instrument speaks of another quality of coin than the florin, as in D. de solutionibus, l. pauca. Although they may be reduced, albeit indirectly and equivalently, to the same thing with effect, considering the custom of the place, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. quae extrinsecus, nevertheless the witness does not have the power to dispose, but to report the words of the parties in their proper form; nor does it suffice to state merely the intent, but he must state the words that intervened: because he ought to depose from hearing, not from simple understanding: because in this he would be more an interpreter and judge than a witness, as in D. de testamento, l. qui testamento, § si. Moreover, the said first witness deposes one thing that is not true. On the 7th chapter: for when asked if the said sale could not have been true, that the witness himself would not know, he answered, no, whereas the contrary is true by the nature of things, since the will of the contracting parties is ambulatory, as in C. de pactis, l. pacta.

† latest. Nevertheless, the return of a bad cause excuses the witness from fraud, for he added the cause: because there was an agreement; yet, because he asserted a negative, he is suspect, as in Extra, de causa possidendi, c. Cum Ecclesia Sutrina. And therefore he ought not to be considered an unimpeachable witness, as is required for invalidating an instrument on the grounds that it is untrue or simulated, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. Optimam, in fine. Another difference exists between the witnesses, namely between Bernard and Simon: because Simon, regarding the second argument, states that Stephen and John promised to return the said meadow to the said Beltramo. Bernard, however, seems to speak of the said three brothers. It must be considered that an agreement to execute an instrument of sale in place of a pledge makes it so that the contract subsequently entered into in the form of a sale is in truth a pledge, as in ff. de mandato, l. 4, § Ab ignoto; C. plus valere quod agitur, l. Emptione. And if this were proven by witnesses who were certainly competent, nevertheless, the testimony of the witnesses should not be credited due to the aforementioned differences, because the articles are alternative and doubtful. And because they do not accord well with the buyer’s petition, nor with the statements of the witnesses, it seems that it must be said that, due to such singularities and differences, it has not been proven that the contract spoken of in the public instrument was usurious or pledged, and especially because the second article contains that Stephen, or the said John, and each of them promised, etc., which is a statement of joint and several liability (insolidum). And Bernard does not state joint and several liability, nor does he speak of the said two, but of the said three brothers. Moreover, the said Bernard seems to contradict Simon, for in the second chapter he says that all three brothers were present, and he cites Simon as a co-witness; because Simon speaks only of the said Stephen and John, therefore it appears that one of them does not recall the truth. To this question I answer thus: it is possible that the petition is true in fact, yet as it has been pleaded, it is not properly articulated. Moreover, it is not fully proven due to the aforementioned singularities. And see that in chapter 6 above, Bernard says that he heard the aforementioned Stephen, John, and Peter, absent, and the said Beltramo, present, that they held the said meadow as a pledge, etc. But the instrument speaks only of Stephen, and likewise the petition; hence, from this confession, the plaintiff cannot base his case, because it appears contrary to what he intends in the petition, or at least very different. The final conclusion is that it has not been sufficiently proven, although some probable matters have been proven. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A prince's privilege must be gratuitous, yet not to the prejudice of a third party.
body: Because testimony of the truth consists in past matters, remunerative words are relative to the past, if they are verified in the past. D. de dolo, l. Aquilius Regulus; and D. si pater. It suffices, therefore, that they were done in the past, where words are appended to the past and the future. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Si iam facta. Moreover, we ought to be gracious and benevolent in obtaining degrees for masters, since no one is wronged. D. de constitutionibus, princ.; l. Beneficium; Auth. et usupallii; C. ex tuarum. Therefore, having seen the gracious words of the Supreme Pontiff, and having diligently noted them, I, the undersigned Baldus, say that the said venerable brother Augustus, strictly speaking, ought to be admitted to the degree of master, having read the said four books of the Sentences for two years, and having made five responsions, nor ought he to await another term again. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a debtor is presumed to be released solely by the cancellation of the instrument.
body: From that alone.

† If the debtor produces a cancelled instrument of the debt, liberation is not presumed, unless it is presumed that the instrument was returned by the creditor; for in this case lies the principal reason for the presumed liberation, as is stated in l. postquam, de pactis, and in l. si chirographum, de probationibus, and in l. fullo, de furtis, according to Bartolus. Since, therefore, in the present case the debtor has denied having the instrument, from which it necessarily follows that he has denied that the instrument was returned to him by the creditor, he is rightly not presumed to be liberated. This is supported by C. de fide instrumentorum, l. plures apocis. There are also other non-fragile presumptions against this debtor, according to what is alleged. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, have subscribed to this and sealed it with the seal of my name. And the following laws are pertinent to the above: l. ultima, C. de fide instrumentorum, and l. 2, C. de iure fisci.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when a subsequent creditor may offer to the first, so that he may be preferred to him, or concur with him? And whether, in the case of a constant marriage, the right of offering is granted to creditors against the wife herself for the dowry.
2. During the marriage, the prescription of the right of offering does not run.
3. When one creditor is put in possession, the others are said to be put in possession, if they are of the same title.
4. A subsequent hypothecary creditor may offer to the prior one, to whom the property was given unsatisfied.
5. Upon dissolution of the marriage, up to what time may the woman be offered by the subsequent creditor.
body: It must be premised

† And for the sake of clarity, since it is established that, during the subsistence of the marriage, the husband’s property, when he is verging on poverty, is added to the wife’s dowry, later creditors, while the husband is alive, do not have the right to offer themselves to the wife, just as if she had not received the goods unpaid. Moreover, because they are thus assigned so that, existing in the wife’s possession, they may serve the burdens of the marriage and not be dissipated, whereas money could easily be dissipated and consumed. And this is held by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus, C. qui potior in pignore habenda, l. cum tibi.
From this follows the inference that, as long as the marriage endures, the prescription of the right of offer does not run. C. de ann. exc. l. 1. § fin.

Secondly, it must be premised that when one creditor is put in possession, the others are said to be put in possession if they hold under the same title, provided it is not lucrative nor quasi-lucrative; for in the preceding cases, where the cause is lucrative or quasi-lucrative, the condition of the vigilant party is the better, as is fully noted in the law *Cum unus*, in the title *De bonis auctoris iudicis possessoribus*. And if the property is given to one creditor without payment, it is deemed given subject to the right of hypothec of another creditor, according to the argument from the Digest, in the title *De re iudicata*, in the law *A Diuo*, section *Si post*. From this follows such an inference,

† That the subsequent hypothecary creditor may offer to the prior one, to whom the thing has been given unsatisfied, and to invoke the thing by means of the hypothecary action, unless the possessor offers to the plaintiff. D. 20.1.17 (Mulier); D. 20.6.1 (Pauca), § Qui pignoris. And this applies to those having a hypothec. But chirographary creditors are not admitted to the concurrence unless within two years, or four years, according to the disposition in C. 7.72.1 (Si); C. 7.72.2 (Sed ad residuum). Having satisfied the prior creditor, they are admitted perpetually, as appears there. But to the benefit of the second decree, other creditors are not admitted by concurrence, if the goods are sufficient for all, concerning which it is disputed in D. 20.1.1 (Cum unus), if the goods are seized by a definitive judgment, or by other authority having the force of a definitive judgment. C. 8.5.4.

It remains to be seen until what time the offer may be made to the said woman, whose marriage has been dissolved, by the subsequent creditor. And first, it seems that it is not necessary for the offer to be made to her: for by obtaining dominion, she appears to have withdrawn from the hypothec. And therefore the woman is sued as any possessor. D. de re iudicata, l. neque pignus. The contrary is also true: because whenever the hypothec did not endure, the thing could be defeated by the subsequent creditor against the first creditor. There the action and the hypothecary exception endure, and are not removed by the inquiry into dominion. D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. ex sextante, §. latinus. It remains therefore to be seen until what time the offer may be made. And truly, that until two years or four years. D. l. si, de bonis, auth. iudicium possessorium. But that law speaks of unsecured creditors, not of those who have a hypothec, and therefore it seems to be said that the second creditor may offer to the first during the entire time during which the hypothecary action can be brought. For this right of offering arises from the right of hypothec, and serves it, and therefore it endures and lives for the same time, and this is the truth. C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, §. eodem iure. However, the fruits of the intermediate time during which the wife possessed as owner do not diminish the principal of the woman, and if the adjudication had not been valid in law, D. de usucapione, l. si fur, §. 1. And these are true according to the common law, but according to the municipal law it must be seen whether the annual prescription from the form of the prior statute, or the five-year prescription from the form of the second statute, stands in the way. And because the statute speaks of an unsecured creditor making an offer, and expressly reserves the right for the hypothecary creditor, it is not necessary to dispute in the case of the hypothecary creditor regarding the statute: because it does not speak of him, but of the unsecured creditor, to whom, not possessing, the right of offering is granted by no law, especially after a pledge has been added to the first creditor, unless according to the form of the said law or letter, as I said above. And therefore it cannot be brought, unless according to the time limit prescribed by the statute, as noted. C. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. cum tibi; and C. de solutionibus, l. nulla tibi; and l. obsignatione. And because the case, about which I am asked, is founded on a hypothecary creditor, it is clear from the foregoing that the offer can be made, even after thirty years have elapsed. D. de pignoratitia actione, l. si rem, §. omnis. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a curator of a minor, who has described certain goods in the inventory as belonging to the minor himself, can himself or his heir prove the contrary.
body: Gasparonus Alonus, a citizen of Asti, was the curator of a certain adult woman, and he made an inventory, in which said inventory he caused certain goods or possessions to be listed as belonging to said adult woman, although in truth they were not hers, but rather those of her father, of whom she was not the heir, and which she never held or possessed. It happened that said adult woman was owed a certain sum of money lent in the assets and inheritance of her father. In the presence of her husband, now the heir of said adult woman, and also in the presence of certain agnates, she ceded by title of sale the rights competent to her in the assets and inheritance of said her father, and against his heirs, to the said Gasparonus, her curator, for a certain sum there actually paid. And in said sale she swore, and also the usual renunciations and cautions intervened. Afterwards, said curator, through a legitimate preceding procedure, caused a curator to be appointed for the vacant goods of the father of said adult woman, because no one appeared who wished to be heir. And he caused himself to be awarded by the judge and official of the commune of Asti the said goods which had been placed in the inventory as belonging to the father of said adult woman, and which in truth were his. Now said curator has died, having instituted certain heirs from the Scarampi family, who said heirs sold the aforementioned goods as belonging to the said Gasparonus to a certain Titius, an outsider. Furthermore, said adult woman died, being then more than 25 years of age, having instituted her husband as her heir, who, as heir, demands that an account be rendered to him of the administration of the curatorship, namely, of the aforementioned goods which were described in the inventory, and that the rest be provided by the heirs of said curator. These heirs of the curator, for their defense, allege that the aforementioned goods never belonged to said adult woman, but that they belonged to her father, and that she never held or possessed said goods. And that by virtue of the rights ceded to said curator, he caused himself to be awarded the aforementioned goods as belonging to the father of said adult woman; and that the curator never held or administered the aforementioned goods in the name of said adult woman. And thus said heirs of the curator are not bound to render an account. It is opposed by the heir of the adult woman, that the price of the sale of the rights, as above, was immediately returned to said buyer, alleging that said sale was fictitious and simulated. It is replied that the aforementioned statements are not true; and if they were true, it is alleged that it suffices to prove that the aforementioned goods did not belong to said adult woman, and that he held them not as curator, so that he is not bound to render an account of them. And that if the sale does not hold, he must necessarily begin a new lawsuit for the aforementioned rights against the possessors of the aforementioned goods. From the foregoing, it is asked: First, whether, if it is proven by the heirs of the curator that in truth the aforementioned goods never belonged to said adult woman, the confession made regarding the same in the inventory by said curator prejudices them. Second, whether the aforementioned contract made by the curator with the adult woman, with the intervention of an oath and in the presence of her aforementioned agnates, is valid and binding. Third, whether the heir of the adult woman can challenge the aforementioned and allege that the contract was fictitious or simulated, as he claims. Fourth, granted but not conceded, that said contract is not valid in law, or that it was fictitious and simulated: because by its virtue the curator caused himself to be awarded the aforementioned goods, and his heirs afterwards alienated the same, whether the heir of the curator is bound to render an account of the aforementioned, so that he is bound to restitution thereof, or whether in that case the heir of the adult woman is bound to sue for that debt of the aforementioned rights, the sale being circumvented, against the possessor of the aforementioned goods. And finally, whether, considering the premises, the heirs of the curator should be absolved, and in the aforementioned matters, what is the law. The words

†Accursius in the Commentary on the law *veteris*, Codex, *arbitrium tutelae*, concerning the understanding of it, says thus: I understand this law in those things which can be concealed and removed, such as wine and grain. But if he stated in the inventory that he found such a house, which is discovered to belong to another, whether he is bound, certainly I do not believe so, according to Jacobus de Arena. Because in our case, let us examine these things of the father, and although the inheritance had been repudiated, it must be seen whether we were in the case of the last law, Codex, *de repudianda hereditate*, which could still be accepted. For then one must abide by the inventory, according to the text of the said law *si*. Otherwise, it is otherwise, according to the statement of Jacobus de Arena. But one thing must be observed, to be added to the aforementioned statement of Jacobus, that although the guardian is not bound to restore the thing of the ward which belonged to another, nevertheless by the inventory it appears that he possessed it in the name of the ward; and therefore, upon the termination of the guardianship, he is bound to restore the possession with the fruits. Digest, *de procuratoribus*, law *qui proprio*, § *procurator*. As in certain cases, Digest, *de negotiis gestis*, law *si autem*, § 1, whether they were commanded by him or by another, from whom he alienated them with fraud or gross negligence; for he is considered as a possessor. Gross negligence here is purged by the accounting of the guardianship, just as fraud is. Digest, *de fideiussoribus tutorum*, law *cum ostendimus*. And therefore this case must be reduced to the calculation of the truth. For from true and solemn acts, truth follows, and the inventory would not harm. But from simulated acts, nothing effective can follow, especially between a ward and a curator, as in the Authenticum *minor*, § *debitor*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an appeal can be prohibited by a city statute.
2. A superior prince, swearing to observe the statutes, is deemed to confirm them.
body: By statute

† The appeal to a superior court from a city cannot be impeded, unless it has been confirmed by statute of the superior court itself, or unless the city possesses all appeals, both first and second, by virtue of a privilege granted by the superior. As is proved by the extrajudicial text *Venientes* in the title *De iureiurando*. And it is noted by Cynus in the Code, title *De appellationibus*, law *Si appellationem*; and by Bartolus in the Digest, title *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, law *Si*.

† Since therefore the illustrious lord of the city of Asti has sworn to observe the statutes of that city, by this he appears to have confirmed those statutes: because an oath confirms an act. *De legatis* 2, *l. cum pater*, § *filius matrem*. And therefore no appeal can be made against the form of the statute. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a testator can remit the necessity of giving security to a usufructuary.
body: All

† They say that the testator cannot remit the necessary caution arising from the very nature of the usufruct, which some call its substance; so much so that they say it is of the substance and of the definition of usufruct. But their opinion is not approved in this point, namely, that it is of the substance. In the first point, it is well approved, as C. ut in poss. leg. l. scire; C. de usufr. l. 1; ff. de pact. l. pactum inter haeredem; ff. de leg. 1; l. nemo potest, de usucap.; l. si homo. And this is true in the caution for using and enjoying according to the discretion of a good man, so that the occasion for wrongdoing may be removed. Otherwise in that caution which is given for abusive usufruct, which can be remitted by the testator, just as the caution for restoring a fideicommissum; for this caution also is based on an estimation, which causes dominion to pass to the legatee of the usufruct. ff. de usufr. earum rerum; l. si uni; C. de sec. nup.; l. hac edictali, §. his illud. This is stated by Cynus in the said l. 1, C. de usu; yet he does not confirm it, but speaks by way of recitation. But the gloss there affirms it, and rightly: because there is a text that the testator cannot remit this; for if this caution did not invalidate the legacy of this abusive usufruct, it could not receive its form induced by the ordinance of the law. And if the opinion of the gloss is true, that the testator cannot do this, certainly he cannot order it to be done; and if he orders it and it is not done, the penalty is not incurred as if attached to an invalid precept, as ff. ad l. Falc. l. quod de bonis, §. frater; and l. Nescennius et Augerius. Moreover, the opinion of the gloss, even if not true, is nevertheless probable, that it excuses the heir from the penalty, when he has had a just cause for litigating or for not remitting, arg. de leg. 2, l. si quis solidum, §. etiam; and this dictates equity, and is sufficiently consonant with reason there with respect to things in which usufruct properly falls. If therefore the precept does not hold with respect to those things, therefore the penalty is not incurred, lest the penalty exceed the offense, as ff. de his qui vt ind. l. rescriptum cum si, ibi alle. For the penalty of total deprivation is taken from the whole, not from a part. l. si is qui ecclesia, §. verum, de re iud. The heir, however, could well, if he wished, remit the surety and be content with the bare faith of the usufructuary. But he cannot be compelled to this by the judgment of the testator, not withstanding auth. sed cum testator; because in the precepts of the testator the nature of the legacy is not repugnant; here, however, it is repugnant. The article on the right of accretion is certain: for it accrues to the said Antonio alone. C. de ca. tol. §. his ita; de vul. sub. l. cohæredi, §. qui discretas. The case is formed, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute excluding someone from the closer relatives on account of agnation excludes all subsequent relatives in the same degree.
2. The ablative absolute introduces a disposition.
body: Regarding the second question, namely whether the said sentence, if it was and is valid in law, was and is nevertheless unjust and inequitable, it appears and must be said in law that, presupposing—but not conceding, as is evident from the foregoing—that the said sentence was and is valid in law, it was and is nonetheless unjust and inequitable. This is so because, by virtue of and through the provision of the statute of Ripalta, which provides that after any woman has been married off by her father, mother, or brothers, she may not, after the death of her father or mother, claim anything from the other substituted brothers, etc., the said Beatrice, daughter of the said Andizona, who was married off by the said Andizona, as presupposed above, was not excluded and has not been excluded from the inheritance of the said Andizona, as is clearly evident from the instruments of refutation made by the said Beatrice. Moreover, the said Michael was and is excluded from the inheritance of the said Andizona, his maternal grandmother, by virtue of the aforementioned statute, for the following causes and reasons: First,

† Because the statute appears to intend that the inheritance and goods of the mother remain with the brothers, excluding the sister and the daughter of the same mother: and according to the disposition of the law, the closer in degree is excluded from some succession by special right, as is the aforementioned Beatrice, who is excluded by the said statute, and is excluded in favor of the brothers, so that the inheritance and goods remain to those brothers. Then also all those following in degree connected through that closer relative thus excluded are excluded, and are excluded by the force of the aforementioned statute, as in D. si quis aliquem testamento prohibeat, l. 1; and what is noted there, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. mulieri et Titio; and D. de fideicommissis liberis, l. cum quasi, §. sed et si quis. Secondly, because those words added in the said statute, namely “to the other surviving brothers,” have not only the exclusive truth of the said Bartolus, but also have inductive force: so that the brothers succeed entirely; for those absolute ablatives, namely “brothers” and “surviving,” induce a disposition when they are uttered by one who can dispose concerning that matter, as in D. de legatis 3, l. de fideicommissis, §. cum esset; and ad leg. Falcidiam, l. in ratione, §. tam et si. Thirdly, because when a disposition is made in consideration of someone, although the words are not expressly directed to him, nevertheless the action belongs to him, as in l. servo legato, §. si testator, D. de legatis 1; and l. fideicommissa, §. interdum, D. de legatis 3. Fourthly, because when someone is removed from a benefit in consideration of another, the benefit ought to be applied to him in whose consideration the removal is made, and not to another, as in D. de his qui ut indigni, l. post legatum, §. amittere; and D. de collatione bonorum, l. cum emancipatus, §. si duo. The aforementioned Michael, by the force of the aforementioned statute, is excluded, and is totally excluded from the inheritance of the said Andizonia, just as the aforementioned Beatrice, his mother, is. And this was expressly held, and is held, by Ricardus Malus in a certain disputation of his on account of the first reason aforementioned; and it was also held by Lord Bartolus, D. ad senatus, consultum tertium et orficianum, l. sive ingenua, near the end; and for this it is very well established by what is noted by Cynus, C. de adulteriis, l. 1, near the end; Franciscus de Rampono, the same by Lord Bartolus, and he reproves the preceding opinion.

By the most excellent Doctor d. Frasci, it was said that whatever can be said concerning the second question is for that part for which, by alleging, he advised. And these are the words of Bartolus for the greater part. Nevertheless, upon examination of the words of the statute, it is alleged to the contrary: because the words of the statute are interpreted as applying to the person of a woman not simply, but of a dowered woman. But here we are not dealing with the person of a dowered woman; therefore, the statute ceases to apply due to the deficiency of the words of the statute. D. quod vi, aut clam, l. aut qui aliter, §. si; D. de suis et necess. hered., l. si vero, §. de viro, cum similibus. Therefore, the final reason of the statute fails: because the reason is the dotation itself. But this reason and its quality cease in the case of a grandson coming from his own person after the death of his mother. D. de hered. instit., l. qui volebat. Therefore, the statute ceases to apply. To this effect, D. de lib. et posth., l. commodissime. Moreover, the law speaks of the succession of certain persons, hence otherwise in other cases. C. de collat., l. illam. Moreover, brothers are those who exclude; but here those who would exclude would be the father, concerning whom the statute does not speak, nor is anything else to be supplied in the fact to the statute, but in law and the reason of law it is well permitted to supply concerning statutes: because reason is always believed to be inherent in laws. D. de legibus, l. sed et posteriores. Moreover, it is true that the tacit inclusion of one well excludes the rest, when those are found to be excluded by the same total reason; otherwise, if the reason is not the same. Moreover, where the express provision ceases, because there is no dowered daughter, the tacit provision ceases, namely, the exclusion of the grandson, as in l. 3, §. qui habet haustum, D. de serv. rust. präd. And thus I hold in l. maximum vitium, and when the quality in which the excluding reason consists ceases, there the exclusion ceases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if a person duly summoned in person fails to appear within the prescribed term, he shall be deemed contumacious, and an interlocutory judgment shall be rendered against him on the plaintiff’s petition after the day of the term’s expiration, the question is whether, if the creditor had the debtor summoned to answer for Wednesday and also for Thursday, and the debtor is contumacious, the judgment rendered on Thursday is valid.
2. If the acts are written by the hand of a notary duly requested, and the writings appear contradictory or divergent, whether all of them are vitiated.
body: Assuming,

† It is provided by the form of the statute that if a person, having been personally cited, does not appear within the term, he shall be deemed a true contumacious defendant, and an interlocutory judgment shall be rendered against him upon the plaintiff’s petition after the day of the term’s requirement. And assuming that the creditor has caused the debtor to be cited to answer in law on a certain petition for Wednesday, and for the following Thursday, the question arises whether the interlocutory judgment pronounced on that Thursday is valid. I answer: No, because the statute provides for the following day, as noted in the Institutes, *De verbis obligationibus*, § *Omnes*.

Secondly, it is asked, if it appears from the acts drawn up by the hand of the notary that there are writings concerning the same matter involving contradiction or diversity in substantial points, whether any of the said writings is to be believed. I answer, no, as is fully noted in C. de fide instrumentorum, l. scripturae. And it is supported by what is noted in C. de codicillis, l. cum proponatur, and in de haereticis, l. fraternitatis, according to Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When one is said to have inflicted a wound in self-defense.
body: Of this

The question concerns a case. D. ad l. Aquil. l. si ex plagiis, § tabernarius. For, since the act was committed immediately after the prior actor had instilled fear of death, it is presumed to have been done in self-defense; and no punishment ought to be imposed. And this is the truth: because an atrocious wound with effusion of blood, from which the intent to kill is presumed in the first striker, and the fear of counter-striking, the plurality of blows threatened death to the said Bartolus, as is fully noted by us, C. unde vi, l. 1, and Extr. de homic. c. significasti, and in l. utrimque, with its subject matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the guarantors for the buyer of salt are bound, if the seller gave other salt to the buyer, who accepted it.
body: Gabriel Palanistinus purchased certain quantities of salt from certain places, and as security for the price thereof he provided sureties. Finally, by order of the Commune of Genoa, other salt of the same intrinsic quality was assigned to him in lieu of the said salt, which he accepted. Thereafter, the aforementioned Gabriel absconded. The sureties for the salt are sued, and they claim that they are not bound, because they had given surety under the condition that the salt purchased would be delivered.

But here the delivery of the very same thing did not follow, but rather of another salt, and therefore, with the thing changed, a new contract seems to exist, just as with a changed price. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. pacta conventa, §. Paulus. Moreover, even if not by right itself, nevertheless by means of an exception the sureties ought to be secure. D. de locato, l. cum in plures, §. dicta. Moreover, a tacit novatio from one thing to another seems to have occurred, and thus the exception of fraud stands in the way, as noted. D. de novatione, l. omnes. Moreover, the words of the instrument state that the sureties bound themselves for the said salt; these words can be explained in three ways: namely, conditionally, if the said salt were delivered; moreover, causally; moreover, restrictively. And according to any of these interpretations, the sureties are not bound. D. de vino legato, l. ex eo; D. de verbis obligatis, l. inter stipulatores, §. sacramentum. Moreover, the words of the instrument state, “according to the instrument of sale.” This term, “according to,” is placed here both demonstratively and relatively. And it is certain that a relative requires its antecedent to be true, and refers to it, D. de contrahenda emptione, l. hæc venditio. But the new salt is not the antecedent of this relative; therefore, the relation is false, D. de verbis significatis, c. Abbate, cum si.

To the contrary, it must be premised that sometimes an obligation is novated, sometimes something else is paid for something else without novation of the obligation, and sometimes there is doubt regarding the intent of the contracting parties. In the first case, the sureties are not bound. D. de novatione, l. aliam. In the second case, always preserving the substance of the truth, I do not believe the sureties are released, but that they are bound. I prove this by several reasons. And first, because the obligation is pure, even before the thing sold is delivered. D. de hac re venditione, in §. offerri; and C. de rebus permutatis, l. ex placito. But the exception of the thing not delivered stands in the way: which exception cannot be opposed to the seller, who has satisfied the buyer. D. de pactis, l. si conventum est, however he may have satisfied, as noted there. The second reason is that the principal obligation endures by the force of the first obligation; the principal debtor is bound. D. emptor ad pretium. Therefore, also the surety. Just as the pledge is bound, it is true that the price was not paid, and it becomes due. Thirdly, because these were not sureties for the performance of the salt, but for the price, which has not been changed, and the new salt succeeds in place of the old. C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si donatae, §. si sponsus. Moreover, all words of the instrument ought to be understood according to the nature of the contract, and according to the rules of civil law. D. de usuris, l. si stipulatus. In the third case, which is doubt, I say that when a simple payment in another thing, without repetition of a new obligation, is not called novation, but satisfaction. D. 2, §. fin., D. si certum petatur. These things considered, I think the sureties are bound: because they have given surety for every cause that can arise while the same contract stands. D. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo, §. si nummos. Hence, even if the said Gabriel had remitted the said salts to the common [people] of Genoa for another cause, than with the intent of dissolving the contract: the sureties, who do not have to dispute about the fact, and are not between the parties to the thing, but only about the obligation which they assumed, are bound. And I concede that they are not bound unless by words, D. de fideiussoribus, l. blanditus. Nevertheless, the words bind them, as I have said. The question is certainly quite doubtful. But what I have written seems to me true, always saving the opinion of a more weighty counsel. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether two procurators, one for business affairs and the other for judicial matters, may be appointed in the same instrument.
2. If an instrument states that two parts of the three parts of the inhabitants of a certain village appointed a syndic, whether it is presumed that all formalities were duly observed.
3. If something is to be rendered annually on a certain day, whether the beginning of the year or that specific day constitutes the time for interpellation.
4. When a person is said to be refusing to pay a legacy.
5. Whether a substitute, claiming that the primary heir was deprived because he did not pay, must prove this.
6. Whether the default of one party prejudices the other, rather than the defaulting party.
7. Whether a grandson, instituted by his maternal grandfather solely in the dowry given to his mother, who predeceased him, may declare the will null on the grounds that he was passed over.
body: If in the same

In the instrument, two procurators were appointed, one for business affairs and the other for judicial matters; the administration was divided between them according to business affairs and judicial matters, and therefore one does not interfere with what was entrusted to the other. Hence, the procurator for business affairs cannot litigate, nor can the procurator for judicial matters contract or conduct business. These are distinct species and headings of administrations. D. 17.1.12.1 (Si procurator); and note D. 13.1.1.1 (Qui proprio), according to one reading; and D. 2.1.1 (Cum praetor).

† If it is stated in the instrument that two parts out of three parts of the inhabitants of such a village appointed a syndic, I believe that, although the notary’s words are ambiguous, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly, and the words are to be understood soundly, and by the words “three parts” all are signified, as in l. nulli and l. sciendum, de verbis obligandis. If someone is invested causa mortis, and is ultimately invested as heir, and that investiture is confirmed in the testament, such investiture is considered to be a last will, as noted in ff. de inofficioso testamento; l. etiam nam et legatum quandoque praecedit traditio, de legatis 2; l. Lucius; and l. leg. vel quia in suum favorem est confirmata, he may choose whether he wishes to be invested by contract or by last will, as in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. recusare, §. Titius; and this if he has a coheir. But if he is alone, it could not be valid as a prelegacy, but as a contract nevertheless, l. legatum, §. heredi, de legatis 1; for in the constitution it is merged, just as a part in the whole.

† If something annual is to be rendered on a certain day, that day interpellates on behalf of the person, not the beginning of the year, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1, de peculio legatorum; nevertheless, if the testator says, “I so command that every year on the feast of the Nativity 10 [units] be given to the church,” and adds these words,

And if he refuses to do so, let him be deprived, with the act left to him. Whether it is said that he refuses by the very fact that he does not pay. Truly, that he does not: but then, when admonished by the judge, or requested by the person, he does not pay. C. ad trebellianam, l. pen.; ff. ad trebellianam, l. recusare. For this is the nature of this deprivation, in Auth. de hereditatibus et falcidia, §. si quis autem non implens; Inst. de actionibus, §. item mixta. If something is left with a burden, and if it is not complied with, it is transferred to another, and therefore it is necessary to take care according to the law regarding the manner of fulfilling, de modo implendo, l. 3; l. si tibi, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; l. quibus diebus, §. vlti. Nevertheless, care will not be taken for him who is deprived, but for him whose interest it is. ff. de damno infecto, l. qui bona, §. si quis quia.

† Whether a substitute, who claims that the first debtor was private because he did not pay, must prove the non-payment. I answer: no, because if the creditor brings an action, and the creditor does not have to prove a negative, he has a claim founded on the obligation. D. de probationibus, l. 50. I hold the same view regarding a mere executor, who has his claim founded on a mandate and on a special office. And thus there is no objection from what Innocentius says in de accusationibus, c. Super his, because he speaks of one who has no foundation other than the mere negative, and therefore must prove it. L. 2, de iure emphyteutico, according to Cynus.

† In cessations, the cessation of one does not harm the other, but only the one who ceases. D. de manum. test. l. si ita fuerit duobus. Suppose that what was due to be given to the priest was given; but the priest did not do what he ought to have done, because he did not say Mass. Certainly the giver will not be deprived, because he has performed his office. For it does not belong to the giver to say the divine office, or to reside daily in the church. D. de manum. test. l. Mevia. Nor is one deprived by the act of another. L. Pater, D. de hered. inst. Which law is notable for this matter.

† A grandson, instituted by his maternal grandfather through a predeceased daughter, in the sole dowry given to his mother, does not seem to have been instituted in any respect, but rather passed over, because he was not instituted out of the testator’s substance, but out of the heir’s own substance; and thus the institution is invalid. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. mea res. So says the gloss. D. de minor. l. 3, § sed utrum, in fine. The gloss [states] that in this dowry the grandson has no cause from the grandfather, but from the mother and custom, as in l. dos a patre. Unless one says, according to Bartolus, that this dowry is imputed to the grandson in his legitime, because one can be instituted. C. de impub. et aliis subst. l. humanitatis. Therefore, such a testament is valid. It supports what Bartolus notes ad l. Falcid. in l. in quarta. But this opinion is harsher, and the later one [is] prior to the former. And the gloss determines, as I said. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It treats of the interpretation of a statute which excludes a dowried woman from all succession.
2. The word "idem" (the same), what it denotes.
body: A certain Germanus de Almon of Vignali died intestate, survived by his sons Palmo, Obtino, and John, and by his wife and the mother of the said sons, Margaret, and by his brother, Gallus de Almon. The said mother obtained the legitimate guardianship of the said sons. Subsequently, all the said sons died, survived by Margaret, their mother, and by the said Gallus, brother of the said Germanus. It is presupposed that in Vignali there is a certain statute which provides that a married woman may not, nor ought to, come to the succession of her father or mother, etc., together with male brothers, etc. And towards the end of the said statute are contained these words: “And the same is understood regarding the grandmother and the mother, that they do not come to the succession of daughters and granddaughters; nor do they have anything of their goods, unless he left it to them, or bequeathed it to themselves, as aforesaid in the case of a married sister or daughter, etc., as is more fully contained in the said statute.” And because there is a question and controversy between the said Margaret on one part and the said Gallus on the other part, to whom the inheritance of the said sons of the said Germanus, or of him who last died, ought to pertain, whether it ought to pertain to the said mother or to the said Gallus, uncle of the said sons and of the said daughter of the said Germanus and of the said Margaret, it is asked, what is the law in the premises.

† This statute ought to have been practiced from ancient times: and if it appears how it has been practiced, it ought to be observed. D. de legibus, l. si de interpretatione. But if it does not appear how it has been understood, we must resort to the words of the statute. For in this point the statute is not fully inserted. For in the first part the statute provides for a dowried woman to be repelled by her brothers, unless by that which was left to her. In the second part it provides for the mother and grandmother to be repelled, unless by that which was left to her. And in this chapter it places only one exception: and it speaks through these words, and the same is to be understood in the grandmother, etc.

It remains to be seen what he wishes to say by “and the same.” For this condition denotes precisely the same censure in various cases, as is stated in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, section *Sed pluribus*. Therefore, it must be understood that, where males exist from the deceased, the sister is excluded only if males exist; the same must hold true in all respects.

To the contrary, it is argued that the statute proceeds further and explains itself, so there is no room for tacit interpretation where we have an express interpretation. Moreover, it is stated that it does not come to the succession of sons and grandsons, etc. For if it excludes from the succession of all, it necessarily speaks of all being dead. Suppose that only one son remained from the husband, and this son died; therefore, the mother would not be excluded, which is false, because the statute so provides regarding the mother on account of agnates, as in the Code, *De adulteriis publicis*. And this negative is derived from the whole, namely, that the mother succeeds to no one; therefore, when all are dead, she succeeds to no one, just as when one is dead, she does not succeed to him, as in the Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, law *Si is qui ducenta*, section *Utrum*, according to Cynus.

Then it follows: “unless that which is required, as aforesaid, in the sister.” He wishes to say that it may be left to the mother and the grandmother, so that the words “as aforesaid” refer to their nearest clause, namely, “unless, etc.” To which, by the same construction of words, are joined the words “as, etc.,” as in the Digest, *De postulationibus*, law 1, section *Deinde*.

Wherefore, although this opinion is rigorous, and the exclusion of the mother is very odious, and has always displeased me, nevertheless we cannot depart from the statute, as in the Digest, *Qui et a quibus succedere possunt*, law *Prospexit*. Therefore, I hold that the father’s heirs are to be preferred to the mother and the grandmother by the disposition of this rigid statute, always reserving the opinion of the more correct view, as in the Digest, law *Claudius Felix*.

The other things said regarding guardianship are trifles. Tacit repetition applies to things entirely equal, but here we are not dealing with repetition, but with an exception, because the testator explains himself.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal who sells and delivers a feudal estate to another, subject to the added condition that it shall be if it pleases the lord, thereby forfeits the fief.
2. Whether the Pope may enfeoff the fiefs of inferior churches.
body: Mortizio, a vassal of the Lord Bishop of Asti, of the place of Astesana, having left no other heir in the degree of succession except Valentine, his daughter, wife of the aforementioned Gandulfo. The Reverend Father, the Lord Bishop of Asti, invested Gandulfo of Bregoguris, in his own name, and on behalf of and in the name of Valentine, his wife, with the Castle and village of all mere and mixed empire, and jurisdiction, or power, in the territory of Asti, of the fief of the said Lord Bishop and of his church. Who Gandulfo, having received the aforementioned investiture, rendered to the aforementioned Lord Bishop the due fidelity and homage for and concerning the aforementioned fief. Who Gandulfo and Valentine, having received and held the aforementioned investiture and fidelity, were disobedient to the aforementioned Lord Bishop: and they had certain men and beasts of certain nobles captured, and retained the captives, and imprisoned them, and held them captive in the aforementioned place, although unjustly. Whom men and beasts, despite the admonitions and the command of the said Lord Bishop, they were unwilling to release or restore. Furthermore, the aforementioned Gandulfo and Valentine made a certain submission and subjugation of the aforementioned fief to the Lord Governor of Asti, both against the express command of the aforementioned Lord Bishop, and against the tenor and form of the synodal constitutions of the Bishop of Asti, which prohibit and condemn such submissions, declaring that such submitters are deprived of that fief which they submit, and determining and declaring the fief open and confiscated, etc. For all and each of these things, the aforementioned Lord Bishop, having cited and required the aforementioned Gandulfo, in his own name and that of the aforementioned his wife, whose interest it was, as procurator; and he being present, understanding, and hearing, and also in the presence of many of his vassals of the church of Asti, whom the said Gandulfo, in his own and aforementioned name, would oppose or contradict, that the aforementioned fief was not, for the aforementioned causes, reverted, open, and devolved, and confiscated to the said Lord Bishop. The aforementioned Gandulfo and Valentine, having viewed the aforementioned submission, and weighed its admonitions and precepts, together with the rebellion and contumacy of the said Gandulfo and Valentine, and following the form of the aforementioned constitutions, decreed that they were deprived of the aforementioned fief and all right of the aforementioned fief, and that the fief itself was reverted, caducous, and confiscated to him and his church. And also similarly, he anew deprived the said Gandulfo and Valentine, and each of them, for the aforementioned causes. To whose declaration and sentence of deprivation, the said Gandulfo neither opposed nor contradicted: and which sentence passed into res judicata. And finally, the said Gandulfo and Valentine were publicly and solemnly deprived of the said fief, and also excommunicated and denounced, through the churches of the city of Asti, for the aforementioned causes, public instruments existing concerning all the aforementioned things, all of which having been thus performed, the aforementioned Gandulfo and Valentine, without the knowledge and against the will of the aforementioned Lord, sold and alienated the aforementioned Castle and Village with the men, power, etc., and the whole aforementioned fief, and gave the power of the said fief to Bartholomew Garreto, who Bartholomew, having obtained or asked no license from the aforementioned Lord Bishop, lord of the aforementioned fief and place, entered and took the aforementioned Castle and Village and the said fief, and publicly detained and occupied them. Which the aforementioned Lord Bishop, observing, and knowing that all the aforementioned things had been done to his opprobrium and contempt, and to the damage and prejudice of his and his church's rights, and that the said fief, by that condemned sale, was again open and reverted by law, and freely reverted anew to the said Lord Bishop: desiring to provide duly for himself and his church concerning the premises, all and each of the aforementioned things being written, causes digested and examined, he publicly and solemnly invested the noble man Simonetto, notary, his vassal and vassal of the aforementioned church, with the aforementioned Castle and Village, and the whole aforementioned fief, for himself and his church. Who Simonetto, having had and received the aforementioned investiture for and concerning the aforementioned fief, rendered and performed fidelity and homage in the due form to the aforementioned Lord Bishop, public instruments existing concerning the premises. After all the aforementioned things, the same Lord Bishop admonished and required the aforementioned Bartholomew Garreto, occupier and usurper of the aforementioned place of Astesana, and as a temerarious detainer, that within a certain term peremptorily assigned to the said Bartholomew, the said Bartholomew should appear before the said Lord Bishop in a determined place, and present himself legitimately, alleging and showing a legitimate cause why he should not be deprived of other fiefs, which he is acknowledged to hold from the said Lord Bishop and his church, on account of the aforementioned invasion, usurpation, and occupation, as above. And on this point, let us see the entire process signed up to the end, the narration of which would be long, but could easily be seen and examined, and the case formed upon it: but finally the said Bartholomew sent an appeal to the court of the Lord Clement, Pope, and obtained letters, both subreptitiously and fraudulently, which are to be seen on the folio signed P. and which state that they were in no way granted, nor could be granted by law. From which letters, and the contents thereof, the aforementioned Lord Bishop appealed and is appealing to the Apostolic See, whose appeal is pending, etc. If a vassal

He sells and transfers under the condition that it pleases one. Master Jacobus de Ardizzone says in his notable summa that it does not revert to the lord, because that which is retained in the body of the patrimony is not said to be alienated: for without the lord’s consent, neither does natural possession pass, nor does any benefit accrue. Certainly nothing appears to have been done in fraud when such a condition is appended. D. de magistratibus et alii qui iurisdictio habent, l. Si quis locuples; D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. Qui absenti, § 1; and l. Si me in vacuam, in fine; D. de conditionibus, l. Sub conditione. And he says that this is a good precaution so that the vassal does not lose his right. To this effect: D. de contrahenda emptio, l. Cum manusata, § Nemo. But it seems truer that if any difficulty is thereby imposed on the lord, because the detainer holds the Castle against the lord’s will, and is a harsher adversary and rebel to him, the fief reverts to the lord on account of fraud. As in D. de iure fisci, l. Si ita fidei, word “immo.” For although the form of the words sounds in the premise, nevertheless the effect of the thing reveals the counsel of the mind. Indeed, he is said to proceed who by some artifice of words deceives the lord, as noted in C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. Si. Not only is the fief lost by the cases expressly stated in the law, but also by those similar to them and greater, as in the Decretals, Book 10, which was the first cause, bene amit., c. 1, § Sed quia. For this man honors the lord in words, but in deeds he scorns him and has done injustice to him in the fief. There, c. § Item si suo; and § Si in ratione literae. For he went out of possession so that another might invade or hold it. D. de dolo, l. Cum quis. Hence we perceive fraud from the effect of the thing, i.e., from the damage to the lord, and injury to the lord from contempt. Hence the text says that the effect of the thing should be followed, D. de iureiurando, l. 3, § Pe. Moreover, he who makes the pursuit of the thing more difficult for the lord certainly considers the damage to the lord. D. de alienatione iudicata, l. 1; and what is noted in D. de verbis obligatio, l. Ita quis, § Ea lege. Hence nothing should remain with the vassal from the thing in which he has deceived. D. de legato commissario, l. 5, after the beginning. Furthermore, this man knew that it would displease another lord, and that the lord would not ratify it, since he had already been brought to judgment. Hence he simulated appending a condition, but in his mind he intended to prejudice the lord absolutely. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. Filiae meae; C. de repudiis, l. Dubium. And just as that which does not endure does not seem to be in nature by advent; so that which endures seems to have been made by the consideration of the mind that it should endure. D. de divortio, l. Quod ait lex. Moreover, if not from contract, nevertheless from those things which subsequently followed, the vassal incurs forfeiture, and the fief is opened to the lord. And it supports this: D. de usuris, l. Si modo.

† Concerning the Pope, there is no doubt that he can grant ecclesiastical fiefs: because the Pope, together with all preeminence, is endowed with jurisdiction, as John of Molino says. And all his things are his, C. de quadrien. praescrip. l. bene a Zenone. And therefore the Pope could validly ratify, both in his own name and in the name of the Church, while the matter remains intact. But in the meantime, that fief was opened and granted to another.

† It is doubtful whether the Pope’s ratification was valid: because the Pope does not intend to prejudice the right of anyone. D. de emancip. liber. l. nec auus; D. ne quid in loco publico fiat, l. 2, § si quis a principe; D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. ex facto; C. de silentio, l. de curione, lib. 12. For he does not intend to burden the Church with a double obligation, so that it would be bound to pay the valuation of the fief, concerning which it made investiture or promise, to one person, and to surrender the fief to another, to whom the Pope granted it. D. de legatis 2, l. Titia; § qui inuita, D. de legatis 3; l. fideicommissum, § si quis ita. And the ratification is not valid: because it was not made with certain knowledge, as noted in C. de rei venditione, l. mater. From which, according to what is proposed, it is concluded in favor of the lord Simoneto.

However, it is true that I would not judge concerning the benefit of the Pope, unless he himself, or his commissioner, did so; and because the Pope, by conferring, seems to recall the matter to himself. Arg. D. de testamento tutorum, l. si quis sub conditione; C. de legatis, l. si; D. de crimine vel instaurando, l. Neratius; Extr. de iudiciis, c. cum venissent. And what is noted in col. 10 of the chapter Apud quem vel apud quos controversia feudi, c. 1: therefore, if one says he was invested by the Emperor, and the other by an inferior, it is the jurisdiction of Caesar: because in jurisdiction the lesser is always drawn to the greater. And this applies in a petitory action; but in a possessory action, the civil power under whose territory the castle is located could cognize, Extr. de iudiciis, c. finalis; and l. si, D. de officio procuratoris Caesaris; and l. 1, C. ubi de crimine agi oporteat; and in Auth. qua in provincia. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the statutes of the city bind not only the citizens, but also the district inhabitants, if the district is occupied by another, or if it is rebellious against the city, and whether the rebellion of any place harms the individual persons of that place.
2. Whether a rebel loses the benefits of the city.
body: It is proposed that the custom of the city and district of Este is such that the husband acquires the dowry upon the death of his wife during the marriage, if they have no children. It is also proposed that two natives of the district of Asti contracted marriage. It is further proposed that during the marriage, that district was occupied by a certain Magnificent Lord and brought under his rule, and that it rebelled against the city. And that during the rebellion, the wife died in the marriage without children. After these events, that Magnificent Lord acquired the city, and all matters were reconciled, and the customs and statutes of the said city and district were confirmed by him. Now a dispute has arisen between the brother and heir of the wife and the said husband: because the brother claims that the dowry should be restored, while the husband asserts that he should acquire it. The question is asked: what is the law? On these points, it must be considered as follows.

† For either the husband is not from the Asti district, and he must use the common law and restore the dowry. C. de test. l. si non speciali. Or he is from the Asti territory, although it has been seized by the said Magnificent Lord. And here it must be noted that either this benefit arises from custom, or from a municipal law written in the city, whose authority alone extends to the district. In the first case, since custom consists in facts, the district itself established it for itself, prescribed it, and used it with its own things and facts. Hence, although it rebelled against the city, it does not lose its own proper custom, arg. C. de testa. l. fi. In the second case, when it uses the municipal law by the authority of a superior, and not its own, then it must be seen whether, by the said occupation, they are exempted from the passive bond of the law of their city. And it must be said that they are not: because this seizure does not remove civil rights. For indeed, a subject, by withholding obedience or by rebelling, is not freed from subjection to the law. c. i. de foro compe. in clemen.

Secondly, it must be considered whether, by the said rebellion, he loses the benefits of that city of which he is a subject in law, although not in fact. And I say that either he is condemned for rebellion by sentence: and then he loses that benefit. L. *amissione*, §. *qui deficiunt*, *de capitis deminutione*. Hence, if at the time of his wife’s death he was condemned and incapacitated, he never thereafter resumes capacity, unless he is restored in full: because restoration in full is equivalent to postliminium, *de restitutione in integrum*, L. *si quis filio exheredato*, §. *penult.*, *de heredibus instituendis*; L. *Sed si in conditione*, §. *solemus*. For when the day arrives uselessly and impossibly, the matter is extinguished, but is not retained in suspense, as in D. *de stipulationibus servorum*, L. *usus*; D. *communia prædiorum*, L. *recepta*. Therefore, restoration in full is necessary, as I said. On this point, D. *de verbis obligatorum*, L. *inter stipulantes*, §. *sacramentum*. Or he is not condemned, and then he is not incapacitated; rather, he makes use of the laws and customs of his city. D. *de poenis*, L. *quod ad statum*. And this is proven in C. *pastoralis*, *de re iudicata*, in the Clementines; *de donationibus*, L. *post contractum*. Hence, then the husband acquires the dowry. And although the corporation were condemned, nevertheless the individuals are not condemned, nor made exiles from the benefits of the city, especially since they were unwilling. Hence Azo says: remove the will from the equation, and every act will be indifferent. D. *de postliminio*, L. 1, §. *si quis tamen*. For violence causes fraud to cease in those compelled; hence they are not properly said to be made rebels actively, but passively. L. *immo*, *de liberali causa*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a lord may cede or delegate a vassal to another against the latter’s will.
2. Whether, upon the grant of a territory, the vassals are deemed to have been granted as well, and what effect custom has in such cases.
3. Whether an investiture made of a paternal fief confers a new right not dependent on the old one.
body: It is proposed that the lords of Viscari hold the castle together with its territory, and with high and low jurisdiction. Within the boundaries of the territory of the lords of La Turre, certain persons hold lands in fief from the See of Győr, and they have always rendered homage to the bishop, for more than one hundred years. Now, however, the lords of Viscari, who hold the said castle of Viscari with its district, and to whom renewals and investitures are made from time to time by the Church of Győr, require that the said lords of La Turre swear them fealty by reason of the territory. The latter respond and declare that they are not bound to do so. And even assuming that they were vassals of the Church of Győr, the Church could not alienate them against their will. Here, first, it is asked whether a lord may cede or delegate a vassal to another against the vassal’s will. Second, whether, if the territory is granted, the vassals are thereby deemed granted. Third, whether custom is to be observed. Fourth, whether an investiture made of a paternal fief confers a new right not dependent on the old one.

† On the first point, the gloss of Accursius resolves the matter in a single word, stating that the lord cannot compel the vassal, against his will, to submit to a new and especially unknown person. Thus, the gloss notes in D. 36.1 (De fideicommissis), l. Inuitus. For vassals are freeborn, as is noted in Inst. 1.5 (De iure personarum). Hence, they cannot be sold or subjected to servitude. D. 50.17 (De verbis obligandis), l. Inter stipulantes, §. Sacramentum. Moreover, just as the lord is not compelled to have a vassal whom he does not wish to have, so too the vassal is not compelled to have a lord whom he does not wish to have, especially if this would be undignified for him. Argument from D. 12.1 (De conditione instituta), l. Filius; and D. 50.17 (De verborum significatione), l. Nepos Proculi. For even a donkey resents being seized by a companion, as is noted in D. 10.3 (De aqua pluviae arcendae), l. 1, §. Veteres. Hence, one ought not to have a less worthy lord than the one whom one was accustomed to having as more worthy. Argument from D. 18.1 (De empto vendito), l. Titius, §. Ad hoc; D. 12.5 (De condictione indebiti), l. Si non sortem, §. Libertus, at the words "sed si delegatus." And because the vassal ought not to be ill-treated; yet it seems sufficiently ill-treated if he is compelled to serve someone to whom it is not fitting. D. 39.1 (De operis liberti), l. Opere. For the lord ought to protect the dignity of the vassal, not stain it, but rather augment it, or at least preserve it; not diminish it, nor make his condition worse. D. 24.3 (De re iudicata), l. 2, in principio; and D. 43.29 (De nova operis nuntiatione), l. 1; and in column 10 of the chapter De forma fidelitatis, c. Dominus vero fideli suo vicem reddere debet, etc.

Two cases are excepted, in which the vassal may be alienated against his will: namely, when he is alienated to another vassal, and when he is alienated due to necessity. According to Layman de Ardizone of Verona, in his Summa under the sub-heading "Whether the lord, during the vassal's lifetime, may transfer or alienate the right which he has in him to another." The case concerning the vassal is excepted because, among those holding by symbol, the transition is easier. The case of necessity is excepted because necessity makes probable that which otherwise would not be, D. 38.2 (De manumissis testamento), l. Qui non potuerit; D. 36.1 (De fideicommissis), l. Cum fidei.

But Jacobus Blancus, in his Summa under the heading "Of the causes for which the lord admits the right of lordship," holds that the lord could not alienate the right which he has in the vassal against the vassal's will, but only with his consent. Hence, just as we say of usufruct that it is a right inseparable from the person, so we say here of the property of services existing in the lord, that it cannot be granted to another against the vassal's will, as appears in column 10 of the chapter De feudo dato in vicem legis commissoriae, c. Si quis investierit; and in the constitution of Frederick, c. Imperialem, §. Praeterea ducalis iarchiae, at the words "nec dominus"; and in the Liber Coradi, c. 2, §. Ex eadem.

And the reason is: because the feudal contract is celebrated by the prince and ex post facto for the benefit of both parties; and the lord and the vassal are correlative terms. Argument from D. 46.4 (De acceptilatione), l. Si. And this is true, unless the alienation is necessary: for example, by death and succession; because such alienation is legal. Moreover, such alienation is permitted as inseparable and not standing by itself, when it is made with the universality [of the estate]. D. 41.1 (De acquirendo vel amittendo dominio), l. Quaedam ad Trebatium; for the universality of the castle can be said to be equivalent and sufficient. C. 5.26 (De iure patronatus), l. Ex literis, according to Jacobus; and D. 18.1 (De contrahenda emptione), l. In modicis. Argument from D. 41.2 (De acquirenda possessione), l. 3, §. 1; C. 7.71 (Ubi et apud quos), l. Finis.

† Therefore, the castle having been granted, the vassals come into the consequence of the territory to whose soil they are attached: because the universality of the territory terrifies and circumscribes them, as in C. de agr. et cens. l. quemadmodum; and l. cum scimus, lib. 11; C. com. utriusq. iud. l. pos.; ff. de legat. 1, l. si domus, §. qui confitetur; and it makes what is noted in ff. de adqu. haer. l. pro haerede, §. 1; de damno infecto, l. si finita, §. si qua sunt iura; and C. de haer. vel act. vend. l. 2. For if the lord alienates the whole castle, the rights of the castle ought not to remain with him, ff. de contrah. empt. l. si aquae ductus. Hence, the rights of the universal soil ought to follow the individual parts, as in ff. de leg. 3, l. si chorus. For in these matters, custom ought to be observed regarding common properties, l. venditor, §. si alii. Some say otherwise in the aforementioned l. 1, C. de donat., but I do not care to recite them. But I consider one thing, that here the castle was expressly transferred together with the village, court, jurisdiction, fidelities, and vassals, and that the Pope confirmed this ex certa scientia. As to whether it is valid in law or not, it must be said that there are certain services which a vassal can perform through a substitute: and the right to these services can be ceded, because the vassal can perform them without indignation. There are some which the vassal cannot perform except in his own person and by himself: and in these, the inferior cannot be delegated against his will. There are some which consist in not doing: and the same applies to these services as in the first case, namely, that it is possible, because it does not concern his person. All this is founded on the reason of the aforementioned l. 2, sol. matr. Finally, it must be considered that the alienation was made due to the necessity of the church of Huesca, which could not receive the due benefits because of its expenses; and therefore the renunciation was valid as to all things, according to the opinion of the aforementioned Doctor of Verona. Examining therefore the beginning, since the lords of la Torre were then vassals of the church, they have become vassals, now lords, of that castle, C. de offic. praef. urb. l. 1, §. cum urbem. However, in this vassalage, as regards the lords of Viscar, they are released in time; but from the church of Huesca, whose fidelity they acknowledged, they are not released.

† Nevertheless, it may be said that from the revocations of that ancient feudal contract between the Church and the lords of Viscario, it is understood that the Church has recognized the right of the vassals to belong to the said lords of Viscario; since the concession has its origin, the power of truth, and the substance of a cession. Whether those of La Torre or whoever they are, they ought either to surrender the fiefs or to swear fealty; for they are not strictly bound to swear to a new lord if they wish to remain his faithful vassals. And thus all inconveniences cease. For if they did not wish to be subordinated to an equal or a lesser lord, let them surrender the fief, and the incongruity will be resolved. For they can surrender it, because they have fallen upon a new lord contrary to their expectation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a superior commands an inferior to execute this or that, or a sentence, what are the duties of the executor.
2. If an equal requests an equal, or a judge of one province requests a judge of another province to execute, seize, or remit, whether and when he is bound to do this.
body: Chaste.

It is written to a judge of a judgment that he execute upon the execution; impeding exceptions are opposed, which he sees to be an obstacle. It is asked whether he ought to execute; it is answered that he ought not. Consider: because sometimes it is written to someone as a cognizor, sometimes as an executor, sometimes as an enforcer, who can also be called an executor: but so that it may be better understood, I make a new distinction. For if cognition of a matter is expressly or tacitly committed to someone, this person has cognizance of the cause, because it has not yet been cognized, as in C. si contra ius, vel uri. publi. l. et si non cognitio. It would be absurd to execute first before cognizing: and the necessary order of law is always understood to be inherent in the mandate. Moreover, one should not begin with execution. ff. de re iudi. l. si cum nulla. and l. 1. C. de excu. rei iu. there, "too hastily, Marcellus." For if the execution of an already rendered sentence is committed, or it is committed with jurisdiction, or without jurisdiction. In the first case, he can cognize exceptions not residing in the sentence, but not yet giving rise to execution. ff. de confes. l. cum fideicommis. Also, if the sentence is null, he should desist from execution and write to the delegator the cause why he does not execute. ff. de iudic. si. l. praetor. de re iudi. l. de caetero. In the second case, this executor is a mere instrument and cannot cognize the cause: because he does not have any active jurisdiction, but he performs the office of a naked and necessary executor passively. And if he knows the execution to be contrary to truth, and to be done without justice and judgment, he should resist, saying, "and my hands are clean from the blood of this just person," and he should do the utmost of his power regarding justice and law. l. vt vim. in glo. But when he cannot do more, the sin is not attributed to him. If, however, he doubts, he should presume in his conscience that what is just is being done. But whatever the case, he does not have cognition of the cause. C. de execu. rei iudica. l. si vt propositionis. extra de offi. dele. cap. pastoralis. §. quid vero. in glo.

† If, however, a letter is written to someone who is being compelled by force, as is the case when an ordinary judge writes to another ordinary judge, ordering him to compel the debtor to pay by seizing pledges or by delivering up the person, or if in a criminal matter he writes that the alleged malefactor be arrested or remanded to him, then the person to whom the letter is written ought not to be ready to execute it; because the one who writes is not his superior, but acts by the authority of the law. And therefore, if he sees that it ought not to be executed according to law, he should write back that he does not intend to do injury to anyone, since it pertains to his office to prohibit illegal exactions and injuries. L. illicitas, C. de officiis praesidis. This is understood as noted in ff. de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possessis, L. cum unus, § is qui; and as noted in Authentica de sanctissimis episcopis, § si vero crimen, with similar authorities. And therefore, in our case, according to what is alleged, execution should be stayed. For execution ought not to be carried out in civil matters, as ff. quod metus causa, L. fin., § ult. supports; see also what Bartolus notes in L. a divo Pio, in principio, de re iudicata, ff. And in summary, when a judge of one province writes to a judge of another province, he never compels him against the common law, because he writes solely by the authority of the common law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an appeal to a higher court, omitting the intermediate court, is valid.
2. Whether an appeal is considered abandoned if a sufficient security has not been provided in accordance with the form of the statute.
3. Whether a judge who rendered the sentence, if he becomes the judge to whom the appeal is made, may adjudicate the appeal.
body: The statute of the city of Asti provides that an appeal must be made within the time periods established by law from sentences rendered by the judge of common justice, to the authority of the city of Asti. And the judge from whom the appeal has been taken, if requested to provide the records for the appeal, is bound to deliver them, or cause them to be delivered, to the petitioner within a certain day after they have been requested; because, once the appeal has been made, the appellant is bound to provide adequate security within the next 8 days; otherwise, the sentence rendered shall be held firm and remain in force, and it shall be deemed that no appeal was made, etc. Furthermore, it is presupposed that when an appeal is made to the lord-podestà, as above, that immediately upon the interposition of the appeal, the judge of maleficia, according to the form of the statute, cognizes the appeal, and the proceedings take place before him, and not before the podestà.
