I state that an appeal made to a superior, omitting the intermediate authority, is understood as having been made to the one to whom it ought to have been appealed, as in D. de appellat. l. 1, § si quis in appellatione. Moreover, this does not appear to have been made omitting the intermediate authority, when it was stated in the appeal, “I appeal to the competent judge,” as noted in C. de bon. auct. iud. poss. l. cum proponas. I also state that apostolic letters were granted and the matter brought before the appellate court; it is not necessary to request them again, nor is the appeal considered abandoned on account of the apostolic letters, because one asks in vain for what one already possesses, as in C. de appellat. l. iudici.

But there is a doubt, considering the statute, whether the appeal is said to be abandoned: because suitable security was not provided within 8 days according to the form of the statute, to which I answer thus: either in that city there is a magistrate, to whose approval the security must be given, and then the appeal is abandoned; or there is no office of the magistrate there, and then it is not abandoned: because there is no one who can be approached for the approval of the magistrate, since the office of the magistrate does not function there, by argument from Extra, de rescriptis, cap. Gratiose, lib. 6. For where the office of the magistrate functions, the magistrate is understood to function there: although he is not called the magistrate, but the deputy of the magistrate, as in l. 2, § si mater, ff. ad Tertul.

But here arises a doubt, namely that the same person is both the syndicus and the holder of the power, who cannot adjudicate an appeal on the ground of another office, since he is the one who rendered the sentence alleged to be unjust, as stated in C. de appellatio, l. eos, in principio. To this it is answered that another should proceed, not he himself, but the judge of maleficia; hence suspicion ceases, ff. de iurisdict. omn. iudic., l. praetor. Moreover, this act of giving security is not an act that touches upon the substance of the case. Hence, according to what is alleged, the appeal appears to be abandoned, except where an appeal may be made to the prince, omitting the intermediate instances. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If there are surviving children from the first marriage but none from the second, and the father gave his daughter a dowry double in amount when she married the second time compared to when she married the first, whether, upon the daughter’s death in the second marriage without issue, the dowry belongs to the father or to the children of the first marriage.
2. Whether a maternal grandfather, providing a dowry for his granddaughter of whom he was also the tutor, appears to have given the dowry with the intent of making a gift, or rather with the intent of offsetting a debt, since he was indebted to said granddaughter.
body: Mattheus of Dermona married his daughter to John of the same place, and promised a dowry for her, but did not pay it. This John died, leaving his said wife pregnant, who gave birth to one daughter. Then the said Mattheus married his said daughter again, and gave her a dowry twice as large. Then this daughter of Mattheus died without children from her second husband. Hence the daughter of the first marriage claims that the dowry pertains to her; but Mattheus says it ought to revert to him, and especially that which he gave more to the second husband than to the first. The question is, what is the law.

† The question arises whether, since there are surviving children, the dowry has entirely left the father’s estate, so that it follows the children, or not. Some say that the daughter succeeds her mother: because the dowry is the woman’s own patrimony, and equity seems to dictate that what belongs to the mother should belong to the daughter. Others say that it returns to the father, since by its nature it is a profectitious dowry, as stated in l. dos a patre, C. sol. matr., and therefore it pertains to the father. Bartolus approves this opinion in l. post dotem, sol. matr., and I approve it as well, at least in the greater part, namely that which was not given to the first husband.

† Finally, this maternal grandfather married off that granddaughter; it is asked whether he appears to have given the dowry with the intention of compensating for whatever he might have owed her, since he was her guardian. I answer: yes, because since guardianship is a necessary office, one placed in such a necessity does not appear to have made a gift, as noted by the learned in l. ult. C. de dot. promiss. But this second branch does not apply here: because this guardian gave nothing of his own, as he told me after I had written the foregoing. Therefore, let the first determination suffice. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To promise ratification on behalf of Titius, or to promise that Titius will ratify, are the same thing.
2. Whether a promise made with these words, "I promise that Titius will ratify," is valid.
3. Although a promise concerning another's act is not valid, nevertheless a penalty and damages could be stipulated.
4. Whether a prorogation can be made and a sentence rendered without one party being cited, if the parties so agreed. See no. 10.
5. If power was given to an arbitrator to prorogue as often as he wished, whether a third prorogation could be made. See nos. 7 and 8.
6. Whether and when plural wording is satisfied by the number two.
7. The word "again." What it signifies.
8. Whether a prorogation can be made with both parties absent and unaware.
9. Whether a prorogation can be made outside the place of the compromise.
10. If a statute requires two notaries in the instrument, whether a prorogation will be proved by an instrument made by the hand of one.
11. Whether the prorogued time can be longer than the time originally given.
12. Whether a prorogation not ratified within the term should be considered as having expired.
13. An award rendered after the term of the compromise cannot be ratified, because it was rendered by a non-judge.
body: The noble men Lord Henricus de Advocatis on the one part, and Lord Ubiectus in his own proper name and in the place and name of the Lords Petrus, Bonifacius, and Johannes etc., on the other part—for all and each of whom the aforesaid Lord Ubiectus promised de rato habendo, and that they will hold and keep ratified and firm all and singular the things written below, under the hypothec and obligation of all the present and future goods of the said Lord Ubiectus himself, and for the restitution of all losses, expenses, and the entire interesse of the suit, etc.—compromised generally concerning all and singular suits, questions, and controversies pending, and which might be moved, between the aforesaid parties on whatever occasion (in such manner, however, that only that concerning which and upon which it shall have been declared and pronounced by the arbitrator and arbitratrix below-written, and nothing else, shall be understood to have come into the present compromise, just as if special mention had been made of them word for word in the present compromise), unto the Lord Gregorius as arbiter and arbitrator, so that he may speak, pronounce, arbitrate, render award, and declare on one occasion and on several upon the said questions, etc.; and whatever shall have been spoken, arbitrated, and pronounced, he may interpret and declare on feast days and non-feast days, in any place whatever, sitting and standing, with the parties present and absent, cited and not cited, the order of law having been observed, not observed, and totally omitted, both at law and by accord pleasing to the parties; and further high and low at the free will of the arbiter himself, as it shall please the same arbiter, arbitrator, and awarder, and as he shall see expedient, etc. Which compromise and bailia the said parties and each of them wished and commanded to endure from now to the calends of the month of June next to come, with the power of proroguing the compromise itself on one occasion and on several, at the free will of the arbiter himself; which prorogations to be made by the said arbiter the said parties and each of them have ratified from now, and of certain knowledge do ratify, etc. Now it happened that the said arbiter prorogued the said term thrice, and not in the place of the compromise, but elsewhere; and with no party present, but both being absent, ignorant, and not ratifying within the time of the prorogation made or ratified; nevertheless, it does not appear from the acts. Thereafter it happened that the said arbiter delivered a sentence by which he condemned the said Ubiectus, and those said persons in whose name he had compromised, in a certain quantity of money and other things. Afterwards, however, it happened that those on whose behalf the promise de rato had been made departed this life, and their heirs refused to ratify it; whereupon the interesse is claimed on the clause concerning interesse, which interesse is liquidated from the pronunciation itself. It is asked, what is the law? For several questions and doubts in law arise from the aforesaid facts. First, it is asked whether the said promise de rato held valid. Second, it is asked, granted without prejudice to the truth that it did not hold valid, whether the promise concerning the interesse was valid. Third, whether the sentence rendered against the aforesaid, in whose name the compromise was made, was valid, having regard to the words of the sentence itself directed against them. Fourth, whether the said sentence could be rendered during the third prorogation of the compromise itself, or not. Fifth, whether, having inspected the sentence rendered upon the counsel of the excellent doctor Lord Paulus, which passed into res judicata, the said interesse can be sought, or not; because each party alleges the said sentence for itself. For by the said sentence the right of action seems to be established, and pronunciation was made upon the non-nullity of the award, which makes for the one acting for the interesse. But conversely it is alleged that the said sentence makes for the defendant, against whom pronunciation was made in part only, wherefore he was truly absolved as to the remainder; and these are the doubts which especially arise between the aforesaid parties.

† I return to the first point, and first it must be seen whether it is the same to say, 'I promise de rato for Titius,' and 'I promise that Titius will ratify.' And it seems that it is so, because in both cases I promise ultimately the same thing. To the contrary: because although I promise the same thing, I do not promise in the same order. For when I say, 'I promise for Titius,' it is the same as saying, 'I intercede for Titius,' taking the obligation upon myself, as is noted in ff. de pac. l. 3. §. qui pecuniam. To this makes what is noted in ff. de pecu. le. l. dominus Sticho. For this word, 'I promise for such a one,' must be understood effectively, namely, of a promise that may be valid; whence all things are presumed to have been done solemnly, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. sciendum, and Inst. de fideiusso. §. fi., and to this makes what is noted in l. huiusmodi, in prin., ff. de leg. 1., and ff. de fideius. l. si quis pro eo, in prin., and what is there noted.

† Secondly, it must be seen whether, if there were no other words than these, 'I promise that Titius will ratify,' the promise is valid. And Petrus and Cynus say that it is not, C. de procu. l. 1, in the fifth question; and they draw a distinction as to whether that pact is framed under a real form, 'I promise to hold ratified'—for then it seems he promises to see to it that it will be ratified—or whether it was said personally that such a one will ratify; which distinction is worth nothing, in the gloss on Inst. de inutili stipu. §. si quis. Others say it is special in the cautio rati that 'he will do and see to it' is tacitly understood. Bartolus in l. quo quis alium, de verb. obli., says that in praetorian stipulations those words, that he will do and see to it, are understood, because it is not necessary that anything be added to praetorian words, as is proved in ff. de evic. l. sed ita quis, and ff. de praeto. stipu. l. in praetoris. And therefore it seems to be considered whether this cautio is praetorian, or is reduced to the pattern of a praetorian one because it is before an arbiter, or whether it is purely conditional because it is before an arbitrator. And because it is interposed on the part of the defendant, whence it does not seem praetorian. But certainly even on the part of the defendant it can be praetorian in a real action, as in ff. de procu. l. pomp. §. sed is; whence, since this compromise is general and comprehends even real actions, it seems it should probably be said that it is understood that he will do and see to it. And this especially because the sentence of an arbiter is a true sentence when a statute orders it to be executed, as in C. de iudi. l. pe. And therefore arbitration has been reduced to the form of a sentence, and consequently to the likeness of a judgment. And this concerning the first principal point.

† I come to the second principal point, and I say: granted that the said promise of another's act did not hold, nevertheless a penalty and interesse could be added, provided that there was an interest in it being ratified; but if there is no interest in ratification, the obligation to the interesse is not incurred, as in ff. rem ratam ha. l. pater dotem, in prin., and that rule makes for this, that if the principal does not hold, nevertheless the penal clause holds, as in ff. de verbo obl. l. stipulatio ista, §. alteri; and in the same manner, as I have said, the promise of interesse holds if there is an interest, because the subsequent stipulation of the interesse does not labor under the same defect as the principal promise, as in ff. de ver. obl. l. si ita stipulatus, §. grisogonus. And so I hold that the said stipulation was valid. And this concerning the second principal point.

† I come to the third point, and it seems that the sentence could be made with words directed against the said absent persons. And this I prove thus: the cautio rati ought to represent the same thing as a mandate; but if the said Lord Ubiectus had had a mandate to compromise, and it had been expressed in the compromise that the arbiter could render sentence with the parties absent, the said sentence directly against the absent party would be valid, as in ff. de arbitris, l. diem proferre, §. si quis litigatorum. Therefore, in the present case also it is deemed valid, because it would be confirmed by ratification. l. 1, C. de senten. et interlo. om. iu., does not stand in the way, because there it was not agreed between the parties that the sentence could be rendered in this manner; for it would be valid if this had been agreed, as in ff. de re iudi. l. si convenerit. Also because, by virtue of arbitral power, it seems this can be done causa cognita; for the presence of the party is not always necessary where judicial dispute is not strictly required, as is noted in ff. de bo. pos. l. 3, §. si causa cognita, and in c. 1, de offi. dele., in Clem. And this I believe to be true upon the third point. I come to the fourth point, for there is doubt concerning four or five matters. First, whether a third prorogation could be made, by reason of what was said in the compromise, 'on one occasion and on several.' Second, whether the said prorogation could be made with both parties absent and unaware. Third, whether the said prorogation could be made elsewhere than in the place of the compromise. Fourth, if two notaries are required by the statute of Milan, whether the said prorogation is proved by an instrument made at Milan by the hand of one notary only. Fifth, whether the prorogued time can be greater than the time originally given.

† I return to the first, and it seems that the said prorogation could be made as often as it seemed expedient to the arbiter, as in ff. de feriis, l. oratione, and ff. de eden. l. veluti, §. haec nos. To the contrary it seems that plural speech is content with the number two, as in regula iur. and l. deleg. 3, l. fideicom. §. si decem; and therefore it seems that the said third prorogation was not valid. Nor does it stand in the way that full power was given to the arbiter, because by this it is not understood to be given regarding the prorogation of time, except insofar as the words permit; the text is noted in ff. locati, l. si lege locationis, in prin., there, 'idque arbitrium etc.' For the understanding of this doubt it must be considered,

† that either from many pluralities an absurdity or great grievance to the party can result, and then plural speech is content with the number two, as in the said §. si decem; or no absurdity results, but rather a just and fitting result containing no great grievance to the party, and then it is understood 'as often as is necessary,' that is, 'as often as is just.' Likewise, it should be known that for this reason we use a restriction in these numbers and times, lest the matter proceed to infinity; otherwise it would follow that the arbiter could prorogue a thousand times, just as a third time, which is absurd, because one resorts to arbiters not for the sake of deferring suits, but of ending them, as in ff. de arbitris, l. quamvis arbiter. Likewise, when it is a question of multiplying or proroguing an obligation, twice suffices, as in the said §. si decem. But what is noted in l. si finita, in prin., ff. de dam. infe., makes much against this, where the interposition of an obligation more often is treated, and it is interpreted 'as often as is necessary,' and noted there; for although a prorogation of time is made, the parties do not thereby seem to be harmed, because there is no danger in the delay of a moderate time, as in §. de iudi. l. si debitori. But certainly there is indeed danger on account of the penalty, as in ff. de mino. l. si minor, §. minores.

† But it still seems that he can prorogue as often as he wishes, as in ff. de verb. ob. l. qui Romae, §. callimachus, in fine. But there there is a universal word, 'at whatever time,' and thus it does not stand in the way. Likewise, Bartolus says that there the payment is not multiplied; the word or adverb of the plural number is understood 'as often as is necessary.' It is otherwise where the performance would come to be multiplied. But the laws that are alleged speak of a legal provision, where the ratio of the law is regarded, because the nature of a law is to dispose universally and perfectly; it is otherwise in the disposition of contracting parties, and especially in that which is of strict law. But there still remains the doubt whether 'on one occasion and on several,' that is, other occasions, is understood so that it is predicated of three, or whether the first prorogation is computed in what says 'several.' And to resolve this doubt, the law si is, qui ducenta, §. 1, ff. de re. du., can be adduced; but there the number is specified, here it is not.

† It seems it must be concluded that when it is a question of binding someone by the act of another, then the sentence is extended as often as is necessary; but in stipulations, especially penal ones, extensive interpretation has no place, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. quicquid. Moreover, these words are doubtful, therefore they ought to be interpreted against the speaker, ff. de pac. l. veteribus, and ff. de verb. obl. l. quotiens in stipulationibus, and ff. de re. iu. l. semper in stipulationibus; it ought therefore to be understood of several immediate occasions, that is, of two, ff. de ver. ob. l. 1, §. qui universalis; and that the said words should be restricted to a twofold act, because this power and these arbitrations ought to be restricted rather than extended, by the argument in c. commissa, de elec., in VI, and C. de reb. cre. l. si quis iusiuram., and C. de modo. mulctan. l. eos, though there it speaks of three times.
† Furthermore, the text in §. haec vox says that by the proper signification of the words the phrase 'not again' includes only a twofold act, namely, by interpretation.

† I come to the second point, and I say that there are three cases. For either the prorogation is made with both parties unwilling, and it is not valid, as in ff. de arbi. l. arbiter ita, in the second response; or with both willing, and it is valid; or with one willing and the other objecting, and then, according to some, it is not valid, but the penalty is incurred, as is noted in ff. de arb. l. non distinguemus, §. dies. Now it must be seen what happens when both parties are absent and unaware. And it seems that they ought to be held as objecting, or at least spurning the arbitration, so that the prorogation is annulled, by the argument of ff. de iu. l. edictum. To the contrary it seems: because absent persons ought to be held as consenting, since they consented beforehand and willed that it could be prorogued in their absence. But to this it is replied that concerning the prorogation it was not said that it could be made with the parties absent, unless we say that from the preceding words and from the general power it is understood to be tacitly repeated or included, as in ff. de pac. l. item quia, §. idem Jul., and l. talis scriptura, de le. 1. But certainly, even granted that the prorogation was valid, nevertheless this must be understood if it was notified to the parties by messenger or letter; otherwise, to what purpose would mention be made of a messenger or letter in l. diem proferre? And the reason is manifest, because that term has the force of a peremptory term for adducing proofs, so that proofs can be made up to the end of the term, and the parties seem to be moved concerning this, as Bartolus elegantly notes in ff. de arb. l. si de meis, §. fi.; since therefore it is necessary to notify this force of a peremptory term to their face or at their house, otherwise it is not valid nor does it prejudice in anything, as in ff. de excu. tut. l. scire oportet, §. oportet, and in c. causam, de ele., in Clem. Moreover, the arbitration given in the first part does not seem to be repeated at the end, unless it is restricted to the same, not upon a new case concerning which consent is not found; and to this makes that notable law, ff. de contrahen. emp. l. qui fundum. 11.

† I come to the third, and it seems that the said prorogation could not be made at Milan, that is, outside the place of the compromise, as in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. si ut proponis, §. praeses, and ff. de arb. l. si cum dies, §. si arbiter. To the contrary it seems, because there it speaks of a citation or an act that requires citation of the party, as in ff. de arbi. l. diem proferre, in prin., and there by Bartolus. Moreover, the power was given that in whatever place, etc., as in the said §. callimachus, in fine.

† I come to the fourth, concerning the statute of Milan, and I say that that statute must be observed, because it provides concerning the solemnity of writings that are executed there, as in C. de test. l. fi., and in l. cunctos populos, by the doctors.

† I come to the fifth, and it seems it can be said with sufficient probability that the measure of the prorogued time cannot be greater than the measure of the principal time, as in C. de fideius. l. scimus, and C. quomodo et quando iudex, auth. qui semel, unless by chance the prorogation were made for a necessary cause that was established, as in ff. de arb. l. si cum dies, in prin., and to this makes C. de dilationib. l. 1. Lastly, I come to the fifth principal question, and I say that the consilium of the said most excellent man does not touch upon the question of the interesse, and therefore there is a new petition, a new disputation. And from this it follows that although that sentence passed into res judicata as to the virile share, nevertheless if in truth the award was null, action could not be brought against those ratifying; therefore there is no interest in its being ratified, and thus the stipulation for the interesse is not incurred. What then shall we finally say for certain in this question? I am in doubt.

† And it seems that a prorogation not ratified within the term ought to be held as cancelled, and so one not intimated is held as not made. Likewise because those words, 'on one occasion and on several,' do not stand except for two occasions; for if he had said 'on two occasions and on several,' it would not stand except for three by virtue of the phrasing, as is fully read and noted in cap. ulti., de filiis presby., lib. VI, by Archidiaconus and Johannes Andreae; and

† I say that the said award delivered after the term of the compromise cannot be ratified, because an award delivered by one who was not their arbiter, so to speak, was delivered by an incompetent judge, as in ff. de iu. l. 2, §. sed si iudex, and what is noted in l. 1, C. de pedaneis iudici., and ff. de appel. reci. l. 1, in princ., and ff. rem ra. ha. l. bonorum, and ff. ad Trebel. l. facta, §. si quis bonorum, and ff. de excu. tu. l. scire oportet, n. consequens, and by the argument of C. locati, l. si cum hermes; C. communia utriusque iu. l. 2 does not stand in the way, because here both parties did not consent. Likewise, there there is delivery, here consent; indeed, even if it were a pact, action would not lie upon a nude pact, as is noted in ff. de pac. l. tale pactum, §. qui provocavit. And therefore I conclude, according to the matters that are set forth, that the said award was in no way valid, and consequently, the promise or compromise having expired, action cannot be brought; always saving a better opinion, to which I have always submitted and do submit myself and my words.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A compromise in which no mention is made of heirs does not pass to the heirs unless an award has been rendered.
2. Those who promise ratification, if heirs are not named in the compromise, whether they are deemed to have promised ratification of the heirs.
3. One who promises ratification of the sentence of a judge or arbitrator is understood to promise regarding the sentence, as it stands in law.
4. An arbitrator, by virtue of the power granted to him, extended the compromise without notifying the parties of the extension; whether an award rendered in the absence of the parties is valid.
5. Words do not override the proper nature of the act.
6. If power is given to an arbitrator to extend once, whether he may extend multiple times whenever he wishes.
7. Whether an extension may be made outside the territory of the compromise.
8. Whether an instrument of extension made by one notary in a place where two are required to receive a rogation is valid.
9. Every pact is a contract.
body: All the power of the arbitrator depends on the terms of the compromise. Let us therefore examine what the compromise is, for what matters it was made, how it was made, and with what bailiff and authority.

And it must be noted that in the said compromise no mention was made of the heir, whence the compromise is personal. D. de arbitris, l. diem proferre, § 1; and l. sed interpellatur, § si ex altera. Nevertheless, once the award has been rendered following the compromise, the award passes to the heir, as in l. diem proferre, § nec utimur. But it must be investigated: for this applies between those who compromise in their own right, namely the compromittors, as to whether it stands with regard to the stipulation ratified. For the words say "in the place and name of the lords Peter etc.," but their heirs are not named.

† It is asked whether it appears that one promises regarding the ratification of the heirs. And it seems that he does, for the law provides that if I, as procurator of Titius, have collected money and promised that Titius will ratify, or if I acted as procurator of Titius and promised that Titius will ratify what is committed, the stipulation is such that the heir does not have ratification, as in D. 45.1.13, l. si sine, § si procuratori, and § si in stipulatione. Consider that sometimes a praetorian stipulation is interposed concerning an act that passes to the heir by its own nature: for example, concerning a true judgment, and then the heir is tacitly included, as there. Sometimes it is interposed concerning an act that does not pass to the heir by its own nature, and then the heir is not included, for example, if I promise ratification in the name of a possessor, i.e., of a usufructuary, for the heir is not included, except in that which can pass to him. If, however, the stipulation of ratification is conventional and not praetorian: either it is committed in the person of the deceased and passes to the heir: for example, if the deceased did not wish to ratify, nor does the heir ratify. If, however, the cause of the stipulation is not committed, e.g., he promised that Titius would ratify, and before he could ratify, for example because he was ignorant of the fact, he died: it is not transferred to his heirs. An ignorant person cannot ratify. D. 45.1.13, l. quo n. Since, therefore, if I promise that Titius compromises, I promise an act that does not pass to the heir, because it is personal, the heir is not included, because no mention of the heir was made. Furthermore, consider why the text in D. 45.1.13, l. eandem, § cato, de verb. ob., says: “He promised that Titius and his heir would ratify.” Does the jurist speak without mystery, and as if foolishly, and Paulus regarding the exclusion of the heir? Why did the jurist place this in the formula of the stipulation? Does it not stand in vain? And therefore consider that sometimes one promises something that can be performed by himself or by his heir; sometimes one promises the act of another, or one’s own act, which cannot be performed without the act of another. In the first case, the promise is in rem. D. 45.1.13, l. si ita stipuler per te non fieri. In the second case, no person is ever understood to be implied, unless when the act of a named third party is promised, it is not understood to be of the heir of that third party, for example, I promise that Titius will not offend you; I promise that Titius will help you. For from the act of the heir of that third party, in this stipulation, which derives its force solely from the sound of the words and not from the measure of any edict, the heir of a stranger is not included, as in § cato, arguing from the form of the letter by contrary sense. And D. 45.1.13, l. si ita stipulatus, § grisogonus, in fi. Consider also that when I promise that another will appear or do something, which is subject to his own will and discretion, if he dies before I am in default of securing that, I am released from the promise. The case is in D. 46.1.13, l. si decesserit, unless something is due to me, which ought not to be due; in which case I am bound, lest I enrich myself at another’s loss, as in d. § si procuratori. From these things it appears to anyone intelligent that the obligation is not committed for the portion of those who died before default, and this is the very truth. There remains the question regarding the living who do not ratify, whether the stipulation is committed for that part which concerns them.

† And here consider that it is also aided by the preceding points, namely that he who promises ratification of the sentence of a judge or arbitrator is understood to promise ratification of the sentence as it stands in law. For the term "sentence" is a name that signifies law, as in l. 4, § condemna, de re iudicata, Digest; l. 2, Codex, de sententiis ex periculo recipiendis; l. si. Therefore, this promise does not extend to the promisor promising that something null and improperly done shall be ratified. For at least it must have the appearance of validity. Moreover, he who promises ratification promises ratification by his own act of what is transacted with him in another’s name, not of an act done with another. Hence, if I promise Titius that my lord, who is called A., will ratify what I do and perform, and the sentence is rendered in this manner: “We absolve Titius from A.,” which sentence is improper, certainly, even if my lord does not ratify, I am not bound, because the sentence was not rendered against me. Digest, de iudiciis solutis, l. si ante exceptionem. The judge, by his own sentence, cannot transfer the form of the judgment, nor the absence of the procurator to the principal. Codex, de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. 1. Especially because where there is no mandate, there can be no transfer of the instance. The text is clear. Digest, de procuratoribus, l. in causae, ver. ceterum. And so it was here: because the arbitrator, relying on the unexpected fullness of the power of attorney, pronounced improperly with words directed against one who was never a party to the case, contrary to the note in l. liberto, § si, de negotiis gestis; and l. si se non obtulit, Digest, de re iudicata; and Digest, de procuratoribus, l. Plautius. Therefore, the condemnatory sentence was improper and frivolous, if anyone wishes to examine the law. One can also know for certain, because it is a matter of legal authority and common prudence. These are the narrative points of the plaintiff. There follow certain narrative points concerning the entire praise, about which my venerable colleague, as I heard, but I do not believe, is angry with me; but I am not angry with him. For I did not mention him, but the advocates. Hence I recited, I did not name from myself. As in Extra, de appellationibus, c. Novit ille qui nihil ignorat. Nevertheless, I commend this controversy, the end of which is the elucidation of truth.

Fourthly, therefore, if the arbitrator, by virtue of the power granted to him, extends the compromise after the extension has been previously approved by the parties, yet not notified to them, so that the way is closed to them, and the power [to act] within the space of time for using the benefit of the period: whether the award rendered in the absence of the parties is valid. And I premise for clarity, that the parties promise to ratify the defect of the arbitrator, and especially express or presumed fraud, as in D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. illud nulla; and on this point all the doctors of the world are in agreement. Now I ask you, whether it is done vitiously and with presumed fraud, that which is done by assigning a time and not notifying it. Indeed, no one, I think, would doubt that this is done secretly. But this would not be fitting for an honest man, because it takes away those things which are due by natural law, namely, that faith and truth be observed. C. unde vi, l. meminerint; C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. si; D. de re iudicata, c. pastoralis; in CLE. Porro, eo ipso, quod quis compromittit, compromittit tanquam in animal rationale, et non tanquam in non utentem naturali ratione. D. de operis liberti, l. si libertus. Since, moreover, there is controversy in the compromise, and the matter requires proof, it is fraud not to hear the parties. C. de edendo, l. argentarius; D. ad Trebellianum, l. servo invito, §. cum praetor. It is fraud not to observe the form which leads to the light of truth. 2 q. 1, c. nos in quenquam. I hold for certain that the award, the term not having been notified, is not valid, for the causes and reasons set forth below. And I premise that when the arbitrator asserts that he is rendering sentence on clear proof of instruments, that he then does not transact, because a transaction is not made on what is clear, but he judges in the manner of a judge; and therefore we are dealing with an arbitrator, not a conciliator, as in §. recepisse; and D. de furtis, l. si dominium, according to Dy; and D. de transactionibus, l. 1, according to Dynus.

† and he calls himself, whatever name he wishes to be called; for calls to the bene placitum do not remove the proper hope of the act. D. de praescrip. verb. l. Insulam. And note in l. Si librarius, D. de re iudicata.

Furthermore, I consider that one never finds in the compromise an act or writing that is within a prorogated term, which is in uncertain parts: whether and when power was given to the arbitrator to proceed without notification of the term. Nor is it probable that the parties imposed this snare, as in l. Si convenerit, D. de pactis. It is never seen that an arbitration was granted to impede oneself. l. Si miles, D. de militum testamento.

The laws supporting this are these: The law says that although a fourth fatal day may be granted in the restoration of an appeal in the absence of the parties, nevertheless the party must know this and be cited, so that he may use his rights. C. de temporibus appellationum, l. 2, § 1, and there expressly noted.

Another law says that a judge cannot render a sentence if he knows that the absent party is altogether unable to appear. D. de re iudicata, l. Quaesitum. But one who is ignorant is altogether impeded from appearing. l. 1, § Item cum ex dicto, D. quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur.

Furthermore, it must be clear and evident to the judge or arbitrator regarding contumacy; otherwise, what is done is null. l. Haec autem, § 1, D. qui ex causa in possessionem eant, according to Bartolus. But here it is clear that there is no contumacy, and that appearance is impossible. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Militum interest, according to Bartolus, because ignorance is established. l. Si, D. de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis. This reason ceases on the day of the compromise, because that day is easily known and is held as a term, within which the parties know and can, according to Bartolus in l. Si meus, § Si, D. de arbitris. Therefore, they must impute it to themselves.

Furthermore, a judge may prorogue the term for a contumacious party. However, if he does not notify, the subsequent sentence is not valid, noted in Inst. de verbis obligantibus, § Omnis, and l. Si vitem, § Si, D. quod vi aut clam, according to Decius and Bartolus.

Furthermore, if he does not pronounce judgment at the appointed time, but afterwards while the parties are ignorant, it is not valid. C. quoniam provocatio non est necessaria, l. Cum non eo die.

And if it is said that these do not apply because of the arbitration granted, I answer that in this case the arbitration does not speak, for we have the words of the compromise before our eyes. For a power given is not seen to be copious. D. de transactionibus, l. Cum Aquiliana.

To this is added: D. de verbis obligantibus, l. Si quis arbiter; D. de aedilicio edicto, l. Quod si nolit, § Si quid; D. de in diem addicto, l. Necesse; D. de legatis 2, l. Si tamen; D. de naturalibus restitutionibus, l. Si; C. de distributione pignorum, l. Creditor. The arbitrator is not a mere executor; therefore, he was required to summon the absent party. This is supported by c. Ultimum, de arbitris, lib. 6. Otherwise, due to the defect of the award and the presumed fraud of the arbitrator, it is ineffective, and at least the exception stands in the way. de arbitris, c. Non distinguimus, § Cum quidam. And this is the very truth.

† Having spoken of the causes, it follows to consider the times. And it is asked, whether, having regard to the form of those words, "once" and "more than once," the arbiter could have prorogated three times. And I shall speak according to law, ignoring custom. And I say that the plural expression is satisfied by the number two, as in the rule of law and in the last chapter, *De filiis presbyterorum*, Book 6, and according to Archidamus and Johannes Andreae, *De praebendis*, chapter *Is cui*, § *Si vero*, Book 6. And this is proved by the force of the language, *Digestum*, *De adquirendo et retinenda hereditate*, and the argument of the law *Pautius*. However, so that we may proceed along the path of legal reasons, it must be considered that sometimes the matter concerns an obligation to be multiplied or extended by one's own act; sometimes by the act of another; sometimes concerning the purging of delay; sometimes concerning something to be done which does not harm oneself but benefits another, as in the case of an edict; sometimes concerning the non-restriction of proof. I omit other cases as sufficiently known, and I take only the second case: when the obligation is incurred by the act of the adversary or a third party. And I say that then the adverbs of number are restricted to the minimum, i.e., to two times, *Digestum*, *De legatis secundis*, law 1, § *Si quis decem*, where it is expressly stated, nor is it expedient to make such a great noise about this. In our case, one compromise concerns a composite and proper act. The other concerns an act not proper, nor within his power. For that the arbiter could burden me so many times by placing me in danger due to the act of another, neither equity nor the words permit. To the same effect is that which compelled me to consult: because in voluntary matters, the will sets the limit to the obligation, which will, by its very nature, is of strict law, except in certain contracts. And therefore, from the words in which the will consists, just as the face consists in a mirror, one must not depart, *Digestum*, *De stipulationibus legatorum*, law *Labeo*, § *Idem Tubero*. Having considered the times, let us consider the place.

† And first, whether the extension could be made in a place so remote from the place of the compromise. And I say that it could not, because there the arbitrator is not present, and especially because it is more than one day’s journey distant from the place of the compromise. D. de arbitris, l. si cum dies, §. arbiter. For this extension, although it does not require full cognizance of the case, as D. de arbitris, l. diem proferre, in principio, nevertheless requires some kind of cognizance of the case. Hence it cannot be made outside the territory of the compromise. And certainly this delay has a certain force of tacit citation according to Bartolus, which cannot be assigned outside the territory; nor do those words “in whatever place” stand in the way, because they are understood to mean “in a suitable place,” not outside the domicile of the compromittors: as D. de constitutione peculii, l. si duo, §. 1. And thus it is also understood in D. de interrogationibus et actionibus, l. voluit, §. 1. For this extension is part of the judgment, and not a simple act of voluntary submission to jurisdiction, just as neither is the award of the arbitrator. Hence it partakes of the nature of a judgment. C. de iudiciis, l. rem non novam. Just as a judge existing outside the territory could not extend the terms of the litigation, because there he is private, and it is not doubtful that this extension is a kind of interlocutory decision. Moreover, it requires some reason of its own suitable and equitable nature, as D. de arbitris, l. non distinguimus, §. diem. And the continuity of the judgment ought not to be divided into several territories. D. de iudiciis, l. nisi concepta, because the rule of that law is general.

† Finally, let us consider whether the instrument of prorogation made in Milan by a single notary is valid, when the statute requires that one notary alone should not be deemed trustworthy for drawing up a deed, but that there should be two notaries. And Bartolus discussed this question in *l. cunctos populos*. And he says that it is not valid, because as regards the solemnity of the instrument, the place where the instrument has its beginning is considered: for it must derive its substance from its beginning. And this is the truth, because he who cannot be requested to act, his instrument is not valid in any place. Moreover, because a single notary alone, according to the law of that place, is tacitly declared suspect by the municipal law. Hence, perhaps it does not prove that the matter is half-proven by reason of the statute, as noted in *Auth. de non alienando*, § *quia vero Leonis*; and *C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, *l. iubemus*, § *iconomus*. Someone will say, this prorogation and its instrument was not made in the contract, nor in the alienation. I answer first, that if the contract appears to be present by fiction, as if made retroactively by the parties, therefore it is present, that is, it is in the contract. *C. de pactis*, *l. iure gentium*, § *quinimmo*; *C. de contrahenda emptione*, *l. pacta conventa*; *ff. de conditionibus institutis*, *l. illa institutio*; *de hereditate instituta*, *l. asse toto*. Moreover, this prorogation is a certain pact of the parties then declared by the arbitrator, namely, that the compromise shall endure. *l. sed si manente*, *de deprecatio*. And
† Every pact is a contract, as is noted in the Digest, under the title "Of Actions and Obligations," law 1.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a compromise and a bailiff ought to be appointed for the same matter.
2. Where a law of prorogation exists, a compromise prorogated from the beginning is deemed one by legal fiction.
body: The law of the compromise must be examined. i.e., the agreement in the compromise. The words state that the said compromise and the bail were intended to last until the close. No. This word,

† A compromise and a bailia should not be placed as the same thing, if you begin from the first, namely from the compromise, because it does not follow that he is a compromissarius; therefore, since a bailia may be granted to those present and absent, etc., because these clauses are contrary to the common law and the order handed down by law in simple compromises. It follows in the words, “with a bailia, once and several times, to prorogue the said compromise.” Nor does it say “the compromise and the bailia,” and thus it can therefore prorogue the time of a simple compromise, not one with a bailia. Nor should you wonder that in the prorogation the bailia, granted beyond the common law, does not appear to be repeated. For this is clearly determined by Guillaume in the Digest, De officio proconsulis, in the law Meminisse, where, if you look, a notable decision is made, but each person of the vulgar does not understand this distinction. The words say “once and several times,” i.e., one time first, and then another. Nor is it explained in the text, but it is restricted by the laws alleged by me. And this is clear from the notable opinion of Guillaume de Cuggiat in the law Manumissiones, Digest, De iustitia et iure, where you may see. And what is added, “at free will,” i.e., as to the power, under the said number. Provided, however, that what I advised is saved. This word was not read to me, which I perceived. But a preceding special definition should not be removed by a general one, and therefore there does not seem to be force in this. Law Quotiens, Code, De fideicommissis hereditatibus, with the law Si quis.

† A prorogated compromise is, by legal fiction, one and the same, if the law of prorogation is the same as it was from the beginning. Otherwise, if it is lesser or greater. From *de prebendis*, c. *Hi qui autem*, lib. 6; *ff. locati conducti*, l. *Cum in plures*, §. *Legem dictam*. Hence it must be observed that here there were several compromises. One with the Bailiff, another without the Bailiff: because repetition expressed in some cases and omitted in others does not induce a tacit repetition of what was omitted. *de legibus*, l. *Licet*; *Imperator*, where the case is found. A compromise duplicated by numbers is not truly one, but several; and whenever it is a matter of multiplying obligations, iterative words are restricted to twice. Dynus in l. *Si finita*, *ff. de damno infecto*; and l. *Fideicommissum*, §. *Si quis ita*. And you, Lord John, gave your counsel under the said rule, sealed, you and Lord Paul, Advocate, and Lord Philip de Regio, and you were [cited as] 20 doctors. Having seen whose counsels, for your honor, I did not wish to call into doubt, before they were produced in public form. And that there are truly several compromises, holds Cynus in l. *Si cum dies*, in his additions, *C. de arbitris*. And this is the truth, because it is not terminated by one term; therefore, there are several terminable [compromises]. The words say, "having cited, and not having cited." These words are placed in the first compromise, whose term is known to both parties. Hence, by the lapse of the term, no party can be deceived. He knows what he ought to do, but the term of prorogation is uncertain: therefore, it must be notified to them; because prejudice may threaten them greatly in producing their rights; because one who is ignorant does not have the power to act, [we wish] consent and knowledge, not ignorance, to bind. *de tabulis*, l. *Generalis*, lib. 10; and *ff. de columnis*, l. *Annus*. For a term is fixed so that fuller proof may be made by the parties, and fuller light of truth may be afforded; and therefore such assignment was not valid unless notified, as the law commands to be done, as in l. *Diem proferre*. That a term may be prorogated is not denied; but the party ought to be certified of the said prorogation, and cited to the act of prorogation itself. And especially because of those words, "by agreement of the parties," it ought to be notified and issued by agreement, so that the words may have effect. *de in diem additione*, l. *Necesse*. And it is expressed in favor of the parties, since it says "by agreement of the parties"; and that which is expressed in favor ought not to be turned into injury to the parties. Nor do I ever find in this writing that the Bailiff was given [authority] concerning notifying or not notifying the prorogation. And he would be a fool who gave it, and put himself in haste. Moreover, this prorogation is, according to Bartolus, a certain momentary and peremptory [act]; therefore, it must be notified. And it is the original gloss in l. 2, *C. de tempore appellationis*, §. 2; and *de electione*, c. *Causam*, in the *Clementinae*. *Testamentum*, n. *Dubium* provokes to the cause and its exercise; therefore, he must notify. *C. de excusationibus tutorum*, l. *Scire oportet*, §. *Oportet*, there the case. But you say, the Bailiff says otherwise. I answer, it is not true that he says, "it is in writing." Nothing can be added to the faith of instruments of contract. The words say, "the order of law being observed and omitted." Can he thereby render judgment directly against him who is defended without mandate? Certainly not, even by mere canonical equity, no. *Innocentius*, *de electione*, c. *Querelam*. And it is the original gloss, very notable, in l. *Perlatam*, *C. de senatu*, there, "let it please to contemplate that gloss: the words do not say 'all solemnity or substantiality omitted,' but 'order being observed.' And these are separate, and the discipline and reason of the separated are separate, as *ff. de calumniis*, l. *Finis*. The words of this compromise are in person on every side, and therefore it does not seem promised regarding the ratification of the heir. Rather, the heir cannot ratify this compromise, and consequently neither the award. *C. de arbitris*, l. *Sed interpellatur*, §. *Si ab altera*. Dynus in c. *Ratum*, cum *Si*. Because this case had so many doubts, I advised rather that the award be null, than unjust, so that if the plaintiff later had the truth, he might sue, and the defendant not be hindered by the pretext of an award not valid by law itself, and [I advised] the truth. And of this opinion I am firmly, and I counsel it. Nor do I doubt in any way. And nevertheless, I submit to correction, yet I wish to know the cause, why, and what is answered not to me, but to my reasons. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the power to extend the time is granted to the arbitrator simply, or once, and repeatedly, or whenever he may extend it.
2. A procurator having the power to substitute once, and repeatedly, cannot do so more than twice.
body: A prorogatory adjournment cannot be granted when both parties are absent, and beyond the term without ratification, and while ignorant. L. genero, de infa.

† Hence, the sense of these words, “that he may prorogue once and more than once,” is this: namely, that he may prorogue, not however only once, but more than once. For to say “once and more than once” is nothing other than to say simply “more than once.” For the understanding of this, it must be premised that if the power to prorogue were granted, and it were not stated “once and more than once,” it would be understood as referring to a single prorogation. On the meaning of words, Law *Boues*, § *Hoc sermone*. Therefore, the word “more than once” is added so that the authority to prorogue does not expire after a single instance; not, however, so as to add anything to the plurality, i.e., so that it extends beyond two instances. Similarly, one may appeal once and more than once, but not three times. And thus advised the aforementioned Philip de Regio, Bartolus de Saliceto, and eight other doctors. Likewise, if it is said that a penalty is incurred once and more than once, it is not incurred three times. Moreover, every prorogation is a multiplication and renewal of the compromises, especially if the arbitrator has so restricted himself that judgment could not be rendered within the time of the original compromise. Digest, On the meaning of obligations, Law *Cum stipulatus*; similar to what Proculus says to me; and note Cynus in Law *Si cum dies*, in the beginning, On arbitrators. Whenever we deal with the multiplication of compromises, we are dealing with the multiplication of promises, and indeed odious ones, because they are penal, and therefore the words must be strictly interpreted. Note: If the power to prorogue is granted, and the time for deception is prorogated, but notice is not given, the prorogation is of no effect, if he has the power to prorogue in the absence of the parties. However, if he prorogues in their absence and does not give notice, the prorogation is considered as not having been made; for it cannot be said that notice need not be given; nor is that act understood to have been performed which was omitted in the mandate, and which is prejudicial, contrary to law, and contrary to good faith. Law *Creditor*; Law *Si quis arbitratu*, since the matter has been brought into controversy. Likewise, the clause “the parties not being cited to the sentence” is contrary to the common law, and is not understood to be tacitly included. And clauses which are prejudicial and contrary to the common law, if placed at the beginning, are not understood to apply at the end. And contrary to another chapter, tacitly repeated: if I give someone the power to bind me once or more than once, he cannot bind me more than twice.

† If one grants to two procurators the power to substitute once, and more than once, they cannot substitute except twice. If one grants the power to extend their mandate once, and more than once, they cannot do so except twice. For the adverb "more" and the noun "more" or plurality are verified in two, and take their stand in two. See in *obligatione contrahenda*, but in this matter, when they explain it by acquired right, and more fully, as in § *hic nos* on this word, *pluraliter*. Spezzano touches upon it, but establishes nothing in the title *de arbitris*, § *sequitur*, verse *quid sit dictum*. I am of this opinion: that the clause added, that he may [act] with parties cited and not cited, operates within the term assigned by the compromittors, who have knowledge of the term and a vested right; otherwise in a prorogated term, unless it has been notified to the parties; because ignorance prevents them from appearing, and the arbitrator is unable to appear; because ignorance is a natural impediment, *l. quaesitum*, *de re iudicata*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A donation is not valid without insinuation (judicial registration) insofar as it exceeds the lawful sum.
2. Whether the presence of the Princess supplies for the defect of insinuation in a donation, just as the presence of the Prince does.
3. If the notary summoned to witness the donation is, by privilege, an ordinary judge, whether he is deemed to have interposed the authority of the said donation, so that it is considered insinuated; and whether consent, authority, or a decree of the judge is required in insinuation.
1. Whether a debtor may pay the assignor, omitting the assignee, and whether he is thereby discharged.
2. Whether the assignor may do anything to the prejudice of the assignee.
3. Whether priority based on time exists among assignees, or between the assignee and the debtor.
body: The fact is as follows: Lady Anerana, under the title of a donation inter vivos, transferred half of the maintenance rights belonging to her in the estate of the late lord Corado de Asinariis, her husband, and likewise half of her dowry rights, and likewise half of all goods in which she is found to be heir or rights existing in the goods of the said late lord Corado, or held by the late lord Corado, unto the most famous doctor of laws, lord Filippo de Casolis of Reggio, as appears from a public instrument with due registration solemnly stipulated, etc., and solemnly furnished with all formal requirements. Which rights, as above, on the same day with no interval having elapsed, in that manner and just as the said lord Filippo had held them from the above-written lady Anerana, the same lord Filippo, under the title of a donation inter vivos, transferred to the Most Illustrious Princess and lady, the lady Countess of Virtù, and as appears from a public instrument furnished and solemnized, etc. After which, a certain time having elapsed, the aforesaid lady Anerana sought, and did seek, that the said maintenance be assessed for her, and on this matter litigation was conducted by her for a certain time against the heirs of the said lord Corado. Finally, by virtue of letters of the Illustrious Prince and Magnificent lord, the lord Count of Virtù, etc., then lord of Asti, transmitted at that time to his podestà in the said city, a submission to arbitration was made by the said lady Anerana on the one side, and her adversary on the other. And indeed, by arbitral sentence the maintenance was determined to amount to 4,000 florins, and thus it was declared that that adversary was the debtor of the said lady Anerana, no mention having been made of the aforesaid lady Countess, nor of the aforesaid lord Filippo; against which sentence, however, an objection was lodged, but the objection itself was not pursued. Finally, the said parties came to a certain transaction, or settlement, no mention having been made of the aforesaid lady Countess: namely, that the adversary of the said lady Anerana should answer to the said lady Anerana or her heirs for 4,000 florins on account of the said maintenance. And thus it was done: for there were assigned to her so many goods as amounted to the said quantity, which lady Anerana sold, and she confessed that she had received the price, namely 4,000 florins; but in truth she received only two thousand, which she delivered to a certain niece of hers, to whom, before the donation made to the aforesaid lady Countess, she had donated under title of donation inter vivos 2,000 florins upon all her goods. Concerning the other two thousand of hers, an instrument of deposit was made under such condition that they should answer to the said lady Anerana or her heirs for the said 2,000 florins, provided that the aforesaid lady Countess remit all rights which she has in the goods of lady Anerana or of lord Corado, but otherwise not. After the aforesaid matters, the aforesaid lady Anerana died, having made a will, etc., under which the inheritance was entered upon, etc. Can the aforesaid lady Countess—to whom no mention of the aforesaid matters was ever made, nor did she ever perform any of those three things of l. 3 C. de novationibus—obtain her rights? Now, in the first place, it is called into doubt whether the aforesaid donation is valid, and if it is not valid, by what legal remedy counsel is given to the aforesaid lady Countess, especially since the penalty of interest and expenses, etc., was inserted in the contract of donation if it should be contravened, etc. Also, in the event that the said donation is valid, whether by the payment of those 4,000 florins made to the said lady Anerana for that maintenance by virtue of that settlement, the certain debt of the said maintenance is extinguished in all respects, since there is an opinion that payment made by a debtor to a assignor then only discharges when that payment must tend to the benefit of the assignor himself, but otherwise if to the benefit of the assignee; and if it is extinguished, by what law counsel is given to the aforesaid lady Countess. Also, if it is not extinguished, by what law counsel is given to the aforesaid lady Countess. Also, if the whole debt of maintenance is not extinguished, whether the aforesaid lady Countess can ratify that arbitral sentence, and thus seek half of the assessment made on account of the said maintenance, especially since in the factual statement it is presupposed that she has already delivered those 2,000 florins to that niece of hers on account of the preceding donation, and especially because the said lady Anerana did nothing in the name of the aforesaid lady Countess, but only in her own name. In the event that it can be proved that the heir of the late lord Emanuele Asinario, heir of the late lord Corado himself, knew of the cession made by the said lady Anerana to the said lord Filippo, from whom the aforesaid lady Countess derived her title, and consequently to the lady Countess herself, whether such knowledge is held to be, and suffices in place of, notification, and thus we are in the case of l. 3 C. de novationibus; and this because that condition was inserted in the deposit of those two thousand florins; for the glosses are continually contradictory. The aforesaid matters concern the rights of maintenance: because first the aforesaid lady wishes to obtain those, and afterwards to turn to her other rights; for obtaining all of which, may it please you to answer in law how her claim is best grounded. First,

† it must be examined whether the donation made to the noble and outstanding doctor, lord Filippo, was valid; for from it derives the donation made to the Most Illustrious lady, the lady Countess of Virtù. And it must be said that if the donation was supported by registration (insinuatio), it was valid in whole; otherwise it was not valid except up to the statutory amount, C. de do. l. sancimus and in l. si quis argentum and l. si quis pro redemptione, § fi., that is, up to 500 gold solidi, as appears there. Nevertheless, it could be doubted

† whether the presence of the Princess supplies the defect of registration, just as the presence of the Prince supplies it, as in C. de test. l. omnium; and there is an argument that it does, C. de don. inter vi. et uxo. l. pe. and C. de quadriennii praes. l. bene a Zenone, and what is noted in Auth. de non alie. § si minus, col. 2; for if the Prince acts in the place of Caesar in his territory, then so does the Augusta Princess; whence they have the same privileges, as in ff. de legi. l. Princeps. Likewise, she excels in authority every magistrate beneath her, just as was formerly said concerning Countess Matilda, as is noted in C. de arbi. l. fin.

† Likewise it could be asked whether a notary, who is also an ordinary judge by the terms of his privilege, can interpose judicial authority in that donation, so that it may thus be seen to have been registered before a magistrate, since he is an ordinary judge, even though he does not preside over a tribunal. And it seems that he cannot, as in C. de dona. l. in hac; for in this regard the prorogation of jurisdiction is not valid, as in C. de te. l. testamenta omnia. Likewise because this interposition of a decree belongs to mixtum imperium, ff. de transac. l. cum hi, § si praetor. To the contrary is what is noted in ff. de iud. l. 1, and that these men, by consent of the parties, have the power of drawing up public acts before themselves, C. de sac. san. ecc. l. iubemus, § his tabellionibus. Likewise, this does not properly seem to be a decree, since it belongs by right of magistracy; but it is rather a kind of authority, as is noted in Authem. ut non fiant pignorationes, § illud, colla. 5; it can be interposed by the defender of the city, as in the said l. in hac. Likewise, since these charter judges have jurisdiction immediately from the Prince, that is, habitual jurisdiction, therefore they can also interpose decrees, C. pro sua iurisdi. l. j., and this is customary to be contained in their privileges; to which is relevant what is noted in l. 1 ff. de tuto. et curato. dandis ab his. And although these privileged judges, whom we call charter judges from the parchments of their privileges, C. de iudi. l. rem non novam, do not have the exercise of jurisdiction except between consenting parties, nevertheless they have the root of jurisdiction from the Prince, arg. ff. de testamentaria tutela, l. tutores non ab haerede. In this matter the tenor of the privileges must be seen; for by the ius commune an inferior to the defender cannot register before himself, in Authem. de defen. civit. § nulla. Regarding that, however, which is asked concerning the penalty, it must be said that he who breaches the faith of a lawful donation falls into the penalty, but otherwise if it is unlawful, ff. de transac. l. qui fidem, ff. ad l. Fal. l. Seyus augerius. Consider: Bartolus says, in ff. de do. l. Modestinus, that in registration the presence of the judge suffices, and his authority or decree is not required. Guillaume de Cunh says that a decree is required. I have said that authority is required, for a decree is so called from creating, that is, from the creation of a new right or a new status; but authority is applied for confirming, not for creating anew; on this see what is noted in C. de sac. san. eccle. l. illud; for if the presence of the judge as judge, and not as a simple witness, is required, therefore something is within the judge's power to decree or authorize, ff. de transac. l. cum hi; to which is relevant what is noted in ff. de bono. pos. l. 3, § si causa cognita, and l. fi. ff. qui ad bo. pos. And yet this is most true, because that registration pertains more to voluntary than to contentious jurisdiction, which was not in the form of a trial between father and son, nor can it be done, as in C. de dona. l. data iam pridem.

† Now I come to the other question, namely, presupposing that the donation is valid, whether the payment of those 4,000 florins could be made to the assignor. The laws that speak on this matter must be considered: because some speak of a spontaneous payment, as in C. quae res pig. obli. pos. l. nomen, and C. de excep. l. 1, ff. de haere. vel act. ven. l. venditor actionis, § nominis venditor; some of an extraction made from an unwilling party, as in C. de dona. l. 3; some of a judicial proceeding and confession, as in ff. de procu. l. actor malit. and l. procu. in rem suam; some of a transaction, ff. de transa. l. fi.; some of a gratuitous agreement, ff. de pac. l. si cum emptore; some of an account, ff. quemad. ser. amtt. l. si patrem, § fi.; some laws speak of a restitution made under the SC Trebellianum, ff. ad trebel. l. factam, § si haeres, and l. 1, § 1 eo. ti., with similar passages. And concerning all these, Iacopus de Arena, Oldradus, and Bartolus say that if the assignment was made for the sheer benefit of the assignee, since an actio utilis has been transferred, which is preferred to the direct action—because the assignor, by assigning, intended the assignee to be preferred, and caused business pertaining to himself to pertain to another—if the debtor is aware of the assignment, and did not receive payment from one paying spontaneously, he cannot exact it from an unwilling party, nor transact, nor agree, by the said l. ult. ff. de transa. by argument a contrario sensu; and thus the assignment remains in the firmness of its force, and the assignee can proceed against the old debtor; yet knowledge is not presumed unless it is proved. Others say that the assignor, while the matter is intact (re integra), can receive payment from a debtor who pays spontaneously; but otherwise if the matter was not intact. And the matter is said not to be intact when one of those three things intervenes of which mention is made in l. 3 C. de nova. And this opinion seems to be that of that third law; otherwise, to what end would the law enumerate those three cases there if mere knowledge sufficed there? For notification is not then of the substance, as that law requires, and yet the assignment had been made principally for the utility and favor of the assignee. And if you say that that law speaks of a mandate, not of an assignment, you speak against the gloss placed there; that opinion is approved by the gloss in C. quae res pig. obli. possunt, l. nomen. But it approves the preceding opinion in the said l. finalis, ff. de transac., and commonly the gloss of that last law is approved, as Cynus reports. In the schools, I touched upon this by investigating and arguing that an assignment cannot bring it about that the debtor, by paying, is not discharged ipso iure; because the assignor cannot make the condition of the debtor worse; but by paying the assignee with respect to the actio utilis he is not discharged ipso iure, but by the aid of an exception, C. de excep. l. 1; whence, because it is in his interest to be discharged ipso iure, it seems that even when knowing he can pay the assignor. But to that l. 1 it is answered that there he paid to another by the will of the deceased; here, by the will of the living, as is noted there; and the doctors hold this solution. But since the assignment cannot change the state of the obligation, nor its origin, it seems it should be said that the debtor can pay spontaneously, otherwise he would be burdened with the burden of proving: because he would be burdened with proving the assignment if the debtor denied it, and he were compelled altogether to pay the assignee; an argument for this reason is in l. 2 ff. sol. matrimo. It must be considered that sometimes an obligation is naturally dissolved by payment, and then it seems that the debtor, even when knowing, can pay the assignor, unless he promised by delegation; for that law makes this distinction; sometimes it is dissolved civilly by a new pact or transaction: and in this manner among knowing parties it cannot be dissolved to the prejudice of the assignee if the assignment preceded the pact; but otherwise if the pact had preceded the assignment, ff. de excep. doli, l. apud celsum, § quod si is, cui, and the said l. fi. de transa.; others say otherwise, as stated above. There is also another reason in their favor: because they say that, the assignment having been made, if the assignor sues in court, the debtor can oppose to him the exception of transferred actions, which perpetually bars the assignor; therefore, if knowing this he does not oppose it, let him impute it to himself, ff. de fideiussoribus, l. exceptione, ff. mandat. l. si fideiussor, § quaedam; for he does not seem to pay in good faith, but rather to donate to the recipient, according to what is noted in l. si procu. de condi. ob causam. But concerning that exception the dispute is still before the judge, because since the right to direct actions has not been destroyed, therefore the exception does not bar the assignor by the case of the said l. 3; nor does the argument a contrario sensu of the said l. ult. de transac. stand in the way, because that argument a contrario sensu ought not to be taken except in so far as it can be taken, that is, it is with the distinction of the said l. 3 de nova. Likewise because the said l. ultima speaks of a new contract, not the execution of an old contract; these things are doubtful, and different people think differently. Furthermore, in restitution under the SC Trebellianum, on account of the authority of the senate, no one doubts that a debtor knowing that the inheritance has been restored cannot pay the heir, in whom the empty name of the actions remained, ff. ad Treb. l. ex asse; for ownership of the rights themselves is transferred under the SC Trebellianum; this the gloss holds in the said l. si cum emptore. Here ends the article concerning one who has knowledge; here begins and follows the article concerning a debtor who is ignorant of the assignment, in which article the reasoning of the SC Trebellianum does not differ from any other assignment.

† But they distinguish: either it is a pact from a lucrative cause, and then it does not harm the assignee; or from an onerous cause, and then it does harm, according to Iacobus Butrigarius and Cynus; and much more strongly does true payment made to the assignor harm. What then do you say in a transaction or an amicable composition of an arbitrator that is not a lucrative title? I answer: in so far as it was given to the creditor, it is the same as in payment; but in so far as it was remitted to the debtor, either the debt was not liquidated, and it is the same as in a transaction; or it was liquidated, and it is the same as in a donation, as in ff. quae in frau. cre. l. 1, § an transigit. In our case, however, since the debt had formerly been liquidated, and the right acquired for the said illustrious lady, in that which was not truly counted out, without doubt the assignment retained its force, presupposing the foundation that the donation was valid.

† One point also is touched upon, namely, whether among assignees there is priority in time: because assignment has the force of quasi-delivery, as is noted in ff. de don. l. ad eum; this question is determined in ff. de leg. 1, l. quocunque, § qui Gaium. And the aforesaid things are true between the assignee and the debtor; but between the assignor and the assignee there is no doubt that if the assignor did anything to the prejudice of the assignee, whether by suing or by contracting, he is bound to reimburse him, as is noted in the said l. fi. de transac. and the said § quod si is, cui, and it is the text in l. venditor actionis, § fi. ff. de transac. l. cum hi, § si integra, second response; but among the primary assignees among themselves, the said § qui Gayum has place. And therefore against the heirs of the assignor rights belong to the said Renowned lady, if the donation was solemn. And this I say without doubt, always saving the counsel of anyone having a better opinion. And thus do I, Baldus, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether damages arising from litigation may be claimed by any type of action once the dispute has been settled.
2. Whether one who produces a false witness is liable for perjury.
body: A certain Master James of Lazisio, or another procurator in his name, asserting that a certain Doctor Antonio of Lazisio was his debtor by virtue of a certain custom written in the volume of statutes of the commune of Verona, caused a sequestration to be made, two years having now elapsed, of a very great number of bolts and pieces of cloth, as if they were the goods of the said his debtor, in a certain dyed-cloth stall, which a certain Bonicontrus the Dyers held in his own name; and he caused the said stall to be closed. Upon this being done, Bonicontrus’s procurator appeared in court and petitioned that the said sequestration be lifted and annulled according to the form of the said statute or custom. And, at his petition, the said sequestration was annulled insofar as it was to his prejudice; the said bolts and pieces of cloth, however, remaining in sequestration according to the form of the said custom. Subsequently, the said Bonicontrus, or another procurator in his name, produced before the judge a certain document, in which he petitioned that it be pronounced that the said sequestered goods belonged to him and pertained to him, always protesting against the said Master James and his procurator for his damage and interest. The said Doctor Antonio of Lazisio never appearing in any way to be, or to have been, a debtor of the said Master James in the principal case, which was appealed in favor of Master Bonicontrus and against Master James. The expenses incurred in the litigation were taxed and are so, all of which having been completed, etc. And because the said stall of the said Bonicontrus remained closed continuously for five months, and the said bolts and pieces of cloth remained in sequestration continuously for twenty-one months, from which the said Bonicontrus was damaged in a very great quantity, both because he could not exercise his person in his art of dyeing, and because he could not sell the said cloths, and they were of greater value at the time of the said sequestration than they were at the time of their restitution to him. Wherefore, the said Bonicontrus, regarding his damage and interest, brought a libel against the said James, petitioning that the said James be condemned to pay his damage and interest, in which also account should be taken of lost profit on the aforementioned occasion, as is more fully contained in his libel. And upon the said libel, the litigation being contested, and legitimate proofs having been made by Master Bonicontrus in the said case, the said Bonicontrus succumbed for the sole reason that the consultant says that no action arises from the aforementioned facts for Master Bonicontrus, as is contained in the consultant’s opinion, thus or otherwise. From this sentence, Master Bonicontrus appealed legitimately. Now, from the premises, it is asked whether, by law, from the aforementioned causes, any action arises for Master Bonicontrus against Master James for the said damage and interest, by which he may proceed against him for the said damage and interest, and act rightly and lawfully against him, and whether the right to sue pertains to him. It therefore pleases your nobility and exalted learning, having first seen the said statutes of the commune of Verona, the libel, the acts, and the proofs on both sides, as well as the opinion of the said consultant and the allegations thereon, having seen them in law, to write and transmit your opinion and allegations sealed with your seal. Moreover, the said Master James of Lazisio, or another in his name, produced against Master Bonicontrus a certain witness, who says that from the month of August 1372 continuously until the feast of Saint Lucy of 1387, he saw Master Bonicontrus standing at the said dyers’ stall selling cloths and exercising his person, and indeed Master Bonicontrus went to Saint Anthony of Vienne and remained on the journey in Master Bonicontrus’s house for a period of twenty-seven days. Now it is asked whether the said witness can be accused of perjury, similarly by him who produced him or by another of them, having regard to the statute of the commune of Verona. And on this, give your opinion as above. Whether

† Whether damages arising from the litigation may be claimed by some form of action after the dispute has been settled, or whether they may not.
