There are various opinions, recited by Cynus in C. de iud. l. sancimus. And indeed, the doctors speak of judicial expenses and judicial damages. But suppose that I had a sequestration made of certain things, which over the course of time have deteriorated in their intrinsic or extrinsic quality, because the price of the things has decreased; am I held liable? The law says that he who, by bringing a vexatious suit in an action for the recovery of property, impedes an action in factum, is liable to his adversary. D. de dolo, l. rem quandam. Another law says that against him who improperly had a sequestration made, relief is afforded by an action for fraud. D. de dolo, l. si oleum. And therefore, since this is a case covered by the law, there is no doubt. And this is true if calumny or fraud is established; as stated in the aforementioned laws. But by what means is it established? Certainly, it is established if the plaintiff proved nothing. But if he had proved it, even by probable presumptions or by one good witness, fraud is presumed to be absent. Hence, the acts speak in this matter, and it is supported by D. de usuris, l. maritus. Consider also whether the time limits are favorable, and whether fraud was expressly or tacitly alleged in the petition, or not, as in l. igitur, D. de lib. causa, which appears from the causes of the libel. On the second point, it must be said,

† Either a false witness was produced entirely on a false article, or on a true one. In the first case, the one who produced him is liable. In the second case, he is not liable, unless he makes use of the deposition of that false witness. C. de falsis, l. si falsos, unless it is proven that he suborned that witness. ff. ad l. Corn. de falsis, l. 1, §. item. And therefore, if the article was true, the said Master Jacobus is not to be blamed, unless he knowingly made use of false attestation. And almost all of this can appear in the records. Likewise, whether it was objected to the praetor or not, is clear from the records. ff. ne vis fiat ei, l. 1, §. hęc uerba. It could also be gathered from the sentences, as in C. de iudiciis, l. rem non nouam, §. fi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the term "mill" includes the millstone, the movable iron, and similar items.
body: I have considered,

Whether a mill is said to contain the millstone, and whether also the movable iron and similar items are said to be contained. For one thing is described as containing, another as being contained. Moreover, I considered this: if the millstone and the iron were said to constitute the form of the mill, then if the usufruct of the mill had been bequeathed to me, it would pertain both to expenses and to the form of the thing. D. de impen. in rebus dotalibus factis, l. 1, §. si. Furthermore, no one would say that a mill is constructed when the millstones have been removed from it; therefore, neither is it destroyed, provided that those things which ought to be attached to the mill, upon which the wheels and millstones revolve, are attached there. For those things which are not attached are rather called instrumental than formal, as in l. granaria, D. de act. empt. And therefore, the qualities of the building must be observed with the eyes. §. ad officium, C. And therefore, regarding the state in which the mill is, this matter, which some say is done and others undone, is better inspected with the eyes and everything reduced to writing; because these tax farmers have come to me, though very reasonably and very discreetly, and they say that it concerns the lord’s revenue. Hence, they will make their statements before the lord. It is necessary to observe this carefully, for they say that according to common usage, this is called a mill. Moreover, that it has been taxed as a mill, and if they were to be changed, they are not to be changed at all. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation causa mortis is void by operation of law if the donee dies before the donor: and what if mention was made of heirs. nu. 8.
2. Whether four witnesses described in the instrument with the clause "and other witnesses" suffice, where the contract requires more than four.
3. Whether a donation causa mortis is deemed revoked by those words of a will revoking all other dispositions.
4. Whether a donation causa mortis is equivalent to a contract, or to a last will, and whether it requires acceptance by the heir.
5. Whether a donation, in which mention is made of death, but with the addition that it cannot be revoked, is considered inter vivos or causa mortis.
6. Whether a statute speaking of a minor comprehends both female and male: and whether speaking of a donation it comprehends both inter vivos and causa mortis.
7. Whether a donation made out of excessive reverence is valid.
8. Whether a donation inter vivos is subject to the deduction of the Falcidian portion.
9. The act of the law succeeds in place of the formal act of a person.
body: The lady Joanna, formerly of Ser Lanfranco of Tarvisio, aged more than twelve and less than fourteen years, made a certain donation to the said Nardo de Nardiis of Tarvisio, receiving for himself and his heirs in this form, namely: by way of a pure, mere, and absolute donation, which is made causa mortis, upon the occurrence of the case of death, and the said Joanna dying without legitimate heirs descending from her; willing that, if it cannot be valid by one donation, it should be valid and ought to be valid by several donations, each of which does not exceed the sum of 500 gold florins. Which donation, made causa mortis, as stated, the said Joanna promised to hold as acceptable and ratified, and in no way to contravene or rescind. And these words were inserted, namely: that she made the said donation pure and irrevocable by any act to be performed by her, unless expressly by a public instrument, expressly and specifically of revocation of the said donation, the said donation was revoked by her; and otherwise, or in any other manner, it is not, nor is it understood, that the present donation is revoked. And similarly she made many other donations. In some instruments there are five witnesses, and in another instrument four witnesses are named; and after them these words are named, namely: and by many other witnesses, however not specified. Then the said Joanna made a testament, in which she instituted other heirs with a derogatory and revocatory clause, in this form, namely: revoking and annulling every other testament and last will. It is proposed that the said Nardo, the donee, died before the said donor, leaving heirs. It is proposed that in the city of Tarvisio there is a certain statute, by which it is provided that if anyone, being more than fourteen years and less than fifteen years of age, sui iuris, was a public merchant, or otherwise acted, did, and contracted commonly as a paterfamilias, who had a general curator, or did not have one, and contracted in any way: or as if: he is bound and sued concerning all contracts, as any person more than twenty-five years of age. The other minors, sui iuris, less than twenty-five years, who do not publicly act or contract as a paterfamilias, although more than twenty-four years, are not bound, nor is anyone for them, even if they have sworn, etc. It is also proposed that the said donation was fortified by an oath. Now, the donor being dead, the heirs of the donee are proceeding on the basis of the aforementioned donation.

But on the other hand, the heirs of the donor say that the said donation was in no way valid for many reasons and causes. And first, whenever the donee dies causa mortis before the donor, the donation is revoked by operation of law, as in Inst. de donat. § 1, and D. si cert. pet. l. Non omnis in principio. But here the donee died causa mortis before the donor; therefore, the donation was as it were lapsed, just as we say in the case of a legacy, as appears from the conjunction of two paragraphs, C. de caducis tollendis § In nouissimo and § Fin. Nor does it matter that mention was made of the heir, because the mention of the heir must be understood according to the subject matter, namely, that this donation causa mortis, once confirmed, passes to the heirs from the person of the deceased, not that a new donation begins from the persons of those heirs, as in C. de actionibus ab herede et contra heredem incipientibus l. 1. And therefore it seems to be required that the day of this donation had arrived and occurred during the life of the deceased, for this donation is made in consideration of merits, and therefore the deceased is considered, not the heir, arg. D. de donationibus causa mortis l. Si filio. But to this it is answered that if a testator leaves a legacy to Titius and his heirs, those heirs are considered to be legatees, as in D. de usufructu accresc. l. Si quis Titio; and to this effect, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. Cui fundus. And this is the first doubt under the ius commune.

The second doubt is whether four witnesses suffice with the addition of "and many other witnesses." And I say that they do: because by those words two other witnesses are signified, therefore six witnesses were present, as in D. de testibus, l. ubi numerus. Nor is it necessary that they were summoned, as in C. de codicillis, l. si, §. in omni. But the contrary is true: because the names of the witnesses must be expressed in the instrument; otherwise the instrument is invalid, as in Auth. de instrumentorum causa et fide, §. sed si instrumenta, and in Auth. de hereditate et Falcidia, §. si vero absunt. For uncertainty vitiates the instrument, as in D. de testamento tutorum, l. duo sunt Titij, and D. de iure fisci, l. ita fidei.

Thirdly, it must be considered whether the aforementioned donation causa mortis is understood to have been expressly revoked by those revocatory words concerning any last will. And it appears that it was: for although a donation causa mortis, in the manner of contracting, approaches more closely to a contract than to a last will, nevertheless, in the ease of revocation, it approaches more closely to a last will than to a contract. Hence, according to certain authorities, a natural action arises from a donation causa mortis, as in the case of a testament, as noted in C. de donationibus causa mortis, l. 1; and as noted there by Cynus and Dominus in l. 1, ff. eodem.

† Moreover, according to certain authorities, the acceptance of the inheritance is required for the confirmation of a donation causa mortis, as stated in the Digest, *De donationibus*, in the law *In mortis*, as glossed by Bartolus. But on this point, say as noted in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, in the law *Etiam*. Moreover, the Falcidian deduction is taken from it, just as from a legacy. Therefore, a donation causa mortis can be called a last will, because it has more similarities with a last will than with a contract, as is fully noted in the Institutes, *De donationibus*, § *Hæc mortis*. Moreover, when it does not appear that another last will preceded, so that these words may have some effect, they seem to be applied to the donation by necessity. But the contrary seems to be the case when it is not merely a last will: then, because the words say "unless expressly," and a special revocation is required, etc. But here there is no special revocation of the donation itself, since no mention is made of it, as in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, in the law *Si quis*, in the beginning, regarding a will.

Fourthly, it must be considered whether the aforementioned donation was a donation causa mortis or inter vivos. It appears that it was inter vivos, because it was agreed that it could not be revoked except in two cases; therefore, only in those two cases is it a donation causa mortis, whereas in all other cases it will be a donation inter vivos, as stated in D. de donationibus causa mortis, l. si alienam, § Marcellus, and l. ubi ita donatur. To the contrary, it seems that these express words state that he donated by a mere donation causa mortis. And it is certain that the act of the parties does not operate beyond their intention, as stated in D. si certum petatur, l. non omnis. Nor does the contrary authority cited present an obstacle, because our case is very dissimilar. For the pact appended here pertains rather to the mode of proof, namely that the express donation must be proved by an instrument specifically mentioning the donation itself, rather than transferring the donation causa mortis to the nature of a donation inter vivos. Furthermore, by this pact, tacit revocation, which occurs by operation of law, is not prohibited. Moreover, this is supported by D. de donationibus causa mortis, l. si alienam, where it is established that what was agreed upon stands, from which it follows that the Falcidian deduction would be made.

Fifthly, it must be considered whether, whether the donation is causa mortis or inter vivos, the statute of the community of Tarasio annuls it. And it seems that it does not, because the law speaks of a male, not of a female: and because it comes to correct the common law, therefore the masculine does not comprehend the feminine, and especially when an oath intervenes. And on this point much has been alleged, fully, elegantly, and whatever can be said. But against this is the truth itself: because the text of the statute says, "the other minors." For if we speak grammatically, to this word, "minor," two articles are proposed, "hic" and "haec." For it is declined as "hic" and "haec minor." Or if we speak legally, as jurists ought to speak, we must not look at the mere figure of the words, but at the intent, as in D. de verb. sign. l. quisquis mihi. There, when it says, "to me Labeo seems to follow the figure of the words, Proculus the intent," and adds, "I do not doubt that Labeo's opinion is not true," as in D. de iur. fis. l. ait diuus. There it says, "we must understand 'quicunque' to include both male and female." And on this, fully noted in l. 1. D. de verb. signi. and C. de ser. fug. l. quicunque. and D. de neg. gest. l. ait prętor. §. haec verba. with countless similar authorities. Therefore, this term, "minor," according to the modes of speaking of the gloss in l. 1. D. de re. iu. is common to male and female, and indeed, because of the weakness of the sex, it is more fitting for a female than for a male, as noted in D. de statu homi. l. in multis. Hence, because this word, "minors," is common to male and female in voice and signification, in intent and reason, there is no doubt that the said statute, as regards the annulment of contracts, comprehends both male and female. Likewise, by the name of contract, it comprehends also donation, both inter vivos and also causa mortis, as in D. de dona. inter vir. et vxo. l. mortis. in prin. which law the gloss introduces to this effect in l. 2. D. de dot. praeleg. and especially when a donation causa mortis has certain pacts which are added to a donation inter vivos, and it is contracted by stipulation: as was the donation in question.

Sixthly, it must be considered: because it is said that the said donation was made out of excessive reverence. And it is true that, if this were established, rescission would be applicable, as noted in l. 1, § quae honorandae, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. But nothing has been proved on this point. It is true that, since donating, especially immovables, is a kind of dissipation, considering also the childish age of the donor, the shrewdness of the donee, and other indicia: there are certain presumptions of extortion and fraud, as noted by the gloss in l. 3, § quid ergo, de contrario iudicio tutelae; nevertheless, from all these presumptions a rescissory judgment could not be rendered, as noted there. I have, however, often seen donations of this kind rescinded by the aid of the praetor, as in l. illicitas, in principio, de officio praesidis, namely when they are donations inter vivos. But when causa mortis, it would not be just to rescind them, just as one does not rescind the wills of adults, as in ff. de liberis legatis, l. Aurelio, § Gal.

Seventhly, and finally, in this question it must be concluded that the said donation, as a donation inter vivos, did not take effect by virtue of the statute. However, regarding a donation causa mortis, there is considerable doubt whether the statute appears to speak, for it acts in such a way that minors are not bound, nor is anyone bound on their behalf. But from a donation causa mortis, they are not bound, nor is anything due on their behalf; since they cannot be sued against their will, nor can their sureties be sued: or, if they are bound, it is revocably, which is not properly to be called being bound, as stated in the Institutes, De obligationibus, in the beginning, although in a broad and improper sense it may be said that they are bound. And thus, it does not obstruct the fact that Cynus, in the last law of the Code, De donationibus causa mortis, does not say so. Therefore, as regards a donation causa mortis, the statute does not speak, but we are in the common law, by which law a donation causa mortis, with the addition of an adult’s oath, is valid: and perhaps even without an oath it is valid as a last will. Similarly, we cannot say that it was revoked, because the form prescribed for revocation was not observed: and this seems to me to be the more correct view, saving that which donation, in which five witnesses did not participate, is not valid, as in the Code, De donationibus causa mortis, the last law. Also, as I said above, I consider this donation to be causa mortis, and especially for this reason, so that the thing may rather be valid than void.

† For if it were between living persons, it would be of no effect, and from such a donation the Falcidian deduction may be taken, just as occurs in the case of a quarter or a half, according to the quality of the heirs making the deduction, as is noted in C. ad l. Falcid. l. in donationibus. And what is said in ff. de tutel. et rationibus distr. l. 1. § 1, and what is noted in ff. ad Trebell. l. 1. § fuerit quaesitus, and C. de in integrum restit. minor. l. si curatorem habens, supports the foregoing. But there remains to me a very strong argument. For, as I have said, this donation is not valid as an inter vivos donation, being impeded by the statute; therefore, it must be said that it is valid in whatever way it can be valid, namely, as a donation causa mortis, at least on account of the oath appended. For when an oath is taken so that the act may be valid, it is valid in whatever way it can be valid, ff. de legat. 2, l. cum pater, § filius matrem. But this is so, if it is valid as a donation causa mortis. And if the donee predeceased, the donation was revoked by operation of law by virtue of the statutory provision, and where the law provides, no other formality is necessary.

† because the fact of law succeeds in place of the solemn act of a man, as in D. de cond. ob causam, l. si pecuniam, § si filium; and D. de manumiss., l. causam, § 1. But to this I answer: because it was acted that it should not be revoked in this manner, hence, since only two cases were specified in the revocation, all other cases appear not to revoke the donation, as in D. de fund. instr., l. quaesitum. Furthermore, I answer regarding one point, that even the mention of the heir is confirmed, although the heir appears to be placed in consequence, as noted in D. de pact., l. si tibi, § si pactum; and D. de verb. oblig., l. stipula ista, § si quis ita. And thus I, Baldus, hold.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when a debtor who tenders payment may demand that a cession be made to him.
2. Whether the benefit of cession may be demanded in the execution of a judgment.
body: Any

† just possessor offering the debt can demand that the actions be assigned to him by the creditor suing by the hypothecary action, as in ff. qui po. in pign. ha. l. mulier. And the reason, according to the Gloss, is because this benefits another and does not harm him, and therefore through the equity of the judge he ought to obtain the assignment. ff. de euic. l. in creditore; ff. de aqua plu. arc. l. 2. §. item varus. But that possessor, although he may offer, cannot however demand that the rights be assigned to him; and therefore with a distinction the lex mulier says 'just possessor'. And so also says Spec. in titu. de ob. et solu. §. 1. versi. illud etiam quaeritur. Moreover, the creditor must assign to the just possessor the personal action; likewise the hypothecary action, if he has any hypothecary action against others. But the right which he does not have, he is not bound to assign, nor on that account is he repelled by an exception: because having to assign would prejudice him, since it would exclude him, which ought not to be. C. ad Velle. l. iubemus. ff. de solu. l. Stichum. §. fin. is not an obstacle, because that applies when the grant arises from a pre-existing contract, while here it arises from another equity. And what Cyn. notes supports this, ff. de pig. l. si domum, and ff. de pact. l. nisi. in glo., and by Dyn. ff. de fideius. and l. Modestinus. de sol., and by Bar. ff. de fideius. l. stipulatus. §. sed ex duobus, and what was noted by Cyn. C. de solu. l. nullo. From the aforesaid it follows that in our case the rights which can be assigned against other possessors must be assigned; but if they cannot be assigned, the plaintiff is not on that account repelled. Otherwise it would follow that if a woman consented to her husband alienating one property and renounced the right of hypothecs, she would be repelled when suing by the hypothecary action against another possessor if he offered the dowry and demanded that the rights be assigned to him, since it is not possible for that to be assigned which she renounced; which is false, because it is contrary to the case of the said l. iubemus. It suffices therefore to assign such rights as one has.

† But if it is asked whether the benefit of assigning actions can be implored in the execution of a judgment, I say that, since this benefit is consecutive upon the right of offering payment, and thus they correspond to each other, it lasts as long as the right of offering lasts, until there is joinder in the suit by lit. contest. or its quasi-equivalent regarding the action on the judgment or the office of the judge. ff. de leg. 1. l. si res obligata; ff. de pet. haer. l. Item veniunt. §. cum praediximus; and by Bart. ff. de sol. l. si quis stipul. fuit 10. in mille; taking into account also the first allegations wisely made. And it must be considered what is subtly touched upon at the end in the understanding of a certain objection. And it is necessary to consider whether the enforcement of the assignment of actions arises at the time of the obligation, and thus after judgment, or when: on account of the rule which is given in ff. de condi. sine causa. l. si fullo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. To what is he who is bound to maintain something liable.
body: Having weighed

† It appears in favor of the buyer that he is not bound by the promise: because every promise made simply, which concerns a thing, ought to be judged and understood as it accords with the thing at the time the obligation was conceived; nor can it be extended to a time of greater or lesser ease, which arises from a great and difficult time, such that it might even be judged impossible. Rather, according to the prevailing and present time, stipulations conceived ought to be understood: as in D. de verb. oblig. l. continuus, § cum quis, ver. non enim. For when a stipulation cannot assume existence or validity according to the present time, it is not extended to a future state of the thing, which cannot occur unless it be difficult, to the point of being considered impossible: it cannot concern that future state of the thing, which is in a manner impossible, so that the stipulation itself may be valid; rather, the stipulation is vitiated, as in the said § cum quis. How, then, in our case, should the stipulation or obligation to maintain the sluice, which according to the present time and the present state of the thing is valid and produces effect, be extended to a future state of the thing that is impossible or so difficult that it appears impossible? Whereas in the said § cum quis, it is rather vitiated than extended. For in the case of the supratitled theme, the changing of the riverbed makes it impossible, or at least so difficult that it can be considered impossible, for the promised act, or the maintenance of the sluice, to merit execution. This supports the aforementioned: because from the words, the more odious interpretation of the disposition ought to be received, rather than that the disposition be vitiated, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. quotiens, and noted in l. quicquid astringendae, facit, D. de reb. dub. l. quotiens. Furthermore, this supports the aforementioned: because whenever a debtor binds himself to an act, there is always in the effect of the promise a condition, unless it is valid from an impassible cause, or entirely difficult, to the point that the promise may be judged in a manner impossible to be kept: in which case he ceases to be bound, as in D. qui sat. cog. l. si, ibi ex concessa causa. Furthermore, this supports it: because every obligation is vitiated if its execution, without fault or delay of the debtor, is reduced to the impossible, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. si homo mortuus, and l. si seruum, § sequitur, and l. si ex legati causa, with similar authorities. For just as the impossible prevents the obligation from arising, so too it terminates it, as in many laws, D. de verb. oblig. l. si homo mortuus. Furthermore, this supports it: because a stipulation or commission made for one case does not encompass another case entirely separate: for the obligation is extended. But in the case of the theme, the buyer did not bind himself except to maintain the sluice. And it is one thing to maintain, i.e., to keep the thing in the state in which it remains; it is another thing to make a new and different sluice. For the interdict which wishes someone to be maintained in possession is for retaining, not for recovering or acquiring possession, as appears in the title Uti possidetis, and in the title Quorum bonorum, etc. Moreover, this promise to maintain the sluice is not a merely potestative promise, but a mixed one: because it also partly depends on chance. For the said buyer cannot maintain the sluice as it is in the river, if the river descends, because the sluice is that which encloses the riverbed and excludes the force of the river from the riverbed: which the sluice cannot do when the river thus changes its bed; because the water cannot be enclosed in the riverbed, and consequently the force of the river cannot usefully or effectively be excluded from the riverbed, as in our case. And it is established in law that nothing is imputed to a debtor who is impeded by chance, which cannot be resisted, so much so that he is released, as in the common laws, which is true especially when the matter concerns an act in the obligation, for then if it fails by chance, nothing is imputed to one wishing to fulfill it, as in C. de necessariis servis, l. si. Furthermore, this supports it: because every promise which concerns a thing concerns one thing according to the state and being of the thing remaining at the time the stipulation was conceived; and another thing according to that state which subsequently occurs, D. de iud. l. stipulatio, and l. seq. Inn. If the state of that which it concerns fails, although it may still be restored, the obligation has failed, as in the said laws. Thus it will be in our case, namely: that because the state of the thing has changed by the changing of the riverbed, the name of the thing does not concern the state of the said buyer; rather, the promise has failed, and he will be released. And so I say and advise, I, Philip of Casoli.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A daughter to whom a dowry has been left, on condition that she marries or enters religion, what should she have if she has done neither?
body: Lord Ubertino of Laudo made his will in the effect of the tenor set forth below, namely: First, he instituted as universal heirs in all his goods and rights the noble Bernabò and Lady Blanchina, his sister, [who are the] son and daughter of the said late Lord Ubertino. Then he added that his last will and intention was that the said Lady Blanchina, his daughter, should have from his goods, in the case in which she contracts marriage with Lord Henry, or Peter, or Padoa, three thousand pounds of Placentine denarii, namely two thousand pounds for the dowry of the said Lady, and one thousand pounds for her paraphernalia. And in the case in which she contracts marriage with any other person, or enters a monastery, that in that case she should have and ought to have only one thousand pounds of Placentine denarii, and not more. And in the said quantities and cases set forth below, and in any one of them, she is and ought to be tacitly satisfied and content by right of the institution of the paternal inheritance, [notwithstanding] the Falcidian and Trebellian shares due by right, the nature of the goods, the right of subsidy, and any other right, nor beyond that anything by any other right, or by any aid of a legacy. Then he ordained that if the said Lady Blanchina should die before carnal or spiritual marriage, that the aforementioned Bernabò should succeed to her, or if her male children survive, granting nevertheless in that case to the said Lady Blanchina leave for her soul of two hundred pounds of Placentine denarii, and not more. He also adds that, being ignorant of his patrimony and assets, he did not wish the said Lady to be able to deduct any Trebellian share; indeed, he forbade that the goods, or possession of those goods, should in any way come to the said Lady Blanchina or her descendants; but he only wished that those goods and possessions of his should be and remain with the said Bernabò and his descendants. The aforementioned will having been made, [the testator] died, leaving the said Bernabò and Lady Blanchina, who, after the will until now, has not been married either temporally or spiritually. And in the goods of her late father, she seeks to be provided with a suitable remedy. From these facts, it is asked, first, what right the aforementioned Lady has, the circumstances being as they are, as they presently stand, in the inheritance and goods of her late father. Second, having seen the right competent to her, it is asked concerning the mode of execution of that right. I take the first,

And conclusively, considering only the truth and justice, we, the undersigned doctors, state and advise that, from the facts set forth above, it is manifestly clear that the dominion over half of the entire inheritance of the said late father has been continued in the said Lady Blanchina, the status of heir being considered. And this is especially so because, although she was first expressly burdened to restore the inheritance universally to the coheir, nevertheless those words of the introductory institution do not alter its nature. But in case of doubt, they import the burden of a universal fideicommissum in the event of the condition left by the said Lady Blanchina to the said Bernabò or his heir, as is proved literally in *l. peto*, in the beginning, in the second response, *ff. de legatis* 2, and *l. fideicommissa*, § *si quis ita*, *ff. de legatis* 3; especially since he prohibited the Trebellianic deduction, which deduction is due solely to the universal heir burdened by a universal fideicommissum: as in *l. 1*, § *inde Neratius*, *ff. ad Trebellianam*, and *l. lex Falcidia*, § *nunquam*, *ff. ad legem Falcidiam*. Therefore, since the condition has not yet occurred, in the meantime she is heir by full right to the said late father for half the portion. Moreover, even if the condition had occurred, because she had married, since the universal fideicommissary, after the inheritance has first been accepted by the burdened party, must take the fideicommissum from the hands of the burdened party through a personal action arising from the will: as in *l. ille a quo*, § *si de testamento*, and *l. 1*, § *de illo*, and *l. facta*, and *l. restituta*, *ff. ad Trebellianam*, and *l. 1*, *C. eodem titulo*. Therefore, although the condition had existed, nevertheless she would remain heir of all the goods for half the portion; however, she could be compelled by Bernabò to restore the fideicommissum, after first deducting the legitimate portion and also the Trebellianic deduction, according to the gloss in *auth. sed cum testator*, which two, joined together, amount to half of half of the entire inheritance. Nor do the words of the will, by which he simply forbids his goods to come to the said Lady Blanchina, seem in any way to deviate from the promises, because from the words which immediately follow, by which he first forbids the Trebellianic deduction, then simply forbids the goods to come to her; and then from the subsequent words, by which he not only forbids her, but also her descendants, so that he might not incur the vice of mutual contradiction, those prohibitive words must necessarily be understood in the case where she would marry, either temporally or spiritually; in which case also the legitimate portion and the Trebellianic deduction would not be prejudiced, which, although the testator wishes to prohibit, he cannot. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person who promises to sell something to another within a specified time, provided he obtains permission, incurs the penalty if he sells it to someone else during that period.
2. Whether a notification that one knows to hold and keep valid, as promised, causes him to incur the penalty for non-fulfillment of the condition regarding permission.
3. If the clause is added that the penalty is incurred as often as the breach occurs, to how many times it extends.
4. The clause appended at the end refers to all the preceding matters.
5. Having premised a certain decree of the illustrious and magnanimous
body: During the time when the Lord, Lord Galeazzo, Viscount of Virtues, etc., was residing in the city of Piacenza, there existed a decree which effectively prohibited the sale of castles and fortifications without the express license of the said Lord, and unless certain solemnities were observed; and if done otherwise, the sale would be annulled by operation of law. It happened that a certain John Manchasola, a citizen of Piacenza, possessed a certain piece of land forming part of one location, having no jurisdiction and no open territory, and absolutely not reduced to any fortification whatsoever. This place, however, is called the Castle of Grazano, and it is so named because it is believed that it was once actually reduced to a fortification and castle, although perhaps no memory of this remains. And since this place was not prohibited from being sold or alienated by any decree of the aforementioned Lord, but could indeed be sold with impunity, both in his own name and on behalf of and in the name of his mother, Lady Francischina, who could also claim rights in the said place and its territory, for whom he promised and solemnly obligated himself to ratify, and that he would see to it and ensure, with effect, that the aforementioned Lady Francischa would ratify and fulfill all things promised in the instrument, with appropriate clauses and renunciations, he promised to the noble men, Lord Lazarus, a knight, and Bernard, brothers of Angussola, in their own names and in the name of their nephew and brother Anthony, to sell all goods and rights which he and his mother, and either of them, have, hold, and possess in the said Castle of Grazano, and in the lands, villages, rights, and jurisdictions, and streams in the said village of Grazano, and Vigozoni, Ulzani, etc., and in the surrounding parts, and all the aforementioned lands, fiefs, and rights which the aforementioned John and his mother, the said Lady Francischina, have, for the price of nine pounds per perch, etc., with a promise of defense, and with clauses and renunciations usually appended to the praise of the wise, etc. And also the aforementioned Lords Lazarus and Bernard, in their own names and that of the said Anthony, promised to buy for the said price. This was done between the contracting parties, with the agreement that the entire said price should be and was to be paid by the said buyers, except for two thousand pounds, for which the said buyers were to receive and acknowledge all the above-sold items as a fief in perpetual emphyteusis from the aforementioned John and his mother, under an annual fief payment of one hundred and twenty Piacentine deniers, at the rate of six pounds per hundred for the remainder of the said two thousand pounds to be paid from the said price. And that the said John was bound, both in his own name and that of his mother, and either of them jointly and severally in the common form to the praise of the wise, to invest the said brothers in emphyteusis for the aforementioned annual fief of all the above-sold items, with a promise of defense, etc. It was also expressly agreed and covenanted between them that whenever the said buyers, or either of them, or to whom or to whomsoever they shall have given within five years, or shall be ready to give, the said John and his mother the said two thousand pounds, that the said John and his mother shall be bound to receive them and to make a sale to the said Angussolas of the said fief of one hundred and twenty pounds, etc., and of everything for which the fief is paid. Then it was agreed and a clause was added that all the aforementioned matters should have and must have place and effect in the case where the aforementioned Angussolas can obtain, it is not said that they obtain, and are able to obtain license from the aforementioned magnificent Lord Count of Virtues to buy all the aforementioned things, notwithstanding the decree of the aforementioned Lord Count currently in force in the said city of Piacenza and prohibiting, considering that no decree is in force which prohibits this sale, as is supposed above, effectively that the sale of castles can be made without the license of the aforementioned Lord. Then it happened that the said John of Manchasolas was summoned before the Podestà of Piacenza at the instance of a certain noble man, let us call him A. When asked if the said John had promised to sell the said castle and the aforementioned things to the said A, and if he had written one letter asserting the said A, written by the own hand of the said John Manchasola before the aforementioned promise to sell to the aforementioned nobles of Angussolas made by the said John Manchasola to the said A, he responded that he had written it with his own hand. From this, the said Lord Podestà of Piacenza commanded the said John that he should sell to the said A. Upon this command being made, the said John and his mother, the said Lady Francis, sold and transferred the said castle and all rights which they had in the castle and in the aforementioned things to the said A. And these sales and all the above-written matters were done several months before Easter of the Resurrection, and thus before the term established for the said parties within which license could be obtained from the aforementioned illustrious Lord of ours that the sale of the said castle could be made, as is contained above in the theme. And then it happened that the said brothers of Angussola, or their legitimately constituted procurator, denounced to the said John Manchasola, and before Easter of the Resurrection, and before the term agreed upon for the license to sell, that the said John should do and see to it for Lady Francis, his mother, for whom he had promised to ratify, and that he should have and approve the said promise to sell as ratified, protesting under penalty, etc., as is more fully contained in the instruments of protestation. The said John fulfilled nothing, nor did he see to it that his mother should ratify, and from these things it is asked, as follows, etc. First, whether the penalty was incurred solely because within the said term of Easter the said John and his mother alienated to them. Second, it is asked whether the penalty was incurred because the said John, having been denounced several times before the said term of Easter established in the contract, or could obtain license to sell from the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count of Virtues, and would see to it and ensure that the said promise to sell was ratified by Lady Francischina, his mother, did nothing. Third, it is asked, with several denunciations made to the said John by the said Angussolas that he should see to it and ensure that his mother should ratify the said promise, and with him fulfilling nothing, how often the penal clause is incurred. Fourth, it is asked, since no license was obtained from the aforementioned illustrious Lord, if the said John, if now required, does not sell, and an offer of the price is made to him according to the form of the promise, whether he will be bound to damages or to the penalty.

† And to the first point, which asks whether, solely because the said John sold within the term of the license, namely Easter, and his mother sold as stated above, a penalty has been incurred or not: in law it seems that it has not, because one cannot be said to act against a promise whose day has not arrived nor passed, since before the day passes no obligation has arisen, as in D. de verb. sign. l. cedere diem. And thus one cannot act against that which does not exist, as in D. de iniur. rupt. test. l. nam sub conditione § rumpendo; D. de iureiur. l. remittit; and D. de verb. oblig. l. decem. But in our case, every promise to sell, and all promises contained in the aforementioned instrument, appear to have been made under a condition, namely: if the license could be obtained from the aforementioned Lord Count. This license was never obtained, as is assumed; therefore, nothing done can be said to be against it, and thus the penalty will not have been incurred; indeed, it seems that it could not even have been incurred, because where there is no delay, as in l. lecta, vers. dicebam, D. si cert. pet.

The contrary view in law appears to be supported, especially because, even assuming to the greatest extent that the said promise was conditional (the truth of which will be declared below), it would still seem probable to say that the promise to sell and to buy made to the said brothers, and by the brothers of Angussola, would be considered committed and purified without any suspicion, if it is due to the debtor that the disposition cannot take effect, or if it is due to the debtor that the condition cannot be fulfilled, since that stipulation is committed against the debtor, through whom it is that the disposition does not take effect, or the condition is not fulfilled. This is the case in conventional stipulation, D. de cond. et demonstr. l. iure civili, and in fin.; D. de verb. oblig. l. in executione, in fin.; and D. de contrah. empt. l. haec vend. and l. Labeo scribit si mihi, to which D. de reg. iur. l. in omnibus causis contributes.

But if we say, without prejudice, that the promise to sell was conditional, as has the argument above first alleged for the contrary party: it was due to the debtor that it did not take effect, or could not take effect, or that the condition could not be fulfilled, which is clear, because, as was first shown above, if the license to sell had been obtained, it would have been useless; since both John himself and his mother, in the meantime, before the condition was fulfilled and before the agreed time had elapsed, had already sold their rights and the castle, and transferred vacant possession to another. Hence, since they had already sold the actions and rights competent to them, and thus transferred useful actions to the said A., they could no longer fulfill their obligations to the said brothers of Angussola; nor could they transfer vacant possession, nor constitute themselves as possessing in the name of the said brothers of Angussola; since they ceased to have the useful actions and possession of the said castle and things, nor could they further grant the said properties in emphyteusis to them; because no one can transfer more right to another than he has himself, as in D. de reg. iur. l. nemo plus iuris. From these it is clear that, considering the state of the thing, and that to which John and his mother had reduced it in the present, which state must be considered, as in l. quod servus, in fin., D. de cond. ob caus. and l. statu lib., D. de statu lib., the license to sell would have been useless, since they could not fulfill what was agreed, and what could not be fulfilled by the agreement in any way.

Furthermore, that this disposition, by the act of John in the meantime, let us say, was reduced to impossibility while the condition was pending, is clear, because those things are impossible to do which cannot be done by law or without crime, D. de cond. instit. l. filius and l. cum quidam. But in the meantime, before Easter, John and his mother, Lady Francisca, sold their rights to the castle to others, namely the said A. The promise to sell could be fulfilled, and to sell lawfully, or to obtain the lawful license of the illustrious Lord Count, as was agreed. And by the said sale to A., the promise to sell and to obtain the license became impossible by law; since they could not sell a thing sold to one to others without the crime of falsehood, which is committed if they sold to two, as in D. de fals. l. qui duobus. Therefore, the thing was reduced to impossibility by them, and by any one of them, John and his mother. And thus the promise to sell is purified to his detriment, since he rendered it impossible, and in favor of the said nobles of Angussola. And thus it was due to John, and by his act, that the true license of sale could not be obtained, and that the promises were not fulfilled. Therefore, he is compelled by this alone to the penalty and to damages. Hence, the first question is resolved, and from this the express response to those things alleged to the contrary is gathered.

† Regarding the second point, however, which asks whether the penalty has been incurred on the ground that: before the aforementioned license was obtained from the illustrious Lord Count by the nobles of Angussola, the said John de Manchasolis was repeatedly denounced, so that he should take care and see to it that the said promise made by John in the name of his mother, concerning the sale etc., should be ratified by the said mother, and he did not do so, etc. It seems according to law that the penalty has not been incurred: because the said promise of ratification, and all other promises contained in the instrument, appear to have been made under the condition: if the license could be obtained from the aforementioned Lord Count, as appears in the words of the instrument, when it is said, “and all these things shall have effect.” For he who says “all” excludes nothing, as in C. man. l. a procu. and ff. de reb. dub. l. si his, qui ducenta. §. vtrum. with similar authorities. And at the time when the said denunciations were made by the illustrious Lord Count, the license had not been obtained, nor was it established that the license could be obtained, and thus it does not seem that the said promise of ratification could have been fulfilled. And thus it seems that by this means the penalty could not be incurred according to law. Nevertheless, in the name of God, I say the contrary.

First, because he who promises and obliges himself to ratify must take care and see to it that the person whose ratification he promises and obliges himself to obtain, shall have it, when he can, as in ff. rem ratam haberi. l. enim. with similar authorities. And if he does not do so, the stipulation is incurred, and what is promised is not fulfilled. Therefore, this John, having been denounced, who had promised that his mother would ratify, ought immediately upon being denounced to have fulfilled and taken care that his mother should ratify his promise. And if he does not do what he ought, and thus the penalty is incurred against him. For since by the convention between them, two times were considered in the promise: namely, the time of the obligation to sell, and the time of fulfilling the promises to sell. And the obligation to sell must precede the time of carrying out and executing the sale, namely, John himself ought to have taken care and seen to it that his mother, in whose name he made the promise to sell, should first ratify it. And from that she should be bound and obligated, before the promise should occur, or exist, or fail. And before the time of executing the promise should arrive, so that there should be a difference between the time of the promise and the execution, which there ought to be, as in l. quod dicimus. C. de solutionibus. And that this is true, let the words of the instrument be observed. For Lord John, in his own name and on behalf of his mother, for whom he promised ratification, promised to sell the castle, rights, and commons, which they have and possess, or which they jointly hold in the villages, etc. And he also promised that he would take care and effect with certainty that the aforementioned his mother would approve, ratify, make, and fulfill all and each of the above-mentioned things. And that she would sell with promises, defending with any other promises, renunciations, and clauses suitable and usually appended, etc. Hence in this promise, we can and must consider it to be the quality and substance of the promise, however it may have been conceived. And this does not depend, nor can it depend: because the essence, or subsistence of the obligation cannot depend, as in ff. de stip. ser. l. vsus fructus. For it is to be present at any time, and thus in the present: because present things cannot depend, nor past things, that they are not, or were not, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. si ad praesens. with similar authorities.

Furthermore, in the promise we can and must consider the content and effect of the promise, or the execution of what is promised, and this can well depend, and can assume dependence from the future, and have it. Just as all dispositions for a certain day and conditional in effect depend: and in execution from a future event, as in ff. de condi. insti. and de condi. et demonst. throughout. and de instit. et substi. throughout C. when. However, this is not the case in our situation, as will appear below at the end of this opinion. Now let us see what the said clause appended in the instrument concerns, and let us repeat the words of the clause, which are formed as follows below. And the aforementioned things shall have effect, and shall have effect, and effect in the case where the aforementioned de Angussola can and are able to have and obtain license from the illustrious prince and magnificent Lord Count of Virtues to purchase the aforementioned things, notwithstanding the decree of our aforementioned magnificent Lord in the city of Piacenza, which is in force and prohibits in effect the sale of castles from being made without the license of our aforementioned magnificent Lord, etc., as contained therein, etc. For from this clause it appears that the quality, or substance of the obligation is not suspended in any way, nor could it be suspended, since it had emanated into being and the nature of things: as has been shown above. But it is the suspension of the execution and effect of the promise itself, as the words of the clause demonstrate, when it is said, “all these things shall have effect, and shall have effect, and effect,” etc. From which it is clear that only those things are suspended by the said clause, if we call them suspended, which concern the place and effect of the execution of the sale and purchase, which is deduced in the promise. Therefore, John ought to have taken care that the promise to sell, which he made in the name of his mother, let us assume that he made it in that name, without prejudice to the truth, under condition, should be ratified by the mother, and thus the event of the condition could purify it, if it were a condition, or thus, that it should be pure, if the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count granted license, or could obtain license. And since he does not do this, the penalty was incurred, and even the promise to resell ought to have been ratified by the mother, before the mother was bound or constrained to sell the rights, as appears from the instrument, which has two times from the contracting parties, namely, the time of the promise, or within which the parties are bound in the promise to sell and to buy. And this was immediately brought into being as to John himself: but as to the mother, it ought to have been brought into being by the ratification of the mother: of which John obligated himself in the instrument, and did not fulfill according to the time of execution of the promise. And this was in no way brought into being by John himself; on the contrary, by him the matter was brought to such a case, that John could no longer bring the execution of his promise into effect. Therefore, the penalty was entirely incurred by him.

Moreover, from the aforementioned words it appears manifestly that the said John promised two things for his mother, first namely, that the promise to sell, which he made in the name of his mother, the mother would ratify. Secondly, that he would take care and see to it that the mother would ratify, approve, make, and enlarge the things written below, which follow in the instrument. Hence the first promise, as to itself and to the promisor himself, did not have, nor could it have, suspension, nor could it be suspended by the clause, all of which are clear from the premises. Hence his doing and fulfilling the promises, of which he secondly promised, that the mother had suspension, or could receive suspension, of which is contained in the instrument from the aforementioned clause. And from this also appears the manifest solution of that which was alleged to the contrary. Moreover, a general clause, which by words comprehending all things looks to all things, operates equally only if it can look to all things by equal reason, as is gathered from C. de libe. praete. l. 1. in fi. But this clause cannot refer to the ratification of the promise to sell, which must precede. l. quod dicimus. C. de solutionibus.

† Regarding the third point, it might seem that if John has been notified a hundred times to take care and see to it that his mother ratifies, and he does not do so, such that he failed each time, a penalty should be incurred against him for each instance due to the words appended in the instrument, which state that the penalty is incurred as often as the contrary is done, the ratification remaining, etc. In support of this, there is what is found in the Digest, *de transactionibus*, *l. qui fideius.* However, in my opinion, the contrary should be said according to law, namely, that the penalty is incurred only twice; because when words multiplying the obligation are introduced into a disposition, they are not verified, nor do they produce their effect of multiplying the obligation, unless in a single act. Digest, *de legatis tertio*, *l. fideicommissa*, § *si quis decem alicui*.

Regarding the fourth point, in which it is asked, assuming that no sentence has been obtained from the illustrious lord, the Count, whether, if the aforementioned nobles make an offer of money or price to the said John, as agreed in the aforementioned instrument, the said John, if he does not sell and transfer, and his rights and actions pertaining to him in the said castle, or does not take care and effectively see to it that his mother, Lady Francischi, cedes and transfers her rights and her actions by reason of the sale, as she promised, is bound to damages or to a new penalty. According to law, it seems that the said John is not bound, because since it is presupposed that the said nobles did not obtain license from the aforementioned illustrious lord Count that the sale of the said castle could be made notwithstanding the said decree, which prohibits alienations of castles and also fortifications from being made without license, etc., of which mention was made above, the said promise to sell and to buy should not have place or effect; because it was expressly agreed between the said nobles of Angussolis and the said John of Marchoasolis, as appears at the end of the instrument, there: "and all these things."

† For since the said clause is placed at the end of many promises made on both sides, it must be referred to all of them, as in D. de lib. et posth. l. si pepercerit, and C. de impub. et aliis subst. l. 1, with similar authorities. Nevertheless, invoking the names of God and the Blessed Virgin, the contrary must be said in law. For, as is assumed, although it is called the Castle of Grazani by common name and usage, perhaps derived from what was formerly said, it is not in fact a castle, nor does it contain any fortification; hence no decree, no statute of the Commune of Piacenza stands in the way of its being sold, nor is there any prohibition. From this it is clear that the aforementioned agreement contained in the said clause is either fulfilled or deemed fulfilled, and ought not to have been fulfilled otherwise.

But it is so, if someone pays a true procurator, unaware that he is a true procurator, so that the procurator causes the payer to be released from the principal, whereby by paying the procurator he obtains release by operation of law. For example, because the procurator has a sufficient mandate, which the payer did not know. And although the procurator does not cause him to be released from the principal any further, he cannot recover from the procurator what has been paid, because that which ought to have been fulfilled is deemed fulfilled: as in D. de cond. indeb. l. si procuratori falso, in the second response noted; to which effect is l. cum quis, § 1, D. de sol. Therefore, the same will apply to a promise conditioned on future performance, namely, that if the cause of performance follows from the beginning, or its effect, that which ought to have been fulfilled from the beginning is absent, so that the promise is strengthened and made effective, since that performance strengthens the obligation, which prevents recovery of what has been paid: as in C. de rer. perm. l. ex placita; D. de praescrip. verb. l. naturalis; and it is noted in D. de cond. ob causam, l. si pecuniam, in princ.

Therefore, the same will apply in our case, namely, that the promise made by John Manchasola to sell to the said brothers of Angussola would have had effect, if until Easter the said brothers had obtained license from the aforementioned illustrious Lord Count that the sale could be made of the said castle, notwithstanding the decree or statute of the Commune of Piacenza, which prohibits the alienation of fortified castles, etc. Namely, that although the said brothers did not procure that the sale could be made, or did not obtain it, nevertheless, because it was not necessary to fulfill this, and the effect, or cause, notwithstanding the statute or decree, followed from the very beginning—because no decree or statute stood in the way of the sale being made of the said named Castle of Grazani, which is not a castle, although it was and is called a fortification from times when perhaps no memory exists to the contrary—and thus the license would be futile and useless, because one would vainly obtain by petition what is granted by common law. And thus the said promise to sell, and all other things that are lacking, which are present and declared above: in law, the promise was and is valid, and not suspended under any future event, as above. And that the sale could have been made without the substance of any decree or statute, the said John cannot deny, who sold and delivered to another, and to the said nobleman afterwards, before the time for obtaining the license had elapsed, etc.

In support of this, it is made that it does not matter whether something is done by man or by law, as in l. fi. si man. ita fuerit aliena. And furthermore, however it is done, this promise seems fulfilled, for we cannot and must not depart from the words, as in l. 1, § si quis navem, de exercit.; l. non aliter, D. de leg. 2. But the words of the clause do not say that all these things shall have effect if license is obtained from the Lord Count. But they say that license could be obtained for selling and buying, since it is of the genus of permitted things. Hence all things seem permitted which are not simply prohibited, as in D. de proc. l. 1, and D. de test. l. 1, in fin. Therefore, it could be obtained; indeed, to that which common law permits, the faculty is said to be granted to each by operation of law, as in D. de acqu. haered. l. Papi, per totum. It is made by l. quo, in fin., D. de cond. instit.

Furthermore, we always look to the minds of both contracting parties in contracts, as in D. de reg. iur. l. semper in stipulationibus; D. de rebus dub. l. in ambiguo, with similar authorities. But from the mind of both contracting parties, namely John, who promised to sell, and the said brothers of Angussola, who promised to buy, it was to be deduced and to revert to the agreement and contract of sale, if the decree of the magnificent Lord, which prohibits the sale of the bought castles, did not stand in the way. And if the decree, which is in force in the County of Piacenza, did not stand in the way, and does not stand in the way, as above assumed in the theme, therefore the sale was pure, and the agreement to sell and buy, according to the mind of the contracting parties, must be judged pure, and is so, as by the said laws.

Furthermore, the said promises to sell and to buy were purely contracted, although a pact was afterwards added, that the said promises should have place and also essence, i.e., place with effect, if license could be obtained, etc. And thus by l. 2, de in diem adiec., they must be considered pure, since no suspensive effect remains, as is clear from the premises; and by this it is established that Lord John did not fulfill what he ought to have done, and that he is liable to the penalty from many headings, and to damages, which is that which is in question.

From the foregoing, all contrary arguments cease in multiple ways. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus. And to this opinion concur the said Paganinus de Sola, the said Philippus de Caso, Bartolus of Padua, the said Signorinus de Homodeis, the said Tadeus de Vicomercato, the said John de Bo, the said Permatth. de Vice, the said Barth. de Sali, the said Pet. Pau. de Treb, the said John de Procelli of Padua, and the learned John, the said ordinary Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One who promises that another will consent or ratify must do so within such a time that what is done may be effective.
body: It seems that action cannot be brought before it is made clear whether the most illustrious [lord] wishes to grant permission or not, as in ff. de verb. obl. l. hoc iure, and ff. de acqui. haere. l. eum qui duobus. §. filius. The contrary seems true: because he who brings it about that the lord cannot consent with propriety incurs the penalty just as he who brings it about that an arbiter cannot arbitrate, as in ff. de verbo. obli. l. si quis arbitratu; for I say that one is unwilling when, hindered by one's own act, one cannot be willing, as noted in l. 1. C. de naturali. lib.

† Likewise, he who promised to make another consent or ratify [must] bring about concerning this such a time that it is effectual, as in l. fi. ff. rem ratam haberi. From which it is concluded that the penalty has been incurred. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a contract is said to be simulated, and especially on account of an agreement to resell.
2. From what the presumption of simulation of a contract is induced, and whether one who swears that the contract is true and not simulated causes it to be presumed simulated.
body: According to these, which are proposed, there seems to be no doubt.

† For the pact that is added for the purpose of resale is a just pact, and it is not presumed to be vitiated or made in fraud of usury; from the sole matters set forth in the case, as C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. 2; ff. de pactis, l. ab emptore; C. plus valere quod agitur, l. ab emptione, and there by Cynus; C. de probat., l. 1, by the same author and others.

† especially, because from the beginning it was sworn that the contract was true and not simulated. For since perjury is not presumed, such an oath must be upheld, unless perjury is clearly proven, or fraud is established by presumptions approved by law, for example, because he promised to sell the thing later at a lower price. And because there had previously been negotiations between the contracting parties regarding an exchange, or other matters are proven which diminish the validity of a true contract, for instance, regarding the fruits of the intervening period to be computed in the price of the repurchase to be made. For from these things, which are not accustomed to be included in ancient contracts nor fall within them according to the nature of the contract, and rather suggest the wickedness of usury, simulation and fraud are presumed. But in our case, no quality of a loan contract is present; but rather one that is true and just; because it appears that the buyer did not wish to profit from the fruits or anything else, because he promised to resell whenever the same price was punctually restored to him, even if it were returned the following day; hence no certain time was set for the repurchase, and thus no advantage was arranged by reason of time. But it was placed absolutely in the power of the seller. And thus the chapter *Ad nostrum* on Sales and Purchases does not stand in the way, nor the chapter *Illo vos* on Pledges, when rightly considered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether money is said to have been received by delegation of the debtor
body: The facts stand thus: In the year of our Lord 1387, on the 8th day of the month of January, Antonio Punis of Perugia and Jacominus, son of the said Antonio, solemnly bound themselves by means of the undersigned public instrument, for the purpose of a loan, to Jacominus de Rampis in the sum of 400 florins, on account of a loan. After this obligation, on the same day and in the same year, the said debtor and creditor came to such a transaction and such an agreement between themselves, namely, that the said Jacominus, the creditor, by an express pact fortified with a solemn stipulation, promised and agreed with the father and sons to pay to the treasurer of the commune of Pavia, receiving in the name of the said commune, every month 175 pounds and 4 solidi, until the Kalends of September next ensuing, for the squadra [contract] for the purchase of bread, wine, and meat of Garlaschini. These may be sold by the said Jacominus, the debtor, for the price of 1,452 pounds, to be given and paid by the said Jacominus, the debtor, from month to month pro rata of each month, for which Jacominus, the auctioneer and debtor, the said Antonio, the father, and Peter, the brother, were sureties. And conversely, the said father and sons, the debtors, and each of them jointly and severally, promised and agreed with the said Jacominus de Rampis, the creditor, that they would not sell, nor make any sale of any places, namely, of the contract for bread, wine, or meat in any place of the said squadra, without the license of the said Jacominus, the creditor. And that all the money which was the price of the sale of those places would be presented and brought by the buyers of those places to the said Jacominus, the creditor. Those moneys ought to be computed by the said Jacominus in those moneys which the said father and sons today, a little before, confessed to have had and received from him as a loan, as appears from the deed of the debt handed over today a little before. After these things, on various days, certain sales were made of certain places of the said squadra by the said father and sons with the license and agreement of the said Jacominus de Rampis, the creditor, for certain prices. And for which sales the buyers promised and agreed, by the will of the said Jacominus de Rampis, the creditor, to pay his creditors, or to give and pay to the said Jacominus himself, according to the pact agreed upon in those sales, within certain terms expressed in that deed. And also certain places of the said squadra were sold by the said Jacominus de Rampis, the creditor. And it is true that some of the said buyers paid the said Jacominus, the creditor, and some, that is, for the greater part, did not pay. After which, the heirs of the said Jacominus de Rampis, the creditor, in the form of a certain statute in force in the city of Pavia, caused a precept to be made and commanded to the said debtors, that they ought to pay the said 1,300 florins by virtue of the said first credit, providing that if anyone appears as a debtor to any tax collector, that a precept be made to him to pay, or that within 15 useful days he must prove whatever he wishes; which term having elapsed, if the debtor has proved nothing, execution shall be made against the said debtor without any other censure. Considering that the said Jacominus de Rampis is the creditor of the same debtors for two causes: one is the cause of a loan, the other is the cause because he bound himself for them in certain quantities and paid for them.

And I say that if there were only the first obligation, it would appear that satisfaction had been rendered to him up to the concurrent amount by means of the delegation of debts. D. 17.1.1 and D. 17.1. inter causas § abesse. But because there is another debt arising from matters belonging to the same contract, this delegation ought rather to diminish the obligation to which it pertains, than an extraneous obligation from which it does not depend nor derive. However, since it has been added that the monies received, which diminish the first debt, must be considered as to whether they are deemed received by way of delegation of debts, not made for that specific purpose, but simply; for if made for that purpose, they ought to be considered as real payment. But because the delegation appears to have been made for another cause, more proximate and immediate, this fictitious payment does not feign anything except with respect to the cause to which it refers: as C. 2.15. si de certa. I say this, retaining also the other prudently made allegations for that party: because the agreement was framed regarding the diminution of the first debt by true and real payment, whereas the agreement does not speak of fictitious payment; therefore, in the fictitious case, we adhere to the common law, which refers it to its origin, that is, to these contracts of the publicani, as if they proceed with a continuous structure. And thus the delegation is referred to the second contract, insofar as an obligation subsists from it, and not to the first. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A libel in which a defamatory action is instituted does not proceed if no time is specified therein.
2. What penalty should be imposed on one who alleges fraud for the purpose of inflicting legal or factual infamy.
body: That the petition produced against Lord Niccolò, Marquis of Palavicino, does not proceed in law, is proved by the reasons set forth below.

And first, because the said petition does not contain the month according to the law on libels. D. de accusationibus and C. de accusationibus, l. in causis. For the laws claim for themselves a place, if fraud is criminally alleged, as D. de iniuriis, l. praetor edixit, § 1, in principio, and D. de dolo, l. item exigitur, where it should be noted,

† But if fraud is alleged with the aim of incurring legal infamy, whether accompanied by the grave infamy of the fact, which bars one from dignities and constitutes the maximum penalty when alleged against someone holding a dignity—for example, against a noble count, as is the case here, since the infamy of the fact is the maximum penalty for a noble, as stated in D. de dolo, l. non debet; whereas for a plebeian or person of low status it would be a minor penalty, or none at all, as stated in C. intra tempus, l. 2. Therefore, whether the allegation is made against the owner with legal infamy, or with both legal and factual infamy, or with factual infamy alone—as in the condition of theft and the interdict *unde vi*, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Caesar; D. de vi et vi armata, l. neque—a time limit must be specified. However, in D. l. libellorum and X. de procuratoribus, c. tuae, this is not required, and this is confirmed by the following reason: because such an action is instituted criminally, as stated in D. de tabulis exhibendis, l. locum, § si quis dolo, and as noted in C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. si quis ad se fundum. Moreover, violence is called a felony, as stated in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. servus, § non in omnibus. Hence, although an arbitrator’s sentence does not inflict legal infamy, it nevertheless inflicts factual infamy among good and serious persons, according to the note in D. de infamibus, l. quid ergo, § ex promissione. Even before an arbitrator, it is necessary that a time limit be specified, since arbitrations are reduced to the model of judicial proceedings, as stated in D. de arbitris, l. 1, and C. de iudicibus, l. rem non novam. And it would be absurd to say that in every accusation, even in a minor matter, a year and month must be specified, but not in this infamous action, which pertains to the atrocity of a crime, as stated in D. de regulis iuris, l. ad ea, and C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. servos. And the foregoing are proven by another reason: it is certain that no exception inflicts infamy, as stated in D. de infamibus, l. Lucius. Hence, infamy ceases in exceptions, except in the exception of procuring, as noted in D. de adulteriis, l. 2, § si publico. And yet, if the exception contains a crime, a specific month must be stated, X. de testibus, cap. praesentiam, lib. 6. It is true that if one did not demand that a time limit be specified, the proceedings might still hold. It is also true that the *speculator* says nothing about time, yet he considers some practical aspect of drafting the libel, and not the subtlety of the law. Moreover, he is rightly compelled to state the time, so that the defendant may deliberate whether he wishes to yield or contest, by argument from those things noted in Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § item verborum; C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam. Moreover, the libel does not proceed for another reason: because in the interdict *unde vi*, the fact of a specific person must be deduced, as stated in D. de vi et vi armata, l. cum ate, and as noted in D. l. licet, § possumus, D. de nauticis, cautionibus, stabulis. But here it is not alleged who ejected, although in the action *quod metus causa* this is not necessary due to the nature of the action itself. Moreover, this libel does not seem to proceed if referred to X. c. saepe, de restitutione spoliati, and to X. c. rem integram, and 2 q. 1, c. in primis, because in those chapters it seems to be required that the thing be occupied with fraud or gross negligence, by argument from D. de abigeis, l. 1, in fine, and l. igitur, de libellis causae. But this is not declared in the libel; therefore, the libel, as vague and general, does not conclude. It is true that regarding the understanding of the said chapter *saepe*, neither Innocentius nor Ioannes Andreas put forward any firm conclusion; but it can be gathered from the glosses of Accursius that a bona fide possessor, who did not succeed in the defect, cannot be sued by any possessory action that takes its origin from a delict, but one must proceed to a petitory action, such as a vindication of the thing or a Publician action. For the possessor has more right by the very fact that he now possesses, and in good faith, than another who merely claims possession, as stated in D. uti possidetis, l. 1, in fine. Otherwise, it would be futile in the said Publician action if possession were called so solely from old possession as if preferable, rather than from that combined with title. And therefore, the text in D. l. si coloni, C. de agris et censibus, lib. 11, requires a defect on the part of the possessor and good faith on the part of the plaintiff in the new possessor. And certainly, if the libel of the plaintiff is considered, this good faith of the plaintiff is not alleged, and therefore the libel seems inept and non-conclusive, as noted in the said l. si coloni. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The cause from which the action arises must be stated in the libellus. And even in a rescript, the cause that would move the prince’s mind to a contrary will must be stated. And no. 2.
body: It must be premised and made evident,

† Wherefore, whenever in a petition or in a conventional agreement such a cause is stated, from which the claim arises and without which the claim does not proceed, the proponent is required to prove that cause; otherwise, he would suffer defeat, as noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, *De Privilegiis*, chapter *Ex parte abbatissae*. And these words of the text are sufficient: Codex, *De Edendo*, law *Finis*, in the word "the origin of the petition is founded." To this effect: Digest, *De Institutione*, law *Habebat*; Digest, *Quod cum eo*, law *Titianus*; and what is noted in Digest, *De Edendo*, law 1, in the principal part, and law *Edita*, with its gloss. And thus it is necessary to prove and to assert the foundation. Therefore, if a cause of this kind is omitted in the supplication or petition, and another is inserted, it is not included even in a real action, unless the cause is expressly stated: as in Codex, *De Petitione Hereditatis*, law *Haereditas materterae*. From these follow two dilations, or conclusions. The first is that the said suppliants must prove fear or simulation. Codex, *Quod Metus Causa*, law *Si per impressionem*; at least by probable and plausible indications, considering the quality of the persons and the quantity of the asserted price, and considering whether the contracting party was in his liberty or not. As in Codex, *Quod Metus Causa*, law 2; Decretals, *Eodem*, chapter 1; Codex, *De Dolo*, law *Dolum ex insidiis*; Digest, *Quod Metus Causa*, law *Non est verisimile*. The second conclusion is that, since in the supplication the cause of the paternal inheritance of the suppliants was expressed, and not the cause of the inheritance of the father of the uncle, it does not seem to be included, especially for the parts of those who repudiated the uncle's inheritance.
