For the said repudiation is deemed to operate retroactively to the time of the death of the person whose inheritance is in question. To this effect: Digest, *Si Certum Petatur*, law *Proinde*. But it would be doubtful whether the whole or a quota of the priest is included. And it seems that the whole, on account of the right of accretion. Digest, *De Inofficioso Testamento*, law *Si non mortis*, § *Finis*; or at least useful, considering the number of suppliants commonly and in common, Digest, *De Re Iudicata*, law *Paulus*; Codex, *Si Plures Una Sententia*, law 1. But this does not seem true: because the right of adition to be consolidated to one is indivisible. Digest, *De Acquisitione Hereditatis*, law *Ex semisse*, and what is noted there. Hence it seems that, since the expression of the cause restricts the writing, Digest, *De Legatis 2*, law *Cum pater*, § *Dulcissimus*; Digest, *De Acquisitione Possessionis*, law *Si is, qui animo*; Digest, *De Re Militari*, law *Milites agrum*; Digest, *De Administratione Tutorum*, law *Ita autem*, in the principal part, nothing of the inheritance of Bartamolo is included in the conclusion of the rescript, although the Emperor, in a real action with an expressly stated cause of ownership, was considered to include every title, as fully noted in Digest, *De Exceptione Rei Iudicatae*, law *Ita et an eadem*, § *Actiones*. Furthermore, assuming that the statute against alienating to clerics were not valid: because clerics and churches enjoy the same privilege,

† However, for the present, with regard to secular clerics, I say, albeit with doubt concerning this matter, which could have moved the prince not to grant contrary to his decree, that it seems that mention should have been made by the petitioner: because perhaps he would not have been so swift in granting; as in C. si contra ius, vel util. publ. l. praescriptione, nisi vel in tacendi fraudem. For it must not be omitted that dying intestate is said to be a certain tacit alienation to agnates. ff. de leg. 2. l. eodem. §. pen. and noted in de verb. oblig. l. si quis ita. §. Seia. I do not speak of one’s own sons, for a father is not said to alienate to them: because they are not aliens, but his own, and masters while the father lives. ff. de lib. et post. l. in suis. C. de impon. luc. descr. l. 1. C. non lic. habitatoribus metropoli. l. 1. C. de usucap. pro empto. l. nihil. Moreover, the lord has the right to have his decree interpreted. ff. de regulis iuris. l. Neratius. and C. de legibus. l. fina. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who publicly exercises the office of a notary should be regarded as a notary.
2. He who denies that a document was written by the hand of such a person is said to allege a forged writing, and he is bound to submit to the penalty of talion.
3. Whether credence should be given to an instrument of a foreign and unknown notary without testimonial letters.
4. Whether a ratification caution removes such exceptions, namely, that this instrument was not drawn up by the hand of a public notary, or similar.
5. Whether a special mandate is required when something is sought to be rescinded.
body: Since the matter has been most fully alleged, I shall proceed to the conclusions in a few words. And first, regarding the first point,

Whether he who publicly exercises the office of a notary public ought to be considered a notary. I say thus: either the question is with him personally, for example because he claims some act as one existing as a notary, and he must prove his title, that is, his privilege. D. de decurionibus, l. Henricus; and l. 2, C. si servus, aut libertus ad decurionatum aspiraverit; lib. 10, C. de fide instrumentorum, l. si non sollemnibus; argumentum in c. 1, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Or the question is about the office between the contracting parties, or between others. And then, if indeed his possession of the office is recent and insufficient, as we say in a similar case, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si qua per calumniam, according to Cynus and Jacobus de Belvisio; for how could the contracting parties, who do not have the notary’s privilege in their possession, produce it? And thus the faith of instruments could be overturned by the lies of the litigants, which is absurd. Indeed, I say more: even if the possession is not long-standing, if he had drawn up some documents in court, it would make him presumed to be a notary, since his person has been approved by the judge. Argumentum, D. quod falso tutor, l. 1, § idem Pomp. Furthermore, if he is of very good reputation, has performed many acts, and has been publicly regarded as a notary in the past, D. ad Macedonianam, l. 4, the judge ought therefore to deliberate on this matter based on presumptions and indications, which suffice where clear proof cannot be obtained. D. de re militari, l. non omnes, § a barbaris. And with this distinction, the laws cited by you for and against are reconciled. Moreover, such an instrument ought to be one from which even the principal could be convicted, if there were doubt about the mandate itself, with the principal denying the mandate; because the instrument of mandate ought to legitimize the person for both parties; otherwise it ought not to be admitted. D. de procuratoribus, l. si procurator absente. It is possible to deny that the letters are not in that hand; nevertheless, a good man would commonly not admit this allegation, because it is presumed in favor of the instrument. “Behold, I write the opinion entrusted to me with my own hand,” someone might say; “it is not written in the hand of Baldus.” If the handwriting were entirely foreign, it would be a good allegation. But if the person is known, it is a frivolous allegation; otherwise, a comparison of handwriting would have to be made in every instrument.
† Moreover, he who denies the pen, says that the writing is false, let him therefore subscribe to the penalty of talion. C. de fidei instrumentis, l. fin.

† This allegation does not please me, nor do prudent men use it, unless the notaries were asserted to be foreign and entirely unknown, as in Auth. de testi. §. si vero ignoti. For such writings are not believed, lest cause and material for fabricating falsehoods be given. C. de fideius. l. quaestionem. Hence, such persons ought to have authentic testimonial letters, or those of their homeland. And thus it would be fitting that this man should have them.

But let us see whether the caution de rato removes all these ambiguities. I answer: yes, insofar as the form of the asserted mandate permits. C. de procur. l. 1. And although Cynus there says that a promise de rato is not valid if it does not state that he will do and procure, according to Petrus, he does not speak the truth in praetorian stipulations. ff. de verb. obli. l. quot quis alium, per Bartolus, because the form given in them suffices so that it may be observed. Moreover, even if it appears that he was constituted for present causes, he is understood to be constituted for actions which are currently available; because actions are the causes of trials, de procu. l. omnium, de impensis, which is said by Dynus.

But doubts remain as to whether, when someone seeks to have something rescinded, a special mandate is required. And I say that it is so, if he seeks to have the act of the principal rescinded; otherwise, if it is the act of a third party. D. de minoribus, l. illud; §. si, D. de in integrum restitutione, l. constitutus. And in all cases where a special mandate is required, a ratification caution is not sufficient, unless the special mandate itself is established by half-proof, and [the party is] bound to swear against calumny; hence judgment cannot be founded thereon. D. de damno infecto, l. qui bona, §. si alieno nomine; C. de iureiurando calumniae, Auth. principales; c. fin., D. de iureiurando calumniae, lib. 6; c. 2, D. de procuratoribus, in Clem. And therefore this power of attorney is not sufficient for proceeding, as one ought to proceed to further stages of the case, as C. de iureiurando calumniae, l. 2, §. hoc etiam huic legi addendum; and note D. de procuratoribus, l. Pomponius, §. sed et his. Finally, it must be concluded that the mandate ought to be drawn up in this manner: because, since if the principal were to deny the mandate, perhaps when the procurator succumbs, the principal himself could be convicted from the same instrument that the matter was ratified, lest the security, etc., be lost, c. 1, D. de probationibus, according to Innocentius. But if there is doubt in the instrument, a ratification caution suffices regarding the matters contained in the instrument, because it makes at least an indication prima facie; but otherwise regarding matters not contained therein, because from the instrument itself it is established that there was no mandate in those things which are contained in it. C. de probationibus, l. ad probanda; C. de procuratoribus, l. maritus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a person, born in one place and having his domicile in another, and possessing property in both, makes a will in the place of his domicile, whether judgment on that will is to be rendered according to the statutes of the place of origin or of the domicile, and thus whether the statute of the place of domicile extends to property situated in either territory.
body: The facts of the case

It is proposed to be as follows, namely: Peter, from the city of Milan, whence he was a native, departed and came to reside in Pavia, and in the city of Pavia with his entire family he dwelt for twenty-four years and more, proximate and continuous, and until his death; there were born to him several sons and daughters by a wife from Pavia, who afterwards succeeded to him, Peter, as hereinafter stated. And this Peter, during the aforesaid time in which he dwelt in Pavia, acquired by title of purchase a house and possessions in the city of Pavia, and also a great part in the city and county of Milan. Then this Peter died in Pavia, leaving several sons and daughters, and having made a will in Pavia, in which he instituted the daughters in dowries, the sons as universal heirs, and also, in the event of the said sons dying without issue, he substituted certain brothers and nephews of the testator, all in one half of the goods, and the other daughters, already provided with dowries, in the other half. The wife of the testator, however, he constituted as dominus, massaria, and usufructuary, as long as she lived in widow’s habit. Afterwards the instituted sons died, and the substitutes from the second codicils entered upon the inheritance, namely, strangers for one half, and the daughters of the testator for the other half. These heirs say that by virtue of such a legacy they are not bound to the said dominus, except to provide sustenance only, principally by reason of the disposition of the underwritten statute of Milan, which exists. It is therefore asked, considering that the said Peter dwelt in Pavia for so long a time, made his will there, and died there, where the said statute is not in force, and that he acquired all immovables in the cities both of Milan and of Pavia while he was residing in Pavia, whether the said dominus ought to have such a legacy with respect to all the goods of the deceased, or at least with respect to the goods left by him in the district of Pavia, or at least with respect to the goods devolved upon the stranger substitutes, as above, notwithstanding the statute of Milan in force, the words of which are these: “If the wife of anyone is constituted by her husband in his last will as dominus, and massaria, and usufructuary, as is the custom, or as dominus only, or massaria only, or usufructuary only, or alternatively: she so constituted shall have nothing from such a legacy, except sustenance according to the capacity and dignity, to be determined at the discretion of the judge.”

If the statute of Milan did not exist, this widow ought to have one half of the sustenance for the share of the daughter, but for the share of the stranger she ought to have the usufruct. For the interpretation of the effect of the legacy varies according to the varying quality of the heirs. For what is established by written custom in the vulgar court, which is today generally observed, in favor of children, is not extended to the favor of stranger heirs, as noted by the learned doctors in *l. Titia*, cum §. *ulti.*, ff. *de legatis* 2. For children are to be treated more mildly by the mother than strangers. ff. *l. de excusatione tutoris*; *l. amicissimos*, §. *Lucius*. Insofar, therefore, as this legacy begins with a stranger heir, we judge of it as of a legacy left by a stranger heir. And therefore the woman ought to have the usufruct of the half pertaining to that stranger. And this is true when the legacy is not considered as one, but as several, and thus the day and condition pass differently; because I said “as long as,” etc. But if it is one legacy made to the wife during her life without division and multiplication, and then the beginning is inspected, and the interpretation of the legacy never varies, since it is uniform in the mind of the testator, as I said in *l. 2.*, C. *si secundo nupserit mulier*; and thus holds Bartolus. And observe well that it is not my custom to vary, but you, the inspector, weigh the terms upon which I speak, if you please; nor are the sons objected against the mother in this matter; because as regards the share of the stranger, they have no right to oppose, since it does not concern them to obstruct the mother in that part in which they do not succeed, arg. ff. *de contrahenda tutela*, *l. si post mortem*, §. *liber*. Certainly this usufruct of the whole half will not be deducted from the mother, unless the accumulation of other legacies would induce the Falcidian deduction. And the reason is, because the ownership of this half of the inheritance is equivalent to a full quarter, as noted in *l. uxori*, *de usufructu legato*.

There remains now a doubt on account of the statute of Milan, which provides that from such a legacy the wife ought not to have except sustenance: whether this statute is drawn to goods existing in Pavia. And from what is said by Bartolus in *l. cunctos populos*, it seems to be said that yes, for he says that this statute is favorable, lest they despoil each other by mutual love, and therefore it is extended to goods placed in any territory, from which the statute provides between subject persons. That said is not true, but altogether erroneous. For a statute which excludes anyone from the common law is always odious, unless it is expressed in the statute that a person is to be included who deserves the favor of princes from some equity. Moreover, a stranger heir is not of this kind, as *l. maximum vitium*, C. *de liberis praeteritis vel exheredatis*. Also, this statute comes more to the interpretation of the will, i.e., to a restrictive, interpretive, indeed constitutive interpretation. For it provides as if to the hatred or favor of anyone, whoever he may be; nor is the saying of Bartolus true in a last will, nor the reason thereof, because the legacy is conferred at a time when the marriage does not endure, nor does the legator become poorer. And therefore the legacy between spouses is valid, as is known, especially to the doctors.

Solving therefore the proposed question, I say that the statute of Milan, which limits the acquisition to be made by virtue of the said legacy, has place in its own goods in the territory and jurisdiction of Milan. But in Pavia the general custom will be observed, since the general custom is observed in Pavia. And therefore the daughter is not bound to one half of the quantity of sustenance with respect to the whole of her part. But how will the stranger heir be bound? Will he be burdened in providing the other half part of sustenance from the revenues of Milan, and furthermore the usufruct of his share of the Pavian goods, so that he may be burdened by a double prestation, which certainly would seem inconvenient? And this inconvenience regards only the stranger heir. Perhaps it will be done thus: suppose that the goods of this stranger’s portion, which are in Pavia, are worth 300, and those of Milan 100. Proportionally he will have sustenance and usufruct, namely, on account of the goods of Milan, one third of the half quantity of sustenance, and two thirds the usufruct of the Pavian goods. And in this difficulty, two qualities of heirs do not introduce two patrimonies and two laws. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a father instituted as heir a posthumous child to be born from his pregnant wife, and substituted strangers to that child, but left the wife as dominus (owner) and usufructuary as long as she remained in widowhood, then, upon the birth of the posthumous child, and subsequently his death, and the substitutes entering into the inheritance, what is due to the wife?
body: Nicolaus Tuderti instituted as universal heir the posthumous child to be born from his wife, Monaldutia, and to this same posthumous child he made a pupillary substitution of outsiders, and he left his wife, the lady, as owner and usufructuary of his goods, provided she maintained her widowhood. It happened that the posthumous child was born, and having accepted his father’s inheritance, he died, and the substitute under the second will accepted the inheritance.

† It is asked what the said lady ought to have by virtue of the said bequest. And omitting the opinion of Dy. and others, who say that the said words import that the said lady has the choice whether to choose dominion or usufruct, according to l. si quis Titio, ff. de usufr. leg., as Dy. notes in l. Titia, §. si, ff. de leg. 2, and Cy. in l. 1, C. si secundo nupserit mulier. And taking as true the opinion that custom observes, namely, that children instituted by virtue of the said words have only alimony for the wife, but otherwise in the case of strangers instituted, as noted by the gloss in C. si secundo nupserit mulier, l. 1. Now it creates doubt in the question: because at the beginning the son was instituted heir here, but now a stranger is heir, which of these we must examine. And it seems that this legacy is judged from the person of the son: because it began to be due from his person, and thus the substitute ought not to be bound to more than the son himself is bound, as l. qui fundum, §. qui filium, ff. ad l. Fal., and de leg. 1, l. si fundus sub conditione, §. si pater. On the contrary it seems, and this is the truth: because they ought to be due from the person of the substitute for the following years. For such a legacy is an annual legacy, which is clear from the condition "until," ff. de ann. leg., l. leg., and de leg. 3, l. qui concubinam, §. uxori. But it is established that annual legacies are for the most part conditional for the first year and the following ones, as l. cum in annis, ff. de ann. leg., and l. si in annos, ff. quando dies leg. ce., and thus we must examine the beginning of each year: as d. l. cum annos, and l. senatus, in fi., ff. de don. cau. mort. Since therefore for the following years it begins to be due from the person of the stranger substitute: as d. l. si fundum sub conditione, §. si pater., therefore it ought to be adjudged from his person, so that it is at least fully usufructuary: as l. uxori meae, C. de usufruc. leg. Bart. To the same effect. Lord Bal. de Perus. in Auth. hoc locum, super l. 1, C. si secundo nupserit mulier, in the gloss there "alimenta." It is true that children are extant, and thus custom interprets such a testament. But when children are not extant, she ought to have usufruct: because the word "domina" does not refer to them, but to the person, and lest the testator be contrary to himself. Nor does it import dominion, but administration of fact: as l. i., ff. rerum amo., de annu leg., l. qui unico, de publica., l. cum se exhibuissent, per Jac., ff. de ver. sig., l. pronuntiatio, per the same, ff. man., l. creditor, §. Lucius, in glo. 1. praedicta. For when the testator did not leave her domina of all things, but of a certain thing: then the interpretation of custom has no place, but we adhere to the signification of the words, as d. l. si Titii fundum. But what if, at the time of the testament, he had children, and they died, and strangers succeeded: say, thus, that the interpretation does not change: because it is interpreted etc., as ff. de lihoc no. Dy. in l. Titia, cum testamento, §. si, ff. de leg. 2.

Case of the following counsel. War arose, and the matter of the question between Lucius the plaintiff, and Maevius the defendant, on account of a fief and homage: to which Lucius asserted that the said Maevius was bound to him for a certain castle, which he held from the same Lucius in fief, and under homage and ligeance, while Lucius the plaintiff was ready to make war against the said Maevius for obtaining his right. A certain greater prince and king, requested both by his son asserting that he was prior in time in the fief and homage of the said castle by his right, and by the said Maevius the defendant: at their request, he caused the king's banner to be placed upon the said castle. Then the said Lucius the plaintiff, not under the king's dominion, although a man and vassal of the same, yet not by reason of the fief of which it is here treated, was requested on behalf of the said king that he abstain from war and offense against Maevius: but that the same Lucius would submit to the king's cognition regarding the matter of the said war and question. Who Lucius responded by a certain letter of his, which was directed to a certain official of the said king, as follows subsequently.

Responsive Letters. Most dear friend, we have received and heard the gracious letters which were reported on your part by Lords Peter and Jac., through whom, if the notification and request proceeded by royal consent, that was from the information of someone who was silent about our rights: wherefore we are certain that if the royal majesty had been informed, or reminded of our right, he would not have proceeded so much to our prejudice as he did: and also he would not have had such intimations made to us. And although we well know the great prejudice that arises therefrom to us: nevertheless, because with our whole heart we desire to serve, obey, and please our lord the king, if it is so that you are certain that our adversary will personally present himself before the royal majesty, where he will be, or before you within your territory to answer for us, and to give an account of those things which we shall say and ask against him in one brief term: we will be in that term before our lord the king, or before you, to receive an account from him, and to give an account to him of those things which he will wish to say or ask against us: we offering to you to send our son as hostages, until we present ourselves before the said lord our king, or before you. And we will cease from all offenses and wars to be inflicted on our said adversary in that case, unless other new matters arise for us from the parts of the kingdom. And if it were so, that it pleases you more, to come to these parts before the said term to receive under your conduct our said adversary, and to lead him before the king in your land before you. We ourselves would come with you before the said lord our king, or before you, to take and give an account, as above. And in the case where you would not be well certain by anything else than by words, or letters, or by hostage, of representing his person: we beg you, that it not displease you, if we proceed against our adversary according to our proposal, and if God helps us, it seems to us that if he refuses to present himself before our lord the king, or before you, who represents his person, it ought not to displease the king, if we procure our right against our adversary as best we can. And although we offer to receive an account from him before our lord, or before you, this is not on account of any homage to which he is bound to the king Dauphin: because we do not hold him for such, but we do it only for the honor and reverence of our said lord the king, to whom we are, and will be, true, legal, and obedient in all times of our life. And you wish to write back to us on these matters within the next 12 days: because thus we have agreed with the said Lords Peter and Jac., your ambassadors.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A petition of the prince is a certain species of violent commanding.
2. I submit myself to the cognition, etc. What do these words import? And what is it to submit, and how it is done, and with what words, and whether it appears to have been made as to a judge, arbitrator, or mediator, or in what manner, and no. 4.
3. Whether one who submits himself to the cognition is understood to submit himself to the decision.
4. A compromise expires upon the death of the arbitrator, or of the compromitter.
5. When power is seen to be attributed to dignity, or to a person: and when it expires.
6. Whether a proper name, or an appellative, is to be considered.
7. The word "our," what it imports.
8. No one can be a judge in his own cause.
9. A vassal cannot prorogue the jurisdiction of another judge without the license and consent of the lord.
10. Whether a sentence passed by the king can be ordered to be executed outside his territory.
body: Beginning from the head, in accordance with the rule that a reason must be deduced from its head, as stated in the Digest, *De edendo*, law *Argentarius*, section *Rationem*; and because it is written that subjects are such as the predicates demonstrate, as stated in the Digest, *De interrogationibus et actionibus*, law *Si defensor*, section 1; and because the mind of the respondent is referred to the questions asked, as stated in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law 1, section *Si quis simpliciter*; and because the subsequent event is formed from the beginning of the title, as stated in the Code, *De impositione lucrativa descriptione*, law 1, book 10. Therefore, it must be examined what is presupposed in the theme, namely, that the Count himself ought to submit himself to the cognition of the king regarding the matter of that war and question. And it must be considered that the king does not make this request on the ground of jurisdiction, since these are words of deprecation, and not of power or compulsion, as stated in the Digest, *De legibus*, book 2, law *Peto*, in the beginning; and in the Digest, *De usufructu legato*, law *Generaliter*, in the beginning. By these words, however, the king’s majesty is not signified, but rather the person in majesty.

And although to request the duke is a species of violent commanding, yet here, as he said only to the prince, and also as it was fitting according to law, he wrote rather by exhortation than by imperious speech, as in the Extravagant Decretals, On Greater and Obedience, chapter Humilis. For he did not say that the prince was drawing the cause, which was not his own, to himself, except with the consent of the parties, and of such consent as would show the perseverance of the mind, as in the Digest, On the Law of All Judges, law Si convenit. For as long as one can be recused according to law as suspected, so long can he be declined, and not afterwards, as in the Digest, On Judges, law Sed et si susceperit. But the lord king wrote, as has been said, with these words, that he wished to submit himself to the cognition. From which words two doubts arise. For first it must be declared, what is meant by the word "submit."

Secondly, what is said regarding cognition. For the word "to submit" appears equivocal. For he who submits himself to an arbitrator may be said to submit himself; and he who submits to a judge by prorogation is said to submit himself: as in D. de iudiciis, l. 1; and he who submits himself in such a way that he cannot bring an action is much more strongly said to submit himself, as in D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. est receptum. But because submission to an arbitrator for one's own utility is highly contemptible: as in C. de arbitris, l. 1, therefore, considering the quality of the person of the said king, it is not likely that the said king consented to an illusory submission, but to a most efficacious one, and to that which is called submission from pre-dominance. Thus words are to be understood so that they accord with persons: as in D. de uso et habitatio, l. plenum, § aequitii; and D. de legatis tertio, l. item in legato, § per vim; and l. si filiae; D. de auro et argento legato, l. Titia, § fi.

It remains to be considered regarding the word “cognition,” whether one who submits himself to cognition is understood to commit himself to the decision. And it seems that he is not: because to cognize and to define are separate, both from each other and with respect to the mind of the law. And when one of the separated things is conceded, the other is not thereby conceded: as in C. *Ubi senatores, vel clarissimi*, l. *Quotiens*; and C. *De falsis*, l. *Ubi*; and what is noted in c. *Auditor*, *De rescriptis*, in the Clementines.

To the contrary it seems: because cognition carries judgment with it, and just as the former leads to the existence of the latter: as in C. *Si contra ius, vel utilitatem publicam*, l. *Et si non cognitio*; and D. *De iudiciis*, l. *De qua re*, so that the subject matter of the cause is not divided, as in C. *De iudicibus*, l. *Nulli*; on this point, D. *De procuratoribus*, l. *Qui procuratorem dat*. But because it is not probable that the Lord King meant only cognition, but rather the effect of cognition: because words are to be taken with their effect, and the effect of judgment is that which is final, or that which is best. It is a definitive sentence, whether well or ill pronounced, as in D. *De appellationibus*, l. 1, in the principle. The same is to be presumed, that the Prince meant only the sentence, lest his cognition be in vain if it did not have a termination. C. *De episcopis et clericis audiendis*, l. *Episcopa*.

Furthermore, because the instance of judgment is indivisible, and is a certain integral thing comprehending in itself beginning, middle, and end. For these three are inseparable, just as the soul to the body. For the soul of judgment can be called the definitive sentence: because it is the final formal perfection. But just as it is true that an indefinite response is referred to the questions asked, so also it is true that where a difference can be noted, saving the reason of right speech, and between the effect of the interrogation and the effect of the response, it is not understood that a response has been given to the questions asked: as in D. *De verbis obligatis*, l. 1, § *Cum adiciat*.

Now therefore let us see regarding the consonance or dissonance of the response, or of the letters of remission. And it is well true that at the end of the letters are these words, that we are, and will be, true, legal, and obedient in all times of our life. Hence from those words “obedient,” it seems to be inferred a response, according to the letter of remission. But weigh what he says, “of our life,” to that which I shall say below. Also weigh that these are general words, which oblige and delight the ears, as in C. *Quod cum eo*, l. *Si*. Also from those which follow, it will appear whether there is conformity or disformity of the letters of remission and the response: because the foundation lies in the letters transmitted to the Illustrious King of the French, who then reigned, by the Illustrious Prince, the Lord Count of Savoy, who then lived.

It must be considered first whether the said letters indicate a compromise to the said Lord King, or rather indicate a prorogation of jurisdiction, or a certain submission, which is similar: yet it is greater than a prorogation, when one prince submits himself to another regarding a certain case. And indeed, the question is common, whether in doubt a compromise or a prorogation of jurisdiction is presumed. For the gloss, which is in l. 1, D. de iudicibus, says that this can be weighed from those things which preceded between them: but if no preceding matters appear, it says that if a penalty is found to have been promised, he is presumed to be an arbitrator; because in compromises penalties are accustomed to be appointed. But if this does not appear, he is presumed to be an ordinary judge, if otherwise he is a judge, so that the matter may be more valid. But if otherwise he does not have jurisdiction, the gloss holds that he should be considered an arbitrator, a gloss which Cynus holds, referring to it itself, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Si qui ex consensu, in fine. The older translators before Accursius, however, said that the aforementioned is true according to the mind of the law, when the matter could be valid in either way. But a compromise cannot be valid as to an arbitrator; then it seems to be a compromise to a counselor, or a transactor, and a composer of the lawsuit, which the gloss also holds in l. Sed in servum, §. Sed si iudex, D. de arbitris. And let us conclude that either the mind of the parties is established, and the mind of the litigants is followed, or the mind of the parties is not established: and then we adhere to the mind of the law, which presumes the act in the manner in which it is accustomed to be done, and in the manner more apt for the validation of the act. To this also contributes what is noted in a similar case in l. Huiusmodi, in principio, D. de legibus 1. For contracts by custom assume a certain tacit form, as C. de fideiussoribus, l. Si. Let us therefore see and weigh first the words of the letter. The words say in the preface, and notification, and request for the consent of the king, etc. Therefore, the notification and request should be examined, whether it was amicable, or whether it was rigorous under the pretext of royal Empire. Also, whether it emanated by way of threat, or by way of narration, or by way of demonstration. For it seems to be said that if the said letters had emanated by threats of the Lord King, or by fear of a greater evil to placate the king, certainly no jurisdiction would have been prorogated; because consent would not properly have been given. For the perfection of will consists in free choice: where there is fear falling upon the most steadfast man, there a prorogation of jurisdiction does not bind, as D. de iudicibus, l. 2, in principio. It is true that there is a certain word to be weighed there: namely, "resisted." For that preamble, i.e., to resist and detest, is an expression of dissent, and a manifestation of fear. But I hold that this is not necessary: provided that otherwise fear is established: without which he would not otherwise have done it, as fully noted by Bartolus in l. De pupillo, §. Si quis ipsi praetori, D. de noxia actione, num. But this allegation does not seem to apply to our proposition because of the words of the letter, which say, "we desire to serve, obey, and please our Lord King." These words manifestly show the good pleasure of the will, as in c. Cupientes, de electionibus, lib. 6. And therefore we must pass to another reason. For the words of the letter say, "let us come before our Lord King, or before you, for taking and making an account, as above and below." It adds, "and although we offer to receive an account of him before the said Lord King, or you: we do this only for the honor and reverence of our said Lord King." And I say that these words, "for taking and making an account," confer no jurisdiction to the king by their own force of speech: but our Lord King is assumed as a certain third party outside the litigants, not as a judge or arbitrator, but as a person whose authority is to be obeyed, and by such words power is not conferred upon the Lord King, except to inform himself, but not so that he may know by way of dispute, nor that he may pass any sentence. But he may, and must, urge the parties to obey his judgment, i.e., discretion. To this contributes what is noted in Speculum, de arbitris, §. Sequitur, verb. Licet numquid iste tertius, where this is expressly determined. Moreover, one must not depart from the signification of words, as D. de legibus 3, l. Non aliter. But the words of the letter say, "for taking and making an account before the king." But it is one thing to do before the king, another to do by the king, as D. de verbis significatis, l. Coram; and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Si quis mihi bona, §. Si coram; and D. de arbitris, l. Diem proferre, §. Coram. For this seems to have been said rather so that, out of reverence for the king, they may be drawn to the will of the king, than that he has subjected himself to his jurisdiction. Argument in ratione sui, D. de arbitris, l. Sicuti. For to submit oneself to another is most prejudicial, as D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Est receptum. And therefore this should not be presumed, unless the words allow it. But this allegation seems to be opposed by the fact that he who promises to do or pay something before a judge, which is executory of a certain debt, draws the whole matter there. For there it is said that a contract is celebrated by reason of the destined payment, as D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Contraxisse; D. de bonis auctoris iudicis possessis, l. Si servus; D. de solutionibus, l. Quaero; D. de deposito, l. Lucius. But to this I answer: because the words of the letter are not directed to the adversary, therefore nothing is contracted with him, as D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Consensu; and l. Ex maleficiis, §. Longe minus, eodem titulo; and what is noted D. de contrahenda emptio, l. 1, in fine; and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1; and C. de donationibus, l. Nec ambigui; and D. de donationibus causa mortis, l. Inter morientes; and what is noted in l. Huiusmodi, in principio, D. de legibus 1. For in contracts it matters with whom one speaks, although otherwise in last will, as D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, §. Dona. From these things, therefore, it seems to be inferred that the said Lord King was assumed neither as a judge nor as an arbitrator: but as a simple auditor of the parties: to the end that he may reconcile the parties by the good pleasure of the parties, but not that from this he assumes Empire between the parties: because the words do not say this, and the mind is not otherwise established: although perhaps there was a fuller mind than the words sound, as D. de verbis obligatis, l. Quicquid astringendae; and D. de supellectili legato, l. Labeo, §. Idem Tubero; and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Si servum, §. Non dixit. And because the aforementioned seem true, this conclusion follows, that the sentence of the Lord King was null by the law itself, as issued by a non-competent tribunal, as C. si a non competenti iudice, per totum. And the aforementioned are confirmed: because the words of the letter say, "before the king, or before us." For the word "us" is a personal word, and the personality of one induces personality in any of the extremes, as in §. Si ex altera; and argument C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. Cum solum. Because one and the same thing should not be judged by different law, as D. de usucapione, l. Eum, qui aedes. Also, by another reason, the said sentence does not subsist by law. For either the Lord King was assumed as an arbitrator, or as an arbiter aequitatis, or as a judge, or as a certain good man auditor of the parties, as I said.

† If indeed he was elected as an arbitrator, the compromise expired upon the death of the party who submitted to arbitration, as stated in the Digest, title *De arbitris*, law *Diem proferre*, section *Si heredes*, and law *Si interpellat*, section *Si ab altera*. Likewise, it expired upon the death of the arbitrator, as in the Digest, title *De arbitris*, law *In compromissis*, and by argument from the Digest, title *De cura furiosi*, law *Cuius bonis*, and what is noted in a similar case in the Digest, title *De tutel*, law *Tutela*. And in the same way, the arbitral authority expires upon the death of the arbitrator, as in the Digest, title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Multae non committitur*, in the beginning. Or if the lord king was appointed as judge by prorogation or submission, then likewise I say that the prorogation or submission expires upon the death of the king.

† For the sake of understanding, it must be known that certain things pertain to the person in dignity, such that the person is the immediate cause, while the dignity is the remote cause. Other things, however, pertain principally to the dignity: and because the dignity informs its subject, they pertain to the person; for the dignity without the person does nothing. In the first place, when the person, who was the final subject of the act, is extinguished, the pending act itself expires; because the person makes room for the act, as in C. de caducis tollendis § ne autem, and D. de solutionibus l. inter artifices. And therefore, whatever pertains to individual faith and diligence, as singular possessions of the mind, are annihilated by death and are not transmitted. Hence, no one transmits faith and diligence. In the second place, those things which pertain to the dignity primarily and to the person placed in dignity secondarily, and in this manner, it is necessary, because, as I said, jurisdiction without a person does nothing, as in D. de origine iuris l. 2 § post originem iuris. There we consider the dignity as principal and the person as instrumental. Hence, the foundation of the act is the dignity itself, which is perpetual, as in Extra de officio delegati c. quoniam abbas. Now, in our case, it must be seen whether any power was attributed to the lord king, and whether his proper person was the final and immediate cause of the attribution, or the dignity, or both comprehensively and simultaneously. And it seems that it is the dignity; because the proper name was not expressed, as in the aforementioned c. quoniam abbas, and D. de stipulationibus servorum l. communis servus, and as we have in D. de pactis l. tale pactum § si, and D. de iure omnium iudicum l. et quia in the final gloss. But here it must be observed: for those who say this seem to follow the figure of the words. We, however, ought rather to look to the intent, as in D. de verborum significatione l. quisquis mihi. For the intent is established more by reason than by words, as in D. de pactis l. iuris gentium § pactorum.

And therefore, whether we consider the proper name or the appellative, it must be said that either the thing can be valid in both ways uniformly, or non-uniformly; or it can be valid in one way and not in the other. In the first case there is no question, since it is valid uniformly. In the second case, make a sub-distinction: either the intention of the speaker is established, and we adhere to the intention; or the intention of the speaker is not established, and then either the appellative name is expressed, and yet we follow that; or only the proper name, and we follow the proper name; or both are expressed, and we follow that which is named first. And these are proven in the aforementioned law *Si communis servus*, and in law 1, *De contractibus iudicum*, and law 1, C. *De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*, and others, and in D. *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Quotiens*, and law *Non unquam*. In the third case, it is valid in the manner in which it can be valid, as in D. *De pactis*, law *Si unus*, § *Finis*, and there by Guillaume de Cuyck, and in D. *De legatis tertio*, law *Legatum si sic*.

But if any authority is granted by a mixed reason of person and dignity, it expires with the person, because one does not subsist without the other. For those things which take their form and origin from a mixture, when the mixture is resolved in part, lose their essence, because they are deprived of the form of the mixture. As is evident in pupillary substitution, which consists partly of fatherhood and partly of power, for it is dissolved by emancipation. And the same is true of all things which consist of a mixture of certain qualities, as in D. *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, law *Moribus*, and in D. *De legatis primo*, law *Titiae textores*.

From this theoretical principle, therefore, the solution of the question is clear. For, assuming that this was a prorogation of jurisdiction or an inviolable submission, nevertheless, by the words of the letter, it was addressed to the king then present, and by the mind of the Lord Count, the fidelity and diligence of the person were chosen. Therefore, the authority and its bond ended with the death of the king. That the words are restricted to the king then present is clear from the words of the letter, where it says, "to our lord the king."

For that phrase, "our," designates the present king, not a future one, as is stated in D. de aureo et argenteo legato, l. si ita; and D. de legatis 1, l. Stichum, qui meus erit; and D. de verbis obligatis, l. quod stipulamur; and l. si a colono. Moreover, the intention of the writer appears evident. For he says thus: "We do this solely for the honor and reverence of our said lord the king." Therefore, he referred honor and reverence not to the dignity, but to the person; because he did not say "for the honor of the king and majesty," but "for the honor of the King"; for these words are personal and proceed from good faith, as in D. de legatis 2, l. unum ex familia, § item Imperator Marcus. Hence, the lord count ought not to be deceived, who presumed more favorably concerning the king then reigning. Furthermore, if the reason of good faith had been mixed, whether placed in the person or in the dignity, it would have been extinguished by the death of one of the connected parties, without whom it would not have been granted from the beginning, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. si ita, § regula. We have therefore considered the quality of royal power and its expiration having regard to the personal aspect. Now let us proceed to other considerations, by virtue of which it will appear more clearly than light that the said sentence of the lord king was in no way valid.

† And first, because since the lord king possesses the Dauphiné, and he himself is both king and Dauphin, he cannot judge in a case concerning the Dauphiné. First, because the case is his own, as in C. ne quis in sua causa, l. 1. Second, because a personal distinction is required between the parties and the judge: for judgment is an act of three persons, namely the judge, the plaintiff, and the defendant, as in extra de verbo signi, c. forus. Hence, the legal proceeding is vitiated if the three persons are confused with one another, or two of them. Third, because the law expressly determines this, ff. de iudic., l. si alter ex eis litigat. For when the matter reaches that point from which it cannot proceed, another remedy of rescission is necessary. Indeed, such a case consumes the matter itself, to which it has now come; or rather, the impossibility of law consumes it.

Secondly, by another principal reason: because the castles in question are feudal holdings of the Lord Emperor himself, the jurisdiction over the castles cannot, as a matter of law, be compromised without the Emperor’s license, nor can jurisdiction be prorogated to the King’s domain. It is established that the Lord Count is a vassal of the Empire. Furthermore, those castles are within the territory of the Empire, from which they originate, and are presumed to be feudal, as is proven and noted in column 10 of the chapter *Imperiale*, § *praeterea*, in the title *De prohibita feudi alienatione*. This is fully noted by Innocentius in the extrajudicial chapter *Caeterum* under the title *De iudiciis*, and by Bartolus in the Digest, title *De novi operis nuntiatione*, law 1, § *et post operis*. Just as a fief cannot be alienated by contract, so too it cannot be alienated by prorogated jurisdiction; otherwise, lawsuits could easily be fabricated, and the fief alienated contrary to its nature, which is absurd, as stated in the Digest, title *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, § *si cum lex*. Indeed, according to Bartolus, even regarding a non-feudal thing, a vassal cannot prorogate jurisdiction to another without the consent of the lord of whom he is a vassal; for he is subject precisely to that lord’s jurisdiction, just as a cleric is subject to his diocesan bishop, according to Bartolus. A vassal, with respect to jurisdiction, is anyone who swears fidelity and performs manual homage. For these persons are more strictly bound than simple subjects, concerning whom law 1 of the Digest, title *De iudiciis*, speaks.

Now I make one final, very strong reason: although we say that a fief passes to the son who is the heir, which is established in favor of creditors, so that he ought to be heir, as in chapter 1, *An agnatus vel filius*, column 10, nevertheless it does not pass to him because he is an heir, but because he is a son. For this is the immediate cause of the transfer, especially if he is the firstborn, if such is the fief in which primogeniture is observed by custom of the country or by the form of investiture, and if the birth itself is considered, as in column 10 of the chapter *J.* under the title *De feudo marchiae*. It is acquired by the benefit of the lord and of the ancestors, and by its own nature, not merely by hereditary right, as in the Digest, title *De interdictis et relegationibus*, law 2. For the body of the fief is not a hereditary body; hence the son, who is preferred, does not institute a *condictio ex lege*, but a contradiction based on the usages of fiefs, as is read and noted in the Digest, title *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Item videndum*, § *nunc videamus*, and in the Digest, title *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Pro haerede*, § *si quia tamen*, and by Decius in law *Ex facto*, § *finis*, in the Digest, title *Ad Trebellianum*.

Now it is so that the act of the father does not prejudice the son in an ancient fief, where deprivation does not threaten due to ingratitude for a delict or due to ingratitude for a contract. From this it necessarily follows, and it is true, that the compromise made concerning the feudal castles was extinguished due to the death of the compromising father. Likewise, the prorogation or submission was extinguished due to the death of the prorogating or submitting party; because whether the compromise or the judgment was founded on a right that ceases with the deceased, and from which a certain right of solemnity seems to be recreated in the son, as we say in the case of a usufructuary: as in the Digest, title *De verbis obligatis*, law *Stipulatio ista*, § *si quis ita*. Although the law fictions that it is one and the same fief in number, because in a fief the person of the father and the son is considered one, and it is rather said to be continued than newly acquired, as in the Digest, title *De liberis et posthumis*, in law *Suis*, because such is its nature, namely mixed with a certain reality, although otherwise in the case of a usufructuary, because it has a merely personal nature, as in the Usages of Fiefs, chapter 1, § *si vero Conradus*. Nevertheless, whatever the case may be, whether you consider the mind of the law or the subtlety of reason, a fief is not a hereditary body. And for this reason, what the father did concerning the fief itself by submitting himself, and such a submissive instance, does not pass to the son by the father’s testament; because it does not descend to him as to a simple heir, according to the doctrine handed down in the Digest, title *De precario*, law *Quaesi*, § *ultimus*.

Since therefore the party submitted himself by litigating his own right, and having ceased that right as if the material were extinct, upon which the instance of the judgment was materially based, and thus the judgment must be dissolved, as in the Digest, title *De suspectis tutoribus*, law *Si finitam*. Just as if the judgment had been undertaken concerning a certain dignity or prelacy, for it is dissolved by the death of the litigant: as in the Clementine *Ultima*, title *Ut lite pendente*.

The following clause follows in the letters of the Lord Count: “And although we offer to render an account of it before the said Lord King, or before us, this is not to the cause of any homage to which he is bound to the King Dauphin; for we do not hold him to be such.” From these words it appears that no compromise nor submission was made between him and the King Dauphin into the Lord King of France. Although the Dauphin was named in the judgment: as in the Code, title *Ubi in rem actio*, law 2, nevertheless the Dauphin was not bound nor submitted by these letters. And just as he had not submitted himself, so neither had the said Count submitted himself; for equality must be observed in judgments: as in the Code, title *De fructibus et litis expensis*, law *Finalis*, and in the Extrajudicial, title *De mutuis petitionibus*, chapter *Prudentiam*. And just as he could not condemn the Dauphin to the Count by virtue of the said letters, so neither could he condemn the Count to himself; because prorogation and compromise do not extend beyond the person, as in the Extrajudicial, title *De officio delegati*, chapter *Penultimus* and following.

And therefore it must be thought that the Most Illustrious Prince and the Most Serene Lord King in this case proceeded rather militarily and according to royal power, than effectively according to the reason of law; since his sentence, according to the rules of the forum and of both laws, cannot be defended by any reason: saving always the royal majesty, and asking humble and devout pardon.

† Finally, it must not be omitted, but carefully observed, that even if the sentence of the Lord King were valid both between the Lord Dauphin and the Lord Count, and between the Lord Count and the Marquis of Lucca—which is not true—nevertheless, the execution of the fact outside the territory of the King, and within the territory of the Empire, could in no way be carried out by the said Lord King; because such execution, which is of mixed Empire, or even of mere Empire: if mere Empire is contained in the sentence, prorogation or submission does not in any way extend to it, nor does there appear to be consent on this point: as in D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, l. ex quocunque, in the fourth gloss. And therefore it would be necessary that a letter be written to the Emperor, that he execute the said sentence, who would have to weigh it under the scales of justice: and if he found it null, he would order to desist from execution, and write to the King the reason why, as in D. de re iudicata, l. a diuo pio, in the beginning. And if, omitting this, the Lord King proceeded to arms, it would not be a just war, as noted in C. de iudaeis and de restitutione spoliatorum, c. olim, through Innocentius, and in extra de iureiurando, c. sicut, through Innocentius; and he would be liable for satisfaction for the injury and damages: because many crimes are included under the name of violence: as in C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. multa facinora, and C. vt armorum vsus inscio principe, l. 1. And thus, from the beginnings or principles to the end of the present matter, it has been discussed by me, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, ordinary lecturer at Pavia, devoted familiar of the said illustrious Lord Count, submitting myself to the prevailing opinion, as in D. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. claudius felix. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required for a *datio in solutum* to be valid.
2. Every condition and every final cause are of the substance of proof.
3. Whether anyone is presumed to misuse his own property, and how this is proved.
4. Reputation must be effective, not slight and bare.
5. Whether a judgment that cannot be declared null by the defendant sued may be declared null by a third party.
6. Whether the nullity of a judgment is evident if citation does not appear.
7. Whether the right to deny is extinguished by the passage of time.
body: Whether the aforementioned proceeding, instituted against Leonellus, the husband of Violantis, who was verging on indigence, is valid or not; and consequently, whether a certain *datio in solidum* or valuation, which ensued on the occasion of the said conveyance, is valid or not.

It must be known that every *datio insolutum* (delivery of an unsatisfied claim) made by a judge requires, specifically on the part of the cause, that the cause be true and that the contract from which action is brought be true in fact. Furthermore, it requires that the cause be just, that is, that it be legally conclusive toward such an effect. D. de in integrum restitutione, l. omnes; C. ne vis fiat ei, l. 1, § haec verba. Hence, a defect on the part of the cause invalidates the *datio insolutum*, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. iuste, and fully noted by Cynus in C. de restitutione militum, l. ignorare. And it is called a defect of justice, with regard to the judicial forum, if no action has arisen from the fact from which action is brought. D. de verbis significatis, l. cedere diem. There is another defect on the part of order, or inversion. D. de re iudicata, l. si cum nulla; C. de executione rei iudicatae, l. 1; D. quod metus causa, l. fin., § ultimo. There is also a defect on the part of the person, for example, if a son in power brings an action against his father, as in D. de iudiciis, l. lis nulla. And wherever entry into judicial proceedings is prohibited, the end of such a judgment is null and void by operation of law, whether the prohibition is due to the persons, or due to time, or due to some other disposition of custom or statute, as in D. de aleatorio, l. 1, § quod autem; C. de feriis, l. si iudica; D. de solutionibus, l. vir bonus; C. qui actiones non possunt, l. si. And among other things, *datio insolutum* requires that it be made according to the measure of the declared debt. Hence three elements: namely, the measure, the debt, and the declaration, that is, the liquidated claim, speaking of adjudication: as in Auth. de exhibendis rebus, § si vero, in the text joined with the gloss. Therefore, it must first be liquidated before it is adjudicated. Otherwise, the liquidation would be in vain, and the solidification of the decree. D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. hoc autem, § 1, in the words constare liquere quae potiori. Now let us see whether this procedure erred in any respect, so as to render the *datio insolutum* and the estimation retroactively null by operation of law. And it is alleged that it did: because no proof of the procurator’s mandate was made to the judge. But I do not find this allegation persuasive: because when a declinatory exception is not raised, the judgment is valid even without proof of the mandate. It suffices that proof of the mandate be provided, which would be raised by a procuratorial exception. D. de damno infecto, l. inter quas, § alieno. It is also alleged that this procedure is null due to holidays. But here it must be considered that either the statute speaks prohibitively, or simply institutes holidays: for example, if it says that proceedings may not be conducted, and then holidays cannot be waived. Or it speaks not restrictively, but simply institutes holidays for providence, that is, for the utility of men, and not for the worship of God. For the worship of God binds unwillingly, since it is of natural law. And then, when it is for the benefit of all, it can be waived. But here it must be considered that these holidays were not instituted in favor of plaintiffs, but in favor of defendants. Nor in favor of judges. And therefore, the defendant, in the absence of the plaintiff, can waive holidays: because this rests solely in favor. D. de iureiurando, l. Labeo; C. de pactis, l. postquam liti; C. de iure deliberationis impetrando, l. 2; D. de negotiorum gestione, l. Nesennius Apolinarius. Thirdly, it is alleged, and this allegation pleases me: because it is substantial and true in law, that when a dowry is found during the subsistence of marriage, it must be established that the dowry is in a case of restitution or collation in trust. That is, that the husband improperly used his own property, or that he is verging on poverty: as in C. de collationibus, Auth. quod locum. For under this condition must this resignation of the dowry be made.

† It is established, however, that every condition pertains to the substance of proof and to the final cause. D. de verb. oblig. l. hoc iure. And note the opinion of Innocentius, Extravagantes de privilegiis, c. ex parte abbatissae. And therefore it ought to have been liquidated. C. de compensatione, l. fin. And without such liquidation having preceded, the payment of the unsatisfied debt and the execution were null by operation of law, nor can they be aided by subsequent proofs. Argumentum in c. appellanti, de appellationibus, in Clementina. Moreover, because it is null by operation of law and irregular, it does not become valid; and this opinion is confirmed. For against one acting in such a manner, it is presumed:

† because it is not presumed that anyone acts maliciously in his own affairs, or tends toward indigence, unless this is proven by the evident nature of the thing, or by manifest indications, or there is a very clamorous voice among the people, which is to be held as a certain notoriety, as noted in C. *quando fiscus, vel privatus*, l. 2; or by informants appointed to inquire into assets, and their legitimately made report, l. *magis puto*, de reb. eor.; or by the gloss in C. *mandari*, in l. *si pro ea*; and as stated by Jacobus de Aretino in l. *paupertas*, ff. de excus. tutor.

It ought to be understood as referring to a reputation arising from probable grounds, concerning which witnesses make mention; otherwise, reputation alone never suffices, neither for proving nor for relieving from the burden of proof. The reputation must indeed be effective and supported by some suitable presumption, not slight and bare. L. 3, D. de testibus. Therefore, unless it is now proven that it was then clearly established, the assignment of insolvency did not hold. Regarding the estimate, even when committing the matter to estimators, the order established by law must have been observed. C. de secundis nuptiis; L. hac edictali, § his illud.

† It is also certain that a judgment which cannot be declared null by the defendant against whom the proceedings were conducted may be declared null by a third party whose interest is affected, as stated in c. 1, de re iudicata, in the Clementines. And therefore the second creditor may properly declare the case null for his own interest. C. de non nullis petitionibus, l. si cui, because a judgment rendered without citation does not prejudice. l. saepe, ff. de re iudicata, and the common rule, l. res inter alios acta. Nevertheless, nullity is expressly stated in the aforementioned c. 1.

But it is doubted whether there is an evident nullity if the citation does not appear. And it seems that there is not: because the citation can be proved, even though no mention is made of it in the sentence. Therefore, it does not necessarily appear that the sentence is null; therefore, it stands. The statute prohibiting the hearing of a plea of nullity comprehends this case. On the contrary, it seems that a sentence which is null, either for lack of solemnity or on account of impossibility, and regarding a sentence which is null on account of impossibility, the statute is not understood to speak. For the sentence of the Emperor can be said to be null on account of impossibility, if it is against the natural law. C. Pastor, De re iudicata, in the Clementina. Nevertheless, it must be observed what I said, that the sale or delivery of unsold property is invalid if the cause is not proved: for this is true when the sale is made by interlocutory sentence; otherwise, if it is made by definitive sentence, which is valid even if the debt does not subsist, on account of the authority of the definitive sentence; because after a definitive sentence, exceptions destroying the judgment are not admitted, but after an interlocutory sentence they are, as in L. Fulcinius, §. Sed is qui, D. Qui ex causa in possessionem. Thereby, by the gloss and Doctor, many other things are subtly and copiously alleged, and on these points by Cynus and others in L. Properandum, §. Si autem reus.

† Finally, I say that the right of denial, since the burden of proof does not lie upon the one who denies, is not extinguished by the passage of time, except in two irregular exceptions, namely, *non numero pecuniae* and *non numero dotis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and in what manner apodixae prove.
body: The Republic

†while seeking to obtain his due, but from whom we must see. And I say that he ought to obtain it from him from whom he would obtain it if the said confessions had not been made. And this is thus explained: by a confession made in a testament, payment to the Republic is not proved; because the confession lacks the day on which the payment is made, the month, the consul, and the solemnity, as in C. de apocr. publicis, l. 1, lib. 10. And therefore such a confession is null by the law itself against the fisc. The fisc therefore acts as if the confession had not been made. Moreover, other confessions, which have the day, year, and month in which he writes that he received, are overthrown by the proof of witnesses. For the writing contains that the counting took place then, and the witnesses described in the receipt say the contrary. D. quemad. testa. ape., l. 1, in fi. and note C. si cer. pe., l. si ex pretio. Here, this writing can be disproved as public, not true. C. de non nu. pec., l. si ex cautione. Moreover, if the right was immediately acquired for another, saving his name: because without his act it cannot be transferred to another, as noted in D. si cer. pe., l. certi condictio, §. si nummos. D. de pac., l. fi. For someone to whom a mandate was given to receive payment cannot free the debtor by bare confession. D. de nov., l. si debitorem. C. de nov., l. non abstulit. D. de man. testa., l. qui filium. D. de admi. tu., l. Lucius, la secunda, §. tutela. Hence this bare writing of receipts, from which the counting does not appear, and is not a public writing, does not prejudice the fisc, unless it were solemn. C. de non nu. pe., l. in contractibus, §. 1, and the contrary is not proved. Among themselves, however, the fisc does not have to intervene, but to enforce its right against its own debtor. And let these things be said, always saving the faith of the truth. Therefore, the collection ought to be made in the order contained in these contracts, and not by leaps. D. de verb. ob., l. decem, and l. fi. D. si cer. pe. And thus first the one first obligated ought to be sued and exhausted, before the others who succeed: unless there were a custom that full faith was given to those receipts, and the contrary was not proved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How a judge is constituted with respect to his origin.
2. A fief cannot be granted with the power of alienation.
body: Regarding this article of jurisdiction, I say,

† That the Illustrious and Magnificent Prince of Achaea, and his council, was and is the competent judge of this case by reason of origin: although some doubt this, as is fully noted by Cynus in l. iuris ordinem, C. de iur. omn. iud. And because this certainty arises from the confession of the party regarding origin, and from the disposition of the law regarding the effect of origin, it was not necessary that a sentence be rendered on the point of written law. As to competence, because where something is certain by statute or law, a pronouncement by the judge is not necessary, as is noted in l. ex quacunque, ff. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit.

† Regarding the principal matter, it must be said that in the petitory action concerning the fief, those who derived their title from Beltramo will fail, because the prince could not grant the fief with that power of alienating the ownership which belonged to the illustrious and most noble Lord, Count of Savoy. C. ne rei dominicae, vel templorum, l. universas. Nor was it confirmed by the Lord Count, because he did not invest simply, although it was done saving his right and saving the mere ownership pertaining to himself. ff. qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur, l. sicut, §. non videtur. And in this, only the intention of the reserving party is shown simply, because reservation resides in the reserving party alone. But as far as the possessory action under the edict of the law is concerned, the plaintiff must proceed, and it was rightly judged by Master Antonio. For that possessory action partakes of the nature of the interdict for recovery, and therefore possession must be restored to the instituted heir, because the property subject to restitution will be treated as such, as in Inst. de interdictis, §. commodum; ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. exitus controversiae. It is not expedient to discuss here the altered nature of fiefs, because, as I have said, there is a defect here in the efficient cause with respect to the prince, and in the formal cause with respect to the Lord Count. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What a tower is, and what is included under its designation.
2. If a house may be raised to the height of a certain tower, in what manner it ought to be raised.
body: A house is distinguished from the construction of a tower, which pertains to the common property of estates. L. Si quis duas. §. Quod in aedibus. For a tower is

† a certain building raised upward, consisting of its own substance. C. de operi. pu. l. turres. And if a garland or a wine press is placed on top of a masonry structure, that part is not properly part of the substance of the tower, nor of its height, because it is not joined by the same material; just as the material of movable stones is not without the mortar placed beneath. But if the entire tower were made of wood, then it would be part of the tower, because it is of the same material. ff. de rei ven. l. in rem. §. 1. And therefore, a masonry structure cannot be raised higher upon masonry if the boundary agreement prohibits it, even though many people loosely refer to the whole thing as a tower. But if it were shown to be the common usage of speech, that usage should be followed; because judgments, and boundary agreements of arbitrators, and especially those of common people, ought rather to be understood in a general sense, than according to the precise points of meanings. ff. de fundo instruc. l. cum delanionis. §. asinam. ff. de do. ante nup. l. si cum ante. per Cy.

† Now let us see whether a house, which can be raised to the height of this tower, ought to be raised to that height, that is, so as to touch the same summit; or whether, by measuring, if the house stands on lower or depressed ground, so that if the tower is one hundred feet and the house were two hundred feet, if it were extended up to the level of the summit, whether this can be done or not, and how equality is to be understood. I answer that equality upwards is understood as that whereby the faces of the summits are equal. But if pressed downwards, equality would be understood in depth. However, we are speaking here of raising upwards, that is, that the party walls and the summits from the ground up to the top are equal. To this effect: D. de aedificiis privatis, l. an in totum, and what is noted there, these words are understood both in law and in fact. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a testator institutes someone in a specific thing, with another person instituted universally, who is bound to the creditors.
2. The custom of the place is observed regarding the faith to be given to sealed letters.
body: If the testator,

† He instituted his brothers as legatees of certain things, and his wife as universal heir; the wife is bound to answer to her creditors, not the brothers: unless the estate were insolvent; for then the legacies would not be valid. C. si cert. pet. C. de leg. l. si universæ. C. de hære. insti. l. quos. and there, no. ff. de hære. insti. l. ex facto. and there, no.
† Regarding letters sealed with a signet, whether they make faith, I say that the custom of the place where they were made must be observed, as in Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum dilecti.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a renunciation made to an official is valid, and whether it is presumed to be made under fear.
2. Whether a prince, who acknowledges no superior, may sell or donate another’s property, yet pledged to him for public debt.
body: From the principle of the title, the subsequent event is formed, as is described in C. de impositione lucris describendi, l. 1, lib. 10. Hence, let us begin with the causes. The cause of the seizure of the goods was, so to speak, the debt of the first word. For it must be satisfied first to the fisc, before other goods may be claimed or held by others, as in C. de privilegio, l. utilitas, lib. 12.

† Then, after these things, the prince at that time appears to have approved those goods for himself, having given the son the option of paying, who rather chose to renounce the goods than to pay, as appears from the refutation of this by a public instrument, which must be believed in case of doubt, because it was made for a cause, namely, to avoid lawsuits that could have been brought against him as heir. D. de minoribus, l. minoribus; D. de alienationibus iudicum, l. non solum. And perhaps because there was more in debt than in patrimony. D. de legatis 3, l. qui habebat. And where there is a just cause, unjust fear is not presumed. Moreover, if the official also exacts extra ordinem, the exactions are not revoked while the debt subsists. D. quod metus causa, l. si, §. vlt. But if military terror inflicts fear contrary to good morals, the renunciation would not be valid. C. quod metus causa, l. 2 and 3; D. eodem, l. metum, §. volenti; and C. de executionibus et exactoribus, l. 1, lib. 12. But this must be proved, as in Extra, de renuntiationibus, c. super hoc. By which illicit fear being proved, the fisc would be an unjust possessor, whoever succeeding into the defect; because the action quod metus causa is written in rem, and useful in rem, which is given to the one who suffered the fear, and lies against every possessor, as in the said §. volenti, and l. si cum exceptione, §. haec autem actio; and arg. C. de agris et censibus, l. coloni; Extra, de restitutione spoliorum, c. saepe. It follows subsequently to see, since the lord of that time donated by absolute power, assuming that he had it, whether the said donated thing could be claimed by the donee. It is to be said,

† That when a prince, who acknowledges no superior, gives another’s thing as his own in good faith, believing it to be his own, and cannot purchase the thing from him to whom he gave it, by whatever title he gave it. C. de quadrien. pręscrip. l. omnis. and l. bene a Zenone. Sometimes he gives another’s thing as another’s: yet on account of a preceding debt, and then it matters whether he sold it with the solemnity of public auction observed, and transfers dominion, as is read and noted, C. si aduer. fiscum. l. edicto. or whether he donated it, in which case public auction cannot apply, and then he does not transfer dominion: but right, that is, the right of credit, and hypothec. ar. ff. de contrah. emp. l. qui tabernas. ff. de leg. 1. l. si domus. §. fi. ff. de vsufr. leg. l. Sticho. C. de leg. l. uxor patrui. From these I conclude that this defendant, or exception, or by the law itself according to what is alleged, is secure, the substance of the truth in fact and in law being preserved, and I submit myself to the truth in fact and in law. And of the aforesaid I specially adduce what is noted by Bartolus, ff. de iu. fis. l. quibusdam. and l. procurator. eo. ti. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a caution (security) given by a manifest usurer, in hand, or before the vicar’s deputy, or the parish priest, is valid.
2. Whether a caution given before two notaries is valid.
3. Whether the diocesan bishop may ratify such a caution given before notaries.
4. For a notary, presumption arises from long and daily practice.
5. Whether the provision of c. quamquam applies to usurers who are in the lands of the Empire.
6. [Continuation of item 5: “of the Empire.”]
7. When a guardian, not being appointed for a ward, loses the succession.
8. A burden attached to the execution does not make the institution conditional.
body: Since a certain usurer, manifestly such, lay ill in a house where he kept a daily altar prepared, although he drank and slept with his family in the house of another parish, he furnished security for the restitution of usuries to the vicar of that parish where the sick man lay, with a notary present, but not by the authority of the ordinary. Then he made a will, instituted his son as heir, and substituted his uncle, adding this clause, namely, with this condition, that the said B., the substitute, and his certain executors are bound and must give and distribute a certain quantity from his goods. And yet that they are not compelled to give while the plague is then prevailing in Parma: but only after the plague has subsided. It is alleged that the testator died, the said minor being still alive, as well as the said substitute, and the wife of the testator, and the mother of the said minor. And that then the minor died within a year, and that the substitute acted as heir, and that the substitute died without having paid the said quantity. From these facts, it is first asked whether the said security was solemnly furnished in the form of the chapter *Quamquam*, although we must know this in order to determine whether the will was valid. Secondly, it is asked whether the said words constitute a condition. For there is doubt: because the mother of the minor claims to succeed intestate for three reasons. First, on account of the tutor not being demanded by the pupillary substitution. Second, because the will was invalid, since the security was not solemn. Third, because even if it had been valid, nevertheless the substitute, dying while the condition was pending, would not have transmitted the right. On the contrary, it is said that the security was solemn, and the penalty for not demanding a tutor does not apply here, and that those words do not constitute a condition. Moreover, since the Statute of Parma requires, for a will to be valid, that there be two notaries, and it is said that he who subscribed was not a notary, it is asked what is the law. Furthermore, it is asked whether the chapter *Quamquam* has application in the secular forum.
