† And that the said caution was not solemn, seems to be proved in the text of the said chapter *Quamquam*, there, where it says, “either to the rector of the parish”; it does not say, “or to his vicar.” But above it had rightly said, “to the ordinary of the place, or to him exercising his functions.” Hence, since these words “exercising his functions” are not repeated after the word “rector of the parish”: therefore we ought not to supply them either; because it is established by law that it is not to be supplied, but observed, even if it be most harsh, as in *l. Prospexit*, *Qui et a quibus*. To the contrary it seems, because it does not matter which of equivalent things is done, but it is the same whether something is done by the principal or by his vicar in office, as in *C. De officio eius qui vicem alterius iudicis*, *l. Subgerente*. For on account of absence one may leave a substitute, where otherwise he could not, as in *ff. De officio eius cui mandata est iurisdictio*, *l. 1*, § *1*. But to these it is answered, that where a constitution expressly commits something to the faith of a certain person, it cannot be delegated to another, as in *ff. De transactionibus*, *l. Cum hi*, § *Sed nec mandare*. But concerning this stipulation to be received under any sum expressed, lesser or greater, for which the faith of the proper priest has been chosen as surety, therefore this cannot be done by another, as in *c. Quoniam abbas*, *De officio delegati*, by Innocentius, and argument from *De arbitris*, *c. Non distinguimus*, § *De officio*, there, “to whom sureties,” and *c. Nam*. For when an arbitration is given on uncertain matters outside of judgment, the skill of the person is almost always seen to have been chosen. Hence one must not depart from the person, because the commission is singular and personal. Moreover, what is permitted to certain persons is prohibited to others, as in *C. De procuratoribus*, *l. Maritus*. The question stands here, how we are to explain that word “rector.” For if we explain it strictly, that is, having the right and title of the rectory: it would not suffice to give it to his vicar, because that vicariate is with respect to officiating in the church; nor does it extend to other things, unless he were a vicar by the authority of a superior, as in *c. Extirpandae*, *De praebendis*. But if we understand it broadly for him who in fact orders and governs the church in spirituals and temporals by the mandate of the true rector, and then such a caution is valid: because broadly this one is said to govern, although he governs in another’s name. Indeed, this one properly governs, but absent perfection, as in *l. Prima*, § *Deiecisse*, *De vi et vi armata*. But it is said that there is no proof of this vicariate of the rector: because there is no proof of the mandate, nor is a mandate presumed unless it is proved. *C. De procuratoribus*, *l. 1*; *De mandato*, in the principle, *l. 1*; *De officio delegati*, *l. Cum in iure*; *C. De iure fisci*, *l. Prohibita*. And if he does not have a mandate, he is a false vicar. *ff. De solutionibus*, *l. Qui hominem*, § *Si nullo*. But to this it is said, that he was publicly held there as a locumtenens. Hence it suffices, as in *l. Barbarius*, *ff. De officio praetoris*, especially in the case of impending death, argument from *C. De inofficioso donatione*, *l. Ultima*; to this, *C. De testamento*, *l. 1*; *C. De senatu et interlocutionibus*, *l. 2*, *Cum si*. However, that he was publicly held as such must be proved, because it is not presumed, since it is a certain fact contrary to nature. *C. De probationibus*, *l. 2*, with countless similar cases. But let us assume that such a rector, such as he was, would suffice.

It is asked whether two notaries suffice. For one notary, unless he acts by the mandate of the ordinary himself, does not suffice, as stated in the text and gloss there, because in this case the law does not require that restitution of usury be made to those to whom it is owed through him, unless he has been sent or summoned by the diocesan bishop. And it seems that two notaries suffice, especially if a priest is joined to them, as argued in the Extravagant *De testibus*, chapter *Tamen res*, and chapter *Relatum*, and in the Authenticum *De haereditatibus et falsis*, section *Si vero obsunt*. The contrary is the true position, because in matters done for simple proof, where individual items do not avail, many help; otherwise in matters done for the essence of a thing, as in law 1, Code *Qui numero tutelarum*. And because in this case the decretal wishes that inquiry not be made through a notary unless he is a notary with the mandate of the bishop. The Pope enacted this to exclude frauds, because if any notary sufficed, this could be done secretly and kept hidden, and not produced unless it were expedient, as in law *Non intelligitur*, section *Tacite*, Digest *De iure fisci*, according to Bartolus. Hence the Pope wished that the cautions of manifest usurers come to the public knowledge of the diocesans. And this is a most special case, due to the hatred of usurers.

But suppose that the diocesan bishop has ratified this caution, which is the case precisely because he ordered the usurer to be buried; or suppose he has made use of this caution and had it drawn up for himself: does this ratification equate to a mandate? It seems that it does not. D. 29.2.1 (Si quis mihi bona), § Iussum eius; D. 40.12.1 (Si vero non remunerandi), § Si post creditam; and what is said in C. 10.2.2, lib. 10. I believe the contrary follows from equity, because the reason and intent of the constitution have been satisfied, and by the rule Ratihabitio et cetera, and C. 4.5.1 (Finis); and D. 4.5.1 (Si filius). For when this notary received the caution, in the name of all those who had an interest, he is deemed to have received it also in the name of the bishop, since the bishop too has an interest on account of the distribution of uncertain legacies. D. 5.1.1 (Cum sit). Or a distinction should be made, so that if the bishop ratified while the testator was alive, the testament becomes valid; otherwise, if after his death, as in D. 28.5.1 (Exigit), de secundis tabulis. The first opinion is more humane, so that it may become valid by reason of the act. Regarding the point concerning the two notaries, the statute must be observed.

It must also be noted that the notarial profession is not always required to be proved with absolute certainty; for it is presumed in favor of the individual on account of long and daily exercise thereof, especially in matters which tend not to prejudice the right of another. This is supported by what is noted by Cynus in the Code, title "Who cannot be accused," law "It is not unknown." Likewise, if the bishop regards him as such, as in the Code, title "On contracting and stipulating," law "The best."

† As for that chapter "Although," which makes usurers manifestly incapable of making a will in the lands of the Empire, I believe that this is so, because a usurer can be condemned by the Church on account of his offense, as in the Authentica "Item, when no community," together with its gloss, in the Code, On Bishops and Clerics. Although they are infamous according to civil law, they can nevertheless make a will, because infamy does not deprive them of their goods. But whether the contrary can be introduced by custom, that is, whether the wills of such persons are valid, because their wills have always been observed in both forums, must be discussed elsewhere.

† Regarding the article concerning the tutor not requested, I say that under the new law a penal year is established, and if the ward dies before that time, the succession which descends from the will is not lost; otherwise, in that which descends from the Senatusconsultum Tertullianum, as in l. sciant. C. de legit. haere. insti. ad Tert. §. si. Regarding the point concerning the condition, I say,

† That these words do not create a condition, because a burden attached to the execution does not make the institution conditional. Moreover, this is not a condition, but a certain obligation of the heir, and before the inheritance is accepted, he cannot be bound. Therefore, that burden is attached after the inheritance has been accepted, and it is not attached purely, but under a condition. Hence, the burden is placed under a condition: but the substitution is not placed under any extrinsic condition, but in a certain fideicommissum. The judge requires the inheritance to be accepted, but does not prevent it from being accepted, because that would be a certain contradiction. For before he accepts, he cannot be bound by the will, nor can the execution be carried out: as in l. si nemo, ff. de reg. iur., together with si; and l. si quis sub conditione, si quis omissa causa testamenti. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, give my opinion and counsel, and I have subscribed to the truth and signed with the sign of my name, always reserving the right to a sounder opinion, because these matters are new.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Although a person legitimated by the prince does not succeed to the fief, it is otherwise if he is legitimated by a subsequent marriage.
2. The prince, nor the Emperor, cannot legitimate for ecclesiastical fiefs.
3. When a marriage is not valid by divine law, nor by human law, but only by dispensation, because the dispensation was granted only regarding the marriage, the offspring is not legitimated: it is otherwise if the dispensation was granted regarding both.
4. Whether a legitimated person can succeed to a fief by virtue of an investiture made to him out of paternal affection.
body: 1. To the evidence

It must be premised that, although a son legitimated by the prince does not succeed to a fief, as stated in the chapter *Naturales*, in the title *Si de feudo fuerit controversia inter dominum et alium*, nevertheless the common opinion is that a son legitimated by a marriage contracted in the face of the Church succeeds to a fief, just as if he were legitimately born. This view is held there on grounds of equity by Master Jacobus de Belvisio and Antonius de Isernia, on account of the force of marriage, as in the extrajudicial title *Qui filii sint legitimi*, chapter *Tanta*. This applies even to an ecclesiastical fief, because this legitimation is most strongly confirmed by the Church and is retroactive, although Bartolus states indiscriminately that legitimated persons do not succeed to a fief or to an ecclesiastical emphyteutic lease, as in the Digest, title *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Ex facto*, section *Si quis rogatus*.

But his statement is to be understood as referring to legitimation by the prince, unless the prince declares that he legitimizes for ecclesiastical fiefs, according to the gloss of that chapter. I say that the prince, i.e., the Emperor or King, cannot, even if he wishes, legitimize for ecclesiastical fiefs. For he who cannot grant cannot dispense, nor restore to full rights: but the Pope does so, as in the chapter *extra qui filii sint legitimi*, c. *per venerabilem*. What is noted in c. *pastoralis*, de re iudicata, in the Clementine *legitimati*: those legitimated by marriage are legitimate in all respects, just as they were formerly, when nature alone prescribed for men, and in the original purity of the law of nations, to which they are now restored, as in the Authentica *quibus modis naturales efficiuntur legitimi*, in the beginning.

And this is true when the marriage proceeds by divine and human law, namely by the common law; but if the marriage does not proceed except by dispensation, if indeed the dispensation is granted solely for the marriage, then children born before are not legitimated. D. 1.5.1, Paulus. But if the dispensation is granted for both, namely for the marriage and for legitimation: then they are legitimated as by the force of the rescript, not as by the force of the marriage, as in D. 23.2.1, § 1. Therefore, when carnal intercourse is contrary to the statutes of the laws, a subsequent marriage is valid even with respect to fiefs, unless it is stated in the grant that it shall not pass except to one legitimately born. Such a marriage, however, must be proved by instruments according to civil law. In Auth. Qui modo nati efficiantur legitimi, § Quam; and Inst. 1.10, § Si forte. Although according to canon law nothing is required except the pure substance of truth being proved, yet because the text says, "such is the force of marriage," etc., but in marriage there is nothing of the substance except expressed consent.

But assuming that the legitimated child does not succeed by virtue of ancient investitures, he may succeed by virtue of an investiture made specifically to him, especially when his merits demand it, or out of parental affection, as stated in the argument in Title 10 of the Collatio, *Quemadmodum feudum ad filium pertineat*, Chapter 1. Moreover, a diocesan bishop is presumed to know the quality of the person whom he invests, *Digestum*, *De regulis iuris*, Law *Qui cum alio*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who answers to another concerning fruits is deemed to acknowledge possession from that person.
2. Minors who answer to the purchaser concerning fruits, where the purchaser bought from their guardian who sold the possessions of said minors without a judicial decree, are not said to have approved or ratified said contract; nor do they incur the penalty of the statute against those who commit spoliation, etc.
3. A guardian cannot grant a precarium.
casus:
CASE. The case upon which counsel is sought follows in the terms set forth below.

In the Statutes of the City and Community of Pavia, it is provided, by a statute of the following tenor, concerning the penalty for one who has committed any violence against another in his possession.

Heading. We also statuate that if any person of the community or university, of whatever status and condition he may be, henceforth dispossesses any singular person, college, or university of any possession of any immovable thing, which was then truly possessed by someone, either personally or through another in his name, and the fruits of whose possession were accustomed to be collected by him, or the faculty of collecting whose fruits pertained and belonged to him, and who can truly be called possessor; or if he molests, disturbs, or troubles him in said possession, or occupies it, or dispossesses him of said possession, or in any other way commits violence against him regarding the possession, in whatever manner, or causes any of the aforementioned modes, or another, to be committed; that he or those who commit the aforementioned acts, or any of the aforementioned, or cause them to be done, shall be punished and condemned in 100 Pavesi pounds, if there is only one. If there are more than one, exclusively, up to the number ten, inclusively, in 50 Pavesi pounds for each of them. And if more than that, however many there are, in 25 Pavesi pounds for each of them, and less according to the quality of the act and the offense, at the discretion of the Lord of the Potestas. Half of this condemnation shall belong to the Community of Pavia, and the other half shall go to the offended party. And nevertheless, the aforementioned offender shall be bound to restore the possession dispossessed or occupied to the offended party, and to cease from disturbance, molestation, occupation, or inquietude; after first having made proof to the Lord of the Potestas, or his judge of malefices, by legitimate proofs or suitable witnesses, of the violence, and also to restore to the offended party the expenses which he incurred on account of said violence. And what is said regarding violence in possession not vacant, as above, shall also have place in vacant possession of any immovable thing or things. And in any case of the aforementioned, the constitutions and laws dealing with violence, and their penalties, shall also have place; and immovable things are understood to be corporeal things which can be touched or handled: such as land, house, orchard, meadow, wood, vineyard, mountain, and plain. Of which, having made said proof, the Lord of the Potestas shall be bound to condemn the offender, and to compel him to the restitution of said possession and thing, and to refrain from committing violence henceforth; and also to restore expenses, after first having made a legitimate taxation, and to maintain the offended party in said possession, and to make him repair the damages which he suffered thereby, summarily, and without clamor and solemnity of law; so that no appeal may be taken from the process, sentence, pronouncement, condemnation, or execution, as above. And the aforementioned shall have place: unless the aforementioned person, who is called the offender, had such a right, on account of which he could have lawfully done it, if he had shown it to the Lord of the Potestas, or the judge of malefices, and abandoned it before said sentence. And if the one claiming the right is negligent in any of the aforementioned, let him be punished in 100 Pavesi pounds, half of which shall belong to the aforementioned offended party. Moreover, the entry and possession seized by said offender, and whatever was done by him, shall be void, null, and of no value, if said offender, as above, has been condemned. Furthermore, we statuate that the community of the place, village, castle, or borough of the territory of Pavia, nor any university, may prove that the land of said place, village, castle, or borough is not Pavia's for said community in any of the aforementioned cases. And if the offender does not appear, or a legitimate person for him, let him be banned from the aforementioned matters which are brought against him, with a space of 8 days given to him; which having elapsed, let him be held as having passed by and confessed; and him not appearing, let condemnation be made as above, and execution. And in the same way let process, condemnation, and punishment be made against those who have committed, or caused to be committed, violence, occupation, or disturbance to anyone in possession, or quasi-right of any servitude, way, or act, watercourse, or any other servitude.

Assuming the aforementioned statute, the case, or fact of the question, is assumed.

A certain Albert died from the fund in the 16th year elapsed, leaving behind him Ambrosia, his wife, and A, B, C, D, E, F, their legitimate and natural children, all under the age of 14, except for one daughter over the age of 12, and lacking a tutor and curator. And leaving in his goods and inheritance three or four plots of properties, which by the said deceased until the time of his death had been held and possessed peacefully and quietly. After the death of said Albert, the aforementioned Ambrosia, mother of said minors, was decreed and appointed as tutor and curator of said minors by the ordinary judge, and having assumed the burden of their tutelage, and having completed an inventory of the goods of said minors, and especially of the aforementioned three or four plots of hereditary property. The case arises that said tutor, in the name of her children as surrogate and curator, without a judicial decree, and without there being any debt, sold certain of the hereditary properties of the late Albert, pertaining to said minors in the aforementioned hereditary name, to a certain Gratio, and constituted herself as tutor and curator in the name of said minors to hold and possess said properties thus sold precariously in the name of the aforementioned Gratio, the buyer; as is evident from a public instrument regarding said sale. Notwithstanding said sale, the aforementioned minors have naturally possessed said properties thus sold until this day. Of which properties, the aforementioned minors annually, as is reported, rendered to the aforementioned Gratio, for the lord's share, part of the fruits.

After these things, when about a year ago, the aforementioned Gratio, the buyer, wished to enter into possession of the aforementioned properties, as is premised, sold, or some of them, as he wished perhaps to deprive the brothers of possession of said properties, the aforementioned brothers, or two of them, fearing they might be deprived by the same Gratio of possession of said properties, repelled said Gratio and prohibited him from entering into possession of said properties; saying that said properties were theirs and pertained to them. Wherefore the aforementioned Gratio brought an accusation against said brothers, who prohibited him as premised, for disturbed possession before the ordinary judge; requesting that said brothers be condemned in 100 Pavesi pounds, according to the form and tenor of the aforementioned statute. And he produced as the foundation of his intention the instrument of said sale made to him, as premised; and furthermore he alleged that at the time of said disturbance, and before for many years, he had held and possessed said properties through himself, or the brothers in his name; and that said brothers had continuously responded to said Gratio for ten and twelve years elapsed regarding the fruits thereof for the lord's share, and had disturbed and molested said Gratio in the fruits in the possession of said properties.

Upon which aforementioned allegations, the aforementioned Gratio produced many witnesses, eleven in number, who witnesses solemnly swore in the hands of the ordinary judge, before whom the question was pending, that all the witnesses in effect deposed that the aforementioned brothers possessed said properties continuously for ten and twelve years elapsed in the name of said Gratio, and responded to him at the due times regarding the fruits owed for the lord's share. But when interrogated regarding the reason, they conclude: because they saw said lands being worked by said brothers, and said Gratio sometimes responding regarding the fruits of said properties. They say, however, that they were never present at any lease made orally, nor in writing, by said Gratio to said brothers.

On the other hand, the aforementioned brothers proved by other eleven witnesses that they had held and possessed, for ten, twelve, and fifteen years elapsed, and from the time of the death of their late father until now, the aforementioned properties peacefully and quietly as their own, and as if they were theirs; who witnesses solemnly swore in the hands of said ordinary judge. And furthermore they proved that said properties were hereditary to their late father, both by the confession of the opposing party, and by witnesses, as premised, produced.

Now it is asked, whether said brothers, on the pretext of said accusation, and things being as they are, as is expressed above, can be condemned according to the form of said statute; or whether they ought to be absolved, notwithstanding the proofs and said sale of Gratio.
body: It seems that the said brothers should be entirely condemned.

† For he who answers to another concerning the fruits of a thing is deemed to recognize possession in the other and to hold possession for him; so that if he denies him entry into possession, he is deemed to have dispossessed him. D. de vi et vi armata, l. colonus. But if he otherwise disturbs him, he is liable under the interdict uti possidetis, as in D. de pacato, l. ab emptione, in the major gloss. Therefore, these brothers have incurred the penalty of the statute. Moreover, on account of the long payment of revenues, they cannot raise a question of ownership, and therefore neither of possession. C. de agris et censibus, l. litibus, lib. 10. Furthermore, they appear to have ratified the sale made by the guardian. For ratification is effected not only by express words, but also by the things themselves and by acts, as in D. rem ratam habere, l. Paulus. Moreover, these two things are equivalent: holding possession for another and answering concerning the fruits. D. qui modis ususfructus amittatur, l. Pomponius. Moreover, the contract and the delivery by the guardian, although they were invalid from the beginning, have been confirmed by ratification. C. si maior factus sine decreto factam venditionem ratam habuerit, l. finalis; and see the argument in l. finalis, C. de his qui a non domino.

† To the contrary, it seems, because it does not appear to be proven from what cause the response regarding the fruits was given. Hence this response is indifferent to every cause and uncertain; indeed, it is formless and does not bind to pay the annuity in the future; especially since it is established that it was paid unduly in the past. C. de pac. l. si certis annis. Moreover, no lease is proven: and the lease is not contained in the instrument of sale, hence it cannot refer to that which is not provided for in the instrument, nor is it proven to have preceded. ff. de usuris. l. cum de in rem verso. Furthermore, two fictions concur, namely, the feigned sale of them and the feigned delivery of them, arising from the same fact, namely, from the same consent of the owners, who would feign that it was sold back by them ratifying, behold one fiction, and would feign possession delivered, behold another fiction, which two improprieties, or fictions, are not said to concur. I. 1. C. de do. promis. C. de acqui. pos. l. aliquam rem. C. loca. l. qui rem. et l. si quis condi. per Cy. et l. ab emp. de pac. per Guil. Moreover, the owner has a just cause for not allowing another to enter his possession: as ff. de ser. ru. præ. l. diuus. et l. fi. ff. de off. proc. cesa. C. unde vi. l. quærebatur. de vsuf. le. l. hæres in fundum. Moreover, he who has a just cause even for disturbing is not punished criminally for disturbing violence: as d. l. colonus. ff. de ac. et ob. l. seruus non omnibus. Moreover, the knowledge of the contract is not proven: because these did not know of the sale of the guardian. and the ignorant cannot ratify. l. quæ enim. rem ra. ha. and ignorance is presumed in another’s fact. l. fi. ff. pro suo.

† Moreover, a guardian cannot establish a precarium, since he is not bound in his own name. D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. quod meo, by contrary reasoning. From these and other authorities, we may say that the said brothers, according to what is alleged, ought to be absolved, as in C. de rei venditione, l. mater tua, and D. de solutionibus, l. filiae. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when the confession of a procurator prejudices the principal.
2. Whether an abbot may recover what was paid by a monk.
body: Procurator

† A procurator having a mandate to receive payment cannot make a confession to the prejudice of his principal. C. de nova, l. non abstulit; ff. de nova, l. si debitorem. But if he has a general mandate with full discretion, he may do all things which the principal is accustomed to do. ff. quod cum eo, l. Titianus; and those matters which are according to custom and the exercise of that mandate. ff. de procu., l. procuratorem, cui libera. But to his own prejudice, a general procurator may confess without distinction; and his confession is presumed true to the prejudice of the confessor himself, and by it he is bound to his principal. ff. de adm. tu., l. Lucius, §. tutelae. However, if the principal has in his possession the accounts of the agent, or if the principal himself prepared them, he is bound to produce them, and especially if the principal is a usurer. c. f. de usu, in cle. de edem, c. praetor.

† If a monk pays something from the goods of the monastery, the Abbot may recover it; otherwise, if from elsewhere. In case of doubt, it is presumed in favor of the church according to some. Others say the contrary when the church brings an action. D. de cond. indeb. l. servus cuiusdam. If the recipient receives in bad faith, he is liable; but if in good faith and has consumed it, he is not liable. However, if the money still exists, it is claimed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that no one may alienate immovable property to a person who does not pay the *collectae* [taxes], etc., if someone has bequeathed to a monastery or pious place an immovable property usually subject to the payment of *collectae* through testamentary burdens, the monastery or pious place is not included under the said statute, and consequently is not bound by the said burdens.
body:
Cases. Ruffinus de Bestosso of Pontestura, being called, placed his goods in the register of the commune, and they were registered in the registers of the men of Pontestura, and from those registered goods he bore the burdens of taxes, levies, and others, together with the other men of the said county, from the time the said register was made until the death of Ruffinus. Then the said Ruffinus died, who left a son and heir called by the name John, who John, as son and heir of the aforementioned late Ruffinus, throughout the time of his life bore and sustained for the said registered goods the burdens of taxes and impositions, together with the other men of the land of Pontestura. And the said John died and made a testament, in which testament he disposed as follows. Moreover, the aforementioned John wished and commanded that from the Cassina of the said John, first made, namely from the half of the said Cassina towards the rising of the sun, there be made one hospital with beds, where the poor of Christ, truly and not falsely needy, as well as the sick, may lodge and be received, and be treated kindly; to which hospital for the poor and needy shall serve the half of the vacant ground, i.e., without buildings, towards the said side, namely the rising of the sun, of the same John. That ground and Cassina lie in the village of Pontestura, near the wall of the said village in the quarter of Leniuca, to which adjoins the public road on two sides, and the house which used to be that of the pleban of Zabandinis. In which hospital indeed all the needy shall be received and sustained, and from the kinship there shall always be, and ought to be, one rector, governor, and custodian, provided he is of good condition and fame, a suitable and honest person, who shall always hold under the name of Saint John the Evangelist, that he govern the hospital, if anyone sufficient shall be from the kinship of the said John, and always the more sufficient of them shall be bound to provide aid, counsel, and favor to him who is, and for the time shall be, in the priory of the church of Saint Agatha of Pontestura, to which the said John constituted one priest, who shall always celebrate there one mass for the repose of the dead, etc. In all his goods, in the third part of his goods he instituted as his heir Sibil, his daughter. But if it should happen that the said deceased wife his wife bore one or more posthumous sons, or born in the meantime coming to light, he instituted them as heirs in the other third part. But if from the said wife he had no posthumous son, he instituted the said Sibil, his daughter, as his heir in the half of all his goods. However, if the said daughter, or posthumous sons, or posthumous daughters, should die in pupillary age, or otherwise at any time without children, he substituted the said hospital for them. In the other part, namely the half or third part, according as the case of succession in the sons and daughters shall require, he instituted the said hospital as heir, and the aforementioned things, etc. Afterwards, when the said John died, the said Sibil, his daughter, surviving, no other sons being born afterwards. And thus it is found that the said hospital is instituted as heir in the half of all the goods of the said John, certain later provisions standing. Petranus de Bestosso, as the more sufficient of those of the said kinship, was invested in the said hospital by the vicar of the Lord Bishop of Vercelli, and by the same Lord Vicar was placed and appointed rector and governor of the said hospital, as appears from a public instrument sealed with the seal of the said Lord Vicar, signed on the outside by C. But from the written disposition it appears from a public instrument signed on the outside by A. It is true, however, that the statute of Pontestura provides that no person of Pontestura, or from elsewhere, whoever he may be or shall be, may or ought in any manner or cause to donate, sell, alienate, or bequeath, or pledge as security, any immovable thing which he has, or seems to have, or certainly has had, or any rights which he has, or has had, in any immovable thing in the place of Pontestura, territory, or jurisdiction, to any person from wherever he may be, who does not pay, or has paid, or refuses to pay fodias, taxes, datias, or collectas; and also to bear the burdens from his goods and things, just as all and each of Pontestura pay, used to pay from their things to the commune and men of Pontestura, and for the said commune; under the penalty and ban of 25 pounds of Pontestura. Then the said statute adds. Moreover, the said alienation, sale, or bequest is null by law and fact. Nevertheless, the said thing sold is not removed from the estimate of the said seller or alienator, so that he does not pay to the said commune and men the fodias and collectas, just as they used to before the said alienation. Then it adds, that the chapter is made saving the right of the willing Lord Marquis. Now it happens that the commune and men of Pontestura wish that the said rector and minister of the said hospital contribute in the payments of taxes, and in the future which have been imposed, and are imposed, and would be imposed on the men of the said community, for solidi and pounds, according as the possessions held by the said hospital were registered in the register of the said commune by the said late Ruffinus, father of the aforementioned John. Now it is asked, whether the said minister, rector, and governor is bound to bear the said burdens for the goods and things aforementioned, with the said community and men of the said community, or not, considering the following.

Opinion on the preceding case. Under the title: "It is permitted to the inhabitants of Pontestura, or from elsewhere, to transfer their places to another, who, or which, shall not have paid, or refuses to pay fodias, taxes, or datias, or collectas, etc., pious places are not contained, such as monasteries, churches, and canonical hospitals founded by authority, and this for several reasons. First, because those words 'to any person from wherever he may be' do not include pious places; because it is one thing to bequeath to a person, another to a place. D. de annuis legatis, l. annua, §. a Titio; D. quod metus causa, l. metum, §. animaduertendum; and noted in c. 1, extra de sepultura, eodem titulo; c. dudum, §. verum, in Clementinis, semper, n. These are placed as separate: a person is an animated substance, whereas a place, and without a person, has an understanding of law. Hence, speaking properly, when the see is vacant, the church does not lack, but the person. So also a woman is said to be vacant, who is without a husband, yet she has her own proper being. Ad l. Iul. de vi, l. qui cetu, §. qui vacantem. And it is one thing a church, another a person in the church. D. de testibus, l. requisisti; quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, l. sicut, §. si, in fine, cum si.

The second reason is that hospitals are exempt from secular laws. C. de episcopis et clericis, l. omnia privilegia. And in a general disposition, the exempt are not contained: as noted, C. de silentio et decem, l. decurionibus, lib. 10, unless express mention is made of privileges.

The third reason is that if this statute were understood to apply to sacred places, i.e., ecclesiastical ones, it would be against the liberty of the church, and would not be valid; because it would follow that churches could not be endowed, nor enriched. D. de senatu et excommunicatione, c. nouerit, per Innocentius.

The fourth reason is that such statutes would be extended to places dedicated to God, which is prohibited, arg. D. de pace, l. nemo; and in specialis, D. de immunitate ecclesiae, §. ult. Therefore, the statute is not valid so that it could not be alienated to churches, if the dominion is free. Whether any mode can be found that such estates are bound for collectas, Bartolus, D. de mutatione et homine, l. rescripto, §. si. Jacobus de Belvisio says otherwise, but of this it is not expedient to speak at present. From all things therefore considered, and the matter being thus, I say that the bequest is valid; and that which is holy of holies to God, I do not think is bound to collectas."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who gives money to someone and receives an annual income from him is said to commit usury.
2. What the power of selling with the clause "to whomever he wishes" contains.
3. How it is to be understood that the contracting parties may take each other back.
body: And that

† the said annual rent may be demanded, is demonstrated. And indeed, a contract entered into upon an annual obligation is valid, as in l. Stichum, § stipulatio, ff. de verb. ob., and l. senatus, § fi., ff. de do. causa mor., and l. cum notissimi, § in his, C. de praescri. 30. vel 40. an.; and in every contract the obligor is bound to give and to pay, as in l. 1, ff. de verb. ob., and insti. de obl. in prin., and de act. in prin., and l. licet, § ea obligatio, ff. de procu. Therefore, the said contract immediately produced an obligation, or the effect of an obligation, as in l. ex hoc iure, ff. de iusti. et iure, l. iuregentium, ff. de pac., and l. 1, § fi., ff. de contrahen. emp. Moreover, the collection of the said annual rent is future, and uncertain as to life, for nothing is more certain than death, and nothing more uncertain than the hour of death, as in l. nam et si cum maior., ff. de condi. indeb., and l. haeres meus, ff. de cond. et demon. Therefore, the doubt of this uncertainty makes a contract valid which otherwise would not be valid, as in l. si ea pactione and l. causa non frumentum, C. de vsur., and as Cy. posits in l. si pater, C. de inof. testa. To this lends support what the gloss posits in c. nauiganti, in the second gloss, at the end, extra de vsuris, and in c. non existimemus, 13, q. 2, l. 1, § 1, ff. de ven. inspi., and extra de sepulturis, c. sacris. Likewise, where it is uncertain whether the profit will exceed the principal sum for a person, that uncertainty makes valid a contract that otherwise is invalid, as in l. si haereditas and l. nam hoc modo, ff. de haereditate, vel actione vendita; but in the present case it is not certain that the fruit, that is, the annual rent, will exceed the principal sum; therefore, etc. Furthermore, that which does not rescind a sale on the part of the seller, its opposite does not rescind on the part of the buyer, as in l. rem maioris pretii and l. contractu, C. de rescinden. ven.; but on the part of the seller, the receipt of a lesser rent does not rescind the contract, as in l. si hęreditatem, ff. de hęre. vel ac. ven.; therefore, etc. To the contrary, it is shown that the said contracts, and the obligations arising from them, do not hold, and thus the said annual rent cannot be demanded. And thus it is certain that usury can be practiced not only in a contract of loan, but also in a contract of purchase and sale, as in extra de emp. et uend., c. ad nostram, and de pig., c. illo uos, and de usur., c. in ciuitate and c. consuluit, 14, q. 4, c. si quis oblitum and c. quicunque. But there money is given under certain usuries; for to receive money year by year for life, as above, at least presumptively, such a contract is usurious: because money is given for money, which is contrary to the nature of a contract of purchase, as in l. 1, ff. de contrahen. emp.; and money is not arranged except for buying, as is held in c. eiiciens, 88 dist.; and money in the hands of the debtor, so far as it is in itself, does not deteriorate, and produces no utility for that debtor, as in l. si nauis, ff. de rei ven., and in the previously cited c. eiiciens, and the well-known l. vsura pecuniae, ff. de verb. signi., where the text states that money is not properly fruitful, because it does not proceed from its own substance, as fruits proceed from a thing; and to that extent such contracts and obligations are called usurious, and are deemed to have been made as usurious in fraud of usury. Moreover, that according to the contract the said annual rents also cannot be demanded is also demonstrated by another reason: for it is certain that unless someone has a specific mandate with respect to contracting a specific obligation, if he contracts an obligation under a harsher condition, or otherwise exceeds the mandate, the obligation is contracted as a nullity to the prejudice of the principal, as in l. grecae, § illud, ff. de fideiussoribus, and as noted in l. fi., ff. de iuri. om. iudi., l. rogat., ff. mandati, and extra de rescript., c. cum dilecta. And the reason is that in contracting an obligation for another, the agent seems to be tacitly prohibited from binding the other person, as in l. qui alieno, § libertos, ff. de neg. ge., and as is commonly said on l. fi., C. eo. ti. But the said syndic was appointed to sell to whomsoever and to whichever persons he wished, for the life of him or of those for whom he wished. And from those words 'to whichever persons he wished', written last, two things are shown: first, that the said words refer to the persons of the buyers, and thus refer to the life of those whom the purchase concerns. This is shown because where the preceding terms concern the determination of certain persons with respect to the disposition at issue, the subsequent qualifying terms indeterminately refer back to the preceding persons, as in l. 1, C. de diuer. rerarum, it is presumed to have been added. Moreover, although it may be said,

† that which is written, l. talis scriptura, ff. de leg. 1, l. Titia, § 1, ff. de verb. ob., since subsequent matters are explained by preceding ones, as in l. si seruus plurium, § 1, ff. de leg. 1; therefore,

† since the power of selling to whomever he wished was free, yet with respect to the obligation was restricted to the life of those buyers, this restriction refers in doubt to those persons whom the contract of sale concerns, as in l. quicunque, ff. de act. et obli., l. quotiens, § 1, fa. her., and as is commonly said in l. 1, C. de sen. et interlo. om. iud. Furthermore, where there is a word demonstrating multiple persons, this word by its own meaning assigns shares to the several persons, and not the thing in its entirety to each, as in l. pluribus, ff. de lega. 2, l. qui haeredi, § fi., ff. de condi. et dem., and l. 1 and 2, C. si plures vna sententia condemnati sunt; but the distributive word 'each' indicates this, as noted in the said l. pluribus; and the words 'for the life of those to whom he wished, etc.' are demonstrative and significative of multiple persons; therefore, they seem to regard and signify according to several distinct shares. Whence an obligation defined with respect to the whole is just as if it had been said 'for the life of P. and J. and Albert', as in l. institutio talis, ff. de cond. insti. But from the arguments stated above, the power was granted to sell for the life of the buyers, and not of others, such as lord Ruffinetus, as appears from the above. But the annual rent was not limited to the life of the buyers; therefore, the said syndics exceeded their mandate, and consequently nothing was done to the prejudice of the principal or principals, as is evident from the aforesaid. Moreover, where a sale in its specification concerns multiple persons, it concerns them not as each individually for the whole, but concerns them with respect to the disposition, as is clear from the above. The principals therefore intended the annual rent to be limited so as to regard the life of multiple persons, and not each individually for the whole, but for the life of the said Banduinus and others, and this so that upon the death of one of them a due portion would be deducted from the annual rent, as in l. Lucius, § Gaio, and l. haeres, ff. ad Treb.; but the said specification concerns each person individually for the whole. Likewise, that upon the death of one, no diminution of the payment should occur; and thus also with respect to the specification of the annual rent the mandate was exceeded by the said syndics, which they could not do to the prejudice of the aforesaid principals, the commune and its men, as in the laws cited above for this point. Furthermore, where money is given to persons who will receive money year by year for life, as above, the common opinion of the doctors is that receiving in the future beyond the principal sum makes the contract usurious, as noted by Cy. in the said l. si ea pactione, C. de vsur. But from an obligation contracted for life, as above, the common opinion of the doctors is that if he said the annual rent would endure beyond the principal for the life of three persons, that it is presumed to endure beyond a period of twenty years, according to the common opinion; arg. l. si vsufr., ff. de vsufr. leg. Moreover, the addition of multiple persons in an annual rent is equated to a perpetual obligation, as in l. sancimus, § fi., ff. de don. But if the aforesaid obligation were truly perpetual, it is certain that the rent would exceed the principal sum; for we see that a doubtful disposition with respect to future time is equated to a perpetual disposition, as in l. sufficit, ff. de condi. inde., and as is commonly said in l. exceptionem, C. de proba.; but the obligation contracted for life, as above, was contracted with respect to the life of the aforesaid persons, and therefore in doubt a long life is presumed with respect to the receipt of the said annual rent. Moreover, the purchase of the said future receipt is made with respect to the value of the fruits which it is likely will be collected in the future, as in l. si fundum per fideicommissum, ff. de le. 1, and l. 1, § si vsus fructus, ff. ad l. fal., since the price equates to the equivalence of the thing, as in l. 1, ff. de contrah. emp.; but the collection of the said annual rent exceeds the principal, and it was and is likely that for the life of so many persons it would exceed the principal, and thus such contracts and obligations were made in fraud of usury; therefore, etc. Furthermore, where to a giving of money, with respect to a preceding giving of money, something is added which serves to augment the preceding obligation, this addition is presumed to have been added in fraud of usury, especially where the creditor was accustomed to practice usury, as in l. cum seruus, ff. de condi. et demon., and l. 1, § honorandae, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. But the addition of multiple persons, namely of the said Ruffinetus with respect to the said second contract, and also of the said persons both with respect to the first and also to the second contract, was added to augment the preceding obligation; therefore, it is presumed to have been added in fraud of usury. Moreover, although it may be said,

† that contracting parties may lawfully deceive one another up to half of the just price, as in l. 2, C. de rescin. uend., and l. si uoluntate, eo. titu., and extra emp. et uendi., c. cum dilecti, this is understood where fraud did not give cause to the contract, nor enter into the contract, but there was deception in the thing itself, because he believed the thing was not worth more, or the buyer believed it was worth more. But here a payment of money is expected, which has in itself the nature of a loan; and because beyond the just price, even if the things had been bought, not so much fruit would have been gathered as is the said annual rent of the said money, which pertains to usury, not to fruit; since from a thing, that is, from money itself, money is not generated of its own nature; and thus it is to be deemed usury, as in the previously cited l. usura pecunię, ff. de uer. sig. And since beyond the just price, in the said annual rent or the said annual rents, there is an expectation that will exceed beyond the just price, it must be called usury, and the said contracts must be called celebrated in fraud of usury, as in extra de usur., c. in ciuitate, which also the first gloss on the said c. in ciuitate seems to hold; and this also Ioan. Cald. seems to hold in c. nauiganti, extra de vsuris; and Inn. on the said c. in ciuitate says that contracting parties should beware of such contracts, because they do not escape the taint of usuries. Gof. also holds this in the matter of an annual rent in tit. de vsuris, near the end, at the verse quid de his, qui dant pecuniam ecclesiae etc., where from the fact that men hope to live and to receive more money than is the money which they gave, such a contract is not licit. And the reason for the aforesaid can be that which Archi. assigns in the previously cited chapter eiiciens, which is placed as a palea in 88 dist.; for he assigns the reason there: because by giving money and receiving money, usury is presumed rather than by receiving a thing, because money is not arranged except for buying. Secondly, because from a field, by plowing it, I take fruit, and from a house the use of dwelling; for by leasing a house or an estate, I seem, as it were, to exchange profit for profit. But from stored money I take no profit, and through this it seems that the sale of the use of money is not a licit contract, although Ioan. wished to hold the contrary in his gloss on c. 1, 14, q. 3, the contrary of which Archi. holds there, and Io. Cal. in the said c. nauiganti. From which laws it is clearly concluded that since the said contracts were and are, and the obligations from them are by legal presumption usurious and made in fraud of usuries, and also in contracting the said obligation the mandate was exceeded, and according to the estimation of the common opinion of men right from the very beginning the annual rent exceeded the principal, and exceeds the aforesaid payments twofold, and the said contract savors of the nature of a loan, and beyond the principal nothing can be demanded, and by the said payment the principal sum first owed and the debt are extinguished, as in l. 1, 2, and 3, C. de pig. ac., with concordances; and beyond that, that which was received as usurious and received by a usurer must be restored, as in l. rogasti, § si ibi nummos, and that which is noted there by the gloss and Bar., ff. si cer. pet., and by the doctors in the auth. ad hoc, C. de vsuris, and in c. quia in omnib. and in c. tua nos, extra de vsuris, and by Ioan. Cal. in c. nauiganti, eo. tit., with countless laws that could be cited for this; it is clearly evident also through the above matters cited for this party by the said commune. But these matters notwithstanding, the contrary seems to be truer upon inspection of the instrument. For the instrument speaks thus: that certain persons bought for their lifetime, or the lifetime of either of them, for 300 florins such a rent from a certain universitas, namely that the said universitas should pay 30 gold florins during their lifetime; and it is presupposed that he who is called the buyer was accustomed to practice usury and to make colored contracts in fraud of usuries. Likewise, it is presupposed that he was young, and that it was presumed through the lex haereditatum, ff. ad l. fal., that he would live so long that the annual receipt of 30 florins would far exceed the principal sum. Likewise, it is presumed that he lived so long that he received 60. Now that universitas says that this contract was usurious, and that in truth he intended to make an unjust contract. The aforesaid solemn arguments are confirmed, because if the instrument of syndicatus is considered, the intention seems clear: namely, that this contract is not usurious in intent, because the money was received not as a loan with the capital preserved, but as the price of an annual rent; and it is certain that an annual rent can be bought and sold both in money and in goods, as in C. de sac. san. ec., l. iubemus, in Auth. de non alie., § uult. For just as something annual can be bequeathed and donated, as in C. de lega., l. in annalibus, and ff. de uerb. ob., l. Stichum, § stipulatio, so also it can be sold for some suitable and just price, namely as much as such a hope could commonly be sold for, having regard to the time of the contract. For the subsequent outcome is not to be considered, but the beginning or inception of the contract. Likewise, hope is not worth as much as the thing itself, since hope is subject to many fortuitous events, just as fruit in the blade is not worth as much as in grain; to this effect, ff. de contrahen. emp., l. fistulas, § frumenta, and ff. de act. emp., l. si iactum retis, and by Bar., ff. de publi., l. cotem, § qui maximos. For those who buy tolls and gabelles, which consist in annual rents in coined money, do they not buy lawfully? And it is certain that they do. Why then can I not establish a certain annual rent upon my property and sell it? Likewise, if I am entitled to receive a certain annual rent from some city, we daily see that annual rent sold; and what difference does it make whether it is paid from the hand of the seller or from the hand of his debtor? Certainly none, as in ff. de pigno. act., l. solutam. Likewise, that contract is not presumed to be usurious since it is not contracted with the capital safe, since the capital itself is non-recoverable, as noted in a similar case in l. 1, C. pro socio; and this is true unless it is likely presumed to be a usurious contract because of an excess of quantity infallibly, or under an infallible hope of the thing owed, as in ff. de transac., l. cum hi, § modus. The person also must be considered, whether he was accustomed to practice usury or not, as in the said l. cum hi, § sed et personarum, regard must be had; and what is noted in ff. ad Treb., l. Lucius, § fi., supports this; and we see a similar thing in one who buys an emphyteusis up to the third generation, because the common people say that it is worth a third less than if he bought by full right, because it is subject to the occurrence of death; l. sancimus, § fi., C. de don., notwithstanding according to one interpretation, and ff. ad l. falci., l. hęreditatum, because those laws speak in a lucrative cause; but in an onerous cause it must be investigated for how much it could commonly be sold under such uncertainty, as is fully noted in l. si seruum, in prin., ff. de condi. furtiua, and in l. 2, C. de rescin. vendi. Let it therefore be concluded that in doubt we ought to abide by the instrument; yet men of more refined conscience would abstain from these contracts. Supplements of Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, under the seal of his name and in his own hand.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A privilege prohibiting the cognizance of a case is invalid.
2. Possession cannot be taken away from a person who has not been cited.
3. How a general confirmation of statutes or privileges made by the prince is to be understood.
4. The dispossessed party must be restored before all else.
body: Copio has alleged on behalf of the said minors, and it is a true conclusion,
† That a privilege or rescript which prohibits the cognizance of a cause is not valid, as stated in the Extravagantes de rescriptis, chapter 2.

And because possession cannot be taken away from the buyer without citation. C. unde vi, l. meminerint, and note in that title, l. si quis in tantam, and l. si. C. si per vim, vel alio modo. And that these abusive privileges, at least as to the matter at hand, are of no effect. C. de sac. san. eccl., l. decernimus, and de origine iuris, l. 2, § ex act. deinde regibus; but that text rather supports the contrary. But distinguish who established it and what was established.

And because our lord confirmed the statutes of the City of Verona, not as unjust privileges, since they are never seen to have been confirmed. D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 1, in principio, per Jacobum de Ravenna and Cynum, D. de falsis, l. Divus, § nec generalem, in 10th column; per quos fiat investitura, c. 1. Moreover, a minor and a church are equated. Hence, the equality of those holding privileges reduces the matter between them to the common law. D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Sed et milites, in principio. Furthermore, in law, even if our lord had confirmed the privileges, he is not understood to have confirmed those from which rights do not arise, but rather occasions for injuries or grounds for delicts. For the prince is always deemed to write with the justice of others preserved, as in X. de sepultura, c. Certificari; and it is supported by X. de confirmatione utili vel inutili, c. 1, and c. Si nuptiae, ex rescripto Petri, l. finalis. And whatever the prince does in truth and in the cause, he is seen to act not on the assertion of one party alone. C. 2, q. 1, c. Nos in quemquam, and c. In primis; and C. 17, q. 4, c. Frater, and c. Episcopus noster. These I add to the other prudently alleged arguments.
† and therefore I hold that the said wards, without order and without proof, having been dispossessed, ought first of all to be restored to their possession. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person who has been unjustly dispossessed by a judge must, above all else, be restored to his possession.
2. When an instrument or privilege is produced before a judge in the absence of a party, that party must be summoned; otherwise, condemnation cannot be pronounced.
3. A statute or a judge’s decree cannot provide that anyone, without being summoned and without having defended himself, is to be dispossessed of his goods.
4. The clause “non obstantibus” and the like: who may or may not avail themselves of it.
5. A privilege, decree, or rescript of the prince stating that something shall be done in a certain way against all persons does not include infants or wards.
6. Whether statutes bind infants or wards.
7. Whether a statute of laymen, even if favorable to the Church, is valid if it has not been confirmed by the Pope.
8. What confirmation confers.
body: The article, or case, is as follows: Antonius de la Scala, while presiding over Verona, granted certain possessions to the nobleman Cortesia de Saratico. These possessions were held and possessed by the said Cortesia, his heirs, and Lord Antonius de la Scala, and his predecessors, as lords, for a period of 50 years and more. It happened, as it pleased God, that the said Lord Antonius was deposed from the lordship of Verona, and a new lordship of our Holy Lord the Count, etc., succeeded, who ordered that the statutes of Verona be observed. Cortesia died, and from his heirs, the Abbot of Saint Zenon demanded the aforementioned granted possessions, and in proof of his right, he produced certain instruments of lease; and without any other proofs being made, and without observing any legal solemnity, the praetor ordered the laborers of the said possessions that they should answer for the fiefs and pensions thereof to the Abbot of Saint Zenon; and that they should declare that they held and possessed the said possessions from and for the said Abbot. These laborers, by virtue of the aforementioned command of the praetor, answered and declared for the said Abbot. And in this manner, the said heirs of Cortesia, who are minors, have been dispossessed and deprived of their rights most unjustly, and against all justice and truth. And to effect such dispossession, the praetor was induced and moved by the force of a certain statute and privilege made by Lords Albert and Mastino, brothers of la Scala, which I transmit to you. Now it is asked, having seen the said privilege, and having seen the donation, and the authority and power of Lord Mastino, paternal grandfather of the said Lord Antonius de la Scala, whether the said minors and heirs of Cortesia ought to be restored in all things by right, or whether they could not have been thus dispossessed.

And that the said wards ought to be restored and placed back in their former state is proved first as follows. For this decree, or statute, of the lords of Mistini and Albert presupposes that those prosecuting the right of the monastery must do so unwillingly, by means of privileges of Emperors, Kings, and any other person, or by instruments of fiefs, leases, exchanges, and purchases; and it requires that it first be made clear that these are privileges or juridical instruments. But this could not be established unless the wards were first legally cited. Therefore, the wards themselves ought to be placed back in their former state. And in support of this is L. 4, § condemnatum, and what Bartolus notes there, D. de re iudicata; and what Bartolus notes there in L. Divus, D. de testamento militis; and L. 1, § 1, D. quod vi aut clam.

For in the production of privileges or instruments, the opposing party must be cited, as stated in 3. q. 9. c. chartae, and as noted by Bartolus in l. Item illa, de constitutionibus peccatorum. This is required, among other reasons, so that the party may have the opportunity to prove the falsity of such documents or the lack of due solemnity. Such falsity and lack of solemnity can be assessed from many sources, as seen in Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. inter dilectos, and in Codex, de tabulis, l. generali, lib. 10. And what is fully noted there is not obstructed by the fact that in the aforementioned last decree or statute it was stated, "notwithstanding any laws," and specifically "notwithstanding the imperial law," Codex, si per vim, vel alio modo. For that clause was added with regard to the exclusion of privileges or instruments, provided that it is first established whether the privileges or instruments are legally valid in themselves. That clause does not apply, for it was simply stated with reference to those privileges or instruments, and thus it must be understood as referring to legally valid ones, as stated in § condemnatis, ff. de contrahenda emptione, and l. non putavi, § non quaevis. And I consider this to be true according to positive law, and that the said decree or statute would be valid. And even assuming that the said lords could have used the said clause, "notwithstanding," which, however, is not true, as I will say below, it suffices that the clause can operate in another respect: for example, concerning the knowledge of the possessors' rights, without it operating concerning the knowledge of the rights of privileges or instruments, since we are dealing with a matter of contempt and injustice, as in c. quae a iure communi exorbitant, de regulis iuris, lib. 6, and l. cum quidam, and ff. de liberis et posthumis. And in support of this, beyond the aforementioned points, is what is noted by Cynus in l. si quando, Codex, unde vi, and by Johannes Andreae in c. ultima, Extra, de foro competenti, in the Novella.

Secondly, thus: for the said decree or statute could not provide that anyone summoned and undefended ought to be dispossessed of his goods; because this is contrary to natural justice, therefore, etc., as in c. Pastoralis, De iudiciis, in the Clementines, and Codex, De iure fisci, l. Defensionis, lib. 10. And it supports what Innocentius notes extra, De constitutionibus, c. Quae in ecclesiarum. For any possessor, however unjust, and even one possessing de facto, must nevertheless be summoned, as in Codex, Si propter pupillum, pen., l. Si deserta praedia, in fine; and Innocentius notes in c. Quatuor, extra, De maioritate et obedientia. And it supports l. 1, § Si, and l. Si, in principio, ff. Uti possidetis. For the aforementioned d. de la Scala, or even the people of Verona, cannot use

† The clause of non-obstante legum: and especially concerning the aforementioned matters. For statutes of inferior authorities cannot employ a clause by which derogation is made to the laws of superior authorities, as is stated in the Digest, ad municipalia, the last law; and in the Extravagantes, de iureiurando, chapter Venientes. And note this through Iacobus de Belvis in the Institutes, de actionibus, section Omnium. And it is supported by law 1, Codex, de iure aurei anuli, and what is said there by the same Iacobus de Belvis.

Thirdly, that these lords Mastino and Alberto were not bound by the said decree or statute in their contracts or acts. For, as we have said, the said decree or statute derives its force from the people of Verona, and it cannot bind the superior of that people, to whom all free power has been transferred by that people by way of law and statute, as is evident from the statute of the city of Verona, which begins: "Item statuimus, et ordinamus, quod nobiles, et magnifici domini Albertus, et Mastinus fratres de la Scala" etc., under the rubric "Arbitrium, et potestas magnificorum dominorum Alberti, et Mastini fratrum de la Scala" etc. And the laws cited above in the immediately preceding reason are applicable to this point, as in the Extravagantes, de maiestate et obedientia, chapter Cum inferior. Or, if we say that it is valid as a decree or statute of the said lords themselves, it still did not bind them: because there must be a personal distinction between the binder and the bound, as in the last chapter of the Extravagantes, de institutionibus; and because no one, in general speech, is considered to speak of himself, as in the Codex, de solutionibus, law Quaestio. And the same applies if you say that this is a statute of the people, to whom the said lords gave their authority, and by the same laws. And it is supported by law 1, in the principal part, Digest, de auctoritate tutorum; and in the Extravagantes, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, in chapter Si una, in the Clementines, joined with law 2, section Omnino, Codex, de vetere iure euocando. And in the matter proposed, Johannes Andeolus holds this expressly in chapter 2, de constitutionibus, book 6; and in the Extravagantes, de raptu, in chapter 1; and more fully and expressly in chapter Cuiuslibet, Extravagantes, de regulis iuris, book 6, in his Mercuriales. Whose opinion is founded on the law Digna vox, Codex, de legibus, by which law the opinion of the Archdeacon, who holds otherwise, is rejected, and the opinion of Johannes Andeolus is approved by my teacher, Lord Baldus, in the said law Digna vox.

Moreover, although the said lords of the Scala had wished to subject themselves to the said decree or statute, which they nevertheless did not do; yet concerning the persons of their successors in co-equal jurisdiction, they could dispose of nothing, as in the said law Digna vox, in the word "iudicamus," with the gloss. And it is supported by the Digest, de arbitris, law Cum magistratus, and what is elegantly noted by Guilielmus de Cuneis in the last law of the Digest, de re iudicata. From which it follows that Lord Antonio della Scala, who made the donation of the said goods to the said Cortesia, was not bound by the said decree or statute. On the contrary, even if the said Antonio himself had made or confirmed such a decree or statute in favor of the said monastery, by that decree or statute possession could not, nor ought to, be claimed from the heirs of the said Cortesia, nor concerning them or their goods should any innovation be made by the aforementioned decree; and especially because the contracts of the said lord made during the time when he ruled ought to have obtained the force of law or the force of statute, as in the Digest, de publicaniis, law Caesar; and in the Codex, de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, law Do. And what is fully noted by Bartolus in the Digest, si certum petatur, law Civitas.

Fourthly, because by virtue of such a decree or statute, the aforementioned spoliation could in no way have been committed against the aforementioned minors, this is proven. For it is not credible that the said lords of the Scala, by the said decree or statute, intended that the persons of minors, so defenseless and without judicial cognizance, should be stripped of the goods they possessed, because they could not have done so even if they had wished. For not even an imperial rescript containing such loss or detriment to those minors would be valid, so that in his province he would be bound and experience the fortune of litigation, and all due caution would be observed. Codex, quoniam inter pupillos et viduas, law Unica.

† On the contrary, it must be well considered. The aforementioned law *Quae pupillis*, which grants a double privilege to wards, widows, and miserable persons: one, that no privilege or rescript is obtained whereby they are drawn out of their province; the other, that even if they are sued within the province, the order of law be observed in proceeding between them, so that, as stated in the text, “all the fortune of litigation and all caution be preserved,” rightly considered. So much so that my teacher, the said Baldus, says there that although the emperor said in the rescript “notwithstanding any law,” nevertheless the rescript would not have effect between the wards themselves, unless there was a special and express mention of the persons of the wards. From this it follows that if this is so in the prince, much more so in an inferior cannot one dispose against the prohibitive laws of a superior. Nor can one use the clause “notwithstanding,” as has been said above. On the contrary, even if the said doctors of La Scala could have used the clause “notwithstanding,” nevertheless by their clauses inserted in the said decree or statute, the persons of the wards would not have been sufficiently comprehended. I reject the law *Nec imperialem*, C. *Si per vim*, which contains the common law of all. For by this, it seems, the aforementioned law *Unica*, C. *Quoniam Imperator inter pupillos*, is rejected, nor do other laws seem to be rejected specially, and those providing for wards in privileges, such as C. *Qui legitimam personam*, l. 2, and C. *Qui dari tutorem possint*, in l. *Universis*. Nor do those words “and all other laws speaking against the aforesaid, etc.” stand in the way, because by this, laws introduced into the privilege of wards are not understood to be rejected, since in them there is a stronger reason than in the laws expressly stated, as in Extra, *De rescriptis*, in c. *Sedes*, and *De procuratoribus*, in c. *Non potest*, in the Clementines. And by this, those other words in the said decree or statute placed there “against whatever singular persons, colleges, and universities, etc.” do not stand in the way. And because from such general wording the persons of the wards themselves ought to be excepted, since no special mention is made of them by the aforesaid: and because this disposition is one introducing new law, and also inequitable, therefore, to the greatest extent possible, it ought to be restricted, according to the doctrine of Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus in l. *Nuntiatio*, ff. *De novi operis nuntio*, and ought to be understood, to the greatest extent possible, so that it is not extended except to cases expressly stated, as in Extra, *De regulis iuris*, in c. *Ea quae a iure*, lib. 6, and what is said there by Johannes Andreae, and what is noted by the same Johannes Andreae in c. *Constitutionem*, *De regulis*, lib. 6. For a new disposition, to the greater extent possible, ought to be understood by subdivision and limitation, so that it does not correct cases which by subdivision or limitation are in any way separable from it, as in l. *Sed et posteriores*, ff. *De legibus et senatusconsultis*, and C. *De litibus contestatis*, auth. *Offeratur*, joined with l. *Sciendum*, ff. *Qui satisdare cogantur*. And especially here must subdivision and limitation be made on account of such wardship persons, since their privilege is enclosed in the body of the law, to which privilege it ought not to be understood that derogation is made by the aforesaid words or similar ones, unless special mention is made of that privilege enclosed in the body of the law, as is noted in l. *Haeres absens*, in the beginning, ff. *De iudiciis*, and C. *Ubi de crimine agi oportet*, in auth. *Qua in provincia*, and what is noted in l. *Decurionum*, C. *De silentiariis*, lib. 12. Nor let anyone say that the said goods came to the wards by contract of the said Cortesia, who was older, by l. 3, ff. *Quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur*, and l. 2, C. *Si adversus creditores*, and l. *Aemilius*, *De minoribus*, cum sequentibus, because this is nothing: because here the privilege of the wards is not alleged in any contract or transaction with the deceased. But in that which ought to have its origin from the wards themselves, namely, the indefensibility of the wards, and in the judicial order to be observed against the wards anew, as in the said l. 2, C. *Qui legitimam personam*, and the said l. *In universis*, C. *Qui dari tutorem possint*, and to l. 1, ver. *Quinimmo*, C. *Quoniam Imperator inter pupillos*, vel viduas. And it serves, C. *De restitutione militum*, l. *Si cum militaribus*, and what is noted there by the gloss and by Jacobus Butrigarius, and what is noted by Bartolus in l. *Cum filius*, § *In hac*, ff. *De verbis obligatorum*. And this is what these defenses or judicial exceptions are called “emerging,” inasmuch as they emerge and have their origin in the time of the trial, as is noted by Innocentius in c. *Pastoralis*, Extra, *De exceptionibus*, and by Bartolus in l. *Eum qui*, § *Qui ita*, ff. *De verbis obligatorum*. Nor do the aforesaid stand in the way.

† That which is said, that statutes bind infants and the insane, as in l. si sine haerede, §. Lucius, and what is noted there by the gloss and by Doctorus, ff. de administratione tutorum, and what is noted by Cynus in l. 2, near the end, C. quae sit longa consuetudo, because this must be understood in those cases where there is an equal reason for disposing against wards and against adults; otherwise, it is otherwise. And thus says Guillaume de Cuneo in this passage in l. ingenuum, ff. de statu hominum. But this is not an equal reason, but rather a most unequal one, as in the aforementioned l. unica, C. quod Imperator inter pupillum et viduam. Moreover, the aforementioned l. si sine haerede, §. Lucius, speaks where the statute is conceived in rem and generally. But this decree, or statute, is personal, and not simply in rem and general; therefore, etc. And thus holds Bartolus in the aforementioned §. Lucius. Certainly, it respects a certain mode in the statute, and not a general provision, that is. And by this it supports l. 1, in fine, ff. de exceptionibus doli, which is noted in l. antiochensium, ff. de privilegiis creditorum. Furthermore, the aforementioned l. si sine haerede, §. Lucius, with its subject matter, has place in the premises, or in dispositions simply made by the common law, but not in prohibitions, as in l. omnes populi, ff. de iustitia et iure, and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. cassa, and de episcopis et clericis, auth. item nulla communitas. But here we are in a prohibitive matter, as in the aforementioned l. unica, C. quoniam Imperator inter pupillum et viduam, ver. quinimmo, and l. finalis, C. si per vim, vel alio modo. Nor does anything avail the derogatory clause placed in the aforementioned decree, or statute, which in no way regards the privilege of wards, nor was there power to append such a derogatory clause, as has been proved above, and by the aforementioned the understanding of the aforementioned l. si sine haerede, §. Lucius, is declared, which by the doctors is not commonly declared. Fifthly, and lastly, I say that the aforementioned decree, or statute, of the lords Mastino and Alberto, providing for the said monastery of Saint Zenon, and concerning things pertaining to the said monastery, was not valid in law, and was, and is, expressly null by the law itself. For laymen have no jurisdiction over ecclesiastical persons, as in Extra, de constitutionibus, c. quae in ecclesiarum. And since to enact statutes is a matter of jurisdiction, and a statute can only be made concerning those things which pertain to the jurisdiction of the enactor, as by Guillaume de Cuneo, l. 1, §. qui magistratus, ff. quod quisque iure in suo loco teneatur, therefore, etc. Moreover, although the imperial law favoring the Church, which does not contradict canon law, is observed by ecclesiastical persons, as in Extra, de non offendenda ecclesia, nunquam, in c. 1, and what is noted there by Johannes Andreae.

† Nevertheless, a law or statute of inferior laypersons, even if it favors the Church, or ecclesiastical persons or things, ought not to be observed, but is null by the law itself, unless it has been approved by the Roman Pontiff, as is the case expressly stated in *Extra*, *De constitutionibus*, chapter *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae*. And this is found in *De hoc*, Distinction 10, in chapter 1, and there by the Archdeacon, from which it clearly appears that the said decree or statute, which was issued in favor of the said monastery of Saint Zenon and the things pertaining to the said monastery, was and is null by the law itself, since it was made by lay persons and by one inferior to the prince, and was not confirmed by the Roman Pontiff, as in the said chapter *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae*. And thus it does not deserve to have the name or effect of a decree or statute; it lacks the efficient and material cause, as in the said chapter *Quae in ecclesiarum* and the law *Decernimus*, *Codex*, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*; and in *Extra*, *De foro competenti*, chapter *Si diligenti* and chapter *Significasti*; and by this, the said law 3, § *Condemna*, *De re iudicata*; and the said law *Non putavit*, § *Quae vis*, *De contrahendis*; and the law *A nullo*, *Codex*, *De fideiussoribus*. From which it follows that such a decree or statute ought not to be understood as confirmed by our lord.

† For by a simple confirmation, vigor is not conferred upon a privilege or status which is in itself null, as stated in Extra, De confirmatione utili vel inutili, c. 1, and the glosses thereon; and in the same title, c. Cum dilecta; and in Codex, De fidei instrumentis, l. Inter dilectos. Moreover, by the confirmation of our Lord, this status, which is disapproved by law, is in no way understood to be confirmed; for a firm confirmation is not extended except to matters proven and lawful, and it is not deemed to have been issued in respect of matters base and unlawful. And the case appears expressly stated in c. 1, Extra, De iureiurando, lib. 6; and for this purpose, l. Si quis sub conditione, ff. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and thereon, on this point, by Bartolus; and it supports what is noted by the gloss, ff. De regulis iuris; and l. Non videntur data, §. Qui iussu; and l. Tale pactum, §. Finis, ff. De pactis, in the final gloss at the end.
