From all these things, and especially considering this fifth and final reason, it must be concluded that the deprivation of possession made to the detriment of the said minors, and the interdiction made to their laborers, did not hold in law, nor could it in any way be effected by the force of the said alleged decree or status; and consequently, that the said minors ought to be restored and placed back into their former status; and that the said deprivation or spoliation ought to be revoked insofar as it proceeded in fact, as stated in l. Meminerint, Codex, Unde vi; and l. 1, near the end, Codex, Si per vim vel alio modo; and it supports Extra, De re iudicata, c. Pastoralis; l. Finis, in the Clementinae, De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, c. Ad audientiam; and De purgatione vulgaris, c. Significantibus; and what is said on both sides by Bernardus. I, Ziliolus de Crema, doctor of laws, say and advise this. And thus, as above, it seemed to me, Philip de Casolis de Regio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A testator, who, having appointed no heir expressly, stated to his executors that he was placing all his goods into the hands of the said executors, yet without naming them as heirs or using the word of institution, whether he appears to have wished them to be heirs.
body: I have seen the opinion of Blasius de Ros, written in the French vernacular and explained to me word for word, and the question is

Whether the said last will is a testament, or whether the said Blasius died intestate. And it appears that the said last will is not a testament, but rather a codicil made by an intestate. For a testament is not properly a testament without the institution of an heir, as is noted in *Digestum*, *De testamento*, l. 1; *Digestum*, *De his quae in testamento delentur*, l. *proxime*; and *Institutiones*, *De legatis*, § *ante haeredis*. Although it is abusively called a testament, i.e., a declaration of mind, as is noted in the said l. 1. But in this writing it is never found that anyone is named as heir; therefore it is not a testament: hence there is room for succession intestate. And if you say that executors for pious causes, when no other heir is written, are considered heirs by interpretation of law, as in *Codex*, *De episcopis et clericis*, l. *si quis ad declinandam*; and *Extra*, *De testamento*, c. *cum tibi*: That is not to be understood as meaning that if 10 [units] are left for the soul, and an executor is given, that such an executor, given specifically for certain purposes, is to be understood as an instituted heir. But rather, he must have been constituted by universal words: for example, to give or distribute the whole inheritance, or a quota part. *Digestum*, *Ad Trebellianam*, l. *cogi*, § *hi qui solidum*. For certainly things or quantities do not make an heir, but succession to the universal right which the deceased had. *Digestum*, *De hereditate instituenda*, l. *ex facto proponebatur*; *Digestum*, *Ad Trebellianam*, l. 1, § *si haeres*; and l. *mulier*, § *fi*. Hence, unless it has the signification of civil law, it is not an heir. *Digestum*, *De edendo*, l. *quædam*, § *his autem*. Moreover, the testator appointed these, so to speak, arbitrators, i.e., executors, only concerning movables. *Digestum*, *De verborum significatione*, l. *mouemtium*. Hence they could not bring actions, which are per se separate species. *Digestum*, *De peculio*, l. *quam tuberonis*, § *in peculio*. Furthermore, in this last will more things are left for other causes than for the soul, and therefore this whole testament and last will must be considered made otherwise than for the soul, i.e., not for pious causes. Argument: *Digestum*, *De contrahenda emptione*, l. *domum*. Nor does that sought-after gloss help, because it said that they should pray for the soul, as is noted in *Codex*, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, l. *illud*. It is established, however, that executors for non-pious causes are not considered heirs: because that [rule regarding pious causes] was received in favor of the soul, contrary to the rules of civil law, by a certain fiction; therefore, the common law is to the contrary. *Digestum*, *De legatis secundis*, l. *si quis Titio*. Moreover, in the said testament mention is made of heirs privatively, and it seems to refer to the legitimate heirs, since it cannot refer to others; therefore it seems he thought of heirs intestate. Moreover, it was easy to name those executors as heirs, if he had wished, for the name of heir was conferred, not to this effect, but to the contrary, as in *Digestum*, *De hereditate instituenda*, l. *ex facto*, § *cogitatum*. Therefore he knew what this vocabulary, "heir," imported. And with full knowledge he omitted to append it to the person of the executors. Argument: *Codex*, *De caducis tollendis*, § *si autem ad deficiens*. Also, the name of heir must be expressed, *Codex*, *De testamento*, l. *iubemus*. But here it was not expressed; therefore we are in the case of an intestate, and thus it would seem to be concluded prima facie.

On the contrary it appears: because the word "I leave," or its equivalent, added to a universality, in no way demonstrates an institution [of an heir] by benign interpretation; because a testament is more favorable than a codicil, as is noted in *Digestum*, *De hereditate instituenda*, l. *his verbis*, in the principal part; and as is noted in *Authenticum*, *De hereditate et falcidia*, § *si vero nulla*; and *Codex*, *Favorabiliter*, l. *quot*. Also, it is the same and equivalent to say, "I make you heir," "I make you lord," "I institute you heir," "in your hands," i.e., "in your power I put all my things": because he who says all, excepts nothing. Nor does it matter by what words the will is expressed, provided the quality of the will is established. *Codex*, *De testamento*, l. *quam indignum*; and l. *testamentum non ideo infirmatur*. Nor should we inspect one clause of the testament, but all: because sometimes that which is said universally is augmented by the genus subjected after the species. *Digestum*, *De legatis tertio*, l. *hoc legatum*; and l. *ea tamen*; *Digestum*, *De funerariis instrumentis*, l. *quositum*, § *ulti*; and as is noted in *Digestum*, *De pactis*, l. *emptor*, § *Lucius*; *Digestum*, *Ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *si servus servum*, § *inquit lex*, ver. *sed non est novum*; *Si quis causam*, l. *sed et si quis*, § *quaesitum*. And I say that a testator, who puts everything in the hand of someone with no other heir instituted, seems to have placed universal power, which is the same as dominion in that person. And thus he seems to have made him lord, i.e., heir: because hand signifies power and property. *Digestum*, *De iustitia et iure*, l. *manumissiones*. Also, the testator said, "I have trust in them for the whole"; and this heir is called a fiduciary heir, as is noted in *Digestum*, *De iudiciis*, l. *quamuis*, in the gloss beginning *appellat haeredes*. Also, because he said, "in their hands I put all my goods whatsoever": therefore rights and actions. *Digestum*, *De verborum significatione*, l. *princeps bona*; and l. *nominis et rei*, which is noted in *Digestum*, *De transactione*, l. *controuersia*. And thus to the universality of the right. Also, because he gave them the power to possess without other authority: which words suggest the understanding of an institution, as is noted by Bartolus in l. *Centurio*. Also, this is supported by *Codex*, *De pactis*, l. *licet*. Also, because he calls it a testament, and it was his intention that it be a testament; therefore he wished to institute an heir, but this cannot be unless the executors are heirs. Also, he wished all other testaments to cease, which cannot be done except by a new testament; therefore he wished to make a will. But you will say, he indeed wished, but could not: because he omitted the institution of an heir. *Codex*, *De testamentis*, l. *nostram*; *Digestum*, *De aditione legatorum*, l. *ex parte*. And if the last testament were null, the first testament would be confirmed; otherwise, if no other testament proceeds, nevertheless this last will, which he wished to be valid as a testament, will not be valid by the law of codicils. *Codex*, *De codicillis*, l. *fi*, unless a codicillary clause were joined. *Codex*, *De fideicommissis*, l. *eam, quam*; *Digestum*, *De legatis secundis*, l. *Lucius*, § *filiam*; and the said l. *fi*, cum si. And if it were valid as a codicil intestate, the acceptance of the inheritance intestate would be necessary. *Digestum*, *De hereditate instituenda*, l. *qui filio*, § *servus*. And the Falcidian deduction would be taken. *Digestum*, *De legatis*, l. *ad pias causas*.

This question has many doubts and angles, and is very doubtful; finally, however, the will of the testator seems to me to be aided by interpretation. *Digestum*, *De legatis secundis*, l. *vnum ex familia*, § *item Imperator Marcus*. And therefore, considering the aforesaid, and considering that the testator said that the heirs would not contravene, which is to be understood of all heirs, and especially of those succeeding by the judgment of the testator. *Digestum*, *De vulgari substitutione*, l. *qui liberis*, § *haec verba*. And it cannot be explained of heirs by the judgment of the testator except of the executors themselves. I say that he openly named them heirs under a certain compendium of words. Wherefore I conclude that they are the heirs of the testator, and the case of intestacy ceases by the judgment of the stronger sentence, to which I have always submitted, and do submit. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The selection of a notary to record the proceedings in a case pertains, under the common law, to the office of the judge who pronounces the law.
2. If a statute prescribes a specific form for the election of a notary to record acts before the judge, whether that form must be observed in the case of a notary who records the sentence.
3. The term "acts" includes the sentence.
body: To the office

† of the one administering justice it belongs by the ius commune to choose the notary who should write in the case, as in c. statutum. §. notarium vero. de rescrip. lib. 6. Nevertheless, if the notary is suspect, he can be recused, as noted in Auth. de trien. et semis. §. et quod sępe. colla. 4.

† But through the form of the statute a certain form of choosing has been handed down with respect to those things which are done before the judge. Whence faith is not given to another, unless to a clerk of the acts (commentariensis) of this kind, that is, to whom the acts have been entrusted, as noted in ff. de iure fisci. l. in fraudem. §. quotiens. But the statute does not seem to speak about acts that are done by the judge, as in the pronouncement of a sentence: because a sentence is not delivered before the judge, but by the judge before others. I contradict [this] on the basis of the reasoning written in the statute: because the same reasoning applies to the sentence: for although the sentence is delivered by the judge, nevertheless the writing concerning it is made before the judge by the notary of the acts, as in C. de arbi. l. ne in arbitris. and noted in C. de libe. causa. l. iubemus.

† The third reason [is] because the sentence is contained under the name of the acts, as noted by Cy. in C. qndo libellus principi dat. l. pe. And therefore I think that the election of such a notary was not valid, and that his unlawful writing cannot stand. And therefore, if an incompetent notary writes, the acts are not valid, as noted by Guli. de Cu. in C. de epi. et cleri. l. repetita. and C. de execu. et exact. l. 2. lib. 12. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a witness who is an enemy with grave enmity provides sufficient indication for torture; and who is said to be an enemy with grave enmity; and what is the case with a witness who says one thing in court and another outside.
body: Of one

† Testimony is not to be believed, nor does it even constitute evidence sufficient for torture, if the witness is an enemy bearing grave enmity, as stated in the Digest, *De quaestionibus*, in the law *Maritus*, and there expressly by Bartolus; or if he appears to be an enemy on account of a most serious injury, because he was an enemy for a notorious cause. Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Licet*; in the Authenticum, *De testibus*, § *Si vero odiosus*; Digest, *De his quibus uti institoria*, in the law *Si inimicitia*; Extravagant, *De accusationibus*, chapter *Cum P. Manconella*. And here there is no doubt, and it is most certain in law. On this point, one may also read fully in the Decretum, Distinction 3, Question 5, chapter *Accusatores*. Furthermore, this witness is not credible, who outside of court states the contrary, as noted in the Digest, *De falsis*, in the law *Eos*, by Bartolus. Moreover, because he alleges a false cause, namely, an expected succession, and thus he ought not to be believed, since there was no succession in prospect. For this, the Institutes, *De pupillari substitutione*, § *Si autem quis ita formidolosus*, is most apt. And therefore, the said Pe. ought to be absolved, and the said defamer and accuser ought not to go unpunished, as stated in the Code, *De calumniis*, in the law *Nostris*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether public duties and burdens ought to be discharged at the place of origin, or of domicile, or where the valuation is made.
body: Where someone

† It derives its proper origin, whether paternal or avuncular, if he was born or conceived while the grandfather was alive: there he is bound to bear public offices, as in D. 50.4.1 (libertus), § praescriptio, and § in adoptiva. And this is true, unless he has transferred his domicile elsewhere: because then, according to the glossa in loco domicilii, he is bound to bear fiscal burdens in the place of his domicile, and not in the place of his origin, as noted in D. 50.4.1 (assumptio). But that glossa is rejected by Decius, Jacobus de Arezzo, and Cynus, who note this in C. 2.12.1 (de iuris omnium iudiciorum), and by Bartolus in l. assumptio, § 1, cited above. And this is true when he has borne patrimonial burdens in the place of his origin for the possessions which he has there: but for the possessions which he has in the place of his domicile, he bears them in the place of his domicile, as in D. 50.4.1 (rescripto), § si, and as noted in D. 50.4.1 (l. 1). And this is true, unless such burdens depend on an assessment which is made for him even in his own place by a superior. For then he ought to pay according to that assessment, and where he is found to have that assessment for the time being. And if he had an assessment in different places, i.e., for different things, he ought to pay according to the form of the assessment, as noted in D. 50.4.1 (incola). But if the assessment ought to follow the status of the person, and ought to be one, and not several: we judge of that assessment according to the new status which the person assumes, arg. D. 50.4.1 (idem Vlpianus). Since therefore this person, concerning whom the question is asked, has been transferred to the city by consent, indeed and by the form of municipal law, as noted in D. 50.17.1 (aedificia), there I say that it ought to be considered that, with the status changed, and also the quality of the thing, it is fitting to change its appellative name. C. 10.1.1 (de imponendis lucris describendis), lib. 10. For these statuses are distinguished by a certain difference of opposition, whence the latest status ought to be considered for the following time. D. 41.2.1 (si quis ante). And therefore I think that the first opinion was more just than the second, and that the appeal ought to be followed as just. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute providing that a brother and sister shall succeed one another as co-heirs appears to exclude the mother.
body: The question is

Whether the said statute excludes the mother from the succession of her son, when the mother, brother, and sister are present. And I see that it does, because the inclusion of the brother and sister appears to be the exclusion of the mother. D. de legibus 1, l. quod in rerum, § si quis post. That which supports the negative is found in Bartolus on l. 2, ad Tertullianum. I say the contrary, because the said statute does nothing other than to provide that brothers and sisters succeed to paternal goods among themselves, considering the difference made by the common law. Either they are joined on both sides or not, as noted in C. de legatis, auth. post fratres. And this was seen as sufficiently equitable by the legislators. But to exclude the mother, who succeeds in a manner by natural law, would be altogether inequitable. C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. nam et si parentibus. Therefore, a statute, which is founded upon a certain species of equity, ought not to be interpreted against humanity; and especially because, to exclude someone from the legitime, a special disposition is required. C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. si quando, § si; D. de bonis damnatorum, l. cum ratio; D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, § si. Moreover, the tacit sense of the law is not admitted against the mother. C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutis, l. precibus. Also, because the correction of laws is to be avoided, and the statute ought rather to be drawn to the sense of the common law than to its correction. C. de noxalibus actionibus, l. si servi vestri; Extravagantes de consuetudinibus, c. cum dilectus. Also, lest the statute appear to cover one altar and uncover another. C. qui potiores in pignore habeantur, l. assiduis, § exceptis. I, Baldus...

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute excluding males from the succession of an intestate son applies to a pupillus, who is unable to make a will.
body: The question is asked.

† whether a minor under guardianship is said to die intestate. The text says that he is not: according to the strict meaning of the words, because he is incapable of making a will, not intestate, just like a madman and a spendthrift. D. 28.2.1. in princ. and noted in C. 6.30.1. in the gloss veluti. But in a broad interpretation, even a minor under guardianship and a madman are said to die intestate. D. 39.4.1. § haec autem. We cannot say otherwise. For everyone who dies dies either testate or intestate. For there are only two categories. D. 38.1.2 and 3. And this is what the text wishes to say in the aforementioned l. 1, at the words “sed has quoque,” D. 28.2.1. Now let us see, if the statute is odious and excludes the mother from the succession of her intestate child, whether we should interpret it strictly and more properly, or broadly and less properly. Bartolus says that it should be interpreted broadly, on account of common usage of language. Others, looking at the matter more humanely, say that it should be interpreted strictly, although in purely lucrative inheritances Bartolus’s opinion could be upheld, and because it is one thing to lose a due inheritance and another not to gain a profit. C. 6.33.1. § in omni. and C. 10.52.1. § lucratiuus, lib. 11. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the brother of the testator, who by the form of the statute excludes the dowried daughter by accepting the inheritance under an invalid will, thereby loses the intestate succession.
2. Whether one possessing the inheritance on an invalid title transmits it.
3. Whether acceptance of the inheritance by these words, “I accept under the will, if it is valid; and if it is not valid, I accept intestate,” is valid.
4. Whether a manifest usurer can be instituted as heir.
5. The mother has one year to petition for a guardian.
body: The question is asked.

Whether the brother of the testator, who by virtue of the form of the statute excludes the dowried daughter by taking under an invalid will, loses the intestate succession. Papinian said in a similar case that he does. Paulus said that he does not. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Clodius. The opinion of Paulus is true if he erred in fact; otherwise, if in law, according to Jacobus de Arena and Doctor. I say that in matters depending on the mind, or on the knowledge of the mind, just as error of fact does not harm, so too it does not harm in matters depending on another legal constitution or statute, as in l. 2, C. de iure et facto ignorantia. I therefore say that he is not deemed to have tacitly renounced on the ground that he is ignorant that it pertains to him. D. de regulis iuris, l. in totum omnia. And this is true while remaining within the bounds of error: but if, under the pretext of this error, he had proceeded to judgment, then the way of correcting his error being closed, prejudice would be generated for himself, as in l. non fatetur, D. de confessionibus. Likewise, if he did not err, but feigned error, he would prejudice himself. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. filium. There it is presumed that he did not err concerning the father’s insanity, although under this color he acknowledged the intestate inheritance. C. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. de tutela. It is asked,

† If he possessed the inheritance, whether it is transmitted, when he has acted as heir. And it seems that it is so. For even so is to act as heir, inasmuch as from every appropriate head expressly to enter upon the inheritance. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro herede; § Papinianus, Auctoritas. C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. minus instructus. For possession always looks to its title, just as to its cause, from which it draws its origin. But this is true, unless we have other presumptions to the contrary. And therefore if a brother possessed from an appropriate head, he does not transmit. Thus said this celebrated Johannes in the said l. Clodianus. And it is the very truth in an extraneous heir, but a sui heres transmits the rights existing of the sui heres, by which rights he transmits the inheritance, being ignorant, as l. apud hostes, with its material.

† It is asked whether such an acceptance of an inheritance from a will is valid; if it is valid, then from the will, and if not valid, then from intestacy. I answer that it is not valid, because the person conferring the right to accept is uncertain in law, as noted in the Digest, title *Si pars haeredi*, paragraph *pe.*, law *Illud*, Digest, title *De regulis iuris*, law *Actus legitimi*, unless perhaps in the case of his own heir: because, since it does not appear that he renounces the benefit of abstention, the truth makes him an heir, as in § *Sui*.
† It is asked whether a manifest usurer can be instituted as an heir. I answer: yes, because no law prohibits it.
† It is asked whether a mother has a year to petition for a guardian. I answer that, setting aside the fables of Bartolus, she does have it, as in the Institutes, ad Tertulianum, §. si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The heir is to be granted possession by means of the action provided in the law *si*, Codex, title *de edicto*, under the reign of Hadrian.
2. What may be objected is considered.
3. A compromise between a guardian and a ward cannot be made, from which an alienation or even an obligation may follow.
4. A judgment rendered without observing the solemnity of the statute is void by operation of law.
5. A prohibition of division is presumed to have been made in favor of the children.
body: Although it has been fully alleged, I will add something: and it is well known that a written heir must be put in possession, unless the possessor has an obstructive title, or another defense granted to him by the edict of the said Adrian, or a just cause: for example, because the will is suspect upon inspection due to erasure, or another visible defect, as in the law "edicto," Codex, on the edict of the said Adrian. Tol.

And therefore I say that the said written heir ought to be pronounced to be put in possession, if there is a contradiction, and then to be put in possession in fact. D. de appel. reci. l. si. It is true that if the written heir releases the possession by pact or by transaction, then he ought not to be put in possession, because he renounced his right, which he could do, as D. de pac. l. pacta inter haeredem. l. 1. §. quod autem quorum leg. ista. This exception is about permitted matters, because it proceeds from the consent of the heir. Nevertheless, it must be considered

It is that a compromise cannot be made between a guardian and a ward, from which an alienation or even an obligation could follow, as is fully read and noted in l. 1, ff. de noua. Nor can it be made between a general curator and an adult, because an adult having a curator is similar to a ward. Hence, the curator represents him as a ward, especially in what is transacted between them; the reason being that the oath does not represent the adult who is of age, because on the contrary the representation of minority stands in the way. C. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. si curatorem habens. Also, because one is forbidden to contract with oneself. ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. si in emptione, §. si, unless with the authority of another curator and of the judge in good faith. C. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum ipse. And therefore the said arbitration does not stand. Nor does the sentence stand in the way: because a just appeal was taken from it, and it is alleged that the appeal is pending.

† Moreover, if it is true that the statutes provide that the judge is bound to observe another solemnity, and it has not been observed, being a grave and weighty solemnity, as in C. de repudiis, l. dubium, the sentence is void by operation of law. ff. de transact., l. cum hi, § cum prætor. That they may be appealed on just cause, Bartolus states in the aforementioned l. ult., ff. de appel. reci., if the possessor had other rights, or if the truth had not been assumed in the facts. I, Baldus, say that the truth must be adhered to.

Many matters must be considered. First, it is certain that the instituted heir must be put in possession: under the edict concerning the things which the testator possessed or quasi-possessed at the time of his death. D. de adquirenda vel omittenda hereditate, l. fin.; and C. de edicto divi Adriani et divi Marci, l. edicto. Unless those things had been left to another, who had obtained possession without defect. D. ad Trebellianum, l. filiam fratribus. Moreover, one is said to possess with a defect if a legacy has lapsed. Arg. C. de fideicommissis, l. quaestionem, §. sin.; C. de legatis, l. non dubium; and it is established in D. quorum bonorum, l. 1, §. rediguntur. Therefore, the requested possession should have been granted, notwithstanding the contradiction of the opposing party; because the contradiction, as alleged, did not have a title that was obstructive. Which I prove thus: the possessor was being disturbed by an award. Now, that award was null by law itself, and thus the award is considered as no award. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. nec ullam, §. omnibus. That the award was null appears: because the compromise was null by law itself, for a ward cannot compromise with his tutor; just as he cannot be a party in court; nor alienate to himself; nor settle. D. ad Tertullianam, l. qui habet, §. si pupillus; D. de nova operis nuntiando, l. 1, and there fully noted. Moreover, a curator cannot contract with an adult on his own authority; but if he had another curator, he could do so with that curator’s authority, observing the form of law and good faith. C. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum ipse; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. in emptione, §. si. Since it is not alleged here that another curator was appointed, the compromise did not hold, especially because an adult having a curator is, in contracting or releasing another, similar to a ward. C. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. si curatorem habens. There is also another reason: because one is not bound to keep faith with an award when the adversary is breaking faith. C. de pactis, l. cum proponas; D. de transactionibus, l. qui fidem; D. locati conducti, l. quaero, §. inter locatorem. Hence, according to what is alleged, the said award does not impede the effect of the possession. Moreover, the division did not hold if it was made against the prohibition of the testator. C. de usucapione pro emptore, l. 2. Unless this had been done in pure favor of the prohibition, and he renounced the prohibition, being of legitimate age. For a ward cannot renounce the favors of a will, lest an underage son rescind the judgment of his father.

I understand that when the prohibition of division was made for a time in favor of minors, who are presumed. D. de communi diviso, l. communi diviso, § si convenit. And that in l. sin., C. de communi diviso, because this precept is not understood, nor even that it was made in favor of age, as the said l. 2, C. de usucapione. l. pro emptore, which law is sufficiently notable for this purpose. And it supports what is noted in C. qui dant tutorem possunt, Auth. minoris debitor, in the gloss, sed quid, verse Item quid si habet secum res communis. Therefore, the petition for possession has its foundations, so that it should have been made from the beginning, notwithstanding an invalid award or transaction, which is considered null. As for the sentence, which is said to have been rendered on non-possession, I say nothing: because I have not seen the records. Hence, I say that a sentence rendered in a possessory action, where the rights of the parties were not fully discussed, would not prejudice the petition for inheritance, if it were brought by the said written heirs, as l. cum fundum, § fin., D. de vi et vi armata. Even if the sentence in the possessory action had become res judicata. C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. post sententiam. Also, if any solemnity, grave and weighty, required by statute had been omitted, and especially one concerning the form of the litigation to be decided, or the decision of the controversy, the sentence would be null, as l. cum hi, § si praetor, D. de transactione, cum si. Prudently and copiously by the noble colleague Alle,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A promisor, who undertook at his own expense and cost to maintain and repair the sluice, the site, and the mills, if necessary, in the event of a great and overwhelming flood that irreparably destroyed the said mills and rendered the remaining sluice, the site of the sluice, and the mills entirely useless: whether he is bound by the force of the aforementioned promise, and to what extent. And number 4.
2. A promisor who undertook to maintain the bell tower is not bound to provide the bells.
3. Whether a debtor, who did not expressly bind himself for the case of fortuitous event, is liable for such event.
4. Whether one who promised to make a roof is bound to make the walls.
5. How "to maintain" is to be understood. The time could not be completed by force; whether a remission is to be made, and in what manner: for example, if you lease a house to me for one year for 20, the utility of which lies during the fair season, which lasts for 10 days: if after the fair you were expelled by enemies, whether a remission of the rent is to be made, and in what manner.
body: In a certain instrument, in which one partner sold his share of certain mills and a sluice to another, reserving a claim for the unpaid price beyond certain quantities agreed upon as fruits of a specific time, i.e., one year, the following words are found formally: "the said buyer is also bound, at all his own costs and expenses, to maintain and have repaired the said sluice, places, and said mills, if necessary, nor shall the said seller be bound in any way for such maintenance and repair." It happened that there was a very great and unusual flood, which irreparably destroyed the said mills, and rendered the said sluice, the place proper to the said sluice, and the mills entirely useless, and caused many other great damages to the said buyer in his houses and land situated nearby, as well as to others having mills on the said Tiber.

† Now it is asked, assuming without judicial determination of the truth that the said instrument is free from any error, whether the said buyer, by virtue of the said words, is bound to the said seller for anything. And it must be said that he is not, for the reasons set forth below. Nevertheless, certain matters must be premised for clarity, which are so morally true that they cannot be denied.

First, that on account of the force of the water and its continuous impetus, mills and sluices cannot be maintained in the same quality unless, as necessity successively demands, they are repaired when they are destroyed in whole or in part; for by this aid, unless divine power intervenes, they can be preserved. And a mill is similar to buildings, which are preserved by being restored. D. de serv. urb. pr. l. eum debere columnam. It is also similar to a human being, who is not preserved except by the restoration of what is lost, as the philosophers say. D. de iud. l. proponebatur. D. de neg. gest. l. sive haereditaria. D. de verb. sign. l. impensae. However, when divine force supervenes, such as lightning from heaven, or hail, or shipwreck, it is impossible to preserve human things, and this is manifest by nature. D. de act. empt. l. si ea res. D. de verb. obl. l. inter stip. §. sacramenta. cum si.

The first reason, therefore, is this: he who promises a human act is not bound for the act of a river; because he does not promise the act of a river, which occurs by divine force, as D. de dam. inf. l. fluminum. §. servius. there: "of the river," etc. and D. de dam. infec. l. quidam. there: "by external force," etc. where the case is literal. And D. de reg. iur. l. contractus. where the case is also literal.

Second, because the fortuitous event was not promised, therefore the promisor is not bound for the fortuitous event. l. sed et si quia. §. quaesitum. si quis cau. l. 1. C. commoda. per Cynus. And the reason is that an exception arises from the case, and one is not understood to waive a future exception, as noted by Guido de Columna in the said §. quaesitum.

Third, because that case was so sudden, so unusual, and so dangerous, that it seemed rather the wrath of God than nature joined to the case. And such cases, which exceed human usage and consideration, do not fall within the promise, even if the case had been promised, D. de contr. em. l. si fistu. §. frumenta. and there noted by Bartolus. And noted D. de neg. gest. l. cum alicui. And D. ad l. Aquil. l. quemadmodum. §. in hac illud. in the word "suddenly," where the text is express. And l. si putator. there: "since to divine," etc. And l. si quis fumo. in the word "rather by force." And l. si ex plagiis. §. fin. in the words "case rather than fault." And Guido de Columna allegates the said §. frumenta for the case of this question in the said §. quaesitum.

Fourth, because the buyer did not undertake the peril upon himself, but a certain care and social solicitude, albeit at his own expense; and only the soil or site was vitiated, whence this detriment did not arise, which is mixed with the vitium of the soil, even if the peril had been undertaken, as D. loc. l. opus. and there Bartolus; much more so where no mention of peril was made.

Fifth, because this case is similar to the case where the soil and site sink into the depths, and the debtor is released. C. de iure emph. l. 1. For this site, as regards the use of the mill and its substance, is dead, and there it cannot be restored, as D. de aqua pluv. l. 1. §. denique. And the buyer did not promise to change the nature of the place, and that a sloping and low place should become level, and that water should not carry away sand and not silt up the place; therefore he is not bound for the act and judgment of God.

Sixth, because this case is called a tempest, which does not fall within the contract unless special mention is made of it, as D. de publican. l. Caesar. and l. secunda. si quis cau. §. penult.

Seventh, because from every promise of an act, a fortuitous event is understood to be excepted, unless mention is made of it specifically, as expressly noted by Bartolus, D. de verb. oblig. l. stipula. ista post princi. For this is inherent by nature.

Eighth, because every promise of an act has this tacit condition, namely, unless a just cause impedes. D. de verb. obl. l. in illa stipulatione si calendis. per Bartolus. Also, this condition is understood: "as far as it is possible for me to keep." D. loc. in l. loca. In Auth. iusiur. quod praestatur ab his. in two places in the text.

Ninth, because the case of the extinction of the site is an unthought-of case, and never before occurring, and which ought not to have been thought of; therefore the promisor is not bound. D. de verb. oblig. l. inter stip. §. sacrament. For he ought not to have looked to so unusual and adverse fortune.

Tenth, because the extinction of the subject extinguishes the substance of the thing and the disposition of man. D. de leg. 3. l. 11. §. si rem. D. de solut. l. qui res. §. aream. And D. de usufr. l. 2.

Eleventh, he who promises to maintain a wall to support the burdens of a neighbor, if the wall falls, is bound to restore the wall of the same kind, that is, of the same span, that is, form, and quality, so that the same thing may be understood. D. de serv. urb. pr. l. servitutes. §. si sublatum. And he is not bound to anything else. Also, he is bound to this only if he can; otherwise he is not bound. D. de serv. urb. pr. l. eum debere columnam. Because every future thing has a tacit condition of possibility. D. de verb. oblig. l. interdum and l. si homo. per Bartolus. And given a lawful time. D. de verb. obl. l. et ideo. And l. continuus. §. item qui insulam. And in the same place. For he is not bound to restore in another place, nor to follow the water. D. de aqua quot. l. hoc iure. §. si aqua. where it is expressed.

Twelfth, because those words, "as it shall be expedient," are of absolute locution, so as to be reduced to the arbitrium and sense of a good man. And first I say that the word "as" or "according as" means the same as "as time requires," "as it is expedient for the time," "as equity dictates." C. de edict. l. edita. D. de relig. l. si quis sepulchrum. §. sumptus. And l. ut si quis. §. si colonus. D. ubi pupillus edu. debeat. l. 2. §. modus autem. D. de exercit. l. Lucius. §. quare est modus in rebus. D. de verb. oblig. l. si ita quis. §. ea. l. C. de annonis, et trib. l. pro locis. And l. mediterraneae. lib. 10. de nauiculariis, et naucle. l. cum nauclerio. in the word "for the freight." But everything that time demands out of necessity, and for the utility of obtaining fruits, was done by the said buyer, as is notorious.

Thirteenth, that there are three cases. The first is maintenance, which signifies punctually the same state and the same quality. But because this is precisely impossible by nature in water, which always erodes and always moves, it follows subjoined and transitively from the first head of construction to the second head of the same, substituted in the possible pact in place of the impossible, namely, to have it adapted. But suppose that the second, by the impossibility of the nature of things, because it cannot be adapted in the same or similar manner. Certainly this case is omitted and is not contained in the obligation. D. de verb. obl. l. quicquid restringendae. Hence consider the order of the writing. For the first part begins with maintenance, and because it cannot last long by itself, it passes to the second head, namely, to adaptation. And if this second head were possible, it ought to be repaired in the same place, given a convenient time. But if it were not possible, there is no obligation of impossibilities; because there is no solution of impossibilities, and no execution, as in the rule of law: no one is bound to the impossible. D. de excus. tutor. l. Titius. §. fin. Also, the word "maintain" signifies expenses in restoring, not in making another new building of a different genus, as if a husband has a mill in dowry, he is bound to restore and replace removed stones. l. 1. in fin. de impensis in rebus dot. factis. He is not bound, however, to make a stone tower or pillars for the solidity of the mills. Hence the laws which speak that the husband is bound, speak of restoring, or speak of moderate expenses which can be made from the fruits of the dowry, sol. matrim. l. si cum dotem. §. si autem in seuissimo. For since he does not know for how long the marriage will last, and he is not bound to make uncertain expense from his own purse, although he could recover if made. And it serves. c. rem in praesenti. §. sed nec ob impensas. These are not necessary in our case, because the obligation is limited to a certain place, and, so to speak, to the place of the place.

Fourteenth, the buyer did not promise the seller to keep the mill, nor the machines, nor did he promise him to restore or reacquire the millstones, hence even if the building called the mill and the sluice had grown in figure: nevertheless no fruits would have been perceived, and the fruits and water would have been lost. Therefore he is not bound, to l. Rhodiam de iac. l. si vehenda. §. idem iure. And fully noted in l. quod te. D. si certum petat. by others. And Bartolus.

† Just as if I promise the Abbot to maintain the bell tower, which yielded no fruits when the bells were removed, I am not bound to maintain the bells, nor to re-equip the bell tower: even though the parishioners, not hearing the bells, do not go to the church to make offerings, as in l. quicquid astringendae, ff. de verb. oblig. If they are destroyed, or thrown down by the force of the winds, I am not bound, nor can it be said to me: you ought to have secured it with new supports, or you ought to have closed the windows of the bell tower: for if that had been done, the wind would not have carried them away. For these are cavils. l. circa medium, C. de sententiis, quae pro eo quod interest. Moreover, the millstone, which is movable, ought not to be repaired, but the millbed, that is, the lower part of the millstone, which is fixed and immovable. Thus, if someone had promised to keep the fortune of a raft, ff. de fundo instructo, l. cum delationis, §. asinam, according to the true case of that §. vnde, a chance occurrence in the millstone does not pertain to the said promisor, but that chance alone suffices to impede the revenues. Fifteenth, because speaking properly and in reality, even if someone had promised to repair the machines and other instruments and utensils of the mill, which was not promised here: nevertheless, in no way could that be said which the Jurisconsult says elsewhere: to restore and preserve the old, as is fair and necessary. But I am not compelled to begin new things. ff. de neg. gest. l. nam et seruius, §. si auio. And there is the case: that to maintain signifies the old, that is, those things which were formerly placed in the substance, not new things, because to preserve and to maintain are the same. Hence, it demonstrates the preceding figure of the place, as it appeared. l. rutilia, and there no. in l. fundi, ff. de contrah. empt. Sixteenth, if we refer ourselves to the judgment of a good man: which lies enclosed in the word expedierit, as ff. de fideicomm. liber. l. thays, §. Lucius. And according to the standard of justice, it must be considered that the final cause of this promise was that the said vendor ought to receive the fruits of that year. Hence, for the sake of the fruits of that year, it was said for a brief time that the buyer alone would make those expenses which occurred to the vendor for the reservation of the fruits, and this is the simple truth. And nothing else was said or thought substantially. Therefore, the sense of the writing must be drawn to this sense of the truth. And this should sound by the common way. For everyone who, on account of the fruits of a brief time, is bound to acknowledge the burden of expenses, is not bound to make expenses for the perpetual utility of the thing. But only those which are for the sake of obtaining the fruits, and which he who has to consider only the fruits of that time is accustomed to make, as if he were a lessee who would promise this. ff. sol. mat. l. fructus, ff. de usufr. l. hactenus, hoc no. Barto., ff. de in pen. in re. do. fac. l. impensae, and by the notes there by Bart., this passage is decided.

† Moreover, when it is asked whether a debtor, who has not expressly bound himself for a fortuitous event, is liable for such an event, Guillaume de Couzan, Raymond de Peypuier, and other doctors in § sed interdum state that a distinction must be made. For either no fault precedes, and he is not liable for the fortuitous event, and this point is pursued by the Doctor in ff. de verb. oblig. continuus, § cum quis; or fault does precede, and then it matters whether that fault did not destroy the fortuitous event, that is, did not lead to the fortuitous event, and he is not liable, as in ff. quod vi aut clam, l. si alius, § est et alia, and l. non omne, ff. de statu hominum. Or it was directed toward the fortuitous event, and then it matters whether such fault was not punishable by the nature of the contract, such as slight fault in a bilateral contract entered into for the benefit of both parties, and he is not liable, as in ff. comm. l. si ut certo, § nunc videndum, and there noted, ff. de negot. gest. l. sive haereditaria. Or it was purged by an action arising from that contract; and then it matters whether the fortuitous event would have occurred nevertheless: and this is certain, and he is not liable, as in ff. ad l. Rhod. de iac. l. sive haeredi, § idem iuris, and l. et in totum, de impens. in re dot. fact. and de act. et oblig. l. is qui. Or it is certain that it would not have occurred; even then he is liable, as in ff. comm. l. si certo, § sed interdum. Or it is doubtful, and then the defendant is absolved, as in C. de pign. act. l. qui fortuitis. But here in this buyer no fault is found: and especially because he could not foresee so sudden and divine a case; just as he could not foresee many other things that happened in the city and in his own house: to whom it may be said, “Prophesy, who struck you?” From these it appears that he who says that the fortuitous event occurred through fault committed in obtaining [the thing] must prove that if that had not been omitted, the fortuitous event would have occurred. Which in our case is false to prove by the nature of things, and impossible. And if he were to attempt to prove the truth, which can be shown by hidden faith, he never lacked support, and cannot change the merits of things in prudence, as Boethius says.

† For if it were said, “You, the buyer, could and ought to have made the sluice-gates,” the answer is: “You know that you are lying, especially because neither does this instrument state it, nor were any words spoken to this effect, nor was it said, nor was it even contemplated.” I believe that the instrument itself is truthful and that what is contained therein stands. But unless I am mistaken in my opinion, one must resist the fraud, falsehood, and malice of the other party by the following ways and modes, which are also in accordance with the law.

First, because a promise determined according to place so determinately includes that place that it excludes all others. D. de eo quod certo loco, l. 3, § si quis ita, at the words “quemadmodum.” But here the work promised was determined as to place, namely, the place of the mills and the dam; for “place” is predicated of the interior part of a thing, not of an external, remote part, nor of that which does not cohere with the body itself. D. de verbis significandis, l. locus. Hence, the truth is gathered from the instrument itself.

Furthermore, no one is bound to incur an uncertain expense. For it was uncertain by the very nature of things, and doubtful, whether the sluice-gates would be of future use or not. Hence, no one is bound to apply doubtful remedies at his own expense, nor to risk his certain patrimony for uncertain gains. Hence, in case of doubt, the law says that it is safer not to sail, and it is safer not to build on sand. Moreover, the truth itself has declared that they were not to be of future use.

Furthermore, the sluice-gates contribute nothing to the dam, which had fallen into ruin, nor to the riverbed, which had become silted up, to such an extent that even if the mills had remained standing on their foundations, they would not have operated.

Furthermore, the water-carriers were about to migrate; yet, due to the flood and the silting up of the dam’s channel, as well as due to the machinery and other utensils, which were lacking in the mills and which the said buyer was not bound to repair, the sluice-gates were of no assistance whatsoever, nor are they of any assistance to the said seller. For the said seller would derive no benefit therefrom, whether by lawful or unlawful means; thus, the argument collapses entirely.

Thirdly, because he who promises to build a house is not bound to build other structures than the house itself, even if access to the house is gained through those other structures. Hence, he is not bound to construct a road. And he who promised to build a pond did not thereby promise to build a stream and an aqueduct, because they are distinct bodies. D. 44.1.1 (de exceptionibus), l. sed si ante. For the expense is different, and the works are different. D. 50.17.1 (de negotiorum gestione), l. eum actum, § sin. And on account of one burden I am not bound to two, even if they cannot be separated; just as if I promise to place a roof on a house, I am not thereby bound to build the walls, although a roof cannot be placed without walls, as in D. 41.3.1 (de usucapione), l. eum qui aedes; although the upper part could not exist without the lower, because it cannot be supported in the air. D. 43.2.1 (de damno infecto), l. quod clavis. Hence, he who promises to maintain a roof does not thereby promise to maintain the walls. And he who promises to maintain millstones does not thereby promise to maintain the mill, because he who promises an accident does not promise its subject, nor conversely. Hence, if I promise a slave in general, I do not thereby promise that he be a cook, or a weaver, or a miller. D. 35.1.1 (de legatis), l. generaliter; and D. 35.1.1, l. Titiae textores.

Fourthly, because the word *manutenere* (to maintain) does not signify maintaining by means of some other thing joined from afar: for just as it could be said, “you ought to have made another dam on top of that one,” which is false; so too it cannot be said, “you ought to have maintained by means of another accident separated from the thing”; but only in the manner customary in that place, as in *l. venditor*, §. *si constat*, *communia praediorum*. And here there were never *spetones* [weirs/dams]; hence, he who promised to repair the mills is not bound to make *spetones* that are uncustomary and unusual; for it is not understood that the unusual was contemplated. *l. Mella*, §. 1, *de alimentis et cibariis legatis*; *ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae*, *l. si prius*, §. *recte*, verse *non enim*, where the case is literally applicable. And this is confirmed by the customs of the city and by natural equity, which interprets contracts of good faith, as in *ff. pro socio*, *l. si locius pro filia*. For when someone leases a mill to millers, he promises to preserve it in working order: if it is destroyed, the lease is not terminated for him, nor is the owner condemned to pay damages [*interesse*], but it remains in suspense until it is repaired; for this is the nature of the contract, as in *l. habitatore* and *l. si fundus lo.*, *ff. quando dies legati cedat*; *l. firmi*, in the beginning.

Fifthly, because in this contract neither the slightest fault [*levissima culpa*] nor fortuitous accidents [*casus*], much less simple accident, is included, as in *l. si certo*, §. *nunc videndum*, *ff. communi dividundo*; and according to Bartolus in *l. quod nerva* and the notes in *l. etiam*, §. *licet soluto matrimonio*, in the gloss; and it is an express text and gloss in *ff. locati conducti*, *l. in nave saufeli*, §. *si ita*; and *l. si maritus*; and *l. si merces*, §. *vis maior*; and §. *qui columnam*.

Sixthly, because one is not bound to undertake the unusual. *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. si negotia*. For he who does what is customary is free from all fault, as is clear in that question concerning a horse left in pastures. And I hold that good faith, together with the diligence which God gave him, would suffice. *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. proculus*; *ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, *l. quamvis*; and the notes in *ff. de iureiurando*, *l. eum qui*, §. *in popularibus*.

Seventhly, because the *spetones* had been previously ordered by the said buyer from the owner before the accident, and they ought to be considered ratified; for they were usefully managed, and indeed begun. *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. Pomponius*, in *negotio*, and there fully noted. Hence, there is no fault if the injustice of a fortuitous accident overturns the work of one who had begun well. *ff. de negotiis gestis*, *l. sed an ultro*, §. 1, and §. *fin.*; and *l. successionem eius*, §. *ult.*. Indeed, what is usefully begun is considered as done, not merely for an exception, but for an action. The case is there literally.

Eighthly, because if a tutor promises to keep the ward’s property safe, that is, to maintain it; and let us suppose that this property is a ship, and it sinks in a storm, it is certain that he is not bound. *C. de negotiis gestis*, *l. tutori*; *ff. de usufructu*, *l. arboribus*, §. *navis*. Much more strongly, the same applies to a partner in revenues, and in any contract of good faith.

Ninthly, because words ought to be understood according to the nature of the contract. *ff. de usuris*, *l. si stipulatus*. But by the nature of this contract, neither accident nor even the slightest fault, if any there were, is included. *ff. locati conducti*, *l. si ut certo*, §. *nunc videndum*, and §. *quod vero senectute*. Which can only be said falsely and calumniously, not according to the truth. Moreover, these words, “if it shall be expedient,” namely, for the time being. For to this word *expedit* [it is expedient], time is always understood to be annexed. *l. 1*, in the beginning, *ff. de exercitoria*; and it is more express in *ff. de verbis obligatis*, *l. continuus*, §. *item qui in simul debent*. For such words are to be understood in this act of partnership of fruits, namely, for both parties, not for one of the partners. *ff. pro socio*, *l. acti*, §. *Labeo*, where it is expressed. *ff. de solutionibus*, *l. cum Stichus*. Hence, these words are like theriac against poison, which implicitly excludes every contrivance by placing the discretion of a good man in the place of theriac, as in *ff. de procuratoribus*, *l. non cogendum*, §. *at qui iustas*; and *l. Lucius*, *de exercito*.

Tenthly, that nothing was promised regarding the *spetones* beyond all the aforesaid. Thus it is necessary, when the conjunction falls between acts denoted by the names of two words, of which the latter can inform and qualify the other, it is certain that it forms it. *ff. de vino legato*, *l. sin.*, §. *cui dulcia*. And it determines and restricts the word to a definite meaning. *ff. de verbis significandis*, *l. si eum fundus*. And the precise word receives a natural and rational modification. *ff. de operis libertatis*, *l. cum liber*, §. *in omnibus*. And similarly, when the conjunction has in itself a local limitation, the whole antecedent is understood to refer to the same place. *ff. de penus legato*, *l. nam quod liquide*, §. *si cui penus*. But here it says, “and to fit and make the said dam,” and the whole refers to the place, and to the buildings of the place, and to its substance. *C. de contrahenda emptione*, *l. pacta conventa*. And thus it is spoken of the repair within the place only, not of the *spetones*. And note that if anyone were to interpret the instrument otherwise, he would be committing perjury in fact and counsel. Hence, if it were expedient, it would be necessary for the notary to interpret this. *ff. de appellationibus*, *l. ab executore*. Whom I believe would tell the truth.

Many other things could be said, which let remain in their proper place: therefore, omitting all things requested outside the writing, conclusively regarding the writing and points of law, having God before one’s eyes, let the mere truth of the law be consulted.

† Furthermore, it is asked: since this flood occurred on the last day of October, and these mills had been leased for a certain number of bushels of wheat to be provided annually, calculated from four months to four months, yet in winter they yielded little fruit; but because of the summer, almost the entire lease obligation was fulfilled, as the whole summer had passed: whether the lease obligation should be remitted pro rata of the number of days remaining in winter, or pro rata of the quality of the days, having regard to the utility. For example, suppose they were leased for fifty bushels. And in summer the lessees profited forty bushels from the fruits, so that due to the winter misfortune they lost only ten bushels: whether, under the pretext of fortuitous event, they ought to profit and become enriched. I say that they should not. The quality of the days should be considered according to the judgment of a good man, as in this other example. I leased to you a house, which was in a fair town, for one year for ten [units of currency]; in the whole year this house was not useful except for eight days of the fair: nevertheless you had those eight days, which are the final cause of the rent: although a case of moving away supervenes for ten days, nevertheless there will not be a remission of the rent for three hundred and fifty days, as the house was leased, but according to the judgment of a good man. Likewise, if I were to lease to you a vineyard from the month of September for one year, and after you had gathered the vintage, I were to move away because of enemies, nevertheless the remission of the hire would not be made according to the number of days: but according to the utility thereof. Argument: Digest, On Verbal Obligations, law Qui certarum, in the beginning; noted in the solution of the law Divortio, On Marriage. Wherever utility is attained, the time for ending the lease is to be considered according to the effect of the utility, not the number of days. From which it follows that neither the buyer, mentioned in the preceding, even if he had expressly assumed the risk, is bound: except insofar as he could yield fruit to the seller in winter, and not for that which yielded fruit in the preceding summer. And this is proportionate to justice. Furthermore, it is asked: suppose that the said buyer had assumed upon himself the fortuitous event and all adverse fortune: and by chance the mills were destroyed, as is stated above: and at the time of the event a bushel of wheat was worth two florins, afterwards it was worth ten: whether the time of the fortuitous event is to be considered, or the time following afterwards. And I say that the time of the event measures the interest, which is in the promise: which promise is referred to that time when it begins to be in obligation, and after the interest began to be in obligation, a novation was made. Digest, On Novation, law Fundum Cornelianum. And thus the time of the condition, that is, the fortuitous event in the condition imposed, in which case the obligation consists, is considered. Nor can the obligation of interest increase after the thing has been destroyed by chance. This is noted in the Code, On Negotiorum Gestio, law Sive haereditario. Furthermore, it is one thing to follow the peril of fortune, another to follow the peril of true fault, and not fictitious or imaginary. For fortune gives damage in hope: and therefore hope alone is to be estimated. Even if the cause of fault were otherwise, which is not true, unless the fault has in itself true fraud, or presumed. Thus say all the doctors, and especially Guillaume de Cuyac in the law Vinum, Digest, If a Certain Thing is Demanded. Furthermore, this case admits of the species of future perception of grain. Hence similar cases, when someone caused damage to the wheat in the ear: because it is estimated how much that hope could then be sold, and nothing more is owed according to the true opinion of Jacobus de Arena, as he notes in the law Cedere, On the Theft of Trees of the Caesars. This opinion is approved by Johannes Andreae in the Speculum, On Injuries and Damage Given, in his additions. Although the Speculum varies there. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the cause must be stated in an appeal from a grievance.
2. Whether a plaintiff may desist from a commenced lawsuit and renounce the instance against the defendant's will; and whether such renunciation prevents a judgment.
3. Whether one seeking a cognizor from a grievance is bound to state the reasons why he seeks it.
body: Because law arises from fiction, therefore, as is briefly stated below: behold, a certain lady Isoldina Dedeatis, wishing to bring an action, appointed her procurator, namely Ugoninus de Garzano, against the nobleman Thomas de Gutariis, citizen of Asti. And in the instrument of mandate, she solemnly promised to pay all and everything in which her procurator might be condemned, under the obligation of all her goods, etc. The said procurator then initiated litigation against the said Thomas; and in the aforementioned case, upon the submission of the libel, the litigation was contested. Later, however, when the public hearing was nearly concluded, and other matters in the case had been argued, the said lady Isoldina purely obligated herself and her goods to Francischino for a certain sum of money. Finally, the said procurator succumbed and was condemned in costs, which costs were duly taxed. After such taxation, the said Thomas petitioned the judge of the commune of Asti that the said sentence be put into execution against the goods of the said lady Isoldina, according to the form of the statutes of Asti. Whereupon the said lord judge and the official of the commune of Asti, appointed for the aforementioned matters, wishing to put the said sentence into execution according to the form of the chapters of Asti, had the creditor summoned by general proclamation, so that he should appear within three days and produce his rights, etc. The said Francischino appeared as a creditor, claiming that he was superior and prior to the said Thomas, requesting that he be paid first from the goods of the said lady Isoldina. Lastly, the said lord judge, having seen all and each of the things to be seen and examined, recognizing that Thomas was the prior creditor of the said Francischino and that the goods of the said lady Isoldina were previously obligated, ordered the said officials and liberators of the commune of Asti, present there, that they give and deliver to Thomas payment from the goods of the said lady Isoldina, according to the form of the statutes of Asti, for the said costs, as the prior and earlier creditor of the said lady Isoldina. The said Francischino, on the contrary, stated that from the said words and narrative by the said lord judge, and from the aforementioned order, justice had been done and was being done, and he demanded a cognitor, which petition for a cognitor was committed to Messer Martino Capello and Raymondinus de Pallidis, judges of the college of judges of the city of Asti. Regarding these matters, it remains to be seen what the law is. And for clarity, I premise,

† That from the form of the statutes of Asti and from the grievance, a request for cognizance may be sought, which request for cognizance is a species of appeal, as in *l. non distinguimus*, § *cum quidam*, D. de arbitris. Hence, it must be examined whether the said request for cognizance is valid. And briefly, it is to be said that it is not. This is proven because when the judge, in the execution of the said sentence, ordered the officials to deliver the unpaid amount to Thomas as the preferred creditor, that order was a certain interlocutory sentence, as in *l. cum clerici*, C. de episcopis et clericis, and especially because it occurs in the execution of a sentence, and thus it is an interlocutory sentence, as noted by Cynus in *l. ab executione*, D. de appellationibus, in the beginning, and by Cynus in the same *l. ab executione*, in the third question. This is different in the case of an appeal from a definitive sentence, as in *l. Seius*, in the end, D. de appellationibus, with similar cases. But Francis himself alleged no cause of grievance in the said request for cognizance; therefore, the request for cognizance does not hold in law, as in *cap. Cordi*, Extr. de appellationibus, lib. 6, and is proven in *l. ait praetor*, § *permittitur*, D. de minoribus. And fully, since the cause of grievance was not expressed, which, as was stated above, had to be expressed, and indeed significantly and clearly, as noted by Johannes Andreae in *c. Appellanti*, Extr. de appellationibus, in the Clementine *Non generaliter*, nor obscurely, as noted and read by Johannes Andreae in *cap. Significantibus*, Extr. de non obtemperando, in the Novella, and in the said Clementine *Appellanti*. And especially because injustice must be revealed by allegation and proof. First, therefore, let us see whether Lady Isoldina could have renounced the lawsuit and the prosecution against the will of the adversary, or not. For if it was not within her power to renounce, that condition which is inherent in the promise of *iudicatum solvi* is valid, if judgment has been given. As for the validation of the prior hypothec, it would have retroactive effect, and would come to the confirmation of that prior hypothec, although contracted under a condition, as in D. qui potioris in pignore habent locum, *l. qui balneum*, and *l. potior*, § *uideamus*, and D. quae res pignori obligari possunt, *l. Titius*. For the time of the contract must be considered in the preference of the creditor in those matters which have a necessary consequence from the utterance, as is proven by the aforementioned laws, and by *l. 1*, D. qui potioris in pignore habent locum. Such is the doctrine handed down, that in those matters which are presumed to be consumed by mere agreement, so that they no longer depend on the power of the creditor or the debtor, the debtor cannot prejudice the creditor. Indeed, the right is already acquired, albeit under a condition. In those matters which depend on a future act of the debtor, or on a mixed act of the debtor and creditor, then indeed the debtor, contracting in the meantime, can prefer another creditor to the creditor who had previously agreed on a future hypothec, as in the said *l. potior*, in the beginning. If, therefore, it is so that it was not within the power of Lady Isoldina to renounce the lawsuit and the prosecution against the will of the adversary and the judge, then the condition was not potestative, and therefore Thomas, the conditional creditor, would undoubtedly be preferred to the second, unconditional one. Now we briefly allege something for, and something against.

† For the fact that it is within the plaintiff’s power to renounce and to desist against the defendant’s will appears to be proven by C. de appellationibus, l. Si quis libellus; and D. de iudicibus, l. Desistisse; and C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. 1; and what is noted in D. de iudiciis solutis, l. Cum lite mortua. To the contrary, it seems, for this renunciation of the lawsuit is said to be a pact, and it gives rise to an exception based on the pact, as in C. de pactis, l. Postquam liti. Therefore, the consent of both parties is required, as in D. de pactis, l. 1, §. Conventionis. Moreover, it is proposed here that we were near, or close to, the conclusion of the case, hence this renunciation is late, by argument from D. de evictionibus, l. Si rem quam, §. Quolibet tempore. And it supports what is noted in C. de edendo, l. Edita actio; and C. quomodo et quando iudex, Auth. Qui semel. And certainly this appears to be proven by the security for costs which the plaintiff provides to persevere until the end of the lawsuit, as in C. de litis contestatione, Auth. Libello, in the corpus from which it is derived. Furthermore, even if the renunciation were binding, the instance is not thereby terminated by operation of law; rather, a judgment can still be rendered, and it is valid: and thus it is within the judge’s power. And this appears to be expressed, for the law states that if I ask that someone be declared a slave, and after proofs have been adduced on both sides I renounce the lawsuit, the defendant can demand that the case proceed to a definitive judgment: because it is more expedient to be defended by the aid of proofs than by the plaintiff’s desistance. This is a notable case. C. de ingenuis et manumissis, l. Si te. Moreover, no one is compelled to seek assistance from the adversary if he has confidence in his own right, as in D. de iureiurando, l. Eum qui, 3. responso. We see something similar in criminal cases, where a plaintiff who desists cannot desist against the will of the judge and the adversary, but must merit an abolition of the prosecution, as in l. 1, §. Accusationem, D. ad Turpiliani legem. From these, and other arguments that can be made and alleged, the judge can proceed to a definitive judgment even against the will of the renouncing party, and condemn him in costs. And if we consider carefully, this is the case in l. Properandum, §. Et si quidem. For although the plaintiff incurs a heremodicy, which is the same as desertion of the case and tacit renunciation—because he says he does not wish to come to the case, as noted by the ordinary gloss in the aforementioned l. Postquam liti—nevertheless there is no doubt that the defendant is definitively bound to pay, and the plaintiff is condemned. The text is in the aforementioned §. Et si quidem. And to this effect is what is read and noted in D. de rei venditione, l. Utique; and D. de iudiciis solutis, l. Si servus. And in the plaintiff, a just cause for litigation is not presumed unless it is gathered from the records: because the plaintiff must prove not only what he claims, but what he can prove, as in C. de edendo, l. Ar., §. Cum autem. On another point,

Whether he who seeks a cognitor against a grievance is bound to state the reasons why he seeks it. And I say that he is bound to state them in his libel, if a libel is offered on this point. But if he were to proceed by a simple word, any petition would suffice for the reasons to be clarified in the course of the proceedings: although it would be safer even to state the reason by word, as in l. 1, C. de praediis cum liberto, 10, where it says, let him expressly state the reasons by which he is strangled. And to this effect are other more well-known laws, which speak of the expression of the reason, where a grievance is alleged, as in D. de minoribus, l. ait praetor, § permitti. For a petition without cause should not be received, as in l. minor autem magistratus, eodem titulo. And this pertains to the office of the magistrate, even if no one requests it, as in l. 1, D. de officio assessoris. Certainly, since this petition is a kind of recourse, it takes on the nature of an appeal: yet I do not say that more is required in this than what the statute requires, as in D. de exercitoria, l. 1, § si is, qui navem, and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si servum, § non dixit praetor. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One who has been ejected from possession under the pretext of a null sentence, or one that is subsequently rescinded, is to be restored to possession.
body: The dispossessed

† By virtue of the alleged sentence, if the sentence is null or rescinded, [the party] must be placed in possession, and it is not necessary to inquire into the title or to prove the justice of the possessor. 2 q. 1 c. Notum; De restitutione spoliatorum, c. Conquerente; C. Si per vim, vel alio modo; L. Si, C. Unde vi; L. Meminerint, and the note thereto, in the same title; L. Si quis in tantam, D. Si qua mulier ventris nomine in possessionem missa; L. 1 § Necessaria, and L. 1 § 1, in the following title. For that which has been done wrongly must be revoked. C. De iure fideicommissorum, L. Prohibitum; D. De testamentaria tutela, L. Iure nostro. Therefore, the order of judicial proceedings is a solemnity established in the middle, so that no one may validly occupy the possession of another without order and reason of law. D. De iudaeis, L. Nullus; C. Finiri reg., L. Si constiterit. To this effect is what is noted in L. and note, 2 q. 1 c. In primis; 1 q. 6 c. Appellatore; 7 q. 1 c. Praesertim; D. Ne vis fiat ei, L. 1 § Haec verba. Since, therefore, by two sentences the award was first annulled or declared void, all possession obtained under the pretext of said award is revoked as void, and must be restored to the defendant against whom the aforementioned execution was carried out; for things done wrongly and nullly must be revoked by contrary command. L. Quod iussit, with similar authorities. It is supported by what is noted in D. De acquirenda possessione, L. Iuste, with its subject matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an offer made by the debtor at the creditor’s house is valid, and when.
body:
If the creditor was truly bound to make a refutation or a discharge, as the woman stated, then the creditor was in delay in accepting, and the creditor must bear the consequences. But if he was not bound, except to make a refutation or discharge from those who were obligated, then the debtor improperly offered payment, and she must bear the consequences. On this point, see the number in the Digest, De transactionibus, l. cum acqui., according to Bartolus.

Regarding the offer made at the house, it must be said that either the creditor was hiding so that nothing would be offered to him, because he was perhaps in the house and did not make himself available; in this case, the woman did not incur the penalty, since she went to the creditor’s house. See the Digest, De constitutione pecuniae; also that title. Or else the creditor was not at fault, and the woman did not wait for him. But she departed with the words mentioned, and then the woman incurred the penalty, because she did not make a lawful offer, nor did she even notify of the deposit. See the Digest, De solutionibus, l. si soluturus; the Code, De usuris, l. acceptam; the Institutes, De hereditatibus instituendis, l. suus, § puto; and the Code, De libellis agnitionis, l. 1, § denuntiare; and the Digest, De excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, § oportet autem. And it supports what is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, De novo operis nuntiando, l. praetor, § si quis paratus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether execution of a sentence rendered between two parties may be carried out against a third-party possessor who has not been cited.
2. A possessor does not lose possession by virtue of a sentence, unless, etc.
body: It is alleged that a certain guardianship was administered by a certain Gasparone, or that a certain curatorship was held over the goods of Bartholomew; and that a certain Thomas purchased a certain estate from the heirs of the said guardian or curator, out of the goods, it is claimed, of the said Bartholomew; and that subsequently an action was brought against the said heirs, that they render an account of the administration, and the rest; and that the said estate was listed in the inventory of the said guardian or curator. Hence a sentence was rendered, that an account of the administration be rendered, and consequently the said estate. It is further alleged that the said purchaser knew that the said cause was being litigated; because he was a witness in the said cause; and because he was present at the time the aforementioned sentence was rendered. It is also alleged that, after the said sentence was rendered without the said Thomas being cited, the plaintiff was put into possession of the said estate by the said Thomas, who held possession. This putting into possession was made in the cause by virtue of the judgment of the said sentence.

† Now it is asked whether the said execution could have been carried out without citing the said Thomas. And that it could have been carried out is proved thus: the said sentence prejudices the said Thomas, because it was rendered concerning the ownership of the said land against his tutors, who were sued, with the said Thomas having knowledge and not objecting. Hence, it rightly prejudices the said Thomas, because, knowing of his right in the judgment disputed with him by the one from whom he derives his title, he ought to have intervened in the judgment. Hence, on account of his knowledge, and the opportunity to prohibit or at least to intervene, as well as the negligence he committed, the said sentence prejudices him, as stated in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Saepe*, § *Sed et scientibus*; and in the chapter *Quamvis*, Extra, in the same title, and there by Innocentius. And Innocentius seems to say this openly in the chapter *Proposuit*, *De concessionibus praebendarum*. And although the said judgment was personal, nevertheless, since in it the ownership of the ward or adult was disputed, and it was pronounced upon as concerning the restitution of the residue, it prejudices just as if the judgment were real. For having a mixed cause, inasmuch as real obligations come into it, this supports what is noted by Bartolus in the said law *Saepe*, when he refers to what he noted in the law *Si finita*, § *Si de vectigalibus*, *De damno infecto*. To this also contributes what is noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Vendito*; and in the Code, *Ubi de crimine agi oportet*, Authentic *Qua in provincia*. Furthermore, Innocentius says that when execution is against the very thing concerning which the sentence speaks, no other citation is necessary, as he notes in the Extra, *De appellationibus*, chapter *Ex ratione*. To this contribute the Digest, *De rei vindicatione*, law *Qui restituere*; and law *Is cui*, § *Qui in possessione*, *De utroque iure possessionis*.

On the contrary, the truth itself seems to indicate otherwise for three reasons. The first reason is that this Thomas did not derive his title from the tutor or curator, but from the heirs. For one contract is that of the deceased, another is that of the heir, as stated in the Digest, *De pignoratitia actione*, law *Rem alienando*. And therefore the act of the deceased does not prejudice those buying from the heir, who did not sell as heir, but as if it were his own property. Argument from the Digest, *De diversis et temporibus praescriptionum*, law *An vitium*, § *Ex facto*. This reason is not pleasing.
