And therefore I assign a second reason, namely, that in the judgment of tutelage or curatorship, ownership is not treated principally, but incidentally. For it is not necessary to prove that the thing belonged to the ward or adult; but it suffices that it be proved by the inventory that it was among his goods, nor is there an express or tacit pronouncement upon ownership. And therefore such a sentence does not prejudice the buyer regarding ownership, nor should a sentence rendered on presumptions harm a third possessor against whom ownership is fully proved. Argument from the Code, *De probationibus*, law *Quod res*. Furthermore, the action for partnership in tutelage or curatorship does not follow the land, as stated in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, law 1, § *Si haeres*. And therefore, by its force, execution is not made against a singular possessor, as stated in the Code, *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Eum*.

It is also to be considered whether the said buyer knew that ownership was being disputed or not. For it is undoubted that if he did not know that ownership of that singular thing which he possesses was being disputed, it does not prejudice him, as in the said law *Saepe*. It is also to be considered whether he knew at such a time that he could conveniently use his rights, as stated in the Digest, *De evictionibus*, law *Si rem*, § *Qualibet*.

Solution: Because execution ought not to be made against a third possessor not cited, where, if he had been cited, he could have had a just cause for objecting, I hold that the said seizure was not valid in law. To this I add what is noted by Cynus in the Code, *De iure et facultate ignorandi*, law 1; by Bartolus after law 1, § *Necessarii*, *Si mulier ventris nomine*; and law 3, Code, *De pignoribus*, by the same; by the gloss in the Digest, *Quibus ex causis maiores*, law *Cum miles*, § 1; by the text in the Code, *Si propter publicas pensiones*, law *Si deserta*; by Innocentius, *De majoratibus et obedientia*, chapter *Inter quatuor*; and by another text in the chapter *Licet episcopus*, *De praebendis*, Book 6. Furthermore, by the most well-known texts in the Code, *Unde vi*, law *Meminerint*; and noted in the same title, law *Si quis in tantam*; and Code, *Si per vim vel alio modo*, law *Finis*. For it is absurd that against one who was never cited, and who was never in court as a litigant, and of whose knowledge no faith is established—which ought to be established by citing him—a sentence is ordered to be executed, and afterwards he is deprived of the thing in fact. Question 2, Distinction 1, chapter *In primis*; and Code, *De iure fisci*, law *Prohibitum*, Book 10; and Code, *De bonis vacantibus*, law *Finis*, same Book. That which therefore has been done contrary to law must necessarily be revoked by contrary authority; because the one who has been dispossessed must, before all else, be restored without observing the order of law, as stated in the Extra, *De purgatione vulgaris*, chapter *Significantibus*; and Digest, *De administratione rerum ad civitates pertinentium*, law 3, § *Gravi*. And it supports this: Extra, *De regulis iuris*, chapter *Suborta*; and Digest, *De rei vindicatione*, law *Officium*.

† It is certain that a possessor does not lose possession by virtue of a judgment, unless through the judge, if he has duly granted admission, as stated in the law and noted in the Digest, title *Qui satisdare cogantur*; and in the law *Sciendum*, section *Fundum*. Furthermore, it is certain that what is done by a contrary act must be revoked, as noted in the Digest, title *De feriis*, law 1, section 1; and in the Digest, title *De evictionibus*, law *Minor*, in the beginning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether witnesses who testify about the payment of money, although they differ as to the time or the occasion of the promise to repay, prove the payment.
body: Gasparonus brings an action against a certain person by means of a civil action on a loan for one hundred livres, and he proves the payment by two witnesses. However, when the said witnesses are questioned as to whether any promise was made regarding the repayment of the said sum, they differ: for one says that there was a promise to repay after a certain third party should return from the province. The other witness, however, said that a promise was made to repay in the short term, and that he hoped to repay before the said third party returned from the province.

† Now it is asked whether the said witnesses prove the payment, or whether, on account of the said difference and diversity, they are rendered singular or suspect, so that they do not prove, as we say in Susanna, as noted in C. de testibus, l. testium. On this point, I say briefly that the judge must consider how much faith is to be accorded to the witnesses, as in ff. de testibus, l. 3, §. magis, and this is noted regarding the quality of the witnesses. But regarding the quality of the deposition, I say that the said witnesses should not be called singular, because they agree in one end of the matter, which arises from the payment. Argument from de poenis, l. qui scientiam. For there are two [witnesses], but the payment itself is proved by both. And this suffices for bringing an action, because it is effective. Moreover, it is a stipulation: and this has not been disproved by any difference of the day or of the circumstance of the restitution from the promise; therefore, it could not be acted upon as invalid, as not proved. It follows, therefore, that an action could be brought on the payment, because the valid is not vitiated by the invalid, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. certi condictio, §. quoniam. And because they depose concerning the same and unique payment, it cannot be said that, with respect to the payment, it is said [to be defective], which supports what is noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in l. 2, C. de erroribus advocatorum, and by Bartolus in l. 1, in fine, ff. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, and others teach in the said l. testium. It is not an objection what is noted there in Susanna, because there a contradiction results. For one crime cannot be committed simultaneously in different places, because it is impossible for one body to be in different places at the same time, as in ff. communis, l. si certo, §. si duobus vehiculum. If, however, the said witnesses did not depose concerning the payment, but only concerning the promise, they would prove nothing. And it supports what is noted in l. cum quid, ff. si certum petatur. And from these things it appears that it is not necessary to prove that the third person, who is called Johannes Martinus, returned from the province, because it has not been proved that this delay was attached. Hence, the action is brought on a pure payment, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. omni.

† Moreover, it is certain that a witness who has been approved cannot now be impeached anew, unless a new cause has supervened, as is stated in the Code, *De testibus*, in the law *Si quis testibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The assertion made by the agent on behalf of the deceased, that he has certain goods deposited with Titius, which he wishes to be given to the poor: whether the deposit must be proved.
2. What if Titius confesses the deposit, whether he can be sued by the poor.
3. Whether the poor can bring an action without assignment.
body: Castus. A certain lady of Ast., acting in extremis, stated that she had deposited certain goods with a certain Thomas, whom she had ordered to give them to the poor. This Thomas denies it. It is asked whether

† Whether the assertion of the lady prejudices the said Thomas. I answer: No, as in C. de prob. l. rationes, and noted in l. inter chartulas, C. de conuenien. fisci debitoribus, lib. 10. From this it follows that, even if this were proved by two witnesses or more, nevertheless the said words would not be believed, as in ff. de test. l. uerba. Secondly, it is asked,

† If it is proven that the said Thomas promised to return and restore the said things according to the will of the said lady, whether he can be sued by the poor. I answer: yes, because in his testament a testator may burden his debtor so that what he owes to him he shall pay to another, as in D. de legibus I, l. si pecunia fuerit deposita.

† where it is said that the debtor may be burdened with the charge of a fideicommissum, if he accepts the tacit legacy of release; otherwise the heir is bound to the legatee to assign the actions against the debtor. And because here we are dealing with a legacy left to the poor, he would have a useful action without assignment, as C. de sac. san. ec. l. si. In the case of other legatees, whether full assignment is required, see C. de leg. l. ex legato nominis. and it supports ff. de leg. 1. l. quidam testator. in the beginning. I therefore conclude that, in the name of the poor, if the debt is proven, the debtor may be sued without any further assignment. To this effect, C. quae res pig. obli. po. l. nomen. joined with l. 1. C. communia dele.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How one who is bound to render an account ought to render it, and which documents must be produced; and if they are not produced, whether an oath in lieu of proof (iuramentum in litem) is to be taken.
2. Whether the procurator of one of the parties, after that party’s death, may serve as a witness in the principal case.
body: For the sake of clarity,

† it must first be premised that a partner is bound to render an account to his partner concerning the acts and administration performed by him: as in ff. de eden. l. quaedam sunt personae. in princ. Moreover, to render an account is not merely to produce the account books, but to bring forth the arrears into the open. The text says this in ff. de verb. si. l. boues. §. fin.; ff. de condi. et demon. l. qui sub conditione reddendarum rationum. and l. cum seruus.; ff. de manumis. testa. l. si ita fuerit. §. si vero. and l. qui filium impuberem. §. item quaesitum.; ff. de tutel. et rationibus distrahendis. l. 1. §. officio.; ff. de fideicommis. lib. l. thays. §. sorore. and §. Stichus, et damas. and §. Titius Sticho. and l. si pater duos. §. Sticho.; and ff. de statu libe. l. si statu liber. punit. §. vlt. and l. seruus si haered. §. Imperator. and l. Sticho libertas. §. seruus testamento.; and ff. de condi. et demon. l. si cui libertas.; and ff. de lib. leg. l. non solum. §. is, qui rationes. and l. fin. §. inter caetera. For all the aforesaid laws state what is contained under the name of rendering accounts; and certainly even a scrupulous examination is contained therein, unless it has been remitted, as in ff. de lega. 1. l. si seruus vetitus. Moreover, one must weigh what and what kind of writings are to be brought forth, and how an account ought to be rendered, and whether, if the writings are not produced, an oath in litem can be taken. And regarding the first point, the texts of the said laws must be weighed. For in l. cum seruus, it is said that the accounts must be brought forth in the manner they are customarily brought forth, that is, to be presented, read, investigated, and calculated, whether they are reported properly or improperly, rightly or not rightly, received or given. But in l. qui sub conditione, it is said that he who is bound to render accounts must state, and proof must be established concerning all things that were done by him, as in l. si cui libertas, it is said that an arbiter must be given by the consuls to inspect the instruments, calculate the accounts, and approve or condemn them. Furthermore, in the said l. si ita fuerit, it says that the volumes of accounts are to be surrendered. But in l. qui filium, it is said that he should render an account according to the good and equitable, such as a good paterfamilias would accept; and in l. si pure, the text says to instruct concerning the particulars; but in §. Stichus, et damas., it says that everything is contained which in any kind of acts would receive credit; but in l. si statulibera ponit. §. fi., it says that the volumes of accounts must be delivered for the purpose of inquiring into, examining, and knowing the accounts; and, in short, every rendering of accounts must contain good faith within itself, as well as the skill and diligence that the nature of the act requires. In this matter, custom is also considered, both general and special. For example, if a moneylender, say, states that he has not prepared an account book, but shows certain scraps of paper or loose leaves, he is not to be believed; because he is tacitly deemed to have a mandate to draw up account books, and because custom is such, as noted by Iacob. But. in l. 1. C. de eden.; c. 1. de vsu. in cle. is relevant; and by the argument of ff. de pigno. actio. l. vel vniuersorum; hence he who does not produce the account books is presumed to conceal them. For this reason, in bonae fidei actions, such as the action pro socio and the like, an oath in litem is taken; argument of ff. de administra. tuto. l. tutor, qui repertorium. And these are the words of Iac. de Are. on l. 1. §. officio. de tutel. et rationibus distra. upon the word cedere, where he says thus: for this see above, ff. de admin. tut. l. Lucius. §. tutelae; so too the book itself must be produced by any administrator whatsoever, as below, ff. de libe. leg. l. fin. §. inter caetera, and ff. de manumis. testa. l. si ita fuerit; otherwise, if he does not do so, he will be liable for the interest to be declared through an oath in litem, as above, ff. de admini. tuto. l. tutor, qui repertorium. Thus Iacob. de Are. From these things, therefore, it appears that one must conclude regarding the premised points that the production made in the said loose leaves, and not in account books, as is customary and ought to be done, shows presumed fraud on the part of the one producing them. And therefore, if he does not produce the account books, as they are accustomed and ought to be prepared, an oath in litem is taken, as appears manifestly from the aforesaid. Moreover, concerning what is calculated and liquidated, it is the duty of the judge to compel the debtor to pay, as in ff. de statu. libe. l. statuliber. §. rationem; and thus the bonus vir to whom this examination is committed ought to arbitrate; nor is credit to be given to perfunctory writings, but to books prepared formally and according to the customary manner, as has been most fully proven above; and C. de dona. l. si quis pro redemptione is relevant. It is true that regarding certain small and slight matters, according to the standing of the person, credit could be given to the oath of the one producing them, but not regarding grave and weighty matters, as is noted by the Gloss and the Doctors on C. de iure delibe. l. fin. §. in computatione; and extra de accusa. c. qualiter. et quando; and it is express in the said l. qui sub condi. reddendarum. That point is very well known, namely that an account must be produced from the beginning and with the dates and consuls, as in ff. de eden. l. argentarius. §. edi. and l. si quis ex argentariis. §. rationum. and l. 1. §. rationes. and l. praetor. in prin. And because in such account books the calends, that is, the beginnings of each month, were customarily entered, therefore the said books are sometimes called a calendarium, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. eius, qui in prouincia. in princi. Furthermore, the protestations made to the contrary on the part of those of the Falleti effect nothing: because the act itself is required, nor does a protestation suffice, as Bar. notes in l. praetor. §. si quis paratus. ff. de no. oper. nun. It does not suffice, therefore, to protest, unless all the books of the entire administration are brought forth into the open, so that the truth may appear without any chicanery, as has been most broadly proven above. And so the account must also be rendered faithfully, as in ff. mandati. l. creditor. §. Lucius. But concerning that which is asked,

† regarding him who formerly was the procurator of one of the litigants, whether, upon the death of the latter, he can testify in a once common cause, since his testimony does not look to the process of the case, but to the principal fact; and since the testimony does not concern the personal advantage of the principal, seeing that, having considered the effect, he was a minister and not someone retaining the advantage. It must be said that he can, as in C. de testa. l. dictantibus, and Inst. de testi. §. legatariis, and by the argument of ff. de fal. l. impuberem. §. penul. in the rationale of the letter there, where it says: 'since there is no advantage of his own'; and what is noted in ff. de iure fis. l. deferre. §. idem decreuerunt; let there be added what is read and noted in ff. fini. regundo. l. eos, and C. de arbi. l. ne in arbitris. §. ipse; therefore, once the office of procurator has been laid down, or ended against his will, he is not prohibited from testifying upon the principal cause. Let there be added what is noted on C. de testi. l. omnibus, and ff. de testamen. l. qui testamento. From these things it appears that concerning liquidated matters execution is to be carried out for the abovesaid year; but concerning non-liquidated matters, a calculation is to be made, upon exhibiting the books of administration for the entire time, according to the arbitrament of a bonus vir; otherwise an oath in litem is taken, as I proved above. That point is certain, that execution of a liquidated matter—that is, of that year—is not delayed on account of the pendency of the suit over a non-liquidated matter, as in l. qui solidum. in principio. ff. de legatis secundo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A title is not sufficient for an heir to prescribe, but delivery, or quasi-delivery, is necessary.
body: The claim

I assume the consent to be well-founded, unless the prescription of the defendants absorbs the proof, and the prescription of the plaintiffs. Hence, according to what is alleged, Nicolinus had title from someone, namely the bishop; but possession from no one: because Auctor and Vbezinus do not possess, and thus one of the substantial elements of prescription is lacking, namely, tradition or quasi-tradition. D. de usucap. l. cum solus. Moreover, the sons of Nicolinus do not prescribe by title on behalf of an heir. C. de usucap. pro herede l. nihil. Furthermore, it is noted that Georgius sold to Bartholomew as if it were the property of minors, and thus in bad faith, because contrary to the prohibitions of the laws, as Inst. de usucap. § error autem. Moreover, this tutor received the same thing in augmentation of dowry from the buyer. In this contract, fraud and bad faith are presumed. D. de auctor. tutor. l. sed si pupillus § per interpositam. And therefore prescription ceases both for the husband and for the wife through the husband. Moreover, the resignation made to the wife does not give her any other title than she previously had in the thing; but it is merely a restitution or resignation. From which it is concluded for the defendant that prescription, according to what is alleged, has not been proven. Hence, the plaintiffs, who prove better, are said to prevail according to what is alleged in the cause of fact. But if the possession of the defendants had had a just cause, the latest prescription would absorb the earlier one. There is no doubt that the petition proceeds. Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a citation of an absent party made in this manner, if anyone wishes to defend such a person, etc., is valid. And see how an absent party ought to be cited: and how by a herald. No. 2.
2. A sentence is null where there was no lawful citation.
body: Citation

The aforementioned act, made by these words, "if there is anyone who wishes to defend, etc.," is defective: because it does not include the person who ought to be cited principally, from whom the form of citation ought to begin, if there is no procurator of the absent party. This is clear in the Authentica *De litigio*, § *Omnem*, where it says, "either in person or through a legitimate procurator." For this is the form when an absent person is cited, whether cited at his home, or by edict, or by herald, as is clear there. However, it must be known that it is not sufficient to cite someone by a herald, unless the proclamation is made in his own neighborhood, as noted in the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Si finita*, § *Iulianus*, in the major gloss on the principle, where it says, "or to be proclaimed in his own neighborhood."

† Hence, if an absent person, who is not from the land where the trial is being conducted, is to be summoned, a summons made by a herald is not sufficient; because true or presumed knowledge does not reach the person summoned. D. ad Sill. l. 1, § occisorum; C. eo. l. si; C. de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis l. ultima; D. de postulando l. 1, § propter casum; De iudicibus c. 1, § porro; In Clementina de electione causam eandem compilata. For this summons lacked substantial form; because it ought to begin with the absent party, whose case it is, or with persons having a mandate, not with friends while omitting the principal party. L. haec autem, § 1, Qui ex causa in possessionem eatur. Moreover, an absent person from the territory, who is from another province, ought not to be summoned by a herald; but notice ought to be brought to his knowledge, if possible. C. de foro competenti l. Romana, § contrahentibus; C. de episcopis et clericis l. omnes, § hoc nihilominus; C. de officiis praefecti urbi l. quod promulgatum. For the law does not approve a deceitful summons. D. quod vi aut clam l. prohibere, § clam facere; and l. aut qui aliter, § si quis. And although it is conceded that a summons may be made by the public voice of a herald, C. de feriis l. finalis; and in the aforementioned authenticum Qui semel; and noted by Cynus, C. de accusationibus l. 4; nevertheless, this is true only if no other reason invalidates this mode of summoning. It must therefore be concluded that either a person was summoned by a herald at the place of his domicile, or where he was bound to reside, or where he had promised to stay, or elsewhere. Or he was not summoned at all; and then there is no doubt, C. quomodo et quando iudex l. ea quae; and the gloss says so in the aforementioned l. 4, C. de accusationibus.

† If the citation is not lawful, the sentence is void by operation of law. Moreover, in our case, it is not merely unlawful: but it was not made against the principal in his absence, nor against any of his procurators. Hence, according to what is alleged, the sentence is void. As for the other point, namely, regarding the order, I say that the order is gathered according to the law in three things. D. de iudicibus. The order of the writing also, if it accords with reason, signifies the order of the acts; otherwise, the writing shall be followed. D. de usufructu, l. quotiens; and in Cap. Duobus, de rescriptis, lib. 6; and D. de fideicommissis, lib. 1, l. Generaliter, §. Quid ergo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether fraud, and when, is presumed in cases of counterfeiting on the part of one who carries, spends, or possesses false coinage.
body:
It is found in the volume of statutes of the commune, under the rubric concerning false coinage, chapter 45, a statute of the following tenor: “Moreover, if anyone shall knowingly or fraudulently spend, or cause to be spent, false coin, he shall be punished with one hundred Imperial pounds. Provided, however, that if anyone is found to have knowingly and fraudulently spent false coin on one occasion, or on several occasions, to the value of ten Imperial pounds, or other coin worth ten pounds, or more than that, he shall be burned. Those carrying false coin to the city of Novara shall be subject to similar penalties.”

CASE. That statute, in each of its parts, requires fraud (*dolus*); yet fraud has not been proven. But let us see whether fraud is presumed from the nature of the act. It seems that it is, because in malicious acts fraud is presumed. Codex, *De iniuriis*, l. *Si non convicii*. To the contrary it seems, because there are certain things which do not result in another’s detriment, and in these fraud is not presumed; hence, although someone has a false instrument in his chest, which he neither fabricated nor uses, he is not punished. Codex, *De falsis*, l. *Si falsos*. There are other things which result in another’s detriment and are prohibited, and in these fraud is presumed, unless the contrary is proven. There, l. *Nec ex vi*, according to Cynus; and Codex, *De sicariis*, l. 1. Our case, however, is doubtful: because although it does not harm another, it could have harmed another. But if he had spent it, that which could cause harm is examined, even if it does not harm another. Digest, *De statu liberorum*, l. *Labeo*. The solution is that, under such circumstances, they could not harm anyone, and the intent to harm is not presumed. Hence, here, because no one can harm another unless another act of a person follows, fraud does not seem to be presumed, except from the quality of the person, or from the custom of doing such things, as noted in l. *Penult.*, Codex, *De probationibus*; for it is presumed that one persists in the same malice. Likewise, a fraudulent purpose is presumed from the quality [of the circumstances]: for example, if he were carrying a large quantity of florins. Such a person is presumed to have the intent that those doing similar things for this purpose have. All these matters pertain to the discretion of the judge, who must also consider whether the person is of good reputation or not, as in l. *Non omnis*, § *A barbaris*, Digest, *De re militari*. However, because the quantity is small, even if there was an intention to gamble, he could have gambled for whatever the debased copper was worth. Digest, *De pigneraticia actione*, l. *Eleganter*, § *Qui reprobos*. And because, if there had been any intention, he seems to be absolved by the just vote of penitence. Digest, *De falsis*, l. *Qui falsam*. This law is of little help, for in our case the offense was consummated by carrying [the coin] to a prohibited place. And in this at least he was in fraud, namely in the fraud of the carrying: since he knew it to be false, hence he seems to be condemnable, saving the benefit of confession according to the form of another statute.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a partnership is considered new, or when an old one is said to be continued.
2. Whether acts performed after the termination of a partnership fall under the action for management of affairs without mandate or the negatory action.
3. Whether a partner may approve the books in part and disapprove them in part.
body: Qum

There are two distinct societies, separated in time, and especially when a new partner is joined in the second society, there are two actions *pro socio*: one for the first society, and on the ground of an account to be rendered by him who administered the society; another for the second, and so on, whenever the first society is terminated and a new society is begun. For it matters greatly whether the same society continues or a new one is begun, as in D. 17.2.14 (*Si quod*), § *Filius*, and D. 43.6.1 (*Sed si manente*).

† It must be noted here that those things which come to the completion of matters already begun do not create a new partnership, nor a new matter; but those things which pertain to a new business do indeed create a new matter, as in D. de negotiorum gest. l. Nam et servus, § Si vivo; and D. de administratione tutorum l. Titium et Mevium, § Altero. And from this it appears whether those things done after the partnership has ended pertain to the action pro socio or to the action negotiorum gestorum; for if they are entirely new, they pertain to the action negotiorum gestorum upon the death of a partner, and not to the action pro socio. Now I come to that which is in question,

Whether one must adhere to the written records of the books in their entirety if a partner approves part thereof; or whether he may indeed accept the written records in part and reject them in part. It appears that he ought to accept them in their entirety, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. cum quaeritur. To the contrary, it appears that he may accept what is to be accepted and repudiate what is not to be accepted, as in D. de deposito, l. publica, §. finalis; and D. de liberatione legata, l. Aurelius, §. idem quaesivit. The doctors say that concerning the same chapter, or one connected thereto, it is necessary that he accept the whole or repudiate the whole. But if the chapters are entirely separate and distinct, he may accept one and repudiate another: unless he has already accepted or approved the entire code of accounts; for then he is bound to stand by what he approved. Thus noted by Cynus, C. de confessionibus, l. unica, in 13. q.; and C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. 2; and Bartolus in the said §. idem quaesivit. But I do not depart from the text, because when he assents to the writing in part, he does not consent in part to the accounts rendered; the judge ought to estimate and consider what is probable, as in the said l. publica, §. fin.; and ought to inquire subtly into the truth. Argument from C. de sententiis quae pro eo quod interest, l. 1. If, however, it cannot appear to the judge through other presumptions, he ought to consider the quality of the writer, as in D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, §. 2; and if he is a good man and of good repute, and the amount is not excessively large, his oath shall be upheld, as in C. de donationibus, l. si quis pro redemptione; and noted in C. de iudicio deliberando, l. finalis, §. in computo; and Extra, de accusationibus, c. qualiter et quando; and l. non omnes, §. a Barbaris, de remissione. In doubt, however, one must adhere to the distinction of the aforementioned doctors, namely: if it is one chapter, or several inseparable ones, then the writing may be approved in part and not in part; but in distinct matters, separation has place. From these things it is concluded what the law is in doubt. Nevertheless, if he to whom the account is to be rendered wishes to prove the contrary of what is written, he ought to be admitted to prove it, as in §. idem quaesivit. And the foregoing is supported by D. de administratione tutorum, l. Lucius, §. tutelae. Furthermore, it is supported because when the chapters are distinct, it is not said that he varies who approves one and reproves another, as in D. de minoribus, l. in causis, §. 1. Hence, we see that he who responds to allegations may confess one and deny another. And it is supported by D. de legatis 2, l. qui solidum, in principio. Furthermore, we see that one may appeal from one part of a sentence and acquiesce in another, as in C. de appellationibus, l. ampliorem, in principio; and Extra, de testamentis, c. Raynaldus. Furthermore, it would be absurd that he were bound to approve a writing if it were false or doubtful, as in C. de probationibus, l. rationes. Wherefore, all things are not referred to the discretion of the judge, who ought to exercise his discretion in a known case, as I said above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A statute punishes those who transport grain outside the district of the city, or to places not subject [to its jurisdiction], or into any fortress; whether such a statute is to be understood disjunctively, as the words sound, or conjunctively.
body: Words

The doctors say thus: Moreover, that if anyone has contracted a certain quantity of grain outside the district of Pavia, or to places not subject [to jurisdiction], or in any fortress, he is held liable, etc. The question arises concerning the sense of these words, whether this is the sense, that he is held liable in three cases, namely, if [he transports] outside the district indiscriminately; moreover, if [he transports] to places not subject [to jurisdiction] indiscriminately; moreover, if [he transports] to fortresses indiscriminately; or whether, in order that he be held liable, it is required that [he transport] outside the district of Pavia to a place not subject to jurisdiction, or into any fortress, so that it would be otherwise if he were to draw [the grain] outside the district to places where the tax is likewise paid. For it is not probable that the Magnificent [Lord] intended to burden those extracting [the grain] with a double burden. Argument: Digest, On Laws, Title 2, Law Titia, Section Who in life. The tenor of the words is in favor of the tax collectors because of the disjunctive, or as in Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, Law If to an heir several; and Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, Law If, When a pupil, Section Disjunctively. But perhaps the mind of the statute is to be considered contrary, because one part has equity, the other rigor. For I do not know which to choose; hence I think it advisable to consult the Lord Referendary, as in Digest, On Peace, Law To the ancients. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the lord of a certain territory may visit a castle held by certain nobles in fief from the bishop, in order to inspect whether it is properly fortified and guarded, perhaps because they were apprehensive about war.
2. Whether a city may command its citizen, who possesses a castle, to fortify and guard it.
3. Whether and when it is lawful to fortify houses or churches.
4. If two persons are condemned to pay by a single sentence, whether it is understood that each is condemned for one-half, or rather for the whole amount.
5. If a certain village is completely destroyed, and a city erects gallows in its territory, which stand for a period of 30 years, and if that village is subsequently rebuilt, what is the legal situation.
body: It is proposed that a certain place called Montaldi lies within the boundaries of the territory of Chieri. Nevertheless, it is claimed to be an ancient fief of certain lords of the said Castle, who hold the said fief from the Lord Bishop of Turin. However, the said feudatories of the said Castle have certain articles and pacts with the said commune of Chieri concerning the making of peace and war, and concerning the payment of a certain tax.

† Moreover, the lords of the said Castle are the original inhabitants of the said territory of Chieri. Now, the officials of the said territory of Chieri, fearing certain armed men who, it is believed, are about to arrive, wish to visit the said Castle of Montaldi, and to inspect and see how it is fortified, so that the entire country may not suffer harm due to negligence in the custody of the said Castle. But the lord of the said Castle does not wish them to enter, nor to visit it by virtue of any right of visitation; because he says that the commune of the said Chieri has no jurisdiction in this matter, except insofar as the agreements provide. Now the question is asked: what is the law? For clarity, it must be premised that visitation signifies a right, and is sometimes called administration, as noted in the Decretals, *extra de electione*, chapter *Cum nobis olim*, at the end; and it is supported by the Digest, *de officio proconsulis*, law *Si in aliqua*; and the Digest, *de conditionibus in publicis horreis*, law 1, book 10. Hence, whoever has no right of administration has no right of visitation. Moreover, whoever claims to have some administration over another’s property must prove it; because the contrary is presumed by law, namely, that every thing is free. For being obliged to receive a visitor is a species of subjection and servitude. Hence, whoever alleges it must prove it, as in the law *Loci corpus*, § *Competit*, in the Digest, *si servitus vendicetur*. Having premised these things, if the question is asked concerning visitation which is a matter of right and jurisdiction, I answer that one must adhere to the form of the said agreements, and it is not permitted to extend beyond what the agreements provide, as in the Digest, *de verbis obligatorum*, law *Quicquid astringendae*. Nor is it lawful to enter another’s castle against the lord’s objection, as in the Digest, *de usufructu legato*, law *Heres in fundum*; and Distinction 1, chapter *Omnes leges*; Digest, *de iniuriis*, law *Lex Cornelia*, in the beginning; and most fully noted by Innocentius in chapter 1, *de immunitate ecclesiae*. However, if danger were imminent, as is proposed, considering that,

† Since the lord of the said Castle is a citizen of the said territory of Chieri, he may be ordered to fortify the said Castle and to keep it so fortified that no danger may threaten the said territory of Chieri on account of his negligence. Cf. D. 43.8.1 (De via publica).

† Moreover, the authorities state that in this case it is lawful for the superior to fortify the towers and fortifications of churches situated within the territory of said community, and those already established: I do not say outside the territory, as in the extrajudicial collection on constitutions, chapter *Ut animarum*, Book 6. And this is for the sake of public safety, which I understand to apply after a delay or negligence on the part of the possessor. Note this fully in Cynus, Code, On the Holy Trinity, law *Nullus haereticus*. Otherwise, one would have to say that they can hold a castle to provoke emulation in the superior, which is false: as in the Code, On the Limitation of Fiefs, law *Quicunque castrorum*, Book 11. However, one must especially take care that no pretext is fabricated by which the said lord could be deprived of possession of said castle; because in this matter one must proceed in good faith, since it is highly prejudicial. This is supported by the aforementioned points, because a citizen is bound to defend his city: as in the law *Postliminium*, section *Filius*, Digest, On Captives and Postliminium. And especially when it benefits the republic and does not harm himself: as in the Digest, On Rainwater, law 2, section *Idem variis*. Hence, public duties are imposed on citizens and inhabitants, as in the Digest, On Public Duties and Honors, law *Rescripto*, section *Si*, and law *Munera*, throughout the law. To this effect, Decretum 23, question 2, chapter 2, where it is said that it is a just war, and there is the highest praise of military service.

Secondly, it is asked: In a certain judgment it is contained that two communities are bound to pay 12 gold florins each year, whereas formerly 20 were paid for each of the said places; and the words “of the man of the said places and of each of them” are inserted in the wording of the judgment. Now it is asked whether the said places must jointly pay the 12, or 12 for each. I answer: Sometimes two persons are condemned indefinitely to a certain sum, and then each is bound for his share, as in C. Si plures una sententia, l. 1, unless it appears from the intention that each is bound in solidum. This can sufficiently be gathered here from the mind of the speaker, by referring each item to each person. Sometimes the word “each” is added, and then each is bound in solidum, as noted in l. Si pluribus, de legatis 2. And so it is here.

Thirdly, it is asked whether, if a certain village is entirely destroyed by hostilities, and the commune of Chieri erected gallows on the said destroyed village and held them for a period of 30 years, and then the said village is repaired and, so to speak, renewed from its destruction, whether the said village can, notwithstanding the said lapse of time, exercise its rights. And I say that it can, because in the meantime, while it was destroyed, there was no people there. And therefore prescription could not begin. For I consider that this case is similar to that of a people against whom prescription does not run: as in C. de praescrip. 40. anno. l. sicut. §. non sexus. And if it were to avail, restitution in integrum would be granted: as in ff. de ser. rusti. prae. l. attilicius. Nevertheless, there is doubt, because these goods appear to have been destroyed, the people being meanwhile absent; and therefore they are conceded to the occupant, as noted by Innocentius in a similar case in extra de prob. cap. in praesentia. But the same author says elsewhere that this is an absence of fact, and not of law; and thus the people, although in flight, do not lose their rights: as he notes in extra de no. ope. nun. cap. cum ex iniuncto. And this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a contract made by the King binds the king who succeeds him in the Kingdom not by hereditary right, but by election.
2. Certain kingdoms are transmitted by line of blood, while others are transmitted by election.
3. The Emperor dies, although the dignity itself does not die.
4. A king who acknowledges no superior in his kingdom holds the most principal principality: and whether he is bound by contracts made by him.
5. The public entity of the Kingdom never dies: and therefore it has no heir.
1. Whether sons lose the fief on account of the father's delict.
2. Whether a vassal who attacks the public entity of the Kingdom loses the fief.
3. Whether and when the command of the Prince is to be observed.
4. By what penalty a contemner of the king's command is to be punished.
5. Whether the time of one possessor accrues to another possessor.
body: On that point

It is asked whether, by virtue of the contract entered into between the said Dionysius, in his own name and that of his successors, and the said Manuel Punzano, also in his own name and that of his successors, concerning the offices of the Admiralty, its jurisdiction, and other emoluments, and by conferring upon the said Manuel and his successors the rights arising from the said office, the illustrious present King is bound, who does not succeed to the aforementioned King and his heirs in this kingdom by hereditary right, but has been assumed as King solely by the election of the people, to relinquish the said office with its emoluments and fief, or of necessity to grant them to the successors of the said Manuel, or to approve the contract according to the form expressed in the said contract, as a matter of law, whether they are bound to do so or not.

It is rightly doubted, and for the sake of clarity it must be premised that sometimes certain Kingdoms are transmitted by the line of blood and pass successively to descendants, as in *extra de voto*, c. *Licet*. But other Empires and Kingdoms do not pass to heirs by succession, because they are conferred by election and not by succession, as in *extra de electione*, c. *Venerabilem*, § *Insuper*, and *extra de pace*, c. *Accipimus*, as is the Kingdom of the Romans. And such a Kingdom is bestowed upon men to such an extent that, as stated in *Codex de vetere iure enumerando*, l. 2, § *Quia vero Imperialem*, and l. 1 in the beginning, and in *Authenticum Quo oportet episcopos* in the beginning, and in *Authenticum De instrumentorum cautela et fide*, § 2, and in *Authenticum Constitutio quae de dignitatibus*, § *Pe* at the end, and in *Authenticum In medio litis non fieri sacras formas*, § 1, and in *Authenticum De consulibus* at the end. And it was said in ancient times, when the Roman Empire was in its flourishing state, that the Imperial crown was invisibly imposed by God, whereas the material and visible one was the Imperial insignia itself, as in *Codex de quadrien. praescri.*, l. *Bene a Zenone*. Secondly, it must be premised that

The Emperor can die in person; but the dignity itself, or the Empire, is immortal, just as the Supreme Pontiff dies, but the Supreme Pontificate does not die, and therefore those things which proceed from the person and the new seat are personal, if they depend on the successive will. But if they immediately transfer with them full right, then the death of the grantor does not prevent the benefit from enduring during the time of the successor, as in the Authentica Constitutio, which is about dignities, § Illud, and in the chapter Si gratiose, on rescripts, book 6. Certain things, however, proceed from the seat, and these are always perpetual and eternal, until a case of extinction supervenes, or the term of life of such concession. Contracts of the Kingdom are of this kind, which are contracted in the name of the King and of the Kingdom, or of his people. For the Kingdom contains in itself not only the material territory, but also the peoples of the Kingdom, because the people collectively are the Kingdom, and without the circumscribed obedience of the peoples, the King could not be said to reign. Digest, On the Origin of Law, law 2, § Exac. And these things are true, unless the King has ordered something to the prejudice of the Kingdom, because such an order falls with the grantor, if it would enormously injure the Kingdom itself. For whatever is said about the Donation of Constantine, which was miraculous, if similar donations were made by kings, they would not bind successors, to whom the protection of the Kingdom, not its dissipation, is entrusted, as in the chapter Grandi, on the negligence of prelates, book 6, and noted in the Authentica Quo oportet episcopos, in the beginning, and expressly in the Extravagant On Oaths, chapter Intellecto. An exception is made, however, according to some, if it were made for the state of the whole Catholic Church, as noted in law 1, V. Cum urb., Code, On the Office of the Prefect of the City, and On Law, chapter Pastoralis, in the Clementines, and On Oaths, chapter 1, in the same compilation. But this is left undiscussed for the present, for it has been fully said elsewhere.

Thirdly, it must be premised that the King, who holds the most principal principality in his Kingdom, because he acknowledges no superior, is the all-containing whole, and can contract in his own name, and in the name of the whole land and his peoples. For he has the fullest power, as is stated in the Digest, *De publicis*, l. *cessat*; and in the Code, *De quadriennali praescriptione*, l. *bene a Zenone*. Hence, he who contracted under the name of his dignity binds his successors; for the nature of a contract is that it is transmissible, except in certain contracts which, by their nature, do not admit of transmission. Hence, it should be known that whether a royal disposition is real or personal is ascertained in several ways. For in the first place, it is ascertained from the form; for if the tenor of the writing makes mention of successors on both sides, this disposition is written *in rem*, and passes to the successors of both parties, whether we speak of successors who succeed by hereditary right, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, l. *iuris gentium*, § *pactorum*; or of successors in dignity and administration: as appears from what Legatus and Novellus state in c. 1, *Qui successores teneantur*, col. 10; and *Extra*, *Praetiti vices suas*, c. *fin.*; and in the Digest, *De pactis*, l. *iuris gentium*, § *pactorum*; and l. *qui in futurum*, § *si ex altera*; and in the Digest, *De probationibus*, l. *si pax*; and in the Code, *Ut actio ab haerede et contra heredem*, l. 1. And in the contracts of kings it is expressly stated that they are binding on the parties and pass to the successors in the Kingdom, if celebrated in the name of the dignity, *Extra*, *De re iudicata*, c. *Abbate sane*, in the principle, lib. 6; and *Extra*, *De iureiurando*, c. *Intellecto*, according to Innocentius. Nor is this surprising, for in the Kingdom the dignity must be considered, which does not die:

† And also the university, or the commonwealth of the Kingdom itself, which even after the kings have been removed, perseveres. For the commonwealth cannot die. And for this reason it is said that the commonwealth has no heir: because it always lives in itself, as is stated in the law and noted in l. 1, §. fin., D. si quis ius dicenti non obtemperet. Just as Aristotle says, the world does not die, but the dispositions of the world die, change, alternate, and do not persevere in the same quality. Hence, speaking with understanding, the person granting here is not dead, namely the commonwealth of the Kingdom itself. For it is true to say that the commonwealth does nothing by itself; nevertheless, he who governs the commonwealth acts by the virtue of the commonwealth and of the dignity conferred upon him by the commonwealth itself. Moreover, two things concur in the king: the person and the signification. And this signification, which is a certain intellectual entity, always perseveres enigmatically, although not corporally. For although the King may fail, what of it? Namely, the King acts in place of two persons, as in D. de his qui ut indici, l. tutorum. And the person of the king is the organ and instrument of that intellectual and public person. And that intellectual and public person is the one that principally founds acts; because the principal act or virtue is regarded more than the organic virtue. Certainly, even if the promisor dies without an heir, the promise nevertheless ceases not to endure in its perfect being, as is stated in the law and noted in D. de deposito, l. 1, §. plane; and D. de solutionibus, l. Stichum aut Pamphilum, in principio; D. ut legatorum nomine caveatur, l. postquam; D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si; D. de administratione tutorum, l. si quis heredem, in principio; C. ad Trebellianum, l. Sancimus, §. cum autem. From these it is clearly concluded that the said contract is transmissible by its form; and also by the dignity and authority of the grantor; and likewise by the commonwealth itself represented, which, as I said, does not die. Furthermore, the said contract is called real by the confirmation of subsequent kings; because confirmation argues, i.e., acutely proves perpetuity in the act, as is stated in the law and noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. privilegia, according to Petrus and Cynus. Also, because it is presumed real on both sides, when such reality of the contract is compatible with the contract itself and of its nature, in c. 1, §. ultimo, Qui feuda dare possunt, col. 10; and in c. 1, de successione feudorum, same column; and which is noted by Innocentius in Extra, de institutionibus, c. cum venisset. Nor does it avail to object if it is said that it is not of the nature of an office that it should pass to the heir, especially when such an office is one that is exercised by the virtues of body and mind, as in D. de tutelis, l. pe; and D. de cura furiosi, l. cuius bonis; C. de caducis tollendis, §. ne autem; D. de negotiis gestis, l. nam et servius, §. si vivo; Si quis ignorans rem minoris emerit, l. 1. There it is said, since the office is ended by death. And that is true in a mere office. But this is an office mixed with advantage and utility, and even when it proceeds with utility, it is called a military service, as is stated in the law and noted in D. de bonis possessionibus ex testamento militis, l. 1. Namely, because annexed to it is mere and mixed imperium, and transmissible jurisdiction by the form of the concession and pact. Hence, whatever we acquire, we rightly prepare for our children by vow, as in D. unde liberi, l. scripto; and D. de bonis libertorum, l. nihil, §. facilior; and D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si. From these it appears that this contract is real on the part of the matter. Furthermore, it is real on the part of the final cause: because in such a fief it is permitted to serve through the heir of one’s own body, and in case of necessity through any equally suitable person, as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. continuus, §. si ab eo, and there noted. Also, it does not avail to object if it is said that King Dionysius, contracting in his own name and that of his successors, did not consider total annihilation, but the perpetuation of his progeny; and that the acts of agents do not operate beyond their intention, as in D. si certum petatur, l. non omnis. For words are restricted to what was considered, as in D. de testamentaria tutela, l. si quis ita; nor do they pertain to the adverse case and the fortune of a tardy man, as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. inter stipulantem, §. sacramenta. Because neither he nor anyone considers that he will die without an heir. And yet the contract endures after he dies without an heir, as has been said: although deeds exceed the will. Furthermore, every thing is regulated by the path of reason, nor is it to be founded upon hope, but upon the things themselves and the facts, as in C. de conditionibus ob causam, l. si repetendi. From all these it is openly concluded that the said contract is considered to be of the nature of reality, and to live, and to live as long as it must live.

It remains, therefore, to consider the second point, namely whether this contract has been absorbed and the fief extinguished on account of the felony committed by the aforementioned Lozelatum, successor in the aforesaid fief, for having hostilely purged the republic of the Kingdom. On this point, it must be said without doubt that such an attacker and traitor to the republic or fatherland has undoubtedly prejudiced himself and his descendants for multiple reasons.

First, because he incurred the crime of high treason by acting against the majesty of the Kingdom or the republic. For the republic itself possesses majesty, analogous to the Roman people, since it is free and has the right to create a king, as stated in the Institutes, *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Item placuit*. And from this it follows that it cannot have an heir, as provided in the Code, *Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*, *Quisquis*; and in the Code, *De hereditatibus*, Authenticum *Gazaros*. And if the sons cannot be heirs, they cannot therefore succeed to the fief, as stated in the title *An agnatus vel filius*, chapter 1, column 10.

Second, this is proven by another reason: because the said sons are infamous with the greatest infamy, and therefore they do not dare to appear in the king’s court, nor ought they or can they be heard; for they are to be avoided by all, like lepers, as stated in the Authenticum *Iusiurandum quod praestatur ab his qui administrationem recipiunt*, § *Finis*.

Third, the reason is that the nature of fiefs is such that whenever a fief is lost, or ought to be lost, on account of a felony committed against the person of the lord, such fief reverts to the lord, as stated in chapter 1, § *Certe*, column 10, of the title *Quibus modis feudum amittitur*.

Fourth, there is a general reason drawn from the nature of all contracts: because a contract cannot benefit one who has, by his very acts and deeds, opposed it, as stated in the Digest, *De locato conducto*, *Quaero*, § *Inter locatorem*; and in the legal rule and in the Digest, *De his qui uti probati*, in the aforementioned law *Postlegatum*; and in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, *Papius*, § *Meminisse*.

For these reasons, I say without doubt that the felony of the said successor in the fief generates prejudice to the children descending from him, and that the fief would have freely reverted to the republic of that Kingdom, and consequently to the king himself, who was elected and newly created and succeeded in the principality with full right, and that the king could dispose of the said fief according to divine and human law, at his own will. For even if it was perhaps perpetual from the beginning, as shown above and by what is noted in the law *Patet*, *De servis legatis*, and because the king’s affairs are said to be the affairs of the community, as noted by Innocentius in *De iureiurando*, chapter *Quintavallis*, nevertheless, by his own delict, the said fief returned to nullity.

† Since it received its foundation from the republic itself, it is most evident that the said fief has become forfeit and has reverted to the chamber of the republic, or of the king, when the republic itself was invaded by an enemy, even in some minimal part of it, as C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, in principio, and ar. C. de liberis et eorum liberis, l. 2, §. si. Moreover, concerning the creation of the said King, to whom it pertains, this is not the place to discuss: but it is presupposed, and I believe, that it is more true that it pertains to the King. 8. q. 1, cap. Moyses, and ff. de iustitia et iure, l. ex hoc iure gentium. From this we presume, and presuppose, a free people, as noted in ff. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. hostes, 63. dist., c. Adrianus, and 7. q. 1, c. incipimus, de foro competenti, c. licet, per Innocentius, and de voto, c. quod super eundem, Innocentius. However, that Kings ought to obey the laws of Emperors is noted by Innocentius, extra de re iudicata, c. cum re. Innocentius also says that Kings ought to follow the laws, and especially the laws of nature. Thus noted by the same author, extra de re iudicata, c. cum te. Therefore, if the said vassal had not committed a delict, undoubtedly his heir would have the benefit of the fief, because, as I said, reparation does not diminish the right of contract of the ancient king. ar. de minoribus, l. in integrum, and l. Aemilius Largianus, and what is noted in l. 1, C. de contractibus iudicii, C. de quadrien. praescriptione, l. omnes, and l. bene a Zenone. It supports extra de praebendis, c. dilecto, 63. dist., ca. Adrianus, 7. q. 1, c. Moyses. But because of the ratification, all honor is excluded. C. ubi senatores, vel clarissimi, l. 1. The fief has freely reverted to the first power, i.e., the lord King, as lord of the fief. The text is express, and the ordinary gloss in c. cum vassallus culpam committat, si de feudo controversia fuerit, collatio 10. And by this it is clear that a response has been given to all questions asked. That also is established, that it is to find a people and province free. ff. de captivis, l. hostes, and l. non dubito. And it supports what is noted by Innocentius, extra de foro competenti, c. licet, and de voto. Furthermore, it must be presupposed that the said King can donate castles and places to his soldiers, as in collatio 10, qui feuda concedere possunt, c. 1, §. si, C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. donationes, C. de crimine stellionatus, l. instar, ff. de evictione, l. Lucius, and noted in C. de legibus, l. humanum, provided that he does not do anything whereby the honor of the crown or the status of the Kingdom is diminished, as extra de iureiurando, c. intellecto. And from this it follows that the donation made to Titus the soldier was valid. Secondly, it must be premised,

† That the command of the king is to be observed, provided, however, that it is just, or at least not unjust. Hence, if the King were to command his subject to kill himself, or to go to a place where he would be slaughtered by an enemy, or to send his son as a victim, in such cases one is not to obey the King: because such commands are contrary to natural law. But if he commands someone to defend the fatherland and the honor of the King, even if this could not be done without danger, one must obey the King: because this will be the right of the King, etc., as noted in the preface to the Digests. By this I return to the point at issue: if the King commanded that one send his son as a hostage, a Christian, into the hands of Saracens or of a cruel tyrant, the command would not be valid. As stated in l. ut vim, ff. de iustitia et iure; and ff. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. postliminium, § filius. And all this is to be referred to the judgment of a reasonable man. And by this it becomes apparent whether one ought to have obeyed that command to send the son as a hostage, or not. See ff. quod metus causa, l. isti quidem, at the end. And it supports what is noted in extra de iureiurando, c. ex rescripto; and c. ne filius pro parte; auth. imo. It remains to see,

† When a precept is binding, by what penalty should the contemner of the King’s mandate be punished? For sometimes the law states that he shall die the death, as in Extra, De maiestatibus et obediencia, c. 2. For he is a violator of the law who does not observe the King’s mandates, as in Digest, De re militari, l. 3, § in bello, and l. Omne delictum, § Contumacia. Another authority states that the goods are taken away from the contumacious person and exile is imposed, as in Codex, De fundis limitosis, l. Si, lib. 11. Secondly, it must be said that if a certain penalty is attached to the Royal mandate, that penalty is inflicted. But if no certain penalty is attached, the penalty is discretionary, as in Codex, De primicerio, l. 1, in fine, lib. 12. Because no sin is so small that it does not become greater through contempt, as in Authentica, Ut omnes obediunt iudicibus provinciarum, § Haec considerantes, col. 5. By Lombard law, however, the penalty is imposed according to the King’s will, as in Lombard law, Si quis literas Imperatoris despexerit, l. Si quis literas, non. It is not necessary that contemners of the King’s mandate be exempt from penalty, since they are rebels by that very fact, as in l. Si desertores, Codex, De desertoribus, lib. 12. And certainly those who have received benefits from the Prince ought to be punished more than others, as in Codex, De conductoribus et procuratoribus sive auctoribus praediorum, l. Unica, lib. 11. Hence, on account of disobedience, a soldier is deprived of his office with infamy, as in Digest, De infamibus, l. 2, § Ignominiae, and § Miles. And the law says that we do not grant pardon to such persons, nor do we alleviate crimes by indulgences, as in Codex, De cohortalibus, l. Si apparitor. Although elsewhere it is written that the immunity of trampling upon the law suffices, as in Codex, De vestibus electoribus, l. Temperet. From these things, therefore, it is clear that if Titius without cause did not obey the King, the King could take away the Castle from him: and not only from him, but also from his sons, to whom the examples of their ancestors are prejudicial, as in Codex, De cohortalibus, l. Si cohortalis, and 10, col. Qui mox seu amittit, c. 1, § 2. From this it immediately follows that the concession of the said Castle made to Lucius was valid, and the donation which had been made to Titius, as being extinguished and dead, never revived, as in Digest, De solutionibus, l. Qui res, § Aream. Subsequently it is proposed: that the said Lucius was a deserter to the King’s enemies, on account of which the King deprived him of the said Castle and granted it to another. Now it is asked: whether this third concession was valid. And it must be said without doubt that it was, as in c. Quamvis, De rescindendis, lib. 6. And it supports this: Digest, Qui ex causa maiestatis, l. Sed si per praetorem, § Sed si dum decreto.

† Now I come to another question, whether the time during which Titius possessed, and then the time during which the King possessed, and then the time during which Lucius possessed, should be added to the time during which the last knight possessed. And it seems to be said that not: because the possession of Titius was naturally interrupted, by the apprehension of possession, which the King made, as in D. de usucap. l. naturaliter. And therefore it is necessary to begin the prescription anew, as in D. de usucap. l. si is, qui pro emptore. §. si quis bona fide. and l. eum, qui aedes. §. si autem demolita. Moreover, for the times to be continued, it is necessary that the latter have a cause from the former, but here he does not have a transmissive cause, but an exclusive and privative one: because the King deprived the first, and transferred to the latter, to this effect. D. de usucap. l. id tempus. in princ. Moreover, the possession of him who is private was at some time vitious, therefore to a vitious possession nothing can be added, nor conversely, as in D. de acquirenda possessione. l. Pomponius. §. si. Furthermore, it does not seem that the King can prescribe anything in his Kingdom as to jurisdiction, or Empire, because he has this by common law as in D. de usucap. l. sequitur. §. lana. and note per Innocentius extra de posth. praela. c. bona. But against the above makes. D. de don. causa mortis. l. qui alienam. for these possessions seem to be under that. tit. l. si rem. and there the gloss expressly notes, that he who revokes, uses the accession of the possessor, from whom he revokes, and henceforth all having cause from the revoking one, arg. D. de acquirenda possessione. l. Pompo. §. si iussu. and great difference is between interruption of possession, and translation, which is a way of law. It seems to me, that the donation of the king gave the beginning of prescribing to Titius, and then to Lucius, and then to the last donee against the owner if there was any of the said Castle. which however the possession of one benefits another does not seem reasonable, because the right of the prescriber was prescribed. and another created anew, as extra de prebendis. c. dilecto. and makes. D. de reivindic. l. a divo pi. §. sic veniet. Moreover the lord King, if the Castle was of some third person, did not have title: and the possession of the king was not altogether without defect, as C. de acquirenda possessione. l. improba. in doubt however Castles are presumed to be the king's: because to them adheres jurisdiction, as in c. 1. quae sint regalia. col. 10. and therefore in doubt it is to be said, that the King could grant, and that the last one is to be preferred to all: because the first were deprived by law. and makes. C. de heredit. auth. idem est de nestorianis. and what is noted in l. Gallus. §. et quid si tantum. D. de lib. et posth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an emphyteutic thing, which the emphyteuta bequeaths or donates, or the right which he holds, without the consent of the owner, reverts to the owner.
body: It is asked whether,

† if an emphyteuta bequeathes his right which he has in the emphyteutic property, or the emphyteutic property itself: whether by bequeathing and alienating it, even though de facto, the property reverts to the direct lord, who did not consent to the legacy nor to the alienation; and that it does not return to the direct lord, laws sufficiently known to understanding men are cited: ff. de lega. j. l. dominus. §. fi., C. de fun. patrimo. l. j., C. de praediis curia. l. fi., insti. loca. §. adeo, ff. de ver. sig. l. in conuentionibus, and what is noted by Accursius in C. de iure emphy. l. fi., extra de loca. §. nunc aliqua, versic. 107 and verse 112. To the contrary are cited all the arguments that Cynus posits in l. vlt. C. de iure emphy. in his addition, and what is noted by Bartolus in l. de quibus de leg. On this point it must be considered that either it is an emphyteusis of the fiscus or of one possessing the privilege of the fiscus, and the donation and legacy hold, because the right of the fiscus is preserved, as is noted in the previously cited legal texts and in c. 1 § donare qualiter olim poterat feudum alienare col. 10. Or it is of the Church, and Bartolus used to say that it could not be donated nor bequeathed, but reverted to its direct ownership; and he held this by l. vniuersas C. ne rei dominicae, vel templorum. I had this question with him in consultations, and I said that such a legacy is valid, because the beneficial profits of the dominium utile are deemed to be bequeathed, and not the dominium utile itself. Hence, if they are such profits as can be bequeathed because they are transmissible to successors, those profits are deemed bequeathed: as in C. de lega. l. vxor patrui and ff. de vsufr. lega. l. Sticho, and what is noted in C. si pignus pignori datum sit l. 1 in the gloss sed nunquid. Also there is another reason, as I shall immediately state. Or it is an emphyteusis of some private person, that is, of a person who ought to be governed by the ius commune, even if he were a great count or baron; and then there are opinions, because some say that it reverts to the direct ownership, and some say that it does not revert. Consider that either we are speaking of a donation that progressed as far as it could to its effect because delivery intervened; and then the question can be doubtful. Nevertheless, I think that the donation is valid, and the rent can be sought from the donee by the action under the Lex Zenoniana, which is quasi in rem, as is noted in insti. loca. § adeo. Or the donation did not arrive at delivery or quasi-delivery, and then without doubt the property has not reverted to the direct ownership, because prior to delivery or quasi-delivery the donor abdicated nothing from himself: as in ff. de verb. sig. l. alienatum. Or we are speaking of a legacy; and then without doubt I say that it does not revert to the lord, and this by a novel reason, whose nature is as follows: either the legacy is valid and belongs to the legatee, therefore it does not revert to the direct lord; or it is not valid, and then the legatee cannot accept the legacy, therefore it remains with the heir of the testator, as in C. de ca. tol. § pro secundo; whence it is just as if the legatee repudiated the legacy, or a donee to whom a donation was made by messenger or letter did not accept—in which cases it is certain that it is just as if it had not been bequeathed nor donated: as in ff. ad l. aqui. l. huic scripturae and ff. si certum peta. l. proinde. Whence the said Cynus, in speaking of a legacy and expressing doubt, did not consider what he ought to have considered. And from these points it is concluded that through such a legacy the property has not reverted to the lord. But if it had reverted by reason of the determination of the line or from another cause, then this would not pertain to our case: as in ff. dele. 2 l. peti. § praedium; and therefore the lord ought to invest him, and accept that which is accustomed to be accepted for similar investitures. And thus I, Baldus, state and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the possessory and the petitory actions for retaining possession may be joined together, especially in corporeal things.
2. How ownership and possession, or quasi-jurisdiction, are to be proved. num. 5.
3. The boundaries of a territory are proved by ancient documents.
4. An oath produces the same effect as a derogatory clause made with certain knowledge.
5. When the possessory action has been proved by both parties, and the case has proceeded to the petitory action, he prevails who proves his case better in the petitory action.
body: It is proposed that the case concerning the commune of Terdona, which is pending in the court, between the said commune and its syndics acting on one side, and the commune of Pavia defending on the other, on account of the place of Cognaro and the like, has been brought as both a petitory and a possessory action on behalf of the said commune and city of Terdona. It is said, namely, on behalf of the plaintiff, that the said place of Cognaro, and its jurisdiction, as well as possession and quasi-possession, belonged and belongs to the said commune of Terdona, both by virtue of imperial privileges and by the nature of its location and territory, as well as from the exercise of jurisdictions and regalia for such a long time that there is no prior memory to the contrary. It is also stated that in ancient times it was in peaceful and patient possession, both by the universitas of the commune of Pavia and by those surrounding the said place. Recently, however, it is reported that the same question and controversy have been raised by the said commune of Pavia, attempting to cast doubt upon and impede the exercise of the said rights and jurisdiction, albeit improperly and unjustly, by asserting in fact that the said rights and jurisdiction belong to the commune of Pavia, and that the said place and territory of Cognaro are part of the territory of Pavia. On these points, both parties have endeavored to prove and produce their respective rights, both in the petitory and in the aforementioned possessory action. Therefore, the first question is:

Whether the petitory and possessory actions could be cumulated, and I see that they cannot: because the possessory action for retention is not granted except to the possessor. But the petitory action is not granted to one who possesses; therefore, he who brings both the petitory and possessory actions simultaneously is contradictory to himself. This is not so with respect to the principles on the part of the plaintiff, for even a dominus who possesses has the real action for vindication of the thing, which is so conjoined with dominium that it cannot be separated from it, as is stated and noted in l. 1, in principio, ff. de edendo, in the great gloss, and by Petrus and Cynus in l. 1, C. de alienis iudiciis. But with respect to the thing itself, if the defendant does not possess, nor ceased to possess through dolus, he is not liable in a real action, and the formal vindication of the thing, or as it is in exercise, is brought in vain, and especially when the plaintiff possesses: because he asks in vain for what he holds within himself, as these matters are proven: ff. de iudiciis, l. non alias, § 1; ff. de rei vindicatione, l. ordinarii; ff. de rei vindicatione, l. qui petitorio; ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. naturaliter, § nihil commune; and l. exitus controversiae; ff. uti possidetis, l. 1, § interdictum; C. de interdictis, l. incerti, and the note; C. de appellationibus, l. 1; and ff. de iudiciis, l. si domi. To cumulate the petitory and possessory actions is therefore to contradict oneself in the exercise of actions, nor are the modes of possessing and the species of disturbances distinguished in bringing the action. For sometimes one disturbs, yet does not possess, as ff. de vi et vi armata, l. vim facit; ff. de acquisitione et obligatione, l. servus non in omnibus; C. finium regundorum, l. si quis super and l. si constiterit; ff. quod vi aut clam, l. prohibere; C. ubi de possessione agi oporteat, l. 1; ff. de diversis temporum praescriptionibus, l. si quispiam; ff. de iniuriis, l. iniuriam, § fi; ff. de empta re, l. qui pendentem; ff. de officio procuratoris Caesaris, l. fi; ff. si servus venditus, l. sicuti, § Aristo. Therefore, the contrary must be said: because when the petitory and possessory actions are brought for incorporeal rights, both remedies are granted to the possessor, as Inst. de actionibus, § aeque, and there most fully by Dominus Dy, and ff. si servus venditus, l. sicuti, § si quaeratur. Hence, because jurisdiction, and a common species thereof, is something incorporeal, the petitory and possessory actions for retention may rightly be brought. And especially when both parties proceed voluntarily in the case regarding both remedies. Moreover, he who causes obedience to be withdrawn from the lord, in a certain manner commits spoliation, and therefore just as the interdict for recovery and the petitory action can be brought simultaneously, as ff. de vi et vi armata, arguing from l. cum a te, § fi, and the note in the said § nihil commune, and Extra de restitutione spoliatorum, c. cum ad sedem, and so in our case, for although the disturbance is considered with respect to jurisdiction in general: nevertheless, it is a certain spoliation with respect to certain obediences which are inhibited and withdrawn, as ff. de dolo, l. cum quis, and Extra de electione, c. querelam. Presupposed

† Therefore, let us examine whether it has been properly acted upon, and whether this has been proven. And first, regarding ownership. It is certain that all jurisdictions pertain to the supreme ownership of the Emperor. Hence, no one can have jurisdiction unless by his concession or permission, speaking according to Roman law. And jurisdictions cannot be exercised except by magistrates, who are called by various names: the creation of whom pertains to the authority of the Prince, as in D. de officio praefecti, l. Barb. in fine, and in Auth. de defensoribus civitatum, § interim. And if one Emperor granted it, it does not prejudice successors: the succeeding Emperor can take it away and grant it to another, as noted in C. de legibus, l. digna vox, and in Auth. quomodo oportet episcopos, in principio, and in Auth. iusiurandum quod praestatur ab his, in rubro et nigro. But it is so that the commune of Tordona, by many privileges of Emperors, has attributed to itself the said place, which is called Cognarium, and all jurisdiction of the said place; therefore, the claim of the commune of Tordona is founded on the petitory, as noted in C. de legibus, l. humanum, nor can it be said by the opposing party to be prescribed, since the commune of Tordona has always, or for the greater part of the time, had the fruits and benefits of the said jurisdiction. For he who has the benefits is said to possess in reality, as in D. qui modis ususfructus amittitur, l. Papinianus, and D. de solutionibus, l. Titia, and as noted in the said l. si quis super finium regundorum, C. de agris et censibus, l. litibus. Since therefore this is proven by the commune of Tordona, it also appears that the possessory is proven, and from the preceding title: because possession always refers to the title from which it arises, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. predia, C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. minus instructus, D. pro socio, l. merito, D. si servitus venditur, l. si a te. And it suffices for one species of jurisdiction to be used, if someone uses that species as contained under the genus, and with respect to the genus, as in D. qui modis ususfructus amittitur, l. is qui ususfructum. Likewise, it is not necessary to prove individual species of jurisdiction, but it suffices to prove acts in some, and aptitude in the others, according to the note in D. de testamento, l. ob carmen, § fin., and Extra de excusatione, c. qualiter, per Innocentius, and in l. possideri, § 1, de acquisitione possessionis, per Bartolus. For acts of the same quality of jurisdiction are contiguous, and whenever we deal with proving a genus, witnesses who prove species contained under the same genus are not called singular witnesses: because in each species the genus is represented. Otherwise, if it were necessary to prove a singular act, according to Jacobus de Belvisio. And to this contributes what is noted by Cynus in l. 2, C. quae sit longa consuetudo. And from these it appears that, assuming the commune of Pavia had an ancient privilege, nevertheless it was absorbed by prior privileges transferred successively, as in D. de adimendo legatis, l. translatio. Nor is the possession of the Tordonesi presumed to be clandestine: because it was never vitious, but by the authority of the Prince, as in D. de noxa, l. generaliter. Likewise, because it does not appear that the commune of Pavia used jurisdiction before them, hence, since possession was vacant, it is not called clandestine, especially in one who subsequently has a title, since he possesses by title for himself, as in D. pro suo, l. si ancillam. Likewise, he is not called a clandestine possessor who possesses for so long a time that he ceases to possess earlier, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si quis ante, D. de usucapione, l. furti, and l. fundum.
