Hence, concluding from the first to the last, the claim of the commune of Tordona is stronger, and seems to be rightly proven, especially since nothing is proven or duly articulated regarding the prior possession of the other, and the foregoing are confirmed by the letters of our Illustrious Prince, who asserts before the commune of Tordona that there is present possession, or quasi-possession. These letters induce a presumption transferring the burden of proof to the adversary, as in c. literas, de probationibus, in Clementina. Since therefore the commune of Tordona has present possession, it ought to have its benefits, as in Inst. de interdictis, § commodum, and D. de liberto causa, l. liberis, § 1, and D. de probationibus, l. circa eum, and C. de servis exponendis, l. moueor, and what is noted in C. de possessionibus, l. si de possessione, and in column 10, de consuetudine recti feudi, § sacramenta, and C. de re vendita, l. si. Finally, the foregoing are confirmed: because that city is said to be in possession of jurisdiction, and is also presumed to be in ownership of the villages and castles under which the villages and castles make collection, as in Auth. qui modis nuncupativus efficitur sui, § si quis igitur ex qualibet, and there noted, and D. de censibus, l. forma.

† To this end also contribute the ancient writings, by which the boundaries of the territory are proved, as in D. de probat. l. Celsus; and in C. de contrah. et committ. stipul. l. Optimam; and in C. de iure deliberandi l. Cum aliquis. And it is made by what is noted in C. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum l. Monumentorum. For from the customary manner of speaking truth is presumed, as in D. de fluvio l. 1 § 1; and similarly from the general custom of notaries. Much is presumed in favor of public archival writings, as in C. de fide instrumentorum Auth. Ad hoc. One thing is also very well known, namely, that the Emperor granted the said place of Cagnario to the said Terdonenses with an oath. Hence it must be known,

† that the oath produces the same effect as a derogatory clause made with certain knowledge, and especially when it is the oath of the Prince: for that which is sworn is inviolable, as in D. de legibus 2, l. cum pater, § filius matrem, and there note III. It is also to be noted,

† But if both parties were to prove their case in a possessory action: nevertheless, since the matter is being litigated in a petitory action, he prevails who proves his case better in the petitory action, as stated in C. de edicto divi Adriani tollendo, l. edicto. Indeed, even if only a possessory action had been brought, all other things being equal, that claim prevails which is more justified by title, as stated in Extra de probat., c. licet causam. And therefore, for the strengthening of a possessory claim, title is of great value, according to the note in C. qui legitimam personam, l. momentanea. This is especially true in possessory actions concerning jurisdictions: because they are in a certain sense mixed, as stated in ff. de interdictis, l. 3, § quaedam. Hence, he who has better supporting arguments has the better possession. And in these possessory actions, not only the substance of the possession is considered, but also its quality, i.e., that they are possessed by right, i.e., with the aid of law prevailing, as noted in ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 1, in principio. And these statements suffice. Let the most just judges see and supply the rest. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mother contracting for her sons, or in their name, is herself principally bound, or the sons, or whether she is deemed to have interceded. nu. 4.
2. A mother does not stand surety for her son, nor vice versa.
3. When a woman is said to stand surety for another.
body: The case is as follows: some time ago, Andreas, formerly of the lord John of Porto, a citizen and inhabitant of the city of Vicenza, etc., invested the lady Ughana, daughter of a certain lord Lippo, formerly the wife of the lord John Georgius, formerly of the lord John of Todesta, acting, receiving, and stipulating on behalf of, in the place of, and in the name of the minor brothers Antonius Richus, Magdalena, and Tarsia, heirs of the aforementioned John Georgius, their father, and also of the children of the aforementioned lady Ughana, their mother, concerning certain possessions. In this instrument, the said lady, acting as if for herself and her heirs, promised to pay and answer to the said lessor, or to his heirs, every year 80 pounds, etc., as these and other matters are more fully contained in the lease instrument. Now, having examined the words of the said instrument...
† It is asked whether the lady herself is bound to pay the said 80 pounds, and what is to be said regarding the expenses. For clarity, it must be premised that

† That a mother does not act as a surety, even for her son, as in C. ad Velleianam, l. Si commissae; nor conversely does a daughter act as a surety for her mother or father, as in C. ad Velleianam, l. Si paternam. For no distinction is made as to whom she guarantees, ff. ad Velleianam, l. 2, in fine, although a distinction is made as to the cause. For there are certain causes in which the Velleian Senatusconsultum ceases to apply, as is fully noted in C. eodem, l. Finis. Secondly, it must be premised that

† A woman is then said to act as a surety when she binds herself for another who is bound, or when she assumes another’s obligation for the benefit of that other, and not for the woman’s own advantage. For whether the benefit accrues to her primarily or secondarily, since she acts in her own interest, i.e., for her own utility, she is not aided by the *Velleian* Senatusconsultum, which was devised solely to remedy the simplicity of women, and in the case where it deals with pure loss, as in D. ad Velleian. l. *aliquando* and l. *si pro aliquo mulier intercesserit*. Thirdly, a certain law must be premised, which seems to determine our case specifically; for the law provides that if a woman hires premises and binds herself for the lease, then she is not aided; but when the lease is made to another, and not to the woman, and she binds herself for that lessee, then she is aided. Thus says the text, C. ad Velleian. l. *si adversarius tuus*.

† Now it must be seen who is said to have leased these premises, whether the sons or the mother. And it seems that [it was] the mother, [given that] the sons do not ratify. For, since the sons do not ratify, this lease remains with the mother in her own name, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. Cum quaeritur; and C. si certum petatur, l. Si absentis. And it supports what is noted in D. si certum petatur, l. Civitas. Moreover, if the fruits of the leased things come to the mother herself, the mother does not seem to be aided, because she in fact made the contract herself, and she ought not to be enriched at another’s loss, as in D. ad Velleianam, l. Si mulieri solvero.

On the contrary, it seems that this lease ought to be said to have been made by the sons themselves through the interposed person of the mother, as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Mulier (which begins Sulpitius). For she, in leasing, performed the act of the sons, and not her own proper act. For she did not lease for herself, but for her sons; from which lease, just as it seems to be acquired for the sons, so too the sons seem conversely to be tacitly bound, as in D. de acquisitione emptionis, l. Iulius, § Si procurator. And it supports D. de solutionibus, l. Filiae.

But to this it could be responded that it is not true that an action accrues to the sons without assignment; because the contract was not celebrated on the sons’ property, but on hers. Hence, a direct action belongs to the mother, and effectively before she assigns it; and consequently, conversely, she herself ought to be held directly and effectively to the payment of the rent, as in D. de pignoratitia actione, l. Solutam, § 1, Liberam.

It therefore seems to be said that either this contract was ratified by the sons; and then the mother seems to have intervened. For even if she had received the fruits in the name of the sons, she is bound to render them to them. But if this contract was not ratified by the sons; then, because only the mother is involved in the contract, rightly the mother herself is then effectively bound, as in the aforementioned l. Si adversarius tuus. Ratification, however, is proved by words and deeds, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Pomponius scribit, Si negotium; and l. Quoniam, in principio, D. rem ratam habere.

What, therefore, in the meantime, before this contract is ratified or rejected, does the text seem to respond? D. de acquisitione emptionis, l. Iulius, § Si quis colludente. And in the meantime it is in suspense, as in D. de condictione indebiti, l. Si procurator, in fine, with the following law.

On the contrary, it seems that relief should be granted to the woman indiscriminately, as if a contract had been made with a ward, namely so that the contract does not limp, as in D. de actionibus empti venditi, l. Iulius, § Si quis apud pupillum. Let the lessor therefore impute it to himself, because he contracted in consideration of the wards, and not of the mother, as fully in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Si pupilli, in principio; and l. Qui aliena, § Quanquam.

Nor is it true that, the sons not ratifying, this contract remains firm in the person of the mother; because the mother did not wish to lease for herself, but for the sons; nor did the lessor wish to lease for himself, but for the sons. And the acts of agents do not operate beyond their intention, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Non omnis, in principio. The aforementioned law Si absentis does not obstruct, which speaks of a contract which is contracted by thing; but here we are in a contract which is contracted by consent, and therefore, consent lacking, such a contract operates nothing, as in D. de pactis, l. 1, § Conventionis; and D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Consensu.

And therefore it finally seems to be concluded that, ratification not having followed, the contract is not valid. But ratification having followed, the mother is safe by the benefit of the Velleian Law, since it does not appear that she renounced the said benefit, as in C. si mater indemnitatem promiserit, l. 1. And thus I hold, always saving the substance of the truth, and having seen also the statutes of the commune of Vicenza.

However, I say that the fruits perceived in the meantime are to be restored by the wards themselves; because wards ought not to be enriched at another’s loss. I say they are to be restored insofar as the said minors were enriched, as in D. de commodato, l. 1, in fine, with the following law.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, and when, a cedent may use the right ceded or the action ceded.
2. The testator wished debts and legacies to be paid first, and then the residue to be restored; how this is to be understood.
body: It must be premised

† As to the point, the assignment of actions is sometimes by necessity, sometimes by will. In the first case, after the assignment, the assignor cannot bring an action, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. facta; D. de solutionibus, l. Modestinus; and l. Stichum, § si mandato, and the note in D. de pactis, l. cum emptore; and l. si paciscaris, § 1, quemadmodum servitus amittatur; and what is noted in l. final, in principio, C. de iure dotium. And the reason is that whenever the law imposes the necessity of assigning actions, or the testator does so, there is a transfer of actions. D. de legibus, l. non quocumque, § qui Gaius; the force of direct actions is weakened. D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex asse. In the second case, when it is by will, it matters whether there is an assignment of actions or a concession without a mandate of direct actions. In the first case, there are opinions. For some say that the assignor can bring an action, except in the three cases noted and set forth in l. 3, C. de nova. Others say that the assignor can be expelled by the assignee objecting. Also by the debtor raising the exception of the right assigned to another, if it was made for the benefit of both, according to Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus, in which case the action belongs to the assignor. C. que res pignori obligari possunt, l. nomen; D. de transactionibus, l. final, referring each law to its members. In the second case, when the exercise of direct actions is given in rem suam: then the text properly speaks in l. 3, C. de nova, although the gloss there says the same in assignment as in mandate. But the opinion of that gloss is not supported by any text, and the reason of the matter is manifest: because mandate is founded on the person, and in the person of the mandator. But useful actions are proper to the assignee himself. C. de procuratoribus, l. qui stipendia. And these are true in one who can assign and mandate by his own right. But if he has a certain form, and in doubt it is presumed that he wishes to observe it, if it refers to that, otherwise his act is not valid. D. de verbis obligatis, l. qui Romae, § Flavius Hermes. Hence we come to the matter of the lessor, as in D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si possessio, § et si possessor, quonam nostram.

† And the form of the test is clear: because the testator wished debts and legacies to be paid first, and the residue to be restored. A similar form is handed down. D. de iure fisci, l. Res, §. Res. Those words, “if anything remains, etc.,” have the force of a condictio, l. Si superficies apparebit, in a question or inquiry legitimately made about this. As D. ad l. Falc., l. Maritus, §. Si; D. de probat., l. Cum de lege; D. de verb. oblig., l. Decem; D. si cert. pet., l. Si. Hence nothing can be done except according to the practice of that form, for he who is instituted heir cannot disregard the execution of the testator’s will, because he is to be considered as a mere minister in a certain sense. D. de usur., l. In fideicommissi, §. Cum Pollidius. Moreover, especially here, the reserved power of the recipient is evident, and joined with the preceding ones, which reservation is according to the nature of execution: because it is formal in the testament, and the recipient knew it, because he himself wrote the protestation, and immediately received the concession and mandate; notwithstanding this election, because they could not nor did it avail more than the testator had ordered. D. ad Trebell., l. Mulier, §. Ut Treb., and l. Sed si ante. It is nevertheless equitable that the debtor paying be secured as to identity, and not be distinguished, at least in fact, under the pretext or guise of the said distribution to a new adversary, who contracted with one. D. de fideicommiss., l. Fideicommissa, §. Pluriumque. And thus the provision of both is implied: namely, of the testator and of the heir; indeed, also of the payer. D. de stat. lib., l. 2, §. Stichus annua. The debts and legacies remaining to be paid, and consequently also considering the said attached protestation, which partakes of the form and executory reality of the said testament, I say that the action remains to the said heirs, especially with the said consent of the distributors, i.e., those to whom the said distribution was made: lest the payment of debts be excluded by some cavils, lest the safeguards be mocked, but the payers must be secured, for those acting with certain tricks should not be circumvented. D. de rei vend., l. Is, a quo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman can renounce the right of dowry, and whether she can renounce mortgages.
body: The case upon which the legal opinion is sought is as follows: 1,

† There was a certain man in the city of Asti, who was named Nicolinus Valetus, who had two sons, namely Godinus and Gulielmus. The said Godinus, during the lifetime of his said father Nicolinus, took as his wife a certain woman named Margarita, who gave a dowry to the said Nicolinus and Godinus, namely 5,280 gold florins. And both the said Nicolinus and the said Godinus, and each of them in solidum, bound themselves and their property in solidum for the said dowry, etc. Afterwards, the said Nicolinus dies, the said Godinus and Gulielmus, his sons and his heirs, surviving him, each for one-half; and the said Margarita, the wife of the said Godinus, also surviving. Thereafter, the said Godinus and Gulielmus, intending to proceed with their division, agreed with one another: namely, because the said Godinus and the said Margarita, his wife, executed an acquittance and release to the said Gulielmus, heir to one-half of the said late Nicolinus, concerning one-half of the said dowry, the form of which acquittance may be seen at the end of the gathering marked with the letter A, which was made in the year 1370 on the first day of February. Which acquittance having been made, the said brothers came to a division among themselves regarding the rest of their property, a copy of which division may be seen in the said gathering marked with the letter A, which was made in 1371 on the fourth day of September. Before the said acquittance and division, upon the death of the said Nicolinus, namely in the year of the Lord 1319, the said Gulielmus and a certain Lady Florina, his mother, confessed that they had received on loan from Secundolus Alionus, the second of his name, 114 gold florins, and they bound their property in solidum, whereof there is an instrument. By virtue of this debt, the said Secundolus, after the said acquittance was made, took in payment according to the form of the statutes of Asti from the property of the said Gulielmus and Lady Florina, namely in the year of the Lord 1371 on the sixth day of June; and he took in payment a parcel of land with rows of vines, which is situated in the estate of Cortacaniari in the valley of Castelliano, which is nine modia, four staria, one tabula. Item, in the said estate, one parcel of meadow in the said valley, which is four modia, six staria, two tabulae. Item, three staria, four tabulae, one foot of one parcel of land and homesite in the said estate. Which properties belonged to the property of the said late Nicolinus; and the said Gulielminus, at the time of the said giving in payment, held and possessed them; and yet it is not established that Gulielminus himself and the said Godinus had as yet come to divisions. But concerning certain other properties they did arrive at a division after the said giving in payment: namely, in that very same year, on the fourth day of September; nevertheless, the acquittance made by Margarita regarding one-half of the dowry had been made prior to the time of the said giving in payment to the said Gulielmus, namely in that same year 1371 on the first day of February. Afterwards, the said Gulielminus dies, his said brother Godinus surviving him as his heir; thereafter, the said Godinus dies, the said Margarita his wife surviving, and two daughters surviving, who were not and are not heirs of the said Godinus. There also died the said Secundus Alionus, the creditor of the said Gulielmus, with Thomas Alionus his son and heir surviving him. And here it is to be noted that before the death of the said Godinus, the aforesaid Godinus, as above, the heir of the said Gulielminus his brother, sold several properties to the said Thomas Alionus, and among others there were 11 tabulae and two feet of vine-strip of the parcel of land given in payment to the said Secundolus Alionus, which were found to be in excess of what was contained in the said giving in payment and what Secundolus himself ought to have had for the said giving in payment; and in the same manner regarding the meadow. To which sale, and to everything written therein, the said Margarita subsequently consented and renounced her right of hypothec in the said properties sold, and promised to observe the sale and all things contained therein; which sale and consent may be seen in the instrument marked with the number 100. Upon the death of the said Godinus, the said Lady Margarita his wife instituted proceedings, or rather her procurator did, against whomever was the heir of the said late Nicolinus Valetus and Gulielminus Valetus, their sons and heirs; and no heir appearing, a curator was appointed for the vacant estate of the said Nicolinus, Godinus, and Gulielmus, and he was condemned for the dowry of the said Lady Margarita, which was as above. This condemnation having been made, unencumbered properties found belonging to the late Godinus and the said Nicolinus and Gulielmus were given in payment to the said Margarita, or to her procurator, for part of the said dowry, and for part of the increase of the dowry, to which increase Godinus alone was bound. And because the said properties were not sufficient from which the whole dowry and the whole increase could be paid, the right to the residue was reserved to the said Margarita; for which residue, because none is found among the unencumbered properties, it was pronounced that the properties were exhausted, and license was granted to her to be able to proceed against the possessors of the pledges. Wherefore the said Margarita, or her procurator, presented a libel against the said Thomas Alionus, from whom they seek to claim back the said properties given in payment to the said Secundolus his father, as being part of the property of the said Nicolinus. For the defense of which Thomas several questions arise; but because they are not decided, I have not written them down, but the legal opinion is sought upon this whole set of facts. The questions were these: First, whether the acquittance made by the said Margarita to the said Gulielmus concerning one-half of her dowry as heir to one-half of the said Nicolinus is valid and holds good. Assuming that at the time of the said acquittance there remained in the hands of Godinus, who was bound in solidum for the dowry, very many properties from which satisfaction could be made to her quite abundantly for that dowry; and whether the said acquittance is of such efficacy that Margarita herself cannot have recourse for the said dowry against the aforesaid properties, which belonged to the said Nicolinus, father of the said Gulielmus bound for the dowry, which afterwards came to the said Gulielmus by inheritance. And whether, an absolution and release having been made by the said Margarita to the said Gulielmus concerning one-half of the said dowry, and there having subsequently been given in payment to the said Margarita from the property of the said Godinus so much as exceeds the other half of the said dowry, full satisfaction seems to have been made to the said Margarita for the said dowry, so that she ought to be barred from her claim against the said Thomas, who derives his title from the said Gulielmus. Item, it is asked, since in the giving in payment made to the said Margarita the amount of the dowry was joined with the amount of the increase of the dowry—for which amount of the increase of the dowry neither Gulielmus nor Nicolinus was bound, but only Godinus—whether the giving in payment is presumed to have been made for the dowry, which is the more burdensome, large, and older debt, or rather for the increase, or for both debts. For the debt of Secundolus Alionus and of the said Thomas is prior upon the goods of Gulielmus to the debt of the said increase, so that for that increase she could not proceed against the said Thomas nor claim the aforesaid properties, since, as has been said, the said Gulielmus was not bound for that increase. Item, it is asked whether the said Margarita prejudiced herself in the properties given in payment to the said Secundus Alionus, as above, through the consent given to the sale that the said Godinus made to the said Thomas regarding that excess beyond what was contained in the giving in payment made to the said Secundolus, which the properties were found to measure; by those words which are stated in the consent itself, that she consented to everything contained in the said sale, and mention is there made of the giving in payment, etc. Item, it is asked whether the said Thomas has the right of tendering to the said Margarita her entire dowry; and whether she is bound to surrender to the said Thomas that which she received in payment and holds for her dowry, and to assign to him the remaining rights, notwithstanding that a year has elapsed since the day of the said giving in payment; since in the statute of the municipality of Asti on giving in payment it is provided that debtors and their creditors are permitted to recover properties given in payment within a year and a day. For clarity, it must be premised,

† that a wife, both during the marriage and after its dissolution, can renounce the right of hypothecs which she held, or was to hold, for her dowry, as in C. ad velleia. l. etiam. and l. iubemus; not extending, however, that renunciation to any contract other than that concerning which it was made, as is stated there. And in favor of this is ff. quib. mo. pig. vel hypo. solu. l. 1. and what is noted in ff. de pac. l. si tibi. §. de pignore. Wherefore, whatever may be the case regarding the release of the dowry, whether it is valid or not, nevertheless the renunciation of the hypothec is valid. And therefore the said Lady Margarita does not have any hypothecary action with respect to half of the dowry against Thomas, since she has released Gulielminus; concerning the other half there is a question. And because she consented to the sale of the properties that she intends to claim back through the hypothecary action, I likewise say that she ought not to be heard, by the same laws, and by what is noted in the Speculum under the title de renuntiatione, and by Iacobus de Arena and Cynus on the said l. iubemus. And even if she were heard, she would be obliged to assign her action (ff. qui potio. in pigno. hab. l. mulier) up to the amount of the remaining debt. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman renouncing the right of mortgage ought to be certified.
body: Whether

It is necessary that a woman who renounces the right of hypothecation be certified as to whether she has this right or not. It must be said that either she has the right of hypothecation expressly by a contract entered into by her, or by another in her name, and which has come to her knowledge. And then it is not necessary that she be certified: because the preceding contract certifies her. D. de actionibus emptio venditio, l. 1, § final; C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. Magnam; and l. 1, § 1; D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvuntur. And see what is noted in the ordinary gloss. Since, therefore, this woman made a discharge to William, there is no doubt that the hypothecation was removed. Or she has the right of tacit hypothecation by mere provision of law, and then say, as is noted in Authent. Matri et avie, when this renunciation is accessory to another principal liberation. Nor does any text, nor any gloss, say that, the principal being removed, the hypothecation remains. On the matter, see D. si tibi, § de pignore; de pactis. Since, therefore, we are in our case dealing with a conventional and most express hypothecation, it was not necessary for her to be certified as to the right, C. de iure et facto ignorato, l. Si. And I believe that no sensible man, thinking well, ought to doubt our case, and I have written this confirming my opinion, so that no one may doubt the justice of the opinion. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the delay is attributable to the judge, a second year is granted for pursuing the appeal.
2. When it is said that the delay is attributable to the judge.
body: When

It is established by the case which occurred in the person of the judge for some notable period of time, that a second full year is granted by law according to the common and equitable opinion, as in the Authentica *Ei qui appellat*. Now let us see whether this case is among those. And I answer: if indeed this judge chose for himself a certain place in Pavia, or the parties agreed on a certain place, or the prince expressly or tacitly assigned him a certain place, and the judge moved to another place, whether for cause or without cause, the appellant is not bound to go to that place. D. *Quando appellatio sit recipienda*, l. 2, § *Dies*; and especially to a remote place. D. *De damno infecto*, l. 4, § *Si tam vicinum*; D. *De arboribus*, l. *Si cum dies*. That place is understood to be fixed which is more convenient for the litigants. D. *De iudicibus*, l. *Si locus*; C. *De rescriptis*, cap. *Statutum*, § *Cum autem*, lib. 6. And this applies even to the judge delegated: because his office ought not to be damaging to himself, nor should he seek his own difficulties for the convenience of others. D. *Si quis ex assignatoribus*, D. *Quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur*. From these matters examined, it can sufficiently be weighed whether the second year is understood to be granted by law or not. For the question is rather one of fact than of law, since the disposition of law is placed in the cause of fact. But certainly neither a delicate appellant nor an onerous appellee ought to be heard. And therefore I require from the appellant that he make a protestation and show his diligence. And since he had a nearby Prince, he ought to have supplicated him; and if he did nothing of these things, the appeal is deserted. D. *De libellis dimissis*, l. 1.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the debtor promised to pay in Rome, and wherever he may be found, and may be sued before any judge by his procurator by virtue of such promise, whether the principal is said to be found where his procurator is.
2. In contracts, no remission is made either to a true place or to a fictitious place.
3. If the statute mentions the place of the contract, whether it is understood to refer to the place of payment designated.
body: The words say,

He promised to pay in Palermo, and wherever he might be sued, and before any judge whatsoever. The question is whether the procurator of this Sicilian merchant, who is found in Genoa, while his principal is not there but in Palermo, is bound to answer in Genoa on a personal or hypothecary action; because it is said that he has grain there which is alleged to be hypothecated to the creditor, since the debtor has bound all his goods. And it seems that he may be sued both personally and hypothecarily. As to the personal action, it seems to be proven by the law *Lucius*, in the Digest, under the title *De deposito*, where the text states: "whenever you wish, and wherever you wish, I will immediately pay you." Where Cynus says that through these words some hold that even if a certain place is not expressed, the debtor may be sued everywhere (Cynus, *De pistorio*). But certainly this must be understood thus: if the debtor is found there,

† for in contracts there is no remission even to the true place of the contract, much less to a fictitious one, as is fully noted in l. haeres absens, ff. de iudiciis. And it is expressly stated in cap. Romana, § contrahentes, de foro competenti, lib. 6, and is proved in l. 1, ff. de eo quod certo loco. But it is doubted,

Whether it is said that the principal is found where his procurator is found. And it must be said that either the procurator has been appointed for this place and this cause, and the principal is deemed to be found by legal fiction, and may be cited and sued there; or he has been appointed generally, and then the contrary holds: because he does not appear to have a mandate to respond in that forum in which the absent principal cannot be sued, even if the procurator were to consent; because he cannot extend the jurisdiction of a judge who is not his proper judge, and a mandate for lawsuits and causes must be understood as being before a competent judge, since words spoken indefinitely are restricted by law. D. de constit. poss. l. si duo, § 1. For by the appointment of a procurator, the condition of the appointing principal is not made worse; because the use of procurators was introduced in favor of those who appoint them, not to their detriment. D. de procur. l. 1, § usus. Hence, as is said, before an improper judge he does not appear to have a mandate; because the juridical and sound understanding of words is referred to those matters which are juridical. D. de cond. indebit. l. si procurator; D. de solut. l. si is, cui, § Flavius.

† Furthermore, it is doubted whether, if a statute mentions the place of contract, it is understood to refer to the place of payment designated. Here it must be considered that a contract has two parts, one obligatory, the other executory. The first is founded on the word “I promise.” The second consists in the word “to pay.” With respect to the first, the place of payment is not the place of contract, because it does not circumscribe the act of promise. With respect to the second, it is the place of contract; and because execution is not carried out except through judicial process, as regards the place of forum, we look to the place of payment, as in *l. contraxisse* and *l. si seruus*, D. de actionibus et obligationibus. Nevertheless, speaking properly, the place appointed for payment is rather the place of district than of contract, D. de conditionibus indebiti, *l. qui certo loco*. Hence, since a statute ought to be understood properly and materially, without extraneous interpretation or fiction, it is not said that the contract was made in Genoa, although the general words of the agreement state, “he promised to pay in all places.” Hence also the statute of Genoa decided this question, and this with respect to the personal action. Furthermore, quite subtly in support of this side, because the words say, “whichever he may be sued,” but do not say that he promised to pay wherever he might be found. Hence the agreement is not said to be before *litis contestatio*, and thus it may be declined before *litis contestatio*, D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, *l. si conuenerit*. But I would not base myself on this reasoning, especially because of the words that follow, namely, “and before whichever judge.” And therefore I base myself on the other allegations made above. Someone will say, jurisdiction is established from what is alleged, not from what is proven, D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, *l. cum quaedam puella*. Hence, if the contract in Genoa is falsely alleged, justice ought to be rendered in Genoa, and the case should proceed. I answer, here it is clear from the open nature of the business that there is no jurisdiction, hence one ought not to proceed, as noted in *cap. 1*, de officio vicarii, and de filiis presbyterorum, *cap. constitutus*. I come to the hypothecary action, and I say that this grain, if it had been sold to another and delivered by consignation or by inspection of the eyes, is not included in the obligation, as in *l. cum tabernam*, D. de pignoribus, which is solemnly alleged, and fully noted by Jacobus de Arena, C. de iure dotis, *l. vbi adhuc*, where it is highly advisable to see the beginning. And it is permissible to decline the forum by saying, “I do not possess,” because one who denies possessing and having the ability to restore the thing is not compelled to *litem contestari*, D. de rei venditione, *l. officium*, and in Auth. de triennio et sexennio, §. *si*, D. de rei venditione, *l. fina*, D. de pignoribus, *l. si fundus*, §. *in ven*. It is not an objection if it is said that he ceased to possess through fraud, for it is not sufficient to allege this so generally, but it must be specified how the fraud was committed, D. de dolo, *l. item exigit*. Nor does the seller commit fraud who sold the thing to another, when the first buyer wished to accept it, D. de minoribus, *l. emilius largianus*. And if the new buyer is the fisc, and is named in the lawsuit, he has his own judges, D. soluto matrimonio, *l. si constante*, §. *si*. I therefore commend the allegations made notably for this side, and I say that the judge of Genoa is not the competent judge according to what is proposed, and which is so in the truth of the matter. I speak of the competence of the judge; I say nothing of the substance of the debt; but let the truth have its place there before its own judge, D. de probationibus, *l. fina*, D. de mandato, *l. si fideiussor*, §. *quaedam*. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A solemn nuncupative will is not revoked by a subsequent will in writing that is not solemn, even if made among children.
2. Whether a confession regarding a dowry or paraphernal goods made in a will is valid.
body:
The case is as follows: A certain nobleman had a son from his first marriage and several sons from his second. He drew up both a nuncupative and a solemn testament, in which he instituted all his aforementioned sons as his heirs in equal shares. In it, he made several legacies and fideicommissa, and among other things, he left to the son of the first marriage 100 pounds as a dowry, which he stated he had received in the name of the dowry of the mother of his said eldest son, his first wife. Then he left to his second wife, during her lifetime, her dowries, of which there is proof by public instrument. And in another part, he left to the same wife 100 pounds, which he stated he had received from the paraphernal goods of the said second wife. Of these dowries and paraphernal money, the said testator assigned to the said second wife certain possessions.

Later, however, over the course of several years, the said testator wished to make a will in writing and in his own hand, and he wrote another certain testament in a book of the testator’s, in which he similarly instituted the same sons as heirs in the same equal shares, and left to the same second wife her dowries and 100 pounds from her paraphernal goods, which he confessed he had obtained from her through the purchase of a fund, as he had previously left and assigned to her the same possessions as in the first testament. To the son of the first marriage, in this second testament, he left and assigned certain possessions from the dowry of his mother, the first wife, without expressing any quantity of the dowry in that legacy. This testament, in the presence of seven witnesses called and requested, the testator himself closed and subscribed with his own hand, and handed it over to two notaries, requesting them that after his death they publish the said testament in the presence of the heirs and draw up a public instrument from it. However, that testament was not subscribed and sealed by the hands of the said seven witnesses, nor by the law, nor published in the presence of the said witnesses, nor in the presence of the notaries, nor even of anyone else. Nor does it appear, nor is it proven, that it was that testament, or that very writing, which was handed over to the notaries in the presence of the witnesses.

After the death of the testator, the said notaries, in the presence of certain nobles and in the absence of the witnesses, described in the said last testament, and in the presence of the sons and heirs of the said testator, published the said testament eight days after the death of the said testator, and from it drew up a public instrument. Then, having accepted the inheritance of the said deceased by the sons of both marriages, the benefit of inventory not being expressly stated, whether from the testament or intestate, and no mention being made of the said testaments, a question arises between the said heirs before arbitrators elected by them, whether the aforementioned testament is valid and binding in law: whether the first or the second. Furthermore, they allege that the said second testament was published in the presence of the heirs who did not object, and that after the publication they accepted the inheritance, so that it appears they accepted the said inheritance from the second testament and not from the first. Now it is asked from the premises, what is the law, and which testament is true, whether the first or the second. The second

† The document, which is presented, written by the father’s hand, does not state the time when the testament was executed by the father’s own hand; and therefore it is not formal, according to the Authenticum *De testamento imperfecto*, in the beginning. For that entire title speaks among children; and yet there is given therein a form, which if not observed, the document is invalid, and thus the first testament remains firm. But if the second had been made according to the form there laid down, although other common formalities were lacking, the second would be valid among the children, as stated in the gloss placed, as in § *Si quidem*. For if it were the first, it would derogate from the second, according to the doctrine. Therefore, much more so, being the second, it derogates from the first. I speak when it is through a document, and perhaps many do not understand that gloss. Furthermore, retaining this theme presupposed without prejudice to the parties, that the second testament would be valid among the children.

And whether the wife of the second marriage, if she could not otherwise prove the paraphernal money lent to the husband, concerning which he seems to confess in the said first and second testaments, could avail herself thereof, or not, given that the confessions made in both the first perfect testament and the second imperfect one do not exist. According to the note by Bartolus in *l. cum quis decedens*, § *codicillus*, D. de legatis 3; and by Cynus in C. de non numerata pecunia, *l. generaliter*; and by Jacobus de Belvisis in Auth. de iureiurando a moriente praestito; and by many doctors in various places stating that sometimes a confession emanates as a cause for bequeathing, and then it does not prove a debt (D. de libellis et legatis, *l. Aurelius*, § *finis*); but sometimes simply, so that the truth may appear, then Peter says that it is valid, even in the absence of the party, just as a writing in a ledger of accounts made in the absence of the party is valid. For this testator, as it were, inserted a ledger of accounts into his testament, as appears from the inspection of the testament. To this adds what is noted by Bartolus in D. de donationibus, *l. nuda ratio*. The contrary is determined by him in § *codicillus*. And it is otherwise in a book of accounts, because it was entrusted to the adversary, hence the entrustment represents him as being present. Solution: If the confession is made for liberation, it is valid; if for obligation, according to the strictness of law it is not fully valid to the prejudice of the party, but only for a solemn judgment (Extra, de successionibus ab intestato, c. *cum dilectus*). And because this confession was often made in the presence of witnesses, and we are dealing with the first testament, which was not revoked; because in the second testament there was a lack of observance of both singular and common law. For the testament was not in writing, although there was some non-solemn writing due to lack of time, as I said, nor was it nuncupative; because the name of the heir was not expressed by the voice of the testator in the presence of witnesses (C. de testamentis, *l. iubemus*). And because in his divisions the quantity is expressed, from this the truth clearly appears, although not solemnly; because it nonetheless makes great faith among others, so that an oath should be deferred in supplement of proof. This is almost expressly noted in *l. si duo patroni*, in principio, D. de iureiurando, where is the case in the reason thereof according to Guilielmus de Cuneo. And because the father was the legitimate administrator of his children, his contract and assertion of the dowry benefit the children (C. de bonis matri, *l. 1*). Hence also, without delay of an oath, the truth, proved by so many supports, cannot be denied (C. de non numerata pecunia, *l. generaliter*; Extra, de probationibus, c. *per tuas*). And to this optimally adds C. de confirmatione tutelae, *l. Lucius*, § *tutelae*. For this father is reduced to the likeness of a tutor, hence his writings should be upheld, as in *l. finis*, C. arbitrio tutoris; de confirmando tutore, *l. chirographus*.

And in the same way, if the son of the first marriage could not otherwise prove the maternal dowry than by the confession made in the first solemn testament, could he avail himself of the confession made by his father, the testator, in the said first testament, or the second?

Furthermore, the said son born of the first wife alleges that the said dowry of his mother ought to be deducted by him in the division of the inheritance as a debt, and as alien property (*aes alienum*). From the first place, notwithstanding the assignment made by the said testator in the said testaments to the said second wife, and this because the said testator and the brother of the said testator, in a division long since made between them of the then common goods, confessed that the mother of the said son of his first marriage had been dowered, and had given a dowry; and in the book of accounts of the brother of the said testator it appears, what the said dowry was, by the writing of the book written by the said brother of the said testator; and also that in a certain other instrument made between the said testator it appears that the father of the said son of the first marriage had and received a certain quantity of money, or certain possessions, for the remainder of the dowry of the mother of the said son of the first marriage, although in the said instrument the quantity of the said dowry is not expressed. Also, because the said testator in the said first testament expressed the quantity of the said dowry.

On the part of the other brothers and heirs, the contrary is said: and that the said asserted dowry cannot be deducted as a debt. I answer: a true dowry can be deducted as a debt, unless the testator ordered the contrary, and if assets are available; otherwise the burden does not hold, as is commonly noted by masters in *l. si cum dotem*, § *si pater*. It is a true dowry, which the instruments declare, as I said, and afterwards the dowry must first be deducted (C. qui potiores in pignore habeantur, *l. assiduis*).

Also, on the part of the said sons of the second [marriage], it is said that the quantity of money and paraphernal goods of the second wife ought to be deducted as a debt, as alien property, and not as a legacy, first by the force of two or three witnesses, who deposed that the said testator before death bought a certain castle for a certain price; and while paying, he confessed in the presence of the said second wife and the present witnesses that it was lent by the said second wife to the said testator from the paraphernal goods of the said second wife, and that he wished to secure her upon the said castle bought. Also, because the said testator confessed this in the said two testaments. Also, because it appears, it seems from other conjectures and also instruments that the said second wife had paraphernal goods. It is asked, what is the law? I answer: All these are confessions, and made to the wife of the second marriage, hence we are under *l. hac edictali*, C. de secunda nuptia.

Also, with this being the case, that the said son of the first marriage, in the name of his said father, had from the lord marquis a certain castle to be held by the said father under certain pacts and conventions contained in a certain public instrument, to which relation is to be had. And subsequently it appears from the form of the public instrument that the said father was confessed to have had and received, with his said son, 200 gold florins, on account of a loan, which he asserted proceeded from the castrense peculium, and it is proved that the said son had long before served in the military stipends, and for which he obligated to his said son the said castle and possessions pertaining to the said castle, with a pact, and under a pact, that the fruits shall go to the profit of the said son, and be compensated with the expenses which are made by the said son for the custody of the said castle, as appears in the said instrument. With this pact, that if such pact or such convention were not valid, that the said father made a donation to the said son of the said fruits from that time. And also it is contained in the same instrument that at the time when the said father wished to recover the said castle, he would be bound to restore to his said son the said 200 gold florins, and the true expenses made in the fortification and repair of the said castle, as more fully appears from the form of the said instrument, to which relation is to be had, and the said instrument should be seen.

The said contract is valid, unless it were celebrated in fraud of usury (D. de fideiussoribus, *l. si quis pro eo*, § 1; D. de castrensi peculio, *l. si forte*). And according to the determination of that law, it is valid. For a contract over adventitious goods, and more strongly over castrense goods, between father and son, is valid. And in the case where the said castle were to be brought into collation with the brothers, expenses made for the perpetual utility of the castle, in the castle itself, and really ought to be reimbursed from the common fund voluntarily (D. de negotiis gestis, *l. ex duobus*). And the pacts of the said instrument are also to be observed, as I said.

It is asked, whether such contract, as to all things contained in the said instrument, is valid, and whether the said castle comes into the division of the inheritance and goods among the sons and heirs, notwithstanding that the said son of the first marriage now says and opposes that the said castle was and is of the goods of the church, and also says that he has recently acquired and has a title from the church by virtue of certain instruments, which should be seen, and to which instruments relation is to be had. I answer: In this, the truth is to be inspected, whether it truly pertains to the church or not; otherwise it comes into the division (D. de evictionibus, *l. si rem, quam*, in principio; C. de familiae erciscundae, *l. si familiae*). In doubt, he is presumed to be the owner who is recognized as owner (D. de solutionibus, *l. Titia*; C. de agris et censibus, *l. litibus*).

And whether in the said division the said son of the first marriage can deduct the said 200 gold florins, and the necessary and useful expenses made by the said son in the fortification and repair of the said castle. And whether what is said and will be said about the fruits of the possessions of the said castle received before the death of the said father, also has place regarding the fruits of the said possessions of the said undivided castle born before the death of the said father, and received after death, and after the said controversy over the division of the said things and goods was raised. The response is given by *l. Titia*, D. de solutionibus.

Also, with this being the case, that the said testator in the first testament, in which he confessed the said dowry to the said son, assigned certain possessions for the portion of the said dowry, touching the son of the first marriage less than is the quantity and portion pertaining to the said son from the said dowry; it is asked: whether the testator could have done this to the prejudice of the said son, and whether the testator could have burdened the son and heirs in this, if he wished.

Also, it is asked: whether the other son of the first marriage, doubly related to the said son, died after the death of the said mother, and during the life of the said testator, transmitted the portion of the said maternal dowry pertaining to him, not having been taken up, to his said living father; presupposing that the said heir did not take up the inheritance of the said lady on behalf of the dead son, nor on his own. The Gloss touches on this in *l. apud hostes*, C. ad Orphit. It is commonly held, as noted there by Cynus.

Also, presupposing that the statute of the land and place of the said testator, and of the said land, excludes female daughters from the jurisdiction of the lords of the said land, married and dowered, from the succession of the said father and mother: whether such statute extends to the daughters of the said lords of the said land, married and dowered; and whether it excludes them from the said succession. These women are of the jurisdiction, because they are not lords of the jurisdiction (Guilielmus in *l. ultima*, D. de rerum divisione). These being excluded, the maternal dowry comes to the brother doubly related, not to the uterine brothers of the second wife.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who acts within the time limit does not forfeit his right.
2. Before an arbitrator, one ought to narrate nothing other than the facts.
3. If the cause over which there is a compromise is to be decided according to law, but the quality [of the matter] is such that an error of law is patent, the sentence is null: and such a sentence the judge ought to pronounce null, and not to reform. And number 5.
1. The hearing of an arbitrator is not called a judgment, nor a lawsuit, nor a cause.
2. Statutes speaking of arbitrators are understood to refer to true [arbitrators].
body: In the first place

It must be known that a person does not lose his right merely because he brings an action before the proper time; rather, he is either repelled in the meantime, or, if the defendant so requests, adjournments are granted, as stated in the Institutes, On Exceptions, § Temporales; and in the Code, On Judicial Proceedings, Law Justas, Book 10. Hence, it is not for the defendant to choose whether he wishes to be absolved at the instance of the trial, or rather to have the adjournments doubled. Or say this: if the case is at issue (lis contestata), it is said that the adjournments are doubled, yet the defendant is condemned, because the action has arisen. But if the case is not at issue, the plaintiff ought to be repelled, according to Innocentius, On Claiming More, Chapter 1. Nevertheless, it is certain that the plaintiff does not thereby lose his action, as is fully noted by the doctors in Law Pecuniam, Digest, On Action on a Certain Stipulation; and it is proven in the Edict of the Aediles, Law Bovem, § Sub conditione.

Secondly, it must be known that in named contracts, repentance has no place. This rule fails in partnership, as is fully noted in the law *Pecuniam*, in the beginning, in the Digest on conditions on account of a cause. And therefore, if I have placed money into a partnership, I can recover it; however, if I do not have a cause for repentance, I am bound to my partner for damages. Institutes, *Pro socio*, § *Manet autem*. And therefore, the lord Dominic could repent, which would appear to be done by suing for the capital that he had placed in the partnership, especially since the agreements were not observed. From which, by relating the agreement to the contract, there results an innominate contract, and because otherwise there was no contract. Thirdly, it must be known that,

† that before an arbitrator nothing ought to be stated other than the facts; nor is it required that the petition conclude with a formal prayer for relief, because there is no judicial proceeding there. And where there is no judicial proceeding, a conclusion is not required. L. 1, § 1, de liberis agnoscendis. Fourthly, it should be known that

† If a case is compromised for decision, to be cognized according to law, however it may be, if the error of law is patent, the sentence is null. But in doubt it must be held as valid. l. pen. ff. de iustit. et iu. Nevertheless, in this case it can be reformed, even the sentence of an arbitrator. ff. de app. l. ex consensu. Because it is so acted between the parties, that a doubtful sentence of an arbitrator is reduced to the examination of law: because by recourse to a good man, Bar. says that this sentence, being contrary to law, is null by the law itself. But he does not speak truly, when it is just at first sight and apparently. Rather, it must be reformed by a judge: because those words "according to law" are understood as "according to law." s. constitutionis: otherwise such compromises would be uncertain. It makes what is noted in c. 1. de procur. in clem. Fifth, it is to be known,

† But if such a sentence is void, because it was rendered outside the time of the compromise, or outside the mandate, the judge must pronounce it void, and not reform it; because nothing has been pronounced, and when nothing has been pronounced, there is no departure from the province. On the contracting of sale, l. si. But if it is void by some other provision of law, then the judge reforms it. No. ff. On the meaning of words, l. illa verba. And in reforming, he may impose the due oaths, because he ought not to omit anything that is contingent. C. On judges, l. iudices. Sixthly, it must be known,

† That the discussion of the arbitrator is not called a judgment, nor a lawsuit, nor a cause; and therefore the reduction to the arbitration of a good man is a first cause. And the direct time limits prescribed by our Illustrious Lord must be observed as in a first cause; and not the decree on appeals, or on second lawsuits, although every recourse is held to have the nature of an appeal. On arbitration, l. non distinguemus. §. cum quidam. The oath does not obstruct, because it is limited by the form. s. de iure tamen. Furthermore, it does not obstruct that he consented that the sentence be rendered according to the closed opinion. C. plus valere quod agitur. l. si. Nor is it understood to be ratified, that which is unknown. C. de arb. l. si. de transac. l. de his and l. cum aquiliana, and l. qui cum tutore. §. qui per fallac. And he who has the power of judging de iure tamen, is not an arbitrator in full, but in the other case, however. Hence, one should not adhere to his sole arbitration; because this is not permitted by the form of the mandate. Merely in this case, recourse may be had to the superior so that the truth may be inquired into. l. si cum. in princip. ff. si quis cau. And if open injustice appears, it is evident that the sentence was rendered by non-arbitrators.

† However, statutes that speak of arbitrators are understood to refer to those appointed by true arbitrators, not by a praetor; for when a statute speaks of an arbitrator, it must be established that he is indeed an arbitrator. As stated in the law *Lucius*, in the Digest, under the title *De militum testamentis*. To this effect is what is noted in question 12, question 2, chapter *Relatio*, on the word *canonice*, and expressly in the Digest, under the title *De verborum significatione*, in the law *Illa verba*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The judge is not bound by the common law to refer the case to the counsel of a wise man; and if he has referred it, he may revoke the reference; nor is he compelled to judge according to the counsel, otherwise under statutory law, or by agreement of the litigants.
2. Statutes, which are said to be precise: and whether they admit of any implied understanding, or gloss.
3. Confidences are also given under the common law.
body: To make the matter clear, it must be considered first what the law is according to the common law; secondly, one must proceed to the statutes.

† I say, therefore, that according to the common law, a judge is not bound to refer a case to the counsel of a wise man, and if he has referred it, he may revoke the reference. Moreover, he is not compelled to judge according to the counsel. D. de appellationibus, l. ad principem, and there by Bartolus. But by the form of a statute, he may well be constrained to do so. Also by the agreement of the litigants. D. de re iudicata, l. si convenerit, and there by Bartolus; D. de electione, l. cum in veteri. Hence, we must base our argument on the statute, and the statute must be observed regarding the election of the first consultant. But it must be examined whether the form of the statute was omitted regarding the election of the additional consultant. For if the provision of the statute had not been observed, an appeal would proceed, if it had been properly interposed, and the petition for apostols would be granted, unless by the form of the statute these solemnities were waived for appeals against interlocutory decisions. It is therefore established that an appeal may be taken from a judge who does not observe the constitution, as D. de minoribus, l. ait praetor, § permittitur, according to the common understanding of the doctors. We must therefore examine only this additional consultant, whether he was properly requested, and whether the form required for the execution of such a petition was observed or not; because if the one requesting the addition of another had not observed the statute, his appeal would be null by operation of law, frivolous, and of no effect. But if he had observed the statute, then we would be within the disposition of the statute annulling the proceedings, or at least the proceedings would be invalidated by means of the appeal. And since the aforementioned sentence ought not, nor could, have been made, as is proven, the judge acted against the statute; therefore, he pronounced judgment wrongly and erroneously. The case seems to be of this nature in the said § permittitur. To the contrary, it seems that the judge observed the first statute, which compelled him to pronounce judgment according to the form of the counsel given; therefore, he pronounced judgment correctly; for since the first statute is precise and penal, and speaks precisely in the case of counsel given, it does not admit of limitation or distinction as to whether an additional consultant was requested or not.

† because precise statutes are so called, inasmuch as they do not admit of glossation or any implied interpretation. Extra, de rescriptis, c. 2. Moreover, one ought not to form a point according to one's own arbitrary will. Digest, de iureiurando, l. ius iurandum; and ad pecunias, § si de qualitate. Furthermore, it is not presupposed that the opposing party was required to provide suspected and confidant witnesses, as is required to be done, even

† According to the common law, in the Authentica *de triennio et semestri*, § *et quod saepe*, in the gloss. Moreover, this addition appears to have been given with the consent of the first consultant. But he is not said to have consented who has revoked his consent. C. *de rebus creditis*, l. *si quis iusiurandum*. For that consent did not pass into an obligation, but into a simple will, whence it could be revoked, and was revoked by the very fact of the return of the counsel. For these reasons, I think that the appellant in this appeal does not uphold justice: always saving the practice, if there were any to the contrary. ff. *de legatis*, l. *si de interpretatione*. For practice is of fact, or of mixed law and fact, and therefore one may legitimately err in it, as in c. 1, *de constitutionibus*, Book 6. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an episcopal constitution devolving execution to him has place, when the hands of the testamentary executors were bound by ignorance of fact. And no. 2.
body: by the common law,

† Then the constitution of the bishop must be considered. Under the common law, time does not run against executors who are ignorant, and therefore the bishop does not intervene: because he is appointed to supply the negligence of those executors. For one who is ignorant does not act negligently, unless it be supine ignorance, as in C. de epis. et cle. l. nulli, in the words “pro sua conscientia.” But one ought to know the disposition and the mode of the disposition, or else there is supine ignorance. ff. si cer. pe. l. quod te. But in our case, even if the executors knew the disposition, namely that a certain part ought to be distributed, nevertheless they do not know the mode of the disposition: because the testator said that the mode and form were contained in a certain schedule. Hence, before it is declared that that schedule cannot be found, the executors are not bound to proceed to any execution; but once it is ascertained that they cannot be found, the heirs ought to be summoned, and, with the bishop present, to proceed as if the use had changed. l. legatum, de vsufr. leg. As far as the constitution of the bishop is concerned, the constitution is sufficiently consonant with the common law: because it says “negligentibus” etc. And therefore, unless the negligence is first liquidated and pronounced, if negligence is denied, the bishop cannot usurp the execution for himself. C. ad Tre. l. pen.

† I, while once reading in Florence with the illustrious doctor Thomas Decius, had to treat this point: whether the jurisdiction of the bishop transfers to his hands the execution of the executors of the will, whose hands were bound in the execution due to ignorance of the fact. And he answered that not by law, but otherwise by custom. But Bartolus in the law *Genero*, *De infamibus*, says that not. On this, it is necessary to speak more subtly. Namely, that the execution of the bishop comes into effect due to the defect of the testator’s provision, and that either the constitution of the bishop disposes in the case of negligence, or absolutely. In the first case, what I said above holds. In the second case, subdistinguish: either the execution sets a time for the executor, saying, if anyone does not carry out the execution: and it is not understood to speak of the ignorant one. Law *Fin.*, § *Si*, *De legatis*, 2. Or it sets a time for the execution speaking impersonally, for example, because it says, and if the execution has not been made, etc. Then, without any knowledge, solely by the passage of time, the bishop becomes executor: because it is true that the execution has not been made. To this distinction, which is very notable, the following supports it: *Digestum*, *De aqua hereditaria*, law *Si servum*, § *Non dixit*. From these it appears that the procedure of the vicar is void and has no effect. As for the other points, you will understand from the foregoing. The Trebellian portion is not deducted for pious causes; debts are paid, and particular legacies are granted. *Codex*, *De legatis*, law *Si universae*. Special legacies are to be paid before generic legacies. *Codex*, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Quotiens*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether action should be taken on the basis of the first sentence, or on the basis of the second confirming the first.
body: The case is submitted, on which legal advice is requested. Behold, a controversy arose between James and William, brothers of Penacii, on one part, and William of Caravatio, son of the late Lord Ogerius, on the other part. By them a compromise was made into certain arbitrators and umpires; and both parties promised to attend to and observe, etc., under the obligation of all their goods, and under a penalty of 100 florins for the aforementioned attendance, binding all their goods. The said arbitrators and umpires, among other things, said, pronounced, and adjudged that all moneys contained in bills made after the death of the said Lord Ogerius, under the name and to the name of the said William, son of the said Lord Ogerius, belong and pertain to the said William. But the moneys contained in bills made before the death of the said Lord Ogerius, whether they be to the name and under the name of the said William, or to the name and under the name of the said Ogerius, pertain to the said William for one half, and to the said brothers of Penacii for the other half. Which sentence having been rendered, the controversy was again moved between the said William, son of the late said Lord George, on one part, and William of Penacii on the other part, on the occasion of a certain bill of a certain quantity of money, the said William of Penacii saying that a fourth part was due to him by virtue of the said arbitral sentence. Which parties, by virtue of a certain statute, compromised themselves; and finally the arbitrators pronounced and adjudged, and condemned the said William to give and pay to the said William of Penacii a fourth part of the money of which mention is made in the said bill. Now it happens that the said William, debtor at the time of the first sentence, held and possessed one house, which house he sold before the aforementioned second sentence was given. Whether, after the legitimate exhaustion of the debtor's goods, an action of hypothec may be brought against the buyer of the said house. And doubt is made, because if it could not be brought except by the second sentence, there would be no place for hypothec; because at that time it was not in the debtor's goods. I answer: Hypothec does not come by the force of the sentence, but by the force of the contract declared by the sentence, which declaration does not remove the conventional hypothec; nevertheless, if the sentence were just, it would not prejudice an external possessor having a cause prior. D. de pignoribus, l. si superatus. Now the doubt is,

† That there is a case in which two judgments are rendered, and from the second a *actio in factum* arises. I say, however, that even from the first a prejudice to the possessor arises. Namely, a judgment of proof: because the second judgment, being conformable to the first, does not remove the rights produced by the first with respect to the possessor; because he is not bound by an *actio in factum*. Hence, the second judgment strengthens the proof arising from the first, which it declares to be true: and thus it increases its credibility, not diminishes it. D. de regulis iuris, l. res iudicata. From these it follows that a hypothecary action may be brought. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How manyfold vengeance is.
2. What vengeance is.
3. Where a constitution or statute permits vengeance to be taken, whether anyone of the progeny may take vengeance.
4. What is included under the term of competent vengeance.
body: In the city of Chieri, between the Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, the Lord Count of Savoy, and the other Most Illustrious Lord, the Prince of Achaea, there is a certain society called St. George, which has among other statutes one constitution confirmed or issued by the Emperor, in which it is contained that if any of the guests named therein strikes any member of the said society, the striker shall not be understood to be a member of the said society after the said striking. And if the person struck wishes to take vengeance for the said striking, the said society is bound to assist him. And that those of the striker’s household ought not to favor the said striker under a certain penalty. And that vengeance having been suitably taken, they ought to do so and see to it with effect that within one month, etc., good peace and concord be made, under the penalty of expelling from the said society him who would not make peace, etc. This chapter was made on the 21st day of September. In the constitution, however, of the said Most Illustrious Lord Count on the article concerning vengeance, these are the words: “if they should take vengeance, or do vengeance in any manner upon him or those who committed the said wrong, or caused it to be committed, or upon any of his kin who was not in the said society, etc.” Now such a case has occurred: William of Merlenginis wounded a certain Jacob of the said society; after an interval of time, the said Jacob wounded Merlotus of Merlenginis, who at the time when the said Jacob was wounded was beyond the mountains. Finally, it was ordered by the rector of the said society that the house of Merlenginis make peace with the said Jacob, or the Merlenginis be expelled from the said society. Peace is refused, because it is said that this was not vengeance, but a new war. Furthermore, it is said that the others of the said household or casato were not culpable, and ought not to be expelled from the said society; and that the statutes of the said rectors are not valid. The question is asked: what is the law? And it is well, before proceeding to the solution of the questions asked, that something be said concerning the meaning of certain words, as in D. si certum petatur, l. 1.

† The law speaks of vindicta. Now vindicta is sometimes taken in a good sense, as in the title De manumissionibus vindictae. Sometimes it is taken in a bad sense, namely for illicit vengeance, as in C. De iudiciis, Nullus. Sometimes it is intermediate between these two: for it is done out of malice, yet permitted by law, as noted in C. Quod metus causa, l. Accusator; and in D. Ad legem Silanianam, l. Et si percussor, §. Si.

† Vengeance is, however, the re-affliction of the offender. "Vengeance is mine, says the Lord, and I will repay." Vengeance is, however, relatively contrary to the offense, and therefore it is properly vengeance only when directed against the offender; for, since it serves in place of punishment, it strikes its own authors. Codex, On Punishments, law *Sancimus*, so that innocent persons may not be struck. Moreover, one who is absent and ignorant could not sin; hence, that he could be offended is contrary to natural law. Codex, On Inofficious Wills, law *Si quis in suo*, § *Fin*. Nevertheless, since here we are not inquiring about the law, i.e., whether he can be offended, but rather about the fact, i.e., whether it constitutes vengeance.

It must be known that, according to the custom of certain places, it is considered vindicta, as in the city of Florence, where all of the offender’s kin take up arms; for their custom is to seek vengeance in temporal matters among their kin, since an injury done to one discredits the entire household. C. si quacunque praeditus potestate, l. 1, and there by Cynus. But under the common law, it is not vindicta, but a new brawl, especially if it is directed against one who is said to be beyond the fourth degree from the initiator of the feud. For with one who is so distant, it is not said that he shares in the passionate feelings, as noted in ff. de iureiurando, l. lex Cornelia, in the beginning. Others extend this up to the seventh degree, as noted in C. ad Turpilianum, l. si familia. Finally, it must be observed here that the constitution permits the infliction of proportionate vengeance. Titius is injured, who is of great and noble lineage; may someone from that lineage inflict vengeance, namely those who can bring a civil action for injuries, and not others? And this is true. But Bartolus seems to say that all may accuse as if it were an injury to their own persons, not as if it were to any member of the populace, as he notes in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus, at the end. The gloss in l. cum fundum, ff. de vi et vi armata, seems to restrict this, and perhaps rightly so, to the person who is corporally injured, not to one who is injured by legal fiction. Hence, the father or son of the injured party, by virtue of the permissive constitution, could not avenge themselves. To this effect it is said that words most odious should be understood in their primary, not secondary, sense. Therefore, those who cannot avenge cannot be avenged against; for the rule is the same for contraries, just as they cannot act, so they ought not to suffer, by the argument of parity of contraries, ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. et si contra.

† Having spoken of the substantive, i.e., vengeance, let us consider the adjective, i.e., competent, or the adverb, i.e., competently or suitably, which is the same thing. Suppose a nobleman, out of arrogance, cuts off the nose of a commoner or disfigures his face; the commoner later strikes the nobleman on the arm. The commoner seeks peace; the nobleman refuses, saying that he did not inflict competent vengeance, but one far lesser; and therefore the statute, which speaks of peace made after competent vengeance, does not apply, because the words do not fit the case. I say that the nobleman speaks wrongly, because the commoner could seek peace even if no vengeance had been inflicted, because satisfaction for his act is given as the creditor wishes. D. de pign. act. l. solu. §. satisfactum. But if the vengeance exceeded the temperate limit, i.e., equality, there would be no place for the petition of peace. X. de rest. spo. c. olim. C. unde vi. l. 1. But here remains such a doubt: suppose the vengeance was inflicted treacherously, whether on this account it is said to be greater. He wrote thus, all other things being equal. Also, if it had been inflicted with a poisoned sword. C. de malef. et ma. l. 1. To betray faith is to betray, or to mix other deceit with the striking. D. de poenis. l. respiciendum. §. delinquunt. This term also must be understood as it sounds in the laws of the common people. D. de leg. 3. l. liberorum. §. quod tamen casius. Having thus briefly outlined these points, if I consider the constitution of the Emperor, only the offender is to be expelled from the society, like a sick beast from the fold. C. de episc. et cle. l. quisquis emersit. Nor can the rectors of this university change the constitution of the Emperor. C. de offic. praef. praet. l. normam. And therefore the others from the said hostel of the Merlenghi cannot be expelled from the society of the assembled. And this as far as this point of expulsion is concerned. As for the point of peace, I say that if the opinion of the common people considers this to be vengeance, peace must be made both for the old and the new offense on both sides; otherwise peace should not be made. For peace cannot be made while war remains. Secondly, because two contraries cannot fall together in the same subject. D. pro suo. l. si ancillam. Therefore, on account of the new war, because the reason of the separated is separated, D. de ca. l. fi., peace cannot be sought. Also, these are not mutual debts which are removed by mutual compensation, because they concern entirely different persons. D. so. ma. l. si socer. §. Lucius. Statutes that a married woman shall not come to the inheritance of her father or mother. co. 40. co. 20. and co. 65. If a woman of the city, or of the posse, or of virtue, was formerly, or shall hereafter be, married by her father, brother, or brothers, uncle, or by her grandfather’s brother, or by any of them: she shall not come to the inheritance of her father or mother with her brother or brothers on the father’s side, nor with their heirs. Henceforth, and that such a married woman shall not be able to act in the paternal or maternal inheritance, or in the paternal or maternal goods, nor against the aforementioned, or any of them, for the legitime otherwise due to her by natural law, nor even for any supplement of the said legitime.
