But by the very fact that she is married, or appears to be married, or has been married by the aforementioned, or any of the aforementioned: she is bound and ought to be content, so that paternal or maternal goods, or even against any of the aforementioned on the said occasion, or by any right, at any time, she shall not be able to have any further recourse. Except that if the father or mother, or either of them, has bequeathed anything to her, or left it to her in any way, which he could leave to her with reason, and that woman can demand or have it. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The disposition of a testator, who, having one married daughter and another in a monastery, when asked whom he wished to be his heirs and to hold his inheritance, answered: the brothers of
2. Carthusia: whether it is valid.
body: A certain lord Rambaldus, having been asked whom he wished to be his heirs and to hold his inheritance, answered: those of La Cartusia. This testator had one daughter married, another in a monastery, whom he passed over.

† It is asked whether the said brothers of the Carthusian order ought to have anything, or not: and that they ought not to have anything is proved, because it is not sufficient that the testator respond to questions, but he must speak of his own accord and express the name of the heir. C. de test. l. iubemus. But this reason does not avail, because for pious causes one can even be instituted heir by a nod, as is noted, extra de testamentis, c. cum tibi, and it is a sufficiently noted gloss. Also, by another reason it seems that it is not valid: because if one son is omitted, the way is open to all to say that no testamentary tables will exist. ff. si tab. testamenti nullae extabunt, l. 1, in fi. Also, the institution is not valid if a son is omitted, as in Auth. ex causa, and this rule fails neither in God nor in His saints, since this does not pertain to the counsel of Augustine. Here it must be considered that the words should be “his own heirs,” and until now the testament in no way is valid; it follows that he has his inheritance, if this is referred to. If by the law of institution, it is superfluous and inequitable, because it had already been said. But if it is understood ampliatively, i.e., how and in what manner he may have it: then by the law of institution it is not valid. But it is valid insofar as it can be valid: so that this clause appears to have been added for strength and to have some effect: and thus it appears he said, “be heir,” or at least “have the goods”: because the nature of the conjunction is to amplify. ff. de leg. 3, l. ea tamen. And because this is suggested by the precise will of the testator, and the favor of the soul: and because words ought to have some effect, and ought not to be interpreted in that direction to which no effect of things follows. C. de inof. testa, l. si quando. Therefore, I say that by the law of testament it is not valid: but by the law of fideicommissum the aforementioned disposition is valid as if intestate: saving, however, the due right of natural law. First, however, consideration must be had of those things wrongly extorted and pertaining to the bishop. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an heir who refuses to pay a legacy to the testator’s wife, unless she provides security for restitution in the event she enters into a second marriage, is to be heard; and whether said security is to be furnished at the time of payment of the legacy, or at the time of contracting the second marriage.
2. When a person is burdened with the obligation of providing security by law, or by the testator contracting, or by the prince, whether security is to be provided in the interim.
3. Security is threefold.
4. Who is to be called a manifest usurer.
body: The case concerning which legal advice is requested is as follows. Titius, having left behind three legitimate and natural daughters born to him and to his lawful wife Seia, departed this life having made a will, in which he instituted the said daughters as his particular heirs: and to the said Seia, his wife, among other things, he made such a legacy. Moreover, he bequeathed and by right of legacy left to the same Seia, his wife, all and every and each of the jewels and garments made for the said Seia by the said testator, whatever they may be and for whatever use prepared for her, both for daily and other use, and both for the adornment of Seia herself and of another. The said Seia demands that this legacy be paid to her by Sempronius, the universal heir of the aforementioned testator. Sempronius is prepared to discharge the said legacy to the said Seia, provided, however, that the said Seia first furnishes adequate security for the restitution of the said legacy to the aforementioned daughters, or to whichever of them survives, if it should happen that the said Seia, their mother, predeceases them. In the event, however, that she should happen to enter upon a second marriage, the said Seia states that she is not bound to furnish the aforementioned security until after she has entered upon a second marriage.

† The question is asked, what is the law: namely, whether the aforementioned security ought to be provided at the time of payment and the release of the aforementioned legacy: or rather only after the transition to a second marriage. That security ought not to be given is proved by several reasons. First, because no law provides for it, we are ashamed to speak without a law. In the Authenticum, *de triennio et semestri*, §. *consideramus*. Second, because this burden of giving security was not imposed by the testator, nor by the contracting party, nor by law; therefore, security need not be given. Codex, *de hereditate vel actione vendita*, l. 2. Third, because she did not receive execution of any action of good faith, but of strict law. That is, a condition from the law *feminae*. Digest, *de secundis nuptiis*. Therefore, according to the natural doctrine of the glosses, security ought not to be given. Digest, *de iudiciis*, l. *in omnibus*, in the gloss, and contrary to the sense of the letter. Fourth, because he who does what he ought, is not meanwhile bound to give security for not doing, or for doing. Digest, *de conditionibus ob causam*, l. *dedi*, in the principle. Fifth, because securities are to be provided only in cases expressly stated in the law. Codex, *de verborum significatione*, l. *sancimus*. And Institutes, *de satisdationibus*. Sixth, because one ought not to be burdened before the time, as in the Institutes, *de exceptionibus*, §. *temporales*. Seventh, because the security is superfluous before marriage, therefore it ought not to be interposed. Law *haec stipulatio*, §. *divus*, *ut legatorum nomine caueatur*. Eighth, because the present status, in which the woman is, is presumed to last, until the contrary appears. Codex, *de servis exponendis*, l. *moueor*. Ninth, because she is not suspect, since she is an honest matron of good family. *De privilegiis creditorum*, l. *si creditores*. Tenth, because it is a pure legacy, not under a condition or mode, and thus it does not obligate. Digest, *de indicta viduitate*, l. *cui relictum* and l. *si*, in the gloss. Eleventh, because it is not in the interest of the heir, since the legacy will not revert to the heir, but to the children. Digest, *solutis matrimonii*, l. *si socer*, §. *Lucius*. Twelfth, because before she marries, she is not a usufructuary, but the owner; therefore, she is not bound to provide security regarding the usufruct. Digest, *de usufructu earum rerum*, l. 2. Thirteenth, lest she be burdened with the burden of satisfaction. That is, now, and when she marries. For the sake of form, as if it were a usufruct, security will then be required: but it is absurd that she be burdened twice, as noted in l. *si ante*, *iudicium solutum*. Fourteenth, because we ought not to look at what may happen, unless some fault or controversy precedes. Regarding fault, it is clear in Digest, *de negotiis gestis*, l. *diuortio*. Regarding controversy, it is clear in l. *harum* and l. *egi*, *si seruitus vendenda*. The preceding is clear from the note in Digest, *solutis matrimonii*, l. 2. Fifteenth, this is clear when considering the text of this edictal law, §. *his*, *de secundis nuptiis*, there: "this is, if she comes to other marriages," etc. Note, *venerit*, that is, already. Therefore, after marriage, and she is not bound to give security beforehand, because by second marriage she becomes suspect. Codex, *de administratione tutorum*, l. *lex quae tutores*. And odious to the children, and to the law. But before, she is not suspect to the children, nor odious to the law, but favorable, and greatly to be revered, as in the Authenticum, *de nuptiis*, §. 1, *si quidem*. Sixteenth, and lastly, it seems to be the case of the law in a similar matter, for if it is the father or mother, who is asked to restore to their children, they ought not to give security before they pass to a second marriage. Codex, *ad Trebellianum*, l. *iubemus*, §. 1. To the contrary, it seems,

† For sometimes one is burdened with the obligation of some restitution by law, sometimes by the contracting party, sometimes by the testator: sometimes by the prince writing a rescript. In the first case, security must be given in the meantime. E.g., an outsider gave a dowry for a woman; by the provision of the law, an action is acquired by the woman. D. 24.3.17 (sol. matr.). Security must be provided. L. Si constante. §. Quoties. D. 24.3.17 (sol. matr.). Certainly, this reason is not the consideration of that §. For the same applies to any giver of a dowry, for example, the woman herself, even if she stipulates for its return to herself; but there the reason is the favor of the dowry, for the husband there gives security, as it seems the text there says, even if otherwise he is solvent. Also there, a certain day. But we can more properly allege the reason, because a delay granted by law is more similar to a delay granted by a testator than by a contracting party; therefore, security must be given in the meantime. D. 46.1.1 (qui sat. cog.). L. Inter omnes. Lest the provision of the law be circumvented. Arg. D. 26.5.1 (de adop.). L. His verbis. And lest the contrary happen to the purpose of the law, if in the meantime he dissipates or consumes what is to be restored, and especially money, which is most subject to consumption. D. 50.17.1 (si cert. pet.). L. Periculum. D. 7.1.1 (de usu). L. Si bene. Someone will say, what then is the difference between praetorian [actions] and these? I answer, praetorian [security] is also given by the most trustworthy person, but these are not given unless the cause is known. That is, if the thing cannot reasonably be kept safe otherwise, and this according to the quality of the persons, as C. 5.3.1 (de pet. her.). L. Fi.

I therefore state that there are three types of security (satisdatio). One is provided for the form of usufruct, and this is regularly to be provided by anyone, even one of the highest solvency. C. de usufr. l. 1, in the last gloss; and l. Usu. Another is provided by express and special ordinance of the law, and the same. D. ut leg. nomine caveatur, throughout; and d. l. Hac edictali, §. His illud. A third is extraordinary, which arises, so to speak, from emerging causes, from various configurations of affairs, and this has place in all actions, but more easily in those of good faith than in those of strict law. D. de iudic. l. In omnibus, lest the debtor dissipate or consume to the detriment of the creditor. I therefore say that the quality of the persons must be considered. For if she is young and suspect regarding the celebration of marriage, she must provide security now, either in the form set forth above in the case, or she must provide security now for the security to be given then: lest, as I said, if in the meantime she should consume, or conceal, or secretly disburse, and afterwards marry, the provision of the law would be absorbed, which would be very inequitable, and by not providing security, the woman would be given the means to defraud the children and to commit delict. But if the mother were otherwise solvent through possession of immovables, or if it were probable that she would not marry, I would not consider her to be burdened with the obligation of security. And it is established. D. qui satisdare coguntur, l. Si fideiussor, §. Ult.; D. ad Trebellianum, l. Imperator. In the second case, when restitution must be made after an uncertain time by the disposition of the contracting parties, it can also be said what was recently concluded regarding l. 2, D. de hereditate vendenda, and regarding l. Dedi, D. de conditionibus ob causam. Say, as in each of them, no. 1. But I say that caution is to be observed for the daughters, or the heir, if he has a mandate from them, or is a related person. And perhaps they themselves can protest that he should not pay without security being received. And by this, he sufficiently has a mandate to receive security. But when security is demanded for the manner of performance, there is no doubt that the heir can demand and plead it, because it pertains to him to defend the inheritance, the authority, and the will of the testator. D. de legatis 3, l. Si tibi; D. de annuis legatis, l. Quintus, §. Pomponius. Let it therefore be concluded that a good man, i.e., the judge in our matter, having inspected the quality of the woman and the quality of the patrimony, must provide for the children ex officio regarding suitable security in the partition, such that in the event of restitution being made, the money is safe for them, i.e., in restoring it, the occasion will be contained in the point, lest the law be placed as a mockery. Another case was touched upon regarding the testator, another case is dispatched by rescript. C. de praescriptionibus imperatoris offerentis, l. Universa. But these cases do not apply to our case; therefore, in our case, let it be concluded that if there is any suspicion against the mother, she must be compelled to provide security.

† He who holds the altar is a manifest usurer by notoriety of fact, that is, publicly defamed by proven public fame and the truth of the fact. Likewise, he who has confessed in court. Likewise, he who has been declared so by sentence. Others are not manifest, but are to be made manifest. On usury, c. *Quamquam*, Book 6. On theft, l. *Furtorum*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made in favor of the poor by these words: “I institute my son as heir, and whenever he shall die without children, I wish that all my goods be distributed among the poor by A. and B., my executors,” is direct or fideicommissary; and what if the son died in pupillary age; and whether the son’s goods acquired from another source are to be distributed. No. 4.
2. What a direct substitution is, and what a fideicommissary substitution is.
3. Whether one who makes a substitution without distinction of time is deemed to have made a fideicommissary substitution, or rather a direct one.
body: A certain Noine A. of Genoa made his will and left many legacies, instituting as his heir by these words: “To Sempronius, his legitimate and natural son.” In all my other movable and immovable goods, or those capable of movement, rights, and actions whatsoever, I institute as my universal heir Sempronius, my legitimate and natural son. Furthermore, I give, bequeath, will, and ordain, and dispose, that if my said son Sempronius should die at any time without children and heirs lawfully descending from him, that all my goods ought to be distributed to the poor of Christ, for the sake of my soul and those of my other predecessors, by G. and H., whom I choose, make, constitute, and will to be my executors and trustees of my present last will. And in the case in which my said trustees and executors should both die before they have distributed as above, that nevertheless all my goods left to my said son, as above, ought to be distributed to the poor of Christ by F. and L., both of whom I ordain and constitute as my trustees and executors of this my last will, after the death of the aforementioned G. and H., to whom, in that case, I give and bequeath and leave, by every right, manner, way, and form by which I can and could best, the authority to distribute as above. With this saving and reservation, that if my said son should die without sons and heirs, as is said above, that one-third part of the said goods ought not to be distributed to the instituted poor; but it ought to come and shall come to Titia and Mevia, both my sisters, whom I institute and substitute as my sisters in the said third part to my said son; I will that it come to them by the right of trust or legacy, if they cannot take it otherwise. The said instituted heir died in pupillary age, and the substitution takes effect.

† Now it is asked whether the said substitution is pupillary. Secondly, whether the said poor of Christ, as substituted heirs, by virtue of the said last will ought to have two parts of the inheritance of the said testator. Also, whether all the goods of the said deceased son, being a pupil, or rather two parts of those goods, since the heir, being a pupil, had more maternal goods intestate. For the sake of clarity, it must be premised,

† That direct substitution is that by which the right to enter upon the inheritance is transmitted to the substitute by virtue of the substitution. Fideicommissary substitution is that by which a person may demand that the inheritance be restored to him by fideicommissum, namely, by the Trebellian fideicommissum. However, a fideicommissum which does not contain in itself a restoration under the Trebellian rule is not called a fideicommissary substitution, but is called a fideicommissum of a specific thing, or non-universal, as these points are proven. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. verbis civilibus; and l. centurio. D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. 1, in principio; and l. mulier, § ut Trebellianum; and Inst. de singulis rebus per fideicommissum relictis, in the rubric and text; with similar authorities. Secondly, it must be premised that he who takes through an intermediate person does not take directly, but by fideicommissum, when it is required that such intermediate person restore the inheritance. But he who takes after an intermediate person, yet not through the intermediate person, but by himself, takes directly, as is noted. C. de fideicommissis, l. eam, quam

Thirdly, it must be premised that where the testator does not distinguish, neither do we distinguish; and therefore, one who makes a substitution without distinguishing times is deemed to have made an indifferent substitution, that is, one suitable for every age, namely, a fideicommissary substitution, as noted in *l. precibus*, *l. centurio*, § *extraneo*, and *c. Raynu.* and *Rayn.* This rule fails if the words compel us to a direct interpretation, for example, if the word "instituted" is appended in the substitution, as in: "If my son dies without sons, I institute such a person." For this word is civil and direct; hence, this substitution, if the age and quality of the son—because he is in the power of his father—is direct, according to *ff. ad Trebellianum*, *l. recusare*, § *Titius*. Whence these words, "instituted" and "substituted," signify a full substitution; and the substitute may choose between the direct and the fideicommissary. And thus Bartolus advised, and I after him very frequently. Now

It remains to be seen regarding the substitution of the poor. Bartolus often advised that executors appear to be directly substituted, having regard to the universality of the poor, and for the poor; so that they could name a substituted heir: for example, a certain hospital as heir, if it seemed good to them. And thus the mother and all those coming as minors intestate would be included. C. de epis. et cle. l. si quis ad declinandam. But the common interpretation does not extend this to goods acquired externally by the minor. And therefore I have often advised that these were executors of a fideicommissum, not of a direct substitution: although a direct substitution can be made under an executor or distributor. For a city and a universality can be directly instituted and substituted, given an executor to distribute among the citizens. arg. extra de testamentis. c. cum tibi. But in this case, because the words say, he instituted and substituted: there is no doubt that the substitution is direct, and I think that in whole, as if this word "instituted" is declaratory of the foregoing, as d. §. Titius. And those words "if otherwise etc." do not diminish the right of the substitutes: because they are added in their favor. And thus the inheritance pertains to the poor for two parts, and for the third part to the other substitutes, namely the testator's sisters. Considering that it was made to the minor with direct words. From which we also interpret that it was made directly of the poor: although there is less doubt about the sisters, than in the poor, to whom also the fideicommissum should be restored without deduction. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Regarding the understanding of the son who has taken possession, you should do the following: and if you feel aggrieved, appear in court to receive the full measure of justice.
2. Who is said to be the defendant in a possessory action.
3. Upon the termination of an emphyteusis, the owner may enter into possession by his own authority, even if the emphyteuta had transferred possession to another.
1. An emphyteuta who has lost his right, if he does not admit the owner, appears to be dispossessing him.
2. If one pair of capons was paid each year for a piece of land, and the name of the contract is not apparent, what kind of contract should be judged.
3. The holder of a census has fallen into forfeiture: but note, that I remember that Master Jacobus, in law 10, Code, on the right of emphyteusis, holds the contrary in the distinctions he makes between the emphyteutic contract and the census contract.
4. One who has been invested and is not acting in bad faith cannot be accused.
5. The owner may invoke the office of the judge, so that he may defend him in the quasi-possession of the right to expel the invader by his own authority.
body: For the sake of clarity,

† it must first be premised that when a judge has ordered something with the clause attached that if he feels aggrieved he is to appear to receive full justice, upon that party's appearance the order is resolved into a simple summons. For this order appears to have been an alternative one, namely that he either do it or appear. And therefore, once he has appeared, satisfaction has been made; and in an alternative obligation it suffices that one part has been executed; this is noted in ff. de no. ope. nun. l. de pupillo. §. meminisse; and so hold the curials of the Roman Curia. Wherefore, upon the order to act, which has been consumed by the appearance, there is no further dispute to be had,

† but one must proceed further and see to the right of the parties. And if indeed this party who appears is nevertheless in possession, one ought not to proceed de facto to expel him from possession; rather, a libel on the petitory action ought to be served upon him, as in Auth. offeratur. C. de lit. conte. and ff. de rei ven. l. qui petitorio. and Instit. de inter. §. conmodum. If, however, it is obscure which of them possesses—for example, there is a dispute between two persons who each say they are possessors—inquiry must be made as to who possesses corporally, and that person is treated as the defendant, and the adversary as the plaintiff, as in l. liberis. §. vlt. ff. de libe. caus. And this is true unless the defendant who opposes is, by opposing, understood to despoil the claimant: as because he is a tenant after the expiration of the lease, or is an emphyteuta who has forfeited the emphyteusis, as in C. de iure emphy. l. 2; for the judge must prohibit violence from being done to the owner, and this ex officio, as in ff. de offi. procu. Caesaris. l. 2. And this is true provided it is first established that he is the owner and that the property is emphyteutic; for before anything has been proved to the judge, he can order nothing, as in C. vnde vi. l. meminerint. and C. si per vim, vel alio modo. l. fi. ff. quibus ex cau. in poss. ea. l. hoc autem. §. 1. and noted by Inn. in c. solet. de sen. excom.

† Secondly, it must be premised that when an emphyteusis has ended, the lord may enter into possession on his own authority, even if the emphyteuta has transferred corporal possession to another, because he cannot transfer it except along with its cause and its defects, as in ff. de acque pos. l. Pompon. §. cum quis; to this makes what is noted in l. 3. C. de pig. And if he can do this on his own authority, all the more so when the office of the judge has been implored. Nor will any other formality of libels be necessary, because the office of the judge is implored for a certain execution of the law; to this makes what is noted in Instit. de libe. §. multum; for this office is not instituted by way of an action, but is implored as a kind of patronage to execute a legal permission, as in C. de seru. fugi. l. requirendi.

† Likewise, if an emphyteuta has forfeited his right and does not admit the returning lord, he is deemed to despoil him, as noted by Dy. in c. qui ad agendum. de regu. iur. lib. 6. and C. loca. l. si quis conductionis; wherefore the judge ex officio ought to compel him, lest it come to brawls and arms with the lord; arg. ff. de vsuf. l. aequissimum. It is necessary, however, that the emphyteutic contract be established by an instrument, arg. ff. et C. de iure emph. l. 1, or by long-standing payment, as in C. de agr. et censi. l. aliquibus. lib. 11.

† Yet it can be doubted whether, if witnesses say that for such an estate one pair of capons was paid every year, this contract is to be understood as emphyteutic, or a contract of superficies, or rather an innominate contract of I give that you may give, by which contract the direct ownership of the estate is transferred, nor does it fall into forfeiture for non-payment, as noted in l. 1. ff. de publi.

† Commonly we call this a census contract, and the common opinion is that it falls into forfeiture, as in Instit. locati. §. adeo. These premises having been laid down, I come to the question proposed regarding the person invested by the most noble man, the lord Franceschino de Gabiano.

† And first I say that that investee could not be accused, because he was not in fraud, but used possession in accordance with his right; for the same permission that belonged to the lord Franceschino is deemed to have been granted to him, as in ff. de no. ope. nun. §. vsufructuarius; wherefore he was not in fraud nor in gross fault, and therefore he is not understood to have inflicted atrocious violence, which alone is punished criminally, as in ff. de act. et oblig. l. seruus non omnibus. Nay rather, if the custom of the region is not contrary, nor has the property fallen into forfeiture, he ought to be defended in possession by the aid and authority of the praetor, as has been proved above. Having seen the acts, it seems to me sufficiently proved regarding the paternal and ancient census, and also regarding the new one; and to this makes C. de praescri. 30. ann. l. male agitur, de vsu. c. cum de in rem verso, and what is noted in C. de pact. l. si cer. annis, ff. de ser. vr. praed. l. seruitutes, extra de elec. c. querelam, and what is noted by Cy. in l. 1. C. ne quis in sua causa. It is true that it would have been safer to conduct the process observing the order of law; and to this makes what is noted by Guli. de Cu. in ff. de in integ. resti. l. omnes. Likewise, the same power ought to be extended to those who succeed one another, as in extra de iudi. c. quia 5; for that permission which has been given by the law to lords, etc., is by public authority, although it is for private utility, and therefore the office of the law ought to be engaged in its execution.

† For the office of the judge can be implored so that he may defend the lord in the quasi-possession of the right to expel an intruder on his own authority, and likewise any succeeding judge. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the oath of a minor, and when, validates or does not validate an act prohibited by statute from being contracted with a minor.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that sometimes a statute prohibits contracting with a minor without consent, let us say of relatives, and the minor’s oath does not validate an act otherwise performed. C. de leg. l. non dubium; de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinos, §. fi.; C. ne fideius. dotium dentur, l. 2. Sometimes a statute does not speak in terms of prohibition, but states that a minor cannot [contract]. And then, if the statute makes mention of an oath—because it says “notwithstanding if he has sworn”—and likewise, because civil law can repudiate an oath on certain grounds, as ff. de iu. patr. l. adigere, §. fi. Or the statute does not make mention of an oath: and then some say that the oath is valid, as in Auth. sacramenta puberum. Others say that the oath is not valid, because the disposition made by Auth. sacramenta puberum cannot be entirely abolished by statute; nevertheless, it can be modified by observing a certain solemnity approving the contract, and by not observing it, repudiating the contract. ar. ff. de don. cau. mor. l. thais. And this is commonly observed, for if the form is not observed, both contracting parties err in form; and because the statute gives form to consent and prevents natural obligation from arising if that form is not observed. And to this effect is what we note in Bar. ff. de fideiuss. l. si quis pro eo. And thus it is commonly held in the secular forum. From this it follows that the said promise and renunciation did not hold; and especially because the minor was not notified of the benefit of the statute, as noted by Cy. C. de rescin. vend. l. 2. Regarding the second point, I say that she is tacitly professed, both from the acts of profession and from the length of time, unless the contrary is proven, and this daughter, or the monastery through her person, comes together with the brother according to common law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an instrument executed in a prohibited place creates faith in another place.
2. The place of the instrument, or of the contract, is examined in the decisive provisions thereof.
body: Instrument

A deed executed in a prohibited place does not carry faith in any place, and the reason is that there is no authority, since it ought to intervene in that place and time, according to the authority on guardianship, l. obligari, §. si. Since, therefore, the authority of the notary is lacking, his writing is not valid. The second reason is that the sentence of the statute annuls the writing just as the sentence of a judge does. But the sentence of a judge annuls everywhere; therefore, also the sentence of the law, in the Authority on not alienating, §. quia vero, C. de testamentis, l. iubemus.

The third reason is common to all the doctors, because in decisive instruments the place of the instrument is inspected, just as in contracts. L. si fundus, D. de evictionibus; and L. cunctos populos. And therefore the instrument in question, although not made by a private person, but by one who has authority from the Emperor, C. de sepulcris violatis, L. 3, §. divus, nevertheless, because it was made by one under interdict, receiving instrumental rogations in that place makes no proof in any place, as if not rogated: because it could not be rogated; yet it makes an indication, as noted in L. admonendi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the legitimation of a spurious grandson is valid to the prejudice of another grandson. Numbers 4 and 5.
2. If a father or grandfather names a legitimate son or grandson in a will, whether he is to be considered as such.
3. How filiation is to be proved.
body: The son having died, and the grandfather having a grandson not legitimately born, while a legitimate and natural granddaughter survived, the grandfather had the said grandson legitimated by the count. Moreover, in his will he called him his grandson and instituted him as his sole universal heir, but instituted the granddaughter in a certain sum. Finally, this testator having died, the son claims to succeed in everything and alleges three things. First, because he denies him to be his grandson. Second, he says that by the recitation of the will he was not legitimated. Third, he says that the count’s legitimation is not valid. On the contrary, three things are alleged: namely, that he is the son of the son, that he is legitimated by rescript, and that if he were not legitimated by rescript, he is legitimated by the grandfather’s will. This bastard, however, was born of a free man and a free woman, yet of a certain widow prostitute. Now the question is, what is the law.

I answer that he who claims to be a son, and whose status as a son is denied, must prove this. D. 22.3.1. But how will he prove it? I answer that it is difficult to prove this with respect to the father. D. 12.1.1.

† The same is not proven by the fact that he called him son, but by the things themselves and the facts: namely, because he supported and kept him as a son publicly in his house, in the sight of the neighbors. Extra, de probat., c. Per tuas; de filiis presbyterorum, c. Michael. I. That he kept and treated him in the manner in which sons are commonly accustomed and ought to be treated. D. de verb. oblig., Quidam cum filium.

† It is necessary, however, that certain preceding circumstances concur, for example, that he was born in the house. D. de his, qui sunt sui, vel alieni iuris, l. filium. Or some other probable circumstances, for example, that he was accustomed to approach the house from outside, as C. de probationibus, l. nonnullis and l. non epistolis. And other probable circumstances, which must be investigated, for example, the probability which is akin to nature, and is a locus from commonly occurring events. And therefore the mere assertion of the grandfather does not prove him to be the grandson. C. de fideiussoribus, l. eam est. C. de hereditatibus institutis, l. si pater. D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. uxorem. D. de pactis, l. epistola. Moreover, where succession is at issue, where one must prove oneself to be such, it is not sufficient to prove quasi-possession, unless some other antecedent is proved, for example, marriage, cohabitation, and other things assisting by probability: because in decisive possessory actions, a possessory claim is not sufficient, unless it is approved by a presumption of law. C. unde legitimi, l. non hoc. l. 1. §. 1. de itinere actuque privato, l. 2. §. quidam. D. de interdictis. I come to the second,

And I say that in the rescript there is no mention of the legitimation of the nephews, and rightly so, because with the father of the nephew dead and legitimated, who must proceed in order of degrees, he does not have his own right when the son is excluded. This is noted by Guillaume de Cuy in *l. benignus*, D. de legitimatione. Moreover, this spurious child is not natural, because access to a widow is punished by the penalty for stuprum, D. de quaestionibus, *l. si quis viduam*, unless it is held in the form of concubinage, D. de concubinis, *l. cum in concubinatu*. And therefore the rescript is invalid. I come to the third point, and I say that for a testament to legitimize someone, it is required that marriage be possible by nature, by law, and in fact, and thus coming according to good morals. Thus Bartolus advised, as in D. quae et a quibus, *l. si rogatus*, § *matrimonii*. But here, with the son dead, and even if alive, married, all these things are impossible, hence it is concluded in favor of the niece against this person, whether because he is not a son, or because he is spurious, and the legitimation was null. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How those words are to be understood, which are placed in the compromise, that he may take away from the right of one party in a large and small quantity: and whether by such words he may take away dominion. num. 4.
2. What is meant by a large, greater, and small quantity. num. 3.
3. An arbitral award is assimilated to a transaction.
body: First,

† I ask to what effect operates the power given to a mere arbiter to take away from the right of one party and give to the other in great and small quantity. And it seems that it operates nothing: because the decision of the arbiter must be stood by, even if it harms entirely, ff. de arbi. l. diem proferre. §. stari. Likewise, those words "in small and great quantity" were given from the intention of those uttering them for augmentation, therefore they do not restrict, ff. de fun. instru. l. quęsit. §. pe. On the contrary it seems, for by referring ourselves to mere arbitrium, these words "in small and great quantity" are held in place of a limitation (taxatio). And because the power is given over so much and not over the whole, therefore if the arbiter harms exceedingly, that is, enormously, recourse can be had to a superior so that he might reform that which was done very unjustly, as is noted in de ver. sig. l. illa verba. And it is certain that an argument drawn from the intention of the contracting parties is valid in law, ff. de ac. et ob. l. obligationum substantia, and l. non omnis, ff. si cert. peta., and l. cum quod, de pac. do. l. inter socerum. §. cum inter., and l. beblius Marcellus. Likewise, that which is granted qualifiedly (secundum quid) is not deemed to be promised entirely, as in l. qui aliena. §. libertos. ff. de neg. ge.; therefore in this case, if more is ordered than permitted, recourse is had to a superior, ff. de app. l. ex consensu. For a judge can well be approached to declare that the award does not hold, ff. quae sententiae sine app. rescin. l. 1. in prin., since the office of the judge has been brought forth for making all declarations, ff. de condi. insti. l. quę sub condit. §. vlt. And that recourse is a certain species of appealing, that is, of having recourse to the help of a superior, ff. de arbit. l. non distinguemus. §. cum quidam. And I think this is true, because by agreement he moderates the equity and the freedom of the arbitrium so that it does not exceed a great quantity, but extends up to it inclusively. Whence in the case of a mere arbiter, that clause, by declaring the intention of the parties, limits [it] up to a great quantity and does not confer power beyond. But immediately it is necessary to ask what is called a "great quantity," and whether ownership is included under the noun "quantity," such that he can take away ownership in great and small quantity. And first it seems that this power is not valid, because it is uncertain, ff. de in lit. iur. §. cum in furti., ar. ff. de ver. ob. l. triticum. On the contrary it seems that it is valid, and is understood of an eighth part, or of a sixth, or of a fourth, ff. pro soc. l. si non fuerit. and l. si societatis, ff. de inof. test. l. si quis in suo, de lega. 2. l. cum filius. §. pater.

† I say that in an arbitrium decisive of a dispute these words must be referred to the judgment and discretion of a good man, so that what he believes to be fitting in accordance with the good and the equitable not rejected by law, he may do that. Likewise that which is equitable and not good; likewise that which is good and not equitable not rejected by law, provided that he does it for the good of peace, as in c. nisi esset. de pręb. But concerning the signification of the words, I do not think that he can harm regarding that which is certain beyond the quantity assessed by the Authentica C. de sent. ex periculo reci. auth. nisi breuiores, or beyond the quantities of taxation in Auth. de defen. ciui. §. et iudicare. C. de pedag. iudi. l. placet; or indeed this measure is committed to the arbitrium of the judge, ff. de in integ. resti. l. Seyo, ff. de transa. l. cum hi. §. modus. For if the case is about a certain county, 300 gold coins are nothing, but if it is about a trifling thing, even 10 gold coins is a great matter for one who is poor and of an obedient life. And if at any time it should be much worn, much debated, much hostile, and traced back to a grandfather, the quantity ought not to be considered so much as the quality; whence vexation must be bought off with the more powerful, de infamibus. l. furti. §. qui iussu. For this opinion, that a great quantity is said to be by the arbitrium of a good man, we have this determined in another matter, C. de reb. cre. l. in bonęfidei, de iureiu. l. amouedi, ff. de iud. l. sed et si susceperit. §. 2, ff. de leg. 3. l. si filiae, ff. de procu. l. vel iudicio, ff. de neg. gest. l. Nesennius, C. eo. l. 1, ff. de vsufruc. l. hactenus. Here therefore the compromissum will stand firm, namely, that he can effectively harm up to a great quantity, but not up to a lesser or the greatest. There remains a greater doubt,

† what may be called greater, and what may be called greatest; but I still firmly believe that it belongs to the arbitrium of a good man through the same legal reasons and through many other similar ones; that which is noted in C. vnde vir, et vxor. auth. praeterea supports this. And these things are true, even with respect to the arbiter, lest he make the suit his own, as in ff. de pac. l. pen. in fi. It follows to see what this power given to a mere arbitrator operates,

† and it seems that it is interpreted more broadly: because the power of transacting has been given to him; and in a transaction even a great lesion is tolerable, ff. ad Treb. l. Lucius. §. fi. The doctors commonly say that when such power is given, the arbitrator can in good faith, from the power committed and granted to him, take away and give by his arbitrium: provided however that he does not exceed the limit too much, for that would be permitted by fraud, nor is it understood to be permitted, as Bar. notes in l. pe. de pręto. stip. Dominus Iacobus Cal. and dominus Raynerius, disputing, said that such collation of power was to be broadly interpreted, not reduced to the arbitrium of another. For which said l. cum filius. §. pater. ff. de dote pręlegata. l. Theopompus most excellently makes. I nevertheless hold what I said above, and this according to the ius commune. But through the form of a statute one could not come against it, unless perhaps it were proved that fraud was absent, or fraud is seen if the plaintiff has proved nothing within the term appointed for this; and therefore the defendant was absolved, ff. de arbi. l. si de meis. §. fi. And by how much more the thing were doubtful,
† by so much more is the arbitramentum assimilated to a transaction, as in C. de fur. l. post decisionem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The heirs cannot oppose the adultery of a woman claiming her dowry from the heirs of her husband, if it was not opposed during the lifetime of the husband.
2. Whether a woman can claim the restitution of her dowry from feudal goods.
3. Whether creditors have recourse against fiefs.
body: Peter contracted marriage with Lady Berta. During the said marriage, she committed adultery and had a son born of adultery, and she kept the said son secret and nursed him as the son of the said Peter for 12 years while the said Peter lived. Moreover, the said Lady Berta had another son and one daughter, born male and female, of the legitimate marriage. After the death of the said Peter, her husband, the said Berta had a daughter by a certain man who was not her husband. Now it happens that the said Berta, being in the presence of many persons, and with the legitimate and natural son present, and with the spurious son present, wishing to unburden her conscience, said and protested that the said spurious son was born of adultery and that he was not the son of the said Peter. Upon hearing this, the said spurious son withdrew and went to distant parts. The other son, legitimate and natural, died and bequeathed his dowry to the said Berta, his mother. However, because the said Berta claimed her dowry from the goods of the said Peter and against the heirs of the said Peter, it is asked whether the heirs of the said legitimate and natural son, who made the aforementioned bequest, can raise an exception against the said Berta on the ground of adultery, so that she loses the dowry, notwithstanding that the adultery was not opposed to her during the lifetime of the husband. Furthermore, since among the goods of the said Peter there are feudal goods, it is asked whether she can claim anything of the said dowry from those feudal goods, or from the fruits thereof, in the case where the exception of adultery could not be raised against her. [The feudal goods are] from a noble, ancestral, and ancient fief. Furthermore, it is asked whether the creditors of the said Peter can have recourse against the feudal goods, or the fruits and profits of those goods. CASE. A woman,

† A wife who was not repudiated by her husband on account of adultery cannot be barred by the husband’s heirs from claiming her dowry. L. 1, § 1, *solummodo* *maioris* [or *sol. ma.*], and there by Bartolus and others. For although this came to light after the husband’s death, nevertheless, as an action for vindicta [punitive damages], it does not pass to the heirs. D. de collatione bonorum, L. cum emancipatus filius. And therefore the said heirs can neither bring an action nor raise an exception for the forfeiture of the dowry.

But whether the said dowry can be recovered from the fruits of feudal goods, in no case can the feudal right itself be alienated. D. 12.1.14; D. 38.2.1; D. 38.2.1 § 1; D. 9.2.1; D. 9.2.1 § si qua sunt iura, and there fully noted by others. Some say that even the feudal right can be seized in the case of a judgment. But it will not last except during the lifetime of the vassal, but the first opinion is more correct. From this it is clear how to respond to all questions concerning creditors. To the penultimate point I do not now respond, so as not to prejudice the matter on which the greater weight of the opinion rests.

† Regarding all creditors of the vassal, I say that upon his death and the termination of the fief, they have no recourse against that fief, as stated in c. 1, *An an agnate or son*, Collatio 10, and in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, l. *Lex vectigalis*. I say that they have no recourse against the agnate succeeding to the fief. However, in the husband’s own property, creditors holding an express hypothec prior in time are preferred over the wife, according to the Code, *Qui potiores in pignore habeantur*, l. *Assiduus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who is the judge in feudal matters.
body: The case stands thus: When the late Nanus of Matchio, either in person or through his legitimately appointed procurator, sold and, by reason of the sale, confessed that he had sold and delivered to Lord Reynald of Pontolio, Podesta of Asti, and the Sages and Rectors of the people of Asti, who held bailiwick and general authority to receive and provide for the affairs of the commune of Asti and for all acts and business of the said commune, as granted by the general council; namely, first, the castle and village of Cena; likewise the village of Ruasis, together with certain other castles and villages contained in the aforementioned sale, and with the opportune solemnities regarding the said properties and concerning the same; and this for the price of one hundred thousand Asti pounds, with the necessary and opportune clauses and renunciations. And immediately thereafter it appears that, when the full and general council of the city of Asti was assembled, and in the name and on behalf of the commune of Asti, as the said Lord Reynald, together with the said council thus fully assembled, and the said councillors and council granted to the said Lord Nanus, for himself and his sons George and William, and their other heirs or successors, whether male or female, brothers, collaterals, etc., and others descending from them in Asti, as is customary in such matters, a rightful, noble, and gentle fief. And which Lord Nanus, in his own name and that of his sons hereinafter named, swore bodily upon the Holy Gospels to the said Lord Podesta, Captain, Sages, Syndic, and Treasurers, in the name and on behalf of the commune of Asti, receiving himself and his sons and their successors as faithful to the said Podesta and to the others who shall exist from time to time in the government of the city of Asti, and to the other magistrates and presidents of the commune, and to the commune of Asti itself; and that the said Lord Nanus, his sons, heirs, successors, or any of them, shall not be in fact or counsel, or in any place, by which the Podestas of Asti, or those who from time to time shall be in the government of the city of Asti, or any of them, shall lose the land of the commune of Asti, or person, or limb, or any jurisdiction, as is customary in such matters, and as is more fully contained in the instrument of fidelity itself, with the pacts hereinafter added. The tenor of the pacts and conventions, to which and for which the said Lord Nanus is bound, for himself and his sons, heirs, and successors, to the commune of Asti, and to which and for which the said commune of Asti is bound to the said Lord Nanus, for himself and his sons and successors, is as follows, namely: that the said Lord Nanus and his aforementioned sons, by themselves and their male and female heirs and successors, hold and ought to hold from the commune of Asti, in noble and gentle fief, the whole and entire land, castles, villages, and places of theirs, which are denoted and specified in the instruments of sale made of the aforementioned properties; as is more fully contained in the instrument of sale and fief itself. And conversely, the said commune of Asti holds, or possesses, or detains, or shall hold and detain, or acquire, that the said Lord Nanus, his sons and heirs, or successors, or any of them, shall swear, defend, and hold by hand, and make peace and war against any persons, colleges, universities, communities, and places, and counts, and Marquises, and certain other persons, who and which should offend in the said fief. Likewise, it was agreed that if any person, college, commune, or university, castellan, Marquis, or counts, or any other of whatever order or degree, for any occasion, by any real or personal action, direct or useful, civil, praetorian, pecuniary, or criminal, or in any other manner, should wish to proceed against the said Lord Nanus, his sons, or heirs, or successors, or any of them, or to demand from them, or any of them, any thing or things: that the said Lord Nanus, his sons, heirs, or successors, shall not be able, nor ought they in any way to be compelled or distrained by the Podesta of Asti, or by other captains, or rectors, magistrates, president, or presidents of the commune of Asti, or for the commune of Asti, or in the name and on behalf of the commune of Asti, to sue, or stand to law, or render justice in the city of Asti, or in any castle, village, or place of the commune of Asti, both by reason of future contracts which they, or any of them, might make or contract in the city of Asti or its territory, as well as by reason of a delict committed in the city of Asti or its territory, or of delicts committed in the city of Asti, its district, or territory, or by reason of domicile which they, or any of them, might have or establish in the city, territory, or district of Asti, and by reason of things situated in the territory or district; they shall be bound to stand to law and reason, and to obey in the city of Asti, according to feudal laws, and otherwise not. And thus the said parties promised and agreed with each other, and did all things with reasons, pacts, and conventions, as is more fully contained in the instruments of the said feudal grant and convention. Now it is asked, whether, notwithstanding the said exceptions, the said Lord Governor ought to pronounce himself the competent judge, and whether he ought to pronounce that the said Lord James is to be restored before all things to his spoliations. And what and how is to be done in the aforementioned matters.

† According to the matters proposed, it is undoubtedly true that the said magnificence, who represents the commune of Asti, is the competent judge. Likewise, the said authority [is competent], although it is necessary that the said authority have a special commission regarding this: because he does not act as a mere authority, nor by virtue of the office of the podestà, but by virtue of the office by which feudal lords must adjudicate when a dispute concerning a fief arises between vassals. Extra, De feudis et beneficiis, c. Imperialem, §. Pe; De pace tenenda, c. Quam, §. Ministrales, which states: "If any lords have war among themselves, the Count or judge, in whose region laws and judgments are made, shall pursue the matter from there." De prohibitione alienationis feudi, per Fed., §. 1, which furthermore states: "If there is a dispute between two vassals concerning a fief, the lord shall have cognizance, and by him the dispute shall be terminated according to the law of fiefs." And this has been said regarding jurisdiction; it is not yet time to speak of decisory matters: because before spoliation appears proven, restitution ought not to be made. Afterwards, thus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute speaking of a wife applies to one who has not yet been brought to the marital home.
2. And what is the case with a betrothed woman.
3. And what if the marriage was null.
body: "If a woman," he says, "is joined to a man through marriage."

† I ask whether a virgin is said to be joined by marriage who has not yet been brought into the husband’s house. And it seems that she is, as in *l. nuptias*, D. de re iudicanda, and D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, *l. Seya*, in the beginning, where it says “marriage contracted,” which is understood from consent. To the contrary: because matrimonial union, or copula, is not said to exist unless carnal copula has intervened, consummating the marriage, as seems to be proved by the gloss which is in Inst. de nuptiis, in the beginning. Hence that passage, “What God has joined, let no man separate,” is explained as referring to perfect union, that is, by carnal copula, C. de conversione coniugali, c. 2. Certainly, rather, it is understood by matrimonial consent, even without copula, without favor of religion. The better reason, therefore, is that if the husband did not bear the burdens of marriage, he does not acquire the dowry, *l. pater*, D. de exceptione doli.

† And in our case it must be said, according to what is proposed, that she ought not to profit: because she is not yet of marriageable age, nor is she said to be joined by marriage, as noted in ff. sol. ma. l. si a me, and it is expressly stated in ff. quod falso tu. au. an. l. in partem; and it applies in ff. de vulg. sub. l. qui habeat; ff. de peti. hęre. l. nec vllam, §. omnibus. And although a betrothed woman is sometimes considered as akin to a wife, this is true in her favor, C. de bonis, quę libe. in l. non sine, not to her prejudice, ff. de infamibus. l. solet. Since therefore the marriage could have been contracted despite the impediment of age, as in c. 1. de despon. impu. lib. 6., the statute does not apply, nor does the intent of the statute, and therefore the benefit of the statute ceases; nor do betrothals pass into the substance of marriage by the mere passage of time, as in the aforementioned c. 1. de despon. impube. li. 6., and there is the case,

That this is not a marriage, and consequently there is no dowry, speaking properly, as we must speak in the statute. And this is evident from the conjunction of two laws: Institutes, De nuptiis, in the beginning; and Law 1, Digest, Unde vir et uxor; and Digest, De adulteriis, Law Si uxor, § Diuus Seuerus. Furthermore, I understand the said statute to apply to a woman who can give a dowry, not to a ward. Code, De lege tutela, Law Si; Digest, De iure patronatus, Law Adigere, § Quamuis. Since, therefore, the said alleged marriage lacks the substance of marriage, and the said alleged dowry lacks the essence of a dowry, as in Law Si, Digest, De nuptiis, and Law Quod Seruius, Digest, De conditionibus ob causam, cum si. I state that the said fiancé, who has incurred no burdens of marriage, gains nothing under the pretext of the said statute, since mention is made therein of burdens; for one clause explains another, Digest, De petitione hereditatis, Law Vtrum; and Law Nihil, Digest, De coniungendis cum emancipato, liberis eius; and Institutes, De rerum diuisione, § Item lapilli. And so I state and advise, I, Balde de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and affixed the seal of my name. And the sentence rendered in the case regarding the acquisition of gain ought to be reformed and corrected, if time permits; because it was rendered through an error of law based on the supposition of the said facts, as contained in the point, according to the truth of the facts.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If several brothers are invested with a fief, in such a way that as long as males survive among them, females succeed upon their failure: whether the daughters of predeceased brothers succeed together with the daughter of the last male, or she alone.
body:
The agreement is as follows. Fagonus, Bartholomew, and John, brothers of the family of Vgonis, citizens of Asti, purchased the castle and village of Asternae with its appurtenances, which were part of the fief of the Lord Bishop and the Church of Asti. They, along with Jacob and Uberto of Mercato, citizens of Asti, were invested in the said castle and village by Lord Bandarchus, then Bishop of Asti, now mentioned below, namely in a direct and noble fief, as an ancient, paternal, and ancestral holding, for themselves and their male and female descendants; so that brother succeeds to brother, uncle to nephew, and collateral to collateral, as long as any male descendant remains from the aforementioned brothers; so that a woman may in no way look to the succession of the said fief, nor can the present Lord Bishop, or his successors who will be in the Church of Asti for the time being, make an investiture of the said fief, in whole or in part, in the person of a woman, as long as a male survives from the said brothers and their descendants. If, however, no male should survive from them, then the women descending from them shall succeed in the said fief, as is established by the public instrument of the aforementioned investiture made in the said brothers, as is premised.

These things being so, the aforementioned brothers died. First, the said Fagonus died, leaving one male son named George. Afterwards, the said William died, leaving one son and two daughters. Afterwards, the said John died, leaving one daughter, who afterwards died, leaving one daughter now living. Afterwards, the said Bartholomew died, leaving two male sons and five daughters. Afterwards, the said two sons of the late Bartholomew died, leaving their sisters and the said George, their blood relatives. Afterwards, the said George died, leaving one daughter, who, the daughter of the said George, was invested by the present Lord Bishop of Asti in the said castle and village of Asternae as in a fief devolved to the said Lord Bishop.

Now a doubt arises between the said daughter of the late George and the said daughters of the said William and Bartholomew, and the daughter of the daughter of the said John, concerning the aforementioned fief. For the daughter of the said George says that the said fief pertains to her in its entirety by virtue of the succession of George, her father, the last male brother to die, and by the testament of the said George. The aforementioned daughters of the said Bartholomew and William, and the daughter and daughters of the said John, also say that the aforementioned fief pertains to them for the parts pertaining to their parents William, Bartholomew, and John, according to the form of the aforementioned investiture, and that they are to be invested by the said Lord Bishop. The parties having produced the aforementioned matters, it is asked, what is the law.

The tenor of the investiture gives this order, that every male is preferred to every woman. Hence, the last male was the vassal of the entire fief, or each one, for his undivided share, seemed to have contracted it to his daughter, as in the chapter *Duo fratres*, "Concerning two brothers invested by a captain," column 10.

† The doubt therefore arises: because if the last male, namely George, was the feudatory of the whole to the exclusion of collateral females, such females, once excluded, do not seem to be admissible to the fief thereafter, as in column 10, “the bishop or abbot,” §. quin etiam. That the male excluded them is not in doubt, as in the title De eo qui sibi et haeredibus suis, c. 1, and it appears from the form of the instrument. No one is admitted to that from which he is shown to have been once excluded. On these points, see the usage in F. de amissione, l. si cum in annos. Moreover, this male is considered as the sole stipulator in solidum, once the matter has come to the point of time alone, and therefore his daughter rather than an agnate should succeed, De successionibus feudorum, c. 1. I believe the first opinion to be more just, that all succeed per stirpes, each in the place of her father, Ff. de haereditatibus ab intestato, §. cum filius. And thus each should be invested by the bishop, and not only the daughter of the last deceased, as argued in Ff. de haereditatibus institutis, l. Lucius; C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; Ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. Gayo; Ff. de rebus dubiis, l. si is qui ducenta, §. utrum; C. de fideiussoribus, l. cum acutissimi; C. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum avus; Ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si; Ff. de liberis et postumis, l. Gallus, §. quidam recte. For this pact, as being real, benefits all the females. As many fathers as made the pact are understood to have made it, Ff. de duobus reis, l. reos, §. cum tabulis. And each is understood to have provided for his own posterity, as noted in Ff. de pactis, l. si tibi, §. si pactus. For this is the law of nature, that a father should take counsel for his children, Ff. unde liberi, l. scripto; Ff. de bonis liberorum, l. nihil, §. facilior; Ff. de adulteriis, l. nec in ea. And the females succeed by portion according to the tenor and form of the pact, as in the title Qui feudum dare possunt, c. 1, §. hoc autem, column 10, which pact, as being favorable, is to be extended, Ff. de liberis et postumis, l. placet; Ff. de pactis, l. iure gentium, §. pactorum. And so I conclude that, upon the death of all males, any female shall succeed in the place and portion of her own stem.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A general release, or refutation, or division does not encompass matters not contemplated; and the action remains with respect to those matters.
body: In the article

It must be said that if fraud and deceit by a brother concealing money or account books intervene, an action pro socio may be brought notwithstanding the award and captious refutation, since it is not extinguished by Aquilian stipulation and acceptance. Likewise, if that money were common by reason of an inheritance, an action could be brought on that ground. Otherwise, if fraud is not proven: yet, since it is sworn, absolution from the oath should first be obtained. This is noted in C. de trans. l. sub praetextu specierum; ff. eo. l. qui tutoribus; and l. cum Aquiliana, ff. de pact.; l. tres fratres, C. de do.; l. nec ignorans, C. de excom.; l. si ex maiore, ff. de condi. indeb.; l. si, §. idem quaesivit, C. de collat.; l. si soror, ff. de act. et oblig.; l. ex maleficiis, §. longe minus, ff. de pactis; l. emptor, §. Lucius, ff. de const. pec.; l. final. The conclusion is this: in general, those things which are concealed are not included. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an infant son transmits to his mother the inheritance of his father that has not been accepted.
body:
Given the statute of the tenor set forth below: “No woman of Asti shall succeed to a deceased person when male agnates exist up to the seventh degree, except in the usufruct of that portion which she would have received under the common law. The same rule applies to the maternal grandfather; yet the woman herself shall be deprived of that very usufruct by law if she enters into a second marriage.”

Furthermore, assuming as true in law the opinion stated in the facts: because, where this question arises, it is held that a son who did not intervene in his father’s inheritance does not transmit it to strangers, but to his descendants, if he has any; and if he has none, he transmits the inheritance only to his mother, as though it were acquired by a special maternal right.

It happens that A. died, leaving B. and C., his sons and brothers related to each other only on the paternal side, not on the maternal side. Moreover, C., still in infancy, died before anyone had intervened in the paternal inheritance on his behalf, his mother and the aforementioned brother B. being still alive.

† Now the question arises between the mother and the aforementioned B. concerning the half-share of the inheritance of the late A., which had devolved upon the late C.; it must now be seen what is the law regarding the said share. This case is perplexing. For if the agnate is called, he cannot be called except by the right of accretion, and then the mother excludes him entirely, because the matter is not one of the son’s inheritance, but of the paternal inheritance. But to exclude the mother entirely is contrary to the statute, which grants the mother the usufruct, and thus the intent of the statute is not satisfied by the right of accretion. C. ad orfi. l. non pro numero. Or if only the mother is called, this is contrary to the statute, which intends that she have only the usufruct. ar. C. de secundis nup. l. fęminę. in fi. But nevertheless, if there is a special custom that the infant transmits to the mother, so that not to another, and this custom is proved, then this custom induces a personal privilege, and in this case it is singular, in that it does not extend beyond the person of the mother. ff. de leg. 2. l. cum patronus. unless the custom were one approving that option, namely that he should transmit because he is a suus heres, and not one privileging the mother; for then we would be directly under the statute, whereby the mother would have the usufruct, and the agnates the ownership, transmitted to them by the existence of their heir, and transmitted from the infant. But according to what is alleged, the custom rejects this opinion, except in favor of the mother, in favor of the statute, that it passes to her. Hence, this being established, the personal privilege of the mother does not extend beyond the person of the mother. ff. de excu. tu. l. amicissimos. §. Lucius. That this is a privilege of the mother, the gloss holds in l. apud hostes. in maiore infante. But in the case of an infant, it must be said that according to the common law, as noted in l. si infanti. per glo et doct. Concluding, I say that if the custom is proved, so that it is established as a privilege of the mother, it benefits the mother and not the agnates; but according to the common law, opinions are diverse. Hence, this case stands according to the custom in a qualified sense, and according to the common law in a qualified sense. For according to the common law, I say nothing. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal may alienate a fief with the condition that the lord consents, or at least subject to the lord’s right; and that in the meantime the person to whom the alienation is made holds it in the name of the vassal.
2. Whether a vassal is deprived of the fief by operation of law itself, or whether a judicial sentence is required, if he transfers the fief to another without title to the prejudice of the lord.
3. Who is the competent judge in a case concerning a fief.
body: The fact occurred in the year of our Lord 1388. The Reverend Father, the Lord Bishop of Asti, made a certain investiture of a fief of a certain castle and village in the persons of Gandulf and Valenta, his wife, or in the name of the said Gandulf and the said Valenta, namely in the person of the said Valenta as if of a paternal and ancient fief held by her progenitors from the said Church of Asti, namely for the said spouses and their legitimate and natural male and female children to be descended from them, etc. Then in the year of our Lord 1389, the said Gandulf and Lady Valenta, his wife, and each of them jointly and severally, namely the said Valenta with the authority and consent of her said husband, she however being of the age of 18 and under 25, renouncing the benefit of minority of age and restitution in integrum, on the condition that the Bishop of Asti, in his own name and on behalf of his Astian Church, would consent to the alienation set forth below, and would give counsel or authority in all and each of the matters set forth below, and would successively invest the noble man Bartholomew de Garretis, the purchaser set forth below, and make investiture to the said purchaser according to the form and tenor of the investiture made to the said Gandulf, her husband, and the said Valenta, his wife, in their names, or that another superior of the said Lord Bishop, the said Lord Bishop not consenting and not giving consent, authority, and license to the said alienation, and not making or refusing to make investiture of the aforesaid in the due manner and form, even saving the right of fief of the said Lord Bishop and the Church of Asti, gave and sold to Bartholomew the said castle, etc., on the condition that the said Bartholomew would hold and possess the said place in the name of the said Gandulf and Valenta until the said Bartholomew was lawfully invested by the said Lord Bishop or another superior having power therefor. Who also, the said vendors, under the said condition, constituted themselves to hold precariously, etc. After which the said Bartholomew, thus superficially invested, held the said castle against the will of the said Lord Bishop, who did not consent, although investiture had been requested from him. After which the said Lord Bishop invested another with the said castle as reverted to the Church of Asti. After which it was petitioned to the Lord Pope that he ratify the said sale, who, the Lord Pope, delegated the matter, however did not ratify it, and died. Therefore, presupposing the said theme as true, and saving the terms of truth.

† It is asked whether the said fief of the said Church of Asti was opened, so that another could be invested, or not. On this point, some say that alienation without consent is void, and even with consent, if it is to the prejudice of the lord, it is void. That consent is of the substance of alienation is proven if the cause of causes is established. D. de cond. ob causam, l. 3, §. subtilius; D. si cert. pet., l. si ego. That it binds to the prejudice of the alienator is proven by Inst. de usufr., §. finitur, and the entire matter of fiefs sings no other song. Immediately, not that the vassal proceeds to the act and consent, so that two intervene: namely, the act and the will, and the transfer of corporal possession, even if abusive and superficial; the fief reverts to the lord, and especially to the church by operation of law, as C. de iure emph., l. 2, and in c. imperialem, §. callidis, de prohib. alien., feud. per Federic. Nor is re-delivery of possession required, because the virtue of the direct lord, remaining in the act by virtue of attraction, does this, as D. ad Trebell., l. si haeres, where it says, “the direct actions suffice.” And this is properly not a new dominion, but a consolidation: because direct dominion has the force of both direct and useful dominion; just as when emphyteusis ends, and when usufruct ends, and when the dowry reverts to the woman, so the main point, as C. de iure dot., l. in rebus, and especially in the church, which also acquires new dominions without tradition, as Extr. de consuet., c. ex parte; C. de sacr. sanct. eccles., l. ut inter divinum. Thus, when the action of the father and daughter is consolidated to one of them. For cession of right, which was with the deficient party, is not necessary; nor is any corporal tradition, as C. rem in praesenti, §. videamus. But when consent is not present in alienating, then alienation is not said to exist, neither in fact nor in name. So it is in the case at hand, for wherever a future condition is appended, which is properly a condition, until the condition is fulfilled, there is no consent, as D. de oblig. et act., l. non solum; D. de verb. sign., l. cedere diem; D. de cond. indebit., l. sub conditione, and l. qui promisit, as noted, C. de rerum perm., l. ex placito. Likewise, if a vassal sold without requesting the lord under the condition, if a ship comes from Asia: and the ship from Asia did not come, he does not lose the fief; because nothing was contracted, arg. D. si cert. pet., l. omnia, and l. perinde, and l. non omnis. Thus, therefore, in the case at hand, there is no difference in saying, if a ship comes from Asia, or if the lord consents. In both cases, the words and the intent of the contract fail when the condition fails, as D. de peric. et comm. rei vend., l. quod si pendente. For the condition existing in your act imposes the beginning of the cession of the day, as fully noted, C. de cad. toll., l. unica, §. 1, and D. de cond. et demonstr., l. Mevius. And in this a condition differs from a mode, as is fully read and noted, D. de cond. et demonstr., in the rubric. Someone says, although the contract is conditional, yet if the tradition is pure, alienation is said to proceed from a title, which is in Spec., as D. de solut., l. sub conditione; D. de usuc. pro dote, l. 1; D. de iure dot., l. sed nisi. And if you say, this tradition was not pure; because it was acted, as Bartolus, that he should hold and possess in the name of the said Gandulf and Valentina, I answer, tradition has three things in itself: namely, the effect of the contract, where the contract holds as to the transfer of dominion by transfer of the substance of possession, and a certain superficial act of a kind of donkey-like detention; and this act, contrary to law, and grave and damaging to the lord of the fief in fact, as intervened in the case proposed, and therefore the lord should not be defrauded with fictitious tergiversations, as said in §. callidis. For this donkey-like detention, the fact exists, which cannot be regarded as not done, as D. de captiv. et postlim. revert., l. in libello, §. factae. Nor does protestation help; because it sings well and scrapes badly, as noted in cle. gratiae, de rescript. What, then, shall we say? Certainly, by the act of the word, the fief did not fall into forfeiture; but by the act of fact, it seems that it fell into forfeiture, as D. de verb. sign., l. alienatum. Likewise, how can the seller be excused from fraud, who received the price? Certainly not at all, as l. fi., C. de praediis curial., lib. 10. Nor do fictions help to excuse excuses in sins; rather, he sins more heavily who defrauds the law than he who expressly acts against the law, as l. si libertus minorem, D. de iure patron. For the understanding of the foregoing, I form one question.

† If a vassal transfers a fief without title to the prejudice of his lord, whether he loses the fief by operation of law, or whether a judgment and the trial of the parties are indeed necessary. The rules in the matter of fiefs state that fraud must be proved before the parties, and that they themselves, by their sentence, must deprive the feudatory of the fief, and it does not open to the lord except by sentence. Therefore, although by alienation it reverts to the lord by operation of law, yet by fraud it does not revert by operation of law, but only by sentence. And just as the petition for inheritance is not open before the complaint of the inofficious will has been brought, as is fully read and noted in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. qui de officio, so too the fief is not open to the lord before the complaint of the vassal’s fault has been pronounced, as I prove fully below. And if it is asked, what is the reason for the difference, that by alienation it reverts to the lord by operation of law, but not by fault or fraud: a twofold reason is given. The first is, because the vassal, by alienating the fief, although in fact he makes himself alien to the fief, arg. D. de peculio legato, l. cum dominus, §. si, otherwise where he does not intend to alienate; for he does not alienate who merely loses possession, as in D. de alienatione iudicio mutata causa facta, l. non solum. The second reason is, because the felony of the alienator is purged by the law of the contract, and thus by the law of consent, as in D. locato conducto, l. quæro, §. inter locatorem, and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. qui res iam dictas; otherwise in the felony of a delict, because that is purged by a condition arising from custom. This condition must be pleaded, and a pronouncement made upon it; because the vassal ought not to lose the fief without certain and concurrent fault, and approval by the judgment of his court, as in c. 1, de feudo sine culpa non amittendo, and in c. 3, quo tempore miles investituram petere debeat.

† For when the question is one of fault between the lord and the vassal, the peers of the court ought to judge, not the lord himself, because he would be a judge in his own cause, as is read and noted in the Extravagantes, De iudicibus, chapter Certum; and in chapter 1, § Ad haec, in the title Hic finitur lex. And then the customs of the kingdom begin, since it is one thing to have been reversed, another to ought to be reversed, just as it is one thing to be free, another to be freed; and it is one thing to have been provided for, another to be provided for, as in the Digest, De iudicibus, law Qui se dicit. So it is in the present case: because before the thing is evicted from the feudatory, the fief is not opened to the lord; although it is most true that between the lord and the vassal there is no fraud, nor any evil. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the first creditor is to be preferred to the second in the debtor's assets acquired after both obligations: and what if the second obligation arises from the cause of a dowry. nu. 2.
