2. Whether one who denies an exposition may be prevented from invoking it to his own advantage.
3. Whether one who consents to the alienation of a certain thing, and thus cannot assign the hypothec thereon, is repelled by the exception of cedendarum actionum.
4. Whether one who denies that anything is owed to the plaintiff, and denies his hypothec, loses the benefit of the assignment of the hypothec.
5. If the first creditor has the right of sale, whether the buyer is bound to follow.
body: Lord Lanfranchus, and Boninus his son Parabola, and with the consent of his said father by public instrument, confessed that they had had and received in dowry from Lady Raysina, the betrothed and wife of the said Boninus, then legitimately betrothed with a ring there present, two hundred pounds of imperial currency. For which dowry the said Lord Lanfranchus and Boninus invested, in the name of pledge, and with the advice of the said Lady Raysina, present and receiving, all the goods which they had and would perpetually have. And they both promised jointly and severally with due renunciations: and they bound all their goods as pledge to the said Lady Raysina, stipulating and receiving, that they would restore the said dowry to the said Lady Raysina and her heirs upon the occurrence of the case of action. And so forth. These are the words of the dotal instrument. The said Lady Raysina died, leaving Antonio, her legitimate and natural son from the said marriage, and emancipated by the said Lord Lanfranchus, his grandfather. Therefore, the said Antonio, the son, is suing for the dowry of his mother against Titius, the possessor of the goods which belonged to the said Lord Lanfranchus, grandfather of the said Antonio and father-in-law of the said late Lady Raysina. This Titius accepted the judgment as possessor, and after the contestation of the lawsuit, being solemnly interrogated in court whether, at the time of the creation of the hypothec, he was an agent or possessor in the goods or domain of the debtor, he responded by oath that he does not believe it. Then the plaintiff proved that the thing was in the goods and domain of the debtor at the time of the hypothec, or afterwards: after the same plaintiff, having published the attestations, made his position, by which it was shown that it was proven; the defendant again responded by oath that he does not believe it. Now, however, this Titius, the possessor, produces certain instruments of a certain prior and older loan credit than the said dotal instrument, from which the said possessor had rights ceded by a certain debtor having an express general hypothec in the goods of the said Lord Lanfranchus, the debtor, from which instruments the said possessor wishes to defend himself. From the aforesaid, therefore, the following questions arise. First, whether the said Antonio, the son, suing for the right of the said dowry of his, having in the dotal instrument a general and express hypothec, is superior in right to the said Titius, the possessor, having prior rights ceded by a private creditor of a loan having an express and general hypothec both in the things which the debtor had at the time of the first obligation and the second, and afterwards, and in those things which he acquired after the second obligation of the said dowry. Second, whether the said Titius acquired. Second, whether the said Titius, the possessor, can from the aforesaid positions and proofs impugn the actions which he brought. I answer, by oath, that he does not believe that he can derive aid for his defense, since by the said Titius, the possessor, nothing is proven by which it appears that the thing claimed was at any time in the goods and domain of the debtor against whom he has ceded rights. Third, because the same Antonio possesses with title. For as heir of one house, which was of the aforementioned Lord Lanfranchus, his grandfather and debtor, for the dowry, and also consented to the alienation of a certain fund which was of the said Lord Lanfranchus, the debtor, he renounced in the hands of the buyer the right pertaining to him in the said fund. And to the same Antonio, the agnates are opposed by Titius, the possessor, by the exception of cession of actions. First, because the plaintiff himself possesses of the goods of the debtor, and thus he would make a cession against himself. Second, because by consent to alienation and by renunciations made beforehand he worsened his rights, nor could he cede against the said fund: intimating that it is not sufficient for the plaintiff to cede only personal actions to the possessor, but rather he is bound to cede also real actions not worsened. Hence, concerning this, it is asked what the form of law requires. And if from the aforesaid theme other doubts can be gathered, let them be subtly observed, although concerning the decisions of the aforesaid many things are treated by the glossators and doctors; nevertheless, the decision ordered by reasons of the Most Serene Father and Lord Baldus, with his seal, is humbly requested.

† As to the first point, it is established that, according to the common law, the first creditor is preferred in full with respect to assets acquired before the second obligation, even if the second obligation arises from the cause of a dowry, since the prior creditor has an express hypothec, as is fully read and noted in C. qui potior sit in pignoribus habendis, l. assiduis, in the major gloss. But if the assets were acquired after both obligations, that is, the first and the second, then there is a question, for the gloss in l. si is qui, ff. de iure fisci, states that in subsequently acquired assets both are equal, which is understood if both bring action or both possess. But if one possesses, the nature of priority is such that the possessor is preferred. Others say, without distinction, that he is preferred who sued on the pledge in all assets whenever acquired, whether they were acquired from a cause that fakes retroactivity or from one entirely new, by l. hac edictali, § in his, C. de secundis nuptiis; and thus, by disputing, la. de Are. held, by l. si, C. qui potior sit in pignoribus habendis.

But these statements are true, unless the older creditor arises from a non-privileged cause, while the later one arises from a privileged cause, such as a dowry; for then, with respect to assets acquired subsequently, the dowry cause prevails. For when the birth of the hypothec concurs at the same time, the privileged party must be preferred over the non-privileged party, as is clear from the notes in the aforementioned law *finis*. And therefore, without doubt, the cause of the dowry prevails. Argument: Codex, *De iure dotium*, law *In rebus*. It supports what is noted by Dy. in chapter *Qui prior* and in law *Privilegia*, with the *si*. But one thing makes me doubt, because the dowry was acknowledged by confession, and it does not appear that it was paid out. For in a dowry acknowledged by confession, privileges do not apply; but true payment must be proven, as noted in the small gloss in the aforementioned law *Assiduis*. And this gloss is quite singular in itself, although it is commonly cited. But to this it is answered that, according to statutes and local customs, such instruments are held as truth when the usual renunciations are contained therein; as noted in law *I*, Codex, *De dote caut.*, *Nonnulla*. This question does not arise if payment made in the instrument were apparent. What if it does not appear at what time the goods were acquired? I answer that the dowry is preferred by virtue of the privilege of the dowry, not by virtue of temporal priority in certainty; because an uncertain time has no priority; as in Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *In ambiguis pro dotibus*. And add here what is noted by Bart. in the aforementioned law *Si is, qui*.

† On the second point, it seems one should first say that, although the defendant denied the plaintiff’s hypothec, he may nevertheless rely on his own prior hypothec, by virtue of which he can bring an action, as in D. de except. rei iud. l. duobus and l. ex sextante § latinus. Therefore, all the more so, he may raise an exception if he is in possession: as in D. de superficie l. 1 § quod ait and in l. regula dolo facit. To the contrary, the case appears to be this: since he denied the right from which his own hypothec derives its origin, he ought first to transfer possession to the adversary as a penalty for his falsehood, as in Auth. de trien. et semis § pe. Moreover, he not only denied the right but also the proof, and from denied proof one cannot defend oneself, having denied it under oath against calumny. Hence, by asserting the opposite, he seems to be acting calumniously with regard to his own opinion, and therefore the judge ought ex officio to reject him. Arg. C. de fide instr. l. 3; C. de testi. l. si quis testamentis. There is also another doubt here: it is alleged that the hypothecary or personal action has ceased, which I do not care to address at present. Nevertheless, notwithstanding the aforesaid, it seems one should say that the benefit of cession is available even to one who has joined issue, denied, and made a conjunction; and even after judgment: as in D. de leg. 1 l. si res obligata; D. de solut. l. Stichum § si mandato; D. qui pot. in pig. hab. l. mulier; and D. qui mod. pign. vel hyp. sol. l. Paulus § qui pignoris, provided that otherwise the case for cession subsists, and the benefit of cession is rather a certain burden attached to the claimant, to whom satisfaction is made, than a privilege of the defendant. The second point is,

Whether he who consents to the alienation of a certain thing, and thus cannot cede the hypothecary rights in that thing, is repelled by the exception of ceded rights. And it seems that he is: because by his own act he has caused it that he cannot cede; and therefore he ought to impute this to himself, as stated in the aforementioned §. si mandatum. To the contrary, it seems from the text of the Codex, Ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. iubemus, and thus it is determined there by Cynus. And this is more correctly applicable when he renounced by bad faith against the possessor, knowing that he ought to cede rights to him by bringing a hypothecary action against him. For then perhaps he is repelled: because fraud and the act of one ought not to harm another, as argued from the Digest, De iure et facti ignorantia, l. iniquissimum.

A third doubt arises here regarding certain possessions which this plaintiff possesses: whether, if he wishes to be paid, he ought to transfer possession to the payer. And it seems that he ought, for the law provides that the plaintiff bringing a hypothecary action, if he is paid, ought to cede to the debtor all the pledges which he holds on account of the same debt which has been paid; just as we say in the case of one who sues a guarantor, who then ought to cede the pledges, as stated in the Digest, De negotiis gestis, l. fideiussores; and in the Codex, De solutionibus, l. cum eorum. So, if in these possessions he has a cause solely of the credit which is paid to him, then he ought to cede possession. Or if he has another external cause by which he justly detains them, then he is not bound to cede possession; because such a cause is weakened by the obligation, as argued from the Digest, De diversis temporum praescriptionibus, l. an vitium, §. ex facto; and from the Digest, De acquisitione possessionis, l. 3, §. ex plurimis.

On the third point, two doubts occur: the first is,

Whether he who denies that anything is owed to the plaintiff, and denies his hypothec, loses the benefit of ceding the hypothec. And the argument is that he does: because he denied that which is of the substance of his benefit. And benefits are easily lost on account of falsehood, as in that which is the cause of the benefit: as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si dubitetur, § 1; and D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. hereditatis, § fin.; and D. de re iudicata, l. sed hoc ita. Although these authorities speak of one who denies his own act, nevertheless in our case the act of the author is denied. And it supports this: C. de non numerata pecunia, auth. contra qui propriam.

† If the first creditor had the right to sell, and sold correctly and properly, the buyer is secure. But if he did not have the right to sell to others, nevertheless he could sell to himself and assign the rights for defense. And in this case, the assignment is not presumed to be simulated. C. mandati. l. per diuersas. §. exce. And therefore, pro rata, as the right was assigned, the buyer can defend himself; and because the proportion is uncertain, as l. fi. ff. de adi. le. declares, it will be determined in execution by appraisers appointed for this purpose: as l. 1. C. de vsu. et fruc. legatorum, et fideiussorum. In the meantime, on account of the uncertain part, the whole will be retained, ar. ff. quorum legatorum. l. 1. §. rediguntur. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made to several minors under the age of puberty takes effect in the share of the one who dies during the period of minority, or only upon the death of all of them.
body: It must be premised

† It is evident that the pupillary substitution, which was made in favor of the said daughters, was made in the following terms, namely: “and if any of the said daughters should die in pupillary age, etc.” By these words, it is understood that a singular substitution was made, not a universal one, nor a collective universal one. And therefore, whenever one dies in pupillary age, whether she be the first, the middle, or the last, she has no pupillary substitute who excludes the mother and the sister of the pupill, as is clear. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. vel singulis. It would be otherwise if the substitution had been made by collective or universal names, such as “if both,” “if all,” or indefinitely, such as “if they should die.” For then the pupillary substitute would not be admitted upon the death of any of the aforementioned pupills, as C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. pen. and there fully on the matter, n. and more fully by Bartolus, D. ad Trebellianum, l. haeres des mei, §. cum ita; and D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. pater filiam, §. duobus; and it is touched upon in D. de in iusto testamento, l. si ego. And therefore, according to what is proposed, the pupillary substitutes succeed to the four and five daughters who died in pupillary age. And because the pupillary substitution is express, the mother and the surviving sister are excluded: as C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. precibus; and D. eodem, l. Lucius, with its material. And this is supported by the fact that the testator used the word “ei” [to him/her], which is of the singular number, and therefore a singular substitution is preferred, as D. ad Trebellianum, l. Iulius fēbus. The objection from D. de re iudicata, l. si is, qui ducenta, §. si, does not hold, because there another case is presented, namely, when the disjunctive is proven negative, as is clear in that law, §. cum ita; and noted in c. in plerisque, de electione, in the Clementines.

However, doubt may be raised: because finally there is no male substitute existing for her; and also he did not repeat those words, “if another should die in pupillary age.” Hence it seems that in this case the substitution should be interpreted as oblique, at least in favor of the mother and sisters, as noted in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. Centurio; and the aforementioned l. precibus; and C. de testamento militis, l. in testamento. But to this it is answered that the whole is one construction of the same reason joined together, and therefore those words, “in pupillary age,” are understood to be repeated in the connected substitution, as in c. si pater, de testibus, lib. 6. It would be otherwise if the sentences, i.e., the substitutions, had been entirely different: for then each substitution would be considered for itself, and the last one made by a common word would be considered, in favor of the mother and sisters, as a fideicommissary substitution. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What those words mean, which are placed in public auctions, that it shall be given to the higher bidder: and who is said to bid higher.
body: Fact. The case on which the opinion is requested is presupposed as follows. The tax on dyed cloth in the city of Pesaro, which begins in the month of June, by municipal law or custom, begins to be put up for auction in the preceding month of November, and thus the bidding commences for four or five months before the tax begins. Now it happens that in the book of auctions of the commune of Pesaro is found written in the form set out below, namely: 1381. The tax on dyed cloth, which begins on the first day of June 1381, was auctioned in the Palace of the Commune of Pesaro on the fifth day of November 1381, by the official. And it was placed under auction, as will be declared below. James Peter of Ancona for one thousand pounds, and above that, below for the pound, let him have who bids more. Andrew John of Fermo on the same day offered one thousand and one hundred pounds, to whom the auction was awarded, i.e., one solidus for the pound, as was promised to him. Above that, let him have who bids more, two solidi for the pound. No one bids. Then the official says, above that, let the bidder have three solidi for the pound. The aforementioned James Peter promised one thousand two hundred pounds. Above that, four solidi for the pound. The aforementioned James on the said day promised one thousand three hundred pounds. Tickets were made of the aforementioned auctions for the said James, which he presented to the depositary. The aforementioned James on the eighteenth day of the month of February 1381 promised to take the said tax at the said auction, i.e., at the rate of four solidi for one thousand five hundred pounds. And to explain certain things according to the common usage of Pesaro, when in the first writing of the book it is said, without auction, it is to be understood that the first bidder is not to receive anything up to that quantity for the pound. For the official causes it to be proclaimed in the Palace, that whoever wishes to bid on the tax on dyed cloth, let him come forward, and then the first appeared, namely the one named, and promised only, as above. The official, however, seeing that no one else promised more, nevertheless said to the crier, say that whoever bids above one thousand shall have one solidus for the pound. And so for each, as above. This solidus, which is given, is called the auction increment, as if this were given because he bids more, i.e., outbids. Furthermore, it is presupposed that from this auction increment, i.e., solidus, a ticket is made for the bidder, or outbidder, by the official appointed, which they carry to the depositary, who has to pay the debts of the commune. Then I presuppose that the said tax was not auctioned with these words: and it shall be given to the higher offeror; but only it was said, whoever wishes to bid, let him come. Then it was promised, as appears above from the discretion of the book. These things being thus presupposed, it is found that the aforementioned James, the last bidder, departed from Pesaro as a guest in the month of April. The official in charge of the auctions entirely wishes that the aforementioned Andrew take the tax in the month of May. Andrew says that he is not bound because of the subsequent bids in the form written above. And thus the second bid was accepted. Now it is asked, whether the said Andrew is bound to receive the said tax. As is subtly alleged, the words used by the official placed in charge of the auction must be considered.

For if the words of the herald state that the work shall be awarded to the highest bidder, and a certain term has been set, and that term has elapsed, so that the prescribed times do not permit further bidding, then it is certain that it shall be awarded to him who offered more, provided that what is to be auctioned and fixed in the bidding has been accepted by the official. But if he has not been accepted, because perhaps he was not suitable, the first bidder is not released. Argument: Digest, *De in diem addendo*, l. *Ubi autem*, § *Idem ait*. The same applies if the times allow for those prescribed by common law or municipal law. For in the meantime a better bidder may be admitted, and the contract established with him. But if no further bidder appears, it remains with him who was accepted. For he seems sufficiently suitable who has been approved and admitted as suitable: as in Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, l. *Qui satisdare*; and Digest, *Mandati*, l. *Inter causas*, § *Absesse*. Therefore, that which was done last prevails, argument: Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, l. *Si quis ante*; and Code, *De pactis*, l. *Pacta novissima*. And the prior bidder is released by the novation of the person and the contract; rather, more correctly, he did not effectively fall into the obligation which from the beginning was in suspense. Notwithstanding Digest, *De in diem addendo*, l. 2, because there the contract was not in suspense, but its resolution; or, if we say that an obligation was contracted, we say that it was contracted in an unbinding and revocable manner. And so I say. On this matter, fully noted in the text and gloss, and by Bartolus, subtly alleged by you in l. *Si tempora*, Code, *De fidei instrumentis et iure hastae fisci*, lib. 10. Since therefore in the case at hand it appears that the last bidder was admitted and accepted, and the bidding was confiscated to him, there is no doubt that he has succeeded in the obligation, and the first is exempt. Here it must be considered that those words, “he who auctions for a thousand, will have one solidus for the pound,” import that it shall be given to the highest bidder. For since a premium is given, a burden is also seen to be imposed. Argument: Code, *De furtis*, l. *Manifestissimi*, § *Sed cum in secunda*; and Digest, *De legatis 2*, l. *Sed in duobus*; and Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, l. *Nonnunquam*. Since therefore a transfer of the contract has taken place, the first promisor is released, or did not fall into obligation, as I said. To this effect: Digest, *De praetorio stipendio*, l. *Valerianus*; and Code, *Locati conducti*, l. *Si cum Hermes*; and Digest, *Locati conducti*, l. *Si cum plures*, § *Legem dictam*; and argument: Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, l. *Si stipulatus est opus in ratione litterae*. And if the official contracted badly, it is his peril, and not that of him who first offered, whose opposition was not accepted, as in Digest, *Si certum petatur*, l. *Periculum*; and l. *Cum quaeritur*, Digest, *De administratione tutorum*. And so I say, and I, Baldus, advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is to be admitted, or preferred, in the succession to a paternal or ancient fief.
2. A donation, or alienation, even by will, is not valid with respect to a fief; but the nearer heir is admitted.
body: Brothers

The sons of predeceased brothers succeed in the paternal fief, whether ancient or not; then, more distant agnates succeed according to the order of degrees, just as in other goods regarding the degrees of succession to a fief. C. 1, § His vero deficientibus. Nor does a testamentary disposition have effect in fiefs, for the text states: "no disposition of the deceased having effect in the fief." De successione feudorum, C. 1, 2 responso.

† Moreover, a donation is in no way valid to the prejudice of agnates. The text states: “He cannot donate or judge for money.” How a fief could formerly be alienated is set forth in c. 1, § Donare, *De prohibitione alienationis*, in the Sextus, or through Lotharius, c. 1. Therefore, it seems to be said that this fief pertains to the nearest relative, as in c. 1, *De naturali successione feudorum*, col. 10, where it is stated: “and this is what is said to pertain to the nearest relatives.” For the reason of order requires that the nearer relative be preferred, as in the Authentica *Post fratres fratrumque filios*, C. *De legitimis heredibus*. Nor do I find that this succession departs from the nature of degrees; and therefore we may use the common law therein, as in c. *Obertus*, § *Strenuus*, *De feudorum cognitione*, col. 10. And this is what Jacobus de Belvisis says in the aforementioned title *De naturali successione feudorum*, on the word “proximiores.” However, he does not say that all should succeed together; but those who are nearer in degree among them, or he who holds the nearer degree, ought to be preferred, according to Jacobus de Belvisis. Therefore, Gabriel is stronger than Bartholomew in feudal matters. But in other goods, the donation is valid, and the will is valid, and both are to be observed, *Extra*, *De testamento*, c. *Raymundus*, and l. 1, C. *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, with its companions. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A judgment rendered against a filiusfamilias is void by operation of law if the father does not consent.
1. A statute prohibiting the assertion of nullity is to be understood as applying to persons who are legally capable.
body: In deciding

† We must state, as the glossa in the aforementioned § necessitate, 3, l. cum non solum, C. de bonis quae libera sunt, holds: that the judgment mentioned is null by operation of law itself. Nor is it regarded as a father’s act in this case, because it deals with adventitious property, as in c. si annum, extra de iudiciis, lib. 6. Nor otherwise, etc. The execution of a legitimate judgment, if less than fully carried out by the judge, ought to be revoked to the extent that it proceeded in fact. ff. de re iudicata, l. si cum nulla.

† A statute that precludes the way of alleging nullity is to be understood as applying to persons who are capable. L. ut gradatim, §. et si lege, De minoribus et hominibus. Nor is the son of a family said to be negligent, because he who can be repelled by an exception is not considered negligent. FF. De negotiorum gestorum, L. si pupilli, §. item quaeritur; L. 1, in fine, FF. De annali exceptione. And he who is not negligent is not prejudiced by the passage of time, as noted in the Authenticum, De appellationibus, Collatio 8, after the principal paragraph. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It treats of understanding. c. 1. de despon. impub. lib. 6.
2. Whether a statute speaking of a wife by the word "copulated" is to be understood as referring to a minor.
body: Shall I begin? Add also whether there was a marriage between the lord Christophorus and the girl, or not.

† And it is certain that from the beginning it was not prohibited by the age of the girl. Therefore, if it did take effect, it must have done so through convalescence. Whether, therefore, it convalesced through the acts alleged by Dr. Christopher concerning carnal copulation is a point of law rather than of fact, namely, whether the alleged acts are sufficient, assuming that they were proven, presupposing the absence of Dr. Christopher during the girl’s adolescence. And regarding this question, there is a case in c. 1, *extra de desponsatione impuberum*, lib. 6, through all the allegations cited. Hence, in order to see on which side the case lies, it must be considered that that chapter speaks of public convalescence; for first it speaks of the convalescence of betrothals, which from the beginning did not hold due to infantile age being prohibitive, up to the words “ideo quoque.” Second, it speaks of the convalescence of marriage, which from the beginning did not hold because pupillary age did not permit it, although it did permit future betrothals, up to the words “praedictus tamen.” It therefore says that betrothals convalesce through cohabitation, in the word “pro cohabitatione,” or otherwise by word or deed of the parties themselves, if it clearly appears from their words or deeds that they are the same persons, not different persons. And yet above it had said that one was from the beginning older than an infant, and it says “of both of them,” not “of the infant, however.” Now it follows in the text “idem quoque,” and it makes a transition to those older than infancy, and it says “idem quoque,” i.e., “in the same manner also,” namely, as regards the convalescence of marriage, the same mode is to be observed, except that one mode is added, namely, carnal copulation. Therefore, marriage, which from the beginning was not marriage due to prohibitive age, convalesces through subsequent carnal copulation. Likewise, through cohabitation, or otherwise by word or deed of the parties, as it had said above, if it appears that there is a perseverance of will, and it repeats in substance the same speech, when it says “the contracting parties themselves.” Therefore, it must appear that there is a new, persevering consent of both, because it says “of them,” and not from light presumptions, but from evident deeds between themselves, or words spoken to one another. For if one does or says something while the other is absent and ignorant, since one alone, just as he does not make a marriage exist, so also does he not give it convalescence: as C. *de nuptiis*, l. *si ut proponis*. Nor can it be said that it speaks there only of the case when both were impubes, because it says “postquam,” i.e., “after,” and thus new signs of consent are necessary. Moreover, it is one thing to say “I do,” another to say “I will,” as is noted in C. *de senatusconsultis et interdictis omnium iudiciorum*, l. *cum iudex eos ad pubertatis tempora pervenisse*. Because these words were uttered so as to comprehend both cases permitted above in brief words and leave neither untouched. Otherwise, we must distinguish and say “him” or “them,” as in ff. *ad Trebellianum*, l. *Iulianus Phœbus*. Furthermore, that this is the intention of the letter appears from the same letter, which says that the interpretation of law is that future betrothals are equivalent, therefore by words of the future tense, i.e., “I will take you as wife when time permits, and you me.” Thus, the words are resolved. But by such words, one never arrives at marriage through the act of only one, but of both, even if they were pronounced between impubes with an oath: C. *de sponsalibus*, l. 1; *extra de sponsalibus*, c. *praeterea*. And if it is said that the older party must consent, I concede that he is obliged to do so, but he has not yet done so; hence, the matrimonial bond and the conjugal tie were not born. For there are two obligations: one, which is called the matrimonial bond; the other, which is called the personal obligation to contract. The first is effective and real, inducing right by law; the second is not, as appears expressly from what is read and noted in c. *de illis*, § *si*, and 30 q. 2, c. *si quis ingenuus*, and there noted. And thus I have said, therefore the acts must be mutual, so that they may seem to deliver themselves to one another, and as if by delivery the real right of marriage is acquired, as we say in the matter of solemn and non-solemn vows. Therefore, marriage was not contracted in our case, nor ratified by convalescence; because it could not convalesce by the word of only one. And if Dr. Christopher, things being thus, had obtained some ecclesiastical benefice, or taken a second wife, it would have been valid; although penance according to canon law should be enjoined upon him for broken faith. Therefore, it is true that she was not joined by marriage; and thus she ought not to gain the dowry: as l. *si extraneus*, ff. *de conditione ob causam*; ff. *solutis matrimonii*, l. *si ante*; ff. *de iure dotium*, l. *fructus*; ff. *de doli exceptione*, l. *pater*. Moreover, in this case, much was most subtly alleged for and against, and many matters were turned over regarding the understanding of the statute, namely, how the word is to be understood

† joined: and whether the statute has application in the marriage of a minor: because Bartolus says that it does not, in l. si constante. Others say the contrary: because it is an alienation by law, and she married a worthy person: as I said above regarding the word "joined matrimonially." They say that, with regard to the dowry profit, it is understood as a deduction, especially according to common usage of speech: although, with regard to the substance of the matrimonial bond, it is understood by consent alone. And so many words were said most subtly, that it would be no small book. I go to the root: because it does not seem to me that the marriage is established. And thus I advise, without prejudice to the award, to which I do not intend to derogate, if it was valid, and valid irrevocably: otherwise the award does not make her a wife: because, according to what is alleged, no one is understood to be subject to reform, which I have said, that in cohabitation lies the weight of marriage. But among other things, the weight of tacit and real testimony stands. Your brother Baldus of Perugia holds thus, and advised under the sign of Papiæ, 17 July, concerning expenses of litigation not to be recovered. C. de re iudicata, l. generaliter, §. 1, in the gloss. Reverend lady, because the parties did not leave me the statute on compromise, but rather took it away, therefore I wrote under a condition: but, mindful of the statute from those found later, I say that the said award can and must be reduced to the discretion of a good man as being unjust. And finally I say that Lord Christopher has no right in this case according to the acts and proofs. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How is marriage proved both by canon and civil law? And what is required in it.
2. If a father names a certain son in his will, is he thereby to be judged legitimate? And whether such a person succeeds to a fief. No. 3.
body: In this case, in which the question is raised, first regard must be had to the status, namely, to legitimacy. Secondly, to the goods, and first to the allods, or to the properties; secondly, to the fiefs.

† Regarding the first point, it must be known that, according to the civil law, in the case of a free woman taken into a house, a marriage is presumed to exist in due order and with the burden of nuptial obligations, unless a protestation to the contrary intervenes: as stated in D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. in libera; D. de concubinis, l. in concubinatu. For the intention and will are declared by the very act itself, and these alone constitute the substance of marriage, as argued in C. de institutione et substantia matrimonii, l. reprehendenda. And from the very conferral of honor, it is determined whether she is a wife or a concubine: D. de lege tertia, l. item in legato, §. parvi. But according to canon law, words expressing present consent must intervene; otherwise, there is no marriage, if the contracting parties can be heard. Extra, de praescriptionibus, c. illud; and see the note in l. cum notissimi, in principio, de praescriptionibus, 30 annorum. Cynus says that in successions, civil law must be observed, as he notes in C. de nuptiis, l. si vicinis. For successions are granted by civil law; therefore, in the forum of Caesar, civil law must be observed, as argued in Extra, de appellationibus, c. si duobus, §. j. But certainly, by Auth. qui modo nuptias efficiunt, §. quandocunque, col. 6, it is determined that between those who hold the middle status, i.e., from the illustrious down to plebeians of lower condition, exclusively, proof by writing is required; but we do not use that law, as noted there. Therefore, recourse must be had to probable presumptions according to civil law. I do not think that one should depart from the judgment of the Church in this matter, whatever Cynus may say, as in Extra, de ordine cognitionis, c. tua; and in c. lator, qui sint legitimi. The judgment of the Church, however, rests well on facts and signs, where there are no witnesses who were present at the contradiction of the marriage; and especially where the issue is not about the bond of marriage, but about the legitimation of children, as noted by Innocentius in c. ex parte, de restitutione spoliorum; and by Archidiaconus, 30 q. 5, c. feminae. For if from the beginning a woman was brought into the house, and was taken, treated, and called as a wife; and publicly wore a ring as a wife; then from these very things and signs we have evidence of marriage. Extra, de probationibus, c. per tuas; D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. mulierem. And a marriage, which ought to be fully proved, as noted in l. 1, §. si ea, D. de venditionibus in possessione mitium, is proved by the aforementioned modes according to Innocentius. But if she was not called a wife, nor did she wear a ring, she is presumed to be a concubine: by the argument from customs or habits; and by the aforementioned c. illud, de praebendis, cum si. It remains to see,

† If a father, in his will, named his son but did not add the word "natural," whether from this he should be judged to be born legitimate or legitimate. And there is no true doubt about this: because it is a case of law. See in the Authentica "Item si quis," Codex, De naturalibus liberis, where it is said that one having natural children from a woman who could have been his wife, naming them sons in his will, such sons will be legitimate and successors. Which Bartolus in one of his consilia thus explains, saying that "who could have been his wife" means: by nature; because living according to law; because not prohibited in fact; because not absent, and according to good morals, having regard to the quality of the persons. Digest, Qui et a quibus, Law "Si rogatus," Section "Matrimonii." From this is taken this word "could." Digest, De verborum significatione, Law "Nepos Proculo." I believe that he speaks of potentiality, however, for good morals are never in a concubine. Also, that the woman then lives or is present is a trick: for even she being dead and absent, they could be legitimated by the father's word; as in the Authentica "Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui," Section "Illud." Coming therefore to the points formed, there is no doubt that the will is valid as to allodial property, same title, Section "Si vero filius."

† What about the fief? I answer that this is a paternal fief, and illegitimate children do not succeed to it, nor does this legitimation operate in any way to the prejudice of the agnates, as in the chapter *Naturales filii*. And rightly so, because they are not recognized by them, as in the aforementioned Authority, § *Et generaliter*; nor are they properly legitimate, except by a certain imagination, that is, a fiction, which has no place in fiefs. Moreover, the father cannot make a will regarding the fief, because he would be disposing of the right of a third party, c. 1, *De successionibus feudorum*, col. 10. Hence, it is necessary that this son be legitimated by the Emperor with respect to this fief, with mention made of the agnates; otherwise, the rescript would not be valid. But if it is a new fief, let the father come to an agreement with the lord and have the son invested. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person who, in a written instrument, confesses to having received and accepted a certain sum of money, not in expectation of a future payment, but in truth, thereby waiving the exception of non-numerated pecunia: may he subsequently raise a complaint of non-numerated pecunia?
2. A statute provides that a dowried woman shall be certain. What if, at the time of the testator’s death, she is not dowried, but is endowed with a dowry afterwards?
body: A certain girl, Leoneta, confessed that she had received and taken from a certain uncle of hers 300 gold florins on account of a loan, asserting that she did not make this confession in hope of a future payment. And she renounced the exception of non-numerated pecuniary sum. Then, after the uncle died within two years, she brought forward the complaint of non-numerated pecuniary sum against the heirs of the uncle, and requested that the aforementioned citation be restored to her. On the other side it was opposed that the aforementioned caution was solemn, and that the aforementioned doubt prevailed, whence the said Leoneta was bound to pay the said doubtful sum. Then the said Leoneta proved by a notary and witnesses of the instrument that at the time the instrument was drawn up no money intervened, nor any payment. It is also said on behalf of the said Leoneta that the said renunciation was not valid, since a woman does not know what the said renunciation imports, and she was not afterwards confirmed in it. But on the other side it seems that the said confession was made for a just cause: because the said uncle had paid the said quantity for the dowry of the said Leoneta, which could be converted by stipulation into a loan: as in C. si certum petatur, l. si ex pretio. But on behalf of the said Leoneta it is denied, and the instrument of loan does not refer to these matters. Now the question is, what is the law.

And as is well known, there are three opinions on this matter. One opinion is that of the gloss, which holds that a person who has renounced the exception of non-numeration of money may nevertheless bring this complaint within two years, provided that he proves that the money was not numerated. For this renunciation must have some effect; it therefore operates to shift the burden of proof onto the renouncing party. This is the opinion of the glossator, which is held by certain modern jurists. For one can tacitly renounce the exception of non-numeration of money by the lapse of two years; therefore, one can also do so expressly.

Another opinion is that, since the renunciation of the exception of non-numeration of money is contained in a public instrument, the instrument must be upheld, and the exception cannot be raised. For by asserting that he confessed not in hope of future payment, one must stand by his own words against himself, as in *l. cum precibus*, *De probationibus*. This is the opinion of Petrus; indeed, it is the opinion of Accursius in *l. 1*, *Codex*, *De dote causa non numerata*. Otherwise, as the gloss there says, the whole world would be mistaken; for by custom, such instruments are everywhere considered valid, as the gloss there states.

The third opinion is that of the moderns, who say that this renunciation is understood to have been made in hope of future payment, as in *l. si*, *Codex*, *De non numerata pecunia*, and that it proceeds with the same facility as a confession. In support of this opinion is *l. ultima*, *Digestum*, *De constituta pecunia*. Moreover, he who confesses that he had, received, and still has the money in his possession, by that very act renounces the exception of non-numeration of money. And yet the law provides that he retains the exception, as in *l. et nota*, *Digestum*, *De solutionibus*, and *l. si ex pluribus*. And although this seems contrary to the tenor of the instrument, nevertheless that tenor contains a tacit condition, as in *Digestum*, *Locatio conductio*, *l. quaero*, § *inter locatorem*.

Furthermore, we say that there are three types of loan: namely, natural, and civil, to which nature cooperates; and civil, to which the passage of two years cooperates. We do not add a fourth loan, namely, civil, to which renunciation cooperates. Since this fourth loan is not found in the law, we should not superstitiously invent it, as in *Digestum*, *De acquisitione et obligatione*, *l. obligationum fere*, § *placet*, and *l. 2*, § *verbis*, *Digestum*, *Si certum petatur*. Moreover, from a renunciation does not arise a certain action, nor is it effectively born before two years; therefore, it cannot be brought. Furthermore, before two years, a confession is in suspense; therefore, the renunciation, which is its accessory.

In our case: because the renunciation was made by a woman in the instrument itself, and with the same fragility as a confession, I think that the woman should be aided, and judgment should be given in her favor in the said complaint, unless a statute or custom were otherwise. Or, if we wish to hold the opinion which places the burden of proof on the complainant, and does not distinguish between male and female, nevertheless I say that this Leoneta is understood to have proved the negative, insofar as it is possible to prove it. For it would be foolish to say that one is bound to prove a negative that is impossible to prove. It is therefore sufficient to prove that at the time of the alleged payment, no numeration took place; for to prove that money was never numerated is impossible, unless by the confession of the adversary, as in *Digestum*, *De probationibus*, *l. actor*, and *De non numerata pecunia*, *l. asseueratio*.

And in this respect, a loan differs from other contracts, which are not accustomed to be celebrated and frequently entered into in hope of future payment, as in *Digestum*, *Depositum*, *l. publicus*, § *si*, and *Digestum*, *De institoria*, *l. Lucius*, and in the *Authenticum*, *De fideiussoribus*, § *pecunia*.

Concluding this point, I say that Lady Leoneta has the right; because there was no other substance of obligation related to the stipulation, as appears from the testimony of the witnesses. However, the right of the heirs of the uncle is reserved, if he paid anything for the said Lady Leoneta as her manager of affairs, which he may recover by the action of management of affairs, as in *Digestum*, *De compensatione*, *l. quod in diem*, § *si*, and *Digestum*, *De pactis dotalibus*, *l. Beblius Marcellus*. Now I come to the second point,

† A statute provides that a woman endowed to certain persons shall not succeed. Now, a certain woman was not endowed at the time of her father’s death, but was endowed afterwards. The question is whether she succeeds. It appears that she does not, because the statute makes no distinction as to time, nor ought we to make one, as in L. in venditione, §. de tempore, D. de bonis auctoris iudicis possessoris. I hold the contrary by a rule of law. For when succession intestate is in question, the condition of the successor is examined at the time the inheritance is conferred, as in Inst. de legatis, §. proximus. But this Leoneta was capable of succeeding; indeed, by virtue of her existence as an heir, she succeeds to her father; therefore she cannot cease to be an heir, according to that rule of law: he who once is an heir, is always an heir; as in D. de minoribus, L. et si sine, §. sed quod Papinianus, and D. de hereditatibus institutis, L. aliquo casu. To this effect is what is noted in D. de libellis et postulationibus, L. Gallus, §. et quid si tamen. And thus, on this point, I advise in favor of Leoneta, saving the judgment of the more learned, as in D. qui potior in pignore habeantur, L. Claudius Felix.

Having written this opinion, I reviewed the tenor of the loan instrument and weighed those words: “and in truth acknowledged.” I considered whether, by that word “in truth,” anything could be changed in the substance of the said opinion. And briefly I say that it cannot; because those words “in truth” are terminated by the word “acknowledged,” so that these words refer only to the confession itself and to the supports of the confession, insofar as the confession could be strengthened by bare words. Nevertheless, no truth can be proved except concerning those matters which occurred at the place and time of the execution of the instrument. Nor could he be asked about any other truth to which he himself was not present, and which lacks a date and consuls, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, de probationibus, cap. Quoniam contra falsum.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the consent of both the lord and the agnates is necessary in the alienation of a fief, and when.
2. Whether a father may prefer one of his sons over the others in the succession to a fief.
body: That

† The phrase “with the consent of the lord of the fief, the alienation is valid” must be understood as follows: if the fief is new, in which agnates do not succeed. But if it is paternal, the consent of the agnates is also necessary; however, here one must distinguish. Either the alienation is made to an outsider, or to another agnate. In the first case, the consent of the agnates is required according to all authorities; the same applies if they remain silent for a year from the day of knowledge, as in c. Titius, si de feudo vassalli feudum contrauerit, col. 10. In the second case, there are differing opinions. For some say that the alienation is valid by its own force of law, because it is not contrary to the nature of the fief if the fief is ambulatory from one to another; indeed, this seems tacitly permitted. ff. de legibus, l. pater, § 15, libertis; C. de fideiussoribus, l. voluntas; C. de secundis nuptiis feminarum, § si. Thus also the metropolis permitted its inhabitants to alienate among themselves, and not among others, as in C. non licere habitatoribus metropolis, l. 1; C. de iure fisci, l. certa forma. For they can also divide among themselves, and what arises from the division is stable until he to whom it falls dies without an heir, as noted in C. familiae erciscundae, l. si familiae, col. 10, si de feudo vassalli feudum contrauerit, c. omnes filii. And this is seen as tacitly permitted from the beginning itself, and agnates can alienate among themselves. And this is held by Bartolus, ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si uni. And although he speaks of emphyteusis, the same reason applies to a fief. Hence he cites col. 10, de prohibita alienatione feudi, § pater; C. de impositione lucrorum descriptorum, l. 1; and he holds the same, ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, § duo fratres. And it seems expressed in the aforementioned c. Titius.

But the masters in the science of fiefs, which is a certain science in itself, say that if one who has no heir has several agnates, and grants or sells to one in fraud of the other agnates, i.e., to the damage and detriment of their succession—for the ancients understood fraud as damage—that may be revoked by the other agnates. Arg. ff. quae in fraudem creditorum, l. ait praetor, § sciendum; in Auth. de non eligendo secundum nubentem, § prospeximus; and d. § Titius. It is true that Laude de Domino, in his laudable Summa, does not stand firm on this point, and alleges to the contrary from de impuberibus and others under l. humanitatis, ff. de assignandis litiibus, l. 1. Nor can a final decision of the question be gathered from his words, as I have said. There is no doubt that if the alienation degenerated from the nature of the fief, because it was made to an outsider, and also with the will of the lord, that the agnates are preferred. But if it did not degenerate from the nature of the fief, that the grant be made among the agnates themselves, it is equitable that if one of the agnates is more friendly and more deserving, the vassal may burden him with his share. Arg. C. de senatus consulto Pegasiano, l. in quaestione testamenti, § vlt.; ff. si quid in fraudem pupilli, l. vnius. For even the father who received the fief, if he had been asked, being a reasonable man, ought to have granted this, de pactis, l. tale pactum, § finali. But the eminent lord Doctor Odofredus says thus: I ask, if there are two or more coheirs to whom the fief opens in equal line, if the vassal should die, whether he may nevertheless give to one, either inter vivos or by last will. And the truth is that he may not, in Auth. de non eligendo secundum nubentem, § prospeximus. And thus there will be no place for gratification. For even the father himself who acquired the fief could not prefer one son over another, as in c. 1, de successione feudorum. For whether the right is formed by pact and acquired in rem, or formed but not yet acquired, it cannot be taken away except by the will of all those whose interest it is, ff. de aqua pluviali, l. in concedendo; arg. ff. de pactis, l. fi. Moreover, one alone cannot remove a form established long ago, ff. de administratione tutorum, l. quidam decedens, because in this matter the favor is not of one, but of many, ff. de servorum rusticorum praediorum, l. profundum; and l. recepta, ff. de coniunctione praediorum, communi diviso, l. Sabinus; C. de libertis et eorum liberis, l. 2. Moreover, the contract of fief is a contract running by its own nature, in which nature is regarded more than institution or investiture, extra de natura feudi, c. 1. The said sale is not among the prohibited cases, since it was made to an agnate of equal degree, and the lord ratified it, as appears from the authorities and reasons alleged above. Therefore it could be done. The contrary opinions, which say that by alienation the thing fell into forfeiture, do not stand, because they speak of prohibited cases. And this is true, that the said sale was upheld, because it could be made among themselves; notwithstanding the said opinion of Lord Odofredus, because it does not seem that a prohibition was made so that one could prevail over another, on account of the equality of affection, as argued in ff. de ritu nuptiarum, l. non solum, § de uno. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Three modes of succession are found.
2. How do the sons of brothers succeed among themselves? And whether with uncles, they succeed per stirpes or per capita. No. 3.
3. Whether cousins succeed per capita or per stirpes.
4. Whether paternal cousins succeed per capita or per stirpes in a fief.
5. Whether the right of accretion has place in a fief among paternal uncles, or their sons.
body: For the sake of clarity and to be stated beforehand,
† For there is succession ordered by the way of the common law: some ordered by the form of contract: some ordered by the proper nature of the act, as is the succession of fiefs. Concerning the first

† It has been customary to raise the question whether the sons of brothers succeed per stirpes or per capita. And this question is threefold. First, when they succeed together with their uncle: and then there is no doubt that they succeed per stirpes in relation to the uncle. And the reason is: because they must succeed in the place of their father; otherwise their uncle, as being closer to their deceased brother, would exclude them: as in the Authentica "Ut fratrum filii," after the principal part, where it says, "entering the degree of the uncle and taking his portion."

† The second question is, when there are sons of two brothers, and their uncle, who was the third brother, dies, it is asked how these collateral nephews succeed to him, whether per capita or per stirpes: and on this point it is usually said that they succeed per stirpes: because they come by representation of their father. And in this way is understood a certain gloss which is in C. de leg. hered. auth. cessante. and there by Cynus.

The third question arises when dealing with the succession of cousins, for example: there were three brothers; one died leaving one son; another left two; the third left three. Then the sole son died. It is asked whether the said cousins come into the inheritance per capita or per stirpes. Some say per stirpes, because the text states that after brothers, the sons of brothers come in per capita. Therefore, those preceding come per stirpes, as in the Authentica de haeredibus ab intestato, § si vero neque fratres. Since we are here among the brothers themselves and not after the brothers, they therefore come per stirpes. This is the opinion of the glossa, adhering to the text in the aforementioned Authentica cessante dominus. Cynus holds the contrary opinion there. And in the Authentica post fratres, he gives this reason, namely, that they do not come in the person of their uncles, but in their own person. And since this intestate succession depends on the root of blood, to such an extent that some say it is the very right of blood, and in this right all are equal, and this right is divided per capita, therefore it is a succession per capita. And for this, C. de legatis, l. leges, in fine. But for the glossa, the reason stands: because it is more reasonable to divide per stirpes than per capita, as is clear in the succession of the descending line. And although in the succession of the transverse line it is established that beyond the sons of brothers it is per capita, nevertheless we are here dealing with the sons of brothers. Hence, that which has the stronger reason of equity should be weighed. Moreover, whenever several succeed in the place of one, they are counted as one, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cui fundus. Also, it is difficult to depart from the determination of the glossa in judging. But whatever may be the case on this point, I come to the second succession ordered by the form of contract, and I speak of fiefs, because in other matters it is not our subject. And I say that the form of the contract must be observed, whether it provides per capita or per stirpes, as in 10. col. qui feudum dare possunt, c. 1, § cum vero Corradus. I come to the third,

† And I inquire concerning a fief granted in the common form: namely, whether paternal cousins succeed one another per capita or per stirpes. And I know that the laudable and eminent Doctor, Master James of Ardizone of Verona, in his subtle and laudable Summa on the Usages of Fiefs, says thus: "Collaterals of the nearest degree succeed, excluding other lines; however, when a brother succeeds together with nephews from a brother, they succeed per stirpes and not per capita. But those who succeed further on do so per capita and not per stirpes." And thus he interprets the chapter *Per successionem*, § *Ad filias*, *De gradibus succedendi in feudum*, Collatio 10, where it says, "then the more distant agnates." For he understands [it] as meaning per capita. Nevertheless, this word is not in the text, as in the Authenticum *De haereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Reliquum*.

But it is more reasonable and true to say that the said division ought to be made per stirpes, and the reason is this: because it arises from the feudal contract; for from the beginning of its succession it had the order of division per stirpes; and the nature of the fief is such that it always looks back to its origin. And agnates come to the succession of the fief by virtue of the rescript of the first parent, as if they were coming to the succession of the ascending line, as stated in the aforementioned chapter *Cum vero Conradus*. And everything that has reference to the ascending line is divided per stirpes and not per capita, as in chapter 1, *De successione feudorum*, and in the Title *De haereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Cum filius*. Hence, these agnates come because they enter into the place of their parents, who would have succeeded per stirpes and not per capita.

However, I do not extend myself beyond paternal cousins to say that more distant relatives come per stirpes; for on this point we would have neither text nor gloss of the original, nor living reason, but only their opinion. Therefore, concluding finally, I believe that when we are among the sons of brothers, as we are in our case, the succession to the fief, considering its order and primary nature, is per stirpes; for, as I said, here there concurs not only the order given by law, but also the order from the contract and the primordial nature of the fief itself; and because up to the fourth degree there is an extension of the paternal succession, as the text says in the aforementioned § *Cum vero Conradus*. Therefore, it is per stirpes. And

† For a better understanding of this point, it must be known that the matter concerns either equality (parilitas) or order. In the first case, the common opinion of the doctors teaches that if one share fails, it accrues to the other, as in usufruct, as in D. de usufr. l. si Titio § 1; D. de usufr. accresc. l. 1 § interdum. In the second case, I say that it is not properly called a right of accrual (ius accrescendi), but rather a certain order of succession. Therefore, when one of the paternal cousins dies, since they are in the same degree and there is room among them for the right of accrual, it accrues proportionally, and not per capita (pro virilibus), as in C. de impub. et aliis substit. l. 1. And thus it should also be said regarding emphyteusis, which would devolve by right of accrual among those between whom equality prevails, as if they were united by legal connection: because if two are united on one side and three on the other, the two have one half, and the other three have the other half, as in D. de contrah. empt. l. si duobus in principio. And this is similar to the edict concerning those joined with emancipated persons, D. de coniung. cum emanc. lib. l. 1 § si quis ex nepotibus. Hence, if anyone considers this correctly, it is not the same for paternal cousins in a fief as in a simple inheritance, in which the aforementioned Brother Jacob held the common opinion of his distinguished teacher, Master Azo. Therefore, it seems just to me that, among equals, when one fails, we consider succession according to the right of quasi-accrual, which is united to it. Argument: D. de acquirenda hereditate l. qui patri; and D. de in ius vocando l. si ego 2 in the response. And thus it seems to me that this should be said according to the truth and subtlety of the law: always saving the opinion of a more authoritative counsel. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A dowry is not said to exist where marriage is absent due to a defect of consent caused by the impediment of age; hence, the statute speaking of one joined in marriage ceases to apply, and so forth.
2. Whether a marriage, which is null due to the impediment of age because one party is a minor, is perfected by subsequent conduct upon proof of the persistence of the now-adult party. And number 4.
3. If a testator left a tenth under the condition that he shall be joined to Seius by marriage, whether the legacy ought to be received immediately upon marriage.
4. Whether a judge’s decree is required for the constitution of a dowry when an adult female contracts marriage, given that she cannot alienate property without a judge’s decree.
body: In this case, it must be considered whether any dowry was constituted by legal disposition in our case, or not. Secondly, the statute regarding the dowry to be acquired must be considered. Thirdly, it must be considered whether the marriage has been proven.

† As to the first point, it is certain that from the beginning no dowry was constituted, the pupillary age being an impediment; and consequently the statute, which speaks of being joined by marriage, ceases to apply, since there was no marriage, neither in act nor in status, as is noted in *l. quod seruius*, *de conditionibus ob causam*; and in *l. si ante*, *solutis matrimonii*; and in *l. dotis fructus*, *de iure dotium*, with its companions.

But it must be considered whether, assuming the subsequent fact, this occurred without prejudice, provided that the persistence of the woman’s consent was proven. And it seems that it did, by c. *De illis*, § *Si*, *De sponsalibus*, joined with c. 1, *De desponsatione impuberum*, lib. 6, in the words “contrahentes eosdem.” For the girl, as she grows older, comes to feel the same way, and the older party cannot dissent; therefore, the consent of both is found. Argument: ff. *De re iudicata*, l. *Quo*, § 1, and l. *Receptum*, *De communibus praediis*.

To the contrary, it seems that a marriage cannot be defective, as noted in the aforementioned c. *De illis*. Hence, the consent of the older party was never matrimonial; for that consent is called matrimonial which is the efficient cause of marriage, as is clear in 27 q. 2, § *Si*, where it is said that consent is the efficient cause of marriage. The consent of the older party, as I have said, was therefore not matrimonial, because it was never the efficient cause of marriage. For consent is a simultaneous agreement in the same thing. ff. *De pactis*, l. 1, § 1, and argument: ff. *De iniuriis testamenti*, l. *Si ego*. And therefore the gloss on the Ordinal says that neither is compelled to remain with the other as regards the bond of marriage. 30 q. 2, c. *Si quis ingenuus*. Hence, that consent is prior to marriage, not perfective of marriage; although it contains within itself the bond of promise, it does not contain within itself the efficacy of perfection.

Moreover, the acts perfective of marriage must be collected or communicated between the parties, not from the side of one only; for those whom God has joined together, human consent cannot separate. Argument: l. *Si ego*, ff. *Si certum petatur*. For things differ in any quality in which they differ, or in nature. ff. *De verbis obligatis*, l. 1, § *Cum adiungitur*.

Furthermore, not all acts are sufficient, but they are said to be companion acts: such as a leading away that is not momentary, but stable, to the husband’s house, or carnal copulation, as noted in the gloss on the Ordinal, 30 q. 2, c. *Ubi non est consensus condignus*. The Archdeacon says that tacit consent is understood through cohabitation. Moreover, from carnal intercourse, otherwise without new consent of both, marriage is not contracted, nor does a presumption of law arise, and as a matter of law, even if a kiss intervenes, as C. *De donationibus ante nuptias*, l. *Si a sponso*, according to Innocent and Johannes Andreae, additions. And similar things are called similar, whose terms are equal, although they are not the same terms, concluding only from one side to the other.

And therefore, since the text permitted [discussion] regarding two pupils, and regarding one pupil and another adult, finally it overturned the common clause in both cases, in which it says “contrahentes eosdem”; and thus in the plural and conjunctive number. Nor is this surprising, because there are two, and one soul ought to be in different bodies in this sacrament of matrimony, as is clear in the aforementioned c. 1, *De desponsatione impuberum*, lib. 6.

But assuming that it was a true marriage, another doubt arises: because the statute establishes the dowry if they are joined in marriage.

† Suppose that a testator bequeaths 10 solidi to a woman, on the condition that she shall be joined to Seius in marriage: whether she ought to receive the legacy immediately upon marrying, or only if she is taken as a wife or carnally known. And it seems that neither is required. D. 50.17.32 (de regulis iuris); Q. 32.1; X. 4.5.1 (non in sola); C. 9.13.pr. (de incestis nuptiis); C. 5.4.pr. (de nuptiis); D. 35.1.13 (haec conditio) and the note in the same title; D. 35.1.14 (cum fuerit); C. 5.12.1 (cum in te); D. 50.17.1.1 (hinc descendit) with similar authorities.

On the contrary, it seems that the statute and the testament appear to have considered the effect of marriage, as noted in the glossa summae of D. 50.17.32; Q. 27.1; and D. 35.1.1 (si ita) in the text; D. 38.2.1.1 (adigere, si patronatus), especially in the case of minors, as we say in D. 23.2.1 (eliescentia). Thus, we examine the bare name. For marriage is deemed not to exist if one does not intend to take a wife. D. 24.2.1 (matrimonii). Hence Marcellus says elsewhere, “I think that the effect of the thing should be followed,” in D. 12.2.3.2 (de iureiurando).

Furthermore, this is expressly supported by X. 2.12.ult. (de conversis iudicibus), verse “ac ex hoc.” Moreover, we must seek the mind concealed in the words. D. 50.16.1 (quisquis mihi). But mind and reason are the same, as noted by Dynus in X. 5.17.ult. (de regulis iuris), lib. 6. Since a statute is presumed to be reasonable, that reason is presumed which can be assigned, as appears in the commentary of Ulpian, which applies to all edicts of the praetors, e.g., D. 28.5.1 (de posthumis) with similar authorities.

Furthermore, since a husband cannot claim the dowry unless he takes a wife, or unless it does not depend on him, therefore he cannot claim anything from the dowry; consequently, he cannot claim the place of the dowry, especially if he stood in the way by promising the dowry by right of absence; because he who did not take a wife and does not bear the inconveniences ought not to enjoy the benefits of marriage. C. 4.2.1.2 (manifeste, sed cum in secunda); and what is noted in D. 23.3.1 (si ante); D. 44.1.1 (pater); D. 18.1.1 (praesertim). But it depends on him, because he voluntarily absented himself, arg. C. 2.1.2 (Iul., offerri); C. 4.4.1 (qui pendentem); C. 4.4.1 (ex placito); D. 19.2.1 (quaero, inter locatorem); D. 23.5.1 (ab hostibus, si cum si).

† I do not hold that a marriage is formed by the consent of the older party prior to the marriage, together with the subsequent consent of the younger party alone; because these consents are not of the same species, otherwise if they were of the same nature. Cf. l. receptum, D. de condictio praedii. Another doubt arises concerning this constitution of dowry.

Let it be assumed that there was a marriage, because an adult woman cannot, neither tacitly nor expressly, alienate immovable property without a decree. D. de iure dotis, l. Titia; C. si maior factus, l. si; C. de administratione tutorum, l. lex, quae tutores; D. de tutoribus et curatoribus daturis, l. 1, § 1; C. de pignoribus minorum, l. praedia. Hence, at least in marriage, a decree must intervene: not on account of the marriage itself, but on account of the dowry. This is the opinion of Bartolus, D. solutione matrimonii, l. si constante; and de pactis, l. Item alias. For an absurdity would follow: namely, that the bare act of marriage could have more power than a decree, against which restitution in integrum would be granted. Moreover, it would open a clear path to defrauding the minor. And it is absurd that laws should induce frauds, when they ought to prevent them. C. de iudiciis viduarum, l. 2; l. meminerint, C. unde vi. Furthermore, every law which does not expressly provide regarding capacity admits a restrictive interpretation as to a capable person, and “capable” is understood as such in law and in fact, according to nature and according to good morals, especially in marriages. l. adigere, §. quamuis, and similar authorities. But because this interpretation would not be restricting the law, but rather breaking it, I do not believe it should be so restricted, provided that the parties are of equal age and status. Moreover, nobility and knowledge make up for many things. D. pro socio, l. societas, § 1, in the gloss. Also, when the marriage has been approved by relatives and not usurped. Hence, in our case, I do not consider Bartolus’s opinion to be true or equitable; because the marriage was contracted with the counsel of the mother and relatives, and it was more favorable to Lord Christopher. And it supports what is noted in the aforementioned l. item quia, by Odofredus, and l. polla, D. de his quibus ut indigis, in the gloss of the Ordinarius, and similar authorities.

Having spoken of the dowry, we must now consider the acquisition of the dowry, assuming that all the aforementioned points favor Lord Christopher. And briefly, regarding the acquisition of the dowry, beyond the aforementioned points, I weigh one thing, namely, the phrase “in the husband’s power.” And briefly, I say that the dowry is not in the husband’s power before he can act with effect. Moreover, unless he is in possession, or quasi-possession, and thus “in the husband’s power” is understood as possession, or quasi-possession, or enjoyment. Yet even with enjoyment, it is not yet in his power; because the burden of marriage must precede, not perfunctorily in the bride’s house, but effectively in the groom’s house; as in l. pater, D. de exceptione doli. And therefore, Lord Christopher has no right, considering what ought to be considered, nor did he prove effective evidence. I have labored, therefore, and in the case, your Baldo, under the seal of his name, has thus advised, saving the substance of the truth, and also your correction. I beg you, however, if you can, that you settle the cause, lest another matter of dispute be stirred up, and for the honor of Lord Christopher, whom I love as a son. Nevertheless, I am Plato’s friend, but truth is a greater friend. I, Baldo.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What exceptions may oppose an heir who petitions to be put in possession under the edict of the divine Hadrian.
2. Whether a compromise between a guardian and a ward, or between a curator and an adult, is valid.
body:
To the most illustrious and Magnificent knight, Lord Clasmatic, honorable vice-governor of the city of Asti and its district, etc., for the most illustrious and invincible Lord Duke of Turin, Lord of Asti, etc.

It is signified and humbly proposed on behalf of your most faithful subjects, Thomas and Manfred, brothers of Monte di Rocha: that whereas they had even judicially requested before Lord Arminio of Parma, then judge of justice of the city of Asti, to be induced and put into possession, and quasi-possession, of the goods, things, and rights which were in the goods and inheritance of the late Lord Manfred of Monte di Rocha, father of the late Bartholomew and Manfred Fraylon, who was the bastard of the said Manfred of Rocha aforesaid; and whereas judgment was pronounced against them by the said judge, and especially declaring that they should not be induced into possession of the aforesaid, as contained in the pronouncement; and whereas the said pronouncement was declared null, and an appeal was taken therefrom on behalf of the dower of the said petitioners, and thus it is of no effect; and especially because it is and was contrary to the capitula and statutes of the city of Asti, sworn by your lordship; and especially because, according to the said capitula, as in other cases, the matter should have been committed to three good men; and whereas it should have been pronounced by the said judge with the counsel of wise and trusted persons of the parties, according to the capitula and statutes of the city of Asti, the said judge, affecting to do what he did, pronounced against the said petitioners.

And from the foregoing follows a great inconvenience, namely, that Bartholomew and Manuel, born of Fraylon, who was the bastard of the said late Lord Manfred, should have the goods which ought to have belonged to the said petitioners, who were the legitimate and natural sons of the said late Lord Manfred; and especially because the said Fraylon, who was the tutor of the said petitioners, robbed and deceived them of great quantities of money and goods; and not content with the aforesaid, the said judge still strives to compel the said petitioners to great expenses and penalties, and the houses, goods, and dwellings of the said petitioners have been usurped in the city of Asti, and other enormities and illicit acts have been perpetrated and were perpetrated against them, from which the said petitioners are forced to be exiles from the said city, which is not believed to be your benign intention.

Wherefore it is requested and required from your aforesaid lordship on behalf of the said petitioners, Thomas and Manfred, that you would be pleased and deign summarily and de plano, by every right, mode, way, and form by which you best can, to pronounce and, by pronouncing, to declare that the said pronouncement or sentence passed by the said Lord Arminio is or was null by the law itself, and also that every condemnation, damages, and expenses, and all consequences thereof and from the aforesaid, be set aside; and especially because innovations and acts were made contrary to the inhibition of the Lord Bishop of Asti and contrary to the oaths which were and are to be observed; and also that the said petitioners should be sent and induced into possession, and having been induced, should be defended and preserved, and that you should cause them to be sent and induced into possession and quasi-possession of the aforesaid goods and things, of which mention is made in the petition submitted by them before the said Lord Arminio; and which were against the father of the said petitioners, and the points following therefrom, removed therefrom being Bartholomew and Manuel, who were born of Fraylon the bastard. Notwithstanding the aforesaid and anything else to the contrary.

And especially because the said sentence was null for the aforesaid reasons and many others; and suspended by nullity and appeal, and contrary to the inhibition of the Reverend Lord Bishop of Asti containing excommunication; and contrary to oaths to be observed by law, and to the prejudice of their souls; or at least, may your lordship deign, considering that the said petitioners uphold justice in the petitory, and in the property and dominion of the said goods, rights, and things, as legitimate and natural sons of the said Manfred, and as instituted in the testament against their father aforesaid, as appears from the opinions of twenty doctors, or about that number, of the most solemn, sealed with their seals; who, notwithstanding certain transactions and arbitrations made and sworn, some of them among the Monte family, or some of them, advised the said petitioners to uphold justice; and especially because Fraylon was the tutor or curator of the said petitioners, and consequently a transaction, obligation, and alienation could not be made between them; and also because the arbitrations were not fulfilled, and pronouncements were made on behalf of Fraylon and the sons; rather, in some cases, the contrary was done, and consequently, even if they had been sworn, the said petitioners are not bound to observe what is contained therein.

Item, because the pronouncements and arbitrations were made without examining and knowing the witnesses and their words; and because they are also to be reduced as most unjust, as in the opinion of the doctors, and as it appears. And especially because by the episcopal power of the city of Asti, this was declared in his sentence, and the said petitioners were absolved from the sacraments. And especially because one of the said petitioners, namely Manfred, as a minor, was not present for all the aforesaid, and many other considerations.
