I also consider that, even if the aforesaid sentence in the possessory passed against the said petitioners had become res judicata, nevertheless, from the fact that the said petitioners uphold justice in the petitory and dominion, and especially because they have the sale and cession of the goods and rights of the said Bartholomew and Manuel, and they pertain to Thomas and his brother, as will be liquidated before you; and of the homage, to which they are bound, which Thomas and Manfred absorb and draw to themselves, they draw the possessory, which ought to accede to the petitory, and to the said petitioners upholding justice in the petitory, to declare that the dominion, property, and all rights, and also possessions, and whatever else of theirs which are comprehended in the petition before Lord Arminio, judge of justice of Asti at that time, be drawn, given, attributed to the said petitioners, legitimate and natural, and that they be induced therein without any litigation, and also without the noise and figure of judgment; removing also the said Bartholomew and Manuel born of the bastard; and also that the houses, goods, and dwellings of the said petitioners, and occupied by them, be restored in full to them as to the lord and possession, and by full right.

The aforesaid requisition and signification having been presupposed and submitted to you, Magnificent Lord Governor of Asti, on behalf of Thomas and Manfred, brothers of Monte di Rocha of Asti, for the purpose of resisting the unjust calumnies and malignities committed and perpetrated on behalf of Bartholomew of Rocha and certain judges who pronounced judgment; to which calumnies and malignities it is hoped that your most just lordship will wish to resist. It is shown first that the said Thomas and Manfred ought to obtain in the possessory, as in the signification, allegations, and legal instruments. First, because the said Thomas and Manfred are of legitimate and suitable age and capacity. Although this has been fully alleged, nevertheless I will add something.

† And it is well known that a testamentary heir must be put in possession, unless the possessor has an obstructive title, or some other defense granted to him by the edict of the divine Adrian or Justinian; or because the will is suspect upon inspection on account of erasure or some other visible defect, as in the law *Edicto*. And therefore I say that the said testamentary heir ought to have been put in possession; because he had an adversary, and then to be put in possession in fact, as in the Digest, *De appellationibus recipiendis*, law *Si*. It is true that if the testamentary heir relinquishes possession by pact or compromise, then he ought not to be put in possession; because he renounced his right, which he could do. Digest, *De pactis*, law *Pactum inter heredem*; Code, Book 6, § *Quod autem*, *Quorum legata ista*. This exception is among those permitted; because it proceeds from the consent of the heir.

† However, it must be considered that a compromise could not have been made between a guardian and a ward, from which an alienation or even an obligation could follow: as is fully read and noted in l. 1, ff. de noua. Nor could it be made between a general curator and an adult: because an adult having a curator is similar to a ward. Hence, the curator represents him as if he were a ward, especially in what is transacted between them. Therefore, the oath does not represent the adult as a major; because, on the contrary, the representation of minority age stands in the way. C. de in integrum restitutione minorum, l. si curatorem habens. Also, because one is prohibited from contracting with oneself. ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. si in emptione, §. si, unless with the authority of another curator and of the judge, and in good faith. C. de contrahenda emptione, l. cum ipse. And therefore, the said arbitration does not avail. Nor does the sentence avail: because it is alleged that a just appeal was taken from it; and it is alleged that the appeal is pending. Also, if it is true that the statutes declare that the judge is bound to another solemnity, if it has not been observed, since it is a grave and weighty solemnity, as in C. de repudiis, l. dubium, the sentence is null by the law itself. ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si praetor. That it may be appealed for a just cause, is stated by Bartolus in d. l. vltima, de appellandis reiectis. If the possessor had other rights, or if the truth had not been assumed in the fact, I say that the truth must be followed. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed and signed with the signs of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The liar, or he who denies possession, loses the possession itself.
body: Because of

† If the falsehood is established, the defendant shall be deprived, and possession transferred to the adversary, when he denied possession, or that the thing belonged to the author, nor was it in his assets, nor at the time of the obligation, nor is it transferred afterwards. I say, possession [is awarded] to the plaintiff by reason of the falsehood, and the defendant becomes the plaintiff. For he does not lose his mortgage, if he cannot retain the thing, but he is the plaintiff, in Auth. de trien. et semis. §. pe. And therefore the defendant ought to be condemned, because he spoke falsely: reserving to himself the right of action, if he has any from his mortgage. And thus the ordinary gloss teaches us, which is in the said §. and Dyn. in the chapter nullus pluribus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The recipient, on account of a disgraceful cause, is not bound to make restitution.
body: That each month of the said eight months, he is to lend, or cause to be lent, in the city etc., to the said Thomas, 100 florins of gold, of correct and just weight etc., and whole, without any retention of toll; so that the said Thomas, with the said money, may support the stipendiaries whom he holds for the guard of the Rock and the Castle of the aforementioned Burgh. The said Thomas is bound and ought to repay and restore the said 100 florins to the said commune etc., and before he restores or delivers the said Castle and Rock to another. And furthermore, that the said Thomas may not, nor ought to, give or deliver, or permit to be delivered or given, the Burgh or Rock to anyone in the future at any time, unless restitution and satisfaction have first been made to the said commune of the entire quantity of money which he received from the said 100 florins each month, as will be said above, with changes etc. Also, that the said Thomas may not, nor is it permitted to him, during the said eight months, assign, give, or hand over the said place to any person, whatever the condition, preeminence, or dignity of the said commune or college, even if they were comprehended by law in general words, without express license etc. And under the penalty of 200 florins of gold in each chapter of this contract, even with solemn stipulation premised, which penalty may be demanded and exacted as often as it is committed, whenever anything contrary is done. Also, the said commune is bound within 10 days from the day of the requisition to be made to the said Thomas, to give men of the said commune sufficient for any of his requisitions for attacking etc., under the penalty, as above. According to what is proposed hitherto, beyond the preceding agreements, since it is generally established that turp conventions, that is, those interposed on turp matters, are of no effect, and also those interposed on a lawful matter, but from a turp cause, with turpitude turning from the beginning on the part of both contracting parties, do not hold by the law itself.

† Therefore, it can be concluded that the aforementioned agreements, insofar as they contain a prohibition on the surrender of the Castle, being based on an illicit matter, are not binding. Moreover, although the thing itself involved in the loan is lawful, since the money was given as a loan, the recipient of the loaned money is not bound to make restitution from that contract, because of the illicit cause, not only due to the turpitude arising on the part of the recipient, but also due to the damages. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What agreements the custodian of the Castle, holding it from the Prince, may or may not make.
body: If to someone

† If the custody of a certain Castle has been committed by the Emperor or the Roman Pontiff to someone, this custodian cannot make the aforementioned pacts with any person in the world, unless with the license of the Prince, as held in ff. ad l. Iul. Maie. l. 3, in the words "aut arcen tenuerit, aut Castra concesserit." The glossa says "tenuerit," meaning not by returning it to the Prince, but by requesting it, having received it from him in custody; therefore, by contracting not to return it, he incurs a crime, and thus such a pact is criminal and shameful. He who makes such a pact turns against the enemy. Argument: ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si; and C. de re militari, l. si qui a Barbaris, lib. 12. If anything has been given or lent by one who knows [the turpitude], it is not recovered. l. 3, de condictione ob turpem causam. And even in a loan it is expressly stated, through the conjunction of two laws, that it is not recovered: nevertheless, I do not approve of him. ff. de conditione indebiti, l. si penes causa, in principio. Nor yet concerning Blasius, because by the authority of law he may not return it, and thus it is left to his conscience, and the common saying is: "I fear scandal, not future judgment, when one thing appears to the discerning, another is read." Let it therefore be concluded that, by law, what has been lent or given on a shameful cause cannot be recovered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a community may sell its property, and when, or not, and with what solemnity.
2. Whether a seller may take back from the buyer the thing sold to him in emphyteusis, or vice versa.
3. Whether a judgment rendered with hasty expedition is valid.
4. The fisc is not properly called an heir.
5. It is presumed in favor of a judgment that it was rendered on the basis of proof, if the judgment makes mention of the acts, even where the proceedings are not established due to the antiquity of time.
6. Whether reputation, in matters of ancient standing, induces notoriety.
7. Whether an example constitutes an indication.
body: The long factual scenario, thus narrated, requires a clear and wisely ordered exposition. The Community of Gaido sold communal property to Lord Maphaeus, and ultimately received it back from him in emphyteusis. Thereafter, the said Lord Maphaeus was condemned to the ultimate penalty, and, having been subjected to confiscation, ended his life by execution. King Robert followed the sentence in part, and in part the execution of the ban declared that said sentence had not stood, and restored the successors to the goods. Many other Brescians occupied and held them, and at certain times thereafter the census was paid by certain persons not having a mandate from the Community of Gaido. The properties today are of little value. The Community of Gaido is sued on the basis of ancient instruments, approved subsequently by many acts; the Community defends itself by seeking to extirpate the root, i.e., the initial sale, as prohibited by a certain statute of Brescia. It is alleged against the condemnation and confiscation; but the plaintiffs reply on many grounds. Now the question arises: what is the law, having considered the matters narrated on both sides? Also to be considered is the petition filed against the Community of Gaido by the actor, concerning the properties, etc. I come to the first contract of sale,

† which appears to have been void for several reasons. And first: because it was made contrary to the municipal law, which prohibits public sale; therefore, the sale does not bind. It must be presupposed that the statute is valid and binding. C. de vend. rebus ciui. l. 1. lib. 11. ff. de priui. credito. l. antiochensium. And then it immediately follows that such things are not in commerce; therefore, their sale is not valid, as ff. de ver. ob. l. continuus. §. cum quis sub hac. Secondly: because a city, a castle, and any university in which there are peoples, and similar entities, are equated with a church, as noted in ff. si cer. pet. l. ciuitas. But the property of churches and of wards cannot be sold without public auction; although the contrary holds for the property of adults according to some authorities. ff. de mil. l. et si sine. and in Auth. hoc ius. Therefore, the same applies to the property of universities. Thirdly: because the decree of a judge did not intervene, which ought to be interposed after the contract and solemnities have been completed, as C. de vend. rebus ciui. lib. 11. Fourthly: because it is not proven that the price was converted to the benefit of the Castle, which must be proven, as noted in l. 1. C. de ven. rebus ciui. lib. 11. Fifthly: because in the syndicate the names of those interested were not expressed, nor did they swear, as stated in the aforementioned law. But to some of these points one can easily reply, and to others not so easily.

I come to the second point, namely, to the emphyteutic contract. And if the sale is invalid, the vendor could not lease his own property, nor acquire the useful dominion, since he held the direct dominion. C. loca. l. qui rem. ff. ad Tre. l. si hermes. But assuming that it had been valid, a question arises concerning the penalty: whether it is incurred each year, or once for all the years, or once for a single year only. And I see that it is incurred each year: because the penalty of double responds to, and accords with, the nature of the thing, since it is annual, and because it is most probable that this was the intended meaning, given that a distribution of years intervenes. To the contrary, that it is incurred once for all years: ff. de poe. le. l. 1. in fi. To the contrary, that it is incurred once for one year only: ff. de arb. l. si duo. and no. ff. de ver. ob. l. si sic stipulat sum. The first opinion would be more correct in our case, if it could be incurred, and with respect to the person to whom it is incurred. I come to the third question.

† On condemnation and confiscation. And it appears that the sentence rendered with precipitous haste was invalid, because it is impossible to complete the entire process in one day, as noted in the Digest, title *Qui ex causa*, law *Sed et si per praetorem*, section *Quotiens*. The contrary is true in such a great crime, since delay could subvert the public order. Digest, title *De iniuriis*, law *Si quis filio*: punishment must be swift, provided that the crime is established. And therefore the aforementioned Lord Maphaeus died subject to the penalty, and his goods, by reason of the crime of lèse-majesté, devolved to the fisc, as in the Authenticum *Bona damnatorum*, at the end. From this it follows that he left no goods in the city; and thus he could have no heirs. Digest, title *De vulgari*, law *Lex Cornelia*. But in place of the heir, by the custom of the Lombards, was the Imperial fisc, as in law 1, Code, title *De bonis vacantibus*, book 10. And therefore, unless the Emperor or the city had restored the goods to his descendants, such descendants would have no right. But it is said that the King restored the exiles; nevertheless, we justly hold that he was not King of the Romans nor Emperor, having been rejected by the Pope and by the just judgment of God, on account of what he publicly did against Pope John and against the universal Roman Church. Hence his privileges were invalid. Code, title *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, law *Decernimus*; whatever is noted by Cynus in law *Bene a Zenone*, Code, title *De quadriennali praescriptione*. Nevertheless, this is not contrary to what I say. Moreover, the donation of Lord Mastino could not make these donees heirs of Lord Maphaeus, because one who leaves no inheritance has no heir. For even a father who takes possession by right of peculium is not called an heir. Digest, title *De stipulationibus servorum*, law *Si servus communis Meuii*, in the beginning, and there noted.

† Nor is the fisc properly called an heir: as in D. de nov. l. quotiens. §. si. and l. noua. in fi. I say this when it succeeds by way of confiscation. D. pro so. l. actione. §. publicatione. D. de duo. reis. l. si. Moreover, the donation of Lord Mastino, assuming that it was valid for the years during which he held dominion in an ambulatory manner, as fortune wanders: nevertheless, for the time during which he did not hold government, he could not donate the annual revenues owed to the commune of Brescia. arg. D. de stip. ser. l. si seruus communis Meuii. and castrensis peculii. §. si. AE. I compare such governments to usufructuaries, since they are not transmitted by law to successors. And what is purchased from them is not properly said to emanate from dignity, otherwise in the case of a Prince, and these are subtleties of law. However, in Lombardy these laws are trifles; new laws are made every day for new rulers. D. de orig. iu. l. 2. §. ex actis. Moreover, a decree was made in the time of Lucano by him. Moreover, the recognition of individuals does not prejudice the whole, as is fully noted in D. de reg. iur. l. aliud. §. refertur. And therefore it seems to be said that these rights, if any exist, pertain to the commune of Brescia and not to these plaintiffs: unless insofar as they are considered to them by the commune of Brescia or by a superior presiding over the dominion, always reserving the truer opinion. Consider also the libel of the plaintiffs, in which if no mention were made that they themselves are successors of Lord Maffeo in their own person, they could not prevail. C. unde liberi. l. qui se patris. But the plaintiffs themselves make mention that they are as heirs of heirs. C. de haere. insti. l. si. Hence the petition is aptly formed, yet it is not aptly proved, if it is established that the said Maffeo was condemned to death, and the condemnation was especially executed. In which case he has no heir even for pious causes, as is noted in c. quamquam. extra de vsu. lib. 6. in nouella. And although it was done hastily and abbreviated, nevertheless law is presumed to have been observed: because it is presumed in favor of a sentence passed in confession, even if delays were not observed: especially if other proofs also support it, particularly in matters of discretion. D. de adm. tuto. l. si bona. de iud. l. si prętor. D. de euic. l. hęrennius. extra de renun. c. in pręsentia. And these are true, if confession is established; otherwise it is not presumed in favor of a sentence passed abruptly and without observing the order of law, but rather then it is presumed against the sentence due to the defect of the process. 2. q. i. c. nos vero quemquam. and c. in pręmis. It accords with what is noted in In. extra de eo, qui fur. ordi. c. innotuit. and Bar. D. de dona. l. filius.

But if, due to the antiquity of time, it cannot be established what the procedure was, it is presumed in favor of the sentence that it was rendered on the basis of proof, provided that the sentence makes mention of the accusation; otherwise, the contrary applies. This is understood as follows: no. Cy. C. de fi. instru. l. emancipa.

† And even when the act is very ancient, they make conjectures together with fame concerning all these matters. Namely, in acts that are very famous and widely known: because fame can be so great and have endured for so long that it induces notoriety, as noted in ff. de negotiis gestis, l. At qui natura, §. Cum me absente; and ff. de rei vindicatione, l. Indici; and l. 2, §. 1; ff. de excusationibus tutorum. Innocentius notes this in extra de iure calumniae, c. Cum causam; and in c. Vestra. And whether one who obtains restitution in integrum appears to be condemned, see Bartolus, ff. de verborum obligatione, lib. 10. And because from the records and in conscience it seems to me that the said Lord Maphaeus was guilty of death and subject to penalty, and that no action can be brought in his name as heir: namely, guilty, I say, of judgment, not of malice: of fault. I do not know, but the law presumes guilt where a conviction or condemnation with certainty is found, and doubt exists regarding rectitude. ff. de poenis, l. 3. And the foregoing are confirmed: because restitution in integrum cannot restore a dead person to have an heir, whom he could not have at the time of death. ff. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Huic scripturae; C. de senatus consulto Pegasiano, l. Si; de bonis libertorum, l. Qui libertinus, §. Posthumus; and ff. de stipulationibus servorum, l. Si servus, §. Servus. And also, a rescript without the clause "non obstantibus" (notwithstanding) appended in the proper form is not valid against res iudicatae. This reason is not good with regard to the Bavarian rescript: because that rescript does not err in form. But nevertheless, the other points I mentioned are true: because it errs due to lack of jurisdiction and power, as C. si a non competente iudice, per totum, objects. Or, regarding lesion in an onerous contract due to supervening utility of the thing, it does not affect the matter, nor should restitution in integrum be granted in the same way. ff. de minoribus, l. Verum, §. Si locupletior; and especially because time does not permit, as C. qui ex causa maiorum, l. Respublica. Hence, the community of Gaido remains in one most powerful defense, namely, in the confiscation of Lord Maphaeus, and before anything is declared thereon. And even if, granted but not conceded, he had no right in the principal matter, nevertheless he would not incur the penalty of the contract: because he is not understood to be bound until it is declared that he is. ff. de verborum obligatione, l. Hoc iure; and l. Hoc te; ff. si certum petatur; and ff. depositi, l. Si quis inficiatus; and ff. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. Illud. I therefore conclude that, since the plaintiff, having no action, sues as if he were the heir of Lord Maphaeus, who could not have an heir due to the adverse fortune of his condemnation; and since they did not found their claim as heirs, nor can they do so, the defendant ought to be absolved. It is certain that if what is owed to the community of Brescia by error or by imposition of the community of Gaido is paid to these other descendants of Lord Maphaeus, to whom it ought not to have been paid, thereby neither is a true obligation extinguished, nor is an abusive obligation created. ff. de conditione indebiti, l. Si poenae causa, §. 1. It is also certain in the matter of proof that what does not avail individually, when many things concur, helps. Consonance. Many judgments presume, and together with fame make full proof in a civil case, whatever is introduced therein: as in the aforementioned l. 2, §. Aetas, ff. de excusationibus tutorum, according to the gloss and Decius.

† Moreover, although an example does not constitute proof, and especially an example of an example, as in C. de diuersis rescindendis, l. si qua, and there by Cynus, it nevertheless creates an indication, as noted in l. 2, ff. de fideiussoribus institoribus. Furthermore, just as a death long past is proven by reputation, C. 5.39, l. si quidem, so too is the nature of the death; hence, all these elements joined together form one perfect sense or indication in the mind of the judge, against which it ought not to be pronounced according to natural reason. And therefore, civil law considers that proven, the contrary of which is not credible nor can be persuaded to any honest man, to whose judgment all these matters are referred. ff. de testibus, l. 3, §. tu magis; and l. ob carmen, §. fin.; and extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. si illud etiam constet. It is also established that a long performance on account of an invalid cause does not bind for the future, as in l. si certis annis, C. de pactis, with its subject matter. This too must be added concerning the Bavarian rescript, which is otherwise invalid: because a rescript that remedies a defect must disclose the defect, so that it appears that the one issuing the rescript clearly and specifically understood the cause; otherwise, it is not understood that dispensation has been granted, as in c. 2, extra de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6; and l. 2, ff. de naturalibus restitutionibus; and de rescriptis, c. dilectus filius abbas, §. Stephani; and ar. ff. de actione empti, l. 1, §. sed si id egit; and de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis ab his, l. tutor si petitus; and l. cum dominus, in principio, ff. de peculio legato. Wherefore, I firmly hold that the community of Gaido ought to be absolved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether hospitals fall under the term “clerics” or “benefices.”
2. Whether a hospital subject to a monastery is, and when, considered a member of that monastery.
3. Whether the valuation of a monastery also includes the valuation of a hospital, or whether the valuation of a hospital is in itself subject to burdens.
4. Possession is acquired by a single act.
body: In the case pending between the proctor of the lords canons of the chapter of the church of Vercelli, acting also in the name and on behalf of the entire clergy of the city and diocese of Vercelli, of the one part, and the lords Abbot of the monastery of S. Andrea and the minister of S. Andrea of Vercelli, on the occasion of a tallage newly imposed upon the aforesaid hospital of S. Andrea of Vercelli; and in the name and on the occasion of a certain declaration made on that account between the said parties by the learned doctor dominus Thodescus de Barilo, who pronounced and declared that the aforesaid hospital of S. Andrea ought not to have been, nor was to be, separated or distinguished in any assessment, nor in any books of assessments and tallages of the clergy of Vercelli, from the aforesaid monastery of S. Andrea of Vercelli, to which it is subject, nor from the assessment of the said monastery; and consequently that the said hospital of S. Andrea and the minister and chapter of the said hospital, by virtue or pretext of any assessment assigned to the said hospital separately from the aforesaid monastery, are not bound in any way to pay the tallage recently imposed, nor any others that might happen to be imposed. And having examined the letters of our Magnificent and Illustrious lord, and having examined certain documents of the assessment that are not public, but private, and having also examined all the acts and proceedings in the said cause, it seems to me, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, that certain matters must be premised for clarity, and thereafter we must come to the resolution of the aforesaid question.

† And first, I premise that although hospitals are not contained under the designation of clerics and churches, as in ca. per literas, extra de pręben. in Clem., nevertheless it is otherwise in this case on account of the intention of the lord, who willed that all be comprehended under a certain most comprehensive universality. Whence, since all hospitals employ this law, similarly the hospital of S. Andrea ought to be comprehended under this discipline and assessment, as read and noted in extra de ver. si. c. cum tibi, and extra de testis. c. requisisti, and 1, q. 7, ca. si quis omnes, and de relig. do. c. Zolo. decen., by the argument of ff. de pi. l. debitor, and ff. de hęre. inst. l. ex facto, §. rerum autem italicarum. Nevertheless, whether it ought to be comprehended as a member of the said monastery or separately, I shall state.

† Secondly, I premise that the said hospital of S. Andrea is a member of the said monastery, and so to speak, a member born from the beginning together with its head, which appears not only from the apostolic privileges, but also from the very name: because it is called the hospital of S. Andrea of Vercelli; for the genitive signifies a right, as in ff. de reli. l. 2, §. in locum, in accordance with what the law says: the father, it says, [judges] from the very name what he owes to the prefect or not, as in C. de offi. praefe. vr. l. 1. And from this it is inferred that the monastery is the head, and the hospital is a member connected to it, which ought not to be separated from its head, as in C. communia vtriusque iudicij, l. possessionum, and C. de agri. et cen. l. cum scimus, li. 11. And just as a father and a son are not said to undergo two burdens, but it suffices that the father undergo it for himself and his son, as is noted in l. 1, C. qui aetate, li. 10,

† so here the monastery, which is in the place of a father, ought not to undergo the burden of its own assessment-rate, which comprehensively signifies the entire and whole patrimony of the monastery and the hospital, and the tax ought not to be repeated for the hospital itself, because this evidently appears to be an excess. And that would be paid twice which is to be paid once, because civil and natural reason does not permit the same thing to be exacted twice from the same cause; for the other exaction would be undue, as in l. nam hoc nam, ff. de cond. ind. And it is certain that when anyone is burdened beyond what is due, he may have recourse to a superior, as in C. de censitoribus, et perequatorib. l. qui grauatos, lib. 11. Whence the sentence delivered on this matter was reasonably delivered, if it is true that the hospital is included under the assessment of the monastery. If, however, it is not included, and the said assessment is otherwise congruous, the sentence would not have been well delivered: because even the same man can have several particular assessments of several estates, but not several universal assessments, as in ff. de censi. l. forma; and it is similar in l. falci., which is imposed upon the goods of a father and a son, as in ff. ad l. falc. l. in ratione, §. quod vulgo. Item, where the goods of a father and a son are united, they are not said to be separated from each other, as in ff. de vulg. sub. l. sed et si plures, §. filio, and ff. de separat. bo. l. 1, §. sciendum, and C. de iure deli. l. quidam eulogio. For it matters greatly whether the valuation of the monastery is comprehensive of the whole and made indefinitely, or whether the monastery was assessed according to one measure and the hospital was assessed according to another, as in ff. de edil. edic. l. cum plura, and ff. de act. emp. l. si duorum. Because this is not established to me; but in doubt it seems it should be interpreted that the assessment was made as it ought to have been made, upon the person of the monastery integrally and comprehensively. For in doubt an ambiguous fact is referred to the law, as in ff. pro soc. l. merito. But if this is so, the monastery has cause to complain, and also the hospital has cause not to pay by itself, because the monastery pays for both under a single aggregate. Nevertheless, that which moves not a little to the contrary is that previously the monastery paid for itself, and the hospital for itself; by which payment voluntarily made, the clergy was established in quasi-possession of its being done in like manner for the future,

† for possession is acquired by a single effective act, as noted by Innoc. in extra de in integ. rest. c. 1. Moreover, the lord, by referring himself to custom, which is of fact, and not to that which is of law, seems to have referred himself to the immediately preceding act, as in ff. de ali. le. l. mella, §. 1. Whence the clergy can say to the abbot and to the hospitaler: 'as you possess, so may you possess; and as you paid, so may you pay.' But to this it is answered: because it does not appear that the abbot made that payment thus separately by mandate of the chapter, whence it could prejudice neither the ownership nor the possession of the monastery, as noted by Innoc. where cited above. Furthermore, the said writing is a private writing, to which credit ought not and cannot be given by law; for if it were a public writing, then perhaps it would be otherwise, as in extra de his, quae fi. a praela. capit. ea noscitur, through Innocen. What then shall we finally conclude? For this question is partly of fact and partly of law, and the conclusion is this: that if the assessment now made upon the monastery itself arises from some proportion of the ancient assessment, which is integral, the monastery has justice on its side, because that which depends on another assumes its quality, as in ff. de don. inter vi. et vxo. l. si donatę, §. si sponsus. If, however, it is a new and emerging assessment, and congruous with respect to the amount, then the clergy has justice on its side; whence the root of this imposition and its manner must be looked to, and in doubt the presumption is in favor of the assessors, since they were chosen by the consent of all, C. de secun. nup. l. hac edictali, §. his illud tamen, provided it appears that at other times payment was made separately; otherwise if it did not so appear, as has been said; to this effect ff. de le. 3, l. praediis, §. balnea, and ff. de fun. instr. l. Seya, §. mando, and l. cum delanionis, and ff. de ser. vrb. prae. l. Olympico. The final conclusion, therefore, is this: as you ought to have been assessed, so shall you pay. Which pertains to the office of the judge to examine, that he may inspect the books of the assessment in which the light of truth resides; and according to the division or union of the said books, let him so pronounce, do, and declare, and observe what was accustomed to be observed in the most recent payments, according to the mandate of the lord: as in the said c. cum non liceat, extra de praes. Whence if the said hospitaler has his own revenues and sustains his own burdens, and applies the fruits to the table of the hospital and not to the table of the abbot, he undoubtedly ought to undergo the burdens by himself, because the administrations and advantages are separate, although in the papal tithe he does that which was accustomed to be done of old. Item, if the privileges are considered, there is not properly a union, but a subjection; whence the hospital is not of the table of the monastery, but has a table by itself, de rescri. c. abbates, in Clem.; whence for the debts of the monastery the hospital is not bound, nor vice versa, ff. de mino. l. denique, §. sed vtroque; and it is absurd to say that the hospital should pay nothing either in the aggregate or by itself, for through this others would be burdened for the hospital, which is discordant; everyone ought to bear his own burden, C. vt nullus ex vicariis, l. j, li. 11; to this makes what is noted by Bart. in ff. ad l. fal. l. 1, §. si cohaeredem. Item, what difference is there whether the hospital is assessed at five and the monastery at ten, or both together at fifteen, in the effect of the payment, not as to the recipient? For he receives just as much, whether separately or in an aggregate, ff. de pac. l. maiorem; but the force is in this alone: lest one be burdened twice for once, as in C. de leg. l. cum questio. This is also determined by Old. in his consilia regarding him who impetrated one taxed benefice according to the taxation of the tithe, to which was attached another not taxed, saying that the letters were subreptitious because the untaxed one, on account of the union, added to the amount that was suppressed, according to Old. The hospital says: 'I wish to pay together with the abbot, but only for that which is imposed upon the abbot, because so it was accustomed to be done.' I answer: where it is imposed with respect to both together, it is true that so it was accustomed to be done; but here it was not so, whence when it is imposed distributively, the one is not included in the other, ff. de vulg. sub. l. cum ex filio, §. filio, nor is the manner of the tithe observed in this case. And the apportioners could have collected both into one; they could also have divided them, because in this I see no difference in effect, provided that both joined together would amount to as much as both separated from each other. By these things, however, no prejudice is done to the right of the monastery which it has in the hospital itself, nor is any power by law newly attributed through the aforesaid to the clergy against the said monastery and hospital, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is said to be natural, and whether. 6.
2. Legitimation, if one mode of illegitimacy is expressed, when there was another, whether it is valid.
3. Whether a grandson through a predeceased son can be legitimated at the instance of the grandfather.
4. Whether a legacy can be left to a spurious grandson by the grandfather.
5. How legitimated persons succeed.
body: A certain A., who was chaste, had two sons, namely B. and C., both of whom had legitimate and natural children; that is to say, B. had Maximam and Ioanna, who are alive today, and the said C. had one son, namely Nicolaus, from a young woman who was not his concubine but who worked for wages with the said A., father of the said C., before, however, the said C. took a wife, whom he married while the said young woman was still alive. And the said young woman was a widow. The said C. died, with the said A. and his brother B. surviving, and leaving Ioanna, Nicolaus, and Maxima. Afterwards, the said B. died, leaving all the above-mentioned persons. Afterwards, the said A. died, having made a will. Then, after making the will, he caused the said Nicolaus, who had been instituted as heir, to be legitimated, with Maxima and the above-mentioned Ioanna present. And he appointed Albert as guardian. On the other side, Ioanna, the ward, appeared; because Maxima cannot claim according to the form of the statutes, since she was married and very well endowed. And the said Ioanna says that the said Nicolaus was never the son of C., because he was not born in the household, and other objections are raised. Nicolaus says that he is the son, and he produces the will of his grandfather, the said A., and he produces the legitimation made for him. Ioanna says that those words placed in the will and in the instrument of legitimation do not prove him to be the son of the said C., and she cites l. non nudis with its companions in C. de prob. et no. and l. j. in C. de falsa causa adie. Nicolaus says: I am in possession of the filiation; you prove that I am not the son. Ioanna says: Where there is a right to bring a petitory action, there is no right to bring a possessory action, etc. And also, bastards are not in the power of their parents, and the name of grandfather and great-grandfather does not apply to a bastard, so that your allegation is invalid. And assuming, but not conceding, that you were the son, I say that you cannot succeed from the will except to one ounce, if the mother had been a concubine and legitimate children were extant. Nicolaus says: My grandfather named me son, and did not say bastard; therefore I am legitimate, as in Auth. ut liceat matri, et aviae, in §. ad haec. Ioanna says: That applies when legitimate and natural children are not extant, and the mother was a concubine. Moreover, those words were uttered by the grandfather, and not by the father; and thus they do not avail. And the reason is: because the consent of the grandfather cannot make her have been a wife, just as the consent of the father can, although in our case such consent does not even apply: because the said father, while the said young woman was alive, took a wife, and thus performed an act contrary to the will of the said A. And that you are natural appears from the legitimation made, because legitimate and natural children are not legitimated. And then Nicolaus says: If I am legitimate, therefore I can succeed. Ioanna says: I say that the legitimation did not hold. First, because it was obtained with tacit truth and express falsehood: because it is stated in the instrument, "in defect of birth." Second: because not all were cited to whom the benefit or detriment pertained, or could pertain, as is required by law. Third: because the rescript of the Lord Emperor does not wish that prejudice be done to legitimate heirs in succession, as appears in the said privilege. Nicolaus says: That applies in intestate succession, but I claim from the will. Ioanna says: This is not true in law; rather, the whole inheritance pertains to Ioanna, the ward, by reason of the share in which I was instituted: because one cannot die partly testate, etc. And insofar as it appears that you were a natural son, I will give you one ounce: indeed, you were not capable at the time of the will, therefore, etc. The said words of the testator do not avail, nor does the said legitimation, for the reasons above stated. Now the question is, what is the law. The first step, which is elicited from this case, is whether the legitimation was, and is, valid in law, or not. The second step is whether, by the very fact that the said legitimation of the said Nicolaus was made after the will of the grandfather and after the death of his father, it cannot tend to the prejudice of Ioanna, the ward; or whether, notwithstanding that it was made after the will of the grandfather, provided it was before the death of the grandfather, it ought to tend to the prejudice of the said ward, and this being posited without prejudice, that the said legitimation would be valid. The third step is, positing that the legitimation would not be valid, whether the institution of the said Nicolaus, natural, made by the grandfather, was valid, in such a way and manner that he has the power to exclude the said Ioanna, and to what extent he has the power to exclude her: whether in whole, as if his institution were valid in whole; or in part, as if the said Nicolaus were not capable of the whole; and in the above-mentioned matters, the question is, what is the law. The fourth step is whether the words of that grandfather make, or prove, him to be the son, and whether legitimate.

† This person was born from a free man and a free woman, and therefore he appears to be a natural child by the presumption of law; and also because people so believe, and by common usage of speech he is called a Bastard, as noted by Cynus in the Code, on the subject of natural children, in the law "Si". And if it is said, rather he is a spurious child, because he was born from a widow, as in the Institutes, on public judgments, § "Item lex", I say that this girl was of low condition: hence, with her, stuprum is not committed, as noted by Azo in his Summa on concubines. But certainly it does not follow from this that he is a natural child. For even a child commonly conceived is sometimes born from a free man and a free woman, and yet he is spurious, as in the law "Vulgo" in the Digest, on the status of persons, at the end. If someone simultaneously has several concubines, although free, and a free woman bears a child, nevertheless the children born from them are spurious, as in the Authenticum "Qui modo" on making oneself an heir, § "Si quis autem". And therefore it seems to be required that, for him to be the natural child of whom the laws speak, he must be born from a woman who is retained in the household with an undoubted concubinary affection. The said § "Si quis" declares that this intention is shown by a protestation and other apparent acts. For a clandestine access judges the contrary, as in the Digest, on concubines, in the law "In concubinatu". And furthermore, it is required that she be held in the stemma, i.e., in the order and status of a concubine, and be treated with some domestic honor, albeit lesser than that of a wife, as in the Digest, on legacies, title 3, in the law "Item in legato", § "Parvi". Bartolus says that children born from such girls are spurious and are not legitimated by a subsequent marriage, as in the Digest, on concubines, in the law "Si". Hence it seems to be said that if this father retained this woman as a concubine, this son is a natural child. But if he did not have affection for her, but fell into the commission by natural impulse, then this son is spurious.

† Let us now consider both points: if he is a spurious child, his legitimation as a natural child does not bind, because an error has occurred in the factual basis. For the law states that, although the petition must be made by the authority of the Prince, if a freedman was petitioned by a freeborn person who tacitly concealed that he was a freedman, such a petition, being obtained by fraud from the Prince, did not alter the status of freedmanship. D. 38.2.17 § patronum (De in ius vocando). To the same effect is the argument in D. 26.7.1 (De tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his). For it is not permissible for the petitioner to conceal anything material. Auth. Qui modo nati efficiantur sui § illud, in the words “declarantur.” And this is true according to the subtlety of the words. But there is doubt on account of common usage of speech and the general opinion of the vulgar, who regard these bastards as such.

But assuming that they were natural children and were legitimated prima facie by the count or by a rescript of the Lord Emperor, let us consider whether a grandson can be legitimated in the person of a grandson through a deceased son. And I say that by rescript one can be legitimated per saltum, i.e., in the grandson, skipping over the son, as in Auth. Qui modo naturales efficiantur sui, § Si quis igitur, in the word “aut auus,” col. 7; and eodem titulo, in principio, in the words “ad nepotes”; and § Si quis igitur habens, in the words “de nepotibus.”

And from this we have that the opinion of those who say that a legacy can be left to a spurious grandson by his grandfather is false; because if this were so, the legitimation of grandsons would be superfluous: which is false.

† Since it is assumed that he has been legitimated, the question arises as to what right he has. And it appears that he has a right equal to that of those born legitimate. But because those born so imprudently sometimes do not find equality sufficient in their minds, but wish to be preferred by will, the question arises as to what right [he has]. The text of the imperial privilege states thus: provided that the legitimations to be made do not prejudice legitimate children and heirs, and that they themselves succeed with equal portions together with those being legitimated. And I understand "heirs" to mean children of any kind. But suppose there are two daughters: one instituted in one ounce, the other instituted in three ounces; can this legitimated person have the entire residue? And it seems that he can. For since the rescript speaks of per capita [virile], it therefore speaks of intestacy; hence, by will, a legitimated spurious child born of a concubine may have more than a child born legitimate from marriage. But the text notably states that a legitimated person cannot have more than the least-having among the legitimate ones, in Auth. Qui modo naturales efficiantur sui, §. Et quoniam. And among all, [he cannot have more than] the least-having, whether by will or by donation, which is notable. The words of the rescript are interpreted, or at least he cannot have beyond the per capita share, arg. not. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. 3. As for the portion of natural but not legitimated children, it is established that, when legitimate descendants exist, they have one ounce, l. 2. C. de naturalibus liberis, and in Auth. Qui modo naturales efficiantur sui, §. Discretis, and not. in l. ultima, ff. de regula Catoniana.

† What shall we say? Is the child born of those little girls who go about to the fairs and the marketplaces, wander through the alleys and streets, and afterwards return to the house of someone by whom they become pregnant, simply and properly a natural child, or is he a spurious child? Is he not to be supported according to civil law, or is he to be supported, and is this speech inhuman? Nevertheless, according to the severity of civil law, because this womb is not guarded (C. de custodia rei ad Carbo, l. si), indeed it has a weariness of fornicating with many, and it cannot be said to be retained in the house (illa, namely, she who is not easily able to mix with another); the father is not certain, whereas this one, who wanders about, can, if she wishes. And the law does not accept these births as so obscure. Hence they are spurious and unknown. And although they are not hateful to the laws, because they are born of a free man and a free woman, nevertheless, as degenerate and unknown, they are held as spurious, as stated in the aforementioned law, *vulgo*. And if they are legitimated as natural children, the legitimation is not valid. And therefore it is necessary to legitimate them in this manner, namely, as born of a free man and a free woman, without expressing "natural." For if it is said "natural," the legitimation is not valid on account of the defect of expression or declaration (arg. ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. qui testamento vel quasi sit obreptum praetori), unless it is said that this error does not infringe the substance of the consent and legitimation, because if he had known this subtlety of the law, he would have done the same thing (l. Barb. Philip. in totum). To exclude this one stings my conscience and natural equity, and it is against the mind of the one who legitimates. And this one can be called natural in a broad sense, that is, not contrary to natural law, nor contrary to civil law, since the procreation itself is natural, and it is not overshadowed by an obstacle of civil law. And whatever civil rigor may dictate, the canonical laws call every child born of a free man and a free woman natural (extra de electione, ca. innotuit). And therefore the legitimation was valid, and this is the truth. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, and for the faith of this I have subscribed and signed with the signs of my name.

Whether a spurious child can be substituted as heir in l. 2, C. de haeredibus instituendis.
Whether, if a spurious child is instituted with a codicillary clause, that clause is valid, see C. de fideicommissis, l. eam, quam.
Whether that clause is divided if it is not valid, i.e., insofar as the heir is not valid, no. ff. de transactionibus.
I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the bishop may, for cause, extend the time granted to executors by the testator.
2. Whether the bishop may dispense against synodal constitutions.
body: The following doubt arises, namely: because a certain testator made a will, in which he instituted his only son, who was an impubes, as his sole universal heir, and he willed and ordained that if his said son were to die at any time without children and heirs lawfully descending from him, that certain goods of the said testator should be distributed to the poor of Christ for his soul and that of his predecessors, by two fideicommissaries and executors appointed and named in the will. It happens that by a synodal constitution, executors of last wills are bound to execute them within one year from the day of the death of the deceased, under penalty of excommunication for laymen, and of exclusion from church entry for clerics; nevertheless, they are deprived of the power to execute them, and that power of disposing devolves to the diocesan bishop. It happens that one of the executors obtained from his diocesan bishop an extension of the one-year period assigned by the synodal constitution to executors for executing last wills, calculated from the day of the death of the testator. It happens that within the synodal year, the distribution was not made by the above-mentioned executors; but after the said year, and within the time of the said extension, the said distribution was made by that one executor alone to whom the said extension had been granted. Similarly, the said distribution, made after the said year and within the extended time, was confirmed by the other executor. It happens that the diocesan bishop, after the lapse of the said year and the said extension, distributed the said goods to another, believing that the said power of distribution had been conferred upon or devolved to him. Now the question is asked: which of these distributions is valid and binding in law, or which of them ought to be preferred.

† If it is asked whether the bishop can extend the term of the executors, there is no doubt that he can: because by extending it, the course of the peremptory term assigned by the episcopal constitution is impeded. The constitution does not impose a law upon the bishop, but upon the executors; and therefore the bishop, as having full power, has the right to extend the term. And this is especially so for a cause, which is presumed in the bishop and in any magistrate in these acts, which are of voluntary jurisdiction. For if one of them had been ill or absent, this would certainly be a just cause for extending the term, because he who was not negligent should not be harmed by the passage of time, and the matter remains intact. As stated in the law and note 1 of the Authentica *de appellationibus*, after the principal, column 8, which supports this. *Digestum*, *de pretio stipulationis*, law 1, at the end; and *de verbis obligatorum*, law *Cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo*. Certainly, Bartolus holds this in a similar case in law 3, § *Dies*, and *de damno infecto*. And thus the testamentary execution will be extended. And assuming that it was not an extension, it is a certain commission made by the ordinary, who can do this even for a stranger, let alone for one whose fidelity has been approved by the testator. *Digestum*, *quod cuiusque universitatis nomine*, law *Item eorum*, § *Si decuriones*; and in the *Speculum*, *de instrumentis edicti*, § *Nunc aliqua*, which calls these executors "appointed executors." Hence it follows that if this person, whether we call him extended or newly appointed, made his distribution, such distribution shall prevail over the distribution of the bishop subsequently made: because the distribution was so perfect, provided it was made to the poor for a pious cause, as noted in the *Codex*, *de sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law *Illud*, and by Bartolus in *de legibus* 2, law *Unum ex familia*, § *Si duos*.

† Regarding the aforementioned constitution of the bishop, there is no doubt that it is valid, as noted by Bartolus in the title *Cum quidam*. Nor should anyone argue that this extension must arise from the testament, and therefore cannot be made unless in the same manner as the first. Concerning a precarium, however, if it remains: because whether it rests on justice or on grace, it can be extended in the person of him who, according to the usual custom, had the power, and whose tenure is extended, as stated in the chapter *Religiosis*, in the title *De testibus*, Book 6. And because the bishop is not compelled to grant grace during his own time. This serves to determine whether it is an extension or a new commission, as noted in § *Hi qui*, in the Authenticum *De prebendis*, Book 6. As for what is presumed by the judge in such matters, Innocentius notes in the extrajudicial title *De eo qui furtim ordinatus est recte susceptus*, § *Si*, and in the chapter *Innotuit*, *De arbitris*. And in my homeland, this custom is observed; I do not know what is observed here. Nor does it object that something could be strongly raised to the contrary: because against a general constitution of the bishop, the bishop himself cannot dispense, although he could abolish it entirely, as noted in the chapter *Licet canonici*, *De electione*, Book 6, in the great gloss. Because this is not a dispensation, but an extension, or at least a commission, which in no way touches the constitution of the bishop, because the synodal constitution says nothing about it. *Codex*, *De appellationibus*, law *Precipimus*, at the end. From these, it is concluded that if the distribution of goods was made by the said executor in the person of the poor, how valid it is according to law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The customs and statutes in force at the husband’s domicile are observed in the acquisition of dowries.
body: The Doctors

The latter say that in such gains we must examine the customs and statutes prevailing in the husband’s domicile, according to l. exigere dotem, D. de iure Archipresbyteratus, Distinctio 10, c. illa, and Bartolus in l. cunctos populos, column 4, verse ex praedictis. For by marriage the woman passes under the jurisdiction and authority of those who make the laws, l. cum quaedam puella, D. de iure omnium iudicum. I do not care where the things given as dowry are situated, arg. D. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. si, and C. de contrahenda emptione, l. 1. Hence, according to what is alleged, the husband has acquired the said dowry as a gain, and therefore he ought not to restore it. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What those words mean, namely, "if the owner and usufructuary."
2. The term "even": what it means; and no. 4.
3. The term "as": what it means; and no. 5.
body: Those words,

The words “domina” and “usufructuaria,” when used simply, receive this interpretation: that they have the usufruct in favor of an instituted heir who is a stranger. And this is observed by custom, unless another conjecture can be gathered from the presumed affection of the persons and from the quality of the words. Cf. D. de usu et usufructu leg. l. si alij. Now, therefore, let us consider the quality of those words, “even for maintenance,” or “even by maintaining herself.”

† For the word "even" is used for "especially"; as if it were said, especially by being maintained, just as was the case during the lifetime of the said testator, by receiving it by his own authority, as in D. 34.2, l. Titia, § 1. For it does not restrict, since it is of an ampliative nature. D. 34.3, l. tamen ea adiectio. And especially after the death of the sister of the said testator, and thus that charity being ended, which could have restricted the legacy. D. 34.2, l. Titia, § si, per Bartolus. And here I consider that either the testator speaks by way of demonstration, and does not restrict the legacy. C. 6.30, l. quidam testamento. Or by way of a mode inserted in favor of the legatee, and the same result. D. 33.9, l. Lucius. Or by way of a final cause, and then the legacy is restricted. D. 7.1, l. si ab initio, § 1. Or by way of a condition, and the same result, because a condition requires itself to exist.

† In our case, the word "as it was" gives rise to doubt. For it seems to restrict the matter to the mode that was observed during the testator's lifetime; yet it is certain that, strictly speaking, it was not a usufruct, although she had a certain freedom of administration, which consists in fact, which the testator wished to continue. I do not place emphasis on what he said, even that she was to be maintained.

† because the word "even" is an augmentative term, and therefore it does not restrict: as in c. etiam ob chirographariam pecuniam. In the rubric and black, the aforementioned are proven. de auro et arg. leg. l. species. ff. de dona. l. donationes in concubinam. §. species. ff. de ali. leg. l. 2. ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. si vni ff. de leg. 2. l. Titia cum testamento. §. fi. ff. de vsufru. earum rerum. l. fi.

But I reflect on that word, as: whether it refers to the substance of the entire legacy, or to the mode and quality of exercising her authority, as she did during her husband’s lifetime. D. de usufr. l. item si fundi. §. si. It seems sufficiently probable, from the affection for the person, that the sister contemplated full usufruct. Arg. D. de lib. leg. l. Aurelius. §. Titius. And the same appears to have been the sister’s intention in the will, and more expressly so: for she used words which cannot conveniently be restricted to mere maintenance. It would be vain to say, “I bequeath to you the maintenance of all my goods,” unless maintenance were placed for revenues. The case is doubtful. But this opinion is more probable, nor should the word “as” be referred except to that to which it can be referred without violating the rules of correct speech, i.e., to that word “usufructuary.” D. de au. et arg. leg. l. Plautius. It is certain that whatever is said for the purpose of amplification does not restrict, by l. legata. in princ. D. de sup. leg. says the said Cynus, from the equality of persons. Those words also expressly stated, “for the purpose of dwelling,” are to be interpreted in the said l. si habuero. Cynus. I said that there the word “purpose” limits the thing according to itself. D. de lib. leg. l. Aurelius. §. sticho. D. de legat. 2. l. cum pater. §. dulcissimis. Nevertheless, on account of the affection for the persons, that purpose is presumed to be impulsive according to Cynus, or at least not restrictive. Hence, since we are speaking here of a wife preserving the honor and vow of her husband, from such affection the words are to be interpreted more benignly, so that they are added for the purpose of amplification, not of restriction, since there does not exist a person who, from the presumed will of the deceased, could exclude her from the usufruct. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A usurer, who for 300 [units] purchased from a certain community an annual revenue of 30 gold florins each year: this person lived only long enough to receive six hundred [florins]; whether he is bound to restore what he received above the price.
1. Whether a syndic of the community, having a special mandate for this purpose, can make such a contract, and whether he binds the community, unless the price has been turned to the utility of the community.
body: The question is

† In such a case, a certain usurer purchased from a certain city an annual rent of 30 gold florins to be paid to him each year during his lifetime, for 300 silver florins. He lived only long enough to receive six hundred florins. The three hundred are claimed back as usury. The question is asked: what is the law?

It seems that this contract is invalid: because a contract of sale requires money on one side and a thing on the other. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. 1; D. de praescriptionibus verbis, l. naturalis, §. at cum. But here money turns over on both sides; therefore, it is not a sale. Moreover, this contract is in rem on one side and in personam on the other; yet it is presumed to exceed the lawful sum, as in C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, §. si.

On the contrary, it seems: because this rent is called "civil bread" and can be sold; for if it is a special rule in the Church that it cannot be sold, then the common law is to the contrary. C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus; Auth. de non alienandis, §. vult enim. Furthermore, this rent is counted among immovables; and thus it can be sold and bought. Argument from D. de re iudicata, l. communis. Furthermore, this contract is not usurious: because usury is the increase of the repayable principal, but here the principal is not to be repaid; therefore, nothing is added to the principal, and thus it is not a usurious contract. Furthermore, even if it were not a sale, it is nevertheless an innominate contract, do ut des. D. de conditionibus ob causam, l. si. Nor does the diversity of names vitiate it. D. de praescriptionibus verbis, l. insulam; D. de regulis iuris, l. si librarius. Furthermore, a contract that can be interpreted in a good sense should not be interpreted in a bad or vitious sense, as in C. de usuris, l. si ea pactione. Furthermore, this buyer subjected himself to the peril of fortune; hence, the price is for the peril. D. de nautico foenore, l. periculi. Furthermore, if this buyer had lived only one hour, would the seller have restored the price to him? Certainly not; therefore, one should not demand from another what one does not consider in oneself, or the contrary of which one would not have demanded. Furthermore, here hope seems to have been bought, and therefore the value of that hope must be considered, and it should not be judged by the event, according to Bartolus, D. de publicanis, l. contem, §. qui maximos. Furthermore, age should be considered. D. ad legem Falcidiam, ad hereditatem, inde. From this, a conjecture of life and death is taken. Furthermore, one transacts differently with an old man, differently with a young man. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. modis autem pro aetate. Furthermore, due to uncertainty, it is not said that the limit is exceeded. C. de usuris, l. si ea. Furthermore, this expression did not happen by fact, but by fate. Because to live is a benefit of God and nature alone; therefore, we ought to give thanks to God for a man's life, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haeres meus, in principio. Furthermore, otherwise it would follow that usufruct could not be bought without the peril of usurious wickedness, if any excess were found, which is false: because it is not rescinded unless there is lesion beyond half the price at which it would commonly be sold to a buyer of that age and quality. D. de usucapione, l. 3, §. 1. And many other similar contracts would be rescinded: which is absurd and inequitable. For if someone were to lease Saltworks and tolls from the republic at a lower price, it would be rescinded in the same way, as if in fraud of usury, as if a lease could be made in fraud of usury, which is false: because a contract where there is potential equality of loss and gain is far removed from usurious wickedness, or from the sweetness of usury, due to the double-edged peril. Argument from D. pro socio, l. si non fuerint, §. 1; and see D. de pactis, l. episcopalia, §. si; D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. necessario, §. ultimo; D. de locato, l. si quis domum, §. huic.

It is not an obstacle that it is noted in Extra, de usuris, cap. naviganti, and cap. in civitate, where fraud is presumed: because there, although the thing was not necessarily certain, it was nevertheless close to certainty; here it is not, and therefore the case is different here and different there. Argument from the said l. periculi; and what is noted in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. 1, and l. sed de eis.

But does a city syndic, having a special mandate to conclude this contract, bind the city if the price is not applied to its benefit? Answer: Yes, if the mandate contains such authority, because he may confess; for where one can bind the principal by mere confession, application of the price is not required. But if he lacks a mandate to confess, nevertheless, since he has a special mandate for this contract, namely to contract in this manner, it suffices to prove necessity. D. de exercendo, l. si. And even without proof of necessity, an obligation is contracted in another contract for which he has a mandate, other than a loan; indeed, even in a loan, unless the purpose for which it is to be used is specified in the mandate. D. de iure fisci, l. si procurator; and in Auth. hoc ius porrectum; and D. de deposito generis, according to the doctors in l. ciuitas, D. si certum petatur, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a tax farmer, or a simple collector of a tax, can remit the duty or tax to one bringing merchandise, so that the goods do not fall into forfeiture.
body: It is proposed that Perinus and Iordaninus, brothers and sons of Bartholomew Michel, merchants of Lucca, in the present year, in the month of May just past, sent certain merchandise to Paris on two beasts, which they consigned to John of Pelatia, knight of the illustrious and magnificient Lord, the Count of Virtues, etc., together with the quantity of money required for the payment of tolls on account of the said merchandise. And the said Iordaninus had letters to the effect that he was a knight of the aforementioned most illustrious Prince. And when he arrived with the merchandise in the city, he consigned it to the toll-collector, who held the toll on the merchandise for a certain quantity of money. By whom, being asked who he was, whence he came, and what he was doing, he showed to the said publican the said letters and the merchandise, asserting, according to the tenor of the said letters, that he was a knight of the aforementioned Lord, and that he was conveying the merchandise to Paris. These things having been heard, the toll-collector granted him license to go about his business; and, having been licensed, he departed, having waived the toll. Therefore, the question is,

Whether the merchandise fell into forfeiture due to the toll not being paid. This question is clearly settled. D. de publicanis (50.6), l. si, §. si quis professus. Especially because the benefit of the toll belonged to the tax farmer, and not to the treasury, therefore the remission of the toll was granted to him only insofar as it concerned his benefit; indeed, even if he were a simple official, he would still be excused, as stated in the same law. And note that, although the toll could be collected without penalty from a solvent person in the absence of an official, as the glossa states in the aforementioned §. si quis professus. Since the penalty incurred by the defendant is applied to the tax farmers who are the contractors of the toll, there is no doubt that they can act to their own prejudice to ensure that the said penalty is not incurred; and if it were incurred, they can remit it, as the learned Cynus advised, based on D. de actionibus emptoris et venditoris (19.1), l. creditor, in principio, and C. de vectigalibus (4.60), l. si quis sine. Therefore, he who showed his goods and was licensed by them incurs no penalty, as stated in the aforementioned §. si quis professus. But if they were not contractors, but mere collectors of the toll, they cannot remit the toll. Nevertheless, he who confessed would not incur the penalty according to one interpretation of the aforementioned §. si quis professus. Others say otherwise on this point, based on D. de verbis obligandis (45.1), l. qui Romae, §. Calimachus. The first opinion is more correct when the carrier of the goods should not have believed himself to be liable on account of the letters of the owner, because owners are accustomed to be lenient with each other in such matters; therefore, having taken into account the custom, he had a just cause for believing himself not to be liable. Argumentum: D. de pignoribus actionibus (13.7), l. universorum. Hence, there was no fraud nor fault in the carriage of the goods. Moreover, he believed the toll collector, who licensed him, when he ought to have believed him, because he was a public official. However, he could not remit the principal of the toll to the prejudice of the treasury. But the goods did not fall into forfeiture, because, as far as he was concerned, he is not alleged to have omitted anything regarding contingencies, and if the toll collector was a mere toll collector. For if he was a contractor, there is no doubt that he could be liberal with his own money, or that his own negligence harms himself. Therefore, this question, in the case of a contractor of the toll or passage fee, has no doubt that the goods are not lost; but in the case of a simple collector appointed by the lord or the community of the place, it has doubt due to the lack of mandate. Nevertheless, according to what they propose, I think the same applies to him based on the arguments cited above. And because a general mandate over some act can prejudice the lord in seeking remedies. C. de acquisitione possessionis (41.2), l. si, and l. 1, §. magistrum, D. de extra ordinem cognitionibus (2.1), and the aforementioned §. Calimachus, and the aforementioned §. si quis professus, according to Bartolus and others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. By what penalty is one punished who causes someone to be seized unjustly. And no. 5.
2. What jurisdiction is said to be held by the judge of tolls, and what he may do.
3. What penalties a pedaneus judge may impose.
4. What is the nature of gerunds, whether it is to declare, restrict, or enlarge.
body: A certain person, at the request of Titius, had the judge of the gabelle order Titius to be arrested at his insistence. Since no mandate had intervened, nor did it in any way pertain to the office of the judge of the gabelle, he had the said Titius arrested and detained in prison. And because the said judge of the gabelle denied that he had ever given the said license, he had the same Titius released. When the said Titius complained of the said injury and of the damages inflicted upon him, he petitioned the Illustrious Prince, the Lord Count of Virtues. At whose request the aforementioned Prince ordered the aforementioned judge of the gabelle to punish him who is found to have erred, on account of the matters contained in the aforementioned petition, according as it may seem appropriate in law, in order to compensate the petitioner for all damage and interest which ought reasonably and by right to be reserved to him on account of the said matter.

† It is asked whether, and what are the parts of the said judge of tolls in cognizing, proceeding, and punishing the aforementioned person, who caused the said Titius, his debtor, to be seized in this manner de facto and detained in prison, considering both the common law and the letters of the prince writing thereon. To which I answer that the said judge of tolls is not presumed to have granted the said license; because a judge is not presumed to have commanded unjust things, especially since the said debt did not arise from any other cause than on account of tolls, and thus it did not pertain to his office. Hence, unless the commission of the judge appears, it must in no way be presumed, as C. de iure fis. l. prohibitus. li. 10. and C. de man. prin. l. 1. and C. de exhi. reis. l. neminem. It follows therefore that the said seizure was injurious. But it must be seen whether it follows that the said seizure was false, i.e., that the said creditor, under the pretext of a false commission, by opening the said prison keepers and circumventing them with deceit, caused the said Titius to be detained. From what appears in the records, it does not seem proven that the said debtor said any words to the keepers. And thus the crime of falsity or stellionatus does not appear, in which deceit and liquid proof are required. If these were apparent, he could well be punished for such deceitfulness, as C. de falsis. l. nec exemplum. ff. de falsis. l. qui nomine. and l. si quis obrepsit. and ff. de iur. fis. l. in fraudem. §. quotiens. ff. ad muni. l. Titius. cum esset sicut qui facit falsam ambasciatam ex parte iudicis, as noted C. de spor. l. 2. ff. de cust. reo. l. diuus. C. quomodo, et quando iudex. l. si vt proponis praeses. ff. de fur. l. si quis vxori. §. apud labeonem. and this case is posited by the law. ff. quod met. causa. l. fi. in fi. in l. and glo.

And it must be said briefly that the aforementioned tax judge, who does not possess *merum imperium* (full sovereign power), even if he has proof of *obreptio* (fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation), cannot deport or exile, nor confiscate goods generally, as stated in C. de sen. et interlo. omn. iudi. l. nulli. Hence, by virtue of his jurisdiction, although an injury has been done to his jurisdiction, he nevertheless cannot exercise *merum imperium* by imposing heavier penalties; but he may well exercise a certain extraordinary jurisdiction or authority on account of the injury done to his jurisdiction, as noted in C. de test. l. nullum, and in the text of d. l. 2. de spor., and according to Cynus, and it is clear from ff. de offi. procon. l. si qui velit, and ff. de offi pręfe. vigi. l. fi. Therefore, he can punish with a pecuniary penalty if something concerning such falsehood is established to his knowledge; and I believe sufficiently that it is established through a certain confession made to him by the said creditor. For, as I said, he can judge the injury committed against his jurisdiction; therefore, he is a competent judge, and in confession the order of law is not required, as noted in ff. de infa. l. ictus fustium. And assuming that he was not then a competent judge, a rescript has supervened, whereby he is compelled by the same judge to persist in the same confession, as noted by Innocentius in extra de ele. c. per inquisitionem.

† As for the penalty of private imprisonment, it is not to be discussed here: because a lay judge cannot impose such penalties, nor does the prince’s rescript allow that anyone be compelled beyond the penalty that is appropriate according to law and jurisdiction; indeed, if one carefully weighs the rescript, it does not speak of punishment except with regard to damages and interest to be recovered thereby.

† whose nature it is, when posited without fault, to distinguish and declare, and not to extend, as noted in l. 1, C. de his qui latrones, per Jacobus de Belvis. My final opinion is, considering the intention of the prince, that this person be punished by the penalty of restitution of damages and interest; and also by some extraordinary penalty in the manner of a fine, as in ff. de his qui notantur infamia, l. debuit. Nor would it perhaps be inappropriate that he be deprived of the right to a debt otherwise credited, as in Auth. ut non fiant pignora, col. 5, and in Auth. ut nulli iudicio, §. fin., and as noted in ff. quod metus causa, l. extat. I therefore say that he be punished in damages and interest; and also that he be punished at the discretion of the judge by a penalty applied to the fisc, because he does injury to the magistrate.

† Regarding the restitution of damages and expenses, and a certain small penalty, taking into account the status of the judge, he should be condemned. And it is similar to what we say in the action for injuries: because it cannot be denied that this person was captured by injury and detained by injury, as noted in ff. de privatis delictis, l. si; and ff. de iniuriis, l. iniuriarum aestimatio. And there it is said that in the case of a person of low status, the estimation of the injury is low and moderate. And so it is in our case, and it is safer for the judge to proceed under this heading than under the heading of correction: because this heading is more clear from the acts. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a son transmits the inheritance of his father or mother, not yet accepted, to ascendants or descendants; and whether he transmits the right of deliberation; and what is the case regarding the benefit of restitution.
body: The case is this: Titia, having a mother and the mother’s sister, and a paternal grandmother, became ill and lost her senses and speech, so that she understood nothing. Nevertheless, before Titia died, her mother died. Then Titia died, having not accepted her mother’s inheritance, with the aforementioned grandmother and aunt surviving. The question is: to whom does the inheritance and the goods of the aforementioned mother belong?
