Whether to the paternal grandmother by right of the grandson, or to the mother’s sister in her own right. Hence, the point at issue lies in the transmission of the maternal inheritance.

† And it is certain that this does not transmit the right of deliberation: because she lacked understanding. C. de iur. deli. l. cum antiquiorib. But nevertheless, the gloss in l. apud hostes says that the inheritance of ascendants, if not accepted, is transmitted to those who transcend them. And so hold some doctors. Others say that the inheritance is not transmitted, nor the right of deliberation: but restitution in integrum is transmitted through the said daughter and maternal grandmother: because she was a minor. C. de resti. mili. l. 1. de reb. du. l. qui duos. in prin. and d. l. cum antiquioribus. per Bar. and ff. de acquhae. l. Pantonius. and l. cum quidam. Here it must be considered whether in our case the said daughter, who had lost her understanding while her mother was alive, is equated with a madman or a lunatic, in whom it is specially provided that, upon dying, they do not transmit the inheritance in any way, unless possession of goods had been sought in their name by a curator. as C. de cur. fur. l. si. §. si autem in furore. Therefore, perhaps the law provides this because one who immediately loses understanding is similar to a dead person. ar. C. de test. l. iubemus. and afterwards did not recover it, therefore, as if dead, he does not transmit. Nor is there any law in the world which grants restitution in integrum to lunatics, whence lunacy hinders transmission more than age. And the law in the case of a lunatic distinguishes only two cases, namely: either he is a sui heres, and he transmits; or he is not a sui heres, and then it is otherwise. Whence then the nearer relatives of the deceased succeed, as d. §. sui autem. in gl. qui defuncto. The same therefore applies to a madman, i.e., one who had previously totally lost his mind. For the reason is the same for these two, as in Auth. hi qui circa medium. And because the law so provides, even against the statute of the law, restitution in integrum is not granted. For one is not harmed by negligence, or absence, or age, but by madness and disease. To this effect is what we note in Cyn. in l. non pro numero. C. ad Senatuscon. orfi. And this opinion is quite equitable and probable according to the law, adhering to the text of d. §. sui autem in furore, where no distinction is made between major or minor: but it speaks indiscriminately, as appears in that l. §. si autem ex alia. This could also be most strongly persuaded, because the mother’s sister survives. But the same applies to other successors of the mother, by what has been said above. And this is, as I said, the more equitable opinion and more conformable to the text of the laws: although, as I said, there are various opinions. And all the above are confirmed by other reasons. For if the benefit of restitution in integrum were transmitted, the law which says that an unaccepted inheritance is not transmitted would be imposed on words, and not on things. Also it would follow that the heir of a major lunatic would always be restored on behalf of the lunatic, since they have the benefits of minors, as we note in l. 2. C. de cur. furio. Moreover, a minor is not restored where the same would have happened to a major. But this would have happened to any major person deprived of sense, therefore the minor is not restored, as l. non videtur. Moreover, it would follow that the condition of a minor not transmitting the right of deliberation would be better than if he transmitted that right of deliberation: for if perhaps only a month or a day remained of the year, he would transmit only that remaining time, and his heir would not be restored. But if he transmitted nothing of the inheritance, he would transmit four years for seeking restitution, which is absurd. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mere executor must carry out his duties without fear.
2. Citation must be made three times, or by public crier, when a serious prejudice is at stake.
body: In the case of the noble lord, the day of Blacina

† I say that the mandate of the magnificence made in his favor ought to be put into execution, and the mere executor ought not to fear the exception [provided] in Extra de app. c. nouit. and c. ex ratione, according to Innocentius. Moreover, that which was done to the prejudice of the said lady is not valid for several reasons. First, because it is not established that she is bound in any way to her adversary. C. de prohi. seq. l. 1. C. de exce. rei iudi. l. nimis propere. C. de pac. l. si pacto, quo pęnam. Second, because it is neither alleged nor proven that she is the heir of her father, as is noted in l. si cum dotem. §. transgrediamur. ff. sol. matr. and l. 1. C. si vt se ab habetur. absti. Third, because the substance of the credit is not clear. C. de ac. et obl. l. negantes.

Fourthly, because a serious prejudice is at issue, he ought to have been cited three times, or peremptorily. C. quoniam, and when the judge. l. three denunciations. Fifthly, because his contumacy does not appear, since he was not accused. C. de iud. l. properandum. in fi. prin. Sixthly, it must be considered whether the said precept was made on the assigned Wednesday. l. si vitam. §. fi. quod vi aut clam. per Dy. and Bart. Seventhly, execution cannot be made against the debtor of the debtor, unless the debtor has been condemned and exhausted. ff. de re iudi. l. a diuo pio. §. fina. §. pen. and fin. and l. non prius. when the fiscus, or private. ff. de iur. fis. non intelligitur contra multa. Therefore, he concludes for the lord, that the magnificent one ought to be obeyed in that which is of his intention. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute excluding daughters while a male heir exists, whether by such statute they ought to be excluded in perpetuity, or rather only so long as the male heir lives.
body: The words of the municipal statute under the title “On the Legitimate Portion of a Son, If the Father Has Only One Son,” and also under the title “On Successions Intestate,” always establish as the primary cause the children, provided that a sister does not succeed while a male heir exists. Also under the same heading: if a father, who excludes his sister from the succession to the parent’s goods, dies without children, and without a consanguineous brother, his son, or his agnate grandson of the male sex, having made a legitimate will, or having entered a monastery or any other venerable place, offering or giving his property, or declaring that he will live without his own means, he shall leave to his sister or sisters, and to their sons of the male sex, half of all the goods which he possessed at the time of his death, from those which came to him through succession or by a lucrative title, or from any ancestor through his father. From these words arises the question which is posed: whether the sister of Albrici ought to have half in accordance with the form of the said statute, or not, since there survives the daughter of the said Albrici, instituted by him as universal heir.

† And first it must be considered whether those words, “while a male is extant,” are to be understood as meaning: until the male lives; so that the sense would be that, upon the death of the male without a male heir from his own body, the sister resumes the rights which she had lost on account of the male’s privilege; or whether they are to be understood as referring to that time from which the succession is first deferred. In favor of the first part it is argued, because the privilege lasts as long as the final and substantial cause of the privilege lasts. But the exclusion of the female was introduced for the privilege of the male; therefore it lasts as long as the male survives. Argument: C. de inoff. testa. l. si; ff. de vulg. substit. l. ex facto; ff. de testam. mil. l. ius militis, §. militia; ff. ad l. Falc. l. si post missionem. The contrary is true, because one who is once simply excluded never resumes the right from which he is once found to be excluded, as noted in C. de sec. nup. l. in quibus. Moreover, when the inheritance has been applied to another, it remains fixed and rooted with him and his successors perpetually, especially on account of personal obligations which adhere like a character. ff. de min. l. si sine; §. sed quod Pap. ff. pro socio. l. ea vero; inst. de bon. poss. §. quos autem. Moreover, dominion once acquired is by nature perpetual and transmissible. C. de donat. l. si avia; C. de prob. l. siue possidetis; ff. de reg. iur. l. heredem; ff. de acq. poss. l. cum heredes; ff. quibus ex cau. mai. l. cum miles. Furthermore, it is a rule of law that when it is a question of the inclusion or exclusion of an heir, regard is had to the time at which the inheritance is first deferred and acquired. inst. de legit. agn. success. §. prox. This part was held by Bartolus in l. filius familias, §. quando impedienti, which is the final law, and §. fin. of the entire Infortiatum, ff. ad Tert. And this is the truth.

Secondly, it must be considered regarding that statute, “if the brother, who [excludes] the sister,” whether it has application in our case; and it seems that it does. And thus the sister ought to have the half of which the statute speaks. For the words seem clear and general; because there is a brother who excludes the sister at the time of the father’s death; therefore there is no doubt, because the words are clear and open. And where the case of the statute exists, there is no room for interpretation. C. de indicta viduit. l. fin. Moreover, in doubt it is better to adhere to the words of the edict. ff. de exercit. l. 1, §. si is, qui navem. Moreover, this determination is general. ff. de test. mil. l. in fraudem, §. fin. Moreover, this seems a great equity, that the granddaughter does not exclude the daughter. C. de bonis matr. l. si viva matre. Moreover, and for another reason, it seems most equitable: because the statute introduced a certain reparation to the sister upon the extinction of the male sex. But we ought not to depart from the intent of the law, as in ff. de pactis. l. quod dictum. And that which is lost by one case is as it were resuscitated by the contrary case, as in Auth. de non eligen. sec. nub. §. Gregoria. Moreover, this is that sister whom the brother excludes. s. ex testamento. For she has neither querela nor action for supplement while the male is extant, as noted by Bartolus in d. l. fin. Therefore, the true terms of the calling of the sister are present; therefore the sister is called by the words and intent of the statute.

On the contrary, the text says that the difference between emancipation and paternal power has been removed; but because this text is placed under the rubric de success. ab intestato, we say that this difference is removed ab intestato, and not by testament. ff. de min. l. si filius; ff. de inoff. testa. l. si proponas; ff. de collat. l. si emancipatus; ff. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum. Moreover, this §. si frater, qui sororem, continues from the preceding, and cannot be referred except to the preceding; and things said in the preceding are understood to be repeated for the declaration of the following. l. nihil, ff. de coniung. cum emanc. lib. eius. Hence it is understood to be of the brother privileged ab intestato. Moreover, the words of the law ought to be taken according to the title under which they are placed, as noted in ff. de cond. inde. l. si; ff. de in diem adiect. Imperator. Furthermore, and this is the living reason: sometimes the brother is the proximate and immediate cause of the exclusion; and then the statute speaks. Sometimes it is not the brother, but the father; and then otherwise: because although the father’s testament is confirmed by statute, nevertheless the testament itself and the father himself are the immediate cause of the exclusion; and therefore there is no room for complaint against the brother. ff. de inoff. testa. l. Papi., §. sed nec impuberis. Although the statute tacitly makes it impugnable, nevertheless the statute does not give, but the father principally gives. ff. de pact. l. legitima; ff. de pet. haer. l. 2 and 3; ff. de verb. sig. l. lege obvenire haeredi. The statute therefore speaks of the brother who is by himself the immediate cause of the exclusion, and solely by the privileges given to him by the statute, and thus ab intestato. For the principal and immediate cause is regarded, and not the remote. l. si mulier, rerum am. The brother, therefore, who does not exclude by himself, but through the father’s testament, is not said to exclude himself, but the father, from whom this exclusion ought to be named. ff. de vulg. sub. l. patris, et filii.

Furthermore, by the very fact that the statute wishes the legitime to be half, it immediately follows that it ought to be without burden, because this is the nature of the legitime portion, since it is considered as if it were a debt. C. de inoff. testa. l. scimus, unless the law specially appended this burden to the legitime. ff. sol. matr. l. si cum dotem, §. si pater. By Jacobus de Arena, I opine that the daughters of Albrici have the stronger rights. But if the statute were otherwise interpreted, those things which had a certain interpretation ought not to be changed. ff. de leg. l. minime. It is clear, therefore, that in the legitime of Albrici, although it follows in the case of a testate succession, the sister has no right. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a mother is excluded from the succession of her son by the provision of a statute when she enters into a second marriage, unless she has been instituted by him, is she considered excluded if she was substituted for the son in a pupillary substitution in the father's will?
body:
Such is the case. The statute of the city of Asti provides that any widow may, with all right entirely removed and the children of the first or any other marriage excluded, by operation of law and by the law itself, with all interpretation of law and fact removed and without any intervention of the woman, act, contract, order, and transfer in dowry, and in any other manner to a second or subsequent husband, her dowry and any goods belonging to her by legacy or disposition of her former husband, or in any other way. Conversely, the second or subsequent husband, his children, heirs, and successors, and any holders of the goods of the second or subsequent husband, stand on the same equity of reason, that the mother is excluded by herself, and any of her ascending, descending, and collateral lines, and those who would have any right from her in any way, from all right of succession to the inheritance of the children of the first or subsequent marriage; and she is excluded, and they are excluded, from all claim to the legitimate portion, or the debt of subsidiary goods, and even the supplement of the legitimate, in the same manner as above, from the inheritance of the son or sons. Likewise, the mother is excluded and entirely stripped, by herself and any of her ascending, descending, and collateral lines, and those who would have any right in any way, from all right of guardianship and claim for a guardian of the children of the first and subsequent marriage. However, if anyone were appointed or given by her upon her passing to a second or subsequent marriage, he is to be considered as not appointed or given; rather, the guardianship is to be deferred to the agnates and cognates of the ward, as the laws provide; and also the inheritance of such ward, and also of another or other sons, after the aforementioned age, intestate or by testament of the deceased mother, is excluded, and the cause and denomination are to be taken from him. Provided, however, that if the woman herself, or anyone of her line having cause and denomination from her, were instituted heir in solidum, or in ownership, or in some quantity, or in a certain thing, or if anything were left to her or them, in which case or cases the disposition of the said statute does not claim a place in the said woman and the others aforesaid. But they may claim, demand, and have that which the chapter is understood to apply to, and has place, both in widows who are married, and also in women who are otherwise widows and now married, and conversely. And for the observance of the said statute, the Podesta of Asti and future ones, and their judges, and soldiers, and any other officials of the city of Asti, and its government and presidents, are expressly bound by the bond of oath.

Then Antonio de Niueis, a citizen and merchant of Asti, coming to his death, made a nuncupative and solemn testament: in which, after many legacies, he appointed and wished to have as guardians of his daughters Master Martin Capella, doctor of laws, citizen of Asti, and Simonetta, the wife of the said testator. In all his other goods, he instituted as universal heirs Beatrice, Joan, Alice, and Emerald, daughters of the said testator. And if it should happen that they, or any of them, should die in pupillary age, or otherwise at any time, he substituted to the same, or those dying, the said Master Martin Capella and the said Simonetta, his wife. The said testator having died, and the inheritance having been accepted by the said guardians, and guardianship decreed to them; and also an inventory having been made of the goods of the said late testator, the said Simonetta, after the year of mourning, married a second husband, to whom she gave in dowry her dowry of the first marriage, and also the legacies made in the testament of the said Antonio, her first husband. Then, while she was married to the second husband, Beatrice, one of the said daughters, died in pupillary age, the other sisters being alive, as well as the said Master Martin and Simonetta. Now the said Simonetta, mother of the said Beatrice, claims half of the inheritance of the said Beatrice by virtue of the said substitution. On the other hand, it is said that she cannot come to the inheritance of the said Beatrice in any way, the aforementioned statute being an obstacle: because she passed to a second marriage, disposing of her dowry and other legacies made to her by her first husband. And that the said testator could not by his disposition remove the disposition and effect of the said statute, because no one can do so that laws do not have place in his testament, etc. And that the testator cannot remit the favor of the heir. For just as the sons are excluded from the inheritance of the mother passing to second vows, so also is she excluded from the inheritance of the children by the disposition of the same statute. Likewise, it would be absurd to say that the mother, by virtue of the disposition of the testator, would succeed to the son, and the son would not succeed to the mother married to a second husband, and in the dowry and other things by virtue of the said statute. Also, this is objected by the said Simonetta, that she ought to come to the said inheritance by virtue of the said statute, where it is said: provided, that if the woman herself were instituted heir, etc. To which it is answered, that she was not instituted heir by the daughter herself: because she died in pupillary age. And that the statute cannot refer to paternal substitution: because the said statute says, provided, that if the said woman were instituted heir, etc. and thus it is understood of the woman already married to a second husband. And thus it refers only to the institution by the son, not to the substitution made by the father, therefore, etc. Also, it is opposed by the said Simonetta, that the daughter seems to have instituted her, when the father made the said substitution: because the father can make a testament for himself and for his impubes child, etc.

From the foregoing, it is asked: whether the said Simonetta comes to the inheritance of her said daughter in any way by virtue of the disposition of the said testator, or whether she is excluded from it by the force of the disposition of the said statute. And if she is excluded, whether the part of the said Simonetta accrues to the said Master Martin, the substitute. Also, it is asked: whether the said statute in any way prejudices the said Master Martin because he is a blood relative of the said Simonetta.

Without going through ambiguities, the said mother together with the other substitute come by the pupillary substitution: because that is the father's testament as regards the ordering. And it is the ward's testament as regards the succession. And thus, properly and truly, neither the common law nor the permissive part of the statute claims a place, as noted in ff. de inoff. testa. l. Papi. §. sed nec impuberis, where the aforementioned words are found. And it is the text in Auth. de nup. §. disponat. and C. de secundis nup. l. foeminae, in fin. An accessory similarly cannot be weighed by itself. ff. de execu. rei iudi. l. si in iudicio. But there it speaks of an accessory of judgment, but of an accessory of a thing it speaks in ff. de rei vend. l. vtique.

CASE. A war arose in the matter of the question between Lucius, the plaintiff, and Mevius, the defendant, on the occasion of a fief and homage: to which Lucius asserted that the said Mevius was bound to him for a certain castle, which he held from the same Lucius in fief, and under homage and ligeance: while Lucius, the plaintiff, was ready to make war against the said Mevius for obtaining his right. A certain greater prince and King, requested both by his son, who asserted that he was prior in time in the fief and homage of the said castle by his right, and by the said Mevius, the defendant: at their request, he caused the banner of the said King to be placed upon the said castle. Then the said Lucius, the plaintiff, not a subject of the King, although a man and vassal of the same: yet not by reason of the fief of which it is here treated, was requested on the part of the said King, that he abstain from war and from making offense against Mevius. But that the same Lucius would submit himself to the cognition of the King on the matter of his war and question. Who Lucius answered by a certain letter of his, which was directed to a certain official of the said King, as follows subsequently.

Responsive Letters.
Most dear friend, we have received your gracious letters, and heard what was related on your part by Messrs. Peter and Jacob: through whom, that if the notification and request proceeded by Royal consent, that was from the information of someone keeping silent on our rights. Wherefore we are certain that if the Royal Majesty had been informed, or reminded of our right, he would not have proceeded to our prejudice, as he did: and also would not have had such intimations made to us. And although we well know the great prejudice that arises therefrom to us, nevertheless, because we desire with our whole heart to serve, obey, and please our lord the King, if it is so that you are certain that our adversary will present himself personally before the Royal Majesty, where he will be, or before you within your territory, answering for you and giving reason for those things which we say and demand of him in one brief term: we will be in that term before our lord the King or before you for receiving reason from him, and giving reason to him for those things which he will wish to say or demand of us. We offering to you to send our son as hostages, until we present ourselves before the said lord King or before you, and we will cease from all offenses and wars to be inflicted on our said adversary in that case, unless other new things come to us from the parts of the kingdom. And if it were so that it would please you more to come to these parts before the aforementioned term, for receiving under true conduct our said adversary, and leading him before the King in your land before you, we ourselves would come with you before the said lord King, or before you for taking and giving reason, as above. And in the case that you are not well certain otherwise than by words, or letters, or by hostage of the representation of his person, we beg you, that it not displease you, if we proceed against our adversary according to our proposal. And if God help us, it seems to us that if he refuses to present himself before our lord the King, or before you, who represent his person, it ought not to displease the King, if we procure our right against our adversary, as best we can. And although we offer to receive reason from him before the said lord King, or before you: this is not on account of any homage to which he is bound to the King of Dauphiné, because we do not hold him for such, but we do it only for the honor and reverence of our said lord King: to whom we are, and will be, true, legal, and obedient in all times of our life. And you wish to write to us on these matters within the next 12 days: because thus we have agreed with the said Messrs. Peter and Jacob, your ambassadors.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An appeal may be made to the Pope from an unjust sentence of the King of France, who is not a subject.
2. Whether the jurisdiction of the King is deemed to have been prorogated, or a compromise made in his favor, by those words: "we shall be before our lord the King for receiving judgment on such matter."
3. Whether a compromise made in the King expires upon his death, or upon the death of the party making the compromise.
4. Whether the instance of the judgment passes to the heirs.
5. Whether the instance is terminated by the passage of time.
body: Therefore, I think,

† That a non-subject of the King of France may appeal to the Pope from an unjust sentence of the King of France, as provided in *Extra*, *De iudiciis*, chapter *Novit*; and if he has the strength to resist in fact, as noted in *Codex*, *De iudicibus*, law *Nullus*; for one who resists is not his subject, *Extra*, *De re iudicata*, chapter *Pastoralis*. Nevertheless, let him see what he does, *Codex*, *De his qui ut indigni*, law *Pol.*; because it is against the greater [authority] and against the dignity of the King of France. *Digest*, *Per prima vexilla*: let no one presume to dishonor the invincible King of the French. However, I do not say that one should not be heard against a natural error; because he has God as his helper, who hears the prayers of the just: when a just king sits upon the throne, nothing evil shall oppose him, as in the epistle *Inter claras*. Therefore, by contrary reasoning, the unjust king has God as his punisher and resistor, and especially in these times, the vengeance of God knows no delay. These things which I have said refer to the case of prorogation and submission, supposing such a case to exist.

But now let us see whether, in our case, there was a submission or a compromise. The King requested submission; but the Count, passing by with deaf ears, seems to have responded nothing to the submission, as Scaevola elsewhere. D. 12.3. (de conditionibus indebitis) l. Stichus; similarly D. 41.1. (de acquisitione possessionis) l. si aliquam rem. The words say: “we shall be before our Lord the King, or before you, for receiving an account from him, and for rendering an account to him of those things which he wishes to say or demand, etc.” By these words the Count does not prorogue, but offers himself to go immediately before the King. And these are enunciative words, not dispositive, nor submissive, as when someone says, “I will choose,” or “I wish to choose”: this is not a choice, but a certain pronouncement. D. 30. (de legatis 1) l. servi electione. Because words ordered to the act of another word of the future, without that second and effective verb, enunciate and do not dispose; therefore it follows that by the words of the letter, and especially alternative ones, no prorogation was made, as D. 45.1. (de stipulationibus servorum) l. item si servus duorum §. ult. I do not know the remainder of the procedure.

Moreover, these words, if they signify anything, signify no more an arbitration than a compromise; nor even a compromise, as with such a one; but if he says himself such, as not in a similar case. C. 4.21. (si certum petatur) l. si ex pretio. The question is common, whether a compromise or an arbitration is understood, and the gloss distinguishes. D. 2.1. (de iudicibus) l. 1. From which it appears that, since no penalty is appended here, it was an arbitration, that is, a prorogation of jurisdiction. For if it excluded the most well-known terms of prorogation by the addition of a penalty, then it would be a compromise; because difference makes a difference; because nothing is placed under a species except through differences. Inst. 3.15. (de locat.) §. 1. For if it were a compromise, it would be terminated by the death of the King. D. 4.8. (de arbitris) l. in compromis; D. 12.1. (de conditionibus et demonstrationibus) l. mulcta non committitur in principio; and by the death of the compromitter. D. 4.8. (de arbitris) l. diem proferre §. si haeredis; and l. si interpellatur §. si ex altera. But if jurisdiction seems to be real and transfusory. D. 2.1. (de iudicibus) l. proponebantur; and l. edictum; and l. tam ex contractibus; D. 46.1. (de fideiussionibus) l. si eum hominem. For I consider that some have jurisdiction by their own right, as ordinaries, in fact and in name. Some have nothing of their own, as delegates. Some hold, as it were, a certain middle ground, as those to whom jurisdiction is prorogated.

I also consider the weight of the cause; for in those matters which are of the greatest weight, the mystery does not seem to be chosen, but faith. Arg. D. 17.2. (pro socio) l. si convenerit; D. 32. (de legatis 2) l. unum ex familia §. pen.; D. 46.3. (de solutionibus) l. inter artifices; D. 50.17. (de regulis iuris) l. in omnibus. Hence it has, as it were, a mixed nature of prorogation and compromise, so that it is a third species, which is called a compromissory prorogation; therefore it is personal. D. 4.8. (de arbitris) l. non distinguemus §. de officio. For sometimes words are so personal that they are separated from all reality. D. 12.2. (de iureiurando) l. veritatis; C. 2.15. (de pactis) l. qui in futurum §. 1. Also, sensual passions, and scourges, and lacerations of the flesh: but goods and evils of the intellect are more participable, as if there were one intellect in many men. D. 43.16. (de vi et vi armata) l. 1 §. quotiens. There is a certain fiction there.

Certainly, neither submission, which is made by words directed to the judge; nor prorogation, which is made whenever the parties agree among themselves; nor can a compromise be made by one party if the other does not consent. D. 2.1. (de iudicibus) l. 1 and 2, with the gloss, since neither was previously subject to jurisdiction. However, if the Marquis consents to the letters, and consented to the manner of writing. D. 16.3. (de deposito) l. publicus §. fin., so that an account might be rendered from both sides. But whether he had consent, it must be proved.

But let us assume that it were proved, and that there was a submission or prorogation. I ask whether it was extinguished by the death of the king while the litigation was pending. The words speak: “before our Lord the King.” This term “our” signifies the King now present, and as it were points out with the eye him who is at present King. D. de acquisitione et amissione hereditatis, l. Quintus, §. Argento. Hence, since the person is taken in place of the final cause of prorogation by one not to be personally future, which is the soul in the substance of man, and not the ideal person, which is dignity: the person itself gives place to the prorogation, and not the dignity; therefore, the person being extinguished, the prorogation is extinguished. D. de cura furiosi, l. Cuius bonis. For those things which are of sincere faith do not find a successor, because they are qualities of the individual and passions of the soul. Therefore, the sacraments of the Church, and similar things, as well as commissary guardianships and offices, where the faith or skill of the person is chosen, are dissolved by death, similarly also wills concerning the future. C. de caducis tollendis, §. Nec autem; D. de divortiis, l. Quod ait lex; D. de legatis 1, l. Si ita legatum, §. Illi si volet; D. de locato, l. 4; D. de legatis 3, l. Fideicommissa, §. Sic fidei; D. de rescriptis, l. Si gratiose, lib. 6. And although the name called was added, it was not added for the cause of extension, but for the cause of demonstration of the present proper subject: nevertheless, the whole was done out of reverence for a certain person, namely, a certain king. For reverence and personal respect have the force of a tacit proper name. D. de legatis 3, l. Fideicommissum, §. Interdum. Therefore, by the death of the king, the authority ended, considering the mental consideration. For every sense takes its beginning from the mind through writing. D. de pactis, l. Iure gentium, §. Pactorum; 1 q. 1, c. Manifestum. It is similar to c. Quoniam Abbas, because the Pope attends more to the dignity than to the person, which is often unknown to the Pope, as D. de rebus dubiis, l. Qui habebat. Likewise, the commission ended by the death of the count, who said, “throughout all the times of our life.” Likewise, it was extinguished by the extinction of the root of the personal cause. D. de suspectis tutoribus, in l. Post finita. For some things descend to our descendants by virtue, which they draw precisely from our loins, circumscribed by the right of hereditary faculties,

† and in the instance of judgment concerning these matters, the heir does not succeed: because it does not appear as if there were a contract with the son, who comes from another head; as in usufruct and dignities. D. de verb. obl. l. stipulatio ista. §. si quis ita. and l. 3. D. de interdic. et rele. And therefore in these castles, the submission to judgment does not pass to the new lord, as if it were a new, irrevocable fief of these castles in a new person, which are held in common from the Emperor. Certain things descend as to heirs of law and blood, and thus by a mixed consideration precisely as to the universal right, who are called successors of the inheritance, and in these the instance passes, as l. si cum hominem. and D. de infamib. l. seruus. Nevertheless, it does not pass in rem if the litigation is not contested. l. 2. de praet. stipu. The King of France is certainly governed by the law understood. 2. qu. 1. c. scelus, quod lotarius. Indeed, the greater the King is, the more excellent must be the understanding in him: because understanding made Kings from the beginning, and by the same arts empire is preserved by which it arose: for from the same we are nourished and are, according to Aristotle.

† That point also must not be omitted, but rather examined: whether the instance is terminated by the passage of time. And it is certain according to civil law that it is so, as in the law *properandum*, Code, *de iudiciis*. Certainly, that law does not apply when the case is before the prince’s consistory, Code, *de tempore appellationum*, authentic *sed lis*; and especially before the most serene King of the French, who is exempt from Roman law and deigns not to be subject to its statutes; yet he does not disdain to imitate the sacred canons. But I fear that from the letters of the Lord Count another intention may be gathered, where he says “within a brief term.” For he signified that his mind was not extended over a long period, nor drawn out into eternity, but within a brief time, that is, one year, Digest, *de verbis obligationum*, law *si quis arbitratu*, according to Bartolus; or three years, as this is to be understood from tacit agreement, Digest, *de arbitris*, law *sed si compromissum*; or, if you extend it more broadly, for life, as in law 1, Digest, *pro socio*. The latter interpretation I believe to be true, when the letters are weighed carefully. This last question seems to be decided from another aspect, namely, from the aspect of confused jurisdiction, Digest, *de iudicibus*, law *si alter*; Digest, *de arbitris*, law *penultima*; Digest, *de procuratoribus*, law *licet*, section *si plures*; Code, *ne quis in sua causa*, law 1; and note the opinion of Innocentius, Extravagant, *de verbis significantibus*, chapter *ex parte*. And thus it seems to me, Balde of Perugia, V.I.D., saving the opinion of the more authoritative counsel, as in law *Claudius Felix*. And therefore I have subscribed, and sealed with the seal of my name, under protest that if I have offended the Royal ears, I hereby revoke it and hold it as not said, as if persuaded by one incapable of understanding, because according to the Apostle, “whoever thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.” Thanks be to God. I, Balde.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The same matter is discussed by the aforementioned counsel, and it is very beautiful.
body: With a humble mind and bent knees I shall speak, because such are the matters which are put forward in indefinite words, as the aforementioned authorities demonstrate. D. de interpellationibus actionum, l. sed si defensor, § 1; and D. de vino legato, l. si, § cui dulcia; and D. de verbis obligatis, l. 1, § si quis simpliciter. Therefore, whatever the nature of the inquiry, the response made individually is to be understood in the same manner. It is otherwise if it is adversative or dissimilar, as in the same law, § cum addicit, and l. quae extrinsecus. For often the response disagrees with the interrogation, and sometimes it opposes it, and sometimes it implies something else. D. de acceptilatione, l. nisi consentiat. And consent is not said to exist unless there is agreement in the same thing and in the same manner of understanding. D. de pactis, l. 1. And therefore, when in the specific matter of conducting business there is disagreement, no business is perfected. D. si certum petatur, l. si ego. From this antecedent I infer such a consequence, or conclusion, that if someone asks me: “Do you wish to prorogue jurisdiction to me?” and I say “I wish to be an arbitrator,” or “I wish you to be a conciliator,” by this I am bound to nothing; because the difference impedes the act, which requires a union, i.e., a communication of consents. And therefore it must be considered, that among all Christian Kings the King of France holds the crown of liberty and glory, who inquired of the Illustrious Lord Count of Savoy whether he would submit himself to the cognition of the King. And it was responded by the Lord Count, as he stated, that with his whole heart he was ready, or desired, to serve, obey, and please the King. And at the end of the letters were these words: “who are, and shall be, true, legal, and obedient in all times of our lives.” Nor ought there to be dispute among such great points of law, nor should one play the sophist in the augustness of the law; but only truth, which the law of nations cultivates. However, just as without words no construction or signification stands, therefore it is necessary to follow the force of speech for the judgment of the intellect. D. de aurea et argentea legato, l. Plautius; D. de sepulchris, l. Labeo, § idem Tubero. For we ought not to follow a concealed intention, but an open one, which both perceive and ought to conceive in their intellect. D. de usufructu legato, l. si alii. Let us therefore follow the words, Extr. de privilegiis, c. porro; de consecratione, dist. 4, c. in Christo pater; de exercendo, l. 1, § si is, qui navem; D. qui et a quibus, l. prospexit. For sometimes an act is performed without reason, where the will is presumed to be such as is found described in the writing; sometimes reason precedes the will, and then from the directive, i.e., from reason, the words and writing receive the force of the intellect. D. de legibus, l. cum pater dulcissimis; and § curat; D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si is, qui animo; D. de re militari, l. milites agrum; D. de pactis, l. quod dictum. Therefore, if the present controversy and its matter pertained to the empire of the said Lord King, here, which nature dictates, it would not need the addition of prorogation, submission, or arbitral power. But because, from the suppositions of the terms, it does not pertain to the King by ordinary and natural law, as is supposed in the theme, it must be seen: whether the King has obtained extraordinary jurisdiction or arbitration. And it seems that neither. For the words of the letter say, “we come before the King for taking and making reason”; as if to say, before so great a lord, in whose presence it is not lawful to litigate rashly: so that it seems that a new power of judging is given rather by his presence and reverence than by right. D. de verborum significatione, l. coram; D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si quis mihi bona, § si coram; D. de arbitris, l. diem proferre, § coram. And therefore it is often said that the King is not an arbitrator, nor has the authority of judging. For sometimes someone is chosen as an inspector, sometimes as a conciliator, sometimes as an arbitrator and decider, sometimes as a judge and definer by the authority of jurisdiction. But multiple possible interpretations create obscurity; because the agent intellect does not illuminate itself. Hence Boethius says that its truth is explained in multiple ways. However, it is understood that that meaning should be taken which is more fitting to the matter about which inquiry is made. Fitness is generated by two things, namely, nature and reason. Nature gives us sense, and consequently consent; because it is impossible to live naturally without consent, even for the wild life of men; but the mode of living and contracting is given to us by reason; because to live under reason is to live as a man, as noted in Auth. de monachis, in principio; and man is more intellect than sense, i.e., sensuality, according to Aristotle. Ambition and the appetite for having deprive men of that purpose; because from many senses of the writing the more just one must be taken. And words which cannot be referred to law are referred to fact. D. de verbis obligatis, l. quidam cum filium, § videamus. Therefore, let us discern the more fitting sense according to the underlying matter. For since the matter of reason attracts a certain interpretation of speech to itself, as D. de usufructu, l. Proculus; D. de vulgari substitutione, l. si mater; and noted in the same title, l. verbis civilibus; and D. ad Trebellianum, l. sciendum; D. de praescriptionibus verborum, l. insulam; and l. si uno loco. And I consider that speech conceived by only one party has no interpretation; because it has no force. C. de conditionibus ob causam, l. si repetendi. But speech presented receives interpretation from four causes, namely, from the persons, from the form of the words, from the fact or matter, and from the final intention of the contracting parties; because it is fitting to observe from whom it is made, and upon what, and how, and to what end. Let us therefore see from whom and to whom the words were spoken; secondly, upon what matter; thirdly, how and under what form; fourthly and finally, what was the final and true intention. Regarding the persons, I admit that it was fitting to the majesty of the King and the honor of the Lord Count to cut off the matter of so great a lawsuit, so that the lawsuit would not proceed in fact, but they would separate with good concord. For this way is friendly to nature, and he who abandons this way usually does not have happy outcomes. D. de usufructu, l. aequissimum, especially with a superior. Seneca says that to contend with an equal is uncertain, with a superior is furious, with an inferior is sordid. But regarding the persons, it must be considered that the Count did not commit himself to the Lord King with the King’s Dauphin; because it must be established on both sides. And it is not established that the Lord Dauphin obligated himself to the Count in any observance, therefore neither did the Count to him. And therefore the Lord King obtained no power between the said Lord Dauphin and the Lord Count which he did not otherwise have. And thus he could establish nothing between those between whom he is considered to have had neither natural nor accidental power, as C. si a non competente iudice, per totum. For if the Marquis of Saluzzo were a vassal of the Dauphin, and the Dauphin and the Lord King could defend his vassal from injury of fact, nevertheless he could not from this assume jurisdiction against the Lord Count, with the pretext that the Count is not a vassal of the King, nor proceed to sentence in a real judgment against him. For in this article the lord of the fief, who is named in the judgment, is an adversary, not a judge. C. ubi in rem actio, l. 2; and in X, de controversia inter vassallum et alium de beneficio, c. si controversia; and noted by Innocentius, Extr. de iudicibus, c. caeterum. It supports this, Cle. de re iudicata, c. pastor; and de foro competente, c. caeterum. Furthermore, regarding the person of the King of France, nothing else can be said than what is said about the Antarctic pole, which is not the prince of our hemisphere. But regarding the Lord Count of Savoy, it must be said that he is illustrious, yet he is a vassal of the Empire, and that he holds mere imperium in his lands from the Emperor. Therefore he cannot abdicate it from himself except into the hand of the Emperor. Fl. de officiis praesidis, l. legatus. Hence he cannot give to the King of France a privative or transmissive power thereof. Likewise, he cannot prorogue real jurisdiction to the Lord King, nor submit himself to him without the consent of the most serene Lord Emperor; because he is a vassal of the Lord Emperor, as noted by Bartolus, D. de novo operis nuntio, l. 1, § et post operis. This is because a fief cannot be alienated without such consent. For prorogation of jurisdiction is a certain species of voluntary alienation, which is prohibited in fiefs, de prohibita feudi alienatione per Lotarium, capitulo imperialis benivolentiae, in the word “vel aliquod commercium”; and de prohibita feudi alienatione per Federicum, c. imperialem decet solertiam, § praeterea si de feudo. And because they cannot compromise regarding the right of a third party, i.e., the Emperor’s, especially in matters reserved to the Emperor. Here I pause: because if vassals say they have different investitors, one must go to an arbitrator or adjudicator in whom the litigants consent, as noted there on the word “duos”; and de pace tenenda, § si duo. Therefore one could go to the King. Certainly, rather one ought to go to the Emperor; because the plaintiff must follow the forum of the defendant. Hence the Marquis of Saluzzo ought to have followed the forum of the Count, i.e., to sue before the Lord Emperor, to whom it pertained, both because the Lord Count recognized the fief from him; both because he was a ligius man of the Emperor; both because the Emperor is the universal lord. 11 q. 1, c. experientiae; de foro competente, c. cum sit generale; 26 dist., c. cum ad verum; 63 dist., c. Valentinianus; D. ad legem Rhodiam de iactu, l. deprecatio. For in doubt, all temporal jurisdiction is his, and by right he is immovable, i.e., perpetual, as in Auth. quo oportet episcopos, § fi. dat cuncta moveri; and the Catholic Church holds this, and to say the contrary is sacrilege. C. de crimine sacrilegii, l. instar. For he has empire over the whole dominion which sees the ascending and descending sun, and which is on both sides, i.e., south and north, as in Auth. ut omnes obeant iudices provinciarum, § hoc considerantes, coll. 5; and in all islands which extend to the recesses of the ocean, as in Auth. ut ecclesia Romana, § quod ergo vestra, coll. 2; and over all land which the law of the Romans and the sanction of the Catholic Church contain, as in Auth. de non alienando, circa fi., coll. 2. For we do not worship an idol, but truth. For the Emperor is the second Sun, who is called the Moon, which by its approaches and recesses makes wonderful changes of perishable and worldly things. Something little has been said about the matter of the fief. Now it must be spoken of the form of the letters. For it is written, and in the manner of a contract, nothing can be added to or detracted from writing, as C. de fidei instrumentis, l. contractus. But it must be considered that general and reverential words are rather flattering than obligatory, as when a friend says to a friend, “I am yours,” as noted C. in quibus causis coloni, l. 2, lib. 11. But in special words there is the weight of the day and the heat; because in special words there is understanding, in general and uncertain sayings and vulgar promises there is no understanding. D. de aedilicio edicto, l. sciendum, § dicimus; C. quod cum eo, l. fi; D. de fideiussione legis, l. generali, in principio. Let us therefore omit the most general and uncertain speeches, and come to the certain ones, where he says, “And for making reason to the same.” Does he who promises to make reason submit himself to the will? By no means, but to the reality of justice. And it is certain that he submits himself to justice, i.e., the substance of good and equity. For the lawgiver sometimes errs, but justice never errs. D. de iustitia et iure, l. iustitia; and l. pen.; D. de appellationibus, l. 1, in principio; Extr. de sepulchris, c. certificari. Likewise it is certain that reason and justice do nothing without a person. D. de origine iuris, l. 1, § post originem. Hence without a magistrate, justice placed in controversy is buried. But it must be observed that he who submits himself to justice cannot suffer injustice, except in fact. For if someone promises to stand by justice, he is not bound to obey unjust commands. And therefore this submission operates little and not strongly, unless justice is established, as noted D. de verborum significatione, l. illa verba; and in c. 1, de procuratoribus, in Cle.; and 21 q. 1, c. 1; and by Bartolus, D. de arbitris, l. si de meis, § recepisse. Hence if the Lord King injured the justice of the Count, this does not come within the submission. For the submission was made with words restricting the King to the weight of justice, not loosening him to the good pleasure of the King. And of this justice and injustice the Emperor or the Pope, who is greater, ought to cognize. Extr. de iudicibus, c. novit, who cognizes between leprosy and leprosy. Help us, O God our savior; the pious mother of the world suffers a schism such as was not before; the heavens are shaken, O Lord, to whom shall we go, O Holy One? To the Hebrews 7, who can have compassion on our infirmities? 5 to the Hebrews. Where, O Lord, is our refuge and strength, alas. For by the name of reason I understand justice, which neither deceives nor is deceived, as l. ultima, C. de pondere auri. Someone will say, therefore there will never be an end to lawsuits, for the vanquished will always deny. D. de verbis obligatis, l. inter stipulatores, § 1. Wherefore the authority of the thing adjudged is placed in the middle, lest it be permitted to each one to raise a lawsuit from a lawsuit. D. de iudicibus, l. si praetor; C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. terminato. For when a sentence passes into res iudicata, justice is not attended to, but the sentence. D. familiae erciscundae, l. cum putarem; D. de pactis, l. eo tempore, in principio; and noted D. de conditione indebiti, l. si non sortem, § haeredi; D. de re iudicata, l. aeterni. Especially because for the sentence of the King it is presumed, as D. de officiis praefecti praetorio, l. 1, § credidit enim princeps. Hence from his sentence an appellant is not heard, if he pronounces it from his jurisdiction. The same also seems to apply if it is prorogated, because one jurisdiction is augmented by prorogation. For prorogation is an addition of the same quality. D. de precario, l. sed si manente. And it is understood to be of the same form and nature, as noted in § hi, qui, Authen. de praebendis, lib. 6. And if it is a submission, it is still very strong. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. est receptum, ad hoc; D. de pactis dotalibus, l. inter socerum, § cum inter patrem; C. de episcopis audiendis, l. si qui ex consensu. And although sometimes the key of justice errs, when there is no appeal there, one must stand by the error, because the error of the prince in that case makes law, as l. 3, in fi., de suppleto legato. But I answer, as I said, here it is different on account of the nature of the feudal thing itself, which touches the right of the Emperor, Extr. de re iudicata, c. suborta. Hence even if the sentence were valid regarding personal prestations, it is not valid regarding real prestation, or perhaps it is valid in nothing on account of the indivisible cause. D. familiae erciscundae, l. in hoc iudicio; and in the rule cum principalis. For when the principal escapes the cognition of the judge, the accessories likewise do; because it cannot be weighed by itself. D. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. si in iudicio. But there he speaks of an accessory of the judgment, but here he speaks of an accessory of the thing. D. de rei venditione, l. utique. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A condition of this kind, if you sell such a thing, or part thereof, for three thousand and three hundred florins, whether it is casual, potestative, or mixed.
2. If a mixed condition fails by chance or by the act of the person who is bound to fulfill it, whether it is to be imputed to him.
body:
Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob. One part [was held by] Georginus, the second part by Ughettus, the third part by Georginus. Georginus sold the part he had in Ponzono to Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob for the price of 6,000 florins. The aforementioned Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob gave to the said Georginus, in payment of the said six thousand florins, their entire part which they have in Donice for 3,000 florins. Furthermore, they gave to the said Georginus, in payment of the said sum, one sixth part of Meladii for the other 3,000 florins. And they made this pact with the said Georginus: that if they gave to the said Georginus within nine years 3,000 florins, he would then be bound to restore the said sixth part of Meladii. And see the instrument which you have on paper.

Ughettus sold to the said Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob the part he had in Ponet for the price of 6,000 florins. For which 6,000 florins they gave to the said Ughettus, in payment, one sixth part of Meladii for 3,000 florins. Furthermore, they gave to the same Ughettus, in payment of the other 3,000 florins, one sixth part of Spig, with the saving and reservation that if Francis de Correcto and his brothers, or another person, wished to buy the said sixth part of Spig given to the said Ughettus in payment, in such a way and manner that the said Ughettus could receive for the sale of the said sixth part 3,000 florins and 300 [denari] within nine years from the day of the contract, that then he would be obliged to sell, and that the said Ughettus would be obliged then to buy from the said Georginus the sixth part of Meladii which he had from the aforementioned Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob, and to give to the said Georginus for the price of the said sixth part 3,000 florins. And see the instrument which you have on parchment.

Now the said Ughettus sold the said sixth part of Spig to Francis and his brothers before the year [expired], for the price of 3,000 florins, and refuses to buy from the said Georginus the said sixth part of Meladii for the said 3,000 florins, as was agreed; because he says that he did not receive from the said part more than 3,000 florins, and is not bound to buy. Pontius says that the said Ughettus sold before the term of nine years, that he should impute this to himself, and that he is not bound to buy the said part from Georginus and give him 3,000 florins, or at least to return the said sixth part of Meladii to the said Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob; because the said Georginus, seeing that he could not have the said 3,000 florins from the said Ughettus for the said sixth part, sold the said sixth part to the said Pontius, Bertagna, and Jacob these days.

On these points, let the instruments making mention of the aforementioned matters, which are in your possession, be examined, and let it be advised by you what is the law, and what they ought to do in the aforementioned matters; because the said Marquis, of whom the place of Meladii is a fief, commanded them that they appear before him with their rights and allegations within the next Friday, which command is in your possession. The matter is pending.

†And from the act of the buyer and the seller. It is noted that a buyer is not easily found, and especially one who buys for a formal price, that is, literally for such a price. D. de legatis 3, l. non dubium, §. fin.; and l. qui concubinam, §. fin., D. ad leg. Falcidiam; l. alienus, D. de praescriptionibus verbis; l. si tibi, C. si in causam iudicis; l. 2, C. de executione rei iudicatae; l. ordo. Moreover, it depends on the snares of fortune. For it can happen that, if the thing should deteriorate by chance, or if the seller should die in the meantime, the condition cannot be fulfilled. C. de iure emphyteutico, l. 1; C. de iure dotium, l. si inter virum; C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. 2, according to Petrus and Cynus; D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, §. gerius; D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. qui societatem. In many causes and cases, things do not find a buyer, even at a just price. D. de dolo, l. rem quandam; C. de rescindenda venditione, l. 2; D. de legatis 1, l. et si aequo; and D. de publicanis, l. cotem s, §. qui maximos. Having premised this for clarity, we must turn to the rules of mixed conditions. For if they fail by chance, the obligation ceases. C. de conditionibus insertis, l. legatum. But if they fail by the act of him who was bound to fulfill them, then he is bound in the same way as if they had been fulfilled. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Labeo scribit si mihi Bibliothecam. And thus it is noted by the gloss in the aforementioned l. qui concubinam, §. fin., D. de legatis 3.

† Therefore, in the case proposed, it seems that one must say: either the thing to be sold was commonly worth three thousand and 300 florins, and then he sold it for less through his own fault, and he must impute this to himself. For he is bound to observe the contract, because it is presumed that he maliciously disposed of it at a lower price. For many buyers are found for things that are sold at the common price. D. de donat. causa mortis, l. mortis causa. Or it was worth less, and fraud or fault is not presumed, because he did what ought justly to be done. And therefore he cannot be sued, because the condition fails, arg. in its own reason. D. fam. ercisc., l. haeredes; §. idem iuris, D. de verb. oblig., l. 5, §. si sortem. Or it is doubtful, then the quality of the thing seems to be weighed. But to me, in our case, it seems that fraud is presumed, for it ought to have been investigated whether he could find a better buyer, nor ought the seller to have hastened, since time was appointed for the benefit of both parties. For by reason of the small or lesser quantity, simulation is presumed. C. mandati, l. per diuersas. And sometimes by reason of time. D. de exercit., l. Lucius. And contrary custom is proved by oath as against fraud, if the judge is moved to defer to the oath: as noted, Inst. de verb. oblig., §. penult. Moreover, whenever within the said nine years three thousand and 300 florins were found for the said thing, he must be compelled to fulfill the act, because the words of the contract are so expressed, thus the words say, he may receive for the sale. D. de haered. instit., l. suus, §. puto. Therefore, he ought not to have hastened to the detriment of the creditor, especially without having investigated the price. For the thing ought to have been proposed for sale publicly, lest any fraud could be committed by favor or fiction, as in the said laws and similar ones. Therefore, examine whether Francis and Louis de Caretto were buyers at the price of three thousand and 300 florins; then the condition is considered fulfilled, and the said Ughetto is compelled to buy. And the same is to be said if such a price could have been obtained from Georgino or any other person, because good faith must be observed, nor ought he to have hastened to the disposition. Arg. D. de negot. gest., l. diuotio; D. de fideicommiss. liber., l. thays ancilla, §. 1. Let him therefore impute to himself if he sold at a lower price. But this can be proved by those who would have given so much, if they say that they would have given so much, except that he hastened to sell. It supports what is noted, C. de fen. quae pro eo, l. 1, ad fin.; and C. de rescind. vend., l. si voluntate. And it supports in its own reason, D. de reb. eic., l. magis puto, §. in primis; and D. mandati, l. si mandauero tibi, vt excuteres. The common price can also undoubtedly be proved by witnesses, as noted in the said l. 1, de sent. quae pro eo, by the gloss and doctors there. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The ecclesiastical judge may, ex officio, inquire even without any preceding complaint or notoriety, where there is imminent danger to souls.
2. Where the testator commands in his will that usury be restored, such words are understood to mean that they are not subject to a pact of non-petition.
3. I confess that I have received 10 for the complete restitution of usury; how these words are to be understood.
4. A liberal remission is not presumed in those who receive usury.
body: To the evidence

It must be granted that there is an inquiry ex puro et mero officio iudicis, with no complainant and no preceding rumor, where there is danger to souls. And this is expressed in the text on usury, and by Innocentius and Johannes Andreae in Extra, de iniuriis, c. Ad nostram, el. 3. And by this it is not necessary to allege anything else, because this is the truth.

Secondly, it must be premised that if the testator in his will ordered that the usury extorted by him be restored, these words have the sense of the law *non obstante pacto de non petendo*. For it would be the same as if, after the pact, the usurer had promised to restore, as in the Digest, *de verbis obligatorum*, law *si dari stipuletur*.

Thirdly, it must be premised that these words, "I confess that I have received 20 solidi for the complete payment of all usuries," can be interpreted in three ways. In one way, by way of confession. In a second way, by way of a pact not to sue. This is stated by two ordinary glosses joined together, D. de solutionibus, l. si ex pluribus, in principio. In a third way, they can be interpreted so that it constitutes a certain captious and simulated liberality, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana. And thus the doctors interpret them, out of hatred for usurers, as is read and noted in D. si certum petatur, l. rogasti, § si tibi; and D. de conditionibus, l. si tibi decem milia. For, on account of the bad custom of moneylenders and the prohibitions of the laws, fraud is presumed, as is read and noted in D. de probationibus, l. qui testamentum. It supports what is noted in l. 6, D. de conditione et demonstratione.

Fourthly, it must be premised that those who receive money for usury do so out of the necessity of their household, as is noted in ff. de pign. act. l. 3; and ff. de pig. l. si fundus, §. fi; and l. 1, §. si rem, ff. de leg. 3. Hence, in those receiving for usury, a liberal remission is not presumed, by argument from ff. de adim. lega. l. rem legatam. It is therefore rather a certain pact made in fraud of usury and contrary to good morals, which in effect or by the law itself does not hold, as in ff. de pac. l. si vnus, §. pacta, quae turpem. And therefore it is established that the pact is not remitted unless the usurer restores what was taken away; unless it is manifestly proven that the usurer offered the money, and he to whom restitution was to be made freely remitted it. Thus it ought to be understood, as is noted by Master Dy. and Jo. And. after him, in c. peccatum, de re. iur. lib. 6. However, as I said, this is not probable in those who are perpetual usurers, because by custom it is presumed against them, by argument from ff. ad l. Iul. maie. l. famosi; and C. si quis Imperatori maledixerit, l. 1; and l. non omnis, §. a barbaris, ff. de re milit. From these premises, the solution to the questions asked appears, namely conclusively, that the said confession does not benefit the one extorting usury; rather, the bishop, by his mere and pure office, can compel him to the restitution of usuries. And this seems to me to be the very truth as regards God and the world, and in every forum, both canonical and civil. Those words, "20 solidi for complete satisfaction," manifestly show that 20 solidi nevertheless intervened, for which a general remission was made in fraud of usury; and therefore the usurer is not released; but a certain simulation was employed, which evidently appears from the quality of the person. And these things are proven by the noted authorities, per Dyn. in cap. peccatum, extra de reg. iur. lib. 6, with similar cases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mother must have the legitime of her children.
2. If the testator, when asked whether he wished those related to him to have the goods, answered, certainly not: but rather I would prefer that the poor have them; whether by this the relatives are excluded, and it is disposed that the poor have them.
3. The executors of the will are not suitable witnesses for the will.
body: It seems

† to me, so that the mother may entirely support the claim, for there is no doubt about the half: because she ought to have the legitime of five children, which is half of the whole, which would have been proven from the legacy to the poor: because the words of the fideicommissum are deemed: and that the last one died a pubes, as fully noted in l. precibus, C. de impub. et aliis sub. Now I say that the mother has the claim in its entirety, because nothing has been proven against the mother.

First, because the witnesses do not agree. For Conradinus stated that, when the testator was asked whether he wished those related to him to have the goods, he replied, “Certainly not; rather, he wished the poor to have them.” He said this, meaning that he preferred the poor to have them rather than his blood relatives; and thus he used words directed solely to the exclusion of his blood relatives, not thereby making a disposition in favor of the poor. But this seems poorly stated according to the law Pamphylus, section Propositum, On Legacies, Book 3. And I do not dwell on this point; rather, I say that the other witnesses report the words differently, in a manner that sounds more clearly.

But they do not seem to prove the case, for they are suspect, since they dispose in their own favor by stating that they were left as executors. D. de test. tut. l. ex sententia. Nor can a witness be rejected merely as suspect, unless he is rejected on account of a defect of mind in his entirety, as noted in C. de transact. l. si ex falsis. And especially so when an executor for pious causes testifies regarding that which contains the right of action in his name as executor. D. de episc. et cler. c. nulli. And indeed concerning the whole matter, and thus it does not obstruct Inst. de testamentis § legatariis. It supports D. de falsis l. vexori § 1. Furthermore, it is sufficiently apparent that one of them is an enemy, and the other is the son of an enemy. Hence, only one witness remains: and that one is singular, and also not very clear in law; because the statement is not clear as to whether it was made with a dispositive or declarative intent, and for what reason, namely, to disinherit the blood relatives, it was made. Although, as I said, I would base my argument on this point if it were clearly proven by suitable witnesses, at least two, for pious causes. Therefore, to me, the said father and son do not appear to be suitable witnesses; because they are suspect in multiple ways, and they make themselves suspect, and passionate, and biased: and the first witness, who said that he knew only in a limiting sense, when cited as a witness, does not agree with them. Argumentum D. de verb. oblig. l. 1 § cum addicit. It is true that these are two different chapters, namely, the legacy and the appointment of the executor, and they are separable, as noted in l. si ex falsis C. de transact. Nevertheless, the credibility of a witness ought to be indivisible. The mother’s own confession is alleged against her. D. de success. abintest. cap. cum dilectus. Because they do not specify the mode of appointment, which can be multiple. And therefore the confession is most uncertain and formless. And although there are thus some indications against the mother, they are nevertheless insufficient; because there are not two suitable and agreeing witnesses, as noted in C. fam. erc. l. fi. And therefore I incline in favor of the mother, who should be left to her own conscience, not finally condemned; but rather, according to the rules of law, she should be absolved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How relatives on both sides shall succeed: and whether they are preferred to those related on only one side: and whether the same rule applies to fiefs as to allodial property.
2. The paternal uncle is preferred to the cousin in every succession, whether of fiefs or of allodial property.
3. Property acquired from outside, likewise sheep and cattle existing on a feudal estate, are not feudal: but are personal property.
body: The case is as follows. First, the lord Beneventanus Guetarius had five sons, namely Francis, Gabriel, Geoffrey, William, and Parciual. Francis, however, was a brother on the father’s side only, and not on the mother’s side. The other four were brothers on both the mother’s and father’s sides, and they stood at one bread and one wine; Francis, however, stood apart by himself. Now it has happened that the aforementioned Francis died and left one son, who is called Bartholomew. Afterwards, William and Parciual died without issue. Afterwards, Geoffrey died and left one son, who was called John; this John is now dead. The question now arises: who ought to succeed the aforementioned brothers, both in allodial and in feudal property? Whether Gabriel the brother, or Bartholomew the nephew? Similarly, who ought to succeed the aforementioned John, son of the late Geoffrey, both in allodial and in feudal property? Whether Gabriel the uncle, or Bartholomew the full blood relative? And let it be known what the law is on this matter. Also, what is allodial property? If possessions acquired after a fief has been acquired are allodial or not? Also, whether grain, wine, the massaritia of the house, oxen, cows, other beasts are allodial or not? Also, whether possessions which are in Asti and other villages, which are not fiefs, are allodial or not.

† It must be premised for the sake of clarity that in allodial holdings and properties, when one of the brothers dies without children, the brother related on both sides succeeds, as does the son of a brother related on both sides, to the exclusion of a brother related on only one side and his son, as is fully set forth in the law *legi*, C. de legibus hereditatibus, the authenticum *post fratres*, through the gloss and C. *communiter de successionibus*, and thus according to Cynus. However, in feudal holdings, those related on the paternal side succeed in the same manner as those related on both sides, because the mother contributes nothing to the succession of a fief, according to Jacobus de Ardizzone, since only agnatic relationship is considered in paternal fiefs. From these principles it follows that Bartholomew, together with Gabriel, succeeds his uncles in feudal goods, but in no way succeeds in allodial goods.

Secondly, it must be known that in every succession, whether of feudal or allodial estates, the paternal uncle is preferred to the first cousin: because the paternal uncle is in the third degree, but the first cousin is in the fourth degree, as in the Authentica *Post fratres*. From this it follows that Gabriel succeeds John in all his goods, and not Bartholomew.

Thirdly, it must be known that things acquired from outside, such as oxen and the like, are not feudal but proprietary. D. 18.1.34 (fundus nihil); D. 50.16.1 and 2, with similar authorities. And from this it follows how succession occurs in them, as is clear from the foregoing. And so I say and advise, I, Baldo degli Ubaldi of Perugia, Doctor of Laws. And at the end I have subscribed and affixed my seal with my name thus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A division made among certain brothers, who promise ratification on behalf of another brother, is entirely void, even as between the others, if it was not ratified by him.
body: HAVING SEEN

† From the instrument of division made between the most excellent and respectable knights, Lord Raymond, Marquis of Busta, for himself and in his own proper name; and on behalf of and in the name of Blasch, his brother, for whom he promised ratification under a hypothec and obligation of all his goods; and against Lord Erine, Ludovic, and John, brothers, Marquises of Busta, concerning their lands, castles, and feudal holdings, several doubts arise, since it is alleged that from the said division the said Lord Raymond was defrauded by more than half the just price. And that the said Blasch never ratified the said division, nor wishes to ratify it. It is asked, what is the law? And on the second point, I say that the said Raymond could not prejudice the said Blasch; the text is in C. res inter alios acta; l. si cum fratre; it supports de acquirenda hereditate, l. duo fratres; and C. de contrahenda emptione, l. dudum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who is bound to deliver to someone a certain number of sacks of wheat and a certain number of casks of wine according to the measure of a particular place is considered burdened with the obligation to pay in that place.
2. Add the following opinion.
body: The Facts. And the noble lord Antonio Turchi of Asti, in his will, made a legacy, namely: He further ordained that whoever shall hold the fief of Montemagno shall be bound to give and pay to his wife, the lady Catherine, every year during the life of the said lady Catherine, provided she observes a chaste widowhood and maintains her honor, twenty-five sacks of good wheat of standard weight; for each sack, four *minae* according to the *mina* of Asti, and five *octales* of good, pure wine. It is further assumed in the facts that the said testator had no goods in Asti from which the said wheat or wine could be procured; but rather in Montemagno, where he also had his domicile and the greater part of his fortune. It is further assumed that the said lady had a large dowry and legacy, and was a wealthy lady. It is further assumed that a similar award (*laudem*) was rendered in this matter concerning the said will, with reference being made to the will. It is further assumed on behalf of the one to whom the said castle devolved, that he was always ready to pay the said legacies in Montemagno; and the delay did not lie with him, but with the said lady, who did not send anyone to the said place for the said wheat and wine. It is also asked regarding the penalty of the compromise, whether it has been incurred with effect or not, especially considering the letters of the said lady, in which she writes that she will send someone to the castle of Montemagno for the said wheat and wine. These letters were drawn up outside Asti in a certain castle from which the said lady was originally descended, outside the territory of Asti. I argue first for the parties; secondly, I proceed to the solution of the question.

And it seems, first, that the said payment ought to be made in Asti, and there, at the debtor’s expense, the wheat and wine of the said lady ought to be measured, for three reasons. The first is in favor of alimony. For the provision of alimony must be made at the place of the alimentary beneficiary, lest in the meantime the beneficiary perish on the journey, as noted in D. de iudiciis, l. sed et si susceperit, § si libertus, in the gloss beginning *vasa erant*; and in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § causae fere. The second is from the designation of the measure. For it says “according to the measure of Asti,” from which it is presumed that she wished it to be measured and paid in Asti, as noted in the said § si libertus, and in l. Titia Seia, in the beginning, D. de legatis 2. The third is because the said lady is noble; and by reason of nobility, the utility is increased, so that it ought to be brought to her house, as in the said l. sed et si susceperit, § sed et si proponas. And for the lady, it seems to support the view noted by Cynus in C. ubi fideiussio peti oporteat, l. 1, where he says that because he bequeathed according to the Parisian measure, etc.

To the contrary, that the said payment ought to be made in Monte Magno, this is proven by several reasons. And first, from the rule of law which says that payment ought to be made at the place of domicile, as fully noted in D. de iudiciis, l. quod legatur. Second, from another rule: because whenever a place is not added to the payment, and the debtor is found at the place of contract, he is compelled to pay there, and ought not to be sent to another place, as in D. de eo quod certo loco, l. 1; D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. contraxisse. Third, from another rule: because whenever the debtor is of a different domicile, the creditor ought to go to his domicile, not the contrary, as noted in D. de constitutione pecuniae, l. item illa. Fourth, from many conjectures, which overcome one conjecture. The first conjecture is: because he burdened the heir with respect to the place, therefore he seems to have had that place in mind. D. de iudiciis, l. fidei, § quid tamen. The second, because in Asti there was no capacity for payment from the testator’s wheat and wine, of which it is credible that the testator imagined, although this is not clearly established. And therefore, lest the heir be unduly burdened, he seems to have had in mind a more suitable place: as in the said § sed si proponas, in the words *et sit sufficiens* and the following, from the contrary sense. The third, from the conjunction of another legacy, namely, of wine, in which he did not mention Asti. Hence it is certain that the wine ought not to be paid in Asti; therefore neither the wheat, lest those things which are united by conjunction be considered under different law. C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. cum solitum; D. de usucapione, l. rerum mixtura. The fourth, because the testator burdened the sons; hence, in favor of the sons, a milder interpretation ought to be made by the conjecture of piety.
