Argument from C. de fideiussoribus, l. voluntatis. The fifth, because if it is special in favor of alimony, therefore the common law is to the contrary. But an annual legacy made to a rich person is not understood as a legacy made for alimony; because it exceeds the limit and nature of alimony: as noted in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si annos. The sixth, because the dignity of the legatee is considered in a small legacy, not in a large and burdensome one, as is this one, as in the said l. sed et si susceperit, in the verse *iam modica*, from the contrary. Nor does it avail that he said “according to the measure of Asti.” For according to that measure, or mode, it can be measured even in Monte Magno without any difficulty. And because the said words were added in favor of the sons; because the measure was smaller in Asti than in Monte Magno. I speak of the measure, having regard to the sack: as I am told in the facts, just as in coins, if I promise Venetian ducats, it does not follow thereby that they ought to be paid in Venice. I would, however, opine that if the lady cannot obtain payment in Monte Magno on account of the power of the heir, that the heir, by the equity of the judge, would be compelled, at the expense and risk of the heir, to pay in Asti from the testator’s wheat and wine, because fraud ought not to aid anyone. Argument from D. de edendo, l. praetor, § si.

From these things it clearly appears that the penalty has not been incurred, since the lady did not send for the wheat; and especially because by her letters she consented to the place of payment. Argument from D. de verbis obligationum, l. qui Romae, § Calimacus, at the end; and D. de iudiciis, l. sed et si susceperit, § si. And also because the penal disposition was conditional, and the condition was not clearly given. D. de verbis obligationum, l. hoc iure. Saving, however, such matters, that he acts in good faith in paying, both on account of the penalty of the compromise, and on account of the penalty of the common law, and on account of God, because he ought not to violate the laws of piety. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legacy must be paid at the domicile of the heir. This rule fails in three cases, as here.
1. A legacy of 25 sacks every year, if made to a wife, whether it is to be considered a legacy of alimony.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that a legacy ought to be paid at the domicile of the heir. This rule fails in favor of alimony. For then it ought to be paid at the place of the alimentary recipient. D. de iudiciis, l. sed et si susceperit, § 1. Moreover, it fails by reason of the quality of the thing bequeathed. Hence, Cynus says that if something is bequeathed according to the Parisian measure, it ought to be paid in Paris. C. ubi fideicommissum peti oporteat, l. 1. And Bartolus says that if one mina of wheat is bequeathed to someone, although the Perugians use that measure, payment ought to be made in Perugia, as he notes in the aforementioned l. sed et si susceperit. Moreover, it fails by reason of the quality of the person. l. item illa, § 1, D. de constituto pecuniae.

† It must therefore be considered whether this is a legacy of alimony, and it must be said that it is not: because it was made to a wealthy woman. C. de transa. l. cum hi. §. si in annos. and there by Guli. and Bar. because it exceeds what would suffice for alimony. And because it is not of the same nature as a legacy of alimony: unless it were proven that the testator had a different intention: and that of the arbitrators. Secondly, it must be considered whether, because he said "according to the measure of Asti," he appears to have intended that it be measured and paid in Asti. I say this regarding wheat, for nothing was said about Asti concerning wine. And this is true by way of conjecture. This designation of place favors the legatee: yet on the other hand, there appear to be several conjectures. The first, because the testator attached this burden to the later [estate of] Monte Magno: and thus burdened the heir with respect to certain assets: Hence he attached the legacy to the burden of those assets. ff. de iudi. l. fideicommiss. §. tractatum. The second [conjecture] favors the children, for in doubt it is presumed that the testator wished it to be provided by them in the place where they can do so more conveniently, that is, where they have their patrimony, from which they can more easily provide it, an argument from those things noted ff. de condit. et demonstra. l. illis libertis. per Bar. C. de fideic. l. cum acutissimi. From the presumed affection for the children, three rules of law favor this side. The first is that one ought to pay in the place of domicile, as fully noted ff. de iudi. l. quod legatur. The second, because whenever the place of payment is not added, the claimant must attend to the domicile of the debtor. ff. de constit. pecu. l. item illa. The third, because since this case arises from contract and arbitration, if the defendant is found there, for that is the principal place. ff. de iu. l. haeres absens. with similar cases. Also, those words, "putting for each sack 4 minae of wheat at the Asti mina," appear to have been added for the sake of difference: because a sack is understood differently in Asti and differently in Monte Magno: because the sack of Monte Magno is said to be smaller. Hence the testator spoke thus for the sake of a lesser obligation, not for a harsher one: nor for the sake of confusing the place of payment to somewhere other than Monte Magno. And because in the mind, what is said, it is fitting to observe. ff. de exhiben. l. pen. C. de fideiuss. l. voluntatis. Hence these words designating a lesser debt should not produce the contrary effect. ff. de leg. j. l. legata inutiliter. Also this is clear from the legacy of wine, which undoubtedly must be paid in the place of domicile. Also if the testator had intended this, he would have expressed the payment. This question hangs on conjectures, and requires the information of witnesses, if something can be proven from outside regarding the mind of the testator. And until it is declared, the penalty is in no way incurred, since the heir has always offered himself ready to pay in Monte Magno: and the lady has not sent [for payment] to that place, although she had written that she would send: and consequently accepted that place as the place of payment. argu. ff. de iudi. l. fideicomm. §. quotiens. de verbo. obli. l. qui Romae. §. calimacus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The time of the instance, whether the case is civil or criminal, or whether it is mixed, when it begins to run.
2. What is called a civil case, what a criminal case, and what a mixed case.
3. Whether slight fault in criminal matters is subject to punishment.
body: Although many arguments have been subtly and commendably alleged for and against this case, nevertheless it should be known concerning the present matter,

† That "instantia" is said in a twofold manner. For in causes nothing is done without litis contestatio, and the solemn form of trials begins the instantia from contradiction, as noted by Cynus in C. de procuratoribus, l. nihil arbitramur; and by the gloss in c. 1, de electione, lib. 6; and it is proved by the reason of the law non novam, C. de iudicibus; and it is established by c. saepe, extra de veritate sigilli, in the Clementines; and C. ubi in rem actionem, l. 2. But in ordinary causes it begins from the solemn litis contestatio, as in C. de iudicibus, l. properandum; in the Authentica de litigiosis, § omnem; noted in ff. de iure omnium iudiciorum, in l. et quia, de officio delegati; c. relatum; and ff. de conditione indebiti, l. eleganter, § si quis post; extra de liti contestatione, c. exceptionis obiectus, according to Innocentius.

† Having granted this, and having considered the matter carefully, I state with certainty that one cause is purely civil, another purely criminal, and a third mixed, as stated in Extra, De procuratoribus, chapter Tuas, Si quidem. Indeed, if the matter concerns a penalty to be applied to the treasury, it is also called criminal according to civil law, as in the law Agraria, Digest, De termino moto; but if it concerns a party, it is called civil. However, if a civil matter arises within a criminal one, regard must be had to what is principal in our case. If the libel concludes principally to the restoration of damages, the instance is undoubtedly terminated by the decree of the lord; notwithstanding the discretion granted to the judge, for that discretion does not pertain to the extension of the time of the instance, as the text notes in Digest, De locato, law Si in lege, in principio; and thus Bartolus decided there. But if it is principally criminal, and not secondarily, the statutes of the commune of Piacenza apply, to which one must adhere, as in Digest, Ad legem Aquiliam, law 1, in the word derogavit. If the statutes set a limit for the cause or jurisdiction, the instance does not endure after the time has expired, as in Digest, De iudiciis solutis, law Cum lite mortua. I come to the principal matter, assuming that the instance were to endure; and because I have not seen the records, I cannot respond on the basis of the records. But insofar as I can comprehend from the allegations on both sides, I say that it must be considered whether a just cause can excuse the lessee from all fault; and then he must undoubtedly be absolved; and fault is presumed to be absent from one who leased in good faith, as noted in Digest, De rei venditione, law In rem, section Tignum, in the ordinary gloss, unless malice or a sought-after pretext were proven, as in Codex, De servis fugitivis, law Quicunque; this is noted by Bartolus in Digest, Si quis testamento liber esse iussus, law 1, section Non autem, at the end of his words. But if fraud or gross negligence is proven, he must be condemned without distinction.

But it is doubtful, if very slight fault is proved, whether it comes in as in the civil Aquilian action, and thus in the criminal action. And Cynus says that in these criminal matters, which by their nature do not suggest the atrocity of slight or very slight fault, they are not punished criminally, as is noted in the law “If one does not say that I seize,” Code, On Bishops and Clerics, at the end. But the judge of the case should carefully consider this, if the times permit; otherwise, he should absolve the defendant from the observance of the judgment, Digest, On Adultery, law “He who is about to accuse.” I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In which place patrimonial burdens must be paid.
2. Payment cannot be made for one thing unless in one place.
casus: CASE. It is proposed that a deceased inhabitant of the castle of St. John, who was subject to the burdens of said castle, and within the jurisdiction of the disposition of the assets of said castle, left his considerable patrimony transferred by one of his daughters and heirs, by way of dowry, for half to B., a son of a family, her husband, receiving it in his own name, and in the name and on behalf of, and by the will, consent, order, and command, and instruction of his said father. And B. is not listed in any tax register; nevertheless, his father, with whom he lives, is listed in the city of Piacenza and there bears the burden. Furthermore, by the disposition of the deceased, the remaining quarter part is destined, by the ordinance of the testator, for the construction of a certain chapel. Now the question arises from the foregoing: whether said daughter, the aforesaid heir, and holder of said goods, is bound and ought to be compelled to pay and bear the burdens of said communal castle of St. John, as said late father of hers was bound.
body: If it is asked,

† Concerning the place where patrimonial burdens ought to be paid: I answer, in that place where the goods are situated, and also where they are assessed, as is read and noted in C. de mulieribus, et in quo loco; l. 1, lib. 10; and ff. ad municipalia, l. incola. To the contrary is made the fact that the collected tax ought to be paid in the place of domicile for goods wherever situated, and thus they ought to be paid in the domicile of the husband, which the wife follows, as in ff. ad municipalia, l. Lucius, §. respondit idem; ff. de muneribus et honoribus, l. rescripto, §. si; and there the ordinary gloss appears on this, which is commonly alleged: because sole possession is not considered, but it is required that the possessor be a citizen or inhabitant, in order that he be bound to pay the collected taxes: because they cannot be imposed on a person who is not subject. And there it is noted by Dy. A distinction must be made between a purely patrimonial burden, which is to be borne in the place of the things, and a mixed one, in the place where it is considered whether the person is subject or not. It is certain, however, that the said husband is not subject to the castle of St. John, nor is he a citizen or inhabitant there; and therefore he cannot be compelled there to pay the said collected tax, according to the gloss, Dynus, and all the doctors commonly. But since those making the assessment in common bind the very goods for the payment of the collected taxes, it is necessary that they be paid in the place where the assessment was made, by analogy to tributes: because that obligation is real. The statutes of places have also been accustomed to provide on this matter, that they cannot be alienated except by one who promises to bear the burdens. Moreover, they have been accustomed to provide that the estates be tributary for the burdens of the collected taxes, as is noted by Bartolus in the said l. rescripto, §. fin.; and for this in Auth. de mancipiis, prin., §. non praemittas. And thus custom observes, namely, that the collected taxes which ought to be paid according to the measure of the assessment are paid in the place where they were assessed by the possessor of those things, or by the things themselves: because, as we have said, the things themselves are burdened, by taking from the things themselves, and by distraining for the payment of fiscal dues, and also by compelling the subject tenants; as is found in the statutes of certain territories.

† It is also certain that for one possession payment ought not to be made in more than one place, as is noted in the aforementioned law 1, *De mulieribus*, and in which place. This is noted there by Bartolus, and in the aforementioned law *Rescripto*, § *Si*, *De bonis autem paraphernalibus*. There is no doubt that the tax should be paid where the property subject to valuation is found by the said daughter; because goods outside the dowry are hers in full right. The following supports the foregoing: D. *De impen.*, l. *Neque*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a disposition speaking of marriage, and of a woman married or united to a husband, requires carnal copulation.
body: To the evidence

It must be premised that there is a twofold marital union: namely, the civil or canonical union, which is perfected by consent between persons of suitable age. 32. q. 1. c. Non in sola, Extra, De regulis iuris; c. Nuptias. And this was instituted in Paradise, for there Adam did not know Eve, yet it was a true marriage; and the natural and corporal union, which is called the confirmation of marriage. 32. quaest. 2. Solet queri de conversione infidelium, Ex litteris, Extra, De translatione episcopi; c. Licet, De bigamis; ca. Debitum. Moreover, the first union, which is called the bond or tie, is twofold: namely, true, when marriage is contracted by express words between persons of suitable age; and interpretative, or presumed, when legitimate words are exchanged between a pubescent and an impubescent person, or between impubescent persons, and afterwards follows an evident perseverance in consent after the legitimate age, as in cap. 1, Extra, De desponsatione impuberum, lib. 6. And the text seems there to require signs from both sides. Which is undoubtedly true if both were impubescent at the time of the betrothal. For the older party cannot withdraw against the will of the younger, as in cap. De illis, § Muliere, Extra, De desponsatione impuberum. Moreover, the second union, which is called the use of marriage, is twofold, namely, true and presumed; for since she has been brought home by the husband, when both are pubescent, intercourse is presumed, although no other certainty appears; but here it is certain, if perhaps she is pregnant, as in cap. Litteris, De praesumptionibus. Now let us see whether this proposition, that A. and B. are united by marriage, although in truth no carnal union intervenes, is a true or presumed proposition. And if indeed we speak of union in the civil sense, the proposition is true. But if we speak of it in the natural sense, the proposition is false. Since therefore the writing can be explained in two ways, it is certain that the ambiguous writing is equivocal; for as Boethius says, that which is explained in multiple ways, its truth is unknown. In this doubt, however, the more equitable opinion must be chosen. First, it is argued: because since the statute does not expressly mention carnal union, but simply speaks of marriage, certainly we ought not to require more than the statute requires, for we ought to be content with the words of the law. D. De acquirenda hereditate, l. Si servum, § Non dixit. Moreover, the law does not distinguish, therefore neither should we. D. De publicaniis, l. De pretio. Moreover, the genus is verified in any of its species. L. 1, D. Si certum petatur. And for this, that it is not necessary that she was brought home, serves: C. De episcopis et clericis, l. Deo nobis, and there I expressly noted. This same opinion is held by Bartolus in l. Nihil, D. De rerum amotione. And this is supported by: C. Unde vir et uxor, Auth. Praeterea; and C. De donationibus ante nuptias, Auth. Cum re. 31. quaest. 2. c. Quod si dormierit, De translatione; c. Inter corporalia. To the contrary, it seems that this statute distinguishes, therefore we also must distinguish, as C. De furtis, l. Apud antiquos. To understand that the distinction of unions, concerning which distinction the statute intends, applies only to carnal union; because some are indeed incestuous, some condemned, some concubinary, some matrimonial. Therefore the statute says that only matrimonial unions have the reward; and this seems to be the true intention of the statute. And this also the words seem evidently to signify. For the statute requires two things, namely, marriage and union. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The son does not lose the Trebellianic [right] solely because he did not make an inventory.
body: In the first article, it seems to us, a better opinion being reserved, that the sister should, as a matter of law, succeed to her deceased brother, the exclusion of the brother by the aforementioned statute notwithstanding; because it does not cover this case, as was prudently alleged above on behalf of the sister herself.

† In the second article, we state that the son does not lose the Trebellianic portion solely because he did not make an inventory, according to the true opinion; just as he also does not lose it in bequests for pious causes, as noted by the gloss, which is also true, in the chapter *Si pater*, Book 6, *De testamentis*, although some hold the contrary, and wrongly. And thus we say and hold in both articles. I, John of Castiglione of Milan, Bishop of Vicenza; and to the faith of the foregoing, I have written with my own hand and sealed with my ring. To the same effect. Confirmation of the above-mentioned counsel of the said Baldus. This most excellent doctor speaks the truth, that the statute does not say "in that degree," but says "in equal degree." Moreover, there is no equality where there is preference, as in the Authentica *De consanguineis et uterinis fratribus*. For these words, "in equal degree," signify law. And therefore I confirm the said counsel, which you sent me among other writings, as to the first point, and also as to the second. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How one who defames another, or utters words that give rise to discord between husband and wife, is to be punished.
2. Whether it is contrary to good morals to say to a married woman, "I had previously betrothed you."
body: Every

A fact or statement contrary to the truth, made to defame another, especially if the reputation of a woman is attacked, and thereby discord is sown between husband and wife, deserves punishment commensurate with the discretion of the judge, as stated in the Digest, *De iniuriis*, in the law *Item apud Labeonem*, § *quod autem non in coetu*, and in § *meminisse*. Likewise, anyone who has made an imputation, having laid false accusations against good men or women, as stated in the Digest, *De crimine stellionatus*, law 3, § *Item si quis imposituram*, and there in the notes.

But let us see whether it is contrary to good morals to say, “I betrothed you.” And it seems that it is not, because this is lawful and permitted. C. de sponsalibus, throughout. Nor by this do I defame the marriage subsequently contracted, as C. de sponsa, l. 1. But certainly every lie to the detriment of another is contrary to good morals, and especially when it slanders the honesty of a woman and disfigures marriages with false insults. C. de adul., l. quamuis adulterii, which some do presumptuously, as is said there: but not without punishment, for here both the man’s betrothal and the women are defamed with the same infamy. ff. de infamibus, l. 1, in fine; and l. quid ergo, §. quod ait. And it also contributes, insofar as it is concerned, to bringing oneself into the hatred of one’s father, as in Auth. ut cum de appell. cogn., §. aliud quoque capitulum; ff. de contrab., l. 3, §. si emancipatus. Nor does it fail to provide grounds for living badly with one’s husband. C. de fur., l. manifestissimi, §. fin. And sowers of discord are to be punished, as noted in l. agraria, de termino moto; and C. de acc., l. 1. Nor can he in his own case claim ignorance, nor allege that he did not act with intent to injure. C. de iniu., l. si non conuicii. For all, individually and collectively, know that it is not permitted in that which cannot be shown to move the judge’s mind. C. de cal., l. nostris. Therefore, the offense ought not to go unpunished. ff. ad l. Aquil., l. ita vulneratus, so that others may be deterred by example. C. ad l. Iul. pec., l. 1. And on this point, as was consulted and judged by the official of the Illustrious Prince and Magnificent Lord Count of Monteferrato, my most singular lord, a new proceeding is to be formed with the proper insertion of the place. And it is to be known that one who has confessed is compelled to confess again, as noted by Innocentius in c. per inquisitionem, extra de electione et de confessione, c. cum super; ff. de edilit. edict., l. cum quaero, §. fin.; and de infamibus, l. ictus fustium, with its following. And this I say of Nicolino; but the messenger, who is not presumed to be fraudulent in another’s act, I think should be excused, for the crime of injury and stellionatus require fraud. The penalty, however, will be extraordinary. ff. de iniur., l. 1; and ff. de priv. delict., in the gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the reservation of the power to declare and to supplement has the effect of extending the term of the compromise.
2. Although the lessor did not have the contract of another lease distinguished, he may nevertheless demand the removal of the things stolen from him.
body: Lord

† My lord Papiensis questioned me and had a discussion with me on two points: whether the aforementioned reservation of declaratory and supplementary power constitutes a prorogation of the compromise. And it must be said that it does, because it is an extension of power, and to extend and to prorogate are the same thing, even if the names are different. D. loc. cond. l. si in; D. de verb. oblig. l. si stipulatus; D. de precario l. sed si manente; D. de arboribus l. si cum dies. It supports what is noted: D. de familia erciscunda l. item Labeo. Moreover, he who reserves intends that the reservation should have some effect; therefore, he intends all that by which one arrives at that end. The laws are most common.

Secondly, he asked me whether, if this lessor did not have the contract of another lease distinguished, he could nevertheless demand the recovery of the things stolen from him. I answer: yes; for these points are entirely separate and irrelevant to one another. C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si maritus; ff. de minoribus, l. Papinianus exul. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman succeeds in a feudal castle, and if so, whether she succeeds in the furnishings assigned by reason of the castle.
2. Whether debts ought to be paid out of feudal goods.
body: A woman does not succeed to the paternal fief, as stated in c. 1, § hoc notandum, quae feuda possunt, col. 10. However, she succeeds in other goods together with her brother, each receiving a pro rata share. C. de lib. et posth. l. Maximum vitium. Of this pro rata share, she may make a will as she pleases, provided that she does not institute a person of infamous character. D. de inoff. test. l. Fratres; D. eod. l. 1. The question now arises,

Whether, just as a woman does not succeed to a feudal castle, so too she does not succeed to the furnishings assigned for the necessity of the castle. And it should be said that those furnishings did not adhere to the castle, in which [the castle] succeeds. D. de actione empti, l. feudi nihil.

Secondly, it is asked, from which goods debts are to be paid. I answer that all are universal heirs, both male and female; the son alone is heir to a specific thing beyond the daughters in the fief: and in this respect he is not liable to creditors. C. de haer. inst. l. quot; ff. eo. l. ex facto; proposebatur. Unless the debts were contracted on account of the fief, for which alone the son is liable. ff. de test. mili. l. si certarum. §. Iuli. However, in this case, if he had received, for example, one hundred on loan, from which he purchased provisions, of which above such provisions would pertain to the son alone. ff. de reg. iur. l. secundum naturam. In the same way as I said sisters succeed, so too does the mother succeed: as in Auth. defuncto. Bastards, however, succeed brothers legitimate in no way. ff. vnde cognati. l. si spurius. and l. hac parte. It is necessary, however, that legitimate sons support bastard brothers from paternal goods, as C. de natu. lib. auth. licet pro rata bonorum, quam possident: or perhaps only the universal heir is sued for alimony. C. si cer. pe. l. 1. and l. fi. ff. de vsuf. leg. and quod no. ff. de transa. l. controuersia. And note that an illustrious male can have natural children, a female cannot: but they would be spurious. C. ad orfi. l. si qua lllustris. Or say, as there. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Pope can grant to someone the vicariate of a castle of a certain city with full jurisdiction, in which castle the city had full jurisdiction.
2. Whether the jurisdiction of the city is extinguished by the said grant.
3. Those who hold jurisdictions by virtue of their office cannot alienate or donate them.
body: The fact upon which legal counsel is requested stands in the terms set forth below. There is a certain city subject to the Roman Church, possessing full jurisdiction, and also a certain castle belonging to the said Church: in which castle the Supreme Pontiff granted to a certain person a vicariate for a fixed term, with full jurisdiction, such as the same Supreme Pontiff held in the said castle. Now it is asked, first: whether the same Supreme Pontiff can, or appears to intend, to grant any jurisdiction, especially since the said city held all jurisdiction in the said castle, and this was not expressly stated in the said grant and petition. Second, presupposing that he could and did intend: whether, on account of the said grant, the jurisdiction of the aforementioned city has been entirely eradicated. Third, or lastly, presupposing the grant to be valid: whether the holder of the said granted jurisdiction can transfer it to another.

I answer that there is no doubt regarding the impotence; he may. As is noted in C. de legibus, l. humanum. Nevertheless, it must be considered whether the petitioner, in obtaining the castle of the city or of another person, made mention of his prior possession or not. For if he does not make mention, the petition is invalid. C. unde vi, l. adverte, and the glosses noted therein; and in l. si qua loca, C. de fundis et saltibus rei dominicae, lib. 11, where the gloss notes that the rescript of those who occupied the lands of Count Ugolino without making mention of the occupation is invalid, because the rescript is obreptitious; thus says the gloss of the Ordines. Nor does a city differ from a private person. D. quod metus causa, l. metum, § animadvertendum. And thus the first point is decided.

† From this it is clear how to respond to the second point, because the Pope is not understood to have granted the rights which the city possesses by ancient custom, unless they had been devolved to the Pope: for example, through deprivation; because he could deprive one of jurisdiction and grant it to another, since he is the lord in the head of all jurisdiction. L. 1, § cum urbem, C. de officio præfecti urbis; ad L. Rhodiam, de iactu; L. deprecatio. He also can divide and come by the plenitude of power. FF. de assessoribus, L. si eadem; and L. 1, C. de metropolitanis. Berito, lib. 11.

I come to the third point, and it must be known that those who hold jurisdictions by virtue of their office cannot sell them: as in the Authentica "Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio," in the beginning; nor can they even donate them, and especially to the emulation of the city, as in the Code, "De fundis limitosis," law "Quicunque castrorum," book 11; and especially to more powerful and harsher adversaries, if they could defend themselves before the prince. Code, "Ne liceat potentioribus," law 1; Code, "De iudicibus," law "Nullus"; Digest, "De officio praesidis," law "Illicitas," section "Ne potentiores." Moreover, a formal usufruct cannot be alienated, and it immediately reverts to the ownership: as in the Institutes, "De usufructu," section "Finitur." On these matters, however, one ought to examine the writings: as in the Digest, "De legibus," law "In civile"; and Digest, "De transactionibus," law "De his"; and Extra, "De privilegiis," chapter "Porro." And it supports what Innocent notes in "De postulando praeparatorio," chapter "Bonae," in the beginning, column 10, at the words "contra Papam autem." I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Legacies on account of preterition are not vitiated.
2. What the words of a testator granting license to take possession of a fideicommissum by one's own authority import.
body: Truth

First, we inquire whether the legacy is valid, and it is valid, by the authority *Ex causa*, Codex, On omitted or disinherited heirs, because legacies are not vitiated on account of omission, even if the codicillary clause is not present there, the force of which it is not expedient to discuss here. And as appears from the records, the intestate inheritance has been entered upon, or administration has been conducted as heir. And this is certain, and ought not to be called into doubt: and upon this is founded the opinion of the most eminent doctor, Master John of Castillon, and it contains the final truth. Or we inquire about the very delivery of possession, and it is certain that such delivery, according to the common opinion, has no place in intestacy: and we are here in a case of intestacy, where the law *Edicto*, Codex, On the edict of the Divine Hadrian, abolishing, has no place, as well as Codex, On codicils, law *Si quis agere*. And because, as has been wisely alleged, it does not pertain to a universal fideicommissary before restitution has been made to him from the Trebellian portion, or we are in cases of exception. Furthermore, it is certain that a judge’s sentence does not merit execution against those not cited: as has been fully alleged above, and therefore, against those not cited, delivery of possession of the goods ought not to have been able to be made by the authority of the aforementioned law *Edicto*.

But one thing must be noted, that we are not here within the terms of the said law edict: but we are within the terms of the law Titia with a will. § 1. de legat. secundo. and C. de pigno. l. 3. and C. de iure emphyt. l. 2. because the testator gave the fideicommissary permission to take possession by his own authority. From this opinion arises the duty of the judge, so that no force and injury be done to him who wishes to use the benefit granted to him by the testator, and also by the law. arg. ff. de conditio. et demonstr. l. quibus diebus. in princip. and l. si. ff. de offi. procu. Caesaris. Hence he can invoke the aid of the praetor through whatever libel. arg. ff. de interr. act. in rubri. Therefore, although a sentence already passed does not deserve execution against one not cited, yet since he is now cited, and the cause has been discussed, the said mission should be made, or permission and judicial authority to go into possession should be granted, which if it were not for the permission of the will, would not be granted at all. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one who associates another in the commission of homicide, or who does so after the fact, is said to render aid.
body: Let us see

The genus of the crime, so that we may know the penalty, is in no way inferred from the matters narrated in the inquisition, namely that these accused persons were murderers, nor that they were present at the murder, nor that they were present at the infliction of wounds; hence they did not cooperate in any way in the act of striking, neither principally nor accessorially, as is noted in incipit 1, de poenis, in the Clementines. Although they gave favor to the killers by associating with them, this act was not joined with the homicide, nor were they present at the place where the wounds were inflicted; hence it is said that they should be punished more mildly than murderers, at least according to equity, as stated in the extrajudicial collection, de homicidio, chapter Sicut dignum, at the words "etiam qui vero"; and according to Decius, in the Digest, law De furtis, law Is qui ope. Certain persons, however, very rigorous in their approach, say the contrary, especially where counsel is joined with aid, as in the Digest, de verborum significatione, law Saepe. Nevertheless, according to equity, I hold the contrary view, and therefore in this matter I follow the opinion of the most excellent doctor, Lord Philippus de Regio, namely that the penalty, short of death, is discretionary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a possessor in bad faith is said to be one who knows that he, or his predecessor in title, is liable to a personal action.
body: This husband

† He had from the beginning good faith and title, and therefore he prescribed by long time according to civil law. C. de usucapione transformanda, l. 1, §. hoc tantummodo. And it should be noted that he who knows that his author, or even himself, is liable to a personal action, is not a possessor in bad faith. ff. de usucapione, l. pignori, §. si, and there, through Bartolus. And therefore, according to what is proposed, prescription is acquired. C. si adversus creditores, l. 1 and 2; C. de prescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, in principio, and there, noted. For payment and knowledge of a personal debt of a third person do not concern the hypothec, whence also this prescription proceeds according to canon law: because no fraud supervenes by which bad faith of the possessor is induced, and thus it does not obstruct c. peccatum, extra de prescriptione. And although it was a solid annual sum, nevertheless it is not a hypothec. And thus one prescription suffices according to the opinion of the gloss, C. de prescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, §. si illud. Although many hold the contrary, and it is a sufficiently difficult question, nevertheless, according to Jacobus Butrigarius, in doubt it is better in advising to follow the opinion of the gloss. And it supports C. de usucapione, l. eos, in principio. Nor does the aforementioned authority, malae fidei, obstruct, by what has been said, when I alleged l. pignori and si, and what there through Bartolus, and ff. de usucapione, l. sequitur, §. si viam, by the same. And although division was made, nevertheless the times are joined. ff. de usucapione, l. cum solus, in the gloss; ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. Pomponius, §. cum quis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an hermaphrodite, or another person having both sexes, or some signs of a male and some of a female, ought to be considered a male or a female, so that as a male he may succeed to a fief.
body: A certain Pagnificus, lord of the Marquises of Malaspina, namely Lord Momellus, in his will, among other things, thus provided and ordained, namely: because he said, “In all my goods I institute as heirs Anto., Ioan., and Bernaboe, my sons: namely, Ioan., if he, Ioan., should develop more in the male sex than in the female; but if the said Ioan. should develop more in the female sex than in the male, I institute him [as heir] to 1,000 florins; and if he can be judged neither male nor female, I institute him as heir to an equal portion in fiefs only: provided, however, that the said Ioan. shall have no mere or mixed empire, nor jurisdiction, nor homage, in the said case over our men and lands.” Finally, it happened that the said Ioan., so called, reached the age of 28 years or thereabouts, and these are the signs of the male sex in him, namely, beard and testicles; but the sign of the female sex is that he does not have a member that appears; rather, there is something like an egg with a certain hole, from which urine exits with great violence, nor is there in him any aptitude for generation, either active or passive. Now, it is asked what judgment should be rendered concerning this person, considering the form of the said will, and also concerning the fiefs; it is asked what is the law, considering the custom of fiefs. To which it is answered as follows.

† namely, because it must be stated for clarity that the greater draws the lesser to itself. As in D. 38.4.1 (Quaeritur hermaphroditus); and D. 48.1.1 (Repetundarum), § 1; and D. 41.1.1 (Quicquam), § 1. Hence, that which is greater prevails, as in D. 35.1.1 (Quaesitum), § 1 (Illud fortasse). But what if it does not appear which sex prevails? Some say that judgment will be made according to the male sex, as the more dignified. Argument: D. 39.5.1 (Qui duos), § 1 (Cum in bello); and D. 48.1.1 (Si fuerit), § 1; and Inst. 2.20.1 (Si tamen). But Master Hostiensis says in his Summa, under the title De testibus, § Qui testis, that it is at his election which sex he wishes to use more; and having chosen one, he will not use the other. Argument: D. 47.2.1 (Sed si alius); and D. 12.1.1 (Titia si non nupserit). And some more modern jurists follow this opinion, to which they adduce reasons. First, because in an equal case there is room for election. As in D. 49.14.1 (Si quis in gravi), § 1 (Si cum omnes). Second, since there is equality of sexes, he should stand by his election, just as we say in marriage, as in C. 5.4.1 (Viduae). Third, because when it concerns his own conscience, no one knows better than himself. Argument: D. 28.1.1 (Cum falsum). And it is proposed in the case that this person is of such an age that he ought to know from himself in which sex he heats up more, in which vigor he strengthens or prevails more; and whether he is capable of male or female operations. This supports what we note in Speculum, De testibus, § 1, ver. Idem, quod est hermaphroditus. In this opinion, Master Hostiensis is followed by Cynus in the said law Quaeritur, in his lecture. It must be considered that this person, speaking properly and perfectly, is not a pure male; because form is known through operation. For Aristotle says that operation indicates form, and transmutation nature. By the same reasoning, he is not a pure female, but is of a common sex, unless by the art of physicians he could be reduced either to the act of male generation or to the use of a female; because it is not said to be impossible if art can supply nature. Hence, according to what is proposed, with no other judgment by physicians, John, who is properly neither of the male nor the female sex, but of a confused one, to which confusion the grammarian did not assign the masculine gender nor the feminine, but the confused, I say here and here, does not succeed by will, except under that clause if neither male nor female can be judged. Therefore, the judgment of physicians is necessary. Let physicians beware, because according to the commentator, the test of true words is that they agree with sensible things. And it is proven in D. 44.2.1 (Confessionibus). And certainly, considering the case set forth above, the distinction of Hostiensis has no place here, either because we are not in doubt, in which election is committed, but in a certain case; namely, that he does not have the generative power of a male or a female. Here it must be considered that when we speak of sex, by sex we understand the generative power, either in which or by which generation is accustomed to take place. Hence, although as to other things this man might be of a masculine mind, it nonetheless does not help this matter; because we are not dealing with prudence, but with things to be prudently considered. But as regards fiefs: it must be considered, either he heats up in a masculine mind, and is useful to the lord of the fief, as in horsemanship, and in performing deeds of arms, and in the prudence of counsel; and then he should be judged a male. Or he is of a fragile nature, weak, and feminine; and then he should be judged a female: so that in the first case he succeeds as a male in the fief, as long as he lives; in the second case, not at all, according to our note in D. 35.1.1 (De quibus), although it is confessed by all that a woman does not succeed in fiefs. But against this it is argued: because statutes concerning simple cases, i.e., of a male only, and of a female only, do not include double cases. As in D. 35.1.1 (Titiae textores). And therefore the statute, or custom of fiefs, which extends fiefs to male descendants, is not understood to mean males in a qualified sense, but only simple males. The same applies to those whom the common people call males. On this point, our note in D. 35.1.1 (De quibus). To this effect, D. 35.1.1 (Hoc legatum). I say that either the hermaphrodite can act most actively, and in the male sex; and then he is judged a male. Or he can act most passively in the female sex; and then he is judged a female. Or he can do nothing in either sex, neither in the male nor in the female; and then he does not succeed in the fief: because this case is omitted in the investiture of the fief. Argument: D. 18.6.1 (Si vina, quae in doliis); and D. 28.5.1 (Commodissime). To this effect, if a testator were to bequeath to one males, to another females, such hermaphrodites are not due, as in the said law Titiae textores. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a mode of performance directed at a third person gives rise to an action for that third person.
body: For clarification,

†It must first be set forth that if a charge or condition (modus) is present in contracts, such that something is to be given or done for a certain third party, an action is regularly not acquired for that third party, as in C. de iu. do. l. si genero. It fails in a contract of donation, as in C. de do. quae sub modo. l. quotiens; but in a last will, he for whom the condition ought to be fulfilled can sue, as in C. de his, quam sub modo. l. 2. ff. de condit. et dem. §. si eum ante. Since we now see that the words state, "for the sake of endowing the monastery of S. Giacomo of Vallombrosa," whether an action belongs to the said monastery: and I say that it does. For whether it be a donation or the execution of a last will, it is certain by the aforesaid laws that an action belongs to the aforesaid monastery. This is supported by ff. de lega. 3. l. fideicom. §. interdum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether legacies left in a will, in which a posthumous child subsequently born during the testator’s lifetime was omitted, and in which the testator finally died without altering the will, are due, either by virtue of the authority *ex causa*, or by means of a codicillary clause, or by canonical equity. And see number 2.
2. Whether a son who repudiated his father’s inheritance may later, upon approaching death, make a will concerning his father’s goods. Also add in the fifth part of the consilia the opinion beginning, “that the said legacies, etc.”
body: Because the last step was difficult, although it was thoroughly examined.

† First, it must be considered whether, if a testator omitted a posthumous child in his will, in which he left legacies, and the posthumous child is subsequently born while the testator is still alive and without altering the will, whether the legacies are due, according to the *authenticum* *Ex causa*. On this point, there are contradictory glosses, for some glosses state that the legacies are valid: C. de success. edict. l. 1; and ff. de manum. test. l. *Uxorem*; and ff. de fideic. lib. l. *Generaliter*, § *Ex testamento*; and ff. de pact. l. *Bona*, § *Bona*, § *Si*; and ff. de leg. 2, l. *Si quis testamento*. In the contrary sense, the ordinary gloss determines, according to one reading, in l. 1, C. de posthum. haer. instit., for the text from which the *authenticum* *Ex causa* is derived seems to refer to ungrateful children, or those who can commit ingratitude, whom the law burdens with the payment of the legacies which the testator left in that will which is invalid by reason of the omission; a consideration which does not apply to a posthumous child, as C. de inoff. test. l. *Si quis in suo*, § *Si*. Moreover, the *authenticum* *Ex causa* arose for the purpose of upholding the testator’s will regarding legacies and fideicommissa; but in the case where a posthumous child is born, it is not probable that the testator intended to burden him, since he did not think of him: arg. ff. de pact. l. *Tale pactum*, § *Si*; and de test. tut. l. *Si quis ita*; and what is noted in l. *Titius*, de lib. et posth.; and C. de revo. don. l. *Si unquam*; and ff. de iur. cod. l. *Is qui*; and de leg. 3, l. *In fin.*; and ff. de leg. 2, l. *Cum pater*, § *Cum estimaret*. Furthermore, in the omission of a posthumous child, the legacies which began to be due from the institution of the heir: therefore, the substitution being removed, they cannot have force, as ff. de iniust. test. l. *Nam et si sub condicione*, § *Rumpendo*. And this opinion, namely that the legacies are not due, is held by many doctors on the strength of the said *authenticum*. Bartolus distinguishes on this point: either the omission was made by one who thought of posthumous children, or by one who was ignorant. In the first case, they are due; in the second case, they are not due: arg. C. de test. mil. l. *Sicut certi* and l. *Stichum vel in utero*. The objection from ff. de inoff. test. l. *Cum mater militem*, as noted there, can be answered by saying that either the testator made mention of children in some part of the will, and did not restrict himself by a proper name, but spoke indefinitely, and then the *authenticum* *Ex causa* applies; or he made no mention of children in any part of the will, and then he does not seem to have thought of those children who were in the body of his pregnant wife, especially if the legacies exhausted the forces of the inheritance; because it is not probable that the testator would wish to burden his children against natural affection: arg. ff. de haer. inst. l. *Lucius*. And therefore, because in this will no mention was made of children, but rather, in despair of having children, he made the will while in a state of illness, rightly the legacies are not due on account of the unforeseen case and the error in the final cause of the disposition and the legacies: arg. ff. de mil. test. l. *Militis codicillis*, § *Miles in summis*. And this opinion seems to me very equitable, and I consider it true. And thus I understand what I myself wrote in the *authenticum* *Ex causa*. Now it seems necessary to inquire about the second question, namely, assuming that the said legacies are invalid by force of the said *authenticum* *Ex causa*.

Whether they are valid by virtue of the codicillary clause through these words: “if they are not valid by the law of wills, let them be valid by the law of codicils”; and “if they are not valid by civil law, let them be valid by canon law.” And it seems expressly stated that this is so in the aforementioned law *Generaliter*, § *Ex testamento*. But the Gloss expressly determines that the said clause has no place when the will is broken on account of omission. And thus the Gloss determines in the Authentica *Ex causa*, and Guillaume de Coucy in the last law of the Code on codicils. And this seems true by civil law, and even more so by canon law; for he who wishes to institute one and exclude a son should seek another for counsel, not Augustine, signifying that such counsel does not befit a good man, since the will itself is unjust. But Lord Dino del Garbo says that legacies left in default of the will, however the will may fail, provided it does not fail due to a defect of the testator, nor due to a defect of the person to whom it is left, nor on account of the thing disposed of, are owed by the intestate successors; as in the Digest, on fideicommissa, law *Lucius*, § *Filiam*. But Bartolus distinguishes in this article, that either the omission was made knowingly, or by one erring, or ignorant, or not thinking of his children. If indeed it was made knowingly, for example because he knew his wife was pregnant: then the said clause operates, so that the legacies are owed. But in the other cases it operates for nothing. Which I hold to be true at least in our case; because the testator, overtaken by thoughts of death, does not seem to have been able to think of sons not yet born, but subsequently conceived from a new wife, just as we say in a similar case when a testator makes a donation *causa mortis* while ill. For it is revoked by recovery; because it is not probable that he wished it to be valid in such a case. I say the same regarding a posthumous child born after the father has recovered from such an illness, referring myself solely to the conjecture of the will, and to that which is probable according to natural reason. It is supported by what is noted by Dino in the law *Ex facto*, in the principle, in the Digest, on vulgar and pupillary substitution. And for this reason I hold that these omitted posthumous children are not bound to the payment of the legacies; because the testator did not think of burdening them, and would probably not have left them, had he thought of them; because he made no mention of his own and necessary heirs in any part of the will. Argument from the Digest, on legacies 1, law *Qui filiabus*, in the principle. Nor does it avail that the testator did not change the will; because he knew, or it was presumed that he knew, the will to be broken; and by this he knew that the right of the children endured everywhere; nor was it necessary to change it otherwise. Hence he does not seem to have persisted in that will which was not valid by law. Argument from the Digest, on actions and obligations, law *Non solum*. Nor does it avail from the law on fideicommissa, *Generaliter*, § *Ex testamento*, by argument *a contrario sensu*, because that argument *a contrario sensu* is taken, unless there is a conjecture to the contrary. But this is a great conjecture to the contrary; because, as I said, the testator, being in illness and fearing death, and the substance and words of the will saying that he wished to order his affairs before death, did not leave to a son whom he knew to be dead. And thus, on account of the lack of children, he proceeded to such last will. Likewise, it does not avail the law *Lucius*, § *Filiam*; because that testatrix wished to burden the daughter and the grandson; yet by the codicillary clause it appears there that she wished to burden others, for he who excepts certain persons seems to think of burdening others. Argument from the Digest, on legacies 1, law *Ab omnibus*, in the principle. Likewise, it must be weighed that in our case the legacies are so great that it is not probable the testator made them if he had thought of future sons. Argument from the aforementioned law *Si unquam*. Hence, although § *Ex testamento* does not distinguish, it must be distinguished by other laws. Nevertheless, in this opinion is the aforementioned Bartolus. But the learned Niccolò de Matti holds precisely and without distinction that the posthumous child is bound to the payment of the legacies by virtue of the said clause. And I refer to the aforementioned Authentica *Ex causa*, and without doubt this is ambiguous. I hold the more humane opinion on account of many conjectures, about which I said above, namely, that the said omitted posthumous children, having seen and examined the tenor of the will, are not bound to the said legacies. Nevertheless, because many hold the contrary opinion, and I myself have often doubted, I come to that point, namely, that the said testator repudiated the paternal inheritance. Finally, coming later to death, he made a will concerning the paternal goods.

† Now it is asked whether he could or could not. For that he could not seems to be proved: because by such a repudiation the right was acquired by the sister, and if it is said that it is a special privilege of one’s own descendants that they may revoke their abstention and enter upon the inheritance within the term, provided the things remain in the same state, as C. de repu. haere. l. si, this seems to be understood when by such a repudiation the right is acquired by an outsider; but if the right had been acquired by another son, then it would seem otherwise. Ar. ff. de exc. tu. l. sed et milites, in princ. For by the existence of his heir, another son, even if ignorant, immediately became heir as regards his own benefits. And therefore, since the inheritance was acquired for him, he who has once become heir cannot cease to be heir: as ff. de haere. instit. l. aliquo casu. And the gloss seems to say that he who has a substitute or a joint heir, after the inheritance has been acquired by them, cannot interfere. To the contrary, it seems that the aforementioned l. si and l. si quis suus, C. de iu. deli., speak indiscriminately; and thus it seems that he could make a will concerning the paternal goods, notwithstanding the repudiation, I mean concerning his share which touched him. Solution: because the words of one repudiating the inheritance are thus: “he who entirely and totally abstained.” I hold that the one repudiating the inheritance cannot be admitted, as ff. de adqu. haer. l. cum haereditatis; and therefore his will does not prejudice the sister, to whom the goods were acquired; and therefore he could not make a will concerning another’s property, as extra de testa. c. filius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman ought to be compelled to return to her husband under a sworn bond not to offend her.
body: It has been most wisely alleged and concluded; thus I, Baldus, conclude.

† saying, that when a wife is reconciled with her husband, the husband should be compelled to swear that he will do no harm to the reconciled wife. Argument from the Authentica *De monachis*, § *Sancimus*, column 1, where it says, “to give him an oath that he will do no harm.” And our doctors cite that text. However, it must be known that neither this oath nor a sacrament always suffices. For often the return would be more grievous than the separation: if an unfortunate woman, not to be governed by a spendthrift and a slave to lusts, cruelties, and barbarities, were to be committed to be torn apart. C. *De senatu consulto Pappiano*, l. *Si*; ff. *De his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt*, l. 1, § *Dominorum*. How much less can it be hoped that the husband will be the author of safety, when it is certain that he lived badly with his wife, whom he accused of theft? C. *De furtis*, l. *Manifesti*, § *Si*. A snake in the bosom, fire in the lap, badly guard their host. And above all these things, it is the most foolish thing in the mind of everyone to commit oneself to a capital enemy. ff. *De excusationibus tutorum*, l. *Propter litem*; *Ut lite non contestata*, l. *Accedens*. For when the sacrament is violated, one must again be believed. l. *Si*, *De bonis*; Auth. *Iudicis*, *Post*; c. *Testimonium*, *De testibus*. Moreover, who is an intervener secure in such danger, or a suitable surety? Furthermore, the husband did not deprive her of these things, but the husband stripped her by expelling her so often, Extra, *De restitutione spoliorum*, c. *Ex parte*, according to Innocentius. And therefore, for this and other reasons, the sentence of alimony should not be hindered. ff. *De solutionibus matrimonii*, l. *Si cum dotem*, § *Sui autem*, and § *Si vero*, and l. *Si ubi adhuc*. Certainly, under the true sense of the words, even the letters of our Lord, although they rather sound the contrary. But I see that the remainder belongs to spiritual cognition, that is, to the bishop, whom God will help. But the conclusion is that the sentence is to be executed, notwithstanding the deductions to the contrary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether clerics, of whom special mention was made in one chapter, can be included in the immediately following second chapter, in which only subjects are discussed.
body: The words of the chapter between the Illustrious and Magnificent Lords subscribed below were, in the first place, as follows: We, Galeazzo, Vice-Count, Count of Virtues of Milan, etc., Imperial Vicar General for lawsuits and disputes, which have hitherto prevailed, with the Author and Redeemer of souls operating between the Illustrious Prince and our most dear Uncle, the Magnificent Lord, Count of Savoy, on one part, and us on the other. Now, with the Father of mercies and graces disposing, by whose ordinance all things are directed for the better, striving to establish a good composition, by which we may attain the desired fruit of tranquility, we declare and will by the tenor of these presents: that the subjects of both parties, both clerics and laymen of every condition, who hold possessions and goods in the domain and territory of the other party, ought to enjoy those possessions and goods in peace and to hold and possess them; and to use the fruits, revenues, and proceeds arising therefrom peacefully, without impediment, all molestations ceasing, as they were accustomed to do before the controversy was raised before the Roman Church, etc. In another final chapter, it is contained as follows: Moreover, that all and each of the subjects of the Illustrious Prince and the exalted Lord Count of Virtues, who have possessions in the territory, from the territories which are ruled and governed by the Illustrious Prince and Lord Count of Savoy, may transport their fruits, namely, all coarse and fine grains, etc., arising from their said possessions, etc.

It is now asked whether this chapter, which does not mention clerics, should restrict the first chapter, which does mention clerics. And it is to be said briefly that whatever the prince ordains in favor of clerics or churches is never understood to be revoked by any other decree of theirs, unless clerics are expressly mentioned. The text is in C. de sacro. sanc. ecc. l. priuilegia. And therefore the first chapter is to be formally observed with regard to clerics. To this also contributes the fact that the said Most Serene Prince also calls clerics subjects in this matter, which concerns protection. 10. dist. c. si in adiutorium. And the words of the lords should be understood according to their true intention and broadly: as in Authen. constitutio, quae de dignita. §. illud. l. 1. de suppel. lega. facit. ff. de leg. 3. l. suos seruos. Moreover, clerics are part of the city, and indeed its most honorable member; nor are they entirely alien to the universal body, since their honor is increased. ff. de condit. et demonstrat. l. falsa. §. 1. And the foregoing are confirmed because a special chapter concerning clerics is not understood to be abrogated by a new general chapter concerning subjects: as ff. de alim. et ciba. lega. l. alimenta. §. basilicae. and l. Stichus nutricis meae liber esto. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person holding a mandate from the Pope that provision be made for him of a benefice pertaining to the collation of any persons whatsoever may be provided with a benefice pertaining to the collation of only one person? Likewise, whether a benefice pertaining to the collation of several persons is included in that pertaining to the collation of any person whatsoever.
2. Whether a benefice pertaining to the collation of a prelate ought to be conferred upon him to whom it is mandated that provision be made of a benefice pertaining to the collation of a chapter.
body:
The case is as follows: A certain B. obtained an expectative grant in the manner set forth below, namely: “Boniface, etc., wishing therefore to confer upon you, as you allege, being born of noble lineage from both parents, a special favor in consideration of the merits aforementioned, we reserve to the Apostolic See one, two, three, or more ecclesiastical benefices, or an ecclesiastical benefice, and if one of them, or of the two, three, or more, is a cure of souls, or a dignity in a metropolitan, cathedral, or collegiate church, and such dignity is a cure of souls, and in the metropolitan or cathedral church it is the major dignity after the pontifical one, or in the collegiate church the principal one; or even if one of them, or of the two, three, or more, is a canonry and prebend, or canonries and prebends in the metropolitan or cathedral church or cathedral churches, and if anyone is assumed to such dignity by election, the fruits, revenues, and proceeds of which do not exceed 200 gold florins according to the valuation of the tenth, pertaining to the collation, provision, presentation, election, or any disposition whatsoever, whether jointly or severally, of whomsoever they may be, which, if any, in the province of Milan, or in the cities and dioceses of Milan, Como, Padua, Verona, and Vicenza, is or are now vacant, or shall become vacant, whether simultaneously or successively, which you shall deem it fit to accept, either by yourself or through your legitimately appointed procurator, within the space of one month after the vacancy thereof has become known to you or to the said procurator, and which, after such acceptance, we reserve to you with all their rights and appurtenances, strictly inhibiting, etc.”

Subsequently, a certain benefice, called a fief, pertaining to the collation of the Lord Archbishop of Milan, became vacant by the death of a certain Antonius. B. likewise accepted it and had it provided to him. The question now arises whether this benefice is contained within the aforementioned grant.

† Regarding this point, it must be said that it is not included. The reason lies in the word “quoruncunque” [whatever persons], which is in the plural number; and the plural number is not satisfied by one. L. Ubi numerus, D. De testibus. Hence, the learned ask: if it is ordered that provision be made for a benefice pertaining to the collation of “cuiuscunque” [whatever person], does a benefice pertaining to the collation of several persons come within this? And they say that it does not; because the sense of this grant is [to apply] to the collation of someone, whoever he may be; and because the singular number does not admit of plurality. Extr. Divort., c. Gaudemus. There it did not say “will adhere to wives,” but “to wife.” D. Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, L. Si. See also Extr. De praebendis, lib. 6, c. Cum in illis, § Si. The learned add that if it is written “ad collationem quoruncunque” [to the collation of whatever persons], then a benefice pertaining to the collation of one person does properly come within it. D. De regulis iuris, L. Pluralis. With a similar case. This is the case in our matter, therefore, etc.

† Moreover, the doctors inquire what happens if someone is commanded to provide for a benefice pertaining to the collation of the chapter: and it is also said, whether commonly or divisively, whether a benefice that pertains to the collation of the prelate is included. They say that it is not, if the question concerns the principal prelate: because the prelate and the chapter are distinct. On those things which are done by the prelate, in the rubric and black letter, *ne sede vacante*, c. 1, lib. 6; and see the gloss in *Cle.*, *Hi qui*, *de aetate et qualitate*; in the gloss to c. *Cathedralibus*, *de regularibus*; in the Clementine, c. *Ut professores*; in the gloss to *Ad urbem*. They also say the same regarding a non-principal prelate: as in c. *Si*, lib. 6, where it is said there, by reason of prebends, and not dignities. Thus holds Johannes Andreae there. Moreover, if any constitution is made disposing concerning the ministers of churches or dignities, and even if the bishop or archbishop is not included: as noted by Innocentius in c. *Dilectus*, *extra*, *de concessione praebendarum*. Therefore, also c. Moreover, those things which are not worthy are not comprehended by general words, unless they are expressly stated. *Digestum*, *de iniuriis*, l. *Item apud Labeonem*, § *Hoc edictum*. And furthermore, c. *Quamvis* is not to the contrary, because there it speaks of an honor attached to the church; but we speak of an honor attached to a person: this is a divided plurality, not comprehended in a divisible unity. And therefore, the said allegations appear true to me.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The payment of an unsatisfied debt to a wife, exceeding the amount of her dowry, is valid as a donation, unless it was made in fraud of creditors.
2. A fideicommissary substitution made to two persons for equal shares encompasses only one half, not the entire inheritance.
body: Having examined the aforementioned point, the instrument of conveyance which remains unpaid, and the renunciation contained in that same instrument:

† I consider that the payment was not a simple one, but mixed with a donation; because to renounce the law *Secunda*, C. de rescind. vend. is a certain donation made between husband and wife concerning that which is beyond the dowry in the thing granted: as ff. de donat. l. si quis delegaverit; ff. de donat. inter virum et uxorem l. si sponsus § circa; ff. de contrah. empt. l. si quis donat. in the gloss. And indeed, that thing was delivered, and therefore the donation was confirmed: ff. de donat. inter virum et uxorem l. Papi. and l. cum hic status § si maritus. Without prejudice, however, to creditors, or to the substitution made by the father of this husband.

But concerning the substitution, it is asked: because the testator says thus, he substituted to them Blasius for one half, and Francischina, daughter of the said testator, or her sons and heirs: nor did he add for the other half. Whether the brother with Francischina and her children is substituted in only one half, or in two halves, and thus in the whole inheritance. And it seems that in the other half, just as an heir instituted without a specified share is considered instituted in the residue. D. de hereditate instituenda, l. Item quod Sabinus, together with si. On the contrary, because one thing appears in fideicommissary substitution, and another in direct substitution, because the reason ceases, lest one die partly testate and partly intestate. Also, the nature of conjunction is to connect perfectly and to the same thing. D. de fundo instrato, l. servo, §. Gayo. Also, these are conjoined in fact and in words: therefore to the same half. For if they were to the other, they would be disjoined in fact. D. de legatis tertio, l. re coniuncti. Also, from the unity of repetition, it seems the same thing is repeated. D. de legatis tertio, l. in repetendis. Also, here there is unity of speech: and all these persons are governed by one principal verb, and are enclosed under the same verbal act: as noted. D. de hereditate instituenda, l. liber honoris, §. Titius. Also, even if there were two sentences: one perfect, and another imperfect: the second, which is imperfect, receives the form of the perfect sentence from it. According to the theory of the learned in the said l. in repetendis. I think the testator in truth thought of the other half, although in the way of legal disputation it can rather be defended: that since mention is made of only one half, only that single half comes into play: although in institutions a broader interpretation is made. The said l. Item quod Sabinus. As for that which this lady asked about from the paraphernalia, it is certain that it pertains to her freely and fully. C. de pactis conventis, l. hac. C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Quintus. From the foregoing it appears that my opinion in law is this, that only one half of the inheritance was included in the fideicommissary substitution above mentioned. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Possession is not to be sequestered when it is established; rather, the adversary is to be enjoined from taking possession by his own authority; and he who has come into possession is to be maintained in it, unless a petitory action is brought against him.
body: Without touching upon the substance of the fief: because a more profound inquiry is required, but coming to the words of the magnificence, which indeed were most just:

† Because where possession is established, the possession is not to be sequestered; but the non-possessor is to be enjoined from taking possession by his own authority. D. de officio proconsulis, l. si. It must be said that, upon the death of the feudatory, the natural possession of the feudal thing remained vacant at that instant; nor does it, by operation of law, pass without apprehension. L. 1, §. Sceuola, D. si quis testamento liberum esse iussus fuerit. And therefore, he who has anticipated in taking possession ought to be defended in possession until another proves his right, in a judgment lawfully instituted on this matter. D. de libris causis, l. liberis, §. si. And these are the words of Innocentius ad litteram, X. de probat., c. in praesentia. Since the said Beltramus has arrived at possession, he ought not to be disturbed in possession, much less deprived of possession, unless an action in rem is brought against him: as the glossa ordinaria states in l. ult., C. unde vi. To this is added the nature of the edict of the Divine Hadrian, which protects the instituted heir in those things which the deceased possessed at the time of death: as l. 1, §. edicto. And Lord Beltramus is the instituted heir, whence possession is to be confirmed to him in the meantime, without prejudice to the question of ownership. C. de carborum edicto, l. 1. And therefore, from what I have been able to conceive in the cause of fact, I hold that the sequestration should be removed, and in the meantime, until the adversaries of the said Beltramus convince him by due legal means, if they can: the said Beltramus is to be protected in possession, as has been proven. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "castle," "village," and "appurtenances" includes jurisdiction, and whether it includes vassals.
2. A later act is presumed to clarify an earlier act that is in doubt.
body: Villa

† Or a castle contains both the corporeal substance and the honor, jurisdiction, and district, as Innocentius states literally in c. Ex litteris, Extra, de iure patronatus; and this is clear from D. de officiis praefecti urbis, l. 1, § Cum urbem. The term, however, which signifies a universality or some singular thing, such as the name of a house or a castle, does not in itself contain mere or mixed imperial power, or jurisdiction, unless the seller had such power within the ambit of those walls, D. de contrahenda emptione, l. In modicis. Nor do vassals come into the sale, nor the dominion of other things than those sold, because the word does not signify this, D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Fundi. Nevertheless, in our case, it must be considered that the jurisdiction of the appurtenances was also sold. Innocentius states that we know of no corporeal thing assigned by law to a castle as its appurtenance. It is, however, customary for all, and by their statutes, to assign a certain territory, which is said to be appurtenant to the castle, Extra, de restitutione spoliatorum, c. Cum ad sedem, according to Innocentius. Therefore, if in the present case the seller exercised any jurisdiction under the pretext of the castle, and consequently the vassal held it, all these things seem to be included under the general term of appurtenances, by argument from D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Si aquaeductus; D. de legibus tertio, l. Praedium, § Pe. et fin.; D. de fundis limitosis, l. Quicunque castrorum; Lib. 11, C. de bonis vacantibus, l. Si quando; Lib. 10, C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. Posses.; D. de legibus primo, l. Si quis inquilinos. And this is especially so because the comparison of the price to the thing openly demonstrates this, by argument from l. 1, D. de rebus dubiis.

And because the later fact is declared in doubt to have preceded the earlier act, arg. C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. minus instructus; ff. de re vendicata, l. quaedam mulier. And it supports what Innocentius notes in de exceptionibus, c. cum venerabilis, in principio; and ff. de verbis significatis, the word “illud” pertains, or even if the castle is a place, and also a sign of dominion over vassals, to whom the sign is given, and the signed thing seems to follow: as C. de donationibus, l. 1; ff. de iure fisci, l. si accepto; Extra de consuetudinibus, c. 2; and in c. 1, de regulis iuris, lib. 6, through Dyther, tacit consent is sometimes held to be equivalent to title. Innocentius says in de iure patronatus, c. cura. Here I say that tacit consent is interpreted as express. C. de petitione hereditatis, l. si filius, as if from doubt to something which is not doubtful: thus the later quality of possession declares what at the beginning was of doubtful intention. ff. de legatis tertio, l. hoc legatum; and ff. de fundo instrato, l. Scaevola, § tyrannide; de legatis tertio, l. cum fundus. To this also contributes the common interpretation and mode of speaking: and the custom of that region would not be without considerable aid to understanding, since such intention is presumed to be singular as is universally predicated, ff. de fluminibus, l. 1, § 1; ff. de fundo instrato, l. cum Delanionis, § asinam; ff. de verbis significatis, l. ut Alphenus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. To what burdens churches are bound.
body: Ancient

† The transfer of lay property [to the Church] is [prohibited], because the churches are enriched day by day, and the laity are crushed by burdens, since the churches do not bear personal, mixed, or any extraordinary burdens. C. de sacratissimis ecclesiis, l. placet; de episcopis et clericis, aut. item nulla communitas. And this is the privilege of the churches: because their liberty consists chiefly in their privileges; for a privilege is nothing other than a privileged liberty: as noted by Innocentius in c. noverit, de sententia excommunicationis; and Cynus approves in aut. cassa et irrita, C. de sacratissimis ecclesiis. But the laity have found remedies, of which Bartolus notes in l. rescriptis, §. si, de muneribus et honoribus. There is, however, one method, whereby citizens bind themselves principally, and with the intention of not reclaiming their goods for any secular or ecclesiastic possessors, to pay general impositions; hence, all goods subsequently transferred to the Church would then be bound: but we do not use these subtleties; rather, we use the simple and rough way. And the laity establish that goods are bound for collections. To advise on these matters is not very safe; nevertheless, regarding the construction of bridges, roads, and walls, and wherever a similar and precise sudden necessity arises, the bishop must compel the churches to contribute thereto with due moderation, in those matters wherein the safety of the churches and the public welfare are provided for. C. de sacratissimis ecclesiis, l. ad destructionem, according to the ancient, modern, and more modern commentators; and because these points have been most legally treated by the excellent doctor Anselmus de Rambaldih, it is not expedient to proceed further. And thus I conclude that tributes, even those which are properly tributes, must be acknowledged, if they are for the tripartite assessment of estates. 11. q. 1, c. si tributum, with similar authorities. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether war is a just cause for retaining the pension.
2. Whether a remission may be sought on account of war, notwithstanding that the instrument states "notwithstanding any exceptions whatsoever, etc."
body: If, on account of

† wars, the said brother Bernardus was unable to collect the fruits of the said quests, such that he suffered an enormous loss, a remission of the rent ought to be granted in proportion to the time and to the loss, to be assessed at the discretion of the judge. ff. loca. l. ex conducto. §. fi., and there Cynus says in his additions the following words: ‘Certain persons leased specific possessions from the commune of Pistoia for a specific time, say five years; the collector seeks the rent on behalf of the commune; the lessees say they are not bound because they could not have the possessions cultivated due to the incursions of enemies who dwell in the castle of San Luca. It is asked, what is the law?
