I distinguish: either the war and the incursions of the aforesaid enemies supervened after the contract of lease, and then the rent is remitted, as here; or the war existed beforehand, and then it is to be imputed to them, who knew the condition and state of the thing, whence they are not excused from the rent. l. qui bona. §. de illo. de dam. infec. Cynus.’ To this pertains what is noted on l. 1. C. de iure emphy. by Ia. Bu. and Cy. Since therefore, in our case, war and an unthinkable event supervened, a remission ought deservedly to be made once the enormity of the loss arising from the war has been proved. For a moderate loss ought to be borne with equanimity. If, however, it is permitted to enjoy neither in whole nor in part, nothing ought to be paid of the rent: d. l. ex conducto. in prin. But against this it is objected: for this is a specific thing leased or bought, namely a doubtful event and a hope constituted in doubt; therefore a remission ought not to be made, just as when that which happens to be won in a game of dice is bought, or the cast of a net. ff. de act. emp. l. si iactum rethis. Solution: that case is different, where a wholly uncertain hope is bought, whose determination rests on the ambushes of fortune, and thus is in an uncertain nature from custom and event; but in our case, where a certain quasi-certain hope is had from the collective custom of rendering, although from uncertain persons—in which, if anyone were disturbed, he would have against the disturber an interdictum utile uti possidetis to be brought by the lessor, or the office of the judge, which the lessee could also bring: ff. de donatio. l. aquilius regulus. It is otherwise in dice and in a cast, where there is no quasi-possession, and there lies solely an action for iniuria on account of the contumely rather than on account of one's estate: ff. de iniur. l. iniuriarum. §. fina. and l. iniuriarum aestimatio. ff. de conditio. et demonstratio. l. quibus diebus. in prin. Whence the matter of dice and the cast is not similar to our case. ff. de eo, quod cer. loco. l. 3. §. fi. in gl. and arg. ff. de alea. l. mella. §. 1.

† Likewise, it is objected concerning what is noted in extra de loca. l. propter., where a remission is not made if it is provided by agreement that it should not be made; but by this agreement it would seem to have been renounced; therefore, etc., as is clear in the tenor of the instrument there, when it says, ‘all exceptions, occasions, impediments, etc.’ For the answer is evident: because general words do not extend their renunciative force to rare and unthinkable cases. ff. de contrahen. emp. l. fistulas. §. frumenta. ff. si quis cau. l. sed et si quia. §. quaesitum. with its subject-matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The first assignee has priority, if the same rights have been assigned to several persons.
body: It must be presupposed that the house was in the debtor’s assets at the time the dowry was received; for if it had been alienated beforehand, it would not have come within the scope of the obligation. D. de pign. act. l. Si is qui, §. Quod dicitur. Furthermore, it must be presupposed that the debt of four hundred pounds, with an express hypothec, if it preceded the dowry, such that it remained in its original form and was not subsequently declared as to its purpose, undoubtedly would have priority in right, he who had preceded in time with an express hypothec, as is fully noted in l. Assiduis, C. qui potiores in pignore habentur. For now, it must be determined in fact whether the instrument was received for the cautionary defense of things purchased before the dowry, and for what purpose it was made. For it was not useful against prior creditors, nor was it necessary against subsequent ones. I do not have full information regarding these modes of drafting instruments in this country; nevertheless, it appears that it is done for a just purpose, so that, upon eviction occurring, one may sue pro rata on the basis of this caution, as if succeeding to this promise in place of the interest for eviction, as declared by this contract. D. de praetor. stipul. l. Si. And from the protestation it appears that it was also done so that he may use the said instrument for defense. But if the alienation, being older, protects the buyer against the dowry, that instrument is futile, as I have said. Hence, in order that you may receive a fitting response, insert more clearly an example of the facts, and state which preceded in time, the alienation of the house or the dowry. And if the alienation preceded, the hypothecary action for the thing is futile, which had previously left the assets. l. 1, C. de iure fideicommissi, l. 10. But if the dowry preceded: then this house would be bound by the earlier right to the first creditor, and by the later right to the woman.

And then it would have to be seen, when rights have been assigned to several persons, who is the stronger. And the law says that the first assignee is: because a right once assigned cannot be assigned again. D. 1.17.1. l. non quocumque. §. qui gemma. And there by Jacobus de Aretino and Bartolus. That is true if the succession is pure. But if conditional, as it is here, it is equally valid in suspense, D. 44.2. l. pecuniam. Or here it was not conditional, but for a certain final cause, and to one to protect one thing, to another to protect another, and this assignment was made proportionally: and therefore it suffices that the debt of 400 pounds be offered pro rata of the value of the thing which is claimed by the hypothecary action. Arg. C. 8.27. l. 1. For it ought not to be offered to several in solidum: because it would be absurd that those who contracted with one should be distinguished in toto. And by this part the way to the hypothecary action is precluded to him, unless it is necessary for each in solidum: but pro rata, although the nature of the pledge is indivisible, as l. in exceptione. §. quam. D. 50.16. and l. quandiu. cum seq. And it was assigned personally pro rata, therefore it suffices that the rate be offered: for without the personal right the hypothecary cannot be assigned. Noted by Dyonisius and others. D. 46.1. l. fideiussor obligari. And by Cynus. C. 8.13. l. usucapio. D. 46.1. l. si pignori. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person who has suffered damage from a seizure of goods wrongfully made against him may claim damages and interest, even though he did not do so at the time when the seizure was revoked.
2. When a civil and criminal action arises from the same delict.
body: A certain

† merchant caused the goods of another merchant to be sequestered, and consequently he whose wares were sequestered suffered damages because they could not be sold. Thereafter, the sequestration was revoked; and the judge who rendered the judgment revoking the said sequestration made no mention of damages and interest. Thereafter, damages and interest are claimed. It is objected that they cannot be claimed, because malicious prosecution (calumnia) by the plaintiff cannot be inquired into except in the very same judicial proceeding, as in C. de fruc. et lit. expen. l. terminato and C. de iu. l. sancimus, according to the Doctors. To the contrary, it will be said that the said malicious prosecutor is liable criminally for the crime of stellionate, because he is in bad faith (dolus) and a specific designation of crime is lacking; therefore, he is liable civilly for interest.

† For wherever a delict concerns private property, both a civil and a criminal action arise from the same delict, C. de fal. l. qui nomine, C. quando ciuilis actio l. 1, and as noted in l. fi. ff. de priua. delic. I have previously advised that an action can be brought under l. rem quandam ff. de dolo and l. si oleum; and now I advise that he who disturbed a merchant in the sale of goods which he possessed is bound to him for interest, as noted in ff. vti possi. l. si duo §. vlti. in fi. vlti. gl., by which gloss even the wisest must abide, and let them look there. And the lex terminata has nothing to do with the fact, nor does that which is noted there in l. sancimus, because here we have dealt with the interest of the principal thing, which can always be claimed. Hence, since the case against this merchant, who is called dominus Iacobus, is clear from the proofs, the judgment rendered in his favor, being most unjust, ought to be reformed; and the counselor who advised in favor of the said Iacobus plausibly considered the force of a suit already commenced from the beginning, but not one that ought to be commenced, ff. de infa. l. debuit enim. That is certain: since the said Iacobus proved nothing, he is presumed to have brought the suit maliciously, l. i. de aduo. diuer. iud., c. 1 de elec. lib. 6 in fin. Likewise, he did not consider by what right the interest comes into play, which is the value of the thing; for the value of the thing is one thing, the expense is another, ff. de condi. et dem. l. quibus diebus §. 1, and what Innocentius notes in c. vlti. extra quod metus causa supports this. And so I, Baldus, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a thing given to someone, so that the donee may provide maintenance for the donor, can be reclaimed on account of the maintenance not having been provided.
2. Whether the donee, from whom such a donated thing is recovered, can purge the delay.
body: † [if] I have given that you may provide me with maintenance, such a donation is valid. But if you do not provide me with maintenance, an utilis rei vindicatio is granted to me. Furthermore, if it is asked whether this donee, from whom the property is reclaimed on account of maintenance not having been provided, can purge default (moram purgare). The answer is that he can, when three things concur: namely, when joinder of issue (lite non contestata) has not taken place, within a short time, and if it does not affect the interest of the adversary. The first words are the words of the text and the gloss; the second words are the words of dominus Cynus in l. 1, C. de dona. quae sub modo. Therefore, since maintenance has not been provided for a long time, nay rather, according to what is submitted, the donee has never observed the condition (modus) attached to the donation, it is evident that the donation has lost its effect; such is the case in the said l. 1. Likewise, in the provision of maintenance, compensation for past time does not properly apply, since he may perhaps have suffered from hunger in the past, which cannot be restored to its prior state through an obligation.
† From these things it appears that the said ser Modestus can revoke the said donations, and that the said donee cannot purge default, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession of payment made to one of two debtors jointly liable benefits the other. Likewise, what is the case in remission. Likewise, what is the case in a pact not to sue. And number 2.
2. What this clause, "all things being computed, etc.," imports.
body: Two debtors were jointly and severally bound by reason of a sale to a certain person named Piacecero, for the sum of one thousand Asti pounds. Now, the aforementioned creditor, through the hand of a public notary, made a settlement with one of the said debtors in the following words, namely: that he had received, and that he received and had from the said debtor fifteen solidi, and this for all and the whole of that which the said creditor could demand from the said debtor, whether with a written instrument or without; renouncing the exception of non-numeration, computed in this confession and payment made between them in the past. Now, the creditor wishes to sue the other debtor, with whom the said instrument was not executed; the debtor opposes the said instrument.

† It is asked whether the said instrument, drawn up with the said words, proves in favor of the said defendant: and for clarity it must be premised that whenever a true payment occurs, sometimes there is a confession of payment, sometimes a pact not to sue, and sometimes it is doubtful how many of these have occurred. In the first case, when a true payment occurs with one party paying, both are released, as in D. de duobus rebus iudicatis, l. ex duobus. In the second case, when there is a confession of payment, either the exception of non-numerated pecuniary sum has not been waived, and then according to the common law it does not prejudice the creditor if he raises this complaint within 30 days; this fails in excepted cases: but if he does not raise the complaint of non-numerated pecuniary sum within 30 days, then he cannot raise it later. C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus. Or the exception of non-numerated pecuniary sum has been waived, and then either after an interval, and the waiver is harmful according to all, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si ex cautione. Or it has been waived immediately in the same instrument: and then opinions are divided. For some say that the waiver has no effect, because it seems to have been made in hope of future payment; others say that rather it has effect, because the contrary was asserted. And this opinion prevails both in law and in custom. Also because the waiver ought to have some effect, whence by it the effect is increased, as noted in l. 1, C. de dote cauta, n. but as that gloss speaks in the case of a confessed dowry, there is a contrary gloss. C. qui potest in pignus habere, l. assiduis, in the small gloss, which says, therefore not confessed. For which gloss it is made. C. de dote antenuptiali, auth. sed iam necesse. And C. de manumissionibus, l. per diversas. But there it is on account of suspicion of fraud, and on account of the prohibition of the law: as noted in D. de probationibus, l. qui testamentum. And D. de legibus 3, l. cum quis decedens, §. Titia. I conclude that the confession of non-numerated pecuniary sum with waiver benefits both defendants owing, not that by this the act of true payment is proved, as in D. de depositis, l. publica, §. si. And D. de constitutionibus pecuniarum, l. si. Nevertheless, by legal presumption, and by law it is presumed that payment has occurred, and on account of the convention of the obligation of two defendants, and the connection of the cause, the exception of fraud is sought for the other absent, as in D. de liberatione legis, l. non solum, §. si liberationis verba, in the gloss and argument. D. de pactis, l. rescriptum, §. si, arguing that the present one by his gesture in conducting the affairs of the absent made himself his procurator at least followed by ratification. D. de solutionibus, l. solutionem, et iudicium. Nevertheless, the gloss notes the contrary. D. de pactis, l. idem in duobus. By that rule, that by a free person directing substantial words in the person of the absent, no right is acquired, unless it is such a contract, which is contracted by thing, or by direct consent by messenger, or by letter, as in D. si certum petatur, l. certi condictio, §. quia. And §. si nummos. D. de depositis, l. publica, in the beginning. D. de verbis obligationibus, l. stipulatio ista, §. hanc consequentibus. D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. 1, in the beginning. D. de legatis 1, l. huiusmodi, in the beginning. D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. quaecunque gerimus. But it must be observed: because this beginning of validity I assumed in the person of one of the conjuncts by the conjunction of the obligation: although there was no partnership between them: whence consequently it is extended to the co-defendant by the same law from the contrary sense. For this confession not contradicted would prove the reality with the intervening instrument, or chirograph. D. de verbis obligationibus, l. si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus. D. si certum petatur, l. lecta. And noted in l. 1, C. de falsa causa adiecta, l. 1.

† Now I come to the third point concerning the pact: and if indeed it is fortified by a confession of payment, it has the same effect as a confession. But if it was made simply, or under a cloud of uncertainty: then it is not deemed to derive its force from a presumed payment, but from its own sole force, which is to refrain from further demand. D. 46.3.11 (Si ex pluribus), in principio; D. 2.14.1 (Tale pactum), in principio. Therefore, in our principal question, we must consider that the instrument was executed with one of the debtors, and the words were directed to his person. And the rule of law is that an extraneous person is never implied in a contract or release: as stated in the aforementioned § Grigonus, at the end. Therefore, this liberating pact does not directly extend to the other debtor: because it is personal, which does not totally extinguish the obligation, but merely terminates it: as in D. 46.1.37 (Stipulatus), § 1. What then is the answer? I reply otherwise: the debtor remains bound as before in strict law; but on account of the duty to assign actions, he cannot be sued except for a part. For the creditor cannot sue for the other part not only because the law prevents it, but also because his own pact prevents it; and thus the exception of the duty to assign actions stands in the way for that part for which the actions ought to have been assigned. D. 2.14.10 (Nisi); D. 46.3.12 (Modestinus); and D. 46.3.13 (Stichum), § Si mandato.

† Now follows the fourth main point: what is the meaning of the words of the said instrument, when it says, “compute,” etc. I answer that this word does not prove anything in a determined manner, unless the computation is produced, because it does not signify anything certain, since it refers to another document: as in D. 2.14.1 § Lucius (Digest, On Pacts, “The Buyer”). And therefore it is considered as that of a simple father: as in the aforementioned law “If from several.” One might doubt, because both confession and pact are expressed, in which capacity it operates. I answer that it operates as best it can operate: within 30 days by the law of pact; after 30 days, however, by the law of presumed payment; or it may be said that the whole is by the law of pact: as in D. 2.14.10 (Digest, On Pacts, “If within”). The final conclusion is that the said instrument indirectly, i.e., by reason of the benefit of cession, benefits in part and does not benefit in part: because cession ought to be made in part: as noted in D. 16.3.1 (Digest, “On Two Debtors”). Hence, in part the creditor has the right; in part the debtor, not by the nature of the obligation, which is not in acceptance, as in a pact, if it is interposed upon a good-faith contract: D. 2.14.1 § Item acceptilatio (Digest, On Pacts, “If one”). But if upon a stipulation, then the obligation is removed by the law itself: and there remains the question whether payment can be set off, but by the benefit of cession, to which it was not renounced nor is it customary to renounce, as noted in C. 8.40.1 (Code, On Fidejussors, in the beginning). And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a confession, or an agreement of a treasurer, or of a negotiorum gestor, prejudices the prince or the city.
body: The order of the facts is said to be as follows.

† Peter Bancherius agreed with the tax collectors of the commune of Milan to relieve them of the payments to be made to the treasurer of the same commune by the said tax collectors each month. He also lent to the aforementioned treasurer one thousand florins of gold. With the passage of time, it happened that the treasurer remained indebted to the said Bancherius for four thousand florins of gold, both on account of the principal sum and the profit tacitly agreed upon between them, because the number of years and months in which the sum had multiplied had elapsed. Then it occurred that, while the Lord Duke was in need of money, the masters of the revenues were content that the entire quantity necessary for the Lord, which was perhaps six thousand florins, be borrowed by the refrendarius, who is the administrator of the funds, from the aforementioned treasurer. For this reason, the treasurer had recourse to the said Bancherius. The Bancherius, having obtained one apodissa (written assurance) containing the fact that the refrendarius was content that the said Bancherius would serve the loan to the said treasurer for that quantity necessary for the Lord, secured by the revenue of the month of April then future as pledge, and having also received a confession made by the said treasurer to the tax collectors for the aforementioned month of April, finding himself creditor of the said treasurer for the aforementioned quantity of four thousand florins, counted out to the said treasurer only two thousand florins, retaining four thousand florins for his credit; although the said Bancherius received the entire revenue of the said month of April. And the said treasurer was removed from office before the event of the said month of April.

The tax farmer, after having collected the revenues or taxes, became the owner of what was collected, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *de publicanis*, law *cotem ferre*, section *qui maximos*. However, for the quantity for which he contracted the taxes, the revenues coming to him were obligated to the public treasury, according to the argument in the Digest, *de actionibus emptoris*, law *Iulianus*, section *offerri*, and law *si ventri*, section 1, Digest, *de privilegiis creditorum*. Moreover, all his goods were obligated until the public treasury was fully satisfied, as in the Digest, *de iure fisci*, law *aufertur*, section *fiscus*. And if the tax farmer deposited or consigned the said moneys to any money-changer, until the money was consumed, there is no doubt that it is obligated to the public treasury, because the obligation still persists in the goods of the tax farmer, as in the Digest, *de deposito*, law *licet*, section *rei depositae*. But if the money does not exist, but has been consumed by the money-changer, and the money-changer has become enriched, undoubtedly the money-changer is bound to the public treasury by a useful action, because the benefit succeeds in place of the thing, as in the Digest, *de usufructu*, law *qui pretio*; Digest, *de legatis* 2, law *imperator*, section *si*; Digest, *de pignoribus*, law *cum tabernam*.

Now, in the proposed case, I say that the money-changer, or Bancherius, became enriched from the fiscal revenues. And I prove this first with regard to the usuries which he paid to himself: because receiving usuries is indeed an odious profit, as in law 1, Code, *de conditione indebiti*. Therefore, he must restore them, not as usuries, but as the principal of the public treasury, as in the Digest, *de iure fisci*, law *deferre*, section *si*, and law *Titius*, unless the said Bancherius had lent under usuries by the will of the Lord, or the Lord had commanded the said Bancherius or the treasurer. For then the lender could retain what was paid on this cause, because he received it by the will of the Lord. And what proceeded from the lips of the Lord, the Lord ought not to make void; although borrowing at usury is a sin in the receiver, not in the one providing the usuries, as in the Extravagant, *de iureiurando*, chapter *debitores*. And it pertains to the honor of the Lord; indeed, it often pertains to utility to pay conventional usuries; otherwise, he would rarely find a lender, as noted in law 1, Digest, *de pignoribus*.

As for the principal of two thousand florins converted to the utility of the Lord, there is no doubt that the Lord is bound, and that it can be set off with him by the said Bancherius. The conclusion therefore is this: that the Lord is bound for the principal of two thousand florins which came to him, and for the usuries agreed upon for the said quantity. But for the other sum which Bancherius paid to the treasurer, the Lord is not bound; rather, it must be restored to the Lord, because Bancherius ought not to be enriched from his own frauds, as has been said, notwithstanding any confessions made in bad faith and extorted; because a manager of affairs cannot convert the money of the Lord to his own uses to the prejudice of the Lord, as in the Digest, *de negotiorum gestione*, law *qui usuras*, and Digest, *de manumis*, law *creditor*, section *Lucius*, at the end, and there is the case. Also, by confessions in which fraud and deceit are present, the condition of the Lord cannot be made worse; because this does not seem to be commanded, nor permitted, as in law *si pater*, Digest, *de privilegiis creditorum*; Digest, *mandati*, law *si mandauero*, section *si centum tibi*, which section, in the reason of its own, and makes well for our question. The confession of the treasurer also does not prejudice the prince or the city, as in the Digest, *si certum petatur*, law *ciuitas*, and *autem hoc ius porrectum*, Code, *de sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, and noted in law *si pupilli*, section 1, Digest, *de negotiorum gestione*, and by Innocentius in the Extravagant, *de deposito*, chapter *gravis*, and Digest, *de exercitoria*, law *Lucius*, and Digest, *de institutionibus*, law *cuicunque*, section *non omne*. And what is paid before the day, when the day arrives, is not repeated, as in the Digest, *de conditione indebiti*, law *sub conditione*. And it is true that the treasurer could not anticipate the time in paying, especially by falling into the time of the successor, as in the Digest, *mandati*, law *si mandauero tibi, vt pro me in diem fideiubeas*, where it is expressed. However, by the consumption or commingling of the money, the payment was reconciled, as in the Digest, *de solutionibus*, law *si alieni*; Digest, *si certum petatur*, law *nam et si sur.*, and law *si filius*, because the day which had ceased came and arrived. This reconciliation is made up to the quantity which the Lord owes; beyond that, it must be restored to the Lord, as in the Digest, *de conditione indebiti*, law *si procurator*, section *Celsus*. And it makes, Digest, *de statu liberorum*, law *Thais ancilla*, section *Titius Sticho*, and section *Stichus, et dammas*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute prohibiting alienations unless made in a certain form, and otherwise rendering them void by operation of law, applies to a legacy, an institution of an heir, or any other testamentary disposition.
body: The case is as follows: A certain citizen of the city of Lucca made his will; at that time, in that very city, the statute of the tenor set forth below was in force: and by that will he left certain immovable property to certain domestics and friends of his, who were not subject to the jurisdiction of the commune of Lucca, without having paid to the said commune of Lucca the Lucchese soldi per pound of which the aforementioned statute makes mention. He also left, in addition to the above-mentioned legacies, that two chapels should be established and endowed from the residue of his goods: one in the church of Saint Fredian of the aforementioned city of Pisa, without having paid, as above, to the said commune of Lucca, from the said aforementioned goods, 10 soldi per pound. It is now asked, following the aforementioned alienations in the manner described above, whether, due to the non-payment to the said commune of Lucca of the aforementioned 10 soldi per pound, the aforementioned immovable goods fell into the right and dominion of the said commune of Lucca by virtue of the said statute, or not. And if they fell into the right and dominion of the said commune: whether the commune itself can seize those goods as its own, notwithstanding the prescription of time. The form of the aforementioned statute is as follows: namely, that any citizen of the city and district of Lucca, who wishes to alienate in any manner any immovable thing to anyone not subject to the jurisdiction of the commune of Lucca, shall pay from the true estimation of the thing which he alienates, or transfers to another not subject to the jurisdiction of the aforementioned commune, 10 Lucchese soldi for each Lucchese pound. And all immovable things which are possessed, and shall be possessed in the future, by those subject to the jurisdiction of the commune of Lucca, which it should happen to be alienated in the future to those not subject, without payment of the aforementioned 10 Lucchese soldi for each pound, by the law itself from that time, as from now, shall fall, and be understood to have fallen, into the right and dominion of the commune of Lucca. And if anyone shall have committed fraud against this statute in any manner or by any device, especially from person to person, he is condemned to the true estimation of the thing, and nevertheless shall pay as above. Notaries, who knowingly shall deliver or write any instrument of any contract, by which anything should be done contrary to the aforementioned, or in fraud of the aforementioned in any manner, shall be punished in 10 Lucchese pounds, and the contract itself shall be null by the law itself. And if it should happen that a person who is not of the jurisdiction of the said commune of Lucca possesses from now on a thing which belonged to someone subject to the jurisdiction of the aforementioned commune, for full proof against this ordinance and statute, it shall be held as if the alienation had been made in its fraud. And the Podestà of Lucca, who now is, and shall be for times to come, is bound and ought to inquire, cognize, and condemn concerning the aforementioned, and each of them, when it comes to his knowledge; in which, and each of them, if he shall be negligent, he incurs the penalty of 500 Lucchese pounds. And this statute shall be derogatory of all statutes, provisions, and reformations, even if there were words in them of which special mention ought to be made. To all and each of which, insofar as they would oppose the above-mentioned, or otherwise dispose, it is entirely derogated. A certain Lucchese left in his will certain possessions to certain persons not subject [to the jurisdiction]. Also, from other goods he ordered that two chapels be made and endowed, and the statute is presupposed, as above, by which it is provided that any citizen of the city and district of Lucca who wishes to alienate in any manner any immovable thing to anyone not subject to the jurisdiction of the commune of Lucca, shall pay from the true estimation of the thing which he alienates, or transfers to another not subject to the jurisdiction of the aforementioned commune, 10 soldi for each pound; and if it should happen to be alienated without payment, by the law itself they shall fall, and be understood to have fallen, into the right and dominion of the commune of Lucca, and the contract shall be null by the law itself. It is asked, what is the law, and whether the commune can seize the possession by its own authority, notwithstanding the prescription of time. And for clarity, it must be considered.

First, whether a last will is included under the term alienation. And it seems indubitable that it is: because alienation is every act by which dominion is transferred, as in l. 1, C. de fundo dotali. But it is certain that dominion is transferred by a last will: as in l. 1 and 2, C. communia deleg. Moreover, this prohibition is general: as in C. de secun. nup., l. hac edictali, and l. si quis prioris, §. centum, where it says, "it will be seen as alienation of things, which is in the testament"; therefore, the statute claims a place for itself: because the words of statutes must be observed as they stand, as in ff. de exerci., l. 1, §. si is, qui nauem, and it is noted there. On the contrary, I see that either we will say that the testator alienated, and this does not seem true: because the day of the legacy does not pass while the testator is alive: as in C. de cadu. tol., l. unica, §. et cum triplici. Also, the legatee cannot accept unless the testator is dead. Also, and even after his death, if he repudiates the legacy, it is not said to be alienated: ff. si cer. pet., l. proinde. Or I would say that the heir alienated, and this does not seem true: because when the text of the statute says, "when he wished to alienate": certainly the heir does not alienate voluntarily, but out of necessity: as in ff. de leg. 2, l. vnum ex familia, in prin. Moreover, it seems absurd that the said statute should be understood in a last will, which ought to be free as regards the testator: as in C. de fac. san. eccl., l. 1, and gratuitous as regards the legatee: as in l. haeredem, ff. manda. So the words of the statute seem to determine this question, namely that the said statute has no place except in contracts: because the words of the statute say, "and the contract is null by the law itself": which clause declares the whole statute: ff. de iurisdi. om. iudi., l. si idem cum eodem, §. fi, and extra de appel., c. secundo requiris, C. de praed. cur., l. fi, lib. 10, and it is proved by such reason. For although the beginning of the law is general, or indefinite: because it says, "in whatever way": nevertheless, after the genus follows the restrictive species: because it adds, "and the contract etc."; hence the species restricts the genus: as in ff. de ver. sig., l. si cum fundum, ff. de leg. 2, l. legatorum, §. qui plures, and because "they acted" and "they contracted" do not pertain to testaments: as in ff. de verb. sig., l. verba gesserunt. As for that which is left to the chapels of the city of Lucca, there is less doubt, because the church is held in the place of a son: ff. de verb. obli., l. si ita quis, §. ea lege, but in the prohibition of alienation, the son is not included: as in l. j, C. de impo. lucra. descrip., lib. 10. Also, because the liberty of churches is not contained under a general word, nor does anything seem to be ordained against it: especially, because it would induce mortal sin. For he sins mortally who ordains anything in fraud of the liberty of the church: as in c. non minus, and c. aduersus, extra de immu. eccl. And these things I say, unless by custom and practice the said statute was extended even to last wills. For as it was practiced, so it must be observed, saving against the liberty of the church; and then whether prescription would run against immunity, and of what time, recourse must be had to the distinction of the doctors in l. vlt, C. de sac. san. eccle., and ff. de diuer. et tempo. praescrip., l. intra quatuor, and l. in omnibus, and by Dy. in c. 2, de reg. iur., lib. 6. For if indeed they are not incorporated into the fisc, as is the case here, since they were not denounced to the fisc, 20 years are required from the time when they were acquired by the fisc, or community, by municipal law; but if they had been denounced to the fisc by some promoter, prescription would be made in the space of four years, and the statute does not obstruct, because it disposes nothing about prescription, it is left to the disposition of the common law. Moreover, it must be observed that the said statute does not invalidate except contracts: and therefore not last wills, which are more favorable, as in ff. de reg. iur., l. in testamentis. But this reason seems to be opposed: because of things confiscated ipso facto, a testament cannot be confirmed: because they have gone out of the body of the inheritance, they have been transferred to the fisc before being transferred to the legatee. Which would be true, if this statute were interpreted in last wills, and prescription had not been made, if the times allowed. How, however, the statute was practiced and customarily understood, is not clear to me: therefore on this article I cannot advise, except as on a doubtful proposition, distinguishing: as above, and knowing that the opinion of Bartolus is, that on account of a tax not paid, which is similar to our case, in things not yet incorporated, prescription is made against the fisc in four years, as he notes in d. l. in omnibus, computing from the day when the fisc began to be able to act. But the former distinction pleases me more: because a tax does not pertain to immovable things: but to movable things, which are more easily prescribed; and that which is said, that things of the fisc are not usucapted, is true in incorporated things, in which usucaption ceases, taken strictly: as in instit. de usucapio, §. res fisci, and I add that which I note in ff. de iure fisci, l. 1, an bona. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether it is lawful to construct a bridge in a river to the prejudice of those having the right of ferrying, and conversely: and what applies to one holding regalia from the prince.
body: The case is as follows, Most Serene Prince. The King of the Romans erected and created the dignity of a county in Palemo, with its boundaries and powers. He wished all these to be contained within that dignity; then, there investing and granting the said county in fief to the Illustrious and Learned Master Antonio, Count of Polenta, together with all the royal riparian rights of the river Tanagro, and other riparian rights of the said river, as is clearly gathered from his imperial privileges. And since long before and after those privileges, the said Lord Antonio had held and maintained a port, and had caused a ferry to be operated on the river Tanagro from one side to the other, both through the middle of Murro and through the middle of Iordo, and the territory of the same castles, through which people, carts, horses, and any other animals with merchandise passed continuously and without interruption. Provided, however, that whenever, due to great floods, the force of the river broke the port, it was relocated to lower places, as is customary in such cases; and sometimes it ceased operation due to wars and dangers to the people crossing there. Nevertheless, when convenience arose and necessity demanded, it was repaired and restored to its former state. Recently, however, when the same Lord Antonio had caused the port to be established in the usual manner, and consequently a stake had been placed and fixed, and other devices necessary in such matters had been set up from both banks of the river, behold, certain men of Claraschi, with armed force and by their own authority, uprooted the stake fixed on the bank of the river beyond the Tanagro, on the side towards Murro.

† It is therefore asked whether it is lawful for the said Lord Antonio to have the said stake driven or fixed, and to hold the port freely with the stake fixed in that bank, by having it there continuously without the condition of the commune and the men of Clarice, and of the consuls of another person, by virtue of the aforementioned customs and privileges; or whether not. And so that the proposed question may be more clearly elucidated, it is argued in the negative: and it appears at first sight that the right to prohibit the port, in such a manner as to have it in that river, belongs to the commune and the men of Clarice, since that river is public and navigable; and the commune has lawfully occupied the right of collecting tolls and of portaging those passing through their port on that river at a place upstream, for this reason: because it has been exacted for so long a time that there is no memory of its beginning. And thus it is held as if by established law or privilege: as is stated extra de verb. sig. c. super quibusdam. §. praeterea, with the concordances there. From which it follows that they seem to have the right to prohibit, on the ground that the condition of the one who has preempted should be considered the better: as is usually said in a similar case regarding a lower mill, which can be prohibited in a public river by the owner of the upper mill, who lawfully preempted, as in leg. et not. C. de servit. et aqua. l. si manifeste. de serv. rust. praed. l. Imperatores. and de eden. l. si quis ex argentariis. si initium de flumine. and ne quid in flumine publico. l. 1. §. sunt qui putant. Again, and for this reason it seems to act against the law: because that port is said to be held not only in the river, but also suspended by a new building made on the bank of the river, which is beyond the Tanagro, and borders on the lands of another territory: since the ownership of the banks belongs to those whose lands they adjoin: but the use is public: as ff. de fluminibus. l. 1. §. ripa. and in l. penult. de rerum divisione. l. ripa. and inst. eod. tit. §. riparum quoque. and ff. de acquirendis rerum dominis. l. penult. §. si. But it is certain that a usufructuary, and much less a user, in a property of which he has the use, would prohibit the making of a new building: as ff. de usufructu. l. novum. and l. usufructuarius. ergo et c. arg. and de acquirendis rebus dominis. l. qui in littore. and l. sequenti. Moreover, if anyone had built on another’s bank, it would not only be ordered to be destroyed by a judge: but also the owner could destroy it by his own authority, being in possession of the said bank, argu. ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. qui vitem. §. qui ad ianuam. and ad. l. aquil. l. quemadmodum. §. magistratus. and leg. et no. ff. de operis novi nuntiatione. l. de pupillo. §. meminisse. Therefore, for two reasons it seems that the right of portaging, as proposed, can be prohibited by the commune of Clarice.

On the contrary, it appears that the Lord Antonio cannot be prohibited by the commune and the men of Clarice from having the port, as is asserted, in the river Tanagro. For among the royal prerogatives of supreme princes, the prince, among other things, are numbered not only navigable rivers, but also ports and riparian rights: as in the book of fiefs, tit. quae sint regalia, c. unico. And they are sometimes in the domain of the same prince, as says Bartolus in his little book on alluvions, in the treatise on the bed. Which is clear, because the laws permit only the prince to dispose of these: as d. l. quominus. de fluminibus. ff. de verbis oblig. l. continuus. §. cum quis. de contrahenda empt. et vend. l. Celsus. in principio. Therefore, since all the royal prerogatives were granted by imperial privileges to Lord Antonio in those parts, and what is more, specifically in the said river Tanagro, mention also being made of the riparian right, it is undoubtedly established that the faculty of portaging belongs to him by his own right: and therefore he cannot be prohibited by the right of preemption, as is read and held literally in d. l. Imperator. in the letter there, unless by his own right, etc. and there the gloss explains "by his own right" as meaning "conceded by him who had the right to grant, namely the prince or the senate," according to what is read and held in the aforementioned l. quominus. de fluminibus. And by this the first argument is not an obstacle: for it speaks when the lower party wishes to be admitted without the prince’s concession to the damage of the upper party, who had long since preempted: in which case, in equal cause, the condition of the occupier is better. Moreover, the lower party is then prohibited by the upper party by the right of preemption only when it inflicts damage by asserting the use of the upper party. Otherwise, when it merely diminishes the advantage, perhaps: because so many people do not go to the upper mill: as d. l. 1. §. sunt qui putant. And fully read and noted by Bartolus in d. l. quominus.

Therefore, the commune of Clarice complains improperly, since its bridge is not impeded by the act of toll collection, nor by those passing to its port: but only its advantage and utility are diminished. And from these also the last allegation is removed, which proceeds only against one who uses solely the public law of nations, or as if by that law a user were to build something new on the bank of a river, which is not permitted because it does not condone, and alters the form of the place against the will of the other. But otherwise in the proposed question, where the riparian right of the said river Tanagro pertains to Lord Antonio by his own right from imperial concession: the prince does not seem to build on another’s bank, than we do, etc. as C. de iure vetusto enucleando. l. 2. §. sed cum omnia. Especially since it is for a cause, namely a port. ar. ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. l. 2. And therefore, by the custom of the commune of Clarice, continued for so long a time that there is no memory of its beginning, it acquired for itself the right of portaging in its own territory, and not beyond. Therefore, also from this head, it vainly claims for itself the right to prohibit in another territory, namely the county of Polenta of the aforementioned Lord Antonio: it is asked, what is the law. And briefly, from the allegations for the second part, which rightly conclude, and remove the allegations to the contrary: I say and counsel that Lord Antonio, Count of Polenta, has the right to have and hold the port, as proposed, in the river Tanagro from both sides of the river: and that he cannot be prohibited by the men and the commune of Clarice: and in testimony of the premises. I, Christopher of Castiglione, doctor of laws, have subscribed, and have ordered my seal to be impressed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A usurer who, after making a will with the required caution, again practiced usury: such a will is invalid, even for pious causes. See also numbers 7 and 8.
2. Which usurers are to be considered heretics, and which are not.
3. The will of a manifest usurer is invalid if the caution has not been provided; otherwise, if he is a concealed usurer, whom it is scarcely possible to convict of usurious wickedness.
4. If a usurer publicly practiced usury with P., but secretly with Ioan., and P. restored the usury, but Ioan. did not: his will, without the caution being provided, is invalid.
5. The concealed quality of infamy arising from other thefts aggravates the remaining thefts.
6. A manifest usurer, who duly gave caution and made a will: if, after the recovery of his health, he received usuries promised to him and given voluntarily, his will is broken.
7. If a father, by right of institution, leaves 5 to his son and another 5 to his daughter, with a certain hospital instituted as universal heir; and he ordered that the said 5 left to the daughter should go to a certain society of the Virgin Mary: whether, if the testator dies and the hospital repudiates, and the son or daughter come in as intestate heirs, and if the daughter dies, whether the said 5 are due to the society of the Virgin Mary.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A certain usurer, wishing to make a will, first executed a security instrument, then made a will, finally engaged in usury, and died without having altered his will. The question is whether one can succeed under such a will, or whether legacies are due, or whether at least a claim can be made for pious causes, or not. And here I shall discuss certain matters concerning the wills of usurers, and I shall resolve the questions proposed. It must be known, however, that some are

† Usurers are heretics, namely those who practice usury by lending, believing that usury is not a sin; because, namely, they do not believe the Gospel law, they are heretics: as in c. 1, § sane, Extra de usuris, in the Clementines. And the wills of these persons are invalid, because they are excommunicated by canon law as heretics: as in C. de haereticis, auth. credentes. Some usurers are not, however, heretics: because they believe the Gospel, that usury is a sin; yet, led by the blindness of avarice, they practice usury. And then they are either manifest usurers or hidden ones: if indeed they are manifest:

† And the wills of these persons are not valid unless they make due provision in due form. c. Quamquam, § Nullus, Extra, De usuris, lib. 6. But if they are concealed, so that they can scarcely be convicted of usurious wickedness, their wills are valid; because they are not prohibited from making a will by any civil or canon law. ff. De probationibus, l. Ab ea parte; and the aforementioned § Nullus, by contrary reasoning.

But here a doubt arises: suppose that a usurer practiced usury publicly with Peter, but secretly with John; he restored the usury to Peter, but neither restored it to John nor gave security for it: whether his will is valid. And it seems that it is valid, because by satisfying Peter he ceases to be a manifest usurer, since sin is forgiven if what was taken is restored: as is stated in the aforementioned §. nullus, in the words “satisfecerint” [they have satisfied]. The vice being purged, his capacity to make a will seems to be restored. C. de nuptiis, l. imperialis. And by the payment of what is owed, infamy is abolished. ff. de procuratoribus, l. si reus paratus. I say the contrary, for this man neither fully satisfied nor gave security: for one cannot repent in part; but it is necessary that he be made clean entirely, because salvation is indivisible. Hence, the text, assuming that he is a manifest usurer, requires security to be given for usury in the definite sense, that is, for both manifest usury, there where it says “de usuris” [for usury]. For this indefinite term is equivalent to a universal one. ff. de pigneraticia actione, l. si necessarias, §. si annua. And it is similar in the case of one who made public gain, for infamy is perpetual. ff. de ritu nuptiarum, l. palam. And in the case of a notorious thief, who is to be hanged on the gallows, even on account of one theft that is not notorious but secret.

† Quality. The quality of being infamous, arising from other thefts, aggravates subsequent thefts. Digest, On Penalties, Law "Capitalium," Section "Famosos." And it infects like leprosy. Furthermore, it is doubted: suppose that

A manifest usurer made a solemn caution and testified; but after the testament he recovered, and exacted or received the usuries previously promised to him, voluntarily paid by the debtor: whether the testament is broken. And truly, that it is not: because this happened by a certain consequence of the prior contract. D. de minoribus, l. 3, § scio. I say the contrary: because it does not benefit him who has cautioned, if he afterwards acts against his caution; for he ought not to derive advantage from that which he undertook to impugn, as in the rule of law. And see, Extr. de usuris, c. Quia frustra; D. de minoribus, l. Auxilium, in fine; C. de usuris, l. Acceptam, § Si.

Having premised the above, I come to the question asked, namely: whether the testament of a usurer is valid if, after giving a caution and making a testament, he again engaged in usury. And if indeed he lent money publicly afterwards, it is certain that the testament is not valid; because, even assuming that he had not previously practiced usury, he would become intestable by virtue of the most recent usurious contract. This is held by Paulus de Leaz in cap. 1, de usuris, in the Clementines. Since it is required in a testator that he be legally capable of making a testament at the time of making the testament and at the time of death, and this person, at the time of his death, is intestable due to his own fault, therefore the testament is not valid, as is read and noted in l. 1, §. exigit, de legatis praestandis.

But if, after the testament, he lent money secretly and not publicly, this is the question of the eminent doctor, Lord Federicus of Siena, in his work, consilium 7, which begins: “The question is such, that a usurer, etc.” He determines that the testament is broken, because the defect does not appear to be purged on account of the crime being quasi-continuous; from which it is also presumed that penance is lacking, and conversely, that it is simulated. See the argument in cap. accusatus, §. 1, de haereticis, lib. 6, de sententia excommunicationis; cap. sacro, eodem titulo; cap. eos, lib. 6. Thus, an illness that has relapsed is not said to be cured, as is noted in the Digest, locata conducto, l. maritus; nor is one said to have fully separated who has returned, as in the Digest, de divortio, l. 3, in the first response; for he has not amended himself who has not ceased to sin again, Codex, de episcopis et clericis audiendis, l. 3, in fine. For indulgence is not granted except to those who have been corrected, Codex, de sententiis passis, l. in quaestione testamenti.

Moreover, the capacity to make a testament is restored by the force of the caution, which must be integral and complete, not partial, but with regard to the future. This caution is not only incomplete, but null. Digest, de verbis obligatioibus, l. cum stipulamur, and l. si a colono. And even if it expressly spoke of restoring future usuries, it would be invalid and inept. For example: “I promise to pay those extorted and those to be extorted.” For it appears that I do not have a right intention, nor am I penitent; and therefore such a caution would not suffice for the capacity to make a testament, see the argument in Digest, de legibus, l. servo alieno, ita, §. ineptas. Although therefore a secret usurious defect does not of itself invalidate the testament, nevertheless, by the addition of a public defect, or a certain veil due to the caution, which is now uncovered by a contrary act, [the testament is invalid].

It must be said that the will is not valid, even for pious causes: because the person is incapacitated: and an incapacitated person cannot make a will for pious causes: as is noted in l. 1, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, especially when the incapacity arises from canon law: and thus the solution to the questions proposed is clear, that the institution of an heir or legacies for pious causes is not valid.

† Subsequently, it is asked: A certain Peter left to his son by way of institution 5 [units of currency], and to his daughter another 5, and instituted a certain hospital as heir. And he ordered that the 5 left to the daughter should, after the daughter’s death, go to the Society of the Virgin Mary. The testator having died, the hospital repudiated the inheritance. The son, or the daughter, entered upon it intestate. Then the daughter died. It is asked whether the said Society ought to have the said 5. And the answer is no. C. de fideiuss. l. eam, quam; and l. si nemo, de reg. iur.

To the contrary it seems, for if there is a codicillary clause in the will, they are due by the law of codicils; if there is no codicillary clause there, they are due under the edict “If anyone omits the cause of the will.” Because when the son and daughter entered upon the will by the right of accrual, as noted by the learned in Auth. nouissi., de inoff. testam., they preferred to succeed intestate. Moreover, pious causes are favored, where entry upon the inheritance is not required; as touched upon in d. l. eam, quam, in the gloss. But here one might answer that the body of the Society is profane, not pious, since it is a college of laymen.

Solution: If the testator was capable of making a will, I say that those 5 are due; otherwise, not. And thus I resolve this question: it is necessary, however, that the testator’s debts be paid first; as C. de legat. l. si universae. The legitime must also be preserved for the heirs of this daughter, if the goods, after deducting the debts, were insufficient for the full payment of these 5. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A paternal uncle acting as guardian cannot claim a salary for services rendered to the wards, nor conversely. And number 5.
2. What a *saccus* is, and in how many ways it is understood.
3. A *veges* of wine is sometimes used to include wine; sometimes for a simple measure.
4. What a *tessera* is.
casus: CASE. It is asked of your immense learning that you deign to give your counsel on doubtful instruments, with the laws and arguments bearing on them. First: whether a tutor, to whom no salary was fixed by the judge at the beginning of the accepted guardianship, nor did the tutor seek to have one fixed for the administration of the guardianship, can, upon the termination of the guardianship, claim a salary. And it is presupposed that this tutor was the uncle of the wards. Second, it is presupposed that the father of the wards, during his life up to the time of his death, was a merchant of dyed cloths, and kept a shop and a stall, and engaged in other trades; now the aforementioned tutor, brother of the said merchant, draws up an inventory, in which he described the goods of the wards; and among other items which appear in the said inventory are these, namely: “Also four sacks of wheat. Also one sack of hemp, in which were six linen sheets for the household. Also thirty sacks of flax here. Also one small bag of wool.” Now on behalf of the wards it is said that the aforementioned thirty small bags of flax should be understood to have been filled with flax in the ordinary sense; that the one small bag of wool named above was filled with wool; and on behalf of the tutor and his heirs it is said that it should be understood that the said thirty small bags were made of flax material, and not filled; and similarly they say of the small bag of wool. Third, it is asked on behalf of the wards, since they lived with their tutor for a period of time, namely one for 25 years, and the other ward for 22 years, and served their said tutor, their uncle, in grooming horses, and many other services in the house, and accompanying him both on foot and on horseback, both within the city and without: whether they can claim for their wages for the said services thus rendered, at least from the fourteenth year onwards, something, and what from the heirs of the said tutor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it must be said that he cannot demand a salary, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Tutoribus*, § *Penultimus*. However, when he departs for the affairs of the ward, he must go at the ward’s expense. Digest, *Mandati*, law *Idemque*, § *Idem Labeo*, and there noted.

† On the second point, it must be said that a sack is sometimes used to denote the material, sometimes the contents. D. 47.2.14 (Qui saccum); D. 16.3.1.1 (Si pecuniam in sacculo); D. 7.1.13.1 (Adhuc), in the word "in sacculo"; D. 18.1.35 (Qui fundum), § Fundi, in the words "ex sacco saccularii"; and concerning a sack and a bag, see the note in D. 42.8.1 (Si), at the end.

Similarly, I observe that the term *veges vini* is sometimes used to encompass wine in general, and sometimes to denote a simple measure. D. de vino leg. l. 2; D. de contrahenda emptione l. comprehensum; and l. quod saepe, § in his.

Similarly, regarding a token of wheat. D. de iudiciis, l. sed et si susceperint; D. de legato 2, l. Titia Seio tesseram. How, therefore, is the sack of flax understood? I answer: I will interpret against the tutor, because he made the inventory obscurely, and the oath of the adversary will be upheld. L. tutor, qui repertorium, in principio; D. de administratione tutorum. And because the common usage of speech is in this sense, as in D. de vino legato, l. si cui vero. But because it is credible, and that which arises from the quality of the person, D. de legato 2, l. cum pater, § immense.

† On the third question, it must be said that nothing can be claimed in the name of salary: because among such persons services ought to be gratuitous. This is established by the Digest, *mandatum*, l. *salarium*, and l. 1, in fine, *de variis et extraordinariis cognitionibus*; and by the Extravagant Decretals. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father cannot be compelled to pay from his own property the legitime portion on account of his son’s condemnation.
2. A son does not have a legitime while his father is alive.
3. Whether a condemned son may claim his mother’s dowry, in which the father holds the usufruct.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether, if a son is condemned for homicide, the fiscus can demand from the father the son’s legitima. And the truth is that it cannot: because while the father is alive, the son has no legitima, as noted in the Authenticum de haereditatibus et falsis, § si quis autem non implens, in the glossa ordinaria, and fully by Cynus and Gulielmus and others in l. si qua poena, ff. de his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris.
† For this son is considered dead while the father is alive, and therefore he has no legitimate share. L. 1. in fin. ff. de contrahenda tutela.

† What regarding the dowry of a predeceased mother? I say that the father has the usufruct as long as he lives, and therefore the fisc cannot seize the goods to the prejudice of the father’s usufruct. D. 50.17.3 § si filius (Quod quisque iuris). I, Baldus. On Successions Intestate. Chapter 46.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is included under the term "uncle" (patruus): and what if the term "great" is added.
2. Whether an uncle (patruus) excludes the mother.
3. When there is doubt regarding the meaning of a law or a person, in case of doubt it is to be decided in favor of the mother.
casus: CASE. Moreover, we establish and ordain that if anyone dies intestate, if indeed the father, mother, grandfather, grandmother, great-grandfather, great-grandmother, or other ascendants succeed such a descendant, male descendants from him through the male line shall succeed. Female descendants, however, if they are dowered, shall not succeed, in the presence of surviving male descendants from such an intestate descendant through the male line, or any of them. If, however, they are not dowered, they shall be dowered from the goods of whose inheritance it is in question, at the discretion of two more suitable blood relatives; or they shall succeed in the portion of the inheritance competent to them by law; and this if in the election of the said surviving males. If, however, there remain female descendants, or male descendants from females, or one together, all dowered and undowered shall succeed together, and their sons or grandsons according to the form of law; provided that their dowries, or those in whose place they succeed, be collated, if from him there was a son or daughter, grandson or granddaughter, great-grandson or great-granddaughter, or other descending person, who or which died intestate, and who or which had no descendants, the ascendants through the male line shall succeed together with the brothers of the deceased, or the sons of brothers who are male, if they survive, to the exclusion of sisters. If, however, it was a brother or sister who or which died intestate, with no descendants or ascendants capable of succeeding supervening, as if male brothers and male sons of brothers jointly related on both sides succeed, if they exist, and if they do not exist, male consanguine brothers and male sons of said consanguine brothers shall succeed, however; and if they do not survive, uncles and male sons of uncles shall succeed, to the exclusion of sisters, and the mother, and the maternal grandfather, and the paternal grandmother, and all other relatives. If such a deceased person has no surviving descendants, or ascendants, or aforesaid collaterals, as stated, other relatives shall succeed according to the form of the common law, declaring that with respect to the aforesaid, a woman is understood to be dowered whether the dowry was paid for her, or promised, or assigned to her in a testament, or otherwise by legitimate will by any of the aforesaid. A certain person died intestate, with his mother, uterine brothers, aunt, or great-uncle surviving him. It is asked, which of the aforesaid shall succeed by virtue of the said statute.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The term "patruus" (paternal uncle), used simply, includes that paternal uncle who is the prior and more prominent uncle in succession; but when the term "magnus" (great) is added, there is a certain distinction. That which is stated without distinction should not be understood with distinction. Since the text says, "a patruus is the brother of the father," as in the Institutes, De gradibus, § Patruis, therefore the great paternal uncle is not included.

† Therefore, according to this, the great-uncle does not exclude the mother; and consequently, all the more so, the son of the great-uncle; for he who is removed first is removed later, as in C. de natu. lib. l. si. For if we extend this term, then the great-great-uncle would exclude the mother, and furthermore, their sons: which is nothing more absurd. When the syllable "n" is added to a word, it alters its meaning. And what is said simply does not seem to be said of that which is altered, changed, or transformed, as in ff. de lega. 3. l. hoc legatum, and l. seruus legatus, §. si ex officio. Moreover, we must extend the succession of the mother, not restrict it, according to no. insti. de succ. agna. §. si, and insti. de bono. pos. §. adhuc. Also, a tacit understanding is not admitted against the mother, as in C. de impu. et aliis. l. precibus. Hence, when

It is doubtful whether the law or the man is to be understood; in case of doubt, judgment should be rendered in favor of the mother, even though the statute says "uncle" (patrui). It is not understood to multiply degrees, but persons. For one can have many uncles; hence this is indefinite in number, but not in degrees. The more they ascend by transference, the more they are removed from the line, and the less they pertain, and the force of succession is weakened; because the effect of those who are more distant is more remote both in law and in nature, as in Auth. Defuncto.

On the contrary, it seems that the intention of the statute is broader, and not stricter. For if it comprehends the son of the uncle, who is in the fourth degree, therefore by the name "uncle" it understood up to the fourth degree according to civil law, on account of the identity of degree; on account of the identity of reason, on account of the indefiniteness of the expression, and on account of the plurality of the speech; because it says "uncles" (patrui). D. de leg. praestan. l. 1. and §. generaliter. D. de testam. milit. l. in fraudem. §. si.

Solution. "Uncle" (patruus) in common speech is said to be a kinsman on the father's side, as in Auth. de haer. abintest. §. per consequens. And therefore, if according to the common speech of that place such great uncles are called kinsmen on the father's side, it excludes the mother; because the sense of the statute is the sense of the citizens, and the common understanding, which we must follow; otherwise we do not extend it. D. sol. matr. l. si vero. §. et viro. And this is also required by the statute there, and the preceding one cited, for the persons excluding the mother are fixed, and as it were named. If therefore it appears, and is taken commonly, it is limited according to the common usage; nor is the statute said to be extended, but declared. If this does not appear, then recourse must be had to civil law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. That the heir may be subjected to the assignment of assets on account of the deceased's debt, and what and how many requirements are necessary therefor.
2. What and how many requirements are necessary for the issuance of a second decree.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having viewed the said point, and examined the records, both old and new proceedings: first it must be known,

† That the necessary heir suffers from the debt of the deceased, once the debt is established, and once it is established who the heir is, and once his contumacy is established: I say first as a principal point, that it is a debt contracted by the deceased, for from the person of the deceased the heir measures his right. C. de haereditariis actionibus, l. pro haerede; ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. 2, §. ex his; ff. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. apud Iulianum; and in Auth. de exhibendis rebus, §. si vero. I also say as a second principal point, that he who is sued becomes the heir; for if he is not the heir, he does not suffer seizure, especially in his own goods, as C. de transactionibus, l. nec intentio; and noted in ff. soluto matrimonio, l. si cum dotem, §. transgrediamur. Nevertheless, if summoned as heir he does not respond, he suffers this first decree by reason of contumacy. Hence it is that even this minor, who is not defended, suffers the first decree. And an absent person, on account of public interest, [is treated as contumacious], as stated in l. apud Iulianum; and C. de restitutione militum, l. ignorare; and l. si finita, §. si forte, de damno infecto. And it is said that he also does not appear who does not appear legitimately; because a good man does not consider him to have appeared who appeared defectively, as noted in l. secunda, quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, according to Bartolus. It suffices, because in this first decree the debt is alleged, and the oath against calumny is required to be proven; because it generates little prejudice, and by comparison with the refund of expenses and satisfaction it is reduced in a manner to a certain kind of threat, and it ought to be revoked. C. de bonis auctoritate iudicis possidendis, Authentica ei qui iurat. The third principal point is that the judge be certain of true or presumed contumacy: of which he must be certified by the records of the case. For this is of the substance of the order and procedure. ff. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. haec autem, §. primo; ff. iudicium solutum, l. 3, in fine; C. de iudicibus, l. properandum, §. si autem res.

† As to the second decree, it is required that the judge be not only informed of the debt by the oath of the plaintiff, but that he be certain of the substance of the debt, and of this with sure faith: because a full prejudice is at issue, and a thing is to be given in satisfaction according to the measure of the debt: as in the laws cited. For it must be certain to him that the thing which is given in satisfaction belongs to the debtor, if it is possessed by the debtor, as C. ne vxor pro marito, l. ob maritorum; C. de priuileg. fisci, l. etiam; de re iudic., l. admo., §. si super; and ff. de noxa, l. generaliter; ff. de acquirenda possessio, I. Pomponius, §. si iussu. And undoubtedly, if the acceptance of the inheritance had been proved here, and all things had been solemnly acted against the heir: because this proceeding has its origin upon notice. Nevertheless, there is doubt, because it is not certain that the inheritance of Nerius, in whose person the debt is claimed, was accepted. The doubt therefore stands on this: whether, if he is truly an heir, yet this was not clear to the judge, except by a presumption from commonly occurring events: because it commonly happens that, when a brother dies without children, the other brother possesses all things, and thus acts as heir, as ff. de acquirenda haereditate, l. duo fratres. Whether he is bound according to the decree, or whether it is void by the law itself: because it is not certain that the obligation was also derived through succession, nor that he himself is the debtor. For he who denies that he is an heir is not compelled to suffer hereditary actions. ff. de interrogatio actio, l. prima. And it must be said that the decree is then void when it is obtained by fraud from the praetor, by alleging a false cause: not when the cause is true. ff. de fideicommissa liber, l. cum vero, §. subuenitur; l. prima, §. haec verba. ne vis fiat ei, signo est allegatum, quod est haeres: and it is not then obtained by fraud from the praetor: otherwise it is not called obtained by fraud, but undiscussed: because the sentence agrees with the truth: although the vigor of judgments requires proof. C. de edendo, l. qui accusare. But this would be a long discussion, and therefore I pass to other matters, and it is certain that by the second decree, execution having been made, there is a position of fact. ff. de acquirenda possessio, l. qui vniuersas, §. item cum praetor. In which the person sent in must be protected, until the judge revokes it. And l. si quis missum, ne vis fiat ei; and ff. si mulier ventris nomine, l. prima, §. primo. Nor is it permitted for the contumacious party to resist the praetor by his own authority, but he must appear before him, and set forth specifically the causes by which he is strangled, as l. prima, C. de praedij curia, libro 10. And the same is true for he who claims a defense from the defendant, as in the said §. si autem reus. And therefore, as to proving possession, it suffices to prove the sending in by the second decree. And it is noted that although the second decree does not bind: nevertheless, because the said lady, although she refuted it, and since it is to the prejudice of her and her successors, the agreement must be stood by, ff. de iu, l. sed et si possessori, §. 1. And it is read and noted in l. 2, C. comm. vtriusque iudi. From which it is concluded that the person sent in is to be restored to possession according to the form of his petition, against any illicit detainer: because the said lady, although she had a title passing through many hands, as the said l. si quis missum. And thus I, Baldus, say.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a layman condemned by a bishop may again be sued before a secular judge, or whether the exception of res iudicata stands in the way.
2. Whether a secular judge is bound to adhere to the procedure of an ecclesiastical judge in criminal matters.
3. Add in the sixth part of the consilium beginning "in the aforementioned matters two things are to be considered."
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. An inquiry was made by the bishop against a layman concerning the union with a certain nun. The layman appeared and denied the offense; and because it was not proven, this layman was definitively absolved by the bishop.

It is asked whether a secular judge may proceed anew against him and punish him if found guilty, or whether the exception of res judicata stands in the way. And it seems that the exception of res judicata stands in the way, first by the text and the ordinary gloss in c. ult. de exceptionibus, lib. 6; secondly by reason: because one ought not to inquire repeatedly about the same delict of the same person. L. licet, §. possumus, ff. de nautis, cauponibus, stabulariis; from various laws, as ff. de accusationibus, l. senatus censuit; and noted by Innocentius, extra de collationibus, c. si; de aetate et qualitate, c. accipimus; de electione, c. cum dilectus. Moreover, the bishop is greater than the [secular] power, as noted ff. de postulando, l. ex ea. Therefore, an inferior judge cannot pronounce contrary to that which the superior has pronounced. ff. de minoribus, l. minor autem magistratus. Moreover, the sentence of the bishop ought not to be made a mockery. ff. de iudicibus, l. si praetor; and noted in c. si saepius, de restitutione in integrum; ff. de postulando, in l. fin. Moreover, in sacrilege the bishop has principal jurisdiction, as extra de foro competenti, c. cum sit generale. Moreover, a layman cannot take cognizance of the said nun, since she is spiritual, extra de ordine cognitionis, cap. tuam; but he ought to refer the matter to the bishop; but the bishop ought not henceforth to interpose his parts, because he has already absolved; therefore the way of secular judgment is precluded, as in Authent. de clericis, apud quos episcopus, in fine; C. ubi senatus vel clarius, l. quotiens; noted ff. de regulis iuris, l. nemo qui condemnare. But if he had been condemned by the bishop and had made satisfaction, he could not be further punished, even if the penalty of the temporal forum and that of the ecclesiastical forum were different; because since any penalty tends to vengeance, it suffices that one penalty has been exacted, as ff. de iniuriis, l. quod senatus. And an acquittal is equivalent to a condemnation when satisfaction has been made. ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. si quis cum totum, §. plane; and noted ff. ad legem Aquiliam, l. ex morte; and ff. de iure patronatus, l. diuus Vespasianus, in fine.

To the contrary it seems: because the bishop cannot take away from the secular judge his jurisdiction, nor command him not to use his right; as noted by Innocentius in c. dilecto, de sententia excommunicationis; and the same for all judges. ff. de accusationibus, l. si cui, §. cum sacrilegium; and noted by Archidamus, 11. quaestio, capitulo de persona. Moreover, it is expressly stated that cognizance of this crime cannot be taken away from the secular judge by the bishop alone, in Authent. de manumissionibus principum, §. si vero canonicum, col. 3.

† And elsewhere it is expressly stated that in criminal cases the secular judge is not bound by the procedure of the ecclesiastical judge; but he himself ought to examine the crime, in Auth. de sanctis episcopis, § si vero crimen, column 8, on this point by Guillaume, ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. magistratibus. Likewise, the constitution of the bishop does not restrict the secular judge, as noted in the chapter Dispendiosam, de iudicibus, in the Clementines. Therefore, neither does his sentence: since every sentence depends on jurisdiction. For this, what is noted by Bartolus in l. Divus, ff. de custodia reorum, is most apt, and there he determines the question literally, although the example which he placed there concerning heresy is rejected: because that crime is reserved solely to the church for judging: because it is against the Catholic faith, and pertains only to the forum of the church. Hence, whatever the church binds, is bound; and whomsoever it absolves, is absolved. And the same applies to all matters pertaining solely to the forum of the church, concerning which see note 11, q. 1, in the Summa. I therefore say that the bishop, by absolving the offender, cannot prejudice or impede the secular treasury of the Empire or of the city; and consequently, he cannot impede the criminal procedure of the secular judge. For everyone is greater in his own forum, as noted, ff. de manumissionibus, l. apud eum. This is the truth according to civil law; but according to canon law, it seems sufficiently probable to say that regarding a delict committed against a cleric or a monk, he can cognize it and fully absolve, according to the said last chapter, de exceptionibus, lib. 6. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The new law concerning the compelling of debtors. Heading.
body: In the name of the Lord. That creditors may easily obtain the debt owed to them, we establish by this present statute, which we wish to be called the new law, valid in perpetuity, that if a public instrument appears regarding the debt, the judge shall order, or cause to be ordered through a bailiff, that the said debtor pay the said debt within three days under a penalty of 30 pounds.
