And if he does not pay, from that time forth the said debtor shall be seized in rem and in personam at the will of the creditor for the payment of the debt: and he shall thereafter be admitted to no defense against payment, except that of payment, or discharge, or extension of the term, which are proved only by a public instrument, or by an instrument of debt cancelled, etc. We will, moreover, that the aforementioned mode of proceeding or execution shall not have place for non-subjects of the commune of Gubbio against subjects of the same commune. Cionus, son of Francis, a citizen of Gubbio, promised to restore to the monastery of Saint Clare of the Gubbio diocese 30 florins, which he confessed to have had and received from the said nuns in deposit, submitting himself, the said Cionus, for the observance and keeping of the aforementioned terms, to real and personal coercion, and to the censure of any statute and municipal law of any place, from which a more facile and expeditious collection of the aforementioned sums could be made, and which are more favorable to the said creditor: and he renounced every exception competent to him, and swore to observe the aforementioned terms and not to contravene them, etc. Now the syndic of the said monastery seeks that execution of the said instrument be made to him according to the form of the said statute of the new law, asserting that the said statute is also more favorable to him, and that execution is more expeditious thereby. Now it is asked whether the disposition of the said statute claims place in the said instrument.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Although a statute cannot abrogate the right of the Church, which it holds by the common law or by agreements, it could nevertheless provide that the benefit of the statute shall not avail churches.
2. It cannot be agreed by contract that the contract shall have ready execution.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Although a statute cannot deprive churches of their right, which they hold by common law or by agreements, it may nevertheless validly provide that the benefit of the statute shall not avail churches or clerics, as noted by the doctors in Authen. cassa. And therefore it seems that, since churches and clerics are not subject by law, and without penalty and prejudice to the enactors, what can be understood generally should be understood generally, as in l. de precio, with its entire brocardic subject matter. To this effect is what is noted by Iac. But. in Authen. statuimus, C. de episc. et cler., in l. noua. Nor does he have the benefit of the agreement, which agreement refers to the statute and must be interpreted according to the statute. Hence, one submitting to the statute is understood to submit in the case included in the statute, not in another case. ff. de lib. leg., l. Aurelius, § testamento. And thus I, Baldus, say.

† That a contract should have ready execution cannot be achieved by agreement, because one cannot renounce the order of judicial proceedings, as stated in the Authenticum offerantur, Codex, de litis contestatione; and in the chapter de causis, de officio delegati; and in the first chapter, de libellis oblatis. Therefore, it must be done by law. But a law, whose provision is limited, does not exceed its boundaries. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the confession of a testator ordering the restitution of usury is proved, and whether from it he is judged to be a usurer, and whether the judge can compel the heir to make restitution, and whether he is bound in the forum of conscience.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. I advise the heir to acknowledge good faith and not to condemn his conscience, which I myself would observe if the matter concerned me; but whether a judge of the judicial forum can order this of the heir, or if he acts with the community, condemn him, is a great question, and there are opinions. Petrus says the heir is to be condemned, even if the testator revokes [the will]. Others say the heir is to be condemned only if the testator persisted in this will; otherwise, if he revoked it. Now let us see the reasons for and against. And for the opposing party, that which Cynus reports, C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter, in 12. quaestiones, there reasons are made. And first, the general reason of justice makes for it, for sin is not remitted unless what was taken is restored, as in c. peccatum, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Secondly, the reason of civil law makes for it, for this proven confession induces [proof], as I will show, therefore, etc. That it induces proof is clear from several reasons. The first is this: the favor of the soul is not less than the favor of liberation; as C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. sancimus. But by the favor of liberation, a confession made between absent parties is valid, as noted, ff. de interrogationibus, actio, l. 1, even if it is made in nullum voluntas [without formal will], as noted, ff. de libertate legatis, l. non solum, §. liberationis verba. To the same effect is what is noted, C. de pactis, l. postquam liti. Therefore, much more strongly is such a confession valid in favor of the soul. Moreover, this confession tends to free the soul from sin, therefore such confession must be adhered to. Moreover, the testator confesses that something exists, even lawfully with him, therefore it is to be extorted from the heir as ill-gotten gain. ff. de calumniis, l. in haeredem. Moreover, when someone confesses that he has sinned, from such confession proof is made, or judgment is induced. ff. de aedilitio edicto, l. quaero, §. fin. From which, with other supporting evidence, an oath can at least be deferred to the adversary in default of proof; as ff. de iureiurando, l. si duo patroni, in the first, by Gulielmus. But there is no doubt in him who confesses himself criminal. Moreover, this confession made before so many witnesses and a notary proves him to be a manifest usurer, as noted in c. quanquam, de usuris, lib. sexto. Hence, the legacy which he makes is not valid by the law of legacy; but it is valid as a certain mandate granted after death. ff. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. Meuius. Or as a denunciation, rather more truly a restitution granted after death, which can also be done by a manifest usurer. Moreover, although in contracts between absent parties a messenger or letter is required, ff. de deposito, l. publia, in fin., yet in last wills this is not required, as ff. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. donatis. Moreover, it is spiritual in hatred of moneylenders, that domestic writing made in the absence of the party, as in c. 1, de usu, in Clementina. Moreover, if the fisc and the community are said to be present everywhere, as noted, C. de quadriperti praescriptione, l. 1. Moreover, although a pact is a common act of two and cannot be made with an absent party to be valid by the law of pact, as ff. de pactis, l. idem in duobus, yet confession is the act of the confessor alone, and it seems it can be made, even between absent parties, as extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. cum dilectus, and ff. de negotiorum gestione, l. Pompo, and l. Nesennius Apolinarius. ff. de pollicitationibus, pactum sit etiam testamentum. ff. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. surdo. By which reasons it seems clearly concluded that the said confession is proven, induces [proof], and must be adhered to in every way. To the contrary, it is proven by several very strong reasons. And first, because a confession made in a testament does not prove that a contract preceded between living persons, unless it is sworn. ff. de legatis 3, l. cum quis decedens, §. codicillis. And in Auth. de iureiurando a moribundis praestando, in rubro, et nigro. But this confession was not sworn, therefore it does not prove. Secondly thus: if this confession proved, the legacy would not be valid; because a legacy cannot be made to a creditor, unless someone takes away his benefit. ff. de legatis 1, l. si creditori. But this is false: because rather the legacy is valid. ff. de donationibus praeter legem, per totum. And C. de falsis causis ad legem, l. 1, and l. si non designata. And ff. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. fidei tuae. Moreover, the law is express, that from such confession an open cause is not proven. ff. de libertate legatis, l. Aurelio, §. fi. Nor does any favor of the soul make here, since no one accepted that confession for the absent party, as noted, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud. The arguments to the contrary do not stand: because they speak when the confession emanated by mode. In this opinion, the conclusion resides with Bartolus in d. §. codicillis. For either this confession proves the debt, and the legacy is not valid; or it does not prove, and then the legacy is valid, but the law says the legacy is valid: therefore the debt is not proven. This opinion of Bartolus presupposes that by this confession a manifest usurer is not proven, for if a manifest usurer were proven, therefore the legacy is null. But Federicus de Senis in his consilia sensed that such confession makes certain, and proves him a manifest usurer, at least by canonical equity, which, where the salvation of souls is concerned, does not permit disputing from the tips of civil law, but from the rigor of civil law. The opinion of Bartolus is true: to which also Cynus applauds, although he does not dare to determine against Petrus de Bellapertis. Yet I do not deny that this confession makes a great indication, even by strict civil law. I, Baldus. See in the following consilium.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether it is lawful for one who has fallen to accept money from a rebel or an enemy of the fatherland, and from whom it may be given.
body: For Banne de Luce of Panzano, for so laudable a deed as it was to have Thomasinus, his cousin, who was a rebel of the commune of Florence, an enemy and hostile to the republic, and hateful to God and the world, and placed in the depths of crimes and sins, be consumed by the sword of divine vengeance, and hoping that for so great a fruit and benefit conferred upon his city, the commune of Florence would not be ungrateful towards him: money having been ordered for him by the office of the bailiff, received on this matter from the chamberlain by their mandate: whether he can retain said money, having obtained it for a just cause, and need not return it. He has the foundation of the common law on his side. For it is established that letters [of authority] are given to administrators of the republic for just causes, such as that one was, indeed most just, and rightly to be embraced, to expend public and fiscal money, and decrees made, which accord with the utility of the republic, are such that what is paid on that account, or what is paid without cause, or not for cause, or as undue, is not subject to repetition by the commune itself, according to those things which are usually held. D. de iust. et iur. l. 1; D. de const. pec. §. plane; D. de relig. et sumpt. fun. l. minime; and l. ap. §. plane; D. quod vi, aut clam; C. de prec. l. et de serv. qui pro prim. liber. metu; D. de decr. ab ord. fac. l. 3; and the note of Asermanus, l. Corn. with many similar cases. With what trepidation, then, does this John live, who submitted his own flesh to the cross for the redemption of the world, and brought salvation to the whole city, lest he be required to return so small a reward, which it pleased the princes to grant to him as a surplus? Certainly this would be very blameworthy, inequitable, and unjust: as I have premised, his deed was supremely laudable. Therefore, if this were attempted to be done, it would be very reprehensible, and thus I estimate it should not be attended to, and that he can keep it. Having this foundation, let us see what could be said against this opinion and contrary to it in law. Certainly the opposition is weak. Someone might say: "For we are not in the field of the common law, but of the laws and reforms of the commune of Florence: according to which two thousand [florins] are promised to be paid: and if they are paid, the authority and efficacy of their power must be inquired into and examined. And since one must not depart from the words and form of them, let us therefore see if the disposition of said reforms supports him or offends him. And it would seem to expressly act against him? Both because the rule provided against such rebels, and their prosecution, and extermination, and the faculty of expending etc., manifestly excludes those convicted of them; yet, because those convicted are imposed with the necessity of prosecuting, otherwise they themselves become rebels. Therefore, they do not go further, but act in view of their own right, and compelled, to avoid penalty. Also, because they are rewarded with a special prize; and because general laws are determined by prior ones, whence the power of expending, although largely granted in the month of September etc., must be restricted to those not prohibited. Also, because when a special and general prize, or benefit, is granted for the same cause, etc., as in l. alimenta, §. basilicæ; and l. libertum, with its material. Certainly if these were true, it would not be expedient to labor: it would have been badly promised, you would have received it badly, you would have to return it: but these are dreams on account of several things. First, because John did not receive [the money] by virtue of that promise, which renders the convicted ineligible and threatens them with penalties etc., but by another subsequent one, which accepts no person. And because that whole foundation is removed, and departed from, and a division introduced, and the conjunction removed, so that John was, and is, eligible to receive; and the eight lords petitioning to dispose, to whom the sum, powerful, and ample bailiff of the commune of Florence on this matter, and concerning it, with free faculty of expending at their pleasure, which the other eight hitherto had on war for the extermination of, and care for, said rebels and enemies of the commune of Florence. Therefore John has for himself, beyond the common law, of which I care not, the most ample bailiff of those who provided for him of the prize of two thousand; and their decrees conforming, and one was called, therefore from said matter of petition. There is only one thing to see in that which can be opposed to him, namely provisions, from which John strives to have a determined, express, singular, and taxed cause with proof added, not to another directly or indirectly: namely, for the extermination, and prosecution of rebels. Therefore they have to watch in exterminating, prosecuting, and destroying to be able [to deal with] the aforementioned enemies and rebels, and on their occasion to provide and expedite etc. The bailiff of exacting is given: therefore those are private. It is established, however, that it is one thing to be able to give, or expend, that something be done: another to give for remuneration already done. One looks to a future cause, the other to power, but at the time of the promise of giving John two thousand. Thomasinus was already killed and exterminated: in whose person prosecution or extermination did not fall: because these no longer dominated him; how then, by what authority, since it is another case from those comprehended, than the bailiff: because it remunerates a deed done, not provides if it be done later, and the reason of separated things is separated, and a case omitted does not accept the reason of the common law, and it is not ours to extend the law: and especially such as disposes of salary and public pecuniary grants, and because one may not depart from the words of the law and constitutions. And the law, which indulges something for the future, forbids it for the past. Such determinate bailiffs in a cause for the future, not faculty and remuneration of the past, would at first sight seem to be to his detriment: not because he is prohibited or convicted, as some say. Certainly to this I answer, counselor, to whom it will be easy, having seen the provisions sent, although long and poorly ordered, but for some declaration of this passage it seems to me, although at present much occupied, that from the words and sentence of the promise such remuneration in the cause, and for the cause, and on the occasion of so great a host and enemy, can be tolerated: although preceding the time of said liberation, yet following the time of the concession of the bailiff, and after said concession, and remuneration on this matter according to [custom]. Now, if the occasion had already been done, remunerating the occasion can be comprehended under the words against the will. In extermination, and for extermination: I understand [it] to be done, or to be done. Also, because such provision concerns future cases, for while they remunerate this one, they incite others to similar operations, which is established to be permitted. Moreover, this cause is not from such, but that, or at least not entirely of the same cause, and of the same nature, and well of the same presumed pleasure. Also, the expression is similar, and it is to be believed that the commune of Florence disposed, and granted in mandate, if it had considered. And because the disposition proceeds by the same cause, therefore in one case disposed, and in another by the same reason seem to be disposed. And because laws do not consist in words, but in the reason of the roots. And it is said that what is expended in extermination, sufficiently includes that they can remunerate the exterminator, and even if the extermination had preceded: and especially because it does not seem that what was preordained to be done first was done later; and because the eight lords themselves thought their decree to be aided by these provisions, therefore it should not be rendered null, or annulled, as if they had provided for an alien cause. But nevertheless, one should not stand on the effect, as I said above. From these things thus ordinarily touched, and without laws, because I know that I speak to a wise man, to whom the laws present themselves, therefore I conclude for John, that he need not return that light reward, worthy of a greater [reward] for so great a deed, considering the peril, weighed by natural equity, against which he fought, and with the fruit rising again, and such intention of the rebel: which if otherwise, by his misfortune, should happen, I estimate that John himself would have made himself a rebel of the commune: because he could not return it, since in truth he did not receive it, although he confessed to having had the money. He would have to go forth naked and exiled. Let him therefore be recommended to you, and spare the writer: because the pen drew more than due, and I care little for the form of words."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who kills an enemy and foe of the republic is to be punished or rewarded.
2. Who may reward the slayer of an enemy of the republic.
3. What the clause “as it shall seem good to them” imports.
4. What the word “for” denotes.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† He who, inflamed by the fervor of public charity for the protection of his natural fatherland, kills the most bloody enemy of that same fatherland, is not called a fratricide, but is termed one fighting for the fatherland, performing a divine work full of praise; for indeed it is fitting to slaughter hostile beasts, and a sacrifice is made to the Creator while the universal creation is benefited, the treasury is freed from infamy, and the fatherland finds rest; nor does he act against the bond of blood: because, since he is an enemy, as stated in D. de captivis et post liminium reversis, l. amissione, § qui deficiunt; D. ad legem Corneli de sicariis, l. 3, § transfugas; and D. de re militari, l. proditores, in fine, kinship does not retain him, but abhors him. For once the status is consummated, the rights of kinship are consumed, as stated in D. de bonis possessis, l. edicto; D. de contrahenda tutela, l. 1, in fine; D. de rebus dubiis, l. si cognatis; D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § et quid si tamen. He is also severed from the republic, because he is a putrid limb, as stated in D. de religione, l. minime, against which one must oppose the sword as against a robber, C. quando licet sine iudice vindicare, l. 1 and 2. Therefore, he is deemed worthy of a reward; for the reward of excellent labor should be called such, as stated in D. de donationibus, l. si pater. But this would contradict what is noted by Bartolus in D. de adulteriis, l. si adulterium cum incestuoso, § liberto. However, there is a difference between an enemy guilty of the crime of lèse-majesté, as in this case, and another enemy who is an outlaw: because the latter offends principally a private person, and secondarily the republic. It is of this enemy, against whom the city is hostile, but who is not hostile to the city itself, that Bartolus speaks.

But it must be considered only whether those who gave the reward could have given it. And it seems that they could not: because it is permitted only to him who holds the principate to call upon the public treasury, as in C. de quadriennali praescriptione, l. Omnes; and l. Bene a Zenone, D. quod vi aut clam, l. Prohibere, § Plane; C. de prebenda salaria, l. 1, lib. 10; ad hoc de pactis, l. Pactum curatoris; C. de transactione, l. Praeses; D. de pactis, l. Contra iuris civilis regulas, § Fin.; C. de sacrosancta ecclesia, l. Iubemus; D. de donationibus, l. Filius. For each one can reward another from his own property, but by no means from another’s, D. qui et a quibus, l. Semper; D. si quid in fraudem patris, l. Unius libertus. Indeed, it is a species of theft to bestow gifts from another’s property without the owner’s consent, as in D. de furtis, l. Si pignore, § 1. For it is not regarded as legitimate administration, because it strips the owner, D. pro emptore, l. Qui fundum, § Si tutor. And the limits of the office of a diligent guardian must be observed, C. de negotiorum gestione, l. Tutori. And all these things are true, unless he has a mandate from the owner, d. l. Filius; or from the law, as noted in D. de poenis, l. Item magnum; D. quod cuiusque universitatis, l. Nulli. And therefore this question turns on whether these reward-givers had a mandate for this purpose, or not, or the power to reward. The words of the law say, “for pursuing, and concerning extermination, and for accomplishing the aforementioned, and any of the aforementioned.” All of which do not apply to the body already examined: because he has already suffered the last of the terrible punishments, and cannot suffer it again: because the dead do not die again. For we live here with only one life, as with a single substantial form existing in us, as noted in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Qui duos, § 1. Therefore, words which confer something to be exterminated in the future do not include what has already been done, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, and l. Si iam facta. Moreover, by death he ceased to be an enemy, although his memory is condemned. Furthermore, this man does not deserve a reward: because he acted compelled by fear of punishment, not voluntarily, D. ad legem Silianam, l. Si quis in gravi, § Caeterum. Furthermore, he seems infamous, who in this way suffers himself to be honored, as noted in D. de postulando, l. 1, § Bestias. But an infamous person does not deserve a reward, but the indignation of grave men, D. si quis omiserit causam testamenti. For even if he killed according to law, he did not do so as a legitimate person, as noted in C. quod metus causa, l. Accusationis, in the glossa ordinaria. Moreover, there is no virtue which is tarnished by the baseness of money, l. Idem est, § Si tibi, D. de conditione ob turpem causam, and there noted. It is doubtful with what mind he did it: whether deliberately for the republic, or out of special hatred and private motive, D. de exceptionibus debiti, l. Apud Celsum. If, therefore, you say he could have been rewarded, show me the law, my lord. Moreover, in the discretion given, those named from this family were expressly excluded as hateful: hence the power of bestowing gifts, which has been specially removed, cannot be extended to them, D. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, § Lucius Titius damna; and D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. Testamento Centurio. Moreover, discretion given within certain limits is of strict law, and cannot be extended, D. de negotiorum gestione. Moreover, even if discretion is given broadly, it is not to be interpreted loosely: but must be restricted with moderation, D. de mandato, l. Creditor, § Lucius; D. de legatis 2, l. Cum filius, § Pater cum filia. But notwithstanding these things,

† because the words of the law state, as it shall seem expedient to them for the aforementioned, and for each of the aforementioned. And they judge that it is expedient for the republic, as an example for all the aforementioned, that, as in C. de delatoribus, l. fin. lib. 10, to exterminate living rebels, they have the right to reward men by way of example, so that others may be given the spirit and the occasion to do similar things. It seems sufficiently supportable that the said reward may be granted, because the word,

† "pro" denotes not only the final cause, but also the efficient cause, as noted by the Archdeacon in Question 1, Chapter *Ordinationes*. And it denotes not only the end, but the order towards the end. Digest, *De adulteriis*, Law *Nec in ea*, § *Sin*. Moreover, he who has taken up arms perpetually for the republic ought not to be worn down by arms all the days of his life, nor to live always in poverty. And because nobility, with the consent of the illustrious city of Florence, suggests this, as stated in the aforementioned Law *Filius*, in the verse *Quid ergo* and in the verse *Nonnunquam*, to this effect. Digest, *De evictione*, Law *Lucius*. Digest, *De captivis*, Law *Mulier in opus salinarium*. And if those who enacted this statute had considered it more clearly, they would have expressed it, I believe, in words. Digest, *De pactis*, Law *Tale pactum*, § *Fin*. For it is more just that he be rewarded than that he be compelled to this. Digest, *De re militari*, Law *Non omnes*, § *Si*. It is more just that this labor be rewarded than that it be sold. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What the inventory of an heir requires.
2. Whether an inventory, in the preparation of which some are cited and others are not, prejudices those not cited.
3. Whether executors are to be cited in the preparation of an inventory.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Inventory

† Many things are required of the heir, all of which the legislator introduced so that heirs might not commit any malice in concealing or suppressing hereditary assets, especially movable ones, which are easily hidden; as in the Authentica *De haeredibus et falsis*, in § *Sancimus*, column 1. Among these solemnities is the citation of those who may be harmed by the concealment of assets, such as creditors or legatees, unless the estate is small.

Let us therefore suppose that some have been summoned and others not; does the inventory prejudice those who have been summoned? It seems that it does not, because when something is lacking in the formalities, the whole is vitiated. D. de regulis iuris, l. et simul; D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si praetor; C. de auctoritate praestanda, l. fin. Moreover, it is understood that the judge’s decree is contained in the inventory; and a decree and a sentence cannot be valid in part and invalid in another part. D. familiae erciscundae, l. in hoc iudicio. The contrary is the truth: because a summons always prejudices the person summoned, but does not prejudice those not summoned. D. si cui plus quam per legem Falcidiam, l. 1, § cum dicitur; D. de iudiciis, l. non incerto. For as regards those summoned, everything has been done with due formality. C. si propter publicam poenam, l. si deserta; D. de re iudicata, l. de uno quoque; D. de minoribus, l. 2, § fin. Furthermore, it is asked,

Whether executors are to be summoned. And it seems that they are not: because they are neither legatees nor creditors. D. 34.2.1 (Si quis Titio). To the contrary it seems, because they conduct the affairs of the legatees, especially of uncertain ones, such as the poor. C. 1.3.28 (Nulli) and C. 1.3.30 (Si quis ad declinandam). Therefore, they are to be summoned. D. 3.5.32 (Sancimus) in Auth. Quosdam pro eis agentes. C. 3.34.1 (Cum quae res agit haeredum). D. 33.9.3 (De alimentis legatis). Nevertheless, even if the poor or the church are not summoned, they are never executed against, except up to the strength of the hereditary assets, which are in reality, not in verification: as noted by the learned doctors in C. 10.43.1 (Quanquam) De usucapione, lib. 6. Furthermore, it is required that third-party creditors be added in place of the absent ones. Therefore, if the document states that they were present in place of the absent creditors, it should be understood that they were also present in place of the legatees. It seems that this is not so: because they are set forth as distinct. The contrary can be said, for after the inheritance is accepted, legatees are creditors of the heir. D. 35.2.1 (Pater filium facit). D. 50.17.1 (Si certum petatur). The document does not say in place of the testator’s creditor, but in place of creditors simply. To this point, D. 5.2.1 (Si quis intentione ambigua). Furthermore, a general proclamation is required, that is, so that it prejudices uncertain persons; nevertheless, it is valid as regards certain persons who are summoned, as in C. 6.30.1 (Si quis se ab haereditate abstineat). Auth. Si omnes. C. 4.18.1 (Humilis). According to Innocent III, X. 2.4.1 (Qui matrimonium accusant). X. 2.26.1 (Cum in tua). Furthermore, it is required that the messenger first report that he has summoned, and that the judge interpose a decree, as in D. 7.2.1.1 (Hoc autem) Quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur. And D. 35.1.1 (Multum) De conditionibus et demonstrationibus. Certainly, no law says that a decree is required, although it is required that the summary inventory be made before the judge. C. 5.31.1 (Qui admissi ad bonorum possessionem). C. 6.30.1 (Omnium). And even assuming that a decree is demanded as an accessory complement and conclusion of the inventory, nevertheless it suffices that the protocol shows the proper report: because we ought principally to give faith to the protocol, as in Auth. De tabulis §. Finali. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Saxoferrato, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The agreements standing, by virtue of which the castle is subject to the city, the castle is not bound to appoint syndics to denounce crimes to the vicar of the city, since cognizance of crimes is to be had in the said city.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

Three matters occur to be considered, namely: the old pacts made during the time of Pope Martin, according to which the commune of Selano is undoubtedly not bound to provide syndics to denounce crimes to the vicar of the city of Spoleto; and the reason is: because according to those pacts, such crimes ought to be cognized in the castle of Selano, and not in the castle of Spoleto, considering the first cause, for that castle has by itself power and a distinct territory: to that power alone did the cognition pertain, and if a determination were made before another, it would be made before an incompetent judge, which could not be done, nor ought anyone to be drawn to what is forbidden and incongruous from cases, as in C. de iurisd. om. iud. l. in criminali. Two matters occur to be considered: the new pacts made during the time of Lord Gomerius, and even assuming as constant that the commune of Spoleto had jurisdiction in the four cases there expressed, namely in homicide, theft, robbery, and violation of women. Nevertheless, even in those cases, the commune of Selano is not bound to provide syndics to report crimes established by the vicar of the city of Spoleto, and the reason is: because although denunciation comes in consequence of the jurisdiction of cognizing and punishing crimes, and also precedes and excites the office of the inquiring judge, as in ff. de custo. reorum. l. diuus. and l. 1. C. de vena. and C. de cura. l. ea qui dem., nevertheless, because in a stipulation nothing comes unless that which is expressed by words, as in ff. de verbo. oblig. l. quicquid astringendae, or that which is tacitly understood by both parties, l. cum quid. ff. si cer. pet. But this is not even expressed by words, but rather the contrary was provided by the contracting parties: because it was expressly acted and agreed between the parties that the commune of Selano was subject to no real or personal burden. ff. de muner. et hono. l. mundorum igitur defensores. and by accident it could be real. For if the commune of Selano were bound to provide syndics, and if it did not provide them, it could be mulcted. ff. si quis ius diui. non ob. l. 1. Also, because the right of jurisdiction and their customary immunity were expressly reserved to the castle of Selano in the latest pacts, which reservation is valid and must be adhered to in every way, not only because the right is ancient, but because it is the latest, C. de pact. l. pacta nouissima. ff. si quis cautio. l. enim. in prin. ff. fami. haer. l. item Labeo. cum si. ex quib. From which it is truly and evidently concluded that the commune of the castle of Selano is not bound by law to provide the aforementioned syndics. Thirdly, custom must be considered, and because it has not otherwise been customary to provide them, the said commune of Selano, relying on such custom, is in no way bound to provide them: because things which have always had a certain custom should not be changed, as in ff. de legibus. l. minime. ff. de aedil. edicto. l. quod si nolit. §. qui assidua. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required for the acquisition of possession.
2. Permission may be granted to an absent person, through a messenger and even without a messenger, to take possession by his own authority.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case of Peter de Missa, there is no lack of right: for truly, according to God and conscience, he has a right on behalf of the ladies for whom he acted, namely, to one and a half parts out of five parts. But it must be seen whether proof is lacking to him, or whether proof made to the contrary operates against him.

† And it appears that nothing has been proven on behalf of Peter, neither his possession nor the spoliation committed by the adversary. And this is shown thus: it requires the intent and the physical control of the person apprehending it, or of another on his behalf. D. 41, 2, l. 3, in principio. It is required that if another was then in possession, that he delivered, or as it were delivered, the possession, or that the praetor solemnly constituted him as possessor. D. 41, 2, l. clam possidere; and l. si ex stipulatione. C. 4, 2, l. meminerint. But here it does not appear that Blaxius ever delivered this possession, even assuming that he sent a messenger saying that Peter should send someone to receive the possession. D. 41, 2, l. qui absenti, § si quis. Moreover, since Blaxius always possessed, he cannot be called a spoliator. For he who continues the old possession is not called an invader. C. 2, 18, c. licet causam. Moreover, by the adversary, continuous possession in solidum has been demanded and proven; because the witnesses of Blaxius say that he possessed in solidum, therefore another did not possess. C. 3, 32, c. cum ecclesia sutrina. D. 13, 6, l. si ut certo, § si duobus vehiculum. D. 43, 17, l. si duo. D. 41, 2, l. 3, § ex contrario. Moreover, Peter ought to have proven possession of a certain time, namely the time of the novitatis, namely of Francis, but the witnesses regarding the time say that they do not know or do not remember, therefore they do not prove that time, which is the foundation of the petition, and therefore the defendant ought to be absolved. D. 43, 1, l. 1, § interdictum autem hoc nullum. Moreover, if Peter had possessed at the time of the said novitatis, he ought to be considered a clandestine or violent possessor, and by the restitutory interdict he would be compelled to restore the possession to Blaxius as the older possessor, and therefore he acts in bad faith; because he demands what he ought to restore in bad faith if he possessed, since here the interdict unde vi is not claimed, but a condition from municipal provision, as is fully read and noted. D. 5, 2, l. si de vi. On the contrary, it is argued thus: it is certain that Blaxius sent a messenger to Peter.

† Moreover, it is certain that permission to take possession by one’s own authority can be granted to an absent person, whether through a messenger or even without a messenger. D. 32.1.1 (Titia cum testamento), § 1. Since, therefore, Peter took possession through his sons, the infant became a possessor. Furthermore, although Blaxius could not transfer possession between absent parties, he could nevertheless declare his intention, which he confessed, namely that he held the property for Peter. For it is apparent that from that time onward Blaxius did not hold it for himself, as stated in D. 41.2.1 (si ancillam) [under the title “pro suo”]. Moreover, possession is lost by intention alone. D. 41.1.1 (non quemadmodum) [under the title “de acquisitione possessionis”]. But Blaxius did not wish to possess in his own right; therefore, he lost possession. Furthermore, the gloss states that he who confesses to possessing for another, if he continues to hold it, or even at the time when he confesses, makes that other person the possessor for whom he admits holding it, as noted in D. 6.1.1 (si ab emptione) [under the title “de pactis”]. Moreover, this Blaxius, by thus detaining the property, managed Peter’s affairs; hence, upon subsequent ratification, Peter acquires the right. D. 3.5.1 (si ego) [under the title “de negotiis gestis”]; D. 3.3.1 (per procuratorem), § non semper [under the title “de procuratoribus”]. And if it is said that the time of the novation is not proven, I answer that, on the contrary, it is excellently proven by the arguments of the jurists: because a friend, that is, Blaxius, or a negotiorum gestor, could not interrupt possession. C. 7.31.1 (fi) [under the title “de acquisitione possessionis”]; C. 7.33.1 (male agitur) [under the title “de praescriptione triginta annorum”]. And if he did intervene, he did so fraudulently, and it does not benefit him. D. 50.17.1 (parem) [under the title “de regulis iuris”]. Furthermore, possession of the mind, which is more noble and more powerful, is presumed to be continuous, as noted in c. sine possessione, through Dynus, and c. 1 [under the title “de servis fugitivis”], l. 1, § cum si. From these points, I conclude in favor of Peter, because he is in the right and has the truth and a friendly reason on his side. And I say the same, especially considering the discretion granted to the captain’s lord solely for the purpose of following the truth and equity of the case, as noted by Bartolus in D. 39.5.1 (filius) [under the title “de donationibus”]. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is meant by the exception of simulation.
2. When an instrument is said to be simulated.
3. A debtor is not considered suspect where a new cause has arisen after the contract.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

It must be known that the exception of simulation is said to occur when a promise has been made in a simulated manner for a cause that is not true or not just. Thus speaks the entire title *Plus valere quod agitur*.

But when a debt is truly due on account of one cause, even if another cause is added in a new instrument by means of an intervening stipulation, action may be brought on the basis of that stipulation itself, and the instrument is not said to be simulated, as in C. si certum pet. l. ex pretio. Even if one person first contracted and a new person transferred that obligation onto himself, this constitutes novation, or not, as in C. de transa. l. nec intentio. Hence, in our case, a distinction must be made: whether a debt previously existed in the person of someone, in which case the instrument is not simulated; or whether it did not previously exist, in which case the instrument is said to be unjust or is doubtful, and then a true confession is presumed, as in ff. deposi. l. publica, in fin., and fully noted by Bartolus in ff. si cert. pet. l. singularia. On another point, it must be said that

† A debtor is not said to be suspect where a new cause has arisen after the contract. As stated in the Digest, *De privilegiis creditorum*, law *Creditores*. It supports what is noted by Dynus in the law *Si constante*, in the beginning, in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*. Regarding the matter of the first point, it is noted in the Digest, *De postulando*, law *Sub specie*. As for what is said, that express mention must be made of such novation in the instrument, as in the Code, *De novatione*, law *Fin.*, I say that it is one thing to treat of novation, another thing to treat of the substance or cause of the second obligation; for whenever the cause itself is substantial and true, the obligation holds; but both are presumed to be satisfied by one payment, and therefore, if the truth of the cause appears from the acts, the substance of the latest obligation necessarily follows.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a defamatory confession proves.
2. A sister's son is not a blood relative of his maternal uncle.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If we consider the confession of the accused, it does not prove against him by necessity: for he may have uttered these words by defaming his own progeny, not by defaming another’s; nevertheless, from this it is sufficiently presumed that he is a heretic in defaming another, as in l. item quid. §. conuinctum, ff. de iureiur. For sometimes one openly, sometimes deceitfully, utters injurious words. C. de postul. l. quisquis. But it must be examined whether there is proof, which the statute requires to exist, and consequently requires to be proven. And certainly the statute is sufficiently obscure: for first it speaks of one who insults by imputing an injury to himself and his ancestors, and this is not our case. Second, it speaks of one who insults by imputing an injury which a carnal brother or nephew from a carnal brother received, and this is not our case. Third, it speaks of one who insults by imputing an injury to relatives up to the second degree. And this pertains to our question: for it seems to be a chapter of amplifications and general; yet in that part where it speaks of homicide, it seems to speak of homicide inflicted by an enemy.

Fourthly, he speaks of one who improperly attributes death either to a judge or otherwise justly, and this chapter is that upon which the inquisition is founded. And because the son of a sister, speaking properly, is not a blood relative of his maternal uncle, and this term in penal matters ought to be understood in a sound manner: since this has not been proven, an acquittal ought to be rendered. Furthermore, the necessary and evident connection of the persons, which ought to be clearly proven in cases of maleficium, where it gives existence to the maleficium, has not been proven; and especially the marriage has not been proven, which could have been clearly proven, although the case is different regarding filiation as to the father. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Lucius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, by a statute of the laity, it may be provided that the benefit of the statute shall not avail churches or clerics.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Although the statute

† the lay authority cannot deprive the churches of their own right which they hold by the common law, or by agreements; nevertheless, it may well dispose of matters in such a way that the benefit of the statute does not avail churches or clerics, as the noted doctors state in the Authentica *Cassa iudex videtur*, where it is held that since churches and clerics are not subject [to the lay power], they do not enjoy the benefit of the said statute; because, since there are many kinds of non-subjects, the words “by right” and “without prejudice and penalty to the enactors” can be understood generally, and therefore must be understood generally. See *L. De praedio*, with its entire brocardic material. To this effect is what is noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in the Authentica *Statuimus*, Codex, *De episcopis et clericis*, in the new text. Nor do they have the benefit of the agreement, because the agreement refers to the statute and must be interpreted according to the statute.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a fideicommissary substitution made to several persons has effect in the person of each individual, or whether it is required that it exist in the person of all of them.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† A fideicommissary substitution is sometimes made simply to several persons; and then it is deemed to have been made individually to each one. Hence, there is no doubt that the plural wording doubles the singular meaning, and the substitution has its place and force, regardless in whose person the condition exists, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Lucius, §. Gayo. Sometimes it is made with a universal and comprehensive sign and condition; and then either we speak according to the literal sense of the words: and it is required that the condition exist in the person of all; because the truth of the universal order requires the truth of the particulars by the force of speech. D. de rebus dubiis, l. si is, qui, and §. vtrum. Or we speak according to the interpretation of the law: and then it suffices that the condition exist in the person of the last survivor as regards his portion. D. ad Trebellianam, l. haeredes mei, §. cum ita. But Bartolus limits this, saying that this is true only when there is no such person who, by the presumed will of the deceased, excludes the substitute. This, however, can be known from natural charity. Argument in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. quidam recte. If, therefore, a closer relative in degree exists, and the substitute is more remote, the substitute is excluded; but if the substitute is equal, because there is no order among equals, nor does degree arise from an equal, the substitute is not excluded, as also in §. cum ita. Therefore, in our case, the collateral nephews coming from the other side exclude the substitute, according to Bartolus. Here consider: when a universal sign is appended to the substitution, either directly, and it must exist in all persons in order to preserve the right of legitimate inheritance. C. de inofficioso testamento et aliis substitutionibus, l. pen. Or fideicommissarily, and then either someone succeeds according to the judgment of the testator, for example, if one of the instituted heirs survives, or one of the first substitutes, and the final substitution does not take place, as noted in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. pater filium, §. si duobus. Or the survivor does not come according to the judgment of the testator, and does not seem to exclude the substitute, as in §. cum ita. But certainly, the sons placed in the condition seem to succeed sufficiently according to the wish of the testator, even though nothing is truly left to them, as in D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius. And this is true if such excluding successors succeed to the last survivor; otherwise, neither natural equity nor the presumed will of the testator dictates that they exclude the substitute, they who will have nothing. Hence, if the last survivor instituted another heir and passed over these, the substitute seems to be called; because one who does not succeed is considered as nothing, as noted in D. de legatis primo, l. filii, §. cum quis. However, Dynus reproaches that gloss and holds another, which is in D. ad Trebellianam, l. ex facto, §. si. But I answer: Dynus speaks when children exclude by the force of the words; the reason is when they exclude by tacit interpretation of the law. Argument in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi, in fine. And then, therefore, they exclude the substitute when they are preferred to him in succeeding; otherwise not, argument in D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. fin., and the said l. Lucius, in fine. For when the final cause of the exclusion of the substitute ceases, the exclusion ought to cease, as in D. de contrahenda tutela, l. si post mortem, §. liberi, and D. ad Trebellianam, l. 2, §. si mater. For there preference exists, etc., unless it is said that something else is in the provision of the law, which ought to provide for all cases. But the testator often omits unforeseen cases. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the aforementioned opinion and distinction is more friendly to equity. Cynus, however, according to Petrus in l. 1, C. de conditionibus insertis, holds that the person who, by the presumed will of the deceased, will exclude another, excludes him, whether he himself succeeds or not. And thus holds Bartolus, and this is truer according to the strictness of the law. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of both laws, and I have subscribed to the faith, and signed with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an appeal from a judgment rendered in a suit for the partition of common property, where the case is heard without the formalities and trappings of judicial procedure, is valid if the appeal was made orally on the same day, while the judge was not seated in his customary place but was elsewhere.
body: In the name of God, Amen.

†From a sentence pronounced in a common division, where the case is heard without the noise and formality of a trial, an appeal was made orally on the same day, the judge not being seated in his customary place but being elsewhere. It is asked whether the said appeal is valid. And it is said that it is: since all legal solemnity is removed. By c. Saepe, in the Clementines, *De verbis significandis*; and in the Extravagant *Ad reprimendum*, in the gloss on the word *figura*; and by the case of c. Dispendiosam, in the Clementines, *De iudicibus*. However, because the appeal is incidental in the case, as held by Cynus in l. Inuitus, in 3. q.; and it is of the same nature as the person, as in ff. *An per alium causa appelletur*, l. 1 and l. Ita demum; and Cynus in the said l. Inuitus, in the 14th question; both because the appeal is a defense, and thus is considered of the same nature as the person, cap. Cum inter, extra *De exceptionibus*, Bartolus in l. Si expressum; also, if we were to say that its preparatory stage is of the same law as the principal, l. Ad rem and l. Ad legatum; or if we say that what touches the primary cause is the same, as in the said c. Dispendiosam; or if we say it is accessory and of right, as in the rule Cum principalis. Therefore, it is concluded that the said appeal is valid, since the solemnities of law are removed and only natural law is considered: so that nothing is necessary but the exposition of the fact, however inept, provided that the intention of the expositor appears, as by the said laws. Rarely hitherto has it been willing to accept [this] on account of your honor. For I believe that although the case proceeds fully and summarily, nevertheless regarding the form of the Apostolic appeal, these fatal words "de plano" [from the bench/summarily] effect nothing. Hence, in benefice cases, in which the case proceeds summarily and de plano, nevertheless the appeal must be made in writing at an interval. Your Baldus [says] that here not only de plano, but without the form of judgment, the case proceeds, in which case all things pertaining to, antecedent to, and touching the cause are regulated by the same rules and are deduced from the same non-existence. And for the said decision, Dynus and the gloss, when it posits [the case] of betrothals and other inquiries in the gloss, and the reason of equity does not permit saying otherwise: both because the cause producing the appeal is called the very negative and the principal right, and the injustice of the sentence; therefore the appeal caused thereby is of the same nature; both because the cause itself, and the instance, and the fear tend to one term, namely, the sentence, and one sentence is to be pronounced in the case of appeal. However, with the rule being questioned, it is extinguished by the appeal, and the whole is one piece; therefore, to one nature and substance, or at least by place conjoined, our client should foster justice: or since the primary cause is greater and more is at stake, because it is the whole law and the whole business; and yet it is terminated without noise and formality, much more strongly in this interposition of appeal, which is less and which is incidental, in which case by reason of its mixture it loses its own nature and becomes and is drawn to the nature of the greater. And many more things can be said, which it does not expedite to narrate and allege to your lordship. I do not see how the said lady M., although she has justice, [can prevail]; and because the solemnities of law are more to be observed in interposed appeals than in the primary case from which it is terminated and caused; and than the instance of appeal, to which term it tends; because indeed every term, from which and to which, is one and the same cause; although not entirely having the first, that certain things are involved in one which are not in the other, namely, the person to whom and the person from whom; nevertheless in substance it is the same. I beg that you aid this party. Your servant, Ayme.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A mill that has existed since ancient times cannot be disturbed by a new building.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† One who has held an upper mill on a public river from time immemorial, of which there is no memory to the contrary, or otherwise by lawful right, cannot be protected by a new builder in the use of the mill, nor have the water stagnated for him, as stated in the Digest, *De flumine*, l. *Quominus*; in the Code, *De servitutibus*, l. *Aqua*; l. *Si manifeste*; in the Digest, *De edendo*, l. *Si quis ex argentariis*, § *Si in Titium tabulatum*. And in this case, the judge ought to observe equity against the new builder and grant him a suitable remedy. Digest, *De variis et extraordinariis criminibus*, l. *De usu aquae*, § *Quatenus clusa inferior nocet et restagnat*: unless it is removed to that extent, it should even be lowered. This matter, however, shall be entrusted to experts in such cases, as provided in the Authenticum, *De non alienando*, § *Quod autem*, together with similar authorities. And thus I rule in the question now at issue, having examined the rescripts of the Lord Count, the common law, and the statutes of the land of Calais.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A judgment may be null in four ways.
2. A judgment, even if interlocutory, is invalid wherever there is such manifest injustice that it appears from the mere inspection of the judgment itself.
3. Execution carried out under the pretext of an unjust judgment must be revoked to the extent that it proceeded in fact.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because our question concerns only nullity, a question of nullity which the judge reserved in his interlocutory decision: therefore he will speak only on the article of nullity. And for clarity I premise that among the other modes by which a sentence is null,

There are four modes of nullity. The first mode arises from the reason of a substantial order being omitted: whether the order is established by common law or by another who has the power to establish law. C. de senten. et interlo. l. prolatum. and extra de rescri. c. cum dilecta. and there by Innocentius. The second is on account of an expressed error, as ff. de appel. l. si expressim. and ff. quae sententiae sine appe. l. 1. §. item qui contra sacras. The third is on account of impossibility: for an impossible sentence is null by the law itself, as ff. quae sententiae sine ap. resc. l. Paulus. But a sentence will be called impossible in many ways. Namely, by nature: as when a judge orders something which nature does not permit: as if he commands a dead body to be produced in court, as ff. qui satis. co. l. si decesserit. And by fact, as if a judge commands one who is in Perugia to appear today in Capua, as instit. de verb. obl. §. loca. or that he give the Golden Mount, as ff. de stat. libe. l. cum habes. §. 1. And by law, as if he appoints a guardian for a person of lawful age, as ff. de tuto. et cur. da. ab his. l. Seye egresse. Also, in the fourth mode, it is impossible according to good morals, as ff. de arbi. l. si cum dies. §. si arbiter. There are also other modes, partly on account of time, on account of obreption, speaking of an interlocutory judgment. ff. ne vis fiat ei. l. 1. §. haec verba. and ff. de fideicom. libe. l. cum vero. §. subuenit. non ob. l. seruo inuito. §. cum praetor. ad Trebe. because it speaks in a definitive judgment.

† It is also to be noted that wherever there is this manifest injustice, such that the injustice of the sentence appears from the very inspection of the sentence, the sentence, at least if interlocutory, is invalid. As in Extra, De sententia et re iudicata, Excommunicato, c. Per tuas; De confirmatione utili vel inutili, c. Examinata; and Extra, De re iudicata, c. Cum inter vos. And it is noted in the Speculum, De sententia, § Iusta, under the words “item est nulla ratione manifestae iniquitatis”: although according to the strictness of civil law such sentences seem valid, unless there is an expressed error, as in Digest, De peculio, l. Eo tempore; and Digest, Familiae erciscundae, l. Cum putarem. And so that the Speculum does not contradict those texts, the Speculum must be understood as meaning when the injustice is expressed; for if an expressed error vitiates, much more strongly does the fraud of the judge, or gross negligence evidently appearing from the inspection of the laws, which is for the judge to ignore the laws. Digest, De origine iuris, l. 2, § Servius autem Sulpitius. Secondly, I premise that it is impossible to proceed to execution without a preceding cause for execution; nor can the judge cause execution to begin, as in Digest, De re iudicata, l. Si cum nulla. For the act of the praetor cannot derogate from the law concerning appeal; therefore the sentence will be invalidated, as in Digest, De feriis, l. 1, at the end of the principal paragraph.

† Moreover, even if total execution had been carried out, it ought to be revoked, insofar as it proceeded in fact, as is shown in the Decretals, in the title *De purgatione vulgaris*, chapter 2. It supports what is noted in the Digest, in the title *De iureiurando*, law 1, in the beginning. Considering, therefore, that execution was sought too hastily, and that the judge’s office did not have jurisdiction for this, and that this appears evidently from inspection of the very instrument mentioned in the sentence, and from inspection of the statute, and considering that this sentence is contrary to the common law, as in the law *Nimis propere*, Codex, in the title *De executione rei iudicatae*, and in the Codex, in the title *De pactis*, law *Si pacto, quo poenam*, at the end, where it is said that concerning the solemn order, petitions are made in vain; and in the Decretals, in the title *De accusationibus*, chapter *Qualiter et quando est*, first there, where it says that from things done inordinately, nothing of an orderly nature can be done. I say and advise, I, Francis, the least of the advocates of Perugia, a disciple of Lord Baldus, that the aforementioned pronouncement on the execution of the said instrument, having been made inordinately, and being contrary to law and impossible in law, as well as being void by law and of no effect or force due to evident error, is and was null and void. And so I hold, saving the judgment and sounder advice, as in the law *Claudius Felix*, Digest, in the title *Qui potior in pignore habeatur*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a private document constitutes half-proof.
2. Whether a judgment in which an error is expressed is void.
body: The facts are as follows: Stidam, a money-changer, lent 10 to the lady Gabriella by order and in the name of the lord Agabetus, and he wrote this in his book. Now, because the said lady Gabriella did not repay the 10 to the lord Agabetus, he had the entry in the book approved by the auditors of exchange. And it was approved before the judge of the captaincy, and he submitted his petition, in which he stated that the said entry had the force of a confessed instrument; and therefore he also requested that execution be ordered against the said lady Gabriella according to the form of the statute. The judge, however, pronounced that the entry was to be executed and ordered execution against the said lady Gabriella. From this interlocutory judgment, the said lady appealed, and in her appeal she raised two grounds: nullity and injustice, as appears from the libel of appeal, which I wrote among other libels. The judge of the appeal, because the decree was not collated within 20 days, as required by the statute, pronounced that the said appeal was deserted, reserving the right regarding the nullity of the said lady Gabriella. Now, the lord Agabetus requested that the said sentence be ordered for execution; on the contrary, the procurator of the said lady said that it should not be ordered for execution, because it was null, as in l. si feriatis, ff. de feriis. And on his behalf, he alleged three principal points. First, because a private writing without a legitimate number of witnesses does not make faith, neither by common law nor by municipal law. Second, because the toll was not paid on the aforementioned loan; and the ordinances of these tax farmers provide that on every contract or promise, from which a right is acquired by another, the toll must be paid; otherwise, it is null by operation of law, and of no value and effect, etc. Third, because this sentence of the judge from whom it came is null due to the omission of the order of procedure, as in l. prolatam and l. nimis propere. For, first, before the amount was demanded, and the case was contested on the amount demanded, and before proof was made on the said amount, execution was demanded; and thus the act was done in disorder, and the executive sentence was passed too hastily.

† To the first, concerning private writing, state that the private writing of one good man, such as a partner, constitutes half-proof. As stated in the law *Nuda*, in the Digest under the title *De donationibus*, and there by Bartolus. First, this writing was approved by the auditors; therefore, it is held to be true, because a cause that has been approved is held to be true, as in the Institutes under the title *Qui manu non possunt*, and in the Digest under the title *De manumis*, in the law *Vindicta*. To the second, concerning tolls, refer to their ordinance. To the third,

† That this sentence is void because it contains an expressed error, for he pronounced it to be committed to execution, and thus against the law of the constitution: because the law prohibits beginning with execution, as in l. 1. C. de execu. rei. iud. And thus, both on account of the omitted order and on account of the expressed error, it is void. The lord Agabetus remains: which would be true if he had chosen the path of the common law, but he chose the path of the statute. But to this the opposing party responds that the statute does not speak of such writings, and thus he chose a path that does not exist, and if he says, I narrated in my petition that this writing has the force of a confessed instrument: even the adversary denied it: and the judge pronounced on the first doubt, and also on the question of fact, therefore the sentence is valid. And when I say to you that rather whether execution should be made or not is a question of law, and not of fact, as appears from no. per Cyn. in I. Aretusa. ff. de statu homi. where it was said there that the jurist does not answer a question of fact. There he himself sets forth what is a question of fact, and what of law: and what is an interlocutory of fact, and what of law, and therefore see there entirely. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The words of statutes are to be weighed: and especially those which give beginning to the act.
2. A woman marrying a second time, with surviving children from her first marriage, how much she can give as dowry to her second husband, so that we may know how much the second husband can gain from the said dowry. And no. 3.
3. What fruits the husband gains from the dowry: and whether he gains the fruits of paraphernal property.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of statutes are to be weighed,

† and first of all those things which provide the beginning and commencement of the action. Hence it is that one must first consider how much a woman marrying a second time may give as dowry from her first marriage to the survivors, so that we may thereby know the amount of the dotal profit.

† And I will first set forth the common law for the sake of clarity, and then descend to the municipal law. As for the common law, either the woman gives in dowry estimated corporeal things according to the estimation, which makes a sale: and such a sale undoubtedly is valid. But the quantity itself remains in the dowry: and this is true, unless fraud or simulation is proved, which is not presumed in doubt; rather, it is presumed that the transaction was conducted for the benefit of both parties, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, l. *Si sponsus*, § *Si circa venditionem*; and l. *Quod autem*, § *Si maritus*; and in the Code, *De secundis nuptiis*, l. *Hac edictali*, at the end of the principal part, in the small gloss which begins *Cum fingat*. For the law *Hac edictali* rescinds only lucrative transactions, but not onerous ones: as appears there, and in the Authenticum *De nuptiis*, § *Optime*, column 4. And therefore, while the marriage subsists, the constitution of the dowry holds, because while it subsists it is an onerous title; but if, upon the dissolution of the marriage, it begins to incline by agreement or custom to a lucrative title, then that title is reduced, by l. *Hac edictali*, as these matters are proved in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, l. *Mulier bona*; and l. *Ita constante*; and l. *Fin.*; in the Code, *De iure dotium*, l. *Nulla*; Code, *De inofficiosa donatione*, l. *1*; *De liberis legatis*. Therefore, according to the common law, the husband himself retains the heritable corporeal things by title of purchase, the price being supplied if the estimation was made lower with the intent of making a gift; otherwise it is not necessary to supply it, as is noted in the said § *Si maritus*, and in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, l. *Plerunque*, § *Si ante*; and also in l. *Si res*, § *Si mulier*, in the same title.

† Moreover, she gains half of the dowry, that is, of its valuation, by force of custom or statute; the other half belongs to the sole child of the first marriage by the provision of this edictal law. And he acquires it not as an heir, but as a son, as § optime and the argument in ff. de adoptionibus; l. si arrogator, § sed an impuberi, and ff. de sepulchro violato, § quaesitum. Hence, even if the heir is an outsider from the mother’s testament, he does not suffer this gain with him; therefore, he does not hold it as an heir, as ff. de operis liberti, l. ut iure, § sed liberi, and de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro haerede, § 1. But it does not seem that the same should be said regarding municipal law. For a woman is prohibited from selling or alienating beyond a quarter of her goods to the prejudice of her children; but to give estimated things is to sell, and it is a true sale, l. plerunque, § si ante, ff. de iure dotium. And thus the statute has place, in which words are to be strictly observed. Moreover, alienation is every act by which dominion is transferred, as l. 1, C. de fundo dotali. But by dowry dominion is transferred, C. de re vendicata, l. doce ancillam, and note C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus, and ff. eodem, l. ubi. However, it must be observed here that while the mother lives, the children have no right in the goods of the living mother; because the succession of children begins only from the death of the parents, C. de pactis, l. fin., ff. de liberis agnoscendis, l. 1, ff. de his quibus ut indigis, l. 1, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Authent. si qua mulier, so that what is done while she lives is valid, ff. de legatis 2, l. peto, § praedium.

† And this title carries with it the fruits, so that the husband profits in respect of the burdens of marriage, and does not even restore those which remain extant, which he makes his own by full right. D. 19.1.13 (Ex diverso); D. 23.3.10.1 (Si ususfructus); D. 36.1.16.1 (Si heres). However, upon the death of the mother, what has been done is rescinded, so that it does not harm the son of the first marriage, except insofar as the reason of municipal law permits, as in D. 20.1.1 (Lex vectigali). Because when the power of the giver is resolved, the right of the receiver is resolved. D. 19.2.13 (Praedium); D. 19.2.1 (Et hic). Consider: here there are two causes, one of which measures the other and is plucked from the body of the other; for from the body, or substance, of the dowry, the profit of half the father is plucked. Therefore, there must be a dowry, so that there may be a dowry profit; since, therefore, the mother cannot alienate to the prejudice of the son, nor give in dowry more than a quarter part of her entire patrimony: it appears that the dowry profit can ascend up to half of that quarter, and not beyond the execution of two municipal laws. D. 28.5.1 (Ille casus). It follows to see what is the law regarding fruits perceived before the said things were given in dowry. And according to some, the wife is presumed to tacitly give her own goods to her husband in dowry; but this is not true: as noted in D. 23.3.16 (Mulier bona). This marriage, therefore, was in the meantime without dowry; nevertheless, by compensation of the burdens of marriage, it is presumed that the wife granted the fruits to the husband; and therefore they cannot be recovered by the heirs of the woman from the husband. D. 24.1.24.1 (Si quis). And I say this, wherever the marriage is without dowry, that the husband is presumed to receive the fruits of paraphernal goods in compensation of the burdens of marriage. Nor does the husband have these fruits from a lucrative cause, but an onerous one, as I said. But if the woman were adequately dowered to support the burdens from the dowry: then what would be the law regarding the fruits? Some opinions say that the husband profits from those consumed with the wife, and restores those extant; others say that nothing is to be restored. On this, see C. 5.13.1 (Ubi adhuc); C. 8.38.1 (Finis). Since, therefore, the husband is not the owner, the wife is the owner; and thus the extant fruits are the wife’s; nor does the husband consume for any other reason than because he consumes by the will of the wife. Arg. D. 47.2.1.1 (Locavi). In the reasoning of the text. This question was disputed by Marsilius, and Bartolus consulted on it; nevertheless, they judged indiscriminately in favor of the husband regarding paraphernalia. I said, and I say, that fruits of things distinguished by themselves as without dowry, if they are consumed in honor of the marriage, or for the sake of common children, are not recovered; because the husband does not seem to be richer thereby, but to have lived more honorably; but those extant, or converted into acquisitions or businesses by the husband, must be restored to the woman. D. 24.1.3.1 (Si uxor annum); D. 35.1.10 (Maritus). I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether reputation is proved by both common law and statute.
2. It is not said to be usury to purchase fruits before the time at which they could be gathered, even if they might be worth more or less at the time of collection.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The indictment formed against Bractem Brameti of the city of Nuceri is not proven, neither by its form nor by individual witnesses; and therefore the said Bracor ought to be absolved from the indictment.

† It is not doubtful under the common law that mere reputation alone is insufficient, nor are single witnesses sufficient, as stated in the Digest, *De testibus*, law 3, § *idem divus*, and in the Digest, *De quaestionibus*, law *De minore*, § *tormenta*. Therefore, it remains to be seen whether the reputation has been proven according to the episcopal constitution. And I say that it has not: because the words of the constitution state that public reputation, or the reputation of the lesser part of the people of the place or neighborhood, suffices; but no witness in the case, knowing this, says that he heard it from the greater part of the people of the place or neighborhood; although they say that they heard it from many and many persons. For "many and many" means four, but it does not follow, nor is it true, that because there are four, they constitute the greater part. Wherefore, no witness proves the reputation, especially that of which the constitution speaks; because proofs must conclude with necessity, as stated in the Extravagant, *De probationibus*, chapter 1, *Praesentia*. Since, therefore, having heard does not conclude, and the witness says that he only knows it: it is manifest that, although they later depose the existence of the reputation by way of statement, they do not prove it. Code, *De testibus*, law *Solam*. And this clearly establishes that the reputation has not been proven, especially that of which the constitution speaks. I also say that the statement that Barem exercised usury is not proven by three single witnesses. And first, it is not proven by Lord Vannus:

† Because purchasing fruits before the time at which they could be gathered at the time of harvest, when they might be worth more or less, is not usury; nor does the witness state this, nor does he give the cause of his knowledge: because it would be probable that they would be worth more at the time of harvest than at the time of the contract; and therefore he does not prove the contract to be usurious, as in Extra de usuris, c. In civitate, and c. Naviganti, § Ille quoque. Dominicus Raynerius does not prove usury: because it would have been lawful for the seller to receive that for his interest, l. Curabit, C. de actione empti; and because one should not worry about one thing, l. 2, ff. de dolo. Although Angelus Pagnoli attempts to prove it, nevertheless his statement is of no value, because the voice of one is the voice of no one, C. de testibus, l. Iureiurando; and therefore it follows conclusively that the accused should be absolved; otherwise the judge would incur a penalty, c. Cum aeterni, Extra, de re iudicata, lib. 6.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the heir of a partner, not having been summoned by the other partners, is bound to abide by the report of a collector appointed by the other partners, or by a private document drawn up without the knowledge of the heir.
body: The point of the disputes arising between Petrutiolo of Spello, acting on one side, and the wife formerly of Perrilio Otioli, and now the wife of Master Perrilio of the same place, on the other side, is as follows: namely, that having seen the petition of the said male party produced before Lord Guadanischo, judge of the commune of Spello, and subsequently produced before the arbitrator in writing, and having seen the exceptions produced against the said petition, both before the said judge and also before the said arbitrator; and having seen the articles produced before the said arbitrator on behalf of the said male party, and having seen the responses made to the said articles by the said other party; and having seen the statements and testimonies of the witnesses examined on behalf of the said male party in the said case; and having seen the exceptions of the said other party produced before the said arbitrator, both against the said witnesses and their statements; and having seen the sentence and award rendered in the said case by the said arbitrator against the said other party, no term having been granted to the said other party by the said arbitrator to allege her rights before the said sentence was rendered, as is required by law; nor was the case concluded by the said parties. And considering that the arbitrator in the said sentence made mention of a certain bastardello written by the hand of Ser Marino Masarli, notary, regarding the revenues of the toll, the said Ser Marino having been appointed to record the revenue not elected by the said other party and the other associates of the said toll; concerning which bastardello and its production made by the said male party before the said arbitrator, the said other party was not summoned, nor present, nor granted a term to obtain a copy and to file a contradiction to the bastardello. Now it is asked whether the said sentence and award rendered and given by the said arbitrator against the said other party for 14 florins and expenses was rendered and given according to law, or not, although the said arbitrator had the power to award and sentence according to law only, as contained in the compromise. In the Name of Christ, Amen. Although it should be believed that a good man judges well and does not condemn anyone without cause, nevertheless he must not deviate from the path of the law, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter Licet causam on proof. And in this first proceeding, it must be considered whether the partnership of a specific year has been proven. And certainly it has not been proven, if one considers the witnesses diligently. But because this is against conscience, I presuppose that it is proven. And therefore I do not dwell on this point, but proceed further, and it is certain that this partnership of tolls passes to the heirs.

But whether he is bound to adhere to the report of the collector appointed by the other partners, or to a private document made without the knowledge of the heir, nor by his command, nor ratified by him, when he was not requested by the partners? And it must be said that he is not bound to adhere, nor does it prove against him: as is read and noted in l. Chirographis, in the beginning, ff. de administratione tutorum. For even a partner ought to require the other partner, when he does something prejudicial to another without the mandate of the partner, which was not entrusted to him.
