For in a common thing, no one ought to do anything in solidum according to his own discretion, but by shared counsel; and what touches all, in C. ut l. fi. de auctoritate praestanda, and l. nam ita divus, and C. res inter alios acta, throughout; and l. Sabinus, with its material; and l. qui admittitur, ff. pro socio; and l. si ex duabus, de negotiorum gestis, with similar cases. And therefore this woman is not then said to adhere to that bastard. Moreover, the quantity of the damage has not been evidently proved by witnesses. If I saw the instrument of partnership and the pacts inserted therein, I would say that the instrument must be followed; but here it does not appear that an instrument of cession intervened. Finally, I say that the truth must be followed in all things, however, regarding the partners or managers, and that he stood at the proper hours for choosing; hence negligence may have accrued to the collector from the other superiors, as in §. si tutores. But certainly this woman receives, therefore she ratified; but this proof is uncertain, because it is not about how much. Finally, I say that the quantity of damage is not fully proved against the said lady, nor does the said private document of the said bastard quasi prejudice her; I speak of law only. For Ser Martinus does not say that he was present at the exactions of the toll, but that he wrote; which is not sufficient to prove that which is in question. For the soul, however, it would be better for these to compose; but according to law, it is as I said. It makes C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali, §. his illud. Baldus.

CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. The fact is proposed thus: Baptista sold to Martin a certain house held in dowry, unestimated by the wife, and Lella, heir of the wife and lady, promised to the said buyer to defend, authorize, and distrain legally, etc., under the obligation of her goods. Now, a lawsuit having been moved concerning the said thing sold by the said Martin, and no denunciation having been made concerning the said dowry, either to the seller or to his heir: the said buyer brings a hypothecary action against an alien possessor, who possesses certain goods which the said seller had at the time of the said sale; and he petitions that the said goods be released to him for the defense of the said house. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The buyer must notify his seller of the litigation brought against him before he is evicted; otherwise, the seller is not liable, nor can a hypothecary action be brought against him or his heir.
body: It is argued on behalf of the defendant that the said plaintiff does not have the right to bring an action, and that his claim does not proceed on these laws and reasons, namely: that he ought first to have notified this lawsuit to his grantor, or to his grantor’s heir, and this by the law *Emptor fundi* and the law *Si controversiam*, Codex, On Eviction, and the law 1, Digest, On the Peril and Commotion of the Thing Sold; and because before the thing is evicted, the buyer-plaintiff cannot sue his grantor, even if notification had been made, as the law *Qui rem emit*, Codex, in the same title, On Eviction, and the law *Herennius*, Digest, On Eviction. From which it follows that the plaintiff is repelled if he did not timely notify his grantor to defend the thing, when he could have done so, as the Digest, On Eviction, the law *Si rem, quam*, § *Ultimo*, and the law *Si d.*, § *Praesentem*, and the aforementioned law *Herennius*. Another reason is: because he acts on an uncertain matter, namely: he asks that the thing be released to him for defense, nor did he state his interest, or for how much his interest is; or he wishes to say that the thing itself defends him in the contumacy of his plaintiff, who cannot be called contumacious before notification. It is replied on behalf of the plaintiff, that the said laws have place when eviction is in question, but in the present case eviction is not in question, but a hypothecary action for the defense of the thing. Moreover, he said that he could bring this action by virtue of a statute giving the mode and form of proceeding: namely, that upon the petition being presented, or the narration of facts being exposed, etc. Moreover, by virtue of another statute, which provides that a hypothecary action may be brought against an alien possessor, notwithstanding that a personal action has not been brought, or that the goods have not been exhausted. Moreover, by virtue of another statute, which provides that in all cases proceedings shall be simple and without the noise and formality of judicial procedure: and that the process shall not be vitiated if it happens that the solemnities of law or order are not observed. Moreover, it is said on his behalf, that no one is found who wishes to be the heir of the vendor; therefore, it is said that notification was not necessary. It is answered on behalf of the defendant, that all the said statutes do not obstruct: because the said statutes have place only when a hypothecary action may be brought, when a personal action may be competent to the plaintiff; but the said Marino would not have a personal action, even if the thing were evicted without notification having been made; much less a real action, which is accessory. It does not obstruct that it is said that no one is found who wishes to be the heir: because this is not true: because he did not prove this. And even if it were assumed that no heir were found, then no one would be obliged to the defense of the thing: and consequently a hypothecary action for defense cannot be competent: because no one was in default. Moreover, it does not obstruct if it is said that the defendant was sued without being summoned, answering if he possessed the thing encumbered: and thus he knew the lawsuit was brought. Therefore, he cannot allege ignorance, nor was another notification necessary: because the alien possessor sued was not obliged to defend the thing, nor was he bound to offer himself to the lawsuit. Moreover, it does not obstruct if it is said that nothing was opposed against the libel, because on behalf of the defendant the claim was denied, and also the narrations were denied, as they are narrated in the claim, to be true, and that what is asked ought to be done: and because the defendant does not have to prove anything against the claim, that what is asked ought not to be done, since it appears from the claim itself, therefore it was not necessary to oppose anything else, but then the claim ought to be torn up by the judge when the parties are present. Now it is asked, whether the said claim proceeds, or not, having seen the said claim, and having seen the allegations of the parties. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Unless it were notorious that an excuse could not be made, the said lady could not be sued hypothecarily. C. de pign. auth. praesente. Regarding the point concerning fruits, I say that the agreement is valid up to the amount of the dowry’s alimony; beyond that, it is not valid, because it constitutes usury. ff. de solutionibus, mater l. insulam, §. usuras, per doctores. However, due to the fact, one can proceed hypothecarily just as for a giving, since a hypothec accedes to every obligation, both of giving and of doing. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And for the faith of this, I have written it, and with the seal of my name, seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an emphyteusis, which originated in the person of one individual and was eventually derived to several others upon the death of some of them, pertains to the survivors or to the church; and whether the right of accretion has place in contracts.
2. An emphyteusis divided in its original root is also divided in the course of proceedings.
3. Ecclesiastical emphyteusis requires five conditions in order that it may pass to the heirs.
4. Whether a son repudiating his father’s inheritance will hold the ecclesiastical emphyteusis.
5. If the emphyteutae divide the ecclesiastical emphyteusis among themselves, whether the portion of one then reverts to the other.
6. If one emphyteuta renounces in favor of another, whether this renunciation is to be understood as made in favor of the church or of the brother.
7. The church cannot invalidate or lease the property to the prejudice of the right of accretion.
8. The older emphyteusis is to be preferred.
casus:
The point of the question is as follows: The Lord Abbot of Bar., Abbot of the monastery of Saint Christopher of Duram, by himself and his successors, with the consent of Lord Benedict, a monk of the said monastery, present there, gave, consented, and renewed, for the unpaid canon, to Lord Guidon, formerly canon, tutor of Francis, and Dyn., sons of the late Ser Cola and Bartolus, releaser, son of the late Ser Nardo, stipulating and receiving for the said Lords Francis and Bartolus, and for their sons and grandsons, up to their third generation completed; so that the share of those dying shall devolve upon and accrue to the survivors, certain pieces contained in the instrument. After the passage of time, the said tutor of the said Francis having died, Dyn., Francis, and Bartolus made a division of the said things, and the said Dyn. and Francis, as to their share falling to them, were renewed by the said monastery; and the said Bartolus, as to his share, was similarly renewed by the aforementioned monastery. Nor does it appear in the instruments of the second renewal made to Bartolus, Dyn., and Francis that they consented. Of these things, each of the aforementioned held and possessed their part in severalty for more than ten years. It is also alleged that the said Bartolus was renewed a second time by the said monastery for the said part together with Lady Jacoba, his wife, the said Dyn. and Francis being ignorant. In the past year, the said Bartolus died, the said Francis surviving, and leaving Nardo, his son. Upon the death of the said Bartolus, the said Nardo, his son, was last renewed by the aforementioned monastery for the said part; and upon his dying without sons, the said part would devolve to the said Lady Jacoba, his mother, and to Angelo Salveri, cousin of the said Lady Jacoba. Upon the death of the said Nardo, son of the said Bartolus, the said Francis, by virtue of the first renewal made to his tutor, entered into possession of the said part, before the said Lady Jacoba and Angelo had apprehended possession of any thing. Then the said Lady Jacoba and Angelo likewise entered into the said possession without the will of the said Francis. And they disturbed and do disturb each other in the aforementioned possession, each asserting himself to be stronger in dominion and possession. Now, however, at the petition of Lord Francis, a sequestration of the fruits of the said part was made, and a term was given to the parties to prove their right.

It is alleged on behalf of Lady Jacoba and Angelo that the said Lady Jacoba and Angelo are in the stronger right: first, because of the division made among the said Francis, Dyn., and Bartolus; second, because of the last renewal made to the said Nardo and the said Lady Jacoba and Angelo. And because they ought to possess the said part for the share of the said Francis, it is said that the said Francis is stronger in dominion and possession in the said part of Bartolus by virtue of the instrument made to his tutor and the pacts united thereto, by which the portion of the one failing accrues to the survivor. Nor does the division and remission of right contained in the instrument of division made among the said Francis, Dyn., and Bartolus stand in the way, because an emphyteutic thing cannot be divided, and Dyn. and Francis, by remitting the right competent to them in the part of the said Bartolus by dividing, could not abdicate such right from themselves; nor do the renewals made afterwards by Bartolus and his son the said Nardo stand in the way, because they could not be made to the prejudice of the said Francis and his right, the said Francis being ignorant and not consenting. From which it follows and appears that, on account of the part, the right accrued to the aforementioned Francis, and he is stronger in possession, and Dyn. excluded, the aforementioned Lady Jacoba and Angelo being excluded. It appears that Angelo and Lady Jacoba have incurred the penalty by the aforementioned molestation, and consequently the fruits are to be restored to the said Francis.

These things having been seen, it is asked who is stronger in the said thing, and to whom the fruits are to be adjudged.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Certain matters must be set forth for clarity.

† First, it must be considered how an emphyteusis, which originated in the person of one individual, and was eventually derived to several persons, pertains to the survivors upon the death of some of them, or whether it reverts to the church. The issue is proposed as follows: it was granted either up to the third generation, or to the entire generation in perpetuity. On this point, it must be said that when some have died, the survivors take the whole; and if only one remains, that one alone takes the whole, and by the right of escheat it reverts to the church. And this is proven by ten reasons.

The first reason is that the survivor, holding the entirety, represents the stock and holds the image of his author, namely the first emphyteuta, and is substituted in his place. Hence, this occurs by the nature of substitution. And by virtue of representation, this is the case in c. 1, §. cum vero Conradus, Qui feuda possideant, Collatio 10.

The second reason is: because a generation takes by reason of death otherwise than by capture; but in a taking by reason of death, the right of accretion has place, as in D. de fideiussoribus, lib. 1, Thays ancillam, §. Stichus servus.

The third reason is: because the word "until" is a repetitive and substitutive term, as in D. de evictionibus, l. si rem, §. si; and D. quibus modis ususfructus amittitur, l. si cum in annos.

The fourth reason is: because whenever one proceeds from one to several, and finally from those several returns to one, the entire right recedes into that one, and especially in collective names, such as the name of agnation and the name of family, which names are similar to a universality, which is preserved in one when all others are excluded, as in D. quod cuiusque universitatis, l. sicut, §. si. This is also shown by our first father Adam, in whom the whole human race was contained, as appears in Genesis, chapter 2.

The fifth proof is: because by reason of civil and natural connection, a certain consolidation takes place, as in C. rem in praesenti, §. videamus.

The sixth proof is from the force of tacit ordination. For when something is left or granted to a family, so that it is not alienated outside the family, as is the nature of emphyteusis, as noted in D. etiam, §. 1, De solutione matrimonii, then among themselves they seem to be substituted for one another in the places of the deceased, as in D. de legato 2, l. Titia Seio, §. Seia. Who decided this question.

The seventh proof is: because it suffices that one of the children exists, so that the condition of failing children is seen to be defective, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. pater Severinam, §. 1. Since, therefore, it does not revert to the church except under the condition of failing children: as long as anyone exists, it does not revert to the church in any way, as in D. de pactis dotalibus, l. inter socerum, §. cum inter patrem; as in l. Beblius Marcellus.

The eighth proof is that he who receives for himself and his generation expressly provided for each of the generation, and thought more of the generation than of the church, and therefore excludes the church for each of the generation, as in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. pen.; D. ad Trebellianum, l. haeredes mei, §. cum ita. For there remains a person who, by the presumed intention of the contracting parties, repels the church, as in D. de probationibus, l. si pactum, §. si.

The ninth proof is by analogy: because the patronage of the church, although not divided in substance, is nevertheless divided in voices, and therefore we say that such a one has half a voice, as in c. 1, De iure patronatus, in the Clementines. Therefore, let it be concluded that the patron died leaving two sons; then one died without an heir: will the survivor therefore have half a voice? Certainly not; rather, he will have the whole and entire voice, and no liberty returns to the church. 16. q. 7. c. Considerandum; and D. de assignatione libertatis, l. utrum; D. de iureiurando, l. si duo patroni.

The tenth proof is by that which is held in fiefs. Collatio 10, An filius vel agnatus, c. 1; and De gradibus successionis in feudum, c. 1. And it is confirmed by the natural example of a tree having shoots. For with all counted except one, the whole virtue of the stock flows into that one. This opinion is held commonly by all, and especially by Bartolus, D. de verbis obligatorum, l. si mihi et Titio.

† But against this it is objected, because in contracts the right of accretion has no place except in usufruct, as in D. de usufr. accresc. l. 1, § interdum, and the aforementioned l. si mihi, et Titio. But I answer: This is true, unless there is an express or tacit agreement of the parties, as in D. de contrahenda empt. l. fundus ille. For in contracts, although the legal right of accretion ceases, nevertheless the conventional right of accretion does not cease; but it has been proved above evidently that this is tacitly understood to have been agreed upon. Moreover, that statement is true in mere contracts between living persons, but otherwise in a donation causa mortis or a mortis causa capture, as in C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, in fine. And what the father received for his sons appears to be the final judgment; therefore, the right of accretion has place, as in C. de familiae erciscundae, l. filiae cuius. It therefore appears that the whole of the survivorship is consolidated by the law of the law, and by the law of signification, and comprehensively by the wording; moreover, the law of nature also accedes. Argument: D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaerede, § qui discretas. And this is the very truth. Secondly, it must be premised that

† That when an emphyteusis is divided in its own root, it is also divided in the course of the action; hence, if it was granted from the beginning to two brothers of the lineage of one, nothing accrues to the lineage of the other, but only to its own root, or rather to its own column, as in the tenth column concerning two brothers of a new benefice in the investigation, chapter 1. Namely, because each looks out for his own kindred, as in the Authentica on not alienating, § emphyteusi, column 2, unless it was expressly stated that from one it should revert to the other. For this agreement is valid, as noted in the Digest on donations, in the great gloss, and in the Digest on deposit, l. Publia, and also on donations which are made under a condition, l. Quotiens. Thirdly, it must be premised,

† That emphyteusis of the Church requires five things, namely that there be descendants and heirs, so that it does not pass unless there are heirs, since it does not require hereditary right, but rather the form of the emphyteutic contract must be considered on this point.

† And in this case, even if the paternal inheritance has been renounced, they succeed to the subsequent emphyteutic right, as is stated in the Code, On Inofficious Wills, in the authority "Wherefore, if a parent"; and on this point, see Bartolus in the law "Of Oaths," section "If children," On the Duty of Children; and see Cynus in the law "Of Freedmen and Freedwomen"; and see the gloss in the law "If to you," section "If you have agreed," in the Digest, On Agreements. And here one might doubt what happens if he renounces the inheritance of his father, but not that of his brother. But this doubt is resolved by the law "He who renounces his father's inheritance," in the Code, On Children. Fourthly, it must be premised,

† Although they may divide the emphyteutic rights among themselves, this does not prevent the lapsed portion from reverting from one to the other. For this division, which is made for the sake of doctrine, arises from that intellectual division which is effected by law itself among the heirs, and is its execution, unless it alters the nature of the thing, as in D. de acquisitione emphyteuticis, l. Iulius Celsus. Fifthly, it must be premised,

† Although in the division itself one renounced to the other, nevertheless this renunciation is understood to have been made not as absolute but as causative, not in favor of the church, but in favor of the brother. Hence, with respect to the church, it produces no effect, as in C. ad Velleianam, I. iubemus. And it is expressly stated in the first column of the chapter Si de feudo defuncti controversia fuerit, c. fi., which begins Titius, where there is a very notable text. Finally, it must be premised that

† that the church cannot invalidate or re-let to the prejudice of the said right of accretion, as in the Digest, *De aqua pluviali arcenda*, l. *In concedendo* and l. *In diem*, at the end, where is the most notable text, because that which is subject to acquisition by reason of death seems to be subject to the last will, and therefore cannot be alienated, as in the Code, *Communia de legatis*, Authent. *Res quae*; and it is expressly stated in c. *Finis*, *Qui successores teneantur*, col. 10. From the foregoing, therefore, it appears,

That the earlier emphyteuta is to be preferred, because the latest does not have a natural investiture, as in D. de publicanis, l. si autem, § si duobus; and C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. si ante; C. de pignoribus, l. si superatus. And I weigh these arguments, which I state, because you will not find them stated so perfectly and so truly elsewhere. And what I said about the ancient investiture being preferred notwithstanding the division and the new investiture is notably and expressly proven in col. 10, de successionibus feudorum, c. 1, § hoc quoque. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, and to the truth I have subscribed and sealed with the seal of my name. And the same as was advised above, I say and advise, I, Honorius of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, and to the truth I have subscribed and caused to be sealed with the seal of my name. And thus, and that which was advised above by the aforementioned Lord Baldus and Lord Honorius, I say and advise the same, I, Julianus Vini of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, in testimony of which I have subscribed to the foregoing and sealed with my usual seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How much a husband instituted by his wife should have, considering the will of the father of the said wife, in which he substituted by fideicommissum to the predeceasing spouse without children, etc.
2. Whether a substitution in the dowry can be made.
3. The dowry does not pass under a fideicommissum, unless express mention is made of the dowry.
4. Add the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain Ser Cola, having 10 and 800 in his goods, and having two legitimate and natural daughters, namely Hermilia and Paulutia, and one granddaughter through a predeceased son, namely Nicolutia, coming to death made a will, in which he gave a legacy to the said Hermilia and to his said granddaughter of 600, which he had given to each of the aforementioned for dowry; to the said Paulutia, however, he gave a legacy of 40, which he had given for her dowry to Daniel her husband. Furthermore, so that the said Paulutia might be equal with the aforementioned Hermilia and Nicolutia, he left and adjudicated to the said Paulutia 200 pounds of denarii from his goods. And in the aforementioned bequests and legacies, he instituted them all, namely Hermilia, Paulutia, and Nicolutia, as his heirs, commanding them to be silent and content, and that they should not ask for more, etc. In all his other movable goods and so forth, he instituted and made his aforementioned daughters and granddaughters universal heirs in equal portions, and if any or some of them should die without legitimate children, he substituted the survivor or survivors, and also instituted and substituted them to one another. Now the case has occurred that, after the testator died, one of the said daughters, namely Paulutia, died without children, having made a will in which she instituted her husband as her universal heir. It is therefore asked, what and with what force of such a will is due to the husband from the dotal goods of the said predeceased daughter, considering the paternal will, in which he substituted by fideicommissum the survivor to the predeceasing heir without children: and presupposing that the said Paulutia acknowledged the aforementioned adjudication, by accepting the legacy of 200 pounds and the inheritance.

† And it appears first, that the husband, instituted as heir by his wife, succeeds in all her goods. For there are three cases: sometimes, when a father provides a dowry for his daughter, he stipulates that it be restored to himself alone; and then the gloss in l. rem. in praesenti. §. videamus. says that, upon the father’s death, even in such a case, the action for the dowry consolidates in the daughter, which opinion some doctors hold and others reject. And since this is not our case, say, as the said §. videamus. through Cy. and through Bar. in l. post dotem. ff. soluto matri. Sometimes, when a father provides a dowry, he makes no stipulation regarding the restoration of the dowry to himself or to the daughter; and then the common law’s disposition applies, which holds that, since the action for the dowry is common to the father and the daughter, upon the father’s prior death, the action consolidates in the daughter, as ff. soluto matrimo. l. 2. versicu. quod si in patris. And this also is not our case. Sometimes, when a father provides a dowry, he stipulates that the dowry be restored to himself and to the daughter: as is the case in our matter, as appears from the dotal instrument; and then, without doubt, upon the father’s death, the dowry consolidates in the daughter and becomes her own property, as in the said §. quod si in patris. and ff. de lega. 3. l. vxorem. §. filiae. and there by Barto. Therefore, it does not fall into the fideicommissum; because the heir’s own property does not fall into a universal fideicommissum. ff. de vulg. substi. l. cohęredi. §. cum filię.

To the contrary, that he could not testate of the whole, but only of the half, it is thus proved: the daughter, burdened with restitution, is burdened either purely or under the condition if she dies without children. In the first case, she deducts only one quarter, and to the extent that there is more in the other. In the second case, there is an opinion among the doctors of civil law: whether she deducts two quarters or only one. And it is commonly held that she deducts two, since they do not fall into the same time of deduction, as noted in C. ad l. fal. l. quanquam. and ff. de inoff. test. l. Pap. §. meminisse. in Auth. de resti. et ea, quae parit. §. quamobrem. in Aut. de hęre. et fal. §. si quis autem non implens. and in l. filium, quem habentem. fa. er. But in canon law it is settled that she deducts two quarters, as extra de testamentis. c. si pater. lib. 6. and in the same title c. Raynutius. and c. Raynal. And the custom of the world stands in this part with the canons, for the Pope can interpret into the laws, since sometimes, when the Empire is vacant, the Pope can enact civil laws in place of the Emperor, argumentum extra de re iud. c. pastoralis. in fi. in cle. whence the opinions of the doctors must yield to the authority of Blessed Peter and not precede it. We therefore follow the aforementioned decretals. From which it appears that, since the aforementioned daughter was burdened under the condition if she should die without children, if the condition occurred, she could not testate of the dowry except up to the half, by the aforementioned laws. For, since the quantity of 600 pounds was prelegated to her for the dowry, and afterwards she was burdened, such prelegatum falls into the fideicommissum ad Trebel. l. Marcellus. §. quidem libris. and de fideicommissis. l. cum virum. cum simi.

† Nor does it matter if it is said that a substitution cannot be made in a dowry, as in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. maritus. For either you ask whether a vulgar substitution can be made, and I say that it can, since it is within her power to accept or refuse. Code, de hereditatibus instituendis, l. cum proponas. Or you ask whether a substitution by fideicommissum can be made, and I say that it cannot, except to the extent that it constitutes the legitimate portion, as in the aforementioned §. videamus, according to Cynus, and the aforementioned §. maritus, according to Bartolus. For a fideicommissary substitution is a burden, as in l. ex tribus, Code, de inofficioso testamento, and every burden is removed by law itself from the legitimate portion, as in l. quoniam in prioribus, Code, de inofficioso testamento. Since, therefore, the aforementioned dowry, calculated according to the number of children, exceeds the legitimate portion, the substitution holds to the extent that it exceeds it. Nevertheless, from that which exceeds, the Trebellianic quarter is deducted, since the substitution was fideicommissary. Therefore, the aforementioned daughter could make a will regarding the said dowry up to the legitimate portion and the quarter of the residue above the legitimate portion, and thus up to half of the aforementioned dowry, the calculation being made, since she would have received only as much as the dowry given to her if she had inherited intestate, since there were two daughters and one granddaughter, and the estate consisted of 10,800. And these statements are true if the aforementioned daughter approved of her father’s judgment by accepting the inheritance and the legacy of 200 librae. But if she did not approve of the inheritance, but repudiated it, a substitution could not be made in the dowry given, which dowry had come from the paternal estate. Code, de inofficioso testamento, auth. unde si parens. If the said dowry is considered as equivalent to alienated property, as in l. ultra, Code, de collatione dotis, l. fin., for a burden cannot be imposed by the father on a dowry given, unless the daughter consents, as in l. quotiens, Digest, de solutione matrimonii. If, therefore, this daughter, by approving of her father’s judgment, consents, the substitution is valid to the extent stated; otherwise, it is not. And if it is said that one instituted in a specific thing deducts the Trebellianic quarter, I answer that this institution from a specific thing was merged with a universal institution by the acceptance of the inheritance, as in Digest, de legatis, l. ab omnibus, §. si a Titio.

But Bartolus holds that a dowry does not pass under a fideicommissum, unless express mention is made of the dowry: as he himself notes in the said §. maritus. And therefore the Lord Baldus says otherwise on this point, as appears in the following opinion. I, Francis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution can be made in a dowry, and whether it passes into a fideicommissum.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A father having three daughters provided a dowry for one, giving to her husband 40 for her dowry. And finally, coming to death, he left to her 200 for the augmentation and equalization of the dowry. Likewise, to the other two daughters he left 600, that is, 300 to each of them for a dowry. And afterwards, in the same will, he instituted them as universal heirs, and to whichever of them should die without children, he substituted the survivors. The said married daughter died from her father,

† It is asked whether anything of the said 600 livres, partly given and partly left to the same daughter, comes into the said universal fideicommissum. And it seems that they do not: because the dowry does not come into the fideicommissum, unless the testator expressly says so, as in D. ad l. Falcidiam, l. Pater filiam, in principio; and D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. A filia; and C. communia de legatis, Authent. Res, quae. For the dowry is not prelegated. And this seems to be the opinion of Bartolus, D. ad Trebellianum, l. Lucius, §. Maritus. And the reason for this is: because this dowry is in place of a debt, hence the daughter, as a creditor, can use the right of retention, as in D. de collatione dotis, l. Si; and l. Qui liberos, de ritu nuptiarum. Secondly, it seems to be said that the dowry, insofar as it was given, does not come into the fideicommissum, as by the said laws; but insofar as it was not prelegated, it does. And the reason is: because insofar as it was given, it went out of the father's goods, and became the proper patrimony of the daughter. D. de minoribus, l. Denique, §. Sed verum. But in a universal fideicommissum, the heir's own goods do not come in; therefore, neither does the given dowry. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. Cohaeredi, §. Cum filiae. But those two hundred which were prelegated seem well to come into the fideicommissum: because they are in the father's goods. For even the dowry returned to the father would come into the fideicommissum, as noted in l. Pater filiam. Also, because he first prelegated, and afterwards requested. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. Quidam; C. de fideicommissis, l. Cum virum. Also, because she was already married and dowered, she can diminish the fideicommissum for the augmentation of the dowry. D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Obligamur, §. Lege; because the father had already fulfilled the necessity of marriage and the piety of dowering. Sixthly, it seems to be said, so that equality may be preserved among the children. C. de collatione, l. Illud; C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. Si. But that all six hundred come in, insofar as they are above the legitime, or nothing, is not absurd; for it is said that in the person of another. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. Lucius. For if the other daughters, not being married, had died first, this married one ought to be admitted by substitution, even in the prelegated items. And therefore it seems to be said that the testator seems to have intended the whole: because the charity of the children suggests this; and because in the will the testator dowered her; however, insofar as it is above the legitime, it ought not to be restored. Also, if she abstains from the inheritance, she is not bound. C. de inofficioso testamento, Authent. Si parens; because he who repudiates the inheritance is not bound to the universal fideicommissum, and is not compelled to enter upon it. D. ad Trebellianum, l. Quia poterat. But to the two hundred livres prelegated, she will perhaps be bound by the said §. Quidam liberis; D. de legatis 2, l. Miles, §. 1; D. de legatis 1, and quid totum. Because they exceed the legitime, and he could burden them. D. de separatione matris, l. Si cum dote, §. Si pater. The objection from l. A filia does not hold: because there the dowry had gone out of the father's goods, here these two hundred livres were in the father's goods. Also, here in the prefaces mention was made of the dowry, there it was not, and thus it does not obstruct. And so I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a will made in the presence of five witnesses is valid according to canon, civil, or divine law.
2. What the phrase "such as it is" signifies.
3. What custom is.
4. The statutes of royal cities are valid, just like the statutes of the entire province.
5. A legacy that is invalid by the law of institution is valid in another way through a codicillary clause.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Lord Raynutius, having made a solemn will, in which he instituted his aunts as heirs, in the presence of seven witnesses. Later, being on his deathbed, yet of sound mind, as is said, and having the capacity to deliberate, in the presence of five witnesses, four men and one woman, he was brought to consideration, and that he himself and his household were held captive and weak in state by Lord Cathalan, his paternal uncle. He was asked whether he had left his goods to the said Lord Cathalan. It is asked, assuming the testator's sound mind and the said bequest to be true, so that there is no other doubt except regarding the solemnity due to the lesser number of witnesses: whether the said Lord Cathalan has a right or not, and to what portion. To this. In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the Book of Ezra it is said that a woman is strong, a king is strong, wine is strong, but truth conquers all. The law says, where the truth is established, we do not care about solemnity. C. de fideius. l. quoniam. and Inst. de fideius. haer. §. si. And Christ in the Gospel of John says, the testimony of two men is true. And the Mosaic law says, in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. And the Pope says, that it be valid.

† A will made in the presence of two suitable witnesses, and approved. Extra, de testamentis. c. Cum esses. c. Relatum. The gloss teaches that those chapters speak only concerning pious causes. And it is clear that the chapter Relatum restricts the chapter Cum esses to pious causes, where it says, "some such cause."

For the expression “such” is a restrictive term, limited to similar things and excluding dissimilar ones. For these expressions, “such as,” are concordant terms, as in Holy Scripture: “As is the father, so is the son.” D. 47.2.11. Others say that in secular courts and outside the Church, the chapter *Cum esses* must be observed. And therefore, before bishops who possess temporal jurisdiction from the Church, it is not necessary to have a number of judges, unless a binary one. But in other secular courts they distinguish: either in cases concerning pious causes, and likewise in favor of widows and the poor; or in other cases, and then civil law must be observed. And thus it is reported that Innocent IV pronounced this in the public consistory. Now, therefore, it must be examined regarding the lesser magistrates of that city and its statutes: whether they are governed by laws, or by canons, or by some third and proper law, namely municipal law. D. 1.1.9. Customs are, in a manner of speaking, natural laws in that place, whence R.

† He states that custom is a second nature. To this effect is the Institutes, *De rerum divisione*, § *Praedonum*; and in law 1, § *Bestias*, Digest, *De posthumis*. And the Decretal states that each province abounds in its own sense. And certain cities have the status of a province, as is noted in the Code, *De praescriptione longi temporis*, law *Si*.

† The statutes of royal cities are valid, just as the statutes of the entire province are. This is noted. On the contrary, it seems: because the aunts were solemnly instituted [as heirs], but the Lord Catalan was not solemnly instituted, nor would he have succeeded intestate; therefore, the legacy made to the Lord Catalan was null. D. de legatis 3, l. si mater; C. de testibus, l. hac consultissima, §. pe.; and in Auth. de testibus imperfectis, §. 1. I do not object to the chapter Cum esses, and c. Ray., and c. Relatum, because they do not speak of an instituted heir, but of legacies and fideicommissa devolved to the execution or protection of the diocesans. For neither can the law Ultra, C. de fideicommissis, which upholds the truth, be understood in the institution of an heir. D. de adimendis legatis, l. 3, §. non solum; and l. ex parte. From this, the inheritance cannot be entered upon. l. 1, D. de iniuriis testatorum; l. 1, D. de testibus. Therefore, it is useless: and the useful is not vitiated by the useless.

† It is to be held by this that the legacy made to Lord Catalan does not have effect by the law of institution. But whether it has effect as a simple legacy. There are many ways in which a legacy can be made: so that we understand that it is a legacy in such a way that it is valid, but by the law of codicils in a fideicommissum. In this matter, it must be said that either Lord Ray. intended to institute Lord Catalan as universal heir: and the institution is not valid; or he intended simply to leave his goods to him, under whatever title of legacy: and it is valid by the law of fideicommissum; or there is doubt, and the same applies. D. de her. inst. l. his verbis. Because what I do simply is valid, insofar as it can be valid: because no one is presumed to have chosen a path to challenge his own judgments, as in l. 3. D. de in iu. test. and C. de test. l. non codicillum. unless there were derogatory words in the first will, and not uncertain ones. D. de leg. 3. l. si quis in princ. test. And therefore, regarding this matter, having seen and examined the statements of the witnesses, no advice can be given except with distinction, as has been said, and these are true. For although we love the truth. C. de condi. et dem. l. cum ita legatis. yet this truth must be seasoned with the salt of the sacred constitutions. C. de fideius. l. si veritas. Nor is it a sin to follow the sacred constitutions, leaving bare truth and ineffective legacy behind: because the truth requires the support of laws: otherwise laws would be foolish, which is ridiculous and rash to think: I do not say the support of words, but of laws, as in C. si quis se ab herede absti. l. 1. D. de depositi. l. bona fides. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a will made in the presence of five witnesses is valid according to civil law, canon law, and in the forum of conscience; and whether it revokes a prior will made in the presence of seven witnesses.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, amen. The facts are as follows: The noble man Lord Raynutius, formerly of Menecutius Egydei, of Lord Andrew of Tudert, was gravely ill unto death in a certain castle of the noble ladies, Lady Gemma and Lady Jacoba, daughters of the aforementioned Egydei; and there, being in the straits of death, at the urging of the said Lady Gemma, he was asked if he wished that the said ladies be his universal heirs, and he is said to have answered that he did. Thereupon, I was requested, who is said to have drawn up the instrument of the testament and last will of the said Lord Raynutius in the common form before seven witnesses, as is alleged, having been summoned, after which one of the sons of the noble knight Lord Catalan entered the mind of the said Lord Raynutius, who was ill, and said to Lord Raynutius, and he himself marveled at the said testament, that he ought to have left it to the said Lord Catalan, in whom stood and depended the entire status of their house and of his friends. Whereupon the said Lord Raynu. replied, I do not wish that the said testament be valid, but I wish that my goods be those of Lord Catalan. And this was done in the presence of four male witnesses and one female, five witnesses being summoned for this purpose, since by the power of the said Lady Gemma more could not be had, nor could they enter to the said testator. Now it is asked: whether by civil, canonical, or divine law the said Lord Catalan has a right: and with a clear conscience he may hold and have the goods of the late said Lord Ray., knight created by the Illustrious Prince Lord Stephen, Duke of Bavaria, Count of the Holy Empire. Who, the said Lord Ray., was a cousin once removed of the said Lord Catalan, and the said ladies were dowered and had renounced the goods of the said late Egydei before his testament was made.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. If anyone considers the origin of civil law, he will find that in ancient times, before written laws were issued, the principle of constitution and the edicts of the praetors were valid, even if seven witnesses were not employed in one continuous context and summoned. This proceeded from natural and free justice, which protected the substance of the last will. This was the case at that time, when truth alone was sanctioned for men. However, as the depravity of men increased, laws, institutions, and edicts of the praetors began to be necessary for the sincerity of testators, so that no fraud might be employed, as in Inst. de test. § 1, and C. de fideius. l. quoniam. And this was introduced by the authority of those who established laws for the public good, whereby, if solemnity is not observed, the testament is called not made according to law: and from this, the inheritance cannot be entered upon, as in ff. de in iu. test. l. 1. Therefore, a departure was made from the simplicity of that rude, plain, and simple age, for the purpose of extirpating falsities, so that perfect truth may be revealed through more ample means, and a way be barred to malice, as in d. l. quoniam. It supports C. qui test. fa. pos. l. hac consultissima. § 1. And in this, human law distinguishes divine law, having been given by God Himself to Emperors and legislators. For the utility of the world and the sound governance of the universe, God gave kings and Caesars the power to establish laws among their subjects; otherwise, He would have made them Vicars in temporal matters in vain, as in extra de maio. et obe. c. solite. C. de leg. l. 1. in fine. Thus, I infer from the cause: what is done by a superior is amended or interpreted. ff. man. l. si hominem. Nor does this contradict the lord, because it offends the words, but not the mind, i.e., the reason or cause. Moreover, in ordering witnesses, will alone is not sufficient: but the will must be just, i.e., solemn. ff. de testa. l. 1. For the authority of law is required in proving it, otherwise it is not valid, as in l. cerdonem. ff. de ope. lib. and ff. de haere. insti. l. pater. ff. de leg. 2. l. condi. § 1. So much so that if a notary draws up a public instrument regarding a solemn will, he is liable to the penalty of falsity, as in C. de test. l. iubemus. in fine, because he was not legitimately summoned, and therefore he should not have written it, as in Auth. de tabel. § 1. coll. 4. Nor does it seem otherwise to be said in the forum of justice and conscience, because where civil law establishes such a statute, it is to be observed even in the canonical forum of causes, and also in the penitential forum of consciences, unless otherwise commanded by sin and deceit. extra de pręscr. c. quando omnes. But here the law establishes that it is not valid; therefore, with others, to whom the will is directed, having no right, he who has the right holds without agreement, since no one usurps what is not another’s. Otherwise, it would be said that many were ensnared and condemned by the defect of civil law, which is a true absurdity, since the law is good and expedient for the human race: and good laws and statutes excuse conscience from sin, nor do we have to scrutinize the reason, but the constitution, as noted by Innocentius de imm. ecc. c. quod plerique. in fine. For as a reason, it suffices that it is so written, as noted in 1. dis. c. ius generale. But of civil law, it is expressly stated that a solemn testament is not revoked by a less solemn one, unless there are five witnesses, and in the second, those coming from intestacy are written, not in the first. C. de test. l. hac consultissima. § pe. For then, since the second is valid according to the law of intestacy, it is necessary that he to whom it is said to benefit be among those coming from intestacy. ff. de iniu. test. l. 2. This is now said according to the law of intestacy, which is instituted in the second, from which the inheritance cannot be entered upon by mere civil law, having a right from intestacy. But this is not our case: therefore, the most solemn testament endures. ff. de testamento mili. l. milites codicillis. § veteranus. And of civil law, this is the very truth. And although we are in the land of the church, as it is said, let us see what the law is according to the canons. Namely, whether a non-solemn testament is valid, which is proven to be true before the judgment of the church, because it is proven by three or more credible witnesses. And in this matter, there are several opinions. Some say that it is valid for pious causes or pious places, otherwise not. Others say that it is valid in the lands of the church, elsewhere not. Thirds say that if it is proven by two witnesses and a priest, it is valid, otherwise not. Fourths say that if the witnesses are credible, it is valid, otherwise not. And these are read and noted in extra de testamentis. c. cum esses. and c. relatum. The opinion which says that it is valid for pious causes or pious places, but not for others, is proven by c. relatum. there, when it says, some such cause. For the word "such" is a restrictive word, therefore, from the contrary sense, otherwise in causes not such. The opinion, however, which says that one thing is in the lands of the church, another in the Empire, is proven, because those two chapters speak of bishops of the lands of the church, for the Pope cannot impose a law on subjects of the Empire. The opinion, however, which says of the priest, is proven significantly in ca. cum esses. The text says, before a priest. Nor is it surprising, because priests are public and sacred persons, as in ff. de iust. et iu. l. 1. § publicum nil. and they are judges of souls, which is no less than being a temporal judge, and a testament made before a temporal judge is valid with a smaller number of witnesses. C. de testamentis. l. omnium. and l. sancimus. Therefore, it is not surprising if the decretal disposes the same in a priest. And thus the Venetians observe, and it seems to be so by the law of nations, that every word stands in the mouth of two or three suitable witnesses. ff. de testa. mili. l. 1. per Iaco. de Are. and Barto. and it supports what is noted in de iur. et fac. igno. l. si post diuisionem. glo. and l. cum quis. The fourth opinion, however, is founded on the fact that, truth being established, solemnity of proof should not be cared for, as in insti. de fideius. haere. § 1. and d. l. quaestionem. But there it speaks of a fideicommissary, not an instituted heir, who should be more solemn, as noted in ff. de adimen. leg. l. 3. § non solum. and l. ex parte. and C. de testa. l. nostra. What shall we say? Weigh that the chapter cum esses. introduces three reasons against civil law: but divine law, the institutions of the holy fathers, and the general custom of the church, from which it appears that solemnity, even external, should not be said, but mere proof, which can be made by suitable witnesses, whose words the light of truth assists. And these three reasons are general, and the whole constitution is understood to be general. l. regula. § 1. ff. de iu. et fac. ign. The reason of a statute amplifies the statute, if it is general. ff. de excu tuto. l. non solum. § qui primipilum. But where is this general custom, of which it speaks there? Certainly, it is not in Italy, rather it is to the contrary, except in some places, as in Venice, except in testaments which pertain to their own protection, to whom the Pope writes. As are testaments in which something is left for the soul. C. de sacrosan. eccle. l. 1. in repetitio. Bar. and mine. in c. ad nostram. 2. de iureiuran. per Innocentius. Because they are for pious causes, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. si quis Titio. The Novellator in d. cap. cum esses. thinks that the subtlety of civil law is derogated in the lands of the church, I understand those which are of the full temporal jurisdiction of the church, and thus that they are merely requested, but canonical law otherwise obtains civil law, and statutes of places, especially if they are approved by the church, or constitutions of the church, because such are of positive justice, and do not have the same force in all places, as natural law has, as in C. de testamentis. l. si non speciali. and l. 1. and noted in ff. de consti. prin. l. 1. But against this, the text of the said chapter cum esses. works, which removes local laws and customs, as if they induce sin and rebel against divine law: because they infringe truth. The legist must hold that it is not valid: the canonist that it is valid, according to the common opinion of canonists: because truth prevails. And because, the presumption of falsity ceasing, the final reason of civil law ceases, and the second succeeds: because the last will is to be observed. 13. q. 2. c. ultima uoluntas. and 11. q. 1. c. siluester. The legist, however, fights in the forum of Justinian, the canonist, however, triumphs in the forum of Blessed Peter. And therefore, I distinguish tributes. In disputes of the forum of conscience, or treatise of conscience, I leave it to theological inquiry. Many other things are touched upon in the point, which I do not pursue at present, which make for the lord Cathalan. And add what is noted by Innocentius de immu. eccl. c. quia plerique. in fine. and I touched upon it. And thus I say, and I advise, following Ioan. An. I, Bald. de Per. V. l. D. saving the correction of anyone deciding better. And therefore I wrote myself, and signed with the seal of my name. Following civil law, however, it is necessary to follow the said l. hac consul. § pe. because Justinian was precise in this. C. de fur. l. Ancillae. But following the common opinion of canonists, truth prevails, as fully said.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the statements of witnesses who testified in a process declared null and were published, are valid in another trial.
2. Whether the indiction of one leaf is understood to be repeated in the following leaf.
3. An instrument without an indiction is null; however, the contrary may be established by statute.
4. Whether a legacy made upon marriage is due when the woman dies before the marriage.
5. Upon the occurrence of the case of a fideicommissary substitution, restitution must be made.
6. Statutory prescription is interrupted by citation.
7. Given a statute that prescription does not run on dowry, whether it runs on a legacy of dowry.
8. Whether prescription, which does not run on women's dowries by virtue of statute, runs against the heirs of women.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On the first point, which is asked,

† Whether, when a proceeding has been declared null, the statements of the witnesses who testified in it and were published are valid in another trial, it is to be said that if the cause of the declaration and its form pertains to the entire proceeding, for example, because the proceeding was conducted in an irregular manner, then, since the witnesses were not properly received, their depositions are not valid in any trial, as in c. Pisanis, extra de re. spo. and c. testib. de testi. in cle. because that which is done in a trial without order does not hold by law itself, as in l. prolatam.

† On the second point, whether the indication of one leaf is understood to be repeated in the following leaf, it must be said that, by the consequence of the letters, the leaves are joined and contiguous, and it is understood to be repeated; otherwise, not. D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, § si initium tabularum, whether described in the leaves between the same persons or between different ones.

† It is certain that, according to the common law, a public instrument is null if it lacks an indication [of the date]. However, the contrary may be established by statute, as is read and noted in the Authenticum "Ut preponatur nomen Imperatoris" and in the Code, Title "De tabulis," Law "Generali," Book 10. On the third point, which is asked:

Whether a legacy is due when she marries, if she dies before the marriage. It seems that it is so: if she was of marriageable age; so that these words are to be referred rather to the capacity to marry. D. de fideiussoribus, l. Thays, §. splendosus; D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. qui habebat; in the small gloss on the word “nuberet.” On the contrary, it seems expressly stated. C. de nuptiis, l. Sancimus; in Auth. de Sancti episcopi, §. si hoc praesenti; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio, §. Titio genero, ver. ante nuptias, noted. The solution depends on whether the testator assigns the day of the marriage or the dissolution of the marriage, or the substance of the legacy. In the first case, it is transmitted; in the second, it is not, unless the reason of the legitime, due by natural law, would remove this declaration. D. ubi pupillus educandus debeat, l. qui filium; D. de alimentis legatis, l. cum unus, §. si; D. de inofficioso testamento, l. quam in prioribus; C. quoniam diu leges cedunt, l. ex his verbis. But according to your case, the time was inserted into the solution, not into the substance of the legacy, and therefore transmission took place.

† On the fourth point, it must be said that, in the event of a fideicommissary substitution occurring — for the same is said of fideicommissary substitution — and thus by its very nature it requires restitution, with the proviso that in certain cases, as stated in C. ad Trebellianam, l. pen., it must be said that the prior hospital is to be restored the inheritance of Angelus under the Trebellian rule by the heirs of Bartholomew; and perhaps even without express restitution, the hospital has both a real and personal action, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. fin., although the first opinion is the safer one. And if the hospital accepts, the fideicommissum is binding, insofar as the assets are divided; otherwise, the prior hypothecary claims are enforced after excussion, C. communia de legatis, l. praeterea. On the fifth point

† Regarding prescription, I say that statutory prescription, being merely odious, is interrupted by a duly made citation against the person cited, not against another, as noted in the Digest, title *De usucapionibus*, law *Naturaliter*; and in the Digest, title *Pro emptore*, law 2, section *Pe*, according to Bartolus, where he treats of statutory prescription.

† On the sixth point, if the statute says that prescription does not run in dowries, whether it runs in a legacy in the name of a dowry. And it seems that it does: because the words of statutes should be understood truly and properly, but before marriage there is not properly a dowry. C. de donat. ante nup. l. si. To the contrary it seems, since a woman is said to be endowed, even if she is endowed in a testament. l. cum in plures. §. pen. ff. de adm. tut. so that not the title of the action, but the effect of the thing should be considered, and the favor should be extended. ar. ff. de long. temp. praes. l. sed si pro dote, which is more equitable. ff. de reg. iur. l. in ambig. and ff. sol. mat. l. 1. in the great gloss there, namely before marriage and so on.

† On the seventh and eighth points: whether a prescription, which does not run against a woman in respect of dowries according to the form of the statute, runs against her heirs. I answer: either the statute states that it does not run against women, and it does not pass to the heir for the future time: which is a personal prerogative. Or it states that it does not run against dowries simply and absolutely: and then, if it is established by the words of the statute that the reason of the statute is personal, it is the same as if the statute itself were personal. In case of doubt, however: because a privilege is said to be granted by title of dowry, and titles are perpetual and are transmitted with their cause: the heir acts under the same law as the deceased. C. de privilegiis dotium, l. 1; Inst. de acquisitione possessionis, §. fuerat. Or better consider this: because in prescription the origin is considered, when it began; but since it was begun, at least the longest prescription begins from the deceased, but with perpetuity; therefore, the life of the action, as the substance of the action without its essence, passes to the heirs of the woman actively: because to live while living is to be. Argument: ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. insulam intra biennium. Certainly, if someone wishes to begin a prescription, the aforementioned statements are true when the time is initiated from the deceased. But if from the heir: then, because a non-privileged person succeeds a privileged person, he does not use the privilege of precedence in future time, as is fully noted in Auth. quas actiones, through Cynus. And according to the theme formed, this proceeds without doubt: because it speaks of the woman, not of the heir. I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it is permitted for one defending himself to strike back: and how witnesses ought to testify concerning the defense.
2. What an insult is.
body: First, by John of Vignolo, on the second chapter, where he says, “finally, when he says that he cannot do more, etc.” Second, by Peter of Pavia, where he says, “who, seeing, as the said Conrad was following him, having his sword in hand,” and finally, “together, etc.,” as in D. 9.4.1, § cum arietes; and D. 9.2.27, § si navis alteram. For it is to be excused in him who did not act voluntarily, D. 38.2.1, § si libertus. He was not, indeed, obliged to suffer himself to be killed. The decretal says: “If it be necessary that either you or I be confounded, I would rather choose that you be confounded.” And certainly no one ever hated his own flesh, as is noted in D. 2.11.2. And it is to be excused in him who defends his own blood, D. 9.16.1.

Thirdly, by Francesco Remondini, who there, while stating that he always extended the sword for his own defense, says that he did so for self-defense. For when a witness establishes a fact for the purpose of defense, he proves it; not only when he adds probable circumstances in explaining the cause, but even when not questioned about the cause, according to Bartolus in his consilia. It is otherwise if the witness were to say that he is not guilty: then he would not prove it, unless he strengthened his statement by providing a cause, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1, § accusationem, ff. ad turpil. Fourthly, by Pietro de Curvaria, who openly states that he acted for defense and not for offense. And he provides a most conclusive reason: because no better or more certain one can be given. This is further supported by Antonio de Sancto Romulo, who, although he testifies based on belief, nevertheless adds a probable reason, which strengthens his statement if it is more conclusive than the former. In the same way, Bartolomeo de Fisco and Ambrosius the servant are corroborated, as well as the sequence and order of events: because the deceased had insulted him. For once the insult is proven,

† which is the motion of the body from place to place with force, and it is noted in C. ad l. Corn. de Sicariis, l. 2. It is presumed that he made an assault for simple defense, as noted in the said §. tabernarius and §. cum arietes. To the contrary, it seems to have been proven by Antonius de Sancto Romulo, who states openly that Peter first followed Conrad, before Conrad turned around and pursued him. By this, the order of the aggression is noted. Therefore, Peter was the first aggressor: and thus he is to be punished according to the order of aggression, d. §. cum arietes. Furthermore, by Petrus de Ceruaria, it is said that Peter first struck Conrad in the chest, and thus Peter began to offend first. For although one may strike and kill an assailant, as is read and noted in C. ad l. Corn. de Sicariis, l. si ut allegas, much more so may one strike first. The order of the facts therefore shows that Peter did not act for simple defense. Indeed, Peter had previously performed two acts: namely, the pursuit of Conrad from behind, and the striking of Conrad in the chest. If Peter was following Conrad, it was lawful for Conrad to turn around and, out of continuous fear inflicted upon him and without interval, to pursue Peter. If therefore Peter killed Conrad with a repeated blow, Peter deserves to be punished. Someone might say that these witnesses are singular, and therefore do not prove in such an arduous case, ff. de quaestionibus, l. maritus. But to this it is answered that they do not prove fully, but they create judicial suspicion, as noted in C. ad l. Iul. maiestatis, l. quisquis. Moreover, Peter confessed, hence one must stand by the confession, as noted in c. Romana, §. si autem, de appellationibus, lib. 6; C. quorum appellatio non recipitur, l. 2; ff. de edicto, l. quaero, §. si. Moreover, in defense, the intent to defend is required, not the intent to avenge. Hence, if anyone confesses regarding his own intent against himself, one must stand by the confession, extra de accusationibus, c. cum dilecti. Nor can witnesses, who did not know the intent and who are ignorant of the beginning of the brawl, enumerate this confession, neither in intent nor in fact. This confession is indeed considered true from its supporting circumstances. For although from what the witnesses saw, testifying in Peter’s defense, the act appears to them to have been for defense; nevertheless, from what they could not see, and which are nevertheless true in fact, it is established that the act was for offense. A witness who does not fully know the fact cannot fully prove it, as noted in ff. de infamia, l. Lucius. Moreover, defense is said in two ways: one way naturally, and in the following, and then even highway aggressors, while struggling, defend their lives from those wrestling with them. Another way civilly and lawfully, and in this way they are not said to defend themselves. C. quoniam liceat unicuique se, si iudicium vindicet, l. 1; C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si quis in hoc genus; C. de his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt, l. si servus. And thus defense is either natural, or civil and natural. I therefore admit that the witnesses prove defense in the first way, but not in the second, and thus they do not prove conclusively. Similarly, a plaintiff by replying would be said to defend himself, yet this defense is not considered defense, but an attack, because he is provoked to the case. ff. soluto matrimonio, l. cum mulier; C. de adulteriis, l. quam Alexander. He therefore who repeats a blow is not said to defend himself: because he was the principal of the crime and the primary cause, but the substance of the evil deed, and he gave effort to an illicit matter. Since therefore the murderer always awaits what he has done, as l. 3, C. de episcopis et audientia, it seems to me that the said Peter comes to be put to death as a murderer. I advise reluctantly and not gladly in condemnation: but justice condemns him, not my voice, and noted in ff. de probationibus, l. comprobatio, and l. palam, ff. de ritu nuptiarum. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws. And for the faith of this I have written and signed with the sign of my name.

The following case is proposed: Domina Salvagia, daughter of Donatus Ser la. of the parish of Ser Angelus, wife of la. Puciarelli of the said parish of Saint Angelus and of the parish of Saint Lucy, feeling herself detained by a grave illness, on account of which she fears, as she says, the event of death; and that she does not have the capacity to make a will, since she is constituted under paternal power, disposed of her goods by way of a donation causa mortis in the following manner, namely: because if it should happen that she dies from the infirmity which she suffers, with the presence, consent, and will of the said Donatus, her father, present, willing, and consenting, she donated causa mortis to Alexander Georgii of the parish of Saint Angelus, stipulating and receiving for the son of the said lady, whom she bore on the night just past, her dowry and all her goods, from 100 pounds of denarii. These 100 pounds of denarii she wished to be given for the love of God for her soul, according to the sense and will of the said Donatus, her father, with this condition, namely: that if the said her son should die in infancy, or in pupillarity, or in any age without sons, that the said her dowry, which is due by law to her husband Jacobus from the said father in the said dowry, and the 100 pounds of denarii which she wished in the said case to devolve to the said Jacobus, her husband, beyond the said dowry due to him by law, and all her goods devolve to Bernardus, Baptista, Gaspar, and Matthaeus, her carnal brothers and sons of the said Donatus. And from now on, in the said case of death, to the said Alexander, receiving and stipulating for the said Bernardus, Baptista, Gaspar, and Matthaeus, the residue of the said her goods, which are due by law from the said part to the said Jacobus, her husband, and from the said 100 pounds, which she wished the said Jacobus to have from her goods, as is said above, in every mode, way, right, and form by which she could best do so, etc. Finally, the said lady Salvagia died, with her legitimate and natural son Christophanus supervening, and the legitimate and natural son of la. husband of the said lady Salvagia. Finally, the said Christophanus died in infancy, with the said Jacobus, his legitimate and natural father, surviving him. Now, the father asks what portion, and which portion, is due to the said Jacobus by the person of the said Christophanus, formerly his son, from the goods granted in the said donation. It is also asked about the validity of the said donation.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a son under paternal power may not make a will, make a gift, or contract, unless with the consent of his father, whether, if the son makes a gift causa mortis to his father, the father may consent on his own behalf: and see below in the following opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This question is doubtful under the common law, and the doubt is increased

† Regarding municipal law, which provides that a contract entered into by a filiusfamilias is not valid unless the filiusfamilias contracts with the express license of the father, let us see whether a filiusfamilias could make a donation causa mortis to the father himself, either directly or through an interposed person receiving it. The glossa maintains that he cannot, in l. 1, ff. de auctoritate tutorum; and the same opinion is held by Decius and Bartolus. And because this consent of the father partakes of the nature of authority, which one cannot directly provide in a matter principally one’s own. For authority, which serves to confirm the consent of another, must come from that other side, and ought not to be relatively attached to the same person, as is the case with the giver and the receiver, namely the father. For when he authorizes, he must act in the person of the son, just as a tutor acts in the person of the ward; but he ought not to occupy the place of an adversary, as in ff. de pactis, l. si plures; ff. pro emptore, l. qui fundum, §. si tutor. For in the mandate which the father has from the law, it is that he should perform the acts of the son, not his own proper acts. C. de bonis maternis, l. 1; ff. de mandato, l. idemque, §. si tibi; and l. creditor, in fine. This does not apply to ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. phistulas, §. fundum, because there it follows in the mere execution of an obligation effectively contained; whereas here we speak of a contract to be celebrated between the father and the son, with the authority of the father. That the consent which is added in matters of paternal power is called authority is clear from Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. furiosus; and note C. de iure deliberandi, l. si infanti; ff. de verbis obligationum, l. si. For the son is not an integer homo (a person of full legal capacity), and therefore the defect must be supplied by the interposition of authority, as noted in C. de bonis quae liberis, l. si, §. necessitatis. Therefore, in one’s own act, one cannot be authorized, according to Decius, the glossa, and Bartolus. And we see the same in all cases where something is attributed by law by way of office, such as C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. quibuscunque modis; C. de contractibus in decem, l. 1; and fully noted in c. si una, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, in the Clementines. By this means, every machination of a maternal grandfather against a grandson is avoided. In the case proposed, C. de testamento militis, l. si, in ratione sui, is pertinent; and C. de donationibus, l. data iam pridem; and what is noted in l. 1, §. quae honorandae, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. For excessive reverence, which he has towards his father, is the cause of the donation being voided, as noted there.

To the contrary, it seems that the father could, by his paternal authority, consent to a donation causa mortis made to himself by the son. First, lest paternal power harm the father and exclude him from common and natural law. For paternal power is ordered for acquiring with respect to the father himself. ff. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 1; and what is said in favor, etc., as in l. quod favore. This is not so in the case of a tutor, a prelate, a magistrate, and an oikonomos, whose duty is not merely an office or ministry in another’s matter. Second, because the solemnity is preserved. For as to substance, insofar as the father is concerned, the father’s consent suffices. l. thays, ff. de donationibus causa mortis. But in his own matter, one can consent. But to this it is responded that this is not true when the consent must represent two contrary extremes, e.g., the stipulator and the promisor. Third, because the integrity of the person results, for the father imparts integrity of person to his son. But to this it is responded that he cannot impart it if he makes himself an adversary by making himself the creditor and the other the debtor. arg. ff. de procuratoribus, l. licet in popularibus, §. pen. Fourth, because what is present in the theme is the equity of the matter, as in l. dos a patre, C. de sacris matrimonii. Fifth, because the power in the dowry was thus given to the daughter by law. But that the daughter could delegate to the father, and cede to the father by reason: since she is considered sui iuris with regard to the dowry. ff. de solutione et manumissione, l. 2; and l. quotiens, C. de iure dotium; Anna de Pace, de conventionibus, l. ex morte; C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. si; and l. Pomp. phy, ff. de familia erciscunda. Sixth, the congruity of compensation. ff. de mandato, l. si vero non removens, §. idem Papinianus. Consider: if this consent of the father is an extrinsic solemnity, and not intrinsic, the father cannot perform these two roles: for it implies a contradiction. But if it can be such simultaneously, it does not imply a contradiction, as in ff. de adoptionibus, l. si consul. What shall we say? Certainly Iacobs de Radis and Petrus and some moderns hold that, according to common law, a filiusfamilias could make a donation causa mortis to the father, with the father present and consenting; and by the same reasoning, others for the father receiving, with the father subsequently ratifying. But this is false, as in l. receptum, in fine, de coniunctione praediorum. As for the first point, the matter is sub iudice (under judgment), as appears from the foregoing. Know one thing: that whenever a person is added to a contract, to whom one can give orders, it is always considered done through an interposed person; and much more so if an interposed person is used through whom one seeks. ff. de auctoritate tutorum, l. pupillus, §. fin. Now let us impose the statute upon the common law. For the statute speaks of license, and speaks in a contract; hence it is necessary to discuss: first, whether the assignment of actions is a contract; second, whether license can be given in one’s own act, etc. Say, as in another following counsel, which immediately follows that one. For Lord Baldus wrote more extensively in the following, as will immediately appear below.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The inheritance of an insane person is transmitted to the father, to the exclusion of the grandfather.
2. The legitime is deducted from a donation causa mortis, in which the son cannot be burdened; and likewise, any heir deducts the Falcidian portion from the said donation.
3. The burdened son deducts two fourths, and so do his heirs.
4. Whether a daughter may donate her profectitious dowry, or the hope of a dowry, to her brothers with the consent of the father.
5. Whether anyone may consent or be authorized for himself.
6. License is understood in multiple ways.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. These questions in some respects have no doubt, and in some respects have doubt.

† For it is certain that, upon the death of the infant, the father may take the maternal inheritance that had devolved upon the infant by right, and succeed to the full right of the infant, to the exclusion of the maternal grandfather, as provided in the law *Si infanti* and in the authenticum *Defuncto*.

† Moreover, it is certain that the legitime is deducted from a donation causa mortis, in which the son could not be burdened. For a burden would be a diminution of his right, since the son cannot be prejudiced in his legitime by an inter vivos donation, as is stated in the Code, on the inofficious testament, in the authority "Unde si parens" and in the law "Quam prioribus." Furthermore, any heir, not to mention the son, deducts the Falcidian fourth from a donation causa mortis, provided an inventory has been made, just as in the case of legacies, as is stated in the Code, on the Falcidian law, in the law "In donationibus."

And because this infant was burdened by way of a donation causa mortis, after death the father, on his behalf, deducts the legitime and the Falcidian portion, i.e., one-half of all the goods: according to the opinion commonly used and approved by the canons, as in c. Si pater, c. Raynaldus, and c. Raynaldus; and among the learned there is no doubt about this, presupposing that the donation was valid according to its nature.

† Now there remains the doubt: whether the said donation was valid in any respect. And this question turns on whether a son under paternal power can, with the permission and will of his father, donate the dowry brought by the father (dos profectitia) or the hope of a dowry to his brothers who are under the same paternal power, saying to such sons: as he said here, “to the sons of the said donee.” And it must be premised for clarity that the Speculator expressly explains this form of donation in Spec. de instru. edict. §. porro, at the words “quod si filia,” and Johannes Andreae in his additions to the same place holds that this can be done with the consent of the common father; nevertheless, nothing is acquired by the father according to Petrus de Cermitis, whose words Johannes Andreae reports and adds,

† For one thing is to authorize: and this is not lawful in one’s own case, nor in another’s case tending to one’s own advantage.
