Another thing is to promise, or to consent: and this is lawful, and valid in law, according to Johannes Andreas; and thus he holds against the gloss, which is in l. 1, ff. de auctoritate tutorum, which says that if a donation is made to the father, it is valid in no respect; but if it is made to the brother, it is valid as to ownership, but not as to usufruct. And thus also hold Decius and Bartolus. And thus the usufruct would belong to the heirs of the donor, as long as the father lives; nevertheless, upon the death of the first heir, as is the case in our matter, because the boy died, it seems that the usufruct is consolidated with the ownership. Beware, it is not so, for the formal usufruct begins with the father of the infant; for the infant held the total concrete property right, concerning which the question arises; and therefore, holding the opinion of the gloss, Decius, and Bartolus, as long as the father of the woman lives, no action lies for the brothers; because the usufruct of the name, that is, the benefit, is with the father of the infant. Johannes de Ravenna, Petrus, and Gulielmus de Cuneo hold that the father may even be authorized among his children, by argument from ff. de auctoritate tutorum, l. accipientis; just as he may grant them a peculium, by which confession he gives them tacit license to lend to one another, ff. de conditione indebiti, l. frater a fratre. And yet, because the father has no natural obligation by paternal right, but rather as appears there, and by argument from the aforementioned l. 1, de auctoritate tutorum. But against them it is argued that the law and note, c. si una, extra de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, in the gloss on the word “mense suae,” and C. de contractibus iudicum, l. 1, and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. quibuscunque modis. Moreover, it is certain that paternal power is a public office, just as the power of a tutor is, C. de sententiis passis, l. si, C. de bonis matri, l. 1; and from an office which one administers, one cannot buy, nor be a donee, ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. si in emptione, §. si; and just as one cannot do so by oneself, so neither by another, for fraud is prohibited from person to person, C. de auctoritate tutorum, l. si pupillus, §. si; especially because the interposed person was such to whom command could be given, and through whom acquisition was sought, C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali; de sepulturis, c. dudum, §. verum; in the Clementina. And because under the commemoration of the father, who is presumed to be commemorated by way of final cause and acquiringly, not by way of simple demonstration of the body to be demonstrated; for it was sufficient to demonstrate by the appellative name of brother, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filio; C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum aliquis; and thus the act seems to have been done in contemplation of the father, whence also the acquisition would redound to him in full right, ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. sed si plures, §. in arrogato. But this is impossible, and therefore the contrary will of the law impedes it, by argument from ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. non solum. Furthermore, the statute requires license, and license is twofold, namely, direct and reflexive. Direct is from the father to the son; reflexive is from the son to the father; for if it is lawful for the son towards the father, it is sought for the father, and thus the son’s license returns to the father, that is, to his advantage. But this is impossible; for everything that is licensed is licensed by another, not by itself, and everything that is supplied is supplied by another, and everything that is enabled is enabled by another, not by itself, as is clear by the natural rule: for everything that is moved is moved by another, and everything that is confirmed is confirmed by another. And in correlatives, if one extreme is destroyed, the other is also destroyed. But the father is destroyed, who is the active person; therefore the son, who is the passive person, that is, the defendant, or promisor in this contract; for take away the person from the act, and you destroy the act, ff. de iure codicilli, l. quidam; de legibus 1, l. 1, §. si filius; ff. de iure codicilli, l. quidam referunt; ff. de acceptilatione, l. si; ff. de stipulationibus servorum, l. usus fructus; Institutes, de inutilibus stipulationibus, post principium, with infinite similar cases. From which it follows that license requires a third person outside the promisor and the stipulator. For if they cannot license each other, because it is an extrinsic solemnity, whence no one can have license from me to contract with me directly, or through an interposed person; for license is said transitively, not intransitively. And thus it must pass into another, not remain in itself, ff. de renuntiatione, l. nisi cum priorem, §. verum; ut C. post translationem, §. versus; for license is given by another, but abusive and temerary license is taken by oneself: not from the effect of the thing, but to the defect of the thing.

† Hence there is a manifold license, whether of abuse or of presumption. 21. quaest. 2. c. placuit. license of dispensation. 1. qt. 5. c. vlti. license of occasion. 27. quaest. 2. c. si tu abstines. license of promise. 45. dist. c. qui sincenti. license of approval. 28. distin. c. de his. according to the argument of those who thus note in c. vlti. de elec. in clemen. These five modes are posited by the dictum iuste. 6. It is called license by common law expression. C. de sac. san. ecc. l. 1. 7. It is called license for ascension to a degree. de nego. gest. l. quae vtiliter. 8. It is called license of translation. d. c. nisi. Ninth, it is called a certain security. no. in l. is, qui reus. de publi. iudi. and the one granting license and the one receiving license are punished in an undue case, as noted in l. penult. C. de commeatu. And tenth, it is called license granted to a capable person. C. de bonis, quae lib. l. non solum. §. necessitatis. And so in our case, since the son of the deceased is not a whole person, the statutes require license to make him whole; hence this license is reduced to the likeness of authority, and thus the negative conclusion follows: because in the instrument there is no mention of express license, and presence is something other than license. Likewise, consent and will are not express license. It must precede with license, whereas will and consent can follow. no. in c. dudum. extra de reb. eccle. unless one says that consent differs in name, but not in substance. Since substance is a generic term, it is placed for that species which is necessary for the validity of the act: but for authority, license, which laws impose on facts, not words. C. communia deleg. l. 1. in fi. just as it suffices if the tutor says, I consent: although he does not say, I authorize: because to authorize is nothing other than to approve. ff. de auth. tut. l. etiam aduerte Considering the nature of the words: because the statute requires license, which signifies by way of antecedent, which license is the granting of liberty to one who does not have it in himself, as extra de regulari. c. licet. and the words of the donation instrument say, with the consent and etc., which word, with, signifies, and in consequence, as l. 4. de fundo instruc. and thus, if previously the son was not a capable person, as the statute requires, it could be said, by subtlety of words, that the form of the statute was not observed; but you, who have to judge, choose that in the gloss which in this passage is more pleasing to consent to. In the first point, however, regarding the legitime or the Falcidian portion, what I said, I assert, and it is undoubtedly true. And holding that the donation is valid, it also follows regarding the two hundred pounds, what is the law: holding, however, that it is not valid as regards the father of the donor, similarly it appears what is the law: holding, however, that the statute impedes, it appears that the whole tenor thereof is against their will. But you choose what pleases you in this tripartite. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The wife is left as usufructuary owner and manager of all the goods, if she lives a widow’s life, etc., a certain monastery being instituted as universal heir to all the other goods after the death of the said wife; whether the said wife during her lifetime is called an heir, so that the legacies left by the testator can be claimed.
casus: CASE. The fact is such: Francis Louis of Ventioli made his testament, in which among other things he left Lady Balda, wife, as usufructuary and manager of all his goods, provided she lived chastely and honestly, and observed the widow’s life. In all his other movable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they were and could be found, he made and instituted his universal heirs the brothers, or monks, chapter, and convent of the order of Certosa, or Carthusian, after the death of the said Lady Balda etc. Finally, he made his codicils, in which among other things he judged and left to Francis Polloli 100 florins. Finally, the said Francis Louis died without children, the said Lady Balda surviving. This Lady Balda held and possessed the hereditary goods of the said Francis, and from them received fruits, revenues, and profits. Now it is asked: whether the said legacy is due, although the inheritance has not been entered upon by the said brothers: because the said Lady Balda still lives. And whether the said legacy can be demanded, or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Lord Bar. states two points in this matter.

† First, he said that the word “domina” (lady) effects nothing other than a certain preeminence, as I note in l. Titia, §. si, D. de legatis 2, and he places this in his consilia, in consilium 5, which begins “Petrus Magioli.” And he speaks truly, unless by this understanding the legacies would be vitiated. Second, he says that the brothers, or the church, must await the death of the wife, and they cannot precede it. Thus I note in D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. hereditas ex die. And thus the usufruct will never be the woman’s: because not before the inheritance is accepted, as C. de caducis tollendis, §. exceptio; and even after, not, as D. de usu et habitando, l. Titium cum morietur. Moreover, while the wife is alive, no legacy is due, which is impious and absurd. This is touched upon in C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. extraneum. Therefore, it must be said that the word “domina,” since no other person is instituted in favor of the legacies, and so that the legacies do not take effect during the life of the said wife, imports that she is truly instituted as domina, or heir, during her lifetime, and thus for a time, while she lives chastely and honorably, as D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. his verbis, in principio. And the aforementioned Bartolus is correct when another person is purely instituted. It supports what I note, according to Dominus Iacobus de Arena, in l. si secundo nupserit mulier probata. Therefore, upon acceptance, or management as heir, by the said domina, the said legacy can be claimed. For thus we must interpret the testament, so that it may be valid, and not perish, the same in codicils. And thus there is no objection from D. de regulis iuris, l. si nemo; D. de fideiussoribus, l. eam quam. This is: the inheritance is accepted. I do not see how the testator’s will can otherwise be saved. For if that domina could not accept, the legacy could not be claimed. But if the testator had not used that word “domina,” but had said only “usufructuary,” then she would not in the meantime be heir, and she could not claim any legacy unless the inheritance was accepted. Others, however, do not hold the opinion of Bartolus in the said l. hereditas. And according to them, acceptance of the inheritance would be necessary to be made by the brothers. I have been doubtful; but in a doubtful matter, it is more just to preserve the will of the testator. For if we even hold that the brothers have no right during the life of the wife, therefore in the meantime no legacies can be claimed, which would be inequitable. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And for the faith thereof I have subscribed, and with the seal of my name, always protesting for the sounder counsel.

Coraxepis, noble and Magnificent knight, Lord Lanerio de Pisis, honoring captain of the city of Perugia, and your, and of the said commune’s judge, Lord Philippo, constituted for malefices, excepts, and by way of exception proposes, the procurator, and in procuratorial name of Andreucius Angelii of Perugia, of the Port of Saint Peter, and of the Parish of Saint Mary of Colle, accused before you by Antonius Ioannis of Perugia, of the Port of Saint Peter, and of the Port of Saint Stephen, the tenor of whose accusation is as follows, namely. Here the tenor of the accusation is missing, which is omitted for brevity. Against the process, namely that which you made upon the said accusation, and the contents therein. And to this end, that you proceed no further, since you cannot, nor ought to, by law, for causes and reasons.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the same offense, where a condemnatory sentence has already been passed, may be inquired into again.
body: EL Drimo

† Because regarding the aforementioned single blow, mentioned in the said accusation, a solemn inquisition was conducted by you, Lord Captain, and your court against the said Andrizolo, and a condemnatory sentence was rendered. And therefore, the same offense cannot be further cognized, unless the conclusion which is presumed in the inquisition is argued, nor is it concluded in our case. And there is a threefold reason: first, the offense of the same person ought not to be investigated repeatedly. Second, because actions brought for vengeance mutually extinguish each other, even if one contains more than the other. Third, because one could proceed just as well to acquit as to condemn, and thus there would be perplexity, in that the same person would be found both condemned and acquitted for the same offense. Therefore, on account of res judicata, the exception of impossibility of cognition stands in the way, which exceptions it is certain can be opposed by a procurator as dilatory of the process, and contained in the acts themselves, which are notorious to us because of the allegations and legal defenses made by you, which do not require proof. And if the contrary were said, an absurdity would follow, that the defendant could first be accused of a simple wound. Thirdly, of another quality. And if there were a thousand qualities, he could be accused a thousand times: which is ridiculous to say, and contrary to the true opinions of all the ancient doctors, except Bartolus, in his new doctrine, who holds the contrary: whose reasons are worth not one obol, unless there was collusion, having made a contract with the adversary to the prejudice of the fisc. But when it is not concluded, but the quality is omitted, perhaps due to lack of confidence in the proof, or because the inquirer did not have information regarding the quality, and especially since the injured party knew, or ought to have known, that proceedings were taking place in the case, Bartolus does not speak the truth, nor is he to be believed. Indeed, the law from which the question of commodatum arises does not deserve to be cited: because it speaks of civil cases, and not those brought for vengeance. Moreover, the inquiring judge principally and directly holds the place of the fisc, and secondarily the place of the injured party, and therefore his sentence prejudices the fisc. And to say that a procurator does not prejudice his principal, proceeding rightly in the case and in the order of judgments, is openly false, although there is also no good equivalence between the inquirer and the procurator. And the reasons of Bartolus do not touch the inquirer. And truly his opinion is false: unless the conclusion and the ignorance of the injured party are proven, which here neither can be said nor is alleged, and it is a lie: because the court has concluded. And therefore, if the court is in doubt, let there be a consultation of the college of Bonacorso or Simil. And these are true: especially considering the statutes of Arles, according to which against a condemnation there is no remedy of repetition of what has been paid, or of exception, if it has not been paid: and because there are different kinds of penalties, nor do they confuse each other, and it would be deafness to be punished and afflicted with contrary penalties. And see for certain that Bartolus says in the course of his lecture that the things to be examined were not examined. And for this negative part, Jacobus Butrigarius, the most subtle doctor, advised. Especially for this reason: because judgment cannot be founded on the quality alone, and the substance of the offense, once passed into res judicata, cannot be rubbed over again. The same is held by Speculum, Johannes Andreae, and all the others.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a refutation, or release, has the force of a donation; and whether it is valid between husband and wife, when made causa mortis, and with a certain pact, etc.
2. A confession issued in favor of prohibited persons is presumed to have been made in fraud.
3. Whether the cumulation of several rights is to be admitted.
4. Whether a contrary allegation, or exception, is to be admitted.
5. Whether one is said to be acting contrary who states that an act ought not to be rescinded, but is null by operation of law.
6. A contract that is null and celebrated under duress may be alleged in the same petition.
7. Where a statute exists prohibiting the opposing party from raising an exception, this does not mean that the exception of nullity, nor of the incapacity of the person, is removed. See also number 8.
8. Whether laborers are competent witnesses; and what is the rule regarding those who derive a benefit secondarily, and not principally. See also number 11.
9. Whether I may impeach the witnesses whom I produced in the case, if they subsequently testify against me in the same case.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is stated as follows: Lady Bartolina, wife of John, beyond the dowry which she had given to the said John, had, held, and possessed by herself during the lifetime of the said John, her husband, a certain landholding; and this is established by the confession of Lady Gabriella, heir of the said John. And from the said landholding, the fruits gathered were brought into the house of the said John, in which the said Lady B. dwelt with the said John; and they came into the hands of the said John. And this has been proven by several witnesses, and especially by Bar. and Lady Erreanella. And this continued for a period of thirty years. Finally, the said Lady B. made a settlement and renunciation to the said John on the 13th day of the month of January, 1379, concerning all the aforesaid fruits. And she did this, as appears in the instrument of renunciation, because she was satisfied and confessed that she had been fully satisfied by the said John, and she swore not to act to the contrary. Although it appears thus, nevertheless, in truth, the said renunciation was made causa mortis, and under a condition and pact, that if it should happen that the said Lady B. should precede the said Lady B. [sic: likely error for "John"] her husband. But if it should happen that the said John should precede the said Lady B., the said Lady B. wished, by herself and her heirs, to claim after her death from the heirs of the said John all the aforesaid fruits received by the said John. And this has been proven by two witnesses, namely one of the witnesses to the instrument, namely Centuriolus, and Lady Simonella. Finally, on the 21st day of December, 1373, the said Lady B. made to the said John, her husband, for herself and her heirs, a settlement and renunciation, release and absolution, and peace, regarding not claiming further, concerning the fruits received by the said John from the said landholding. And she did this because she so willed and it so pleased her, although at first she said otherwise, but later, out of reverential fear of the said John, her husband, she did this. Of which renunciation it appears by the mandate of Ser Amato Addoli. Finally, after the death of the aforesaid John, the said Lady Bartolina claimed back the said fruits formerly received by John, her husband, before the Lord Vicar of the Lord Bishop, and she says that the said renunciation is not valid.

† And first, the first refutation does not stand in the way: because it was a cause of death, which is extinguished by the death of the donee, as in l. si cum uxori and the following law, ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem; and if it was confirmed by oath, because although the oath confirmed an invalid donation, as in c. cum contingat and c. licet mulieres, nevertheless it does not alter the nature of the contract, so that it is not extinguished by the death of the donee. And especially since the said B. did not revoke it, but John himself, by his death, made it revocable: although during John’s lifetime that refutation would be lost, nevertheless after the death of the said John, the donee, it is not valid, as in l. sed interim and l. sed si mors, ff. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem. Add that the said John in the meantime did not make those fruits his own, as in l. cum quis, ff. de conditione ob causam. Secondly, it is opposed against the said refutation that it was made under reverential fear, and this is proved by witnesses, who say that the said John said at that time: “I want you to make me the refutation of Tagliefrutte.” That word imports necessity: because that which is commanded is ordered, and c. 14, quod praecipitur, and therefore it ought not to be valid, as in l. 1, § quae honorandae, quarum rerum. And it is also apparent from the contradiction of the lady Bar. from the beginning. Thirdly, it is opposed against the said refutation that no delivery took place, and although this does not seem fully proved by witnesses, rather the contrary: namely, by the confession of the said B. in the refutation itself, because she confessed that she had received etc., nevertheless it seems that the presumption of law is proved,

† When a confession intervenes between prohibited persons, such a confession is presumed to have been made in fraud: as [stated in] l. cum tex. ff. de prob. contra nanque refutatio. Two arguments are alleged that it is null. First, as appears from the subscripted refutation, it was gratuitous; and thus it had the force of a donation, for he who remits gives: do. 8. qu. 3. c. talia. And therefore it is not valid by the law itself, as [stated in] l. si sponsus, and l. 3. §. sciendum, and l. 1. C. eo. Although it is confirmed by the death of the donor: as [stated in] l. 1. and 3, and l. donationes. C. eo. ti. But this does not intervene here, nor does it object. If it is said that it is confirmed by death, therefore it was not valid from the beginning, according to the rule quod et c. quia nec dicit gl. in l. 3. ff. de leg. 3. While the husband lives, it sleeps in the interim, or it is confirmed afterwards by the tacit will of the preceding woman, as noted in l. si vxor marito. ff. de do. inter virum. Others say that the revocation not followed draws back: as d. l. 3. implies, that it is drawn back, and that it is valid, as a donation inter vivos. Although Dy. reproves it, per dictam l. sequitur. But the text in l. cum hoc status. in fi. prin. quod quasi ex tex. haeredi. But whatever it is, even if it is drawn back, it does not apply to our case with this. Secondly, the donee predeceased, and thus this donation, whether it was valid or not, was not revoked: as d. l. 1. and 3. And also, since the said refutation of the said fruits is not valid, the libel was conceived in this form, it is valid: because the nature of the fact is made, by reason of the fact it is concluded. Thus it is valid, why does he ask that the said dom. Bart. pronounce the said refutations to be invalid: otherwise there would not have been a contract of donation, and no satisfaction would have been made do. B. And that it is not valid to revoke, by the death of the said Io. And also that the said Ioan. is enriched by the said refutations, and the lady B. is impoverished, and for this reason the revocation is, and is not valid, and that the said refutation, which appears in the form of pure refutation, was, and is, conditional: if and when the marriage of do. B. predeceased the said. Secondly, and that the said condition had failed due to the death of the said Ioan. predeceasing, and that they were, and are, made by fear, and violence of the said Ioan. And that the said Gabriella, heir of the said Io., be condemned, and the condemned be compelled to give, and restore the said refutation, for void, and cancelled. And that the said G. heir be condemned to restore the said fruits, if they exist: or if they do not exist, to the due estimation, be condemned, and the condemned be forced, and compelled. And on behalf of dom. Bart. to found the intention, several things are deduced. First, that the said Ioan. is the husband of do. Bart. And this is proved by the confession of the party do. Gab. That during the said marriage for a period of ten years, lady Bar. beyond the dowry given to the said Ioan. had, held, and possessed a certain tenement of land, from which the said fruits were perceived by Ioan. and brought into his house. And this is proved first by the witnesses themselves: namely a certain Bartho. also on behalf of lady Bart. etc. Chetarellem, also on behalf of lady Gabr. And also, and thus since the intention of do. B. is proved, it is clear that do. Gab. must be condemned to restore the said, for which l. maritus. ad leg. Falci. But against do. B. principally are alleged, first the ineptitude of the libel. Secondly, the said refutations are alleged. Thirdly, that the intention of d. B. is not legitimately proved, nor could it be proved, notwithstanding the statute of the community, and the synodal constitution. As to the first, the libel is alleged to be inept due to the accumulation of several rights, which cannot be done: as l. 3. §. eligere. but one elected etc. vt de noxa. in delictis. §. si detracta. Secondly, by reason of contrariety, for in the libel several things are narrated. First, of the refutations, that they are scandalous, and revocable by the death of the donee. Secondly, that they were made in fraud of usury. Thirdly, that by fear. Fourthly, that they were simulated. And thus in these three last cases he says they are valid, but ought to be rescinded. And thus it is evident that the said refutations are said to be valid, and not valid. And thus alleging contraries. And thus he is to be repelled. l. 1. C. de fur. et de app. l. sollicitudinem. As to the merits of the causes, two, or three, are alleged. First, that against the said refutations exceptions ought not to have been admitted, nor the said proofs, notwithstanding the synodal constitution, which permits those exceptions to be opposed against the instrument of confession, which is permitted by the municipal statute. But these exceptions are not permitted by the statute, therefore neither by the synodal exception in the forum. Nor similarly are proofs admitted. Secondly, that although they can be opposed, and proved by witnesses, it does not appear that they are proofs of law, which are opposed against the refutations. Nor that the said Io. had the fruits. Thirdly, that although this appeared, it does not appear that it is proved that the said Io. was enriched by the donation of such fruits, and d. B. was impoverished, which is necessarily required, that such a donation be valid, as l. de his. C. de do. et l. quod aut sunt. ff. de do. inter vir. et in multis. ll. illius ti.

† In response to the aforesaid, it is answered: and first, regarding that which is said about the accumulation of several rights, it is answered that this is true when they are contrary and are extinguished by election, and in one of which an exception of res iudicata arises, while in the other it does not, as stated in the aforementioned §. eligere. Otherwise, accumulation is admitted: as is the case in our present matter, where Dynus, in the rule Nullus, under the second heading on contrariety, states that in the aforementioned circumstances there is no contrariety.

For sometimes such qualities, namely filial fear in fraud of usury, or that they were null, as in the well-known case: because I say that the donation does not avail by the law itself. Then, although I add afterwards that the act was also simulated through fear in fraud of usury and celebrated under a condition, I do not for this reason seem to say that the act is valid, but that the act ought to be rescinded, for what is ordained for the purpose of impugning cannot operate its validity: as in the law *Siue haereditatem*, D. de negotiis gestis; and according to Doctorus in the rule *Quod ob gratiam*. Rather, I seem to say that it does not avail.

† Hence, if I state that a prelate alienated church property without the required solemnity, and thus it is void by operation of law (ipso iure), as in c. Secundum, Extra, 12 q. 2, and Auth. Hec, P. Portet; even if I subsequently add that it was also done by act, l. Quod simulata, I do not thereby appear to be saying that it is valid, but rather that it must be rescinded. For if an alienation made without observing solemnity is void by operation of law, when it is done through fear, as noted in the gloss in c. Abbas, Quod metus causa, al. 15 q. 6, c. 1, Extra, De iureiurando, c. Peruenit, and Quod me, Cau.; if I say that a testament made in the presence of two witnesses is void by operation of law, even if I add that it was made under fear, and c., I do not thereby say that it is valid, but that it must be rescinded. Indeed, more strongly, that it is void by operation of law. And that I can say an act is null and celebrated under fear, seems to be the case in c. Dilectus, Quod met. cau., thus inducing the point, namely, that the transfer from one religious order to another is a certain contract of partnership, and thus a contract bonae fidei, as in Inst. De actionibus, §. Act. And thus, fraud giving cause to such a contract renders the contract null, as in l. Eleganter, in principio, ff. De dolo, 12 q. 2, c. Si quis episcopus, in fine. And in [the case where] I can say the transfer was made by fraud and fear, I am not said to be contradictory, nor does a libel precede, which is clear: because it is defined, as in the aforementioned c. Dilectus, that otherwise it would not be tolerated; because no definitive sentence is pronounced upon an ill-conceived libel, as in c. Examinata. When, through such qualities, fear and simulation are valid, namely, that by adding them I appear to say that the act is valid, but must be rescinded by the action quod metus causa and other competent actions, as in c. Ad audientiam, Quod met. cau., and this is the gloss in c. Abbas, c. Ei, and l. Metus, §. Sed quo ait praetor, ff. eo. tit. Moreover, that the aforementioned libel precedes, is proven. For either you say that this contract arises nevertheless on account of those qualities simultaneously accumulated, and then [there is no contradiction]: because all render the contract rescindable, therefore no contrariety. Or you say that this contrariety arises from the accumulation of the aforementioned qualities, and that I say the contract is null by operation of law; and then similarly there is no contrariety: and this for the aforementioned reason. And that the aforementioned matters can be simultaneously accumulated in the same libel,

† And to say that the contract is null, and that it was simulated under duress and conditionally, in fraud of usury, is proved by the laws and the canon. Therefore, that it may be said in the same libel that the contract is null and celebrated under duress, is proved by Gratian in the cited chapter *Abbas*, and it appears to be the case in the chapter *Dilectus*. And that it may be said to be null and conditional, is proved in the case *Exhibita*, Extra, *De rerum permutatio*. That it may be said that the contract is null and usurious, is proved in chapter 1 and chapter *Debitores*, Extra, *De iureiurando*. That it may be said that the contract is null, simulated, conditional, and made in fraud of usury, is proved, Extra, *De emptione et venditione*, chapter *Ad nostram*, and chapter *Illo vos*, *De pignoribus*. Therefore, it is clear that there is no contradiction among the aforementioned points; otherwise, the cumulation would not proceed, as stated in § *Eligere* and chapter *Ut quis duas*, *De prebendis*, Book 6.

Furthermore, that it may be said that the contract is null and simulated, is proved in the law *Etiam si uxori*, Codex, *De donationibus*, and the law *Creditor*, in the same title, and the law *Si non verum*, and the law *Si filii tui*. Or, alternatively, when I say that the donation is null and does not hold, because it was made between husband and wife, and I ask that it be declared null, and also that it was celebrated under duress, simulation, and condition, for the sake of delay, and in fraud of usury, and I ask that it be rescinded on competent grounds, then perhaps it could be said that I am contradictory. And thus the opposition is understood. Or even, I say that in this case I can say that I am not contradictory, because words must be understood according to the subject matter. Hence, although they ask that a null act be rescinded, the word "rescinded" must be explained, and it must be shown to be rescinded, as in chapter *Secus viam* and chapter *In Genesi*, *De electione*, and it is the gloss in chapter *Cum dilectus*, in the same title, and chapter *Auditis*, and *De rebus ecclesiasticis*, law *Si quis presbyterum*.

Sometimes I say that the donation is null, and I ask that it be declared null, or even that I say it does not hold, having been celebrated under duress or similar circumstances, etc. I do not say that the agreements are to be rescinded on competent grounds, etc., but only ask that it be decreed that it was made by simulation and under duress. And then I am not contradictory; rather, all these things stand together, since I do not ask for rescission. For it is possible that a contract which is null is also simulated and celebrated under duress, for which the laws cited above support.

Secondly, for the part of Lady G., heir of John, let the aforementioned refutations be read. But it is responded that they are not valid, nor do they in any way obstruct, due to the aforementioned authorities. And if it is said that the said Lady B. should not have been admitted against the said refutations to oppose such exceptions, nor to make such proofs, notwithstanding the synodal constitution,

† which provides that, against an instrument of confession in the ecclesiastical court, only those exceptions shall be admitted which are admitted in the secular forum according to the form of the statute: but the aforementioned exceptions, and proofs against the said refutations, are not admitted according to the form of the statute in the secular forum; therefore, they ought not to have been admitted in the ecclesiastical forum according to the form of the constitution. Nevertheless, the intention of B. is not founded in law, because it is legally proven that the said John received the said fruits, nor that the said John became richer by the donation of the said fruits, and B. poorer. To each of the aforementioned points, it is responded as follows. First, as to the first point, in two ways; and first, that although it is true in the secular forum, it is otherwise in the ecclesiastical forum. Indeed, such exceptions ought to be admitted on account of justice denied by the statute: as in c. Licet, de foro competenti; and c. Noverint, extra de iudiciis. Nor does it avail if it is said that the synodal constitution also prohibits this; because although one constitution seems to prohibit this, another seems to permit it: or say, that the statute and the synodal constitution speak by way of action (via agendi): when opposed by way of exhibition (via exhibendi) to impede execution. But by way of action, the synodal constitution, which is of strict law, does not prohibit. And thus it has place in the case which it expressly mentions, but not in another: as in l. Quicquid astringendae, ff. de verbis obligatis; and c. Cum dilectus, extra de successionibus ab intestato. And thus it will have place when, by way of excommunication, one wishes to oppose against an instrument other exceptions than those permitted by the statute in the secular forum. Otherwise, however, if by way of action: as in our case, which is a case omitted by the synodal constitution; and thus we remain in the disposition of the common law, by which such things may well be opposed by way of action: as by the laws above alleged. For which, l. Commodissimi; and l. Si vero, §. De viro, ff. soluto matrimonio. Nor does the rule obstruct, that to whom an exception is denied, action is more strongly denied: as in l. Nec intentio. Because that rule is not simply true: as in c. Debitores, extra de iureiurando, with many similar cases. Or say, that this rule has place when an exception is prohibited by common law, which receives a broad interpretation: as in l. De quibus, C. de delegatis. Otherwise, if by municipal statute, which receives a strict interpretation. Second, that although, notwithstanding the statute and the synodal constitution, other exceptions than those permitted by the statute, which render the contract invalid, cannot be opposed; nevertheless, exceptions which render it null, or which lead to nullity on account of revocation made by disposition of law, or which prevented the contract from having effect: as is the case here, that the donation never had effect on account of the death of John, may well be opposed,

† because exceptions of nullity, although not permitted by statute, may well be opposed, as the glossa states in c. 1, de sequestro possessorio et fructuario, in the Clementines; and as is noted in l. 2, ff. de poenis; and as is noted in l. si quis excusato, § si quis condemnatus; and according to Bartolus in l. diuus Traianus, ff. de testamento militis; and as is noted by Baldus in l. 3, ff. de negotiorum gestione; and it follows from what is noted in l. non erit, § dato, ff. de iureiurando. And the reason is that when a statute says that no exception may be opposed against an instrument except such and such, it is required that the instrument subsist in law. For by the term "instrument" is understood an instrument that has subsequently obtained legal validity, for which see l. 4, § condemnatum, ff. de iudicibus; and it is understood as an instrument celebrated between persons who are legally capable, as in l. 1, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, there: "let each one have," although the word "capable" is understood, for which see l. cum testamentum, ff. de probationibus. Since, therefore, the aforementioned refutations are useful, as appears above, it follows that the statute has no place in these matters; otherwise one would have to say that an exception could not be opposed against an instrument made by a ward and a madman, since that exception is not permitted by the statute, which is absurd, as stated in the aforementioned l. habeat and l. cum cesset, and c. cum dilectus, extra de successionibus ab intestato. As to the third point, namely, that it is not legally proven that the said John receives the fruits, rather it is proven, as I said above, that although it is said that faith should not be given to the aforementioned Bartolus and other witnesses, because they are laborers,
† And because they perceive an advantage, in that they are released from the restitution of fruits. The said B. I. responds in a twofold manner. First, that there is no opposition.

Secondly, because he cannot challenge them on account of their persons: since the opposing party produced them as witnesses in the same case, and thus approved of their persons, therefore, etc., as in c. *presentium*, Extra, *de testibus*; and as noted by Bartolus in l. *post legatum*, *de his qui ut indigentes*; and especially since there is no prohibition in law that laborers cannot testify, therefore, etc., as in l. 1, D. *de legibus* 3. To the other point, it is replied that it is not true that the wife derives benefit therefrom, because this is not the principal purpose of the action, nor is there any benefit involved: as in c. *cum dilectus*, Extra, *de ordine cognitionis*. Therefore, from this judgment it cannot be said that they derive benefit, and in another judgment their statements would not carry weight, which would be against them on account of the rule *res inter alios acta*, etc. Thirdly, it must be replied that even if they were to derive benefit, their testimony is nevertheless valid, because they would derive this benefit secondarily, not principally. And we should not consider that which is secondary, but that which is principal: as in l. 1, D. *de origine iuris*, and there by Bartolus and the gloss. And nevertheless the testimony is valid, even if they derive benefit secondarily. This is clear in Inst. *de testamentis*, § *in legatis* and § *qui testamento* in principio, C. *de testibus*, where the legatee testifies in the testator’s case, even though he derives benefit secondarily; for which supports the law *si duo patroni*, D. *de iureiurando*, and by the doctors in l. 1, D. *solutis matrimonii*.

As to the other point, which is said, that it is not proven that the said John is richer from such donation, and that the fruits are not consumed, I reply to the second point that indeed they are not consumed, because this has not been alleged nor proven, and consumption is a matter of fact, which is not presumed: as in § *factis*. Nor does l. *qui tutores* object, because the case there is different. As to the first point, it is replied that indeed it is presumed by law that the said John is richer from the perception of the said fruits, because he would have spent the same amount of his own, and the said lady B. is made poorer, because she has less of her own, therefore poorer, as in l. *ea quae*, D. *de donationibus*; and this is especially presumed, unless it is proven on the part that those fruits were spent and converted into some cause, from which it appears that the husband is not enriched, as in l. *quod autem*, post-principio, *de donationibus*. For this, the law *de populo*, D. *de solutionibus*, and l. *is cui bonis*, D. *de nova*, in the gloss, are most apt. Moreover, from the fact that he does not appear richer, he is nevertheless bound, because they are consumed against the will of lady B., which is presumed: because it is not likely that lady B. wished to squander her money. *de probationibus*, l. *cum de indebito*. And especially since women are the most avaricious kind, and especially it is not presumed that they consent to things tending to their household: as in l. *si stipulata*, D. *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, unless the contrary is proven, which is not in our case, since indeed the contradiction of lady B. to the consumer is proven by witnesses, namely Contuciolus and her servant Symonella, who say on the 11th argument that insofar as John predeceased, she did not wish to be able to claim the said fruits from the heir of the said John. By these words she seems to protest that such fruits should not be consumed. In the meantime, I hold my proposition. Moreover, the laws which say that the husband makes his own the fruits consumed and perceived from goods, speak of fruits perceived from paraphernal goods. And this is in compensation for the labor which he sustains in the perception of fruits and cultivation of possessions: otherwise in paraphernal goods, such as those goods which the woman retains for herself and does not commit to the administration of the husband, for which l. *si*, C. *de pactis conventis*, with the gloss. Because fruits perceived from such goods he is bound to restore: as in l. *si*, D. *ad legem Falcidiam*. There is a triple distinction in the patrimony: one is dotal, the fruits of which the husband makes his own, as in l. *fructus* and l. *divisione* and other laws placed there, D. *solutis matrimonii*; another is paraphernal patrimony, as spoken of in the said l. *si*, C. *de pactis conventis*; another is free patrimony, the administration of which has not been given to the husband, and the said l. *si*, D. *ad legem Falcidiam*, speaks of this. And that there is a difference between paraphernal and other goods, is also clear from the gloss in l. *si maritus*, D. *de procuratoribus*, and from the gloss in the said l. *si*, *de pactis conventis*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Which fruits the husband acquires, and which he is bound to restore.
2. A donation causa mortis becomes void if the donee dies before the donor, and the fruits of the intervening period are to be restored; and what if the donation is thus sworn, or a donation between husband and wife, whether it is confirmed by oath.
3. The exception of the incapacity of persons is not understood to be removed by a statute prohibiting all exceptions whatsoever.
4. A bill of complaint containing multiple grounds for nullity is upheld.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Donation

A gift causa mortis is converted into a cause of action if the donee dies before the donor, as stated in C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, in fine, and l. non omnis, ff. si certum petatur; and the fruits of the intervening period must be restored, according to l. cum quis, ff. de conditione ob causam, and in other cases, l. in superioribus allegata. Nor does an oath stand in the way. For a gift causa mortis is reduced to the nature of a last will, which, although sworn, is clearly deemed caducous by its very nature, C. de non numerata pecunia, l. fin.

† A donation between husband and wife proceeds in a similar manner: for if the donee predeceases, the law revokes it and converts it into the cause of caducity. And therefore there is no perjury here: because it is not an act of man, but of the law. C. de donat. inter virum et vxorem, l. a marito; and note ff. de legatis 1, l. talis scriptura; and through Cynus in l. 1, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis. Lord Federicus of Siena in his consilia, consilium 135, seems to wish that such a donation is understood to be made by oath and immediately valid: because he says that the donor cannot afterwards donate that thing to another. And thus it certainly does not matter whether the donor or the donee predeceases. This does not seem true: because one thing is whether it can be revoked by the donor who swore; another is if the donee predeceases, and thus it is converted into the cause of caducity.

† The exception of the unfitness of persons is not understood to be removed, even though the statute says that no exception can be raised against the instrument: because it is understood to be about fit persons, as in l. ut gradatim. §. et si lege. with similar cases.

† A petition containing several grounds of nullity, and aptly conceived, is upheld, and it suffices to prove one of them, as is stated and noted in the Code, On contracting sale, l. si mater tua. And the reason is: because several concurrent grounds of nullity do not diminish one another. Digest, On the institution of heirs, l. si non lex elies. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, and I have subscribed to the truth and affixed my seal; I do not dispute, however, regarding the acquisition of fruits: because in this point it is presupposed that there was no act of acquiring, except by a simple donation, as will be shown later. And thus we are not in this matter. l. ult. C. de pac. conuen. with its gloss. Therefore, the aforementioned fruits, taken in honor of marriage and for more abundant living expenses, are said to have been consumed and are to be restored. Digest, On donations between husband and wife, l. si stipulata, § 1; Digest, On the Falcidian law, l. penult. In this doubt, however, whether they have been consumed as among household members and between spouses, and thus are not to be restored, or whether they have been converted to other uses of the husband, let the discerning and good judge consider.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father makes a will, by which he institutes his son as universal heir and substitutes his daughter to him, if she does not request a guardian for her brother within a year; whether she is deprived of the inheritance.
1. Whether the son is presumed to know his father's will, etc.
2. One may allege such a fact, or quality, from which, or by which, ignorance results.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Peter Lombard, summoned by Lady Lita in an action for the recovery of an inheritance, states that it cannot be imputed to Lady Bartolina, who was substituted in her father’s will, that she did not seek a guardian for the instituted minor heir, because she was ignorant of her father’s will and of the fact that she had been substituted; therefore, the one-year period does not run against her, as provided in the law *Annus* and in the principle that ignorance of another’s fact is presumed, as stated in the rule *Cum quis in ius alterius* and noted in the law *Sed et si me praesente*, D. de conditione indebiti. Moreover, because a daughter, by reason of her filial relationship, is presumed to be ignorant of the will and content with its provisions, as held in the law *Eius, qui in provincia* and in the case *Cum si*, and according to the doctrine of Bartolus in § *Duo fratres*.

But it seems to the contrary: namely, that this daughter is presumed to have known the said testament and to have been content with it. And first: because there is a gloss in *l. cum heres*, D. de lib. leg. Secondly: because even those things which are forbidden by the father to be opened during the life of the son concerning the father’s last will, the son is nevertheless presumed to know, as in *l. quidam ita*, § *si quis filium*, D. ad Treb. Moreover, the gloss, resolving the contrary, expressly affirms that in the son knowledge of the testament and of the father’s last will is presumed, and it admits the reason: because the father and the son are considered the same person, as in Auth. de iureiur. a moriente praestito. Therefore, by reason of this fictitious identity of persons, knowledge of acts performed by the father in the person of the son is presumed. Moreover, a blood relative is presumed to know the acts of blood relatives, as in *l. Octavi* and *l. de tutela*. Therefore, this daughter is presumed to have known the said paternal testament. Moreover, by reason of cohabitation, presumed knowledge of acts performed by those with whom one cohabits is induced, as noted in *c. postquam*, Extr. de elect. Therefore, from the cohabitation of the father and the daughter, it is presumed that the daughter knew the said testament. Moreover, when an act is done in the house of habitation, or notification is made to the house, knowledge of those present in the house is presumed, as in *l. de pupillo*, § *si quis ipsi praetori*. Therefore, since the said testament was made in the house of the said testator, in which the said daughter dwelt, it is presumed that the daughter knew the said testament and was content with it. Moreover, by reason of neighborhood, not to mention cohabitation, knowledge of acts performed is presumed, as noted by Bartolus in *l. 1*, D. sic rerum pet. and noted in *c. quosdam in Africa*, de praesum. and in *l. domini horreorum*. Therefore, by reason of the cohabitation, cohabitation, and neighborhood of this daughter with the father, and in the father’s house, knowledge of the said testament is presumed. And if it is said that this cohabitation, cohabitation, and neighborhood do not appear, here calumniously alleged, nevertheless it can be answered that this cohabitation is presumed, as you alleged yesterday, lest otherwise a harsh separation be induced, which is not presumed, as C. com. utriusque iud. *l. possessionum*, with similar. Moreover, when an impediment of fact exists, time runs even for the ignorant, as fully noted by Cynus in *l. quotiens*, D. de precib. imp. off. But this not knowing the testament, or the contents of the testament, is an impediment of fact, not of law; therefore, time runs against the ignorant. Now it remains to respond to the said Bartolus and to *l. eius qui in provincia*, with similar. And I say that the said law and the said Bartolus have place with regard to the acquisition of the inheritance, in which knowledge or ignorance of the testament are not considered, since by the disposition of the law of suitability, acquisition of the inheritance is effected by the law itself; but in an outsider, knowledge of the testament and its force is required, so that it may be entered upon, and therefore knowledge is presumed in an outsider after the inheritance has been entered upon, because otherwise he could not have entered upon it. But as regards other acts, namely legacies and fideicommissa, and guardianship, Bartolus does not say, nor does *l. eius qui in provincia*, that ignorance is presumed, and in his own case. Moreover, to *l. eius qui in provincia*, it can be answered that that ignorance, of which mention is made there, denotes the contingency of fact, and not the ministry of the law. And thus Balduinus said there. Moreover, there it speaks of a necessary or his own person being absent, whence indeed if ignorance is presumed in an absent person, of which mention is made there, as in *c. cognoscentis*, de const. per gl. Moreover, in our case, this daughter, Lady Bartolutia, did not have suitability at the time of her father’s death; because according to the form of the statute, a daughter can be dowered, in the testament anything can be left to her, therefore it is clear that she can be passed over and disinherited, and she must be content with the legacy of the dowry alone. Therefore, it is clear that she is called an outsider: and consequently knowledge is presumed according to the doctrine of Bartolus, and thus Bartolus does not argue against, but for. Moreover, it was articulated by the said Peter that the said Blasius, father of the said Lady Bart., made a testament and substitution, and it is articulated at the end that of the aforesaid there is public voice and fame. Therefore, it is presumed that the said Lady Bartolutia knew: because of those things of which there is public fame, knowledge is presumed, and ignorance cannot be alleged, as noted by the gloss in *l. si tutor*, C. de peric. tut. and Bartolus in d. § *duo fratres*. From the foregoing, therefore, it is concluded that the said Lady Bartolu. is presumed to have known the said testament and substi. fac. by her brother, Lord Blasius, notwithstanding the allegations.

I believe the contrary to be true, for even assuming that as regards knowledge to be presumed there is no difference between one’s own and an outsider, whatever Balduinus says, nevertheless before the commission of the act and the intent, knowledge is not presumed, as noted by Balduinus in *l. eius qui in provincia*, near the end. Moreover, knowledge is presumed: either because present at the act; or because protested; or public fame. Of none of these is there articulation, nor proof. And if it is said, it is presumed that she was in the house, therefore it is presumed that she knew: true, if such is the act that it cannot be done in any part of the house without coming to the knowledge of all in the house, as an acclamation, which the lord makes, as he is struck, as noted D. ad Sil. *l.* But the act of testating can be done secretly in one chamber, indeed it is presumed that the substitution is made secretly, whence unless it is proved that at the time of the making of the testament she was present at the act of testating, ignorance is presumed: especially in a woman, in whom ignorance of law is more easily presumed, as noted by Bartolus in *l. si*, C. de iur. et fact. ign. This, however, is true, unless she could have consulted those more expert: as *l. iur. igno.*, C. qui admi. ad bo. pos. Let your subtlety and knowledge see and supply the rest. Nevertheless, here it must be seen whether the ignorance of this Lady Bartolutia can now be alleged by Peter, since ignorance or knowledge of men is a matter of notice. And especially because she does not say that she was ignorant, and her intent is not presumed, nor can it be known by this Peter except by externals, which do not appear; but for now I omit it. Now object what was said above: namely, it is articulated that Blasius at such time made a testament. Also that under such form: so that the inheritance pertains to this mother, and first two things are confessed. Also articulated that of the aforesaid there was and is public voice and fame. Response is given regarding the confession. He credits, he denies; not therefore. If it is public fame, knowledge is presumed by the said *l. si tutor*, D. de periculo tut. To this I answer: because although it is articulated regarding the form of the testament, it is not specifically regarding the substitution. Namely, that the said sister was substituted, but that the substitution was made *de stirpe*, or these are words of law and doubtful, as to how they ought to be understood, whence this sister was ignorant that she was substituted: because she did not know that this was imported by that word, *in stirpe*. Therefore, ignorance of law excuses her. d. *l. si*. And if it is said, she could have consulted those more expert. I answer, she was not bound, nor ought she to have: because while the ward was living, she ought not to hope for the case and adverse fortune of him. And if it is said, rather because we see this in the mother, in whom there is a greater presumption that the son will survive her according to the course of nature: as *l. nam et si parentibus*. And yet the mother, unless she petitions within a year, is deprived of succession, nor is she excused on this account. For to this I answer that it does not object, because the mother ought to believe and know that which the law presumes, namely, that she will succeed intestate. But the sister ought not to believe that she is substituted: because the law does not presume this, as noted by Balduinus in *l. suo consiliorum*, in consilio iri. and alleges D. de usuc. *l. non solum*, § *vulgo*, ver. *hoc amplius*.

† Furthermore, the objection raised lastly, that this party cannot allege the ignorance of another, does not hold; for on the contrary, he may do so, or rather, he may allege the fact or quality from which such ignorance results. For when the law presumes something, or presumes upon that which consists in one’s own mind, and must be alleged, nevertheless that which the law presumes must be alleged. D. de adulteriis, l. si adulterium cum incestu, § 1. Or, if it consists in the mind of another, then it suffices to allege the quality from which that which the law presumes is inferred; as in l. omnes, § Lucius, D. quae in fraudem creditorum. Thus says Baldus on the same book, in l. quod adhibitus, C. qui sibi ascribunt. The case at hand is thus: for the law presumes that he who succeeds to the right of another has a just cause for ignorance, as in c. cum in ius, supra alleg., and in l. fin., pro suo modo. Since this pertains to the mind of another, namely, that which the aforementioned Peter alleges, it suffices to allege the quality from which this is inferred, as he does; for he states that this succession occurs by substitution of substance to Blasius, and thus to the right of another.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. A paterfamilias, having four male sons, instituted them as heirs and also provided dowries for two daughters in his will; he substituted the aforementioned male sons, and finally, in the last place, he substituted in this manner: if all the aforementioned male sons should die without legitimate issue, the said goods shall devolve and ought to be in the stirpes. Finally, after the testator died, the sons die successively, and one of the aforementioned daughters dies. Finally, after the sixteenth month from the death of the testator, this fourth son dies in pupillary age, since no tutor had been appointed in the will, nor was any requested to be appointed; he now remains above 25 years of age. Moreover, the uncle and the sister are litigating for the right to the inheritance, through the inheritance of this last deceased son. The case was concluded, and it does not appear whether that sister was of age or a minor. Nor does it appear that she knew or was ignorant of her father’s death. And it does not appear when the year granted to her for requesting a tutor begins to run. However, the contrary was opposed in court before the conclusion of the case against the mother herself, namely, that she and that sister were not the heirs, and that the mother, even if that sister was of age, is excluded because a tutor was not requested. It is asked whether this opposes the mother, namely, what is opposed regarding the sister’s right and also regarding the tutor not being requested. And if this does not oppose, whether the mother can obtain victory in this judgment.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To whom the inheritance of the last deceased son is to be awarded, given the existence of a substitution and the like: whether to the mother, to the sister, or to the uncle of the said minor who died in pupillary age.
2. Whether the person to whom the inheritance is awarded is deprived of succession on account of not having requested a tutor.
3. Whether ignorance of the paternal testator is presumed in the sons.
4. Who is bound to request a tutor, and within what period of time he is bound to make such request.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having seen and considered the above points narrated in order, three matters arise for investigation. First, to whom the inheritance of the said son, the last to die, was devolved: whether to the sister, to the mother, or to the uncle of the succeeding son. Second, whether the person to whom it was devolved for his benefit is deprived of it for not having requested a guardian within the time established by law. Third, whether the penalty for not requesting a guardian passes from one degree to another, and what period of time it induces for mere exclusion.

† Regarding the first point, it seems that a brief statement of the law is required, to the effect that the said sister is admitted to the inheritance to the exclusion of the others: because the son who died last passed away in pupillary age, and from this pupillary substitution contained in the summary will—since it was not entirely tacit, but at least expressed in general words suitable to comprehend a pupillary substitution—succession takes place by means of the substitution, even to the exclusion of the mother, as noted by the gloss in *Lucius*, D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione; and in *Si*, C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus; in *Precibus*, in the gloss *Si magna*, in the verse *Item nota*. And if it is said that in the aforementioned substitution no mention was made of the appellative name, i.e., of the daughter, I say that it is equivalent: because those words “come into” and “ought to be in the stock,” and the substitutions appended to the aforementioned ones, comprehend the said daughter both according to the common law and according to the presumed intention of the testator: because all direct lines, and not those proceeding from the collateral line, are said to be of the stock: as in C. de inofficioso testamento, *Si quis in suo*; C. de naturalibus liberis, *Cum quis*; and the text in both places supports what is noted by the gloss in D. de consanguinitate et affinitate, *Quod lectio*; and C. *Si*, in the same title. Secondly, this is supported, as stated, by the presumed intention of the testator, which has primary place in conditional dispositions, and orders and disposes them: as in *In conditionibus primum locum*, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. No one is presumed to prefer the successions of strangers to his own, as in C. de fideiussoribus, *Cum acutissimi*; C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, *Generaliter*. And this concludes the first point. Regarding the second point,

† from which I assumed the status, namely, the inheritance of the substitution having been offered to the sister: it must be considered whether the negligence of not requesting a tutor induces deprivation of the said status. And it seems that it does not: because it does not appear that she knew of her father’s death: and time does not run against one who is ignorant: as in l. 1, § biduum, D. quando appellatio sit; in the gloss on the word “sententiae latae” at the end, and there it is stated. Also, because it does not appear that she knew of the said substitution, and in doubt ignorance is presumed: because he errs most justly who is not proven to have seen the will. D. de interdictis et actionibus, l. de aetate, § ex causa. To the contrary, the truth seems to be, namely, that the said sister is deprived of the said inheritance for not having requested a tutor within a year: as in l. sciant, C. de legatis hereditatibus non ob. [notwithstanding] what is alleged to the contrary regarding ignorance:

† Because knowledge is truly presumed, or knowledge of the will and of the matters contained therein, one must resort to presumptions; for by presumptions knowledge is sometimes proved, as if at the time the will was made the son or daughter was in the house where the will was made; because household members are presumed to know what is done in the house. C. de rep. l. consensu. §. super. unless the will was made under a secret seal. i. inscrip. vt inst. de pup. subst. §. sinaute quis. Sometimes ignorance is proved by presumptions: as if the son was in a distant country, so that notice of the will could not reach him except by messenger or letters. ff. si cer. pe. l. eius, qui in prouincia. ff. de admi. tu. l. quidam decedens. §. ex quo innotuit. But if nothing appears from presumptions, ignorance is presumed. C. de pericu. tu. l. si tutor. C. de iure deli. l. quam sororem. et l. verius. de proba. cum si. In our case, however, knowledge is presumed, since at the time of the said conditional will the said daughter was in the house in which the said will was made. Therefore, if the said sister did not demand a tutor within a year, she is deprived of the succession by operation of law. ff. ad turpil. l. 2. §. si mater. et C. qui pe. tu. l. fi. Nor does it avail against the foregoing that it does not appear that she was of age; because she is presumed to be of age. C. de in integ. rest. mi. l. si minorem te. extra de proba. c. in pręsentia. in gl. pe. et no. C. de probat. l. cum de. Just as we say regarding a procurator, who is presumed to be of age unless he appears to be a minor from his appearance, as there by Cyn. And it supports what is noted regarding a minor in l. de aetate.

I come to the third point, and indeed, although the sister is excluded because she did not request a tutor, the mother is also excluded, since she subsequently neglected to request a tutor for four months: as stated in l. 2, § confestim, D. ad Tertium non obvenientem; and in l. sciant, D. de legitimis heredibus. For although that law speaks generally, it must be understood to apply to other legitimate successors, not to the mother, because it seems more imputable to the mother than to others if she neglects the interests of her children. C. qui petunt tutelam, l. matris pietas. And this is apparent, because she is required to request a curator for the unborn child, where the period of one year does not run. D. ad Tertium, l. 2, § si cum pregnans. Hence, it does not seem that more than one year can be granted to the mother, but rather a shorter space of time. And this is held by Bartolus in the aforementioned § confestim, and in l. 3, D. qui petunt tutelam.

But the truth seems to be to the contrary: namely, that the equity of the law grants the mother a full year, on account of the word "cuncti" (all), which is found in the aforementioned l. sciant, which is universal; because he who says "all" excludes no one. And this opinion is held by my aforementioned father in l. precibus, and he says it is more equitable.

I consider that in this matter the laws speak precisely. For the constitution of the Divine Severus says that if the mother did not request immediately, she falls from the succession of the impubes. D. qui petunt tutelam, l. 2, § diuus. Another law explained this word "immediately," which is understood as when first possible in law and in fact, as in the aforementioned § confestim. Another law says that the mother's diligence is required in requesting tutors. D. qui petunt tutelam, l. 1. Another, that a diligent office is demanded. C. qui petunt tutelam, l. cum matribus. Another law says that the mother is required to request curators for the unborn child; it is not sufficient to request for the child once born, even if it is born within the year: as is evidently hinted there. This also seems to be held by Richardus de Malevisis. Therefore, it seems that if the mother is in mere notable negligence for several months, she ought to be repelled from the succession, nor would it relieve the mother, even if it appeared that she had managed the affairs of the impubes in the meantime; because the management must be with the title of guardianship, not de facto: as noted in the aforementioned § confestim, in the gloss quod potuit.

On the contrary, I believe the truth to be: namely, that whenever the mother requests a tutor within the year, she succeeds by the disposition of the law nouerunt, as in the aforementioned l. sciant. Indeed, even by the laws, a term of one year is appointed in the aforementioned § confestim. And I argue thus: either such a term of one year is added to the one who is unable, and this is false; because no term runs for him. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. 3, § si ad diem. Or to the one who is able and negligent: then it has its purpose; because delay can be purged within the year. Hence, that text, § confestim, is not understood as referring to an impediment that does not exceed one year, but to the omission of requesting. That is, that one cannot omit beyond one year without the penalty of deprivation of inheritance. But others say that the lapse of one year induces a presumption of law, and in law against the mother, so that she is presumed to be in delay, and cannot prove an impediment. Which, with all due respect, does not seem true according to l. cum a matribus. It is supported by 2. q. 1, c. annorum, concerning him who must pursue an appeal within a year, to whom it is not imputed if it did not depend on him. And in him who must be promoted to priesthood within a year, to whom the year itself does not run if he was detained by a just impediment and could not be promoted. Extr. de electione, c. commissa, § 1, lib. 6.

Furthermore, it seems frivolous also that some say that the law sciant does not speak of the mother, since it speaks generally, as in C. de administratione tutorum, l. si, § personis. And there is not greater delay on the part of the mother than of others, especially on account of her sex. Furthermore, succession is owed to her by a quasi-natural law. I therefore put that the law sciant speaks even of the mother. And it also tacitly makes mention of the laws speaking of the mother, which it extends to all successors, and appends the term of one year, not to the beginning of the request. And thus it is understood by the aforementioned Richardus de Malevisis. But the excuse of the mother, if she requested within the year, and thus it is understood that what is said of the year applies even to the requesting of possession of goods, where she has one year. l. 1, § largius. And thus let her be excused by analogy: and in this case. For inheritance and guardianship are correlative. D. de rerum divisione, l. quo tutela. But the law sciant could be explained thus, according to others: "Know that if they did not request a tutor within one year, or before, when they first could." It does not seem well said, because according to this, the mention of the year would be made in vain. And therefore, and more truly, and more equitably, I hold what I said. That is, that the mother has a full year to request a tutor, or to accept guardianship. And if it is said that more is required of the mother: on the contrary, more is also owed to her. And for this part I allege a singular text speaking of the mother and granting her a year, Inst. ad Tertium, § sed quemadmodum, § si. Even that which seems to determine this question, and also in l. 2, C. si adversus delictum.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a judgment rendered after the expiration of the term is void, and when it is valid.
2. An interlocutory judgment ordering entry into possession, or holding by hand, is void if no proof has preceded it, even if proof is subsequently produced.
3. Whether a judgment can be confirmed by the appellate judge.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† That sometimes a time limit is imposed upon the judge: and then the suit does not end permanently, but the negligent judge is punished, as in C. omnes causae tamen ciuiles, l. 1. Sometimes a time limit is imposed upon the suit, or the prosecution, and then that which is done afterwards is not valid. ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. consequens; C. de iudicibus, l. properandum. Because a sentence, or prosecution, would be carried out, which is impossible. Sometimes a time limit is imposed both upon the judge and upon justice. And then similarly, by operation of law, it is not valid after the term, because the acts of judicial order have perished. l. cum lite mortua, iudicium solutum. Now in our case, a time limit was fixed for the prosecution, and also for the judge, as I will prove; therefore, the sentence passed afterwards was null by operation of law: as was most wisely alleged by the Lord James de Fornariis of Pisa. I prove that a time limit was imposed upon the litigation: because the statute proceeding further says, and shall not endure further, etc. The statute proceeds further with respect to two things: namely, with respect to the prosecution, that it shall not endure; and with respect to the judge, that he be punished. But if it had proceeded with respect to the judge, and had said nothing about non-endurance: then the sentence would be valid, and this is the truth.

† Furthermore, it must be known that interlocutory orders for entering into possession or for maintaining possession are void by operation of law when no prior proofs have been adduced. The reason is that such orders must be founded upon contumacy; but he against whom nothing has been proven is not contumacious. L. 1, § haec verba, Ne vis fiat ei; L. haec autem, § 1, Quibus ex causis poss. ea. And therefore Innocentius stated that a judge, to whom nothing has been proven, can grant nothing. Extra, De senatu et consiliariis, Excommunicato, c. Solet, in fine. To this effect serves what is noted by Cynus in L. 1, C. De errore calculi. Moreover, the writ of sequestration must be issued according to the measure of the debt declared, as in Auth. De exhibendis reis, § Si vero. And therefore, if no debt has been liquidated, the writ of sequestration lacks a foundation, and it errs in substance and in order; because it is a matter of order that, in such a writ of sequestration, faith be first given to the judge, as has been said. Furthermore, a writ of sequestration ought not to be issued against one who is not bound, unless excussion has been made and a pronouncement rendered thereon; but here no pronouncement was made; therefore, the procedure was irregular. Thus holds Bartolus, ff. De novo operis nuntio, L. Praetor, § Habes. Hence it is clearly concluded that the first sentence was void by operation of law.

But a doubt arises: because this sentence appears to have been confirmed by the appellate judge; for he pronounced that judgment had been rendered well and appeal ill, which sentence appears to be of some effect, although it was issued against the right of the litigant; since the error in the sentence was not expressed. D. de appellationibus, l. si expressum. But certainly that is true when the appellate judge proceeded properly to confirm the sentence. Here, however, he did not proceed properly: because he could not confirm except from what was alleged and proved in the first acts, as in c. appellanti, de appellationibus, in the Clementines. Moreover, this is an intolerable error in the second sentence, just as in the first, subject to the same grounds of nullity: because nothing was proved to the judge to whom the appeal was made; therefore, it was both civilly and irregularly based on fact. See D. unde vi, l. meminerint, and C. si per vim vel alio modo, l. final. Furthermore, a sentence issued by the judge from whom the appeal lies, after the instance has ended, cannot be confirmed; just as one issued by a private person cannot. For when the litigation is dead, the judge is reduced to the status of a private person, unless a new instance is brought, as I have proved above, and it supports what is noted in c. 1, de sequestro, posited in the Clementine, and D. de feriis, l. 1, at the end of the principal part. And therefore I conclude in favor of the said lady Tadea. Moreover, when a sentence is null, and certain acts were performed solely by reason of that sentence, then the appellate judge may judge according to the contents of the sentence; but if everything is null, i.e., the procedure and the acts, because they were conducted at a time when they should not have been, or were not made at all, then confirmation is impossible. C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. prolatam. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A widow who had sworn chastity in the guardianship instrument was deprived of her son’s succession on account of fornication.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. On the first point, I have written on another folio; on this second point concerning this woman, I believe that she previously renounced the guardianship, which is what one who seeks a guardian does. Therefore, I assert that a guardian was not sought from her, since her prior renunciation gave rise to the cause under the edict. He had sexual intercourse with her, indeed on the presumption of her being his mother, and before a guardian was sought: because he was alone with her alone.
