And because nature impels a man to be alone with a woman for these natural motions, and because no reason can be given for why he was alone with her in a chamber, except through most gentle Venus, to which nature compels us for the end of generation and the preservation of the species—just as nature compels the superior elements to the composition of a mixture, although they are natural—nevertheless, this is also confirmed by the laws, whether we presume marriage, as in D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. in liberis, or adultery; immediately the mother fell from guardianship, although the glossa says the contrary, namely that a widow does not lose guardianship of her son through adultery, because it is not provided for by law. However, Jacobus de Belvisio, in Auth. de restitutione, and in ea quae parit undecimo mense, §. si, holds that she is deprived of it by operation of law, which is the more correct view, because in the instrument of guardianship she had promised chastity by her own oath, which she did not observe. In doubt, an honest presumption is to be believed, and it is the truth itself, because on account of honesty it is to be believed, D. pro socio, l. merito. And the statement of the canonists has no place with regard to guardianships. The discreet opinion of the jurist, which is set forth in the aforementioned l. in liberis, is observed. Hence it appears that, due to the mother’s deprivation, this tutor could not be sought afterwards according to the canons as the adulterer, nor according to the laws as the husband, because he ought to have been sought beforehand, as in Auth. de nuptiis, §. si autem tutela, Collatio 4. And especially upon viewing the statute, which begins, “Item prouisum.” I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Substitution in the person of those who die last is valid.
2. Alienated property is imputed to the legitime.
3. The mother is owed her legitime in the goods of her son.
4. The burdened heir must have his due portion.
5. Property prohibited from alienation may be alienated on the occasion of providing dowries.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the first question

† It is reasonably doubted: whether the substitution is valid in the person of the last to die. And it seems that it is not, by L. sed si sic, §. si aut., de legatis 3. For a fideicommissum cannot be left to an heir of an heir, unless he is burdened as heir of an heir, and not in his own name. But these were not burdened, but only as children, and not as heirs; therefore the fideicommissum is not valid. The contrary is true, namely that the testator instituted the later ones after the earlier ones in successive degrees, and therefore he could burden the last to die: as in ff. de legatis 2, L. peto, §. fratre, and the aforementioned L. sed si sic. And this concludes the first question.
† As to the second point, I say that alienated property is imputed to the legitime, as in no. ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Marcellus, §. res, qu
† As to the third point, I say that the mother must have her legitime, as in the Authentica de trien. et semiss. § 1, and there noted.
† Regarding the fourth point, I say that the heir must have a canonical portion. Extra, De testaments, c. Requisition, with Si.
† Regarding the fifth point, I say that they could be alienated on account of dowries. C. de fideiuss. auth. res, quae.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An appeal must be made from a lower to a higher court; if the appeal appears to have been abandoned, the lower court may enforce its judgment.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The priors of the lands have the power granted to them by the form of the statutes, and no other, unless some rule follows from that which is granted; hence, if indeed the priors choose a husband, in such a way that he requires another confirmation by a superior, an appeal may be made to them in support: because the superiors say that, since they have the power to appoint and to depose with cause.

† And the rule is that an appeal must be made from the lower to the higher authority, as stated in l. 1, ff. de appellationibus, and fully noted in c. 2, de confessionibus, lib. 6. Just as jurisdiction over the hearing belongs to the prior, so too will the adjudication in the appeal case belong to him; if the magistrate who heard the case did not do so with the advice of the council, the council itself shall be the judge to whom the appeal is made. But if the decision is confirmed by the superior, then that confirmation shall be subject to appeal, unless another person has been expressly appointed for this purpose. See Auth. de iudicibus, § appellationis; and C. de appellationibus, l. eos, cum si. And when it is established before the judge from whom the appeal was taken that the appeal has been abandoned, he may enforce his sentence, as noted in C. de appellationibus, l. eos, in principio, and l. si contra, § quamvis, de appellationibus, in cle. and per. Bartolus in l. 1, nil noua, appellatione pendente.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the heirs of the husband can oppose the wife on the ground of adultery in order to recover the dowry, and further in the following opinion.
body: H

† That the aforementioned dowry can be recovered, and thus that a condemnatory judgment should be obtained, appears to be proven. For, in order for the heirs of the husband to be able to raise the defense of the wife’s adultery to prevent the recovery of the dowry, it seems to be required that the husband has convicted the wife. Thus it seems to be the intention of the gloss in Auth. ut nulli iudici §. adulteram and in Auth. ut liberi mariti et aviae §. quia vero plurimos. But the husband did not convict her; therefore, etc. Moreover, it seems that the husband ought to have repudiated her and complained, as in ff. sol. ma. l. rei iudicatae §. 1, ver. morum nostrorum, etc., and as noted there by Dy and Bar. But since he did not do this, therefore, etc. Notwithstanding these arguments, it seems that the contrary should be said. First, under civil law, by l. consensu §. vir quoque, C. de rep.; under canon law, by c. plerunque, extra de dot. inter vir. et ux., where the case of this question appears. And holding this opinion, one could respond to the contrary arguments.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Deciding to the contrary of the same, as was done in the preceding opinion.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This dowry ought to be restored, for the husband, who remained silent for a long time by not accusing his wife of her misconduct, appears to have approved of it, according to the law *rei venditae*, § 1, *solutis matrimonii*, and by your authority. And this applies when the husband knew of the deed; otherwise, perhaps, if he was ignorant of it, as noted by Cynus, Code, *de adulteriis*, law *si*, and Code, *rem in praesenti*, § *taceat*, by Cynus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judgment rendered contrary to the tenor of the instrument is valid; and whether a judgment rendered on a bad cause can be justified by a good one. And see below, opinion 306.
2. Whether a son who has possessed his father's goods is said to have meddled with the inheritance.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

The first reason alleged in the opinion is contrary to the tenor of the instrument, where it says, in every case, etc., joined with the gloss which is in l. dos a patre. The second reason also alleged in the opinion is not very good: because in the promise to cede rights upon the inheritance having been accepted, arg. C. de iure delib. l. si auia. But it must be considered that a judgment rendered on a bad cause can be justified by a good one. ff. quod cum eo. l. Titianus. And therefore, if it is prescribed by common law, or by statute, the appellate judge ought to confirm the judgment of acquittal.

† And although my conscience suggests that the sons accepted the paternal inheritance, and thus there is no prescription of the hypothecary right, as in l. cum notissimi and C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus, §. si; nevertheless, this does not appear from the records, since the sons could have possessed [the property] for the restitution of the maternal dowry, de sol. l. Titiani. And this is stated by Oldradus ad litteram in l. 1, C. de repu. haere. Nor is the son presumed to be an heir with respect to disadvantages, unless it is proven: as noted in l. si cum dotem, §. transgre, sol. ma., in the glossa ordinaria. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Substitutions and fideicommissa made in general terms do not include the own property of the burdened party.
2. The institution of Titius and his descendants, as to what those words import.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is not doubtful that in a fideicommissary substitution made in general terms, the property of the person burdened is not included. ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, § cum filiae. And therefore it must be considered what were the property of Matthew, because the substitution made by Cola, his father, does not extend to them.

† And therefore it must be investigated what it means to say: I institute Cola and his descendants. And Bartolus clarifies the matter, stating that Cola comes first, and the descendants come after him, that is, if Cola does not become heir. For between these there falls an ordered affection, whereby the prior love excludes the latter. D. 28.6.1 (Gallus), § 1, and there fully by Bartolus. Others say that the father and the son come together. D. 7.4.1 (Si quis Titio) and D. 7.4.2 (Si mulieri); and C. 6.28.1 (Si). But according to Jacobus de Arena, either the latter was already born, and thus the affection and love fell upon him, and then they come together; otherwise it cannot be said that this conjunction, "and," is placed rather subjunctionally than principally copulatively, that is, that Cola, the testator's nephew, should have it during his lifetime, and afterwards his descendants should have it; because this is an ordered and due affection, as D. 28.5.1 (Lucius). And this interpretation is friendly to nature. D. 35.2.1 (Cum ita legitur), § In fideicommissis. But arguing from the force of the conjunction properly taken, there would be a division between Cola and Matthew, both during life and at death, since he acquired it for himself. But to me it seems, from the word "descendants," and because Matthew, Cola's son, is not proven to have been in existence at the time of the said Matthew's testament, nor could he then be hoped for with certain hope.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A judgment rendered on the basis of a single false ground may be confirmed by the appellate judge on the basis of a true ground. And see above, consilium 303.
2. Whether a son possessing paternal property is said to have intervened in the inheritance.
3. A son is not presumed to be an heir with respect to disadvantages.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Judgment

A judgment rendered on a single ground that is not true in law may be confirmed by the appellate judge on a true ground. Text, Digest, *Quod cum eo*, l. *Titianus*. And this is the second point. As for the first point, I say,

† But if Io. and Entendolus intermeddled in the paternal inheritance, there is no prescription. C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus; §. si, C. de praescrip. 30 annorum; l. cum notissimi. But if they did not intermeddle, then prescription has run for the hypothecary period of 30 years. But it must be considered: whether it is proved to the minister, because they possessed the paternal goods. And it must be said that if they had no other cause for possessing, they would be deemed to have intermeddled. C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 1. But here they had another cause, namely for the maternal dowry, for which they could possess. Likewise, the goods as if pledged. Thus says Odofredus in the said l. 1. Therefore, if he swore that he held the said goods not with the intention of intermeddling, but for the maternal dowry, they are not presumed to be heirs. And these persons will be safe by the exception of prescription. It supports what is noted by Laurentius de Arena, de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro herede; and noted in ff. de solutione matrimonii, l. si cum dotem, §. transgrediamur.

For a son is not presumed to be an heir with respect to burdens and disadvantages if he abstains from the inheritance, as stated in l. 1; and even if they do not swear, they are not presumed to be heirs, as is evident there. The point of the question, upon which an opinion is requested, is as follows: namely, the lady Masgia and her son Amagias, and each of them jointly and severally, confessed and acknowledged that they had received from Nicolaus, who paid and gave for the dowry, and in the name and cause of the dowry of the lady Cathelina, the sum of one hundred, and they made a donation propter nuptias to the said Nicolaus, who received for his said daughter the sum of 25 florins, which they ought to gain if the said Amagias survives with children or without; and they promised, each of them jointly and severally, to the said Nicolaus, stipulating for his said daughter, to restore and pay the said dowry and donation in every case where the dowry is to be restored and the donation paid; and the obligation and renunciation are in this form: under obligation, etc.; Renunciation, etc.; and the precept to encumber, etc. Notwithstanding the said confession, the aforementioned Nicolaus promised and agreed with the said lady Masgia and Amagias, stipulating for himself and their heirs, to give and pay to them, notwithstanding the aforementioned confession, at the request of any of them, in the will of the said... under obligation, etc. Then, after some years, the said Masgias alone absolved the said Nicolaus from the said... confessing that he had been satisfied according to his will. It is asked, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The benefit of the *lex Velleia* has no application in the case of a dowry.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Suffered

† It is difficult, and consists in understanding. L. viri uxoris, §. si, C. ad Velleianam; and L. si non singuli, C. si certum petatur; and L. si id, quod ego, De duobus reis. And it is certain that the benefit of the Velleian Law has no place in dowry. C. ad Velleianam, L. si. Furthermore, it is certain that since nothing was promised to this woman, she intervened for another. Furthermore, it is certain that when someone intervenes for another, it suffices that payment be made to the principal debtor. D. De constituto, L. unde falsam. It follows from what is noted in C. De non numerata pecunia, L. tam mandatori. Hence, it seems to me that this woman is bound to the restitution of the dowry actually paid, because of the privilege of dowry; otherwise in the case of a donation, because it does not appear that she was certified, although the word “renouncing” etc. is added, because this brief expression does not convey certification to the renouncing party. D. De verbis oblig., L. sciendum, with its glosses. And it is noted that the rights against the heirs and the goods of Amagia should be ceded to the one paying on behalf of the Lord of Masgia, as is clear in the aforementioned laws, and C. De solutionibus, L. Modestinus, and L. Stichum, §. si mandato. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a will is valid without seven witnesses under civil, canonical, or consciential law, even if the mother has been instituted as heir.
casus: CASE. A certain person named Marcellus Anterioli of Ancona, being a merchant in the parts of Syria in the land of Damascus, constituted in the last article of death, as he asserted, a certain testament fortified by a solemn number of witnesses and strengthened, although the witnesses do not appear to have been requested by the said testator in the aforementioned private writing, and named, although in their testimony they say they were requested. It was written by the hand of a certain private person from the said habitation of Ancona. In which testament, thus asserted by the opposing party, he instituted heirs without making any mention of his goods, but simply named those he wished to be heirs: a certain person named Ianuellus Peterelli, his kinsman, and a certain person named Domina Oliuerta, mother of the said testator. And beyond the aforementioned, he left many legacies to certain spiritual persons of the said habitation. And among the other legacies which he made, he left to a certain person named Domina Auselicia Cionis, his ex-wife, beyond her dowries, 200 gold ducats. Nor does it appear by virtue of the said testament that the said Marcellus wished expressly to make a codicil, but only to make a will. Finally, the said testator died in the said place, with the said Ianuellus and Domina Oliuerta surviving him, the heirs described in the said testament. And Ianuellus and Domina Oliuerta, by virtue of the said testament, accepted the inheritance of the said Marcellinus; and also with three of his brothers surviving him, related to him on both sides. Whom brothers of the said testator, in a certain other first will solemnly celebrated in the habitation of Ancona, together with the said Domina Oliuerta, their mother, and the mother of the said Marcellinus the testator, the said Marcellinus instituted as heirs. It happens that the said Domina Auselicia, wife of the said testator, from the heirs described in the said testament, as is asserted, lastly made by the said Marcellinus in the said place of Damascus, demanded the said legacy of two hundred gold ducats in ordinary court, in which court, and in every part thereof, as you will see from the records, the said Marcellus was always denied to have made, and thus to have made the said last testament, which is asserted by the said Domina Auselicia, or her curator in this case, that the said Marcellus made in the parts of Syria in the land of Damascus; which not only the will, but also the solemnity of the said testament of the said Marcellus was totally denied by the said heirs. The curator of the said Domina Auselicia, to prove that the said testament was made in the parts of Syria in Damascus, and its tenor, made certain articles: and upon these, first response having been made by the said Ianuellus and Domina Oliuerta, he had six witnesses examined from the number described in the said testament asserted by the opposing party. It is alleged that the said testament being thus made, from its tenor, is not sufficiently proved, as required by written law, by the witnesses examined in the said case upon the said chapters; nevertheless, because the said will, denied in the form aforesaid, ought to be validated by a number of at least 7 witnesses, since there was contention between the aforementioned parties regarding the will and solemnity, nevertheless, because two of the said six witnesses are incapacitated, one of whom deposed in Florence, the other in Perugia, and they were not rightly, correctly, or solemnly examined, according as required by law, as will fully appear to us from the exceptions appended against them and their statements and testimonies. Thus, it must be that the said exceptions appended against the said witnesses were outside the term given against the witnesses. From the premises, it is asked, having seen the acts and things done in the said case, and others which ought to be subtly considered in this case, what are the duties of the judge in judging. And whether in the aforementioned case there is place for the tendering of the oath of the said curator, then living, the said Domina Auselicia being in the said case, and today the procurator of the said Domina Angulia, heirs of the said Domina Auselicia, her daughter and legatee, in default of proof.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. These

A private writing, unless proved by seven witnesses, is not valid as a testament, because it lacks the requisite will and solemnity, as noted in the Digest, De testibus, l. Haeredes, Palam, in principio; in the Code, De bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas, l. 2; in the Code, De testibus, l. Si unus and l. Si non specialiter; in the Code, De fideiussoribus, l. Si; and although the first writing intervened, it is useless as to proof, as noted in the Digest, Quomodo et quando testamentum aperiri debeat, l. 2, in principio; and in the Code, eodem titulo, l. 2; and in the Code, De edicto divi Adriani, l. Edicto; in the Code, De testibus, l. Publicati. And therefore, by six witnesses, nothing is proved in the solemn form of a testament. Hence it must be observed that here the defendants are sued as heirs under a solemn testament: and the defendants deny the testament, and therefore they ought to be absolved, because it is not proved. I speak according to civil law. It is true that the mother of the testator was instituted. To prove this, five witnesses would suffice, if it had been done in the due manner, and the witnesses were induced in that manner and on that ground, as in the Code, De testibus, l. Hac consultissima, § Si quis autem; and if the first testament had not been made, in which those coming intestate were instituted. But because in the first testament those coming intestate, namely the mother and brothers, were instituted according to the testament, and the dispositions therein are of no effect; because the testator, what he could do by codicil, he wished to do, as in the Code, De testibus, l. Non codicillum; but what he wished to do, he could not fulfill. Hence, when will and power are repugnant to each other, nothing is done, as in the Code, De codicillis, l. Si quis agere; in the Code, De fideiussoribus, l. Eam quam; and he whom he wished to institute as heir, he inscribed as heir: as in the Digest, De hereditate instituenda, l. 1, § Qui neque, and § Si autem. And thus the civil law wills. But in canon law there are opinions, Extra, De testamentis, c. Cum elles, and c. Relatum. And because the testament was made among infidels, who are living, and we must believe according to the law of nature: as noted by Innocentius, De voto, c. Quod super; and the custom of the place is to be observed. In the Code, De testibus, l. Si posset persuaderi, that legacies ought to be paid, at least according to good and right conscience. In the Code, De fideicommissis, lib. 1, l. In testamento. But let the judge dispute with himself about the forum of conscience. In the forum of civil law, however, I say that the defendants are to be absolved from the claims; because it is not proved, nor is there a place for the administration of an oath, where mere proof is not sufficient. Institutes, De fideicommissis hereditariis, § Si. Because therefore by imperfect proof the disposition of the testator is not perfectly proved, the defendants are to be absolved by sentence. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, etc.

Libellus of Lord Baldus in the matter of spoliation concerning the fact, which immediately below appears, after which follows the consilium of Lord Bal. Before you, etc., saying, that in the years of the Lord 1300, etc., let the year and month be stated, holding, possessing, ruling, and governing the said Louis by his officials, familiars, and superiors: the Castle of Montis Leonis, the province, the boundaries of its castle, etc. Certain persons, let names be stated, in a secret and treacherous manner made a certain ordinance, conspiracy, and agreement with certain of their accomplices and followers concerning invading and taking the said castle, and despoiling the said Louis, and expelling those holding for him. After all the holding of the said castle, and putting the said agreement into effect, the said officials, familiars, and superiors of the said Louis were unjustly ejected by force and machination from the holding and possession of the said castle by the audacity of fury, truly, in consideration of a noble and powerful man, let the name be stated. And thus doing, they despoiled the said Louis of the holding and possession of the said castle unjustly and wrongfully, in a predatory and tyrannical manner: and finally on the following day the said spoilers and invaders seized possession of the said castle, and with armed hand entering the said castle, they introduced themselves, and with the knowledge and consent and ratification of the violent and vitious possession of the said castle they made and constituted, so much so that the said Louis was despoiled, and fearing, afterwards he wished to return, nor could he go or send, on account of which according to the form of law, the said Louis is in peaceful possession: as at the time of expulsion he was to be fully and peacefully restored, and with armed hand restored and reintegrated, and the said noble is to be deprived by sentence of every right, if any he might claim. He also explains that the said noble contradicts restoring and returning the possession of the said castle to the said Louis against the duty of reason: wherefore the said procurator, and procurator of the said Louis, asks that the aforementioned noble, in the name of the same procurator, be condemned by us and by our sentence to restore the said castle and its possessions with the fruits perceived and which could have been perceived, and every cause; and also to be deprived by you by sentence of every right, if any the said noble had or claimed to have at the time of the said invasion. He asks furthermore that the said procurator, with reimbursement of expenses, in every way, manner, and form by which he can best obtain justice and reason for himself, asking, saving the right to add, diminish, interpret, and correct, according to legal promise.

CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. When the noble man Louis of the Counts of Marsagno held and ruled, both by himself and by his officials, the Castle of Montis Leonis, on a certain day, however, while he was absent, his officials being there, a certain other noble man from the opposite side, having made an agreement with certain officials, expelled the officials of the said Louis, invaded the said castle, and afterwards took it in this manner, namely, because certain men of the said castle expelled the said officials at night, and on the following morning the said noble man from the opposite side approached the said castle, and entered it, and held it for some time, and afterwards committed the said castle to be guarded under certain pacts by the noble man Raynucius of Miglano. Who Raynucius thus acknowledged, and promised to restore to the said noble man from the opposite side after a year. Finally Louis ceded all his rights to the said Raynucius, his consort. It is asked, what is the law regarding the possession of the said castle, and in whose hands the possession thereof ought to be consigned, or be. And what ought to be the possession of the same.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An interdict is granted to one who has been factually dispossessed against the person who dispossessed him, ordered the dispossession, or ratified it.
2. Whether the interdict *unde vi* can be assigned.
1. A petition is brought when a certain portion of land is claimed, or when a part occupied by a son is to be raised by means of a cadastral survey
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On this point, I, Baldus, having been consulted, say that, after the officials and household of the said Lud. were expelled, the said Ludouicus was immediately dispossessed of the possession of the said castle. D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. Peregre, § Quibus spoliatis. And he would have been advised to seek relief both by the interdict unde vi and by the constitution Si quis in monumentum against the compeller. Nor is it to be inquired whether Ludouicus held justly or unjustly, or whether he was the owner or not. C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. Si quis ad se fundum; C. si per vim vel alio modo, l. 1; and in c. Reintegranda. And although the interdict unde vi is personal and is not granted except against the expeller, D. de vi et vi armata, l. Cum a te, nevertheless the action arising from those canons is in rem, and lies against anyone having a cause or occasion derived from the invader, as is fully noted in the aforementioned c. Saepe. And these points are to be noted. Innocentius says, regarding those who lose possession of churches and cannot prove their canonical institution, that they may seek to be restored not only against the violator but against anyone whose possession derives from the violent invader, without any title being proved. Hence I say the same regarding jurisdictions and vassals, and this is held by Rosellus in the title Unde vi, l. In libellis. And therefore, without doubt, the said nobleman of the contrada is bound, if he had any possession, to relinquish it to the said Ludouicus, even if it were not proved that he was a participant in the crime of dispossession; yet that he was a participant is made probable by the immediate seizure following. The preceding discussion is noted; the text is notable, D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. Si ventri, § Finis. It is also very notable that one may be sued not only he who ejected, or commanded, or ratified, but also he who consented, De restitutione spoliatorum, c. Cum ad sedem. And so it is read and noted, 2 q. 1, c. Notum. But there is doubt whether, if Ludouicus does not act, but the said Raynutius, by reason of the right ceded to him, wishes to possess by changing the cause of recognition, whether he can do so. For he cannot precede or interrupt the possession of his grantor. C. de acquisitione rerum possessionis, l. Si. Nor does it matter whether the question is one of possession or ownership, because one cannot dispossess his own author of possession, as is fully noted by Dyther in c. Qui ad agendum, De regulis iuris, lib. 6.

† To the contrary it seems, because the interdict *unde vi* can be ceded. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. *quod si infra diem*, §. *Iul.* And if an action is given by reason of a cession, it is given against that nobleman of the opposite party. Therefore, much more strongly is an exception given. C. de exceptionibus, l. *licet*; D. de regulis iuris, l. *inuitus*, §. *cui damus*. This is a beautiful doubt between two invaders: nevertheless, the condition of Raynulf is the better, because he possesses. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. *cum mulier*, with its material. And the statement of Doctorus does not avail, who says that this occurs by the act of him whose possession is interrupted: for it is the other who is dispossessed, into whose place this detainer succeeds. Hence he prevails by the right of his author, not by his own bad faith. And thus the objection from what we have in l. *itaque fullo*, C. de furtis, does not avail, and so it is true in my judgment. And so I hold by l. *inuitus*, §. *cum quis*, D. de regulis iuris, saving the liberty and power of the men of the said castle. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc. CA SVS.

† Before you, discreet and prudent men who exercise the office of the armarius and the cadastre of the commune of Perugia, says, narrates, and proposes Master Francis, son of Master Bald of Perugia, of the Porta San Pietro and of the Porta Santa Lucia, acting as procurator and proxy in the name of the said Master Bald, saying that in the castle of Master Philip, son of Master Maffei, formerly of Perugia, of the said Porta Santa Lucia, there are disputes, clarifications, namely concerning lands, roads, instruments, and landholdings; namely, one landholding of vineyard land with a working area, with vines existing and planted therein, and with appurtenances, of the village of San Cristoforo, called Pistille, in the locality of Vadeloreto, without which from the head. The heirs of Gregory Marcellator for one part; and for another part Petruccio Nicole; and for another part Matteo Gostantii, from three sides by another side the river Tiber. And also one landholding of vineyard and non-vineyard land is situated in the said appurtenances and locality, etc., let the boundaries be placed. And he says also that after the death of the said Master Philip, the said landholdings of land, bounded as above, came to the said Master Bald, except for the parts occupied. The said Master Bald has, holds, and possesses. He says also that the said river Tiber has occupied and continues to hold lands, parts of the said landholdings of land. Wherefore the said Master Francis, in the name aforesaid, requests that you choose and appoint one measurer or surveyor, who shall measure, at the expense of the said Master Bald, the certain landholdings of land; because, upon report made by the said measurer or surveyor, those parts are to be removed, cancelled, and abolished from the book and cadastre formerly of the said Master Philip; and the remaining parts are to be entered, recorded, and registered in the book and cadastre of Master Bald. He requests that the aforesaid be done for him, in the name aforesaid, and for the said Master Bald, according to the form of the order and statute of the commune of Perugia and of the said armarius and cadastre, and in every manner, way, right, and form by which he may best do so. I, Bald.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute may prohibit that one may distrain, leave, or alienate into the persons of another territory.
2. Given a statute that if a certain foreigner is afterwards made a citizen, whether he may then acquire.
3. If a statute disables a foreigner from acquiring, whether an heir may be instituted.
4. Whether a vassal may make a will in a fief.
5. How a fief is presumed to be ancient.
1. One wishing to succeed in the place of any person must prove that person dead for burial, or otherwise, etc.
2. Whether a Milanese woman married in Parma is said to change her domicile.
3. A fief does not pass to women, unless the lord wishes to invest the daughter with honor, and according to the custom of the father.
4. How a fief is granted.
5. Whether an heir is presumed to have the writings of the deceased.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. For clarity, it must be premised that certain things belong to one’s own patrimony, whether original or adventitious, which a master of perfect age may sell, alienate, donate, and exchange; regarding this patrimony, an adult may make a will and codicils. On this patrimony, the Institutes speak in the title *De rerum divisione*, § *Si quis a non domino*; § *Per traditionem*; the Digest, *De acquisitione rei donatae*, l. *Acquiritur* and l. *Traditio*; the Code, *Communia de legibus*, l. 1; and the Digest, *De rei venditione*, throughout; the Code, *De manumissionibus*, l. *In re mandata*.

† But concerning this type of dominion, a doubt may arise: whether a statute can prohibit that property be distrained, alienated, or left to persons of another territory. And it seems that it cannot, if the owners of the things are not subject to the municipal laws of that place. For to those not subject, a law cannot be imposed, as in the law *Cunctos populos*, together with its material. To the contrary, it seems: because this law is *in rem*, not *in personam*; because it says that no immovable thing can be alienated outside the district. And even if it were said that no subject person, and even so, can alienate outside the territory, nevertheless, because the extreme which is prohibited is subject, the statute holds; because to its own person, i.e., its own subject, it can impose a law, as in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, in the laws *Quorum* and *Praeterea*; and in the Code, *De cupressis ex luco Danensi*. And where two extremes are required, if one is invalid, what is done does not hold; because the receptive cannot be without the active, nor can it receive unless it is transferred into it; as in the law *Si ego*, Digest, *Si certum petatur*, regarding solution. If the words of the statute begin with the subject person, because they are directed to him, for example, "no citizen of Piacenza can alienate to a Parmesan," the statute is valid; otherwise, if the words begin with the non-subject, e.g., that the non-subject cannot acquire; because it is directed to the non-subject; because he cannot be incapacitated by those who enact the statute. Or say that the statute is valid in both cases, because correlatives have the same reason, as in the law *Si*, Code, *De indicio dividundo*.

But here arises a doubt: what if a foreigner has become a citizen by a decree of the elders, with the authority of, or the consent of, the prince? I answer that this foreigner has received the use of the Palatine toga, and therefore he can acquire and contract, as is stated in the Digest, *De iure fisci*, law *Sed si accepto*. And note that this citizenship is a benefit which is accepted like a legacy, but it is not said to be ratified; because it does not proceed from him, but into him, and all its force depends on those who enact it; it cannot properly be ratified by him, unless that which ratification feigns to have been done by the ratifier. It is beyond doubt that a privilege does not proceed from the privileged person, but from the one granting the privilege, from whom it derives its existence, although through the acceptance of the privileged person it assumes the unchangeable acquisition of the benefit, as is stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Si quis hereditatem*.

† Subsequently, it is doubted: if a statute states that one cannot acquire by contract or in any other way, whether one can acquire by way of institution as heir. And it seems that one cannot, on account of the general words inserted alternatively, “or in any other way”; for he who excludes everything excludes nothing that is not excluded. D. de rebus dubiis, l. Si is qui ducenta, §. Utrum; C. de rebus aliis non alienandis, l. Si. Moreover, this prohibition is made in favor of certain persons, namely citizens, whose interest it is on account of grants and taxes; not on account of the nature of the thing itself, nor on account of any odium. Therefore, it is understood to apply to alienation even by institution of an heir: as C. de secundis nuptiis, l. 1, ac edictali; and l. Si quis prioris, §. Certum; C. non licere habitatoribus metropolis, l. 1; D. de legatis 2, l. Peto, §. Fratre. To the contrary, it seems: D. de acquisitione rei donatae, l. Quidam. Moreover, lest anyone die partly testate and partly intestate: as noted in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. 1. It seems to be said, truth being preserved, that the said statute is not understood to apply to the institution of an heir; because it does not apply to intestate succession, in whose place the institution succeeds, non obstantibus §. Fratre; because there, in the case of alienation, the thing was left to the family, whereas here it is left to no one. Moreover, here the mention of contract, which serves to restrict, so that it may operate in declaring the quality of the genus, and this unless the statutes of the ancients provide otherwise. The second quality of things is that castles donated by the emperor are not held in fief, but in full ownership. And the same applies to these as to other purely patrimonial goods, although these are castrensia; because they have been transferred with full right, and are not of the fisc, nor of the donor, but of the donee. l. Bene a Zenone; and C. de donationibus, l. Si ea.
The third matter of things is the fief: and if it is ancient, the testament concerning it is not valid, because it pertains to the agnates.

† And it is presumed ancient, because for many generations past it was so conducted and so named: for antiquity provides the ground for prescription and presumption, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, De usucapione, l. Celsus. Likewise, from the correspondence of servitudes a fief is presumed; nevertheless, these must be proved, and past possession does not suffice to prove presumptively, but present possession without violence and secrecy is required, as noted by Bartolus and by me in the Digest, De conditione instituta, l. Penult. And a fief is a certain servitude contrary to the nature of things, which at one time were free, and are today presumed [to be such]: as noted in the Digest, De operis novi nuntiando, l. Si prius; in the Digest, Si servus venditus, l. Alteri; in the Digest, De usufructu, l. Si cui, in the beginning. Regarding the acts to be examined, I cannot extend myself: for I am infirm and afflicted in body, but not in mind, by the grace of God; in doubtful matters, conscience is very good and pleasing to God, as noted in the Digest, De negotiis gestis, l. At qui natura, § Cum me. As to the fact of the lady’s agnate, the prior agnate, it must be said,

† That he who wishes to succeed to the place of another person must prove that person dead by burial, or by some other certainty, or by a sufficient presumption thereof, as C. de cap. l. nec nos. Moreover, the person must be produced: as l. cum exhibuissent. ff. de publica. Moreover, confession accords with natural principles; and therefore it is presumed true, and is valid even between absent parties: as l. quotiens. C. de naufra. lib. 11.

† It is also said that Lady Agnes became a foreigner, because she was married by me, and thus changed her origin, as is noted in the law *Origine*, Digest, *De municipibus et originibus*; but this allegation is not true, because there it speaks only with regard to the forum of jurisdiction, not with regard to property, since with respect to property she retains her original domicile, as is noted in the law *1*, Code, *De mulieribus et in quo loco*, Book 10, and this applies to non-feudal property.
† for feudal goods do not pass to women, unless the lord wishes to invest his daughter with the fief out of honor and love for her father. § which is not alleged here.

† Moreover, a prince’s fief is not proved by witnesses, but by written instrument: as in *l. bene a Zenone*, although lower fiefs are proved by written instrument. Also by peers of the court. Also, if it is an ancient fief, it is proved by other suitable witnesses. See what is noted in the prologue, book 6, in the *Novella*. Also, public reputation is of great weight, yet alone it is not sufficient, as noted in *C. de rei vend.*, *l. inducia*, and the aforementioned § *cum me*. Also, under the *ius commune*, dominion is not proved by declaratory words between absent parties: as in *C. de iuris et facti ignorantia*, *l. cum falsa*.

† Furthermore, regarding the assertion that the heir is presumed to possess the written documents, it is responded that possession is not presumed: as stated in l. 1, § Scaeuola. Also, according to what is noted in c. 1, extra de usu, incle. Moreover, it is difficult to prove the tenor of a privilege due to other requirements, namely, the Imperial seal and other solemnities. And because it is necessary that they recognize the letters by the bulls and other matters which must be investigated with subtlety, as is the case regarding the faith of instruments, c. inter dilectos. Nevertheless, commonly these castles have been accustomed to be fiefs of the Emperor: as in c. 1, quae sint regalia, colla. 10. And from frequency and generality, truth is presumed, unless a contrary custom is proven, as is noted, that in this country, as is asserted, there are not fewer castles that are not feudal than those that are feudal. And therefore, it is uncertain whether they are feudal or not. Furthermore, concerning the Parmesan goods, there is no doubt that they pertain to these nobles of the Rubei family, unless something else appears regarding the substitution made to the said Marchisoto. When I said that possession carries great weight, understand this unless it is violent, as in C. de proba, l. si de possessione and l. vis eius, because a favorable presumption is excluded by crime. It supports what is noted in ff. ad l. Aquil., l. in l. Aquilia si deletum, and l. fi., ff. de in lit. iu, and ff. de fur., l. qui tabulas, and l. quidam tabularum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the Abbot of Viane of Saint Peter has had a hospital built under the name of Saint Anthony of Viane, whether what was left to the said hospital, and what was acquired under the name of the church of Saint Anthony of Viane, was acquired by the said monastery of Saint Peter, or by the monastery of Viane.
2. Viane.
3. Whether a destroyed hospital ceases to be a hospital.
1. Whether, if the census is not paid, the property falls into forfeiture.
2. What is built on the soil of a church to whom it belongs.
body: It is alleged that a hospital was built under the name and title of Saint Anthony of Viana on a plot of land measuring four perches, which territory the venerable Abbot of Saint Peter of Pavia is said to have granted to a certain Brother Gandulfus so that the said hospital might be constructed there. Furthermore, after the said hospital had been built on the said territory, the said Abbot appointed a certain Faciolus de Thoma as minister in the said hospital. However, it does not appear that any of the aforementioned persons, neither Gandulfus nor Faciolus, erected the said hospital; rather, it is presumed as a settled fact that the said territory belonged to the said monastery of Saint Peter.

† It is asked whether the property left to the said hospital, and acquired under the name and title of the church of Saint Anthony of Vianen, were acquired as to direct dominion by the said monastery of Saint Peter, or by the monastery of Vianen. And it seems that they were acquired by the said monastery of Saint Peter, because that which acceded to the hospital of the same law becomes part of the hospital itself, since the accessory follows the nature of the principal, as in D. de legatis 2, l. cum et fundus, and in the rule accessorium. From this it follows that if the said hospital is irrecoverably destroyed, so that it cannot be rebuilt, or if the census was not paid, and therefore the principal place reverts to ownership, the same applies to the houses and other things acquired by the said hospital, wherever they are located; because, with the extinction of the use of the hospital, the final cause of useful dominion is extinguished, and the property reverts to ownership with its encumbrances, improvements, and any accessories. C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. 2; and D. de iure dominii, l. si proprietati.

On the contrary, it seems that this legacy or acquisition, made by the largesse of the faithful, was left in contemplation of the Order of Vianen, because it is acquired by the person in whom the testator’s affection is directed. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filio; D. de hereditate instituta, l. quidam cum filium; C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum aliquis; D. de vulgari substitutione, l. sed plures, § in arrogato; C. de usufructu, l. fin. For if the one elected as minister of the said hospital was a brother and professed member of Saint Anthony of Vianen, or even a free man voluntarily serving the said order, and in good faith for his soul, and through him as through a servant or negotiorum gestor of the Order of Vianen, whatever is acquired, and from whatever cause, is acquired by the master, or by him who has dominion over the person and the statute thereof, as in l. 1, D. de his qui sui iuris sunt; l. fi, D. de stipulationibus servorum; 12 q. 1, c. non dicatis.

Moreover, let it be granted that this acquirer has two masters, namely the Abbot of Saint Peter by reason of the hospital, and the Abbot of Saint Anthony by reason of profession; it must be considered in whose contemplation he acquires, as in C. per quas personas nobis acquiritur, l. fin. Indeed, the legacy would remain with the hospital, vacant of the contemplation of the Order of Saint Anthony of Vianen, through the hospital itself, which at that time is an inanimate thing, and would be acquired by the religion of Saint Anthony, just as that which is acquired by a vacant inheritance is acquired by the future heir, D. si certum petatur, l. eius qui, § pe. For the hospital itself, although vacant, functions in place of a person, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. mortuo. And in the appellative name, whenever it tends to the final cause, the intention of the disposer is recognized, so that acquisition may take place, as in l. si servus, D. de stipulationibus servorum. And especially because we are here dealing with encumbrances, but with a certain house located at a distance. D. de usufructu, l. Item si fundi, § huic; and in c. 1, § si quis de manso, in the title de controversia investiturae.

And it must be observed that a hospital is either destroyed in law, and ceases to be a hospital, and no annuity is due for it; or it is destroyed in fact, and then either it has been transferred to another place, and it will be proven to continue, as argued in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si donatae, § si sponsus; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filiae, § 1; and D. de legatis 2, l. idem servandum. Or it has not been transferred to another place, and then either it is destroyed irreparably, and then it does not continue under the name of hospital, D. de usufructu, l. si usus fructus civitati. Otherwise, if it perished by chance, or is repairable, and then the hospital continues in potentiality, but not in act; nevertheless, in the meantime no pension is due for it: as in l. 1, C. de iure emphyteutico.

† Now I ask: granted that the census ought to be paid and was not paid, does it fall into forfeiture? As if all would say that it does. But the contrary seems truer, unless the lord reserved for himself the direct dominion, which is not presumed in this type of contract: because whatever is not reserved seems to have been transferred. Therefore, also the direct dominion: which does not fall into forfeiture, as in Extra, de restitutione spoliorum, c. Olim; de relictis dominis, c. Constitutus; and by the gloss and Innocentius, and more clearly by Bartolus in l. 1, §. Hic titulus, ff. de publicanis, where he elegantly treats this point. And from this the first conclusion is strengthened, that in things newly acquired nothing is acquired by the monastery of Saint Peter. And what I said about the house by way of example, I say likewise if a castle had been left, as in l. 1, C. de usucapione transformatione data. For he through whom acquisition takes place cannot be a monk in two monasteries, but only in one. 19 q. 1, c. Statutum. From these things it is inferred to other private matters, because since the aforementioned newly acquired things belong fully by right to the Vianese monastery, they could be transferred to another, observing the solemnities, forms, and customs of them, as in c. Dudum, Extra, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, lib. 6. After I had written these things, it was told to me that Gandulfus and Faciolus were not brothers of Saint Anthony, but laymen, and simply hospitalers appointed by the Abbot of Saint Peter of Viterbo. Through the orphanotrophos, acquisition is made for the hospital, just as through the tutor acquisition is made for the ward. C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Orphanotrophos. And through the hospital, which is subject to the said monastery. ff. de annuis legatis, l. Annua, §. 1. And although the hospital is destroyed, what was acquired is not lost to the said monastery of Saint Peter, which truly acquired it. After the said hospital came under the rule of the brothers of Saint Anthony, it pertains to the religion of Saint Anthony. Hence, to each one is acquired as much as the reason of law and the will of the testator permit, as in ff. de stipulatione servo, l. Si servus communis Mævii; and de castrensi peculio, §. Finis. It is certain that any person professed in an approved religion is equated to a slave, and acquires for his religion just as a slave does, as noted by Innocentius, de privilegiis, c. Cum olim; and it is noted by Bartolus in l. 1, §. Si usufructus, ff. de stipulatione servo.

† Moreover, it is certain that a building erected on the soil of a church accedes to the soil and becomes of the same legal status as the soil itself, as noted by Innocentius in the aforementioned chapter *Cum olim*. And it is a rule of both civil and canon law that whatever is planted, sown, or built upon the soil accedes to it; the term "roots" refers, if applicable, to that which is sown or planted. In the case of buildings, however, the foundations take the place of roots. Furthermore, if one builds upon what had already been begun, as stated in the Code, *De rei venditione*, law 2.

† Moreover, if it is doubtful who built, it is presumed to have been the owner of the soil; because, as I said, the building accedes to the soil. As for things acquired from outside, whether they are presumed to have been acquired in consideration of one or the other, and whether they were acquired in ancient times or recently, this must be examined; because both the quality of the person at that time and whose labor was involved are relevant. For differences among ministers cause acquisitions to differ. Also relevant is what is noted in c. fin., extra de rescriptis, in the decretal Is ad quem cura pertinet, where it is presumed that he to whom the care belongs built it. ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. cum seruus, according to Bartolus. Furthermore, it is certain that what is left to a minister is considered to have been left in consideration of the house, as stated in l. anima, § 1. Moreover, the monastery and the church of Viterbo have a privilege, which provides as follows: “We strictly forbid all and each within the district, regardless of status or condition, except the brothers of your monastery who have obtained permission from you, the abbot, on the pretext of some oratory or altar under the name of that blessed Anthony, in whose honor the said monastery is recognized to have been constructed, as well as alms, vows, or legacies for the construction of the said monastery or for future constructions, to seek or receive in the name of the same saint in any way whatsoever. We decree that all and each questors who receive vows or legacies against your will, unless they have been canonically admonished by us or by any of the brothers of your monastery to restore them to us within a certain peremptory term to be fixed by us or by any of the brothers of the said monastery, shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication, and such contravention constitutes a species of sacrilege, as in C. de crimine sacrilegii, l. instar.” I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One having twelve children is excused from burdens, even patrimonial ones.
2. Whether one immune from public offices by privilege is also immune from the contribution for the repair of the city walls.
3. Whether a church is bound to contribute to the repair of the city walls.
4. Whether the repair of the walls is an extraordinary or an ordinary public office.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† If we speak of the common law, a father having twelve children is excused from burdens, whether public offices or even patrimonial ones, as in C. de decurionibus, l. Si quis decurio pater, and it is read and noted in l. Semper, §. Demonstratur, ff. de iure immunitatis. And the reason is the necessary upbringing of the children, as the text there elegantly states. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that this privilege can be removed by the custom of the place, as in the aforementioned l. Semper, §. Quoque. And if this can be done by the custom of the people, much more so by a decree or constitution of the lord, as in ff. de officio praetoris, l. Barbarius, in fine; C. de adoptionibus, l. 2.

And therefore, let us come first to the privileges of the Emperor, secondly to the decree of our Magnificent Lord. For the privileges of the Emperor state that the Palatine Counts and the Imperial minters are exempt from all public burdens. And it is doubted whether by this they are exempt from the contribution for the repair of the city walls. And I say that they are not: because the repair of the walls is necessary, not merely useful. So much so that even the Church is not exempt from repair, as in C. de sac. san. eccl. l. ad distributionem.

But if the city wished to build walls anew of its own accord, for the ornament and pomp of the city, the churches are not bound to contribute, as is noted there by the gloss, by Cynus, also by both Jacobs, by Arena, and by Butrius. To this point the text in the Authentica *De manumissionibus principum*, § *Deinde competens*, in the words “of roads and walls,” is well suited, where the text places these two things as equal, in the case of necessity. On this, note 16, question 1, chapter *Placuit*. To the decree of our lord, into whom flows the fullness of discretion, who can impose a law upon his own property, and yet does not impose it upon himself. *Digestum*, *De fideicommissis liberis*, law *Lucius*. And in effect it is contained in the said decree of the lord, that those holding themselves exempt from the burdens of the commune of the city of Cuneo, by reason of the benefits of immunity, do not enjoy it, except only as regards personal and extraordinary burdens of the said commune. As to ordinary burdens, such as tolls and customs, and other collections to be imposed by the said lord, they cannot claim to be protected; but they are effectively obliged. They are therefore immune from two burdens, namely, the personal and extraordinary ones of the said commune, but not from others.

† Hence it must be considered whether the repair of walls is an extraordinary office. And indeed, that it is so: because an extraordinary office is one that is not contained in law or certainty. An ordinary office, however, is one contained in canon, i.e., rule: not one that is imposed suddenly, as C. de iudic. l. 1. This is held by Petrus in d. l. ad instructionem, because sometimes more is imposed, sometimes less, as the quantity requires. It therefore seems expressly clear that by the decree of the lord they are excused on account of the number of children. On the contrary it seems: because this is a mixed office, which is imposed on persons according to the quantity of their patrimony, as collected: as ff. de muneribus et honoribus l. rescriptae. §. si. and l. munerum. §. mixta. Moreover, this pertains to the protection of all citizens: therefore all ought to contribute, as ff. ad l. Rhodiam de nautis l. navis onustae. Moreover, a man is born to the city before children are born to him, and greater is the charity, as ff. de captivis et postliminio §. filius. Moreover, it ought not to be called extraordinary: because it is contained in the perpetual edict, as d. l. ad instructionem. Therefore all ought to contribute to the repair of roads and bridges, as C. de decurionibus l. vacuatis. And then the burden will be borne more lightly: because it is borne by many, as in Auth. de naturalibus in curia deputandis. And it is noted. C. de exact. tribu. l. actores. and C. de immunitatibus nemini concedendis l. per victimam. where it is expressly stated, unless the contrary was expressly contained in the rescript of the Emperor, which is credible, that he specially makes one immune from the repair of walls. I, Baldus. A certain man made homage and fidelity to our most illustrious lord, the Duke of Milan, etc., concerning certain castles. It is asked, whether this man, who made fidelity, can make war against the lord concerning other cities and lands which he holds, and for which he did not make fidelity.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal, regarding non-feudal goods, may wage war against his lord, or defend himself, or make a truce with the lord's enemies.
2. Whether a vassal is bound to contribute to his lord's purse expenses.
3. A vassal having two lords: to whom he is bound to obey.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† This question can be understood in two ways: in one way, whether he can wage war by resisting; in another way, whether he can wage war by initiating it. In the first case, he who defends himself lawfully does not act contrary to the oath of fealty. And the reason is: because the lord, in unlawfully offending him, acts against the nature of the fief. For the nature of a fief is this, that the lord ought to return in turn to his vassal what he demands from him, as in c. 1. §. dominus vero. de forma fidelitatis. And therefore, if vassals are treated in an unruly and wrongful manner by their lords, they can wage war in the last resort and as a subsidiary measure, that is, as a final remedy; so that arms, which are the executors of justice, may protect those whom mere reason does not assist on account of the power of the lords, as in c. dominus. §. si vero vassallus. de milite vassallo, qui contumax est, and noted in C. de Iudaeis. l. nullus, and through Inn. in c. sicut. de iureiur. In the second case, that a vassal cannot initiate war against his lord, nor form an alliance or friendship with his enemies, because this is expressly contrary to the oath of fealty, as in the said c. 1. de forma fidelitatis, and 22. q. 5. c. de forma, and noted in c. enim. extra de iureiur.; and especially if he is a liege vassal, who swears fealty against every man, as in c. si quis inuestitus. de capitulis extraordinariis feudorum, and in c. pastoralis. extra de re iudic. in clemen.; for since he is bound to look after the honor and status of his lord, as in c. 1. in quibus causis feudum amittatur, and is bound to this by natural custom and instinct, he certainly cannot attack the one whom he is bound to protect. For this is a rule both natural and civil, which is handed down in ff. si seruitus vendi. l. alius, and ff. de condi. indebi. l. frater a fratre. §. porro. Whence a vassal, by the very fact that he makes an alliance with the enemies of his lord, is deemed a prevaricator, as is read and noted in ff. de offi. praefe. vrb. l. 1. §. cum patronus; and he who is not with me in faith is against me, C. de iudicis. l. celicolarum.

† It is true that a vassal is not bound to contribute to the lord in out-of-pocket expenses except according to the proportion of the fiefs, just as we say in a similar matter concerning just public charges that are imposed upon a person according to the share of his patrimony, as in ff. de mune. et hono. l. rescripto. §. fi.; whence a vassal is not bound to make a tax contribution for the assistance of the lord except from the castles and men of the fief.

† And if he has two lords, he is bound in his own person to defend each one with respect to the fief which he holds from that lord, and not to be involved in negotiation and counsel against him; otherwise he is a perjurer and loses the fief as an ungrateful person, as is proved by the aforementioned laws and canons. And natural discernment itself, which is the mother of canon and civil law, dictates this. For it is not possible for two opposing things to exist at the same time in the pillar of the same subject, as in l. vbi repugnantia. ff. de reg. iur. and ff. pro suo. l. si ancillam. And it is similar if someone has two domiciles, say one in Perugia and another in Assisi, and these two cities are at war with one another: for in respect of the property he holds in Assisi, he shall pay the tax in Assisi; and for the property he holds in Perugia, he shall pay in Perugia; but with respect to his person he can settle his allegiance according to his conscience, as in c. domino guerram. in tit. hic finit lex deinde incipiunt consuetudines regni, unless one city has clear justice and the other does not, as the text says there. Likewise, if one city were subject to the other, he must obey the superior, as in l. contra pupillum. §. qui ad maius. ff. de re iudi. and de app. c. comparati. What is noted by Bernard. in c. quoniam Abbas extra de offi. de leg. in gl. magna. uersi. sed pone in feudis is relevant: if someone has several lords, he is bound to the older lord in matters that regard fidelity and active service, as in c. fi. §. contra omnes. in the title hic finit lex; and one must stand by that text. I, Baldus. A certain case: By a statute of the commune of Crema it is provided that no one may sell or by any title transfer any inheritance to anyone not subject to the jurisdiction of the Podestà of Crema; and if an alienation has been made, that inheritance shall pass to the nearer agnates of him from whom the said inheritance proceeded. A certain man of Crema entered upon the inheritance of his paternal uncle devolved to him intestate, and afterwards sold it under the designation of the inheritance of his aforesaid uncle to a certain citizen of Lodi, by reason of which the nearer agnate claims the inheritance according to the form of the aforesaid statute; the buyer opposes. The principal doubt arises from the meaning of this word, "inheritance." For the plaintiff says that "inheritance" is called by the law in countless places both entered upon and devolved. He also says that the definition of the word applies equally to an entered inheritance as to a devolved one: so that it is a succession, etc. The defendant, on the contrary, says that a statute, especially one deviating from the common law, can never be understood extensively, and that improper usage constitutes an extension, and that this noun "inheritance" is never taken properly except in the devolved one, and even in an entered one it is always taken improperly. And he grounds himself upon the statement of Bar. in rubri. ff. de acqui. haere. Likewise, I speak regarding the statute that says "no woman may marry with an inheritance": whether the interpretation of this phrasing is that this word is joined transitively or accessorily, so as to be construed with the verb "may marry," as the letter stands, as if it said "she may not transfer an inheritance by marrying," or absolutely, so that it is construed separately, namely "no woman with an inheritance, that is, having an inheritance, may marry," etc. Whence, I leave this point undiscussed, because inquiry is now made of me concerning this.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The term "inheritance" is understood in many ways, and whether and when it is to be understood as referring to an inheritance that has been accepted or not accepted.
2. A statute providing that no woman shall marry with an inheritance outside the territory is to be understood in this manner.
3. An heir who sells the assets of the inheritance is said to have accepted it.
4. Payment ought not to be delayed on account of the debtor's illness.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Certain expressions, or sayings, cannot be understood except with reference to an inheritance not yet accepted; for example, when we say that a free man cannot acquire an inheritance for us. D. 41.1.1 (Homo liber). Likewise, when we say that an inheritance is not subject to theft. D. 47.2.1 (Haereditariae). Likewise, when we say that an inheritance does not have possession. D. 38.2.1 § Scaeuola. Likewise, we say that a hereditary slave cannot stipulate in the name of a future heir. D. 45.3.1 (Servus haereditarius). Likewise, when we say that we do not acquire possession of a hereditary thing through a hereditary slave. D. 29.2.1 § Veteres. Likewise, when we speak of acquiring or repudiating an inheritance. D. 29.2, in the rubric. However, after the inheritance has been accepted, the goods belong to a living person, and a living person does not have an heir. D. 28.6.1 § Filio; D. 42.1.1 § Praeterea sciendum. Indeed, because a lying inheritance sustains a definite personality, but an accepted inheritance belongs to the heir. D. 28.5.1 (Servus haereditarius). Moreover, an inheritance is the right of succession; but once succession has taken root, it is no longer called the right of succession, because succession has already occurred. D. 50.16.1 (Nihil aliud); D. 43.2.3 § Bonorum. Furthermore, if a curator is appointed for an inheritance, it is understood to be a lying inheritance. D. 3.5.1 (Debitor). Certain other expressions, however, cannot be understood except with reference to an accepted inheritance; for example, when we say that this person sells the inheritance. D. and C. 4.10, throughout. This person donates the inheritance. D. 39.5.1 (Haereditatem pater). This person is the owner of the inheritance before accepting it, unless he is a sui heres, such as a son. D. 29.2.1 (Cum haeredes); D. 4.4.1 (Cum miles); Inst. 2.19 § Sui. Thus, it is clear that in the broad sense, inheritance is said to include even an accepted inheritance, and this is how it is understood in C. and D. 5.3, throughout.

† On this point, I say that either we are speaking of an inheritance that has devolved and is to be disposed of or transferred to another, and then the inheritance is understood as having been accepted, because prior to acceptance it cannot be alienated or transferred separately, unless perhaps the hope of it, as in D. 17.2.3 § de illo (pro socio) and D. 41.1.34 § ex asse (si mulier) (de iure dotis). Or we are speaking of an inheritance in another respect, and then it is properly and strictly said to be an unaccepted inheritance, which is supported by what is noted by Cynus in C. 2.4.32 (de pacis) and D. 50.17.100 (stipulatio hoc modo) (de verbis oblig.). Since therefore in our case we are speaking of an inheritance to be transferred, we necessarily speak of an accepted inheritance; then, or subsequently, it would be drawn back, and thus it would be contrary to the statute, as in D. 45.1.118 § si (si ex re) (de stipulationibus servorum) and D. 45.1.119 (proinde) (de stipulationibus servorum), and D. 50.17.100 (si certum petatur), although it may be alleged to the contrary what is read and noted in D. 3.5.3 § hæc verba (de negotiis gestis). But I answer that by this common word, namely “inheritance,” both senses are appropriately signified. Moreover, the intent of the statute is to be understood according to common usage of speech, as noted in D. 35.2.1 § quid tamen Cassius (liberorum) (de legibus tertio) and D. 50.16.100 (ut Alfenus) (de verborum significatione). And therefore one falls under the statute, however he sells, delivers, or binds. Otherwise, if he did not deliver, nor quasi-deliver, as in D. 50.16.100 (alienatum) (de verborum significatione) and C. 6.30.1 (praeterea) (de fundo dotali).

† It is certain that an heir who can accept the inheritance accepts it by selling the hereditary assets; and thus acceptance precedes the sale, at least intellectually, as stated in the Institutes, *De haeredum qualitate et differentia*, § *fin*. I would say otherwise if he performs an act that is not a species of alienation, because the law speaks only of alienation, as in *l. si*, Codex, *De praediis curialium*; and the example is clear in the Digest, *De donationibus*, *l. donationes concubinam*, § *species*.

† Note that payment is not delayed on account of the debtor’s infirmity. D. de haereditate instituenda, l. Si quis instituatur, in fine. CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. On the aforementioned point, it seems that one should effectively argue and hold that the buyer is not bound, neither by promise, nor by acknowledgment, nor by confession, for the causes and reasons set forth below. And first, because a promise based on error, an acknowledgment of the impossible, and a false confession, and that of a matter concerning which there is no action against anyone, these are shown as follows. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a course of action can be prescribed.
2. In the forum of conscience, if a testator commands that debts be paid, it is not understood to refer to a debt extinguished by prescription.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is posited that, in ancient times, a perpetual fictitious census was due for certain possessions; finally, those possessions were bequeathed to certain religious persons; then those religious persons sold them to Titius under a pact and promise to pay the said census in perpetuity. Now the said buyer refuses to pay, because he says that it has been prescribed, and the said census has not been paid for fifty years and more, nor was any interruption made, nor any recognition of the debt in the interim. The question is asked: what is the law?

And it seems at first sight that the said buyer is bound by the promise, because he solemnly promised. D. de verb. oblig. l. si diuortio. Also by confession or assertion, because in the instrument he confessed and asserted that it was true, as C. de non num. pecu. l. generaliter. And Extr. de probat. c. per tuas. And D. si quis cautio. l. sed et si quis. §. fi. Also because he renounced the exception of things not so done, of bad faith, and of every other exception, which he also promised not to prove, as noted in C. de non nu. pecu. l. si ex cautione. And l. 1. And C. de dote caunu. And C. de pact. l. pe. with its material. Also, although it is described, he could nevertheless depose himself into the old obligation, as noted by Cynus, C. de transa. l. cum mota. And D. de iureiuran. l. si duo patroni. §. 1. Also the seller wished to acknowledge good faith, which does not agree with disputing on the points of law, as D. mand. l. si fideiussor. §. quaedam. Also the pact is valid that no one shall use the exception of prescription, as D. de edi. edic. l. quod si nolit. §. si quis ita. Also, although it is prescribed, nevertheless the natural obligation endures, as noted in D. de fideius. l. vbicunque. D. de neg. gest. l. at qui natura. Also this pact prejudices the seller; he sold for a lower price, hence it is unjust to protect the buyer, because he would enrich himself at another’s loss. D. de ser. expor. l. si venditor. in fi. Also the acts of agents are referred to the intention of the contracting parties, as D. si cert. pet. l. si ego. Also it is absurd to circumvent the contracting party under the pretext of error, and especially because these sellers made this pact for the saving of their consciences, hence it cannot be denied that it is in their interest, as D. manda. l. quintus. And noted in l. si in vendi. §. fi. D. communia praedio. Also this is supported by D. de dona. l. vt donares.

On the contrary, it seems that the buyer is not bound, because a promise based on error is void, as D. de fideius. l. si quis postquam. Also because a completed prescription cannot be interrupted, as noted in D. de sol. l. cum quis. §. si quis pro reo. Also liberation induced by prescription is equivalent to liberation induced by pact, as D. de admini. tu. l. si pupillus. in fi. where the text is noted. To the same effect is l. vlti. D. rem ratam haberi. where it is said that prescription is a species of perpetual and perfect liberation. Moreover, here the sellers did not know that they were liberated in time, hence due to error the act was invalid, as is read and noted in D. de pact. l. si cum te. And l. debitorem. And in the said l. si diuortio. And l. sed et §. fin. Also for this the last law of D. de consti. pecu. is most helpful, which is a singular law for this purpose. Also for this is the general rule, because an agreement arising from just ignorance is voided. D. de condi. indebi. l. fin. §. idem quęsiit. C. de dona. l. nec ignorans. D. de pact. l. tres fratres. D. de act. et obli. l. ex maleficiis. §. longe nimis. D. de exceptio. doli. l. 2. §. circa. Also the immediate action is voided by the prescription, for as the gloss elegantly says, the cause can be true and the action false: because it is prescribed. D. de eden. l. 1. in princ. in the great gloss. Also the prescription of the buyer benefits the successor, even the singular one: because exceptions are transferred: or are transferred by accession, as D. de iureiur. I. etiam si rem. D. de actio. empt. l. si in venditione. D. quemadmo. seruit. amit. l. si partum. §. 1. And the seller cannot, after he has sold, renounce the exception. The text is notable there. D. de pact. l. fin. And it is not an obstacle that exceptions were renounced, because error makes the renunciation invalid, provided that the error is established. D. de transa. l. non est ferendus. §. fin. And l. de his. Also it is not an obstacle that he promised not to prove error, because this is not proof, but relief from the burden of proving, because it is presumed that one ignores the fact of another. l. fi. D. pro suo. Also a general renunciation is not sufficient, as expressly noted by Bartolus, D. de ver. obli. l. si quis cum aliter. in fin.

† And it supports the aforesaid, because if the testator commands that a debt be paid, it is not understood to refer to a debt extinguished by prescription. D. 46.3.100 (*Si is, cui*) and D. 46.3.101 (*Flavius*). Innocentius understands this even in the forum of conscience, as he notes in c. *Cura*, Extr. de iure patronatus. Furthermore, these sellers made an agreement that something would be given to another; this agreement is rather one of doing than of giving, because unless there is an interest, no action can be brought on it, although perhaps an exception may be raised on it, as in D. 45.1.118 (*Liber homo*), § *fin.*, because "to be given to me" contains the notion of being given; but "to be given to another for my sake" contains the notion of having an interest. From these points it is concluded that if there is an error of the seller and the buyer, the buyer may defend himself as a procurator in his own interest. Otherwise not, by argument from D. 32.1 (*Si quis ita legaverit*) and D. 18.1.1 (*Si venditionem*). If, however, the seller is to receive an increase in the price on account of this agreement, it does not pertain to our question. D. 21.2.1 (*Si res, quam*). How prescription is proved, or whether it requires a human act, and whether acts must be proved, or whether it does not require a human act, and then it is proved: and it is a proof established by the course, or passage, of time, just as age and a year are proved by days and by inspection of the calendar, as in D. 40.12.1 (*Lecta*), D. 40.12.1 (*Si certum petatur*). What I have said about the exception of fraud does not pertain to our case: because the claim of a fictitious right is supported by the origin of truth; unless one says that even he who has prescribed has the exception of fraud. D. 16.3.1 (*Quaecunque*) and what is noted in D. 19.1.1 (*Qui si debetur*), D. 19.1.1 (*De conditione ob causam*). Furthermore, in another’s affair, ignorance is more readily presumed than donation, unless one has been informed, as in D. 50.17.1 (*Qui in alterius*), D. 50.17.1 (*De regulis iuris*). This information suffices if it occurs after the time has elapsed: because, having knowledge of the fact, i.e., of the time, knowledge of the law is presumed. The same would be presumed if the fictitious payment had been made for three consecutive years: because it is presumed to have been paid retroactively in each year, and the prescription interrupted. For this presumption does not limp, therefore also c. *Ut*, C. 10.10.1 (*Quicunque*), C. 10.10.1 (*De appositis publicis*). These things can be said according to legal disputation as to sense: but as to prescription of the thing, recourse must be had to C. 7.33.2 (*Male agitur*), C. 7.33.2 (*De praescriptione triginta annorum*).
