But this is not questioned at present, and see Cynus in the said l. *Male agitur* and in l. *Competit*, same title, and what is noted in Speculum, de locatione, § *Nunc aliqua*, vers. 41, and vers. 19, and vers. 57, and vers. 58, with the two following verses, and vers. 62, for the question of the field of Carestello. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a lease for many years is called a single lease.
2. When and at what time the rent is to be paid.
3. The ownership of the emphyteutic thing can be acquired by prescription, and the one who acquires by prescription cannot be sued by a personal real action, nor by a hypothecary action.
4. For what period of time the release from a census is prescribed.
body: To the evidence of the Psalms, it must be appealed,

† A lease for many years is one: because it concerns one thing, there is one contract, and one obligation on the part of the lessor; and consequently, on the part of the lessee, even though the payment of the rent is divided by years or periods. I say this to this extent: because in case of doubt, it is presumed to be divided by years, and not by semesters.

† because the rent of things is due at the end of the year, unless another time has been specified, or custom holds otherwise, as in D. 24.3.12 (Divortio) and D. 43.26.1 § Si pensio. And it seems that a time is tacitly specified, sometimes from the insertion of the cause, as in D. 36.2.1 § Si in habitatione; sometimes from the collection of fruits in a rural estate: but in an urban one, as each person inhabits it. Cf. D. 19.2.1 § Qui impleto. Hence, in a rural estate, continuous payment is not due, which was promised for the entirety of the fruits, unless the fruits have been collected: especially if it is to be paid out of these fruits, as in D. 45.1.1 § Sacramentum and D. 12.3.1 in fine. And the aforementioned words apply to a lease that passes to the heir, but not to one that does not pass to the heir, such as a lease of services, where there are as many leases as there are years, as in D. 45.3.1 (Si servus communis) and D. 49.4.1 (Fin.).

† I further premise, for the sake of clarity, that if anyone prescribes ownership of an emphyteutic thing—which a purchaser can do, who buys from an emphyteuta and possesses in good faith for a very long time—this person cannot be sued by a personal, real, or hypothecary action, even if he is a universal heir, beginning the prescription from himself: because, having become the owner, he cannot properly be understood to have leased his own thing, as in C. loc. l. qui rem. But if he were a possessor in bad faith, in whom the truth is considered, not the legal fiction of speaking in a very long prescription, as noted by Dy. in c. malaefidei, then certainly he would not prescribe ownership, as in C. de praescri. 30. ann. l. male agitur.

† but he would prescribe the liberation of the census for the past forty years, not for the future time, as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in the question of the ancient Pisans, which he disputed; although it seems to some that it prescribes for no time, because of bad faith, as noted in l. 1, C. de usucap. transformanda; while to others it seems that he prescribed the liberation in perpetuity for all time. Argument: ff. de usu. l. eos. in princi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a depositary may oppose the compensation of a loan, or at least the exception of fraud.
body: For the sake of clarity, it must be premised that,

† Suppose you lend me ten coins on a mutuum contract, and I deposit the same ten coins with you. It is clear that I have an action of deposit against you, and you have an action of mutuum against me, because there are two contracts, two forms of obligation, and two distinct substances of the contracts, as stated in D. si certum petatur, l. si tibi. However, a doubt arises: whether the depositary may retain the deposit on account of the said mutuum, or set it off by compensation. I hold that he may, for the right of retention is proven by D. de condictione indebiti, l. si non sortem, §. si certum, and by the note in C. de commodato, l. sub praetextu, regarding compensation, because one who sets off is similar to one who pays. The law states that it makes no difference whether he paid or set off, D. qui potior in pignore habenda sit, l. si debitor, and D. de administratione tutorum, l. inter tutores. Furthermore, it is certain that once the time for payment of the mutuum has arrived, he who does not pay is deemed to be doing that which prevents payment from being made to him, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Iulianus ait si heredi. Moreover, he acts in bad faith (dolo) who demands what he is immediately going to restore, a rule which is also applied to the action for dowry, D. de solutione matrimonii, l. rei iudicatae, §. heredi. Since the action for dowry is more privileged than the action of deposit, which is available for the same amount in kind, it follows a fortiori, or by analogy from similar cases, that the same should be said regarding the action of deposit, arguing from similar to similar, D. de negotiorum gestione, l. ex facto.

On the contrary, it seems that the action of deposit does not admit compensation, as stated in C. de compensatione, l. final, and as is read and noted in Inst. de actionibus, §. in bonae fidei. The rule "he acts in bad faith" does not apply here, because he who avails himself of a privilege of the law does not act in bad faith; namely, because he who denies the deposit is said to interrupt the possession, or quasi-possession, of the deposited thing, and to dispossess the depositor; therefore, the depositor must be restored immediately. This reasoning is given by Dy. in c. qui ad agendum, Extr. de regulis iuris, lib. 6. But if this reasoning were true, it would follow that the same would apply to the action of commodatum, which is available for interest, which is false. The law precisely states that compensation has no place against the action of deposit, which the doctors understand to apply even if the deposit was in ready money, although ownership transfers when money is deposited by number and not by species, D. de deposito, l. dies sponsaliorum, §. 1.

It must be considered whether the action of deposit is properly brought here. For the deposit was made so that it might be converted in the redemption of the properties; if therefore it is converted, one must sue on another ground, namely by the action on agreed words (actio praescriptis verbis) based on a tacit agreement, not by the action of deposit, as is expressly proven in D. de dolo, l. si oleum. This action on agreed words does not succeed in place of the action of deposit, because the suit is not brought according to the form of deposit, D. de conditione ob causam, l. si extraneos. Another reason occurs: because this deposit arises from the mutuum, and therefore it must partake of its nature, D. si quis cautio, l. si eum, §. final, and l. qui iniuria. This appears from the convention of both contracts, and from the fact that it was done immediately on the same day and for the same end, D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. si ventri, §. final. Hence, retention is not contrary to good faith, and for the same reason, neither is compensation, D. familiae erciscundae, l. Mevius, §. eum. Furthermore, for this mutuum, the very money deposited is bound; and although it were consumed, nevertheless the goods of him who receives the mutuum are generally bound. If therefore he demands the deposit back, he must offer the mutuum. Briefly, this circuitry must be avoided, D. si certum petatur, l. cum fundus, §. 1. Finally, I conclude, considering equity and also the reasons of law, D. si certum petatur, l. si me et Titium, that this woman be repelled by the exception of bad faith (exceptio doli), and thus the defendant be absolved from her petition, the obligations being confused on both sides.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a rector who held office in the past may again hold it immediately.
2. Which of the candidates elected is to be preferred, where the greater and sounder part has not consented.
3. How the word "law" is to be understood.
4. Whether it is required in an election that the sounder and greater part elect.
5. The opinion of the ordinary gloss excuses from calumny.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is posited that the election of the rector and scholars was made with an equal number and equal merit in discord; nevertheless, one of

† He had been rector in the immediately preceding year, and still was so until another hour; and therefore it was said that he could not be elected again immediately, and this for a twofold reason, and first by the common law: because honors, especially those of jurisdiction, are not to be continued, unless the election were made in concord with no one dissenting, as in Auth. de defensione civium §. si, and ff. de muneribus et honoribus l. honorum §. gerundorum, where it is said, "nor can anyone continue in honors." C. de decuriis l. qui nisi, when no other suitable person is found, as in the said §. gerundorum, where it is said, "if there are not others suitable to perform this office, from those who have already performed it." But to this it was answered: because he who has once been rightly recognized should not be rejected for this sole reason, that he has already been proven, as in C. de assessoribus l. licet. But that law is understood in another office, not in the continuation of the same office. This is also confirmed by the statute of the university, where it says, "let him perform the office until the year of rectorship." The word "until" is a limiting term, and therefore, lest fraud be done to the law, he cannot be elected again, as in c. Venio deinceps §. huiusmodi, and there noted, extra de electione lib. 6. It is presumed that such an election was made through ambition, hence it falls under the Iulian law on ambitus, and noted in the said §. gerundorum. But the gloss on C. de assessoribus l. nemo de domesticis says that this is true if ambition or substitution is established, or if he conducted himself poorly in office. But if he conducted himself well, the election holds according to the gloss which is in the said l. licet at the end, and especially if this was accustomed to be done. For custom is to be observed above all in elections, and particularly in municipal honors, as in ff. de muneribus et honoribus l. ut gradatim §. sed si lege. For what custom approves is held as law, as in ff. de petitione hereditatis l. Imperator, and extra de consuetudine c. Cum dilectus, and in c. Cumana de electione. Solution: As regards the former rector, his election is not valid, even if it were made by the majority, unless custom were proven, and he were elected by the majority, and not by an equal division, and he had no other impediment.

I come to the election of the other, and it seems that one should first say that his election is valid, because the electors of him were the full chapter: because the votes of those electing the unworthy accrued to those electing the worthy, since they knowingly elected the unworthy; but here knowledge is presumed, as in c. Nulli licere, Extr. de electione, lib. 6. When, indeed, they are not only presumed, but it is notorious: because he had notoriously been rector, and was still governing. Moreover, the decrees or statutes were notorious, and very frequently practiced, hence the electors cannot be excused by the veil of ignorance, who thereby lost the power of electing, as in c. Cum Vitoniensis, Extr. de electione. That this rector was not worthy to be elected appears from the fact that he was not suitable, being prohibited by law. Arg. ff. ad Tertullianum, l. 2, § Si mater.

To the contrary it seems: because this election did not hold, because the greater and sounder part did not consent to the same. For these two things seem to be required conjunctively, namely, that it be the greater and sounder part, hence one without the other is not sufficient, as in Extr. de electione, c. Ecclesia vestra, § Finis, and ff. de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, § Si praetor.

Solution: It must be said that we are not here simply in the common law, but in the statutes of the university confirmed by the lord, which provide that he who has been named in the greater number of the aforementioned ballots shall perform the office until the year of rectorship. But this one, concerning whom the question is asked, was not named in the greater number of the said ballots, and that which is to be proved by the recitation of writing is not sufficient if uttered by living voice, as in l. 1, C. de iure emphyteutico, and C. de non numero personarum, l. Generaliter. Since, therefore, the form regarding the number of ballots was not observed, the election was void by the law itself, as in c. Quia perpetuo, Extr. de electione.

Furthermore, the statute of the university provides that a simple scholar, who is a master of arts, nay, certainly not even a licentiate, is considered as next to being bound. l. Ex eo, ff. de testamento militis. Moreover, one of the connected things being prohibited, the other also seems to be prohibited. ff. de sponsalibus, l. Oratio.

From these it is concluded that, since both elections were null by the law itself, a new election must be made, in which all shall participate, as in the aforementioned c. Cum Vitoniensis. And the words of the statute are so clear that they do not admit interpretation, nor legal fiction, especially because they refer to fact, and not to legal fiction, as in c. Quia circa, de electione in clerico; ff. quibus ex causis maiores, l. Deinde; ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 1, § Si vir uxori; ff. de negotiis gestis, l. 3, § Haec verba, to which l. 1, circa principium, ff. de his quae in testamento delentur, is most apt, there where it says "when"

† He says, however, that the law must be taken as it is seen with the eyes, not understood, namely, what is written. Through which text this question seems to be clearly declared. Moreover, the statute speaks in natural words, not civil ones. D. de capite diminuto, l. tutelas and l. legatum. Furthermore, the writing shows itself, and it is a matter of fact. D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum, § 1. Civil words are pregnant and admit of interpretation, but natural words do not, because they are very clear, and one must not depart from the words of the law. D. de exercitoria, l. 1, § si is, qui navem, and in c. is, qui contra, Extr. de electione, lib. 6. Moreover, the words of the law are to be considered according to the common civil law, he says. Namely, the civil law,

† that which has been healthily established by the greater part of the order. C. de decur. l. nominationum forma. lib. 10. Note: it requires two things, that it be the greater part, and that it be done healthily. Likewise C. de praediis curia. l. si. e. lib. ibi, when it says “by the report of the greater part of the curia proceeding without any malice,” that is, in good faith. Hence, the greater part and a sound mind are required. C. de legi. l. si. quod extraordinarium eo lib. ibi, when it says, “but in a public place, let a sentence be pronounced concerning the common utility of the provincials, and let this be confirmed by the solemn authority of the assent of the greater part.” And thus utility and the greater part are required. And C. de vendendis rebus ciuitatum. l. si. lib. 11, where it says, “we command each one of them who convenes to designate individually the sentence which he thinks useful for his fatherland.” And ff. quod cuiusque uniuer. nomine. l. nulli. And ff. ad muni. l. cum maior. And ff. de re. iu. l. aliud. §. refertur. And ff. de pac. l. l. maiorem. In the second response. That law can be alleged both for and against, because it adds, “but in an equal number, the praetor will follow the authority of him who excels in dignity, that is, in better opinion, according to one exposition among them.” Likewise, whatever diminishes the votes of one party accrues to the other, as in c. si quando. de elec. lib. 6. And c. quanquam. in the great gloss. eo. ti. To the same effect is what is noted in ff. de re iudi. l. Pompo. §. si uni. in the last gloss. But the Lord Oldradus says at the end that these words, namely, “but this does not apply in ordinary cases, since dignity is not considered among them,” as in C. de uete. iu. enucle. l. 1. §. cunque. And de Palatinis sacrarum largitionum. I. iubemus. lib. 12. Likewise, if one half desires what is possible, and the other half what is impossible, that which is possible prevails. This is proven by a certain similarity: if there are more persons who have the power to elect, and some are absent through contumacy, the power of election devolves upon the others, as in ff. de fideicommis. liber. l. si legatario. §. a duobus. Likewise, those who elect contrary to law are regarded as if they were not of the chapter, as in cap. 2. in fin. de elec. lib. 6. And there it is noted. But notwithstanding these, I say that the universitas has its own law confirmed by a superior, to which one must adhere, as in l. 1. C. de vendendis rebus ciuitatum, which law requires a plurality of ballots. Hence, it wishes that a majority be decreed from a certain notoriety, because nothing is so proper to law as clarity, as in Auth. de testis imperfe. and C. de testies. auth. quo siue. That which is not contained in writing is a fiction, which has no place in statutes. Likewise, just as two discordant persons accomplish nothing, so do four, or any subsequent even number, because as one stands to one, so do two to two, as in ff. de pact. l. vter quam si vnus. §. si duos. Moreover, where a form is prescribed, whatever is done without observing the form is considered rejected. ff. de verbo. obli. l. qui Romae. §. flauius hermes. And extra de rescri. c. cum dilecta. Some say it is void by the law itself, others by sentence, de elec. c. quanquam. lib. 6. And these two are equivalent, praeter and contra, as noted in c. si cui. de elec. lib. 6. Then it will be said to be done praeter when something is done which is not statuted. Likewise, these ballots serve in place of witnesses, and if one witness is lacking, the act does not subsist, as in C. de testamentis. l. si unus. Likewise, custom, even if not yet prescribed, excludes fraud, and those who believe their election is aided by the custom then in force will not be said to knowingly elect an unworthy person. ff. de edi. edic. l. quod si nolit. §. qui assidua.

† Moreover, the opinion of the Glossa Ordinaria excuses those who elected the former rector from calumny, as stated in the aforementioned law *Licet*. Just as if all electors ignorantly choose an ineligible person, they are not deprived of their power, so too does this apply when arguing from the whole to the part, as in the aforementioned chapter *Si compromissa*. Therefore, having considered all matters, I hold that neither election is confirmable, and that which was not done properly must be solemnly repeated, as in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Qui per salutem*. Moreover, the true number properly consists in the fictitious count, as in the chapter *Quorundam*, *De electione*, Book 6. Moreover, one must not depart from the words of the statute, as in the Digest, *Solutis matrimonii*, law *Si vero*; § *De viro*; Digest, *De exercitoria*, law 1, § *Si is, qui navem*. And that in the proper matter of elections one should not depart from the words of the statute, is noted in the chapter *Qui his*, *De electione*, Book 6. Someone might say that those who act against the law are regarded as if they were not of the chapter, as is read and noted in chapter 2, *De electione*, at the end, Book 6. And there are two rules: one is that whatever impugns one part of the electors, impugns the other, in the same title, chapter *Si quando*. Moreover, whatever weakens or annuls one part, consolidates the other, in the same title, chapter *Quanquam*, in the great Gloss, Book 6. But to this it is responded that this is true where someone knowingly elects an unworthy person; but it has already been proven that here there is no unworthiness, because custom makes him worthy. And even assuming there were unworthiness, there is no knowledge, because the opinion of the Glossa Ordinaria excuses from calumny, as noted by Innocentius, *Extra*, *De constitutionibus*, chapter *Ne innitaris*; 50th distinction, chapter *Domino Sancto*. The Gloss says this in the aforementioned law *Licet*. Therefore, those who elected the preceding rector were not in bad faith, and consequently not subject to deprivation; and certainly one does not accrue to another unless it decreases from another; because he who is admitted to a part makes a part, as in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Plane*, § *Si duobus*. Since therefore both parties are equal in number, and not unequal, they mutually obstruct each other; because just as one stands against one, so two stand against two, Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Item si unus*, § *Si duos*. Moreover, the ballots do not predominate in number, and whether they serve in place of witnesses or in place of instruments, neither is valid; because since they are contrary and adversarial, one part has no power over the other, as in the Code, *De fidei instrumentis*, law *Scripturae*; and Digest, *De testibus*, law *Hoc carmen*, § *Finis*. Moreover, here at least one more ballot is required, and if the ballot serves the office of a witness, one witness is lacking, as in the Code, *De testamento*, law *Si unus*; and Code, *Qui testamento facere possint*, law *Hac consultissima*, § *Finis*. Moreover, both elections were made contrary to the law, because they did not do what was statuted, as in the Digest, *De verborum obligatione*, law *Qui Romae*, § *Flavius*. And in similar acts, "contrary to" and "against" are the same, as is read and noted in the chapter *Si cui*, *Extra*, *De electione*, Book 6. Moreover, all laws proclaim that something must be added in case of equality, so that preponderance may arise, as in the chapter *Dubii*, *De rescriptis*, Book 6; Digest, *De pactis*, law *Maiorem*; and it is read and noted in law *Si uni*, Digest, *De re iudicata*. And the aforementioned are confirmed by the text of the laws: Code, *De decuriis*, law *Nominationum forma*; Code, *De praediis curiae*, law *Finis*; Code, *De legibus*, law *Si quod extraordinarium*; and law *Ultima*; Code, *De vendendis rebus civilibus*, law *Finis*; Digest, *Ad municipalia*, law *Quod maiorum*; Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Aliud*, § *Refertur*; and Code, *De Palatinis sacrarum largitionum*, law *Iubemus*, Book 12. Since therefore in this contradictory contest no middle disposition is found, a solemn election must again be made by all, as in the chapter *Compromissarius*, § 1, *De electione*, Book 6; *De arbitris*, chapter *Quid tamen*; *De electione*, chapter *Cum Vitoniensis*; and argument from Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Qui per salutem*; and *De officio delegati*, chapter *In literis*, by Innocentius; *De re iudicata*, in the rubric, by Innocentius and others, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the notaries of the bishop may draw up instruments by mandate of the bishop: and whether faith is to be given to them.
2. Whether credence is to be given to letters and the seal of the bishop.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† On the first point, it seems to be said that, although the notaries of the bishop may draw up an instrument by virtue of a mandate given to them by the bishop, or a commission to receive security from an usurer, according to what is noted by Bartolus in *l. ex sententia*, D. de testamentaria tutela, and in *l. 2*, D. de stipulationibus servorum et ancillarum, D. de adoptionibus, *l. si consul*, and de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, *l. iubemus*, §. *oekonomos*, nevertheless this instrument must have its essential formalities and witnesses, as is noted in C. de tabulis, *l. generali*, and D. de editionibus, *l. 1*, §. *editiones*. But here it lacks the formalities which govern the mandate to receive security on this article. Moreover, this instrument was not drawn up pursuant to a mandate; therefore it does not prove the mandate. Furthermore, in this regard, C. de editionibus, *auth. si quis*, provides that what is asserted to have been done by a notary is not given credence, nor does it make full faith. To this is added what is noted by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, *l. optimam*.

And now I come to the letters of the bishop sealed: and if indeed the seal is not authentic, credit is not given to the seal; but if it is authentic, since here the matter is not principally treated regarding the prejudice of anyone, because receiving caution benefits the testator and harms no one, since a testament is favorable, as noted in the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Gallus*, section *Videndum*; nor can the intestate successors claim any probable interest, because they ought not to be concerned with the inheritance of a living person, as in the Code, *De pactis*, law *Si*; and in the Digest, *De ventre in utero iudicando*, law *I*, section *De nuptiali*. Hence, credit should be given to the letters of the bishop: because this pertains to his office, as in the Digest, *De publicanis*, law *Si publicanus*, section *De rebus*; Digest, *De custodiendo reo*, law *Divus*; and in both places by Bartolus; and in the chapter *Ut ecclesia*, *De electione*, Book 6, by the Archdeacon; and most fully noted in the Speculum, *De probationibus*, section *Si*; and by Innocentius, *De fide instrumentorum*, chapter 2. Here also we are in a favorable act; hence, according to the Archdeacon and Ioannes Andreae, credit ought more readily to be given, and especially because the testator was moved by just reason to believe; hence he seems to have satisfied the decree *Quanquam*, Extra, *De usuris*, Book 6. And to this it is very helpful that which is noted in the chapter *Dudum ecclesia*, Extra, *De electione*, in the gloss which begins *Quia cum*, Extra, *De electione*, chapter *Praeterea*. And if the notary’s instrument alone, and the bishop’s seal alone, did not prove, nevertheless both joined together, because they are two authentic persons, namely the bishop and the notary, seem to prove, Extra, *De probationibus*, chapter *Quoniam contra falsam*; and argument from Extra, *De successionibus ab intestato*, chapter *Cum dilectus*; and in the Authenticum, *De haereditatibus et falsis*, section *Si vero absunt*, column 1. I consider that, in order for letters sealed by the bishop to be believed, as in Extra, *De probationibus*, chapter *Post cessionem*, it is necessary that these letters be strengthened by at least two witnesses; for credit ought not to be given to the seal alone, as noted by Innocentius in the said chapter *Post cessionem*. For the seal could easily be affixed to the grave prejudice of the legitimate successors, which is by no means to be permitted, as in the Code, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Quaestionem*, section 1; *De falsis*, law *Si creditor*; Digest, *Ad Velleiam*, law *Seyra*; Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, Institutiones, law *Repetita*. To this it is helpful, Code, *De testamento*, law *Omnium*, at the end. But it is also certain that if the notary says he was requested, or commanded, or entrusted, credit is not given to him unless the instrument contains the required number of witnesses, as in the Authenticum, *De tabellis*, section *Finis*. From these last arguments, therefore, it seems to be said that credit is not to be given to the letters sealed by the bishop in this case, which can be drawn to the occasion of harming the intestate successors; nor does it matter whether the legacies are simple or for pious causes; because the person of the testator is reproved by canon law, and is *intestabilis*, as in the said chapter *Quanquam*. Moreover, the heir cannot make the said testament, which is null due to the hatred of the testator, become valid, as in the Code, *De legatis*, law *Non dubium*; Code, *De testibus*, law *Non dubium*; and which is noted in a similar case, Digest, *De ritu nuptiarum*, law *Adiuo*; and Code, *Ne fideiussores*, *De decem denariis*, law 2. And in this testament, without the intervention of solemn caution, no natural obligation arises, nor the office of the secular or ecclesiastical judge, because the testament cannot be confirmed by the acceptance of the inheritance. Moreover, if the right does not fail, but only the proof fails, then a natural obligation arises; otherwise, if both the right and the proof fail. But this opinion is very harsh, since the testator, moved by just reason, believed he had sufficiently satisfied. For just ignorance makes a testament valid, as in the Code, *De testamento*, law 1; because the law says, "We wish knowledge, not ignorance, to be binding," as in the Code, *De decuriis*, law *Generalis*; and law *Finalis*, Digest, *De decretis ab ordinariis faciendis*; and in the chapter *Ut animarum*, *De constitutionibus*, Book 6; argument from the Code, *De posthumis haeredibus instituendis*, law *Si*, where it says, "so that he may not suffer the penalty," etc., unless it is said that this man was too credulous and foolish, and therefore this testator must impute it to himself, as in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Qui cum alio*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a caution furnished by a usurer before the notary of the bishop, by his command, is valid. And see above in the preceding counsel.
1. Whether credence is to be given to the letters of the bishop, sealed, in which is contained the commission made by the said bishop to the notary to receive the caution from the usurer.
2. Whether an appeal may be taken from a definitive sentence in canon law, to be restored and seized
body: Furthermore, as stated

†If the caution was valid, thus he proves it. In the notarial instrument, mention is made of the mandate, for the notary states that he acted by the mandate of Christ. Then I argue thus: where in the instrument there is mention of solemnity, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly, as the notary states in l. j., C. de fide instrumentorum et iuramento astae fiscalis, l. 10, especially in these extraordinary matters, in which summary faith suffices, as in l. j., §. ibidem, ff. ad exhibenda, and l. thesaurus. Moreover, it is certain that the lender is bound by this caution both by promise and by confession, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter. Hence, since he is burdened in this regard, he ought to be relieved in this regard, as in l. eum qui, ff. de iureiurando. Moreover, in this instrument it is stated that neither he nor his heir can deny the mandate, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter. Furthermore, the notary can draw up an instrument at his own request or mandate, as the notary states in Auth. de tabellionibus, §. nos autem. Furthermore, such is the custom, to which one must adhere, as in ff. de testamento tutorum, l. ex sententia, according to Bartolus. Furthermore, this notary acted usefully; therefore, it ought to be ratified, as in ff. de negotiorum gestione, l. Pomponius writes. Furthermore, I say that this business of receiving the canon pertained to the bishop by necessity of office, and thus it was his business with care and solicitude. Hence, he ought to have ratified what was done in his name, ff. de negotiorum gestione, l. si pupilli. Furthermore, this mandate can intervene at that instant, through a messenger or letter of the bishop, as in ff. de muneribus et honoribus, l. honores, §. si. Therefore, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly, as the notary Innocentius states in c. Innotuit, de eo qui furtive ordinem suscepit, notwithstanding the chapter Quam contra falsum, for there it speaks of a contradictory judgment, but we are here in a voluntary matter and by consent.

† Now I come to the second point, namely, whether credence should be given to letters sealed by the bishop, in which is contained the commission made to the notary. And it seems that not, because they lack witnesses, as noted by Innocentius in c. Post cessionem, Extra, de probat. On the contrary, the truth itself seems to indicate otherwise, first, because credence is given to letters sealed by the bishop, where no prejudice or injury arises to another, as in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Si qua per calumniam. And there Jacobus Butrigarius holds that witnesses are not required. To the same effect it is said that it suffices that the judge’s secret is entered, as in C. de testibus, l. Nullum. Moreover, consider more subtly that either the letters make mention of a fact or internal act, that is, of one’s own will; and then letters suffice without witnesses, the text being in ff. de negotiis gestis, l. Nesenius Apollinaris. Or they make mention of another’s fact or external act, for example, of a crime or contract of someone; and then they do not prove that, because they are enunciative words, not dispositive; because one could not dispose of another’s fact by inducing it, as in ff. de verbis obligatis, l. Inter stipulantem, in princ., and ff. de custodia reorum, l. Divus. Hence they are simply enunciative words, which cannot be drawn to the effect of disposition, and therefore such enunciative writing is not believed, unless the consensus of both parties accedes, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. Optima. From this distinction it is necessarily and evidently gathered that in our case the letters prove the will of the bishop, even without any external witness, which will is proved by the letters of the writer, as in ff. de procuratoribus, l. Si procurator absentem, especially when fortified with his own seal, customary in similar cases, as noted in l. 2, C. de rebus alienis non alienandis. Moreover, here we have the testimony of the bishop and the notary, and the obedience of him who made the caution. For even if he had not given caution, nevertheless he believed in good faith two authentic persons, as noted in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio. And just error excuses him from the penalty of intestacy, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. Titius, § Lucius. And where infirmity presses, there counsel for further deliberation is not sought, as in C. qui testamento facere possint, l. Hac consule, § At cum humana. Also, one ought not to be deceived by the authority of the bishop’s letters, C. de his qui vetita aetate impediuntur, l. Prima. Moreover, lenity is shown to him who is led by writing, ff. de interrogatione actionis, l. De aetate. Also, for the salvation of souls, something is sometimes deemed true, as noted in Extra, de electione, cap. Dudum ecclesia. From which it is concluded that the said caution was solemn, or ought to be held as solemn, actively as regards testifying, and passively as regards obligating, and thus the testament was valid, especially for pious causes, which a pious son and heir ought not to infringe, as in ff. de fideicommissis, l. In testamento. And to what I said, that credence is given to the bishop’s letters, it contributes that which is noted by Butrigarius in C. de arbitris, l. Ne in arbitris, with the following law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The interdict *unde vi*, the action for restitution based on canon law, the action based on the law *conquerebatur*, the action *quod metus causa*, and the remedy under the chapter *saepe* concerning the restitution of the spoliated, against whom these are granted, are discussed in the title *saepe*.
2. An appeal may be taken from a judgment rendered upon an improper petition.
3. An appeal is also taken in an action for the vindication of a thing.
4. A judge cannot cumulate civil possession and natural possession.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† To make the matter evident, it must be premised that sometimes the interdict *unde vi* is invoked; sometimes the *condictio* from the canon *reintegranda*; sometimes the *condictio* from the law *conquerebatur*, C. *unde vi*; sometimes the action *quod metus causa*. The interdict *unde vi* is granted against the one who used force, and it is personal; nor is it granted against a singular successor, as in D. *de vi, et viar.*, l. *cum matre*; against Auth. *hæredem*, *de eo, quod pervenit*; as in l. 3, in the beginning, of the same title. But because those who expelled others transferred possession to another in fraud of the interdict, relief was provided by the decretal *sæpe*, where it is established that, notwithstanding the strictness of civil law, if anyone knowingly received such a thing, since he succeeds the spoliator in the fault as it were, he is bound to restore it to the spoliator. And this decretal requires that he received it knowingly, and although according to civil law one does not succeed in the fault unless he is a universal successor, insofar as it came to him, or he acted with fraud so that it did not come to him, nevertheless according to canon law the same applies to a singular successor; because he would succeed the spoliator in the fault on account of the thing and on account of fraud, as in X. *de iudic.*, c. *quia* 5. The canon Auth. *reintegranda* establishes that unless the fault of violence is purged, which is read and noted in D. *de usucap.*, l. *sequitur*, § *tunc in potestate*. Any possessor in bad faith is bound by the remedy of quasi-recovery of possession, as is clear from c. *reintegranda*, 3 q. 1, which chapter requires that spoliation intervened from the beginning. But another remedy is that by l. *conquerebatur*, and that law requires occupation by one who knows that the thing does not belong to him, but to another, which is presumed to be known, i.e., to belong to another, simply by the fact that he knows it does not belong to him. And that law speaks of one who occupies vacant possession, which nevertheless belongs to another in law.

† Now, in all these matters, it may be doubted whether an appeal can be taken from a definitive judgment. And because our case concerns the canon *saepe* or the canon *reintegranda*, whether we call it a *condictio* arising from the canon or an office of the judge by canonical authority, it must be considered whether an appeal is permissible. It seems that it is not permissible under civil law, as in C. *si de momentanea possessione*, in the rubric, and *nigro*. Consider that we are not dealing with civil law, because these two remedies were never known to civil law; hence civil law never considered them, nor could it have considered them, nor could that title *si de momentanea possessione* have considered them. And if they were not considered, then they were not enacted. This is confirmed by another reason: since these remedies were invented by the praetor, we follow praetorian law, not civil law, as is clear from the discussion of all bonitary possessions. Moreover, canon law is contrary to civil law in these two remedies, which are of canonical intention, not civil, as expressly appears in the aforementioned canon *saepe*. Therefore, I argue thus: from a possessory action, which was invented by canon law and not civil law, an appeal can be taken, because canon law must be observed and served as the foundation, such that even the magistrate of the secular forum derives his foundation from it; therefore, canon law must be observed in any forum. But it is certain under canon law that an appeal lies from a definitive judgment rendered on a possessory action, as in c. *cum ad sedem*, Extra, de restitutione spoliatorum. Therefore, without doubt, concluding from the first to the last point, it can be said that an appeal is permissible here, even in the forum of Justinian. If it is said that civil law must be observed, it can be answered: if civil law is observed, then you proceed without an action, which is impossible, as in l. *si pupilli*, § *pen.*, ff. de negotiorum gestione, and C. de interdictis, l. *finalis*. Furthermore, the *condictio* from the canon *saepe* and from the canon *reintegranda* is more similar to the *actio quod metus causa*, which is an action in rem, than to the interdict *unde vi*. But I see that an appeal lies from a judgment rendered in the *actio quod metus causa*, as is read and noted in l. *si cum exceptione*, § *haec autem actio*, ff. quod metus causa; therefore, so it is in the present case. Moreover, when a judgment suffers from a defect of form, an appeal can be taken from such a judgment, insofar as it was rendered in fact, although truly this is rather a nullity, as in ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. *qui testamento*. But here the judgment suffers from a defect of form, for whether we speak of the interdict *unde vi* or of the *condictiones* from the aforementioned canons, condemnation ought to be made, if the thing is not restored, for the amount of the interest in possessing, as in ff. de vi et vi armata, l. *in interdicto*. And this ought to be claimed in the libel, as there noted by Bartolus, ff. uti possidetis, l. *si duo*, in fine. But here the judge did not follow this form, but exceeded the measure by condemning to the true estimation of the thing. Moreover, no case is ever found in which an appeal cannot be taken from an excess of measure, as in C. quo appellationes non recipiuntur, l. *ab executione*. Furthermore, it must be considered that, since the monastery of St. Peter instituted both a petitory and a possessory action, and did not prosecute the petitory action, it is as if one who does not sue on a petitory action is not bound to give security that he will defend in the possessory action, because he does not raise a controversy regarding it. Hence, the law *is a quo* and similar laws speak when both parties have sued on a petitory action of equal standing, for example, *rei vindicatio* or *publiciana*, or a petition of inheritance. Whether the *condictio* from the aforementioned canons lies against him to whom the *publiciana* is given. For the *publiciana* is greater than any possessory action, and he who does not possess as a thief, which the aforementioned canons seem to require. Moreover, from the aforementioned canons, a singular successor is not sued more than a universal successor would be sued under civil law. But the latter would not be bound if he did not have the ability to restore the thing, because he should not profit, yet he should not suffer loss, as in the aforementioned l. 3, in principio, ff. de vi et vi armata. And it is supported by ff. de solutionibus, l. *si stipulatus*, § *si lanceam*, and ff. de usucapione, l. *servi nomine*. Moreover, having seen the libel, this libel seems inept, especially as regards the possessory action, since the time at which the direction was made is not alleged in the libel. This is noted by Bartolus expressly in l. 1, § *rectissime*, ff. de vi et vi armata.

And from a judgment rendered on a frivolous bill, one can undoubtedly appeal, because it is not said that one appeals from the possessory action, but from the procedure. D. de empt. et vend. l. cum dilecti. And thus says Guillaume de Coulanges in l. si ex causa § nunc videndum, D. de minoribus.

† Furthermore, even in the case of a sale of a thing, there is no doubt that an appeal may be taken, as is read and noted in the Digest, Title "On the Sale of a Thing," law *Qui restituere*. Moreover, this plaintiff admits that for fifteen years and more, before the present suit was brought, he did not possess the property, at least not in a natural sense; therefore, he lost the possession, if he had any, not by spoliation, but by his own negligence, as stated in the Digest, Title "On Acquiring Possession," law *Clam possidere*; § *Qui ad nundinas* in the Digest, Title "On Usucaption"; law *Furtum*, § 1 in the Institutes, Title "On Usucaption"; § *Quod autem*. Furthermore, since he purchased from Francis, he cannot be said to have become richer, as noted in the Code, Title "On the Sale of a Thing," law *Mater*; and therefore, especially after the lapse of one year, the action cannot be usefully brought. And these points seem clearer than daylight. Nor do I omit that this petition was not properly drawn up in any possessory action, as appears from the discussion in all the standard legal textbooks. Speculum, in the Title "On Restitution for Spoliation," § 1.

What more is needed? Here, the loss of civil possession was attempted, and the judge mixed in natural possession, which he could not do, as is noted in the Digest, *De usucapione*, in the law *Cuiuscumque*, section *Si fundus*, and in the Code, *Ubi in rem actio*, in law 2. Finally, I conclude from the foregoing that it appears not only that an appeal could have been brought, but also that it was most justly brought. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a contract is presumed to have been entered into in fraud of usury.
2. On the understanding of c. ad nostram, de emptione et venditione, and of c. illo vos, de pignore.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. An instrument drawn up in the form of a sale contains that Mafiolinus and Codeus of S. Benedict made a sale and transfer to the said Laurentius de Pelegrinis of certain houses and lands contained in the said instrument for the price of 800 florins, then actually and truly counted; and by this instrument of sale thus made, the said Laurentius made a certain instrument, in which it is contained that the said Laurentius, by special grant, conceded to the said lords Mafiolus and Codeus, and to their heirs and those having cause from them, that they may and can redeem and recover the said things within the term of eight years; and that the said Laurentius is bound and obliged to make a retro-datum and re-sale of the said things for the aforesaid price and within the term aforesaid; and in case the said Laurentius should refuse to make the said retro-datum and re-sale, that it shall be lawful for the said parties of S. Benedict to offer, deposit, and consign solemnly and legitimately the aforesaid price, which deposit having been made, the pensions and revenues shall cease and ought to cease in favor of the said Laurentius until the time of the recovery of the said things or of the legitimate disposition of the aforesaid price. Moreover, another pact was added, that if the said parties of S. Benedict do not recover the said things within the term, that the said Laurentius is bound and ought to give and pay to the said parties of S. Benedict 300 gold florins for complete payment and entire satisfaction of all that they could, might, and could have demanded and required from the said Laurentius on account of the aforesaid matter. Since, however, neither the retro-datum has been made nor the pension paid,

† It is asked concerning the validity of the aforementioned contracts, and whether they are presumed to have been celebrated in fraud of usury. And since I had been asked about this point on another occasion, I advised that the aforementioned title of sale was to be presumed simulated and made in fraud of usury, being moved to say this by the following: when the stipulations are referred to the nature of the title of sale and purchase, the first instrument could not per se be usurious; because it has the pure and proper form of sale and purchase, and the price was actually paid in cash; from which it appears that the contract was to be considered effective in its form, if from the circumstances of the contracting parties at the same place and time fraud did not appear, nor was it presumed to have existed previously. But that judgment is to be made regarding contracts from their form, and especially when the form is supported by the cause, is clear: C. de probat. l. cum precibus; and Extr. de usur. c. in civitate. Moreover, he who contracts seems to confess that all things contained in the instrument are true and not simulated, as C. de non numer. pec. l. generaliter. And he who alleges that the contract is simulated must prove the simulation, as noted in C. plus valere quod agitur l. emptione. For no one is presumed to say with his words what he does not think in his mind, as ff. de supellect. leg. l. Labeo § idem Tuber.

† Furthermore, there are two decretals which judge a contract to be feneraticium [a usurious loan disguised as a sale], *extra de emptione et venditione*, chapter *Ad nostram*. There it is said that fraud is presumed from the fact that whenever, from the seventh year up to the ninth year, the debtor would give the creditor 60 unciae. Another decretal is *extra de pignoribus*, chapter *Illo vos*. There it is said that if a usurer buys a thing on the agreement that after a time he shall restore it to the seller, receiving something in excess, although fruits are computed, the contract is presumed from the agreement itself to have been celebrated in fraud of usury. But neither of these decretals seems to touch our case: because here there is not such a smallness of price. And thus chapter *Ad nostram* does not obstruct; nor is there an agreement that fruits be computed into the principal, and thus chapter *Illo vos* does not obstruct. On the contrary, the opposite appears from the instrument of lease. For it was agreed that the buyer, who afterwards leased, should receive and retain for himself the pension of the intermediate time, which is according to the proper nature of a sale, and not contrary to the nature of the contract. Agreements derogatory and contrary to nature cause a presumption against the contract: because they deviate from its species. But agreements consecutive to the contract indicate truth and consonance, as in *Digestum*, *de contrahenda emptione*, law *Fraudi partem*; and *Digestum*, *de acquisitione vel amissione servitutis*, law *Si sterilis*, § *Si tibi*. Moreover, an agreement to resell is not contrary to the nature of a sale: as in *Codex*, *de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem*, law 2. Moreover, nor is an agreement that if the buyer dislikes it, the thing shall be unsold or unbought. Hence, at first sight, it would seem that the said contract ought to be presumed just and valid, especially because he who alleges fraud and deceit must prove it. But notwithstanding these things, I am firm in the opinion that this contract is presumed to be pignoratitium [a pledge]. For here several things concur. First, an unjust price by the form of the instrument of supplement of 300 florins. For it was agreed that if the buyer wishes to possess perpetually, he must supplement 300 florins. Moreover, this sum is excessively high, for if one were injured, whether so greatly injured, it would be enormous injury; therefore, the smallness of the price is an argument of deceit, as in *Digestum*, *de transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, § *Cum modus*; and *Codex*, *de manumissionibus*, law *Per diversas*. Moreover, there was an agreement to resell. Furthermore, there was an agreement to gain fruits beyond the principal. For the principal was over 800 florins agreed upon, but the things were worth 1,100, and the pensions were corresponding to 1,100, and thus there was a greater fruit or pension agreed upon than there ought to have been. Moreover, fraud is presumed if for a part sold, not simply for a part given. *Codex*, *de manumissionibus*, law *Ab Anastasio*; and noted in law *Si tibi*, in the beginning, *Digestum*, *de pactis*, by Guillaume and Cynus. Let us consider not only the cases in the terms of the said decretals, but the reasons of them, and if in our case there is the same reason, or a greater one for presuming fraud of usury, then from the equal or greater, we say the same is established, as in *Digestum*, *ad legem Aquiliam*, law *Illud*; and law 1, § *Interdictum*, *Digestum*, *de fonte*; and *Digestum*, *de verborum obligationibus*, law *A Titio*; and *Digestum*, *de legibus*, law *Nec leges*; and law *Possunt*. Let us see, therefore, what is the reason of the said chapter *Ad nostram*. And the final reason is, because the thing sold ought to be resold for a small sum from the seventh year up to the ninth year, which scarcely ascended to half the just price. And it is not probable that buyers make such an agreement to resell for a quantity much less than they bought, as the gloss says there. Note that the smallness of the price is an argument of deceit. You will say, our case is the contrary, because he promised to resell for a greater sum. I say that this greater sum is an argument, because it tends, *infra*, within eight years, to the profit of fruits, insofar as it touches pro rata up to the said sum not disbursed, as if for the benefit of time and the interval of 8 years. But to this it might be answered, because they ought not of necessity to wait this time, but it was in the power of the buyers, and in the necessity of the seller. And an agreement which is appended in favor ought not to be converted into odium and presumption of fraud from contract to contract. And for certain, this question cannot be determined by the said chapter *Ad nostram*, neither in case nor in reason, unless arguing from remote things: if the agreement deviates from the nature of the contract and from common custom, it leads to a presumption of simulation from contract to contract. But this agreement seems honest. Who, indeed, never pays the entire price and profits the entire fruits, when rather he ought to be held to proportional usury, as in *Codex*, *de actione empti*, law *Curabit*. From contrary qualities, therefore, fraud is presumed, which is proved by the fact that it was done immediately, even by another instrument, as in *Digestum*, *de privilegiis creditorum*, law *Si ventri*, § *Si*. Moreover, just as the disproportion of sums had the fraud of man, so it had the fraud of the law, as in *Digestum*, *si quid in fraudem patroni*, law 1; *Digestum*, *ac si transigat*; and *Digestum*, *de iure patronatus*, law *Si libertus minorem*. Now I come to chapter *Illo vos*. There, indeed, a thing was bought under an agreement of disapproval, so that if it disapproved within a year, so that restored 23 lire, which were the price of the thing, and 60 solidi in excess, the dowry ought to be restored, computing into the price to be restored the fruits perceived in the meantime. The decretal judges this contract to be usurious, whatever was the intention in the heart of the contracting parties, there, on account of the 60 solidi, in which the measure is exceeded, the whole contract is induced to be usurious. But in our case there is a much greater excess. Therefore, especially, for a time of 8 years, this contract was pignoratitium. Moreover, whenever it is acted that dominion be transferred freely, as it ought to be transferred, a sale is not presumed, but another contract, as in *Digestum*, *de contrahenda emptione*, law *Cum manufacta*, § *Nemo*. From which things considered, according to those which are proposed, I advise that the said contract and all things following from it be judged pignoratitium and celebrated in fraud of usury, and that the said 800 florins be restored to the successors of the said Lord Laurentius, with the said principal not having been diminished; but the penalties appended in the said contracts, because in fraud of usury, are to be null, as in *Digestum*, *ad legem Falcidiam*, law *Seius et Augerius*; and *Codex*, *de legibus*, law *Non dubium*. There follows a certain other petition by virtue of another sale made by Lord Laurentius, in which it is petitioned that the price of the said things sold by the said agents for the said Lord Laurentius be restored to the said new buyers. This petition does not seem aptly proposed: because the said agents did not petition that the thing be delivered to them, by those things which I have seen. Moreover, action for double cannot be brought: because nothing is proposed as evicted by sentence, as in *Digestum*, *de evictionibus*, law *Habere licere*; *Digestum*, *de rei venditione*, law *Vtique*; *Digestum*, *de negotiis gestis*, law *At qui*, *natura*, § *Cum me absente*. Safe, however, remains the right of acting aptly, in due place and time. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To whom the burden of providing a dowry pertains: and whether a daughter who has received a dowry from her grandfather, or from another person, ought to be provided with a dowry by her father.
2. Whether providing a dowry for a daughter or granddaughter is a gift, or whether it is said to be a debt.
3. How large the dowry to be given by the father ought to be.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. This matter is divided into two parts: namely, into the dowry of daughters, and into the dowry of granddaughters, great-granddaughters, or even further descendants.

† In the first case, sometimes the burden of providing a dowry is imposed on someone other than the father; and then the burden of providing the dowry pertains to that person, and not to the father, while he is alive and has the means to provide it, as in D. de col. bo. l. dedit dotem. And the reason is: because this is not a burden imposed by natural law alone; but by civil law, derived from the right of paternal power, as in D. de ritu nupt. l. qui liberos in potestate. And this is proven by evident reason, because otherwise it would follow that this dowry would be adventitious, not perfective; and that she ought to have two dowries, or be endowed twice: once by the father, and once by the grandfather; or by the grandfather by the right of sacred power, and by the father by the right of natural stimulus. Which is false, as is clear from the note of Jacobus de Arena in D. de iust. et iur. l. veluti, and D. de lib. agn. l. si quis a liberis. And this is clear by natural reason: because whatever is the cause of a cause, it is necessary that it be the cause of the caused thing. Moreover, we see that all burdens begin with parents, from whom the thing begins to be, as in D. fam. ercisc. l. si maritus.

† Nor does a father or grandfather who provides a dowry for his granddaughter confer a benefit, but rather he fulfills a natural obligation, as stated in l. 1, C. de impo. lucra, described in lib. 10, C. de codi., l. si. And this payment is not strictly a debt, but occupies an intermediate position, as in C. de iur. et fac. igno., l. si emancipato.

† And if you ask how much the dowry ought to be, I answer that, since it takes the place of the legitime portion, it must in quantity extend up to the measure of the legitime, according to C. de sac. san. eccle. auth. si qua mulier. And if the son had many daughters, that mode in the distribution of the dowry will be observed which is observed in the distribution of the legitime portion, arg. in l. 1. §. si pater. ff. de coniug. cum eman. lib. Therefore, these things having been premised, as to the first point, it is truly to be said that either it was agreed between the parties that the maternal dowry should be converted into a paternal one, and thus a certain novation would be made. Nevertheless, in effect, this dowry is called rather a permutation than a giving of dowry, and the daughter has not been satisfied; because not the title of the action but the origin of the obligation ought to be considered, as ff. de don. l. quicquid. Hence, speaking really and truly, there is here a certain simulation, or a departure from the truth: and she who has not been endowed ought not to be repelled under the pretext of a paternal dowry; because words ought to be understood really and effectively, and fraud ought not to be committed from contract to contract. Moreover, if the father said that he wished to endow in order to equalize the portions, he signified his mind, but frivolously; because equalization does not apply where two proportional terms do not apply, as l. si filius. ff. si cer. pe. And therefore, a prelegacy left by a father, simple and unlearned, who did not have knowledge of the law, and who believed to place equality among the children, ought not to be drawn to equality, as C. de col. l. illam. and C. communia vtriusque iu. l. fi. And thus equality is to be preserved among children by natural and civil reason; namely, so that the right of one is not taken away and given to another. It is. Equality is to render what is due to each; fruits pertain to him who sustains the burdens of marriage, nor is the heir bound to restore them, as ff. so. ma. l. insulam. §. vsuras. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. More things ought to be proven when action is brought against a city on the basis of a loan or quasi-loan.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Let it be manifest to all through the series of this public instrument, that in the year of the Nativity of the same 1399, in the 7th indiction, on the day titled the 3rd of the month of June, in the city of Tudela of the Kingdom of Navarre, and of the diocese of Calahorra, before the most excellent Prince and most Serene Lord our Lord, Charles, by the Grace of God King of Navarre and Count of Évreux: the most distinguished man, Lord Charles de Bélemont, Vexillarius of our said Lord the King, natural son, legitimate heir, and successor of the memorable and illustrious Prince, Lord Louis of Navarre, sometime Duke of Durazzo, being personally present in the presence of me, the public notary, and the subscribing witnesses, with as much reverence as he could, humbly proposed and said by word before our Lord the King of Navarre, that whereas the aforementioned Lord Louis, sometime carnal and natural father of the same Lord Charles, while he lived and led life among men, for the dowry of Lady Joan de Cliche, consort of the same Lord Duke of Durazzo, had handed over, or likewise disposed, in the city of Florence and with the community of the same city, with the priors, rectors, and governors then of the same city, in the treasury, or heap, as it is called in the vernacular, the Monte di Firenze, of good gold of right and legitimate weight, 4,000 Florins, or Ducats of gold; the profits, revenues, annual pension, census, income, or honest profit arising from which the aforementioned spouses, while they lived among men, had and received jointly and successively. And finally, the said Lord Louis, Duke, being in extremis, yet of sound mind, made his last and irrevocable testament, in which testament, or last will and disposition, as the same Lord Charles, Vexillarius, asserted, the said former father of his, among other things contained therein, by certain mention and form, disposed and ordained concerning the said 4,000 ducats, as clearly appeared by a certain clause contained therein, by the force and virtue of which he said he had right and it pertained to him in the same sums, or quantities, of 4,000 Florins. And these things having been proposed and done, the same Lord Charles exhibited and presented before our aforementioned King the said public instrument of the testament, or last disposition and will, of the said Lord Louis, Duke of Durazzo, his father, not vitiated, not cancelled, not abolished, nor in any part of it suspect, or altogether free from every defect and suspicion, as clearly appears from the inspection of the same testament, humbly supplicating, etc.

† From the words of the said witness, and from his writing, the debt is not proven, as in C. de prob. l. instrumenta, and l. exempla, and l. rationes. Especially, because when action is brought against a city on account of a loan, or quasi-loan, more things ought to be proven, as in ff. si cer. pe. l. ciuitatis, at least by presumptions, as noted by the doctors in authen. hoc ius porrectum. Nevertheless, these are account books to which recourse is had as to public faith, upon oath against calumny: when presumptions suggest it, the account book ought to be produced and inspected, so that the faith of the truth may appear, as in C. de eden. l. iustum, and noted in the same title, l. j, and l. fi. non ob. extra de proba. c. 1, because here production is not sought as of an instrument, but as of an account book; because this is a certain kind of business, and those exercising these acts are in a manner money-changers, as in ff. de priuile. credit. l. si neutri, §. in bonis. Moreover, whenever something is proven, production serves to supplement the proof, but if it is not probable that the truth is denied. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A lessor who does not observe the contract with the lessee cannot bring an action against the lessee.
2. A contract is not presumed to be simulated solely on account of the low price.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† This was a named contract. And therefore it is clear that the contract is to be observed by the lessor, if the lessor observed it towards the lessee; but if he did not observe it, then the contrary applies, as in D. 19.2.1, Quaero, § Inter locatorem. And therefore for the past time the lessor can claim nothing, because he did not observe the contract on his part.

† However, I do not believe that a contract is presumed to be simulated solely on account of the smallness of the price, as in c. Ad nostram, Extra, de emptione et venditione. And therefore, the lessor, for the future period for which he wishes to observe the contract, could have justice, if it does not prejudice the adversary due to the long delay of time, as in the aforementioned § Inter locatorem, when that time arrives. I, Baldus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The case is as follows: In the year 1389, a certain lease was made by the Abbess, with the consent of her convent, for a period of nine years. Finally, in the year 1381, another lease was made by the same Abbess and the said convent for another period of nine years. In the year 1388, another lease was made for a period of two years, after the lessees had previously renounced the rights competent to them by virtue of the preceding leases. Upon the expiration of those leases and the time comprised therein, and after the aforementioned Abbess had been removed or deposed, and another substituted in her place by the present Abbess and her convent, it is demanded by the said lessees that the possession be relinquished, since the term of the grants has expired. The lessees defend themselves by virtue of a certain promise made to them by the Abbess now deposed, as well as by the convent, which promise is proved in the form set forth below. The present Abbess replies that neither she nor the monastery is bound by virtue of that promise, because it was less solemn and was personal, not real. The question is: what is the law?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an annual lease contract is only one.
2. Where two are for one, and that one alone.
3. A perpetual lease of a church cannot be made.
body: It is necessary to remain silent for the sake of evidence.

† For although the contract is annual, it is one for the entire period of several years. This occurs because there is one annual stipulation, and then that which cannot be done simultaneously cannot be done with the enumeration of years, because the periods are joined together, whether the agreement is repeated or not, because whatever is one and the same cannot be reduced by verbal division to real plurality, since there is one subject and one intention. D. de verb. oblig. l. si stichum. §. stipulatio. D. de don. cau. mor. l. senatus. §. fi. Nor can any art of words or precaution be made so that one is many, nor that fraud be committed against the law in the conception of the law by the force of living and dividing speech:

† because whenever there are multiple stipulations for one thing, nevertheless there is one thing on both sides. D. de evictionibus, l. qui libertatis. It does not matter. D. de verborum obligationibus, l. scire debemus. Because that is true unless one of the extreme parts contains a defect, as we have said, when a donation is made beyond the lawful sum. For the division of words does not therefore divide the disposition, nor does it make lawful that which is not lawful under a summary proceeding, as noted in l. nomen, § 1, D. de legibus tertio, and l. si libertus, § 1, D. de iure patronatus. Nor should it be circumvented, l. Oratio, D. de transactionibus; l. cum hi, § si cum lis. Hence that clause, that there are as many contracts as there are years, is not valid in the leasing of church property, as noted by Dy. in l. codicillis, D. de legibus secundo. And consider that all time which is extended is joined as if to a third, from which substantive act, and by the accession of time it is one and the same, as D. de precario, l. sed si manente. From which it follows that if nine years are added to two years, the authority of the contract ends at the end of the nine years from the day of the first agreement: because that which cannot be done principally cannot be done by extension. For whenever the extension is of the same form and nature, it is then one and the same, as noted in c. hi, qui, Auth. de praebendis, lib. 6; l. cum in plures, § lege dicta.

† From which it follows that the agreement for perpetuity is invalid, because that which is temporary by form and that which is temporary by nature cannot be extended to perpetuity, as in D. de pactis, l. Epistola, §. Si. From these things it appears that by the extension of time another contract is not made, but rather a certain continuation, unless the law repels it; and because the beginning shows its end, both temporal and formal, recourse must be had to the origin of the produced act, and from then on it is necessary to count, that the times continue in natural force, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. Cum stipulatus sim a Proculo. Moreover, if the renewal were made properly, i.e., by novation, and by the law itself, because then it would have been done between the parties, then a new consideration would arise from a new contract, to be begun and terminated, as follows, as in D. de pactis, l. Si unus, §. Pactus; D. de praet. stip., l. Valerianus; and l. 4, D. de damno infecto, per Bartolus; D. de arboribus, l. Si cum dies, in principio, per Cynus. Therefore, one and the same thing seems to be, either by reason of the context in time, or by reason of the continued consent in the mind, D. de pactis, l. Iure gentium, §. Quinimmo. But here continued consent in the mind appears through successive leases, as has been proved above; therefore, it is to be considered one and the same contract, which, in that which exceeds the nine-year period, since it is contrary to the canon, is not to be observed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How is the statute to be understood, which provides that endowed females shall not succeed when males are extant? And whether, if a daughter is passed over, she has the right to declare the act null. And see the following opinion below.
2. Although a statute does not admit of extension, nevertheless the ancient law extends to this matter.
3. Whether a daughter, to whom less was given in dowry than to her other sisters, can be said to be not endowed, and whether she can demand a supplement.
4. Whether the term "brother" in statutes includes a nephew.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Since in the case of the Pisan convent of the Carthusian Order, after all the allegations have been copiously set forth, and certain points previously elicited and discussed with exactitude by earlier consultants have again been brought into doubt, and since it is still doubted as before, nothing remains to be done except to retain the arguments of the earlier consultants, expressed concisely, as before, in accordance with the saying of the most eloquent Ulpian, who writes in the Digest, *De dote praelegata*, law 1, at the end: “Whatever is added to the demonstration of the cause of the thing is superfluous for the purpose of demonstrating it.”

† It is therefore asked first: whether the statute disposing of intestate successions, which establishes that the first cause is that of children, etc., on which the claim of those religious persons is based, finds application in our case: considering that Costius died testate, and the aforementioned testament, as being odious, does not seem to find application except in the case where male children of the first or second degree, or of lower status, would succeed intestate: in which case dowried women and their offspring are excluded. Where, therefore, those male children succeed by will, as in the present case Lotus succeeded to Costius, it is doubted whether the statute finds application. Regarding this doubt, it is answered, as has been answered elsewhere, that although Lotus succeeded to Costius not intestate, but with a will, nevertheless Lotus is [bound] by the aforementioned statute: and rightly so, because whenever one benefit is granted in consideration of another, if that which was the consideration for the grant is removed, the remaining benefit granted in consideration thereof is also taken away, because the cause ceases, etc. as in D. ad exhibenda, l. 1, filio, §. mater; D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si is, qui anno; D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. dulcissimus; D. de iure patronatus, l. adigere, §. quamvis; and fully read and noted in C. de episcopis et clericis, auth. generaliter. But the cause for which dowried women and their offspring, passed over by the father without cause, are admitted under the common law to bring an action for nullity of the testament, and to other ordinary remedies, is that they suffer injury, inasmuch as they are disinherited and passed over, the legitime which is due to them intestate not being left to them. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus, §. quoniam aut quarta, and §. si quis mortis; and l. mater decedens; and C. eodem titulo, l. cum quaeritur; and l. quoniam novella; l. omnimodo; and D. de bonis possessionibus contra tabulas, l. post mortem, §. liberi; l. illud, §. 1; and l. si in adoptione, §. exemplo, with similar authorities. For it is answered that neither to such dowried women nor to their offspring is any legitime due intestate, notwithstanding the statute: no injury is inflicted upon them, and consequently the way is barred against the testament itself. And for this reason it is commonly said that those passed over, whom the testator is not bound to institute, have no remedy against the testament, as in D. de iniusto rupto irritoque testamento, l. si quis filio exheredato in principio; and D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Qui posthumos, §. si quis fuerit. Namely, because when something is prohibited, all that follows therefrom is prohibited, as in C. de legibus, l. non dubium in fine; and what is fully read and noted there. For it is certain that when the antecedent is destroyed, the consequent is also removed, as in C. de furtis, l. apud antiquos, with the notes there. Therefore, etc. Moreover, it is said in l. qui ab intestato decedit, that one who dies intestate tacitly leaves all his goods to his intestate heirs, as in D. de legatis 3, l. si fundum fideicommissum, §. ultimo; D. de legato 3, l. 1, §. sciendum; D. de iure codicillorum, l. conficiuntur in principio. If, therefore, the Pisan law made the testament for this deceased person, and he tested according to that law, it is expressly said that the dowried women themselves and their descendants complain of the Pisan law, and not of the testator, who was the executor of that law, as noted in a similar case by Bartolus in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. et quid si tamen. Whose opinion is confirmed also by another reason, for statutes, although they do not receive an extensive interpretation to a similar case, nevertheless no one doubts that the rule of the common law extends to the statute itself, although formally it is argued that dowried women and their offspring do not succeed intestate in the presence of male children, notwithstanding that statute. But the general rule is that he who is removed from intestate succession, whenever succession by will is discussed, is also excluded even if he wishes to come against the testament, as in D. de bonis libertorum, l. si necem, §. si deportatus; and D. de contraria, l. 1, §. filium; and more fully. It has been proven. Dowried women and their offspring are therefore excluded not by the prohibition of the statute, but by the common law.

† Although it is true that a statute does not admit of extension, nevertheless the ancient law extends to this matter, as is shown in the Digest, in the title *De servo corrupto*, in the law *Non tamen*, § 1, read together with the law *Si quis servo* in the Code, in the title *De furtis*; and what is read and noted by Bartolus in the Digest, in the title *De legibus*, in law 1 and law 2, and by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, in the title *De consuetudinibus*, in the chapter *Cum dilectus*, and other common legal authorities, is abundantly alleged in other consilia, which I do not repeat for the sake of brevity. From all of which it is inferred that the statute concerning intestate successions finds its application in the case proposed, and thus the first doubt is resolved.

Secondly, it is asked whether, since Thora was endowed with a sum less than double, and the natural daughters of the late John, son of Costino, could Lady Ioannina, daughter of the said Thora, be said to be undowered: for, with respect to the other two, she does not appear to have been sufficiently endowed; and also considering the assets of Costino, which were great. And consequently, whether she appears not to be excluded, because she is undowered; or at least whether the right of supplementing the dowry applies, as if the statute concerning the supplementing of the dowry ought to be understood civilly, that is, as concerning one endowed according to the assets of the patrimony. In response to this doubt, it must be concluded, as above, that the said Lady is rightly called endowed, insofar as concerns the matter at hand: since it was determined, and she was endowed to the praise of her father, for whom it is presumed in case of doubt. Argument: Digest, On Tutors and Guardians, From those who are appointed, l. *scire oportet*; § *sed et si quis*; l. *is qui*, in the beginning; On what is done in fear, l. *institu quidem*; § *si*; On testamentary guardianship, l. *testator*; and Code, On those who do not give sufficient security, l. *pe*; and On the hearing of bishops, l. *de creationibus*; Institutes, On the security of a tutor, § *in confirmando*; and l. *utilitatem*, On the action for recovery; l. *ult.*; Digest, On the guardianship of the insane, l. *si*; *Euilescit*, n., etc. As in Authenticum, On Marriage, § *si vero*; Code, On goods which are free, l. *cum oportet*; § *non autem hypotecam*, part, n. *affectionis causae*, in order to remove suspicions of fraud in the father. Digest, On the rites of marriage, l. *pe*, § 1. Nor ought it to be asked whether Thora has likely received what was due to her, if the parent has freely given more than is due to others, as in Authenticum, On Marriage, § *illud quoque*; and in the Gospel, especially since the Pisan statute strictly binds the father simply to endow, without expressing a certain quantity.
