It suffices, therefore, that she is an endowed daughter; nor need one care further, since it is enough to serve the words of the edict, Digest, On execution, l. 1, § *si is qui navem*; nor is the father compelled by any law to offer equal dowries to his daughters; rather, he may offer unequal ones, due to the diversity of persons and the condition in which it happens that the daughters are placed, since the dowry ought to be constituted also according to the condition of the husband, and a greater one ought to be given to a noble than to a commoner, as in Digest, On dowry law, l. *cum post*, § *gener*; Code, On promised dowries, l. *si voluntate*; and not Digest, On verbal obligations, l. *divortio*. Furthermore, the father’s assets are not estimated from the total sum, but from the quality of the patrimony and the condition of the persons. And Bartolus writes fully, Digest, On the action for dowry, l. 2, § 1, in the great gloss. But these things are not established, therefore, etc. Since, therefore, Thora appears to be endowed, the statute on intestate succession speaks of her; and it is in vain that supplementation is claimed from her person, as is read and noted by Dy, Digest, On legacies, book 2, l. *Lucius*; and l. 1.

Thirdly, and lastly, it is asked whether Nicolaus, born of Gemma, can claim half of that which accrued to Lothus and Castius, given that Lothus died without children and with a will. Hence, the statute appears, which begins, “if the brother calls him to that half.” For the clarification of this doubt, that common theory must be premised, which holds that statutes are of strict law, especially when they are contrary to law, so much so that in such municipal laws, that which is not written in this book is noted as if omitted. And consequently, that which is not changed, etc., and the case omitted, etc., as in D. 50.17.10, § de viro, ad municip. L. consti., de testam. milit. L. quod constitutum, D. de verb. oblig. Si minor, C. de testam. L. sancimus, and L. precipimus, de appell. D. 50.17.10, L. si cum dotem, in princ., de lib. et posthum. L. commodissime, de cond. ob causam. L. si extraneus, and other common laws. And also that which must be premised, that because the Pisan statute uses words simply and properly, in these the appellation of brother does not include the nephew from him, although abusively and in any way a progression is made from one person to another, as is read and proven. D. de leg. 3, L. Lucius, § quaesit. D. de ri. nup. L. non solum, § si puellae. Si n. voluissent, expressissent, as in C. de cad. toll. L. 1, § si nautem ad deficientis. Just as in the preceding parts they made express mention of nephews, whenever they wished to be understood regarding them. Hence, with these known, that acts in the preceding are understood to be repeated for the declaration of the following, as in D. de coniung. cum emanci. lib. L. nihil, and de leg. 1, L. quae filiabus, in princ., and L. servus plurium, § si cum si. From these, therefore, it can undoubtedly be inferred that that statute does not comprehend the case in question, since he whose succession is in question is not a brother, but a nephew: nor are they sisters, but rather those born of them, who desire to be admitted to the succession. But neither must that be omitted, that that § si frater is placed under the heading de success. ab intest. but the words of the law must be understood according to the subject title, as is read and noted. D. de in diem adiec. L. Imperator Lotha, § si uno, in princ. D. de condi. inde. L. si, in princ. Thus, and otherwise, although the text in Auth. de haered. ab intest. § nulla generally says that the difference of emancipation and paternal power has been removed, nevertheless, because this text is placed under the heading de success. ab intest., we commonly hold that this difference is removed by will and not intestate, as is read and noted by the gloss. C. de lib. et posthum. L. gallus, § et quid si tantum, de inoff. test. L. si proponas, de minor. L. Si filius, de col. L. si emancipati. Again, and that § si frater speaks when a brother excludes a sister, and consequently when the brother is the proximate cause, when the effect is attributed to the proximate cause, and the principal and immediate cause is always inspected, and not the remote, as is read and noted by the gloss. D. de dolo, L. cum quis, and rerum amot. L. si mulier. Hence, that § does not speak in this case, because the brother does not immediately exclude, but the father, that is, the father’s will. For although the statute is confirmed, nevertheless the will itself is confirmed, and the father is the immediate cause of exclusion: for even if the statute tacitly renders the will unassailable, nevertheless the statute is not said to give, but the father is he who principally confers, as in D. de verb. sig. L. obvenire. D. de pet. her. L. 2 and 3, de cond. ex lege. L. unica, de pact. L. legitima. The brother, therefore, who does not exclude for himself, but through the father’s will, is not said to exclude: but the father, to whom such exclusion must be attributed, as in D. de inoffic. test. L. Pap., § impuberi, and Extr. de testam. C. in fin. In many ways, therefore, and in many modes, it is proven that in the case proposed the words of that § si frater have no place, and consequently neither does the statute itself, as in L. hos accusare, § omnibus, D. de accusat. and de legat. 3, L. Non aliter, de suppellect. legat. L. Labeo, § Idem Tubero, de exerc. L. 1, si is, qui navem, with many other similar cases, especially since even if Lothus had not made a will, Nicolaus, the instituted heir, would have been excluded, therefore, etc. Christophorus de Castillione. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a daughter shall not succeed while males are extant, if the daughter is passed over, whether she has the right to break the will.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Regarding the first doubt, it is argued that the aforementioned daughter, or her descendants, is not excluded on account of the breaking of Castius’s will. First, because there are two rights sufficiently distinct: the right to break and the right to succeed. Hence we see that a *sui heredes* passed over breaks the will by operation of law, before he can succeed, as in D. de lib. et posth. l. si filius, qui in potestate. And although by statute one right is removed, it should not be said that something entirely separate from it is removed, as in D. de serv. pr. praed. l. si domus. Moreover, it makes a difference to have the right to break, and whether we are not to succeed, as is clear in the case of a disinherited son, who, having obtained the *querela inofficiosi testamenti*, may renounce, as in D. de inoff. test. l. qui de inoffic. and l. quemadmodum. Furthermore, it makes a difference in our case from another angle, because the benefit of breaking may be subject to contract, as in D. de contrah. l. filium § erit. Moreover, this daughter should at least be able to come by contract, which is said to be from the will, as in C. de collat. l. ut liberis. To the contrary is the truth. And thus I advise, against the consultation, that this daughter, or her descendants, be excluded: because only he can break to whom the legitime is due, but the legitime is that part which one would have had intestate, as in C. de inoff. test. l. cum quaeritur. But intestate, this daughter is excluded by virtue of the statute and c. Moreover, this daughter is deprived by her own act; therefore, she is excluded both from civil and praetorian law, as in D. de bon. poss. l. non est ambigendum § si. Moreover, in support of this is l. si post mortem § liberi D. de contrah. Moreover, it is established that if an emancipated son is instituted, after which his own [son] is passed over, that grandson passed over does not break his grandfather’s will, since he would not have succeeded intestate, as noted by Bartolus in l. Gallus § quid si tantum D. de lib. et posth. Since therefore dominion is not contained in this daughter by reason of *sui iuris* status: the will cannot be attacked, nor by reason of injury, because the father had free houses with respect to her, since this daughter is unknown to the civil law of her city, just as the emancipated son was unknown to the civil law of the Twelve Tables. Regarding the other points, I stand with the first consultant, Jacobus de Solanis. I, Baldus, serve.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a fief is granted to a person and his male children, if no male heirs exist, the fief reverts to the grantor’s ownership, excluding or not including females; but if the fief is granted to a person and females, females succeed in the fief.
2. When a fief is granted to a common lineage, or a mixed lineage, or an uncertain lineage, whether females succeed in the absence of males.
3. To what degree agnates are admitted in fiefs.
4. Testamentary succession has no place in fiefs.
5. The customs of fiefs receive a passive interpretation from the common law.
6. Whether an heir may act against the act of the deceased in fiefs.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† All are agreed on this point, that if a fief is granted to someone for himself and his male children: that, when no legitimate male descendants exist, it reverts to its original ownership, excluding—or more accurately, not including—females. And this is based on three reasons: first, because of the quality of the words, namely “males”; second, because of the nature of the subject matter of fiefs; third, because of the final reason, since females cannot serve equally in fiefs as males can, as stated in c. j. §. illud qui, feud. de pos. Moreover, all are agreed that if a fief is granted for oneself and females, females succeed. And this is for threefold reason: first, because of the quality of the words with respect to the form of the grant itself. It is possible, namely, in fiefs to provide for one of the heirs, since it consists in fact, as in ff. de pac. l. auus. Second, because the nature of the fief accedes to the nature of the words and is regulated by them, as in c. 1. de eo, qui sibi, et suis fil. masc. et fem. For the nature of fiefs is mobile and accidental: and even agreements transmit their proper nature, as in ff. de pos. l. 1. §. si conuenerit. Third, because the praetor says, “I will uphold agreements.” And in fiefs the agreement must be upheld, even if someone stipulates for another using direct words: because the Emperor so wills, lest there be dispute among noble persons over points of law; or because it so pleased the prince; or because an agreement was added by delivery, and thus a natural act intervenes, as in d. c. 1. §. cum vero Corradus. And ff. de acqui. re. do. l. ea, quae ciuiliter. ar. ff. deposi. l. publia. in prin. And ff. de preca. l. certe. §. procurator.

† But on this point the ancient authors of true philosophy are in disagreement, among whom is rightly and memorably placed the law of Fauem. Pet. and Cy., namely, if a fief is granted to a common class, for example, to Peter and the men of his household; or to a mixed class, for example, to Peter and his heirs; or to an uncertain class, for example, to Peter and his descendants. Whether at least in the absence of males females succeed increases the doubt, because a fief made transitory is no longer placed in the transitory category, but becomes transmissible, as in ff. de leg. 3, l. pater, § quindecim; C. de fideicommis., l. voluntas. Therefore, the aforementioned great men said that heirs, and even females, succeed in it; indeed, they said that even strangers and heirs who are not heirs of the blood, provided they are called to universal succession by law, succeed. For the fief passes with the universality, as in ff. de contra. emp., l. in modicis; nor does it follow from it, because the contained is not separated from its container, as in c. 1, an filius vel agn., col. 10. Other great doctors say the contrary: because in the degrees of succession to a fief females do not come; not because they are odious, but because they are not fit for the burdens of the fief, as in ca. j, de gradib., col. 10, and l. in multis, ff. de sta. ho. Moreover, words that are not formally determined are determined naturally according to the nature of the thing and the contract, as in ff. de ver. obl., l. ita stipulatus, and ff. de vsur., l. si stipulatus. La Grande, around the middle, when he says, "its own nature." Therefore, they say that in fiefs there is no place for the succession of females on account of the nature of the thing. For what is naturally inherent should be considered as expressed, as if nature itself were speaking, as in ff. si cer. pe., l. cum quid, and ff. de ver. ob., l. triticum. Furthermore, a common class and a mixed class are predicated equally of male and female. This is true where no distinguishing reason occurs; but here a reason for distinguishing occurs, for if a testator bequeaths to his slaves the office of a runner or singer, females are not included, to whom such an office does not belong. Words must be understood according to the persons subject to them, as in ff. de vsu, et habi., l. plenum, § sequitur. Briefly, this question is disputed in C. de ope. libe., l. liberti, and ff. ad Treb., l. ex facto, § fi. And it is commonly held that there is no place for the female. And this is the truth.

† Hence, when males fail, the fief returns to the source of its ownership, unless agnates exist up to the seventh degree from the first investee; for then they would succeed as in an ancient fief, unless they had renounced, as in cap. 1, § rursus, quibus modis feudum amittitur, coll. 10. Indeed, some say that not only up to the seventh degree of the deceased, but also in perpetuity, the legitimate degree of agnation is preferred to the lord of the fief, which is more correct; although agnates under common law do not succeed intestate beyond the tenth degree.

† It is established that in a fief there is no place for the succession of the remainder. As in cap. 1, de success.; and in §. donare, qualiter olim feudum potest alienari, ca. 1. The objection from Extra, de feodis, in the chapter Inter dilectos, does not hold, because there was not properly a fief there: although some service was rendered, for example, a tithe; or there was a special favor of the Church, which is not pleasing according to l. Cum quidam, §. fin., ff. de usu. Or say that in c. Inter dilectos the lord did not exercise his right of withdrawal: as in Auth. de alienatione et emphyteusi, §. 1. For these matters of reverence depend on the discretion of the lords, as noted in l. 2, ff. si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticarius; and l. Post diem, de lege commissoria. Moreover, in a fief are contained all the conventions for which service is rendered, whether castles, or other possessions, or feudal men who adhere to the possessions, just as farmers and tenants who cannot be absent from the place: as noted in Inst. de iure personarum; and ff. de legibus, l. Si quis inquilinos, §. fin., qui in quibusdam locis, as at Milan, are called massarii: but the force is not in the word, but in the sense, as C. de testibus, l. Quoniam indignum. Declaring that which I said in my counsel, according to the order of degrees, I say that succession, just as by investiture, and just as the succession of an inheritance, proceeds: as in c. 1, de gradibus successionis in feudis, col. 10. And where nothing contrary is provided by custom, the expert in law may and must determine the case arising according to the written law, i.e., according to the common law.

† Moreover, the customs of fiefs receive a passive interpretation from the common law: as in c. Ubertus, § strenuus, de feudis, coll. From these it consequently appears that the brother’s son succeeds together with the uncle in the place of his father, as in c. 1, de successione feudorum; and they may make alienations and agreements among themselves, as noted above in c. 1, per quos fiat investitura et per quos recipiatur, on the word “proximiori.”

Whether, however, an heir may act against the act of the deceased in an ancient fief, and what the rule is in a paternal fief, is noted in the cited chapter 1, *de successione feudorum*, § *hoc quoque*, according to the gloss beginning: *Quid igitur erit*. But there is no need to dispute this point, because these nephews come in the person of their father. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The renunciation is not valid if an adult girl renounced her mother’s inheritance with an oath and with the consent of her father or grandfather.
2. A minor cannot make a renunciation or settlement concerning immovable property without legal solemnity.
3. No one loses ownership of his own thing through a transaction or settlement, even if he is barred from bringing an action by means of an exception.
4. A father having a daughter in his power cannot alienate her property, especially directly in his own favor or indirectly, in the case of adventitious goods.
5. A bishop can grant a relaxation of an oath.
6. Prescription does not run during the time of paternal power.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. A certain girl named Maffia, born of a first marriage, who had succeeded to her mother’s estate, was endowed by her father and paternal grandfather with certain possessions and properties formerly belonging to her mother, which at that time pertained to the said girl by hereditary right. As for the other goods, she made a pact, settlement, remission, and transaction, and swore not to contravene it. The question is asked: what is the law? The bishop subsequently granted a relaxation to himself. Here, first, having seen and examined the words of direct refutation, it is asked whether the said girl, now a woman of forty years, can return to the said possessions and maternal goods, or not.

† And it appears that she cannot [rescind], because an oath appended to any contract by an adult, male or female, voluntarily and without fraud, must be observed: as in Auth. sacramenta pub., even in a contract of mere donation, as noted in l. 1, ff. de contrahenda et reicienda tutela. Moreover, because the father and grandfather consented, due to whose presence and consent the girl is not presumed to have been harmed or circumvented, as in C. de transactionibus, l. transactionem, which is also noted in C. de his qui, ut indigni, puniuntur.

† To the contrary is the truth, for the sake of whose evidence I first premise that a minor cannot make a renunciation or settlement concerning immovables without legal solemnity: as C. si aduer. transa. l. 1. and C. de praediis min. l. si ad resoluendum.

Secondly, I premise that through a transaction or settlement, one does not lose ownership of his thing, although he is barred from bringing an action by means of an exception, as in C. de transa. l. si pro fundo, and noted in the same title, l. siue apud acta. This is especially so because the agreement does not aim at transferring ownership, but solely at creating an exception. And there are three things that do not operate beyond their nature, as in ff. de usur. l. si stipulatus; nor beyond their form, as in ff. de verb. obl. l. quicquid astringendae; nor beyond the intention of the contracting parties, as in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. in l. ruptilia polla. But such is the agreement that serves to raise an exception, for to except presupposes its contrary, namely, to bring an action, so as to weaken the force and efficacy of the action, not to abolish it by operation of law itself; because an exception is the exclusion or elimination of an action, as in ff. de excep. l. 1. For if the exception of the agreement abolished it by operation of law itself, it would not be an exception of law, but an exception of intention and fact, as noted in ff. de condi. ob cau. l. qui se debere.

Third, I premise that in the case of adventitious property, a father or grandfather having a daughter in his power cannot alienate it, especially directly to himself or indirectly, as is noted in l. 1, D. de pactis tutorum. For what cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly either, unless a circumvention were introduced by law: as in l. quaeritur, D. de bonis libertorum. Indeed, it is entirely forbidden to him, as is noted in C. de bonis matri monialibus, l. 1. One might say that he cannot alienate, but can consent when the daughter alienates, because we can do certain things by consenting which we cannot principally and effectively bring into being: D. de manumissionibus vindicta, l. si pater, § fin. But I answer that here the principal act, namely the remission itself, was invalid, considering the thing and the age. Moreover, the cause of the refutation was invalid: because he made the refutation for his own property regarding other properties, and thus the cause was erroneous or extorted; hence, this contract, indeed this disposition, did not hold: as in l. si, D. de constitutis pecuniis, for two reasons. First, because it is not said to have been done voluntarily when there was error, even in law: D. de iuris omnium iudiciorum, l. si convenerit.

Secondly, because the Lord Bishop relaxed the oath, which he could do, moved by just exhortations: as noted in the chapter on oaths, c. 1. He considered that in the girl there concurs the fragility of her sex and the imperfection of judgment due to her minority; that she did not dare to contradict her father and grandfather, as noted in l. 1, § quae honorandae, ff. quarum rerum actio non datur. Nor does it avail to object that only the Pope can remit an oath; for this is true of an oath that does not pertain to the disputation of the forum, and when it is relaxed by grace or by dispensation. Moreover, here it was relaxed by the authority of the Pope, that is, by the authority of the canons, for the dead voice of the law effects the same as the living voice of the prince, as ff. de iustitia et iure, l. nam et ipsum. Furthermore, it does not avail that no judicial decree intervened, for it was obtained by suppression of truth (obreptitium); because the facts and the right of succession were not laid before him. Hence, the judge exercised jurisdiction over both law and fact. And thus the decree is null; for although decrees that are not just ought to be rescinded between adults, or between an adult and a minor, or between a woman and an adversary of whatever age or status, as ff. de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis ab his, l. tutor si petitus. Moreover, dominical rights are not included in a general refutation. ff. de libellis legitimis, l. Aurelius. In the remaining preceding points, which are clearer, concluding finally that the said Lady Maffia, according to what is alleged, has justice in the lands, I do not say in the fruits consumed in good faith, which never belonged to the said Lady Maffia, but to the possessors in good faith, for in fruits even error of law is protected, as noted in ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. sed si lege, § scire. Doubt might arise concerning the prescription of time,

But this doubt is resolved: because prescription does not run during the time of paternal power, as is stated in the Digest, under the title "On the Annual Exception," law 1, at the end; for it would seem sufficient that the father possessed in bad faith, as is stated in the Code, under the title "On Usucapion Transformed," law 1, section 1, and as is noted there. Moreover, in prescribing over another's property, an error of law is not sufficient, as the rule of law states. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required for a person to be able to bring an action on a hypothec.
2. A lease granted without observing the form of the common law and of the statutes is void and must be revoked, insofar as it proceeded de facto.
3. The defect of litigiousness does not apply to personal actions.
body: The statute of the city of Vicenza provides that if a debtor has alienated the pledged property, the creditor shall be put in possession notwithstanding the said pledge, unless the possessor proves that the principal debtor has unencumbered assets sufficient, or to the extent that they are sufficient, for the satisfaction of the debt. In the present case, the buyer was summoned by a conventional writ, without mention being made of the mortgage, nor of the statute, nor of the possession transferred to him by the debtor; he was contumacious, and a judgment was pronounced against him; following this interlocutory judgment, execution was carried out, and its rescission is sought. The question is: what is the law? First, it is asked in what respect this statute differs from the common law. I answer that this statute does not require execution. Second, because it shifts the burden of proof onto the defendant.

† For regarding the first point, I say that access to the hypothecary action is not open unless through excussion, if the debtor is present, as in C. de pign. auth. hoc si praesens. But by this statute, this form is not required; rather, another form, more expeditious and good, is provided. Regarding the second point, I say that, in the hypothecary action, before proceeding to the joinder of issue on the same, it must be clear to the judge that the debtor does not possess sufficient assets. This fails if this were notorious, because by notoriety a negative is proved just as an affirmative, as noted in ff. de verb. obli. l. decem. Moreover, notoriety relieves from the burden of proving; for that which is manifestly evident need not be proved, as is read and noted in ff. qui satisd. cog. l. si vero. §. qui pro rei qualitate. But by this statute, the burden of proving the affirmative is imposed on the possessor, namely, that the goods are free, i.e., without controversy in the possession of the debtor. And perhaps according to the old common law, where, speaking properly, such excussion was not made, as in ff. de iu. fis. l. Mochiis, it was the intent of that law. Say, however, that there was a special case there, as noted there, or that this applies in tacit and legal hypothecations introduced in subsidium, not in conventional ones, which are made with greater caution. For whatever may be said on this point, it need not be considered in the present case. Having considered the intention of the statute, let us come to the case formulated.

And it seems that one should say that the said seizure is valid: because it is established that, on account of a single act of contumacy, the plaintiff may be put in possession. I do not say in true possession: because there a peremptory title is required, as noted in D. de damno infecto, l. si finita, §. Iulianus; and C. de his qui ad ecclesiam consugiunt, l. praesenti. But it is otherwise with regard to tenebrous, or, so to speak, custodial possession, as in X. de iudicibus, c. 1. Moreover, it is established that, in this respect, a general libel suffices, which is clarified by circumstances, as in C. de annalium exceptione, l. si. For every cause suffices with regard to citation, as in D. si quis vocatus in ius non ierit, l. ex quocumque.

On the contrary, I see and argue four reasons. The first is from the material cause: because here the matter of the statute was not pleaded. The third is from the efficient cause: because here the condition from the municipal law was not pleaded. The fourth is from the final cause: because here the effect to which the action was directed was not expressed. A libel does not exclude any part of itself. And because the defendant had an apparent defense arising from the inadequacy of the libel, he ought not to have been considered contumacious, but the libel ought to have been torn up, and the proceeding declared to be null, as in D. de officiis assessorum, l. 1; and X. de iudicibus, c. examinata. And because nothing was proven by the plaintiff from which he ought to derive the benefit of the statute, according to what is proposed, this bailiff has no justice in this seizure: because the form and proof were omitted.

From these things it appears that the said seizure issued abruptly, without observing the form of the common law nor of the statutes. And therefore it ought to be revoked, insofar as it proceeded as a matter of fact, as noted in D. de evictionibus, l. minor, in principio. For those things which are done extra ordinem ought to be revoked, as in D. si mulier vendiderit, l. 1, §. 1; and D. qui causam in possessionem dederint, l. haec autem, §. 1.

† The defect of a litigious person has no place here: because the action is personal. See the condition from law, or from the office of the judge, as fully noted by Innocentius, Extra de constitutionibus, chapter Cum M. Fertariensis; and Extra de iudicibus, chapter Quia 5. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when an official may contract both in his place of origin and elsewhere where he holds office, whether perpetual or temporary.
casus: CASE. In the name of God, Amen. The point is this: Lord Andreas de Trottis, senator of the city of Siena, while holding the said office for a certain time, bound himself for the magnificent man Antonio Columen, Nicolaus Spinelli of Siena, and Francis de Rampelano of the county of Siena, to pay every sum of money to which the said Antonio was liable, exceeding 600 gold florins, according to the award and declaration to be made by certain arbitrators elected by the said city between the said Antonio, Nicolaus, and the aforementioned ser Francis. And the aforementioned Lord Andreas bound himself as a principal private person, while he was in office; and he renounced all aid of law and privilege: as is contained more fully and at length in the said obligation, written by the hand of ser Galgano Cerboni, as appears fully above. We send to your fatherhood a copy thereof, word for word, which we pray you to examine point by point, and to declare upon all the points. Now the said Lord Andreas says that the said obligation did not hold in law; and thus he cannot be harassed in any way during the time of his syndicate by virtue of the said obligation, since he could not bind himself while in office with his subjects, nor contract, nor make a compromise, nor be bound to anything according to their declaration. Now the question is: what is the law, having seen the point and the aforementioned obligation, etc.?
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

I premise that it is noted by Jacobus Butrigarius and Bartolus in the law *Principalibus*, the following law, in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, and that it is noted by Cynus in the law *Eos* and the law *Quisquis* in the Code, title *Si certum petatur*, where they distinguish as follows: either the official is in his place of origin, and he may contract there without distinction, as in the law *Praesidis* in the beginning, in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, and according to one reading, as are the priores and ancients of the city. But if they hold a perpetual office, and the same applies, as in the aforementioned law *Praesidis*, according to another exposition; or he was an official for a time, and wishes to contract with non-subjects: and then, if lending money on loan, he cannot, as in the aforementioned law *Principalibus* and the law *Praesidis* at the end; or with subjects: and then, if lending money on loan, he cannot, as in the aforementioned law *Principalibus* and the law *Eos* in the Code, title *Si certum petatur*; or if receiving, or contracting otherwise, and then he may, according to their necessity, as in the aforementioned law *Principalibus* and the law *Praesidis* at the end, according to another understanding, and there by Guido de Cavalcanti; or for the sake of profit, and he cannot, as in the law *Quisquis* in the Code, title *Si certum petatur*, and the law *1* in the Code, title *De contractibus iudicum*. And this is true if the time of the office is determined with certainty. But if it is doubtful, then the same applies as in the case of a perpetual official, that he may, as argued in the Digest, title *De conditionibus indebiti*, law *Sufficit*. And thus holds Cynus in the aforementioned law *Quisquis*. And this applies to an official who presides over jurisdiction, as in the aforementioned laws, and the law *Qui officii* in the Digest, title *De contrahenda emptione*. But if he were of his own jurisdiction and contracted for temporal administration, or contracts in the office which he administers: as are officials appointed in public to sell the tolls and communal revenues of the city. Then neither by himself nor through other persons may they buy, nor contract. Law *Non licet* in the Digest, title *De contrahenda emptione*, section *Si*. And by Cynus in the Authenticum *Quibuscumque* in the Code, title *De sacris ecclesiis*. Because he represents the republic, and he would be both buyer and seller. And of this it is noted in the law *Cum ipse* in the Digest, title *De contrahenda emptione*, and the law *1* in the Code, title *De contractibus iudicum*, by the gloss. But if it does not concern the office, and then he may contract. Moreover, the aforementioned is true when the official contracts by himself, but for the city he may, if administration is committed to him. Law *Ciuitatis* in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, and in the Digest, title *De usuris*, law *Gayus Seius*. If only the execution of jurisdiction is committed, as in the law *Plene*, section *Prohibere*, in the Digest, title *Quod vi aut clam*, and in the Digest, title *De pace*, law *Item magistri*. But let us see all those who are prohibited from contracting while presiding over an office. And certainly, he who lends money to a judge is presumed to corrupt him, and it is a certain form of bribery, even if the title of loan is added, as noted in the aforementioned law *Quisquis* in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*. Moreover, when he himself buys, or when he lends, there is suspicion of influence, and he is terrifying to the parties by reason of the office. Code, title *Si rector provinciae*, law *Unica*. It applies if by any of the aforementioned powers, law *Unica*. And lest he neglect his duties for merchandise. Now, regarding the matter at hand, it seems that the said Lord Andrew could obligate himself in the manner in which he obligated himself, because the aforementioned prohibitive reasons cease. For neither for the sake of his own profit, nor does another obligate himself to him, so that influence may be presumed. But he obligates and binds himself to the other, without any benefit or profit to himself, and thus bribery could not arise. Therefore, the prohibitive reason ceasing, the prohibition should cease. The virtue of the law consists in its reason, as in the law *Adigere*, section *Quamvis*, in the Digest, title *De iure patronatus*, and the law *Quod dictum* in the Digest, title *De pace*. Furthermore, in the aforementioned instrument he renounced all aid of the law, and received the aforementioned guarantee. Hence it seems he could renounce such a privilege. And if such a benefit were applicable, as in the law *Si quis in conscribendo* in the Code, title *De pace*.

To the contrary, the truth seems to be that such promise and obligation did not hold. First, because the doctors in the aforementioned law *Principalibus* and law *Quisquis* understand simply that, however the official contracts with subjects, it is prohibited: when he was an official for a certain time. For this, the aforementioned law *1* in the Code, title *De contractibus iudicum*, and the law *Aufertur*, section *A praeside*, in the Digest, title *De iure fisci*. Moreover, in our case, the reason assigned above may be present, lest he be terrifying to the parties. For he did not obligate himself simply, but to a certain quantity, namely, to the declaration of the arbitrators, his subjects in jurisdiction. Therefore, in such arbitrators he could have exercised oppression, lest they award against him, and also to the other party to whom he obligated himself, similarly his subjects. And thus he was terrifying to them by reason of the office. Therefore, such obligation did not hold. Moreover, other reasons may be assigned: because the contract and obligation of the said official did not hold beyond the aforementioned reasons assigned above, because he should attend to the office enjoined upon him, not to those things which might in any way distract him from the office, as says the gloss in the aforementioned law *Qui officii* in the Digest, title *De contrahenda emptione*, argument of the law *Militis* in the Code, title *De locis*. Therefore, he should not attend even to building, as in the aforementioned law *1* in the Code, title *De contractibus iudicum*, and the aforementioned section *Quod a praeside*. And Cynus considers this reason in the aforementioned law *Quisquis*, when he says that he cannot contract for trading, even with non-subjects. Similarly, it is noted in the law *Ab administratione* in the Code, title *De legibus*, and the law *Filius*, section *Veterani*, in the Digest, title *De procuratoribus*. Similarly, it is also noted in the Code, title *De testamento*, law *Consultadiualia*, and in the title *De episcopis et clericis*, law *Repetita*. And these reasons concern public favor, to which officials cannot renounce. Law *Ius publicum* in the Digest, title *De pace*, law *Quos prohibet* in the Digest, title *De postulando*, and the aforementioned section *Veterani*. Thirdly, another reason may be assigned, that the office must be free, even for the administration of justice, so that the official does not become timid in rendering justice to each one, nor gracious because of such obligation, nor in contempt of his office, as in the Digest, title *De officio praesidis*, law *Observandum*, and the law *Plebiscito* in the Code, title *Ad legem Iuliam repetundarum*, law *Finalis*. Therefore, we see that, while they are in office, they can neither be sued nor sue, for the aforementioned reasons. Law *1* in the Digest, title *De in ius vocando*, and in the Digest, title *De iudicibus*, and the law *Pars litterarum*. For no burden can be imposed on a free act, by which it is detracted from free will. Digest, title *De verbis obligatis*, law *Si stipulatio*, and the law *Titia* in the beginning, and in the Code, title *De sponsalibus*, law *Finalis*, and in the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Titio centum*, section *1*. And by this, the response to the contrary arguments formed above is clear. For neither as a senator could he obligate himself: because it does not pertain to his office, since this was not committed to him. For he does not obligate himself for the republic, nor was administration committed to him in this matter, the aforementioned law *Prohibere*, section *Plane*, in the Digest, title *Quod vi aut clam*. Moreover, as a private principal he could not intervene and obligate himself, for the reasons already stated. From which I conclude that, by law, the said Lord Andrew, both before and after the completion of his office, can defend himself from such obligation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who has the power to make a will and to dispose of goods by testament, leaving them solely to closer relatives, will not be able to make a will concerning said goods in favor of others.
2. The term "solely" is exclusive and prohibitive.
3. Who are considered relatives.
4. Who are included under the term "relatives," and whether males and females are comprehended. No. 5.
5. How the term "line" is understood, what it is at No. 9, and how manyfold it is, and at No. 10.
6. Who are considered descendants from the paternal line.
7. How the words "from the progeny of the father" are to be understood, and what falls under said words.
body: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, amen. In the question which is being contested in the city of Treviso between a certain Homobonus, maternal uncle of Gregorius de Baseglis, instituted as heir by the said Gregorius; and a certain Lady Ioanna, born of Francia, daughter of the late Ser Gregorius de Haseglis, paternal grandfather of the said Gregorius whose inheritance is at issue; and a certain Lady Druda, daughter of the late Ser Petrus, who was born of the late Ser Dominicus de Baseglis, which Ser Dominicus was the paternal great-grandfather of the said Gregorius whose inheritance is at issue: each of the said ladies asserting that the inheritance of the said Gregorius the second belongs to her, either intestate or by the testamentary disposition of a certain Lady Quayota, paternal grandmother of the said Gregorius, whose property constituted the inheritance of the said Gregorius the second whose succession is at issue. In which disposition, so far as pertains to our purpose, the said Lady Quayota instituted as her universal heir the said Gregorius, her grandson born of Franciscus, her predeceased son, adding that if the said Gregorius should die before the legal age, all her goods should devolve upon the sister of that Gregorius, who was likewise called Quayota, the said Quayota then giving, etc. And that if the said Gregorius should reach the legal age and not have a legitimate heir descending from him, he might then make a will and leave his goods only to his closer relatives descending, however, from the line or issue of his father Franciscus de Baseglis. And nevertheless, with respect to the aforesaid Quayota, if it should happen that the great house with the entire estate, etc., should come to the same Quayota by the death of her brother Gregorius dying before or after the legal age without having a legitimate heir descending from her, as was said, she might not make a will and leave the said house with the said estate except to closer relatives descending from the line or issue of her father Franciscus de Haseglis. But the said Homobonus contradicts them, saying that by the will of the said Gregorius the goods belong to him, and that the revenues of the aforesaid house ought to be distributed as the said Gregorius disposed in his will, as these and other matters appear more fully in the acts of the said case, which for the sake of brevity are not written here, but are to be held as inserted, since all have been examined.

† And in this question, for the investigation of the truth, I premise that we do not have to treat of the Falcidian, nor the Trebellian, nor of what is due by natural law, on account of the disposition of the statutes of the said city; and we must follow the disposition of the statutes or the testatrix entirely, wherefore it must be looked into. And because it depends upon the words, or upon the intention which is gathered from the words, as in l. cum virum, C. de fideius., let us therefore see first whether from the words uttered in the will of Lady Quayota the said Gregorius is prohibited from making a will and leaving his property to anyone other than the relatives from the line or from the issue of the father, etc. And it seems not: because the testatrix spoke affirmatively, that he 'may make a will,' etc., and thus by the word 'may' (possit). But it is well known that things which pertain to permission do not impose necessity, as in ff. de offi. praesi. l. saepe and ff. de iudi. l. non quicquid. And if they do not impose necessity, it follows that he was able, if he wished, to leave it to whomsoever at his pleasure, and thus to the said Homobonus. To the contrary is that permissive words uttered negatively by one who has the power to prohibit induce a necessity upon the prohibited person to abstain from these things, as in ff. de offic. procon. et lega. l. 4 in fin. and l. solent around the beginning, there, 'for neither can you' (nec enim potestis), and de of. proc. Ces. l. fi. ad fi., and de of. eius, cui man. est iurisdi. l. 1, § 1, and ff. de le. 1, l. nemo potest, with similar laws. But in our case she prohibits making a will and leaving the property to anyone outside the relatives of whom mention is made in the will; therefore the minor premise is also proven,

† proven from the meaning of that word 'only' (solummodo), which is exclusive and prohibitive of all others. For the testatrix said: 'he may make a will and leave his goods only to his closer relatives,' etc. Therefore she does not permit others, but prohibits, as in l. cum praetor in princ. ff. de iudi. And that this word is exclusive the masters of grammar know, but it is proven in C. de pat. qui fil. dist. l. 3; insti. de vsu. in princ.; ff. de adi. leg. l. 3, § cum Titio; the gloss noted in l. rationes, C. de proba.; and it is also proven in extra de procur. c. si duo, lib. 6. And this part is true. The first conclusion therefore stands: that outside of the relatives descending from the line or issue of his father, this Gregorius could not make a will concerning the goods coming to him from his grandmother Quayota; regarding his own property acquired elsewhere, however, if he had any, I do not think he was prevented from including it. Let us see therefore which relatives are included, that we may know which are excluded. And regarding this it must first be seen concerning the sense of that word 'closer relatives' (propinquioribus); secondly, concerning the sense of that word 'from the line' (ex linea); thirdly, of that 'or issue' (seu prole); fourthly, of those words 'only descending' (tantum descendentibus).

† Regarding the first, it must first be seen who are called relatives simply and absolutely speaking. And it appears to me that those are of the number of relatives who are called by civil law to succession intestate, as the case seems to me in l. 1, C. vnde vir, et vxor, and this is proved by the text in C. de impo. lucran. descri. l. 1, verse et his, joined with the gloss on the word propinquitatis; although sometimes that word, on account of an adjunct, or on account of preceding or subsequent words, is restricted to fewer persons, as in the said l. 1. And thus from that simple word, 'closer relatives' (propinquioribus), I say that those who are of the head or degree of cognation are not excluded, and consequently neither that Lady Ioanna nor that Homobonus the uncle are excluded solely by those words, when she said 'to his closer relatives.' But whether the subsequent words have to restrict and limit this, I shall state below.

† Secondly, regarding this word 'closer relatives' (propinquioribus), it must be seen whether we speak of the nearer in degree, so that this Gregorius is thereby constrained to pre-elect them, or whether he can also choose more remote ones. And the doubt arises because whether one speaks in the comparative or in the positive, the same sense seems compounded in the positive thus, 'whom no one precedes,' as in institu. de legi. agna. succes. § proximum and ff. de suis, et legi. l. 2, § haereditas ad fi.; yet Iacobus Butrigarius in l. 1, C. vnde vir, et vxor said that where it is said in the comparative that one from among the closer relatives ought to intervene, it is understood of the nearer ones, to the extent that one further off in degree would not be sufficient. Thirdly, regarding this word 'closer relatives', it must be seen

† whether males, or also females, are comprehended. And I think that in our case females as well as males are comprehended. The reason is that the matter of which we speak is indifferent to male and female, since females also are capable of successions, in Authen. de haer. ab intesta. § 1 et seq. Likewise because it is uttered here in the dative case, wherefore as a common word it comprehends male as well as female, and thus both. Likewise because the laws, when they use that word, understand it of male as well as female, as in l. 1, C. vnde vir, et vxor and the said l. 1, C. de imp. luc. descri. Likewise because the intention of the testatrix was such, which is clear because she willed that if Gregorius died after the legal age and the house came to Quayota, his sister, the said Quayota could not afterward leave it except to her closer relatives, etc.; for from those words it is clearly gathered that if Quayota, the sister of Gregorius, had survived, Gregorius himself could have left his property after the legal age to his Quayota by the disposition of the said testatrix. These things are proved in her will, in the verse nihilominus. And thus stands the conclusion that that word, 'closer relatives,' also comprehends females; nor does the matter of whether the masculine comprehends the feminine touch our case at all, since here the words are uttered rather in the masculine than in the feminine. Having examined that 'closer relatives,' let me pass to the subsequent word 'from the line' (ex linea).

† Regarding which it must be observed that, so that the construction may be good and correct, that word 'from the line' is construed and conjoined with the participle 'descending,' which follows later, or with the taxative 'only,' so that thus, by conjoining the words in order, the disposition of the testatrix says: that Gregorius may make a will and leave his property only to his closer relatives descending however, or however descending from the line or issue of his father Franciscus. Therefore, by that disposition she excludes non-relatives and includes relatives, but not all, rather only those who descend from the line or issue of Franciscus, his father. It must therefore be investigated who those are. And here it must be observed that there is here a word under the disjunctive, 'or' (seu); although it disjoins the words between which it is placed, nevertheless the disposition regarding one of the disjuncts is extended to the other, as is clear in l. si quis ita, ff. de auro. et arg. le., and noted by Cynus in l. cum quidam, de verb. sig. This having been so posited,

† let us see who are descending from the line of the father. And here I say that those words can have a two-fold sense: one is that the word 'father' is taken materially or effectively; according to this sense only the children of the father, that is, of Franciscus, and the descendants of the children are comprehended, and thus not ascendants directly or collaterally. This sense and interpretation does not please me as much as the following one, on account of the other part under the disjunctive which follows, 'or issue,' which would add nothing, but repeat the same thing. The other sense, therefore, is that the word 'father' is taken subjunctively or contentfully: so that the sense is that Gregorius may leave his property to his closer relatives descending only from the line of his father, that is, under which the father is subjected; and this interpretation seems to me more according to the mind of the testatrix.

† And what follows, 'or from the issue of the father,' must similarly be understood in a two-fold way: in one way actively, namely, from the issue of the father, that is, from those begotten by the father; and so Uguccio expounded, and in favor of this exposition is C. de insti. et subs. l. sub conditio; also l. generaliter in fi., with what is noted there, and extra de condi. appo. c. fi.; and so it is held in common usage of speech, which also ought to be observed, as in l. cum de lanionis, § asinam, ff. de fundo instru. Likewise it can be understood 'from the issue of the father' passively, that is, from the issue from which the father was begotten, and thus for the lineage and stock of the father; the first sense is more admitted by proper meaning and common usage of speech, and therefore I hold that as the better. From which I infer that from that part of the disjunctive, 'or issue,' neither the said Lady Druda nor the said Lady Ioanna can come to the claim of the said goods. It remains therefore only to see whether, by virtue of the first part of the disjunctive, either of them can come, as being of the line of the father, taking it according to the sense and interpretation which I set forth above. And because the greater part of this question lies here, it must therefore be seen what a line is.

† Secondly, in how many ways a line is taken. To the first it must be said that a line in this matter is a collection of persons descending from the same trunk, containing degrees and distinguishing numbers; and this according to Ioannes Andreae in his commentary on the tree of affinity, and it is proved in l. scemata, ff. de gradi.

† To the second it must be said that it is threefold according to the same: namely, of ascendants, of descendants, and of collaterals, as is proved in the said l. scemmata. And here it must be observed that if we were to begin from Adam, we would all be of the line of descendants. And to that extent, in our case and topic, if we begin from Franciscus, the father of the said Gregorius, who was named in the disposition of the testatrix, the line of descendants would have been his children ad infinitum; but the line of ascendants was the father of the said Franciscus, the great-grandfather, the great-great-grandfather, the fourth ancestor, and all the others ascending; and this in the line of agnates, but in the line of cognates ascending it would be the mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and great-great-grandmother, etc. And the same is to be seen in the descending line, for those born of a son are in the line of agnation, those born of a daughter, and so successively, are of the line of cognation. And the same in the transversal line or that of collaterals: for some are agnates, and these can be said to be of the line of agnation; some are cognates, and these of the line of cognation. Now to the point: when the testatrix said 'to the closer relatives descending from the line of his father Franciscus,' it must be understood of that line which is direct, and under which, beginning from the trunk, Franciscus the father of the said Gregorius is contained. The trunk, however, was Ser Dominicus, from whom descended Gregorius his son; from which Gregorius descended Franciscus; from which Franciscus descended Gregorius who has now made a will and instituted Homobonus. This is the direct line of the father of the said Gregorius. There is also another direct line under which the father of the said Gregorius is not contained, namely, the line which is of Lady Darda. For from the said trunk, namely Dominicus, descended another son called Petrus, and from Petrus Lady Darda. Therefore the line under which Franciscus is contained is distinct from the line of Lady Darda. And because every line begins from a limit, as in the said l. scemata, from the trunk whence it is derived, just as from the threshold of an inn different ways begin by which one goes to the different small rooms that are in the house; since therefore Lady Quayota the testatrix said, 'to the closer relatives descending only from the line of the father,' she excludes all other lines of relatives not descending from the line of the father, whether you wish to understand it as initiated from the father, and thus descending, or whether you understand it from the person of the father contentfully or subjunctively, which initiates in the trunk, namely in the person of Ser Dominicus, in which the said Franciscus is contained. And from this it is inferred that since Lady Darda is not of that line, but of a different one, she is not comprehended under the words uttered by the said testatrix. Nor is this obstructed by the fact that she is of his agnation, and thus at least can also be said to be of the line of Franciscus by agnation: because I answer that agnation properly does not have a line, but only by the broadest term and thus improperly, as in ff. de leg. 3, l. non aliter and ff. de uerb. sig. l. eum, qui uectigal; nor did the testatrix care about such a line, since she referred to the line of substance, not of quality; therefore she said 'from the line of the father,' not 'from the line of the agnation of the father himself.' I admit therefore that Franciscus is of one line and Lady Darda of another, and thus in the agnation of the father himself there can be two lines, as is the case in our matter. Similarly, from the aforesaid it is inferred that since Lady Ioanna is not of the line of the father of the said Gregorius, namely of the father Franciscus, but of another, namely of Gregorius, maternal grandfather of the said Lady Ioanna, she is not comprehended in the number of those relatives to whom the testatrix willed and permitted the property to be left. Nor does it obstruct that she is of the transversal line, because that is true as to Franciscus himself, to whom she is cognate, but it does not follow: therefore she is of the line of Franciscus himself; since that transversal line leaves the line through which one descended to Franciscus himself, and diverges from Gregorius into Franciscus and successively into Ioanna. From these things, therefore, the solution of our question is clear: that since at the time of the death of the said Gregorius there was no one in the nature of things from among those relatives upon whom Lady Quayota willed and permitted him to testate, the said Gregorius could make a will in favor of anyone else whatsoever and leave his property to him. And thus the institution made of Homobonus is valid, and the legacy made of the revenues for pious causes is valid and holds. And so I conclude, and this is the end of this consilium. Baldus. Addition of Salicetus: Nevertheless, although it is not necessary to add it, yet for the greater satisfaction of the said ladies it can probably be said that they have nothing to complain about; for Lady Quayota, who permitted him to make a will and leave his property to his closer relatives only, did not provide what was to be done if he left it to others. Wherefore if Gregorius did not institute those relatives whom the testatrix permitted, he did not do what he could, and in instituting others he did what he could not; therefore the institution does not hold, according to that saying: 'what I could, I would not; what I would, I was unable to fulfill.' And if the institution does not hold, the inheritance devolves to those coming to him intestate, as in l. 1, C. de haere. insti. and in l. si pater, de insti. et subst. sub condi. fac. And if it is so, that Homobonus, maternal uncle of the said Gregorius, is preferred intestate, who is joined to him in the fourth degree, and Lady Darda in the fifth; and this not only by the ius commune, but also by municipal law. For since those goods came to the said Gregorius from his grandmother, Lady Quayota, the statute, etc., placed under the rubric de bonis defunctorum ab intestato, verse et si quid, has place: that the property comes to the closer relatives of the deceased man or woman whence that property came. Since therefore Homobonus is closer to the mother of this Gregorius from whom the property came to Gregorius, it follows that in these goods, according to the form of the said statute, he would succeed him intestate. Wherefore those women have nothing to complain of if Homobonus has by will that which he would have had intestate. Since, in the case where the said Gregorius tests in favor of other relatives, the grandmother did not dispose that the goods ought to come to those relatives to whom she permitted them to be left. I think nevertheless that the will holds, as I wrote above. Praise to our Savior. Bartholomaeus de Saliceto.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A proceeding instituted in violation of a statute prohibiting certain persons from being admitted to bring accusations, etc., is null if such persons have been admitted, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen. The statute of the city provides that no noble or powerful person may make an accusatory denunciation, or complaint, against any person of the city or episcopate of Ancona, or from elsewhere: except solely for an injury inflicted upon the person of the accuser or denunciator, or his kin, or upon the things which he possesses. And the magistrate, or the judge of crimes, is bound not to admit any person of the aforementioned condition to any accusation, or denunciation, or complaint, under penalty, etc. Now it has happened that a certain noble, included within the prohibition of the statute, caused a certain denunciation to be made against several persons who were said to have committed certain excesses, not however against the person of the said noble, but concerning things not possessed by the said noble. Concerning which denunciation, proceedings were carried out by a procurator, and the said denounced parties were condemned as contumacious, who, through their procurator, claim that the said proceedings are null, because they were conducted contrary to the form of the statutes. It is asked whether the said proceedings, as stated above, were null by operation of law. And whether, if a capital penalty has been imposed, the penalty can be retracted by the procurator.

And it seems that one should say that there is some process: because the summoned parties did not appear, nor did they allege that proceedings could not be taken, nor did they raise a declinatory exception of forum. For they ought to have appeared, and to have alleged and proved their defense in court, as is stated in D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, l. ex quacunque; and D. de iudiciis, l. si quis ex aliena; D. de procuratoribus, l. qui procurator, dat., §. fin.; C. de exceptionibus, l. si. These are common laws and the rule of civil law dictates this. Moreover, in this process no express error is found; therefore, the process and the sentence hold, as noted in D. de appellationibus, l. si expressam; and l. 1, §. cum contra sacra; D. quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur; and l. 1, C. de errore calculi. And the reason is manifest: because error cannot be alleged after sentence, otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits, D. de iudicibus, l. si praetor, in principio. Therefore, it would be in vain to allege error or ignorance, if the error could not be proved: C. de iuris et facti ignorantia, l. error. Moreover, for the contumacious party, the cause of judgments is abundant, C. de iudicibus, l. sancimus.

Furthermore, it does not seem that in the case of the chapter *Haec defensio per procuratorem*, as in §. crimen, and C. de accusationibus, l. reos, according to Cynus, and it was a common question, and Bartolus places in l. penultima, §. crimen, D. de publicis iudiciis, the contrary can be defended as probable. For the laws say that if the accuser is not legitimate, the accused shall not be harassed, Extravagantes de accusationibus, c. 1. Also, he who remained silent about being a nobleman, by remaining silent, committed fraud upon the praetor, and also by proceeding fraudulently; therefore, the process is null, D. de falsis, l. si quis obrepserit. Moreover, this informer was prohibited from informing and accusing, and thus was prohibited from entering into the judgment; hence the sentence is invalid, D. de aleatoribus, l. 1, §. quod autem. Moreover, the procurator is admitted to this defense, because it does not touch the substantial matters of true defense, but is only about procedures. This appears because he did not comply with the exception of res judicata, Extravagantes de iudicibus, c. examinata, in fine. The objection regarding renunciation does not hold, but because it was a peremptory exception, which must be determined together with the principal issue, not by itself, l. 1, C. de ordine iudiciorum. For it is implicit in the procedures from the crime, and therefore the prohibiting reason is examined: because it is fuller and greater, D. de iudicibus, l. per minorem.

Moreover, the matter is not understood to be liquidated by contumacy, which is null, D. iudicata solvitur, l. vir bonus; and l. finalis, §. penultima, C. de iuramento calumniae. Moreover, this process has no permissive foundation, and was done against a prohibiting law; therefore, it does not hold, whatever followed from it and on account of it: C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. non dubium. Moreover, the statute prohibits ordinary jurisdiction; therefore, much more strongly, extraordinary information, l. 1, §. accusationem, D. ad turpia; and C. de delatoribus, l. ex varia; and D. de iure fisci, l. ubi deferre. It is true that sometimes where the accuser is lacking, it is supplied ex officio by the inquisitor, but that would proceed from some special law, for example, in favor of a minor; for as a rule, this cannot be granted, as noted in l. querela, C. de falsis. Moreover, the crime alleged is private, which appears from the form of the statute, which does not permit any person of the Roman people, as noted in l. penultima, C. de conditione ob carmen. Furthermore, the inquisitor succeeds in the place of a public person, not a private one, and the office of inquisitor is not favorable, but rather odious, and contrary to the rules of civil law, D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. rescripto, §. si quis accusatorem; Extravagantes de simonia, cap. non habens; Extravagantes de accusationibus, cap. licet eligatur. How then was this process without foundation: indeed, against the foundation of municipal law.

Moreover, it can be said that this exception, as being odious, can be opposed after sentence, because it is introduced out of mere hatred of magnates, D. ad Macedonianam, l. tametsi. And this was held by Jacobus de Arena in his disputation, which disputation I have in a similar case. Nor do I omit that the accuser obtained to proceed against the denounced parties through a procurator; therefore, let him use the same condition, C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. fin., which speaks both in civil and criminal matters. Moreover, the name of querela is general, and comprehends every kind of complaining, as noted by Odofredus in l. cum arbitror, D. qui satisdare cogantur. And from these things, it seems sufficiently clear that the said processes do not hold by the law itself. However, the question of the crime is not entirely suppressed, but as to the process, D. de accusationibus, l. libellorum, §. quod si libelli; and D. de adulteriis, l. accusaturus. Note that the statute enumerates the first cases, when against the person, and this word signifies those things which are not separated from the person, as noted by Bartolus, D. de publicis, l. licitatio, §. quod illicite. Another case is concerning possessed things, and this head was not alleged, nor is it true: and he who alleges nothing obtains nothing. There are, namely, four cases: alleged and true; also true and alleged; and especially those which are indicative of jurisdiction, and which must be proved before the joinder of issue, according to the order given by law, must be clear; otherwise, the process does not hold, l. quaero, D. de eo qui pro tutore; and noted by Innocentius, de foro competenti, c. cum sit generale; and c. verum.

Therefore, it is rightly concluded that in the libels, an omitted case is considered as omitted: and that from it, or upon it, a sentence cannot be founded, l. fundus, de communi dividundo; and l. finalis, de fideicommissis, liber. Nor is it in our discretion to change the nature of judgments, D. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. non possumus. And therefore, according to what is proposed, always saving the deliberation of the great council of our illustrious lord, I conclude that the process is erroneous and bad, and that the said condemnations are to be saved in the substance of the defense, Extravagantes de purificatione vulgaris, c. significantibus; and C. de accusationibus, l. absentibus. Someone will say, the statute fixes its feet in the imposition of a penalty, therefore that penalty suffices, and the act is valid, D. de divortio, l. ait lex. Solution: there it speaks when the act is of the genus of permitted things: but here it is of the genus of prohibited things, and by the mystery of the law, without the mystery of man, the person was removed from the act, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. nemo martyres. Also, here different persons are regarded: because the penalty is placed, the nullity of the judgment to the process, and remedies in different persons, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus, §. oeconomicus. Moreover, there are certain acts which cannot receive validity, so contrary are they to the form of law, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the subject matter. The law *hac edictali*. And whether, when it is done against a provision beginning with a prohibition and ending with a prohibition, what is done is valid.
2. The law *hac edictali* does not prohibit sons from being substituted to the father by the second mother in that which he could not acquire.
3. Whether what is taken away from the father in the case of the law *hac edictali* applies to the sons of the first marriage.
4. Whether those things which are in the case as if unwritten ought to be restored with fruits.
body: Furthermore, it must be known that

† Another disposition begins with what is permitted and ends with what is permitted; and then, although the wording of the words may be different, there is nevertheless only one and the same disposition. D. de verb. oblig. l. Qui bis idem. And this is true, unless there intervenes a diversity in effect, because then, just as there are several numbers, so there are several effects. C. de nova. l. si. Moreover, a discrepancy of sense and understanding is that which induces a true difference, as D. de fideiuss. l. si ita stipulatus fuero opus; and D. l. cum in plures, §. lege dicta. From these it appears that recapitulation does not make the thing different, nor does a plural essence, as C. de leg. l. cum qu. But this is not our case; rather, sometimes a disposition begins with what is prohibited and ends with what is prohibited; and then neither extreme is valid for what is done, e.g., if both the degree of institution and that of substitution are contrary to law, or both are void in the cause as if not written; because "as if not written" and "null" are the same. D. de his quae pro non scriptis habentur, l. si in metallum; C. de caus. toler. §. in primo. For that which is null has not even the image of a thing, as C. de latr. lib. toler. l. unica; nor can anything be founded upon that which is nothing, as noted in C. de acquirenda possessione, l. nulla. And therefore, if a father has two spurious children, he cannot substitute one for the other; because there is a defect in both extremes, both the first and the second. D. de vulg. sub. l. si is, qui. But here one might doubt whether our case falls under this member, in which the husband is preferred to the children of the first marriage contrary to the law hac edictali. For certainly this extreme is prohibited, as in l. hac edictali; nevertheless, in place of this chapter, the chapter de liberis is substituted, which chapter seems to be permitted; because it is lawful to love one of the children more than another, and to give him more, without diminishing the legitime in any way, as in Auth. de nupt. §. optimae. Nor is it new that the degree begins with the substitute, where the instituted heir fails according to the understanding of the law, as D. de lib. et posth. l. et si pepercerit, §. si. For although there intervenes a subordination of words, in sense and efficacy there intervenes only a degree having validity, in l. 2, C. de haer. inst.

And from this follows the conclusion that the law *hac edictali* prohibits the children of a second marriage from being substituted to a parent in that which he could not take. For this substitution is valid by the law of vulgar substitution on account of the division of will and capacity made by the law, although some say that if one is capable for a part of the inheritance, the entire vulgar substitution expires, as if that vulgar substitution did not permit a testamentary disposition to lapse in part, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. *cogi*, §. *hi, qui solidum*, and noted in l. 1, C. de secundis nuptiis. Moreover, in our case, the substitution made to the husband was vulgar; because a substitution made with the words “if he shall not be able to take” expresses the case of vulgar substitution, as in C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. *cum proponas*. Therefore, I say that either the substitution made in this manner is in fraud of the law, and is void by the law itself; because the device of fraud is rescinded by the force of the law, as in D. de iure patronatus, l. *si libertus iuniorem*; and fraud is deceit, which vitiates a will, as in l. 1, in fine, D. de doli exceptione. Nor ought the law to be circumvented by any abusive nature of caviling, which shows false things as true and, with sought-after and abusive colors, strives to confuse the truth. But truth cannot be extirpated from the nature of things, because it is perpetual and immortal. Or the aforementioned substitution was not made in fraud of the law, as in this example: because the woman left to her husband not so that he might retain, but so that he might distribute as a minister and executor, and then it was not done in fraud of the law, because he is a mere minister, to whom pertains the solicitude of the imposed duty, and not gain, as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. *Sulpitius*. This law is alleged by Iacobo de Arena, and by me in many places: as in D. de usuris, l. *in fideiussione*, §. *cum Pollidius*. Hence, he could above all be a mere executor of the paternal will, because nothing is acquired to him. Or it is doubted with what mind the testator uttered the words; and then one must first resort to the writing, which is the best interpreter of the human mind, so that what the sound represents to the ear, the sound represents to the intellect, as in D. de supellectili legato, l. *Labeo*, §. *item Tubero*. Then one must resort to the order of the writing; because order prepares the intellect, opens the sense, and applauds the truth of the intellect, as in D. de usufructu, l. *quotiens*. For the word first born in the heart is like the firstborn in inheritance, who is, so to speak, prior in fact than another is in the nature of things, as in D. de statu hominum, l. *Arethusa*. For now, if we consider the order of the will and argue from the order, because it is not a fatal order, but an intellectual one, we comprehend that the testatrix preferred her husband and subjoined to him the children in default and in her first affection. Indeed, on account of the ease of restoring to the prohibited person, or of concealing the whole, it is presumed to have been done in fraud, as if through an interposed fictitious person, as in l. *quaeritur*, D. de operis liberto. In frauds to be presumed or not, recourse must be had to the discretion of men having sense, for from excessive caution fraud is presumed, considering the quality of the persons, as noted in l. 6, D. de conditionibus et institutionibus. Behold, therefore, in our case, fraud is presumed on account of excessive affection, which is proper, not common, nor laudable, as in D. de probationibus, l. *qui testamentum*; D. de legatis tertio, l. *cum quis decedens*, §. *codicillis*.

But it is doubted whether that which is taken from the husband is to be applied to the children of the first marriage. And say, as in §. optime. But what is taken from the children, as in our case: on account of the presumed fraud, it seems to be the same, that they do not receive more at first on account of the rule: because those coming by special right do not accrue more than if they were coming by common right. D. de cond. et dem. l. mulieri, et Titio. For that which is taken in the name of a penalty cannot return to him by right of accrual. Secondly, because children who are not too dearly loved should not have more than those who are more dearly loved. C. de lib. praet. l. maximum uitium. and D. de leg. praest. l. saluus Iulianus. The other two members, namely when it begins with what is permitted and ends with what is prohibited, or vice versa, I do not pursue, because it is not expedient. Or say that it is enacted to the prejudice of the one committing the fraud, that nothing accrues to him, but to those who are capable. And this is true, arg. D. de fals. l. filius si sequens quo. Indeed, the penalties of second marriages were introduced in favor of the children, and in compensation for the injury which they suffer from the one marrying. And the rule is this: Whenever one does not offend against the public, but against a private person, and a penalty is imposed in compensation for the injury, which is applied to the one injured, as l. 1. D. de litig. and C. de leg. l. si. Thus it is therefore in the case at hand, because the children of the first marriage are those who are neglected, and suffer injury from the desertion of the affection due to the children. Hence it is that if those children die, the penalty is remitted: because there is no one to whom compensation is made: as C. de sec. nup. l. feminae. §. si. and in Auth. de non elig. secundo nub. §. Gregoria. and there the glossa magistra. And by this the objection does not hold, which I wrote in my lecture on l. hac edictali. because that is true when it is not done in fraud, or in derogation of the law, as is the case here. Which appears from the order of the words. For all this proceeds from the root of condemned affection, arg. D. de acq. et obl. l. si. D. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. 2. and 3. For the footsteps of words signify the order of the will, and its quality: and whether one would otherwise have done it, or not: as D. de haer. inst. l. Paccumeius Androtenes. And the same is to be said wherever a person is interposed under a sought-after color. And the objection does not hold, which I noted in the said l. hac edictali. concerning the spurious great-nephew.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether those things which are not in the cause are to be restored with their fruits as if unwritten. I answer: yes, in the same manner as they ought to be restored to other owners of things; because the title is considered as no title. D. quod met. causa. l. sed et partus. in princip. D. de rei vend. l. fructus. with its subject matter. I say the same in the matter of this edictal law. I, Baldus.
In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain woman named Lady Mita, wife of Mutius of Pitigliano, was accused of adultery, which is said and see in part 5, consilium 437, beginning "ut praesens."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the procurement of a benefice as vacant by reason of the abandonment of an appeal, before judgment has been pronounced on the abandonment, is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The restoration of a deserted appeal is sometimes granted by strict justice: for example, on account of a legal impediment, and in such case it is retroactive, and whatever was changed is restored. Sometimes it is granted by mere grace: and in such case what was transferred in the meantime is not invalidated, as in cap. Quanvis, extra de rescriptis, lib. 6, and ff. de minoribus, l. In causis, §. Interdum. Whether an appeal is deserted through the negligence of the procurator is noted in C. de appellationibus, Auth. Hodie, in c. 1, ut litis non contestatae, and C. de appellationibus, l. Praeses. Hence, whether the procurement of a benefice as vacant by reason of the desertion of the appeal is valid depends on the records, and therefore let the records speak.
