And before this is declared, the matter is sub iudice. ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Dicimus. Therefore, the consulting jurists say well that if the restitution is by grace, otherwise if it is by strict law. If therefore it appears expressly from the records that the said appeal was deserted, and finally the benefice was conferred upon another, the said grace of restoration would not be valid: because the sentence would have already passed into res iudicata, and the matter would not be res integra. It is true that Master Bartolus, in his consultation, held that a pronouncement must be made concerning the desertion: and that before such pronouncement is made, the appeal is pending. And this opinion is correct. He did not hold that the conferral made to another was valid, but the glossa which is in l. Eos, C. de appellationibus, does not require any interlocutory decree to issue on this point: because here we are speaking of a strict restitution in integrum; but by grace, the said John Jacobus obtains the said benefice, which was vacant by reason of deprivation, which had passed into res iudicata. Hence I, Baldus de Perusio, concur with the aforementioned doctors according to what is proposed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the father, or mother, uncle, or aunt, or those in the collateral line, are said to belong to the line, or offspring, of a son.
2. The father does not succeed the son in feudal matters.
3. Whether an heir burdened with a fideicommissum may freely make a will if the person in whose favor the disposition is made fails to exist.
4. The reasons by which reconvention was introduced.
5. What is meant by the continuity of the cause.
body: It is asked whether the line, or the offspring of the son,

† it is said that the father, or mother, uncle, or aunt, great-uncle, or great-aunt, or any ascendant in the direct line, or in the collateral line. And it seems that this is not so, from the proper meaning of the word *de*. For it signifies the matter concerning which something is decided or arises, as in l. 1, § nunc videamus, D. de coniug. cum eman. lib. But an ascendant does not arise from a descendant, but rather the reverse:

† and therefore in matters of fiefs the father does not succeed the son: because he is not of his root or substance, as in c. 1, §. cum vero, Corradus, qui feud. da. pos. col. 10, and in the title de gradibus, the same is compiled. Therefore, an ascendant is not of the offspring, nor of the descending line, either directly or collaterally. And thus, if mention is made in a will of his nearer relatives by line, since the brother of the father and the maternal uncle are not contained in the offspring of the testator’s father. To the contrary, it seems from l. 1, C. de conditionibus insertis; and because it is certain that the father is included, for I do not say that he is of the nearer relatives by line or offspring of his own, since no one is nearer to himself, as no one makes a degree to himself. Nevertheless, the father, with respect to the son, includes nearness of kin and line. Which is thus demonstratively proven: the father is the head of the line, as in Inst. de gradibus and D. eod. l. iure consultus. But it is certain that the head is part of the body, as in D. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum, l. cum in diversis. Therefore, the father is part of the body and line of nearness of kin. Now I prove that the same applies to collateral ascendants: because they are the heads of that line, therefore they are included under the term "line." Likewise, "nearer relatives" or "nearest," as in D. de bonis possidendis, l. cum quidam, and Inst. de legatis agnatorum successione, §. proximus. Therefore, it follows that whether the line is stated affirmatively, this general term includes negatively: it is valid in excluding and affirmatively including. And the above are confirmed by a visual example: imagine a man on a cross with arms outstretched; there the head is the ascendant, the feet are the descendants, and the arms are the collateral parts, and all from one trunk. Secondly, considering the mind of the deceased, whose prudent counsel is observed: because he did not consider extraneous persons, but of his own kind, uncles. And aunts, paternal uncles, and maternal aunts are not included by that term: because it does not seem that the sense was of such extraneous persons, as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. Lucius; C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, cum avus; C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter. And terms are to be interpreted according to natural reason: because natural discretion is the mother of virtues, and judges best in doubtful matters, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. voluntatis.

† In another point it is touched upon: whether, if the person in whom the disposition is made fails, the heir burdened may freely make a will. And it seems that he may, as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. et cum triplici. Hence, if the testator prohibits making a will outside a certain class of persons, and those persons are not found in existence, the said heir burdened by the fideicommissum, if it fails while the condition is pending or by chance, as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. in nouissimo. The son is of the substance and seed of the father; but the father is not of the substance and seed of the son; because nature and reason do not begin from what comes later.

† It is asked, by what reasons is reconvention introduced? I answer that reconvention is a certain inherent or cohering action, as in double actions, as in ff. fa. er. l. in hoc iudicio; l. nulli alij; and generally many cases are decided, as in l. 1. ff. de qui. re. ad eundem iudicem eatur. Others [introduce it] on account of the quality to be preserved, as in c. prudentiam, extra de mutuis petitionibus. And know that in the first member, a sentence rendered in part does not bind by the law itself; but in the other members it binds; but one may appeal from this, as in ff. quae sententiae sine ap. rescin. l. 1. §. si. Arb. Nevertheless, he ought to pronounce sentence on all matters, and collectively, more on account of the form of the compromise than on account of the nature of the thing. ar. ff. de verb. ob. l. scire debemus; and ff. de arbi. l. de rebus.
† And know that it is called a connection of causes when knowledge of one cause is prepared for another, as in a petitory and a possessory action.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Certain types of military service are found to be for sale, and these can be alienated.
2. The term "for," what it signifies when attached to a final or impulsive cause, or when there is doubt.
3. Whether an agreement to sell implies necessity.
4. Whether an agreement is interpreted in favor of the buyer or the seller.
5. When material is drawn to the materialized, and vice versa.
body: I therefore premise that this right, which belongs to Sempronius, may be called the militia of Ferrara.

For certain military offices are venal and marketable. Moreover, they may be alienated under any condition or manner, as is shown in C. de pignoribus, l. si; and ff. de legibus 3, l. his verbis, § alumno; C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo, § fin.; and in l. 3, § nec castrense, ff. de collatione bonorum, ver. sed an id, quod; whence it is said in l. licite potuit vendere, et emptor emere. Furthermore, it must be known that every pact which is modificative of a contract has the power to inform it; and that limiting words appended in a pact are to be observed, as in ff. de servitutibus explicandis, l. cui pacto; and C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. si; and ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. si ita quis, § ea lenali, aut causae impulsiuae, aut dubitatur. In the first case, the cause must exist and be fulfilled; in the second case, it is not necessary, as you will see.

† It is also to be known that the word "for" is either attached to the cause of the fistat: because it is not properly a cause, but rather some motive for contracting or disposing, as in D. de don. l. 2. §. si. In the third case, when there is doubt: then either the words are attached to the cause of the recipient: and then it is an impulsive cause, as in l. Titio centum. in prin. D. de condi. et de. C. de iu. do. l. si mulier dotem. or to the cause of the giver: and then this word "for" denotes a final cause, as noted in C. de epi. et cler. l. generaliter. per Cy. and others. Or it is attached in favor of a third person, for whom one cannot stipulate or agree: and then similarly it is an impulsive cause, since from it no obligation arises, nor even an exception, and thus no right arises, nor any necessity of fulfilling, as in D. de don. l. donationes in concubinam. §. species.

Whether those words, "for selling," properly import necessity in the city, for necessity is sold in selling: for example, to Peter or John, as in l. 1, C. de epis. aud. Moreover, this pact redounds to the benefit of the said parties; therefore, if it is not observed, damages are due by tacit understanding, as in ff. de verb. oblig. l. stipulationes non dividuntur, § Celsus. Furthermore, a new doubt arises, that it is a serious matter to deceive faith, not only speaking of faith in which salvation is placed, but also of the faith of pacts, as in l. 1, post princ., ff. de const. pecul.

† But rather it seems that the entire statement should be interpreted in favor of the buyer: because the seller, who wishes to bind the buyer to something that is not of the proper nature of the contract, must speak so clearly that it cannot be interpreted otherwise than in his favor. For that which cannot be understood in a different way is obscure. D. de pactis, l. veteribus. And thus these doubtful words ought to be interpreted in favor of the buyer, not in favor of the said Sempronius, so that they may be enunciative or designative words, not restrictive ones: for in doubt we must adhere to the nature of the contract, as D. de usu, l. si stipulatus. But the subject matter of the contract of sale and purchase is to transfer the thing to the buyer in such a way that, once dominion has been transferred, the liberty to dispose of the thing is also transferred, as Inst. de rerum divisione, §. si quis a non domino. Therefore, these words come demonstratively, and not diminutively, nor restrictively, and thus the said buyer has free power. And to this it adds: because if it is paid on unworked material, it ought not to be paid on worked material: because double toll ought not to be paid, just as we say that what has been tithed once ought not to be tithed again. Moreover, the buyer succeeds to the place of the seller, therefore he ought to use the same right, but against this is D. de publicanis, l. licitatio, §. mercatores. Moreover, that word "necessary" greatly works to the contrary: because it regards the utility of the republic. Furthermore, every cause can be final, if the contracting parties so will, otherwise they would not contract. And thus they can convert an impulsive cause into a final one by pact: and conversely a presumed final cause into an impulsive one, if it is established that they were in every way able to contract, whence the pact regulates and governs the contract, as D. de depositis, l. 1, §. si convenerit. Moreover, the reason of the person must be considered, whence if an Abbot gives money to a monk for garments, the monk cannot retain it for himself for another purpose, but ought to convert it into garments necessary for his life. And it is held in D. de usufructu, l. item si fundus, §. fin. and D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, circa medium. And in §. ult. D. de usu et habitando, l. plenum, §. sed si sic, the law says that if I give you 10 so that you lend it to me, there are two species of contract. D. si certum petatur, l. si tibi. And thus if toll ought to be paid on the donation and the loan, it would be paid on one for the same thing. D. de donationibus, l. Aristo. Moreover, the law says that worked material and raw material are not the same. D. de acquisitione rei dotis, l. quicquid. Omitting the aforesaid, the cases in point seem to be otherwise, for on unworked material neither the buyer nor the seller pays anything, because this statute does not say so, because under the common law nothing ought to be paid beyond the price, but if a price has been agreed upon for raw material, and that price is paid on worked material not estimated, and the statute provides that toll ought to be paid on sale and purchase: whether in this case it ought to be paid. And it seems that it should, because true estimation makes mention, and a named contract results, and obligation is contracted by consent. And it seems expressed in D. de iure dotis, l. ita constante. To the contrary, because this is an exchange, as D. de conditionibus ob causam, l. fin. and exchange is one thing, true sale another: as l. 1, D. de rerum permutatione. Moreover, we blush to speak without the common or municipal law, as in Auth. de triennio et semis, §. consideremus. C. de collationibus, l. illam. Moreover, these tolls are odious, and against the common law, and therefore an omitted case is held as prohibited, as C. rem in praesenti, §. taceat. Moreover, let this be by the authority of the law, as D. de re iudicata, l. a Diuopio, §. 1. and in Auth. de fideiussoribus, §. quod autem, for the 1st part it is held in l. 1, C. de rerum permutatione. But there it speaks by interpretation of similarity, not by the proper figure of the fact, which is in statutes. Therefore, a libel not formed according to law ought to be rejected, because from that party who alleges the law, the law ought to be proved, as D. de probationibus, l. ab ea parte, according to the common saying of advocates.

† Set forth the law for me, my lord. When the matter is drawn to the material, then we examine the material; but when the material is drawn to the matter, then we examine the matter. D. de legibus 3, l. quaesitum, § illud.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the lessee is liable for damages.
body: They propose the following points.

† The aforementioned complainant is not entitled to any interest, because there are three modes of being bound, or of owing, namely: by commission (ex commisso), by promise (ex promisso), and by legal disposition (ex dispositione legali). Now, he is not bound here by commission, because he committed no wrong; since it is lawful for everyone to conduct business freely in any place, unless the goods were illicit, as in C. de commerciis et mercatoribus, l. mercatores; and ff. de operis liberti, l. libertus negotiatoris; or if something were committed in fraud of the customs duties, as in ff. de publicanis, l. commissa; C. de nautico faenore, l. cum proponas; ff. de locato, l. penultima, §. nauem. Furthermore, no action can lie here by promise, because these words do not sound [in that sense], nor does the meaning of the words tend to this. For outside the meaning and the words, no obligation is contracted, except in tacit contracts, as noted in C. de pactis, l. post venditionem; ff. communia, l. si is qui, §. si libero; or by the nature of tacit repetition, as in ff. de pactis, l. Item. Also, because of the understood intent, as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. triticum and l. quicquid astringendae; and ff. si certum petatur, l. cum quid. Since therefore there are no words of this kind of obligation here, nor is he bound by tacit understanding, nor should one proceed by circumlocutions, interest is claimed, as in C. de senatusconsulto, quod pro eo quod interest, l. 1, §. 1. Rightly, nothing is claimed in law, because nothing is owed. Moreover, no action can lie here by legal disposition, because we blush to speak without law, statute, or custom. He who alleges a law must prove it, whether he grounds himself on an affirmative or a negative not having a preceding legal disposition, as in ff. de probationibus, l. ab ea parte; and C. de collationibus, l. illam. From the foregoing, therefore, the conclusion appears manifest, that this pretension has no root, nor foundation of reason, and therefore the defendant ought to be absolved, as in ff. de pactis, l. epistola, §. fin. It supports the foregoing: because although each may do in his own thing what profits him, even if it harms another, as in ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 2, §. Item; variously, regarding the tavern of a man of Ferrara, ff. de legibus 2, l. Lucius, §. quisquis. By which law it is proved that the exercise of this tavern is lawful, useful, and honest. If the testator bequeaths iron for the use of this tavern, without determining the quantity, only so much is considered bequeathed as is found for the use. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the penalty is incurred if the arbitrator, or the compromise, is not obeyed, or when only one is disregarded, or when both the arbitrator and the compromise, or the award, are disregarded.
2. The clause "the agreement remaining ratified" has no place unless the penalty has been incurred. And no. 5.
3. Whether acts performed by a false procurator, who is now a procurator, can be ratified by the principal.
4. Whether the penalty incurred in one year is to be paid if the compromise is in other chapters.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A compromise was made by stipulation, secured by a penalty, and one party promised the other that she would cause the arbitrator to accept and render his award. Finally, the matter was again brought before a judge, and the litigation was joined before the arbitrator accepted; afterwards, although the party objected, the arbitrator accepted and rendered his award. It is asked whether the party who went to the judge incurred the penalty, and whether the compromise is valid.

† Regarding the first point, it must be premised for clarity that sometimes the compromise is scorned, and not the arbitrator; sometimes neither the compromise nor the arbitrator is scorned, considering the effect, although at first glance it may appear to be scorned. I give an example of each member. Behold, after the arbitrator has accepted, and obedience is not rendered to the arbitrator, but recourse is had to the ordinary judge, or the delegated judge. Thus the arbitrator is scorned, and here undoubtedly the penalty is incurred, unless the hearing of the arbitrator is scorned by the common consent of both parties, as in D. de arbitris, l. litigatores. That which is done with consent does not merit the penalty, as in D. locati conducti, l. cum plures, § lege dicta. It appears that the defendant dissents by protesting and contradicting; for if he consented tacitly and voluntarily accepted the judgment, the penalty is not incurred in effect, as in D. de iudiciis, l. sed et si susceperit, in principio. Example of the second member: namely, when the arbitrator is scorned, but not the compromise. This occurs when the arbitrator commands something that does not pertain to the matter compromised: such as going to Saint James or to the Apostles’ tombs, as noted in c. 1, de iudiciis, lib. 6, by Innocentius. And then the penalty is not incurred, because it is irrelevant, as in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, § nunc de officio. For the limits of the compromise, just as the limits of a mandate, are to be diligently observed and not extended, as in D. de arbitris, l. si de meis, in principio, and l. quid tamen, § fin. Now I give an example of the third member: but sometimes the compromise is scorned, and not the arbitrator; and this example is proper to our case. For the compromise was made and placed in effect, as in D. de arbitris, l. 5. But the arbitrator was not yet placed in effect, because he had not yet accepted, tacitly or expressly; and therefore it does not seem that, speaking properly, it can be said that the arbitrator was scorned, just as we say that the praetor is not scorned who has not yet attained the praetorship; nor is he called a soldier who is not girt, as in l. pen., D. de milite testamento. Moreover, the time of the compromise does not run before the arbitrator accepts; nor is it properly consumed before it arises, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio usus fructus. If certainly by this contrary act the effect of the compromise is impeded, which is contrary to what was promised in the instrument; and he who is bound to observe the award is bound to observe the compromise. Regarding the fourth member, give an example when the arbitrator summoned [a party] to appear in a shameful place, or on a holiday; for he is scorned, but in effect he is not punished, as in D. de iudiciis, sel., l. vir bonus; and D. de arbitris, l. si feriatis, and l. si cum dies. He who impedes the arbitrator from being able to arbitrate incurs the penalty, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. si quis arbitratu. But the arbitrator can proceed in the absence of a party; then he who does not appear does not incur the penalty, unless the interrogation of the absent party was necessary; because he does not impede the arbitrator from pronouncing sentence, or terminating or ventilating the business, as in D. de arbitris, l. non omnibus. From these, it is finally inferred regarding the question proposed, and I say that the penalty is incurred by the contrary act, as in D. de arbitris, l. item si unus, § multo post; and noted in c. quandiu, Extra de appellationibus, in Clementina. And the compromise is consumed; and the penalty arises not from the award, which is null when the compromise is consumed, but arises from the fact that the compromise was scorned, as is proven in the said laws. But it is probably doubted whether, because the parties returned anew to the same arbitrator, the compromise is repaired or renewed. And it seems that it is, as in D. de milite testamento, l. tribunus, § ultimo; and D. de secundis tabulis, l. qui ex liberis, § testamento. And with the same penalty tacitly understood, because this act seems similar to a prorogation, as in l. pen., § si inter, D. soluto matrimonio. And what Innocentius notes de iure, c. Quintavallis, because the will is not presumed to be changed with effect, as in D. de probationibus, l. cum tacitum, and l. quinquaginta. But the contrary must be said: because the other party contradicted; and in the act of reforming, the consent of both parties is required, as in C. locati conducti, l. si non obstat, § inter eos, because there in the principal matter. In marriage, all things were solemnly repeated and recounted, and therefore the same is understood in the accessory, which follows the form and origin of the principal disposition. Add that sometimes an arbitration is considered null for the consent of both parties, as in l. 2, C. communia utriusque iudicii. Also add that what is struck down can be repaired and healed, but not what is consumed, as in § pactus ne peteret. For after death, medicine is prepared too late, when it finds nothing to help. This decretal, in iure, consumpta, de officio delegati, c. significantibus; and l. Paulus, quae sententiae sine appellatione rescindantur; and C. de caducis tollendis, § in primo; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. interdicit. And when the substance is extinguished, qualities or accidents cannot remain in the being of nature, although sometimes they remain in the being of obligation, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. si servum, § effectus; and l. inter stipulantem, § sacramentum. Notwithstanding, D. si quis cautio, l. 2, § 1, because there there was a departure from the first contract. Also notwithstanding, D. de eo quod certo loco, l. centum capita, and l. si, because there it speaks of an accessory, which does not stand by itself, and therefore is taken away together with the principal. C. de usu, l. eos, in principio. Whether a procurator constituted to choose an arbitrator can confirm him whom he previously chose without mandate, or ignorant of the mandate. But all these things seem to be removed in one word by the customary clause that the penalty, whether paid or not, the compromise remains firm. For even if we were to say that the penalty does not remain, nevertheless the compromise remains without penalty. Also, a compromise to an arbitrator can be made without penalty, and the award is valid by virtue of transaction: as in l. si duo, § fin., D. de arbitris. Also, speaking intellectually, there are two compromises: one of which proceeds, namely, with penalty; the other follows, namely, without penalty, and the award is capable of emolument: as in C. de arbitris, l. pen.; and noted in D. de arbitris, l. 2. Therefore, the compromise endures, and its repair is not necessary.

But that response, with the clause “the agreement remaining ratified,” has no place unless a penalty has been incurred; but here the compromise has been discharged, because novation has occurred through the submission to judgment and the withdrawal from it, cf. D. de minoribus, l. minoribus 25 annis omissum. Moreover, it is answered by the notes in the said law qui fidem. It remains to consider another point.

A certain person appointed a procurator to choose an arbitrator. This appointed procurator had already made the choice, unaware that he had been appointed for this purpose. Later, he ratified this choice.

It is asked whether he could have done so. And it seems that he could not: because one thing is to elect, another to confirm; as is clear in the elections of prelates. And therefore, if the Pope delegates confirmation, he does not delegate election, nor conversely; and confirmation pertains to the superior, election to the chapter. Likewise, presentation pertains to the patron, institution to the diocesan bishop; thus it is in the case at hand. Moreover, he who wishes to know something must consider its opposite; but he who has a mandate to confirm does not have a mandate to elect; therefore, nor conversely. Furthermore, this person who compromised seems to have been a false procurator; therefore, the act done by him as a false procurator cannot be ratified by himself; as is read and noted in the Digest, On Exceptions, l. Modestinus.

On the contrary, it seems expressly proven that it is valid from the day of confirmation; because everything that depends on its own being can be ratified. Digest, Common Predications, l. si; Digest, On the Office of Proconsuls, i. observare, §. ult., because as long as the power to confirm lasts. And to confirm is put for to do; as in l. tribunus, §. ult.

Solution: Either he compromised, or he was a negotiorum gestor, and there is no doubt that it can be ratified by himself by reason of a subsequent mandate; because he acts in two capacities, as in the Digest, On Those Who Are Treated as If They Were Not, l. tutore; and argument from the Digest, On Adoption, l. si pater, §. qui duos. Or, as a procurator when he was not one, and then it is doubtful; because those things which pertain to the foundation of jurisdiction, done by a false judge or arbitrator, cannot be ratified, as noted in l. instar posse, so that what was done previously may not be valid due to defect of jurisdiction or quasi-jurisdiction. Nevertheless, my aforementioned conclusions stand firm: because one thing is to speak of the firmness of the award, another of the incurrence of a penalty.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 0. † Whether a penalty incurred in [?]
body: It follows to see, if there are multiple heads [of dispute], whether the submission to arbitration [compromissum] is dissolved in the other heads by one of them. And it seems it should be said that either the heads are connected, or they are entirely distinct. In the first case, let the submission be dissolved in all of them; in the second, not; ff. de mino. l. etiam. §. fi. But indeed, it seems that since there is a single penalty which looks to the whole, the submission to arbitration is dissolved in all of them, as in ff. iudi. so. l. cum quaerebatur; and because the judgment appears undivided with respect to the principal cause, and also the instance: unless it was agreed that it could be renounced upon one separately from another: which is understood in other heads, not in a definitive sentence, by which the instance has been consumed; and this in C. quoniam prouoca. non est neces. l. 1. Say that a penalty which is incurred only once seems to novate the entire submission to arbitration, as in l. apud celsum. §. si in arbitrum. de exce. doli. I did not consider concerning these things when I gave the first consilium, because they were not related to me in the fact, but afterwards I reflected upon it from the common usage of instruments:

† because that clause, "the agreement remaining in force", operates in favor of the one observing the agreement, as is noted in ff. de transa. l. qui fidem. and l. 2. C. de iure emph., but does not operate in favor of the one breaking the deed. I, Baldus. It is provided by statute that a husband has the usufruct of paraphernal property. Now it happened that a woman passed to second vows [remarried], and lost a certain ownership, and the usufruct remained to her according to the lex Foeminae, C. de secun. nupt. In these goods the woman did not claim the usufruct, nor did she give security for using and enjoying at the judgment of a good man, because she did not possess; but the children of the first marriage possessed with the knowledge and tolerance of the woman, and they possessed and gathered many fruits, and the woman died; from whose heirs the husband claims the gathered fruits, or their valuation. It is asked whether he can.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether long-suffering is regarded as equivalent to delivery between closely related persons.
1. The interdict *unde vi*: against whom it lies.
2. CASE. The stepdaughter, concerning Successions Intestate.
body: I was saying.

†e non. Because he did not possess, nor did he give security, and security is necessary for the gaining of fruits, or at least possession; but I hear that, contrary to my opinion, it was advised by some, and they moved themselves subtly, saying that security is then necessary whenever the usufructuary claims the usufruct and claims possession of the thing from which he wishes to receive the fruits. But where he leaves the possession with the owner, or quasi-owner, he could nevertheless receive the fruits, even if he has not given security. For if he wishes to claim the usufruct without possession of the thing, security does not seem necessary; because the usufructuary may not claim the usufruct, and yet the heir can demand the past and received fruits. This usufruct, by the form of the statute, seems to be acquired by operation of law without any other delivery, etc. That which is perceived from the thing of another, i.e., from the usufruct of another, must be restored to the formal owner of the usufruct; because security is of the substance in the constitution of a usufruct, not in one already constituted. According to the note in l. 1, ff. de usufr. Moreover, the force of the law is such that a real right is sought without delivery, or quasi-delivery, as noted in ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. idem respondit. Moreover, regarding the acquisition of the benefit, security for the use is not necessary. I answer: because use itself is not necessary, since the statute does not require it. And the words of the statute are not to be glossed, but followed. Moreover, glosses are not necessary unless the texts are lacking or the interpretation of the letter is doubtful; and even then, the glosses must be authentic and approved, as noted in ff. de off. præsi., l. licet. But notwithstanding these points, I remain in my original opinion, and I say that the husband cannot claim these fruits for several reasons. First, because the husband did not claim the usufruct, and thus they are forfeited by the delay of the one not claiming, not by the contumacy of the one not paying. Such doctrine is handed down, that if I am in delay in claiming, and the thing is not mine, I am not bound to restore the fruits. ff. ad Treb., l. mulier, §. si hæres; and note ff. so. ma., l. si mora, per la. de Are. The second reason is: because if we said the contrary, I would be forced to be the procurator of another, which is absurd, as in ff. ad Treb., l. postulante. The third reason is: because although security is not entirely of the substance, nevertheless before the security the usufruct is not fully formed; because before delivery, or tolerance, the usufruct is not fully acquired, as noted in l. 5, C. de usufr. The fourth reason is: because the benefit depends on the substance of the usufruct. The fifth reason is: because one thing is usufruct, another is benefit, and one cannot be claimed for the other. ff. de peric. et commo. rei ven., l. necessario, §. fi. The sixth reason is: because this security is a burden, and a thing cannot be recognized without its burden, as in l. neminem, ff. de leg. 2. The seventh reason is: because the words of the statute must be understood with their cause and their own defects. But it is so that this security is either a causing cause or a caused cause, and in either case, it must be fulfilled, as in ff. de usuc., l. si homo. It does not avail to say that delivery, or quasi-delivery, is not necessary here; for whatever may be said about this, nevertheless security is necessary, or at least a promise to give security, and an offer of security, as in ff. de usuc., l. si homo. Moreover, it does not avail to say that the statute does not dictate this; because by not making mention of the usufruct, it includes those things which are of its nature. For this comes tacitly by necessity, whence it is held as expressed, as in ff. si cer. pe., l. cum quid. And the above are confirmed by the force of grammar, which composes and does not divide. For this noun, "usufruct," is one compound word made from two whole words, and yet they are not two distinct things, i.e., use and usufruct, but one thing. And therefore neither can be claimed by itself, lest there be a division of the will. his

I add another reason, because between closely related persons long patience is held to be equivalent to remission, as in D. de donis inter virum et uxorem, l. si seruus communis; C. de bonis, quae libera, l. cum oportet, §. pe; D. de probationibus, l. procul. From these it clearly appears that it cannot be said otherwise, and that my opinion stands on the very truth. I, Baldus. The point on which the opinion is requested is as follows. A certain Sempronius pledged a certain tower of his, which was accustomed to be guarded, to a certain Seius, and delivered possession of the same tower to him. Finally, the said Seius sub-pledged the same tower, and delivered possession of it to a certain Gaius. The nephews of the said Sempronius, through his son, together with certain of his friends and accomplices, took possession of the said tower by armed force, not permitting the guards of the same tower to exit or enter, whereby the guards themselves, compelled by hunger, were forced to deliver possession of the said tower to the said nephews besieging the said tower. And this was done with the knowledge of the said Sempronius, who was in possession and wished to prohibit the said nephews.

† It is now asked in what manner, and by what remedies, according to law, and against whom, the aforementioned Gayo is to be assisted. Spoliation is required in the interdict *unde vi*. This interdict lies against the spoliator and his principal. Likewise, it lies against one who ratifies the act, if the spoliation was committed in his name or for his benefit. However, one person is not liable for another, as stated in *Extra*, *De restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *Cum ad sedem*, and in *L. 1, §. Deiecisse*, *De vi et vi armata*. But according to canon law, if possession was vitiously transferred by the spoliator to another, the person to whom it was transferred is liable; but if nothing came to him, he is not liable, *Eodem titulo*, chapter *Saepe*, and *De iudicibus*, chapter *Quia 5*. Nor is a father liable for his son, or a son for his father, unless it is proven that the spoliation was committed with the father’s knowledge and after consultation with him, *Argumentum* from *Digestum*, *De adulteriis*, *L. Et si amicorum*. This can be proven by evident presumptions and signs, as noted by Bartolus in a similar case in *L. Si venter, §. Finis*, *De privilegiis creditorum*. In *L. Si autem contra patrem*, nothing is proven, nor is it found that he possesses anything; therefore, he is not liable for an injury inflicted by his son or grandchildren, as stated in *Codex*, *De actione emptoria*, *L. 6*. And from these points, let the expelled party consider what he can prove. It is certain, however, that he has a hypothecary action against any possessor, as stated in *L. 1*, *Codex*, *Si pignus pignori datum sit*. And thus I conclude on this point. I, Baldus.

It is asked whether an uncle related through both parents is preferred in succession to a nephew who is the son of an uncle related through only one parent. For example, Margarita died intestate, leaving first her father’s brother related through both parents, and Antonio, the father’s brother of the aforementioned Margarita, related through the father’s side only. The following statute is presupposed: “We also statuate and ordain that if anyone dies intestate without descendants, leaving brothers united on both sides, or brothers united on the father’s side only, that all shall come equally to the succession of the deceased brother. But if he leaves also the sons of another predeceased brother, whether united on both sides or on the father’s side only, that those sons of brothers shall come to the succession of their uncle together with the aforementioned brothers of the predeceased uncle, by representation (*in stirpem*) and not per capita (*in capita*).”

In the Name of Christ, Amen. When, as is alleged, Perinus was related to the father of the aforementioned woman, recently deceased, through both parents, and consequently was more closely related than the other uncle, being connected by a double right, whereas the other was connected by a single right only. It is certain that, according to the common law, this Perinus is preferred to the other, Antonio, who is related through only one parent, as is usually said when dealing with the inheritance of a deceased brother: as in the Authentica *De consanguineis et uterinis fratribus*, § *Itaque*; and it is read and held by implication in the Code, *Communia de successionibus*, Authentica *Itaque*, and there the gloss fully explains. For two bonds prevail over only one, as noted in the Code, *De edicto divi Adriani tollendo*, l. 1, § 1; and in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Nam et si parentibus*. Hence it is that those related through both parents are called in the first order. Therefore, they are placed before the prior ones in succession, as in the Authentica *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Si igitur defunctus*; and in the Code, *De legatis hereditatibus*, Authentica *Cessante*. Since, therefore, after brothers and the sons of brothers, the closer relative is preferred, as in the Authentica *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Illud*; and neither brothers, and by implication, in the Code, *De legatis*, Authentica *Post fratres*; it is clearer than daylight that the aforementioned Perinus, as the closer uncle, is preferred to the other according to the common law. Nor does the presupposed statute stand in the way of the foregoing. For it speaks only when dealing with fraternal inheritance to be divided among brothers. This results in its not being extended to the case in question; rather, as an omitted matter, it is left to the disposition of the common law; because municipal laws correcting the common laws never receive an extensive interpretation; rather, what is omitted must be considered as omitted, as is fully read and noted in the Code, *De sacrosancta ecclesia*, Authentica *Quas actio*; and in the Code, *De testamento*, l. *Sancimus*; and *De appellationibus*, l. *Praecipimus*. Although, indeed, in correlatives, correction in one operates in the other by way of inclusion of one in the remainder, and not by extension to a new case; nevertheless, in separate matters, no relation of the correcting law should be made, and thus the omitted case is entirely similar, as is fully read and noted in the Code, *De indicta viduitate tollenda*, l. *Finalis*. And so have advised the undersigned doctors, namely, first: Lord Christopher of Castillion; Lord Signorinus of Homodeis; Lord Gualterinus of Zazii; Lord Jacobus of Mangiariis; Lord Tubertus of Trottis; and they have signed with the seal, as testimony of the aforesaid. I, Balus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether homicide committed by a madman is punishable.
2. Whether a joined person is admitted to excuse, and the proof of madness in criminal cases.
3. When madness is alleged as an excuse for a crime, or to decline jurisdiction, or for both, it must first be pronounced and investigated upon that article of dementia.
4. Confession never legitimizes a person, but assists, when it is from a legitimate person.
5. Privileges granted to minors are granted to those of unsound mind and to madmen.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Behold, the indictment against Ioanninus de Vailate appears to have been formed, in that he is said to have struck Bartolinus Cabini of Crema with two wounds, with great effusion of blood, from which wounds the said Bartolinus died, and is now for the defense of the said accused, it is said,

† that the said accused, at the time of the said beatings, and both before and after, was furious and insane: to such an extent that, on account of the frenzy, it could not be said that he committed fraud. For things done on account of frenzy are not considered voluntary, but rather accidental; and this accident is not punished by the penalty of the Lex Cornelia de sicariis, because what is fatal is not counted as fault, and the frenzy itself is punishment enough, as stated in D. de off. præsi. l. diuus; D. de iu. om. iu. l. si quis id, quod §. si; D. ad l. Corn. de sicc. l. infans; D. de reg. iur. l. in nego. Since, therefore, such a homicide is not voluntary but accidental, the furious person ought rightly to be absolved definitively and perpetually; because where there is no will, nor intent to commit a crime, there is no authority to punish; for will and intent distinguish crimes. Where there is no guilt, there ought to be no penalty, as stated in D. ad l. Cor. de sicc. l. in l.; and D. de fur. l. qui iniuriæ; D. pro so. l. cum duobus §. damna fatalia. These are the most recent laws. And this is established by natural reason, that the furious person rather suffers than acts. For frenzy is indeed a passion of the mind and body; nor ought that which happens due to the misfortune of the act to be drawn into punishment; because affliction ought not to be added to the afflicted, as in c. ult. de homi. in cle.; as in C. de epi. aud. l. tam dementis.

† Behold, therefore, the related party came to excuse the said Ioanninus, alleging madness, and [acted as] curator, and in the curatorial name of the said Ioanninus, who is mad. For they are under the legitimate care of the agnates, as in the Institutes, De cura, § Furiosi. And they are called mad in a broad sense, whether the madness is apparent and existing, or existing but not apparent: which is called the obscured appearance of the mind, whether it be imbecility or dementia; it is not force, as in the Authentica Ut hi, qui obligatas, near the middle. Certainly, there is no doubt about this either: when the related party, even if he does not assume the care of a true curator, nor make an inventory, is nevertheless admitted to full defense; because it is permitted by natural law to defend one’s own blood, as in the Digest, De appellationibus, l. Additos; Digest, De iustitia et iure, l. Ut vim. And immediately upon the allegation of madness, it is necessary that a pronouncement be made on this emerging issue; because persons must be established in court before proceeding to other matters: as in the Code, Qui dandis tutoribus possunt, l. In universis; Code, De iuramento prestando, l. Claram; Digest, De iure codicillorum, l. Quidam referunt; Code, De petitione hereditatis, l. Liber necne; Code, De adulteriis, l. Quam Alexandrum; Code, De origine iuris, l. 1. And if otherwise proceeded, the process is null, as noted in the Digest, Qui satisdare cogantur, l. Arbitro. For it is absurd that anything be done with the necessary order omitted, or rather perverted, as in the Extravagantes, De iudicibus, c. Exhibita. I therefore say that before the joinder of issue, or quasi-joinder—for in inquisitions there is no proper joinder of issue, which requires the intent to join issue, and thus requires a joining mind, but fame is an inanimate thing: hence fame cannot truly join issue—but it is established by a certain natural law that it be part of the joinder; for joinder, speaking truly, is the impulse of the parties, as in the Code, De iudiciis, l. Rem non novam; Digest, De minoribus, l. Ait praetor, § Permittitur; Digest, De conditione indebiti, l. Eleganter: si quis post. I therefore say,

† And this is most certain: if madness is alleged as an excuse for a delict, or to avoid trial, or for both purposes, it must first be investigated and a pronouncement made on the article of dementia or madness, and of curatorship; otherwise, the proceedings do not merit the name of proceedings, because one is not properly proceeding, or one proceeds in an irregular manner. The further one proceeds, the greater the error, as in C. de sen. et interlo. om. iud. l. prolatum. Behold, we have this: if someone is said to be a minor and has requested a curator, and the opposing party argues that he is rather a major and should not be admitted with a curator, lest the law be circumvented—because he would seek restitution in integrum—it is in the interest of the adversary not to be deceived by the color of feigned age, as in C. si minor se maio. dixerit. l. cum circa, and this is the ordinary gloss in l. 2, § quod obseruari, C. de iu. calum. Now, therefore, resuming my argument, I say that it was necessary at the outset of the trial to premise the law concerning persons; without this, no beginning is properly founded, and consequently the entire proceedings collapse, because those things which are the foundation are lacking, as in c. innotuit, extra de eo, qui furt. ordi. susce., according to Innocentius. For nothing is done rightly or correctly without the composition of order; because where there is no order, there cannot be substance, whether we say that order is a substantive or that it is an adjective, because it pertains to the very being of the thing. And from these points I immediately draw the following conclusion: I say that sometimes it is doubtful whether someone is mad, and a pronouncement must be made on the doubt. Sometimes it is established that he is mad; then no pronouncement is necessary to invalidate the proceedings, because by operation of law it is not binding. The confession of a madman is null, because he does not know his own voice, and what he speaks, he does not feel; because he is not capable of mind, nor of dolus, nor of culpa, as is fully read and noted in C. unde vi, l. si quis in tantam, in the great gloss.

† Therefore, the confession made by the said inquisitor does not hold by operation of law: because a confession must be made by a legitimate person. Never does a confession possess a legitimate person, although if the person were legitimate, it would have to be joined together: as in c. Pisanis, de restitutione spoliatorum, extra de iure; c. atsi clerici, de foro competenti; c. si diligenti, confessiones. It must agree with both natural and legal persons, as in ff. de interdictis et actionibus, l. confessionibus; and note in l. 1, C. de confessionibus. And in this point of law, the judge must be very circumspect and sagacious, so as not to strike at innocence, as the text says: "ne subiectam innocentiam feriamus" (so that we do not strike at the subject's innocence). 

Recapitulating, therefore, either the said confession does not hold by operation of law, or it must be overcome by restitution in integrum: not indeed against the delict, if there were one, but against the process, because without any preceding indications of bad faith, the confession was suddenly and abruptly made by voice: but not by signification: because no effective voice is found in the insane. And remove the mind from the equation, and the word remains without understanding. ff. soluto matrimonio, l. 2, § voluntate; ff. de regulis iuris, l. furiosi; ff. de his qui sui iuris sunt, l. patre furioso; ff. de statu hominum, l. qui furere.

† And it is also not to be doubted that all privileges granted to minors are granted to the insane and the mad, and even more numerous and more readily, as that gloss says, no. 2, which is in l. 2, ff. de cura. furio. Likewise, just as an adult having a curator does nothing without him, so neither do the insane or the mad. C. de in integ. resti. mino. l. si curatorem habens. ff. si cer. pet. l. certi condictio. §. quam. ff. quibus ex cau. in pos. ea. l. Fulcinius. near the middle, both with the common and with the proper matter of the said laws. And because the matter concerns the safety of a person, it ought not to be hastened, but deliberated upon. And we ought to be more ready to invalidate the proceeding than to extinguish a human body. Moreover, the cause of madness is a cause of status, and therefore, as if it were a prejudicial matter, it ought to be cognized before all else, as in Inst. de act. §. praeiudiciales. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is the competent judge when it is alleged that a certain contract is usurious.
2. Decrees of the lord are approved when the lord immediately commands that they be observed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. It is proposed,

† That which was brought before a secular judge, namely that the contract is usurious, a pledge contract, and made in fraud of usury. The secular judge, having examined those to be examined, declared the contract to be usurious and ordered the pledges to be restored. It is objected that the sentence was rendered by an incompetent judge: because the cause of usury is ecclesiastical, not secular, and in it one must proceed according to the statutes of the canons, and not according to the statutes of the laws: as in c. Dispendiosam, De iudiciis, in the Clementines, and note 11, q. 1, § 1. To the contrary it is alleged: because pledge contracts are provided for by civil or praetorian law, therefore they pertain to the civil forum by reason of their origin. And certainly this appears if we begin from the most ancient law of the civil law. For before the canons were known, pledge contracts were litigated in court, nor is this found to be corrected. Therefore it is not prohibited to stand by it: as C. De appellationibus, l. Praecipimus. Moreover, the question of simulation of a contract into another contract, or of a contract into no contract, properly falls under the jurisdiction of the secular judge, as noted in C. Plus valere quod agitur, l. Emptione; it is made by C. De manumis, l. Per diversas; and D. De aqua pluviali arcenda, l. Emptor. Others say that since here the matter is principally about the peril of souls, secondarily the ecclesiastical judge has jurisdiction, and not the secular judge: because although the cause of usury is not spiritual, yet by reason of the sin it pertains to the Church. And this is clear from manifest reason: because if the secular judge had this jurisdiction, he could make the crime of usury by pronouncing that the contract is not a loan contract. Furthermore, jurisdiction should not limp, so that it may pronounce for one party but not for the other: therefore, concluding from the first to the last, the lay judge should have jurisdiction in neither party, as in c. Is potest, D. De regulis iuris, l. Nam contrariorum eadem est disciplina. On this it seems a distinction should be made, that either it is expressly clear that the contract is usurious: and then the secular judge also has jurisdiction: because that which is notorious does not need proof. Or it does not appear that the contract is usurious, but it is doubtful whether it is or is not: then in this doubt the ecclesiastical judge should cognize: because in doubt we must follow the surer way. Argument: D. De libellis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § Si eius; D. De aqua hereditaria, l. Quod si dubitet; D. De inofficioso testamento, l. Qui de inofficioso. It can and should be said that the secular judge has jurisdiction not as in a usurious cause, but simply as in a simulated one, and he will not pronounce on usury. And even if he were to pronounce on usury, it is not vitiated by excess: because those things which are in excess do not usually vitiate writings, as l. Non solent, D. De regulis iuris; and D. De auro et argento legato, l. Pediculis, § Labeo. But on the simulation, and he will compel the defendant to restore the thing which he is found to possess without cause, as l. 1, § Necessario, D. Si mulier vendito nomine. And thus in the case proposed, if the pledge is clear, it was well pronounced: just as if I had pledged my book to a Jew, and then had paid off the book, I can recover it before the magistrate, as D. Si certum petatur, l. Si quis nec causam; § Res pignorum, D. De furtis, l. Si quis uxori, § Eum creditorem.

† Now it remains to consider another point. Namely, regarding the decree of the Lord, I say that immediately, since the Lord commanded them to be observed, they are approved, as in the prologue of the sixth book. It suffices that the prince writes concerning observance, even if he does not write to all. And it is established in the Digest, On Laws, Title 1, Law "And in that manner." I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the writings of a notary already accused of forgery, but not yet convicted, are to be believed.
2. The issue of forgery stands as a defense to a petitory action, although not to a possessory one.
3. Whether a grandson legitimated by his father excludes the substitutes appointed by his grandfather.
4. The legitime cannot be prohibited to a son, so that he may testify concerning it.
5. Whether the Fideicommissum Trebellianum can be prohibited to sons.
6. A settlement, even if sworn, does not prejudice the fideicommissary heir.
7. A general compromise does not affect the specific matter settled.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Upon

† As to the point in question, whether faith should be given to a document drawn up in the form of a will by Dr. Maffei de Bruscia, in which document, among other things, it is contained that the said Dr. Maffei made a will, in which he instituted as his heirs Peter Girard, Francis, Marcilius, and Louis, his legitimate and natural sons: with this condition added, that if any of the said sons should die without legitimate and natural male children descending from him, the said survivors being substituted, as is more fully contained in the said document: for it seems to be said that the said document should not hold as suspect of falsity, as C. de probat. l. iubemus and l. sciant cuncti; and ff. de eden. l. praetor § 1. For a document must be free from any defect, as C. de edic. di. Adr. toll. l. si. But this document is defective: because where the author of the document does not have credibility, there the document has no validity, as extra de haere. c. fraternitatis; and there fully by Innocentius; and we in c. damnamus § si de summa Tri. by Bertrand. Moreover, this notary was humble and deplorable, i.e., infamous: to whose documents faith should not be given, as d. l. praetor § 1; and ff. de infa. l. 2 § miles; and ff. de senato. l. Cassius. Furthermore, this notary had already been accused of falsity, hence his office, credibility, and instruments were suspended in the meantime: as ff. de mun. et hono. l. reus delatus.

† Moreover, although the charge of forgery does not bar a possessory action, it does bar a petitory action and a personal action arising from a will: as in C. de edicto, Adr. tol., l. 2. To the contrary, it appears that instruments executed before condemnation for forgery are valid; because with regard to status, not the nature of the crime but the sentence is considered: as in ff. de poenis, l. quod ad statum pertinet, non genus criminis, sed sententia spectatur, and again in ff. de poenis, l. quod statum. And furthermore, even if it were granted that he should be deprived of authority, he has nevertheless not been deprived of authority, as expressly noted by Odofredus in l. 2, §. miles; nor is he deprived of his office by operation of law on account of infamy, as noted by Bartolus in ff. ad legem Iuliam de repetundis. Moreover, it is not alleged that he was defamed with respect to this specific document, but generally; and one document may be true and another false, as in C. de transactionibus, l. si ex falsis, and there noted; and it does not prove this wrongdoing, that it happens to be absent from this case, as in C. de accusationibus, l. si quis hominiorolii. Moreover, instruments already executed are valid, even if he is later condemned for some other offense. For what was lawfully done at that time is not undone by a subsequent wrongdoing, as in l. donationes, C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem. Moreover, the instruments of acts already performed in the past cannot be invalidated, as in ff. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. in libello, §. factae, and l. 1, ff. de novo operis nuntio. Solution: If the instrument was executed while the notary’s status was intact, it is not thereby vitiated because the notary lost his status due to adverse fortune and deserved fault. It is true, however, that the judge may inquire into the truth of the document; because it is not entirely without defect that it was executed by a suspect person. Nevertheless, for the full rejection of the document, mere suspicion is not sufficient, as in C. de contrahenda et communi stipulatione, l. optimam, in fine; and therefore, unless at the time of the execution of the said document the notary was deprived of authority or suspended from office, the said documents should be upheld, absent proof to the contrary. We have a similar case in a guardian condemned as suspect, whereby his earlier acts remain valid: ff. de minoribus, l. Aemilius Largianus.

It remains to consider another point, namely: whether a grandson legitimated by his father excludes the substitutes appointed by the grandfather, provided we are speaking of a direct vulgar substitution. He does not exclude them, because the laws *Cum acutissimi* and *Cum auus* do not speak of a fideicommissary substitution. Or, if the substitute is a legitimate son and a natural son, the result is the same, because there is no person who, according to the presumed will of the deceased, is preferred and more ardently loved. If such a person does not exist, or if a spurious son is legitimated, the result is the same, because a privilege of the prince does not alter wills. Or if a natural son is legitimated, then he excludes the substitute who is entirely an outsider, and this by the force of naturalness rather than by the force of legitimation, which consists in a fiction. Codex, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law *Generaliter*, section *Si*. The objection from the Digest, *Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, law *Haeredibus*, section *Si*, does not hold, because that rule proceeds from the necessary understanding of the will, since the intention cannot be referred to the impossible, it must be interpreted loosely. From these things it is concluded that there is room for a fideicommissary substitution, and that Girard could not make a will regarding the fideicommissum, insofar as he came into the fideicommissum.

† It remains to be seen: whether he could make a will regarding his legitimate portion. And it must be said that he could, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari et extraordinaria substitutione*, law *Si is, qui*. For, since the legitimate portion is due by natural law, it cannot be denied to a son, as in the Authenticum *de hereditate et falcidia*, section *Si quis autem non implens*.

The Trebellianic portion may be prohibited, according to the law *Marcellus*, § *quod autem*, D. ad Trebellianum. Others hold that it cannot be prohibited, because the benefit of the Senate cannot be taken away; and in this matter the Senate has greater authority than the Falcidian law, so that the deduction cannot be forbidden. The glosses are contrary. This is disputable on both sides when an inventory has been made; but if that is omitted, it would seem sufficiently correct to say that the Trebellianic portion could be forbidden by the aforementioned constitution *Sed cum testator*.

† Moreover, it must be known that a settlement made by an arbitrator does not prejudice the fideicommissary, as stated in D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, § hereditatem, and most fully in D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, § duo fratres. An oath also has no effect; for an oath does not increase consent, but confirms it as it finds it, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si.

† On another point, whether a general compromise affects the matter already settled, it must be said that it does not. L. post rem. ff. de transac. And thus the first sentence is to be put into execution. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A will requires free will and the capacity to make a will.
2. Whether presumptions, or enunciative words, prove compulsion and fear inflicted upon the testator.
3. Whether one who declares that he wishes to use his last will, and in the absence of the last, the first, appears to accept the inheritance.
body: It is alleged that Girard made two wills on the same day. The first will he made in the house of Master John of Mantua; later that same day, he was forcibly taken to the house of his nephew Peter by the said Peter, accompanied by armed men, against the will of the said Girard, as expressed by certain words which he uttered: for he said that he did not wish to go to the house of the said Peter, because he knew what sort of man he was. On the same day that he was forcibly taken, he altered his will and left his goods to the said Peter, his nephew. He made no mention of his brother, Lord Federigo, except that he bequeathed to him 50 florins. Wherefore the said Federigo says that the said will...

† The act performed in the house of the said Peter is invalid due to the pressure exerted upon the testator and his will, since he would not otherwise have acted thus: as is evident from the aforementioned premises. For the resolution of this doubt, the writings of the doctors should be consulted, and particularly those of Master Bartolus in l. 2, §. fratris, ff. si quis aliquem testa. prohibue. Nevertheless, concluding: if the said Girardus would not otherwise have thus made a will, had he been in his freedom, the said testament is invalid; because the will and the capacity to make a will must be free until the death of the testator. And it is not permitted that one does not restore discretion, as C. de sac. san. ecc. l. 1; C. de pact. l. si; and ff. de ver. obl. l. stipulatio huiusmodi concepta. And similarly, the first testament would not be valid if it had been made through fraud and pressure exerted upon the body and mind, as l. 1, in fi., ff. de excep. doli. And regarding the right of the son who is said to be legitimated: because there is no controversy concerning his own right, nor is it sought from me, it does not pertain to me to respond; because one ought not to answer questions not asked. And perhaps these litigants are disputing more about the right of a third party than about their own right. As for the legitimation made after the death of the testator, what is the law, I refer to l. Gallus, §. et quid si tamen, de lib. et posth. Concluding, and referring myself to the points about which inquiry is made. For one must answer what is asked. I say that if the aforementioned pressures are established, neither testament is valid. But if there was pressure in one and not in the other, that one which was made without pressure is valid, because force or fear is not presumed unless it is proven. Furthermore, I say that although someone was in prison or under another constraint, if the prison was not employed for the purpose that he should make a will, but for another cause, the testament is valid, as ff. de testa. l. qui a latronib. and noted ff. quod met. caus. l. qui in carcerem. For the place is not the middle of breaking the testator, but fear and compulsion.

† I do not omit that point, namely that by these declaratory words sufficient, i.e., necessary proof, is not required, but rather strong suspicion, which, when joined to another presumption, completes the proof, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on successions of intestates, chapter Cum dilectus. But this suspicion is joined to another presumption: because it is alleged that the said Girard was carried away by armed men to the house of the said Peter. Therefore, the said testament is rendered suspect, as having been made through fear or violence, and thus it should not be upheld.

† It is finally asked, because the said Peter, when questioned as to which testament he wished to use, stated that he wished to use the last one, and in the absence of the last, the first, whether by these words he appears to have entered upon the inheritance. For an alternative generates certainty, and he who is uncertain as to the testament cannot enter upon the inheritance by virtue of the testament, nor can he repudiate it: D. 28.5.1 (Quod si dubitet); D. 45.1.113 (multis interest); and fully noted in D. 28.6.1 (illud). But an alternative generates ambiguity, as D. 47.10.1 (prætor); this also supports the point, because one is bound to choose something certain, and not to demand alternatively: C. 6.23.1 (si); D. 35.2.1 (cum filius), § item variis. To the contrary it seems: because this is not properly an alternative, but a disjunctive or conditional statement, and it is a kind of protestation, which is valid on that ground on which it can be valid: D. 36.1.1, § quod autem; and D. 28.2.1 (Gayus), § si eius; hence it is valid on that ground on which it can be valid, especially since it begins with a valid ground. Moreover, because the doubt consists in written law, and not in fact: as in the aforementioned D. 45.1.113 (multum interest). Moreover, D. 36.4.1 (recusare), § Titius, supports this.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. From what time the prescription of a fideicommissum begins to run.
body: Furthermore, regarding that,

†What is required, in order that the prescription of the said fideicommissum may begin to run, is to be answered as follows: it does not begin until the condition of the said fideicommissum, or of the fideicommissary substitution made by the said Maffeo, has occurred; as is stated in C. de annali exceptione, l. 1, in fine; and in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, §. his illud; and in C. communia delegationum, l. si, §. si autem ob avaritiam. Nor is prejudice generated by the fact that the said P. did not possess the goods of the said Maffeo; as is stated in C. unde legitimi, l. non hoc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession made by a husband to his wife concerning the dowry is valid and proves the matter.
2. Whether a woman who has confessed to the dowry enjoys the same privileges of the dowry.
3. The opinion of the gloss should be adhered to.
4. One may validly waive the exception of non-payment of the dowry.
body: The question is,

Whether a confession made by a husband to his wife during the subsistence of the marriage, concerning a dowry previously not promised, is valid or not. If the marriage had been dissolved, it would be valid; for then it is deemed to have been made in hope of a future payment, but with a liberal intent and for the purpose of making a gift: as in D. de verb. oblig. l. si diuortio. But if the said confession is made during the subsistence of the marriage, it does not appear to be valid as a payment; because in the contract of dowry, true payment is not proved by confession, but by the reality of delivery, just as in a loan: as in C. de dote cauta non numerata l. 1, and the notes thereon; and D. si cert. pet. l. 2, ver. ueluti. Moreover, it is not valid as a gift; because without any agreement, that is, without delivery, or that which is equivalent to delivery, between husband and wife, no benefit accrues, nor can an action be brought: as in D. de don. inter vir. et uxor. l. Papinianus. Furthermore, that which from the beginning does not subsist, unless it takes effect through delivery, does not become valid: as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de do. ante nup.; and the argument from D. de pact. l. si diuisionis placitam. Also, because it is presumed rather to have been from the husband’s goods than from the wife’s: C. de don. inter vir. et uxor. l. Etiam; and D. eo. l. quintus. Also, this confession appears rather simulated than true, due to the quality of the persons: D. de prob. l. qui testamentum; D. de leg. 3, l. cum quis decedens, §. Titia. Also for this reason: C. de don. ante nup. auth. sed iam necesse.

† Moreover, the ordinary gloss states that in a dowry confessed but not paid, the woman does not have the privilege of the dowry: as in C. qui pot. in pign. hab. l. assiduis. § 1. But certainly, although she does not have the privilege of priority or of tacit hypothec, so that if she contends with other creditors, she is preferred by virtue of the privilege in personal hypothecary matters; nevertheless, by this the common law is not taken away: because where the privilege ceases, the common law remains: as in ff. de excus. tu. l. sed et milites. in princ. and ff. ad l. Falc. l. si post missionem. Moreover, Auth. sed iam necesse does not oppose, because there it similarly speaks of priority with respect to other creditors, and when the contest is between creditors and the woman. But where there is no other creditor, or the goods suffice for all, then the confession made on account of the dowry must be upheld: because the nature of the dowry presupposes marriage, and the nature of an act never invalidates the act, but validates it: as in C. de donat. ante nup. l. fin. ff. de pact. l. iurisgen. § adeo. ff. de verb. oblig. l. ita stipulatus. la grande circa medium. ff. de usur. l. si stipulatus. ff. de contrah. empt. l. pacta conventa. Moreover, the law qui testamentum does not oppose, because there it speaks among intestates, not between husband and wife; because donation between them is not prohibited on account of some base cause, but lest they strip themselves through mutual affection. ff. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. 1. The solution, from the quality of the persons and the quantity, seems this matter to be considered, as noted in l. 3. C. de dot. promis. But if nothing else appears, and the time for opposing the exception of unpaid dowry has elapsed, the confession must be upheld, nor do I depart from the gloss which is in the said l. 1. C. de dote caut. non numerata.

† Because where the gloss determines, one must adhere to the gloss, since error is rarely found in the decisions of the glosses. Furthermore, the law *Si forte*, *de castrensi peculio*, and the Code, *de collationibus*, law *Si donationem*, do not oppose this, because there the cause was not naturally present; here, however, the cause of the dowry and of marriage are naturally inherent in each other, as in the Code, *de pactis*, law *Iuris gentium*, § *Quinimmo*. Moreover, here the cause is true, because the marriage is true; but there, the cause which is specially acquired for that effect does not appear, nor can it be feigned. I conclude that, because in case of doubt one must adhere to the words of the instrument, and simulation is not presumed, as in the Code, *de probationibus*, law *Cum precibus*, if the way of exception is barred by the lapse of time, one must adhere to the confession, provided that other creditors are not thereby defrauded; because the case is found in the Authenticum, *de aequa donatione*, § *Aliud*, from which the said Authenticum *Sed iam necesse* is derived.

† Know that when the Glossa states that one may renounce the exception of a dowry not paid, and that in such case it is not necessary for other periods of time to run, because renunciation operates instantaneously what the passage of time would achieve, it is as is noted in C. de dotis promissione, l. 2. I, Baldus, say:

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Church is bound by a loan, if the creditor does not prove that the money lent was applied to the benefit of the Church, given a statute that instruments are to be executed notwithstanding any exception.
2. How money applied to the benefit of the Church is to be proved.
3. Every excess of expenses is considered useless.
casus:
The case is proposed that a certain Benedict, prepositus of the collegiate church of Saint John of Alberia, as appears from a public instrument, protested in the presence of many persons, including the undersigned Antonio de Buxeto, that he needed three hundred florins to be committed to the repair of the said church, its houses, and its mill, which was the only one, unless it were repaired with necessary materials; and for the purchase of certain oxen, etc., as is more fully contained in the instrument. Upon hearing these words, the said Antonio, out of gratuitous loan and love for the causes narrated above, with the mind and intention of serving the said church, as is asserted in the instrument, etc., gave by way of loan to the said prepositus the said three hundred florins, to be converted, for the causes mentioned above, to the utility and necessary affairs of the said church. The said prepositus promised, without consulting the canons of his church, to turn and expend the said moneys for the utility of the said church and for the necessities mentioned above. He bound himself in the name of the said church and his successors, with a hypothec on the goods of the said church, to repay the said three hundred florins at a certain term, now elapsed.

Now, the said prepositus having been removed on account of certain of his delicts, and another having been substituted in his place in another location by mandate of the Apostolic See, the said Antonio, the creditor, demands from the said successor the said 300 florins. Against this creditor, the said successor raises the objection that the church is not bound by the contract of the loan, nor is he bound in the name of the church. First, because it does not appear that the said 300 florins were converted to the utility of the church itself. Second, because the said Benedict could not, without the consent of his chapter, make the said contract and thus bind the church. Third, because it is not probable that the said money was taken for the necessity or utility of the said church, since it is an excessively large sum, given that this benefice is not valued at 45 florins.

The question now arises whether the successor is bound, especially since a certain statute of Terdone, confirmed by the bishop and the clergy of the said city, is in force, providing that public instruments must be put into execution notwithstanding exceptions of nullity, falsity, payment, or any other exception of whatever kind and species, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Just as a city and a church can be bound by the exception of a loan only if the money was converted to their benefit; otherwise, the church is not bound, but rather the person raising the exception, and consequently such a contract does not bind the successor in dignity or office: as in D. si certum petatur, l. ciuitas; C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. hoc ius porrectum; and noted in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. si pupilli, after the principle. However, that the money was converted to the benefit of the church must be proved by the creditor: because from this the creditor founds his claim; and because this is a substantial cause with regard to the existence of the obligation, it is therefore necessary with regard to proof: because the foundations of the claim must be proved by the affirmer and the plaintiff: as in l. qui accusare and l. actor quod asseuerat. Since an affirmative is opposed directly to a negative, this is not properly to raise an exception, but to deny. And therefore the statute, which speaks of repelling exceptions, does not touch this case: because, as I said, it is not properly raising an exception. Moreover, because this is a defense of law, and of right, and thus apparent, it does not require proof, unless the plaintiff proves the contrary. Furthermore, even if it were an exception: because it is nevertheless apparent and existing by the office of the judge, the plaintiff would be repelled. Noted in C. de transactionibus, l. vbi pactum. Wherefore, following the sound understanding of the said statute, which is not to be glossed: because statutes do not receive extraordinary glosses, but must be understood from the marrow of the intellect, where the contract has a figure: as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum, §. pro aurelio. Moreover, a plaintiff acting without color should not be heard: because he approaches the praetor without cause: as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi; D. de minoribus, l. minor autem magistratus; C. de praediis curiae, l. 1, lib. 10. For the praetor is not to be disturbed, unless it is expedient, as in l. 1, D. de postulando. Furthermore, the said statute must be understood for another reason, because the contract is celebrated by a capable person, but this prelate is not a capable person, unless the conversion follows. For he does not have a mandate from law or canon in this matter, nor does his confession harm the church, as in C. de noua, l. non abstulit; and D. de deposito, l. si quis inficiatus. Moreover, when it is a matter of binding one through another, he who wishes to bind in such a manner must be careful that it be converted to the benefit. And this is proved: as is read and noted in D. de noua, l. doli mali, in fine; nor is a word sufficient, where a fact is required: as in D. de castrensi peculio, l. si forte.

But how is this conversion proved? I answer, in two ways: one way by the clear nature of the fact; for example, by the sight of someone seeing it expended for that cause: testimony. For sight is superior to all testimony, as in the Institutes, De gradibus, § Sed cum magis. Another way it is proved by presumptions and a posteriori; because it appears that the repair has been made, but it does not appear from what money. For it is presumed from that money which was lent for this purpose; nor do buildings repair themselves by chance, but with great expense and labor. To this effect: Codex, De usuris pupillariis, l. Si; Codex, De administratione tutorum, l. Quae tutoris; Digesta, De negotiis gestis, l. Ex duobus; Digesta, De privilegiis creditorum, l. Si ventri, § Si.
