† However, it must be noted that the limit not be exceeded in expenses: because every excess is considered useless, as that law states, ff. de exercitoria. l. Lucius. From this, it is conclusively proven from the said loan, the facts being as they are, that the church is not bound. It supports this what is noted by Innocentius, extra de deposito. c. grauis. To the same effect, C. de dona. ante nup. auth. sed iam necesse. and in Auth. de aequalitate dotis. §. aliud. To these is added the fact that the chapter was not convened; a prelate without a chapter is a monstrous thing: because it is a head without members. And if those of the chapter are dead, the college must be restored by others: and before it is restored, nothing can be done except out of great necessity, so that the customary form may be preserved. It supports the above what is noted by Bartolus, ff. de ver. ob. l. cum seruus. I, Baldus. A certain distinguished knight, Lord William de Biuilaquis, at a time when he was living inhumanly, was married to a certain distinguished lady Tadea de Petra Malla, and had children by her; during the marriage he kept in Amasia, or as a concubine, a certain Felicina de Mlo, by whom he begot a single daughter named Margaret, now living, whom he brought into the light. He is said to have subsequently joined this same Felicina in marriage to a certain Honestinus, likewise de Mlo, to whom he is said to have made a certain private security, sealed with his seal, written and signed by his own hand, of the tenor noted below. In the year of our Lord 1394, on the 26th day of June, I, William de Biuilaquis, promise to Honestinus de Pudriano to the best of my ability that he shall have from Felicina de Girmis, from paternal goods, 200 florins, of which the said Honestinus shall make a dowry charter to his wife Felicina. If I cannot do this, I promise to give to the said Honestinus the aforementioned 200 florins from my own money up to the feast of St. Martin next coming: of which, in this case, the aforementioned dowry of the said Felicina shall be made in my name. With the pact and condition that the said Felicina shall give me recourse against paternal goods with the will and consent of the aforementioned Honestinus, her husband. And for the observance of these things, I oblige my present and future goods, both movable and immovable, wherever they may be. And in testimony of all the above, I have written them with my own hand and had them fortified with my customary seal. Now it is asked whether this security is null, or valid, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a private writing requires the addition of the time and place.
2. A confession is stronger than a presumption of law, and a presumption of right.
3. Solemnity is presumed in contracts; the contrary holds in judicial proceedings.
4. Whether a donation made to a concubine to provide a dowry for their common daughter is valid.
5. A marriage settlement contract does not require insinuation.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† It is asked whether the addition of time and place is required in a private writing. And it must be said that either the question depends on the place or the time. And one party affirms that the act was done at a certain place or time; the other denies it. And then it is necessary that the place or time be proved by writing or by witnesses, supplying what the writing lacks: as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. eum actum; and C. de probationibus, l. matrem tuam; and C. de petitione hereditatis, l. si post motam. But if there is no controversy, because the party confesses as to the place and time, or confesses simply, which is to be admitted as full proof; because where there is confession, there is every relation of proof: as is singularly noted in Auth. de aequalitate, do. §. aliud.

† Where the glossa states that a confession is stronger than a legal presumption, both in law and in fact. And regarding what I said about the place, the glossa ordinaria, noted in c. Abbate sane, de re iudicata, lib. 6, supports this, where the glossa says that the place is required in instruments because a promise could be made in one place and not in another; but the text there said that the place is required so that there is the ability to challenge the writing as false; because if it were indefinite and not restricted, it could not be challenged, as C. de contrahendo et committendo stipulatione, l. optimam, at the end, and noted in ff. de editionibus, l. 1, §. editiones, and insti. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. Item verborum, and in c. cum Ioannes heremi, de fide instrumentorum. And both reasons are good, true, and natural, but in our case, the question is not about solemnity or truth; because solemnity is presupposed, as C. de contrahendo et committendo stipulatione, l. 1.

† And in contracts it is presumed: that formality, although the contrary holds in judicial proceedings. And note. Inn. in c. innotuit. de eo, qui fur. ordines suscepit. Moreover, it is not a question of truth: because the seal, which is the image of the substance of the person, together with that which accords with the nature of the transaction, is held as personal presence; and especially the seal of so distinguished a military man, as is noted in l. 2. C. de reb. alienis non alienandis.

† Therefore, the question remains whether this contract is valid as to cause and person. And it must be said that the cause does not in itself invalidate the contract, because it is pious, honest, and privileged. D. 50, 17, l. 1; D. 12, 6, l. cum is, § si mulier. For if there were no marriages, the human race would be a brutish race, of beasts and cattle, as noted in Auth. de nuptiis, in principio, col. 4. Moreover, by reason of the person, the said contract is not prohibited, because the person is not in herself prohibited from receiving: D. 36, 1, l. sed et qui magna. Nevertheless, it must be considered whether, taking into account the origin of the base cause and considering the military status, this is prohibited, so that from several concurring factors the defect is increased. Furthermore, these common women by their deceptions defile the souls of the lost, and they use their images. Therefore, they are called fochariae, as C. 5, 28, l. 1, and women are expressly prohibited from being concubines, even if the man is free and the woman is free: D. 29, 1, l. miles ita haeredem, § mulier. Moreover, the said Lord William was not only a soldier, but also respectable, and properly Illustrious, because he was at the side of the glorious one: l. unica, C. 12, 1, de praepositis laborum. But it must be considered that, since it is a donation with respect to one person and not with respect to another person, in whom the donation must finally be resisted: D. 39, 5, l. ut mihi donares. For the effect is considered from the person to whom it is acquired, not from the pipe through which it passes, but from the container: D. 35, 2, l. cum dotem; and D. 36, 1, l. cogi, § hi, qui solidum. And therefore, insofar as it regards the husband, this is not considered a donation, but a marital gift: l. 1, in principio, D. 12, 4; D. 39, 5, l. si donaturus, § 1. From this it follows that it is not required

† insinuation: because a dowry contract requires nothing but payment. But it must be considered whether the said instrument was made in favor of a concubine; and it is not valid, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. si post. If the concubine changed her ways and actually withdrew from concubinage, then it is valid, by argument from C. de familia erciscunda, l. in ipsius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an assignment is valid when the assignor does not have a cause of action, for example, because the assignor was a creditor in gold coin and assigned rights regarding a quantity not deposited.
2. How a contract of loan for consumption (mutuum) or deposit is to be recognized.
3. Whether one who makes use of a deposit is said to commit theft.
body: A certain A. deposited 200 florins of good and just weight with Bartholomew de Calcaginolis, which are worth 32 soldi for each florin, which said B. promised to keep safe and manage at his own risk and peril, and to restore them at the free will of the said A. Now the said A. assigned the rights to 100 pounds to another party. And it is objected against him regarding the said 200 florins that the assignment is invalid, and consequently he cannot sue; because the said A. assigned rights to that which he did not have an action for, namely the 200 gold florins deposited, and he assigned rights to 100 pounds which he did not deposit, and for which he had no action. For the depositor was a creditor in gold money, and he assigned rights to a quantity not deposited: namely, 100 pounds which he did not deposit, and for which he had no action. Although the deposit contained a certain quantity, namely 200 gold florins, yet because the instrument states that it is on account of a true and pure deposit, and that he promised to keep them safe and guard them, and to return and restore them at the free will of the said A., etc., and it is a mere deposit, and in hope, and thus the assignment is invalid. And it was alleged in this way, that either a quantity is deposited so that the same may be returned: and it is a deposit. Or otherwise: and then it is not so, according to l. Lucius Titius, with the following law, § 1, ff. de deposito. On the other hand, it is said that it is a loan; because the said money was not deposited sealed. Now
† It is asked whether the said cession of rights is valid.

† To the aforesaid question it is answered that the said cession of rights is valid. For the declaration of which, I premise that sometimes a contract is entered into, or a matter is treated, as being a loan, or as being a deposit. And that which has been agreed upon shall be observed, as in l. Lucius, in fine, ff. de deposito; or nothing has been agreed upon: and then either the power to use the money is expressly granted, and then, by the very operation of the contract, it is a deposit, until the person to whom it is given has used the money, or he has subsequently used it: and then it will be a loan, or a certain condition. §. si, cum l. seq., ff. si certum petatur. Or the power to use was granted afterwards: and then immediately when the power to use is granted, even before it has been used, it will be a loan: as in the same laws. Or the power to use was not granted expressly, but tacitly: for example, because the money was given unsealed and not marked: and then it is a deposit, although it exceeds the limits of a deposit: as in l. Lucius, cited above, near the middle. Or the power to use was not granted tacitly, nor expressly: for example, because the money was given sealed, and then it is properly a deposit not exceeding its limits: as in l. dies sponsaliorum, §. 1, ff. de deposito, and l. si sacculum, §. 1.

† For then he to whom the money was given cannot use it; rather, he would commit theft by using it, as stated in the aforementioned law *Si sacculum*. And these points can be gathered from the gloss in the aforementioned law *Dies sponsaliorum*, § 1, and by Jacobus Butrigarius and Albericus there. And thus I infer from the foregoing that the aforementioned contract, concerning which in the possession of the aforementioned case, was a deposit exceeding the terms of a deposit; therefore, if the depositary had used the deposited money, it would thereafter have become a loan (*mutuum*), and thus the said assignment could undoubtedly have been made. But if he used the said money, and the same, namely, that the said two hundred florins are worth 320 imperial pounds, and an assignment was made of 100 pounds *ex* and of the said 200 florins, and thus paying the assignee so much from the said florins as amounts to the value of one hundred pounds, the debtor would obtain release from him. For it appears that an assignment was made of florins which are of the value of those one hundred pounds. Argument: Law *Si stipulatus fuerit decem in mille*, Digest, *De solutionibus*, according to the reading which Bartolus places there, considering also the intent of the contracting parties, which must be observed even if the words were used improperly: as in Law *Sed et si possessori*, § *Item si iurauero*, and what is noted there by Guillelmus de Cuneo, Digest, *De iureiurando*. And also, so that the thing may rather stand than fail, we must take or follow this interpretation, as in Law *Quotiens*, Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, and Law *Quotiens*, Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*. And thus I conclude that the said assignment is valid. I, Baldus. Paulus Argonus.

The case is as follows: A., acting as procurator, appeared before the judge to whom appeal lay, in his procuratorial capacity on behalf of L., on account of a certain sentence rendered against the aforementioned L., and interposed an appeal in the following manner, namely: Before you, Master Bartolomeo de Cantii, Vicar General of the Lord Podesta of Pavia, A., procurator, and in the procuratorial name of the said L., interposes the underwritten appeal of the tenor set forth below. IN THE NAME OF THE LORD, AMEN. Before you, Master B. de Cantii, Vicar General of the Lord Podesta of Pavia, the above-mentioned L. asserts and proposes, in every way, by every right, and in every form by which he may do so most effectively: against, and adverse to, N., and against anyone else who may lawfully intervene in the judgment on his behalf; that the said L. has recently learned that certain P. and B., arbitrators and arbiters, have issued a certain asserted arbitral sentence against the said L. and in favor of the said N., etc., the said L. stating that the said arbitrations and arbitral awards were and are null, of no value and no effect; and insofar as any such might be found, he stated and states that they were and are inequitable and unjust, and inequitably and unjustly rendered against the said L. And that the said precepts, arbitrations, and arbitral awards, if they can be so called, ought to be reduced to the judgment of a good man, etc. Wherefore, the said L., feeling himself aggrieved and injured by such arbitral awards in every way, by every right, and in every form by which he may, could, and can do so most effectively, petitions and requests you, the aforementioned Master Vicar, that in every way, by every right, and in every form by which you may do so most effectively, you pronounce and declare by your definitive sentence that the said precepts, arbitrations, and arbitral awards, if they can be so called, were and are null, etc., and insofar as any such might emerge as inequitable, etc. Subsequently, at the end, this is valid. Which appeal and nullity the said Lord Vicar admitted and admits, insofar as he is bound and ought to do so by law, and not otherwise. And on this account, the aforementioned Lord Vicar ordered this charter to be made, and the said procurator requested it to be made in his procuratorial name, with the following present, etc. Now, and two days ago, it is asked whether the interposition of the said appeal and nullity was duly made and is valid in law, or not.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an appeal may be interposed through a messenger, and in that case how the words are to be formulated.
2. The term "procurator" is an indefinite term.
3. What effect is produced by this clause of mandate: "in every manner, way, and form by which it may better have validity."
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The interposition of the said appeal and nullity does not appear to have been duly made. First, due to a defect in form, because he who appeals in another’s name must frame the initial words in his own procuratorial capacity; for it is not the principal who speaks, but the agent himself, and therefore the tenor must be grounded in him; otherwise, the appeal errs in form and in person. D. de acquisitione et obligatione, l. Quicunque gerimus: “Unless they begin in our own person, they render our act void.” Moreover, because he did not speak as the messenger or minister of the principal, but rather substituted the person of the principal as speaking actually and presently; and the words cannot be adapted to the aforementioned law, since he speaks proemially of himself, yet subsequently is discredited directly as to the person. Hence, he does not appear to have acted either in the name or office of a procurator, because he used words that cannot be adapted to either a procurator or a messenger. For a procurator ought to say: “I, as procurator, in a procuratorial name”; and a messenger ought to say: “I, as a messenger,” as in D. de appellationibus ab executoribus, §. Si; and D. si quis alteri vel sibi, l. Multum. Furthermore, either these words are personal or impersonal, i.e., without a person. If they are personal, the writing would not be true. If they are impersonal, the writing would be invalid, as in C. de constitutionibus, Auth. Si quoniam. Since, therefore, the form of the said appeal is not apt nor congruous, the said appeal appears not to proceed in any manner, according to the theory of C. de formulis, l. 1; and D. si messor falcem, l. 1, §. 1, as was said above. Moreover, the Lord Cynus says in D. de procuratoribus, l. 1, in his golden apostils, that in judicial proceedings concerning causes, a messenger cannot intervene, although he may intervene to allege causes of absence, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Si libero, §. Si. And the reason is: because in judicial proceedings one quasi contracts, as in D. de peculio, l. 3, §. Idem scribit. And because it is necessary that sentence be passed on the person of the procurator, not the messenger, nor the principal, because the latter never appeared, as in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. 1. Since, therefore, the words neither conform to the law nor seem consistent with the truth, the said appeal and nullity, due to an error in the acts, appear to err in form and in the very substance of truth.

Nevertheless, notwithstanding these points, I say that the said interposition of the appeal and nullity can be defended in law, and that it proceeds in law, and that this superficial error does not prejudice the truth. And first, from the general rule stated in C. de errore advocatorum, l. Si: “For even if there were some error, it is corrected by reference to the records,” as in D. de re iudicata, l. Ait praetor. Another reason is: because although he says proemially, “I, procurator,” he subsequently and conclusively speaks as a messenger. And the latter governs and regulates the former and antecedent parts, because the effect lies in the conclusions. For the conclusion is the exit and the deterioration of the entire discourse, as in C. de fidei instrumentis, l. Contractus; and D. de verborum significatione, l. Si cum fundum; and D. de legatis secundis, l. Si cum pater, §. Dulcissimis; and D. de vino legato, l. Si, §. Cui dulcia. Thirdly, this is proven because words ought to be adapted to the nature of the act, and the nature of the words ought rather to be construed improprietarily than the nature of things, as in D. de iniuriis, l. Sed et si possessori, §. Sed et si rerum; and D. de verborum significatione, l. Quisquis mihi. And therefore, the aforementioned speech, although it speaks in a procuratorial name, is nevertheless understood as that of a messenger.

† Moreover, the term *procurator* is an indefinite term, and it is predicated of any mandate, as noted in the *Extra*, *de procuratoribus*, chapter *Petitio*; and see the argument in the *Digest*, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Pater Severinam*, section *Conditionem*; and in the *Code*, *de libris praetoris*, law 3. For truth ought not to be vitiated on account of imprudent speech, as stated in the *Digest*, *de officiis praesidis*, law *Illicitas*, section *Veritas*. Furthermore, there is no doubt that an appeal may be interposed through a messenger; for what is done through a messenger is more properly so called than what is done through a procurator, because it partakes less of fiction, as held in the *Digest*, *de procuratoribus*, law *Certe*, section *Procurator*.

† Moreover, this law did not bind itself to one species of mandate: but it said, by every way and form by which it can be done better; therefore, that form and name are valid by which and by what it can be valid, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. qui Romae, § Calimachus, in fine. From all of which it can be said that the interposition of nullity and of appeal could be interposed by that manner and form, even if it were necessary to stretch the force of the name improperly: because the matter is founded in the substance of truth, and there is no need to care about the tips of words, as in X. de verb. sign. c. intelligentia, and in 1 q. 1 c. Martione et Basilides. And as if he had said, my lord says thus: as is read in the Gospel there, he said more, etc. And thus I hold, saving the reason of right speech, D. de aur. et arg. leg. l. Plautius, and of the sounder opinion, as in D. qui pot. in pign. hab. l. Claudius. And to the aforesaid it contributes what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1, § nuntiatio, D. de nox. oper. nunc. For words are referred to the office to which they can agree, if that office is in the nature of things. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a case for restitution in integrum can be compromised. And number 7.
2. Whether a statute concerning compromises binds minors.
3. Whether the execution of a sentence should be delayed on account of restitution in integrum.
4. When a matter is said to be concluded in a case.
5. After a matter is concluded in a case, nothing may be alleged that would impede the sentence.
6. A woman acquiring property from non-dotal funds, nor from a gift by her husband, acquires it for herself.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Regarding the question whether a party who has obtained a judgment in his own person, which is said to have become res judicata, ought to be compelled to submit to arbitration: first considering the statutes of the commune of Novara, which provide that if any lawsuit or dispute exists or shall exist between any ascendants or descendants, without distinction of degree, or between collaterals up to the fourth degree inclusive, computed according to canonical law, that the authority of Novara, having diligently examined the causes, places, times, persons, and also other circumstances of fact and business with a discerning eye, may compel and force the aforementioned discordant parties to make an arbitration agreement in the form that it deems appropriate, appointing one or more arbitrators as it sees fit, using all legal remedies. Certainly, when it does not seem appropriate to bind them to make an arbitration agreement for some reasonable cause, it shall proceed summarily, simply, and de plano, without the noise and formalities of judicial procedure, in their cases, and shall hasten to terminate those cases as quickly as possible. Then, having seen the letters of our Magnificent and glorious Prince, in which it is contained that, in the case where the persons named in the petition and those letters are such that, by virtue of the statutes of the commune of Novara, they could otherwise be compelled to submit to arbitration, and an action for restitution in integrum is pending, of which mention is made in the said petition, notwithstanding any frivolous cavils whatsoever, the authority of Novara shall compel the parties, as named in the said petition, to submit to arbitration before two common friends, etc. Having also seen the acts and proceedings in the aforementioned case, and considering the state of the case itself, and having diligently seen and examined the allegations of both parties, it must be considered what the law is. And in this case, it has been elegantly alleged by the parties, and on behalf of the minor it holds: because the rights of minors are in a sense immortal. Moreover, a tutor who does not allege the rights of the minor is in gross negligence, which should not harm the minor; especially when it was not proven, he did not oppose on the ground of non-probation. Therefore, he may rightly petition for restitution in integrum. Furthermore, he may petition that an arbitration agreement be made; because it matters greatly whether the minor petitions for an arbitration agreement to be made, or whether it is petitioned against him, as in C. de proc. l. non eo minus. For age and privilege cause the judgment to limp, as in ff. de mi. l. si iudex circumuento. In which judgment the minor obtains two things: namely, that he may oppose on the ground of his right, and rei vindicatio, l. fi. and C. de ser. fu. l. cum seruum. But after restitution in integrum has been introduced in the judgment, both parties are reduced to equality, as in C. de repu. quae fiunt in iudicio. l. 1. and C. de fruc. lit. expen. l. fi. and fully noted by Bartolus in l. 1. §. item nuncupatio. de no. ope. nun. The allegations having been made on the article,

† in the case of restitution in integrum, it ought to be compromised. Which allegations are removed by the rescript of the lord ordering the compromise of the said case of restitution in integrum in the case where the persons etc. as above. Moreover, whether the case of restitution in integrum is to be compromised, since it is of mixed Empire, as C. where, and with whom. l. if. and it is not to be called into doubt: because arbitrators act in the place of a delegate from the prince, who can give a new nature to the acts of men, as l. 1. C. who for their own right. in if. who prince properly, and expressly wrote about this case of restitution in integrum. And even if he had not written, the statute on compromise seems sufficient. For minors are bound by statutes speaking in common matters, and also by any which can be adapted to minors, as ff. de admi.tu. l. if without heir. §. Luc. Hence, saving the reason of rectitude, general laws are observed by all, as C. de leg. l. laws most sacred. and ff. de leg. l. 2. and 3. there it says, according to which all say they live, who are in the city. Hence there is no doubt about the disposition of common law, but about the mandate of the prince: whether the said rescript contains our case or not, because mandates of princes are stronger than all laws. For whatever pleases the prince has the force of law, as ff. de consti. prin. l. i. sacrilege crime is invalidated, who contempts the prince's authority, as C. de crimine sacrilegii. l. instar. Furthermore, wards and minors are bound by the constitutions of the city.

† Hence, the statute concerning compromises properly binds them, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. si sine haerede, § Lucius. Nevertheless, notwithstanding these points, considering the status of this restitution sought and the time at which said restitution was requested,

I say that the times do not permit, nor does equity dictate, that the execution of the sentence be delayed on account of the petition for restitution in integrum. Against this, I prove first by the text in a similar case: l. si rem, quam, §. quolibet, D. de evictionibus, where it says, "so that, however, it not be done near the condemnation itself." For, since all disputes had been agitated, weighed, and written down, there was no longer any right of recension of the acts preserved.

† For whenever nothing remains to be proved, the case is said to be concluded. Codex, On Delays, law Cum a nobis; and Codex, On Adultery, law Quam ius indubitati; and Digest, On Minors, law Denique, § 1; and Codex, On the Time for Restitution in Integrum, law Petendae. And this maturity of understanding is comprehended from the words of the statute; and then it is confirmed by the letters of the illustrious lord, and it is treated as a great prejudice to the ward, who would obtain the same thing through the ordinary judge as through arbitration. Therefore, a concluded case should not be compromised; because the minor does not appear to be harmed if the praetor promises restitution in integrum, as in Digest, On Restitution in Integrum, law Non vero. Equity also supports this: because one should not go to arbitration for the purpose of deferring lawsuits, but for the purpose of deciding them, and so that an end may be imposed on lawsuits more quickly: as in Digest, On Arbitrators, law Quamvis.

† Moreover, after the case has been concluded, nothing may be alleged that would impede the sentence which alone remained to be rendered: because there are no parts of the judge’s function in cognizance, since it has already been cognized; for it is no longer a matter of cognizing, but of having cognized, as noted by Innocentius in the extrajudicial collection on the cause possessed, chapter *Pastoralis*. Furthermore, when a definitive judgment has been rendered, restitution in integrum does not suspend its execution, unless there is manifest injustice, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on restitution in integrum, chapter *Suscitata*, and in the final law of the Code on the order of cognition. Moreover, in the principal fact, these women appear to have a right, since they hold a maternal title: for it is sufficiently probable that the mother possessed, or their father on their behalf, as established in the Digest on acquisition of possession, law *Qui iure familiaritatis*, and in the Code on agricultural and census matters, law *Cum similis*, book 11.

† And that which a woman acquires during the subsistence of the marriage from non-dotal money, nor given by her husband, becomes hers, as is noted in C. de fidei instrumentis, l. scripturae; and C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. uxor marito. According to Bartolus and others, whatever may be said regarding the restitution of the price. Therefore, having considered all the conclusions, and following especially the modifications of the most illustrious lord’s rescript, I believe that the aforementioned restitution in integrum can be denied by the judge, time, cause, and equity being weighed; otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits, which is absurd: as in ff. de iudiciis, l. si praetor, in principio. Moreover, that which has once been adjudicated should not be further committed to arbitration for judgment; because the case is no longer pending, as in ff. de conditione indebiti, l. eleganter, § si post; and ff. de transactionibus, l. post rem; and expressly noted in C. de transactionibus, l. si diuersa. To this also contribute the words of the rescript, which require a deeper inquiry into matters treated in themselves: as in ff. de pactis dotalibus, l. Beblius Marcellus; namely, in those cases in which the exception of res iudicata does not stand in the way: as in ff. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. Claudius Felix. Because the thing, which was purchased by their mother, became that of the purchaser through delivery, or quasi-delivery, intervening. Nevertheless, although I believe that this is the truth, that delivery intervened: as in C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1; and ff. si seruitus uendicetur, l. si at; yet this delivery, or quasi-delivery, is not sufficiently proven; because possession of the vendor does not appear. And therefore, through precarium, nothing was transferred: as in ff. de acquisitione possessionis, l. quod in eo; and l. interdum; and extra de restitutione spoliorum, c. olim. And therefore, truth moves my conscience, not proof; because it is not sufficiently proven. Nevertheless, the definitive judgment rendered in favor of the plaintiff suffices for him; yet whatever may be the case, this is not our article,

But the only remaining question is whether a compromise can be made. And I say that it cannot; because after the conclusion of the case, where, as I have said, nothing remains but to render judgment, even if a minor may seek restitution in integrum, as in the Digest, On Minors, law Minor, omitted within twenty-five years; nevertheless, after the case has been concluded and judgment rendered, the decided dispute cannot be revoked, nor can one return to the beginning of a new question; otherwise the pronouncements of the praetors would be illusory, which is absurd, as in the Digest, On Judges, law If the Praetor, in the beginning. Does the right of the wards therefore perish? I answer: the right of the cause does not perish, but the right of action, as in the Code, On Judges, law Diligence, section If. Moreover, the right of the wards is not said to perish, which does not belong to them; and therefore the statute speaks very discreetly and very legally, and the words of our most noble and illustrious lord, which are full of the virtue of justice, follow the same modification. Furthermore, it is not because one is a minor that one is injured, as in the Digest, On Oaths, law Nam Postea, section If a Minor; Digest, On Minors, law But a Minor Magistrate. And therefore, all things considered, because it does not appear that any interest has been proven on behalf of the minor, and the instruments of purchase are for the contrary party, and secure possession is referred to title, either by the express nature of the words or by tolerance, it does not seem to me that any reason founds a cavil for restitution in integrum, which seems to me to be a cavil according to my conscience; although the allegations to the contrary are from the apex of the law, as in the Digest, On Mandate, law If a Surety, section Certain. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Duke of Milan has the same rights in the lands of the duchy as the Emperor has in the lands of the Empire.
2. The law *Bene a Zenone* and the law *Omnes* claim application in our Duke of Milan and the procurator of the fisc.
3. The delict of the husband does not harm the wife's dowry, and therefore it does not come into the publication of the husband's goods.
4. When, with the universality deducted in the disposition, it is understood that the right of a third party is reserved.
5. The Emperor is the source of justice and the orient; therefore, it is impossible that any injury arises from his rescript.
6. The donation of the Prince is a just cause for prescription, even according to canon law.
7. The law *Omnes* and the law *Bene a Zenone*: when they have application. And see also below at the end of the opinion, number 9.
8. The fisc, which has confiscated all goods for itself: whether it must be sued by a personal action as an heir; and whether one can proceed by a hypothecary action against external possessors.
casus:
CASE. The facts are as follows: it is true that the Most Serene Lord Wenceslaus, Roman Emperor and always August King of Bohemia, in the year of our Lord 1380, in the month of February, granted one singular privilege to our Most Illustrious Lord, the Duke of Milan. By which he created the aforementioned Lord Duke, his heirs, and descendants in his line, general vicars of the Holy Empire, irrevocable and perpetual, in the city of Milan, Pavia, and its territory, and in all other cities, lands, and places, both within and overseas, which were held and possessed by the said Lord Duke. And in that privilege are contained the following words, namely: "Furthermore, the pursuit and punishment of rebels, who are, were, or shall be, of the Empire as well as of the Imperial cities, and especially of the aforementioned places, and generally all and singular royal rights whatsoever, which are deemed to belong to our Serenity and the Holy Empire by law, right, or constitution, or edict, or custom, or otherwise in any way, shall pertain to our vicar and his descendants, and to him and those to whom he shall entrust them, by full right; so that all profits, revenues, and proceeds, however they may arise from publications, confiscations of goods, imposition of penalties, exactions of new and old taxes, or otherwise in any way, from the aforementioned cities, castles, counties, lands, places, rights, and appurtenances, shall pertain to us, to each and every one, by right itself, without any restitution or reason to be made to us henceforth, and shall be converted into your private patrimony and treasury, as you shall wish." All of which, and each of which, having been considered with deliberation and certain knowledge, with all authority, and by all other means by which we can do better, and from the fullness of our power, etc., as is more fully and seriously contained in the said privilege.

After the granting of that privilege, it happened that certain subjects of our aforementioned Lord Duke committed rebellion and the crime of lèse-majesté, for which he was condemned to death, and all his goods were confiscated and seized by sentence of the chamber of the aforementioned Lord. After the confiscation and seizure, the aforementioned Lord Duke transferred the goods by the title of donation to a certain Paganinus de Blasono, his faithful subject, by his patent letters. Which goods, thus donated, the said Paganinus held and possessed continuously for a period of twelve years, under the pretext of the said donation, whatever condition ceasing. In which goods a certain third party claims to have a right, saying that those goods had been mortgaged to him, or that they pertained to him by another right before the commission of the said crime and before the confiscation. The said Paganinus, however, claims to be secure by the prescription of four years, as having cause from our aforementioned Lord. Now it is asked: whether, from the granting of the said privilege granted to our aforementioned Lord by the aforementioned Most Serene Lord Emperor, the benefit and privilege of the law Bene, from Zeno, on the four-year prescription, has been transferred to the aforementioned Lord, and consequently to the said Paganinus, the donee, and as having cause from the aforementioned Lord. And on this point, let it be seen, the aforementioned privilege, etc.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Just as the Emperor has total plenitude of power over every land that is under the empire, so too the glorious and most illustrious Prince has, in certain cities and provinces, that portion of the plenitude which the Imperial Serenity not only committed to him, but truly and fully granted, nay more, transferred, as stated in the Digest, On the Origin of Law, law 2, § last. For in the Emperor all power shines forth, since God’s providence believed it fitting for no one more than the Caesar to guard the safety of the commonwealth, nor for any other to suffice for the matter, as stated in the Digest, On the Office of the Prefect of the Watch, law “For the safety.” And this transfer made by the Emperor is most complete, although it does not uproot the foundations of the Empire, according to that passage: “Therefore nothing is lacking to me,” Digest, On Law and Jurists, law “Manumissions,” and in the proemium of the Digest. There are two causes of the Empire over the illustrious Caesar: one divine, from which he receives authority; and the other human, which is conferred through election, as stated in the Code, On Laws, law last, and Code, On the Abrogation of Laws, law “So great.” Hence the Emperor is the natural lord, because by divine law he rules over the east, west, south, and north, as in the Authenticum, On the Mandate of the Prince, after the first title. And every dignity that is derived from the Emperor partakes of his nature, because whatever is derived from someone by production, and not by adverse subtraction, partakes of the origin of its flowing cause; nor is it less effective in the effect than in the cause, Digest, On Dowry, law “He who, when,” and Digest, On Guarantees, law “Tutor.” For as each thing is, so it generates another according to nature, as says that light of truth, Aristotle, On the Soul, book 2. From these follow two conclusions: one, that our glorious lord, after the Prince, has all the power that the Emperor has. For the benefit of the prince ought to be free from all diminution, because it is not only something favorable, but most highly favorable, as in § “That,” in the Authenticum, Constitution Concerning Dignities, and Code, On Military Peculium and Administration, law 2, and On the Constitutions of the Prince, chapter “Benefit.”

The second conclusion is that, on account of the conjunction of both powers, namely, that of the grantor and that of the granted power, flowing and having flowed, the grant of the Magnificent Lord enjoys the same privilege as the grant of Caesar; so that the laws *Omnes* and *Bene a Zenone*, concerning which Driennus writes in his treatise on prescriptions, claim application to our Magnificent Lord just as they do to Caesar, because he rejoices in the grants of Caesar and the Supreme Empire. Nor do I think there is any doubt about this. For it is established that he is more than a procurator of the fisc, since he is two fiscs and greater; in which procurator the aforementioned laws *Omnes* and *Bene a Zenone* have application, according to Bartolus, who thus notes in the Digest, *De iure fisci*, law *Si procurator*. Therefore, we ought not to dispute the difference of power, but rather the effect of the privilege, and suppose that the Emperor had done these things in his own person, and inquire what the law would be, upon which arguments for and against could be based.

† For the fact that the rights of dowries and hypothecs are not prejudiced, and this lies within the bounds of natural reason, because that which arises as a consequence of a delict committed by the husband ought not to be extended to the detriment of the innocent wife, as is stated in Extra, De pignoribus, c. Ex litteris, and c. Poenis fiscalibus creditores praeferri, l. 1; and because the cause of the dowry is always and everywhere secure, as is stated in Digest, Soluto matrimonio, l. Si marito publico iudicio damnato; and this is expressly stated in Digest, De bonis damnatorum, l. Sed et aliae.

† Moreover, since a universal estate is brought into the disposition, the right of alien property is always understood to be reserved, as in C. ad l. Iul. l. si tutore; ff. ad Treb. l. recusare, §. si fisco; ff. de iure fisci, l. 3, §. sed cum causa; and l. Valerius; C. de bonis praescripto, l. si quis post hac; C. de donatione inter virum et uxorem, l. res; C. de privilegio fisci, l. 1. Furthermore, a privilege of the prince should not be interpreted to the injury of another, as in ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. ex facto, in principio; ff. de administratione tutorum, l. impuberi filio Centurio.

† For since the Emperor is the fountain of justice, and the eastern fountain from which laws arise, it is impossible that injuries should arise: as C. unde vi, l. authoritatem, and l. meminerint. Moreover, these petitions seem to have been abolished, as C. de petitione bonorum sublata, l. 1, lib. 10. This argument, however, ceases to apply when one does not take pity on the labor and frailty of women, at least in matters of dowries, as C. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. assiduis, and C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. quisquis. From all of which it seems to be concluded that the right of hypothecation remains valid, unless it were prescribed.

† because a donation by the prince is the most just cause for prescription: and this opinion seems to be confirmed by canon law, as in 16 q. 3 c. placuit. Moreover, concerning this cause the law appoints judges: therefore the cause can be brought forward: as in C. ubi causae fiscales l. cum vendente.

† Moreover, because the aforementioned laws all speak well, as Zenone observes, when the fisc grants another’s property as such, and not by reason of an error regarding the final cause or ignorance, which is presumed whenever a princely privilege would be drawn to injury: as in C. de precibus imperatoris offerentibus, l. rescripta, because the altars of justice must not be stripped of their ornament and dignity, although sometimes, out of favor for the military and public honor, Imperial majesty has introduced many things outside the ordinary course by royal power, which must be observed: as in ff. de legatis 2, l. qui solidum, § praedium, and ff. de rei venditione, l. Item si verberatum. But where there is error, the rule is different, as there according to Cynus, because error in this case specifically impedes the transfer of ownership. For special law, and that which is diminished by privilege, is more easily removed than general and common law: as in ff. de testamento militis, l. eius militis, § militia. Moreover, all solemnities required in such acts, if not observed, render the act invalid: as in C. si adversus fiscum, l. edicto, and ff. de rescindenda venditione, l. fundus, qui Lucii Titij. Moreover, because that which is not done properly is considered as not done: ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si praetor, and ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. qui Romae, § Flavius Hermes.

† The solution, I say, is that the fisc, which has confiscated all the goods to itself, ought to be sued by a personal action, as if it were an irregular heir. And because the fisc is solvent, recourse may not be had to a hypothecary action against an alien possessor: for the fisc is always present, as in the Authentica Punctae. Nevertheless, on these points I would gladly hear the opinions of others: for that which is sought by many wise men is found more perfectly.

And it should be known that when the fisc is sued as an heir, the law *bene a Zenone* does not apply, because the action is not brought under the condition of that law, but by a useful hereditary and perpetual action. Provided, however, that if the sovereign acted with certain knowledge and from the fullness of his power, the recipient is secure. But if there was perfect ignorance or the importunity of the claimant, he is not secure, and the act of the prince would have been in the execution of justice rendered in the granting of grace. As noted in the Institutes, *de usucapionibus*, § *si*. And recourse must always be had to the intention of the prince, because he is like the living law in his lands. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. I promise that I will make you content. What is the effect of these words?
2. Mediators are not bound by the contract.
body: In the Name of Christ. Amen.

† It is asked in the case of Otto of Mandello: because it is said that he caused Count Monfredo of Barbiano to be released, promising that he would make Filippo of Pisa content, in whose name the said Count had been imprisoned; and that he would not depart from Ferrara without making him content. It is asked, what kind of promise this was. It is presupposed that Lord Otto and a certain other nobleman, Lord Marcus, were appointed as arbitrators in this matter.

To this, it must be premised that these words, “I will make you content,” refer either to payment, or to the declaration of a doubtful question, or there is doubt. In the first case, he who binds himself is obliged to satisfy the debt; because this matter signifies payment: as in *l. peto*, in the beginning, D. de legibus 2. In the second case, he is not bound to anything else except to the declaration; because to this alone is the arbitrator bound, and to declare or decide, by which he has performed his office: as in D. de arbitris, *l. qualem*, §. *si*, with the following law. In the third case, recourse must be had to presumptions, which give understanding of what the intention was, which is declared from the preceding and following matters: as the common laws say, D. de testamento, *l. haeredem palam*, §. *sed si notavi*; and D. de legibus 1, *l. si servus plurium*, §. *si facit quod non*; in *l. 1*, D. de iudiciis, where the good gloss says that from the prolocution the sense and understanding for the declaration of the following matters is known, as in D. de verbis oblig., *l. Quotiens in stipulationibus ambigua*. But if it does not appear, or because of uncertainty, the act is vitiated, as in D. de verbis oblig., *l. triticum*; and note, D. de pactis, *l. veteribus*. Or simply we will say that one assumed as an arbitrator does not seem to have promised *iudicatum solvi* [payment of the judgment]; because it would seem that the substance of the obligation was placed in his will; and because it would seem that the arbitrator was assumed in his own matter, which is not probable: as in D. de arbitris, *l. pe*. And because this does not pertain to the office of an arbitrator, that he should take upon himself the obligation of the debtor, for he would be rather a surety than an arbitrator. And because it does not seem that what is foreign to the nature of the thing was considered. And because his office would be damaging and dangerous to himself, which it ought not to be: as in D. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, *l. si quis ex assignatoribus*. On the contrary, if he were a surety for the judgment, he would be released by the sentence: as in D. de fideiussoribus, *l. Graece*, §. *post litem*.

Furthermore, general words should not be drawn to unusual meanings, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, *l. fistulas*, §. *frumenta*. Also, that obligation of not departing from a certain place savors of servitude, and is not consonant with the law; always saving the custom of arms in this matter, as noted in *l. nam et servus*, in the beginning, D. de negotiorum gestione. I omit the allegations regarding a naked pact, because it would fall into a clothed pact through the performance of the other party: as in C. de rerum permutatione, *l. ex placito*; and D. de praescriptionibus verbalibus, *l. naturalis*, with its material.

From all of which it is concluded that, if there is nothing else in the case than what has been narrated, the said Lord Otto is not bound; because it is not probable that he wished to bind himself in the aforementioned case by loose speech, as in *l. fin.*, C. quod cum eo. I readily admit that the simplicity of arms does not permit disputing on the points of law. Also, we ought to be content with promises and dispositions, not extending them further, as in D. de verbis oblig., *l. si ita stipulatio facta*; and C. de hereditate instituenda, *l. quotiens*. A similarity supports the foregoing:
† because mediators are not bound by contract, as in c. 1, de test., lib. 6.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the period of one year granted to a vassal to demand investiture runs from the time of knowledge, or from the day of the lord’s death, or from the day the inheritance was entered upon.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The text states that if a vassal, after the death of his lord or of another person from whom he may succeed, unless prevented by just cause, does not demand investiture within a year and a month, he is deprived of the fief as contumacious. The question arises whether this year is computed from the day of death, or from the day the inheritance was accepted, or from the day of knowledge, when he knew that his lord was dead, or conversely, when he knew that he succeeded to the fief by the death of the vassal.

It seems that it runs from the day of death, for the text makes mention only of death, as in c. 1, *Quo tempore miles*. But rather it seems that it runs from the time the inheritance was accepted, as in C. *De iure delatorum*, l. *Si*, § 1. For before the inheritance is accepted, fidelity is not owed by the heir of the lord; and conversely, the heir of the vassal, before accepting the inheritance, is not an heir, nor is he bound generally as a general heir, nor particularly as a feudal heir; therefore he is excused on account of great impediment, because the obligation ceases in the meantime.

Moreover, knowledge seems to be required, because this intent seems useful, at least as to its beginning, as in ff. *De edicto edictorum*, l. *Cum sex*. For all obligations to do, beginning from the heir himself, seem useful as to their beginning, and all excuses, as in ff. *De excusationibus tutorum*, l. *Quinquaginta*.

Furthermore, this penalty is placed in the cause, namely in contempt and contumacy; but he who is ignorant is not contumacious; therefore he is not punished; for the text says that we wish knowledge, not ignorance, to bind, as in C. *De tabellis*, l. *Generalis*, in the tenth book, and in ff. *De decretis ab ordine factis*, l. *Finalis*.

But rather it seems that acceptance of the inheritance is not required; for the agnate succeeds to the fief even if the universal inheritance is repudiated. It is sufficient for him that he is an heir in a certain thing, namely a feudal heir, as in c. 1, *An agnatus vel filius*. For if acceptance of the inheritance were required, he would not be bound to fidelity unless he were an heir, which is false.

Solution: This time runs for the heir of the vassal from the day of knowledge and power; but if the lord has no heir, it does not run in the meantime, as argued in l. *Labeo*, ff. *De nautico faenore*, because there is no one to whom the oath may be offered and from whom investiture may be demanded. And thus the debtor is hindered by just cause, not by his own act, but by the act of the creditor. It supports what is noted by Dynus in ff. *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Continuus*, l. *Cum quis*. Hence it is concluded that if the lord dies leaving an heir, the time runs from the day of knowledge; otherwise, if he dies and has no heir. Although it would be safer for the vassal to make a protestation in the meantime that the delay does not lie with him, as in C. *De annalibus exceptionibus*, l. *Ut perfectus*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What and how many things are required for a notary to be bound to produce an instrument.
2. The edict concerning production applies even to a singular successor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A creditor, having the goods of his debtor pledged, brings an action against an outsider who possesses the thing pledged to him, and intends to produce as the foundation of his claim the title and the instrument of purchase made by that outsider possessor from the debtor himself concerning the aforementioned thing, requesting that the notary who drew up that instrument be compelled to deliver it, provided that the creditor first takes a corporal oath before the judge that it is in his interest, on account of the aforementioned cause, that the aforementioned instrument be disclosed and delivered to him by the notary. From these facts, the question arises: what is the law?

† And it seems, in the first place, that the notary ought not to produce such an instrument, nor can he produce it by edict to the creditor. For in the production of instruments, any interest whatsoever is not sufficient. Hence, for instruments, the action for production is not granted, which would be available for any interest whatsoever, as in l. 3, § est autem, D. ad exhibendum. Therefore, the notary is not bound by the action for production, which is an extraordinary remedy. But then it is said to be by the office of the judge, which is an extraordinary remedy, and it would not concur with the ordinary remedy, as in D. de edendo, l. quaedam, in principio. To this, note that for the notary to be bound by this extraordinary remedy, two things are required: namely, that it is in the interest of the petitioner, and that the notary was requested by the petitioner himself, or his procurator, or author, as noted in D. de edendo, l. praetor, in principio, and l. si quis ex argentariis, § pertinere. But this instrument was not drawn up at the command of the creditor, or his procurator, or a similar person. And to this effect, it is well stated in D. de evictionione, l. si res, quam.

On the contrary, it seems that because the debtor who obligated himself can demand this, so too can his creditor; which I demonstrate thus: The creditor has all the goods obligated; therefore, this instrument is also obligated to him, as in D. de legatis tertio, l. qui chirographum. Also, because although the general rule is that the defendant is not bound to produce for a claim founded on mere intention, yet if the intention is partly proven and partly remains to be proven, then he is bound to produce to assist the intention, or to supply it, according to Guillaume and Cynus in l. ultima, C. de edendo. But this comes to assist or corroborate the intention, as in C. res aliena pignori data, l. cum res, and D. de pignoribus, l. si ab eo. For in a hypothecary claim, a conventional obligation is required, and this is established, and the dominion or quasi-dominion of the debtor is required, as in D. de probationibus, l. ante omnia. And to prove this, the instrument in question is relevant; therefore, it ought to be produced, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. si praediorum. And I say this latter part is more true and more equitable, as in D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Titius. Nor does it obstruct that this creditor did not command it, and therefore he is deemed or considered the same person as the debtor, as is confirmed by the aforementioned laws, and in D. de iureiurando, l. etiam si in rem.

† Moreover, the edict concerning the duty to produce documents applies even to a singular successor, as stated in the Digest, De edendo, l. quaedam, §. his autem. Production is not made: because it is not good that truth be denied, as in c. Si quis miles, De contentione inter dominum et vassallum, col. 10. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether expenses incurred by the father for the son can be reckoned into his own portion.
casus: CASE. In the name of Christ, amen. Having seen the acts and the proceedings of the case pending between Master Jacob and Master John of Rimini, his son, the following case emerges. The father sent certain sums of money to the aforementioned Master John, his son, who was at university; and the father possessed and received the usufruct of certain adventitious goods of the said son. When the son, having been enrolled in medicine, returned to his native country, a dispute arose between father and son; and they made a compromise between themselves before certain common friends, regarding both law and fact; and they were granted full arbitral power, the father claiming on one side the expenses incurred for the son at university, or, insofar as he spent more than was his intention; and the son claiming from the father maintenance for himself and his family, as well as his adventitious goods and their fruits, and the dowry of his wife. The arbitrators awarded and sentenced, absolving the son from the father’s claim, except for the restitution of certain books and some sums of money received on loan; and also condemning the father to restitution of the said adventitious goods and half of the fruits received by him, and imposing silence on the son regarding other matters, so that henceforth the son may not harass him concerning maintenance, etc., as is more clearly apparent in the sentence and award of the said arbitrators. From this sentence, the said Master Jacob appealed, stating that it was inequitable and unjust. Now the question arises whether the said sentence should be upheld or not.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The words of Rizzardo Malombra in the law *quae pater filio*, Digestum, *de familia erciscunda*: “What if he is in power?” Odo says: “Much more so.” As for what some say regarding books, some say by this law that books should be considered as given. They respond to this law: because what was supplied, he will claim back as consumed, but here they remained. And thus holds Roffredus in his questions in the question beginning *donatus*. And the same is followed by Marcus Silvestris. Others, more modern, hold the contrary: because legal books are equated with arms, since arms are compared to laws, and laws to arms, as in the Institutes, in the Proemium; Code, *de novo codice componendo*, near the beginning; *de officio diversorum iudicum*, law *scimus*. Therefore, etc., as below, *de colonis*, law 1, § *nec castrense*; and Code, there, law *si*. And noted by Dytherius in the said law *Lucius*, § *idem respondit*. But Rizzardo Malombra distinguishes: either the father intended to give, or not; and this is certain; or it is doubtful, and in doubt he says one must resort to presumptions, which should be gathered from the father’s resources, from the price or value of the books, and from the number of children, argument from below, *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *utrum*; and below, *de legatis tertio*, law *si filiae pater*. And for this, which is noted, Code, *de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *et si de tua*, at the end. The gloss of Rizzardo Malombra says: What if the father gave books and other things necessary for study to a son in his power? It seems that it is valid, by the law *et aliae*, since some of these follow concerning a son in his power. Moreover, a father can give to a son existing at the camps: as Code, there, law 4, in the beginning; and Code, *de castrensi peculio*, law 1, book 12. But if they are advocates, they are said to serve in the military, and they are said to have a quasi-castrense peculium: and by reason of law it is established in certain things that which is in the castrense peculium, as Code, *de advocatis diversorum iudicum*, law *fori*; and law *advocata*; and law *fin.*; Code, *de inofficioso testamento*. From which it appears that a father can give to a son studying and wishing to serve in the military of advocates. Moreover, thus the Macedonian Law ceases on account of study, i.e., when the son receives on account of study, just as on account of castrense peculium: as below, *ad Macedonianam*, law 1, at the end; and law 2; and law *servus*, § *quod dicitur*. Jacobus says: Oldradus in the law *si filia*, § *idem si scribit*, Digestum, *de familia erciscunda*, notes that brothers are bound to buy books and make expenses from the common fund after the death of the father for a son sent to study by the father, and this by the text of this law, and below there, law *ex parte*, § *filius*. Although also contrary by the law *Lucius*, *idem respondit*, below, *ad munera*; and to the law *et si filium*, below, *de muneribus et honoribus*. I answer: because they speak of new operational burdens acquired after the death of the father. Dytherius. Also it applies to another point: if the father pays a debt for the son, whether the brothers count what was paid by the father in the action *familiae erciscundae* to him for whom it was paid; and say that yes, when the son was naturally bound to the father, argument from below, *de peculio*, law *Stichus*, word *idem est*. Oldradus. Having seen and read the opinions of so many learned men, that opinion seems more equitable, that either we speak of expenses consumed, and the father does not recover them: because it is not fitting to repent of natural affection: as Code, *de captivis et postliminio reversis*, law *liber captus*. Or they remain, or they are three, which pertain to the burden of the father on account of food or clothing, and the same, because the father does not recover: because he seems to have acted not so much in managing the son’s business, as in discharging himself by paternal bounty, as Code, *de negotiis gestis*, law 1; and law *alimenta*; and law *quod pupilli*; and noted, Digestum, there, law *Nexenius*. For it is the burden of the father to feed his sons, as Digestum, *de familia erciscunda*, law *si maritus*. Unless it expressly appears that the son had goods, and that the father made expenses with the intention of recovering. Argument in the said law *Nexenius*. Because when the son has patrimony or an art whereby he can live, the praetor should not decree alimony from paternal goods: as Digestum, *de petitione hereditatis*, law *si*. But if they are books or things which are not consumed by use in a short time, then from the number of children and books, and from the possibility of resources, sometimes a grant into peculium is presumed, sometimes a gift, as Digestum, *de peculio legato*, law *si*. And because I believe that the arbitrators weighed equity, their award is to be confirmed, not invalidated: because an arbitrator’s award is presumed to be supported by equity, as noted by Dytherius in the counsel beginning *Tholomeus Manetis*. And this for two reasons: namely, in favor of arbitration and out of hatred of litigation. Moreover, let the father impute it to himself, who presumed better of the adolescent, to whom he committed administration as if to a spendthrift, as Code, *de sententiis passis*, law *si*; and law *ult.*; Code, *de legitima tutela*; and Code, *de bonis quae liberis*, law *cum non solum*, near the middle. The philosopher says that youths are excessive in everything, and therefore before mature age they are prone to spending money, whence the father should complain of himself: because it becomes the part to regulate, not to be regulated; and this is fitting for every wise man. Let it therefore be concluded that if nothing else appears, one must stand by the award, just as by a transaction, as Digestum, *ad Trebellianam*, law *si*; Digestum, *de verbis obligatorum*, law *si quis cum aliter*; Digestum, *pro socio*, law *unde si Nerva*; Code, *quibus ex causis maior*, law *in contractibus*. I do not extend myself further: because I am seriously ill. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Certain indications are required for torture.
2. What indications are called, and what kind they ought to be.
3. To seek reasons, where we have sense, is a weakness of the intellect.
4. No credence is given to a confession made under torture, unless it is persisted in.
5. What just fear is, and how it is proved.
6. Whether reputation supported by evidence, and defamation, suffices for torture.
7. The king ought not to be more lenient than the law: and in malefices, dignity is not privileged.
8. One must always proceed to torture with the moderation of the intellect.
9. Malefices can harm humans.
10. A maleficium can be removed by another maleficium.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because this question of torture, and the question of the Queen of the old Kingdom of Aragon, is very weighty and grave, it is necessary to premise certain things for clarity.

† And first, that in the torture of the illustrious Queen, certain indications are required, and such as cannot be called into doubt as to whether they are indications or not: as C. de quaestionibus, l. milites, §. oportet.

† ought to be. It is necessary that there be indications clearer than light for persuading what something is, not to speak of fully proving it; for these would not be indications, but the light of truth. For indications are, properly speaking, those which proceed by circumferences. Those, indeed, which prove directly, are more than indications; for they attest to the word of a man’s act, since conjectures have place in uncertain, not certain matters, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. continuus, § cum ita. If conjectures indeed consist in the discretion of the judge, as per the last, but the truth of things proved concludes of necessity to the parties and to the judge, who must judge according to the acts and proofs, D. de off. praes. l. illicitas, § veritas. Hence it is that, when fear has been proved by ocular faith, conjectural proof of spontaneous renunciation is not admitted, as in Extr. de renunt. c. super hoc. For that which appears expressly need not be proved, as in C. de poenis l. qui sententiam and l. cum res. For more credit is given to the senses than to words, as in Inst. de grad. § sed cum magis. And as Averroes said,

† To seek a reason where we have sense is a weakness of the intellect. This is so true, indeed, that one fully convicted does not need torture, because it is superfluous to apply torture then, as noted in Codex, *Quorum appellatio non recipitur*, *Observare*. Although, by custom, they are tortured so that they may not appeal, nevertheless, the evasion of a frivolous appeal would not impede corporal execution; because it is now a matter of notoriety, as in Digest, *De appellationibus*, *Non tamen*, according to Bartolus, and in *Venerabilibus*, § *Secus*, *De appellationibus*, Book 6. This is especially so if the person is cunning, and the charge is such that sometimes it is permitted to transgress the laws, as noted by Innocentius, Extra, *De constitutionibus*, Chapter 1, and Codex, *De appellationibus*, *Additos*, in the words *damnatos immanitate criminum*. And this is proven in Digest, *De in iusto testamento*, *Si quis filio exheredato*, near the middle. These objections are raised.

For, as the matter is presented, this illustrious lady confessed under torture, or at least under probable or necessary fear of torture: to such a confession no credence is to be given, unless she persists in it and the terror of torture ceases: as in D. de quaestionibus, l. 1. But this illustrious lady did not persist in her confession; rather, when liberty was granted to her to excuse herself, she retracted her confession; therefore, such a confession, having been retracted, is not sufficient: as in C. de custodiendo reo, l. 2; and as noted in C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. Si quis; and fully by Cynus in D. de quaestionibus, l. De tormentis; and by Bartolus in l. 1, § Si quis ultro, D. de quaestionibus. To the same effect is Extravagant Quod metus causa, c. 1; and what is noted by Cynus in l. 2, C. Quod metus causa. But to this it is answered that there is a certain torture which is carried out with the knowledge of the law: and this does not vitiate [the confession]. There is another which is carried out as a matter of fact, and without the knowledge of the law, and this vitiates [the confession], unless one persists voluntarily. Therefore, either the indicia proceed, and the confession is valid; or the indicia do not proceed, and it is not valid.

† For it is certain that just fear is the fear of credulity, or of capital enmity from a powerful man, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, De sententia excommunicationis, chapter Quod de his. And if it is said that one may fear, and subsequently a grievance follows, it is rescinded by means of an appeal, or a supplication, or by the mere office of a superior, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, De appellationibus, chapter Consuluit. And if just fear is caused by natural discretion, it is committed to the office of the judge, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, Quod mens causa, chapter Cum dilectus. And that fear is presumed from a just cause for fearing, and that there is extortion, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, De electionibus, chapter Bonae memoriae Maguntino. And one who is constrained, so that he cannot flee, is presumed to be compelled, especially by threats and imminent terrors, as in chapter 1, De fidei commissis, in the Clementines. Moreover, no one who is in the power of enemies is presumed to act voluntarily, as in chapter Pastor, Extra, De re iudicata, in the Clementines; nor is he who dares not use a free mind and a free tongue without danger to his life, as in chapter 1, De baptismo, in the Clementines. Furthermore, fear is proved by the place from what is probable. John Andrea says this in De appellationibus, chapter Bonae. Furthermore, fear is proved by the effect, by which the effect of the mind is proved: as in Digestum, De arbitris, law Licet, and law Non distinguemus, section Cum quidam. Furthermore, an impression is presumed from chains. Digestum, De verborum significatione, law Quae neque sequantur, and law 1, Codex, De custodiendis reorum. Furthermore, Albertus Magnus says in Book 15, De proprietate rerum, that a free people has a free mind and a free tongue. Indeed, the aforementioned statements are true with this addition: that if such and so grave indications have been given, that it is necessary for the one rendering judgment to resort to torture, then it is not said that the judge burdens, but the law, as noted in Digestum, De probationibus, and law Palam, Digestum, De ritu nuptiarum.

And some say that reputation supported by evidence, or very bad reputation, suffices for torture, as noted in C. de exhibendis reis, l. nullus. Certainly, Cynus did not say this, but rather that it suffices for imprisonment, until the truth of the fact is investigated. Solution: it must be said that the king’s conscience is to be left here with the counsel of holy and expert men who fear God; because when a just king sits on the throne, nothing evil will oppose him, as in the epistle inter claras. But if, abandoning the good mirror of conscience, he should act otherwise, he would sin grievously, as in c. cum eterni, de re iudicata, lib. 6. Moreover, the sentence is to be mitigated where the judge proceeds from presumptions, according to Innocentius, who thus notes in extra de praesumptionibus, c. illud. And it is also certain that from the concurrence of presumptions guilt is presumed, as in extra de pignoribus, c. illo vos, and noted by Dyther in l. 2, ff. de excusationibus tutorum, and cf. extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. cum dilectus. Nevertheless, one witness does not suffice for condemnation, as noted by Cynus in C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. si quis, because he does not make half-proof in criminal cases; because this term is not found in criminal accusations, but it is called indicium according to Cynus, and therefore it could be removed or overthrown by contrary indicium; but half-proof would so easily be overthrown, cf. ff. de regulis iuris, l. nihil naturale, and ff. de in integrum restitutione, l. diuus, because indicium is less than half-proof, as the gloss elegantly says in d. l. cum probatio. Although sometimes indicium is placed in the place of truth, as in l. si, C. familiae erciscundae, where this is discussed. I omit not one thing, that the king’s clemency ought to temper the strictness of the laws; because most blessed is that king who sits upon the throne of equity.

† provided that it is consistent with the law of nature; otherwise, it is not fitting, for it ought to be more lenient than the law, as is read and noted in the Constitution *de iudicibus*, § *oportet*, and in the Digest, *de officiis praesidis*, law *observandum*. It is also established that dignity does not grant privilege in cases of malefice, according to Innocent III in the chapter *ut fama* of the Decretals, *de sententia excommunicationis*. Nor is this surprising, because guilt excludes all honor, as stated in the Code, *ubi senatus vel clarissimi*, law 1. Indeed, honor aggravates the malefice, as stated in the Code, *de episcopis et clericis*, law *presbyter*.

† Nevertheless, one must always proceed to torture with the moderation of reason, as C. de custodia rei, l. 2; C. de emendatione propinquorum, l. 1. Therefore, torture must not lack the indication of reason: and it is better to desist than to punish excessively. Moreover, it is proper to kings to dispense, whence the Apostle of the Lord says that they should render what is just and equitable, knowing that they also have a Lord in heaven. And the civil law says that the excessive harshness of masters is to be tempered, not followed, ff. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 2, § dominorum. Furthermore, an act beyond measure is reduced to measure, as noted in ff. de usuris, l. placuit. Finally, it must be known that in such malefices one proceeds with a lighter veil, as C. de maleficiis et mathematicis, l. si. And therefore, from suspicions one may proceed to imprisonment, until the truth is examined; but once the truth is discovered, the innocent must be released, the guilty punished, as C. de exhibendis reis, l. 2, where it says, until the cognition held shall have found the distinction. To the same effect: l. 1, C. de custodia rei; and de officio rectoris provinciae, l. iustissimos; and C. de officio praesidis, l. congruit. And in Auth. ut nulli iudici, § si quis vero comprehensorum; and ff. de appellationibus, l. si cui, § cum sacrilegium. So that the wicked will not escape the snare of the hunter.
† But whether it is possible that certain malefactors harm men by means of incantation,

† and whether they can change the sense of the same. It must be said that yes, with God permitting, whose judgments are hidden and unknown to us. Finally, it must be known that a maleficium can be removed by another maleficium, if it cannot be resolved in any other way, namely by an opposing incantation, even of demons, as is noted in the Summa Confessorum by Master John of Ripa, under the rubric on the impediment of ligation. For the mind ought not to depart from God, whatever is uttered by the mouth, according to the opinion of many theologians. For it is lawful at times to drink from turbid water and from a torrent, where the spring of flowing water is lacking. For medicines are not taken for the sake of pleasure, because they are horrible; but solely for the sake of recovering, retaining, or acquiring health, as is manifest from art and nature. And often a wound is added to a wound, so that both may be cured.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A sentence not passed judicially, or without citation, and before the judge has ascertained whether it is within his jurisdiction or not, and whether it is valid.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† Because it was not judicially established for the said judge at the time when he judged on any of his delegation: although he states this in the sentence, he is not believed unless it appears, c. Cum in iure, Extra, De officio delegati. And the judge must ascertain his jurisdiction before pronouncing sentence, just as other acts, as l. Unica, C., Qui pro sua iurisdict.; and l. 2, C., Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit; and there by Cyriacus and Baldus after him in l. Si quis ex aliena, De iudicibus; and in c. Ex parte, Extra, De verborum significatione; and there by Innocentius; and by the same in c. Venerabili, De censibus. And to the foregoing add c. Pastoralis officii, in principio; and c. Super literis, De rescriptis, near the end. Nor does it suffice to know it afterwards to exist in truth. Argument from what is noted in the gloss in c. Saepe, De appellationibus, on the word “peremptorie,” under the heading “et hoc intellige”; and what is noted by Bartolus in l. Hoc autem § 1, ff., Ex quibus causis maiores; and what is noted by the same Bartolus in l. Multis, ff., De conditionibus et demonstrationibus.

I come to the proof of these points, and I say that, considering the acts, the judge did not ascertain his delegation, for the rescript of that contract was produced to the said judge in the same hour and in various places. First, in a non-judicial place, and with the party absent. Second, in the place where the ordinary judge of crimes also had his tribunal. But with the party absent; and it is a matter of law that such production does not hold with the party absent, 3 q. 9, c. Chartae. Hence, this operates only as if it had not been produced; because null and useless are equivalent, c. Inter corporalia, De translatione episcoporum; and l. Quo qui satisdare cogitur. Nor does it avail if the party was cited to see it produced anew, since afterwards it was not produced, but the sentence was produced abruptly.
