Moreover, it is a matter of law that he against whom a rescript is obtained must be cited, and a delay must be granted to him to prove the falsehoods and to produce his rights, l. 2, C., De dilationibus, which was by no means done.

Furthermore, such citation to see the rescript produced, and the mandate of the procurator, and the rights of the adversary, and to hear the sentence simultaneously, did not hold in law; because it was against the order of law; because first the truth of the petitions, and the validity of the commission and the relation, ought to have been ascertained and pronounced. And when the order of law is perverted, the act does not hold, as in c. Exhibita, Extra, De iudicibus. Nor does it avail if it were said that he had this in the commission; because when the words of the rescript appear against the order of law, nevertheless one must not depart from the order of law, as in c. Causam quae, De rescriptis.

Moreover, it is not established for the judge that citation was made of the defendant to hear the sentence, although the notary attests that a relation was made to him. And against someone as contumacious the judge cannot proceed unless he knows him to be legitimately contumacious, which was not the case here. To this add the laws cited above.

Furthermore, the said judge, whom he admonished as his procurator to hear the sentence, and whom he condemned as procurator, perhaps did not know as procurator of the defendant; because no faith was made to him, neither by deed nor by word, regarding their mandate; and thus he did not judicially and legitimately ascertain the persons substantiating the judgment; therefore he judged erroneously. Nor does he say that he appeared as procurator of the defendant, although the judge admonished him as procurator while present there. From which he declares the aforementioned sentence null; because the party was not informed of his power, and legitimate citation was not made, and the tenor of the commission was not inserted in the citation with the force of the mandate, if it appeared to have emanated from the lord of the city, who could not commit the sentence, as is perceived, since he was neither Emperor, nor could even they remove the defense of the said defendant, argument from c. Pastoralis, De res iudicata. Nor was a term given for receiving and opposing, nor for alleging anything, as has been said.

Furthermore, the citation to hear the sentence was made for one hour, namely after the third hour; and in another, he judged in the third hour against the said Bartolus in l. Si, ff., Quod vi aut clam.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the understanding of the last law, § "who necessarily," in the Digest, title "If a woman in possession in the name of the womb."
2. Whether a possessor may be expelled by military force, even by virtue of a rescript.
3. Whether one must abide by a judgment from which no appeal was taken, or whether it may be declared null.
4. When a possessory action is said to be mixed, and whether it is so called from that circumstance.
5. Whether a judge inferior to the prince may commit [a case] without observing the order of jurisdiction, or with appeal removed.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Although the aforementioned point has been fully alleged, and the truth has been sufficiently touched upon by way of allegations:

† However, because this question appears to be a case of law, as the glossa ordinaria states in D. si ventris nomine (39.5), where it is said that if a woman has been put in possession and that possession has been transferred by fraud or to another, in l. 1, § qui necessario, which section has two interpretations, it is necessary to examine which interpretation is more correct; once this is seen, it will appear what the law is regarding the proposed question. Behold, therefore, the law says that if a woman put in possession on account of the womb transferred the possession to another by delivering it in any manner or title, and afterwards it appears that she was not legitimately put in possession because she was not pregnant, such possession is not taken away from him to whom the praetorian delivery was made, or by the hand of the officials. But the owner and true possessor will act more properly and civilly if he converts such holder by means of an interdict. And this is explained in one way as the interdict uti possidetis, because the one put in possession did not possess, but the adversary did. In another way it is explained, namely, by the interdict si ventris nomine, etc., and as it is explained by the interdict uti possidetis. That section sets forth a certain general doctrine, very notable, that he who possesses civilly and naturally cannot expel the holder by his own authority, nor without the order of judicial proceedings; but he must bring the interdict uti possidetis when the detainer has a cause from the possessor. But from one put in possession, or another third party.

And that this possessor ought not to be expelled by military or predatory force, unless due order is observed. And this reading is held by Master Bartolus; he holds the same in l. 3, C. de pign., in his commentary. And according to this, although the chapter might have justice on its side in this: because since he was not cited, and thus possession could not be taken from him, as C. unde vi, l. meminerint; and l. si quis in tantam; and C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. fi.; and C. de pac., l. si pacto, quo poenam; and C. si propter publicas pensitationes, l. si deserta; and l. cum miles, § 1, ff. qui ex causa mai.; and there noted; and also because the said missio ought to have been revoked in fact, insofar as it proceeded in fact: because just as the judge was ready to grant it, so he ought to be ready to revoke it, as ff. si mulier ventris nomine in possessione calumniae causa fuisse dicatur, l. 1, § et hoc edict.; and noted in l. minor, in princ., ff. de evict.; and by Baldus de Ubaldis in l. 1, § item nuntiatio in omnibus, ff. de operis novi nuntiatione, there noted. Nevertheless, after the transfer of possession to the other party has been made, and the said possessor did not defend his possession, when he could have defended it both in law and in fact, as C. quod cum eo, l. si servus; and C. de iure fisci, l. prohibitus; and C. de metatis, l. devotum; and when he was negligent for a long time and suffered the building to be erected, he lost possession through his own fault, as ff. de usucap., l. fur., § 1. There is no reason why possession should be taken from the bona fide purchaser without a libel being offered, nor without a trial being ordered, since in any interdict a libel must be offered and the cause contested, as Inst. de interdictis, § hodie; and C. de momentanea possessione, l. 1. And especially since the said bona fide possessor would have restitution for expenses made for the perpetual utility of the thing, as fully noted in l. in fundo, ff. de rei vendita. Nor does the rescript of the said Marquess avail: because rescripts obtained contrary to law are not valid, as C. de precibus imperatoris offerendis, l. 1; and l. rescripta; and the said l. meminerint. And therefore I conclude that all innovations made under the pretext of the said rescript ought to be revoked: saving and reserving the rights of both parties in other respects; neither party by this falls from its right: for although the hand of nullity might be invoked in fact before any cognition of the cause, nevertheless the penalty of the law meminerint has no place, because the party does not claim to have taken the law into its own authority; and this is the true opinion.

But it is doubted: because the sentence was pronounced against the said [party] and no appeal was taken, whether for this reason the said sentence must be upheld. And it seems that it should, by the general rule. For he ought to have appealed if the sentence displeased him, as in C. si saepius restitutio in integrum postuletur, l. 1. Moreover, the said sentence appears to have been rendered in a possessory action, from which no appeal could be taken, as in C. si de momento possessorio, l. 1. But the contrary must be said: because the said sentence was pronounced without a libel being presented and without the cause being joined; and thus it can undoubtedly be declared null. The case is in the unique decretal, de re iudicata.

† Moreover, this is not a pure possessory judgment, but a mixed one: since the prince ordered that the right of both parties be cognized both in the petitory and in the possessory; and the commissioner reported on both; as we say in a similar case, when a sentence is pronounced under a condition, e.g., l. si quis in tantam. It makes what is noted in extra de resti. spo. c. cum ad sedem. Furthermore, execution could not take place within the time for appealing, as in c. non solum. extra de ap. li. 6. Moreover, it is not necessary to dispute about the appeal at that time: because, as I said, the sentence was rendered contrary to the order of judicial proceedings, as in l. prolatum. It makes what is noted in c. saepe. de verb. sign. in cle. in that question:

Whether a lower authority may cognize or delegate jurisdiction without observing the order of judicial proceedings. The glossa ordinaria there holds that it may not; nevertheless, because lords observe the contrary and it is the common custom of lords, where the prince of the city has expressly delegated, the delegation shall be upheld; provided, however, that he may not delegate with appeal removed, because this cannot be done except by the Pope and the Emperor alone, as in C. de sen. et interlo. om. iu. l. cum soli. Moreover, a rescript of the prince must be understood as presupposing prior cognizance of the case, even if he delegates the execution of a matter to be judged, and not one already judged, as in C. si contra ius, uel uti. publicam l. si cognitio; and extra de iudi. c. exhibita; and extra de rescri. c. ij. and c. causam quę. Finally, I conclude, as I said above, that the said buyer ought not and could not be deprived of his possession with all judicial order disregarded, especially since he had a right of retention on account of expenses, and also because the Emperor is never understood to deprive anyone of legitimate defenses, as noted in C. de adul. l. ita pudor. and l. 1. §. 1. ff. quod ui, aut clam, lest occasion for injury arise, from which laws arise. And also because the said person, according to what is alleged, was a necessary possessor.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required for the prescription of ecclesiastical things.
2. A seller or exchanger cannot claim that he has a right of servitude in the thing sold or exchanged, unless it has been stated.
3. The prince ought to punish the multitude more mildly, but the principal offenders of the crime more severely.
1. Whether a contemner of the king's mandate should be punished.
2. The repair of damages is proved by oath.
3. Cities and universities can commit offenses.
body: In the Name of the Lord, Amen. Venerable father in Christ, and lord, Lord Gerard, cellarer of the house of blessed Anthony the Greater, and also preceptor of the house of blessed Anthony of Reverso, in the name of the said house of blessed Anthony of Reverso, holds certain meadows and possessions situated in the boundaries of the territory of Ripularum, and pertaining to the said house of Reverso. The commune and the inhabitants of the said place of Ripularum claim the right to demand [grazing rights] in the said meadows, both by long-standing custom and by their statutes.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned allegations are valid in law or not. And indeed, that the custom should be followed: because servitudes, both urban and rural, can be acquired by custom, as in D. 8.3.24 § si constat. They can also be acquired by prescription, as in D. 15.1.14 § si quis diuturno. They can also be acquired by indirect proof, by practicing the gloss quae est in D. 22.1.10. On the contrary is the truth itself: because in matters concerning the prescription of church property, or in obtaining it by custom, a title is required from which good faith arises, as in c. ad decimas, X 5.16.6, and X 4.3.1, and in c. malae fidei, X 1.3.32. Moreover, a statute or custom of laymen concerning church property is not valid, as in X 1.10.1. Indeed, those who enact laws against the freedom of ecclesiastical things seem to enact laws against the freedom of the Church itself. Thus says the text, C. 1.3.1. And therefore, those who enact such laws or usurp custom are excommunicated, or at least subject to the royal ban and outlawry, as in C. 1.3.2. Moreover, these laymen can also be in quasi-possession of a servitude: because quasi-possession of servitudes is not acquired without the tolerance of the owner, as in C. 3.33.2 and D. 7.1.1. For he who possesses superficially against the objection of the owner does not possess essentially: because he does not possess the right of servitude, as in D. 15.1.14 § si quis diuturno. For in corporeal things, tolerance of the adversary is always required at the beginning of acquiring quasi-possession, although it is not required afterwards in its continuation: because the beginning of possession must be considered, as in D. 43.17.1.

† Now remains another point: because the aforementioned men of Ripulo and the commune exchanged certain meadows with the aforementioned house of Blessed Anthony of Reverso, and nevertheless, in those things which they gave in exchange, they do not wish to pasture. It is asked, what is the law. I answer that they cannot: because he who sells or exchanges his thing must deliver possession free and clear of all burden of servitudes, as in D. de actione empti, l. si, and l. ratio, in principio; and this is expressly noted in C. de evictione, l. ex praediis. Moreover, a seller or exchanger who did not reserve a servitude for himself can impose no servitude, as in D. de servitute praediorum rusticorum, l. si in venditione. This also appears from necessary reason: because the meadows of the said community did not serve the said community; for one’s own thing serves no one; therefore, by delivering the said meadows, they delivered them free, and thus they cannot pasture in them, as in D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. iure communi. Now let us see by what penalty those of Ripulo are to be punished: for they have sinned in multiple ways. First, by violating the liberty of ecclesiastical things, whence they ought to be placed under ban, and may be plundered with impunity by order of the superior until they submit, as in c. 1, §. ultimo, de milite vasallo qui contumax est. Moreover, they ought to be punished because they took up arms without the prince’s command, as in l. 1, C. ut armorum usus, lib. 6. Moreover, they have fallen under the Lex Iulia de vi publica, which applies even to violent disturbance committed with arms, and especially by a multitude of men, as in l. 3, D. ad Legem Iuliam maiestatis, and l. 1, D. ad Legem Iuliam de vi publica. Moreover, they ought to be punished as rebels if they were subjects of the Lord Count of Savoy: because they used both his banners and his missions in a contrary manner. And it is written that he who does not obey the prince shall die the death, as in Extra de maiore et obediencia.

The Prince, by way of indulgence, dealt more mildly with that reckless person, who is punished according to common practice; yet he dealt more harshly with the principal offenders: for when many are involved, an example must be made, as stated in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Aut facta*, section *Si*. For mercy must be shown to the multitude, because, as the blessed Augustine says, severity must be mitigated where the slaughter of many lies; but with those who are the principal authors of the crime, the utmost severity must be observed, so that they may be drawn as an example, and the punishment of one may serve as a deterrent to many, as in law 1 of the Code, *Ad legem Iuliam de repetundis*.

† Add, whether a contemner of the king’s mandate ought to be punished with a penalty. It seems that he should: for this is the sentence of God, whose judgment the Prince follows, as is read in C. de nuptiis, l. ultima, and c. 1, regum: “Let him who does not obey the Prince die the death,” as in the said c. 2, extra de maiestate et obedientia. Moreover, the mandate of the Prince is law, and certainly general, if it is enclosed in the body of the law; otherwise, it is special to that business upon which the mandate itself is directed, as in Auth. de mandatis principum, in principio, col. 3, and C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. 2, and ff. de constitutionibus principum, l. 1. And thus the contemner of this mandate, as a violator of the law, deserves to be punished capitally, as C. de impositione lucrativa descendentium, l. si filius, lib. 11. Nor is this surprising. For even he who does not observe the mandates of a military commander, and all contumacy nullity against his own proposal, is punished with the loss of head, as ff. de remilitantibus, l. 3, §. in bello, and l. omne delictum, §. contumacia. But this statement is harsh, that anyone should be punished capitally for perhaps slight disobedience. The law also sometimes imposes a lesser penalty, such as deportation, on the violator of the law, as C. de funeribus limitandis, l. si filius, lib. 11. And sometimes without any penalty, as in Auth. de nuptiis, §. ascripticio, col. 4. And elsewhere it tolerates the importunity of the trampled law, as C. de vestibus et elephantis, l. temperent, lib. 11. And therefore it must be distinguished thus: if a certain penalty is attached to the king’s mandate, then for the contempt it suffices that that penalty be inflicted, as in the above-quoted l. in quibus, where a certain penalty is established against the violator of the law, when we ought to be content with the penalties comprehended in the laws, as ff. de verbis obligatio, l. si stipulatio ita facta fuerit. Or if no certain penalty is attached, then the penalty will be extraordinary, and then arbitrary, as C. de thesauris, l. unica, §. pe, lib. 10, and ff. de effractione, l. 1, §. expilatores, and ff. de poenis, l. sanctio legum, since the contemner of this sort commits a crime akin to sacrilege, as appears in C. de diversis rescriptis, l. sacrilegii, de crimine sacrilegii, l. 1 and 2, C. ut diurnum ordo servetur, l. 1, and de errore minuendo anno, lege, l. pe, in fine, and de privilegiis eorum qui in sacro palatio, in fine, lib. 12. The penalty for this crime is extraordinary and arbitrary, namely according to the quality of the person and the condition of the matter, as ff. ad legem Iuliam peculatus, and de sacrilegio, lege, l. §. 1, and l. sacrilegii poenam, in principio. Thus, therefore, the contemner of the royal mandate, in which no certain penalty is added, should be punished extraordinarily, severely or lightly, according to the quality of the person and the condition of the matter contained in the mandate. And so I have found it written that it is observed in the great court, and thus the penalty of contempt may correspond to the offense, as in Auth. ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio, §. sic igitur, in fine, §. 1, col. 2, and ff. de poenis. I do not deny, however, that regard must be had to the fact that in this case, even for slight contempt, a severe penalty may be imposed at the discretion of the judge, as ar. C. de primicerio, l. si, lib. 12, because no sin is so small that it does not become greater on account of contempt, as in Auth. ut omnes obediant iudicibus provincialibus, §. hoc considerantes, col. 5. But by Lombard law, the penalty is imposed according to the royal will, as in l. si quis literas Imperatoris despexit, l. si quis litteras, l. 3, Non obstantibus, l. ultima, C. de nequam poena, because there is a special provision, whose offense is committed and coerced otherwise than common discipline requires, as in the above-quoted l. omne delictum, in principio. It is nevertheless more cautious to attach a penalty to royal mandates altogether. For it is necessary that we be not only restrained by the prohibition of offenses, but also that we instill just fear in transgressors, as in Auth. de depositione et demum inquilinis, §. 1, col. 6. Nor ought it to be that the contemners of this iniquity escape penalties, as in Auth. de funeribus, C. senatus consultum eorum non innixum a creditoribus, circa finem, col. 5. Either, therefore, the question is about the penalty for simple contempt, which is not arbitrary out of fear of the prince. Or to the contempt is annexed another offense, or other offenses, as in the case proposed, the crime of sacrilege, as extra de foro competenti, c. conquestus. It is also a crime under the Lex Iulia de vi publica. It is also the crime of abduction, on account of the animals taken away; and then, on account of the accumulation of so many and so enormous offenses, the most atrocious penalty should be imposed according to the strictness of the law, as C. ad legem Iuliam de vi, l. quia multa facinora, not one offense by the addition of another, as in l. 1, de raptu virginitatis.

† On the restoration of possession. It is also established that when [the facts] cannot be proven individually, an oath shall be accepted, as in C. unde vi, l. si quando; and ff. quod vi, aut clam, l. semper, § in hoc interdicto; and see Innocentius, extra, quod metus causa, c. ult.

† It is established that cities and corporations can commit offenses, as stated in the Digest, under the title "On What is Done Through Fear," in the law "Fear," section "It should be noted." Indeed, even provinces can, as the law states in the title "On the Province of Campania," in the same law, section "And although," in the words "Campania." It supports what we note in the Digest, under the title "On Fraud," in the law "But by that fraud," section 1. And there can be such an offense by which a city is deprived of its name as a city and ceases to have the rights and privileges of a city, as in the Digest, under the title "On Usufruct," in the law "Whether usufruct." It supports what is stated in the Decretals, under the title "On Sentence of Excommunication," in the chapter "Heavy," according to Innocentius, and in the Decretals, under the title "On Restitution of Spoliation," in the chapter "To the Pisans," and under the title "On Prohibition of New Works," in the chapter "Since from the oath," according to Innocentius, and in the Code, under the title "On Military Matters," in the law "Both those who confer," book 12. Nor should it be omitted that to profane the banners of the Prince is a capital offense, as in the law "No one on private estates," etc., laws 1 and 2, and it begins, "That no one [should] royal sails," others have it as a rubric.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an appeal may be made from a subdelegate to the delegate, who reserved to himself nothing of the jurisdiction, etc.
2. If the delegate pronounces that the appeal is invalid, and an appeal is made from him to the Pope, whether the said appeal to him impedes the execution of the sentence passed by the subdelegate.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The Bishop of Vero, as principal executor or delegate, committed the case to his Vicar, reserving nothing for himself regarding jurisdiction. The Vicar rendered a sentence; from that sentence an appeal was made to the Lord Bishop who had subdelegated.

† It is asked whether the said appeal was valid. And it must be said that it was not: because the appeal was made to one who had entirely ceased to be the judge of the case, and thus the appeal was made from the judge to a private person, whom an appeal does not bind under any law, as in the chapter *Super quaestionum*, § *Porro*, *de officio delegati*; and in the chapter *Si delegatus*, § *Ad eum*, *de officio delegati*; law 6; and noted in the *Speculum*, *de appellationibus*, § *Nunc tractemus*, verse *Quid si delegatus*, and the following verse; and according to Innocentius in the chapter *Si pro debilitate*, *de officio delegati*. But if the delegate had not committed his jurisdiction in its entirety, but had reserved some part of the jurisdiction for himself, then one may and must appeal to the sub-delegating delegate himself: according to Hostiensis and all the others. Finally, it happens that the said Lord Bishop pronounced that the appeal interposed to him was not valid; from which pronouncement an appeal was made to the Pope. Now

It is asked: whether the said appeal interposed to the Apostolic See impedes the execution of the sentence passed by the said subdelegate. And it must be said that, by virtue of the appeal, because the said sentence of the subdelegate had become res judicata, it therefore does not impede the execution of the res judicata, since the first appeal was not duly interposed. For one is not first to inquire into the merits of the appeal, but rather into its form and time. To this effect: C. de appel. auth. hodie; and ff. quis, et a quo appelletur, l. si; and C. sen. rescin. non posse, l. 1 and l. si. Therefore, it is not necessary for the subexecutor to cease from the execution of his sentence, for a year is granted, as in extra de offi. dele. c. quaerenti. And these statements are true, unless the sentence itself were null by law and evidently null; for then execution ought to be carried out. And this is not by virtue of the appeal, but by virtue of nullity, when the sentence is null in existence and appearance; otherwise, even then execution would not be impeded, as in l. si, C. de ordi. cogni. and l. 4, § condemnatum, ff. de re iudi. From these it is concluded that the said subexecutor may proceed to execution notwithstanding the said appeals. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The exception of nullity arising from a defect of jurisdiction is always [admissible].
2. Whether a partner can be a judge in the case of a partner.
3. Whether a sentence can be valid in part and invalid in part.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case pending between Bartholomew, son of Paul, and certain others acting on one side, and Nicolaus Baldutii on the other side, the defendant having been summoned before the chamberlain of the butchers’ guild, the matter was so fully and subtly consulted by the advocates of both parties that nothing more can be said beyond measure. And although the aforementioned opinions are in some respects for the plaintiffs and against the defendant, and in others the reverse, namely for the defendant and against the plaintiffs: nevertheless, in effect they conclude almost as one, namely.

† That, assuming the jurisdiction of the chamberlain, execution may be sought of the sentence passed against the said Lord Nicolaus, the defendant; nor may the exception of nullity of the sentence be opposed, notwithstanding the reformation, since the nullity does not arise from a defect of jurisdiction. But if it is such a nullity as denies jurisdiction, it may always be opposed; nor is it properly said to be opposed against the sentence, when the sentence itself is not established, if jurisdiction is not lacking, as in the cited chapter 1, *de sequestro*, in the gloss at the end. It remains now to see whether there was here a defect of jurisdiction.

† And it seems that this is so: because the aforementioned agents in their petition, however framed, state that the said Jac. Herculani, then chamberlain of the said guild of butchers, was a partner of the said agents. To this assertion made in the libel, one must adhere. C. de lib. cum l. precum. ff. fa. haer. l. qui familia. C. de omni agro deser. l. unica. lib. 11. si socius, ergo dominus. ff. proso. l. merito. If he is the owner, then he is a judge in his own cause; therefore, the sentence is null due to lack of jurisdiction. C. ne quis in sua causa. l. 1. ff. de iur. om. iu. l. qui iuris. and de sy. c. ex parte. per Inno. Thus, he could not cognize the case himself, nor through a deputy appointed by him, according to the laws cited above by my lord d. Petrus. And since he who does not have jurisdiction does not confer jurisdiction. And he who has jurisdiction in one matter does not have jurisdiction in another: and he who has no jurisdiction at all cannot render any sentence. C. qui pro sua iuris. l. 1. and there per Cyn. and others. And an exception in the principal jurisdiction operates similarly in the secondary jurisdiction. ff. de neg. gest. l. qui aliena. §. quanquam. What is more: if he is a partner, then he is suspect. de obiecto delicti. c. cum R. canonicus. But the law must proceed without suspicion, as 3. q. 5. ca. quia suspecti. C. de iudi. l. apertissimi. Hence, with respect to the co-partner agents, he could not cognize the case. Moreover, if the sentence is null with respect to one party because it is in his own cause, then it is null with respect to the whole: since a sentence with respect to the same article cannot be valid in part, invalid in part. ff. fa. haer. l. 3. hoc iudicio. C. si aduersus rem iudicatam. I. 1.

To the contrary, that there is no lack of jurisdiction here, seems to be proven thus. This vice-chamberlain, who rendered the sentence, is appointed by virtue of the statute of the universitas of butchers and the craft of the said guild; but the universitas does not give jurisdiction to the rector whom it elected, but the law does, as noted in the gloss in c. 2. ne praelati uices suas. and per Imo. de consti. c. cum accessissent. Hence, although the chamberlain himself [is involved], the vice-chamberlain is not thereby prohibited, since he is said to derive nothing from him, but from the law. Moreover, granted that it is said that this vice-chamberlain, or the chamberlain, by reason of the appointment made by him of the vice-chamberlain, acquired universal jurisdiction, not special jurisdiction with respect to a certain case: and thus in him is found the foundation of jurisdiction, not only with respect to other cases, but also with respect to the certain same case, insofar as it does not concern the things of the chamberlain himself who appointed, but of the agents, since it is between craftsmen, namely concerning a matter pertaining to the craft. de consti. pe. l. 2. in fi. And I believe this last part to be truer, namely: that the said sentence can and ought to be committed to execution for the parties of the said agents. And thus for four parts, since he had jurisdiction over them, the vice-chamberlain who rendered the sentence. But for the fifth part, which touched the said Jac. Herculani, their partner, and the assertion of the said agents, the exception of nullity seems to stand in the way: since it arises in this case from a lack of jurisdiction, because it is in his own cause.

† Nor does it follow from what I said, that a judgment cannot be valid in part and invalid in part with respect to an article; for this is true when the cause’s instance holds over the whole; otherwise, if it were perempted in part, then it suffices that pronouncement be made in that part in which the judge’s authority holds. D. 24.3.11 (Si constante), §. Si. Hence, if the defendant is summoned in an action for the recovery of property, and it is established that he possesses only half, the judgment of the judge who condemned him in that half is valid, even though he said nothing about the other half; because, for that part which he does not possess, the judge’s authority does not hold. D. 6.1.173 (Fin.), according to Bartolus in the said §. Si. Thus, in the present case, the judgment is divided with respect to the same article, since jurisdiction did not exist with regard to the part concerning the same chamberlain; and consequently, neither did judicial authority, nor instance. Furthermore, it does not follow that, because he was a partner, he was therefore suspect. For although the judge was suspect, nevertheless, even though he may be declared such on account of suspicion, the judgment rendered by him in the meantime is valid. X. 2.1.14 (Iudex ab apostolica), according to the gloss. Moreover, it does not follow that the plaintiffs appear to contradict themselves in their petition, where they state that the said Jacobus Herculani, their partners, expected the said pigs, and that they then pertained by right of ownership, or quasi-ownership, to the said plaintiffs; for I understand this in favor of the plaintiffs, so that the contradiction of the libel may be avoided; because, provided the petition is tolerable, it must be admitted. X. 2.1.10 (Examinata), according to Innocentius; and as to the interpretation of the libel, the plaintiff is favored, as noted by Dynus in X. 5.12.1 (Cum sunt partium). And thus I believe it to be the law in the aforementioned question. And thus I say and advise, I, Franciscus, son of Lord Baldus of Perugia. And thus I subscribed and sealed this to the faith. But if the truth be otherwise, let that be followed; for the judge is one of truth and equity.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What are called new taxes, and what are ancient, and for what period they are prescribed. And no. 3.
2. What is meant by notoriety.
3. What is meant by an ancient fief.
4. General custom and the confirmation of the prince induce good faith.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of the rescript of our most illustrious lord command that vain tolls be revoked, adding these words: "not intending thereby to derogate in any way from the said statutes or from any ancient customs of the said community of Piacenza." Moreover, it must be added that the aforesaid most illustrious lord had confirmed the old statutes.

† Now it is asked, which tolls are called new, and which ancient, and which may be exacted, and which may not be exacted. And it seems that ancient tolls are those which have been prescribed by a space of time, of which contrary memory does not exist. For the exaction of tolls does not have a continuous cause, just as neither walking nor acting, as in D. de serv. rust. praed. l. foramen. And this is proved by that evident reason: because such tolls are said to be servitudes, or in the manner of servitudes. The text is noted in 18. q. 2. c. servitium. Therefore, the same time is required in prescribing servitudes which never continue to themselves, but are broken by necessary and natural interruption, as in l. hoc iure. §. ductus aquae. D. de aqua quo. et est. And speaking properly, prescription does not fall upon them: because prescription is the continuation of time. etc. as in D. de usuc. l. 1. and 2. but it is rather a certain custom, which does not require the continuation of any possession, but successive acts inducing custom, as in D. de legi. l. de quibus. §. inveterata. Moreover, the exactions of tolls are against the law, therefore they cannot be prescribed, as in Auth. ut nulli iudi. §. 1. nisi tempore. of which I have spoken, as noted in D. de ver. sig. l. minus proprie. Also, to exact tolls pertains to royal rights, not to cities, as in c. 1. quae sint regaliae. col. 10. Also, in this prescription, the knowledge of him to whom the tolls pertain is required, as in C. de serv. et aqua. l. 2. For unless he to whom the superiority pertains knows, he who uses seems to use secretly, and in bad faith: especially because he ought to know that the thing pertains to another, because even he himself possessed it previously, as in l. clam possidere. in prin. D. de acqui. pos. Also because he ought to suspect that he can be repelled by the authority of the law, and the power of the prince, as in extra de resti. spo. c. olim. and extra de proba. c. licet causam. Bartolus says, that the knowledge of the president of the province suffices. D. de publica. l. publicanus. §. in vectigalibus. Which does not seem true: because it pertains to the president to defend the rights of the prince, not to dissipate them, as in D. quod vi, aut clam. l. prohibere. §. plane. just as for prescribing a servitude, the knowledge of the procurator does not suffice, but that of the owner: because the procurator cannot prejudice the owner in matters acquired, but only in matters seeking: unless he has a special mandate, or a universal one with liberty, as in D. de peculio. l. quantuberonis. §. aliae causae. D. de offi. procur. Caes. l. 1. and especially from a gratuitous cause. C. de pac. l. pactum curato. C. de acqui. pos. l. si. C. si per vim, vel alio modo. l. 1. in fi. whence the knowledge, or consciousness, of the president does not prejudice the fiscal right, whatever Bartolus says to the contrary. It seems that the prescription of 40 years suffices, because in this time the right is prescribed: I do not say against the fisc, but against private persons to their prejudice, as in C. de praescr. 30. an. l. competit. and the knowledge of those private persons suffices: because against them, however, it is prescribed: nor is the consciousness of the prince, or president, required: because their right is not touched, as noted by Innocentius in de postu. praela. c. bone. Also, this prescription is against uncertain persons, and against the very, so to speak, multitude, whence this cannot be justly notorious: because it is patent to the multitude. For this is the description of the notorious,

† namely, it is notorious, that which is openly known to the common people, so that there is no need to prove it, according to that saying: "Their sound has gone out into all the earth." And many hold this opinion, for although according to the common law tolls and duties belong to the Emperor, nevertheless this is not observed in Italy: because the Emperor does not in fact collect them, and therefore every city and municipality having public land pertaining to itself, by reason of that public land, collects tolls, guidages, and pedages. We see this to have been usurped, nor can we, so to speak, re-navigate the whole world; it is a coarse term of rustics. For it is most difficult to destroy things confirmed by custom, as in the Digest, On Promises, l. Imperator. For the custom of most faithful antiquity must be followed, as in the Code, On Wills, l. testamenta omnia. Moreover, our magnificence had confirmed the statutes, after which confirmation certain innovations were made. Then he removed those innovations: adding, without derogating from the ancient statutes and customs. From which it appears that he removed the new and confirmed the old. He decreed this most justly: for the case is found in both parts in the Extravagant, On Oaths, c. tua nos.

† Moreover, if it is asked what is new and what is old, it is sufficiently clear from the rescript: for that which was renewed by confirmation is new; whereas that which was previously in use is old. This is proven with respect to both limbs. D. de constitutionibus principum, l. in rebus nouis, where it is said that in establishing matters, the utility must be evident, so that one may depart from that law which long ago seemed equitable. This is also expressly apparent. D. de legibus, l. ideo, because whether we consider the force of confirmation, or the force of the rescript, or the proper signification of the words, that which has been customary for forty years is called old. To this effect is C. de iure fideicommissorum, l. super creandis, lib. 10, and Extr. de decimis, c. quanuis, in the major gloss. And therefore, concluding, I say that since our lord confirmed the ancient statutes, they are understood to be strengthened by this decretal letter of our lord; and this strengthening operates retroactively, as in Auth. de filiis ante dotem instructis, na., §. si, and D. de liberis et posthumis legatis, l. Aurelius, §. testamento.

† Moreover, that which lasted for several generations and has passed away is called ancient, as is evident in the case of fiefs. But this custom has passed down to posterity; therefore, it is ancient. And we are not attacking a new matter, but an ancient one, as stated in C. de iudiciis, l. rem non nouam, in principio; and in C. de furtis, l. apud antiquos. This word, "ancient," is understood according to the subject matter at hand, and also according to the intention of the one asserting it, which is established here by reference to the statutes, as in C. de senibus, quae sine certa quantitate, l. haec sententia. Furthermore, whether we consider the usage of speech according to the common law, which employs the term "longissimum" (very long), and thus calls a period of forty years more than ancient, or whether we examine the usage of speech of the common people, the same must be said. For the common people, when speaking of this period, call that thing ancient which has been given to the course of so much time. C. ne rei dominicae, vel templorum, l. universas. The objection based on what is said about the prescription of time, of which there is no memory of the contrary, does not hold; because even if that opinion were true in the case of possessors in bad faith, as in Extra de rescriptionibus, c. quoniam omne, it is nevertheless false in the case of possessors in good faith.

† Moreover, general custom induces good faith. Likewise, the confirmation of the prince, or his decree, as in the Digest, On the River, l. quominus, and it is expressly stated there. Since, therefore, the prince most justly decreed, the rescript of the prince must be observed, as in the Digest, On the Peculium Legacy, l. si peculium, §. sicut qui rei suae, that is, he who could impose whatever law he wished upon tolls, guidages, and revenues which truly pertain to him, as one exercising a sort of monarchy over his lands, as in the Digest, On the Dotal Agreement, l. ob res, §. extraneus. And thus I, Ioaunes Zenobius de Vbaldis of Perugia, doctor of laws, knight, and count of the sacred palace, declare: saving the judgment of a more authoritative sentence, as in the Digest, Who Has a Better Right to Pledge, l. Claudius felix, and by reason of correct speech, as in the Code, On Gold and Silver Legacies, Plautius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the Emperor is bound to observe pacts and contracts made with a certain city or baron, and what is the case regarding his successor.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The words of Cynus in his golden lecture, C. de legibus, l. digna vox, are as follows. Finally, it must be done that Guido of Susa formulates this question:

Whether, if the Emperor enters into certain pacts with a certain city or baron, he is bound to observe them, both he himself and his successors. And it seems that he is not, as in *l. princeps*, D. eod., and D. de legatis 3, *l. si quis*, in principio; and because an equal has no authority over an equal, as in *l. nam magistratus*, D. de arbitris, and *l. ille, a quo*, § *tempestiuum*, D. ad Trebellianum. For this part, it serves below, D. de curatore, *l. euacuatis*, lib. 10. On the contrary, it seems that he is, for it is a serious matter to break faith, as in D. de constituta pecunia, *l. 1*; and the natural laws urge that pacts be observed, and faith is to be kept even with enemies, as in D. de legibus, *l. ultima*, and D. de censibus, *l. 1*. Moreover, this is supported here by *l. quia honestas ligat etiam principem*: as is evident here from what I said above; and nothing is more owed to a man than to keep pacts, as in *l. 1*, D. de pactis. For this, it serves below, D. qui testamento facere possunt, *l. ex imperfecto*, and D. de legatis 3, *l. ex imperfecto*, and below, D. de testamento militis, *l. quae a patre*. Moreover, the contract of the prince is law, as below, D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, *l. ultima*. Therefore, etc. And this opinion is held by Guido himself. For which, it serves Extra, de probationibus, cap. 1. Others distinguish whether there was justice on the other side, or whether there was injustice and fraud there: and in the first case, the pact and composition are valid; in the second, they are not, by argument of those things noted below, D. de transactionibus, *l. 2*, and D. de conditionibus indebiti, *l. in summa*, in principio. And it can be just for subjects to resist, if on the part of the lord there is unjust and notorious violence, as below, D. de iure fisci, *l. de prohibendo*, lib. 10.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A man who granted a dotal estate in emphyteusis with the agreement that all improvements should be restored solely to the wife, and that the said man would be liable for the expenses incurred by the emphyteuta: whether he is bound if the expenses are great; and whether the man is understood by this agreement to have made a donation to the wife, or to have managed her affairs.
2. Add the following opinion.
body: Case. A husband gave a dotal estate in emphyteutic lease on the condition that all improvements should be restored to the wife upon dissolution of the marriage, while he himself was bound to reimburse the expenses. It happened that the emphyteuta incurred great expenses on a thing of little value. The question is: what is the law?

I answer that a man is understood to have permitted moderate expenses, not those incurred rashly or beyond measure; because this promise must be understood with the moderation of blameless expenditure, as in the Digest, On Pledge and Hypothec, law *Si servos*; and in the Digest, On Negotiorum Gestio, law *Sed an ultro*, section 1, even if the thing has been greatly improved beyond the amount of the expenses; because it does not appear that this was considered, as in the Digest, On Servitudes, law *Si cui*; and it supports the rule in the Digest, On Negotiorum Gestio, law *Ex duobus*, which leaves it to the discretion of a good man, as in the aforementioned law *Si servus* at the end.

† Subsequently, it is asked whether, by this pact, it is understood that the husband made a donation to the wife, or that he managed her affairs. And I say that, in case of doubt, it is understood that he managed her affairs up to a reasonable quantity of expenses, as if he had made the expenditure for himself. For an act indifferent to donation and to the management of affairs is never presumed to be a donation; because donation is a loss, as in D. de solutionibus, l. si cum aurum. It remains, therefore, that the expenditure made by the husband can be recovered up to a moderate amount; beyond that, the husband does not recover from the wife, nor is he held liable in the pending matter. But if it were an express donation, the husband would not be liable in any way; because it would appear that the husband intervened for the wife with the intent to donate, by assuming the obligation in favor of the wife, as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem. The aforementioned rule that one should not be enriched at another’s loss does not apply. For this fails in an emphyteutic contract. And note, through Bartolus in l. 1, D. de superficie. It also fails wherever one expends on another’s thing, not by managing the owner’s affairs, as in D. de conditione indebiti, l. si in area. Also, this expenditure was made beyond the limit, therefore it is reduced to the limit, as noted in D. de usuris, l. placuit. Also, it is expressly stated in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. ex duobus. On the matter of expenditures, fully noted in D. de re vendicata, l. in fundo. And it applies in the same title, l. habitator. I, Baldus. To the same effect.

CONSILIVM CCCLXXIII. In the Name of the Lord, Amen. A husband granted a dotal urban estate in perpetual emphyteusis on the condition that, in the event of the restitution of the dowry, it should be restored to the wife freely and unencumbered by the emphyteuta; in that case, the husband is bound to have all improvements estimated for the emphyteuta by two lawful men chosen by the parties. Later, the emphyteuta made certain improvements. And finally, the case of the restitution of the dowry occurred. Whereupon a dispute arose between the common daughter of the aforementioned husband, as heir, and the mother, the aforementioned wife. An arbitral sentence was rendered between them, whereby the aforementioned mother was to be the usufructuary of the said estate, and the daughter the owner, with the burden of indemnifying the said mother against the aforementioned improvements, if any were due by law. Then the woman and the aforementioned wife claimed the said dotal estate. And a sentence was rendered in her favor, the effect of which was that the aforementioned estate, mentioned in the libel, belonged and pertained by full right to the said woman and wife; and that the said emphyteuta was bound to release and disencumber the said estate to the said woman or her lawful procurator; in such a way, namely, that the said emphyteuta should have and hold retention of the said estate by name and on account of the expenses made by the said emphyteuta in the said estate up to a certain term, within which the said emphyteuta could and might obtain and have the said expenses and improvements made in the said estate from the heirs in the goods and inheritance of the aforementioned deceased husband, according to the form and tenor of the aforementioned concession. After the expiration of that term, whether the said emphyteuta had obtained the said expenses and improvements from the aforementioned heirs and inheritance or not, nevertheless from that time forth the said emphyteuta is bound to freely release the said estate to the aforementioned wife, without any deduction of expenses and improvements; because so it was debated and agreed in the said instrument of concession. It is therefore asked whether the recovery of the said expenses and the said improvements is available against the aforementioned heir. And it seems that it is, because it was so specially agreed in the said emphyteutic contract. For pacts in an emphyteutic contract are to be observed, as in C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. 2. Moreover, the alienation of a dotal thing, even made with knowledge, is valid to the prejudice of the alienator personally for the observance of that contract, as in D. de usucapione, l. cum vir. Moreover, the emphyteuta of a dotal thing, who has knowledge, is a wrongdoer; therefore he has no retention against the woman claiming the dowry, as in Inst. de rerum divisione, §. ex diverso; C. de re vendicata, l. domum; and what is noted there in D. eodem, l. in fundo. Merely in subsidiary recourse against the heirs of the husband, especially by pact, he has a right of action, as in the said law and wife.

On the contrary, it seems that, since the municipal statute provides that anyone may stipulate and pact for another, and consequently, by the pact of the husband, the emphyteuta was bound to the woman for the restitution of the dowry with respect to the said estate conditionally, i.e., upon the dissolution of the marriage; just as if he were a quasi-corresponding debtor. Therefore, since he expended on the dotal thing without the woman’s will, or for the expenses of the dowry, the retention of the dowry itself is a singular privilege, but against the woman he has the recovery of expenses by the action of negotiorum gestio, similar to that of the husband, as if he had made expenditures in the dotal thing with the intent of recovering and managing the woman’s affairs, as all these things are proven. C. de re uxoria actione, l. sed nec ob impensas; and D. de impensis in rebus dotalibus factis, l. quod dictum, §. si dos; and l. voluntarie, in fine; and D. de solutionibus, l. divor., §. donationes. And by this, it does not obstruct what is commonly said, namely, that for expenses even made in good faith, no action is given, but only retention. D. de conditione indebiti, l. si in area. For that applies whenever one expends on another’s thing as if it were his own, believing he has managed his own affair and not another’s. And consequently, not with the intent of obligating another to him for so much; because in that case, since no one is contracted with in subsidiary recourse, retention is given. But in the proposed case, since he knew that he was making expenditures on a dotal thing, subject to restitution in the event of the condition, in which case he is believed to have expended with the intent of recovering and then managing another’s affair; whereby it happens that, regularly, for such expenditures in the event of the condition, he has the benefit of retaining. And if perhaps he should voluntarily restore the thing, as if he had paid more than was due, for the expenses he would have the condictio incerti, by which he would condemn the holder of the improved thing, as in D. de legatis 1, l. quod si nulla; and D. de conditione indebiti, l. qui exce., §. si pars. But in the dowry, in favor of the woman, retention ceases, and consequently the condictio incerti; and the action of negotiorum gestio is available, as by the laws cited above. Therefore, it is believed that the husband intervened for the woman by that pact, and consequently, since the woman is absolutely freed, as is proposed, from the said improvements: that exception of res iudicata, which benefits the woman, also benefits the heir of the husband as surety, as in D. de exceptionibus, l. exceptiones, §. rei. Nor does that sentence harm, insofar as it reserved the petition not for improvements against the heir of the husband; because res inter alios acta, etc., does not apply. If anyone says that the husband wished that estate, in the case of the restitution of the dowry, to be rendered free and unencumbered to the woman by the emphyteuta, and consequently it seems that he assumed the burden of improvements and intervened for the said woman with the intent of donating to himself; for that which is to be noted is that, as I said, the burden of improvements and expenses made in the dotal thing does not prevent the dotal thing from being rendered freely and unencumbered to the woman. But after it is rendered, provision is made in the pending matter in the thing itself by the right of action, as I said. Therefore, that pact contains nothing new in the dotal thing for that reason, notwithstanding. Nevertheless, the husband is understood to have stood surety for the future obligation and action of negotiorum gestio to be contracted against the woman; since a surety can also be added to a future obligation, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si stipulatus, §. adhiberi. Indeed, even if it were believed that the husband intervened with the intent of donating the expenses to the wife, it would still be of no moment; and the action against the woman would be restored by the law itself, since donation between husband and wife is forbidden, even of expenses made in the dotal thing, as in D. de impensis in rebus dotalibus factis, l. in voluptariis, §. 1; nor is it confirmed by death, as if beginning from a promise, as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Papinianus. Moreover, by virtue of any donation beyond 60 solidi, because not insinuated, it is certain that even from this head, it cannot be confirmed in any way by death. Finally, the arbitral sentence rendered between mother and daughter does not obstruct. First, because res inter alios acta, etc., and therefore it did not deserve to be alleged in the case pending between the daughter and the heir by the said emphyteuta, it profits the emphyteuta nothing. Moreover, the woman was also definitively absolved from these improvements. That sentence creates right and absorbs the force of the other arbitral sentence; especially because the daughter, by that arbitral sentence, was not bound to anything other than exonerating the woman and the aforementioned mother, who was later by that judicial sentence exonerated and absolved from the said improvements. That sentence passed into res iudicata. From which it is concluded for the heir against the emphyteuta, notwithstanding the allegations for the part of the emphyteuta, to which it is sufficiently clear from the foregoing that response has been made.

In the name of the Lord, Amen. A husband granted an urban dotal estate into perpetual emphyteusis with the clause that in the event of the dowry having to be restored, it would be restored freely and unencumbered to the wife by the emphyteuta: in that event, the husband is held to all improvements, to be valued for the emphyteuta by two lawful men chosen by the parties. Afterwards, the emphyteuta made certain improvements; and eventually, the occasion of restoring the dowry occurred. Wherefore a dispute arose between the common daughter, heir of the aforesaid husband, and the mother and aforesaid wife. An arbitral award was rendered between them, whereby the aforesaid mother would be the usufructuary of that estate and the daughter the owner, with the burden of holding the said mother harmless from the aforesaid improvements, if any were due by law. Thereafter the woman and aforesaid wife demanded the said dotal estate, and a sentence was rendered in her favor whose operative text provided that the aforesaid estate, whereof mention was made in the petition, belongs and pertains by full right to the said woman and wife, and that the said emphyteuta is bound to surrender and clear the said estate to the said woman or her lawful procurator: in such manner, namely, that the said emphyteuta has and ought to have retention of the said estate in the name and on the occasion of the expenses made by that emphyteuta upon the aforesaid estate until a certain term, within which the emphyteuta himself can and may recover and have the said expenses and improvements made on the aforesaid estate from the heirs out of the property and inheritance of the aforesaid granting husband according to the form and tenor of the aforesaid grant; which term having elapsed, whether the said emphyteuta has recovered the said expenses and improvements from the heirs and in the aforesaid inheritance or not, the aforesaid emphyteuta shall nevertheless thenceforth be bound to surrender the aforesaid estate freely and without any deduction for expenses and improvements to the aforesaid wife, because it was so negotiated and agreed in the said instrument of grant. It is therefore asked whether an action to recover the said expenses and the said improvements lies against the aforesaid heir. And it seems that it does, because it was specially so agreed in the said emphyteutic contract; and all uncertain pacts in an emphyteutic contract must be observed, as in C. de iure emphy. l. 2. Furthermore, an alienation of a dotal property, even when made to one who has knowledge, is valid to the prejudice of the alienor and binds him personally to the observance of that contract, as in ff. de vsuca. l. cum vir. Furthermore, an emphyteuta of a dotal thing who has knowledge is [subject to] mala fides; therefore, he has no retention against the woman recovering her dowry, as in instit. de rerum diui. §. ex diuerso, C. de rei ven. l. domum, and what is noted there, ff. eo. l. in fundo; deservedly, in subsidy, he has recourse against the heirs of the husband, especially from the pact, as in d. l. et vxor. To the contrary it seems, since it is provided by municipal statute that anyone may stipulate and contract for another, and thus consequently by the husband's pact the emphyteuta was bound to the woman for the restitution of the dowry with respect to the aforesaid estate conditionally, namely, upon dissolution of the marriage, just like a quasi-co-debtor. When therefore retention is impeded in a dotal matter without the woman's consent—namely, on account of dotal outlays—retention of the dowry itself is barred by a singular privilege, but he has recovery of expenses against the woman through the action for unauthorized management of affairs (actio negotiorum gestorum) after the manner of a husband, as if he made the outlays on the dotal property with the intention of recovering them and managing the woman's business, as all these things are proved in C. de rei vxor. act. l. sed nec ob impensas, and ff. de impen. in reb. do. factis. l. quod dictu. §. si dos, and l. voluntarie in fine, and sol. ma. l. diuor. §. donationes; and by this it is not an objection which is commonly said, namely, that on account of expenses, even those made in good faith, no action is given but only retention, ff. de cond. indeb. l. si in area; for that proceeds whenever someone expends on another's property as if on his own, believing he has managed his own business and not another's, and consequently not with the intention of binding another to himself for so much, because in that case, since one quasi-contracts with no one in subsidy, retention is granted; but in the proposed question, he who made the outlays knew that the property was dotal and subject to restitution upon the occurrence of the condition, in which case he is believed to have made outlays with the intention of recovering and then managing another's business; whence it happens that regularly on account of such outlays upon the occurrence of the condition he would have the benefit of retaining, and if by chance he were voluntarily to restore the thing, as if he had paid more than was due, on account of the expenses he would have a condictio incerti, through which he would recover the value of the improved thing, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. quod si nulla, and de condi. inde. l. qui exce. §. si pars. In the case of a dowry, however, in its favor retention ceases, and consequently the condictio incerti ceases, and the actio negotiorum gestorum is available, as in the laws cited above. Accordingly, the husband is believed from that pact to have intervened for the woman, and consequently, because the woman has been absolved, as is proposed, from those improvements, that exception of res judicata which benefits the woman also benefits the heir of the husband as guarantor, as in ff. de exce. l. exceptiones. §. rei. Nor does that sentence hurt, insofar as it reserved the claim for the improvements against the heir of the husband, because a matter conducted between others, etc.; nor is it an objection if someone says that the husband wished that estate, in the event of restoring the dowry, to be returned free and unencumbered to the woman by the emphyteuta, and consequently seems to have undertaken the burden of the improvements and to have intervened for that woman with the intention of donating to her; for that must be noted, that as I said, the burden of improvements and expenses made on a dotal property does not prevent the dotal thing from having to be returned freely and expeditiously to the woman, but after it has been returned, provision is made pending the right of action in the thing itself, as I have said. Therefore, that pact contains nothing new in a dotal matter for that extent; notwithstanding it, the husband is nevertheless understood to have stood surety for the then-future obligation and actio negotiorum gestorum to be contracted against the woman, since a guarantor can also be provided for a future obligation, as in ff. de fideius. l. si stipulatus. §. adhiberi; nay rather, even if the husband were believed to have intervened with the intention of donating the expenses to the wife, it would still be of no effect, and the action against the woman would be restored by law itself, since donation between husband and wife is forbidden, even of expenses made on dotal property, as in ff. de impen. in rebus do. fa. l. in voluptariis §. 1; nor is it confirmed by death, as originating from a promise, as in ff. de dona. inter vir. et vxo. l. Pap. Furthermore, also by force of [the law on] any donation beyond 60 [or 500] pounds, because it was not registered (insinuata), it is certain that also on this ground it cannot be confirmed in any way by death. Finally, the arbitral sentence rendered between mother and daughter is no obstacle. First, because it is a matter conducted between others, etc., and therefore did not merit being alleged in the case pending between the daughter and the heir through the said emphyteuta, it benefits the emphyteuta not at all. Furthermore, the woman was also definitively absolved from these improvements; which sentence creates the law and absorbs the force of the other arbitral sentence, especially because the daughter from that arbitral sentence was not bound to anything other than to exonerate the woman and aforesaid mother, who was afterwards exonerated and absolved from the said improvements by that judicial sentence; which sentence passed into res judicata. From which things indeed the conclusion is drawn in favor of the heir against the emphyteuta, notwithstanding the allegations on the part of the emphyteuta, to which it is sufficiently clear from the aforesaid that an answer has been given.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an arbitral award granted concerning the release of prisoners extends to a prisoner who was subsequently convicted.
2. The sentence is retroactive.
body: Whether

† An arbitrium granted concerning the release from prison of those existing in prison is to be extended to those existing in prison, against whom a sentence was subsequently pronounced. Doubt arises: because by the sentence a new right has been acquired, to which the arbitrium does not seem to extend. D. 20.1.13 (Si fundus), § Si pluris. And because the sentence has passed into res iudicata. D. 12.2.1 (Nam postea), § Si damnetur. Solution, as follows below: Having seen the present reform and the condemnation made against Cambucio Spaualdi de Castro Montonis by the Lord Captain after that ordinance, I say that, notwithstanding the aforementioned subsequent condemnation of the said Cambucio, who was in prison at the time of the said reform for a past offense previously confessed by him, the said Cambucio may be released from the said prisons by virtue of the present ordinance. And these points are proven first by the reason of the generality of this reform, which speaks generally of all those in prison and does not except anyone. S. Nisi quosdam. But it is certain that where the determination of the law is general, its effect is also general. D. 49.16.1 (In fraudem), § Si. Moreover, it is certain that an exception in certain cases confirms the rule in the rest. D. 39.4.1 (Quantum), § Idem respondeat domo. The same is proven secondly: because the special arbitrium granted to these persons for release could not be taken away from them by the Lord Captain pronouncing afterwards. Ar. D. 40.1.1 (Si hominem); D. 3.3.1 (Si ita quod si hoc).

Thirdly, it is proved from this: because the sentence is drawn back in time, for the condemnation is feigned to have occurred retroactively from the day of the joinder of issue, as argued from the Digest, On Donations, law *Post contractum*; Digest, On the Sale of Things, law *Si post acceptum*. Fourthly, it is proved that the status of liberty of this prisoner was implicated, which was not abolished by the sentence. As argued from the Digest, If an action is brought on a delictual cause, law *Si*. Finally, it is proved that these persons have discretion over the cause: therefore, over all law. Fifthly, because although he was not condemned at the time the discretion was given, he was necessarily to be condemned. Hence, with regard to the understanding of the law, the same must be stated concerning him as concerning one condemned in retrospect: that one who is proximate to condemnation ought to be considered as condemned, as argued from the Code, On Adultery, law *Quamvis indubitati*. Sixthly, it is proved that a mandate conferred during pending litigation extends itself up to and including the sentence. Digest, On Proxies, law *Qui procuratorem*. Finally, it is proved that these persons have discretion over the cause: therefore, over all law that descends from it. Digest, On Oaths, law *Duobus*, section *Colonus*; and law *Si*; and law *1*, section *1*; Digest, On Actions Not Given, Digest, On Compromises, law *Post rem*, section *1*. And thus it is clearly concluded that this person can be released from prison. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A daughter in her father's estate must have her legitime, and the fruits of the legitime without any burden.
2. A gratuitous release must be insinuated like a donation.
3. Whether an oath validates a donation not insinuated.
4. Whether a donation is said to be insinuated, in which the judge interposed a decree.
5. On what matters the judge's decree appears to have been interposed.
6. Immovables cannot be concealed.
7. When a contract is broken, all clauses of the same contract are broken.
8. Whether habilitation is required regarding an oath of a prohibited donation.
casus: CASE. The facts are proposed as follows: A certain person named Jacobus de Toscanella made a will in this form: In the name of Christ, amen. And among other things, he disposed as follows: Furthermore, he left and bequeathed to Bartholomew, his daughter, five hundred pounds to be paid to her when she marries, and in that same quantity he instituted her as his heir, commanding her to be content and not to demand more from the goods of the said testator than that said quantity. And moreover, he willed that the said Bartholomew should have, during her lifetime, the house of the said testator, thus bounded, in which she might dwell in case of necessity and widowhood. And in the meantime, until she marries, she should have food, clothing, and habitation in the aforesaid house from the goods of the said testator. At the end of the said will, he instituted heirs in this form: In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, present and future, he instituted and left Martin, his brother, and the male children of the latter for one-fourth part, and Peter for another fourth part, and John for another fourth part, and Abraham, his nephew, for another fourth part, as universal heirs. Moreover, for the execution of all and each of these things, he made the aforementioned Martin and Peter his executors and trustees, granting them full authority, etc., and he asserted that this was his last will, which he willed to be valid by the law of wills. And if it were not valid by the law of wills, let it be valid by the law of codicils, or by any other last will by which it can be valid and binding. After this, the said Jacobus died in the same millennium and year; the said Bartholomew, his legitimate and natural daughter, surviving. Afterwards, a certain instrument was made by the said Bartholomew, of the tenor set forth below, namely:
body: It is certain.

†If a daughter is in the father’s estate, she must receive her legitime and the fruits of the legitime without any burden. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Sancimus, § Repleti; and l. Quoniam in prioribus; and ff. eod., l. Papius, § Si communi. And although the daughter may reject the father’s judgment, nevertheless she will not lose her legitime, unless she expressly remits it: as C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quando, § Si; and noted by Guillaume de Cuyck, ff. de transactionibus, l. De his. Having premised this, we posit, by way of example, that the father’s goods of this girl were worth three thousand florins. And thus the legitime of this girl was one thousand florins in substance and dominion over the paternal things, as I said; for the action for the recovery of the inheritance and the judgment of the division of the inheritance are given to the son for the legitime, if he takes this mode of action: as the law openly states, ff. familiae erciscundae, l. 2, § Si quarta. Nor is this surprising, because in effect he is heir and owner: as ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Linea margaritarum. And it is openly proven that, by reason of the legitime and the trebellianic portion, the judgment of division is rendered: ff. familiae erciscundae, l. Filium quem habentem; and there, noted in the gloss beginning “Fama et re,” before the end. Afterwards, I consider that this legitime is increased by fruits, to such an extent that even consumed fruits come into restitution: as C. familiae erciscundae, l. Non est; and there, the gloss noted; and C. Legitima. It is not a universal or quasi-universal thing, and in universal judgments, consumed fruits come under the name of revenues: as C. familiae erciscundae, l. Cohaeredibus; and it is as is noted, ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. Si urbana. Then, the species of this contract must be inquired into, whether it is a mere renunciation of rights and inheritances. For we sometimes repudiate an inheritance gratuitously, sometimes for something received: as ff. si quis omisso causa testamenti, l. Si pecunia. And if this were the case, there would be no need to treat of insinuation; because to renounce an inheritance is not to make a donation: C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Si sponsus, § Si quis rogata. But it would be necessary to treat whether the Authentica Sacramenta have place in a mere repudiation or renunciation of an inheritance, or whether it is not a renunciation of the inheritance and legitime, but a release of the universal heir, who was bound to the girl for the supplement of the legitime. For if it is a release, it must be considered that this renunciation and release would be in part gratuitous and in part not gratuitous; and for that part which would be gratuitous, it would be a donation, and it requires insinuation beyond the legitimate mode, as noted, ff. de regulis iuris, l. Si quis obligatione; ff. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur, l. 1, § 1. And note, ff. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, in principio.

And Bartolus often advised that a gratuitous release must be insinuated, just as a donation: every liberality is a gift; and to the extent that it truly ought to be insinuated, if it has not been insinuated, it is void by operation of law. C. de donat. l. scimus; ff. de donat. l. ut mihi donares. And therefore the donor may recover and act against his own deed, which is not supported by any validity or obligation.

But let us consider in the case at hand whether the oath is an obstacle to him. And it must be said that the oath is not sufficient where insinuation is required and is not made: as is fully noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Si quis pro eo*. For insinuation is required in order to prevent frauds, especially those of relatives, who fabricate many causes against girls. And therefore recourse is had to the judge, so that donors may not be oppressed by fictitious cunning devices in the month; concerning which, if they become apparent to them, they ought to forbid that the donation be entered into the records: Code, *De donationibus*, law *Data iam pridem*. And it is noted by Guillaume de Coulanges in the Code, *De sacrosancta ecclesia*, law *Illud*.

But let us consider in the case at hand whether insinuation appears to have been made: because the judge interposed a decree, and he is an ordinary judge. And it seems that it was, because any ordinary judge suffices, who presides in that territory. C. de donat. l. in hac. And it is said to be insinuated, that which was done before the judge: even if the decree had not been appended. C. de testam. l. omnium. I say the contrary: because the cause was not exposed before the judge: for the party must expressly state that he intends to make a donation, so that it may be known to the judge what is being done and what is being contracted. C. de praediis curiae l. 1. lib. 10.

For indeed, the judge does not examine that which is not narrated to him in good faith, and he does not appear to interpose a decree. For he errs in the cause of fact, or is ignorant. D. de tutoribus et curatoribus datis ab his, l. tutor si petitus; D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana. For if the judge knew the cause of fact, and the dissipation of the girl’s goods, and the waste, he would undoubtedly not have permitted it, nor would he have interposed a decree; because it is presumed from the mind of the judge that he intends to do nothing [wrongful], because he swears this: as in Auth. iusiurandum quod praestatur ab his, §. equus; and C. ad legem Iuliam de repetundis, l. finalis. Moreover, I boldly say that the said donation was not insinuated really and substantially, although this contract was made superficially before the judge. But if this contract is a cession and transfusion of real rights, the same must be said all the more strongly; because the thing is partly distrained, partly donated. C. de manumis, l. per diversas; and l. ab Anastasio. And this donation was hidden from the judge, whence a captious decree is broken by the interpretation of the prudent. D. l. cum Aquiliana; and D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si praetor.

† Moreover, it must be observed that immovable property cannot be concealed. L. 2, *Quando et quibus quarta pars debetur*. And the legitime of this son, which lies open to view in immovable things and demonstrates itself, this girl confessed to having; and it appears to the bodily eye that she does not have it in those very strongholds, and it is clear to the judicial eye and understanding that she does not have it in so small a sum. Hence, since it is thus established through the examination of the husband, the generality in the mind of the remission and cession must be moderated according to the substance of the final cause. C. *De exceptionibus*, L. *Si ex maiori*. Furthermore, he who confesses that he has, and does not have, is deemed to acquire the right to demand what was confessed. C. *De dotis promissa*, L. *Si voluntate*. But let us see: this girl promised that if anything should come to her, etc. Therefore, whatever she recovered, she would be bound to restore; therefore, the exception of fraud stands in her way. L. *Dolo*, with similar authorities. I answer: this promise suffers from the same defects; and therefore it operates to no effect.

And I say the same regarding the promise of a penalty: for all are clauses of the same contract; and therefore they are infringed by one and the same reason, according to what is noted elsewhere at the end. D. si quid in fraudem patroni, l. si patronum ex asse, where there is a notable gloss. Concluding therefore on the matter, and on the counsel requested: I say that this woman has a remedy of nullity available to her, insofar as the donation tacitly exceeds the legitimate portion. And this is to be restored to the same woman with fruits, by reason of the legitimate portion due to her in her father’s goods; and especially for the entire period of minority, during which delay has been committed against her in the lands. D. de legatis 2, l. Titia Seio, § usuras; C. in quibus causis in integrum restitui, l. in minorum; and D. de adimendis legatis, l. 3, § si quis Titio.

† Nor is it necessary, in making this claim, to first seek a relaxation of the oath, which is invalid regarding a donation prohibited without insinuation; although it would be more cautious to seek such relaxation on account of the rule of the canonists. It suffices that the law condemns both the act and the oath. D. de legatis primo, l. si quis inquilinos, § 1; and by argument, D. de conditionibus, Inst. l. quae sub condi, § fin. And if he wishes to seek relaxation on this point, he should state that the oath is null as a matter of law; but he seeks its relaxation as a precaution, and so that he may pursue his rights in court more safely and securely.
