And thus I opine in the aforementioned matters, nor can it be said that there was a mere renunciation of inheritances and of the legitimate portion; because one who makes an agreement concerning an inheritance is deemed to have accepted it. Likewise, by granting or selling rights, one is deemed to have accepted the inheritance, Inst. de haereditatibus qualiter et quibus differant, § fin. I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, advise as has been concluded above: and under my faith I have subscribed, and with my own hand I have sealed with my seal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A coin is said to be false for three reasons.
2. By what penalty one who uses false coin is to be punished.
3. What an inquiry concerning theft ought to contain.
4. When a receiver of stolen goods from a thief is said to commit theft.
body: The case is as follows: The Lords della Scala issued an edict that a certain coin then in circulation should no longer circulate, nor could it be spent; and they caused a new coin to be struck. Now, a certain official of theirs in charge of preserving and spending money, having in a large quantity of the aforesaid old and reprobated money, commingled it with the new, and paid it out in payments to stipendiaries; and ultimately he retained for himself, and converted to his own uses, some of the new money belonging to the lord himself. Now it is asked whether he, by spending that reprobated money, can be punished for forgery (de falso). Secondly, it is asked whether by retaining the new money of those lords he commits theft, and whether an inquest can be brought against him for theft.

† It must be known that money is said to be false from three causes, namely from a material cause, where it is debased: as if brass is mixed into gold, or another material similar in color is mixed with silver by evil deceit (dolo malo). For this is falsity: for money ought to be of chosen material, ff. de contrahen. empt. l. 1. And whatever is mixed with the said material is called debased material, and it is falsity: as in ff. de falsis l. lege Cornelia cauen[tum]. Likewise, it is called false from a formal cause, whence in golden material the image of the prince, that is his countenance, is required for the form: as in l. fina. C. de vete. numismatis pote. libro 11. and the note in rubri. of the same title. And in another material, say silver, the name of the prince is required for the form, by whose authority the moneyers (Fabricenses) make the coin; for that subscriptio is the formal form, it is not of the substance: as in the said l. 1. Hence in the Gospel: "Whose image and superscription is this? They say: Caesar's." If anyone, therefore, puts on money the name of a prince who is not the prince of the moneyer, he is a counterfeiter; and this falsity is committed in the formal cause. Likewise, it is called false from the efficient cause. For if another baron mints sound money under his own name, yet because it is not lawful for him without imperial or royal authority, or by authority of custom which sometimes has the force of law and of Caesar in granting permission: certainly that money does not have false material, nor false form; nonetheless, the maker is punished for false money, because falsely and boldly he usurps royal authority to himself, C. de incen. l. fi., for minting money is a regalian right, as in titu. de clerico violatore pacis, c. si ministralis, colla. 10, quae sint regalia, at the word 'monetae'.

† And from these causes money is false originally; and if anyone uses it, he is punished for forgery from the use, even though he did not make it himself. Yet he is punished more mildly for the mere use than for the making, ff. de fal. l. falsi. §. ordine. For to this end, in order that the user may be punished for forgery, it is necessary that the money itself be false in one of the three aforesaid ways, namely by reason of the material, because there is an alloy, shaving, clipping (pignoratura), or other such thing, ff. de pig. act. l. eleganter. §. qui reprobos; or by reason of the image, or of the inscription falsely placed upon it, or by reason of a false efficient cause. And if we consider well, those things do not pertain to our case in any way: because the money has an origin of genuineness from all three aforesaid causes; whence it was true money from its origin of truth, and the one spending it was spending true money, because what is once true is always true when the origin is inspected. But the spender committed a delict, because he spent old coins for new, and that crime is extraordinary. And it is not punished under l. Cornelia de falsis, but under the crime of stellionate, without infamy; and by a sound understanding he expounds 'falsis', that is, 'unjust': otherwise the inquest would not be true, for neither in the lex Cornelia de falsis nor in the lex Iulia de peculatu is this case enumerated, as is clear in the said l. cor. and ff. ad l. Iul. pec. l. 1. And certainly a title of crime is lacking for this delict; and therefore this extraordinary crime is to be punished moderately, by the tempered and equitable discretion of the magistrate, ff. de effra. l. 1. §. expoliatores. And although he is said to have contemned the mandates of the lords, nevertheless that contempt does not extend to capital punishment, except in cases contained in the law. But recourse must be had to the mandator, and he should estimate what penalty ought to be imposed, who will know how to temper the sentence according to the depravity and magnitude of the delict. For he who contemns the mandates of the king ought not always to die, or be confiscated of all his goods, but the penalty is to be imposed according to the king's discretion, as in C. de thesau. l. 1. §. pe. and l. de hoc, and l. sanctio legum, de poe.; and so it was advised to be judged in the courts of kings, as I have learned from those knowledgeable in these things. And certainly I have rightly said that it is not forgery, because the money displays and reveals itself, and fraud is not committed against one who sees; and if a quasi-fraud is committed, the penalty is lesser. Likewise, a departure from a mandate does not carry capital punishment or confiscation of goods, but a fine: as in l. eos, de modo mulctan. And this as to the first point.

† Concerning the second point, namely concerning theft: it is certain that the inquest sets down a conclusion, namely that it is theft, but it does not state why, because it is not set forth in the inquest whose money it was, nor how it proceeded, nor whether it was by number, weight, or specific lot (speciem), ff. deposi. l. die spon. §. fi., l. Lucius; for if ownership had been transferred, neither theft nor peculation is committed, ff. de condi. ob cau. l. pen.

† Concerning the third inquest, I say that no crime appears; for I can knowingly receive a thing from a thief with the intent of making a gain, and then I commit theft; or with the intent of managing the affairs of the owner, so that the thing may be safe for him, and then I act lawfully; and in doubt it is presumed to be done with good intent. For he was in an office here, and for an official it is always presumed that he acts with a good and praiseworthy mind: as in l. 1. C. de offi. ciui. iudi. at the word 'quod non arbitramur'. And although it remained for two months, from this it is not of necessity inferred that there was an intent to steal (animus contractandi) when he is accused of a crime; nor does it appear that he had the intent to steal; and in doubt we ought to presume good and not evil, l. merito, pro socio, etc. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son who has received a gratuity may deduct two fourths.
2. Whether a donee, by virtue of the right of donation, may deduct two fourths.
3. Whether excluded daughters constitute a portion for the other brothers with regard to the augmentation of the legitime.
4. Whether a dowry is to be considered the legitime of daughters.
5. A prohibition of alienation among certain persons does not include sons among themselves.
body: A certain Alexander had two sons, John and Bartholomew, and two daughters from his first wife; from his second wife he had Jacob and four daughters, all of whom he endowed according to the form of the statute, so that they could not demand more. He instituted them as heirs in their dowries. He instituted his sons as equal heirs in his will; and to the said John, who was over 25 years of age, he substituted Bartholomew and Jacob, and he prohibited the said John from alienating any immovable property, and if he should alienate any immovable property under any title, the said testator willed that such and those alienated things should devolve upon the said other brothers, or their children and heirs. After the death of the said testator, the said John donated all his goods to his brother Bartholomew, retaining for himself the usufruct during his lifetime. After the death of the said John, a doubt arises: whether the said donation was valid; and if it is valid, whether the said donee, who is also the brother of the donor, could by virtue of the donation deduct two quarters, or only the portion due by natural law, or what right applies.

† There are diverse opinions regarding the deduction of two fourths. Some say that only one Falcidian fourth is deducted; others, both; others, the larger one. Others distinguish, saying that if requested purely, one [fourth] is deducted; if requested under a condition, several [fourths] are deducted; because they are not merged, since they do not occur at the same time, on the Falcidian [law], as is touched upon here by Cynus and others. C. ad legem quanquam. ff. de inofficiosa testamento. l. Papi. §. meminisse. in Auth. de restitutione et ea, quae parit. §. quamobrem. in Auth. de haereditatibus et Falcidia. §. si quis autem non implens. ff. si cui plus quam. per l. Falcidiana. l. 1. §. interdum. C. familiae erciscundae. l. filium quem habentem. But it has been determined by decretals that a son burdened with restitution may deduct his legitime and the Trebellianic fourth; indeed, the legitime is deducted from the Trebellianic fourth; the heir deducts the Falcidian fourth due; by natural law, it is deducted from the body of the goods after deducting debts; but the Trebellianic fourth is deducted from the universality itself, which is the inheritance without separation of debts. And if we examine this subtly, they are deducted as if not from the same universality, but from different ones; because one universality is pure and clear goods, another is a burdened inheritance, and thus there is a double universality, greater and lesser; if, however, the lesser is included under the greater; and therefore in effect both deductions are drawn from the same subject, universal, and intellectual body of the patrimony. Whatever the case may be, the custom of the world stands in this matter for the canons, for the Pope can interpret laws; since sometimes, for example, when the empire is vacant, the Pope can enact civil laws in place of the Emperor, arg. extra de re iudicata. c. pastoralis. in fine. in cle. Hence the opinion of the doctors must yield to the authority of Blessed Peter, not precede it. Therefore, in this doubt, the decretal extra de testamento. c. Raynutius. and Raynerius in c. si pater. de testamento. lib. 6. follows. Thus I have often advised that it should be observed in fact, and thus it is observed.

† And having made this promise, I say that the donee, by virtue of the donation, if it does not exceed the lawful limit, or if it has been insinuated, may detract from the legitime and the trebellianic portion, because the right to the legitime and the trebellianic portion can be ceded and donated, as stated in the Digest, ad trebellianicam, law 1, § in donatione. But how much is the legitime? For if we count nine children, it is half of the ninth part; but if there are three, it is a third of the third. However, it seems that daughters should be included. For although they are not admitted under the name of legitime, they are admitted under the name of dowry, which is substituted in place of the legitime.

† Therefore, women are included among those entitled to the legitime. This is the opinion of Bartolus, D. de inoff. test. l. pater filium, and I heard him maintain this view in his lectures. For one who is admitted to something cannot be said to be deprived, nor to be in a case of lapse; and although her legitime is diminished, it does not increase the legitime of another; because there is no room for the right of accretion unless someone is excluded in toto, and especially among those united solely by legal kinship. Arg. D. de leg. 2, l. proculo. But others say that the legitime is one-third of the statutory share devolving on intestacy, as if it had devolved under the common law; because the rule concerning the legitime portion extends to the case of intestacy; hence it makes no difference whether it devolves under the old law or under the new law, i.e., by statute or custom. D. ad l. Falc. l. 1, § lex Falc.

The question arises whether the dowry is considered the legitimate portion of daughters, or whether it is not legitimate, but something else. In the first case, the opinion of Bartolus is true. In the second case, another opinion applies, for which the following supports it: C. de haereditatibus instituendis, l. quotiens. Rizzari Malus calls it a substitute for the legitimate portion in the question he disputed. And therefore, the opinion of Bartolus is true, which I believe to be correct; however, Jacobus Butrigarius, in his disputation, becomes greatly entangled, and it concerns the subtleties of the law. Moreover, by the death of a male heir, the legitimate portion of daughters in the father's goods is not increased, as noted by Cynus, C. de adulteriis, l. puta.

† I say further, that a prohibition of alienation to any person does not include sons among themselves. C. de fideicommissis, leg. voluntas. And therefore a brother could give to a brother the right and the hope. C. de donationibus, l. spem. For it appears that the testator intended that the property should not be alienated to outsiders, but not among themselves. D. de legatis tertio, l. si pater, § 15. For he made this prohibition in consideration of persons, so that outsiders should not possess these things, but not out of hatred for his own family: and thus the prohibition has personal causes of prohibition, not real. And thus it does not contradict. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § sed si in pluribus. And so I say, and I advise, I, Bal. de Peru., doctor of both laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the grounds for which ecclesiastical property may be alienated.
2. What is required in the alienation of monastic property, and what if the prelate has sworn not to alienate without the counsel of the Roman Pontiff.
3. Add the opinion beginning "Viso puncto," and on exchange, in part 5.
body: The facts are as follows. By means of this, the counsel of a wise man is sought in the city of Camerino. There is a certain monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, which is a member and immediately subject to the monastery of Saint Severinus and its Abbot. Now, the Abbot of Saint Severinus has granted one house, which he holds in emphyteusis under a certain annual pension, as is customary, to a certain John, the emphyteuta. The prior of the aforementioned monastery of Camerino, namely of Saint Benedict, wishes to free that house, to grant it free and clear, and to transfer it to the said John, and to confess that it has been converted to the benefit of the monastery, or by whatever other juridical mode this might be possible. It is asked whether this can be done according to law, and if so, what mode must be observed and what form. In the name of Christ, amen.

† The property of churches or monasteries cannot be alienated except in four cases. The first is on account of necessity: for example, if a debt presses upon them; as in 12 q. 2, c. Sine exemplo; 10 q. 2, c. Aurum; Authent. Hoc ius porrectum, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis; and in the Corpus, from which this is derived. The second case is on account of piety, such as for the redemption of captives or alms for the poor; as in 12 q. 2, c. Aurum. The third case is on account of utility: for example, if one alienates worse property in order to purchase or acquire better property; and thus it is permitted to exchange for evident utility; as in the aforementioned c. Siue; and see the argument from l. Si, ff. de iure dotium. The fourth is on account of inconvenience; as in 12 q. 2, c. Tertulas et casellas. In these cases, one may alienate full ownership, not merely naked ownership; as is fully noted in 12 q. 2, in the gloss on the Summa. Therefore, I say that a church or monastery may exchange naked ownership for another thing that is better, more fruitful, more useful, and more necessary to the church. For we sell certain lands due to their sterility; as in ff. de rebus eorum, l. Si fundus; and we purchase others due to their proximity; as in ff. de minoribus, l. Si in emptione. And this was advised by Dy. de Musello, that the naked ownership of a church may be exchanged for another thing, if the exchange benefits the church; because such good compensation is given to it that the condition of the church is evidently improved. Therefore, by this method, an emphyteuta may acquire full ownership, just as any other person exchanging who is not an emphyteuta.

And in the alienation of the monastery’s property, the consent of the Abbot, the consent of his chapter, and the authority of the bishop are required; and if the Abbot is exempt, who has sworn not to alienate without consulting the Roman Pontiff, he cannot alienate without the will of the Pope: as in 12 q. 2, c. Abbatibus; 17 q. 4, c. In venditione; Extra, De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, c. Ut superius; by Innocentius, Extra, De transactionibus, c. Statuimus. And it is necessary that in such alienations a discussion precede; because they ought to be done with great deliberation and maturity: as in the said c. Sine exemplo, 12 q. 2; and the said Auth. Hoc ius porrectum, C., De sacris sanctis ecclesiis. And in an exempt monastery, no prelate can exercise any power without the consent of the Abbot: 12 q. 2, c. Luminoso. If, however, under some exempt Abbot there is a priory having distinct goods, and the prior of that place wishes to alienate, he can do this with the consent of the Abbot; because since that Abbot acts in the place of the bishop in authorizing: as noted in c. 1, Extra, De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, incipiens; and thus it seems that in our case it could be done, because the house in question is not from the table of the Abbot, but from the table of the Prior; and thus the Abbot’s oath not to alienate without consulting the Roman Pontiff does not extend to that which is not from his table: as in the said c. Ut superius, by Hostiensis. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, advise, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pupillary substitute is deprived of his right if he did not petition for a guardian within a year; and whether the mother is excused on account of the substitute.
2. Whether the mother has a year to petition for a guardian for her son; and whether such a year is continuous.
3. A child born in the household is presumed to be the son, unless impossibility is proven.
body: The point is such that it will be apparent from the copy of the will, which we send. That testator, Valentinus, having two legitimate and natural sons, namely Cynus and Antonius, and having Cassia as his wife, in whom he placed little confidence, as appears in the will, coming to death, instituted as his two universal heirs Cynus and Antonius, who were minors. And he willed that if one should die, the other should succeed; and if both should die without legitimate heirs, he willed that the wealth should devolve upon Divitia and Ioannitia, the sisters of the testator. And he did not provide for a guardian in the will, as you see. The said substitutes did not petition for a guardian to be appointed for these minors within five months from the death of the testator, but within a year; nor did Cassia, the mother of the minors, petition. First, Cynus the minor dies; and Antonius, his brother, remains, to whom we believe Antonius succeeds in the goods of the former on account of the words of substitution, and then one of the pupillary substitutes, namely Divitia, petitioned for a guardian to be appointed for that minor Antonius, who had survived; the other pupillary substitute, who was ill, did not petition, nor did her procurator promise to petition. Cassia, the mother of the minor, petitioned to be admitted to the said guardianship and to be preferred to the others by the Authentica *Matri et aviae*. It was opposed by that substitute, that she was not suitable, because she had lived dishonestly during the life of her husband and after his death, and a term was given to the substitute to prove these things. In the meantime, before the term, Antonius died. First, his mother claimed his inheritance, saying that the substitute aunts of the minor did not petition for a guardian to be appointed for the minors as soon as they could after the death of the testator, but delayed for five months after the death of the testator; therefore she says the substitutes should be excluded, because it was incumbent upon the pupillary substitute to petition for a guardian before the mother. Bartolus determines this, and after a long disputation in *l. Si minores*, ff. *Qui petunt tutores*, and this is what the mother of Antonius, the deceased minor, says. The substitutes excuse themselves and say: that although Divitia, one of the substitutes, petitioned for a guardian to be appointed for the minor after five months from the time of the testator’s death, she says she petitioned justly and within the time established by law. For they concede to the substitutes a year by the new constitution, as in *l. Sciant omnes*, C. *De legatis hereditatibus*; and that which is said, that they ought to petition as soon as they have access to the praetor, as in § *Confestim*, I answer that this has place only in the case of the mother and the freedman; but to the substitutes a year is granted by *l. Sciant*, and thus it seems Bartolus confirms in the said repetition of *l. Minores*. The other substitute, Ioannitia, excuses herself: both because she has a year, and because she was ill, and was prevented by the death of the minor. And if it is opposed by the mother that she is not said to have petitioned, because they did not petition for the said mother to be made guardian and to make an inventory, and without the making of an inventory she cannot administer the legitimate portion, as in *l. 2*, § *Sed quod diximus*, ff. *Ad Tertullianam*, it is answered that the substitutes could not do this, because they were prevented by the death of the minor; and they add that even if they had petitioned for a guardian, because they could not have the guardians make an inventory and administer, nevertheless this should not prejudice them in the succession, unless after a year, following the said *l. Sciant* and the learned Bartolus. And these are alleged for and against in the whole succession. It is also doubted on account of the substitution made by the lord Valentinus from the sons to Divitia and Ioannitia, who was the mother in the middle: whether it was direct or fideicommissary; and whether the mother could deduct the Trebellian quarter. And it is answered by the substitutes that the mother can subtract nothing, because the substitution made, although it is concise, was made by the direct word, namely by the word “die,” on account of which the mother comes to be excluded, by c. *Si pater*, extra *De testibus*, lib. 6. Secondly, how it is to be understood that one ought to petition for a guardian *confestim*, and some say *confestim*, i.e., after nine days from the death of the deceased. For before that they were not compelled to petition, by the Authentica *Nec ante*, C. *Sepultura violanda*. Others say that all things are reduced to the new law, and in all cases we must observe the year, by *l. Sciant*. Others say that it remains in the discretion of the judge, what is to be observed according to law. In the name of Christ, amen.

† A pupillary substitute who does not petition for a guardian within one year is deprived of the right of substitution, as stated in the law *Sciant*, Codex, *De legatis et hereditatibus*; therefore, he has a term of one year. And because the law assigns a certain term, we cannot restrict or shorten it, according to the noted opinion of Dyonisius in the chapter *Adultum*, and the law *1*, Digest, *De iure deliberandi*, as held by Laurentius de Arena; this is supported by the chapter *Commissa*, *De electione*, Book 6. Therefore, if the ward dies within the year, it is impossible that the substitute be excluded, because a supervening event, before the penalty is incurred, prevents its incurrence: Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*, *De iactis*, the law *Pe*, § *Idem iuris*; Digest, *Qui satisdare cogantur*, the law *Si decesserit*. For deprivation of the inheritance is a penalty. And therefore, an event occurring before the lapse of the year excludes this penalty. This is further supported by the fact that where a short time is set by statute, which is understood to be at the discretion of the judge, as in the law *Continuus*, § *Cum ita*, and § *Item qui insulam*, and the law *Si ita quis*, § *Seyea*, at the end, if the ward dies within that time, the penalty ceases: as in the Digest, *Ad Senatusconsultum Tertullianum*, the law *2*, § *Confestim*, at the words *Quid ergo*. Therefore, since a year is set, if the ward dies in the meantime, the penalty of deprivation ceases. Argument: Digest, *De naufragio et fenore*, the law *Labeo*.

But does the period of a year apply to the mother, as it does to others? It is not relevant to our case that the mother is not excluded on the ground of not having requested a tutor; rather, this is because the substitution was expressly pupillary, due to the word "should die," which is a direct term, as in the chapter *Si pater*, wisely cited by you. Nevertheless, whatever Bartolus says, the one-year term is common to the mother and to all under the new law. Hence, that which was formerly established for the mother as "as soon as possible" has now been reduced to the term of a year and determined by law, whereas it previously lay within the judge's discretion. For the text *Sciant cuncti* states "all," and since it says "all," it excludes no one, thereby including the mother. Nor is it true that the mother should be in a worse condition than other relatives; for the term "all" equates everyone, and this is commonly practiced. From the foregoing, it conclusively appears that the substitutes are admitted and the mother is repelled, because the substitution is pupillary. For the words are consistent, the time permits it, and the reason of law does not oppose it.

† On another point of fact, I say that a son is presumed if he was born in the house with the neighbors aware thereof. L. *Filius*. Unless impossibility is proven, as is stated there. And although the wife is proven to be an adulteress, nevertheless, in case of doubt, the son is presumed legitimate, as in D. 48.5 (*De adulteriis*), L. *Miles*, § *Defuncto*, and there is the sole text, and therefore he can claim his legitime, unless negative proof necessarily excludes the opposite. It supports what is noted in D. 12.1 (*De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*), L. *Lucius*. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A minor who has taken an oath must be informed of the benefit of restitution in integrum, so as not to act against the contract; and whether he ought first to seek a dispensation from the oath before violating it.
body: The case is as follows: Angela, widow of the late Racti, dower of Peter of the city, and I, and Lewis, her sons, under 25 years of age, but over 14, gave, sold, and delivered to Maghaloctonicas of the old city, of the region of Baracis, a certain house situated in their city within their boundaries, and the said sellers promised to the said buyer that Peter, son of the said Angela, within the said time of me and Lewis, would ratify and confirm the said sale. And in the said contract it is contained that if the thing were worth more, however much more it were worth, they gave and intended to give as a gift for good services and merits, etc. Now it is asked whether the said sale holds or not, considering that the said sellers at that time, and even now, are under 25 years of age. And also considering that the said Peter, for whom they promised ratification, does not wish to consent to or ratify what was promised by his brothers: and also another of their brothers named John, and under 14 years of age, who is now dead, was not requested by the said buyer. Also considering that the said sellers were deceived beyond half the just price. Also it is asked, if the said sale is valid for the part of the said me and Lewis: and whether it is valid for the part of the said Peter and John: and insofar as it is not valid, whether the said buyer has, or ought to have, or could have recourse against the said sellers, who promised ratification for the said Peter. In the name of Christ, amen. The opinion of Master Dynus de Musello was as follows:

† namely, that unless he has been informed of the restitution in integrum in respect of the benefit, although he may swear and promise not to act against it on any occasion, whether in law or in fact, nevertheless he can still seek restitution in integrum; and the same is held by Johannes Andreae in the chapter Cum dilectus, De emptione et venditione, in the Novella. But Bartolus holds the contrary in the Authentica Sacramenta, for there is no mention of such renunciation there, and by law 1, in the same title, and in law 2, De rescindenda venditione, here below. But the opinion of the Decretists is held by Thomas de Foresto, and it can be well defended in civil law. But in canon law it is strange how the aforementioned Johannes Andreae holds with the opinion of the Decretists, and Cynus in the aforementioned law says that this opinion is safer; but it seems to me that it is safer to seek the relaxation of the oath, so that the minor who has been harmed by more than half the just price through his ignorance might obtain the benefit of law 2. For since the oath contained an error of fact, which is presumed in a minor in case of enormous lesion, as noted by Petrus and Cynus in the aforementioned law 2 and in question 14, such error of fact does not prejudice him; for in an oath consent is required, but there is no consent on the part of one who errs. The first point is proved by the Code, De non numerata pecunia, law final. The second point is proved, as in law Si per errorem, Digest, De iuramentis omnium iudicum, and Digest, De conditione indebiti, law final, section Idem quaeritur, and Digest, De transactionibus, law Cum Aquilio, with its following provisions, unless it were proved to the contrary that the minor knew and swore with certain knowledge not to act against the occasion of minority, nor any other; for the special mention of the benefit of age includes the mention of the benefit of restitution, and thus it is inferred that he is certain of the effect; although the words of the law are not fully understood, just as he does not really understand what it means to say Velleianum; nevertheless it suffices that he understands that he cannot bind himself; for the law does not wish this except when he renounces. But those words, "and if it were worth more, he gave," etc., according to Bartolus, must be restricted as being captious to a small amount; and therefore they do not exclude the benefit of that second law, according to which I believe it to be true in the case of one who errs and is ignorant of the value and quantity of the things. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A posthumous heir, who is thus instituted on the condition that he be born: whether he is said to have been passed over, such that he may succeed, and having been born, died before the testatrix.
2. The poor are counted among extraneous heirs.
3. The poor are equated with minors.
4. The word "may": what it signifies.
5. The word "shall receive" is a direct word.
6. The Falcidian fourth cannot be deducted against the will of the testator.
body: The question is subtle,

For the testator instituted a posthumous son, if he were male and came into the light, in such a way that he could succeed. And she bore a male child: but one who could not succeed, because he died while the testatrix was still alive. Therefore, this one who was born was passed over in this case; hence, the will is broken according to civil law. D. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus § omnibus; and D. de iniust. testam. posthum.; and although it may become valid according to praetorian law, D. l. viua testatrice, it is therefore an invalid will, D. l. posthumus; and see D. de vulg. subst. l. si quis eum § fina. Nevertheless, for this reason one cannot succeed according to civil law; but possession of goods should have been claimed within one hundred useful days by an outsider. It is held that if this was not done, the matter stands as if intestate. D. de succ. edict. l. 1 § largius. And that possession of goods is necessary is clear, because a will broken according to civil law cannot become valid according to civil law; for thus civil law would be contrary to itself, and it would be more suspended than broken. Thus, according to civil law, there would be a species of becoming valid again. Moreover, where there is an omission, the solemnity of civil law is lacking. Therefore, civil law would not reject the will if the praetor, moved by equity, confirms it; because the injury of omission has no effect; and therefore the edictal possession of goods is necessary, as noted in C. unde leg. l. certum; and D. de iniust. testam. l. cum in secundario; and l. filio praeterito.

† However, the poor are counted among extraneous heirs, since they are not in the testator’s power, nor do they become heirs to him: therefore, they do not have the greater period of one hundred useful days. But to this it can be answered thus, and a remedy provided, for just as the poor who are in some hospital are concerned, and the hospital itself is equated with a minor, and by these means restitution in integrum is granted to them, as in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. orpha, and in Authen. de ecclesiis, tit. § orphanotrophi.

† Thus, the poor in general, who are under the care of the bishop, are equated with minors, and therefore relief is afforded to them by the remedy of restitution within four years: because this time is fixed for churches and the poor; for although they are always minors by interpretation of the law, nevertheless the time for restitution is not extended to infinity, but is restricted to the natural time for restitution, namely four years. Chapter 1, *De restitutione in integrum*, Book 6. Argument to this reason in *L. Non finita*, § *Fin.*, *De tutela et ratione distinctionis*. But it seems that the aforementioned points do not bear on the matter at hand, for the words “so that succession may take place” are verified: because power arises from two principles, even if the effect does not follow; as noted in the said *L. Cum in secundo*, *De iniusto testamento*, and *L. Quod Servius*, *De conditione ob causam*.

But I answer that sometimes this word, *possit* (may), signifies a potestative power: and thus that it is within the power of the person of whom it is predicated to bring it into effect: and then it is taken strictly for an efficacious power in acts produced. D. 27.1.1 (*Is potest*); C. 6.52.1 (*Nec nos*). And so it is here; sometimes it signifies absolutely: and then, according to the dialecticians, when any proposition is informed by the possible, it is understood as the possible being, that which can naturally happen. D. 46.3.1 (*Si pater*). But when a proposition of the possible is formed by a man in a dispositive act, it is understood as the possibility according to the nature of that act. But in our case it is not possible according to the nature of the act that the inheritance of a living person be acquired: and therefore those words, “so that he may succeed,” refer to the time of the death of the testatrix. D. 28.5.1 (*Pe*); D. 28.5.1 (*Tu*). From which it truly follows that the said posthumous child was omitted by common law, which fails in him: as in D. 28.6.1 (*Si pater*). However, because by praetorian law the testament convalesced, let us suppose the testament not to be vitiated by this omission. But also for another reason the institution of the posthumous child was null. Namely, because the daughters of the first degree were omitted, since nothing was left to them in the first degree by right of institution: as in Auth. *Ut cum* (C. 6.26.1), § *Ad quoque capitulum*. But by this the second degree, in whom the instituted heirs are found, is not vitiated. Therefore, the first degree being vitiated, either by reason of lapsedness or by reason of omission, the testament begins from the second degree: as D. 28.2.3; and C. 6.26.1, § *Pe*.

Secondly, let us therefore see whether here the second degree, i.e., the vulgar substitution, can be assigned. For a substitution made to an instituted heir, if he cannot be heir, as was the case here, is vulgar, as C. 6.23.1 (*Cum proponas*). But it must be considered that the words which are apt for institution are the same for vulgar substitution, namely, direct words. D. 35.2.1 (*In ratione*); D. 28.6.1 (*Si filio*); D. 28.4.1 (*Cohaeredi*), § *Si*. It must therefore be considered whether here there are direct words. And it is certain that here the daughters were substituted in certain sums by direct words, for no word is more direct in law than the word *instituo* (I institute). D. 28.4.1 (*Verbis civilibus*); C. 6.23.1 (*Quotiens*), § *Si duo*, at the end. Because this improper institution cannot be extended to the whole, the testatrix prohibiting it according to Bartolus, although we could say the contrary in the case of a son: as in Auth. *Ut cum* (C. 6.26.1), § *Caeterum*. For in the case of a son, even if prohibited from claiming or having more, a degree could be founded; otherwise it would follow that the degree itself was null, because the son was omitted therein. The objection from § *Si duo* does not hold, because it speaks of an outsider, but in the case of a son the law supplies, so that he may have his share, i.e., his legitime, and the share draws to itself the fourth part by the necessary right of accretion, as noted in D. 3.1.1 (*Servi scimus*). Therefore, every share draws to itself a share. Nor does a certain thing draw to itself the whole. Nor does the whole draw to itself a certain thing. D. 28.5.1 (*Si quis haeres institutus fuerit excepto fundo*). But that is properly not called the right of accretion, but the right of not diminishing: because over the whole there is not found a vacant portion which could accrue. But assuming that the degree of vulgar substitution was not founded in the aforementioned daughters, it seems that it could not be founded in the executors for the poor.

† Here it must be considered that the word "take" is direct, directing the execution to the substitute himself: as in the Digest, De usufructu, l. Si quis ita. But the executors were ordered to take and sell the goods universally; therefore, they are directly the substitutes. And this is expressly held by Bartolus in l. Centurio. Moreover, the testatrix wished her daughters to be heirs in a certain quantity; therefore, by leaving the residue to the poor, she seems to leave it by way of direct substitution; otherwise, the exact contrary of her intention would follow, namely, that the testatrix wished the sons to be universal heirs and the poor not to be, but to come in by right of fideicommissum. And the judgment of the testator is changed; indeed, it would be turned into its opposite, which is absurd. And for this reason, I conclude that the executors are to be regarded in the place of a vulgar substitute.

It must therefore be considered whether the daughters can deduct the Falcidian fourth from the legacies. And it seems that they can, because it is the common law of all heirs who have made an inventory that they are entitled to the Falcidian fourth. But the poor, although they did not make an inventory, ought nevertheless to be summoned to make an inventory within a certain time, as in the Authentica *De hereditatibus et Falcidia*, § *Papiens*. And thus, having done so, they resume the right of deduction: as above regarding the legitime of daughters, because the legitime is considered to be merely by right of legacy, it is not subject to the Falcidian deduction. Codex, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Scimus*.

To the contrary it seems: because since the poor are heirs, the will of the testator must be fulfilled in all things; nor ought the executors of the last will, although the law fictions them as heirs, to deduct the Falcidian fourth against the will of the testator, and against the natural obligation incurred: as in the Authentica *De ecclesiis*, title, § *Sinautem pro redemptione*, where it says, "according to the will of the testator, all things proceed." And thus equity is to be observed in the case concerning the children. For thus it is apparent from the aforesaid that the will and natural wish of the testatrix would certainly be circumvented, since the executor for the poor is a universal substitute, and the legacy left to the daughters, which was made to them, is due to them; so that the will of the testatrix is observed to the letter, lest the legacy be diminished on account of a smaller dowry. Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Quidam testamento*. Because those words "of the dotal goods" are uncertain and serve the place of demonstration, not of taxation; and thus they do not diminish the substance of the legacy, as in law *Lucius*, Digest, *De alimentis legatis*.

And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws, advise, and I have subscribed to this for the faith thereof.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the judgment by which it is pronounced who is the heir is definitive or interlocutory, and whether an appeal may be taken from it, given a statute that no appeal may be taken from interlocutory decisions.
2. How a grievance is to be proven, so that an appeal may be taken from it.
3. When something is said to be proven.
4. Given a statute that a judge may not commit the reception of witnesses, if he does commit it, their reception is of no effect, even if it was committed with the consent of the parties; because they could not waive the said statute.
body: On behalf of a certain lady named Nicolutia, a certain petition was produced against Hugolinus and Giordanus, as against the heirs of a certain Paulus Unguesti. And the said Hugolinus and Giordanus were cited as heirs of the said Paulus, so that they might appear to respond regarding the right of the said lady Nicolutia in the aforementioned petition. The said Hugolinus and Giordanus appeared within the term, and stated that they had accepted the inheritance of the said Paulus with the benefit of inventory; on account of which they protested that they did not wish to be sued, and that during the term granted by law for compiling the inventory, no novelty should be undertaken against them. Then it was objected on behalf of the said lady Nicolutia that the said Hugolinus and Giordanus could not be heirs of the said Paulus with the benefit of inventory, since they had already involved themselves in the inheritance and had administered the hereditary goods of the said Paulus for more than several years, which the said lady offered to prove. A certain term was assigned to her for proving this; and within the said term, certain positions were produced on behalf of the said lady, and witnesses were examined thereon. By virtue of which proofs, the judge pronounced that the said Giordanus and Hugolinus had been and were heirs of the said Paulus without the benefit of inventory, and condemned the said Hugolinus and Giordanus in costs, as is contained in the sentence, which the bearer of these presents brings to you. Now it is asked whether the said pronouncement, or sentence, is an interlocutory or a definitive sentence. And if it is interlocutory, whether it is such from which an appeal could have been taken; since the statutes of the city provide that no appeal may be taken from an interlocutory sentence, a copy of which is brought to you; and if an appeal could have been taken, whether the appeals in the case of appeal, or of nullity, uphold justice. And it seems that they uphold justice: since the judge committed the examination of witnesses to a certain Ser Vani Notis; and through the said Ser Vani, the examinations are found to have been taken; and the statutes of the commune of Gubbio provide that the judge could not commit the examination of witnesses in a case to anyone, which ascends to the quantity of 50 pounds of small denarii; and the notary writes down the examinations of the witnesses examined by another than the judge, imposing the penalty of falsehood, which statutes the bearer of these presents also brings to you, since this commission was made by the will of the parties. Furthermore, it seems that the said sentence is not valid: because the tithes were not paid, as the statute requires. And the bearer of these presents brings to you the petition, the examination, the commission, and the said witnesses, and the sentence, and a copy of all the statutes, of which mention was made above. Therefore, all the aforesaid having been seen, it is asked whether the said sentence was valid; and whether an appeal could be taken from it; and whether in the case of appeal the appeals uphold justice; and whether the sentence and the condemnation in costs were just. In the name of Christ, amen.

† A judgment declaring someone to be an heir is sometimes definitive, namely when it is pronounced principally for its own sake, as appears in an action for the recovery of an inheritance. It is sometimes interlocutory, when it is pronounced incidentally for the sake of something else, because every judgment rendered on an emerging or incidental matter is interlocutory. And every order that pertains to the case but does not definitively settle the principal action, as noted in Auth. de litig. § ad excludendas, and D. de minoribus l. intra utile. This is not obstructed by the fact that the law calls a certain type of interlocutory judgment “definitive” with respect to the article on which it is rendered, as noted in C. de rebus creditis l. et generaliter, and l. si quis iusiurandum. For there the term is used improperly, because a definitive judgment is one by which the judge fulfills his function toward the parties in the principal case, not one rendered on a single article, especially in the preparatory stages of trials. C. de iudiciis l. ita demum. Likewise, a judgment declaring that proceedings should precede is interlocutory, Extravagant de appellationibus cap. ex parte M. Conversely, a judgment declaring that proceedings should not continue is interlocutory, as noted in D. de iureiurando l. iusiurandum, and l. ad pecunias § fin. But may an appeal be taken from such an interlocutory judgment declaring someone to be an heir without the benefit of inventory? It seems that it may not, because the statute provides that no appeal may be taken from a grievance inflicted before the joinder of issue. But this interlocutory judgment was rendered before the joinder of issue in the principal case; therefore, no appeal may be taken. To this effect it is noted in C. de dilationibus l. a procedente, and C. quorum appellationes non recipiuntur l. ante. The contrary is true, namely that an appeal may be taken. And this is certain under the common law, because from such an interlocutory judgment the effect of the petition is increased; and thus it affects the principal matter, because it makes the action for the full amount enforceable, whereas previously it was limited, namely up to the extent of the heir’s assets. Likewise, in legacies it excludes the benefit of the Falcidian deduction. Therefore, it may rightly be appealed, because even if it does not decide the entire case, it nevertheless, so to speak, resolves a portion thereof; therefore it may be appealed, as noted in l. intra D. de minoribus, and D. qui satisdare cogantur l. arbitror. Nor does the statute of the Commune of Gubbio obstruct this. For this statute prohibits appealing from an interlocutory judgment that can be remedied by an appeal from a definitive judgment; it prohibits such appeal, and nevertheless the statute provides that a grievance inflicted may be redressed in an appeal that happens to be taken from a definitive judgment. Therefore, it speaks of that interlocutory judgment which can be remedied. It speaks and disposes by prohibiting and serving, connectedly. But this grievance cannot be remedied; therefore it may be appealed. For understanding, it must be known that the benefit of inventory not only moderates condemnation, but also suspends the convention. For sometimes, while it is being prepared, it delays the process; but when it is completed, it moderates condemnation. C. de iure deliberandi l. fin. § donec, and § licentiam; in Auth. de haeredibus et Falcidia § sancimus. If, therefore, one who ought not to be harassed, nor compelled to endure litigation, is compelled to undergo this annoyance, and the damage cannot be remedied, D. de captivis l. in bello § factae; C. de appellationibus l. si quis provocaverit. From this I clearly conclude that the interposed appeal is valid. But let us examine its justice, whether it is justified or unjustified from the same records, and without any proof, as the statute requires, and also canon law in cap. appellant de appellationibus in Clementina. For from the production of the old records the grievance must appear clearly, for a judge is not presumed to inflict a grievance on anyone, as C. de inofficiosa civium iudicia l. 2. And sometimes the proofs are clear; sometimes they are clear through extrinsic proof.

For if someone is not admitted to the common law, for example to prove a case, when he ought to have been admitted, and he offered to prove it immediately, or offered witnesses, and they were not received: by this very fact the grievance will be proven; because the observance of law has been denied to him, Extra de appel. ca. interposita. For the justice of judgments consists in proof, ff. de restitu. in integ. l. omnes. and in the examination of truth: as is clear there, hence if there is any mandate contrary to the common law, the grievance appears by that very fact. Hence if it is mandated to one who has come with the benefit of inventory that he proceed in the case: the grievance appears by that very fact, indeed if it were an expressed error, nullity would appear. ff. de excu. tu. l. qui in testamentis. But if it is said that he came back later, and the time for the inventory has lapsed, this must be proven: because the acceptance of an inheritance is not presumed. ff. de interdi. ac. §. quia plerunque. and note, ff. solu. ma. l. si cum dotem. §. transgrediamus.

It follows, therefore, that we must examine whether this has been proven or not. Here it must be known that something is not said to be proven unless it has been proven properly, solemnly, and in civil order and manner, as stated in the *Clementina* on witnesses. And for this it is required that the person receiving the testimony be competent to receive it, as noted in the *Codex* on the fiscal law, *Instar*, Book 10; in the *Codex* on the cause of liberty, *Iubemus*; in the *Codex* on the faith of instruments, *Auth. Apud eloquentissimum*; and in the *Codex* on evidence, *Is, apud quem*.

† Hence, since the statute provides that the judge may not delegate the examination of witnesses, but must personally attend and examine them himself, it follows that the witnesses were not duly received. But a doubt arises here: because the delegation was made by the consent of the parties, therefore the testimony should be upheld, as in l. Theopompus, ff. de donationibus praeteritis; extra de testibus, c. Tuas (alias Tuis). To this I respond that here the law fictions that the notary wrote falsely; and thus it fictions that the truth is lacking; hence the consent of the parties appears to effect nothing. l. 1, de his quae pro non scriptis habentur. Moreover, this statute was enacted so that falsities might not be committed; and thus for the public utility. Hence one cannot renounce the said authority, apud eloquentissimum, in Auth. Ut sine prohibitione matris, in fine, in the great gloss. Moreover, this statute prescribes a certain form and prohibits another; and a prohibitive law, which goes beyond annulling or punishing, cannot be renounced, as in C. ne fideiussiones dentur, l. 1, and similar cases. It accords with what is noted in Clem. Saepe, de verbis significandis, and C. de iuramento calumniae, l. 2, §. Sed quia veremur. The contrary does not hold: cap. Tuis (alias Tuis), and what is noted in l. Unica, ff. de feriis, because the oath that is remitted is fictionally deemed to have been taken. Hence there, an oath is fictionally present; and thus solemnity does not lack, nor does the truth of the law by fiction, as in ff. de iureiurando, l. Remittitur. The contrary does not hold: l. Theopompus, because there it is not a mere witness, but also an arbitrator, a moderator of the dowry, because there the presumption of law accords with the witness’s statement and the truth; but here the fiction of the statute is against the truth. And thus the contrary does not hold, and this insofar as it appears from the records that the cause of this article exceeds the amount of one hundred pounds. Otherwise the delegation would be valid, as in l. Scire oportet, ff. de excusationibus tutorum. And so I say and advise, I, Balde de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the faith of this I have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is meant by "full" in various senses.
2. What is meant by "full discretion."
3. "Free" is said in three ways.
4. "General" is said in two ways.
5. What a full, free, and general mandate, or discretion, may encompass.
6. Whether those possessing full, free, and general discretion over war, and over matters dependent upon it, may grant immovable properties, or fiscal properties, to those who have recaptured castles.
7. Spontaneous motion is not presumed in a Prince.
8. If the first confession made to Titius regarding a certain estate is invalid, and subsequently a valid concession is made to Gaius of a certain territory, under which the said estate lies, with this exception, that it is understood that what is conceded to another is thereby conceded, whether the said estate is included.
9. What is meant by "arrival at the place."
body: When, on account of a certain fact, for example concerning war, a full, free, and general mandate is granted to certain persons, and similarly a mandate is granted regarding matters dependent thereon, it must be considered what those to whom discretion has been granted may do. This is to be determined from the meaning and interpretation of their very words. And first, the word "full" must be considered.

† For "full" is said to mean valid, so that what is done by this authority may be effective. D. de acquisitione rerum, l. si de meis; D. de responsis, l. 1. Likewise, "full" is said to mean comprehending all necessary and useful things. D. de arbore, l. si cum dies, § plenum. Likewise, "full" is said of that to which nothing can be added. 16 q. c. bene quidem; and see Hostiensis in c. per venerabilem, Qui sint legitimi. Thus also "plenarium" seems to be that which does not require addition, as noted by Archidiaconus in c. licet, De praebendis, lib. 6. Sometimes, however, "full" is said of that which is so free that it can prefer the inequitable to the equitable. D. de legatis 3, l. fideicommissa, § quanquam.

† Here it must be considered that either full discretion is granted to someone with the transfer of full ownership made therein: and then full discretion is understood as mere will, "thus I will, thus I command"; the will is the reason. And anything is permitted to him who has full ownership; hence he may cast his things into the sea. D. 12.1.14 (Meuius); C. 4.34.1 (In rem manda). And so it is in the aforementioned § Quanquam, nam cum heredi, where full discretion is given to the heir, i.e., the owner, it is understood as mere will; otherwise, if full discretion were granted to someone, as in a minister or official, because then it is understood to be committed to equitable, not mere, discretion. D. 36.1.1 (Lucius Titius testamento). For he who commits something to someone chooses his faith and diligence. Hence he ought not to be deceived who presumed well of the commissioner. D. 32.1.1 (Vnum ex familia), § Item via et c.; and D. 39.5.1 (Item si libertus).

† Thus, "free" is said in three ways. For sometimes it is called free when one can prefer the unjust to the just, as in the aforementioned §. quanquam. Sometimes it is called free when something is done not by any compelling necessity of judgment, but solely by will, as in C. de transac. l. si quis maio. Here it must be considered that either one has power in the act by one's own right: and then it is understood as freedom of judgment. C. de act. et ob. l. sicut. ff. commo. l. in commodato. §. sicut. Or one has power in the act by another's right, i.e., by virtue of a mandate or commission: and then it is understood as equity of judgment. Hence, although free administration is granted to a procurator, he must nevertheless render an account of fault and negligence. C. mandati. l. a procu. Nor is what he does by dissipating, or squandering, or for his own utility and not that of the principal, valid; because this does not proceed from good faith. ff. manda. l. creditor. §. Lucius. Moreover, if they transgressed with little good faith, it would not be censured. ff. de condi. et demon. l. quamuis. ff. de manu. test. l. qui filium. That which is lacking in the diligence of the superior is supplied by good faith, which preserves, as is noted, ff. de iureiu. l. eum, qui. §. in popularibus. in glo. parua. In the third way, "free" is said of that in which variation and inconsistency are admitted, and which can be done and annulled repeatedly, as in ff. de procu. l. ante litem.

† The term "general" is said in two ways. In one way, namely, indefinite and without any restriction, as if by statute the priors of the city had general bailiwick in all matters of the city, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. an generaliter. In the second way, it is said to be general not simply, but with a certain limitation:

† For example, if a general discretion is granted to someone regarding the administration and governance of a ship, or regarding the administration of grain: and in this case it must be considered what the commissioner, to whom this mandate is given, may do. Certainly, if he wishes to extend his mandate to another species, he cannot do so. D. de institoria, l. cuicunque, §. non tamen omne. But the mandate extends well to the individuals of the species committed; hence, if the administration committed cannot be properly administered unless money is acquired by loan, certainly he may acquire money even with interest for the purpose of executing the mandate, as stated in the aforementioned l. cuicunque, §. sed si pecuniam. This comes from a certain necessary, or useful, and expedient consideration. It must be considered that in those matters which cannot be expressly mandated, but come tacitly by consequence, and as members and appendages of the thing mandated, four things are to be considered, without which the effect of those things which pertain to the thing mandated does not stand.

First, it is required that the act tends to that cause in which the power is permitted: as in the aforementioned §. non omne. And it can be by a proximate cause, and by a remote or mediate cause; for example, if discretion is given to hire mercenaries for war, it is of the substance of war to impose taxes. For military affairs cannot be conducted without money: as in Auth. ut iudices, sine quoquo suffragio, §. oportet vos; also to acquire money by loan for paying the mercenaries, if the money of the common treasury is not sufficient. D. quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, l. 1, §. quibus. And generally, whatever is ordered to the thing mandated, whether it is ordered to it by itself and principally, in which order it is called a cause; or by accident, which is called an occasion, is included in the mandate. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. cui iurisdictio; and D. de procuratoribus, l. ad rem mobilem, and l. ad legatum. Those things, however, which do not have an order to that which is commonly not included, because they are entirely foreign, namely, the nature of a mandate is to draw appendages with it; but foreign things are not completed, as noted in D. de procuratoribus, l. qui proprio, §. item quaeritur. Thus, in partnership, the cause is sought, but an occasion that is too foreign is not considered. D. pro socio, l. socium, §. final; and D. de mandato, l. inter causas, §. non omnia.

Second, an evident utility or necessity is required. For it is in vain to strive, and to spend for the sake of pleasure does not pertain to the mandate. D. de exercitoria, l. si, §. quod certe.

Third, it is required that the sum or quantity permitted in the thing allowed is not exceeded; for it ought to be commensurate, and not immoderate. Codex, l. §. quare. What if he exceeds in part, not in whole? I answer: that which is beyond the measure is reduced to the measure. D. de usuris, l. placuit. It is easier, however, in money than in lands, where the computation is more difficult and the portion obscure. D. de adimendis legatis, l. si.

Fourth, the congruity of place and time is required. Codex, l. §. interdum.

† Having premised the above, it is asked whether those who have full, free, and general discretion concerning the war between two cities can grant immovable or fiscal property to those who recapture a castle. And if indeed a castle were taken from the enemy city and given away, a reward could more easily be given as if in place of a non-gratuitous exchange. See the authority of C. de nauicular. l. nauarcorum, lib. 11, and l. 1, § 1, ff. de iust. et iur., according to Guillelmus de Cugliate. But when one insists on the limits of defense, ambushes are repelled chiefly by one’s own citizens, who are bound by natural law to defend their fatherland, as l. veluti, ff. de iust. et iur. teaches; and therefore it would perhaps be shameful to make an agreement regarding a reward. For that which ought to be done by virtue, if done for money, is done shamefully, as l. si, de cond. ob turp. causam, and l. idem est, § si tibi iudicium, in the glossa ordinaria, indicate. It does not seem that the discretion extends to that which is not, as it were, honorable; ff. de verb. sign., l. nepos proculo. Moreover, when a certain form has been prescribed for alienation on the occasion of remuneration, such alienation cannot be made. C. de sacr. sanct. eccl., l. iubemus. But in the alienation of immovables, a certain form has been prescribed: C. de vend. rer. civ., l. si, ergo, etc. Furthermore, these are not accustomed to be granted by the commune of Perugia; therefore, they are not included in the mandate. ff. de pign., l. obligatione generali; C. quae res pign. oblig. poss., l. alumnos. It is also proven that when the Prince has granted [such property], the grant is not valid: C. de pet. bon. subl., l. 1, lib. 10; C. de oper. publ., l. si alum., unless the clause “notwithstanding” were present there. d. l. 1.

† Or unless the Prince grants it by his own motion: which is not presumed in those things which are prohibited on account of ambition: as in c. si motu proprio, de præbendis, lib. 6. If, therefore, the act of the Prince is not valid, it is not valid from an inferior.

But let us suppose that the grant made of the larger territory, in which that estate is situated, is invalid, with this exception that what has been granted to and possessed by another is not included: is that which has been uselessly given to another to be regarded as excepted? I answer: the intention of the grantor is to be considered rather than the effect of the disposition. D. de peculio legato, l. cum dominus; §. si, D. de adimendo legato, l. legatum sub conditione; D. de communibus praediis, l. si in venditione; D. de legatis 1, l. quod in rerum; §. si quis post. But if that which is possessed by another at a certain time is excepted: either it was not possessed at that time, nor was it due to him, then it is not included; otherwise, the contrary applies, as in the aforementioned l. in venditione, at the words "a quo non abhorret." Hence, there, where right and special possession are lacking, the whole is included under the general grant. D. de legatis 1, l. Titiae textores. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, and I have subscribed to this for the truth.

† Adventus is said to occur when someone arrives at a place either in person, or through his procurator, or otherwise through a messenger: as in c. 1, de electionibus, lib. 6, in the word “post adventum”; provided, however, that if this term is referred to the lord of jurisdiction, he must have free exercise of jurisdiction there: as in ff. de officio proconsulis, and l. si aliquam, and l. meminisse, and l. 1, de officio praefecti Augustalis. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, give my opinion and counsel, and I have subscribed to this for the sake of faith.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When and in what manner witnesses may be received for the perpetual memory of the matter.
2. Whether witnesses received before an arbitrator make proof in another trial.
3. While a case is pending before an arbitrator, the judge ought not to be approached.
4. Whether joinder of issue is necessary, if a party objects, where witnesses are requested to be received for the perpetual memory of the matter.
5. Whether an arbitrator may again examine and re-examine witnesses, to determine whether they told the truth before the judge, just as the judge equally could.
6. Whether witnesses of the trial are to be recalled.
7. A witness who wavers in his first testimony is not believed.
body: The point of the question, on which the legal opinion is requested, is as follows. A certain Francis, while at Vannes and in his last illness, said these words in the presence of seven witnesses: “I will that if my daughter Lucia should die without children, half of all my goods shall belong to Lady Florence, her mother.” Then the said Francis died. Then the said Lucia, his daughter, died after him in her minority, nine days after the death of her father, with Lady Jacoba, the mother of the said Lucia, and the said Florence, the mother of the said Francis, surviving. And Lady Jacoba entered into the inheritance of the said Francis, her late husband, through the person of the said Lucia, her daughter. Now, when a dispute arose between the said Florence and Jacoba, with the said Jacoba alleging and denying that the aforementioned legacy had never been made to the said Lady Florence by the said Ser Francis, her son, they finally unanimously compromised the said question to the said P., who, as arbitrator, set a term for the parties to produce, claim, and prove their rights before him. However, Florence, being in possession of half of the said goods by reason of the said legacy, fearing, on account of the great mortality then existing in the city, that the witnesses who had been present at the said legacy might die, had the said Jacoba summoned before the ordinary judge to have the oaths and examination of the said witnesses taken.

And briefly, they were examined for the perpetual memory of the matter, with the curator of the said Lady Jacoba appearing and objecting, who was, and still is, under the power of her father. And the said witnesses proved at the bench that the said legacy had been made to the said Lady Florence in the form aforesaid. Now it is objected that the said witnesses are not valid for the part of the said Lady Jacoba, because they were examined when the case was not yet contested, with the party appearing and objecting. To this it is said that the judicial order should not have been observed after she appeared and objected: as in c. per venerabiles, § praeterea, Extra, Qui filii sint legitimi. It is answered on the contrary for the part of the said Florence that this does not avail, since the said Lady Jacoba appeared through a procurator, being herself under the power of her father, a curator could not be appointed for her; and rightly so, because a curator, nor a tutor, is given except to free persons; and rightly it is said that the said appearance was not valid. It is answered for the part of the said Lady Florence that the aforementioned objections do not avail; and that although the case was not yet contested, the witnesses could be examined, after she was in possession of the goods; because it is not within the power of the party to initiate the lawsuit: as in l. pure, in fine, ff. De doli exceptione, where the case is literally applicable in c. Signi, and c. Alberi, Extra, De testibus, and there Innocentius expressly holds this regarding witnesses who are produced on the part of the possessor, who fears that a controversy may be brought against him. It is answered for the part of the said Jacoba that the aforementioned points do not avail in law, because the said Lady Florence could make her proofs before the said Lord Arbiter; and when the cause ceases, the effect ceases, as in l. adigere, § quamvis, ff. De iure patronatus, and l. generaliter, C. De episcopis et clericis. And when the cause of the law ceases, the law itself ceases. It is answered for the part of the said Lady Florence that this does not avail, because although there was a cause submitted to arbitration, she could go to the judge: as in l. litigatorem, l. si quis rem, ff. De arbitris. For it would have been dangerous for the said Lady Florence if she had caused the examination to be made before the said Arbiter.

For they would not have given their testimony in another court: as is noted and very clearly stated by Innocentius in the said chapter, and by Albericus, explaining the difference between an arbitrator and a judge. For he says that a witness examined before an arbitrator is presumed to be bolder in telling falsehoods than before a judge, because the arbitrator does not have the power to punish them, whereas the judge does. Moreover, the case is found in the last law of the Code on Wills, that if the same witnesses were to appear, it would be within the power of the adversary. This is noted by Florentius, because they could have been made infamous and hostile, on account of which the proof of the said Florence might have been destroyed; otherwise, the proof of the said Florence would have failed. And since it has not been entirely removed, in case of doubt the cause is presumed to be impulsive, and the law remains: as is noted by Cynus in the said law *generaliter*, and by Decius in the chapter *decet concessum*, Extra, de re iudicata, book 6. Now, three of these seven witnesses seem to wish to say the contrary of what is found written and proven by them at the instance of the party, because there is a certain rumor that they say this. But the contrary, on account of the profit obtained from the opposing side; and this is well proven by rumor. Now it is asked, whether the said witnesses are valid in law, notwithstanding the aforementioned objections against the said examiner? It is also asked, whether the notary is to be believed, or the said witnesses, who say that they said the contrary; and whether, for this reason, even if they said the contrary, the right of the said Florence would be vitiated? It is also asked in law, whether the appearance in court of the said lady Jacoba, who was under the power of her father, is valid; because a curator is not appointed except for free persons.

† While a case is pending before arbitrators, the judge should not be approached; nevertheless, the path is not so obstructed that the act is void by operation of law; on the contrary, the petition presented before the judge is valid. D. de arbitris, l. si quis rem, § litigatores; and l. item si unus, § si multum post.

But whether the contestation of the lawsuit is necessary when the opposing party objects: it seems that it is, as in the chapter *Per venerabiles*, *Qui filii sint legitimi*. In the gloss, the contrary view appears: because where an exception of witnesses is sought for the perpetual memory of the matter, the judge’s inquiry is also sought and implored, namely that the judge investigate the truth from the witnesses before the action becomes moot; and this is concluded to the judge, not to the party; and therefore, without the contestation of the lawsuit, the case proceeds, as in the chapter *Quoniam frequenter*, *Extra*, *Litis contestatione non interposita*, to this effect, as in the Authentica *De testibus*, § *Pe*. And this is the truth.

But whether an arbiter may examine and reflect upon whether they told the truth before the judge, and again, by examining them, just as the judge may examine witnesses who testified before the arbiter at the instance of a party, as it seems from C. de testib. l. si, it appears that he may not; because it is more probable that they told the truth before the judge, who has the power to punish; because he who is more feared more effectively elicits the truth from a witness. I answer: this case is not found to have been decided.

And some say that judicial witnesses are not to be recalled: because they cannot vary; but witnesses of discretion are. But Cynus, in the Code, on edicts, in the law "is, apud quem," says that the new judge examines anew: as in the Code, on the time of appeal, in the law "per hanc." That does not apply, because it speaks of different witnesses.

† Whatever the case may be, no credence is given to a witness who wavers or varies in his initial testimony: as in C. de falsis, l. qui falsa, vel varia. Thus, if he testifies repeatedly, credence is given to the earlier statement, or at least no credence is given to the later one; because it is established that this occurred before perjury, argumentum extra de testibus, cap. testimonium.

But whether the notary or the witness is believed: I say that the notary here acts in the place of both notary and witness on account of the secret examination. And therefore the notary is more believed. To this effect in l. j. in fin. ff. quemadmod. test. aper. according to Jacobus de Arena, and in l. si quis decurio according to Cynus and Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If a legacy is left to a certain girl for the purpose of assisting her marriage, and the said girl marries before claiming the legacy: ought she to receive the said legacy?
body: Considered,
†The heir of the testator sees the legate as being in his aid, etc. See in the 5th part of the consilia, no. 495, beginning “considerato,” etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is this substitution? I institute my son: and if legitimate and natural children were born to him, and if any of them were to die while still in pupillary age, I substitute the survivors.
2. Whether a grandfather, who did not institute his grandson, can substitute for that same grandson by means of a fideicommissum.
body: For the clarity of the case, it is necessary to set forth the inscribed facts. A certain Peter Putii Griffoli of the Castle of Papiano in the county of Perugia made a will, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they may be and may be found, he instituted and made M., his legitimate and natural son, his universal heir; and if the said son M. should die without legitimate and natural children, he substituted to him his nearest male blood relatives, one or more, then surviving, from the paternal line only; and if legitimate and natural children were born to the said son M., and any of them should die in pupillary age, he substituted to him the survivors; and if the said children to be born to the said M. should die in pupillary age, he substituted to these pupils the said nearest blood relatives from the paternal line only, then living, and no others, etc. This testator, not ignorant of his patrimony or assets, ordered and expressly forbade that any Trebellianic or Falcidian portion could or ought to be deducted in any manner, and this was his last will, etc. Then the said testator Peter died, now ten years and more ago, with the said son and heir surviving him. After the death of the said Peter, M. took as his wife the said Vicina of Venatico, from whom he had Antonio a year before his own death; then the said M. died, now two years or so ago, with the said Antonio, his son, aged eighteen months or so, surviving him, and with the said Vicina, his wife and mother of the said Antonio, surviving; and after a short time of two years, the said A. died, aged perhaps three years or so, with the said Vicina, his mother, surviving, and with Martin and Griffolio, his carnal nephews of the said testator Peter, born of Banniculo of Todi, brother of the said testator Peter, and nearest male blood relatives of the said testator and of the said M. and of the said Antonio from the paternal line. Now the question arises, having seen the will, whether the inheritance of the said M. and Ranchone comes to the said Martin and Griffolio, or to another entirely or in part; and if the lady Vicina, mother of the said Antonio, succeeds in the said inheritance in any respect, and to what extent? First, it must be seen what kind of substitution this is, which was made to the children of children; second, whether it could have been made.

† Regarding the first point, I say that this substitution cannot be considered pupillary, because the nephews would fall under the paternal power; hence, they could not be substituted to by the grandfather in a pupillary manner, as stated in the Digest, title "De vulgari et pupillari substitutione," law 2, section "Posthumus." It therefore necessarily follows that such a substitution is fideicommissary after the inheritance has been accepted.

Let us therefore see whether a grandfather, who instituted his son and not his grandson, could substitute for the grandson by means of a fideicommissum.
