And certainly the law seems to determine this question thus: either the testator burdens [the heir] under the name of heir; and then he can [do so]; or under his own name, or that which serves in place of his own name in our case; and then it is not valid, as in D. 36, 1, l. si fuerit and l. si sic, where it seems expressly stated. For since the grandfather, unless he left [property] to the grandsons, could not burden the heirs with the charge of a fideicommissum, C. 6, 32, l. ab eo. Bartolus in the said l. si sic does not firmly hold the same [opinion], because he saw that the matter was doubtful; and he says first that perhaps it is not valid, unless perhaps we say that by burdening the grandsons by fideicommissum, it is tacitly induced that the father is requested to restore [the property] to them, as in l. denique, §. interdum, D. 33, 7, and l. procul, D. 7, 1, and l. alio, D. 33, 1. This is what he himself says. I say it with doubt: but it does not seem well said that if the father substituted for his son, if he should die without children, that he is therefore seen to have substituted the children for the son; since a tacit burden is not understood in the person of the son. D. 28, 5, l. Lucius, and there noted. Likewise, he who is burdened is not therefore understood to be tacitly substituted. D. 28, 5, l. ex facto est, and l. sed si sic, and the said l. ab eo. And this is expressly held by Laurentius de Arena in the said l. Lucius, §. cum quis, and ad Trebatium, l. ex facto, §. fin., and what is noted there by Cynus in l. 1, C. 8, 40. But for the other side serves l. Titia Seio, §. Seia, and what is noted there by Dino in leg. 1, l. si seruus, §. qui Margaritam, at the end, §. secundo. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, advise, and I have subscribed to this in faith.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Within what time limit must he who claims to have been prejudiced in the measurement, the valuation, or the appraiser lodge a complaint, and what must he prove.
body: He who

† is aggrieved in a measurement or valuation wrongfully made can complain about this within a year; and once an unjust valuation or measurement is proved, that which is beyond or short of the proper measure is [corrected], as in C. de censi. et peræquato. l. qui gravatos. lib. 11. But after a year he cannot complain, with the exception of minors and absentees, as is stated there. Moreover, it is not sufficient for the complainant to prove the old valuation, because the prices of things change over time, ff. de fal. l. precia rerum; C. de iure dot. l. si inter; and thus, according to the variety of times, the assessment of the commune must be changed, and everyone ought to bear burdens according to the strength of their estate, C. de col. fundo. l. hominis. lib. 11. and de anno. et tribu. l. indictiones. lib. 10. etc. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, state and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When several brothers remain in communion, a dowry received by one of them ought not to be restored from the common fund, unless it is proven to have been converted into common property.
body: Although the sons

Whether they remained in partnership with their uncle, or the brothers remain in partnership among themselves: nevertheless, if one receives a dowry, he ought not to be reimbursed from the common fund, unless it is proven that it was converted into common property, as noted in Speculum de iure, Part 4, § Sequitur, under the heading "Quid in communione." Since it is alleged that part of the dowry was spent on the wife’s clothing and ornaments, and not on the common fund, such expenditure ought undoubtedly not to be made from the common fund, nor reimbursed; but the clothing and ornaments, as they are, remain with the husband. Digest, De solutione matrimonii, L. In his; Digest, De donationibus inter virum et uxorem, L. Sed si vir lamiam. Regarding other expenses for banquets and similar consumed items, the affection between the brothers must be considered; for he who suffers that common grain and wine be expended for the common honor cannot recover his share, because he did not have the intention of obligating anyone. Digest, De negotiis gestis, L. Nescennius; Digest, De manumis, L. Creditor, § 1; Digest, De administratione tutorum, L. Cum plures, § In primis. But if these expenses were made from the dowry money, there is no action for the husband to receive payment from the common fund; because one cannot be compelled to make such expenses for a brother, or a nephew for an uncle, or vice versa. Digest, De muneribus et honoribus, L. Qui originem, § Si. And there the author notes that the law distinguishes elsewhere, which is relevant, from which patrimony the expenditure is made. Digest, De petitione hereditatis, L. Sed si lege, § Adeo. Just as the dowry follows the husband, as in Digest, De familiae erciscundae, L. Si maritus, so the expenses and burdens of the dowry are imputed to himself, as in Digest, De duobus reis, L. Si id, quod ego. For such expenditure concerns a proper and simple cause. But that which profits the common fund must be considered. But we, what to one of them... Digest, Pro socio, L. Actione, § Labeo, at the end. And it supports this: Digest, De familiae erciscundae, L. Si filia, § Nec solum, where the dowry given to the son is not recovered, except insofar as it was converted into the father’s property or the common property. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The word "and" and what effect it has on instruments.
2. A general clause does not refer to those matters which are specially declared.
3. A confession prejudices those who have a cause of action against the confessor.
4. Whether a writing not subscribed by a notary proves anything, if he did not publish it.
body: As the instruments are thus, one being an instrument of confession and the other an instrument of promise: nevertheless, because they were made immediately and simultaneously, and the general clause refers to everything, I ask whether both said instruments must be produced together and estimated together by the authority of the judge; because the clause, etc., joins both instruments. Or it may be said that they can be produced inseparably, just as a confession of price and a promise made notwithstanding the confession are two instruments and are produced separately. D. de edendo, l. Praetor, in the gloss. And that clause which refers to everything pertains to the second instrument; because the first was absolute, which is evident from that clause, "remittentis" and so forth.

† For under this etc. all things which are by custom or by nature are included, as the authorities say in l. si duo patroni and in l. Gallus § 1, the first part being the more correct opinion. But whatever the case may be, let us see whether one should adhere to the confession in specific things, or whether, on the contrary, a departure from the confession is permitted both in specific things and in non-specific ones. And it appears that, considering the clause “in the entire inheritance which he could have in whatever goods etc.” and considering those words, namely “the things and goods which he received from the goods and inheritance etc.,” that the said word “received” does not refer to things considered as specific:

† because a general clause does not refer to those matters which are specially declared. D. de verb. oblig. l. stipulationes commodissimum; and thus one must reconcile the matter, for it would be absurd to refer the clause "notwithstanding" to the preceding pure and free particular, as in Extr. de donat. c. cum dilectus. And this is most true: because the specified things were confessed not as paternal hereditary assets, but simply under the words "of goods and heirs"; [the clause] refers only to that which is confessed under the name of the father's goods and inheritance. And therefore, in other matters, the confession remains more firm: not weak, because a derogation in certain respects seems to confirm the rest, as in D. de milit. testam. l. tribu. §. ult. But this dowry begins with delivery: and therefore the woman swore. Otherwise, to what purpose would she have sworn, if she had delivered nothing, since she promised nothing? Therefore, I hold this part as consonant with law and truth. And thus I hold, Baldus de Perusio, V.I.D., and I have subscribed to the truth, etc. Moreover, it is asked whether, by this instrument proved against a third party, it is proved that these specified things were dowry.

And it must be said that this is so: if this third party derives his title from the husband; for the confession of the predecessor prejudices the successor, just as does a contract and a judgment. D. de pign. l. si superatus, cum si.

† Furthermore, it is asked, because the notary was prevented by death from subscribing or publishing, whether the said writing proves? I answer that it does not: unless a comparison of the handwriting has been made according to the form of law, and faith has also been given by witnesses to the instrument, or by others who have derogated from the notary, thus reduced into public form by the authority of the ordinary judge, with those to be cited having been cited, as in Extra, de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum P. tabellio, and Codex, de testibus, l. Publicati. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the appellate judge should pronounce on the abandonment before the judge from whom the principal sentence can be put into execution.
body: The point, on which counsel is sought, is as follows:

† namely, a definitive sentence was pronounced against Peter at the petition of Lady Joanna: from which sentence an appeal was taken both by Peter himself and by Lady Decha for her own interest; and the interest of the said Lady Decha, mother of the said Lady Joanna, was proven, and the proceedings on these appeals continued until a definitive judgment; and a commission was issued to a consulting judge, as to what sentence should be rendered on the appeal of Lady Decha: on the other appeal, the time limits have elapsed, namely 40 days, within which the appeal case must be terminated, or the first sentence remains firm according to the form of the statute. And no pronouncement having been made by the judge to whom, on the appeal lodged by the said Peter, the judge from whom, having executed the first sentence, caused the said Peter and his sureties to be arrested. It is asked, whether he could lawfully make the said execution, etc., what is the law. An appeal impedes execution insofar as it is pending, and only against that person: as noted in D. de man. l. creditor. in principio. And both parties can appeal from the same sentence: as in X. de test. c. Raynutius. and c. Raynaldus. And if one party renounces his appeal, or abandons it, execution can be made against such renouncing or abandoning party; nor does the appeal avail him, which is found to be extinguished. C. de appel. l. eos. in principio, in the great gloss. This is true if the abandonment is clear; but if it is uncertain whether it has been abandoned, then until a pronouncement is made on the abandonment, execution ought not to be made. And a pronouncement on abandonment is sometimes necessary, sometimes not. C. quomodo, et quando iudex. l. si praeses. and what is noted in c. ultima de appell. in the Clementines. In the present case, however, a pronouncement seems necessary before execution could be made; because the statute speaks of useful time, hence the lapse of fatal days cannot appear from the counting of natural days; but it requires external knowledge of the case, whether an impediment intervened or not, as in l. 1. D. de diuer. et tem. praesc. And therefore, before this is declared by the judge to whom, I do not believe that the judge from whom can make execution; because it does not appear to him that principal jurisdiction has been devolved to him. And therefore I say that the said arrest does not hold, as being temerarious and undiscussed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation made by a father to his daughter and her heirs, if the daughter herself dies during the father's lifetime and leaves children, passes to such children.
2. A son is understood to be charged with restitution after death, if he dies without children.
3. If a wife is instituted and charged with restitution, whether it is understood that this applies if she dies without common children of hers and the testator.
4. Whether a codicillary clause operates to any effect in a will that is void due to the omission of a grandson.
body: The facts are as follows: Cola Putii of Spello made a donation inter vivos to Salmitius of Spello, in consideration of the merits and services rendered by the wife of the said Salmitius and by the daughters of the said Cola to the donor, in the name and on behalf of his wife, of certain goods and his possessions; and he promised not to revoke the said donation for any cause, as is fully established by the public instrument drawn up concerning the said donation. Now, with the passage of time, this Cola Putii, coming to the point of death, made a will, instituted Titius as his heir, and died having made the said will. This Salmitius, to whom the said donation was made, by virtue of this donation wishes to take possession of and hold these goods, and perhaps wishes to sell them. The heir instituted in the said will impedes the sale by the said Salmitius, claiming and stating that he has a right and dominion in these goods and possessions by virtue of the said will. And inasmuch as this heir objects, and the said Salmitius has not found a buyer, it is now asked whether this heir can legally impede the said sale, and whether he has any right in the said goods and possessions, and what is the legal view on this matter? Two notable points are to be observed here.

The first point is whether, if a father makes a donation to his daughter and to the heirs of his daughter, the donation is invalid as regards the daughter while she is in his power; and if the daughter dies, it is entirely annulled as regards her. But does it ever hold as regards the children of the daughter? It must be said that, if the daughter predeceases the donor, it does not hold; because the donation was not made to the grandchildren through the daughter, but to the heirs of the daughter; and therefore, since it failed in the person of the daughter, it could not be transmitted to the heirs, as provided in Codex, On Inofficious Donations, Law 2. For the term "heir" is understood to mean an heir, that is, a successor, not, that is, children, unless they are heirs. Digest, On Pacts, Law "If to you," Section "If you have agreed," in the gloss. The second point is:
† If a son is asked to make restitution after death, it is understood that he died without children. L. Cum acutissimi. C. de fideicom.

† What if someone instituted his wife as heir and requested her to restore the inheritance after his death: does this apply if she dies without common children of hers and the testator? And it seems that it does not apply to an outsider. L. acutissimi, as noted, C. de inst. sub. L. generaliter. On the contrary, it seems that he does not wish to prefer an outsider to his own sons: as is evident from the reasoning of the aforementioned laws: because he preferred an outsider by instituting him, he seems also to prefer him by substituting. FF. de condi. et dem. L. Publius, § 1.

Thirdly, it is asked: since a testament in which grandchildren through a daughter are passed over is null, as in Auth. cum de appel. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum, does that clause, “if it is not valid by the law of testaments, let it be valid by the law of codicils,” have any effect? And it seems that it does not; because the said testament is null as being inofficious; and therefore the institution by way of fideicommissum ought not to be valid, as is noted in C. de libe. praete. auth. ex causa. For the right of declaring a maternal grandfather’s testament null succeeds in place of the complaint of inofficiousness raised, and so too the rest, C. de inoffic. testa. l. Titia. This is the opinion held by Gul. de Cu. C. de codicil. in l. fi. The contrary is held by Cy. in auth. ex causa. According to Dy., almost all the moderns hold the same. The question is doubtful; nevertheless, I adhere to the common opinion; and I say that the codicillary clause is valid, and therefore the legitime is due to the grandchildren through the daughter; but the residue to the legatees and the heirs instituted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A confession made in the absence of the opposing party proves release.
2. Whether a confession made in the presence of a surety is deemed to have been made in the absence of the adversary.
3. Whether an instrument is valid if the notary is not requested by both parties.
4. If two notaries are requested regarding the same contract and draw up different instruments, whether such instruments are to be believed.
body: First, it must be considered whether a confession made in the absence of the opposing party is valid for proving a release. Second, whether it is said to be made in the absence of the party if it is made in the presence of a surety.

I come to the first point. Some say that it is not valid unless one party is present. For a confession requires the presence of the adversary, just as a pact does. D. de confessionibus, l. certum; § si quis, C. de confessionibus, l. 1; D. de pactis, l. idem in duobus. It is supported by D. de interrogatoribus et responsionibus, l. finalis; and D. de liberatione, l. Aurelius, § finalis. Otherwise, unless such a confession is transmitted by a messenger or by letter. D. de depositionibus, l. publica, § finalis; D. de donationibus, l. nuda. The contrary view seems correct, namely that such a confession is valid for mere proof, even if made in the absence of the adversary, as stated in Auth. de testibus, § et licet; and it gives rise to an exception, as noted in D. de liberatione, l. non solum, § liberationem. Although a pact is not valid in the absence of a party, unless a messenger or letter intervenes, because a pact is a contract; but a confession is not a contract. D. de acquisitione et obligatione, l. consensu; and see C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud; D. de acceptilatione, l. si acceptilatum, § finalis. To this it is added, as noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Pomp. scribit; D. de edicto edilitio, l. quæro, § finalis; and C. de fideiussoribus ab intestato, c. finalis. Solution: it must be said that, as regards the effect of inducing or disposing of something, it is not valid between absent parties, unless the disposition depends on the will of one party only: as in ratification or disapproval, as stated in the aforementioned l. Pomp. But as regards the purpose of proving payment made and repelling a contrary fiction, it is valid, as stated in the aforementioned § et licet, whatever Petrus says in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter.

† On the second point, it is said that an act is not considered to have been done in the absence of the adversary if it was done in the presence of a surety: for through the surety the principal exception of fraud could have been raised. The case is in the aforementioned law *in duobus*, § *si*.

But does the instrument drawn up concerning the said confession have validity? It appears that it does not, because the notary ought to be requested by both parties, as in the Authentica de tabellis, § dos autem. But here he was not requested except by the sole surety; therefore the instrument is invalid and does not bind. Solution: When an act is performed for the benefit of both parties, then the notary ought to be requested by both parties; but sometimes it is done for the benefit of only one party, and in favor of only one party it suffices that he be requested by that one, as noted there. Hence, because the said confession was in favor of only one party, it suffices that the notary and the witnesses were requested by that party. For I say the same regarding the witnesses.

† Finally, it is asked: two notaries were simultaneously requested to draw up the same contract; these produce various instruments; are such instruments to be believed? I answer that if, due to such variation, each of the notaries is singular in his own writing, neither will be believed. For although one notary is believed, this is true only unless the parties have employed several, as stated in the Authentica *De haereditatibus et falsis*, § *Si vero absunt*, and by argument from law 1, Digest, *De officio consulis*. Moreover, writings that vary in substance or effect, regarding which the dispute arises, concerning the same matter, derogate from one another. Code, *De fide instrumentorum*, law *Scripturae*; and what is noted in chapter *Cum Ioannes Heremita*, by Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether payment of a dowry promised to several persons, and also to the husband, can be made to the husband alone.
body: The statement of the fact is as follows: Franciscus, Petrus, and Laurentius, brothers and sons of the late Mutius of Borgo San Sepolcro, and Ser Sanctes [son of] Ser Franciscus of the said place, in their own name, and as the agent and in the name of the agency of the lady, the wife of the late said Mutius—all the aforesaid in the names as above, and each of them in their own names and in the name of Master Bartholomaeus and Solus, sons of the late said Mutius, concerning whom they promised ratification and that they would bring it about that when the aforesaid Master Bartholomaeus and his associate returned to the Borgo, or either of them, they would ratify and approve the present contract—were content and confessed that they had had and received from Matthaeus and Massus, brothers and sons of the late Vannes Buminuti of the said Borgo, giving as dowry for the said Magdalena, their niece, and formerly the daughter of Buminutus [son of] the aforesaid Vannes, and the wife of the said Franciscus, 380 gold florins to be presented at the Borgo. Which dowry the abovesaid brothers and Ser Sanctes, in the names as above, promised to the aforesaid brothers, stipulating in the name of the lady, their niece, to return and restore in every case and event of the dowry having to be restored, etc. Thereafter, immediately, notwithstanding the aforesaid confession, the aforesaid Matthaeus and Massus, acknowledging that they were the true debtors for the said dowry, promised to give and pay to the said Franciscus, Petrus, and Laurentius, brothers, and to Ser Sanctes, in the names as above, being present and stipulating, the whole of the said dowry in its entirety: namely, 380 gold florins within certain terms, as is contained in the instrument. Then, the said marriage having been contracted between the said Franciscus and the said Lady Magdalena, the aforesaid Matthaeus and Massus paid the whole of the said dowry to the aforesaid Franciscus, husband of the said Lady Magdalena, without consulting the others named in the said instrument of promise; and they were released by Franciscus himself. Finally, the said marriage having been dissolved by the death of the said Franciscus, the said Lady Magdalena surviving, and the occasion for restoring the said dowry having arisen, the said Lady Magdalena brings action against the said others who confessed that they had received the said dowry, since the estate of the said Franciscus, formerly her husband, is insolvent. It is asked whether the aforesaid or others, to whom payment of the said dowry was not made from the promise of it made by the said Matthaeus and Massus, can demand from Matthaeus and Massus themselves the portion falling to them, or in any way trouble them for their portion, notwithstanding the payment of the entire dowry made to the said Franciscus, the husband, and the discharge obtained from him, against whose assets recourse cannot be had since they are insolvent; or rather, whether those paying the aforesaid husband Franciscus are released, and nothing can be demanded from them by the other creditors, notwithstanding that the inheritance of the said Franciscus is insolvent. Please render a consilium upon these matters.

† If in the instrument the said quantity of 380 florins was promised to each of the aforesaid stipulating parties in solidum, or otherwise, whether it could not be paid in its entirety to the husband to the prejudice of any of them, just as with multiple debtors; for it is deemed paid to one by the will of all, C. de duo. reis. l. fi., ff. de no. l. si rem aliquam. §. fin., ff. de iureiu. l. duobus, C. si cer. pe. l. si non singuli. But if the dowry was promised to several without expressing that it was to each in solidum, then it is doubtful, because it seems promised to each pro rata, ff. de duo. re. l. reos. §. contra tabulas, although whosoever receives it is bound to deliver it to the husband, because he is deemed to have stipulated for the sake and in consideration of the husband, ff. de duo. reis. l. si id, quod ego. in gl. If, therefore, an obligation was acquired for each pro rata, it could not be paid to the husband in solidum to the prejudice of the others, ar. ff. so. mat. l. si cum dotem. §. transgrediamur. The contrary, however, seems truer: because they previously bound themselves in solidum in consideration of the future promise, and afterwards they received the promises not for their own sake, but for the sake of the husband, as in the said l. si id, quod ego; whence they are deemed to have tacitly consented that the whole amount be paid to the husband, ff. mand. l. idemque. §. si cui, since the business principally pertains to him, ff. fam. er. l. si maritus. Therefore, payment having been made to the husband, the cause of the prior promise by which they bound themselves in solidum to the restitution was fulfilled. And therefore, in conclusion, it seems it should be said that from the first obligation of restitution of the dowry each is bound in solidum, although the dowry was paid to the husband alone; for this seems tacitly agreed upon from the nature of the dowry, that the dowry could be paid to the husband in solidum, arg. ff. de condi. et dem. l. Titio centum. §. Titio genero. If, however, there were not an instrument by which each bound himself in solidum, then each would be bound pro rata, as in the §. contra tabulas. And therefore the words of the instrument must be inspected. For the action is brought on the first instrument fulfilled by the subsequent payment, as in l. cum enim. de noua. etc. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A father who has something written or promised to his son, whom he holds in his power, which is owed to the father himself, appears to grant this to the son as part of his peculium; otherwise, if the son is emancipated, because then it is presumed to be a donation.
2. Whether the son is bound to share the fruits of the dowry.
body: It is to be noted

† that when a father does business in the name of his son, or causes to be ascribed to the son himself that which is owed to the father himself, or causes a promise to be made to the son; if indeed the son is not emancipated, but in the power of the father, the father is deemed to grant it to him as peculium: and therefore, unless the father afterwards in his will pre-legates the peculium, such money belongs to all the heirs in common according to their hereditary portion: as in C. fam. erci. etc. and l. certum and l. Titij filii. de pe. leg. and there by Iac. de Are. and de leg. 3. l. nomen. §. filio. If, however, the father did such things in the name of an emancipated son, a donation will be presumed, l. 1. ff. de don. Resolving therefore the first doubt, I say that because Fideibocannus and Bonaventura were not emancipated, the said 400 florins belong to the said Antonius for a third share, and this concerning the first part, or first point. Upon the second point it is to be noted,

† that if the father bears the burdens of the marriage of his son, the fruits of the dowry ought to belong to the father himself on account of the burdens which he sustains. And therefore, if the father collected them, there is no doubt that it ought to be common to all the heirs according to their hereditary share, because they belong to the father by full right. The same is true if the son collected them in the name of the father, because they are peculium profectitium when the son collects them in the father's name, and therefore it is common to all the heirs, as in the said l. certum. If, however, the father willed that the said fruits belong to his said son, then it must be considered that the father can renounce the usufruct which he has in adventitious property: and then that belongs to the son, and not to the coheirs, as in C. de bonis, quae lib. l. cum oportet. §. sin autem res; and thus it seems that Antonius has gained the said fruits of the dowry, and ought not to share them. Nevertheless, the truth is thus: that either the dowry was counted out to the son and given to him from the beginning, and then it is something adventitious, and the father could renounce the usufruct, and it would belong to the son by full right, as in the said §. si nautem res; or the dowry was given from the very beginning to the father himself, and thus was made the father's by full right; and then either the father gives back that dowry to the son, because the son keeps his wife with him, supports her, and bears the burdens of the marriage—and the result is that the son and husband is not bound to share anything with his brothers, as in C. fam. er. l. 2. and ff. eod. l. si maritus—or the father bears the burdens of the marriage and the son collected the profit: then such profits are common to all the heirs of the father, because a donation from a father to a son is not presumed if the son is in his power, but a bare commission of administration is presumed, as in the said l. Titii filii, ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. pater; and therefore in that case what was bought from such profits would have to be shared, unless it were proven that the father intended to donate to this son. For then it would be confirmed by the death of the father, unless it had been revoked by the father, as noted in C. fa. er. l. filię eman. and C. de inof. don. l. 2. Therefore, the second question cannot be answered unconditionally, but under the aforesaid distinction. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A testator bequeaths something to be distributed among certain maids when they marry, and the said maids die before they marry, except for one who is married; whether the entire legacy devolves to the married maid.
body: The facts are as follows: Paul of Stidia, being on the point of death, made a will, in which, among other things, he disposed thus, because he commanded that all his lands, territories, and all possessions situated in the County of Gubbio, located in their respective places, be distributed among the daughters of Manittius and Lord Manifi, and the daughter of Paciolus Sauli, and the daughter of Ugonitius Cocarelli, and the daughter of Realis Puctiolus Albrici, and the daughter of Nicolellus Paschus, and the daughter of Angiolinus Aucumbali of Gubbio. And to each of them equally, and to each of them there shall be given only for dowries, when they shall marry, or when they shall enter into any monastery, if any of them should take the monastic habit, for an equal share: as appears in the said will. Now the daughter of the aforementioned Realis claims her portion of the said possessions and fruits from the heirs of the said testator. And it is said on behalf of the said heirs that the said daughter ought not to have the said part: on the ground that the said Realis, at the time the said will was made, had two other daughters older than this one, who does not claim; and because at the time the said will was made, and at the death of the said testator, this one was an infant, and now, when she claims, she is married, and now already two years and more have passed. Now the question arises, having seen the said will and the aforementioned point, whether the said daughter of Realis is admitted to the aforementioned claim in law: and if she is admitted, whether in whole or in part, etc.

† This daughter of the real estate rightly claims: because since the condition of marriage exists in her person, and did not exist in separate persons, the whole is due to her, who now lives, as ff. de leg. 2. l. si quis Titio. §. fi. and l. cum quidam. ver. plane. de condi. insti. l. vter ex fratribus. Also, the legacy is to be understood in such a way that it is given to her among the children of the said real estate, in whom the time or condition for initiating marriage is found to have existed from the beginning. Therefore, with the others dead, it is due to the survivor: because those who predeceased do not transmit the fulfillment of the condition to their heirs. And it makes ff. de legatis. 2. l. cum ita legatur. §. fideicommisso. there where it says, or after all of them have been extinguished. And I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A father having several sons, and among them one brother in the Order of Preachers, whom he instituted as heir to a certain sum, and forbade him to claim more: but he instituted his other sons as universal and equal heirs to himself; then he generally substituted all his sons to one another. It is asked whether the said brother, a preacher, is included in the said substitution.
body: A certain man, having one son in the Order of Preachers and four other secular sons, made a will: in which he left to the said brother 100 pounds and instituted him as heir therein; and he willed that he could not claim anything else in his goods. Then he instituted the said other sons as universal heirs in equal parts; and he made a substitution in this manner. And if any one, or several, of the said sons, whether born or to be born, or any one, or several, of his daughters, whether born or to be born, should die at any time in pupillary age, or if afterwards they should not reach the age of 25 years without legitimate children born of their body, he substituted pupillarily, vulgarly, and by fideicommissum the surviving sons, or their male children, by stocks and not by heads. Then the said testator died, with all his said sons remaining above 14 years of age, and afterwards Peter, one of the said sons, died intestate, with Agnella, his daughter, surviving. Then Dominic, his son, died last, having made a will, in which he left to the said brother John, his brother, 100 pounds, and that he could not claim more in his goods. Then he left his mother as universal heir, novc rcamdicti, of the said brother John, with the said brother John and the said Ametermia, daughter of the said Peter, surviving. Let it be known to you that Amatuemus and Peter were brothers of the said brother John from both parents; and Dominic and Laurentius only from the father. Now it is asked, what is the law: and how much should the said brother John have in the paternal goods, and in the goods of the said sons, his brothers:

† How was the testator’s intention regarding the son who was in the order of Preachers? That is, as to the effect of the substitution, whether the father intended him to be admitted together with his brothers, or not, is sufficiently doubtful from the substitution. For it is against the religious, and it is so, because the father forbade him to demand more, and therefore he does not seem to have loved him in making the substitution, whom he seemed to hate in instituting him, cf. D. 35.1.1 (Publius), § 1. For general words are restricted so that odious persons are not included, D. 35.1.2 (Lucius), § Lucius Titius damnam. And thus it seems likely that the father intended to substitute those remaining in the secular world. For just as he does not seem to have substituted for the brother, because that form, “if he should die without children,” would be inappropriate in the case of a brother who is a Preacher; it is adapted to the habit, and not to others, as noted in D. 26.1.1 (Credendum), § 1, and D. 28.5.1, in the beginning. Likewise, he does not leave out the brother who is a Preacher. For a common substitution ought to be understood commonly, and not differently, D. 28.6.1 (Iam hoc iuris), § Sed si aliter.

On the contrary, it seems that those words, “that he could not demand more,” were inserted in favor of the other sons; but favor is not due to the dead, nor is it likely that the father intended to exclude the religious son after the other sons had died, cf. D. 35.2.1 (Paulo Calimaco), § Pomponius. Hence, those words, “that he could not demand more,” seem to be understood as things standing thus, cf. D. 16.3.1 (Quod Servius), and cf. D. 2.14.1 (Tale pactum), § Si, with its gloss. The substitution therefore made to all, and of all the sons, excludes none of the sons. And therefore it seems to include all. On the contrary, however, it is argued from D. 35.1.1 (Legatorum), § Qui plures, where general words are restricted by the species. To the same effect, D. 28.6.1 (Cum heredi), § Qui patrem, and § Qui discretas.

Solution: In doubt, because the strongest reason is that which is made for the son and for religion. I believe that the said brother is included in the substitution: and that he holds to the deficient part together with his brothers. Likewise, in doubt, I presume the intention to be such as it ought to be: and thus favorable to the sons, cf. D. 2.14.1 (Tale pactum), § Si, with its gloss. Therefore, the legitime and the trebellianic portion of the succeeding heirs being deducted, succession takes place according to the number of children, notwithstanding the repudiation which the said religious made of his father; and this is not extended to our case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a partnership is dissolved among the partners, accessory things must also be divided according to the manner of the principal things.
2. Where several persons are expressed in a contract, each comes in virile share, if the nature of the contract permits this.
body: The facts are as follows: there are three partners in the spice trade, namely Santonius, who holds three of the six parts in the said partnership, another holds two parts, and the third holds one part. Now, one of them leased an apothecary shop for the said partnership, for the purpose of exercising the said trade for himself and his partners. Finally, upon the termination and division of the said partnership, the said apothecary shop and the said lease remain, because the term of the lease has not yet expired. Now it is asked: in what manner and in what proportion does the said apothecary shop belong to the said partners for the remainder of the future time during which the lease continues? Having considered the said point and the said instrument,

I say that the said apothecary should be divided as to the usufruct according to the shares of the partnership, so that the said Santonius had one-half part. For since the cause of partnership was accepted in the apothecary, and it is accessory thereto, the same shares should be made of the accessory as of the principal, cf. D. de vulgari substitutione, l. si in testamento, and l. pater filio, with similar authorities. Moreover, because in the instrument mention is made of the appellative name of the partners, therefore what was acquired by virtue of the partnership is to be divided according to the shares of the partnership. D. pro socio, l. si non fuerit, l. quid enim, in materia.

† Notwithstanding the objection that where several persons are named in a contract, each is liable for the whole, as in C. loc. l. si diuisa. For that rule is true only if the nature of the contract permits it; but here it does not permit it, except for the share of the partnership. And even if only one person were named in the instrument by reason of the partnership, the same would apply. And in support of the foregoing, in its own reasoning, see C. de agri. et censi. l. quemadmodum, lib. 11. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a condition attached in a will to a legacy of two daughters, if the condition is removed for one in codicils, is also considered revoked for the other in the will.
body: A certain Faurentius de Simocilli of Foligno made his will, in which, among other things, he left to Cathelina and Bonaventura, his daughters, four hundred florins, worth two hundred florins for each of them, and certain portions and annuities, on the condition that if any of the said daughters should die in pupillary age, or afterwards at any time, he ordered and commanded that certain alms be made from the share of the deceased daughter, and that the said share be distributed in certain ways to pious causes, as is contained in the said will. With the said will, the said Cathelina died during the lifetime of the said testator, who, regarding the share of Cathelina, his said predeceased daughter, disposed otherwise in codicils which he later made, than he had disposed in the said will: revoking the said condition, and annulling it, and ordering it to be abolished from the will: and he wished the said share to be distributed in the manner and form inserted in the said codicils. After the death of the testator, it comes into doubt whether the condition appended in the said will for the share of the said daughter Bonaventura, who is still living, appears to have been revoked: having seen the said will and codicils, it is asked, what is the law: As regards the person of the said Bonaventura, I believe that nothing has been changed in the will:

† because the codicils do not speak of his person, nor of the condition ascribed to him: therefore, it remains that the testament has not been altered in its form. D. de militum testamento, l. Tribunus, § 1; D. de aditione legatorum, l. 3, § Condicio, with similar authorities. For although a condition could be removed, nevertheless these codicils do not dispose anything regarding the condition in the person of Bonaventura: and thus the testament stands firm. D. de alimentis legatorum, l. Alumnae, § Qui filias, at the end; § Qui, which text is notable for this purpose. And so I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In statutes, words are to be taken in their proper sense, and according to the common usage of speech.
2. Whether a granddaughter is properly so called who was conceived after the death of her grandfather, so as to be included under the statute, etc. And see below, opinion 407.
3. A negative argument is not drawn from statutes.
body: The point is this: Pontius, having several male children, made his will, in which he instituted them as his universal heirs and substituted them mutually, so that if any of the aforementioned should die without male children, then in the case where the predecessor dies leaving a daughter surviving him, he left to said female daughter 200 florins for a dowry, and in these matters instituted her as his heir? For the remainder of the inheritance of the aforementioned predecessor, he willed that it should devolve upon the other male children. After the testator’s death, one of the instituted sons took a wife and had a single daughter; and while she was still living, he died intestate. The question is whether this daughter could claim the aforementioned legacy and the inheritance of her said father, having regard to the statutes of the city of Perugia speaking on this matter?

In municipal law, words are to be taken in their proper sense: that is, the same meaning is to be understood as the law gives to the terms used by the statute, because one must not depart from the proper meaning of the words. D. 50.17.3; D. 47.16.1, *non aliter*; D. 14.2.1, *si is, qui navem*. Unless common usage of speech extends the force of the language to an improper meaning: for if custom interprets a term, this is a necessary interpretation, from which we ought not to depart. D. 50.17.3; D. 32.1.1, *librorum*; D. 32.1.1, § *quod tamen Cassius*; D. 40.1.1, *cum delationis*; D. 40.1.1, § *asinam*; D. 50.17.1, *si de interpretatione*.

Let us therefore consider whether she who was conceived after the death of her grandfather is properly called a granddaughter. For if she is properly called a granddaughter, she is excluded by the statute. But if she is not properly called a granddaughter, she is not excluded. For in municipal law it is not permissible to draw a negative argument, so that a granddaughter truly and naturally so called does not succeed; therefore, a granddaughter less properly and abusively so called does not succeed.

And especially since a statute established against the common law is, as in our case, as stated in *l. quod contra rationem* and *l. quod non in ratione*, D. de legibus. And therefore, because the statute is also of strict law, we ought not to extend it beyond what the words disclose, as in D. de verbis obligandis, *l. quicquid astringendae*; and D. de testamento mulieris, *l. quod constitutum*. And also because injustice would follow: and the law expels all injustice, as in C. de vetere iure enunciato, *l. 1*, § 1. And also because the right of succession ought to be extended, not restricted, as in Inst. de bonis possidendis, § *ad hoc*. Therefore, it is necessary to examine whether this person can properly be called a granddaughter. And it seems that she can, both according to law and according to customary usage of speech. For it is sufficiently clear in the computation of degrees. For the first granddaughter is in the fourth degree from her great-uncle according to civil law: and this does not occur except through the person of the grandfather, to whom the granddaughter is in the second degree; hence it is clearly shown thereby that she is properly called a granddaughter, just as she is properly said to be in the second degree, as in Auth. de gradibus, in principio, and § *quarto gradu*; and D. de gradibus, *l. iure consulto*.

But the contrary is evidently demonstrated. For if this person is not called a granddaughter in a matter that is favorable and to be extended, as regards succession: as in D. unde cognati, *l. 1*, § *si quis proximior*; D. de in iustum testamentum, *l. si quis filio*, § *sed haec ita*; D. de suis et legitimis, *l. Titius*; in Inst. de haeredibus ab intestato, § *cum autem*; D. de bonis liberis, *l. Paulus*, § *Paulus*, vers. *responsum enim*; C. de inofficioso testamento, *l. si quis filium*, in principio. Therefore, much less in a matter that is exclusive and odious, such as this one, as in *l. maximum vitium*, C. de libellis praetoribus. And this is confirmed because, since the grandfather died at a time when this person was not yet in existence, it is certain that at the time of his death he was not her grandfather; for in correlatives of two, both are required, as in D. de operis libertatis, *l. libertinus*, § *posth.* For after death one cannot begin to be something, as in D. de operis libertatis, *l. libertinus*, § *posth.* And although certain laws call this person the grandfather’s granddaughter, this designates rather the order of birth and of the dowry. For otherwise it cannot be described, which has its root in the very right of blood. Therefore, regarding succession, and thus with respect to successions, and speaking absolutely, this person is entirely alien as a granddaughter and is not considered a granddaughter in the matter of successions, in which we are. For words are to be adapted to the subject matter, as in *l. Imperator*, and if the statute said that the granddaughter succeeds the grandfather, it would not be understood to refer to this granddaughter conceived after the grandfather’s death; therefore, conversely, if it says that the granddaughter does not succeed, it would similarly not be understood to refer to her, that she does not succeed; because the rule and understanding are the same for contraries, as in *l. si*, D. de legibus 3; and *l. si contra*, D. de vulgari substitutione. And she is not said to be dowered by the grandfather, since he was not her grandfather, and she is a posthumous granddaughter alien to him, as in Inst. de legatis, § *posthumo*. For this word “granddaughter” is both a civil and a natural term, as in D. de capite diminuto, *l. tutelas*. And between him, who is in existence, and her, who is not, no natural relationship exists. For even civil law must be accommodated according to its proper and true signification and intrinsic reason. Moreover, to whom the signification of possession is not applied, to him the signification of deprivation is not applied, as in D. de suis et legitimis, *l. in principio*. But to this person, as a granddaughter, the possession of succeeding is not applied; therefore, neither is deprivation: therefore, to this person, abusively called a granddaughter, the grandfather could not, by dowering her, impose a law excluding her from paternal succession. I do not say that this person is not dowered, as in *l. cum plures*, D. de administratione tutorum; but this involves two concurrent fictions, which ought not to concur, namely, that the dowry is given before marriage; and that before the person is in existence, the dowry is given. Or that before one is in existence, it is understood that he dowers her, who is born long after his death. So many fictions ought not to concur, as in *l. 1*, C. de dote promissa. And I say that she is not dowered by the grandfather, when at the time of his death he was not her grandfather. And these words are referred to the time of death, as argued in D. de testamento tutorum, *l. tutoribus*.

And it should be noted that Antonius substituted by fideicommissum to the son dying, leaving a daughter: for which reason it seems that he burdened the son himself, and the legitimate heirs of the son, for restoring the inheritance: by which he also seems to have tacitly called the legitimate heirs to the intestate succession of the son: as in D. de iure codicillorum, *l. 2*. This daughter of Antonius’s son, therefore, as the intestate heir of her father, will restore the inheritance, deducting the legitimate portion and the Trebellianic portion, as in Cap. *Raynutius* and Cap. *Raynaldus*. And she obtained this from the person of her father, which she could not have obtained from her own person; because she herself was not burdened in her own person; but her father was, to whom the words of the statute are not directed. And often one obtains from the person of another what one cannot obtain from one’s own person, as in D. quae res pignori obligari possunt, *l. Arist.* The point, therefore, and conclusion stands in this, that this dower-giver was never really and truly, speaking literally, nor even in the civil sense of the term, her grandfather. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws. And under my hand I have subscribed, and sealed with the seal of my name, concluding that she shall succeed; because the statute ceasing, we are in the common law, notwithstanding that the statute says, or any other dower-giver; because afterwards it adds “saving always,” etc. For here, on the part of this girl, no male exists; and thus according to common and municipal law, she can succeed, remitting the dowries into the inheritance according to the form of this verse: “saving always.”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a mother shall not make a will without the presence of her son, if she has one, otherwise the inheritance shall pass to those who come intestate, if the mother makes a will in the presence of her son who has been outlawed, whether the will is valid.
body: The statute of the City of Assisi provides that no woman may make a will or otherwise establish her last will without the presence of her son or sons, if she has a son or sons. If, however, she has no sons, but has nephews or nieces through a son or sons, or through a full brother or brothers, and if she has made a will otherwise, the will is null by operation of law. Now, a certain Lady Angelutia, daughter of the late Vannis and wife of the late Putius of the City of Assisi and its county, had three daughters, namely Caterina, Cecha, and Machiola, who were dowered by their father, and one son, namely Jacob. This Jacob was exiled from the City of Assisi and its county in both property and person. She also had three full nieces, minors under fourteen years of age, descended from the aforementioned Machiola, and two full nephews, brothers, descended from a full brother of the said testatrix, who were not exiled nor condemned in any matter and were of full age. As the said Angelutia approached death, she made a will in the absence of the said Jacob and her said nephews, in which, among other things, she left a certain sum of money to her said daughters by way of institution; she left a certain sum to her son Jacob; and she instituted Bechus Accolus as her universal heir. Afterward, the said testatrix died, survived by her said daughters and her son Jacob, who was exiled. Finally, the said Jacob died, survived by his daughter Francisca, who had been dowered by her father, the said Jacob. The question is asked, having regard to the aforementioned will and the aforementioned statute, whether the said will is valid or not. Furthermore, it is asked, having regard to the will of the father of the said Jacob, who was exiled and condemned in any of his daughters and sisters of the said exiled person, for what share, and which of them, considering all the aforementioned statutes and wills.

† Because the outlawed person cannot be present, as the statute requires, it is as if, with respect to this matter, he did not exist in the realm of reality, as stated in the Digest, *de contrahenda tutela*, law 1, at the end; *de bonis libertorum*, law *si necem*, section *si deportatus*; *de liberis et posthumis*, law *Gallus*, section *et quid si tantum*. And therefore, one must proceed to the subsequent chapter of the statute, which states: “and if she were without a husband, sons, or another son, etc.” For she is considered to be without a son with respect to this matter, who has a son that is incapacitated with respect to this matter, as stated in the Digest, *de excusationibus tutorum*, law *non solum*, section *si libertus*. Since, therefore, the aforementioned nephews did not make the required declaration nor were they present, the said testament was null, from which it follows that the goods of the said testatrix belong to the next of kin coming in intestacy. Because the outlawed person did not accept the inheritance, it cannot be confiscated. Nevertheless, he transmitted the unaccepted inheritance, as to his share, to his daughter, as stated in the Code, *de his qui ante apertam tabulam*, law *unica*. And because the daughter is not outlawed, she must effectively hold the inheritance; nor does the fisc have any right in this matter. Thus, the said intestate inheritance shall be divided into four parts, and each shall come for a fourth part, because there are three daughters and one granddaughter from another son. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, and I have subscribed to this for the faith thereof.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. With regard to sentences and precepts that have acquired the force of res iudicata, a rescript from the prince cannot be obtained whereby the effect of the pronouncement is impeded.
1. The priores and camerarii cannot enact an inequitable statute, from which a final, perpetual, or indefinite prejudice arises to any specific person.
body: On behalf of Zanninus Zechichi, the procurator of Vanatellus Petri, a merchant of Perugia, the renewal of a certain license formerly granted by their predecessor against the sons of Luca Angelini is requested before the lords consuls of the merchants. Against the said renewal, an ordinance is raised which was enacted in favor of the said sons of Luca by the lords priors and chamberlains, by which jurisdiction against the aforesaid sons of Luca is prohibited to each and every official, and moratoria are practically granted, as is contained in the said ordinance. It is objected that the said ordinance is not valid, and that the lords priors and chamberlains did not have the jurisdiction to establish the said ordinance. It is asked on the part of the said lords consuls what the law is, and whether the said license ought to be renewed; having examined the statutes of the commune of Perugia and the ordinance, it is asked what the law is. Having examined the said legal issue and having carefully inspected the said reformation, I say that, notwithstanding the said reformation, the said license must be reformed or renewed; and this for a threefold reason.

† First, because regarding judgments and precepts that have passed into the authority of res judicata, a rescript cannot be obtained from the prince whereby the effect of the pronouncement is impeded, as in C. sent. rescin. non pos. l. fi.; and if it cannot be obtained from the prince, therefore neither can it from the priors and chamberlains. The second reason is because even if it were made by way of a law or statute, it would not extend to cases finally decided, in Auth. vt cum de app. eo. in patre, and noted in extra de consti. c. cognoscentes per Compost.

† Third, because the priors and chamberlains cannot make an unjust statute from which a final or perpetual prejudice, or one for an uncertain time, is produced against any specific person; for although they may grant a dilatory exception for a certain time to a specific person, yet they cannot do so for an uncertain time and in a way that could be perpetual: C. de preci. impe. offer. l. quot.; ff. quod quisque iuris, l. 3, §. si is, pro quo; and in the same, ff. de pollic. l. totiens, per Bar.; and the said l. 1, in prin., quod quisque iur. Hence, since the said reformation does not hold as to the principal matter, it does not hold as to the penal consequence: ff. ad l. fal. l. Seius, et augerius. Likewise, the consuls of the merchants hold their jurisdiction from the commune of Perugia, and therefore it cannot be taken away from them by a lesser council, namely of the priors and chamberlains, because the deprivation of a charge must arise from the same source whence the conferral of the charge arises, as in Auth. de defen. ciui. §. interim, etc. And thus I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws and advocate of the merchant guild of the City of Perugia, etc., state and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If two documents concerning the same contract are found, written by the hand of the same notary but mutually discordant, what the law should be: for example, because one is found at the tax office, while the other is found in the notary’s records. And see no. 4 below in the following opinion.
2. A public instrument may be derived from an abbreviation and reduced to proper form by the authority of a judge supplying, ex officio, what is lacking.
3. The judge must administer the oath to the party who has the stronger presumptions.
body: Puncta

† Such is the statute enacted in the City of Cortona, which provides that the Vicar or Rector shall be bound to enforce and observe all public instruments made in due form concerning contracts, in favor of the person to whom they were made or requested, or his heirs, unless the instrument was made in fraud and such fraud is proven. And if any abbreviation or protocol of any deceased notary is found in his own handwriting, the Vicar or Rector shall be bound to give it credence as if it were a public instrument, and to hold it firm and binding for the party concerned. This provision shall apply to past and future cases. Furthermore, it is provided that if any defect is found in any protocol, rogation, or abbreviation in the register of any notary, whether living or dead, provided that the entire substance of the contract is contained therein, it shall be held and believed as if the entire form and substance had been appended; and the judge of civil causes, to whom the cognizance thereof pertains, shall be bound to order the execution of such defective contract notwithstanding the defect, as if the entire form of the contract had been appended therein.

There is another statute at the tax office (gabella) worded as follows: It is statuted and ordained that all notaries of the City of Cortona and its boroughs within five days, and those of the county within eight days from the day the contract was celebrated, shall be bound effectively to assign to the official of the gabella or his official notaries, and to send under a brief summary of words, all contracts which they draw up or request; namely, the names of the contracting parties, the quantity, the subject matter, the day, and the year, so that it truly comes into the hands of said official without defrauding, etc.

Now it is added that two abbreviations written by the hand of the same notary are found: one in the book of the gabellas, containing and worded as follows: namely, William, formerly of Ceri, and Nerius, formerly of Andrea of Cortona, concerning the goods and inheritance of the late Lord Christopher, formerly of the Vgutii family, came to a transaction; and Lord Nerius gave to said William all rights which he might have in the inheritance of said Christopher for six livres, which said Nerius confessed to have received, etc., on the twenty-second day of February. The other abbreviation is found in a certain folio in the book of the same notary, written by the hand of said notary, the tenor of which appears from the form of the copy sent to you; in which the place, day, and witnesses are lacking, and they differ in price, because it states the price as 450 livres, as contained therein.

Now it is requested that said abbreviation found in the book of the aforementioned notary be put into execution by virtue of the aforementioned statutes, notwithstanding any defects existing therein. It is also considered that there is fame in the city of Cortona regarding the aforementioned matters, and one witness lives who was present at the aforementioned events. Furthermore, it is asked to whom the oath should be deferred, whether to the heirs of said Nerius or to the defendant, notwithstanding that the sum is large, since the defendant has in his favor fame and a witness still living.

† I answer the aforementioned consultation that a public instrument may be drawn up from the said abbreviation, and reduced to proper form by the authority of the judge supplying, ex officio, those elements that are lacking, both those pertaining to law and those consisting in fact, by means of extrinsic proofs and presumptions. Extra, De fide instrumentorum, cap. Cum P. tabellio; and there by Johannes Andreae, [stating that] a public instrument [may be] supplied in those matters lacking by the deliberate action of the judging authority, or by another writing drawn up by his hand in the same or similar business, or by witnesses, or by the confession of a party, or by similar presumptions. D. De legatis 1, l. Si filiabus; and l. Si servus plurium. D. De usufructu, l. Qui semisses. D. De legatis 2, l. Unum ex familia, §. Finis; and l. Cum pater, §. Cum imperfecta. D. De petitione hereditatis, l. Utrum. D. Quod fallit tutor, l. 2. D. De pignoratitia actione, l. Universorum; and note in the Speculum, De instrumentis, edition, §. Verum quid si abbreviatura? and Hostiensis and Johannes Andreae in the said cap. Cum P. tabellio. Therefore, it is not an obstacle to the fact that the said instrument may be drawn up from the said abbreviation by the authority of the judge, even though the day, place, and witnesses are lacking therein; nevertheless, it must be supplied by the authority of the judge, having regard to the presumption or proof of the truth by witnesses in a sufficient number; or if the number of witnesses is less than sufficient, by supplying [the deficiency] through the oath of the party, and through reputation, and other concurrent signs according to the said laws. And if reputation concurs as a corroborating factor with one witness, and especially if the reputation is corroborative by some similar legal presumption, nevertheless it makes full proof, and [this applies] to proof by sight in civil cases. And D. De testibus, l. 3, §. Eiusdem; and what is noted there on the word "confirmat." D. De excusationibus tutorum, l. 2, §. 1; and there by Dyachenko. Extra, De testibus, cap. De testibus; and by Cynus, De probationibus, in l. Proprietatis; by Bartolus, D. De quaestionibus, l. 1, §. 1; and in l. Admonendi. And this is also stated by the Speculum in the title De notis criminalibus, §. Fama, ver. Fama; and in the title De testibus, §. Restat, ver. Hoc tamen fallit. Cum glossa, 4. q. 3. Item, Speculum. And thus, in this case, an oath will not be necessary.

And if the judge wishes, or deems it expedient, that the proofs require supplementation, he may more safely defer the oath to the party who has so many supporting aids in his favor; for he ought to incline toward that side for which more supporting aids and arguments concur, and he is easily moved to supplement them by deferring the oath to the one who has such aids in his favor; and not to the one against whom they are directed, as stated in the tenth collection on the custom of the right of fief, §. sacramentum, where the text is noted for this purpose; and see the argument in the aforementioned law 1, §. 1, Digest, de quaestionibus; and the aforementioned law 3, §. eiusdem, Digest, de testibus. This is not on account of the nature of the case. Rather, it is said that the matter is not of minor importance, because it is replied to this that the magnitude of the case is considered according to the condition of the persons, as in the authentic nisi breuis res. Likewise, according to the brevity of the article upon which the oath is to be deferred, namely, whether it is upon that which serves to found the entire intention of the party by itself, or upon that which serves to clarify the obscurity of the foundation and to aid the intention, which is considered lighter and easier. This is proven in the law heredes palam, §. sed si not., and there it is noted, Digest, de testibus. Likewise, the magnitude of a civil case does not remove the legal remedy by the disposition of any law; but it is a certain masterly saying founded on the comparison of great civil cases to capital cases. This comparison applies when the case concerns all assets, or the greater part of the patrimony of the one to whom the oath is to be deferred; because from this suspicion arises in §. item inimicitiae, which is said not to occur in its proper terms. And this is the case in fact; and regard must also be had to contrary presumptions, which remove suspicions, as in the law non omnes, §. a Barbaris, Digest, de re militari; and that from that upon which it is sought to swear, the intention is not radically founded, but rather a certain obscurity and ambiguity has arisen concerning the notarial writings drawn up concerning the business, which is removed by easier proofs, as if the intention were simply founded, as in the aforementioned §. sed si notam, with its gloss.

And similarly, the omission concerning the sum, namely the number fifty from the document presented at the tax office by the same notary, is to be supplied. This is not obstructed by the fact that it does not agree in all respects with the aforementioned abbreviation left among the protocols of the said notary, because the tax office produced it less fully. Therefore, in that which is lacking there, the original must be followed, as in D. de edendo, l. ubi; and in that which was written less fully in the original, it must be supplied from that which was added more fully at the tax office. C. de testamento, l. error; D. de codicillis, l. si; D. de regulis iuris, l. si librarius; and the aforementioned l. utrum, D. de petitione hereditatis. And thus, by the industry of the judge, reducing the said variations to harmony, so that truth may prevail. D. de probationibus, l. si; C. de iustis compositionibus, l. quibus. Nor does it follow from the diversity of the summaries that there were different contracts, since it is not found in the notary’s protocols that there was anything but one contract between them. D. de legatis tertio, l. patronus, § Sempronius; and § liberti, D. de manumissione testamento; l. qui habebat. And it follows from this that there is an error in one of them, and that there is only one and the same contract, with the error removed, as in the aforementioned § Sempronius and § liberti. This must be done by signs supporting one of the aforementioned diverse forms, preferring that one, and in that part, and the other in another, to which external aids and signs contribute: and to which external proofs and conjectures attest, as in the aforementioned § sacramentum; and D. de testamento, l. ob carmen, § si testes; and D. de hereditate instituenda, l. his verbis, § sin. And from all these, gathering one true meaning, and according to that, having the instrument reduced to public form. C. de novo componendo, § colligentes in unam sanctionem, which are composed in various constitutions, and making the sense clearer, etc. One addition to the aforementioned, that to him who did not attend the act, and who cannot swear of his own consent, an oath should not be administered, as noted in l. in bonae fidei, C. de iureiurando. Therefore, it should not be directed and administered to the heirs of the contracting party; but rather to him among them who survives, namely the aforementioned William. And I, Francis de Albergotis of Arezzo, the humblest doctor of laws, advise as above stated and advised.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Certain matters pertain to the solemnity of the transaction; certain matters to the solemnity of the instrument; certain matters to the substance and perfection; and certain matters jointly to the solemnity of the act and the writing.
2. Whether a notary can supply what is lacking in an instrument.
3. One writing is supplied by another; and from the conjunction of witnesses or instruments, proof results.
body: On the same matter

† Having thus briefly touched upon the matter, it is to be considered that some things pertain to the solemnity of the transaction or contract; some to the solemnity of the instrument; some are not properly said to be of solemnity, but of substantiality and perfection; some are simultaneously and mixedly of the solemnity of the act and of the writing. Regarding the solemnity of the transaction or contract, we have an example in *l. quaecunque*, § *si*, *de publicis cum suis*. Regarding the solemnity of the instrument, we have an example, as in its own name, the Emperor’s name, and *l. generali*, *C. de tabulis*. For perfection with respect to will or consent, which is properly called substantiality, we have *C. de fideiussoribus instrumentis*, *l. contractus*; *ff. de testamentis*, *l. si is, qui*; *de legatis 3*, *l. fideicommissa*, § 1. Regarding the mixed category, we have an example in a testament made by public instrument: for seven witnesses are in reality of the solemnity of such an instrument and of the solemnity of the testament, as is fully gathered by the noted *C. de testamentis*, *l. quaestionem*.

† Therefore, having premised this, I understand the statute to apply when it is in accordance with the will of the testator, or of the instrument otherwise, but imperfect as regards the solemnity introduced by the pure civil law. However, if the instrument lacks the indication [of the parties], or lacks the day, the statute does not intend that the instrument be vitiated. The same holds if the witnesses or the place are lacking. For it wishes that credit be given to the notary alone, which can rightly be done by custom or statute, as in Extra, De fide instrumentorum, chapter Cum dilectus; in the Authentic Ut proprio nomine Imperator, which begins "Puta in nomine," at the end of which it is said that such custom or municipal law must be observed.

It must also be considered that when two documents are produced concerning the same matter, one is supplemented and determined by the other. *De legibus*, Title 2, *Sempronius*, Proculus. Just as the best proof results from the conjunction of several witnesses, so too from the conjunction of several instruments. *Digestum*, *De eodem*, *Si quis ex argentariis*, § *Si initium tabularum*; and from a mixed conjunction of witnesses and instruments, as noted by Innocentius, *De fide instrumentorum*, *Cum Ioannes heremita*. It should be known that in this mixed proof, the name of proof must be applied to that which has the greatest weight in the matter. *Digestum*, *De statu hominis*, *Quaeritur*. Hence, the aforementioned witnesses accede to the instrument, as to the principal, to confirm its faith; and by means of this very instrument, proof must be made, and it deserves the execution granted to instruments by statutes, since the origin of the proof lies in the instrument, whereas the witnesses come to assist. *Codex*, *De edendo*, *Si*. From which it is concluded that the instrument in question is valid and deserves execution by virtue of the statute beginning, *Item si aliquod protocollum*, etc. For this instrument must be said to be aided by the statute and confirmed by witnesses. *Codex*, *De probationibus*, *Iubemus*. When witnesses come for the declaration of the instrument, principal proof is not said to be made by the witnesses, but by the instrument, as in *Digestum*, *De probationibus*, *Heredes palam*, § *Sed si*; nor is the action based on the proof of witnesses. *Digestum*, *De iureiurando*, *Sed si possessori*, § *Si*. Rather, strength and efficacy are attributed to the instrument. *Codex*, *De testibus*, *Publicati*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An inheritance cannot be accepted unless the heir first knows whether the inheritance devolves upon him by will or intestate, together with the following counsel.
2. Whether a son is presumed to be ignorant of his father’s will, and what applies in the case of an outsider. No. 5.
3. In matters residing in the mind, one must proceed by means of presumptions.
4. Whether acceptance is presumed to have been made formally.
5. Wherever something is necessary to establish a claim, given that it is presumed by law, so much so that it is not necessary to prove it in case of doubt, it is nevertheless always necessary to allege it.
6. A renunciation made by a coheir does not prejudice the creditors, nor the coheir.
7. It is not permitted for anyone to go against his own act, even if it did not hold in law.
8. If a son has renounced his father’s inheritance, which he later accepted jointly or as a substitute, whether the son can again accept it.
body: IOhannes instituted his sons Simon and Petrus, both over 25 years of age, universally and equally as heirs. Upon his death in the city of Forlì on the 5th day of the month of September 1378, the said Simon accepted the inheritance. The said Petrus, being in the city of Fermo, likewise accepted his paternal inheritance on the 29th day of the aforementioned month, and concerning this a public instrument appears. Thereafter, the same Petrus, being in the city of Ascoli, repudiated the said paternal inheritance on the 30th day of the month of September 1378, and concerning this it appears by a public instrument. Upon the death of the said Petrus, a dispute arises between Iacobus, who was instituted by the said Petrus as appears in his testament, and Franciscus, the son and heir of the said Simon, concerning one half of the inheritance of the said Iohannes. For the said Iacobus, the instituted heir, bases his right on the aditio and acceptance of the paternal inheritance made by the said Petrus, and also on other acts done by the said Petrus himself, who [disregarded] the repudiation made by himself, namely in that he appointed a proctor after the said repudiation to sell and alienate the paternal goods falling to his share, as appears through the instruments drawn up thereupon. Franciscus, however, the son of the said Simon, bases his right on the repudiation made by the said Petrus, asserting that the aditio and acceptance first made is invalid. Concerning the first point, four principal questions are asked: First, whether the aditio is valid, having examined the form of the aditio, or rather the instrument drawn up concerning this. Second, if it is doubted whether Petrus knew that it was necessary for him to know whether he was an heir under a testament or intestate, and whether for the whole or for a part and for what quota; and upon whom lies the burden of proof—whether on his heir affirming that he knew, or on the adversary denying it? Third, presupposing that the said aditio held valid at that time, whether the repudiation made by him harms his heir, or ought in any way to bar him? And it is to be noted that in the repudiation the said Petrus clearly expressed that the inheritance had devolved upon him from a testament, which he had not done in the aditio. Fourth, it is doubted whether, by virtue of the acts he performed after the repudiation, he acquired the inheritance notwithstanding the repudiation, namely by appointing a proctor to alienate, etc., as I have stated above, according to l. fi. C. de repu. haere. Regarding the first point, to the effect that the aditio does not hold, l. is potest and what is noted there by the gl. and the doc. ff. de acqui. her. is adduced. Regarding the second, that the burden lies upon the party affirming, etc. Regarding the third, that a repudiation made after an aditio does not prejudice, lex sicut maior C. de repu. haere. is adduced. Regarding the fourth, it is said that lex vltima C. de repu. haere. admits of several interpretations. In the question which is in dispute between Franciscus, son of the aforementioned Simon, regarding the inheritance of Iohannes his grandfather on the one side, and Iacobus, instituted by the said Petrus, on the other side, I will pass through the substance briefly.

† Around the first article therefore, in which it is doubted whether the aditio of the paternal inheritance first made by the said Petrus is valid, it seems it must briefly be said that it is not, through l. is potest and what is noted there by the gl. ff. de acq. haer. For it is certain that no one can accept an inheritance unless he knows, among other things, whether the inheritance belongs to him under a testament or by intestacy, as is noted there in l. is, ad quem, under the same title, whether he is a son or an extraneous heir; because in this respect no distinction is made by the laws, neither by the text nor by the gloss.
