In the case of a necessary heir, perhaps something else may be said and legally proved, according to certain authors in l. si seruus testamento, §. fi. de stip. ser., and l. eius, qui in prouincia, §. fi. ff. si cer. pe., and l. quaesitum, de acq. haer. do. And between them there is a great difference: because the necessary heir is heir whether he wills it or not, whereas a son has the benefit of abstaining. Whence, for him truly to be an heir, a voluntary aditio or acceptance is required, just as in the case of an extraneous heir, arg. ff. de leg. 1. l. nam nec emancipatus, and what is noted there by Dy., and de acq. he. l. cum bonis.

† This being presupposed, I say that in case of doubt it must be judged, to omit other matters, that Petrus was ignorant of his father's testament. This is proved first through general rules: because in doubt, ignorance of fact is presumed, ff. de prob. l. neruis, extra de reg. iur. c. praesumitur. More specifically, because if this knowledge were presumed, why would the law require it? Surely it would suffice that ignorance were not proved. Furthermore, this is proved by the notable gloss which is approved by all in l. si quis extraneus, ff. de acqui. here., and in l. in repudianda, where the gloss doubts how the knowledge of the aforesaid matters will appear; and finally the gloss intimates that although precise and true knowledge is not required, nevertheless it will appear because friends said so, or there was a rumor; and there the doctors declare it so; and for this is the text with the gloss in l. cum quidam, §. quod dicitur, ff. de acq. haer. It is clear, therefore, that in case of doubt, knowledge is not presumed where nothing else is presented. Furthermore, still more specifically, that Petrus was ignorant appears from the form of the aditio. For first he asserted that he knew his father was dead, but concerning a testament he said nothing; therefore he seems to have been ignorant, ff. de iud. l. cum praetor, C. de proc. l. maritus, with similar laws. For if he had known, it was easy to express it; and it is likely that he would have expressed it, just as he did regarding the death; to which purpose extra de decimis, c. ad audientiam, and what is noted there, is well suited. To which it also contributes that in the repudiation which he made afterwards, because he expressed that the inheritance had devolved upon him under a testament, it is therefore to be presumed from the custom or practice of a paterfamilias that he would likewise have done so at first, if he had known, ff. de leg. 1. l. si seruus plurium, §. fi. Indeed, it is quite conjecturable that after he accepted, he believed that it had devolved upon him intestate; therefore afterwards, when he knew it had devolved under a testament, he repudiated, perhaps on account of the burdens imposed in the testament, or other things contained in the testament, arg. for this that it is not likely that he changed his will without cause, ff. de prob. l. 3. and l. eum, qui. From the form of the aditio and repudiation, no other cause can be conjectured; wherefore this one is to be presumed. Furthermore, which is common enough in practice, where he stated in the aditio 'the surviving sons, etc.', he did not add 'instituted heirs.' Furthermore, from this it urges more specifically, if they are carefully observed, that all the words of the aditio conclude that the inheritance pertained to him intestate, and that he so believed, or at least doubted whether it had devolved under a testament or intestate. Which is clear: for first he says his father is dead; next, that he and his brother survive as lawful and natural sons; next, that his inheritance has devolved through the death of the said Iohannes; he does not, however, say through a testament, because their being sons and the death of the father is the mediate cause, not a testament. Likewise this is further made clear when he says 'according to the form of law', as if the inheritance were deferred to him by law and intestate; because in succession the first claim is that of children, as in Auth. in successione, a good argument for this being ff. pro soc. l. 3. §. de illo, where a just inheritance is understood to be that which is devolved by intestacy; and it is the same to say 'according to the form of law.' And words in doubt ought to be taken in their proper sense, and especially when this interpretation is supported by other conjectures; and thus his syllogism rightly concludes 'intestate.' Furthermore, it cannot be denied that the said Petrus doubted whether the inheritance of Iohannes had devolved upon him under a testament or by intestacy; which is shown, for it is said in the said aditio that he accepted the said inheritance 'in every way, etc.' The ways of accepting are two: namely, under a testament, or by intestacy. Therefore, if he doubts, he cannot accept, and the aditio did not hold, as in said l. is potest; and through the aforesaid, every doubt seems to be removed. Nor let anyone say that the aforesaid are curious arguments or considerations, because in a doubtful matter of this kind it is through these most subtle considerations:

† since these things consist in the mind, namely knowledge and ignorance, that one must proceed, arg. from the previously cited l. si seruus plurium, §. fi., and l. haeredes palam, §. sed si notam, de testa., concordant with ff. de testib. l. 3. §. eiusdem, de quaestionibus l. de minore, §. tormenta, joined with extra de testi. c. cum causam, with similar laws. For this reason also, because Petrus was sufficiently absent, since he was in the city of Fermo, away from the place where the father died and the testament was made, namely in Forlì; and between the death itself of the father and the aditio of the inheritance a short time had elapsed, namely 15 days, whence he could quite probably be ignorant.

† Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that, from the fact that he accepted, it is presumed to have been done solemnly, etc.; because that is false with respect to extrinsic solemnity, as in ff. de publi. l. quaecunque, and fully noted in l. sciendum, de ver. ob.

† Nor even if it is said that an heir is presumed to know what the deceased did, arg. of what is noted by the gloss in ff. de libe. lega. l. cum haeres, and ff. ad Treb. l. haeres, §. si quis filium; because that must be understood of an extraneous heir, who otherwise could not succeed except through a testament, or probabiliter doubt whether a son, by the very fact that he is a son, is an heir according to the Apostle, ff. de lib. et posth. l. in suis, and de acqui. her. l. necessariis, with similar texts. And thus Petrus concludes in his aditio. Or it must be understood of one present and who was in the place where the act was done. But this man was absent and outside the province, nor is it proved that it was otherwise announced to him, neither by messenger nor by letter, nor that it was notorious or a rumor in the place where he was; nor was he a notable man or a matter concerning which fame or rumor ought in doubt to be presumed. And thus I do not see how knowledge ought in doubt to be presumed; on the contrary, the opposite is probabiliter proved, ff. de acqui. here. l. cum quidam, §. quod dicitur; to which extra qui ma. acc. pos. c. si extra, de consti. c. vt animarum, lib. 6., extra de postu. c. 1. and 2. serve well, by which lex de tutela C. de in integr. restit. and ff. vnde cog. l. octaui are also removed. Or say with respect to the aforesaid glosses of l. cum heres [and] l. quidam—and I think this is their meaning—that they intended to say that because an heir accepted knowing that he was instituted, it is likely that he knows the rest contained in the testament; because it is not likely that he knew of the institution and not the other things contained in the testament, arg. l. in ciuile ff. de leg., and because it is supine ignorance; but not that by the very fact that someone accepts, he is presumed to know the testament, especially in the case of a son, who otherwise, no testament having been made, could accept. And that the aforesaid is the meaning of the aforesaid glosses is clear by reducing it to practice. For they speak of one who asserts that he is heir, and wishes today to be heir, and whom I likewise assert and confess to be heir; but there is a question whether he knew the contents in the testament. And the glosses say that he did, because it is not likely [otherwise]; for if he asserts that he is heir, and I confess that, this cannot be unless he first knew the testament; and it is absurd to say that he saw a part and not the whole, but that he knew it. But suppose that I deny that you are the heir, because I say that you, especially being a son or a closer agnate to whom the inheritance is deferred by intestacy, were ignorant of the testament at the time of the aditio; you say that you knew, or your heir says that you knew—which is stronger, as will be said below—certainly those glosses do not intend that you are presumed to have known. On the contrary, l. si is, ad quem succeeds, and the previously cited gloss of l. si quis extraneus and l. in repudiando and l. cum quidam, §. quod dicitur, which expressly intend the contrary, if they are well noted, as was said above; and thus they ought to be understood, otherwise they would be mutually contradictory. Furthermore, where other closer arguments do not please, take this: that that one should prevail in doubt; but here we have several indications of ignorance of the testament, according to what has been shown above. Regarding the second principal doubt, enough has been said through the foregoing.

† Note however, that wherever anything is necessary to substantiate one's claim, even positing that it is presumed by law so that in doubt it is not necessary to be proved, nevertheless it is always necessary that it be alleged, if it is a matter that consists in fact. And this appears especially regarding those things that exist in the mind, as are these about which we are treating. This is proved first: because otherwise it would follow that the judge would supply regarding the fact, against l. illicitas, §. veritas, and the notes to C. vt quae desunt aduoc. l. vna; to which instit. de actio. §. aliae and what is noted there well contributes; in the Publician action good faith is required, which consists in the mind, and which certainly must be alleged and set forth in the libel, as is clear there through Dy. and through Roffredus and in the Speculum under the said title. But nevertheless, if it is alleged, it is presumed, because it resides in the mind, as the gloss notes in the said §. aliae; to which what is noted by the gloss and Cynus on C. de proba. in l. siue possidetis well contributes. For if I possessed in the past, I am presumed to possess today, provided however that this is alleged; which is better proved in l. si adulterium cum incestu, §. idem polioni, and what is noted there by Bar. ff. de adult., where the text is found. For this is also l. cum de in rem verso in fi. ff. de vsur.; and see what I wrote concerning this in the Speculum under the rubric on the drawing up of libels, at the beginning, through the said Baldus de Perusio. To the purpose, if this Petrus in the instrument of his aditio had asserted that he knew his father's testament, it does not seem there would be any doubt that, given his absence and nothing else appearing, ignorance of fact is rather presumed. Furthermore, if Petrus were alive and asserted that he had known this, it could still be doubted. But since he is dead, certainly his heir cannot declare nor assert it, because that man's conscience is unknown to him, a good argument being ff. de rei vendi. l. Pompon. otherwise si frumentum, §. fi., de ver. obl. l. inter stipulantes, §. sacram., and what is there through the gloss and the doctors. And through the aforesaid, a clear answer seems to be given to the opinion of certain authors who seem to maintain that when an heir asserts that he knew, it ought to be so presumed in doubt. Concerning the third point, I will repeat that which was said on the first point, with a small addition.

† And first it seems that a repudiation made after an aditio harms nothing, as in l. sicut de repu. here.; but that law must perhaps be understood to the prejudice of creditors, not for one's own advantage, which the penultimate and last glosses placed there seem to intimate.

† And through this: because, positing that the repudiation did not hold, nevertheless it is not permitted for anyone or his heir to come against his own deed, even that which did not hold by law, ff. de adopt. l. post mortem, and l. per fundum, ff. de ser. rust. prae., with similar laws. Likewise through this: because one who repudiates is considered to treat the property as abandoned, arg. ff. pro derelicto, l. 1. and 2., and especially because he never had possession of these things; and thus l. si quis vi, §. differentia, ff. de acque poss. ceases to apply. Likewise for this: because nothing is so natural as that each thing be dissolved, etc.; but by sole and bare consent the inheritance and the ownership of the hereditary things is acquired, therefore by bare consent it ought to be able to be lost, l. nil tam naturale, ff. de reg. iur., and what the doctors note on C. de pact. in l. 1; and this I understand more particularly in things acquired, or an inheritance acquired through the bare will of aditio, not also through a subsequent taking of possession, arg. of privileged rights, for which l. ab emptione, ff. de contrahen. emp., and what is noted there, is applicable. Likewise it seems to proceed especially in our case, where the inheritance had been accepted by a co-heir; in which case, when Petrus repudiated or treated it as abandoned, that share was immediately acquired by the co-heir, as in C. de cad. tol. §. is ita; so that henceforth without his own deed it cannot, and could not, be torn away from him. Likewise, through the words placed in the instrument of repudiation, Petrus seems to confess that he never accepted, or if he did anything by which the contrary could be presumed, that in truth he never had the intent to accept; and thus he had not truly accepted; and thus against his own confession he, or his heir, ought not to be admitted; rather it ought to stand against him to his prejudice, and especially because it seems to tend toward a release and to have the effect of a release: namely, so that he could no longer make a claim against the co-heir, arg. l. tamquam liti, C. de pac., and what Innocent notes there, and c. cum pridem, extra de pac., and c. veniens, extra de test., and what the gloss notes in ff. de lib. leg. l. non solum, §. liberationis verba, and especially where the abdication of a real right is at issue. Concerning the fourth point, it must be said and it seems,

† that if the repudiation was valid, he could no longer accept, neither expressly nor tacitly through the acts that he performed afterwards, as in C. de repu. haeredi. l. sicut. I respond to l. vlt., under the same title, which seems to present a case to the contrary, where it speaks of a slave: it is said that that law has several interpretations; nevertheless, one of two opinions seems to please the gloss. One is that in the said l. si filius, he does not have a substitute or a co-heir joined with him, just as it touches upon in l. si quis suus, ff. de iu. delib., and in l. 2, C. de iur. et fac. igno.; and many of the doctors follow this one, as Dynus and Raynerius. The other is that it has place where the substitute or joined heir had not yet accepted, as is noted in the said l. 2, C. de iu. et fac. igno., which the aforesaid doctors also approve, and Iacobus Butrigarius seems to agree with it in the said l. 2; indeed they add that it is the same if a subsequent statutory heir had already accepted, namely so that the son could no longer return to the paternal inheritance, through l. filii mater, §. fin. ff. ad Tert. But whichever of the aforesaid you hold, we have our proposition, because in our case this man had a joined co-heir who had already accepted the inheritance; nor do I believe that in giving counsel one should depart from the opinion of the glosses, which also possess the authority of such great men and doctors. But that the said opinion, especially the second, relies upon laws and reason is clear: first through the said l. filii mater, §. fi. For a son is admitted to a repudiated maternal inheritance within a year; if, however, another accepts within the year, say a statutory heir, he is no longer admitted; therefore the same holds in the three-year period which is granted concerning a paternal inheritance. Nor does it stand in the way if you say that he ought to be more privileged regarding the paternal inheritance: because although regarding certain subtleties of law there is a difference between the maternal and the paternal, nevertheless regarding those things which rest upon equity, such as an intermeddling after repudiation, there seems to be the same reason. For he is just as much the son of his mother as of his father, indeed more certain, arg. l. Lucius, de condi. et dem., and for this in Auth. de here. ab intest. §. 1. Furthermore, that the same holds in a maternal inheritance, the text intends in l. fi. de rep. haeredi., there: 'so long as the paternal estate remains in the same state'; likewise, 'matters remaining in their own state.' Nor is it valid if you say that 'in its own state, etc.' is understood, namely, because they have not been alienated: first, because if the text speaks indistinctly, therefore it ought to be understood indistinctly; second, because they seem sufficiently to alienate from the fact that they have in any way whatsoever been acquired by another, ff. de ver. si. l. alienationis verbo, C. de re. alie. non alie. l. fi. Furthermore, that the opinion of the gloss, Dynus, Raynerius, and Iacobus de Belviso is true is proved by reason. For presupposing that principle, namely that a son is admitted after repudiation, it is outside the rules of law by virtue of the privilege of a son, as is clear in the previously cited laws. But if it is so, it ought to be interpreted strictly, and so that it is understood to be granted without injury to another, which can conveniently be adapted, as in l. 2, §. merito, §. si quis a principe, ff. ne quid in loco publ., extra de rescr. c. ex tenore. Let us understand, therefore, that he is admitted after repudiation while the inheritance is still lying vacant, not after it has been accepted by another and a right acquired by another: first, because this is against the strictness of law, that that which has been acquired by me should without my act be taken away from me, ff. de reg. iur. l. quod nostrum, with similar laws. Likewise because the correction of laws is to be avoided, l. praecipimus, in fi.; therefore it is against natural equity. For suppose that I, a joined son or a substitute, accepted after his repudiation, and with his knowledge and sufferance held and possessed the goods of the inheritance for almost three years; I cultivated, repaired, expended both labor and costs; the son, toward the end of the three years, seeing perhaps the goods of the inheritance in a better state, says that he has repented, and wishes to accept the inheritance: certainly that he should be admitted is against natural equity, and with the greatest injury to another. Wherefore let us conclude that the aforesaid opinion is true as much from strict law as from equity. And it is to be noted that although certain ancient and modern doctors resolve the contrary from the said l. fi. de rep. haered. otherwise, namely that that law speaks of the paternal estate and the contrary holds in the maternal, nevertheless I find no one saying that even in the paternal estate a son ought to be admitted after it has been accepted by a joined co-heir or substitute. I confess therefore that the aforesaid solution is true, but nevertheless I say that it is not contrary to the aforesaid. In our case therefore, in which the joined co-heir had already accepted, it seems it must be concluded that the aforesaid Petrus is not to be admitted after the repudiation. In a doubtful matter also, favor must be shown to the aforesaid Franciscus, who treats of retaining his grandfather's inheritance and thus of avoiding a loss. For Iacobus, as far as concerns that inheritance which he seeks, is an extraneous person, and thus treats of capturing a gain; wherefore, etc., as in l. fi. C. de cod. And so I, Angelus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, say and advise, and in faith thereof I have subscribed myself.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son may enter upon the inheritance before he is certain of his father’s death, or of his father’s will; and what the rule is for an outsider.
2. Whether a son, or an outsider, is presumed to know his father’s will.
3. Whether a son’s renunciation of the inheritance is valid.
4. If a sui heres has renounced the inheritance, and a co-heir or an instituted heir has intervened therein, and then, within three years, the sui heres who renounced wishes to intervene, whether he may do so.
5. The interpretation of the law *Filius mater*, § 1.
body: But the other of the two opinions seems to please the glossator. One is that, since the aforementioned consultant, whose name I do not know, has deeply touched upon the matter regarding every point, it is not expedient to recapitulate what has been touched upon, but rather to proceed to the conclusions. And in the first point, considering in his heir a twofold intervention, namely, legal and necessary, having regard to the principles of civil law; and voluntary, having regard to the praetorian benefit, the interpretations of wise and prudent jurists, and the constitutions of princes concerning that same praetorian benefit.

† As to the first point, knowledge of the death or of the will is not required; for that which occurs by operation of law does not require the knowledge of a person. C. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. apud hostes; de stipulationibus servorum, l. liber honoris, §. ult.; de militum testamento, l. ex militari, §. si, and the following law; de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multum interest; de conditione ob causam, l. si pecuniam, §. si servum; ff. si certum petatur, l. eius qui in provincia, in fine. Indeed, between the death of the testator and such existence in the successor to whom such inheritance is purely devolved, no intermediate step is found in the primitive civil law, as ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Iulius, per Dige. But if knowledge were required, there would be an intermediate step there; therefore, etc. As to the second point, the same intention is required in a sui heres and in an extraneus, as ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. gerit, and l. in totum. Moreover, intermixture in the case of a sui heres does not make him heir; for he was already heir by operation of law, as l. in suis, ff. de liberis et posthumis; but it is a kind of renunciation of the praetorian benefit. For since he could abstain by virtue of a benefit, which is rather a certain separation of his own goods from the paternal ones, rather than an eradication of the paternal succession, ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. si filius qui nostri; C. unde liberi, l. qui se patris, it must be understood that renunciation intervenes with knowledge of the testate and intestate status, as ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Clodius Clodianus; ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. pen. Therefore, whether we consider intermixture as the execution of the existence of a sui heres, or as a renunciation of the praetorian benefit, it is necessary to know that a will was made, and that it was made in such form, and the other substantial requirements, as leg. et nota, ff. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. illud.

† And it is not presumed that an absent son knows the will: for from the distance of place ignorance is presumed, and from proximity knowledge. C. de falsis monimentis, l. 1; ff. locati conducti, l. dominus horreorum; ff. de decretis ob ordinem faciendis, l. si; ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. plane; and the said law eius, qui in provincia, l. si. It is not presumed that notice has been given to an absent person, or that a messenger has been sent, unless it is proved, as is proved. ff. de legatis 2, l. si tamen quibusdam; ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. hoc iure; ff. de in diem adiecto, l. necesse. For to presume this would be to divine; hence facts are not presumed to be known, since they subsist in another’s fact. ff. pro socio, l. fin. It does not obstruct the case. de liberatione legata, l. cum heres. There, the heir who accepts is presumed to know the will: because it is understood that the acceptance is made as if from the will, and with the heir’s testamentary tablets opened. If, however, the clauses are sealed and unknown to him, unless it is proved that he knew them, he cannot accept; and under the old law he could not accept unless he knew them by inspection of the tablets themselves. But today it suffices that he knows them in whatever manner. C. de caducis tollendis, l. in novissimo. And having knowledge of the institution, it is presumed that he knows the other things contained in the same tablets: because the whole must be published to the heir. ff. de edendo, l. 2; ff. de transactionibus, l. non est ferendus. It appears from these that there was no acceptance made without mention of the will, because without any extrinsic implication it sounds as intestate; hence it is not valid, as stated in the said law Clodius. Assuming this to be true,

† that the intermeddling made from the beginning did not hold: because it was not made under the title under which the succession was declared, it follows that the subsequent repudiation made under the proper title was valid; because the useful is not confirmed by the useless, as is known in the said law Clodius, in the gloss ordinaria, and in the Digest, De inofficioso testamento, law Nihil, section Si cum filius, and law Sub hac. Just, therefore, as a useless abstention does not prevent a valid acceptance, so conversely a useless intermeddling does not prevent a valid abstention; because designation, or narration, is permitted from the invalid to the valid.

It remains to consider that which is concluded in the question. If a *sui heres* repudiated the inheritance, and a co-heir or substitute intervened therein, yet did not sell the assets; and then, within three years, the *sui heres* who had repudiated, moved by repentance, intervenes, it is asked whether he may do so. Jacobus de Arena says that he may not. He states that when the inheritance has been applied to another, it is added: “since ownership of things is acquired by acceptance.” D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. cum herede. Likewise, if the things have been sold by acceptance, this is proven. D. ad Tertullianum, l. filii, § 1, which speaks of sale. L. ultima, de repudianda hereditate. And these two are equated, namely that the goods are sold and that they are applied to another, as in l. 2, de iure et facto ignoranti, according to Jacobus de Arena in his distinction. Behold, he expressly determines for the first part, and it is proven because, since the co-heir or substitute has begun to be heir, he cannot cease to be heir. D. de minoribus, l. et si sine, § sed quod pa. And because ownership acquired by another cannot be taken away by the act of another. D. de hereditate instituenda, l. pater, de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § et quid si tantum, in the gloss and in the rule id quod nostrum. And that the things are not in the same state, because the same state is said to exist when it remains within its limits of abstention, without the effect of acceptance by the substitute or co-heir being joined. For this state is one in which something is immediately assumed; if anything is added, from which the effect is increased, it is not the same state. D. de conditione ob causam, l. quod seruius. And it is confirmed because that which, through fault, as is this case of imprudent repudiation, draws after it execution by the transfer of ownership to another, does not admit of purification. D. de verborum obligatione, l. si seruum, § si sequitur, according to Dynus. And this is effectively proven. For if he could intervene, the sale of the things would be irrelevant: for he would not come to the things sold, but to their value, which is with the co-heir or substitute. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. si et rem, et pretium. Therefore, the immediate reason for exclusion is the transfer of the inheritance to another rather than the sale. However, that persuasion regarding improved things does not move me. D. de minoribus, l. intra utile, § vendentibus. And it is confirmed according to the gloss, because the accepting substitute excludes the *sui heres* from the benefit of that l. ultima, as noted in D. de iure delibandi, l. suus. But a co-heir is a kind of tacit substitute: as in D. de legato 2, l. Titio, et Mævio, § siue. Therefore, the same applies to both.

To the contrary, because the law requires for some conclusion one thing that cannot exist without another, it necessarily requires both. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. illud. But for the exclusion of intervention by virtue of the old l. si quis suus, l. ultima, it requires that the goods be sold; which the substitute or co-heir cannot do unless he accepts; therefore, it requires acceptance and sale joined together. For if acceptance alone without sale were sufficient, the Emperor would foolishly mention sale there, when the *sui heres* would be excluded not by the sale, but before the sale. For the cause that precedes in time is that which applies to itself the denomination of the effect; not the cause that occurs after the effect is consummated. D. de verborum obligatione, l. si ita quis stipuletur, siue nauis. And therefore it would be false to say that sale is the cause of exclusion. Rather, it is the preceding act, namely the acceptance of the co-heir or substitute. Moreover, given a co-heir to whom accrual takes place, it would necessarily follow that the benefit of that law and the three-year period would have no place; which seems false, because that determination is general, as in l. in fraudem, § fi, de nullitate testamenti. And I admit that substitution made in the meantime accrues, but mutably, and thus it can decrease due to subsequent acknowledgment. D. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. 2, in the gloss. And this is held expressly by Bartolus in the said l. si quis suus.

The objection from l. filii mater, § 1, does not hold, because it speaks of a non-*sui heres*. And if it is said, what is the reasonable distinction: since all are now purified, in Auth. de hereditate ab intestato, § fi. I answer: the reason is that in a *sui heres*, abstention contains a benefit, to which one can renounce; and after a right has been acquired by another: as in D. de minoribus, l. si iudex. But in an alien, it contains common law, to which one cannot renounce. From this it follows that if the testator had reduced the *sui heres* to the status of an alien, given an alien co-heir or a vulgar substitute; because then repudiation would be by civil law, and not by praetorian benefit; in which case l. filii mater, § 1, would have place. But in a *sui heres* co-heir, without a vulgar substitute being given, the opinion of Bartolus is true, that a *sui heres* does not exclude another *sui heres* from abstention, as noted in C. de iure delibandi, l. quidam.

† I do not omit, however, that Bartolus, in his interpretation of that law *filii mater*, errs in this respect, because he states that a repudiation is induced by suspensive words through the passage of a year. For, since the subsequent heir can immediately enter upon the inheritance, the repudiation is therefore induced immediately: but it is revocable until the year has passed; because the deliberation regarding repentance from that repudiation does not extend to the last moment. And this is the true interpretation of that law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The office of the Conservators of the coin, and the office of the Massarii, was in Perugia, and to each office, according to the form of the statute, was due a third part; when both were joined together, whether more is due to the conservators and their notaries than was first established.
body:
The reason is that another assisted, or the goods were distributed, and then his own [claim] was excluded. To make this evident, it must be premised that a certain chapter of a certain statute has the following tenor, namely: "Furthermore, we establish and ordain that the said Conservators of the Mint may, and it is lawful for them, to pay and retain for themselves, as their salary for the office and conservation for a half-year term, for each of them 15 gold florins. Furthermore, let there be given and paid to their notaries, for each of them, 12 gold florins, and to their clerks, for each of them, 12 gold florins, notwithstanding anything to the contrary: and this shall have effect in the present and future."

Having premised this, it must be known that the office of the Conservators of the Mint is a certain office in itself; and each of these usually lasts for a half-year term. Now, since this City of Perugia has been restored to liberty, these two offices have been joined together; and the other Conservators of the Mint and Massarij were appointed, for the greater part of six months. The question is asked: whether these officials may have a greater salary? and whether they may establish a greater salary for their notaries and servants than was the case before the offices were distinct and separate, although still for a half-year term.

Having seen the arbitration granted by the reform of the commune of Perugia to the Conservators of the Mint, f. Francisco do. Berrandi, and associates, on the 14th day of January of the present year, concerning the fixing of salaries, etc., and having seen the aforementioned statute, I say that, notwithstanding the said statute, the said Conservators may fix a higher salary than that limited by the statute, if it seems to them appropriate according to the quality of the times and the labor; because in matters which do not have a fixed standard due to the passage of time, discretion operates significantly: as in D. de poenis, l. hodie. To the same effect, because in their time there was a double office joined together: and therefore greater labor, and a higher salary, in Auth. ut iudices sine qualibet suffragio, §. illud. Also, because discretion granted must have some effect: as noted in C. de officio testatoris, l. si quando; to this effect, D. de donationibus, l. si filius; D. de legatis 2, l. cum quondam, cum si. Salaries, therefore, are moderated according to the state of the times and the judgment of a good man: and beyond the ordinary determination of the statute, they may be fixed by the force of this discretion. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an institution of an heir is conditional if made by these words: "I institute my son, if he does not misuse his property."
2. Whether a spurious grandson can be instituted by his grandfather? And what if he was legitimated? Item 3.
body:
Such is the case. A certain Master Andreas made a will, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and so forth, he instituted Pet., formerly of John, who dwelt with the said testator in his house with full right, as his universal heir, provided that he does not misuse and squander his substance by whoring, gaming, idling, or in any other bad manner. And if he were not capable of receiving the said inheritance, then, and in that case, and in any of the aforementioned events, he instituted Benevenuto Venturini as heir, who shall restore the inheritance to the said heir Pet. in the case where he was not capable of the said inheritance. And if Pet. did not observe the aforementioned conditions, and in that case, the said Benevenuto shall sell the said inheritance and distribute it for the sake of his soul, wherever it seems best to him. And if in the meantime John, son of the said testator, should return, he willed that half of the said inheritance be restored to him by the said Benevenuto; the other half, however, shall be distributed as stated above. And he willed that the aforementioned conditions should have effect until the age of 25 years of the said Pet. had been completed. And he left the said Pet. under the protection, defense, and care of the said Benevenuto until the said time. The said Pet. could not sell, alienate, or encumber any of his said goods until the said age was completed by him, without the express consent and will of the said Benevenuto, curator appointed to the said Pet. in the present will by the said testator. And this is his last will, which he willed to be valid by the law of wills; and if it were not valid by the law of wills, let it at least be valid by the law of codicils, or of any other last will by which it may better be valid; revoking and annulling all other wills, etc.

Now, in the facts proposed, it is stated that the said Master Andreas died, and the said Pet. survived, and held a certain emphyteutic house granted in emphyteusis to the said Master Andreas for himself during his life, and after his death for the said Pet. and for the said Benevenuto. And he kept merchandise in the said house, etc. Furthermore, it is presupposed in the facts that the said Pet. was instituted heir by the wife of the said Master Andreas; and that the lady had a dowry instrument, in which all the goods of the said Master Andreas were pledged for the dowry, with license to enter the tenement, etc., with most full covenants. Furthermore, it is presupposed in the facts that the said Master Andreas did not have, at the time of his death intestate, nor afterwards at the time of the death of the said Pet., any closer relative than the said Andriola. Furthermore, it is presupposed in the matter that the said Pet. was a spurious son of a certain John, spurious son of the said testator. After the aforementioned events, the said Pet. died before completing the age of 25 years, and instituted Massio as heir. Now a dispute arises between the said Massio and the said lady Andriola; and it is asked, who has the stronger claim to the said goods and the aforementioned inheritance? And many allegations have been made on both sides, which for the sake of brevity I now omit. First, it must be seen whether the said institution of the spurious grandson was conditional or otherwise.

† And it appears that the condition arises from the very nature of the words uttered. For those words, “if he does not dissipate,” create a condition, as noted in the Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, in the law *Absenti*, § *Si quis*, according to the Gloss and Doctoris. On the contrary, it appears that where words, according to their proper meaning, cannot achieve what is at issue, they are understood outside their proper meaning: as in the Digest, *De usufructu*, in the law *Procul*. Furthermore, because the last word must be adhered to: as in the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, in the law *Si tibi*, at the end. But here, at the end of the testamentary disposition, the testator explains himself. For, by premising the alienation in a certain manner and form, he seems to make him heir; that is, to declare that the act was done in the preceding provisions, by argument from the Extravagant, *De testaments*, chapter *Cum tibi*. And this is the truth, considering the mind of the testator, by argument from the Digest, *De manumissionibus testamentis*, in the law *Meuia*, namely, that the testator truly wished that he should be owner and heir, as long as he did not dissipate and lived frugally. But if he did dissipate, what the law would be is not our question. Secondly, having considered the will of the testator, one must consider the power of his will, whether he could institute this person as heir. And if, indeed, when he instituted an heir under the condition “if he can take,” the institution would be valid, but it would contain within itself a condition: Digest, *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in the law *In tempus*. But the testator did not add this to the form of the institution.

And therefore two points must be considered: first, whether this spurious grandson could take under the will. Second, whether he could take by virtue of Imperial legitimation in the territories of the Church. And this matter has been much debated. It is set forth by the Speculum in the title On Succession Intestate. Roffredus disputed it. And Jacobus de Belvis disputed it, and he raises this question in l. 1, C. de natu. lib. And they are of contrary opinions. Bartolus holds with Jacobus de Belvis that the institution is valid: as is noted in l. Gallus, §. quid si is, ff. de libe. et posthu. And the conclusive reason is: because in any grandson whatsoever no prohibiting law is found, as is noted in C. de natu. lib. l. si. Nor does the reason of the law stand in the way: because the grandson was not conceived by the fault of the grandfather; nor is there fraud upon the law: because through the spurious or natural grandson nothing is acquired by his father: since he is not in his power; nor does the signification of the words of the law stand in the way: because the name of son does not signify grandson in a matter distinguishing between son and grandson: as in the said l. si. In those things which are inseparably inherent in the son and adhere to his bones, no extension is made to grandsons: as in l. 3, §. si emancipatus filius, ff. de contratab. just as a proper passion, such as the curvature of the nose, or the pain of the sons. To me this seems most unworthy, that a spurious grandson from a spurious son could be instituted: since he labors under both his own and his father’s fault. And therefore the said last law speaks within certain permissive and limiting bounds, and it does not speak of a spurious grandson, but only of a natural one, who is from a legitimate concubinage. On this, however, we have something permitting or prohibiting, as Odofredus says in the said l. si, gloss. Nevertheless, the gloss says in Authen. quibus mod. natu. effi. sui, §. fina., coll. 7, that where no express prohibition is found, it is gathered that it is permitted. And that gloss greatly supports that opinion, that this grandson is capable as regards the grandfather. To this effect: ff. de vulga. subst. l. si is, qui intentione sui. To me, in this spurious grandson, in whom from his own person I find no permissive reason for the whole or part, the following distinction pleases me. Either he is instituted as a grandson: and the institution is not valid, by argument from C. de fideicomm. l. eam, quam; C. de haere. instit. l. nec apud peregrinos. Or as a stranger, because he merited well, and the merits are proven to have preceded: and then it is valid, by argument from C. de inoffi. testa. auth. vnde si parens. Or there is doubt, and in doubt natural affection induces a presumption that it is as to a grandson: and thus it is not valid, by argument from ff. de pac. l. si tibi, §. si pactus. For this affection is from an evil and condemned root, the fault is not purged, but continued, by argument from C. de hęre. auth. idem de Nestorianis. And if we were to say the contrary: behold, the law could be perpetually defrauded. For no one would ever institute his own spurious son: but he would say, I institute his descendants. And if the spurious grandson ought to succeed from this, material for adulteration would be given to the father of the grandson: and he would strive for any kind of procreation of children, both nefarious and incestuous: which I do not believe the supreme prince, lover of chastity, would have wished to concede. Therefore, in my judgment, this grandson, who appears not deserving, but rather deserving blame on account of the quality of his life, could not take the inheritance from the grandfather solely by the quality of the institution, or re-institution, I believe, and I advise accordingly: always reserving the sounder opinion.

But could he have inherited by virtue of Imperial legitimation? I say that he could not, because at the time of the testator’s death he was not capable; hence he did not inherit from the will, as is noted in the final paragraph of the Digest, under the title *De regulis iuris*. Moreover, because a spurious son stood in the way and did not consent, or because the son was dead, the grandson could not become his own heir of the grandfather through the legitimation of the grandson made after the grandfather’s death; and thus neither of them consented, as is noted in the Digest, under the title *De legitimis*, in the law *Benignus*, according to Guillaume. Furthermore, legitimation made by a count cannot take away successions granted to another, as stated in the law *Gallus*, section *Et quid si tantum*, and there by Bartolus, and in the chapter *Quamvis*, under the title *De rescriptis*, Book 6. Moreover, legitimation is properly called a gift of the prince, as in the Authenticum *Quibus modis*, section *Si vero is, qui solummodo*; and therefore the count, by Imperial authority, could not extend his gift into the lands of the Church to the prejudice of those who do not consent. This is supported by the Digest, under the title *De natalibus restituitis*, in the final law, and there by Jacobus de Arena, and in the Decretals, under the title *Qui filii sint legitimi*, in the chapter *Per venerabilem*, according to Innocentius, although Jacobus de Belvis disputes this, and Jacobus advised the same as Jacobus de Belvis. For he could not properly legitimize in the lands of the Empire with regard to succession, except indirectly, for example by approving what does not stand under civil law. Just as the Emperor cannot give away the property of barbarians, so he cannot give away the patrimonial property of those exempt from his jurisdiction. Therefore, it must be concluded that the said institution and legitimation were of no effect, and that the inheritance of the said testator belongs to the persons enumerated in the Code, under the title *De incestis nuptiis*, in the law *Si quis incestus*. And if those persons do not exist, then it belongs to the fiscus, as is said in the final paragraph of that law, which, although commonly known, is nevertheless notable. Nor does it matter that the capable substitute was appointed for the incapable person, which could be done, as stated in the Code, under the title *De hereditatibus instituendis*, in law 3. For it was not done in fraud of the law, so as to restore to the incapable person; and therefore it is not valid, according to the argument in the Digest, under the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Heres meus*, section *Quod in fraudem*. And this is clear from the express wording of the will; and therefore it does not require proof. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, and I have subscribed under my hand and caused it to be sealed with the seal of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a grandson is said to be so with respect to the matter of succession, who was conceived after his grandfather had already died. And see above, opinion 398.
2. The facts being thus stated, it is that Antonius has several male children.
body: He made his will: in which he instituted them as universal heirs, and substituted them for one another, so that if any of them should die without legitimate male children, and in the case where the preceding one should die while a daughter female survives him, he left to the said female 15 florins as a dowry: and in them he instituted her as his heir. But the remainder of the said inheritance of the said preceding one he wished to pass to the other male children. The testator having died, one of the instituted male sons took a wife: and had a single daughter: and died intestate while she survived. It is asked, whether this daughter can claim the said legacy and the inheritance of her said father? Having seen the Statutes of the City of Perugia speaking on this matter.

† Because the statute has three heads with respect to the matter at hand: one head concerns the grandfather providing a dowry, another concerns any other person, and the third concerns a non-dowered granddaughter to be dowered by her uncle, and thereby excluded from the remainder of the succession. Let us examine each head separately. The head concerning the grandfather does not apply here: because, with regard to the subject matter and the case of successions, one is not called a grandfather if the granddaughter was not conceived during his lifetime, even though, with regard to the source of memory and the absolute enumeration of degrees, she is called a granddaughter. D. 22.2.1.1; D. 38.16.1.1; Inst. 2.19.1; D. 38.2.1; D. 28.5.1; D. 28.5.1; C. 6.25.1; D. 35.2.1; D. 35.2.1. Since, therefore, words are to be understood according to the subject matter, whether they are used by law or in a contract: as noted in D. 8.4.1; D. 19.1.1; D. 19.2.1; and since we are dealing with successions, let us understand "grandfather" according to the subject matter in which we are engaged: not according to a grandfather in whom the laws of cognation never existed. D. 34.5.1. The head concerning any other person providing a dowry does not prejudice this girl: she can, namely, not accept this legacy, and have her legitime because of what was left, so that she does not accept such a legacy, and thus, since she is not considered dowered if she does not consent, she succeeds to the legitime, as D. 4.3.1. It is not objected that another statute requires daughters and granddaughters to observe the will of their father and grandfather. For this person is not to be considered in the place of a grandfather, who, by no natural bond, nor by perfect and caused natural affection, can yet be called so: as has been said: because, namely, certain things are more liberally granted on account of natural affection, which are not to be granted when affection ceases, as D. 35.2.1. And thus he is not properly called a grandfather in fact or affection: but an outsider, as I proved above. Although, therefore, an ascendant could impose a law on a descendant in whom agnation is found, according to the form of the statute: it is otherwise with an outsider: because not everything that is permitted to parents is permitted to outsiders, as C. 6.59.1. The head concerning the uncle is to be understood equally, and according to the discretion of a good man, as D. 33.1.1; D. 32.1.1; D. 33.1.1; D. 33.1.1. Since, namely, there is only one girl, she is to be dowered generously, so that she has at least her legitime. A good man will never judge that the legitime of a son is to be taken away, which is said to be a debt: and is owed by necessary and natural law, as D. 47.2.1; C. 6.25.1. And it succeeds in the place of alimony, as noted in C. 5.4.1. By Cynus. Moreover, where there is no one else to make a share, the entire inheritance of an intestate father, completely deceased, who made no will, nor codicils, is owed to a single son, or to several, by natural law. D. 28.5.1; C. 7.31.1; C. 7.31.1. And thus, if the uncle gives little to the girl, and retains much for himself, he would not be performing the office of one who judges rightly, as D. 17.2.1. I. 1.1. Furthermore, in the meantime, before the uncle dowers by paying, or effectively promising, the girl herself succeeds in the whole: hence, until marriageable years, she is the universal heir: because the statute says that she is excluded from that time, after she has been dowered: therefore, in the meantime, she is not excluded: because one excluded after a time is considered included before the time, and vice versa, as D. 35.1.1. Saving the fideicommissary substitution made by the grandfather among the sons. Conclusively, I say that, although one might doubt regarding the Trebellianic portion, whether they should have it until marriageable age: regarding the legitime, and the fruits of the legitime, I do not doubt that she should have it, by abstaining from the legacy made by the grandfather, who is called a grandfather in name, and not in fact, as has been fully said. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Law. Always saving the better advice.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a curator should be appointed for a minor accused of a delict, otherwise that the proceedings are null.
body: The facts of the case

† Thus the case is stated: A minor under five years of age, who is established by the records to be a minor, yet over twenty years of age, accused someone of having struck him with an empty hand; from which blow blood flowed, in the presence and with the consent of the guardian. By the accused, who appeared in person, an exception of nullity of the process is raised, on the ground that it was invalid, because a curator ad litem should have been appointed, and the father’s consent alone is not sufficient. The question is whether the said exception is an obstacle. I say that the said exception is an obstacle, by the authority of what is noted by Guillaume in the *speculum* on accusations, § 1, at the words “if, however, a minor,” and by Goffredus in the rubric “Who may not accuse without appearing,” stating that on account of this defect he has seen many proceedings annulled. The same is held ordinarily by Guillaume in the law *Si longius*, D. de iudiciis, and this on the grounds assigned by them in the said places. And so it seems to me, Andreas de Monte Albano. I also, Baldus de Perusio, considering that the father’s authority, where the father does not seek, nor can seek, a usufruct, nor claims any pecuniary interest, thus say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Where two wills of the same person, written by the hand of the same notary, appear to differ in some respect, one must adhere to the will that agrees with the first and original writing.
body: A certain Cicholo Patrician of Spello made a will, in which he instituted his wife Ziliola as his heir during her lifetime; and after his death, he substituted as heirs the priors of the brotherhood of the commendatory of St. Mary of Mercy of Spello, with this law and condition added, namely that as long as she lived and observed an honest and chaste widowhood, she could freely and entirely sell, alienate, encumber, and dispose of the goods of the said testator under any title that pleased her, as it seemed good and pleasing to her, the aforementioned condition not being an obstacle in any way, without the intervention of any person of the commissioners or legatees. After the said Cicholo died, the said Ziliola sold some goods from the said inheritance. Finally, the said Ziliola, coming to death, made a will, in which she instituted Cicholo Putii of Spello as her heir, who accepted the said inheritance. Finally, the priors of the aforementioned brotherhood brought the said Cicholo, heir of the said Ziliola, to judgment, claiming to be the substituted heirs of the said Ziliola by virtue of the will of the said Cicholo Patrician; and they produced a certain will written and published by the hand of Ser Jacobus Corvus of Spello, notary. This will is one and the same as the will of the said Cicholo Patrician, which is produced by the said Cicholo Putii, heir of the said Ziliola; and it agrees with it in the year, indiction, pontificate, day, place, and witnesses, but it does not agree with the words contained in the institution of the heir, since it states that Ziliola, his wife, is instituted as his universal heir, and that he made her so during his lifetime; and after his death, he substituted the priors of the brotherhood and commendatory of St. Mary of Spello. With this law and condition added, namely that as long as she lived and led an honest and chaste widowhood, she could freely do whatever she pleased with the goods of the said testator, without the contradiction of any person of the fideicommissaries or legatees. This will also agrees with the notary’s book, in which the same will is written. And the will of the said Cicholo Putii, heir of the said Ziliola, heir of the said Cicholo Patrician, agrees with the Bastardello [draft], in which the said notary first wrote the will of the said Cicholo Patrician, lacking those words: “without the contradiction of any person of the fideicommissaries or legatees.” And the Bastardello, in which the said will was first written before being placed in the book, does not agree with the book in those words. And that will, or that which the said Cicholo Putii has, the said Ziliola had from the said notary in public form already 25 years ago or thereabouts. And the will that the said priors have, they had from the aforementioned notary already 5 months ago, and no longer. Now it is asked, to which of these wills faith should be given, to the will extracted from the Bastardello first extracted into public form, or to the will extracted from the book? And whether the said Ziliola could sell from the aforementioned goods by her own right and in perpetuity; and whether the said sales, if any appear to have been made, are valid in law by virtue of the said wills, or of any of them, or not?

† First, the original and matrix document must be relied upon: as in the Authentica de Tabulis, in rubro et nigro. For it is called the matrix script of the original protocol; according to the exemplar, as noted in the Digest, de fide instrumentorum, l. 2. And it must be relied upon, just as the first statement of a witness is relied upon, as in the Authentica de testibus, §. et quia vero. And if the notary has restored the instrument to public form, it is to be relied upon insofar as it agrees with the matrix script. However, if there is some diversity in it by which the effect is not varied, it is not vitiated, Extra, de conversione coniugali, c. dudum. And therefore, in the question proposed, greater faith is to be given to the testament agreeing with the original, and the omission of those words, "without contradiction" and so forth, does not vitiate it: because it does not vary the effect of the matter. For the agreement of documents is to be considered with regard to the effect, not superficially: as in the Code, de poenis, l. quod sententiam, where it says, "agreeing in one end of the matter." That text is noted for this purpose. And therefore, according to the tenor of the said document, the buyer lawfully appeared. And thus I say, I counsel, I, Baldus de Petusio, Doctor of Both Laws, and I have subscribed to this for the faith thereof, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legatee who dies while the claim is pending does not transmit the legacy.
2. A substitute who, within one year from the day of his knowledge of the ward, assumed guardianship, succeeds to all the goods upon the ward’s death; otherwise not. And what about the grandmother, if the substitute does not accept guardianship of the ward, whether she herself ought to petition for a guardian so that she may not be excluded from the succession.
3. Whether knowledge of the will is presumed. OPINION 411.
1. A mother who does not petition for a guardian for her son is excluded from his succession, notwithstanding that he had a lawful guardian.
body: Lucas Francischini of Pergola died having made a will in which he instituted his son Andrea as his universal heir; and if the said Andrea, his son, should die without children before he reached the age of twenty years, the said testator willed that Vannes Iunctae magistri Ioannis of Pergola have, and ought to have, from his goods upon the occurrence of that event, as is to be stated, one hundred pounds in coin; and as to the residue of all the goods, if the said Andrea should die without legitimate children under the age of twenty years, he substituted to him Nicolaus, Iacobus, and Petrus, vulgarly, pupillarly, and by fideicommissum. Thereafter, after the death of the said testator, the said legatee Vannus survived, and then died while the said Andrea was still living. Finally, the said Andrea died without children, and before he reached twenty years, and in pupillary age, with Baldutia, his paternal grandmother, surviving, who never sought a tutor; and with the aforesaid substitutes Nicolaus and Petrus surviving, of whom Nicolaus undertook the tutorship of the said pupil. It is now asked whether the heirs of the aforesaid Vannus can claim the said legacy of one hundred pounds. Secondly, it is asked to whom the goods and the inheritance of the aforesaid Andrea the pupil, or of the aforesaid Lucas, ought to go; and what about maternal goods, or goods acquired from elsewhere than from the father? And what of the portion of the said Iacobus, who died before the said pupil, what is the law? This is asked.

† On that first point, it must be said that since the legacy was conditional, namely if the said Andrea should die without children, and the said legatee Vannus died while the condition was pending, such legacy vanished; nor can such legacy be claimed by the heirs: as in C. de cadu. tol. §. sinautem sub condictione, de regu. iur. l. quae legata, and what is noted in de his, quae ante aper. tabu. cum si.

† On the second point, it must be said that the said Nicolaus, who undertook the tutorship, if he undertook it within a year from the day of knowledge, succeeds the pupil by virtue of the said substitution to all the goods of the pupil, both those coming from the father and from wherever else they come: ff. de vulg. sub. l. sed si plures. §. ad substitutos. But if he did not undertake the tutorship within a year from the day of knowledge, then the said substitute would not succeed to anything: as in C. de legi. haere. l. si sciant. But the grandmother herself would succeed to the whole; nor is she repelled on account of not having sought a tutor, because since she did not primarily hope for the succession, the right of seeking a tutor did not pertain to her.

† Knowledge of a will, however, is not presumed, so that it must be proved: C. de iure delibe. l. quoniam sororem, and what is noted in ff. de lib. leg. l. cum haeres. §. j., si cer. pet. l. eius, qui in prouincia, and l. fi. pro suo, and de proba. l. verius, cum similibus; unless it were proved that he was present at the will, because then knowledge would be presumed from presence. Nay, the truth is that the substitutes come in by all means, because they could not undertake the tutorship before the grandmother renounced it; whence the year begins from the day on which the grandmother had renounced the tutorship, and not before. Since, moreover, the grandmother immediately renounced the tutorship and Nicolaus undertook it, l. sciant has been satisfied, and therefore the substitutes succeed by the express pupillary substitution, because the grandmother is entirely excluded. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, say and advise, and under my faith I have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A mother who does not seek a tutor for her son is excluded from his succession, notwithstanding that he had a legitimate tutor.
body: The fact is this: A certain Petrus de Montido had two sons, namely Master Ioannes and Lellus. From the said Master Ioannes, Ioannes was born, specifically of Lara his wife. After the said Master Ioannes died, the said Lara married a second husband named Toxius, and from the said Toxius she had a second son named Frudosus. And from the said Lellus, Collutius was born; from the said Ioannes, Michael was born; from the said Frudosus, Angelus was born, namely from him and Lady Stelucia his wife. Thus, having died first Petrus, second Master Ioannes, third Ioannes, fourth Frudosus, fifth Michael, the said Angelus died, with the said Stelucia surviving, who never sought a tutor for him, nor undertook the tutelage, nor held it; and she remained so for several years, with Colutius son of Lellus surviving, and Cincius son of Frudosus surviving. It is asked, to whom does the inheritance of the said ward belong?

† I respond: if the said Stelucia was under 25 years of age at the time of her husband's death, the inheritance belongs to her, C. si aduer. delictum. l. fi., where it is stated that a minor is not excluded on account of not having sought a tutor. But if she was then over 25 years of age, even then no one is excluded where the said ward has legitimate tutors, according to the gloss on l. 3. C. ad Tert. But according to the moderns she is excluded, because the presence of a legitimate tutor does not preclude exclusion unless she renounces the tutelage, as in Authem. ma. et aui., and this is the true view. Therefore, the mother having been excluded, the next of kin comes, namely the said Cinctius, regarding the degree, even though he is related only through the mother; and therefore by reason of degree he is preferred, as in Authem. post fratres, and in the body from which it is taken. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that a dowried woman, etc., shall not succeed, whether a daughter succeeds in the goods of her father or brother.
body:
The facts are as follows: Masciolus, by name, of the county of Assisi, contracted a lawful marriage with Lady Rosa of Bai, of the said county of Assisi. From this marriage thus contracted, the aforementioned Masciolus had two children, namely Andricus, and his daughter Cecha, and Passara of the said Bai; and he gave her in dowry 40 denarii. Then the case occurred that Rosa, her mother, and the said Andricus died intestate, with the said their sons and the said Masciolus, their husband and father of the said children, surviving them. Subsequently, Masciolus died intestate, with the said Andricus and Cecha, his children, surviving him. Finally, Andricus died intestate without children, with the said Cecha, his sister, surviving him, who now lives. From these facts arises a question between the cousins of the said Cecha on one side, who say that the said Cecha does not succeed in any way in the goods and inheritance of the said Masciolus, her late father, and of the said Andricus, her brother, since she was dowered by her father, as is stated above, notwithstanding the statute of the city of Assisi, which provides that a dowered woman, etc., which statute is opposed. On the other hand, it is responded on the part of the said Cecha that she, notwithstanding the said statute and all the above-mentioned matters, succeeds by right in the goods of the said Masciolus, her father, and of the said Andricus, her brother. Now it is asked from the narrated facts, what is the law: the words of the aforementioned statute are these: "If any woman shall have been dowered by father, or by mother, brother, or grandmother, or by anyone, she may not, nor ought she, or a son descending from her, to recur, or come to the inheritance, or succession of any of those dowering her: nor to ask, or have anything of the goods, and upon the goods of any of the aforementioned dowers in any manner, so long as from the aforementioned, or any of the aforementioned, there shall be, and remain, a son, grandson, or great-grandson, or male heir born of lawful marriage, descending from him, or her, coming into the aforementioned succession. But the said dowered woman ought to be content with her dowry: and she, or anyone proceeding from her, or succeeding, or descending in the goods of any of the aforementioned, may not ask, or have anything: wills, or last wills made, always being saved."

Having seen the point and the statute, the question stands in this: whether those words of the statute, "so long as from the aforementioned, etc.," are to be understood as "from the aforementioned father, grandfather, etc.," or rather are to be understood as "from the aforementioned, of whose succession it is treated." For if they are understood in the first way, the dowered daughter does not succeed: but the cousin brother of the deceased, who is a male descendant of the grandfather of this deceased woman. But if they are understood as "from the aforementioned, of whose succession it is treated": then the daughter succeeds; because from him, of whose succession it is treated, no male exists.

I solve: I say that it ought to be understood as "from the aforementioned, of whose succession it is treated": because such interpretation has less iniquity. And the signification of that word "from the aforementioned" can be preserved in it, since above it made mention of succession, and consequently of those to whom succession is made. D. de legibus, l. in ambigua; D. de regulis iuris, l. semper in dubiis. And this is true, unless custom interpreted this speech more broadly. D. de legibus, l. si de interpretatione. Therefore, it does not matter from whom she is dowered: but it matters well whether from him, of whose succession it is treated, there exist male descendants, who exclude the woman. But collaterals do not exclude: because it would be absurd, as C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; D. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; D. de liberis praeteritis, l. maximum vitium, cum si. And this is also confirmed by those words, "coming into the aforementioned succession with the said dowered woman." And thus it implies those descending from the deceased. He, therefore, who would come with her by common law, excludes her: but not he who excludes the daughter, who would not come with the daughter: because he is an outsider. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who is bound to reserve something for someone after his death ought to give security: and nu. 2.
body: Whether he who, after death, is bound to reserve something for another ought to give security for its restitution after death.

It appears that the answer is in the affirmative, as in the case proposed, C. leg. Cum Archimedoram. To the contrary, it appears that the answer is negative, because a vow to seek death is induced. C. de pa. l. Si. Hence it is that, although a father is bound to reserve the legitime for his children, he is nevertheless not bound to give security for such reservation. ff. de lib. agno. l. Si. Because while the father is living, the children have no right in the legitime, as is noted there by Dy. to the same effect. ff. ad treb. l. Imperator. We have a similar case: a father who gave a dowry for his daughter and recovered it is bound to reserve it for her subsequent marriage; nevertheless, in the meantime, he ought not to give security to the daughter regarding this. C. de rei ux. act. l. Si tam in praesenti. and auth. Sed quamvis.

Solution: Either we are speaking of a *satisdatio* (security with surety), or of a bare caution, that is, without a surety or pledge, when the delivery of pledges intervenes. But if indeed we are speaking of *satisdatio*: then it matters whether they are persons between whom a civil obligation does not arise: as between a father and a son in power: as ff. de condi. et demon. l. Frater a fratre. And then either the father dissipates the property. And then the administration of the property is removed from him. Or he does not dissipate it: and then [he is not bound to give security]: but the father possesses freely. ff. ad treb. l. Impe. Or [we are speaking] of persons between whom a civil obligation can be made: as between a mother and a son: and between strangers. And then it matters whether the burden of reservation arises from a preceding disposition of the testator: and security must be given in rem. ad Treb. l. Imperator. ff. qui satis. cog. l. Inter omnes l. 1. §. Si quis sub condi. vt le. no. c. In which security every quality and conclusion of the last will is so repeated, that such a promise is not considered in the place of a contract: but in the place of a last will as regards transmission: as ff. de leg. 2. l. Bellissime. And thus the contract caused by the last will assumes its nature: because it is substituted in its place: or the burden of reservation arises from a preceding order of the contracting parties: and then a caution must be interposed. ff. de act. em. l. Si quis seruum. §. Et præterea.

And I understand that caution must be given at the discretion of a good man, so that if the person is suspect, he gives security. If, however, he is suitable, he does not give security: as is noted ff. man. l. Si mandato. §. Si. Nevertheless, he is bound to obligate his goods verbally: I do not say that he is bound to deliver them in place of a pledge: for a verbal obligation of goods benefits the creditor, and does not prejudice the debtor, as is noted in l. Si. C. quæ res pig. ob. pos. Therefore, it ought to be interposed, arg. ff. sol. mat. l. 2. ver. Nisi. ff. de aqua plu. l. 2. §. Idem Varus. And what is noted in l. 2. §. Si dubitetur. ff. de iud. Or the burden of reservation arises from a legal disposition: and then either the law proceeds further by ordering security to be given simply and absolutely: and then security must be given. And if security is omitted by a person, it is supplied by the law, because a promise is feigned. ff. de adop. l. His verbis. ff. de vulg. sub. l. Causa cognita. But if the law proceeds further not simply and absolutely, but with distinction, then where the law distinguishes, we likewise distinguish there. For either both offer security: and the plaintiff is preferred, because he has the stronger right. For a right in action is stronger than a right in passivity. ff. de exce. dol. l. Pure. in prin. and in doubt, he is preferred to whom the right pertains in the first place. C. de edi. di. adria. tol. l. 1. ff. dele. 2. l. Si quis seruum. §. Certum. ff. de bo. li. l. Si filius. §. Et sine dubio. Or one offers security in the due form, the other does not: then he who gives security in the due form is preferred. Or neither offers: and then in equal negligence, or in power, the plaintiff is preferred, who has the right to the thing, more than the defendant, who has the right of hope. C. de secun. nup. l. Hac edictali. §. Is illud. Or the law does not proceed further, but only orders [the property] to be reserved: but does not order security to be given: and this is properly our case,

† Because the statute commands that the dowry be reserved for the children of the first marriage pro rata. And the question arises whether security for restitution must be given: and it seems that it must, D. de iudicibus, l. in omnibus; D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si constante, §. quotiens; D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. si creditores. To the contrary, it seems that it need not: because from this statute arises a conditio ex lege municipalis, which is of strict law. D. de conditionibus ex lege, l. 1; in Inst. de actionibus, §. actionum. But in actions of strict law, security is not to be given to a future creditor, as is noted in the aforementioned l. in omnibus, unless either suspicion is imminent, as in l. si creditores, or fraud of the debtor intervenes: because he has obtained an unjust right. C. de praescriptionibus impetratis offerentium, l. universa. But our question concerns a conditio ex lege, and therefore it must be said that in our case security is not to be provided. For the statute fixes its footing in the reservation: and it does not dispose anything regarding security. Moreover, this statute is burdensome and contrary to the common law, whence I will not extend it, nor multiply the inconvenience, arg. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. si vero, §. de viro. But any security is beneficial, and does not harm the one giving security: because it is not interposed to the detriment of the one giving security. And that one is perhaps to be interposed. Hence, the mother shall give security for the preservation of the dowry according to the form of the statute, without the burden of suretyship or delivery of a pledge. She shall, however, give security under a hypothec of her goods and rights. And thus the name of the husband shall be bound: but the husband himself is not compelled to give security to the children of the first marriage: because he did not contract with them, as C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. sicut; D. de communi dividundo, l. incommoda, §. sicut. For if the security does not have its origin in the same person from another cause: one is not bound to give security for the origin of a new contract: because he does not have pre-existing matter, from which the necessity of giving security depends: because regularly no one is compelled to contract. And so it is here: because this man did not contract with the stepchildren, but with the wife: unless the wife preferred that the promise of restitution be formed in the person of the children, as in the aforementioned l. 1, §. 1, D. de solutione matrimonii. For then, if it does not harm her, he is bound to promise: as is fully noted there. Therefore, a simple security of the mother suffices for the children: which having been given, this second husband may sue on the right ceded to him against the heirs of the first husband. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one may depart from an oath in a contract in which a form prescribed by law or statute was not observed.
body: The case is as follows. Sidam Massius of Gualdo, on one side, and a certain donation from the same place, on the other side, compromised to certain arbitrators regarding every lawsuit and controversy that might exist between them on account of the division of common goods, or otherwise in any way whatsoever; and the said parties swore to hold firm the award to be rendered by the said arbitrators and not to go against it. Then the award was rendered by the said arbitrators. It is provided by the form of the statute of the said town that contracting parties are bound and must have contracts and instruments exceeding 50 pounds registered in a certain book existing in the chamber of the massars of the commune of Gualdo within ten days from the day the contract was celebrated. And if the aforesaid is not observed, from now on the contract contrary to the said form shall be invalid by the law itself; and no action of claiming or suing arises for any party from such a contract by virtue of a contract not registered, as is stated above. Since the said compromise contract was above 50 pounds and, due to the negligence of the father, was not registered according to the form of the said statute, it is null by the law itself. The question is asked: whether it could be demanded that it be pronounced null, notwithstanding the oath given in the said compromise contract, and without the said Massius having requested absolution from the aforesaid oath; since the said Massius does not go against the compromise and the award by the form of the said compromise and award, but only by the negligence of the party who did not register, nor cause to be registered, the said contract.
