† Where a form has been prescribed by law or statute for a contract, if it is not observed and an oath is taken: sometimes one may depart from it by means of the oath, sometimes not. For if a certain form is prescribed in favor of the contracting party, one may depart from it if an oath is taken. Extra de iureiurando, c. Cum mulieres; and in the Authenticum Sacramenta puberum. But if the form is prescribed for evidentiary purposes, from such a form one cannot depart, even if an oath is taken, as is fully noted by Bartolus, ff. de fideiussoribus, l. Si quis pro eo. And therefore, if a contract requires insinuation, if it is not insinuated, the oath is not valid; because one cannot renounce insinuation, as is noted by the doctors, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. Illud. So it is in the present case; hence, if insinuation is not made, no right arises from such contract, nor does proof result; nor is he considered perjured who makes use of the authority of the law. ff. qui satisdare coguntur, l. Pe; C. de non numerata pecunia, l. Sin. And especially because a preceding oath does not remove a defense which subsequently arises from following negligence or from another new cause. ff. de iureiurando, l. Sed si possessori, § 2. From which I conclude that he ought not to be considered perjured; because he reasonably makes use of the benefit of the statute, since he holds the office of apostolic vicar: and he may relax the oath, as is read and noted, ff. de iure patronatus, l. Adigere, § fin. And although to compromise, insofar as it is an elective act regarding persons, is not a contract, nor is the transaction of the arbitrator’s award; nevertheless, the promise to abide by the award is a contract, and this promise ought to have been registered, otherwise it is null, and thus the award remains without any bond of obligation; and consequently it is invalid, unless the parties subsequently consented to fulfill the award. C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. 2, with the gloss, etc. I, Baldus.
Regarding the question whether the concession that the dowry instrument was simulated, made by the wife to the husband, etc., see in the fifth part, consilium 471, beginning "Super," etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If there are several merchants who are partners, and one of them, with the consent of the others, hires common goods belonging to all of them, and that merchant is robbed on the way, whether the risk should be shared.
2. When a common seal is affixed to all the bales, the bales are presumed to be common.
body: It is proposed that certain merchants agreed among themselves that each of them on his own would buy as much quantity of saffron (or crocus) as they could; and that, once the saffron was purchased, it would be carried to the city of Venice; and that the profit and loss that should result from the said merchandise would be in common. When each of them had bought two bales of saffron, one from among themselves sent those six bales toward Venice. The event occurred that the said saffron was robbed on the journey, and four bales bought by two of them, who were Florentines, were restored to them; the other two, which belonged to the carrier, because he was from Camerino, were withheld from him.

† It is asked whether the risk is common? And in this question it must be considered whether that saffron was made common property or not, and whether its carrier was in fault or not. For if they made the bales mutually common, and the carrier was not in fault, but by chance fell among robbers, the risk too is common, and the four bales that remain are common, as in ff. pro so. l. cum duobus. §. quidam sagariam; for this arises from the nature of partnership. If, however, the bales were not made common property, such that the partnership was not in their ownership, but in the profit to be realized from them, then the thing perishes to the owner and not to another: ar. ff. loc. l. in naue saufelli; and this arises from the nature of ownership, as agrees with that which is noted and read on a similar matter in C. loc. l. si damnum. by Cy. But if he was in fault by traveling through places notoriously unsafe for him, then let him impute it to himself; to this effect, ff. loc. l. pe. §. naue; ff. pro. so. l. cum duobus. ad fi.; ff. de condi. ob causam l. si pecuniam. in fi.; for the law wills that everyone be wise and diligent. For nature gives man reason and intellect precisely so that he may use them, nor indeed in vain did nature give this sublime gift to men. Therefore according to the kinds of contracts come the kinds of faults, ff. commo. l. si ut certo. §. nunc uidendum.

† If, however, it is in doubt whether the said saffron was made common or not, it seems that it was made common, since a single mark common to all the bales was applied; because by the application of a mark mutual possession seems to have been delivered, ar. ff. de peri. et commo. rei ven. l. 1. §. si dolum. To the contrary it seems that it was not confused, but remained unmixed and separate, ar. ff. de rei ven. l. Idem Pomp.; and because in doubt that communication of ownership does not seem to be presumed, as noted in l. j. ff. pro so. To this makes what is said in a loan (mutuum): for where there is no commingling, a mutuum is not constituted, but where there is commingling, it is; ff. de so. l. si alieni; ff. si cer. pe. l. nam et si fur. Solution: if the partners asserted that each of them held his own bales, it is not presumed from the beginning to have been made common, ar. ff. pro socio. l. itaque. If, however, a common mark appears, and nothing else said or done appears to the contrary, I presume that communication of ownership was made. For every contract is presumed to be unconditional unless it is proved conditional, ff. de verb. ob. l. si ista stipu. §. chrisogonus. in fi. §.; therefore the contract of partnership is presumed celebrated over the present thing and ownership, and not merely over the future price; for that which looks to the future is deemed conditional, de ver. ob. l. interdum; de condi. et demon. l. 1. in fi. Therefore, in doubt, I presume the contract to be unconditional, and that ownership was reciprocally transferred from both sides. I, Baldus.

Or suppose the facts are otherwise, and more true, namely that two Florentines and one from Camerino, having no partnership among themselves, agreed to buy saffron, and that each should buy separately from the others that which each could buy. Now, all three together bought one thousand five hundred pounds of saffron, and each paid his share from his own money; and they made six bales; and they agreed that all three should send the saffron to Venice together through the hands of one of them; and that whatever proceeds resulted from the said saffron, whether loss or profit, should be divided equally among them; and the said bales were not marked with any seal of any of them; but they made on the said bales one other sign or external mark. The one from Camerino transported the said bales to the seaport, and there he was to have them shipped, and then return to his home; and no writing was made concerning the above, nor were any witnesses required, nor was any instrument drawn up; and thus, simply and on pure faith, they conducted the aforementioned affairs. Finally, this one from Camerino, transporting the said bales, was captured at the port, or in the port, with the said bales. Now, each of these claims the said bales from the one who robbed them. This robber, however, wished to know the truth, whose the said bales were; and all three said that each had a third part, that is, that two bales belonged to each of them; and thus they confessed before the robber. Hearing this, the robber restored four of these bales to these two Florentines as Florentines; he retained the other two for himself, and retains them, because he says they belong to the one from Camerino. Now it is asked whether the loss of the two bales lost should be common to all three, or only to the one from Camerino?

The nature of partnership is such that if one of the partners sets out on business for the partnership and, encountering robbers, suffers losses, the risk is common to all the partners, even with respect to his own personal property, as stated in D. 17.2.14 (*Cum duobus*), § *Quidam sagarium*. This holds true unless he was at fault for traveling through dangerous places; for in that case, even if the loss occurred in goods belonging to others, let alone in his own property, the risk falls upon him alone. He ought to have guarded against ambushes, not only those apparent, but also those probable, D. 17.2.14 (*Et si ut certo*), § *Sed ubi*, together with the following law, D. 17.2.1 (*Socius socio*).

Let us therefore first examine whether these individuals were still partners. For it is proposed in the case that each had his own bales, kept distinct from one another; and the partnership had this condition and understanding, namely, if the saffron were sold. Hence, the intervening accident occurring with the saffron prevents the partnership from being formed; and thus the risk is not common, by argument from D. 18.1.1 (*Necessario*) in the title *De periculo et commodo rei venditae*. For the partnership is proposed not regarding the present saffron, but regarding future profits or price. However, everything contributed for the future carries a tacit condition that it shall survive, D. 45.1.10 (*Interdum*) in the title *De verbis obligatorum*; D. 35.1.1, in fine, in the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. For the partnership was not established for the purpose of holding the saffron, but for its sale, D. 17.2.1 (*Si id, quod in principio*), where this appears to be expressly stated.

Secondly, it must be examined whether this person was at fault. And it seems that he was, because war had begun between those of Camerino and those of Matelica; hence, since he was from Camerino, and suffered the loss due to his own hatred for his homeland and that enmity, and not for the sake of the partnership, let him impute it to himself, by argument from D. 19.2.1 (*Si merces*), § *Culpae*, and D. 24.3.1 (*In his*) in the title *De solutione et liberatione*. Hence, if what is proposed in the case is true, let him impute it to himself who was at fault; for he did not foresee the accident that threatened his ruin. And therefore, let him bear the loss alone, because he committed the fault alone, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the fruits of paraphernal property are to be restored by the husband and the brothers.
2. When a minor reaches the age at which he could have entered into a partnership, he must hold his share with the others as a partner.
3. What items are to be shared in a partnership, and number 4.
4. Whether the profit that accrues to the husband by virtue of a statute from the wife's dowry is to be shared.
5. A partner is bound to render an account of everything.
6. Whether expenses incurred on partnership property for its permanent benefit are recoverable.
7. The daughter of one of the partners ought not to be endowed from the common fund, unless it has been agreed upon among the partners.
body: To the first, I say that

† The fruits of the paraphernal property must be restored by both the husband and his brothers, who received them: as is noted in C. de pac. conuen. in l. si, in the gloss quid in naturalibus, and in C. de iure dot. l. ubi adhuc, in the gloss sicut ergo, s. medietatem. For the other half these, who are laborers, ought to have by right of labor and services: because in case of doubt, half of the fruits is attributed to the thing, and half to the labor, ff. pro soc. l. cum duobus, §. in coeunda.

† To the second point, I answer that once he has reached the age at which he could form a partnership and contribute his labor like others, he ought, as a partner, to receive his share, or at least some compensation for his labor. For a son can be a partner, as is clear, once he has come of age. D. 17.2.1 § si filius (Si id quod). In the meantime, those who contribute no labor should be maintained at the father’s expense. But if they have contributed some labor in common, perhaps by tending the beasts or the pigs, they should be maintained in common. For even a minor may have some labor to contribute: as D. 13.6.1 (Caeterum); D. 14.3.1 § possunt (In rebus). In the reasoning of that §.
† To the third point, I say that the inheritance does not come into common ownership, as is stated in the Digest, title *Pro socio*, law *Nec adijcit*, together with the following law.
† To the fourth point, I say that he ought to communicate. D. pro socio, l. coiri, in the word "emptione."

† To the fifth point, I say that the aforementioned Putius appears to have gained the said third part by a cause pertaining to him alone, so that it is not to be shared. D. 38.2.1 (Si maritus). For there is a certain acquisition on account of death, by reason of the death of the wife, which does not fall within the partnership. D. 17.2.1 (Nec adiecit), in the word *causa mortis*. And consequently, the fruits are not common. S. Medietas fructuum, otherwise, because they were acquired by the right of labor. But the truth is that this gain is to be shared, as in D. 17.2.1 (Quod si eo tempore), where the case is notable.

† To the sixth point, I say that he is bound to render an account of all things in such manner as it can be rendered. For witnesses cannot be had for all things: but in certain cases, namely in small matters, his oath is accepted. Likewise, even in small matters, if the quality of the person, the probability of the case, and the inclination of the judge concur with this. C. de donat. l. si quis pro redemptione. C. de iure deliberandi. l. fin. §. in computatione. in the gloss.

† To the seventh point, I say that expenses made for a permanent benefit are recoverable; nevertheless, the fruits, insofar as they are due to be restored to the wife, will be set off against the husband, whether under the common name of himself and his wife, or under his own proper name, I do not care. Argument: Digest, On the Sale of Things, law *Sumptus*; and what is not, in the same title, law *Cum in fundo*.

† To the eighth point, I say that the daughter of one of the partners ought not to be endowed from the common property, unless an action has been brought under the heading *pro socio*, as stated in the Digest, title *Si socius pro filia*. For this would not be a division, but rather a taking, that is, to have a share before the division. And so holds the Speculum in the title *De iudiciis*, section *Sequitur*, under the rubric *Quid si unus ex fratribus*. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If by statute daughters are excluded from succession, and it is said that they are to be content with their dowry, if they are dowered, and if not, that they ought to be dowered at the discretion of their relatives, etc., if it happens that a daughter dies before she marries, and some dowry has been assessed for her by her relatives, may the mother, succeeding to her, claim anything in the goods of her father’s estate?
1. Whether that which is due to a son in lieu of a legitime, or of a dowry, by statute, is transmitted to the mother.
body:
To make the arguments clear, it must be premised that the following statute is in force: namely, we deem it to be for the honor of the city and its glory to have wealthy subjects; and that the assets of women are not diminished by their aggregations [into marriage], whereas the councils of women are sometimes found to be contrary to good morals and to work against their own interests. Therefore, we have enacted that if any person dies intestate, survived by a son or sons of the male sex, or by a grandson or great-grandson, and so on, by any descendant from him who is male, provided that he is connected to the deceased person through the line of the male sex, continued through the same sex, such persons shall be admitted to the succession of the aforementioned persons in its entirety, even if there is a daughter or daughters, one or more; or a granddaughter or granddaughters, and so on, any descendant from that predeceased person connected to that person through a male son, or grandsons, or other male descendants, shall not be admitted to the succession of the deceased person together with one or more of the aforementioned males. But to the aforementioned daughters and the others aforementioned, whom we said should not be admitted to the succession, we have provided in one or more ways that they shall nevertheless have from the goods of the deceased person that which would be supplied to them as having been given for a dowry. However, if no dowry had been given, they shall have only that from the goods of the deceased person which six of the nearest relatives of the woman’s kinship, three from the mother’s side and three from the father’s side, if they could be found, and if they could not be found, two from the father’s side and two from the mother’s side, having been able to be found, have agreed upon by arbitration; between whom, if any discord should arise, judgment shall be had recourse to, and the authority of the power who shall be for the time being; and to his word obedience shall always be paid, due diligent consideration being had, if the woman wishes to choose another life by spurning the temporal world, what and how much is to be granted to her, inspection being made of the quantity, quality, and assets of the person; provided that, on account of what has been said, dowries ought not to be constituted for any woman from the goods of the maternal grandfather or great-grandfather, and so on, of any descendants. But in those cases, let that be observed which laws and rights establish, so that they be admitted to the succession of the deceased person together with the son or sons, or so on, with the aforementioned male descendants; nor is it permitted in wills of ascendants to leave to alien persons or places that which exceeds one-third part of their goods; and if it is done, it shall not be valid; but two parts ought to be applied to those coming intestate. However, this is not to be understood when the testator leaves something for the restitution of things wrongly taken away, and that it is permitted to the father and other ascendants to disinherit sons and grandsons and other descendants for causes approved by law.

The case being such as follows, having premised the said statute: Titius died, leaving a single male son by his first wife, and leaving two daughters by his second wife, and likewise leaving his second wife intestate, no dowry having been constituted for the said daughters, nor anything designated for the said daughters for a legitime, or in the name of a dowry; finally, these daughters died in pupillary age, and thus being under the age of marriage, survived by their said mother, who made herself heir of the said daughters. Now it is asked whether the said mother, as heir, has any right to demand something from the goods of the said father of the daughters by virtue of the said statute, or by any other law: In this article of doubt, if I wished to extend my discourse at length and occupy pages, I could insert here what Ricardus de Malegno wrote in a certain question which was disputed at Padua, which begins, “The custom and statutes of cities, etc.,” in which he concludes that the due supplement of goods is due to the daughter immediately upon the death of the testator, and if she dies, it transmits to her heir, and cannot be taken away by statute, since it succeeds in place of the legitime, which is due purely, all delay and burden being removed; therefore, the same applies to that which is due by virtue of the statute, that it be due purely; and thus it transmits if the daughter dies in the meantime. But I consider that such a great man perhaps did not determine the matter well. And since Dyonisius seems to hold the opposite opinion in l. Scimus, in fine, C. de nuptiis, I reject those opinions, since they contribute nothing to the proposition, or very little.

In our question, I consider the words of the statute, which, insofar as they exclude sons from the succession to paternal goods, are odious to brothers: as in C. de lib. et posth. l. maximum; and de leg. haer. l. lege. Insofar, however, as they admit them to something, they are favorable: and odia must be restricted, and favors amplified: as in ff. de lib. et posth. l. 2; and l. cum quidam. If, therefore, the statute provided for daughters in paternal goods in two ways: in one way, for those already dowered, that they be content with their dowry, and this up to the word “caeterum,” where it provides for daughters contrary to fact and law. For the word “caeterum.” In another way, for those not dowered, in the word “caeterum,” where it contradicts the foregoing in fact and in law; since this is not a conjunction. It establishes what is noted in l. 2, § lenocinium, ff. de adul.; and l. mariti, § si, eod. tit.; and l. 2, § si, ff. ne quis eum, qui in ius voc.; and c. and l. 2, § 1, de donat.; and l. patris, et filii, § si, de vulg. et pup. subst. Hence, provision is made for daughters already married, that they be content with their dowry. But for those not yet married, provision is made concerning the dowry only; for it does not there mention marriage: hence it is not expedient to wait for marriageable age. But the statute provides for daughters not yet married, that immediately upon the father’s death they may demand that the relatives comprehended in the statute provide for themselves from the paternal goods. And this is suggested by the favor of daughters, which ought to be amplified. Natural reason also suggests it, which wills that, upon the father’s death, daughters have a right in the paternal goods: as in Auth. de haer. et fals. § 1; and § prohibemus; and l. cum ratio, in princ., de bon. damn.; l. scripto, in fin., unde vi; and l. in suis, de lib. et posth., cum sim. But how much is to be paid later, let it be declared later by the relatives; nor ought the time of marriageable age to be awaited; because this statute does not dispose of it; nor does it say anything about constituting a dowry. What if the daughters did not wish to marry, nor enter a monastery? It must be said that they are excluded entirely from the paternal goods: certainly not. Thus, therefore, it will be pure what is owed to the daughters, although it is to be declared later by the relatives.

And that right, thus applied to them as solatium, if they should die before reaching their mother, is transmissible to the mother. This is established in l. 2 ad Orf. I prove this: it is certain that where an option of a certain slave is left to someone, it is owed to no one, as in C. de op. leg. l. cum optio. For it is necessary that he first declare his will; and the legacy is considered as conditional. C. eo. de lega. l. si duobus in prin. ff. de op. legati. l. illud. Or rather, that which more properly belongs to the daughter in our case: this right, competent to her in the paternal goods, succeeding in place of the legitime and partaking of its nature, which legitime was owed purely and without delay to the children, per l. quoniam in prioribus. And thus it is pure, simple, and without delay, although it awaits the declaration of the parents: not so that they may have a right in the paternal goods by the declaration of the parents, but so that by their declaration it may be known in how much of the paternal goods they have a right. For if the words of the statute are rightly observed in the words "ceterum," where it is stated only that they should not be deemed to owe anything of the goods of the deceased person to the relatives, it is not a question of whether the daughters have a right in the father's goods, but of how much of the paternal goods they ought to have, which is transmitted to the mother. For, as I said, the daughters, immediately upon the father's death, by virtue of the statute, had the right to approach the judge to compel the relatives to declare how much of the father's goods they ought to have: not whether they ought to have a right in the father's goods. And since that right is pure, it is transmitted to the mother, who, from that right thus applied in the paternal goods to her daughters, may demand that the relatives of the daughters, comprehended in the statute, declare how much the daughters ought to have had in the paternal goods. And those goods, thus declared to have been due to the daughters, will be applied to the mother. And I am content with these few words, for it is written: "Few words are said to the wise man, to whom I speak, and he will understand much," as noted in Auth. de consangui. uter. fra. circa principium, colla. 6. And thus I say and advise, I, Bartholomew de Capitibus Vaccæ of Padua.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a commission to arbitrate made to someone, both by last will and between living persons, has a condition, and when.
2. Whether a daughter transmits a dowry not yet assessed to her mother while the status remains. etc.
3. The debt of the subsidiary benefit of goods is transmitted.
body: On the point raised and proposed, namely that the statute is valid, it must be examined what the statute intends. And therefore, first, the statute provides for male descendants by admitting them to male succession to the entire exclusion of daughters, and this up to the words “but to the daughters.” Second, it provides for the daughters themselves in three cases. First, when they are dowered, by establishing that the dowry shall remain with them. Second, when they are not dowered, by providing for them according to the discretion of the relatives. Third, by positing a spiritual case, namely that if they enter a monastery, etc. The first case lasts up to the word “however.” The second case lasts from the word “however” up to the words “always, taking into consideration, etc.” Our question concerns the word “however”: whether the provision of this word is conditional, such that if a daughter dies before such discretion is exercised, she transmits nothing.

† And for the sake of clarity, three cases must be distinguished. Sometimes a commission is made to the discretion of someone between living persons; and then it has an implied condition: if the matter is compromised on substantial points. See: if he has exercised his discretion. C. de contrahenda emptione, l. si; ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. si quis arbitratu. Sometimes it is made in a last will; and then either there is an express condition, if he shall exercise his discretion, and it is conditional as to whether and how much; or there is no express condition; and then it is not a conditional disposition, but an uncertain quantity. At first sight, according to the interpretation of the law, there is no uncertainty; because it is as much as it ought to be according to the discretion of a good man, ff. de legibus, l. 1. Sometimes a commission is made by law. And here it must be considered whether this commission is reduced to the likeness of a last will, or to the likeness of a disposition between living persons. There I say for certain that the law disposing of successions is reduced to the understanding of a last will; and not in the manner of a contract. ff. de regulis iuris, l. si quis; de legibus, l. si fundum per fideicommissarium, §. iul.; de legatis, l. codicillis, §. pe. For he who does not expressly make a will seems to order that which the law orders concerning succession, as noted, C. de colonis bonorum, l. 1, §. vel maxime.

† From which theory, in the question proposed, it is concluded that the ordinance of the statute is not conditional: because it is not in the power of the relatives, but in the power of good men; therefore, although the portion is obscure at first sight, nevertheless it is not a conditional disposition: and therefore it is transmissible to the heir. Nor does it avail to object from ff. de verborum obligationibus, l. qui Romae, §. Augerius, where it is stated that after death it cannot be declared. For there the text speaks of a contract or of an express condition; here, however, there is no condition. Likewise, it does not avail to object if it is said that the final cause of providing for the girl at the discretion of the relatives has ceased, since the girl has died; for I deny this, because, in place of the legitime due by the common law (auth. succedat), it must be of the same nature. It is certain, however, that

† The debt of the legitimate portion is transmitted. C. de inoff. testa. l. si quis filium. ar. de suis, et legit. l. apud hostes. For if the inheritance is transmitted to the mother, then much more so is the legitimate portion, which is owed by natural law. For the final cause is nature itself; an accident contrary to nature, namely marriage, does not prevail. And thus it does not obstruct, because it speaks of another case, namely when a girl wishes to enter a monastery. For if such a case, or condition, exists, ff. de condi. et demon. l. titio cen. §. titio genero. and in Auth. de san. epis. §. sed hoc in praesenti. Furthermore, it does not obstruct the verse “always having due consideration,” because it speaks of another case, namely when a girl wishes to enter a monastery; for if such a case, or condition, exists, that verse applies. But we are not in that chapter of the statute; rather, we are in the general chapter, in which the statute does not speak conditionally. For it is one thing to attach a condition to the substance of the act, and another to commit the declaration of the quantity or portion to discretion. The case is in d. l. 1. ff. de leg. 2. And the foregoing are confirmed, because although one may argue from law to the words of the testator, as ff. de manu. test. l. si ita fuerit. §. conditionem autem, that text, which leads to the conclusion, is very notable. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, when a son is instituted under a non-potestative condition, and in his default is not disinherited, that condition must be rejected to the extent of the legitime, or whether the testament may truly be declared null.
2. How the statute providing that, where male heirs exist, dowried daughters shall not succeed, etc., is to be understood.
3. Whether the statements made in the preceding sections are to be understood as repeated in the following sections. And no. 6.
4. The word "however" is adversative to the preceding statements. And no. 7.
5. A statute may diminish the legitime of children.
body: Superiors

† That which was recently called into doubt is this: assuming that the said institution was conditional in the sum of 400, is it rejected by the laws *quoniam* in the earlier provisions and *omnino* in the Code on the inofficious testament? It must be observed that in the common law, either that condition would be rejected, insofar as it concerns the legitime, according to the aforementioned laws, following the opinion of the gloss in the law *suus quoque* in the Digest on the institution of heirs, and in the law *si pater* in the Code on institutions and substitutions under a condition of favor; or, according to the common opinion of the doctors, it could be said that the testament is null, as if the daughter, instituted under a non-potestative condition and not disinherited, were passed over in the event of her default. And in such a conclusion, the aforementioned law *quoniam* in the earlier provisions does not speak. On this point I do not insist, because it is not expedient for our case. And the doubt is great: and I have already seen the opinions of great doctors both for and against.

But the doubt which arises here consists in the rights and the mind of the statute placed under the heading “that dowered women and so on,” which begins “daughters or women etc.” And where succession intestate is treated, there is no doubt that a daughter would not be excluded, except by male brothers, or male children of such brothers, etc., as is expressly stated in the beginning of the said statute. But here succession by will is treated: because John, formerly the father of the posthumous daughter Victoria, instituted her to 400 pounds, etc., and if he died having made a will: in which case the doubt arises whether the aforementioned statute requires the existence of brothers, or children, in that part in which it wishes and provides that the daughter be content with what is given or left by the father, and thus according as it has been given or left, etc., and be excluded from the petition for the supplement of the legitime, and the faculty of breaking the will, etc.; or whether it is to be understood simply that such a woman is excluded, even if there are no male brothers, or male children of such brothers, etc. And here it must be observed that the aforementioned statute has two principal parts. The first, which speaks of intestate succession, from the beginning of the aforementioned statute up to the words “but by will.” From then on it speaks of succession by will, although afterwards in the following passages some matters of intestate succession are inferred, which do not pertain to our case. For the first point, that the superexistence of male brothers, or children of brothers, etc., is required.

† All laws establish that what is stated in the preceding provisions is to be understood as repeated in the subsequent ones, as in l. Titia, §. Idem respondit, D. de verb. oblig.; l. Quemadmodum, in fine, D. ad l. Aquil.; §. Hoc tamen capite. Hence, those words placed in the principal part of the statute, “extantibus fratribus masculis et c.” [when male brothers exist, etc.], must be understood as repeated in the words “ex testamento autem” [but from the will], even though no mention is made there of brothers, etc. In support of this, because the aforementioned words, “extantibus fratribus masculis etc.,” constitute a condition, since they are placed in the absolute ablative, as in l. A testatore, D. de cond. et demonstr.; l. Euictis, D. de usu fructu; and a condition added to preceding provisions is understood to be repeated in the subsequent ones, at least when it does not cause invalidity, as in l. Cum pater, §. Ab intestato, D. de leg. 2; and l. Licet, D. de leg. 1; and l. Si, §. 1, D. de fideicomm. liberis. Furthermore, in support of this, because general words following are restricted and declared by the preceding ones, as argued from l. Si servus plurium, in fine, D. de leg. 1; l. Haeredes palam, in principio, D. de testam. Also in support of this, because a statute, which is of strict law and odious, ought to be restricted, declared, and adapted to the common law as far as possible, as argued from l. Ut gradatim, §. Et si lege, D. de mun. et hon.; and l. 2, C. de noxa.

† For this, the word "however" also strongly supports the argument, as it is placed in the statute, viz., "however, from a will, etc." The nature of this word is to oppose what precedes, as in l. hoc amplius, §. his autem, and there noted, ff. de damno infecto, and in those cases which are of the same kind, as in l. mariti lenocinium, §. si, ff. de adulteriis. From these, it appears that the provisions in the aforementioned statute, in the words "from a will, etc.," should be understood and restricted to the case where male brothers exist, as stated in the first part of the statute. But notwithstanding these points, the truth seems to be to the contrary, when the words and intent of the statute are considered. For this, first, the generality of the disposition in the statute in the words "however, from a will, etc." supports the argument, in which there is no further mention of male brothers, which was made in the first part of the statute, which deals with intestate succession. For in doubt, one must adhere to general words, as in l. 1, §. generaliter, ff. de lege praestanda, and l. 1, §. in re igitur dubia, ff. de exercitio, with many others. For this, the diversity of reasoning between the first part and the second part of the statute also supports the argument. For the reasoning of the first part is solely the favor of agnation in those persons mentioned in the beginning of the statute. But the reasoning and favor of the second part is the final will, so that its style may be free, as in auth. and l. 1, C. de sacrosancta ecclesia. Now, it is restricted by laws that call sons to the legitime.

For the statute intended to diminish her portion. This is permissible according to the noted opinion of Dino del Garbo in the chapter *Indultum*, *De regulis iuris*, Book 6, and according to Cynus in the law *Sancimus*, Codex, *De nuptiis*, albeit with a certain moderation, namely, if what was given or left to the woman was such that she could conveniently marry, etc.; otherwise, she could sue for a supplement, as is expressly stated in the second part of the aforementioned statute. For, assuming that male brothers existed, no one would say that the testator could not dispose of his goods to another person. Therefore, the generality of the statute supports this; and the chapter *Pro hoc* also supports it, because these words, “if male brothers exist,” etc., placed in the beginning, are words narrating a fact and establishing a condition, as has been said.

But other things stated in the first part of the law or statute are not understood to be repeated, even if the law is penal and thus odious, as is gathered from the text with the gloss in l. 2, in the beginning, joined with l. 4, § eritque differentia, D. de vi bonorum raptorum. Therefore, etc. This seems consonant with the intent of the aforementioned statute, whose intent, if properly weighed, is expressed in the words “aforementioned,” “from a testament, however,” and so forth. It makes a new disposition in many respects different from the preceding one: first, in that it speaks of a daughter even if not dowered; second, in that it speaks of superiors for a grandfather, there, “and thenceforth,” etc.; third, in that it limits, provided that what is given or left to the woman is only so much as would conveniently enable her to marry, etc.

And even if the word "autem" is correctly weighed, it will well oppose here, and in those things which are of the same kind: for intestate, it was repelled entirely according to the form of the first part of the statute; but from a testament or codicils, it is admitted. And I said well in those things which are of the same kind. For the provisions in the verse "ex testamento autem etc." have well place when male brothers exist, etc. But also when they do not exist, by the laws immediately alleged. From these, the intelligent response to the objections is sufficiently clear, without wishing to amplify the words: because here the entire matter of the things said in the preceding could be discussed, whether they are understood as repeated in the following, which is long and diffuse. And also about the meaning of the word "autem," which has many meanings in law: sometimes it is used initiatively, sometimes restrictively, etc., in which I do not insist further: and I refer to the notes by Bartolus in l. hoc amplius, §. de his autem, ff. de damno infecto, etc. I, Francis de Romponibus, doctor of laws, the aforementioned, as I said above, subscribed with my own hand and sealed. I, John de Lignano, feel the same as above, and subscribed with my own hand and sealed. I, Anthony de Presbyteris, doctor of laws, as stated above, advise, and affixed my seal in sign of the aforementioned, etc. I, John de Casali, doctor of laws, now citizen and inhabitant of the city of Ferrara, subscribed with my own hand: and affixed my seal, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution, by which a substitute is appointed for a ward on the condition that he dies without children, is considered direct within the period of puberty, or whether it is said to be fiduciary for the entire period.
2. What the word "distribuatur" (let it be distributed) signifies.
body: The statute,

† and the declaration mentioned above, do not make provision in our case, because they do not speak of a situation where neither the father nor the son made a testament. Hence we know the statute, and we ought to observe the ius commune; and especially because the statute is odious, and therefore is not to be extended; ff. de lib. et posth. l. cum quidam; solu. ma. l. si vero. §. de viro; C. de pa. qui fi. di. l. 2. Let us see, therefore, what obtains under the ius commune. And the question stands solely upon this: whether the said substitution is direct within the time of puberty—since the wards died—or whether it is fideicommissary. Which appears to be proved: because whenever the times are not distinguished by a substitution, then the substitution is contrarywise fideicommissary for all time, as noted in C. de impu. et alijs sub. l. precibus; but here the times were not distinguished; therefore, the substitution is to be deemed fideicommissary. Likewise because where that condition "without children" is added simply, a substitution is usually made fideicommissary, and not direct, because the testator appears to have wished to burden the heir dying without children, as in the same law. Likewise because the phrasing of the words is single; therefore it must be understood in one and a uniform way for all time. But that cannot be unless it is fideicommissary, which is suitable for every age and every time, as noted in l. centurio, and as noted in Instit. de pup. sub. §. extraneo.

† Likewise this appears from the word "let it be distributed" (distribuatur), which requires the agency of one giving; therefore it is an oblique word, not a common one; therefore that substitution is fideicommissary by the force of the oblique speech; C. de vsufruc. l. si quis ita; and ff. de vsufr. leg. l. si fundi trebatiani. To the contrary it seems that the substitution is direct in pupillary age. First, because when it can be valid by direct law, it is therefore to be deemed direct rather than oblique, as in c. si pater. de testamentis. li. 6; but here it can be valid directly, for executors seem to be instituted to distribute to the poor; C. de epis. et cle. l. si quis ad declinandam; extra de test. c. cum tibi. I resolve it: because in doubt we ought to follow the intention of the testator, even a tacit one, and even against the mother, as noted in the said l. precibus in the small gloss, and C. de test. mil. l. in testamento; but here the intention of the testator is evident, because he said "the whole remainder" (residuum vero totam); and speaking in this way a direct substitution is signified, because if it were oblique, it would be subjected to deductions, but a direct one does not admit the Falcidian portion. Since therefore he who wills an effect also wills the means from which such an effect follows, l. 3. de mil. test., de acque haer. l. istud, it is concluded that this substitution ought to be judged direct; therefore, if there is permission in certain matters, it seems to prohibit in the others; C. de proc. l. maritus; C. de pac. conuen. l. fi.; de neg. gest. l. qui alia. §. libertus; de mili. testamento. l. tribunus. §. vlt. But here the husband provided for the wife in a specific bequest; therefore it was the testator's intention that she should have no more from his goods; and although he did not know how to say "pupillary substitution," nevertheless it must be held as expressed; C. de testamentis. l. indignum; C. fami. haer. l. quotiens. On this we certainly have gl. or. insti. de pupi. substi. §. qua ratione; ff. de vulg. sub. l. verbis ciuilibus; and Cy. in l. precibus; and Io. An. in the said c. si pater; and Bart. holds this in l. centurio, and he also gave counsel to that effect. And knowing this, I believe the same on account of that word, "the whole" (totum). For this cannot be unless it is a direct substitution, because the legitime would be withdrawn by the mother; de substit. c. fideicommissaria. The word "let it be distributed" does not stand in the way, because it does not concern the substance of the substitution, but the manner of making the division among the poor, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A wife to whom a legacy has been paid, and the fruits of all her movable and immovable goods, ought not to have that which is received from the names of debtors: but what about the offspring of horses and cattle? nu. 2.
body: Andreas of Florence, among other things, left in his will to B., his wife, the income and proceeds of all his movable and immovable goods, under certain conditions and modes that are uncertain.

† Now it is asked whether the said wife, by virtue of the said legacy, ought to have those things which are received from the names of debts. In response to which I say that she does not. This is proven by the fact that he says "of his own," etc., which must be understood as referring to those things which pertain to the testator by right of ownership or quasi-ownership, and not to those which are in the names of debts, as in l. Quintus, §. Argenta, D. de auro et arg. leg. Moreover, he said "of his movable and immovable goods"; but names of debts are neither movables nor immovables; rather, they constitute a certain third genus in themselves, as in l. Vel a Diuo Pio, §. In venditione, infra de re iudicata, and in l. Quam Tuberonis, §. Pe, D. de peculio. This is also held by Jacobus de Arena in l. Mouentium, de verbis significandis, and specially in the same terms in de fructibus et interesse, §. 1, vers. 2. From these authorities it is concluded that the said lady ought not to have the usufruct of the names of debts. The objection from D. de usufructu legato, l. Uxori meae, does not hold, because there the usufruct was left simply; in our case, the words "movables and immovables" were added, which serve to restrict the meaning of the words, as has been said. Furthermore, the pronoun "his own" was added, which serves to restrict the meaning of "goods," so that it is understood to refer to those movables and immovables which pertain to the testator by right of ownership, as in the aforementioned l. Quintus, §. Argento. And although in the aforementioned l. Uxori meae the pronoun "my own" was added, and yet it includes names of debts, this is because that pronoun "my own" has as its subject a comprehensive term encompassing all things, not restricted by any addition. But in the present case, the pronoun "his own" refers to the substance of movable and immovable goods only; and thus it is restricted, and not general, encompassing all things. The objection from the glosses, which state that actions and rights are judged as movable or immovable according to that which is the subject of the action, does not hold, because that is true when rights and actions must of necessity be applied to movables and immovables, because nothing has been disposed of regarding them; for example, the law says that the immovable goods of a minor cannot be alienated, but it disposed of nothing regarding names of debts; we shall judge them as equivalent to movables and immovables, following that which is the subject of the action. But this does not occur in our case. For he leaves the usufruct of movables and immovables to his wife, but he leaves the rights and actions to the heirs, as appears from the tenor of the will. And thus it is not necessary that we apply the names of debts to any of the aforementioned, i.e., to movables and immovables, but they should stand in a third genus by themselves, as in the aforementioned §. In venditione, as has been proven above.

† It is further asked, what is to be done regarding the offspring of sheep and horses, whether they come to the said lady as usufructuary, or to the heirs? To which I say that they belong to the said lady. And it is understood that, with respect to those which consist in the flock, she must replace in the place of the dead or useless ones, according to the form of l. foetus. §. si. cum l. se. supra de usufr. etc. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Bal. de Peru. Utriu. lu. Do. and I have subscribed to the truth thereof, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a paternal uncle related on both sides is preferred to one related on only one side, just as among brothers and the sons of brothers, the one related on both sides is preferred to the one related on only one side.
body: The case is as follows: Titius died, having instituted as heir his impubes male son, and he pupillarily and through a fideicommissum substituted Seius and Lucius, the brothers of the testator himself, and the sons of each of them by stocks and not per capita, whenever he should depart without children. At length the said instituted son died without children and pubes, intestate, with the said Seius and Lucius, his paternal uncles and brothers of the said testator, surviving, of whom one was from both parents, the other from the father only. It is asked whether both uncles succeed equally to the said instituted son, their nephew, or whether the said uncle, who is also the brother of the said testator from both parents, is preferred; it is asked what the law is, etc.

† In substitution the duality of the bond is not considered, but the tenor and arrangement of the testament are considered, as in Auth. de consan. et vterinis fratribus, § quia igitur, colla. 6. And therefore that question does not proceed with respect to substitution, but with respect to intestate succession; and the question stands on this: whether, just as among brothers and brothers' sons one joined on both sides is preferred to one joined on one side only—because a twofold ground and cause is stronger than a single one only, and one employing a twofold ground excludes him who could employ only a single right, as the text says in the said Auth. there, "and those using a twofold right exclude those who can use only one"—so it also happens among paternal uncles. For that a twofold ground is stronger than a single one seems to be a natural reason, which seems to extend from similar cases to similar cases. Therefore, from the nature of similarity, it seems to be so, for that is deemed tacitly provided for in which the same reason is found, C. de reuo. do. l. his solis; for the mind of the legislator always seems to consider the reason, ff. de excu. tu. l. scire oportet, § et si maxime, ff. de l. aqui. ad l. illud so. This seems to be true from the nature of correlatives, for just as a collateral nephew stands to his paternal uncle and to the right of succession, so on the contrary correlatively the paternal uncle ought to stand to the succession of the nephew. But in the nephew with respect to the paternal uncle, duality is considered in the active succession of the nephew to the uncle; therefore, conversely, the same applies in the passive succession to be made to the nephew. For correlatives cannot be separated, even where the correction of the laws is at issue, C. de in vidui. tol. l. fi. And it is confirmed by a third reason, because it is inequitable that one should succeed to another in one way, and that the latter should succeed to the former in another way, since the rights of intestate succession ought to be reciprocal, as in C. de legi. haere. l. lex. 12. tab. vers. et cum aliqua; for equality must be preserved, as is clear there, and eo. ti. l. memini, post prin. To the contrary, it seems: for the said paternal uncles are in the same degree; therefore they succeed equally through the rule of the ancient law, as in ff. de suis, et legi. l. post consanguineos, § haereditas, second reason there, where it says, "if there are several of the same kind, it belongs to all"; but these are in the same degree of agnation and cognation, because every agnate is a cognate; therefore they succeed equally. For although one joined on both sides is an agnate, and consequently a cognate from the paternal line, and likewise a cognate from the maternal line, nevertheless from the twofold ground of cognation the effect is not increased. For it is sufficient that there be in someone the quality that is substantially required, although it may be present in one by one ground, and in another by several grounds and causes; for one ground suffices just as much as several, arg. ff. de succes. edic. l. 1, § sed videndum, ver. et post hos. And this is proved by a clear reason, for it is special in the case of brothers and brothers' sons that a distinction is made when they succeed, whether they are joined on both sides or not; therefore the common law is to the contrary. And that it is special in them appears through the text in Auth. de consan. et vteri. fra. before the end there, where it is said, "this law therefore is placed in this case," etc., and below there where it says, "and so in cases of this kind," etc., and it speaks there of a brother; but of the sons of brothers another Auth. speaks, namely vt fratrum filii. In these, namely brothers and brothers' sons, when they are called to the succession, the law is content to posit its distinction, whether they are joined on both sides and preferred to those joined on one side only; and further, it proceeds establishing that in others the first distinction is not observed. In others, I say, namely those more remote, as in C. de leg. hae. autem. post fratres, and in Auth. de hęr. ab inte. § si igitur defun. vers. si vero neque fratres, where it says that if the deceased does not have brothers or brothers' sons, the agnates succeed according to degree; but in our case the deceased does not have brothers or sons of brothers, and the uncles are in the same degree, namely in the third; therefore they succeed equally and are called equally. Moreover, that an uncle is more remote than a brother's son appears because a brother's son excludes an uncle, as in Auth. post fratres, versi. hi. autem si sunt remotiores; therefore nothing is considered except degree. And upon this reason Bar. grounds himself, who holds this position in d. l. post consanguineos, where he resolves in favor of this position. And it is confirmed, because this distinction of those joined on both sides was not known under the old law, for it began to be recognized through Justinian, as he openly says in Authe. de consang. et uter. fratr. in § quia igitur considerantes. And Justinian enacted a new law, which has no place except in the cases expressed in it, arg. C. de colla. l. illam; for since the law does not extend that distinction, but rather confines and restricts itself to succeeding brothers and sons of brothers, it must not be prolonged further, as in ff. de legi. l. ius singulare; for only the legislator can extend those things which are established as a privilege, as in C. de insti. et sub. l. generaliter, § fi., C. de fideius. l. cum acutissimi. Someone will say: if one joined on both sides succeeds to a brother, with the one joined on one side only excluded, and thus the one joined on one side is repelled and does not succeed to the brother, who is closer, therefore much less does he succeed to the brother's son, who is more remote. But I reply that this reasoning does not proceed: because by this reason we would say that he does not even succeed to the brother's grandson, who is still more remote, which is false; for to him he without doubt succeeds equally with the other great-uncle who is joined on both sides, as in d. Aute. post fratres. Because therefore we have no law introducing this distinction and preference among uncles, we shall stand by the ancient law as uncorrected—indeed, as confirmed, because the ancient law is expressly confirmed in those more remote than a brother and the sons of brothers. But an uncle is further and more remote, if not in degree, in the enumeration nevertheless of the disposition of the law. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, it follows that the said uncles succeed equally ab intestato. Nor is a law found that says the contrary; for what law made this difference or distinction between uncles? Certainly no law says this. The argument a simili does not stand in the way, because there is no similarity where there is not an equal disposition of law. Likewise, the argument concerning correlatives does not stand in the way, because the reason and nature of correlatives is not always the same; whence we say elsewhere that a testament is valid among children before two witnesses, but not among parents, C. de test. l. hac consultissima, § ex imperfecto, and § pe. Likewise, the argument from inequity does not stand in the way, because to enlarge successions is not inequitable, but equitable, in insti. de bo. pos. § quos autem. From which I conclude and hold that both uncles succeed, following in this the opinion of Bar., strengthened and clarified, as is evident above. Likewise, C. communia. de succe. auth. itaque, and what is noted there by Cy., does not stand in the way, because it must be understood that those joined on both sides are preferred in the cases expressed in the newest law of the Authentics; nor indeed can we extend the newest law of the Authentics to the correction of the ancient law, except in cases expressed by the law, because the correction of the laws is of the strictest law, as noted in Auth. quas actiones, C. de sacrosa. eccl. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the interdict for recovery is available for incorporeal rights.
2. Dispossession in incorporeal rights is contested and induced by contradiction.
body: In these acts, two points are principally to be examined. The first concerns the proceedings, having regard to the libel submitted in court, which at first sight appears to concern a possessory action on behalf of Lord Pathera. The second concerns the proceedings, having regard to the instrument of concession or composition made by the abbot and the monks of the Holy Trinity of Brindisi, which proceedings concern the prosecution of a petitory action. Regarding the first point, it must be observed that in the libel produced on behalf of Lord Pathera it is narrated how payment was made by the abbot; and how Pathera was in quasi-possession of that right; and how it is now being withheld; and restitution or reintegrand was sought.

† Regarding the first point, it must be observed that, although a direct interdict for recovery does not lie for rights in corporeal things—which lies only for things of the soil, as in D. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, § interdum, together with the following law—nevertheless, a useful interdict lies, D. de mortuo inferendo, l. 1, § item si; D. de vi et vi armata, l. 3, § unde vi, § pertinet; D. de servitutibus, l. quot; and Extr. de electione, c. quaerelam, and there by Innocentius; de causa possessionis, c. cum ecclesia. If, therefore, this lies for him, he could have brought an interdict for recovery for this right of servitude, because it appears to have been brought here. For this lies for him who possessed and was dispossessed against the dispossessor who commanded or ratified the act; this is proved by Extr. de officio delegati, c. consultationibus; de re spoliata, c. cum ad sedem. Thus it was here, for he narrates that he was in quasi-possession and they subtracted it, and thus dispossessed him. And restitution is concluded; and thus a bare possessory action for recovery, although at the end of the libel he adds, by praying, that he not be disturbed in the future, which seems to partake of the nature of the interdict uti possidetis, l. 1 and l. si duo, D. uti possidetis, and l. unica, C. eodem, and there fully noted. Nevertheless, that adapts to the narration, because he narrates that he was dispossessed by subtraction. The interdict uti possidetis, which is given to one who is disturbed and troubled, as in l. statim cited above, does not accord with the conclusion, because he asks to be reintegrated and restored, which accords with the interdict for recovery, or with the condicio, from c. reintegrata, 3 q. 1.

But here it will be objected that in personal prestations and solutions, neither possessory nor petitory actions proceed, and they are correlative, D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1, in principio, and § si, in Inst. de acquisitione, § sic itaque. That a possessory action does not proceed against an obligated debtor seems to be proved by the text D. quorum bonorum, l. 1. Here it must be observed that Peter, in l. certis annis, C. de pace, moved by this reasoning, held that a possessory action is not given in prestations, because a petitory action is not given there. And he said against c. querelam, otherwise, that in c. querelam, de electione, a querela was required. But, with due reverence, he misunderstood c. querelam, because there it speaks of a real servitude by which one church is bound to another, and thus there is a real right, because one church owes to another; but here, in our case, there is a real right of servitude by which the monastery of Brundulo is bound to the church of Gradem, namely, to an annual prestation of two measures of wheat. But Peter’s opinion does not apply in our case, because this real right is owed by the monastery of Brundulo to the church of Gradem. Nor is Peter’s opinion true, because in personal prestations a possessory action would lie. This is demonstrated, because there prescription is found, D. de praescriptionibus, l. cum de in rem verso. Therefore, also a possessory action, since without possession prescription does not run, D. de usufructu, l. sine possessione, and in c. sine possessione, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. And this is held by Guillaume de Cuyac in l. solet, D. de officio praesidis, in d. c. querelam, de electione, and c. peruenit, de censibus.

Here also an objection will be raised against the libel, for here suit is brought for an annual prestation of two measures, because they were previously paid, and no cause is alleged why they should be paid. And thus the aforementioned c. peruenit, 18 q. 6, c. servitium, C. de pace, l. si certis annis, stands in the way. For there are certain modes of inducing obligation, as in Inst. de obligationibus, and in the following rubrics. But a solution, or annual prestation, is not among them. Moreover, a solution by itself does not induce an obligation, because it induces liberation; for by the solution of what is due, every obligation is removed, in Inst. quibus modis tollitur obligatio, in principio. Therefore, it does not import an obligation, D. de solutionibus, l. 1, § hominum. Moreover, time by itself does not induce an obligation; therefore, both joined together, D. de excusatione tutoris, l. spadonem, § qui iura. Here it must be observed that the objection would proceed where suit was brought for an annual prestation solely on the ground that it had been paid previously, no cause of obligation being alleged. But here suit is not brought for an annual prestation; rather, suit is brought by a useful interdict for recovery, because the church of Gradem says it was in quasi-possession of this right, and was then dispossessed, and thus concludes by asking to be restored and reintegrated, and placed in its former state. And it is not necessary that the cause of the petitory action be explained, however much the robber and the dispossessed person must be restored, C. si per vim vel alio modo, l. si; Extr. de restitutione spoliatorum, c. in litteris, and c. item cum quis.

It is concluded that, the obstacles being removed, this libel presented on behalf of the church of Gradem concludes in a possessory action for recovery, at least so I see, not attending to the words added at the end, which partake of the nature of the interdict uti possidetis, because they should be considered as not added, weighing only the conclusion, by which they ask to be restored. The notes by Innocentius, de iudicibus, c. examinata, are helpful. The petition being thus supposed in the conclusion in the possessory action, it remains to proceed to the justification, or proof, of the same. Where it must be observed that the burden of proving that he possessed and that he was dispossessed by him against whom he directs the action, or that it was done by his command, or that he ratified the dispossession done in his name, lies upon the one bringing this interdict. This is proved by Extr. de officio delegati, c. consultationibus, joined with c. ad sedem, de spolio. And these proceed in the interdict for recovery, such as was brought here, by the canon reintegranda, or from the chapter saepe. For all these concur of necessity. And these being proved, the restitution of possession is fully founded. Notwithstanding any exception of ownership or crime, de ordine cognitionis, c. cum dilectus; de restitutione spoliatorum, c. in litteris, and c. item cum quis, and c. conquestione. But all these are proved by the church of Gradem, namely, the quasi-possession, which it has otherwise paid. The dispossession is proved, because the subtraction of several years, and even today it is subtracted.

† Indeed, in these incorporeal rights, spoliation is induced by contradiction through the formal joinder of issue, as noted in the compilation on rescripts, c. Mandato; and those things which are not [so induced] are discussed by Innocentius in c. Olim, tit. 3, de restitutione spoliatorum. And thus it is concluded that the Gradese Church is to be restored to the quasi-possession of this annual prestation, and to all things subtracted from the day of spoliation, ff. de vi et vi armata, l. 1, § Ex die; de restitutione spoliatorum, c. Contra ius. And there I noted that it was legitimately proven, as is asserted: because in the indirect procedure the statements of the witnesses are not [formally] recorded. That which must be considered, however, is whether they prove sufficiently. I have written based on the evidence produced to me, assuming legitimate proof, and thus the first part and procedure are concluded. Regarding the second part of the instrument of composition, or transaction, initiated by the Abbot of the monastery of Brundulo with the Lord Patriarch, because that instrument was produced with the formal joinder of issue in the possessory action for recovery, it partakes of the nature of a petitory action: and only the possessory action was pursued, although a petitory action may be added for justification ex superabundanti. Nevertheless, because nothing is concluded even from the necessary [elements] from that [petitory addition], but only from the possessory action via the interdict brought, it is not necessary to examine that [instrument]. But if it pleases [the court] to do so ex superabundanti to agitate consciences, so that the truth of the conscience of law may appear thoroughly, if a petitory action were brought directly and principally in judgment, I shall write [my opinion] when the reverend father and my lord, the Lord Patriarch, commands. I have touched only upon the necessary points, considering the procedure. And so I say and advise, I, John of Lignano, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute excluding a dowried daughter from succession when males are present: whether it appears to dispose of, and deprive, the legitimate daughter.
2. Whether daughters excluded when males are present, etc., transmit [their rights] in the interim while males are present.
3. A statute excluding a dowried daughter when males are present: whether it entirely nullifies the existence of her inheritance in the interim, or suspends it purely, conditionally, or for a future day.
4. A conditional right of accretion is also transmitted to the heir.
5. Whether the right of accretion applies to the legitimate portion.
body: An ancient statute of the city of Perugia provided that if any woman was, or shall be, endowed by her father, mother, brother, paternal or maternal grandfather, or uncle, she could not, nor ought, to revert to the inheritance or succession of the aforementioned persons, or of any others of them, as long as any male son survives from her, or from him, in that inheritance or succession to which the woman would wish to revert; and it adds, saving the testament and last will of the aforementioned persons, which shall be observed; and afterwards it adds, saving that women may come to the succession of parents, brothers, or other persons to whom it pertains to them by right. Nor does the law *Si haeres masculus non supersit* [If no male heir survives] hinder this, by remitting their dowries into the inheritance. Now it has happened that from a certain very noble house of the Gracani of Perugia, after the death of Lord Philip, the last knight and male, no male exists; likewise, no females exist who are descended from the progenitors of the said house through the said agnatic line, but there survive from them certain sons and grandsons; and posthumous children born from other agnatic lines, or houses, who wish to come for the supplement of the legitime of the mothers or grandmothers of the said house of Gracani, who were formerly endowed by their progenitors, and to demand the said supplement; it is asked whether they can do so.

† And first of all, it must be considered whether this statute disposes of the legitime. And it seems that it does not, because by general words, to the effect that one cannot come to the inheritance or succession, one is not excluded from the legitime, unless this has been specially stated. C. de inoffic. testam. l. si quando. §. si. The same, therefore, and much more strongly, must we say regarding a statute. For if a liberatory pact, which is favorable, does not exclude the legitime, then neither do the general words of a statute, which is undoubtedly mixed with favor and hostility. ff. de lib. praet. l. maximum vitium. To this effect is what is noted by Guillaume, ff. de transac. l. de his. Bartolus seems expressly to determine the contrary, ff. de cond. et demon. l. Titio genero, in the question which begins “quaero statutum,” where he seems to determine that this statute excludes a dowried daughter from the legitime when males are extant. For it seems that the daughter, by reason of the dowry, is disinherited by l. arg. ff. de haered. instit. l. qui volebat, or that her legitime is diminished and reduced to the dowry itself, as noted, C. de nupt. l. scimus, by Cynus. For the statute considers the dowry to be the congruous portion of a dowried woman, and the legitime is nothing other than a certain congruous portion fixed by the discretion of the law for those to whom succession is due by natural law or quasi-natural law. C. de inoffic. testam. auth. nouissima. For it is called a subsidiary right to goods, but a dowried woman has the dowry and her husbands as a substitute. C. unde vir et uxor, l. 1. And it succeeds in place of alimony. But dowried women rarely lack alimony. Therefore, the statute considers this dowry to be the legitime portion without cause when males survive. C. de adul. l. publico, by Baldus de Ubaldis, by Cynus. Therefore, whether because they sometimes have the entire legitime established by statute, or because they seem to be excluded from the common law in the meantime, it seems that they cannot claim more in the meantime. And if they claim more in the meantime, the exclusion by the municipal law, which is considered peremptory for an uncertain time, stands against them. ff. de cond. et de. l. sufficit. Indeed, even without exception, the municipal law itself stands against them, which, since it excludes succession principally, does not require an exception, since the action could not be founded, according to what is read and noted, C. de transac. l. ubi pactum.

To the contrary, it was consulted by the excellent doctors, Doctor Thomas de Corsiis, Doctor Francesco, Doctor Bechi of Arezzo, Doctor Fontanus de Mancianellis, and the Florentine College. For they say that if the words of the statute are rightly considered, they do not exclude the daughter simply from the paternal inheritance, but from it in a certain manner by the existence of certain persons, and by the consideration and favor of those persons, they impede her for a time. This is what the words of the said statute say, in which it is contained, “as long as any male son survives.” By these words, time is designated, as C. de leg. l. 1; de excus. tutor. l. Titius; de cond. et de. l. si quis ita. And it is not proper to extend temporality to perpetual exclusion. ff. de pact. l. epistola. §. si. It is clear, therefore, that the daughter is not entirely excluded from the legitime, but that her claim is suspended for a time, namely, until the males survive. This is the very truth in this first point, nor does Bartolus say the contrary, if it is well observed; indeed, he says that the statute diminishes in time, not in quantity, and thus the prima facie right of the judge, ff. ad l. Falc. in l. Falcidia, is not held to be pure; because the word “which” imports a temporal impediment, which is different from that which imports a perpetual and precise impediment, because the first impediment is removed by the course of time, either simple or qualified, but the second is not, as is noted in the rule “non firmatur,” lib. 6, by Bartolus. Now it must be seen regarding the second point,

Whether these daughters, in the meantime, transmit their rights to their own children: and whether we say they are excluded, it is established that they do not transmit; whether we say they are incapable, similarly they do not transmit; whether we say they have a conditional right, as Bartolus holds in the said § Titio genero, they still do not transmit; because general rights to succession are not transmitted. If we say that the order of preference of males over females is given, with this order remaining, the one who dies later does not transmit, as is openly proved here, C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus. For he who cannot acknowledge does not transmit, as is clear there. But this daughter does not have the right of acknowledgment while the males are alive; therefore she does not have the right of transmission. And this is held literally by Bartolus, descending, ff. ad turpem quaestionem, l. si, in q. which begins, quaero, quid si filia decedat. But this inquiry is deeper, with due respect to the teacher, to be considered. It is necessary to consider the common law, which grants the legitime: as l. quoniam in prioribus, and l. quam nouella, and l. scimus, C. de inofficioso testamento; in Auth. de tertia et semisse, § 1; and in Auth. de restitutione, and ea quae parit, § quamobrem. It grants by the law itself, as to the name of heir in the legitime, so that by name the dominion continues from the father to the sons and daughters in power, ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. in suis.

† It is therefore necessary to examine whether this statute utterly invalidates this existence of her inheritance, or merely suspends it. And it is certain that it does not eradicate it utterly, as I said above in the first point, but rather suspends it. And then it is further necessary to consider what kind of suspension this is: whether it is one that legitimately reduces pure right into conditional right, or whether it is judicial. But if we say that it reduces it into conditional right, it would follow that this is not a diminution in time, but a change of substance; because pure right and conditional right differ as contradictories: because in one birth [of the right] is found, whereas in the other birth is not found. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. non ad ea. But if we say that an uncertain day does not here create a condition, the rule of law is broken. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. dies incertus. If, however, we say that it creates a contradiction, therefore it is not transmitted in the meantime. D. de cond. et demonstr. l. dies incertus; and l. quibus diebus, §. quidam Titio. There it seems expressly stated, when the day of the legacy ceases, l. ex Titio. Indeed, by the order of preference given by the statute, the male is to be regarded in the place of the instituted heir, but the female in the place of the substitute; therefore, dying in the meantime, she does not transmit. D. de vulg. et pupill. substit. l. sed si plurales, in princ.; D. de suis et legitimis hereditatibus, l. si ex pluribus.

To the contrary. For it must be known that when the person to whom the legitime is due is not impeded in it on account of an intrinsic defect of her own right, but on account of an extrinsic defect of another person, who suspends this right and defers the law itself, the person dying in the meantime transmits. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium, it is expressly stated. But here, since the ordinary common law proceeds regarding the legitime and defers it to the daughter, and the common law itself is not corrected by the statute in the substance of the legitime, nor in its quantity according to the doubt in time on account of the extrinsic person, namely the males, rightly this right, with its suspension, is transmitted to the children of the daughter. C. de his quae ante apertionem tabularum, l. j. quotienscumque. For there is no defect in the right of deferring, but there is a suspension in the right of acknowledging or demanding; there the law dispenses so that the impediment to transmission, which would be said to be temporary or suspensive, becomes precise and perpetual, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. ventre, and there it is clear in the gloss which is in the first rule, which is summarized there by Bartolus, and in the rule of Jacobus de Belvisio in the second rule, which is: whenever one’s own heir has an impediment to the access of another, or an inability of law or fact, that in the meantime... and Bartolus holds this rule there, by which the reason seems rarely to be silenced. To the same effect: D. ad Sillanianam, l. si quis in gravi, §. si, with l. se; D. de contracta emptione, l. illud, §. illis, and what is noted there. To the same effect: because when by the death of another a right is not sought for another, but a right previously acquired can be enforced, there the dying person transmits. C. quoniam dies legati cedit, l. ex his verbis. And so it is here, because the death of the males tends to the enforcement of the claim; but it does not defer the legitime, since the common law has already granted it. It can well be said that the right of the males causes the legitime of the daughters to sleep in the meantime, but not to expire or be eradicated; rightly, therefore, the daughters dying in the meantime transmit this right which they have in habit, but not in act. Argument from D. de milite ex militari, §. si, with the following law; D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. liber homo, §. ult.; C. de suis et legitimis hereditatibus, l. apud hostes; and C. de curia fundi, l. si, §. j.; D. de iure fisci, l. Lucius.

Moreover, Bartolus in the consultation beginning “Bartholuce” advised that the removal of the impediment of the males by their death fictionsally retroacts the impediment as not having existed; or the passed-over daughter, according to him, could not proceed unless there were that fiction, since she succeeds: therefore the law fictionsally assumes. And this can be taken as constant.
