But then I argue: the death of the successor does not impede this fiction; rather, it fictionsally assumes that she has the right notwithstanding the death of him who, if he were alive, would succeed, and fictionsally assumes him dead retroactively, and the heir, as in D. ad Sillanianam, l. si exheredatus. Therefore, the impediment being removed, that the daughter died in the meantime: from which it is fictionsally assumed retroactively, she transmits by the said l. si exheredatus, which is unique for this purpose. And it is noted.

Now it remains to respond to l. cum antiquioribus, which Bartolus alleges for the case in the said l. finalis ad Tertullianam. Certainly that law says that repudiated right is not transmitted; but this is not repudiated right, but is the right of the heir, which is transmitted with its quality and nature. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si quis filium. Also, that law speaks of regular transmission; but we are here at least in irregular and abnormal transmission. Also, the ablative “remittendo dotes” etc., as if making a condition which cannot be fulfilled by the heir, D. de legatis a testamento, does not obstruct. For I say that in this case it does not make a condition. The text is express in l. praetor, in princ., D. de collatione hereditatum, l. bonorum; and C. eodem, l. si soror. Furthermore, we consider that this dowry is computed in the legitime by the law itself; therefore the daughter has a part of the legitime purely; in the other part she has hope through the death of the males. Dying in the meantime: certainly, even if she dies at her proper time, her part accrues.

† For the right of accretion, even if conditional, is transmitted to the heir, as is fully stated in the law and notes in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Qui patri*. In the proper sense, the legitimate portion of the daughter herself is made her own by way of concurrence, as long as the son lives, and she is, as it were, joined to the son in this legitimate legal union. And also, just as the son is joined to the grandchildren by the edict on joining, by the very fact that he takes away from the grandchildren the share that would be competent to them by reason of his existence, when dividing with them, dividing with them. But in our case, this right of joining, or right of division, exists with a certain temporality, namely, for as long as he lives. Hence, upon his death, the legitimate portion is restored and consolidated; and this right of restoring and consolidating the legitimate portion is transmitted to the heir. However, this is not because the law, by suspending the daughter’s right for a time, burdens her, and therefore deprives her. For one thing is to suspend, another to remove. See the Code, *De pactis*, in the law *Si unus*; § 1 of the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*; and the law *Cum hic statuit*, § *Sive*. And in those laws having a cause for a time, and an end by law itself from that time, and after the concurrence of the right of accretion is finished by reason of the concurrence: Digest, *De usufructu accrescendi*, law 1, § *Interdum*; and that which is noted in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Plane*, § *Si duobus*, according to Dyachenko. Nor does it obstruct that the ancient statute speaks only of the daughter; because posthumous children come through the person of the daughter, namely, by the right of transmission, which is from children to children: as in the aforementioned law *Si quis filiam*, which is specifically to this effect, etc. Also, as I said regarding the right of accretion of the legitimate portion, I believe it pertains to herself; hence, one should not extend the legitimate portion of one to the legitimate portion of another, but rather to its own nature by a certain consolidation. And it supports this: Digest, *De coniunctione cum emancipatis liberis*, law 1, § *Si quis ex nepotibus*. Also, prescription of time does not obstruct. For in prescriptions, the right is not considered as it is in habit, but as it is in exercise: as in the law *Cum notissimi*, § *Ibidem*, and § *In his*, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*. And since the said Philip died recently, it is clear that the prescription has not run. But it opposes him, who spoke of the right of accretion, which is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Pater filium*, in questions 2 and 3.

† Where he says that in the legitime the right of accretion by legal conjunction, which is a singular succession, has no place, from the argument of l. 2. For in the contrary opinion are Dynus and Jacobus Butrigarius in public disputation: and it was heard, because the privilege of the legitime due is necessary that it have the right of accretion, as all the doctors note, C. de inofficioso testamento, auth. nouissima, and C. de haeredibus instituendis, l. quotiens, per Jacobus, and in Auth. ut cum de appellatione, cog. §. ceterum, and in Auth. de naturali, and Auth. de publico, §. quod si legitimorum. Indeed, in our case there is the right of not diminishing, which the concurrence of males had taken from the daughters of their legitime, the death of the males restored. The right of not decreasing has place from any conjunction: and in any succession, which is rather the loss of its impediment, than the extension of succession. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The things given or sent to the bride by the blood relatives of the husband remain hers, otherwise if sent by the husband.
2. The emphyteutic lease of the church is not confiscated on account of the offense of the emphyteuta.
3. The aunt, who has accepted guardianship, is preferred to the sister in the succession of the ward.
body: The fact is as follows. Ser John, son of Ser Laurentius of Menauia, took as his wife Lady Nicolutia Sechi of Menauia; and according to the custom of the said place, certain blood relatives of Ser John gave him certain dowry gifts, which are called *mente*. Moreover, the mother of the said Ser John sent to the said Lady Nicolutia a silver *franzola* and a silver *scaziale*. Then the said Ser John married the said his wife; and afterwards the said Ser John died. It is asked, to whom should the said *mente*, and the said *franzola*, and *scaziale* belong:

† To which thus Renen. that those things which are given or sent by blood relatives or by the husband’s relatives are presumed to be sent and given by way of donation: and therefore they ought to remain with the said Nicolutia, as is read, and no. ff. de tut. et radistr. l. 1. §. sed non nullos. and §. pręterea. ff. de adm. tu. l. cum plures. §. cum tutor. and l. tutor secundum dignitatem in soluendis. and what is noted there, for wherever there is a sending or a gift, it is called a donation. Or if the husband sends such things: and it is not presumed to be a donation, but a sending: to the end that she may come to him more adorned. ff. de don. inter vi. et vxo. l. sed si vir ex lana. §. pe. ff. commo. §. interdum. I believe the same applies in the case of any sender under the name of the fiancé, for such things are to be returned as having been sent for use: and not for ownership, no. Iac. Bu. C. de dona. ante nup. l. ex his. cum in te. cum l. se. From these it appears that it ought to remain with the said Nicolutia: and with the heir of the said Ser John, her husband. And this I say, your Bal.

† Property held under emphyteusis by a church cannot be confiscated on account of a delict against the will of the church, which holds ownership; but it may be reclaimed, as stated in the Authentica de alienatione et emphyteusi, after the principal paragraph, and in the Digest, de damno infecto, l. finita, § si de vectigalibus, according to Bartolus; and it is supported by what is noted in the gloss to the Digest, de verbis obligatorum, l. si ita quis, § ea lege. And therefore, by reason of the said Assize, joined with the church, which is properly the altar, the said property cannot be possessed as a matter of law. It is supported by what is noted in the Code, de bonis liberorum, l. 1.

† It is true that if the maternal grandmother accepted the guardianship, she succeeds the said Tancredella, to the exclusion of Zecha, sister of the said Tancredella on the paternal side only. And this is established by the text in the Authenticum *De haereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Consequens*. Hence, if not with ascendants, and there it is avoided; for just as a relative united on both sides excludes one united on only one side, so too do the grandfather and grandmother, because they are equated with a brother united on both sides, as there and in the Authenticum *Defuncto*. And although the grandmother and the consanguineous brother, or consanguineous sister only, are in the same degree, they cannot nevertheless be in the same quality. For the grandmother and grandfather are owed the legitimate inheritance almost by natural right, but not the sister united on the other side. *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Fratres*; joined with l. *Finalis*, ff. *Eodem*. For even if parents [are involved]. I say more, that even if the grandmother did not accept the guardianship, it does not prejudice [the case]: because the mother was in between, as noted in C. *Qui petunt tutelam*, l. *Nepotibus*. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, advise, and I have subscribed under my hand.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If two wills of the same testator appear, drawn up by the same notary, at the same time, and before the same witnesses, in one of which no substitution is contained, but in the other there is, whether faith should be given to it.
body: The case is as follows,

Two wills are produced, drawn up at the same time by the same testator, in the presence of the same witnesses, and by the hand of the same notary. In one of them is contained the institution of an heir without substitution; in the other, however, is contained both the institution and the substitution. The question is asked: to which should faith be given? Or should one of them, or both, or neither, or one be considered suspect? The question is asked: what is the law, etc.

If a diversity appears in two writings of the same will, and one is a protocol without any erasure, suspicion, or apparent addition, while the other is a later writing, then the first writing is believed as the original, because the origin of the writing must be inspected, and the exemplar, as in the Authentica *de tabellionibus*, at the end, *exemplar*. It is not the example that ought to be inspected. And just as the witness is believed in his first statement, so the notary is believed in his first writing, as noted by the doctors in the Digest, *de statu hominum*, law *Imperator*, immediately. For the notary who publishes an instrument is equivalent to a witness, whose statement is open and published, according to the argument in the Digest, *de testibus*, law *Domitius*.

Sometimes both writings are protocols, or both are in the proper hand of the public notary who was requested, and it does not appear which is the primary protocol. Then, either the writings are contrary, but one is vitiated and the other is not; and then that writing is followed in which no vitiation appears. Code, *de edicto divi Adriani*, law *Tollius*, at the end. Or both are vitiated, and then neither is believed. Code, *de probationibus*, law *Iubemus*. Or neither is vitiated at first sight, and then either they are contrary, or one contains more than the other. In the first case, neither writing is followed, just as equal and contrary witnesses are not believed. Code, *de fide instrumentorum*, law *Scripturas*. In the second case, when one contains more than the other, that one is believed which binds more. Digest, *de legatis secundis*, law *Nesennius*, insofar as both writings agree. Argument, Digest, *de arbitris*, law *Diem proferre*, section *Si plures*. Or because there is no doubt about the smaller sum, but there is uncertainty about the larger, therefore in doubt we favor the defendant, as in law *Arrianus*.

And it does not apply to the case, or there is more, i.e., more is found written in one and less in the other: for example, because in one there is a clause or substitution which is not in the other; and then I believe the substitution to be valid: because that which is found omitted in one writing is supplied by the other, made or written by the same hand, as in the Digest, *de edendo*, law *Ubi exigitur*, section 1, where it is said that the same writing, less fully published, ought afterwards to be published fully; otherwise it would be published in vain, if faith were not given to it. And thus in the case at hand I say and advise that the will in which the substitution is contained cannot be considered suspect, although in the other writing, more subtly published, the notary’s name is not usually present: for example, because they do not publish the whole; or out of malice, or ignorance, or because a certain part ought not to be published to the requester. They act prudently, however, if they place the words "and so forth," because something remains in writing. But if the notary is so coarse that he does not place "and so forth," it is not thereby vitiated. Code, *de precibus imperatoris offerendis*, law *Si*; Digest, *de edendo*, as in the word "less fully"; *de fide instrumentorum*, chapter *Cum continet*. And especially in our case, since the instrument and the examined witnesses have had a lucid consonance in themselves. Nor is it believed that a will was made more than once, for repetition is not presumed, as in chapter *Cum Ioannes Heremita*, because facts are not presumed unless they are proven.

And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws. And to the faith I have subscribed, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a mandatary may be a witness in a crime against the mandator.
body: In the mandatee

†and whether he can be a witness in that crime against the principal, it depends on whether it pertains to the instruction: and he can. D. de poenis, l. qui ultimo. Or whether it pertains to proof: and then it matters whether he accepted the mandate: and he cannot be a full witness, because he is an accomplice in the crime. C. de accusatoribus, l. fin. C. de testibus, l. quam liberi. And note C. si liberam causam, l. si filium. The principal and the agent commit one delict, as is fully noted by Cynus, C. si reus vel accusator mortuus fuerit, l. 1. Or he did not accept the mandate, but was merely requested and tempted to commit the delict: and then this person is not properly called criminal, because he persisted with an innocent mind and deed. Indeed, he is highly praiseworthy, because he did not consent, but rather revealed it; the text is explicit, C. de furtis, l. si quis servo. And it applies, C. de paricidiis, l. utrum; and C. si quis in imperatorem maledixerit, l. 1. And D. Maleficium, however, requires will and intent to offend. D. de furtis, l. qui iniuriam. But in this case, whom the exhortation did not make worse, no wickedness is found. Therefore, he is a most upright witness: and he provides grounds for torture, as C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. si quis, in the beginning, in the last gloss, especially if other corroborating circumstances support it, such as flight, as in Auth. de exhibendis reis, §. si vero. And some, D. de edicto edicto, l. quæro, §. si. D. de custodia rei, l. divus. It is written by Solomon, “The wicked flees when no one pursues him.” It applies, D. de suspectis tutoribus, l. impuberibus. And note by Cynus in l. 1, C. de raptu virginum. As for what is said that two witnesses are required to prove grounds for torture, as noted, C. familiae erciscundæ, l. fin. And in c. sicut, de simonia, by Innocentius, this is true when they do not testify directly on the crime principally to be proved, but on the grounds of the crime. And it applies to what is read and noted, D. de quaestionibus, l. maritus. And note by Cynus, C. de quaestionibus, l. fin., in the second question. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, U. l. D. et c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the first appeal is properly interposed, but the second is not, the second must not be called an appeal; otherwise, the contrary holds. And then the fatal period of the court begins from the second. And number 1.
2. When the first appeal is interposed on the fifth day in writing, and also on the eighth day, and the second appeal, which of them is valid.
3. When the first appeal is made orally, and the second in writing, which of them is valid.
body: To be considered

There are four cases: the first, when the first appeal was properly interposed; the second, not. And then the first appeal is examined: because it has being, and formal being. The second, however, which has neither being nor formal being, ought not to be called an appeal on account of the force of appeal. D. de poenis, l. si quis ad §. testamentum; D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. qui testamento. For an appeal which does not hold has no beginning, nor origin. And that which has no origin has no end. D. de verborum significatione, l. quim mortui; D. de verborum obligationibus, l. 10. And only the first appeal is in prosecution: therefore only it is in defect or invalidation. Arg. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. si filius; D. de inofficioso testamento, l. cum de secunda institutione te; Inst. §. posteriore.

The second case is to the contrary: when the second appeal is validly interposed, but not the first; then the course of the peremptory time begins from the second appeal, not from the first, which was null. For an appeal interposed in the second place ought not to be called second, but unique, because it has no other before it that could be called an appeal. Hence, it ought to be called not so much second as sole. Argument: Digest, *Qui potior in pignore habeatur*, law *Qui generali*. Moreover, time is concomitant, as in Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Oblatae*. Hence, that which is not an entity in its nature has no time; because where there is no principal, there is no accessory. Moreover, from which the principle is removed, the process and the end of being are removed, as if an axe were applied to the root. And it is not manifest that that which is not ceases before it begins. Nor is privation prior to habit. Law *Si*, Digest, *Si certum petatur*; and more expressly, Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Titio usufructu*.

The third case concerns two appeals of the same kind and form: for example, because he appealed in writing on the fifth day, and similarly appealed in writing on the eighth day; and here it is doubtful whether the second appeal is valid; and it seems that it is not, because the first appeal drew to itself the effect entirely; and therefore it was pronounced: and from the jurisdiction of the judge from whom the appellant was absolved, for that which has once been broken cannot be broken again. And thus to double the appeal, and thus it does not harm. Extra, de appellationibus, c. Dilecto. Nevertheless, it profits nothing: because the second appeal is superfluous: and he would be a fool who pursued it, because it did not draw to itself effect, the first appeal having preceded in this matter. Argument, Digest, de verbis obligatorum, l. Si ita quis stipuletur, sive in animis. Especially if, concerning the first appeal, the judge issued letters of dismissal, then henceforth he is not deemed to act in the place of the judge from whom, but in the place of a private person; hence it is futile to add anything regarding deprivation, since he has been reduced to the status of a private person, as in c. Appellationibus, § Si vero iudex, de appellationibus, lib. 6.

The fourth point concerns appeals that are not similar, one being interposed by a living voice and the other in writing. In such a case, it matters whether, at the time of the appeal, the appellant reserved nothing for himself; and then the first appeal is to be considered. For when the time for introducing the appeal began to run, as in the Authentica de iudicibus, §. appellationes, column 6, it is necessary that they proceed in their course, as in the Digest, de usufructu transferendo, l. 1, §. hoc termino. Time does not have an interruption in its course; because it would not be continuous, but discontinuous and interrupted, as is said in another matter in l. foramen. Or he will have reserved to himself the benefit of appealing in writing, and then it must be seen what this appeal effects; and this appears from the event. For if no appeal is made in writing, it signifies nothing, as in l. 1, Codex, de institutionibus et substitutionibus. But if an appeal in writing follows, then Bartolus puts forward two opinions which he prefers. The first is that such an appeal is not a second appeal, but a reduction of the first into writing, and that this second appeal is retroactive to the time of the first appeal. First, because the first was not uncertain in writing with the commemoration of the second, as in the Digest, de hereditate instituenda, l. asse, tota; and ad legem Falcidiam, l. si praemisit. And that whoever prosecutes a written appeal is seen also to prosecute an unwritten one, because it is one appeal essentially, although superficially they appear to be two appeals according to Bartolus, which is true; because when they are of the same substantial form and reason, although writing is added for caution. But nevertheless, notwithstanding this, I believe Bartolus speaks truly in his second opinion, not in the first, because from the second appeal the effect is not increased; there the first applied the whole effect to itself. It is not objected by l. si domus, cum sequentibus, because two remedies are cumulative unless one provides more fully than the other, Digest, de contractibus; l. si post mortem, §. lib., Codex, de inofficioso testamento; l. contra maiores; and l. eum, qui. Nor is the reservation objected, because whenever nothing is added to the first act by which something is included or excluded in the second act that was not included or excluded under the first, then the reservation effects nothing. Second, if something is added in matter or with form that was not included under the former; because then the reservation effects much, as in l. item Labeo, §. 1, Digest, familiae erciscundae. And therefore if the later appeal corrects something of the first, then only the later one is to be considered, Digest, de iure et iudiciis, l. ius civile. And note this in a similar case, Digest, de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. qui provocavit. The same if it comes supplementarily, supplying the defect of the first, Digest, de praetoria stipulatione, l. Valerianus, §. vocati; cum in plures, Digest; l. dicta, Digest, de rescindenda venditione; l. si id, quod, §. 1, Codex, de appellationibus; l. si quis libellos, Digest, de hereditate instituenda; l. si ita scriptum fuerit; tunc et satis de milite tribuimus, §. si, Digest, de hereditate; and note 2, question 6, chapter Si vero is, qui appellauerit; and l. si quis libellos. Concluding, and presupposing that the first appeal was duly interposed according to the form of the constitution, I say the appeal is deserted; because time is a necessary concomitant of the first appeal, and cannot be separated from it. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, and advocate of the merchant guild of the city of Perugia, although unworthy. And to the faith I have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether that clause, “if it is not valid by the law of wills, etc.,” has application when a will fails due to a defect on the part of the testator arising from the omission of an heir or from disinheritance.
body: Gloss

† In the Authentica "Ex causa," it is held in favor of this clause, and the rule "if it is not valid, etc." does not apply when the will fails due to a defect of the testator: for example, because he disinherited, or because a father passed over a son; but when the will does not have an intrinsic defect of passing over or disinheritance, but rather has an extrinsic defect of the will: then the clause operates. And among the moderns, one doctor holds with the Gloss, as does Guillaume de Cuy in the law "Sin," Codex, De collationibus. However, Lord Dynus in the law "Posthumus," § "Si paganus," Digest, De inofficioso testamento, and the same is held by Cynus, Bartolus, and almost all. And I, following in their footsteps, hold thus. Therefore, it is necessary that this daughter, who is said to be null, restore the inheritance. And there is no doubt that she must deduct the legitime; but regarding the Trebellian portion, there is doubt because of the statement of Raynerius and Francis. But Lord Bartolus advised that the Trebellian portion ceases, because that condition, "if it is not valid," is true in the present: and thus it does not have the nature of a condition; because immediately the will was null. And the same I hold. And therefore, said daughter in this case ought to be content with the sole legitime. The remainder pertains to the heirs of the shares, to whom the fideicommissum is transmitted: as in the law "Cum filio," Digest, De legatis 1; Codex, De fideicommissis; the law "Si in personam." And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A sui heres transmits his legitima, just as he transmits the entire inheritance.
2. Whether a son transmits the supplement to the legitima.
3. A son does not transmit that which exceeds the legitima.
body:
The brothers, namely Marinus and Simonellus, sons of Ioannellus of bona Cassa, are in question. From Simonellus was born a certain son named Rigazius; from Marinus was born another son named Ioannes; from Rigazius was born Margarita. Thus, while Ioannellus was still living, Simonellus died, then Rigazius, then Marinus, then Margarita, with the aforementioned Margarita’s uterine brother alone surviving. Having examined the testaments of the said Simonellus and Rigazius, and the statutes of the commune of Perugia under the rubric “On last wills to be observed by daughters,” it is asked what and how much of the goods of the late Simonellus and the said Rigazius the said Ioannes and the said uterine brother ought to have, and what is the law.

The testament of Simonellus in no way favors Ioannes, because Simonellus made Rigazius, his son, and another of his sons named Simonellus, his heirs. And if both should die without sons, he substituted Marinus, the father of the said Ioannes. The said Simonellus, however, died while his father was still alive, but the said Rigazius died later, leaving a daughter; hence the condition of the substitution is deferred. See Trebatius, l. haeres meus, § communita, C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus; l. 1; and the notes on l. falcidia, l. pater filiam, § duobus.

The testament of Rigazius, however, favors the said Ioannes and the heir of Marinus. For Rigazius left to his daughter 500 florins by way of institution, not as a dowry, and if a male child were not born, he instituted the said Marinus. And since a male child was not born, the said Marinus acted as heir of the said Rigazius by the aforementioned testament; and therefore he transmitted the said inheritance to Ioannes, his son.

† It is nevertheless true that the aforementioned daughter of Rigazio cannot be deprived of her legitime; and therefore, the legitime, as her necessary portion, passes by operation of civil law to her uterine brother as heir. For just as a sui heres transmits the inheritance, so too does he transmit the quota, i.e., the legitime: as stated in l. apud hostes, with its associated material. But here a doubt arises. For there are three cases regarding whether these five hundred florins constitute the legitime: and there is no doubt that they are transmitted, just as pure legacies are transmitted: and whatever is acquired under a singular title, she, this daughter, would have in the place of a legatee. C. de her. inst. l. quotiens; and see the note in l. si quis priore, ad Treb. And if it is said that it is not transmitted, as in l. Titio cen. §. si, I respond that the legitime and natural portion is left under the name of dowry, which, if omitted, would render the testament null; this legacy is not considered conditional, but casual, because it is not presumed that the testator, in case of doubt, chose the path of a condition, which would render the testament void in itself, according to the true opinion of the doctors, and see the note in ff. de inst. et subst. l. si pater; but rather the path of a cause and wording. But in the legitime, every cause from which an obligation arises and which causes delay is removed, as in l. quam in prioribus, de inoff. and therefore it remains a pure and transmissible bequest. The objection of §. Titio genero does not hold, because there it was not left to the daughter, but to the son-in-law; although the daughter is tacitly admitted, this is by a certain fiction, which ceases when the principal fact also ceases. Likewise, the objection of §. sed hoc presenti, in Auth. de sanct. episc. does not hold, because it must be understood that he imposed a condition or a final cause. The fourth point concerns the legitime. For, as I said, in case of doubt, the tenor is not seen to have chosen the path to impugn his own judgments, as in l. 3, de lib. test. Thus, also in the legitime, the mode is rejected, even if modal words were inserted into the bequest. C. de his quae sub modo, l. 1. Bartolus says that even the condition is removed in the case of a son, as noted in d. l. si pater, and de her. inst. l. suus, and per l. scimus, §. cum autem, de inoff. test., according to his opinion, which is commonly rejected in that condition which induces the defect of omission. For, by §. aliud, Auth. ut cum de app. cog., every omitted heir declares the will null; otherwise it was under civil law, because the omitted heir did not declare it null, since it sufficed that something was left to him under any title; however, the omission was not weighed there, but the delay: and that was removed; otherwise it is under the latest law, d. §. aliud. Or it may be said that the tacit condition is removed: because where the principal condition is removed, if the year and day are removed, the consequence, i.e., the condition, is removed. But an express condition is not removed: because the law institutes the omitted son; but it favors the institution, which could be annulled, so that it may not be annulled.

† The second case is, if there is less in these 5 florins than in the legitime, whether the action for supplement is transmitted to the uterine brother, who is an extraneous heir, without being recognized or prepared; and it seems that it is not transmitted: because it is substituted in place of the querela, which is not regularly transmitted. It fails when it comes to children. C. de inoff. test. l. si quis filium.

The third case is, if there is something in the sixth chapter of the *Florentine* code that is more than in the legitimate portion, the excess is not transmitted: because it lapses due to the death of the person and the mother, which is the immediate cause of the legacy remaining, as stated in the aforementioned § *Titio genero*, according to Petrus and Dyacum in the law *firmo*, at the end, when the legacy is ceded. And thus I conclude in the question, always reserving the sounder opinion, I, your Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws and Jurisprudence.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute speaking of a testament not being broken is said to be favorable, so that the masculine gender encompasses the feminine. num. 2.
2. A tacit reason is not considered as expressed.
body:
Lady Pinna, a citizen of Pisa and wife of Peter, a citizen of Pisa, made a will in Pisa; in which, among other things, she said thus, namely, that she disinherited her mother, Lady Simona, a public woman, also a prostitute, who lived and acted luxuriously, and because she sinned against her body, living promiscuously in the manner of a harlot, offering herself indiscriminately to everyone, and she made the ungrateful Lady Simona alien from all her inheritance and succession: and she said that she is disinherited from all her inheritance, succession, and goods: and entirely excluded, and as unworthy and ill-deserving, as is fitting, [condemned] to perpetual poverty. In all her goods, movable and immovable, rights and actions, present and future, she instituted and made Francis, formerly of Iusfredi of Sala of Pisa, and James, formerly of Brusio of Monte Statuario, her universal heirs.

The careful statute of the commune, under the rubric “On Intestate Succession,” is valid as follows: Regarding the mother, it shall be observed thus, that while she lives, so long as she does not marry, she shall have the usufruct, or quasi-usufruct, of the goods of a son dying intestate, or of a daughter without children, for that share which, according to Roman law, would succeed to the son or daughter in ownership intestate, provided that before receiving the aforementioned usufruct she has not married another, provided, however, that sisters do not take a share when brothers are present: with caution to the heir, which is provided by the law *Usufructuarii*. But she shall also succeed to the daughter or son dying intestate at that time, however, in goods which are not of the patrimony: when neither his brother, son, and paternal cousins, nor any other person who would succeed with them, or before them, survives. In goods not of the patrimony: when persons of the patrimony, commonly understood in the fourth degree, namely the son or daughter of the full sister of the deceased, or grandson or granddaughter, do not survive, the mother shall be preferred to all other agnates and cognates, except the uterine brother and uterine sister of the deceased, and their male children of the first degree, who are admitted per stirpes: with whom the mother shall be admitted together, provided, however, that when the uterine brother or his son is present, the uterine sister or her children do not succeed.

But if a son dies having made a will, in the case where the aforementioned constitution provides that the mother shall succeed to him intestate in usufruct or ownership, he shall leave to the mother one-third part, or the value thereof, of those goods in which she would succeed; otherwise, the mother could infringe the last will. But any other woman, ascending or descending through the female sex, shall not be able to retract in any way the last will of one descending from herself. And in another part of the statute, under the rubric “How an ambiguous constitution is to be interpreted,” it is stated conjunctively thus, namely, because many often, adhering too strictly to the letters of the statutes, are compelled to interpret the words of the statute too strictly: Therefore, taking an example from the benignity of the law, we decree that the meaning which is free from defect shall be accepted, and the more benign interpretation shall be preferred, without doubt, etc.

The aforementioned Lady Joan, the testatrix, died, leaving behind her the aforementioned Lady Simona, her mother, who had gone to second marriage. The aforementioned Francis and James, the instituted heirs, entered upon the inheritance from the aforementioned will, and are proceeding against the prior regarding the hereditary goods. It is opposed that they are not heirs: and that the institution made of them does not hold: since in it the mother is disinherited without just cause. And this is proven in the Corpus, Digest, *Ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur*, § *Scimus*, and § *Sequenti*.

To the contrary, it will be said that the will is valid by virtue of the aforementioned statute of the father. In § *Filius autem*, etc., where it is expressly stated that the mother cannot infringe the last will of the son except up to one-third part, provided that it does not exceed the value of 200 pounds. Therefore, by the law itself, it is valid in its entirety; nor can it be broken by the mother, except as is said.

Against this, it is replied that the statute, the instrument, speaks in the masculine, namely, *son*: therefore it does not comprehend the feminine son. It is asked, what is the law: and whether the heirs written below in the will are, or can be, heirs, or can act as heirs, or not, etc. Of the son it is written: of the daughter, however, it is omitted, it is asked, etc. And as to the letter, it seems omitted: because it is not written; but truly, certain things, although they cannot be read, are perceived by understanding, as in Digest, *De his quae in testamento*, law 1. Nor is recourse to be had only to the literal meaning, but to the intellectual, which we call interpretation, as in Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Iusta*, often. For he who signifies more, I say, understands, than he speaks, as in Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Fideicommissum*, § *Si filia*; Code, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law *Si mater*; Digest, *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, law *Hoc iure*; *De liberis et posthumis*, law *Placet*; Digest, *De testamento tutorum*, law *Si quis ita*, with infinite others.

† Let us therefore see whether it is so in our case, that although the word does not sound of a daughter, nevertheless the reason of the statute, or its interpretation, includes a daughter. And for this understanding, recourse must be had to this, that we see whether the said statute is favorable or odious. For if it is favorable, the masculine comprehends the feminine. D. de legibus 3, l. Lucius, § quaesitum. But the odious does not comprehend. I.e., it does not include. As D. de venditis in possessionem missis, l. 1, § quasi, according to the theory of certain doctors. Others distinguish more broadly, as Dyn. in l. 1, de verbis significandis, and Bart. ibid., and Io. Andr. in c. generali, de electione, lib. 6, quid sit in via Brocardica. It seems to be said that we are in a case of favor, and not in a case of hatred, because a statute which disposes of not breaking a testament should be called favorable, not odious, since it is of public interest that testaments not be broken. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § institues. Nor is this statute entirely exclusive of the mother; but it is restrictive, and assigns a certain quantity, which succeeds in place of the legitime. Just as laws which order that a testament not be broken, but that the due supplement of goods be supplied, are favorable. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo, and l. sumus, so this statute is favorable. Moreover, granted that the statute said that the mother could not break the son’s testament, or succeed against the testament, it is not odious; because the favor of the testament is considered more than that of the woman, or mother. Who, indeed, would say that a soldier’s testament, because it excludes the mother by passing her over, is odious? Certainly, the law does not call it hatred; but privilege, and favor. D. de testamento militis, l. 1. Again, who says that a pupillary substitution is odious, because it excludes the mother? Certainly, rather it is called favorable. D. de inofficioso testamento, l. pater, § sed nec impuberi, and what is noted, C. eodem, l. ex tribus, and this in the case of intestacy. But a statute whereby the mother would be excluded intestate could sometimes be called odious, where no person was designated in whose favor it was made; but it would speak simply. For it must be considered that either hatred is the cause of favor; and then the disposition is called odious; or favor is the cause of hatred of another; and then the disposition is called favorable. Hence this consideration is formed a priori, not a posteriori. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. qui exemplum. And to this contributes what is noted by Cy. C. de adulteriis, l. publico.

† Finally, it must be considered, when the masculine is extended to the feminine, which is a matter of interpretation, whether the interpretation arises from the dignity of the masculine gender, from the parity of affection, or from the precise identity of reason: for if it arises from dignity, the masculine comprehends the feminine: it is an extensive interpretation. If, however, it arises from the parity of affection, it is a conjecture. If, however, it arises from the precise identity of legal reason, it is an explicative interpretation, because reason and intent are the same in laws, as noted by Dy. in c. si. de re. iu. l. 6. and l. non minus, et rei. §. verbum ex legibu. de ver. sig. and noted by Cy. in l. 1. qua sit lon. consue. and ff. so. ma. l. cum mulier. and elsewhere in many places. Others say that if the reason is expressed in the words, then Cy. says the same applies if it is tacit and presumed. For then it is an explicative interpretation, which proceeds from the identity of such tacit reason: because such reason is rather integral than legal: and therefore it has no place in statutes according to them.

† I, however, say that where the reason is tacit, although not expressed in words, such reason is considered as expressed in the laws, just as in the acts of men, as in the Institutes, On the Law of Patrons, On Tutelage, in the beginning; Digest, On the Law of Marriage, Law "Libertatem"; §. Senatus; Digest, On Exceptions of Tutelage, Law "Scire oportet"; §. Sufficit. Hence, that in which the reason is found will be said to be tacitly enacted. Code, On the Revocation of Donations, Law "His solis," in the word "satis tacite." And for this, the best law is Code, On the Toleration of Individual Indivisibility, Law "Si," in the beginning; because the reason of this statute is not, nor can it be other than, the favor of the testator. And it cannot be drawn into a more certain discretion; therefore, this statute, which speaks of children, will be extended to daughters, since the mind of this statute can be adapted to them; and both regarding sons and daughters, Julius says, the cause of sex is not equated by itself; because what is said of one is seen to be provided for the other, in which there is the same reason, because the reason, which is more general than the words, must be observed, if the bark of the letter is not inspected, but the marrow. 1st Question, 1st Distinction, Chapter "Marchio." And it makes that which is read and noted in Law "Si," Digest, On the Rules of Law. To this it contributes: because the last part of the statute does not distinguish the sex of the testator, from which it is probable that it did not wish to distinguish in the preamble part, which is joined with the text by copulative speech. Digest, On the Penalty of Heirs, Law "Utrum." To this also adds the statute, which permits a benign interpretation. Digest, On Legacies, Law "De leuibus," in the beginning; and what is noted there. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In the collection of taxes and tributes, no legal procedure is required, nor is a summons necessary, but the matter proceeds directly.
2. On whom taxes may be imposed.
body: Although a judge to whom nothing has been proven can command nothing, as noted by Inn. on de sen. excom. c. solet. at the end;

† and although against one who has not been cited no precept of giving or doing can be issued, nor can anything be disposed against him, as in l. de vnoquoque. ff. de re iu., in l. nam ita diuus. in §. meminerit. and l. fi. with similar laws, so much so that even in notorious matters a citation is necessary to hear the sentence or command according to Inn.; and although even in fiscal causes the order of law is to be observed, as in C. de dila. l. omnes. and qui conduc. rerum fis. li. 10; nevertheless, in exacting public functions, say tributes, or tolls, and taxes, no formal order is required, nor is a citation required; rather, in instruments, general precepts and the denunciation that whoever owes must pay are valid, although elsewhere general precepts of this kind do not have the force of res judicata, as in C. communia. vel epist. l. programma. For in these matters judges and examiners proceed summarily by compelling and exacting, not by citing and conducting formal proceedings, as in l. cum eo. ff. ad l. Iul. pe., in Auth. de man. Prin. §. et festinare., in Aut. iusiuran. quod praestatur ab his. there, and primum, and in Auth. de man. Prin. §. deinde eos., in Auth. de col. verse 1, C. de iu. l. 2, C. de exac. tri. l. missi opinatores. with similar passages. And this is what the ordinary gloss intends to say on ff. ad muni. l. incola., where it states, nor was it denounced to the men of that land, namely that it is in the said tax, and it is ordered to them that they pay it. For public affairs would be poorly expedited if tallages could not be exacted without citation and legal process, and meanwhile the commonwealth would be endangered. And I say that notoriety is threefold: namely, of fact—and here a citation to sentence is required; and of law, although even here, if such notoriety arises from proofs, a citation to sentence is still necessary; but if it arises from res judicata, a citation is not necessary if it is formally the execution of a sentence, but otherwise if it is directed to something else. And it is notorious in law and by law that diocesans owe tithes and subjects taxes; here a citation is not necessary. What is noted by Inn. on de sen. excom. c. dilecto supports this. Moreover, he who is aggrieved, if he appears and alleges the cause of grievance, ought to be heard, C. de offi. ciuilium iud. l. 2; and the precept resolves into a simple citation, de coha. cle. through Inn.; and the same holds wherever proceedings begin with execution, ff. de no. ope. nun. l. de pu. §. nuntiasset., but de ope. no. nun., namely that a precept is permissible without a preceding citation, for it summons to the cause after the manner of a citation.

† Whether, moreover, priors, who otherwise are not inhabitants, are bound to pay taxes in the places where they hold possessions is noted through the gloss and Dy. in l. rescripto. §. fi. de mune. et ho., and Dy. says there that a tax cannot be imposed except on citizens or inhabitants. Nevertheless, it seems it should be said that those making an assessment there are bound, from wherever they may be, because by making the assessment they are deemed to have professed that they would pay the taxes, as noted in the said l. incola. The same would perhaps hold if there were a statute that all estates were obligated and attached for the tax, because then the thing itself, not the person, would be sued, c. postulasti. extra de fo. comp. through Inn., by the argument of l. Imperator. ff. de publi. and de neg. ge. l. qui alienam. §. fi.; and such a custom is observed in these parts, and C. de exac. tri. l. si diuinandum. and de fun. pa. l. vniuersi. li. 11 support this. And in this, governors and officials ought mutually to support one another and assist each other on account of public utility: just as in the human body member assists member, so in the body of the Church officials, who are called members, ought mutually to extend a hand to each other, which ff. de bo. auth. iud. pos. l. cum vnus. §. is, qui. supports. Here, however, it must be considered that an order is not to be given to any corporate community to pay the debts of individuals, as in l. in tamen. §. vniuersitas. with similar passages, and in Auth. vt non fiant pignorationes. If, however, the precept speaks thus: 'I command the community and the men', it seems to apply not only to the corporate body, but to the individuals whom the matter touches, and that the precept itself concurs from the subject matter, so that words uttered indefinitely are referred to those to whom they ought to be referred and whom the business touches, by the argument of ff. de leg. 2. l. legatarium. §. qui plures., so that those are understood to be warned and cited within the bounds of the decree who are worthy to be warned and cited, as in l. si quis seruum. §. si quis seruum. §. si inter. In this, nevertheless, one would have to look at the form of the issued letters, whether they address them merely as the whole body, or as the whole body and individuals, which c. 1. de posthu. and de maio. et obe. c. huic. through Inn. support. For letters either say 'to the corporate body and to the individuals', or they say 'to the corporate body only', or 'to the individuals only', as is clear from the aforesaid. In our case, the precept was given 'to the corporate body and the men'; I understand this as to the whole body and the individuals, so that speech may be heard in accordance with the underlying subject matter. And although individuals were not cited singly, this does not seem to be required, because strictly speaking this is not a citation, but a formal demand and an assessment. And even if it were a citation, nevertheless a person who is not expressed by their proper name is deemed to be expressed by another designation, just as if we were to say: 'Cite him who possesses such an estate', as in l. certum. ff. si cer. pet. with similar laws; which in our case, from the form of the letters, is not disapproved. And so I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc., say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The condition applies, where a fideicommissum exists in the person of the last survivor, to a substitution in his portion, even though a son of a predeceased brother survives.
2. Add the opinion beginning *quidam nomine nautius*, in Part 5.
body: The facts are as follows: A certain Colla Magichi of Assisi made his last will and testament, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows: In all his movable and immovable goods, and so forth, he instituted Nicolaus and Antonius, his sons, as universal heirs. And if the said sons should die without legitimate children, a certain woman is to have from the goods of the said testator, when she marries, 100 pounds of denarii. Furthermore, from the said goods, the youngest son, Libellus, or his heirs, is to have from the residue 100 pounds of denarii for a certain chapel to be built in the church of St. Mary of the Angels. And the residue he left to St. Trucius of the Island and the church of St. Francis, and also to St. Clare of Assisi, in equal parts. After making the will, Colla died, with the said Nicolaus and Antonius surviving him. The said Nicolaus and Antonius took possession of the inheritance of the said Colla. Finally, the said Antonius died, being over 20 years of age, leaving a pregnant wife; from whose womb was born a certain Nazzit, son of the said Antonius. Finally, the said Nicolaus died, leaving no issue, but having made a will, in which he instituted Vannutia, his full sister, as his universal heir. The said Nicolaus, at the time of his death, was 25 years of age and more. Now it is asked whether the said substitution has effect, to what extent it has effect, and to what extent the said Nicolaus could dispose by will of his said goods.

† Because the condition of the fideicommissum existed in the person of the last survivor, the substitution takes place in his portion. D. ad Trebellianum, l. heres meus, §. cum ita; and l. Lucius, §. Gayo; and noted in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. pater filiam, §. duobus; and C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. 1. And although the son of the predeceased brother survives, he does not thereby exclude the fideicommissary of the portion of the brother who died without children. This is testified in the said §. cum ita, because he does not exclude, unless it is the fideicommissary of his own share. Therefore, there are two fideicommissa: one is defective, the other is purified, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. falcidius, §. ultimo. And if it is said that it is absurd that strangers should be preferred to one’s own kin, as in l. cum acutissimi, §. de fideicommissis, I answer that this absurdity is introduced by the testament. For we cannot depart from the said §. cum ita. And if it is said, rather, because in that §. a granddaughter was instituted, whereas here there are strangers, and therefore, since the son of the son survives, there exists a person whom, according to the presumed will of the deceased, excludes the substitute. I answer that it is not so, because the son of the son does not succeed to his uncle: and especially in the judgment of the grandfather, for why would he exclude the substitute, when he himself does not succeed to the uncle? Therefore, rightly, he does not exclude. D. de contractibus, l. si post mortem, §. liberi. Therefore, the places capable of receiving the substitution come from the fideicommissum, from which the legitima due to them is deducted by the sister instituted as heir by this last surviving brother; regarding the other legacies of individual persons, he must have two fourths. c. Ray. And these things are true for this reason: because the last one died without children, but I do not know if this was the mind of the testator. I believe, however, that the mind of the testator was that the succession of strangers would be removed by the birth of his own kin. arg. D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si. But on account of this belief, I cannot deviate my conscience from the text of the said §. cum ita, unless it could be proven to the contrary by other indications: because these mendicants, whose life ought to be founded on the purity of conscience, must meditate diligently: and adhere more to conscience than to the knowledge of the laws. By the foregoing, however, I do not say that the minor brothers are capable, except in that case, and as the decretal says, exiuit, or exijt. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Bal. de Peru., Doctor of Laws and advocate of the commerce of the city of Perugia, though unworthy. And to the faith of this I have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the possession of the deceased passes to the heir without apprehension.
2. By statute, possession can be transferred to the heir without apprehension. And number 3.
3. Whether the faculty of recovering possession can be ceded: and what in the faculty of retaining and continuing possession.
4. Whether one possessing in another's name can deprive the owner of civil possession by transferring it to another.
body:
A certain creditor, having several debtors in the same instrument, who were bound jointly and severally, and who had renounced the benefit of division among two or more debtors, and had bound themselves, and their movable and immovable goods, present and future, to the said creditor, and had constituted themselves as possessing their goods precariously for the said creditor: one of them died, leaving an heir; and one of these obligors sold a property to someone. After this sale was made, the heir of the creditor assigned, gave, delivered, and mandated to a certain third party all rights, all his claims, and real and personal actions, useful and direct, tacit and express, mixed and hypothecary, competent and to become competent, which he has or could in any way have in the said instrument and by its force, delivering to that third party the instruments of the said debt, so that the said third party could thereafter act, demand, litigate, and proceed, and collect the said debt from the said debtors, and against them and any of them, and against any of their goods and those possessing them, just as the assigning heir could do, from now on constituting the said third party in the aforementioned matters in his place as procurator, for his own interest, etc. This third party, who acquired the rights in the said debt in the manner described, took possession of the alienated property by judicial authority, without making any excussion, either of the goods of the alienator or of the others, which was necessary to be done before proceeding against external possessors.

It is argued to the contrary that excussion was not necessary, because by those words, namely, "constituting themselves as possessing precariously," civil possession was transferred to the creditor; and consequently, excussion was not necessary, because he does not sue, but pleads in defense by retaining possession, which he could have entered by his own authority. But to act more formally, he did so by judicial authority. And thus, since the creditor, to whom civil possession had been transferred, could seize it without any excussion, in the same way the heir, to whom possession passes by municipal law, which was with the deceased at the time of death, and thus the heir, to whom civil possession was transferred by the assignment made in the manner and form described above, i.e., to that third party, transferred it to him. And thus he could take possession, since this right of entering possession by one's own authority, or the right of taking possession by one's own authority, can be assigned; and consequently, that civil possession, by virtue of the confirmation, which was with the deceased creditor, and which is transmitted to the heir by the form of the statute, can be assigned by the heir to the one to whom he assigned the rights, and transferred to him, so that the assignee, as heir having civil possession of the alienated thing, could enter it.

On the other hand, it is said that that civil possession, which was with the creditor by virtue of the constitution of precarious possession, did not pass to his heir, notwithstanding the statute. And even if it had passed to his heir, it did not pass to the assignee by assignment, since assignment is not a mode of acquiring civil possession, which possession is not acquired except by possession, or almost by delivery.

It is argued to the contrary that it was transferred by assigning personal and real actions, tacit and hypothecary, in the manner described above; since those rights, which are transmissible to heirs, are transferred by assignment; and just as the right of entering is in rem, so that against anyone to whom the thing passes, the right belongs to the creditor, so also should that right of entering belong against anyone to whom the thing passes to the one who has the right assigned by the creditor; since this right of entering can be assigned by the creditor.

Now it is asked whether that assignee could take possession of the alienated property by judicial authority without any execution having been made against the goods of the alienator or the goods of the other co-debtors; and whether a libel was necessary, or by what means he could proceed by merely writing the truth with allegations; the statute providing that possession passes to the heir, speaks in this form. We establish and ordain that possession of goods, or quasi-possession, and rights of any deceased person, male or female, by right and immediately, passes to the heir, whether his own or an outsider.

There is also another statute, or two, in this form, namely: We also establish and ordain that the assignee is in all respects and in every way in the place of the assignor. We also establish and ordain that action may be brought by assignments; and according to the pacts and conventions set forth in instruments or promises, reason must be made of them; and in all respects and in every way they are in the place of those who assigned the rights and actions.

Although in the narration of the above facts some allegations were not necessary, because everything is most clearly known to the one who should consult, yet, as the quality of the fact dictates, it is deduced in a clearer manner, and the following are said and alleged for the assignee.

† For in the first place it is presupposed that the civil possession, which was held by the deceased creditor by virtue of the aforementioned constitution of precarium, and this right of entering by one’s own authority, was transferred to the heir even without any delivery or corporeal apprehension; and this by virtue of the above-mentioned first statute, which speaks of possession transferred, which could most appropriately dispose of the same being transferred: as in l. omnes populi, with its subject matter, ff. de iust. et iur.; nor does it avail to object that no, ff. pro socio, §. idem respondit socium, in the gloss nunquid ipso iure and c. quia, for that gloss speaks of possession held and maintained by another, as appears there in question 2 of the said §. in causa dictae glossae, ibi, and est ratio, and c. which there by Raynaldus; and in our question it is presupposed that the said possession was held by the deceased creditor at the time of his death: therefore the said possession was transferred to his heir by virtue of the said statute, and thus the learned doctors have advised in the civil law, namely Vincentius, of good memory, Raynaldus of Forlì, Ricardus de Saly, and Argentinus, the aforementioned Lord Raynaldus.

But now it must be seen whether, by the said cession made in such a way and manner by the said heir to the said third party, the said civil possession and the said right of entering into the said possession were transferred and ceded to him, so that the said third party could enter, as is posited in the case, and it seems to be said that yes. For, first, such rights are transmissible to the heir even without any other apprehension, by virtue of the said statute, as has been said; therefore, they are cessionable. L. ex pluribus, de administratione tutorum. It supports what is noted in L. quod si minor, in principio, ff. de minoribus, cum suis. Second, for this view, the case seems to apply, and what is there noted by Bartolus in §. si, de operis novi nuntiatione. Third, for this side, I adduce the note by Innocentius in C. cum venisset, de in integrum restitutione; because just as he, for whom judgment is rendered on the right of choosing, and thus on an incorporeal thing, begins and is deemed to have the intent to possess, although he does nothing corporeal, because there was no case of doing something: so too the said cessionary is said to have, by virtue of the said cession, the intent to possess the said right ceded, although at the time of the cession he performed no corporeal act. Therefore, by the subsequent apprehension, it will be said that, by virtue of the said cession, the said civil possession cooperates with the preceding intent, just as the preceding apprehension operates with the subsequent intent, as is noted in L. si rem, ff. de acquirenda possessione, and L. certi condicio, §. si, and what is there noted, that the subsequent apprehension operates with the preceding intent. Fourth, for by the act of words both possessions are transferred, as appears from L. quod meo; therefore, the civil possession, which was with the cedent, by the act of words in the said cession made in the aforementioned manner and way, can be said to have been transferred. For even a natural obligation can be ceded, as is noted in L. eius, ff. ad Trebellianum, although Bartolus interprets that gloss differently. Fifth, for since the said civil possession, which was with the deceased creditor, by virtue of the statute was transferred to the heir, as above, the said civil possession of the hypothecated thing, existing with the heir, was not interrupted for the heir by the subsequent alienation of the thing made by the debtor, nor was the heir deprived of his civil possession; so much so that he could enter the said alienated thing without any excussion, as fully explained by Jacobus Butrigarius and Bartolus in the said L. 3, C. de pignoribus. Therefore, if the heir was not deprived of his civil possession by the alienation of the debtor, then either it must be said that the said civil possession was transferred to the said third party immediately at the time of the cession; because no act of delivery or corporeal act intervened at that time, yet when the cessionary enters the said possession by authority of the said cession and with the consent of the cedent, the said civil possession is said to have been acquired by the cessionary at that moment; so that at the moment he enters, the said civil possession is said to have been acquired, and from this the said entry is corroborated and judged valid, just as is clear regarding a donation exceeding the legitimate mode, which is null, but is perfected by insinuation, and by being perfected it is insinuated, as is gathered from L. data, C. de donationibus, and expressly for this purpose L. filius in patre, in principio, in the version "herede," auth., and what is there noted in the gloss and by Petrus de Ancharano, ff. de liberis et posthumis, L. cum validatur, and more clearly by L. Titius et Seius, ff. de verbis obligatis, and what is there by Bartolus, where one can sue without an action, when the action arises separately in the protestation itself. Sixth, for the cession having been made, and the delivery of the instruments preceding the cessionary, as is posited in the case, in which instruments the total right of the cedent consisted, it follows that the said civil possession, which was with the said cedent, was transferred to the said cessionary, from the argument of those things noted by the doctors in L. 1, C. de donationibus; then as if delivery had intervened, or that which is held in place of delivery on account of the delivery of the instruments. Seventh, and lastly, a clear and open case of the said statutes, joining them together; for it is certain that the said possession, by the statute, can be transferred without any corporeal act, as the above writings speaking of cassation make clear by the word of truth, that the cessionary is in all respects and in everything in the place of the cedent; it must be said that that possession, which was with the cedent, was transferred to the cessionary by virtue of the said statutes, according to what is noted by Bartolus in L. si maritus, §. 1, ff. de adulteriis, and in L. si quis pro emptore, de usucapione; so that just as the cedent, by reason of his said civil possession, could enter, so too the cessionary by virtue of the statutes. And so forth.

The allegations prescribed were those of Messer Alvise de Luchis, a most valiant advocate of Vicenza, doctor of laws. The allegations made above are notable, worthy of praise, and elegant, arising from the subtlety of his intellect and from the matter of good laws. However, these must be examined more widely. And first, it must be known that, although the possession of the deceased does not descend to the heir without apprehension, because it is a matter of fact and intent, not of intent alone; because no one begins to possess by will alone, as ff. de acquirenda possessione, L. cum haeres, ff. si quis testamento liber esse iussus fuerit, L. 1, §. Scevola, L. cum miles, in principio, quibus ex causis maiores, in the gloss, ordinatio. Although some say that possession continues with one's own heir, as is noted de liberis et posthumis, L. in suis, "liberis creditur possedisse," C. qui etate, L. 2, lib. 10, in the gloss, and C. pro usucapione, L. nihil.

† Nevertheless, whatever is established by the common law, possession may be transferred to the heir and another successor by statute and custom without actual apprehension of the thing, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *Ex parte* on custom, and there the case is found. Secondly, it must be premised that although he who asks for something precariously retains possession, he who grants it precariously possesses it civilly, that is, with the intent to possess. Moreover, he possesses it civilly, that is, by the invention of civil law, as in the Digest, *De precario*, law *Et habet*, section *Eum qui precario*, and there it is noted. Thirdly, it must be premised that one who possesses civilly may also enter into physical possession without the authority of the praetor. Codex, *Quod cum eodem*, law *Et servus*, which is the law properly to be alleged for this purpose; and Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, law *Clam possidere*, section *Si*, together with the following law.

Fourthly, it must be premised that, although the right to recover possession could not be assigned or transferred to anyone other than the person who had been dispossessed (Digest 50.17.149; and see the note in Digest 43.16.1; in the gloss of Ioan.), nevertheless, the right to retain and continue in possession may be assigned and granted (Digest 43.8.2 § idem Nerva; in the ordinary gloss). Fifthly, it must be premised that an omission made by a judge, not in the course of judicial procedure, but in altering a sentence, license, or faculty granted in a contract, does not have the authority of res iudicata, but is considered merely by the law of contract; because it cannot carry the weight of res iudicata, which it does not possess in its form and order (Code 1.17.1; and Code 4.2.1; Digest 40.12.1; Institutes 1.11 § multis; Code 7.4.2; Digest 43.17.3 § in the gloss). From all these, however, it seems to be concluded that the person sent by virtue of a convention is to be protected in possession rather than by the authority of a command or mission, unless he sought to have it confirmed to him after hearing of the case by the praetor (Code 10.29.1), unless this is prevented by what I shall say immediately.

Sixthly, it must be premised that the gloss in the final law of the Codex, *De acquirenda possessione*, states that if he who possesses in another’s name transfers it to someone else, the person in whose name the possession is held loses civil possession, just as the foot follows the natural body. Therefore, if the owner lost it, he could not have ceded it to another. And this opinion, Cynus says, is observed in practice on account of the authority of the glosses, and by the law *Peregre*, § *Quibus*, of the Codex, *De acquirenda possessione*, and in the Digest, *Quibus modis ususfructus*, the law *Pomponius*, and the law *Cum quis persuaserit*, of the Digest, *De dolo*, in the ordinary gloss. But Jacobus de Ravanis, Cynus, and Jacobus Butrigarius say that civil possession is not lost, because to transfer and to lose are the same thing. For he who departs so that another may enter, betrays and transfers, by argument from the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, the law *Fistulas*, § 1. And just as by betraying he does not harm the owner, so neither by transferring, for the reason is the same. Moreover, natural reason dictates this. For whatever right or power my tenant or any other of my ministers has in the continuation and possession of mine is sought, therefore his act harms me. Codex, *Ut per vim vel alio modo*, law 1, § *Penultimum non obstat*, *De acquirenda possessione*, law *Si de eo*, § *Si forte aliud estimandum*. For that section must be understood when the tenant had a cause for surrendering possession: for example, because he departed out of fear of armed men, whether he would return. For this is a causal abandonment of possession; otherwise in a fraudulent one, because he concludes or transfers, for this was not entrusted to him. Law *Creditor*, § *Si mandatum*, *Ad hoc*, Digest, *Locati conducti*, law *Item quæritur*, § *Item exercitu*. And according to this opinion, the said cessionary would have entered into possession by legitimate right. Digest, *De pigneraticia actione*, law *Qui ratiario*, *De servis exportandis*, law *Titius*, *De acquirenda possessione*, law *Prædia*, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Claudius*, and law 3, *De pignoribus*. And by Dynus in chapter 1, *De regulis iuris*, book 6, *De legatis*, law 2, law *Titio cum testamento*, § 1, Codex, *De iure emphyteutico*, law *Finalis*, and argument from *De actione empti*, law *In venditione*. Moreover, in retaining possession, no excussion is necessary; for he who holds is considered in the place of the thing. Digest, *De operis novi nuntiatione*, law *De pupillo*, § *Qui remissionem*. And in the Institutes, *De interdictis et commodis*. And this opinion is pleasing to the aforementioned excellent doctors. But Bartolus says that possession is lost; but it is recovered by the *condictio ex lege*, which is subsidiary; therefore possession is lost, as in the said law *Finalis*. And this is observed in practice, as he says, in which recovery excussion is not necessary, because a hypothecary action is not brought; but an action *ex lege*, in which the dispossessed, or he having a cause on that account, must be restored before all things; since this right can be ceded. Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Quod si in diem*, § *Iulianus*. Therefore, according to the gloss, the said immission, and especially without first establishing that it was of the debtor’s goods, did not proceed according to law; but according to others, it did. The opinion of the others is more equitable, yet in advising I do not dare to depart from the gloss, and therefore it is necessary to bring the *condictio ex lege*. In certain places, however, there are statutes that those holding in another’s name cannot in any way interrupt possession; and then the said immission would be valid. I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, advise as is advised above, and contained therein, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When one of two or more instituted heirs accepts the inheritance, the share of the others, which is vacant by reason of non-acceptance or otherwise, accrues to the accepting heir.
2. Whether the acceptance of an inheritance is an act.
3. Whether the heirs of the husband are bound to account for the fruits collected from the wife's paraphernal property.
4. How the estimation of fruits is to be proved.
body: Regarding the doubts about which inquiry is made, the text of which I omit to transcribe here for the sake of brevity, especially since they are apparent at a glance on another page handed to me by the party for whose consideration I am writing, I will set forth only the truth, as I was requested, in a concise manner, in the order in which the doubts were presented to me.

† And in the first doubt, it appears that the inheritance of the said lady belongs in solidum to her son, who was instituted for a part. I prove this as follows: Whenever there are two or more instituted heirs, and one accepts the inheritance, if the share of the others becomes vacant through non-acceptance or in some other way, the one who accepted succeeds to the whole. L. una cum utrique suo in testamento: as is evident from the case. And here the son accepts the inheritance, as is evident from the acts, and this stepfather did not accept the inheritance. Which I prove as follows:

† Although the acceptance of an inheritance, with regard to its disposition, is termed an act of the mind, it is nevertheless an act of fact, not of law; and I speak of human acceptance, not legal acceptance, which arises from sui status, concerning which my lord Argentinus speaks fully in l. si filius, qui patri, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione. Therefore, as to the effect and declaration, I state that the acceptance of an inheritance is an act of fact, or requires a fact, as in l. potuit, C. de iure deliberandi, with the glosses there, and l. pro haerede, in principio, ff. de acquisitione possessionis. But this stepfather was not a suus to the testator; nor did he accept the inheritance by way of presumption, because facts are not presumed, such as acceptance, as has been said above, l. sciendum, § denique, ff. ex quibus causis maiores, with similar authorities. Nor did he accept by way of proof; for if anyone wished to say that it is proved by attestations that he accepted the inheritance, this would be said to be proved by two witnesses, namely Borthinus, notary, formerly of Boterinus, in what he deposes under chapter 14, and also Henry, formerly of Manfredus of the Falcibus, in what he deposes under chapter 15. But by these witnesses the acceptance of this stepfather is not proved, as is clear from their singularity in time, place, and matter. That this may be more clearly considered, let the confessions of the solutions, upon which these two witnesses base themselves, be examined. Now, singular witnesses do not legally prove, as in l. Marcellus, post principium, ff. de re amissa; l. videamus, circa principium, ff. de iureiurando; c. bonae, et alia; and c. in Genesi; and c. cum dilecti, extra de electione; and c. licet causam, extra de probationibus. I therefore conclude that this stepfather did not accept the inheritance for his share; and consequently, it accrued to the aforementioned daughter of the lady.

† On the second doubt, which is, assuming without prejudice, and not conceding, that the said stepfather is an heir in part, whether the heirs of this stepfather, or the same stepfather, who possessed for many years the goods of the said lady, both dowry and paraphernal, are bound to the fruits collected from the said goods. And it seems to be said briefly, that they are bound to the natural fruits, not to the instrumental ones. And thus: when something from the wife's goods comes to the husband during the marriage, from which he is enriched, the husband must restore it to the wife, as in l. si stipulata. ff. de dona. §. 1. ff. de dona. inter vir. et vxo. unless between them there is a labor of seeking, as noted by the gloss. no. posita in l. fin. on the word, usuras. post prin. gl. C. de pac. conuen. which gloss, if well considered in the said, and reason, seems to decide the present doubt. And it makes for the above. l. pen. ff. ad l. Fal. In this first step therefore, I do not think the Argentines have fully proven them as singular, per no. per Cyn. and in l. 2. versi. sed quaero. C. quae sit longa consue. although this step is somewhat doubtful per the common gloss in l. ob carmen. §. si testes. ff. de test.

† On the third doubt, which is whether the estimation of the fruits, and insofar as it is proved by witnesses, and briefly I consider the estimation of the fruits to be proved, in the book, l. of that currency, of which mention is made in the attestations. For there are two solemn witnesses, greater than any exception, who rightly depose that the fruits collected, or which could have been collected, were worth every year, computed one with another, l. of the aforementioned currency. Nor does it matter that this estimation is not common, but singular, and of affection: for from the fact that a witness says his own interest only, if he does not say singularly his own interest, it is not singular, nor of affection, as noted by the gloss in l. una, C. de sen. quae pro eo, quod inter. in the gloss on the word, subtilitatem ad factum sui. I admit, however, that it does not have the common opinion of all: but of those who have, so to speak, a known thing. And thus it suffices, when it is a matter of estimating a thing by common estimation: which I urge thus. Behold, the law says that a thing is worth only as much as it can commonly be sold, or by common estimation, as l. precia, ff. ad l. Fal. and it is usually said in l. 2, C. de rei ven.
