Certainly, the gloss says elsewhere that this is true, as much as it can be sold to a person knowing the condition of that thing; this is the gloss in l. mortis causa capimus, §. fin. and it is the first gloss of that §. fin. ff. de dona. cau. mor. Thus is understood the gloss of l. si seruus, in prin. ff. de cond. furti. and in l. quantitate, §. magna. and l. quaerebatur, circa princi. ff. ad l. Fal. I will therefore say in our case, that however much the witnesses say that they themselves had accepted for the effect for the said quantity the said possessions ignorantly, yet whether others ignorant of the cultivation of the lands would have leased for such a price, is sufficient for this, that the estimation is common. Nor does this hinder, which is inferred, that it is singular affection, as is sufficiently clear to one understanding the aforementioned. It supports what is noted in a similar case in l. cum quidam, §. quod dicitur, ff. de acque hę. on the word, multorum. What more? This determination is confirmed by the doctors in d. l. 1, in fi. in the reading of Cyn. and thus I conclude that the said estimation is well and legitimately proved, and thus in the aforementioned, truth being inspected, it seems to me, Ioanni Capitaneo de Molino, least of doctors of laws, to be said, saving always etc. And thus I say, and I counsel, I Argentinus of lord Rayn. etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Acceptance of an inheritance cannot be made more than once.
body: Because the witnesses of Posn testify regarding the act of inserting the same addition, as has been fully proven by the aforementioned eminent doctors.

† For the acceptance of an inheritance is an act that cannot be performed more than once. For in the first act, the right of acceptance draws with it its effect: or it is an act that, by law or in fact, does not admit of plurality, witnesses deposing variously being considered singular, as is noted by the gloss and others in l. ob carmen, in fine, ff. de testibus and de accusatione, c. qualiter, through Innocentius. Since, therefore, it is not established that there was acceptance by an act of word or sign, nor administration as heir by an act of deed, the untransmitted portion accrues to the coheir in inheritances. ff. de actionibus hereditariis, l. si servus communis ab extero; C. de iure deliberandi, l. quidam Eulogio; C. de caducis tollendis, l. unica, § is ita, with its subject matter. It is not an obstacle that a certain document was made by a certain notary concerning a certain payment, because that document is denied to be true: and it is said to be impossible, as is proposed to me in the facts, therefore, etc. C. de transactionibus, l. ex falsis. Moreover, not every document of a notary is held to be a public instrument, unless it has the due form and solemnity of law; otherwise it is called a private document. C. qui potior in pignore habeatur, l. assiduis, which does not prove against a third party, as is fully noted in ff. de edendo, l. quaedam, § nummularios. And thus I say and advise, I, Balde de Perusio, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Mere sovereignty may be acquired by prescription.
2. For what period of time mere sovereignty is prescribed.
3. For what period of time jurisdiction is prescribed.
4. For what period of time a fief is prescribed.
5. What acts are required to prescribe mere or mixed sovereignty, and jurisdiction.
6. Whether prescription extends to cases not arisen, and since there are four kinds of extensions, namely from time to time, from person to person, as at no. 7; also from thing to thing, as at no. 8; also from place to place, as at no. 9; whether it extends from one to another.
7. Whether prescribed jurisdiction is transmitted.
8. Whether a parish priest in his parish may prescribe the right of institution.
9. Whether a subordinate may prohibit the exercise of jurisdiction prescribed in a subordinate court.
10. There are four causes for the devolution of jurisdiction.
body: Furthermore, the castle of the ancestors was held, computing the time: ten years for the father, twenty for the grandfather, thirty for the great-grandfather, and forty for the great-great-grandfather. In the Kingdom of Apulia, they were used everywhere, both high and low, during the said time, with the saving that no homicide having been perpetrated in the interim, there was no act of using. Now a homicide is newly committed, which she wishes to punish. The Queen contradicts, not from the plenitude of power, but because she denies that it extends to prescription and use. The question is, what is the law? This matter is thus divided. For first it is asked, whether mere empire is prescribed? Second, if it is prescribed, in what time is it prescribed? Third, whether prescription extends to causes de facto not emerged. Fourth, whether prescribed jurisdiction is transmitted. Fifth, whether prescription deprives the superior of the right to transmit to the inferior, or rather disposes concerning the inferior by subjecting him to the jurisdiction of a new person. Sixth, and last, whether the inferior can impede the prescribed jurisdiction in the inferior by prohibiting, or abdicate by taking away the proposition. I return to the first point, in which there is a double opinion.

† For some have said that *merum imperium* [full sovereignty/high jurisdiction] is not acquired by time. And this is proved by many reasons. And first, by the reason of prohibited usurpation: for he who acts as a magistrate, and is not one, incurs the crime of *laesa maiestas* [treason]; because he occupies the rights of empire. D. ad l. Iul. mai. l. 3. in fin. By which crime, when ensnared, he is not only prohibited from acquiring new rights, but must also lose old ones, and especially jurisdiction and honors, since he is infamous and incapacitated. C. ad l. Iul. maiest. l. quisquis. C. de sacrosan. eccl. l. decernimus. Just as true jurisdiction is not held by heretics, D. 8. dist. c. quo iure. de haeret. Auth. credentes. and note in c. quod super. de voto. extra. so it is not held by those accused of *laesa maiestas*, who are equated with heretics, as C. de haeret. Auth. Gazaros. extra de re iudic. c. apostolicae. lib. 6. And it is confirmed, because if he could prescribe, he would derive jurisdiction, benefit, and honor from his own wickedness: which is incongruous. D. de furt. l. itaque fullo. D. de neg. gest. l. sine haereditaria. For the same cause cannot simultaneously produce odium and reward, from which the unworthy are always excepted, as D. de leg. 2. l. Lucius. §. Lucius Titius Daman. Similarly, the same water cannot simultaneously drip sweet and bitter water, for the same subject cannot receive this simultaneously due to contradiction, C. de furt. l. 1.

Secondly, it is proved by the reason of parity, or production: for it is established that sacred things, priests, and public magistrates are of public law, as D. de iust. et iur. l. 1. §. ius publicum. and as if born from the same womb. Since therefore a profane place is not prescribed into a sacred one at any time: and he who is not a priest could in no way prescribe himself into a priesthood, even if he performed the office of a priest for a thousand years, as D. de decur. l. Herennius. therefore he who is not a praetor can at no time prescribe a praetorship, D. de off. praet. l. Barbarius. And it is confirmed, because neither does a notary prescribe the notaryship, or tabellionage, by the course of time: rather, he is punished for forgery. D. de fals. l. eos. §. fin. and C. de falsis. l. ex initio. Likewise, no one prescribes marriage. D. de ritu nup. l. qui in provincia. §. diuus.

Thirdly, it is proved by the reason of the form of jurisdiction given by concession. For since it is a power introduced from the public, no one [acquires it] except from the public, i.e., by confession, or confirmation of the superior, as in Auth. de defen. ciui. §. interim. C. de man. prin. l. vnica. C. de diuer. off. l. probatorias. with l. seq. lib. 12. And it is confirmed, because he cannot exercise the empire itself unless he swears an oath in the hand of the superior, as in Auth. iusiu. quod praestatur ab his. Likewise, if *merum imperium* could be prescribed, therefore clerics could prescribe the jurisdiction of Caesar over laymen, which is altogether prohibited. C. de test. in l. consulta. de ep. et cle. l. repetita.

Fourthly, it is proved by the reason of avoiding abuse. For if *merum* and *altum imperium*, which is in capital cases, could be prescribed, therefore the right of creating notaries, legitimating bastards, creating magistrates, granting dispensation of age could be prescribed: since these are likewise of *merum imperium*: which seems false, since these are among the reserved rights. It applies in Auth. quibus mod. natu. effi. sui. §. si. coll. 7. The consequence holds, for if jurisdiction can be prescribed, therefore the license to appoint judges, and thus to create another judge, can be prescribed, D. de iuris. omn. iud. l. imperium. §. fin.

Fifthly, it is proved by the reason of impossible acquisition: for if *merum imperium* can be prescribed, therefore condemnations and fines will be confiscated to himself, and applied to himself: which is impossible. C. de modo. mulct. l. mulctarum. C. de bon. vacan. l. 1. lib. 10. D. ad mul. l. si mille. Whose effect is prohibited, the thing itself seems prohibited: for where we speak of the prohibited and the permitted, we especially attend to the effect, arg. C. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. mulier.

Sixthly, it is proved, because the authority to commit delicts is not prescribed. D. de poenis. l. si diuturno. But a private person acting as a magistrate always multiplies delicts, and whenever he harms a man, he incurs the law C. de sicar. [on assassins]; whenever he binds, he incurs the law D. de vi publica [on public violence]; and whenever he imprisons, he incurs the crime of private imprisonment. D. ad l. Iul. de vi. l. lege Iul. §. hodie. C. de priu. carc. l. 1. And these are evil in themselves and absolutely, which can in no way be justified, extra de iureiu. c. et si Christus.

Seventhly, from the lack of true possession, because jurisdiction is not possessed without title, because the name jurisdiction signifies right. And I argue thus: that which is not, cannot be possessed: But jurisdiction in someone without cause is not, therefore it cannot be possessed, therefore neither prescribed, as in c. sine possessione. And it is confirmed, because from whom being is removed, possession of such being is removed. For possessions are many. But the essentiality of jurisdiction is removed from a private person: therefore also quasi-possession, because it is impossible to possess something present without it being, D. de public. l. si ego. §. si partus. This nobleman, however, lacking title, does not prescribe, especially because he is a son. C. pro haerede. l. nihil. Nor can just error fall in jurisdiction without title, as c. ad decimas. extra de resti. spo. lib. 6.

Eighthly, it is established that a doctor has jurisdiction over scholars. Suppose therefore that someone acted as a doctor for a long time, has he prescribed the doctorate? And can he doctorize anything? Certainly not: because he does not accept such use. D. de iure fi. l. sed accepto. Likewise, he does not have insignia: therefore he cannot be preferred to another, because there is nothing in the effect that is not in the cause, D. 1. q. 1. c. Marchio. And it is proved, because a certain form is given for the creation of such honors: not observed, they are held in the place of private persons. C. de nu. et actu. l. actuarios. lib. 11. And in the election of officials, the form constituted of old must be observed. C. de iur. fis. l. super creandis. lib. 10. D. de condi. et demonstra. l. publius. D. de neg. gest. l. quae utiliter. de admini. tuto. l. quidam decedens. and in prin. extra de ele. c. quia propter.

Ninthly, I argue from a sufficient enumeration of parts: for either this prescriber intends jurisdiction from himself: and this is impossible, because in himself he is a private person: and because no one gives title to himself, arg. l. 2. D. de stipu. ser. or from the Prince, or King, and this is false, because silence does not give title. C. de transa. l. si pro fundo. for silence is nothing, but title, or jurisdiction, is something. Likewise, in prohibited matters, he who is silent seems to dissimulate to the better, but not to consent. l. si vas. §. vetare. or from the territory itself: and this does not seem so, because empire is in the territory as in a subject, and patient, not as in a conferrer, especially since territory, insofar as it is territory, is an inanimate thing, like a field, and a house, for these do not serve gifts. but receive them made by men. D. de nego. gesto. l. qui aliena. §. si or from the university of subjects. and this does not seem so, because in the university of subjects is the election of a rector to be confirmed by the superior: for jurisdiction is not in the university, but in its superior. And from this proceeds the giving of a curator, and in his hands must the renunciation be made. D. de offi. praesid. l. legatis. C. de defen. ciui. l. nulli. §. penulti. Likewise, by what name shall we call this man? Certainly he cannot be called by his proper name, other than defender of the town, but the defender of the city is also prohibited from *merum imperium*: therefore also this one. C. de defensione ciuit. l. defensiones nihil. and l. defensores ciuitatum. and if we changed his name, it would avail nothing, as l. 1. C. de priuileg. scholar. lib. 12. there on this.

Tenthly, I argue from causes, and some causes are principal, others accessory: principal causes of becoming are two, efficient, and final. of being are two, namely material, and formal. I take the efficient cause, which is absent, because neither law, nor prince, nor senatusconsultum gives jurisdiction to this man, which is called institution: nor confirms, which is called confirmation. nor approves, which is called approbation: declaration here, or ratification, therefore the first cause is lacking, namely the efficient, which is called the most powerful principle over all causes. D. de officio eius. l. 1. Here also form is lacking, here consent is lacking, here intellect is lacking, which acts for the end, and thus causes fail. Likewise the sequence of causes, namely place, and time, and such, extra de re iudi. c. Abbate. lib. 6. Since therefore prescription is founded on place, and time, and these are lacking, therefore prescription is impossible.

Eleventhly, I argue thus: a thing which does not have in itself the form of being, lacks name, and reason. D. de falsis. l. si quis legatum. but this prescription does not have in itself the form of being. and first, discontinuation of possession, since the discontinuous is that which consists in the acts of men, as D. de serui. l. seruitutes. de ser. urba. praed. l. foramen. de praescrip. c. de quarta. per Inno. Likewise, on account of an unjust beginning, which vitiates the whole process of time. D. de acqu. pos. l. clam possidere. in prin. Likewise, the superior does not lose, therefore the inferior does not prescribe. D. ex quibus causa maior. l. nec utilem. in fin. Likewise, in prescription, right and fact are required, that is, just possession, not against divine, or natural, or civil law: and especially in corporeal things, which have much right. C. de agri. et censi. l. quema. l. si is, qui pro emptore. and l. vbi lex. But to use jurisdiction by one's own authority is against all. C. de Iudaeis. l. nemo. and D. quod me. cau. l. extat. Likewise, that which is alien, everyone knows does not pertain to himself. C. vnde ui. l. fina. but that jurisdiction is alien, because it is in the sole alien, that is, the lady queen's, therefore he who uses it as his own is of bad faith, therefore he prescribes at no time. c. 2. extra de reg. iur. lib. 6. for whatever is within the bounds of the kingdom, is of the lady queen in full right. D. de offi. praefe. urb. §. contra urbem. for she is the mistress in our time: since now she alone reigns in the kingdom, extra de arbit. c. dilecti. iuxta not. C. de arbi. l. fin.

Twelfthly, I argue thus: either this man prescribes against the superior: and this is impossible, that superiority be prescribed against superiority. For prescription is, and there is no ascent above supreme power, because there is no degree above the supreme, and useful prescribed right must be preferred to direct, because it is not acquired against the unwilling. C. de praescri. 30. anno. l. si quis emptionis. therefore one castle, and one baron of one castle would be above the king, which is foolish to say. Likewise, the inferior does not prescribe against the superior, especially jurisdiction of appeals, extra de iureiu. c. venientes. C. de appel. l. si appel. per Cyn. Likewise, it is not probable that the prince, who gave strength to prescriptions, would give it against himself, and against the statute of his empire. D. de pecu. leg. l. si peculium. §. sicut. and if civil law were not, there would be no prescriptions. D. de vsuca. l. 1. pro suo. l. fin. de verbo. sign. l. transac. finita. C. de edi. di. Adri. l. sin. §. penul. cum si. or this man prescribes against the inferior: and then, although the inferior consents, he does not prejudice the right of the superior. C. de acqui. pos. l. fi. C. de poenis. l. seruus. and l. debitorum. arg. D. loca. l. in oper. nun. casus legum in medio proponamus. and l. competit. C. de praescri. 30. ann. says fiscal rights are not prescribed. therefore neither empire, of which the fisc is the predecessor. Likewise l. prima. C. de decur. et statu. lib. 12. removes custom, by which criminals could imprison others: therefore here it cannot be prescribed. Likewise l. omnes iudices. C. de decu. lib. 10. removes custom disposing against privileges of princes. Likewise l. nihil. C. de palatinis. lib. 10. removes custom introduced against exempt persons, except concerning reverence. Likewise, the right of the prince is said to be exempt from all prescription, extra de cap. mon. c. dilectus. ver. vt ita. Likewise, the chapter vt nostrum. says, if anyone exercised acts pertaining to the office, or dignity of another, that from this he does not acquire any right for himself. likewise the law says, that no one can disturb the jurisdiction of another by usurping his office. C. de execu. et exa. l. 2. lib. 12. Likewise, the providence of the superior prohibits usurpatory offices. C. de ex. mili. ante. l. 1. lib. 12. Likewise, and even if the lady queen had expressly donated this jurisdiction, nevertheless without any cause she could freely revoke it, because this is a privilege of the prince. C. de omni agro deser. l. qui fundos lib. 11. which law is much to this point. Likewise, no one can prescribe the right of imprisoning, therefore neither greater cases of *merum imperium*, as C. de coharta. l. 1. lib. 12. Likewise, he who wishes to use *merum imperium* against the prohibition of the king, can be killed with impunity as a rebel. C. de deserto. l. 2. lib. 12. Likewise, if no one can prescribe the benefits of public sense, as C. de fundis patrimo. l. iubemus. lib. 11. therefore much less the public benefits of jurisdiction of *merum* and *mixtum imperium*, such as fines, and confiscations of goods. Likewise, they are regalia, therefore applicable to none but the prince, nor can they be compared, as cap. 1. in tit. quae sunt rega. coll. 10. for this is plain from the name, as C. de feriis. l. a nullo. Likewise, the gloss is ordinary, that no one prescribes against the supreme power of the prince. D. 16. q. 4. c. volumus. and de postula. praela. c. bonae. per Inno. hence if the queen commands that no proceeding be made, obedience must be paid to her, because against obedience nothing can be prescribed. de praescript. c. cum non liceat. and these suffice for this part.

On the contrary, that *merum imperium* could be prescribed, is proved by many reasons: first from the rule, For whatever can be acquired by succession, can be acquired by prescription. D. de praescri. l. eum, qui. and l. quaecunque. D. de contrahen. empt. l. clauibus. nor is it wonderful, for the nature of both prescriptions is one. D. de verbo. signifi. l. alienationis. D. de vsucap. pro empti. l. 2. time, so to speak, performs the role of the person in alienating, since it wastes and corrodes the rights of the negligent, and is transferred to the diligent. C. de omni agro deser. l. qui agros. lib. 11. for all things, as Aristotle says, are terminated by their period. But in the latest law of nations, which all nations use, it was introduced that jurisdictions be admitted: as we see in the sons of kings, dukes, counts, and barons, D. 7. q. 1. c. quoniam periculosum. de voto. c. licet. therefore the same can be born and transmitted by space of time. And it is confirmed, because duchies, and marchionates, as they now are in Germany, and in other places, were not from the origin of the world, and nations, but were born and justified by most ancient use. for antiquity makes all things lawful, just as nature, nor is cause to be sought. D. de aqua plu. arc. l. fi. D. de aqua quoti. et aesti. l. hoc iure. §. ductus aquae. for he who asks for cause, asks for origin, which cannot be had in those things which the present ages of men have exercised. D. de proba. l. si arbiter. For memory dies, and is born, just as man, who is in man. D. de furt. l. quidam tabularum. D. de aqua plu. arcen. l. 2. §. penul. and in Auth. haec constitutio innouat. post prin. col. 8. therefore applying to the proposition, if they can be transmitted, therefore they can be prescribed. Sol. it is proved thus, all that is prescriptible can be prescribed, but all jurisdiction is prescriptible, therefore empire, which is a species of jurisdiction, can be prescribed, for when the genus is permitted, any species is seen to be permitted, unless a prohibition is found. D. quibus ex causa ma. l. nec non. D. de testi. l. 1. de proba. l. ex ea parte. for the position of the genus posits its proper species, as if it enumerated them. D. de lega. 3. l. si chorus. and note in c. ex ieris. de iure patr. per Inn. that jurisdiction is prescriptible, is clear, where there is custom, there is prescription, but custom gives jurisdiction, therefore prescription gives it. C. de emanci. liberorum. l. 1. and D. de iur. om. iudi. l. more maiorum.

Thirdly, it is proved: *merum imperium* is accustomed to be granted, therefore it can be prescribed, because prescription is equated to a privilege, extra de verbo. sign. c. super quibusdam. §. 1. and custom is equivalent to truth, as note. C. de serui. et aqua. l. 1. in prescription they have authority from the prince, therefore they are equivalent to grants. C. de veteri iure enucle. l. 1. §. omnia. Likewise, possession defends the possessor, until the contrary is proved. C. de ser. expor. l. moueor. for what all observe, individuals cannot fail to observe. D. de regu. iur. l. aliud. §. refertur.

Fourthly, it is proved thus, long obedience is held for election. D. 1. tit. argu. D. de vsur. l. cum de in rem verso. patience, or tolerance of the superior with the obedience of the inferior, or with protestation, is held for a fact not only as to the protestation, otherwise the protesting one, But as to the patience of him, who could have prohibited the one rendering service, from rendering it. For there are three cases, one of patience, another of performance only, another mixed, where the superior suffers, and the inferior obeys, where from the long obedience of the inferior, and patience of the superior, a cause is presumed. D. de acqui. her. l. 6. §. 1. and conversely. C. de peti. her. l. si filius. it suffices therefore to allege the concession of the superior, which is presumed, from which the superior is, and is sought, and his subject obeys: and especially because in corporeal things an express title is not required. D. si serui. vendicetur. l. si quis diuturno. unless in spiritual things, as in c. ad decimas. extra de resti. spo. lib. 6.

Fifthly, it is proved, the university prescribes the right of establishing regarding *merum imperium*, as in capital penalties. D. de extraordi. crim. l. sacularii. §. sunt quaedam. therefore it prescribes *merum imperium*, which by common law is not in universities, but in the governors of the province. D. de offic. praesid. l. illicitas. §. si vniuersas. de seru. reipublicae ma. l. 1. de constitu. capitu. cum omnis. And therefore by common law universities cannot banish anyone, since it is of *merum imperium*. C. de sentent. et interlocu. omn. iudic. l. 2. in fin.

Sixthly, it is proved: where there is territory, there lies jurisdiction, which is annexed to every territory. C. vbi, et apud quem. l. fin. And this is clear from the name itself, because everyone has the right of terracing in his own territory. D. de verbo. signi. l. pupillum. §. territorium. and everyone is greater in his own territory. D. de manumis. l. apud eum. in glo. but castles, and towns have their own proper, and distinct territories wherever there are tribunals, and magistrates, extra de restitutio. spolia. cap. cum ad sedem. per Inno. from the reason of territory granted, or prescribed, even *merum imperium* is obtained.

Seventhly, it is proved: whatever pertains to someone by way of sign, pertains by way of the thing signified. D. de ser. urb. praed. l. haec autem iura. he who holds the window retains the servitude. thus he who for a long time held gallows erected, has empire by way of sign. Likewise by the way of effect, because he used it in contingent cases.

Eighthly, it is proved. For this prescription can be considered in two ways, one way as proceeding from all to the receiving person, to whom obedience is rendered. and in this way this is the custom of all, and the territory, as D. comuni. praedio. l. venditor. §. constat. another way, as proceeding from the possessor to the prejudice of the superior, whose right is usurped. and in this way it is prescription, not custom: for Titius possessing, and Seius suffering are two persons: and two persons do not make custom. Now in the proposition this doubt. i.e. prescription, and custom are simultaneously annexed and joined. if therefore custom gives *merum imperium*, therefore also prescription annexed to it, namely that custom protects the president against subjects, and prescription protects him against the queen, arg. C. de his, qui a non domino ma. l. fi.

Ninthly, it is proved thus, the law of nations holds for title, as is clear in those things which are in no one's goods, and therefore dominions are granted to occupiers: for both of things, and of jurisdictions, they began from possession. D. de acque pos. l. 1. And today wherever jurisdictions are vacant, as in the kingdoms of infidels, among whom there is no true dignity, nor true jurisdiction, it would be granted to faithful Catholics occupying, as was in the kingdom of Spain, as note. in decretis. And the same if any Christian King became a heretic. for since he would lose true jurisdiction, and it is vacant, it would be granted to the Catholic occupier, because this arises from the law of nations, which is impossible. D. de iust. et iur. l. ex hoc iure. and the necessity of those things introduced those jurisdictions, because it is impossible to live without magistrates. and without justice. D. de ori. iur. l. 2. §. post originem. and in Auth. vt omnes obediant iudi. prouin. in prin. much more valid are jurisdictions which proceed from the consent of obedient subjects spontaneously. C. de agri. et censi. l. si coloni. and l. Lucius. For what prohibits anyone from submitting himself to his own prejudice? certainly nothing. C. de transac. l. fi. The lady queen, by neglecting for so long, seems to have her own as derelict, or at least to have granted it to another. D. de dam. infe. l. praetor. in prin. de proba. l. procula. therefore the said nobleman has, and had *merum imperium* in the castle in the territory aforesaid.

Tenthly, it is proved, for the presidents of nations, and all officials say they observe the customs of the places. D. de offi. procon. et leg. l. obseruare. §. pe. extra qui fi. sint leg. c. gaudemus. therefore from custom jurisdictional authority depends, C. de exact. tribu. l. missi opinatores. lib. 10. C. quemadmodum tes. ape. l. 2. D. de tes. l. 4. §. fi. for custom must be most faithfully retained, ancient. C. de test. l. testamenta omnia. for custom must be observed in election, acceptance, in entry, progress, and exit of office, in syndicating officials, and in all things to be done. For custom is the form of the thing, and a second natural law, as customs cannot be changed. D. de pollicita. l. Imperator. since therefore the prescription of all is custom, therefore empire cannot be effectively granted by it.

Eleventhly, it is proved, because everyone can submit himself to another, even a greater. D. de iur. om. iu. l. est receptum. therefore much more a peer, or lesser, for he submits himself to his own prejudice by domicile, delict, or contract. Likewise by tacit, or express prorogation of jurisdiction, as C. vbi de cri. agi opor. l. 1. although feudatories cannot submit themselves from the fief to others than their lord, just as a colonist cannot recognize a holding from another than his lord. C. de acqu. pos. l. fi. How much therefore as to subjects, and obedient ones, without doubt it is prescribed.

Twelfthly, it is proved, the lady queen ought to be the guardian of justice: and therefore just as she defends jurisdiction from custom alone, so she ought to maintain the jurisdiction of others from custom alone, because she ought not to limp. for since it is an act prescribing, preceptive, patient, and medium convening, therefore from this results a congruent prescription. now let us bring forward laws and decretals formally proving this: I see prescription in land, and sea: for a castle is prescribed, as C. de funditus bannitis. l. quicunque castrorum. Likewise, the right of fishing alone in some part of the sea is prescribed. D. de diuer. praescri. l. quisquam. Likewise, the right of punishing is prescribed. C. de diuer. offi. l. viros. lib. 12. Likewise, the right of correcting. extra de offic. ordin. c. in refragabili. §. accessus. Likewise, the right of impeding, lest another be approached in delicts, with him set aside. de offic. archidia. c. dilecto. Likewise, the office, and power of delegating. D. de iur. om. iud. l. more. Likewise, the office of giving tutors, and curators, and interposing other authorities. C. de emanci. liber. l. 1. Likewise, the right of electing the Emperor, as note. in cap. ad Apostolicae. de re iudica. lib. 6. which speaks of the king of Bohemia, and in c. Romani. de iureiu. in cle. in gl. which speaks of two Emperors, says, that in doubt they have supreme jurisdiction from custom, as if to say, more than by force of election: which is to be noted. to this add, that custom is the origin, form, and principle of all jurisdictions: and therefore it is rightly to be observed. C. de causa. larg. titu. l. praecepit. de petitio. bon. sub. l. 1. lib. 10. and d. l. missi opinatores. D. de orig. iur. l. 2. in prin. Likewise, it is certain that some can be principal lords of cities, and castles, and have other lords under them. supra de heredit. Auth. si vero dominus. in Auth. de statut. contra libertatem ecclesiae. §. si vero dominus. coll. 10. and this is not from universal custom, or principal concession. Likewise, it is expressed in fundamental jurisdiction. i.e. that it is prescribed 10. col. if controversy be between lord, and knight. c. et si quis per 30. and de fundo dato inuicem legis commiin fin. Likewise, the gloss is ordinary in Auth. de defen. ciui. §. nulla. in fi. great gloss. Likewise, the gloss is ordinary, that powers of lands having presidial jurisdiction from custom. C. de praescrip. longi. tempo. l. fina. Likewise, the gloss is ordinary, Bart. extra de offic. ordina. cap. quando. and Ioan. 9. quaestio. 3. c. conquestus. what shall we say, said Hostien. that speaking of prescription properly, *merum imperium* cannot be prescribed, because it is public, and supreme right, extra de fo. comp. c. cum confugat. therefore although this one had jurisdiction against the city, or castle, he would not nevertheless exclude the superior. and these are two different things, to prescribe from someone: and to proscribe against someone, for prescription of custom is from the university by tacit consent, not against the university, properly speaking, because it is not caused by hatred from proper consent. D. de leg. l. de quibus facit quod no. D. de reg. iu. l. nec ex praetorio. nor can such custom be removed by statute of the people, because it is introduced by the consent, and favor of both parties. Likewise, because to statute is of jurisdiction: and jurisdiction resides with the lord, not with the people. Likewise, the people changed the status, de minore capitulo ex causa. §. penul. Others say that even against the superior it is prescribed: and therefore the superior is excluded, unless he be a prince, who has absolute power. hence cities, and Castles are well prescribed, says Innocen. de postula. capitu. bonae. more easily, however, they are prescribed by a public person, than by a private, for in those having a symbol, or quasi, the transition is easier. and the opinion of Host. seems to speak of a private person, not of a magistrate. simil. n. similibus gaudent, and they accord with them, but not with dissimilar, and in a way contrary things. I say, that sometimes jurisdiction is prescribed, nevertheless it prescribes against no one, as if someone builds a city under his own name: and there the inhabitants exercise Empire, or the new people themselves exercise all jurisdictional rights: and this Empire is not against rights: for just as a father has sons in his power, if he builds on soil which is granted to the occupier, as Venice sometimes prescribes against someone. and then there is triple prescription. i.e. translative, as if I prescribe your county; ascensive, as if a subject ascends to the jurisdiction of the superior; and accumulative. i.e. when both can use. in doubt, however, he who prescribes excludes the other, as d. l. si quisquam. for the nature of prescription is to run against the negligent, and therefore it excludes him, C. de bon. quae li. l. cum oportet. §. fi. and note. simil. verba. D. de mi. l. etiam ei. in gl.

Let it be concluded that *merum Imperium* can be prescribed,

† but for how long a time, and what kind of act we see. And premise that in the exercise of jurisdiction there is required the act of the person exercising it: and this cannot always be continuous. And the act of the person suffering it, and this is twofold. viz. obedience in doing, and this is discontinuous. And obedience in omitting, and this is continuous. And thus in the sufferer there is a continuous act, just as a slave serves continuously, even when he sleeps, or applauds? because the mind of man possesses, and is possessed. But it is not so in lands, because the mind is not in the land, nor does the land obey man, and therefore servitudes are rather of suffering than of obedience. D. de serv. l. quotiens. Furthermore premise, that for prescriptions civil possession in act suffices, if natural possession is in potency. But if the pursuit of natural possession is difficult, then in a person civil possession suffices: but in another movable thing possession is lost. D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. si rem mobilem. But in immovables civil possession endures, although it is with difficulty to recover natural possession, unless the man fears, or shows signs of fear. D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. clam possidere. §. fin. and of this I have spoken. C. de serv. fut. l. i. Let us return to our proposition. And it seems to be said, that either the one prescribing has title, and good faith, and prescribes. 10 years between present parties. And 20 between absent parties, or he has good faith, and not title, and then he prescribes 30 years, as l. si quis emptionis. But jurisdiction is equated to dominion. D. de statu hom. l. qui fure. On the contrary it seems, that they are not required, because we are in the prescription of incorporeal things, as D. si serv. l. si quis diuturno. But there it speaks of rights below dominion, but jurisdiction is a right above dominion. D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. universas. §. praetor. Furthermore l. si quis diuturno. has no place in prescriptions of persons, or status, nor even in personal servitudes, as l. fin. C. de praescr. long. temp. It is proved that it is not required, because as regards subjects it is more custom than prescription, and in prescribing custom title is not required, because the consent of both parties has something, although unnamed. To this it contributes that the note in d. c. cum dilecto. gl. in l. cum de in rem verso. D. de usur. says, that in prescribing servitudes of free persons long time does not suffice. And the same note C. de agr. et cens. l. litibus. and l. scimus. per Andreas de Baiso.

† What shall we say? Observe: either I wish to prescribe jurisdiction fully in the domain of ownership, so that I can sell it or grant it in fief; or [I wish to prescribe it] in fief. In the first case, if I wish to transfer to myself the jurisdiction which another holds, then, just as one who prescribes a fief prescribes whatever is planted or rooted therein, so this jurisdiction, as though planted and annexed to the territory, is prescribed in such a way that it cannot be divided. Cf. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis; and l. aquae ductus; X. de iure patronatus, c. ex literis; de re iudicata, c. cum Bertoldus. But if I wish to create a new empire and subjection over free peoples, then thirty years are required. For example, if the inhabitants of this castle were not bound to the king except for 26 denarii in one year, and in all other respects were sui iuris, and I wish to prescribe them as subjects, the longest period of time must intervene, because they change their status. But in the first case they do not change their status, but only the ownership, although this sometimes causes harm. Cf. D. de fideicommissis, lib. l. inuitus. In the second case, when I wish to prescribe in fief, and thus a subordinate jurisdiction, the text in c. si quis per 30 requires thirty years.

† I say that either the matter concerns a fief being transferred, or one being newly formed. In the first case, a long time suffices; in the second, a very long time is required. Hence, if you hold a fief which I have purchased in good faith from another with the consent of the lord of the fief, I shall prescribe against you by a long time, and I shall be the sole and undivided feudatory, just as in the meantime I was the sole and undivided possessor of the fief, as stated in the aforementioned law *Quisquam*, *de causa possessionis*; and in the chapter *Cum ecclesia*. For possession regulates and governs prescriptions. *Digestum*, *de ictu, actuque privato*, law 1, § *Iulianus*. But Guillaume de Cuy in the law *Imperium*, and Cynus in law 1, *de emancipatis liberis*, say that prescription for extending jurisdiction is acquired by a long time, because the extension of ordinary jurisdiction is favorable and is easily effected by any consent. *Digestum*, *de iudicibus*, law 1. But if it is to be newly acquired by one who otherwise has no jurisdiction, then a time is required of which there is no memory to the contrary, because it has a discontinuous cause, as in § *Ductus aquae*. I do not approve of this statement, because in prescribing a prescription I consider three things. First, the act of the superior who knows and suffers. I call "superior" him to whom that place belongs by the nature of the place, i.e., by its situation, as in *Digestum*, *de iudicibus*, law *Insulae*; as is here the Lady Queen, because the whole soil of the kingdom is hers, as in the chapter *Cum urbem*. For without this knowledge, prescription does not proceed. *Extra*, *de postulando*, chapter *Bonae*; *de aqua et aquae pluviae arcendae*, law 2, § *Peperit*, according to Bartolus; *Digestum*, *de publicanis*, law *Si publicanus*, according to Bartolus. And certainly this knowledge and suffering has a continuous cause. *Digestum*, *de contrahenda stipulatione*, law *Magnam*. Second, the act of the prescriber, and this in its general nature is continuous, because the tribunal has perpetual statutes, and its bans are always in force. *de haereticis* and law *Ariani*. But in individual acts it is not continuous, because judgment is not always rendered. *de feriis*, law *Finis*. Third, I consider the act of the inferior who obeys, and as regards obedience, suffering, and silence, there is no doubt that it is continuous. Argument from law *Dedi*, in the beginning, *Digestum*, *de conditione ob causam*. For the rebellion of one does not take away possession from all, but the rebellion of all universally does so; see *Digestum*, *de captivis*, law *Hostes*, according to Bartolus. Certainly it is not so in the servitude of a water conduit, because estates are not said to obey. Hence passive possession is not founded on intent, but is established by fact. And therefore natural quasi-possession is considered there, not quasi-civil, as in *Institutiones*, *de actionibus*, § *Aeque in electione*. Jacobus Butrigarius proves this in § *Ductus aquae*. I introduce time for the cause, but here I allege a cause from elsewhere for the firmness of the cause. Time properly does not have a cause in itself, nor is time placed among causes, which are only four; although Seneca in a certain epistle says there are more than four, and among other causes, natural and accidental, he places place and time. But here a doubt arises: when there is a certain legal disposition to which the act specially pertains, and right is presumed there to be in bad faith without title, as in the aforementioned chapter *Ad decimas*. Therefore it is false that I said about the thirty-year prescription. Solution: The jurisdiction, whatever it is, is not the same as the jurisdiction of the Lady Queen, just as when I prescribe a servitude on your land, I prescribe a right which is not yours, because your thing does not serve you. For the understanding of the reason of that chapter, see Bartolus in law 1, § 1, *Digestum*, *de ictu, actuque privato*.

It remains to be considered regarding the quality of acts. And know that the acts must be of the nature or within the power of that jurisdiction which is being prescribed; otherwise, possession is not acquired from them. For example, if I prove that my ancestors appointed notaries in such a castle, I do not prove that I have any territorial jurisdiction, but rather one derived from privilege, and this is distinct from the cause of territory. Hence, possession of one does not imply possession of the other, just as I do not prove that I possessed an inheritance by possessing something extraneous to it, unless it is proven that such thing pertains to that inheritance. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. gerit. But if it were such a thing that naturally, that is, by common law, pertains to territory, such as cognizance of causes, then having proven such use, quasi-possession of that dignity or jurisdiction is proven. Extravagantes de officio Archiepiscopi, c. ut nostrum, according to Innocentius. And although it is proven that someone, as Bishop of Perugia, legitimated bastards or granted licenses to doctoral candidates, it is not proven that he is in possession of the dignity, unless a privilege is produced, by which it is proven that this right belongs to the aforementioned dignity, according to Johannes Andreas, which is noteworthy. And the reason is: because it does not prove this to be so, and c. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. pro haerede, § Pomp. C. unde legitima, l. non hoc. And therefore, if his privilege or prescription were taken away, he would nevertheless not lose possession of the dignity, because they are not from the same head. Argumentum D. de servitutibus urbanis praediorum, l. si domus and l. si edes. It is clear, therefore, that these are different habits, because habits are known by privations, D. de bonis liberis, l. si filius in principio.

† Hence, let us see whether prescription is extended: and since there are four kinds of prorogations, if jurisdiction to cognize of wrongs was prescribed from time to time within a month, can it cognize after the month? And say that it cannot, by the authority of prescription. Arg. D. de leg. 2, l. Statutum, § Stichus; C. communia de leg., l. Si. But if he was impeded on account of a just impediment, then by the reason of the common law it can cognize. C. de adul., l. Fin.; D. de mino., l. Intra utile, l. Prospexit, § Seius; D. qui et a quibus. Which is not pleasing, rather it is excluded, arg. D. de condi. inser., l. Legatum. And this is true, unless the parties themselves prorogated, for this can be done except in fiefs, where prorogation is not valid: because it is made over the thing of another, namely over the lord’s own right. D. de iud., c. Certum; Extr. de for. comp., c. Verum, per Innocentius. And office and prorogation are said to be one and the same, if, however, it is of the same form and nature; otherwise, if of another, as c. Hi qui, Extr. de praeb., lib. 6, in the gloss. Or. and arg. D. loc., l. Cum plures, § Legem dictam. Likewise otherwise if it comes to extinguish the office or effect which was induced by the first course: because then it is not said to be the same. D. de verb. obl., l. Cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo; D. de praet. stip., l. Si Valerianus. And these are true, if the limit of time is attached to the jurisdiction, and the action is extended, the jurisdiction is extended, because it extends to incidental matters. Arg. C. de iud., l. Quotiens.

Secondly, let us consider the matter of persons in relation to persons: here Innocentius states that prescription does not extend, because the persons are not contiguous. Digestum, l. aedes, de capiendo monachum; c. Per dilectos, through Innocentius. Petrus holds that the universal right of custom extends to all persons, but the singular right of prescription does not. Codex, Quae sit longa consuetudo, l. 1, through Cynus; and the aforementioned c. Per dilectos, after Innocentius. And the reason is found in the law: Digestum, De legibus, l. Iura non in singulos. And thus, one who prescribes jurisdiction over a foreign praetor: because they ought to be in different subjects; but if both ought to be in the same subject, i.e., in the same magistracy, jurisdiction would be prescribed against all. Digestum, De officiis praesidis, l. Ex territorio, which is one and the same. And all jurisdiction is prescribed if fruits arise, even if they are not received by nature, but by law. Digestum, De rei venditione, l. Si navis. But a universal act exercised includes all, whereas singular acts do not, as in l. 1, Codex, Quae sit longa consuetudo, through Petrus and Cynus; and Codex, De sacrosanctis ecclesiis, you say that the act itself is more to be considered than the exercise of the act. For by one singular act, nevertheless, if the cause and intention of the user is universal, universal possession of the case is acquired. And therefore, by singular witnesses in singular matters, one and the same universal thing is proved: because what is common results from all. Extra, De accusationibus, c. Qualiter, through Innocentius; De haereticis, c. Quicunque, through Jacobus de Belvis; Digestum, De testibus, l. Ob carmen, §. Finis, in the gloss.

Thirdly, let us consider the matter of things; this may be understood as extending from quantity to quantity within the scope of jurisdiction, or as stating that such matters do not accrue to a prescribed right, but that one who prescribes must be content to stand by the prescribed limits. Argument: in the Authentica *De defensione civium*, § *Iudicare*, Codex *De officio praetoris*. See also L. 1. Therefore, it may be understood as extending from genus to its species. And this is not an extension, but an inclusion and predication; thus, as in L. *Imperium*. Conversely, from species to genus: because all, or the majority of, species represent the qualities of the whole. Argument: L. *Arg.*, Digest *De legatis tertio*; L. *Si chorus*. Thirdly, it may be understood with respect to a subordinate case: for example, if an Archdeacon has prescribed jurisdiction in patronal churches, whether, if the patrons do not choose, he is deemed to have prescribed the right of collation. And it seems that he has not, because upon this case, which never occurred throughout the entire prescription, a common act cannot be founded; therefore, neither custom nor a singular act; therefore, neither prescription. Some say that the bishop succeeds to negligent patrons in the presentation competent to them, and thus the bishop will present to the Archdeacon, and the Archdeacon will institute; which is not pleasing, because this would be to change the form anciently established in L. *Quidam decedens*, in the beginning, Digest *De administratione tutorum*. And therefore I hold that, since the Archdeacon has prescribed episcopal jurisdiction in his archdeaconry in the principal matter, he has also prescribed it in the accessory; which is otherwise taken by force of the Authentica. For even prescribed rights have tacit accessories. Digest *De coniunctione praediorum*, L. *Refectionis*, § *Si*. And this is confirmed, because if the institution did not pertain to the bishop, devolution would not occur to him. Moreover, if this devolution were made by the bishop, it would be made by a leap, and without a beginning. Moreover, the delay of the creditor ought to benefit the debtor; the delay of a third party, the patrons, ought not to give right to the Archdeacon. Moreover, this right, which is held consecutively, and a subsequent acquisition from the beginning of the title, is held as such. Digest *De impositione lucrativae descriptionis*, L. 1, Book 10. Moreover, this time for performing is introduced in favor of the church, and of him who has the right to order it with a rector; therefore, it is acquired by him. Argument: Codex *De legibus*, L. *Pe*. However, the contrary could be said: because from two rights, the bishop loses only one, namely, the right of instituting; the remainder remains in the quill; therefore, we stand in the common law in prescription, just as in privilege, which is not extended. Digest *De vulgari substitutione*, L. *Ex facto*; Solus Maximus, L. *Si cum dotem*, in the beginning. Nor, when the privilege ceases, do we stand in the common law. Digest *De excusationibus tutorum*, L. *Sed et milites*, in the beginning. Nor will anyone say that ordinary jurisdiction is favorable; therefore, it is to be extended; because this is odious in the mode of acquisition, because the mode of acquiring by prescription is not favorable; by one reason of the mode, the effect is restricted. And this I believe to be truer, because jurisdiction in this step ascends. And it is similar that the chapter succeeds, while the see is vacant, in the natural jurisdiction of the bishop; not in the prescribed, or in the privileged, which exorbitates from the rule of the common law. Digest *De legibus*, L. *In his*; Extra *De foro competenti*, C. *Verum*, in the Novella at the end. For the right which is given to a prelate by election, upon his death, returns to his chapter as to its own stock; otherwise in foreign rights prescribed or privileged. Which note.

Fourthly, let us consider places. A place is twofold: namely, definitive or circumscriptive, and it is not permitted to transgress these boundaries. D. de aedil. edict. l. quid sit fugitivus, § idem Cecilius. Another is an occasioning and demonstrative place: for example, because the offense was committed within the castle, not outside, nor beyond one mile. And this place does not circumscribe jurisdiction, but rather the offense, as in D. de accusat. l. libellorum. In case of doubt, I hold that a place within jurisdiction does not limit prescription inwardly, because the whole is contiguous. D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. 3, in principio; D. de serv. rust. praed. l. una est via. And he who cuts off an ear has prescribed to the entire *merum imperium*. D. de furt. l. ultima, in principio; D. de agr. et cens. l. cum scimus. And universal possession does not require all acts, but requires aptitude. D. de serv. urb. praed. l. haec autem iura; l. si servitus; and l. stillicidii, § si, quemadmodum serv. amitt. And a non-occurring case does not restrict prescription, or the quality of its jurisdiction, as in C. de decur. l. in filiis, lib. 10, even if the case were to occur. D. de serv. rust. praed. l. attilicinus; and the aforementioned l. 3, de act. poss.

† Now let us see whether the prescribed jurisdiction is transmitted. And it seems to be said that either a personal title is alleged, and it is not transmitted; or a real one, and it is transmitted; or it is doubtful, and then, because the nature of prescriptions is that the party avails himself of the accession of his author, I think it is transmitted, unless the right is personal, such as the usufruct of another’s jurisdiction. If anyone, however, exercises jurisdiction by concession, it does not pass to successors, because a concession is personal, i.e., a commission; but a grant is presumed to be real, i.e., transmissible. Hence, in a commission, the accession of time has no place, because it is extinguished with the person. But in a donation it is so: and in a fief, and in the lease of jurisdiction, and in the sale of fruits, C. loc. l. viam veritatis. ff. de serv. leg. l. pater. per Bar. But mere offices are not transmitted, as ff. de cura. fu. l. cuiusl. Therefore, a commissioned militia is not transmitted, but a purchased one is transmitted, de col. l. illam. §. si. ff. de mil. test. l. 3. §. si quid. ff. de acce. l. diem functo. 11 On the fifth principal question, namely

† Whether a prescription induces the deprivation of another. Say that either one prescribes before being subject to another, as if over another, or as if apart from another. In the first case, he does not deprive another according to the order which he prescribed for that thing, from which he cannot be hindered by a superior. 11. q. 1. c. Per personas. According to the Archdeacon, because inferiors do not derogate from superiors, nevertheless superiors ought not to suppress or oppress inferiors. C. de officiis praefecti urbi, l. 1; C. de appellationibus, l. Nihil, li. 12. In the second case, he does not deprive him of his being, but of his rank in being, because he makes himself lesser by submitting himself to a lesser person, which is to submit oneself to oneself. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. A receptum; and by that very submission he becomes base. Therefore, he ought to preserve the rank which he established for himself. D. de adoptionibus, l. Qui liber; D. de minoribus, l. Ex causa, § Pomponius; C. de liberis et eorum liberis, l. Si, § Si. In the third case, I hold that the prescriber claims the right entirely for himself, which he alone has used. D. de diversis prescriptionibus, l. Si quisquam.

And therefore it appears that if the parish priest has prescribed the right of institution in his parish, the bishop should in no way interfere. This holds true if he held possession by excluding the bishop; otherwise, if by mere tolerance, because negative rights are not acquired by prescription except against those who suffer them under prohibition, not against those who merely tolerate, as in C. de servis et aqua, l. 2, according to Petrus and Cynus. Therefore, in this case, although the parish priest has custom in his favor, nevertheless the bishop is not thereby excluded from the common law. And he to whom the patrons present shall appoint these persons, because the power is cumulative, not absorbed, and thus it is practiced by Florentinus himself and the parish priests, which is to be noted. Sixth, and last principal question 13

It appears from the aforesaid that the matter is most clearly resolved by the Archdeacon in the cited chapter *de persona*. And note that four causes are subject to devolution by operation of law, namely: appeal, nullity, and negligence, as stated in the Authenticum *de quaestore*, § *si vero aliqui*; furthermore, death, in the cases expressly provided for in law, as in the Extravagant *de haereticis*, chapter *ad abolendum*, according to Innocentius. Finally, know that Nicolaus Matarellus disputed this matter; but, by your grace, I have said better and more learned things to you. Thanks be to God. Neither praise yourself nor blame him; this is what fools do, whom empty glory torments. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a simple division is deemed to constitute a renunciation of the restitution granted after the death of the parties making the division.
2. Whether a renunciation of a fideicommissum is valid.
3. What clauses imply a tacit renunciation of a fideicommissum.
body: The facts are alleged to be as follows. Francis died having made his will, leaving his legitimate sons Jacob, Anthony, and Benedict, instituted as heirs in equal shares. Anthony and Benedict were under the age of fourteen, whereas Jacob was of age. In this will, he left many legacies, and among other things, he stated that if any of his sons should die without children, or in pupillary status, that his share of the inheritance should devolve upon his surviving brothers, or the heirs of the others; and if all his heirs should die without legitimate children, then he wished, etc. Afterwards, the said Jacob, having reached the age of twenty-five on one side, and the said Anthony and Benedict, having reached the age of fourteen but being under twenty on the other side, divided the paternal goods which they had received by the said will, in such a way that the said Jacob had one part, promising to do nothing, nor in any way contravene; and the parties promised against the division to do nothing; and one constituted the other as procurator, and the other constituted the one in his own right with respect to the part allotted to the other. And they gave and granted to each other an action, and promised warranty against eviction with respect to any person. Furthermore, in the said division, they made release and settlement among themselves in this form: the aforementioned Jacob, Anthony, and Benedict, brothers among themselves, made settlement, remission, discharge, and agreement not to sue further, and most complete release and absolution, concerning that which one from the other could demand, exact, or pursue now and in the future, on the occasion of any agreement, or by any reason or cause, affirming that the brothers, and each of them, were well and fully satisfied of all and the whole of that which one from the other ought to receive on the occasion of the said goods, and of their said father, and of any other inheritance and possession; promising to observe and keep all and each thing in the instrument of division under a certain penalty. And from this, the said Anthony, having reached the age of twenty-five, made his will, in which he instituted the said Benedict as universal heir; and he left one hundred to the said Jacob, who Jacob attempts to impugn the said will made by Anthony, and the said institution made of the said Benedict; because Anthony died without issue; and thus he says that there is place for the fideicommissary substitution; and that he ought to have a share of the goods of the said Anthony with the said Benedict, and also the legacy. It is asked, what is the law? namely, whether the said substitution made by the said Francis is direct, pupillary, or fideicommissary? but assuming that it is fideicommissary after puberty, what and how great a share of the goods comes into the restitution of the fideicommissum to the said Jacob? Thirdly, whether that restitution was renounced by the said division, assuming that from the will of the said Francis, legacies were paid by his heirs and fideicommissaries. This matter is not new, but obscure on account of the doubt of the doctors. Nevertheless, the aforementioned are two indubitable cases.

† The first case is that, by a simple division, it does not appear that restitution of collations after the death of the dividing parties has been waived; and this holds whether the division is made by a judge, because a judge cannot derogate from a future right, or whether the division is voluntary and conventional; because acts which derive their force from a past cause do not, however, include the future, as in D. de legatis 2, l. compater, § haereditatem; D. de transactionibus, l. qui cum tutoribus; D. de verbis obligatorum, l. si a colono and l. si stipulamur; and as is noted in C. quae res pignori obligari possunt, l. fin.

The second case is that if the right of the fideicommissum is expressly remitted, the remission is valid. C. de pact. l. 1. To such an extent that the injured minor is not considered, since this hope is rejected by him and from him. C. de transa. l. fideicommissi. For when equal benefit and prejudice are required, neither is injured: as C. de inof. testa. l. si pater puellae. And these two cases are outside our case: because here there was neither a bare division standing in the mere limits of division, nor was there an express renunciation by the fideicommissary. Let us therefore see whether the clauses placed here imply a tacit renunciation of a future and uncertain fideicommissum; but it must be said that they do, because of that clause, "unless they shall do the contrary," etc. as noted in ff. de ver. obli. l. qui Romae. §. duo fratres. according to one reading. And this is held by Dy. Gul. de Cu. And this is true, said the learned Dy., because those dividing knew the testament, since one who is ignorant does not seem to remit. ff. de ac. et ob. l. ex maleficiis. §. longe minus. And thus the learned Dy. advised, and Io. An. holds. This is more strongly confirmed because here not only does the promise hold, but also the remission, and the quieting, and the general settlement; therefore it is valid generally in all things, as l. emptor. §. Lucius. ff. de pac. For although two contracts are written in one document, namely the division per se, there, "furthermore," etc., and it is noted that there it says "on the occasion of his said father." For what can these words signify, unless the paternal testament, which proceeds from the father? Also, here are those words, "could now, or in the future." And therefore the right of the fideicommissum necessarily seems to be included; otherwise, this speech would accomplish nothing, whereas it ought to accomplish something, as ff. de fun. instr. l. fundus, qui locatus est. and l. si quando. de lega. 1. For words are not introduced unless their virtue, i.e., meaning, accomplishes something. ff. de suppel. leg. l. Labeo. §. idem tubero.

It is argued to the contrary thus: a special clause restricts a general clause. ff. de condi. inde. l. si. §. idem quaesivit. de excep. l. si ex ma. C. de exceptio. l. licet. But the special clause is the division itself, to whose strength the other clauses are inserted: for they are placed incidentally; therefore, they are understood according to the nature of divisions, and as long as this division lasts, these clauses last: not beyond, because when the principal is destroyed, the appendices are destroyed, as noted in l. si patronus. §. 2. ff. si quid in frau. pa. But after the restitution of the fideicommissary, that which was divided among several persons returns to the same person, and thus the division is confused. ff. de sol. l. Stichum. §. aditio. and l. si haeres. ad Treb. Therefore, it seems to be concluded that since in this contract there is no mention of the testament, nor of the fideicommissum, the right of the fideicommissary is not considered to be remitted to him, as l. de his. ff. de transa. For rights which begin after the death of another require a special remission, as l. si quando. C. de inoffi. testamento. For it does not seem that the case was contemplated, which cannot be hoped for except with unfortunate fortune, such as the death of a brother, and similar things, arg. ff. de condi. et demon. l. cum tale. in prin. and l. pater seuerinam. §. socrus. It is proved: the cause of the liberation itself declares the effect of the liberation; for that to which the cause is adapted, the effect can be adapted: and the effect takes its status from the cause. ff. de sol. l. si ex plurib. de transa. l. cum Aquiliana. and l. cum. §. causa. But the cause of the repudiation is not this giving, but the satisfaction, which was uncertain as to whether and to whom, as de leg. 1. l. filius. §. diui. But when it is uncertain whether, but certain to whom, as in a fideicommissum where the commission is from one side only, that fideicommissum can be restored in the meantime, not, however, by the authority of the Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, but by the liberality on which the testament relies, as C. de fideicom. l. post mortem. ff. ad Treb. l. sed si. ante. argu. l. 3. §. qui fideicommissam. ff. de haere. instit. In our case, therefore, satisfaction did not fall, therefore neither can the deliberation made from that cause extend to this fideicommissum. For an oath adds consent, but is strengthened to confirm the contract, as C. de non nu. pe. l. si.

Solution: either the dividing parties were ignorant of the testament, or they knew it, or it is doubtful. In the first case, it is certain that this remission does not harm, as d. l. de his. nor the division, as d. §. haereditatem. In the second case, it is certain that it harms according to Dy. Gul. and Ioan. And. But Pe. says it does not harm, since no mention was made of the testament. For it was easy to remit, if he had wished. l. vnica. §. si autem deficientis. C. de cad. tol. In the third case, ignorance of fact is presumed, as l. eius, qui in prouincia. ff. si cert. pe. For in his heirs, knowledge of the testament is not presumed according to Bart. But that law does not say this: because this was for abundance in d. l. eius, qui. However, after the inheritance has been accepted, knowledge of the fact of the testament is always presumed, as noted in l. cum haeredes. ff. de liberatione leg. For he who pays a legacy cannot excuse himself by saying he did not see the testament, unless it is clearly proved, as C. de cond. indeb. l. si. in fi. But it must be observed that these were minors, in whom knowledge of law is not presumed, i.e., that they knew the force and power of that constitutional fideicommissum, nor were they certified, as noted ff. de verb. ob. l. sciendum. In the gloss and by Dy. To this they are specially induced. ff. qui satis. cog. l. de die. §. minori. And although an oath presents one as an adult, they cannot be said to know it, according to Dyn. and others.

What is finally to be concluded? Pregnant words induce danger for the one who utters them. C. de do. promi. l. si. in fi. But because I do not find that the pact was gratuitous, but from the cause of satisfaction, I believe the right of the fideicommissum is not included in the restitution, nor in these pacts, and especially because in a minor remitting some right, knowledge is never presumed, unless he has been certified of the right of its effect, as noted ff. de rei vendi. l. 2. per Cyn. Nor is it presumed that he wishes to throw away, as l. cum de indebito. ff. de prob. And he who renounces, throws away, ff. de noua. l. si quis delegauerit. Notwithstanding what is noted by Bar. in §. duo fratres. in 6. q. because it must be understood in those who are presumed to know the law and the fact. Otherwise in minors. Also, it speaks of renunciation, where a restrictive cause was added, argu. ff. de acqui. pos. l. si qui animo. It is proved: if he felt otherwise, let him do so. For I think true what I said. And in 8. qu. also when he speaks of procur. in rem suam, let him speak ambiguities, because this is understood according to the nature of division, as C. man. l. per diuersas. §. excep. And therefore conclusively I stand on this, that the right of the fideicommissary was not remitted, and in doubt let us favor the testament. That doubt is not that this substitution was, and is, after the puberty of the fideicommissary, as noted in l. precibus. C. de impuber. et alijs substitu. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether bastards are said to be of the household and of the close relatives, so that a bastard son is included in the statute speaking of parricide. nu. 3.
2. Whether one who has been permitted to be injured may be killed.
body: For the sake of clarity, certain matters must be sent to P in the form of questions.

† And first, whether bastards are said to be of the household, and of relatives up to the fourth degree, assuming that this bastard son is the son of the offended party. And it seems that they are not said to be of the household, nor are they said to be relatives. And this is supported by several reasons. And first, because civil terms, such as these terms "of the household" or "family," do not apply to bastards, among whom there is no civil significance, as noted by Bartolus in l. fin. C. de verbis significandis; nor can such base men be called relatives, except improperly, and by extension of the word. C. de natu. lib. l. si. in fi. Since, in them, not only in bastards but also in natural children, no legitimate connection is found, one cannot properly assign a degree there, as is clear from the same law, postprin. Now it is certain that statutes contrary to the law do not receive an extensive interpretation, as ff. sol. ma. l. si vero. §. de viro. Therefore, this statute is not extended to natural children, much less to bastards. But this is proven, because if a bastard is not admitted even in part to bring an action, as noted by Innocentius and Ioannes Andreas in c. nonnulli. in fin. extra de reciprocis, therefore much less to kill. For it would be absurd to deny civil acts and permit criminal ones. C. de iudiciis. l. nullus. Thirdly, this is proven: the word "relatives" pronounced by the law must be understood as referring to those legitimately related, not to an unjust connection, which does not even deserve the name. Hence, it cannot possess those things attributed to the name, as ff. de in ius vocando. l. quicquam. §. fin. and l. sed si hac. §. patronum. C. de advocatis. l. verba. ff. de ritu nuptiarum. l. lex Iulia. §. nec distinguitur. Fourthly, and lastly, this is proven, because whenever it is a matter of favors, bastards are not included; but where it is a matter of excluding them from civil favors and benefits, then they are included, as noted in the glossa ordinaria in c. 1. de baptismo in cle.

To the contrary, it is argued thus: according to common usage of speech, bastards are said to be of the household, and the common people so designate them; therefore, considering the vulgar sense, which derogates from every strict meaning, bastards are said to be of the household. l. liberorum. §. quod tamen Cassius. ff. de legatis 3. Secondly, it is proven thus, for sometimes "being of the household" can be understood in two ways: namely, naturally, and according to legal fiction, for nature is common. ff. de accusationibus. l. hos accusare. §. omnibus. And the mode of generation is the same in the legitimate and the bastard, for both are from seed, as noted ff. de iustitia et iure. l. 1. §. hinc descendit. on the word, "conjugated." But in statutes, one should rather look to natural truth, if it can be adapted to the tacit reason of the statute, than to legal fiction, which cannot separate the immutable truth of nature with other bones. ff. de liberis et postumis. l. filio. For the roots of nature cannot be eradicated. And by the law of equality, even bastards are written as sons; and if sons, therefore relatives in the first degree, as extra de eo, qui duxit in matrimonium quam pollicitus per adulterium. c. cum haberet. And if you judge that this term "of the household" is civil, and thus the law using civil terms must be understood civilly, as ff. de capite diminuto. l. tutelas. I certainly deny this, because rather the fact is noted, as C. si quicunque praediorum possessione. l. 1. where "with his own household and those of his," hence even one born from a concubine is said to be domestic, as ff. de verbis significandis. l. Masurius. otherwise beginning "concubine." And this is manifest from nature, hence it does not need proof of laws. ff. de verbis obligandis. l. ubi autem. And in principle, when nature alone prescribed for men, one name was for all sons. Later, differences of names arose from the injustice of embraces; finally, the benefit of legitimation supervened; and thus more species of sons began to exist, yet the genus is represented in any species, and if it were in bastards, it is not totally eradicated from them, as in Auth. qui modo naturales efficiuntur sui. post prin. §. 2. otherwise 3. coll. 7. and qui modo naturales efficiuntur legitimi. §. 1. coll. 6. Thirdly, it is proven thus: where nature alone prescribes for men, as in those things which proceed from the instinct of nature; as that one loves his own flesh, and that one hates his enemy; there civil status is not considered, but only the natural. Hence it is that in the statute on parricide, even a bastard is included, although it was consulted to the contrary in Florence, and wrongly. The words are of Master Cynus in the said §. nec distinguitur. in his additions. So it is in the case at hand; therefore, the bastard son is included. Fourthly, it is proven from a certain statute of the city of Florence, which extends the name of household and relatives to bastards, by which it gives to be understood the common and general usage of speech. Also, what is given to be understood in one case, is given to be understood in its similar, as ff. de legibus. l. non potest. C. de revocatione donationis. l. his solis. and ff. ad Trebellianum. l. qui filium. and noted in l. 1. C. ut quae de sunt aduocatis partium. cum si. Fifthly, and lastly, it is proven thus, because in indifferent matters we should not make a difference between the legitimate and the non-legitimate, as ff. de ritu nuptiarum. l. adoptivus. §. serviles. verso. unde nec vulgo. and C. de interdictione matrimonii. l. libertinum. But we are in an indifferent matter, because in this matter affection is considered, which is natural, as ff. de iustitia et iure. l. ut vim. And sometimes a bastard is more affected towards his father than a legitimate one; therefore, by reason of natural affection and innate charity. The same is to be understood in both: because the part of affection usually induces parity of permission, as ff. de ritu nuptiarum. l. non solum. §. de uno. And this is the truth, because it is clear that Gaspar, the bastard, could take vengeance for his father on the person of Ugutione; for the most just pain reaches even to the bastard son and the sword of paternal anxiety passes through him. To the contrary arguments, it is responded: because cases must be distinguished according to the subject matters and reasons.

† Conversely, it is asked whether one who is permitted to be offended is deemed permitted to be killed: this is an ancient question of Martinus de Saxonia. And it seems that the answer is no, because the powerful person has the right to offend the offender just as a debtor stands in relation to a creditor. I say "debitor" in the generic sense: but where the obligation is not most harsh, but most mild, as in D. de pign. act. l. obligatione generali. Hence, here he cannot be killed: but otherwise he may be lightly offended, as it were by way of correction, as in C. de emend. serv. l. 1. Secondly, this is proven, for the power of the supreme sword, by which life is taken away, does not seem to be granted to anyone unless it is specially granted by the authority of the law. C. de malefic. et mathematic. l. si; D. de officio eius, cuius man. est iurisdict. l. 1. Thirdly, this is proven, because if he could be killed, the punishment would be greater than the fault and the crime, which ought not to be the case according to that rule, "tooth for tooth." Inst. de iniuriis § poena gravior. Fourthly, this is proven, because an offense is a bodily affliction concerning death; but one who is dead is not said to be offended, but more than offended, just as it is one thing to impair the eyes and another to totally obscure them, as in D. de serv. urb. praed. l. binas aedes. Fifthly, and finally, this is proven by such reasoning. It is certain that the ability to be offended is a punishment. It is also certain that by these general words this punishment is not determined: therefore, it is left to the discretion of a good man as to what kind and how much offense is permitted. D. de effr. et expilat. l. 1 § expilatores.

To the contrary, it is argued thus. It is certain that the statute contemplates any offense, even the most serious, when the offended party had been offended with a scar or debilitation of a limb. But no one can moderate heavy blows, nor is it within the power of the striker to temper serious wounds so as not to cause death, as in c. ult. de homic. lib. 6. Secondly, this is proven: to whom the antecedent is permitted, i.e., to wound, the consequent is permitted: hence, it was formerly permitted to a father to kill his son, and by this it was lawful to kill. D. de lib. et post. l. in suis. Thirdly, this is proven, because the desire for death can cause another to be handed over to the mountain, the law permitting. D. ad Sil. l. et si certus § si appetitus; D. ad l. Aquil. l. sed et si quae mecum; D. de verb. oblig. l. qui servum; D. de leg. 1 l. quid ergo § si heres hominem; and note C. quod met. causa l. accus. Fourthly, this is proven, because here a duel is permitted to the offended party, therefore he can kill, as in D. ad l. Corn. de sicar. l. 3 § transfugas; C. de his, qui confugiunt ad eccles. l. si suus. Fifthly, this is proven: because l. generaliter speaks generally, and therefore to warn men, and to destroy those who feed on blood, it must be understood generally and most strictly, since this is expedient for the republic. l. 1 C. ad l. Iul. repetund.; D. de aleator. l. 1 § quod autem.

And this is the truth itself, considering that this permission was not made by the statute except for the most serious fault, and which according to the rigor of civil law would be capital, as in l. is, qui cum telo. Therefore, it is concluded that the said Gaspar, having been killed, could have been killed: and what has been done lawfully does not deserve punishment. C. de adulter. l. Gracchus. It is not an obstacle that the said person had been restored in integrum: because that is with respect to the fisc, not with respect to the adversary, as noted by Bartolus in C. in ius vocand. l. venia. And by this, many laws are answered.
