But the first conclusion regarding the permission of bastards seems to be obstructed by those words of the statute, which say "understanding the degree according to civil law." For a bastard according to civil law does not merit a degree. But I answer that those words are not placed to exclude natural law, but canonical law, as in Extra de consanguin. et affinit. c. non debet. And this is clear from the end of that statute, which speaks of bastards: and therefore by this statute this question is settled. And because a son is said by the Philosopher to be love, l. liberorum and l. isti quidem, and the statute wished to cure just anguish and sobs by the aid of vengeance, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the house of one person is burned down, and the fire grew and spread so much that the neighbor's house also caught fire, whether the neighbor can claim compensation for his damage.
2. Whether one is presumed to have started the fire, or whether, in case of doubt, fault, fraud, or fortuitous accident is presumed.
body: A certain Ponine Rtestorius of Cortona had his own house, which, due to slight care and custody, was set on fire, whereby the neighbor's house was burned down.

† It is asked whether he is bound to pay the damages caused, etc. A fire sometimes arises by chance without any fault; and then affliction should not be added to the afflicted; hence from such a fire one is not bound to another. D. 17.2.3 (pro socio), l. cum duobus, § damna fatalia. And this neighbor, whose house has been burned or demolished, can bring an action. D. 9.2.1 (ad leg. Aquiliam), l. si quis fumo, § quidam dicitur; and D. 43.24.1 (quod vi aut clam), l. si alius, § est et alia; and there by Bartolus expressly. And therefore it affects the case. Jacobus de Belvisi says that when one house is demolished for the safety of the whole neighborhood, so that the fire does not consume everything, that it is to be contributed to that damage by all the neighbors; as is done with the jettison of goods for saving a ship. L. 2 ad leg. Rhodiam de iactu; and he speaks of demolition, not of burning. And both of these say what is true. Or a fire arises from fault; and then either from the fault of a certain person, or of an uncertain one. If indeed from the fault of a certain person, he is bound to repair the damage of burning, otherwise called arson, because fault even proceeding in one’s own thing usually binds in another’s thing. D. 9.2.27 (ad leg. Aquiliam), l. qui occidit, § in hac; and D. 9.2.27, l. si servus servum, § si quis insulam; because one should not draw another into danger. D. 9.2.27, § si fornicarius, and there noted. But if of a certain person, the owner of the first house burned is bound, because the act of a certain person must be proved. L. licet, § fi, D. 14.2 (nautae, caupones, stabularii); and since this on the part of the defendant contains a mere penalty.

† In doubt, however, those are presumed to have set the fire who were accustomed to making fire there, and from them the truth concerning the fault and the guilty party ought to be inquired. D. 19.2.1 (Dominus horreorum). Whether, however, in doubt fault is presumed, or that the fire arose by accident: for usually, as it most often happens, D. 48.13.3 (De officio praefecti vigilum) and D. 18.6.1 (Si vendita), it can be said that if it is not established by any judgment who set the fire, and the owner was accustomed to be watchful and diligent, that the owner is not liable in doubt. Arg. D. 49.16.1 (Si omnes), §. A barbaris; D. 14.2.1 (Argentum). Or if he was a man of little circumspection, or negligent, so that he himself made the fire, he is liable. D. 19.2.1 (Si quis fundum), §. Si colonus. He ought to be diligent in himself and his household, as D. 9.2.27.1 (Si servus servum), §. Proculus; and D. 47.11.1 (Fur adversus naves). He does not answer for an external event nor for the accident of winds, if by the force of the winds the fire burned more than usual. D. 9.2.27.1, §. In hac. It is relevant: D. 39.5.1 (Qui aedes), §. Si vero, with its material. C. 9.17.2. And Inst. 4.3.1, §. Capite. Thirdly, and lastly, if the fire arose from the quality or quantity of the fire, which is presumed from the place by the effect, and the said tenant did not exercise the diligence that men are accustomed to have, he is liable for this damage on account of fault. But if this happened by fortuitous accident, he is not liable, unless it is established by his own act, or by fault, because perhaps he kept boys there who set the fire; otherwise, not. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One who prepares poison to kill someone, and actually attempted to poison him, by what punishment should he be punished. nu. 6.
2. In delicts, the beginning is considered, just as in other acts.
3. How a judge ought to exercise discretion in imposing punishment on one attempting to commit a delict.
1. Arbitrary punishment. Whether it can be extended up to death. nu. 7.
2. One holding poison for the purpose of killing is liable. l. cor. de sica.
3. A judge in matters of discretion may condemn to the punishment of imprisonment.
4. The milder punishment is to be chosen, where there is doubt among the learned regarding the punishment itself.
body: Cechus

He prepared poison with the intent of killing Sempronius, and he attempted to administer it to him; it is asked by what penalty he ought to be punished. It must be known what the title of the crime is, and from this we shall know by what law he will be punished, and finally, in the third place, the kind of penalty will appear: for once the name of the crime is known, the law is known, and once the law is known, the penalty is known. D. de crim. stel. l. 2; §. ubicumque, de falsis; l. quid sit, de poenis; l. sanctio legum. And although it is more serious to poison a man than to kill him simply, as C. de veneficis, l. 1, nevertheless it must be considered here that the act was not consummated, but only attempted and arranged; and it is one thing to attempt, another to carry into effect. Does an attempted crime not carried into execution have the name and definition of a completed crime? For the names of things, as defined, do not apply unless to things perfected, which receive their form from consummation. Hence we do not call him a murderer who attempted to kill by poisoning, nor do we call him one who made an agreement, i.e., who agreed turpitudinally, but him who formally consummated it, or at least began it initially, as if he gave the poison to drink; then, insofar as it depends on him, he completes it, since nothing further was to be done by him; for it is

† In delicts, as in other acts, there is a twofold principle: one remote and preparatory, the other proximate and substantial. D. de cond. ob causam, l. Si pecuniam. For the law, in severely punishing delicts, considers the cause of the wrongs. C. ad l. Iul. de ui, l. Quam multa. And the effects of things, as D. de poenis, l. Aut facta, §. Eventus; and l. Si quis aliquid, §. Qui abortionis; and l. Cicero, D. de poenis. These cease in our case, where there was a remote principle, because he did nothing toward the event, he harmed no body, which was in no way injured: hence it is that one who conspires with some of his accomplices to kill someone is held liable. L. Corn. de sicariis, s. Hodie poena mortis, because he has completed the homicide. C. de episc. audient., l. 3; Inst. de publ. iudic., §. Etiam lex; and in Auth. de pace iur. firm., l. Hac edictali, §. Homicidium; de pace tenend., c. 1, col. 10. However, if he merely conspired and did not consummate, he is not held liable to the penalty. L. Corn. de sicariis; nor to the penalty of that law, but is punished more mildly; he is held liable to the penalty. L. Iul. de ui privata; as C. ad l. Iul. de ui privata, l. Nec interest. Hence it is that they frequently speak in the past tense of the fact, to show that the penalty of the delict requires the perfection of the act in the matter. L. In passo, as D. ad l. Corn. de sicariis, l. 1, in princ., cum si. And especially the statutes of the territories require the act to be perfect, and do not admit an extrinsic extensive interpretation to the imperfect, because there is no legitimate ratio of comparison from the perfect to the imperfect, since it is better to have completed the delict. Let us observe here that sometimes the consummation of the delict is impeded by nature, and one is punished more mildly, as D. de poenis, l. Si quis aliquid, §. Qui nondum; sometimes L. Dicunt, l. Si quis non dicam rapere, C. de episc. et cler. Let us therefore consider the conspiracy to kill Titius, who is absent from me; certainly my conspiracy, things being thus distant, cannot have effect by the nature of things, for on account of the absence the body can suffer nothing from me. D. ad Sill., l. 1, §. Occisorum. Wherefore it is manifestly concluded that the death penalty cannot be imposed in this case, because this name of crime does not have its own species, but is called by the general name of extraordinary crime, as D. de extraord. crim., l. 1, §. Si; or is called by the general term of crime of injury, for which an arbitrary penalty is to be imposed, as C. de iniur., l. Si. For he commits a grievous injury who lays ambushes to another’s life, especially with poison, as C. de repet., l. Consensu, §. Si qua igitur; ad Sill., l. Et si cer., §. Appetitus.

It remains, therefore, to consider how the judge is to exercise his discretion. And it should be known that an arbitrary penalty can be reduced by custom to a certain penalty, as stated in the Digest, *De extraordinariis criminibus*, law *Saccularii*, section *Sunt quaedam*; and noted in the Digest, *De his qui notati sunt infamia*, law *Quid ergo*, section *Poena gravior*. However, this custom is not established by a single act, although an example may be introduced as persuasive, not compulsory, as in the Code, *De senatu*, law *Nemo*. But in the absence of custom, the judge must exercise his discretion equally and after hearing the case, so that he is not less lenient than arbitrators, as noted in Chapter 1, *De re iudicata*, Book 6; nor excessively severe, but with some moderation, as in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Respiciendum*, section *Scaevola*, words *Plane*. If, however, he kills by means of torture, what further punishment could be imposed beyond the death that ensued? Hence I say that he cannot kill or mutilate, as in the Digest, *De effractione*, law 1, section *Fin.*, there, *Dummodo* and following, because there it speaks thus on account of the frequency of offenses. The multitude of individual offenses, let us say, exaggerates the matter, as in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Aut facta*, section *Si*. Hence it has been permitted to judges sometimes to transgress the law, as noted by Innocentius in Chapter 1, *De constitutionibus*.

† Furthermore, it is not to the contrary that which is stated in the Institutiones, De iniuriis, §. Poena, where it is said that an arbitrary penalty may be extended to death; for that statement is true only in respect of completed offenses, but not in respect of uncompleted ones, as is stated in the aforementioned §. Finis. And it accords with what is said by Speculum in the title De accusationibus, under the heading "Quid si primo," where it is stated that capital penalties are not imposed by general custom for uncompleted offenses. The same is held by Cynus in the law Is qui cum telo, Codex, De sicariis, and in the law Si quis non dicam rapere. And this is sufficiently in accordance with natural equity, which those who possess discretion ought to observe most strictly, as if it were a certain law of nations, by argument from the Digest, De re militari, law 1, and De eo quod certo loco, law Quam si Ephesi.

† Moreover, it is not to the point that those who hold poison with the intent to kill are subject to punishment. L. cor. de sica; L. 1, § praeterea; and L. eiusdem, D. de sica. The penalty for which, in terms of its utility, is death, especially for one who is convicted under the chapter on poisoning, as stated in L. eiusdem, § pe. quia. Because this is not observed by custom, as noted in Auth. de pa. iur. fir., § si iniuria, because customs and local statutes require delicts to be established by acts, as I have proven above. And this equity is observed throughout the lands and should not be changed, as stated in L. minime, D. de legibus; and those things which ancient custom has established should be tolerated. Furthermore, that law on poisoning is understood to apply to one who had the effect, as in L. 1, § fin., Q. quisque iuris. But here there was no effect, because the said Francis revealed the matter to the court and to those who were to be poisoned, by which revelation the delict was diminished, since the malicious intent was revoked, which greatly helps in extraordinary crimes, as noted in L. ex hoc edito, § fi., D. de alieni iudicii mutandae causa factae. And to this point it is most fitting that what Innocentius notes in Extra, de homicidio, c. ad audientiam, and the argument in D. de falsis, L. quid sit falsum, although in the edict on calumniators it is of no avail, as argued in D. de calumniis, L. 2 and 3, § si quis igitur, and in D. de infa., L. qui operas. Moreover, it supports this because L. humana requires an act with will, as noted by Innocentius in de sica, c. tua. And therefore the penalty, which is attributed to acts, such as the penalty of irregularity, is not incurred by mere discussion among canonists, as in c. ad audientiam, according to Innocentius; namely, if to discuss and to order require an act, as in D. de adulteriis, L. et si amicos. Otherwise, that thought seems worse than the act, although sometimes it is punished by the penalty of the last supplice, as in D. de his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt, L. fi., in princ. But there it is special, as in D. de partitionibus, L. et si sciente. Because there it is special: therefore, the common law is to the contrary. And it supports what is noted in c. perpetuae, de electionibus, lib. 6, and in D. de conditionibus sine causa, L. annulo. To this point it supports L. saepe, in fi., D. de verbis significationibus, there, and the act followed. And in D. arbori furtim caesae, L. cedere, § sub secare, with many similar cases. It is therefore sufficiently concluded that the penalty of death or of a member cannot be imposed, but because the crime is most heinous in daring and example, another penalty should be imposed.

But which ones? And it is certain that those which are pecuniary, which are in a frequented region. Likewise, I hold that persons of low status in the community may be flogged. Argument: L. 2, § si vero, De crimine maiestatis, especially if it is known that they suffer from poverty, as in C. De servis fugitivis, L. Quicunque; D. De poenis, L. In servos, § si; D. De officiis proconsulis, L. Si quis; De infamia, L. Ictus; De iurisdictione omnium iudicum, L. Magistratus; De officiis praefecti urbis, L. Imperatores. They may also be condemned to temporary imprisonment, because he who has discretion in his hand, that is, governs by his will, is not entirely subject to the law. Argument: D. De origine iuris, L. 2, in principio; Nam omnes leges et constitutiones from the beginning of the world, and from the dawn of human society, were discretionary, and a trace of this remains in cases in which the sanction of the law does not specifically provide, as in the aforementioned § expilatores and L. Sanctio, D. De poenis.

† Hence I say that in matters of arbitration the judge may condemn a free man to a penalty of imprisonment, but not perpetual imprisonment. Cf. D. de origine iuris, l. 2, § exactis. Although the prison was not instituted as a penalty, but for custody, and therefore no person of free birth is condemned to perpetual imprisonment by civil law, as C. de poenis, l. incredibile; D. eodem, l. in mandato. But to temporary imprisonment, yes, as D. de poenis, l. si cum praefinitione. But that law seems to presuppose the ignorance of the judging authority, as the gloss says in the aforementioned l. incredibile. And therefore this part is not well secured, and this penalty of imprisonment is not a capital penalty, unless it were perpetual imprisonment, X. de accusationibus, c. qualiter et quando, according to Innocentius. But perpetual imprisonment does not apply here, both because it is prohibited and because it is not a capital crime. Hence I do not omit to say that this Francis ought to be punished more mildly, since he surrendered himself, than the blind man, namely in an afflictive penalty, such as flogging. Cf. D. ad legem Iuliam de ambitu, l. 1, § qua lege; and cf. D. de re militari, l. qui cum uno, § interdictum; and l. miles igitur. You therefore, Lord Potestas, choose what pleases you, provided you know that a capital penalty cannot be imposed.

† Because where there is doubt concerning the penalty, due to the diverse opinions of the doctors, the lesser one is safer for the magistrate. It is established by what is noted in l. si, C. quae res vendi non possunt. In the gloss on the Ordines, the doctors commonly hold that where another penalty can be imposed, the penalty of imprisonment is not imposed, because imprisonment was not devised as a terminal penalty; but where no other penalty applies, there the penalty of imprisonment may be inflicted in a subsidiary capacity. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, advise, and I have subscribed to this in faith, and sealed it with the seal of my name, advising most faithfully what I myself would do. And see thereon Gandinus, the practical assessor, who says the same in the title de homicidio, under the heading sed pone quaestionem. ego dedi tibi pecuniam etc. And there see what is pleasing.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the assets acquired by the son through his medical practice after the father’s death are to be shared with the brother, or with the nephew with whom he cohabited.
2. Whether the books purchased by the father for the son’s medical practice are to be shared.
3. Whether the fruits of the dowry property are to be shared.
4. Whether the expense incurred for clothing is to be shared.
5. Whether an account of the expenses incurred for the wedding of one of the sons is to be drawn up among the brothers.
6. Where the dowry has been converted to the common benefit, the other brother is liable for the expenses.
body: First, I shall speak regarding the first question, which seems to contain two points within itself. The first is whether acquisitions made

† by Francesco the physician after the death of the common father are to be shared with the other brother, or the nephew through him, with whom he is said to have cohabited, or not? The second is whether books purchased by the father of the said physician for the physician himself are to be shared, or not? And as to the first point, a distinction must be made as to whether the acquisitions made by the aforesaid physician came from the common property—such as, perhaps, from the price of common property voluntarily sold, or from the fruits of those common goods, or from common money with which he traded, or otherwise in any manner whatever on the occasion of those common goods—and in that case it is clear that they must be shared with the brother or nephew, as is clearly proved in ff. pro soc. l. 1. §. j., and l. sed si non mandatum, and l. idemque. §. si ex fundo. ff. de vsu, et habi., and l. si ita. §. fi., and de vul. et pup. substi. l. sed si plures. §. in arrogato; otherwise it would follow that the physician would be enriched through another's loss or sacrifice, which would be contrary to the civil laws, as in ff. de condi. inde. l. nam haec vera. And on the other hand, where the physician acquired this by his own knowledge and his own industry, it can be alleged that these are not to be shared, but he ought to have them as a prior share. And this seems to be sufficiently well proved both by legal texts, by arguments, and also by authorities. It is proved by legal texts in insti. per quas perso. nobis acquir. §. 1, at the words, 'ne quod ei ex suis laborib. etc.', as in C. de bo. quae lib. l. antepe. circa prin. Likewise, this same point seems capable of being proved by an argument of this sort: for it is certain that if this physician had gained anything from his own knowledge or industry during the father's lifetime, this would be and would be called adventitious peculium, as in de bonis quae li. l. cum oportet. circa prin. in the text at the words 'quae ex liberalitate fortunae etc.', and the gloss notes this there, that adventitious peculium was never to be shared after the father's death, as in C. de colla. l. vlt., alias ut nemini. Therefore, since during the existence of the period when he was connected to the brother through the primary power, as noted in ff. de dona. inter vi. et vxo. l. 3. §. verbum, he does not share with the same brother, as has been said, much more will he not share acquisitions thus made after death at that time when he was not in the same power with the brother, an argument being drawn a maiori ad minus by denying, which is probable in law according to Castro, as in C. de rei vxo. act. l. vna. §. j. Moreover, this same point is proved by an argument drawn from a legal presumption in this manner: for what anyone acquires for himself, the laws presume that he acquires for himself and for his own advantage and benefit, and not for another, as is proved in insti. per quas person. nobis acquiri. in prin. at the words 'per nosmetipsos etc.'; and a reason can be given for such a presumption, because in acquisitions and goods of this kind everyone loves himself more than another, as in instit. de do. §. j. at the words 'cum magis se quis velit habere etc.' To which also pertains what is provided in law, that everyone is presumed to be greedy, and in doubt not to transfer his own money to another, as in ff. de probat. l. cum de indebito. in prin. Likewise, this same point is proved by the authority of the distinguished doctor of Piacenza, namely Durantis, who touched upon this question and wrote that this opinion and the points supporting it should be held, in the Speculum in the title de iudi. §. sequitur. de Auth. From the aforesaid, therefore, it seems manifestly concluded that acquisitions made by him are by no means to be shared. And this seems to apply when it is certain whence such acquisitions arose, as is proposed in the question. But if it were doubted whence such profits arose—although this is not proposed in the question and does not need a present answer, yet so that nothing of the contingent matters may be omitted, I did not wish to pass it over in silence—in this case it can be said that this question is rather of fact than of law; so elsewhere says the law in C. de do. inter vi. et vxo. l. ex uobis. Concerning which question of fact it can be spoken of in two ways: for if it is doubted whence the brother acquired such profits, it can be said that this must be presumed from the status of the persons, the quantity of the common goods, and the amount of the profits; for if the son is idle or negligent, and the inheritance is wealthy or large, I believe it must be presumed that such profit arose from the common goods, to which pertains C. de don. inter uir. et vxo. l. etiam., and ff. eo. tit. l. 5, and extra de peculio edic. c. 1. If, however, the son is diligent and an industrious practitioner, and the common inheritance happens to be small or modest, it will be presumed that he acquired such goods otherwise, to which pertains ff. ad l. fal. l. si hęres insti. in prin., and de haere. uel ac. uen. l. uenditor., there noting 'not on a certain thing, but is perceived because of trading etc.'; for neither to the poor is industry or the increase of patrimony, which is acquired for laborers from many occasions, to be forbidden, says the law in C. arbi. tuto. l. si defunctus; and thus, having considered the aforesaid and other circumstances, an upright man, to whose discretion it is left, is presumed to hold, or insofar as pertains to this, ff. de test. l. testium, at the words 'cum magis scire potes etc.', C. de fruct. et lit. expen. l. non ignorat. In another way it can be said that if the other brother seeks that such profit be shared, and the brother who made the profit denies that the profit arose from the common goods, then the brother demanding the sharing of the goods has the burden of proving that such profits arose from the common goods, as in ff. de prob. l. ei, qui probatione; if the brother fails in proof, the aforesaid profits will not have to be shared, as in C. de eden. l. qui accusare.

† Regarding the other point, falling nonetheless under the treatment of the first question, namely whether the books are to be shared or not, it can be said briefly that they are [not] to be shared, but rather the physician himself has them as a prior share. And this can be proved in multiple ways. In one way thus: the law says that if a father expends anything or does anything concerning the honor or promotion of a son to any dignity, he is seen to have done this for the son's prerogative, as in ff. de colla. bo. l. 1. §. sed an id., and fam. hęrc. l. si filia. §. idem scribit; if it is for the son's prerogative, therefore he ought to have the value, nor ought they to be computed in his portion, as in ff. famil. haer. l. quę pater. In another way it is proved thus: the law says that if a father donates anything to a son, or gave it during his life, although such a donation is not valid from the beginning because paternal power is an obstacle, as in C. de do. l. sine emancipati., nevertheless it is confirmed by the death of the father, as in C. de do. inter uir. et uxo. l. donationis; and the son has that as a prior share, as in C. de colla. bono. l. illud; and the father, in giving books to his son, is presumed to have donated them for reasons of affection, as in ff. fami. her. l. filiae. with similar laws; therefore, etc.

† Concerning the second question, in which inquiry is made concerning the fruits of the dotal estate, I believe a distinction must be made as to whether the married brother alone bore the burdens of marriage, or whether they bore them in common. For in the first case, the husband himself ought to collect the fruits of the dotal property, as in C. de iu. dot. l. pro onerib., and ff. eo. l. quamuis. in fi. In the second case, however, the fruits ought to be common, as in ff. de excep. do. l. fi. in prin., and de dona. inter uir. et uxo. l. si quis pro uxore. in fi., and C. eo. ti. l. fructus; and deservedly they ought to be his, because it is according to nature that advantages follow him whom disadvantages follow, as in ff. de re. iur. l. secundum naturam, and extra eo. ti. c. qui sentit. li. 6. To the third question I answer,

† that this question is rather of fact than of law. For either the expense for the clothing was made from the husband's own gains, or from the common goods. In the first case it is clear that that husband ought to refund nothing to the other, since he is seen to have done it from his own, as was said above, and nothing was taken from the other, to which pertains ff. de condi. indebi. l. nam hoc natura. In the second case, however, the husband is bound to make restoration, to which pertains ff. de mune. et hon. l. 3. §. fi., and ad munici. l. Lucius. §. idem respondit hęredes, and C. de statuis, et imag. l. fin. Concerning the fourth question,

† in which inquiry is made concerning the expenses incurred for the wedding by the father, I answer that regarding these expenses, however unequally incurred, no account ought to be taken between the brothers, but rather the whole ought to be imputed to the inheritance, as in ff. fa. hęr. l. si filia. §. neratius, and de libe. agno. l. si quis in totum, with similar laws. To the last question I answer by distinguishing:

† for either the dowry was converted to the common benefit of the household, or not. In the first case, the other brother is not bound to share in such expenses, since those belong to the burdens of marriage, which burdens the husband alone ought to bear, as in C. de iure do. l. pro oneribus. In the second case, the other brother ought to contribute to expenses of this kind, because with whomever the dowry remains, there the burdens of marriage ought to be, as was said above in the second question. And by expenses in this case I understand them only to the extent that instruments or ornaments of this kind were deteriorated because of use, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when profits and fruits derived from the dowries of wives are to be collated among several brothers, and what items are to be shared among them.
2. Whether ornaments made for wives from common property are to be divided among the brothers.
body: Certain brothers come to the division of paternal and maternal goods; these are four in number, and all are married. Some of the aforementioned brothers received their dowries in lands, while the fourth received his dowry in money. Those brothers who received their dowries in lands increased the value of their dowries by purchasing, building, and recovering dotal property. Although these four brothers had separate dwellings, they incurred expenses from the common fund. Now, one of these brothers, who holds his dowry in money, states that since expenses were incurred in acquiring, building upon, and recovering the said dotal properties, he should be indemnified for the said improvements, since those properties ought to remain as before with the married brothers and their heirs. In the name of God, amen. To the first point, I say, for clarity.

First, that the fruits of dotal property ought to serve the burdens of marriage: and they accrue to the husband’s profit, as in l. pro oneribus, D. de iure dotis et societatis matrimonii; l. si cum dotem, §. sin autem in severissimo; and l. si filia; and l. si maritus, D. familiae herciscundae, cum similibus. And the aforesaid are true in respect of any fruits whatsoever, etc., these things being in common. Moreover, it is said that brothers who had dowries in possessions increased the dowries, if indeed they purchased something while all these brothers were partners in all goods. If they purchased in their own name, they are bound to communicate [the purchase] to their brothers, as in l. si quis societatem contrahit, in the last paragraph, argumentum, D. pro socio. But if [they purchased] in their own name and that of their brothers, there is no doubt that they must divide [the purchase] with them. And this comes into the action for the division of an inheritance, as in l. certi iuris, C. familiae herciscundae; nor does it avail for the proposition that they held [the property] separately. Moreover, since through the said brothers, in contracts of debts for various causes, by standing in various offices and procuring various and diverse businesses, and marrying off daughters, it is now asked whether these debts are to be divided equally; and I say that they are not, as in l. ex parte haeres, §. filius, D. familiae herciscundae, unless they were partners in all goods by agreement, as in l. cum duobus, §. pa. and §. idem Pomponius, D. pro socio. Therefore, whoever contracted the debts shall pay them, and cannot impute them to others, l. his consequenter, §. sumptum, D. familiae mercatorum. Moreover, concerning the goods acquired by the said brothers, or any one of them, it is asked what is the law? To which it is said that if goods were purchased by some brothers, or given to them as a gift, will these be communicated? And I say that they will not, for in the action for the division of an inheritance these do not come [into division], but are adjudged as personal property, as in l. heredes, §. pro emptore, and §. pro donato, D. familiae herciscundae. Moreover, if [the goods] were not contracted in the name of all, and for the utility of all, he who contracts retains [the goods] for himself; nor does he reckon them to others, as in the said §. filius reipublicae, and l. ex parte, D. familiae herciscundae. Thus, credits not obtained in the name of all, but by his own industry, and things acquired by him are not communicated to his other partners.

† Moreover, because the wives of the aforementioned brothers have ornaments made from common goods, it is now asked whether these are to be divided among all the brothers. To this it will be said that the wives of the aforementioned brothers shall retain the ornaments made from common goods. I say that if they are ornaments suitable for wives and husbands, and do not exceed what is appropriate or the custom of the region, in this case they are not subject to division, but accrue to the benefit of the wife; for this is a burden of marriage, and dowries ought to serve the burdens of marriage, as has been said above. And equality will be preserved in this, since it benefits all. See *l. pro oneribus*, cited above, and *l. cum delationis*, § *asinam*, D. de funerariis impensis.

To this question, when the brothers make common expenses, having all done so, it is established that the fruits collected from the dowries, whether the dowries are in money or in possessions, must be placed and shared among all, since said fruits serve, as has been said above, the burdens of marriage. Since therefore these brothers sustain all the burdens of marriage, the fruits accrue to all these four, as in *l. filia*, § *hoc amplius*, D. de familiae erciscundae. Therefore, a brother having a dowry in money may claim the fruits; for his wife is maintained from the fruits of the aforementioned dowry. However, fruits or interest do not accrue except from the time the litigation commenced, as in *l. 1*, C. de usuris legatis, and D. de usu, *l. patronus*, in the second response, D. de legatis tertio. Therefore, Azo says in his Summa, in the fourth column, under the heading *Item veniunt*: "But also dowry fruits, etc."

And by this it is sufficiently clear that the fruits collected from the last past summer belong to those who bear the burdens of marriage. And if all bore the burdens together, one is not bound to make restitution to another, since they appear to make expenses for the wives in common and to bear the burdens of the wives in common. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In how many ways possession is disturbed.
2. Whether he who formerly possessed is presumed to possess today.
body: It should be known

For example, someone is disturbed and sometimes troubled by the entry of another against his will, who did nothing else but enter. D. 43.27.1 (Divus). For neither the foot nor anything else may be placed in another’s possession against the will of the possessor. D. 7.1.13 (Sicuti), § Ariston. Sometimes by another act, for instance by hindering cultivation, plowing, or gathering fruits, etc. D. 43.16.1 (Vim facit); D. 43.17.2 (Si duo), § Videamus, in fine. Moreover, because he cuts down trees without the knowledge or against the prohibition of the possessor, he commits disturbing violence. D. 39.3.1 (Nam et si ramos), in principio; D. 39.3.10 (Denique), § Arbores; D. 39.3.11 (Si immaturam); D. 39.3.12 (Duobus), § Colonus; D. 12.2.1 (Vim facit), there “and that which is another,” etc. And not only the one who commands is liable, but also the one who performs the act, if the release of one does not free the other, nor is the naming of the principal in this action required; for a mandate does not excuse from fault, as stated in D. 39.3.10 (Denique), § Si colonus, and § Iulius; and see D. 5.1.1 (Si quis id quod), § Finis; C. 9.18.1 (Non eo minus). For these actions are personal, and therefore it is not expedient to name the owner in the action, see C. 3.13.2; and see D. 43.16.1 (Quotiens) and § Deiecisse; and D. 15.3.1 (Servus). Nor does it matter that in D. 18.1.1 (In rem), § Tignum, the work was done by a craftsman on a thing possessed by the principal, whereas here it was not. From these it is concluded that the accusation instituted against the alleged Seyer proceeds, for completing the offense is not an obstacle. For since they were neighbors, they either knew or ought to have investigated who was in possession, and should not have rushed to commit injury, for rashness is a fault. D. 50.17.1; D. 7.1.13 (Sicut), § De praedictis; D. 9.3.1 (Quid occidit), § In hac. It is relevant that neighbors are presumed to know. D. 43.12.1, § 1; D. 19.2.1 (Dominus). Nor does the statute § Cum vero ingrediens stand in the way, for it speaks of a case where one merely enters and does not perform another act to the prejudice of the possessor. If, therefore, he does so, because he cuts down trees, the statute ceases to apply, and we are in the common law. This appears from the words and the intent of the statute: the reason is that the statute does not wish proceedings to take place because no prejudice has been inflicted on the actor. However, with trees cut down and damage given, it cannot be feigned that no damage was given; nor can it be restored to its former state by that legal fiction. D. 49.15.1 (In bello), § Factae. And therefore it can truly be concluded that the first accusation is pending; and upon it, proceedings should be had for taking proofs and the other things which have not been done. D. 5.2.1 (De qua re). And thus, as the merits of the causes show, the judge will pronounce judgment.

The second question is whether Albertinus has proved possession at the time of the felony. And it seems that he has not, because one who formerly possessed is not presumed to possess today. C. de probat. l. siue possidetis. For possession is a matter of fact. ff. ex quibus caus. maior. l. denique. And in fact, just as the beginning is not presumed, so neither is the continuation. ff. de iureiur. l. eum, qui. §. qui popularibus. And especially when proceeding criminally, where proofs must be clearer than light. de probat. l. sciant. On the contrary, that possession is presumed to be retained with the intent to keep it, and the continuation for ten years; and therefore it suffices to prove the beginning of possession: which being proved, unless it appeared that another had invaded in the meantime, I am presumed to have possessed for ten years. C. de serv. fug. l. 1. and by Dyn in c. possessor. de re iud. lib. 6. de us. l. quaeritur. instit. de usucap. §. quod autem. And the laws which say that one does not presume from ancient possession speak of the present time, where the possessor denies that he now possesses; otherwise, however, if he asserts it. Wherefore it seems to be concluded that civil possession is proved, because then it alone suffices for bringing an action, as ff. de acq. poss. l. clam. §. si. and d. §. denique. Nor is there anything further to be seen in the question, whether by the documents it is proved of possession with the added documents concerning it, because the text regarding the principal possession speaks ambiguously. It helps de usuc. l. celsus. per Bart. Therefore, the reader should first look carefully at the documents, and since they consist in the facts, let him take counsel from himself. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person who protests to a tenant that he shall not surrender possession to Titius, otherwise protesting in his own interest, may be accused of disturbing possession.
2. What practice is to be observed when one protests to a debtor that he shall not pay, or do something else to which he is bound to do.
3. Whether the place where the protest was made should be stated in the accusation, and what place. No. 4.
body: In the point proposed, Titius accused Seius by means of the interdict *uti possidetis*, or concerning disturbed possession: and in proof of his possession he introduces a certain protestation made by Seius, the accused, to Titius’s tenant, in the following form, namely, because the accuser protests to the tenant that he should not relax or restore the said possession to anyone; and if he should do otherwise, he now protests that he reserves his interest and intends to bring an action against him for this.

It is asked whether, by virtue of the said protestation, he could be accused. Moreover, because by this protestation Seyus claims to possess, and he who claims to possess is bound by this interdict, L. 1, § restituendae, and § hoc autem interdictum, D. uti possidetis, where this interdict is granted against him who claims to possess; for he who protests for himself seems to wish to protect and preserve the right concerning which he protests; for a protestation is a precaution protecting the one who protests, as in D. de administratione tutorum, L. quidam decedens, and noted by Johannes de Monarchia in C. in generali, De regulis iuris, lib. 6, and there by Ioannes Andreas. Therefore, this Seyus, by protesting, is bound by the interdict uti possidetis, and consequently can be accused. Furthermore, it appears that this Seyus, by this protestation, disturbs and molests this T. in his possession through the aforementioned defamation inherent in the protestation; but he who disturbs and molests is bound by this interdict, as in L. si duo, § vicinus, D. uti possidetis. Furthermore, it appears that this Seyus, by the said protestation made to the tenant of the said T., as appears above, has established the said T. in his possession. For whoever does something whereby he does not leave the free possession of his adversary, he commits force, and is bound by this interdict uti possidetis, as in L. vim facit, D. de vi et vi armata, according to one reading. Therefore, it appears that the said [person] can be accused by virtue of the said protestation. But it is argued to the contrary, and thus by such a protestation as made here, the one protesting does not seem to disturb or molest the said T. in his possession; but he has protested concerning his own interest, which may be on account of a debt or other just cause, C. quae res pignori obligari possunt, L. nomen debitoris, with similar authorities; because no one commits an injury who uses his own right, D. de iniuriis, L. iniuria, § 1, and D. de petitione hereditatis, L. illud, in the first response, De electione, C. cum ecclesia. For this reason, he cannot be accused. Moreover, since the said indiscriminate protestation, without any just cause, is of no weight or effect, D. de confiscationibus pecuniarum, L. utrum, in fine, L. fideiussor, D. de fideiussoribus, and there by Bartolus. Now the practice is,

†When one protests to a debtor that he should not pay the debt, or do something else which he is bound to do, he should read the same instrument of debt, or another instrument, or leave a copy thereof. D. l. nomen. and de electione, clerici causam. and by Bartolus in l. non solum, §. morte, de operis novi nuntiatione, where he treats the nature of protestation. Therefore, by the said indiscreet protestation, he is not bound, nor can he be accused. And by the aforesaid, answer is made to the first and second arguments made to the contrary. Moreover, by this indiscreet protestation, and one made without cause, no prejudice can be suffered, as in l. stichum, in fine, ff. de nova. Thus holds Bartolus in the said §. morte. Therefore, an action for damages due to disturbance cannot be brought. ff. ut, if two, §. if. Since therefore there is no interest [damages], he cannot be accused. And by this, let there be an answer to the third argument made to the contrary. Moreover, I find a case similarly formed, and in its proper matter: where it is asked whether the interdict uti possidetis has place only against one who defames, for example, saying that I am a possessor in bad faith, or do not have jurisdiction: can I sue you directly by uti possidetis, or indirectly by a useful action? Innocentius holds that no, extra de restitutione in integrum, c. 1, in the middle of the great gloss. Bartolus says that sometimes by such defamation my possession is not impeded. And Innocentius speaks truly, and this seems to be our case: since by such protestation no prejudice is generated, as has been shown above. Sometimes by such defamation my possession is impeded: because I cannot find laborers, or men do not wish to come to me as having jurisdiction; certainly then it seems to constitute force. ff. de vi, et vi armata, l. vim facit, there, whether by doing something altogether, by which, etc. And thus holds Bartolus in l. huius, ff. uti possidetis. Which would be the case if this person had made a discreet protestation with a cause, although not true, yet plausible: because one made without cause has no effect to impede the right due to him. C. de petitione hereditatis, l. 1. and l. hoc autem, in principio, ff. cui plus quam per l. fal. Although then he is liable to him whose interest it is, that this protestation was not made, for damages. ff. de eo, per quem factum erit, l. 1, §. 1. Thus holds Bartolus in the said §. morte, in the matter of prohibitory protestation. From which it is clearly concluded that the said Seyus cannot be accused by virtue of the said protestation, nor consequently condemned.

Secondly, it is asked whether the place where the protestation was made ought to be inserted in the accusation, and I answer that when the matter is pursued criminally, the place and time of the disturbance must be inserted in the accusation, as stated in l. 1, § rectissime, D. de vi et vi armata, and in l. libellorum, D. de accusationibus, and what is noted there; but when the matter is pursued civilly, as in l. si duo, in principio, D. uti possidetis, and then, because the prejudice is civil, the place and time are not required as a matter of necessity, as in l. 1, in principio, D. de edendo, and what is noted there, and in l. testium, D. de testibus. Therefore, in our case, since the matter is pursued criminally, the place and time are required.

But which place ought to be inserted, the place where the protestation was made to the tenant, or the place of the thing, in whose possession the disturbance is said to have been made? And certainly Petrius, as cited by Cynus in l. 1, C. ubi de possessione agi oportet, holds that the place of the protestation ought to be inserted. Bartolus in l. libellorum reproves Petrius and holds that the place of the delict, or to which the delict is referred, ought to be stated in the accusation and confined, that is, delimited; because in those matters which have a successive cause, the place and time of the committed wrong ought to be considered. l. semper, §. omnium, ff. quod vi aut clam. He holds that it will be a matter of caution to confine both places. And thus I believe in the case at hand, that it suffices if it is so confined, of which mention is made at the time of the protestation; although the place of the contestation is not confined. Nevertheless, mention of the protestation ought to have been made in the accusation, for mention of the quality and mode of the disturbance ought to be expressly made, otherwise the accusation does not proceed, as l. 1, §. interdictum, ff. uti possidetis. By analogy, in an accusation the place of the command of the wrong is not required, but the place in which the delict is consummated, as ff. de furtis, l. qui servo, §. si quis uxori, and §. neque verbo; and Bartolus, note, in l. furti, §. ope, ff. eodem titulo. From which it is concluded that the aforementioned accusation is not vitiated by reason of the place of the protestation not being described in the accusation. I, Baldus. Add what Innocentius said in c. qualiter et quando, el secundo, de accusationibus; and Baldus in the word "testis" in the repertory of Innocentius, that he who brings an action by the interdict unde vi must prove the day of the spoliation. The same is held by Bartolus in l. 1, §. interdictum, ff. de vi et vi armata. And see the notes by some in c. cum Io. Heremita, extra de fide instrumentorum; and in c. olim causam, in principio; and in c. cum ad sedem, de restitutione spoliatorum.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the recipient himself is counted when an emphyteusis is granted until the third male generation is exhausted.
body: Granted to someone an emphyteusis until the third male generation of the same line is finished,

† Now it is asked whether the recipient himself is included in the computation, or not. And the glossa ordinaria seems to say that he is not included, as in Auth. de non alien. §. alienationis, in gloss 2, which begins “hic not. coniuncto,” joined with §. alienatur. For the gloss says that the third generation comprehends the son and the grandson; but it cannot be understood to refer to the great-grandson. To the same effect it is said that words must be understood and referred to the nature of the contract, as in ff. de usur. l. si stipulatus. And according to Dy. in l. ex facto, §. fin., ad Treb., and in l. in executione, ff. de ver. obl., but emphyteusis has this nature, extra de consan. et affi., c. non debet in arbore consanguinitatis. And this is proved: if he were counted, the word “up to” would be placed exclusively; nor would the grandson be comprehended, because the recipient is one generation, the son the second, the grandson the third; but the third is not included; therefore it would directly conclude the contrary. §. emphyteosim. And therefore the truth is that the person of the father, or his stock, is not counted in the number; because he is not a generation, but the cause of generation. Just as neither husband nor wife are affines, but the cause of affinity. insti. de nupt. §. affinitas. and ff. de condi. ob causam, l. si seruum. Therefore no doubt arises. Nor does it stand whether the person is counted as the first generation; but it stands in this: whether those words, “up to the third generation,” are placed inclusively or exclusively. And the aforementioned gloss expressly holds that it is placed exclusively; but I say that whenever emphyteusis is received for the third generation, then it is true that it includes it. The same if it is said “up to the third generation finished.” For this word, “finished,” demonstrates this, that it lasts up to the end of the third generation. And thus the third generation is included by the force of the speech, because by the newer law emphyteusis can be granted in perpetuity, as noted in d. §. alienationis; because thus d. §. emphyteosis does not object. But if emphyteusis is granted by simple words “up to the third generation,” and it does not say “finished,” nor “begun,” then it is doubtful whether this word, “up to,” which is appended above the degree by a person, is placed inclusively. For when it is placed above the degree by law, it is certain that it is placed inclusively, as insti. de suc. agna. §. fi. and l. certum, C. unde legi. It is proved in d. c. non debet. and c. stari, de haere. li. 6. But when it is appended by a person in an obligatory contract, it seems to be appended exclusively, as in l. non in plur., de pac. I believe that it is appended inclusively, because it is presumed in doubt that he wished beforehand to take for the third generation, as l. si pactum, ff. de proba. and arg. C. de leg., l. in annalibus. It supports what is noted by Cyn. in l. liberti, C. de ope. li., according to the opinion of Io. It does not object l. veterib., de pac., because there it speaks of that which would increase the obligation, but here it does not increase, but makes it more transmissible. And this is so, because the pact is presumed real, and not personal; and by the same reason it ought to be presumed personal rather than real, as l. iurisgem., ff. de pac., and l. qui futurum, §. fin. It supports what is noted by Cy. according to Pe. C. de con. et const., l. veteris. And thus, having seen the said Spe. who does not examine this passage. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Bal. de Peru., Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Definition of usury.
2. To whom the usurer is assimilated.
3. How the usurer is bound to make restitution? and what is required for this, so that the usurer may be fully discharged.
4. The preamble of a statute does not create law.
5. Whether a constitution invalid in the principal matter is valid in its execution.
6. Whether usurers can be compelled to produce their account books.
7. The temporal lord ought not to permit anyone in his lands to lend money there at interest.
8. The usurer is like the worm of wood.
9. Usury is called most wicked.
10. Whether anyone is bound to produce his book, or accounts.
11. The usurer is like a lion and a scorpion.
12. Whether a Christian can demand from a Jew usuries promised, or permitted by civil law.
13. The cause of usuries is principally of the ecclesiastical forum.
body: It is manifest that natural law, confirmed in the New and Old Testaments, prohibits usury, compelled by the most firm divine scriptures, authorities, and reasons.

† For usury is a lucrative predation contrary to nature, which is most frequently encountered in the contract of loan for consumption. I say "lucrative" in order not to include interest, damage, or loss arising to the creditor due to delay or fault, etc. For this is not usury, but rather principal. L. qui negotiationem, in the beginning, D. de adiectis. That interest may be lawfully claimed and lawfully retained, as noted in C. de summa trinitate, L. 1.

† I say the same thing is predicated, because every usurer is a robber. Here I note several similarities. For the usurer is similar to a heretic, if he believes it is not a sin; indeed, he is called a heretic. But if he believes it is a sin, then he is a robber. Moreover, whether he believes it or not, he is similar to a leper, who infects others through the contagion of his disease. And therefore usurers are lepers: and they ought to be expelled from the company of the healthy, because bad morals must be extirpated from public affairs, as laws 2 and 3 state. Indeed, it can be said that the usurer sins against nature. In the Digest, title *De rerum divisione*, because it is impossible according to nature that what is once one should be twice one. What the usurer strives to do by accumulating and aggregating more than natural limits allow. For nature cannot make that which is once one be twice one, and therefore all usury is against nature. How then are they permitted by law? I answer, that is due to some certain adjunct not subject to doubt: for example, for true and certain interest, not doubtful, nor constituted in ambiguities, as in the Extravagant *De usuris*, chapter *Salubriter*, and in chapter 1 *De feudis*. Therefore, the prince and the laws tolerate usuries not for the salvation of souls, but for the necessity of livelihood, for it is impossible to live without money, as in the Digest, title *De legatis*, law 3, *Si chorus*. And no one wishes to lend his money for free: hence, out of necessity, one comes to usury, otherwise men cannot live without such aid, as I said. Thus says the gloss in the law *Si convenerint*, *De pignoris actione*. Moreover, in a case of strict necessity, one ought to strive to come to the aid of another for free: because in time of necessity all things ought to be common; I say all things consumable by use. In the Digest, to the Law *Rhodia de iactura*, law *Navis onustae*. Hence, piety would be removed from the midst, if usury were permitted. And this is against charity, which is the bond of perfection, and the rope of heaven and the world. The second point is, that every usurer is a robber, but not every robber is a usurer. For example, I pledged a fund for 10 and the accrued usuries, the entire debt being consumed, you receive the fruits. It is theft, not principal, nor usury. In the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Si quis nec causam*; § *Res pignori*, *De furtis*, law *Si quis uxore*, § *Eum creditorem*. By receiving usury he did not commit theft, but this one is therefore a creditor with diminished credit, he did not commit theft, because he converted it into the debt itself: and therefore it arose.

Let us now see how a usurer ought to make restitution of usury. I answer that, in order to be fully absolved, he must make integral restitution; it does not suffice for him if the debt is remitted. For such remission is captious and sophistical when committed in the very act of the crime; for one cannot repent while persisting in the offense. However, a gratuitous and true remission would certainly be valid on its own. Others say that a gratuitous and true remission is valid, because he who remits gratuitously makes a gift. On this point, see *c. Peccatum*, *De re iudicata*, Book 6. I state this for the present, because the constitution speaks of the restitution of usury, and does not speak of gratuitous remission. Hence, this appears to be a case omitted by the constitution; and thus we are left with the *ius commune*. Therefore, I do not say that the constitution is invalid, but rather that it does not comprehend this case. Argument: *Digestum*, *De negotiis gestis*, law 3, § *Haec verba*; and *Digestum*, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Iulianus la picula*; *Digestum*, *De conditione ob causam*, law *Si mulier*.

Let us see whether it is true that the said constitution is valid. For if we love the truth, if it speaks of an offer (*oblatio*), it must be made at a fitting place and time. *Digestum*, *De solutionibus*, law *Si soluturus*; *Codex*, *De usuris*, law *Acceptam*. But if we speak of payment (*solutio*), which is made to the creditor receiving it, it suffices wherever it is made. But if it is merely an addition to the payment, as in *Digestum*, *De eo quod certo nomine*, law 3, § *Idem Iulianus*, then the said constitution is not valid, because it is irrational and contrary to the *ius commune*.

Furthermore, it must be observed that the said constitution does not address simulated restitution; hence, let us adhere to the truth if a true counting of money appears. Although it could be said that in this case true counting is not proven by confession due to legitimate suspicion, argument: *Codex*, *De donationibus ante nuptias*, authentic *Sed iam necesse*. For, due to the prohibition of the constitution, a stipulation of fraud is presumed, as in *Digestum*, *De probationibus*, law *Quam testamentum*. And to this episcopal constitution, the similarity of the said case of usury applauds, as in *c. Quamquam*, *De usuris*, Book 6. Briefly, whatever is observed in fact, I do not know; nevertheless, this constitution is not valid when the justice of truth prevails.

† Add that the preamble of a statute does not create law, but rather establishes law in respect of what follows; for example, a statute states: "Because usurers make instruments for double the amount, therefore we do not wish execution to be carried out unless the true portion is proven." For by these incidental words "because," etc., nothing is proven; hence it is not proven thereby that the instrument is for double the amount, as in D. de rei vend. l. emptor § ancilla, because these are impulsive words, not determinative. It would be otherwise if the constitution spoke determinatively, for example, that it should be presumed to be for double the amount; for the presumption of an episcopal constitution or of a law at least transfers the burden of proof to the adversary. Although, therefore, it is not present that the authority of the constitution could have a necessary nature, as in l. 2 D. de usufr. ea re quae usu consu.

But whether, where a constitution is invalid in the principal matter, it is valid in its execution, it seems that it is, because the sentence of the pastor, although unjust, must be observed. The contrary reason is that he who is not bound to obey does not contain discipline, as in D. 24.2.1 (Iubemus) and D. 35.1.1 (Quod de bonis), § 1, and D. 35.1.2 (Quod Seius), and Augerius, D. 43.3.1 (Cerdonem). The first part is safer, but this one is truer: hence such decrees are resolved into threats, as in C. 1.3.1 (Praeses).

Having premised these matters, let us consider the power of the temporal lord, in what manner he may deal with usurers, and whether he can compel them to produce their account books. For whether they are equated with money-changers, bankers, or merchants, they can be compelled to do so at the request of the interested party, as noted by Jacobus de Belvisio, according to l. 1, Codex, de edendo. Moreover, usurers are bound to pay public duties on their credits and to have them assessed in the tax register, if the superior right remains intact, Codex, de immunitatibus nemini communibus, l. si, lib. 10. Nor can an inferior authority exempt them from this by the prince’s authority, as noted, Codex, de electionibus, l. vacuitus, c. 11. And by this method they can be compelled by the lords of lands and places having fiscal rights to exhibit their account books, even under the same penal sanction, as l. creditorum, in principio, Digesta, de actione empti.

† But it is certain that the temporal lord ought not to permit anyone to publicly engage in usury on his lands, or to lease stations or booths there for the purpose of usury. In the chapter *Usurarum voracitas*, *De usuris*, in the Council of Lyon. And rightly does the text use the word *voracitas* (voracity).

† because the usurer is similar to a woodworm, for the woodworm appears soft to the touch: but it has teeth so hard that it gnaws and devours all wood; so too the usurer is a worm gnawing at patrimony, and although it naturally happens that the mind detests greater crimes, yet the opposite is true in the case of the usurer, because the greater the usuries, the sweeter they are; and just as fire burns infinitely, if it had combustible material brought near to it, so the usurer, like the mouth of hell, devours and gnaws the more he has in his purse, and harms most severely when he is not perceived.

† Moreover, usury is called the most wicked. Dist. 47, c. Si certum. Well, and there, according to Archidamus and according to the secret account books, it is proven that someone is accustomed to exercising this most wicked art. Nevertheless, the account books which he made of his own motion and strictly retains, he is not compelled to exhibit, said Archidamus. Dist. 45, c. Qui sincera. This statement is not simply true: for he is compelled by reason of the case, as in c. 1, De usuris, in the Clementines, and in l. 1, C. De edendo, according to Bartolus, and as touched upon above. It supports what is noted in Inst. De inutilibus stipulationibus, § Item verborum, in the practice of interrogations to be made. D. Ad exhibendum, l. Thesaurus.

† Sometimes a person draws up accounts for himself alone; in such cases, he is generally not compelled to produce them to another. An example is found in private memoranda, which people commonly make for themselves for their own memory and recollection of matters transacted. Sometimes a person draws up accounts for himself and others, as when a partner or a procurator draws up accounts, because he does so for his own benefit and that of another. And sometimes it is for the benefit of another, as in the case of a clerk or a court registrar; and such a person is bound to produce them, as stated in the Digest, in the title *De edendo*, in the law *Quidam* at the beginning, and in the law *Praetor*, section *Rationes*.

† And note that the usurer licks with his tongue and stings like a scorpion, and like a famished lion always seeks whom he may devour, and commits fraud in all predicaments, when he receives what he did not give; or more than he gave; or gave bad grain and receives good; or in a place where he did not give, and [at a time] when he did not give. Moreover, in a moneylender there can be no civility, where no humanity falls.

† But it may be doubted whether a Christian can demand from a Jew usuries promised, or permitted by civil law. For Ambrose seems to hold that he can, when he says, “demand usuries from him whom you can harm.” On the contrary, that a Jew cannot receive from a Christian: as in Extra, De usuris, c. Post miserabilem. Therefore, neither conversely, because “what each one has in law,” etc., as in Extra, De constitutionibus, c. Cum omnis; and L. Finis, D. Quod quisque iuris. The objection from Ambrose does not hold, for it is to be understood of a public enemy or heretic. 8. Dist., c. Quo iure. It must therefore be shown that no kind of person can practice usury: because it is contrary to the tables of the Old and New Testaments, and few would attend to the cultivation of fields if usuries were lawful. Also, to enrich oneself without cause according to him, but with cause thus. But I answer: the cause is determined to something specific, for example, to ten for a hundred truly lent, therefore outside the limits of nature. It does not exceed its natural boundaries: as in D. Si certum petatur, L. Rogasti, § Si tibi. Nor can it be called a donation, because it is implicit with another respect than true and simple liberality. Also, it is not perceived, for as in D. De rei venditione, L. Si navis. Therefore, it is expedient that moneylenders be restrained under the rules of law, as in the Proemium of the Decretals, c. Rex pacificus. And thus it is concluded that temporal lords can not only openly attack manifest usurers by the diocesan authorities, but also, lest the evil example grow in the republic, can provide for it: not, however, judicially to cognize, but it requires a higher inquiry,

† because the primary cause is principally of the ecclesiastical forum, as is fully set forth in no. 11, q. 1, in the Summa, and in the chapter *Dispendiosam*, *De iure in clerico*; and it is similar to the rule that certain things are permitted without a judicial inquiry being notorious, which generally would not be permitted, as in the chapter *Statutum*, *De officio delegati*, Book 6. And thus I, Baldo de Perugia, at the request of Lord Carlo de Mala Testis of Pavia, say and advise.
The question is,

Whether a notary becomes infamous and, consequently, of little credibility in his writings and so forth, on account of defamation alone. Add in part 5, consilium 402, beginning: “It is asked whether by mere…”

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the restitution of the dowry ought to be made from the common patrimony of the brothers.
2. Whether brothers are presumed to be partners in goods.
body: The brothers, one the elder and the other the younger, stood together; and the elder received all and distributed them; the younger took a wife and bound himself to the restitution of the dowry; the elder married off his daughters; after time had passed, they proceeded to the division:

It is asked whether the restitution of the dowry ought to be deducted from the common patrimony: and I say that it should, for two reasons, because just as the other revenues came into the hands of the elder son, so too this dowry appears to have come. Arguing from the custom of the paternal family, D. 20.1.1 (l. vel universorum); D. 39.4.1 (l. cum delationis), § Asinam; D. 35.1.1 (l. prœdiis), § Balneas, and § Titio, and § qui demum. And because it is presumed that what has been harvested is so. Arg. D. 22.5.1 (l. procul). Therefore, it ought not to be deducted from the common patrimony. D. 38.2.1 (l. si filiam), § nemo; D. 17.2.1 (l. ac), § si unus; D. 17.2.1 (l. si socius pro filia); D. 38.2.1 (l. si maritus).

† But whether two brothers living together are presumed to be partners in property: I answer that, by reason of brotherhood alone, they are not presumed to be partners on account of undivided goods. D. 17,2,1, § fratres. But partnership is presumed from acts of partnership frequently performed, because partnership can be contracted tacitly; and because it is contracted by consent, as in l. Margaritam, and there noted. And thus I say, and I, Baldus of Perugia, advise. V. l. D. et c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Two brothers, advocates, who possessed all their property in common and received the fruits by sharing the burdens and profits, whether they are bound to communicate to each other the property purchased in their own names, and whether they are said to have contracted a partnership: and by what acts a partnership is established. nu. 4.
2. Partnership is a correlative contract.
3. How the quality of the partnership is to be considered.
body: To the brothers

† They lived together for a long time, and held common property together, and received the fruits together by sharing the burdens and the profits, because they were jurists: and one of them purchased property in his own name: now they come to division, and the other demands that the aforementioned property purchased in his own name be shared. For the general evidence

It must be premised that partnership is a correlative contract, sometimes expressed by words from which it originates, and sometimes arising from deeds. A partnership contained in words is clear, because the certainty of the words declares the certainty of the understanding. D. 17,2,4. But a partnership contracted by things from the deeds themselves extends to those matters to which the deeds on both sides extend; nor is a partnership contracted by only one party acting, because a partnership requires a joint act where it is contracted by deed. For it is necessary that each party in the partnership contribute something, either truly or lawfully. D. 17,2, ult. and D. 17,2, si non fuerint. Hence, the quality of the deeds on both sides declares the quality and mode of the partnership. Thus, it should be said concerning two brothers who profit from their legal expertise. For if they are accustomed to share profits, not to mention small ones which are consumed by use in the household, but notable ones which are converted into the purchase of estates or some other perpetual utility, then these are common. And if one of them, the other being unaware, made instruments for himself alone, he is bound to share them. D. 17,2, si quis societate contraxerit. Indeed, even if each were to make clandestine contracts for himself, he ought to share them, because common consent is required in order to derogate from the action pro socio. Just as common consent is considered in contracting a partnership, so too in extinguishing the action pro socio. D. 17,2, actione, §. diximus. In this same partnership, as in any acts to be proved, we must consider the genus and differences, as noted in C. 4,19, actor. If we consider the genus, it appears that there was between them a general partnership; which I prove thus.

† If anyone wishes to ascertain the nature of a partnership, let him consider whether the acts are contrary to other acts which are introduced into the contract, as set forth in l. pe. C. communi di., and this will be known through the argument from contraries. For those acts which are dissociative have as their contraries acts which are associative. These brothers were general partners: and this is considered with regard to the genus. However, since the species derogates from the genus,

Let us see whether, in this case about which we inquire, namely in the quasi-castrensia profits, i.e., of offices and advocacies, a partnership was contracted between them. And it seems that it was not, because from this profit they traded for themselves and had deeds drawn up in their own names only. To the contrary, because these clandestine differences or distinctions do not diminish the general partnership. For it is necessary to renounce the partnership in such a way that the other party, to whom the renunciation is made, knows of it. D. de pro socio, l. ac, §. renuntiatum; D. si certum petatur, l. si socius. And it is expressly stated that things bought in the name of one are to be shared, in the aforementioned l. si quis societatem. Therefore, according to what is alleged, everything on both sides is to be shared from the time when each placed something of his profits into the partnership until the time of the death of the first to die. This is supported by what we noted in §. altero and in c. 2, de fratribus, de novo beneficio investiturae, Collatio 10. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether it is permitted, and when, to entrust money to a merchant for the purpose of sharing in the profits, and what kind of contract this is. And whether. 2.
body: To commit

It seems to be lawful and permitted to lend money to a merchant for the purpose of obtaining a share of honest profit, as stated in the *Extra* under *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem* and *De donationibus*, chapter *Post divortium*, and under *De restitutione*, chapter *Per vestras*. Bartolus, commenting on this passage, states that if it is converted into an honest partnership, hence he understands that text in the context of a social contract. A social contract is said to exist when the intention is that profit and loss be shared. *Digestum*, *Pro socio*, law *Si non fuerint*. And therefore, Gosia says in the title *De usuris* in his *Summa*, under the word *aut*, etc.: "If you wish to give your money to a sailor, or to one going to the fairs, or to another merchant, you may place your money without sin, and the other his personal labor; for often what is lacking in money. *Digestum*, *Pro socio*, law 5, § 1. And you share money, losses, and profits." These are the words of Gosia. Where there is no sharing of risk, there is no partnership, as stated in the aforementioned law *Si non fuerint*, § *Finis*; and consequently, it must be that another contract exists.

Let us therefore examine what kind of contract this is: I give money to a merchant, so that he shall give me eight per hundred from the profits which he makes with the money. For the gain on the money can be greater for such a merchant, and it can be lesser, and it can be equal; hence, from the event of profit, if he trades more, it is profit. Thus, he cannot say it is compensation for the money. For even in a true partnership, the capital is safe. In the event of prosperity, what remains is divided; but the capital is not divided, rather it is assigned entirely to the giver, as is fully noted in l. 1, C. pro soc. [Code, On Partnership], which says that this is observed according to custom. And there by Jacobus de Arena and Cynus, who also say that this is the law. I answer that this is a contract of loan (mutuum); and then whatever accrues to the lender is usury. D. si certum petatur, l. rogasti, §. si tibi. Or of deposit; and the same, because it passes into a credit with the transfer of ownership. l. dies sponsaliorum, D. de deposito. And l. Lucius. But it cannot be a contract of mandate, because the mandatory ought not to receive profit; but even immense profit must be returned in full, and he is not entitled to it for himself; hence, it is not a mandate if he receives gain, because a mandate must be gratuitous. D. de mandato, l. 1. Here it must be seen whether, if this merchant had lost the money, he would be bound to restore it. And it seems that he is, as in l. incendium, C. si certum petatur. To the contrary it seems, as in l. 1, C. pro soc., because he is not bound except for his labor, but not for the money. But that law speaks of a contract of partnership. Here, however, there is no partnership in this money, because the entire ownership has been transferred to this merchant. But it favors the merchant more that he is bound if the money is lost. D. de praescriptionibus verbis, as in l. Titius, §. sed nec ipsius. Therefore, the risk falls on the giver, and not on the receiver; it seems to be a lawful pact. D. de nautico faenore, l. periculum. Since the money was thus simply given for use, a loan is presumed, as is noted in D. si certum petatur, l. cum quid. And the risk is that of the merchant, as in the aforementioned l. incendium, even if the money were lost by fortuitous event; hence, the money is always safe for the creditor; and of this he himself is certain. It is otherwise in a partnership, for he is uncertain about his own capital, unless the business prospers. For if it perishes by adverse fortune, it perishes at the risk of the giver. This being presupposed, that the merchant’s money is in doubt, but the giver’s money is certain to be restored to him, the contract is lame, and a lame contract is considered usurious according to Hostiensis, as is noted by Arch. 14, q. 3, c. Usura. To this also contributes the form of the words “eight per hundred,” because usury is accustomed to be made in this way. For in a partnership, a certain quantity cannot be fixed, but an uncertain one, as in the aforementioned l. si non fuerint. And it contributes. D. si certum petatur, l. lecta. And the aforementioned Recuperatus de Sancto Miniate, at the time of his death, for this cause ordered that certain quantities of florins be restored to certain merchants, being led by such a conscience. For even if this question were doubtful in law, nevertheless in the forum of conscience, according to the law of a good man, I would hold the safer part. To this it contributes well what is noted in D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. item ex facto, in the gloss which begins l. quoties. Nevertheless, the merchant will do well if he does not demand to the letter, being discreet in demanding. And thus I say, and I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, advise. Etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that the court may compel the defendant or the plaintiff to take an oath, if the defendant denies that he owes anything and requests that the plaintiff be interrogated by the judge as to whether he had a deposit, whether the judge may compel the defendant to answer.
body: Statute.

† At Perugia it is provided by statute that if the plaintiff wishes to tender an oath to the defendant concerning the cause or debt, or the defendant to the plaintiff, the podestà shall compel him to swear, etc. Now, P. deposited five hundred florins with M. and seeks to recover them from him. M., in answering, says that he owes nothing to the said P. Thereupon P. requests the judge that M. be interrogated under oath whether he received that deposit from him; M. says that he is unwilling to answer in that manner, but only whether he owes it or not. The question is whether he ought to be compelled. I respond: wherever equity moves the judge, the judge may interrogate, ff. de interro. ac. l. vbicunque. And just as it lies in his discretion to consider whether it is equitable to interrogate in order to cut short lawsuits, so the form of the interrogatories lies in his discretion, ff. de iureiu. l. iusiu. et ad pecunias. §. quod qualitate. For let us suppose that you indeed deposited ten with me, but I restored them to you in secret: if the judge has this awareness, he ought not to interrogate you extra ordinem as to whether you received them, but rather whether you owe them. If, however, the judge has indications to the contrary from certain evidence, he may well interrogate concerning the fact; in which case the person interrogated ought not to answer concerning the obligation, but concerning the fact.
