But if the trial were ordered lawfully, the depositions would be answered in due form; yet if it is extra ordinem, it lies in the discretion of the judge, as I have said. And the gl. in d. l. vbicunque. refers itself to the obligation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an emphyteusis accepted for oneself, one’s sons, and heirs passes to daughters who are excluded from the inheritance by the form of the statute, when males are extant.
body: First

† It must be considered, when someone received an emphyteusis for himself, his children, and heirs, whether daughters are included, who according to the form of the statute do not succeed in the inheritance when males are present. And it must be said that they are not. For the understanding of this, it must be known that a father sometimes stipulates for a son as a son; sometimes for a son as an heir; sometimes as a son and heir, with these qualities joined together by conjunction; sometimes for a son as an outsider. We are not in the first, second, or fourth case, which are explained by the gloss in l. si tibi, §. pactus, and ff. de verb. obli. l. quod dicitur. But we are in the third case, not concerning one quality, but concerning qualities joined together; therefore, both must be truly present in reality, namely, that he is a son and an heir. Hence, a son only, i.e., if he is not an heir, is not admitted; nor an heir only, i.e., if he is not a son but an outsider, is admitted. ff. ad Treb. l. ex facto, §. si. Moreover, in stipulations and all contracts of strict law, such as the contract of emphyteusis, words and writing must be taken in their proper meaning; nor should any extension be made. And therefore, the term "heir" is understood as a universal heir of the whole or of a share, in which the definition of heirs is represented. i. iu. successor. ff. de eden. l. quaedam, §. is autem. Not an heir improperly called, for example, in a specific thing or some quantity, as noted in ff. ad Treb. ff. si quis priore. C. de hęre. insti. l. quotiens. and l. ex facto, eo. ti. And it appears that Guidutia did not succeed in this emphyteusis, because they are not universal heirs; for another succeeded in the whole and the emphyteusis, i. Auth. de non alie. §. emphyteusim. And he died without issue; hence, the whole accrued according to the terms of the agreements. And according to Bartolus, also by the nature of acquisition mortis causa. ff. de ver. ob. l. si mihi, et titio. And although the donation made by P., who was the heir, had been valid, it would not have been valid except during his lifetime. ff. de pig. l. lex uectigali. And therefore, it could not be renewed for the donee in the case of its extinction. For among those having a cause from the same prior time, preference is given in dominion and by the publician action, just as in a pledge. ff. de publ. l. siue autem, §. si duob. And therefore, concluding, it necessarily follows that Jacob is preferred to the canonist by any person who has paid, because it does not matter from which possessor payment is made. ff. quemad. ser. amit. l. qui fundum. That exception, whereby when mention is made of generation in an emphyteusis, it cannot be transferred outside the generation against the will of the lord. Nor is he compelled to contract anew, whenever a new contract or renewal does not descend from the old one. Moreover, if mention is made of an heir in the concession of an emphyteusis, a true emphyteusis of the church cannot pass to a singular successor. ff. de ver. sig. l. in conuentionibus, per Bartolus, and C. de fideicom. l. voluntas. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a will is valid, in which the father left to his daughters that quantity which appears to be due to his fideicommissaries, and in that same quantity instituted them as his heirs.
2. Whether the substitution made to the sons and the posthumous child, etc., as appears in the beginning of the opinion, is fideicommissary.
3. How much the legitime of the children amounts to, and what must first be deducted from the father's inheritance.
body: The point of the question, on which your wisdom is asked for counsel, is as follows, namely: A certain Vivianus, formerly of Mariti, a resident of Perugia in the Porta Sancti Petri, made his testament, in which, among other things, he disposed as follows. He also left to Lady Angela Rubei, the wife of the said testator, the said Lady, as Massaria and usufructuary of the goods of the said testator, on the condition that she remain and live together in the house of the said testator with the underwritten his sons and heirs. And if she should choose another life, the said testator wished and ordered that the said Angela have only her dowry, and nothing else from the goods of the said testator. He also left to Cathelina and Bartholomaea, daughters of the said testator, from his goods that quantity of money, or that portion of the goods of the said testator, which it seems and which will be given to them by the underwritten fideicommissaries, instituting them, and each of them, as universal heirs to himself in that portion and those portions; ordering also that they cannot demand more from his goods; and if they should demand more, they fall from the said legacy. And thus in the same manner he wished and ordered in the case in which the said Lady Angela should hereafter bear one or more female daughters. He also chose and left as his fideicommissary executors of all and singular goods and legacies, etc., the said Lady Angela, John, and Raynerius, etc. In all his other movable and immovable goods, etc., he instituted Marinus and John, his sons, as his universal heirs; and also the posthumous child, and posthumous children to be had and born by him and by the said Lady Angela, his wife; and he substituted them mutually, namely, if any of the said his sons, or posthumous children, should die without legitimate children descending from their own body, he substituted the survivors. And if all should die without legitimate children descending from their own body, he ordered that his goods in the said case be given for the love of God and for the soul of the said testator to those miserable persons and pious places, which it seems and pleases the aforesaid his fideicommissaries. And this is the true will of his, which he wished to have effect by the law of testament; and if it should not have effect by the law of testament, or if it should have effect, let it have effect by the law of codicils, etc. Then the testator dies. Then the posthumous child is born. Then the said Marinus and John, sons and heirs of the said testator, die. And the aforesaid posthumous child is in pupillary age. Now it is asked whether the said testament is valid; and how, and to what extent, the said daughters and wife of the said testator, and of the said deceased sons, [are entitled].

† Regarding the aforementioned point, speaking clearly, I say that the legacy made to Catheline and Bartholomew of that sum of money, or that portion of the goods, which is given and appears to be given to them by the sureties of the testament, is valid, according to the Institution *valuit et habita*.

Thirdly, it must be known that the petition for inheritance, whoever the petitioner may be, prevailed in law, notwithstanding that the said quantity was not declared. For in the legitime, by such words, the heirs are undoubtedly instituted, as in C. de inoff. test. l. quam in prioribus. Nor can the executors diminish the legitime, as in C. de inof. test. l. scimus and l. omnimodo. But beyond the legitime, the said testators and executors could, if they wished and if it seemed just to them, give to the said daughters, moderately, however, and for a pious and necessary cause, such as a dowry, as in C. communia de legatis, Auth. res, quæ. Moreover, that the said institution was valid, notwithstanding the uncertainty of the quantity, is a case in l. 1. de legatis 2. Therefore, presupposing this as true, that the will is valid.

Secondly, it must be considered whether the substitution made to the sons and the posthumous child is deemed pupillary or fiduciary. On this point, I state clearly that it is deemed fiduciary at all times, because there are no direct words therein, as noted in the law *Precibus* and in the law *Centurio*. This is the common opinion, which I hold in my consultations. From this it follows that the aforementioned Marinus, John, and the posthumous child died intestate, and that their sisters succeed them intestate. Nevertheless, they are to restore the goods left to their said brothers, after deducting the legitimate portion on behalf of the brothers; this restoration they shall make to the poor and pious places, without the designation of executors, or even to the executors themselves receiving for the poor and pious places, as provided in the law *Nulli* and the law *Si quis ad declinandam*, concerning bishops and clerics. Now it remains to see,

†How great is the legitime of all sons and daughters. I answer that, after deducting the first dowry of the wife, which is a debt, and the funeral expenses, as in l. Pomp. §. quanta, de inoff. test., the legitime is one-half of the residue; because there are five sons, as in C. de inoff. test., auth. nouissima. From this it will clearly be concluded that if the patrimony, after deducting debts and funeral expenses, was worth 12 hundred florins, the said female daughter with their mother ought to have at least six hundred. The other six hundred florins ought to go to the poor and pious places, with the burden of providing for the wife for one-half, since alimony was left. For universal fideicommissaries are bound for the burdens only pro rata. ff. ad Treb. and l. matrem, qui ecclesia, and l. matrem. Nevertheless, by right, the legitime of the males ought to have one-third part, as in Auth. de haer. abintest. §. 2. But the legitime of the daughters is their own proper property; nor is it to be shared with the mother; therefore, of the said six hundred florins touching the said sisters, or the mother of the said daughters, they ought to have one hundred and forty from their person. And of the remaining 460, the mother ought to have 120, and each of the said girls likewise 120 for each. And this is the clear conclusion and division. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What a plaintiff bringing an action for the recovery of an inheritance must prove.
2. Whether a singular title excludes an action for the recovery of an inheritance.
3. A singular title has much more right in a particular thing than a universal title has in universal things. It fails, etc.
body: What he must

† prove who sues by a petition of inheritance: and whether a singular title excludes the petition of inheritance. When an action is brought by a petition of inheritance, the plaintiff must in the first place prove that he is heir, either under a will or intestate; ff. de pet. hęr. l. 1, 2, and 3. Moreover, for someone to be an heir under a will, several things are required: and especially that he knows of the will: as is noted in ff. de pe. hęr. l. illud; and this applies both to an extraneous heir and to a sui heir, speaking of effectual intermeddling; ff. de acque hę. l. gerit. However, he who denies the will is presumed to be ignorant of the will, unless knowledge is proved; and therefore he cannot enter upon the inheritance, because he cannot do so under the will, nor intestate since he is ignorant, because the testamentary cause takes precedence; C. com. de suc. l. antepe. But if someone can succeed by a twofold path, namely testate and intestate, he can say: "I accept the inheritance intestate," if he has no substitution, because he is seen tacitly to renounce the testamentary cause; ff. de acqui. hę. l. illud; C. eo. l. suum. If, however, he does not know of the will, he cannot do that. Moreover, that he does not know is believed against him by his own statement, because he says that he does not know or does not believe; C. de lib. causa. l. cum precum; and because it resides in the intention, which is presumed from words: as in c. humanae aures, and ff. de suppe. leg. l. labeo. §. idem tubero. From these points follows the true conclusion that if the plaintiff in a petition of inheritance denies the will, once the will is proved—because he ineptly sues as if intestate and pursues an incompetent right—he ought to succumb; ff. de pac. do. l. Beblius. in fi. Reserving, however, his right to sue anew, and reserving the competent path chosen, where it is discussed; and ff. de institutoria. l. habebat; and de acque hęr. l. claudius; and extra de iudi. c. exhibita.

† Thirdly, it must be known that the petition of inheritance, even though one is the true heir, is excluded by a singular title of the possessor, even if the plaintiff in the petition of inheritance was admitted to proofs of ownership: because when proofs exclude the nature of the proceeding, nevertheless from that fact the proceeding's nature is not exceeded, nor is an effect increased on that account which the nature of the proceeding cannot encompass. And Cynus holds this in l. cogi. in the 4th question. The reason, moreover, why a singular title excludes the beginning of the petition from the threshold of the trial is that a possessor under a singular title is not an adversary, nor a contradicter of the claimant: because he does not need to deny to him that he is the heir. For even granting that he is the heir, nevertheless this titled possessor has his own compatible title; whence he can say: "Lord plaintiff, I am not bound to enter into conflict with you, because I do not deny your title. But behold my title, which is not impaired by yours; wherefore we are not contradicters in matters of law, and consequently we ought not to be adversaries to one another." For qualified possession makes an adversary in a petition of inheritance by denying that he is the heir; because when he would now be compelled to join issue as a contradicter, he ought to say: "But, Lord, I am not bound to join issue, because I do not intend to deny you, nor even to affirm you, but I allege title as a purchaser"; C. in quib. cau. ces. long. tem. pręs. l. hereditatem; and there the Gloss sets forth this reasoning better than elsewhere in the Corpus Iuris. For the plaintiff in a petition of inheritance claims a universal succession. And if he does not have a contradicter, nor an adversary, in this universality, he cannot establish it. Whence, when he does not have an adversary in the universal title, the defendant is not compelled to join issue. Furthermore, the reason why the title excludes the petition itself in effect and peremptorily is that a singular title in this respect weakens the efficacy of the universal title, and is not weakened by it. And the reason is that a universal title has in itself less right over the thing claimed than a singular title. Since for a universal title it is sufficient, and it includes a title not directed toward any real right; it is otherwise in a singular title; ff. de pe. hęr. l. item veniunt. Others say that the reason is that in an equal case the condition of the possessor is the better.

† But they do not know what they are saying, because a singular title has more right in a singular thing than a universal title has in a thing taken singularly; C. de euic. l. 1; and thus it outweighs by its own nature. It fails, however, in certain cases. The first is where a title is held as no title, because it is equivalent not to be such and not to be held as such; ff. de peti. hęr. l. nec vllam. §. in omnibus. For a title excludes a petition of inheritance because it has the most right: therefore, this title, which has no right, does not exclude. And this applies to the present case, as where a female guardian sold the property of pupils without solemnity. Other cases are noted in the said l. hęreditatem. From the aforesaid, two conclusions follow. First, that the nuns, who say they are heirs to the settlement and deny the will, exclude themselves by their own denial, since the will has been proved, and between children two witnesses are sufficient, and thus it has been proved by several. Second, because the sale by the female guardian does not protect the possessors, because it is null unless cause and solemnity are proved; ff. de publiciana. l. quęcunquibue. §. fi. Whence the nuns would prevail, were it not for the fact that the will has been proved against them who deny it. And therefore the defendant ought to prevail, things being as they are. The nuns also ought to cling closely to God and to the truth, because if the will appears with its legacies, and the executrix sold on account of the legacies, the purchase was lawful; C. quando decre. opus non est. l. 2. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On understanding. The sole law. C. That no one. In the matter of the emperor's hope. Exc. li. 10.
2. There is no need for an external interpreter where the judge interprets his own sentence.
3. What is meant by a pressing war.
body: A sentence was issued by the magistrate of Lanua, whereby it was declared that A. and his property and goods were free, exempt, and immune from all and several head taxes, various capitation duties, single mutual contributions, tolls, impositions, collections, corvées, and perangaria, whether real, personal, or mixed, ordinary or extraordinary, and any others whatsoever that could be named or devised, provided that he observes all those obligations to which he is bound according to the form of the capitulations and conventions. Furthermore, it was declared that the said A. was not entitled to such immunity in times of urgent necessity, famine, grain purchase, or war. And the following is added in these words, and in the spirit of the sole law, with its gloss, C. ut nemini liceat se in empt. spe. excus., lib. 10. Nor also in the repair of fountains, bridges, roads, etc. Illustrious men and masters of the law, you have asked me.

† First, concerning the understanding of the unique law cited and the gloss placed thereon on the word *urgentis* (of urgent) *necessitatis* (necessity), which says *famis* (famine) or *guerrae* (war), and thus *superindictis* (having been superimposed/added), etc. And I say first that the summary intention of the *niger* (the black text, i.e., the main text) is described by the *rubrum* (the red text, i.e., the heading), albeit in less brief language. And therefore, when public necessity urges more strongly in comparison to the purchase of legumes or grains, all are bound to contribute according to the mode of their patrimony, notwithstanding privileges, even those with the authority of sentences, or any other strength of firmness, to such an extent that even the inhabitants of Augusta are bound to contribute. This is what it says. On this law, Anselmus of Saxe, as Barulus figures the case there, states: It sometimes happens that public wheat and barley are not sufficient for the soldiers; and thus, necessity compelling, money is necessary for purchasing barley or wheat. To gather this money, all must be constrained, and no one is excused by any privilege, or by the authority of the Senate and the Divine House of Caesar or Augusta. This author therefore sets forth an example when, on account of an army or war, it is necessary to purchase provisions. The gloss, not content with this example, adds an example of famine, which often occurs by the disposition of the heavens or by the judgment of God. For the common people, oppressed by excessive penury, must be aided by the purchase of grain and crops, so that food does not fail them. For this is publicly useful and necessary. D. *de legibus*, l. *ciuitatibus*, in the beginning; C. *de episcopis audiendis*, l. 1; D. *ad legem Iuliam de annona*, l. 1. For man lives chiefly by bread, and the republic is sustained, as is noted in C. *de feriis*, l. *publica*. And those who do not come to the aid of the people in necessary foodstuffs are said to kill the people. D. *de liberatione agnoscenda*, l. *necessarie*. The aforementioned gloss sets forth an example of urgent purchase, but did not join cases of different reasoning. Therefore, whether it is necessary for the republic to make a provision of grain on account of war, lest it fall into famine or penury, or whether it has already fallen into it by judgment due to sterility, or by human action due to hostility, the aforementioned law has application. L. 1, C. *nemini licere*, etc. Now, the gloss does not intend to say anything there about the stipends of soldiers or infantry, if the city has made war or armed conflict, because this is not the matter of that law. But the conferring of stipends is treated in Auth. *vt iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, §. *oportet nos quoque nostros*, with the two following sections; §. where the text says that military expenses and the pursuit of enemies require much diligence, and these things cannot be done concerning money. And in the following section, it says that we consider the Empire to have sufficient revenue, so that contributors should confer only fiscal tributes; for tributes were rendered to the republic in metals and gold, as in Auth. *de collationibus*, in the beginning, column 9, and as is noted in C. *de annona et tributo*, in the rubric, book 10. It is therefore most certain that that gloss does not speak of this duty of stipend, but only of the duty of purchasing commodities. And thus it said in the singular number, and thus it is *superindictum* (added). It would have said *superindicta* (added) in the plural, if the case had required joining two of different quality and reasoning: for one thing is to speak of stipends, which have an ordered provision; another is to speak of the purchase of commodities, which is rare and seldom occurs, and cannot be encompassed by certain provision. Argument: D. *de contrahenda emptione*, l. *fistulas*, §. *frumenta*. And rightly do I say that that gloss is notable, because it determines the question raised by Cynus in l. 1, in question 10, C. *de iure emphyteutico*. Therefore, what the text there says, *urgente necessitate* (urgent necessity compelling), it says, namely, of victuals: not of every necessity, as in l. 2, C. *de patribus qui filios*, and l. *obesus*, D. *de praedictis minorum*, and D. *de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt*, as in l. *sed dominorum*, in the word *fame*; D. *ad legem Romanam de iaculis*, l. 2, §. *sed cum*, in that gloss which begins *ad comedendum*. There is also another urgent necessity, namely, for the good of peace, which is opposed to war. Extr. *de desponsatione impuberum*, c. 2. But of this, nothing pertains to our purpose. There is also another necessity of adverse case. D. *de publico*, l. *Caesar*; C. *de dilationibus*, l. 1. And note in Auth. *de non alienando*, §. *nos igitur*; D. *de manumissione testamento*, l. *qui potuerunt*; D. *de officio consulis*, l. 1. But of these, nothing pertains to the point regarding our case, because they differ in genus and reasoning from our theme. And rightly do I admit that in time of war certain things are permitted which are not otherwise permitted, as in c. *domino guerram*, under the title *hic incipit*, Collatio 10, and also in the proemium of the Institutes and the Authenticum. However, one case should not be drawn to another. D. *de libellis et postulationibus*, l. *commodissime*; and in c. *suspectum*, Extr. *de rescriptis*, book 6. And the gloss says, *famis* (famine) [means] that cattle are killed by famine. C. *ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *de pecore*. Where nothing is sadder than to be killed by famine; nothing is compared to famine. It supports what is noted by Innocentius, D. *ne clerici vel monachi*, c. 1. And he adds *guerrae* (war) to the text, referring to when war induces the necessity of purchasing commodities in the Republic for consumption. For on account of wars, estates remain uncultivated. In Auth. *de armis*, in column 2, 6, where it says, "those who run over the land, fearing to lose their lives on account of fear, use, etc." And thus necessary victuals are not available for the people, of whom lords and superiors must take the greatest care: and nor should they despise those oppressed by poverty, as in Auth. *vt iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, §. *itaque deo*, where it says, "lest they seem to despise men oppressed, whom God has entrusted to us." And C. *de mendicis validis*, l. 1, book 11. The gloss adds, and thus it is *superindictum* (added), namely, this duty of purchase and contribution made on account of famine, i.e., extreme penury caused by the fault of the heavens or war, which arises from the fault of men. D. *de locato*, l. *si merces*, §. *culpa*; and l. *ex conducto*, §. *sed si labes*. The gloss therefore referred itself solely to the necessity of coercion and the price. And the alternative used by the gloss did not refer the diversity of contingency to extensive diversity. And this is the truth. And from this, as I think, satisfaction has been given to the first question concerning the understanding of the text and gloss of the aforementioned l. 1.

I come to the second point, namely, to the understanding of the words of the sentence. And because the judge proceeded, that is, by declaring and determining, referring himself to the understanding [of the law] not as making it, but according to it, it is to be understood. Nor is this surprising, when the understanding of the sentence proceeds from the law and operates according to it, especially since a reference was made expressly to the written law. And it supports what is noted in *causam*, Extra, *de officio delegati*. And it is expressed in the Digest, *de auro et argento legato*, in the law *Titii amita*; *de re iudicata*, in the law *miles*, § *decem*. The words of the sentence say that they follow the mind of the words: and these words sound interpretively. Code, *de necessitatibus*, law 1, in the beginning, there: "we follow the footsteps of the will," etc. Therefore, the sense of the text and the gloss is the same, which sentence is consonant with the laws of the one declaring the law; because the sentence ought not to lead us to an incongruity. Law *puto*, § 1, Digest, *familiae erciscundae*. And it is noted by Cynus in the law *si*, Code, *de annona excusatione*. From which it follows that, since the judge in the pronouncement of the sentence, of which he is the efficient and formal cause, interprets himself, there is no need for an external interpreter, or an extrinsic understanding. Digest, *de appellationibus*, law *ab excusatione*, from the contrary, or from that adverb *male*. And because there, after the sentence is completed in the proof of the words: "But while it was in the making, it receives every mode and form." Code, *de sententiis*, law *cum eorum*. Finally, the word pronounced demonstrates the sentence passed. Moreover, while the judge is speaking, the matter is imperfect; at the end of the words stands the final end of the cognition. The sentence is a principal article, perfect in its structure and context, containing the substantial and accidental definitions, if they are made in the same context. Law 1, Digest, *de re iudicata*, with *si*. It is clear therefore from the above that war is not contained per se, but per accidens, when it gives rise to the necessity of purchasing the aforementioned goods. Otherwise, if war brought abundance, or plentiful plunder due to the prosperity of fortune, where it is customary for wages to be doubled. Nevertheless, the free and exempt persons are not bound to these, so fully, as our case states. For the words say, "to any others, which can be said or conceived, whatever name they are considered to have, and by whatever reason, occasion, or cause." Therefore, it left no case untouched; because it sensed every article expressed. Digest, *de testamento militis*, law *qui testamento militari*, in this word, "however with this intention." It supports what is noted in the law *sed et si quis*, § *quaesitum*, Digest, *si quis cautio*.

I come to the third point, which is said to be an urgent war. And I say that there is a difference between urging and being urged: for if a city, in order to gain glory, initiates a war, it is said to be urging, not being urged, because it is in the active mode. But if it defends its own territory, it is said to be urged. Hence, elsewhere the gloss says: admitted, not forced. C. de cond. ob caus. l. 1. He who defends himself is said to be compelled by necessity. Extra de except. c. cum inter priorem. Innocentius, ff. ad l. Aquil. l. scientiam, §. qui cum aliter. And C. unde vi. l. 3. If, therefore, a war is called urgent, it is one which the law of the people protects. And if the war were not fought, possessions and districts would be lost; nor do I care whether near or far. ff. de iudic. l. insulae. Nevertheless, for every small war, those who are exempt from levies are not to be collected, and those who, due to war and urgent necessity, are compelled to pay, should be subject to subsidiary liability: so that the privilege and immunity may benefit them; such that whenever the resources of others are insufficient, or if they are available only with great scandal, then the exempt may be burdened to contribute with the others, as noted by Dyther in l. 1. ff. de iur. immun. Otherwise, they are not said to be compelled. Argument from ff. de leg. 1. l. ab omnibus, in principio. And de mun. et hon. l. vt gradatim, §. quotiens. And Extra de iur. imm. ecc. c. aduersus. And what is noted in C. de sacr. sanct. ecc. l. neminem, in ultimo.

Furthermore, in the case at hand, there is no place for this consideration: because the said privileged person cannot be burdened on account of war, except on account of the necessity of the city’s taxes or subsidies; for naval provisions, which are incumbent due to the war which the city suffers, I think he is bound. But for the stipends of armed men, I do not think he is bound, on account of free and general immunity and franchise; and on account of those words, “said” or “devised.” For I presuppose the immunity to be valid; and its validity is not disputed, because it was granted by the prince or the royal city, and it is not obstructed by what is noted in l. euacuatis, C. de decur. lib. 10. For a city, free from superiors, can grant franchise to inferiors; because it performs the role of the prince on its own throne, as ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. prohibere, §. plane. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws, etc.

Regarding the matter of the Lord of Cortona, the chapter states that the Sienese ought to maintain in the city of Cortona 40 foot soldiers and 25 armed men. Add that this opinion is found in the fifth part of the consilia, number 407, beginning "Regarding the matter, etc."

It must be premised for clarity that certain offices are purely and truly real, that is to say, by their nature and effect, etc. Add that this opinion will be found in the fifth part, consilium 408, beginning: "For clarity, etc."

Case: E leased to T in these words: "From the 13th of May, from the feast of Saint Martin next coming, for nine years." See in the fifth volume, consilium 412, beginning: "F leased to T in these words."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the exception of res iudicata is an obstacle, and when it is not.
body: For the sake of clarity, it must be premised that,

†The exception of res judicata then stands in the way, because it is the same thing, the same cause, and the same persons. D. de except. rei iudicat. l. cum quaeritur. and l. cum de hoc. Where therefore one of these three changes, the exception of res judicata does not stand in the way: because one does not act against the judgment. D. de except. rei iud. l. et an eadem. §. actiones. And in this case, a judgment rendered at the discretion of an arbitrator does not give rise to a claim for penalty, because one does not act against the judgment. Secondly, it must be premised that sometimes an acquittal is rendered in a real action: because possession was not proven. Then, if it appears that the defendant subsequently possesses, he may be sued on the basis of the new possession. D. de except. rei iud. l. si quis ad exhibendum. D. de rerum am. hab. l. procurator. Sometimes, because he did not prove the right which he claimed to pertain to himself: and then either by that right it is concluded in the old action, as it is concluded in the new; or by a different right it is concluded in the new, than in the old. If by the same right, then the exception stands in the way. D. de except. l. fundum Titianum. and l. fundi. Because wherever it appears that that very thing which was settled in the first trial is being rehashed by way of the final cause, in the second trial the exception stands in the way. If, however, by a different right, the exception does not stand in the way. D. de evict. l. minor. §. 1. Now let us see. The honorable lady sued as an heir, and requested partition; she did not prove the death of her brother, nor the joint ownership, because it arises for her from death and acceptance; the defendant was absolved: now she brings an action of guardianship as an heir, and thus a personal action, for the rendering of an account of administration. The question is, whether she may do so: and it seems that she may not, because she has already been excluded, because she did not prove herself to be an heir: therefore she cannot anew rehash that very thing, since judgment has been given in a preliminary issue. D. de pet. her. l. si quis libertatem. C. eod. l. fin. and note D. de except. rei iud. l. si a te. in princ. D. de iureiur. l. qui iurasse. §. si pater. To the contrary it seems, for sometimes an acquittal has a perpetual cause of truth: and then it stands in the way perpetually. Sometimes the cause is mutable into the contrary by the passage of time, as possession, and the life of a man, and then the exception of res judicata does not stand in the way, if however the plaintiff is cautious in alleging the state of the present time, and not the past: D. de iureiur. l. eum qui. §. in popularibus. For if I consider even the estimation of possession, a new trial may be decreed. Likewise, if I consider death from a new acceptance of the inheritance, now, being certain of the death, of which he was first uncertain and could not accept, an action may be brought: because a new act of the man conferring the right to sue has supervened. Thus it should be understood. d. l. si quis ad exhibendum. with its gloss. and l. si ex testamento. and l. si in rem meam. C. de pet. her. l. hereditas materterae. C. ad exhib. l. non ignorabit. per Cyn. de excus. tut. l. spadonem. §. qui absolutus. Nor can the defendant say that he could have been sued earlier: because he would allege his own falsehood, nor that the plaintiff was an heir earlier: because he would allege the injustice of the judgment rendered in his favor. D. de leg. 1. l. si servus plurium. §. 1. Wherefore, the judgment formerly rendered in a real action, restricted by expressed causes and limiting times, does not now stand in the way in a personal action of guardianship to be decreed against the heir of the guardian, in which there are clear proofs from the inventory. C. arb. tut. l. fin. because the first judgment may be just, provided, however, that the petition newly proposed is just and true: nor is one subject to penalty, because one does not act against the judgment: because therefore she could not then sue as an heir, now she may: then it was established concerning the death. It is clear from the records, because it could not be proven that the death was established, if death is not proven: therefore if subsequently the death is established, an action may be brought on the basis of a new and effective acceptance of the inheritance. C. de cap. et postlim. rever. l. nec nos. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Laws, and Counselor.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether laborers are liable to the penalty for disturbance of possession.
2. The discretion to punish is not understood to be granted where there is no offense.
body: Given the statute of the commune of Pavia, which imposes a certain monetary penalty on those who disturb anyone in the possession of a thing that he truly possesses, it is proposed that A. and B. were hired by C. to cut down a certain felling forest possessed by D. next to another wood. C., the hirer of the labor of the said A. and B., were thereupon accused, namely the said hirers of labor and the said hirer of labor. Now it is asked,

† without calling into doubt the possession of the said [property]. Whether the said lessors, or the said lessee, are therefore liable to the penalty of the statute, or rather to a simple action under the *lex Aquilia* or to the interdict *quod vi aut clam*: and it seems that they are liable to the penalty of the said statute; because the statute does not distinguish whether error intervened or not. Therefore we ought not to distinguish, as in D. *de publicanis*, l. *de pretio*. Moreover, injury should not be done to another under the guise of error, lest the fool be in a better position than the expert, as in l. *quod servus*, D. *quod vi aut clam*. Also, because they ought to have inquired, at least by domestic inquiry, and among those in the vicinity, whose said wood it was, and who possessed it; for if they had inquired, they would easily have known, as in C. *de ingenuis manumissis*, l. *si aviam*, and D. *de fluminibus*, l. 1, § 1. And not to inquire about that about which one is accustomed and ought to inquire is a species of gross negligence, as in D. *de nova operis nuntiatione*, l. *doli mali*, § *fin*. Furthermore, he who causes damage to another’s property is liable not only civilly by the action of the *lex Aquilia*, but also criminally to a penalty imposed on the fisc. This is the singular gloss in l. *fin*, D. *de privatis delictis*.

On the contrary, it seems that no damage was given, if the wood was coppice, provided, however, that the timber was not carried away by them. Otherwise, if the wood was not coppice; for then some damage would have been given, as in D. *ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *si servus servum*, § *si olivam*, and D. *quod vi aut clam*, l. *nam si ramos*. Also, in the interdict *quod vi aut clam*, damage is not distinguished from non-damage; because the disturbance itself is considered as damage given, as fully noted in D. *quod metus causa*, l. *extat*.

On the contrary is the ordinary gloss on the text in D. *de re vendicata*, l. *in rem*, § *tignum*. For these lessors of labor are excused, because they are accustomed to work in such matters and to let their labor, as in D. *de iniuriis*, l. *item apud Labeonem*, § *si quis astrologus*. And having regard to their art, they applied themselves to a lawful thing. Also, if any fault could be imputed to the said workmen, it was in omitting to inquire; which fault in omitting does not fall under the action of the *lex Aquilia*, because it is very slight; as that notable text says in l. *si cuius*, § *praeteritis*, D. *de usufructu*. Moreover, for very slight fault one is never punished criminally by an ordinary penalty, such as this one, and a pecuniary penalty. And this is singularly noted by Cynus in C. *de episcopis et clericis*, l. *si quis non dicam rapere*. And by this the lessors of labor are excused.

The lessee, however, is not excused, because he ought to have known the boundaries and limits of his property; nor ought he to err in his own fact, as in C. *de finium regundorum*, l. *si constiterit*, and l. *fin*, D. *pro suo*, and D. *de acquisitione hereditatis*, l. *duo fratres*. From these it appears that very slight fault has a certain latitude of its lesser degree, or minimum. Nevertheless, it is in doing, and therefore one need not care for trifles; for since he transgresses so moderately, he is not blamed, as in l. *quamvis*, D. *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. And thus, therefore, very slight fault and minimal fault are not the same, as in the said § *de praeteritis*, if it be understood subtly.

Moreover, these lessors of labor are rustics, and rusticity is pardoned, except in natural law, as in C. *de iniqua vocazione*, l. *Nerva*. But to believe a good man hiring their labor, since everyone is presumed to be good, is not to do anything against natural law, as in D. *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *Titio*. And it supports what is noted in C. *de servis fugitivis*, l. *quicunque*, § *pen.*, where a lawful contract excuses the erring party; and there I said: it applies to the aforesaid, because the law says that we wish knowledge, not ignorance, to bind, as in C. *de tabulis*, l. *generali*. For penalties are not imposed on those deceived on account of the slipperiness of ignorance; as in D. *de decretis ab ordinariis factis*, l. *fin*. Also, he is not said to disturb who does not have the intention of disturbing; as elegantly noted in l. *si duo*, in the beginning, D. *uti possidetis*, unless they were neighbors, who are presumed to know, as in l. *si ita*, D. *de fundo instrato*, and l. 1, § 1, D. *de fluminibus*, and noted in l. 2, C. *quoniam fiscus vel privatus*, and l. *do hor.*, D. *locato*, and l. 1, C. *ubi de ratiociniis agi oportet*. And by Bartolus in l. 1, D. *si certum petatur*.

That which must not be omitted is that if these workmen exceeded the limits of the mandate in putting the sickle into another’s harvest, the master is not liable, because he did not mandate it, nor did he approve of it, as in Extravagant *de restitutione spoliatorum*, c. *cum ad sedem*. Notwithstanding c. *ult.*, *de hominibus liberis*, lib. 6; for there the mandatary exceeded the limit in a personal offense, here in a real one. Also, there the limit could not be set in the entry of the sword, which sword obeys the body more than the soul. And other things are usually deadly: and death is connected and inseparable from the atrocity of wounds. And therefore that which harms is inspected, because fraud precedes accident, otherwise otherwise, as in D. *ad Sillanum*, l. *qui posthumos*. Nor are the workmen themselves liable, on account of ignorance, as I said above. And if it be said that rather they ought to be punished by an arbitrary penalty, because the statute gives discretion.

I answer that the discretion to punish is never understood to be granted where there is absolutely no offense. For discretions apply to the selection of penalties between one penalty and another, as stated in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Hodie*. But where there is no offense, there is no penalty whatsoever. And therefore, the choice or discretion among penalties does not apply, since the accused is protected by his own innocence, and the credibility of innocence affords the greatest security, as stated in the Code, *De iniuriis*, law *Si non convicii*. However, where the type of crime would not correspond to the quality of the penalty, it is necessary to deviate from the ordinary penalty to an arbitrary penalty, ascending or descending to a penalty, or from a penalty, as is appropriate to the degrees of culpability and the status of the person involved, as stated in the Code, *Ut intra certum tempus criminalis quaestio terminetur*, law 2; and in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Hodie*; and in the Digest, *De his qui notati sunt infamia*, law *Quid ergo*, section *Poena gravior*. And see what is noted by Bartolus in law 3, section 1, of the Digest, *Si quis testamento liberis ex iussu fuerit*. Furthermore, it would be absurd to say that one who hires out his labor for one day or a few days would be bound to investigate the possession; because the investigation would occupy more time than the labor itself, as stated in the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Inter quos*, section *Si dominus*. The one who gave the order would also be excused if he did not order with certainty regarding the place; because he is not understood to have ordered things that are contrary to law, as stated in law *Si pater* of the Digest, *Quae in fraudem creditorum*; and in law *Si procurator* of the Digest, *De conditione indebiti*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The cause of usury belongs to the ecclesiastical forum, and how the ecclesiastical judge ought to exercise his jurisdiction in this matter.
2. Whether a relaxation of the oath is required beforehand so that one may bring an action or seek the remission of an arbitral award as being inequitable.
3. From what circumstances the simulation of a contract is presumed.
4. When a contract of sale and purchase is presumed to be simulated.
body: Let us see whether the right of the Lord Bishop can also be founded on the facts narrated: I do not doubt that the said Archbishop is the competent judge to take cognizance of, and to adjudicate upon, the matters contained in the libel of Lord Barzaroli, inasmuch as the case concerns usury.

For in this case we measure the forum of the Church, as in c. Dispendiosam, De iudiciis, in the Clementines, De foro competenti; although according to Bartolus, 11th Question, in the Summa, De iureiurando, c. Ad nostram, Extra, Book 3. It suffices, however, that jurisdiction is concluded from the facts narrated. D. Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, l. Ex quacunque; D. De iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Cum quaedam puella, § Quaestionis. But it is doubtful how he ought to exercise his jurisdiction, since he is a judge. And it seems that he ought to admit the exception of the matter having been referred to arbitrators, and to judge according to the arbitrators’ award; because such persons had jurisdiction by virtue of the form of the statute; for a statute can confer jurisdiction upon them between laymen. C. De iudicibus, l. Cum specialis; and De appellationibus, l. Cum speciali, note, doc.; D. De evictionibus, l. Si dictum, § Compromiserim. Since such a sentence contains absolutely no express error, it ought to be held as true. D. De regulis iuris, l. Res iudicata; and it ought to be put into execution. C. De ordine cognitionum, l. Finis. And since it is a definitive sentence, one must abide by the sentence, even if the matter had been conducted through fraud. D. Mandati, l. Si de iussor, § In omnibus; D. De furtis et eripitis, l. Cum putarem; D. De peculio, l. Eo tempore, in principio. Otherwise there would be no end to lawsuits, which is most absurd. D. De iudicibus, l. Si praetor; C. De transactionibus, l. Fratris; De fructibus et litis expensis, l. Terminato. For under this pretext of usury, all sentences could be drawn to the forum of the bishop, and their execution impeded; and temporal jurisdiction would almost always depend upon ecclesiastical jurisdiction; which would be tyrannical and contrary to the canons themselves, as in c. Cum ad verum.

† Moreover, it was sworn in the compromise to obey the award; which is equivalent to having sworn to pay that sum which is contained in the award, as is read and noted in D. de verb. oblig. l. 5, § si sortem. Therefore, unless such an oath has first been requested to be released and has been released, one ought not to be heard coming against one’s own oath; especially since, by the form of the statute, no complaint can be made regarding such an award. Extravagantes de iureiurando, c. debitores. Hence, such an oath is absolute and does not contain within itself a tacit condition, if he shall judge equitably; since inequity cannot be alleged. To the contrary, it seems that such an award would open the way to the evil of usury; therefore, it is not valid without being corrected by the judgment of the bishop, as in c. ultima, de iudicibus, lib. 6. For thus a transaction is invalid by the law itself, by which the crime of usury is fostered, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, de deposito, unless it was sworn to and the release of the oath was not requested, as the Novellator states there; otherwise, lawsuits would be fabricated so that the transactors could stand by that sentence. D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si cum lis. We see this every day: for instruments guaranteed have the force of a sentence, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de confessionibus, and by the statutes of Tuscany; nevertheless, recourse is had to the bishop on account of the evil of usury, who cognizes and prohibits as the superior, and thus the general custom stands. Moreover, the plaintiff here invokes the mandate which the testator made concerning the restitution of usuries; by virtue of which mandate every contrary defense is removed. Argumentum D. de verb. oblig. l. si dari. Moreover, if it suffices that the libel concludes with a presumption regarding the entire matter, much more so regarding jurisdiction. D. l. omnes, § Lucius, D. quae in fraudem creditorum. Moreover, the quality is expressed here, which of necessity includes ecclesiastical jurisdiction, as I said above; hence, the foundation of jurisdiction is sufficiently and most sufficiently expressed in the libel. And other arguments to the contrary do not seem to obstruct; because here there is a defect in substance on account of the sin or crime of usury connected therewith. D. de verb. oblig. l. generaliter; and l. si plagium, D. de fideiussoribus; l. si aere, § si reo. For a sentence is said to be impossible, and every disposition contrary to good morals. C. de his quae poenae nomine, l. 1; D. quae sine appell. rescind. l. Paulus. But here it is thus answered:

† And even if, by the nature of the case, the matter itself falls within the forum of the bishop: nevertheless, on account of the manifest calumny of the plaintiff, as is said to appear from the libel itself, he ought to be repelled from the threshold of the judgment, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, de officio vicarii. Calumny appears, however, from the multiplication of contracts. C. de non numero plurium petitionum, l. cum fideiussor; l. Gad velle; l. si mulier. From the supplementation of just price. C. de rescindenda venditione, l. 2; ff. de pignori, l. si fundus, §. si. From the remoteness of time. ff. de usuris, l. cum de in rem verso. From a transaction. C. de plus petendo, l. 1, §. si. From an award, for which it is presumed, as noted by Doctorus in consilium which begins, Tholomeus manens; and from the last contract, unless the contrary is stated. For it would be absurd that a question of simulation could not be settled by a secular judge. C. plus valet quod agitur, l. emptione; nor by transaction. C. de transactionibus, l. si. Because in the same way, neither by judicial oath, which is false. ff. de iureiurando, l. 3, §. quaecunque. For transactions may be made concerning past alimony due by last will; but in other matters concerning past and future things, since it is not prohibited. ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi. It is not said that a way can be opened for the collection of future usuries according to Innocentius, which are illicit: but rather that they are removed, as noted. C. de transactionibus, l. praeses. But to this, in one word, it is answered that the libel ought to be admitted, so that the truth may be sought. l. si eum, in principio, ff. si quis cautio; l. nam et postea, in principio, de iureiurando, in glossa. From this depends whether an injunction should be issued: because if there is a judge, and a higher judge can issue an injunction, otherwise not. ff. de iudicibus, l. apud. Since these things seem connected: and such is the order. ff. de iudicibus, l. per minorem; and it makes. c. si iudex laicus, de sententia excommunicationis, lib. 6; and in Auth. de sancta ecclesia, §. si vero crimen. Before I come to the second point, I first premise that the judge ought to consider the form of the petition and the conclusion of the libel. For in the conclusion of the libel, the form of it properly stands. C. de fideicommissis, lib. 1, §. si; and ff. cod. dig., l. vt fundus; and noted, si certum petatur, l. vinum; and de triticaria, l. in hac; de simulatione, c. licet Helias.

Secondly, I premise that a contract, and the form of sale and purchase, sometimes has being and form, namely when it is true and just. This is presumed in case of doubt, unless something else is proven, at least by presumptions of law or other indications for proof, as in C. de probat. l. cum precibus; and Inst. de rebus div. § per traditionem; D. de public. l. quaecunque; and note Inst. de act. § alias. Sometimes the contract is simulated, although it does not appear simulated at first sight, as in C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione. For example, because in truth it is a loan and a pledge, and the price and the thing were simulated. And similarly, simulation is presumed, for it is proven from clear traps and presumptions. To prove this, it suffices that the following concur simultaneously: that the alleged buyer was accustomed to practicing usury, the minority of the just price, and a pact to repurchase, as in Extr. de empt. et vend. c. ad nostram. And if it were perhaps proven that he was accustomed to making similar instruments in fraud of usury, then from the custom of the person and from the custom of offending, perhaps two would suffice, namely the custom and the pact to repurchase, as in Extr. de pign. c. illo vos; D. de pign. act. l. vel universorum. Sometimes the contract is true, yet not just: for example, because it is a true sale, yet this is arranged between them, that it be repurchased, so that in the meantime the buyer may profit from fruits which exceed the legitimate measure of the price. And that this contract is true is clear, because from it arises the action of sale and purchase, and the action on agreed words on account of the pact, as in C. de pact. inter empt. l. 2. Since this is possible, that the contracting parties so willed, truth arises from their very will. Yet, because fraud is admitted, and the contract is in effect similar to a pledge, if it is celebrated with a usurer, fraud is presumed. That which is noted in the said l. emptione supports this, and in l. 1, C. de probat., according to Lauro de Arezzo and Cynus. Against this presumption, however, if the vendor were to confess that it was a true contract, the confession would stand, which excludes all suspicion of fraud, as noted in Auth. de aequali, do. § aliud. I say these things not by way of counsel or determination, but by way of allegation, so that I may cause one word to be noticed, which is in the books, when it says that the third party was not in the words "anni." From which it is argued by the advocates that there ought to have been a true sale, l. ultima, C. de praesc. cur. li. 10. Thirdly, I premise that which acts speak, namely that in the libel no action is proposed except the condictio indebiti, or the condictio ex canone of usuries paid; but rescission of the award is not sought, nor is silence imposed upon the award itself; therefore, nothing is sought which is prejudicial to the award; and why should the execution of the award be withdrawn, since no rescissory judgment is brought, as in C. de fals. l. satis aperte. And if it be said that here it is sought, because the award says that the contracts were true, while the petition says that the contract was simulated, I answer: if it says without prejudice to the truth that the award does not narrate the truth, it is nevertheless valid if it is not rescinded, as in D. de re iud. l. post rem; and since it has execution ready, because it is a true definitive sentence according to the form of the statute, execution ought not to be impeded in the meantime. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a daughter may claim the supplement of her legitime, when a legacy exceeding her dowry has been left to her in the will, given a statute providing that a dowried daughter does not succeed together with her brothers. And no. 3.
2. The legitime may be taken away, diminished, and increased by civil censure.
body: The statute of the city of Mantua provides in this form: Daughters, nor any woman, shall not succeed intestate, nor together with nephews, nor from nephews, and other male descendants in the direct legitimate line, whether legitimated or not, in the goods of their father, or mother, grandfather, great-grandfather, or other ancestors. Likewise, sisters, nor their sons, nor any woman coming from the side, shall not succeed to brothers, when other legitimate, or legitimated, brothers are extant; nevertheless, the brothers are bound to dower them from their own goods, and from paternal goods first, as long as these last; afterwards from the goods of the brother, or brothers, if they are not dowered; in which goods the sisters shall have an express hypothec: and they ought to be dowered honorably according to the capacity of the patrimony. Now Titius, having three sons, and one daughter, and a granddaughter from a predeceased son, made a testament, and instituted his said sons as universal heirs; to the daughter, however, he bequeathed dowries, and fifty; to the granddaughter, however, because she was already dowered, and given in marriage, he similarly bequeathed fifty by right of institution. And he ordered them to be silent, and content beyond the dowries handed to them; and by the same testator in another testament first bequeathed. It is now asked, whether the said granddaughter, notwithstanding the command of the testator, can sue for the supplement of the legitime. In the name of God, amen. On the aforesaid point.

A private statute excludes daughters from the succession of ascendants, to the prejudice of surviving descendants in the direct male line. And this was also pleasing to antiquity, as stated in the Institutes, *De legibus agnatorum successionibus*, § *Quod ad feminas*: "for through males dignity and family are preserved; whereas in females it ends, since they pass into an alien family." See also the Digest, *De venditionibus inspicendis*, l. 1, § *Denuntiare*, where it is said that it is a public interest; and *De postulando*, l. 1, in the beginning, read together with § 1 of the Institutes, *De legibus agnatorum successionibus*, and the Institutes, *De poenis*, § *Si*. However, because Emperor Justinian did not wish to be a censurer and accuser of nature, he invited males and females alike; and he abolished the distinction between agnation and cognation, and of sex, and of paternal power. See the Codex, *De legitimis heredibus*, l. *Meminimus*; Codex, *Ad Tertullianam*, auth. *Defuncto*.

Therefore, since what pleased antiquity contradicts the new censure of the law, the statute must be interpreted strictly, as in l. *Quicquid*, *De verbis obligatorum*; l. *Constitutionibus*, Digest, *Ad municipalia*; Codex, *De noxa*, l. *Si servi*, according to the doctrine in l. *Omnes populi*, Digest, *De iustitia et iure*; and in l. *Cunctos populos*, Codex, *De summa Trinitate*.

Therefore, since daughters and those of lower rank are repelled from intestate succession, it is not said that they are repelled from succession against a will; hence, a passed-over daughter could declare the will null, and bring an action *contra tabulas*. Likewise, an expressly disinherited daughter could bring a complaint of inofficiousness. Nor is this surprising, because the statute does not speak of such succession. Nor is it our place to depart from the words of the law, as in l. *Non aliter*, Digest, *De legatis tertio*; l. *Praetor*, § *Docere*, Digest, *De solutionibus*; l. *Si vero*, § *De viro*.

However, one remedy was removed by the principal censure, namely, succession intestate. It is noted that [this applies] against a will, although, if reduced to the cause of intestacy, it does not benefit herself but others, as in Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Papius*, § *Si quis his*. But the petition for the supplement of the legitime, when a woman is ordered to be silent and content, is not intestate succession; rather, it is a claim against the will. And it is still called succession by will, from which it is sought, given that a will has been made. Hence, it does not appear that she is excluded from the petition for said supplement; and especially since it takes the place of alimony, as is fully noted by Cynus, Codex, *De nuptiis*, l. *Sancimus*.

Alimony, which is owed by law to descendants, Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, l. 1, at the end, cannot be taken away by a civil statute, as in § *Sed naturalia*, Institutes, *De iure naturali*. Hence, it seems that at first glance the supplement can be petitioned.

† The contrary is the truth, because the legitime can be taken away, diminished, and increased by civil sanction, because it was introduced not by natural law, but by civil sanction: which is clear, because it has been altered afterwards, as in the auth. nouissima, C. de inoff. test. And it is established in this manner, when there are not curial sons, that it be a third or a half of that which the son would have taken intestate, considering four or a greater number of children, as in the said auth. nouissima. Since therefore the quantity of the legitime is disputed, and introduced as a part and a quota of the whole, which he who was claiming from that whole would have had intestate: therefore a daughter, who was not capable of succeeding to that quota, could not be supported: because it is impossible to give a third, or a half, or any other quota of the whole, where nothing is found of the whole. Because when the whole is extinguished, or does not exist, no parts of it can be found. l. si quis cum totum, §. si ancillam, ff. de except. rei iud. There is, however, a part in the whole. ff. de reg. iur. l. cum toto, and the said l. si quis cum totum, in princ. Hence, when there is no whole, it is impossible to find parts. Therefore, a woman has no right to claim the legitime, which is due in the manner of a quota of the patrimony.

† and therefore I conclude that this woman cannot demand the supplement of the legitime: because in her case there is no legitime, since the statute simply excludes her, which it may do, as is fully noted by Johannes Andreae in c. Raynaldus, although Dythericus holds otherwise, and not well. c. Indultum, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Let the woman therefore be content with the dowry, which is sufficient for maintenance. But if it were not sufficient for maintenance, she could not demand it by way of a defect or as a cause for supplement, but because she does not have sufficient maintenance, she could demand whatever would suffice for maintenance: since these are due by the law of nature, by which all animals are taught. And thus they cannot be taken away unless a just cause exists. D. de liberis agnatis, l. Si quis a liberis. I could blacken many more pages in the cloister: but this is the truth, and thus, as has been written on this question, I advise, Angelus de Ubaldis of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legitimated son excludes the substitute.
body: A certain person instituted his son Peter as heir and substituted for himself in the following manner: if the said Peter should die without legitimate children, or descendants from his own body, then he substituted Martin. The question is asked whether a natural child legitimated excludes the substitute.

† Considering the words of the will, and considering that natural affection is also owed to natural children, and also considering legitimation by marriage, it appears from the dotal instruments that the said legitimated children can exclude the substitute, unless perhaps the testator was of such nobility and authority that it would be a disgrace for him to have such universal successors. D. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si quis rogatus. Iacobo de Belvis places such legitimated children in all respects and in every way equal to those born in lawful wedlock, as he elegantly notes in Auth. de triennio et semestri, §. si tamen. The testator’s intention was also this, on account of those words: “Or else from his body.” For that phrase, “or else,” is interpreted as “or,” and thus it shows natural affection, as if saying, “or legitimate, and natural, or descending from his body, though natural.” For the phrase “or” and “whether” is used alternatively, or declaratively, or ampliatively, having sense and meaning. Those words, however, “without legitimate children,” are understood to include natural children as well. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. fideicommissum. And afterwards he adds, “or descending from his body.” For it is not understood to refer only to natural children, so that the words may have some effect, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. heredes, §. si. Except that in fiefs of dignities, which do not pass to persons of humble status.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a confession made by a husband in a will, with his wife present, regarding her dowry is valid.
2. Whether a husband's confession made in a will, with his wife present, is considered as a legacy or as a confessed dowry.
body: Confession

† The act of Viti, made in the presence of his wife in the testament for the cause of the dowry, is valid: and it induces proof. It is valid by reason of the cause, and it induces proof by reason of the presence of the woman, according to the noted opinion of Cynus in the title "De non numero personarum," in the law "Generaliter," and in the law "Cum quis decedens," § "Codicillis," in the Digest, under the title "De legatis tertio." And in § "Titia." And if it is not valid for proving the cause of the dowry, it is nevertheless valid as a last will for disposing, as in the law "Lucius," § "Quisquis," in the Digest, under the title "De legatis tertio," and in the law "Aurelius," § "Finis," in the Digest, under the title "De liberis et legatis." And thus, with regard to the said 200 pounds, it will be valid as a confession, or as a last will. However, in the fact it is presupposed that this woman entered into a second marriage: but from this she does not lose, but rather she loses the legacy entirely according to civil law, because within the year of mourning, as in law 1, in the Code, under the title "De secundis nuptiis." But according to canon law, that law is abrogated, as noted there, and therefore she is not punished because she married within the year, but because she married despising her children, and thus she is punished in the ownership: she nevertheless retains the usufruct. On the use of the thing, in the law "Si pecuniae," in the Code, under the title "De secundis nuptiis," in the law "Feminae," and in the authentic "Ibi posita." It must therefore be considered,

Whether it is considered as a legacy or as a confessed dowry. And I say that the woman may bring an action for the dowry and prove the confession made by the husband in her presence; for the exception of non-numeration or of the dowry has no place, because the times do not permit it. C. de dote, cap. Non numerata, l. Finis, and the authority there cited. Nor does the statute concerning possessions not being transferred unless the right of the community of Gubbio is reserved, stand in the way, because the statute speaks of immovable things, not of a sum of money, in which the community claims no right; therefore, the right which does not exist need not be observed. ff. de legibus, l. Si quis legaverit; and the argument in l. Ita tamen, in principio, ff. de administratione tutorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How districts and appurtenances are to be proved.
2. The party who better proves the boundaries, whether necessary or probable, ought to prevail in the case; and what if they are proved equally; and no. 8.
3. In what appurtenances consist.
4. For how long time passages, or saltworks, jurisdiction, and mere or mixed empire are prescribed.
5. Older possession is preferred to newer.
6. The inhabitants of a corporation may testify in the case of the corporation, where the benefit does not accrue to them.
1. Whether a vassal may testify for his lord.
2. Who shall prevail in a possessory action, when both have proved their case.
body: How

† I shall prove the relevant points, and I preface the discussion of the district for the clarity of the entire matter by noting that places and territories are sometimes evidently and notoriously distinguished: sometimes by roads and hills; sometimes by rivers; sometimes by mountains or valleys; sometimes by stones or very conspicuous signs. And in these ways territories are commonly distinguished, as noted by Johannes Andreae according to Gozzadinus, Extra, de probat., c. Cum causam. Sometimes the boundaries of jurisdictions are also proved by express or tacit assertions of the parties, as noted, Cod., de contrahenda et communi stipulatione, l. Operis; and Cod., de iure delictorum, l. Cum aliquis. Sometimes they are proved by the opinion and judgment of the common people and the inhabitants of the surrounding area, who in this matter are more suitable witnesses than others, as l. 1, § 1, ff., de fluminibus. And the simpler and more rustic they are, the more credible they are; because they do not testify except about the possession of fact, as if their eyes were always present upon those places, as noted, ff., de verbis oblig., l. Stipulatio, § Sin quoque. Furthermore, sometimes boundaries are proved by the sentences of judges and arbitrators, as ff., de arbitris, l. De arbitro; l. Inter castella; and Inst., de officio iudicis, § 1. Sometimes they are proved by the collection of revenues, as Cod., si regum, l. Si quis super. Assume therefore that witnesses say that they saw a party possessing from such a river towards the source of such a castle, or from such a large and conspicuous stone, and one that is unchangeable: is that river or stone said to be a boundary or not? And it must be said that it is presumed that it is so; because it is customary to do so. For custom indicates a great part of what is, as ff., de edicto edilitio, l. Quod si nolit, § Qui assidua; and ff., de funere instruento, l. Cum delationis, § Asinam; and ff., de legatis 3, l. Si chorus, § 1. Furthermore, sometimes boundaries are proved by the postings of custodians, as ff., de funere instruento, l. Si ita, § Ville custos. Also by the exercise of jurisdiction, the collection of tolls, and similar things. For by these things the district is proved both on land and at sea; indeed, in the sky and in the air. And this is a great sign of mere empire, which consists in four things, just as there are four elements in the air, as I said: in fire, as when someone is burned for a crime; in water, as when someone is put in the rack and thrown into a river, as l. 1, Cod., de parricidiis qui filios occiderunt, with its concordances; in earth, when someone is beheaded for a crime.

† Because, returning to the point, I say that the party which better proves the necessary or most probable boundaries ought to prevail in the case, because the justice of proof makes the better prover superior. C. de edictis divi Adriani et divi Traiani, l. 1, and there this doctrine is materially stated. When both parties found their claim, if one does so better than the other. But if they found their claim in an equal manner, the judge may, by a distinct movement of his own mind, looking only to God, and not adhering through the path of any carnality, friendship, or any passion, choose which party he wishes to prevail, as is singularly noted in ff. de re iudicata, l. duo iudices dati. But if he does not wish to adhere, because his mind does not incline more to one than to the other: then there is room for that dispute concerning two equally proving parties in the interdict *uti possidetis*, of which it is noted in C. uti possidetis, l. 1. But take note, because that dispute has no place in the judgment *finis regundorum*, because it is a petitory judgment: as is noted in C. de interdictis, l. incerti. Hence the judge cannot say, "As you petition, so let you possess," because this sentence contains nothing: as in l. 3, C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum. But what is it? He may avail himself of the aid of surveyors and the counsel of prudent laymen, and especially of elders, who are more credible witnesses in this matter, where their memory is concerned: as in de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 1, and ff. de probationibus, l. si arbiter. Moreover, concerning these ancient facts, instruments are better than witnesses, provided that the instruments were made with the consent of the parties who were then in place, into whose place the successors have stepped as shoots from the root: as in ff. de finibus regundis, l. eos, and de probationibus, l. census, and there it is noted. These things therefore being theoretically premised, the rules of law must be adapted to the practice of our question: and the statements of the witnesses must be diligently examined or scrutinized.

† However, it must also be premised that pertinences consist not only in fact, i.e., possession, but also in law, i.e., jurisdiction. As stated in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, in the law *Verbum pertinere*; and in the cited chapter *Cum ad sedem* in the Extravagant, *De restitutione spoliatorum*, where Innocentius states that, nevertheless, by the name of pertinences are understood those things which have been assigned by statute, or custom, or grant, so as to be attached. And he adds these words: "To a castle nothing is assigned by law as its pertinence, but nevertheless by men and their statutes and customs a certain territory can be designated for a castle, which it ought to have in jurisdiction, and to leave to others." But in the Speculum, in the title *De restitutione spoliatorum*, § *Quia vero*, under the words "What about those collecting tolls," it is said,

† That certain things are not accustomed to be obtained except by the privilege of the prince, such as tolls, or passages, or saltworks: and where the privilege is not established, possession, or quasi-possession, of such length of time that there is no memory of the contrary, is required: as in Extra, De verborum significatione, chapter Super quibusdam. Yet I do not believe this. The same applies to the prescription of contentious jurisdiction: because that belongs to the first magistrates by common law, as far as simple jurisdiction and certain small fines are concerned: as in the Authenticum De defensione civium, § Et iudicare. But mere and mixed empire can be prescribed by the longest time, as in the Code, De diversis officiis, law Viros, book 12. Not, however, passages and the like, which are reserved to the prince: as in the title Quae sint regalia, in the Usus Feudorum, column 10.

† Furthermore, it must be premised that an older possession, which was peaceful in ancient times, even if it later began to be disturbed, is stronger than the new disturbance by the adversaries: because the older it is, the more just it is; and the force of disturbance ought not to aid those who disturb, as stated in the Extravagantes, De probat., c. Licet causam. Having therefore premised these things, I consider that the witnesses on both sides are very varied and discordant regarding the possession and the quasi-territory, and how some attempt to prove jurisdiction and quasi-possession of jurisdiction. And I begin with the nobles of the community of Gabiano: because they are the plaintiffs, and they prove their territory or dependencies beyond the Po River up to the place of Vallegio and the place of Chamzagna. Moreover, some witnesses say that if any beasts were sent within the said boundaries, the lords and men of Gabiano sent men to seize them, and caused those to whom they belonged to restore the damage and pay the penalty, and so say some. Moreover, Guil. de Gubio says that the said nobles held and possessed, and quasi-estates, goods, and possessions, and things in the vicinity of Vallegio, inclusive, coming towards Gabiano up to the bank of the Po, freely as their own territory and power, and of the power and district of Gabiano. Moreover, Io. the judge, supra, 4, c. Moreover, supra, 14, says that the men of Fontanelli by force and violence sent their beasts to destroy the meadows. Moreover, it is to be noted that on the part of these nobles is produced an ancient public instrument, by which it is provided that there was already a lawsuit concerning the said boundaries: and it was declared: to which declaration one must adhere, as stated in the Digest, De arboribus, l. Inter Castellianum. Now let us see the witnesses, namely on the part of Fontanelli. And certainly their witnesses in effect testify to the contrary, and there are eight witnesses, or about that many, who testify by sight that the territory of Fontanelli extends up to the river Po. And they seem to testify in vain, and De possess., c. Cum ecclesia. Now the question arises, what is to be said in this matter. For it cannot be denied that the variety of witnesses and proofs on both sides make the lawsuit obscure and full, as says the ordinary gloss, Digest, Quod metus causa, l. Tatis.

† Moreover, it cannot be denied that there is a doubt in law as to whether witnesses of a corporation may testify concerning territory. Nevertheless, the common opinion is that they may, provided that no benefit nor detriment accrues to them; otherwise, if they were to receive an immediate benefit, as noted in the Speculum in the title De testibus, § Oportet, at the words "Sed nunquid in causa universitatis," and in the Digest, De rebus dubiis, l. In tamen, § Si universitas, and De testibus, l. Parentes, according to Cynus.

† Likewise, regarding a vassal, whether he may testify for his lord, is similarly doubtful in law: nevertheless, it is similarly to be said that these persons are not repelled on any ground, namely that they are domestics. See also the exception, that he is a domestic. But may not a community command one of the community, and yet he is not repelled according to the *speculum*? Hence, if you consider the *speculum*, it appears to contradict itself. Solution: it is to be said that this is a matter of discretion: for if the witness is of good life and reputation, and deposes to probable matters, and especially if his statements are supported by the testimony of other witnesses, as though corroborated by good reputation, life, and other witnesses, he proves well from without. D. de testibus, l. 3, § tu magis; and D. de edendo, l. si quis, ex argumento § 2, ver. quid enim si, etc.

Now it is necessary to gather all the aforesaid points and proceed to the conclusion. I state that when the matter is entirely doubtful due to the entanglement of proofs and possessions, and the mixture of acts on both sides, he prevails in the case who holds the older possession, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on proof, chapter *Licet causam*. And if it is not established which possession is older, and one party holds a title while the other does not, he who holds the title prevails both in the petitory and in the possessory action. This is expressly determined by Jacobus de Arena in the Code, on the recovery of property, law *Quo*.
