And because the nobles of Gabiano demonstrate their title and cause through a compromise and the subsequent award, which has the force of a transaction, and consequently the force of a matter adjudicated and a definitive sentence, as noted in the Authenticum *Ut differentes iudicentur*, section 1, regarding their instruments there is no doubt that they hold the right. And if there is doubt whether the bodies [of land] are the same, one must go to the places and subject the matter to ocular inspection, as stated in the Digest, on the rules of law, law *Si irruptione*, section *Ad officium*. As for the other matters, the said nobles and the commune prevail by virtue of older possession proven by less suspect witnesses, as stated in the Code, on the edict of the praetor Aedilitian, law *Edicto*, section 1. And because it has been proven that the men of Fontanellis were disturbers, they are therefore later in possession, as noted in law 1 of the Code, on appeals. It is therefore concluded, and necessarily follows, that these nobles of Gabiano and the commune of Gabiano uphold justice: and judgment should be rendered in their favor, and perpetual silence imposed upon the other party. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws and Canonist.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. body: A certain person bequeathed to his natural son one house on the condition that he could not, etc. See in the fifth part, consilium 141, beginning: "The point is of this nature."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the widow, who is a guardian, and a testamentary co-guardian has been appointed, and the widow enters into a second marriage, may she request that her mother, who is also the grandmother of the ward, be appointed as guardian in place of the existing guardian?
body: A certain man in his will left his wife, named F., and another person named Jo. as guardians of his daughter, who was a ward; after the death of the said testator, the said F., his former wife and also the mother of the said ward, together with the said Jo., his co-guardian, assumed the guardianship with the decree of the judge and made an inventory. Later, the said F., having entered into a second marriage, requested that her mother, who was also the grandmother of the said ward, be appointed as guardian of the said ward in her place; and thus the judge appointed the said maternal grandmother as guardian of the said ward, who assumed the guardianship and made an inventory. Now it is asked whether the said F., the mother and guardian, could have requested that her mother, who was also the grandmother of the said ward, be appointed as guardian of her said daughter; and whether the said grandmother is the guardian of the said ward while the said Jo., the testamentary guardian of the said ward, is still alive?

† The aforesaid question is highly doubtful. For three things seem to stand in the way of the said grandmother. First, because the testamentary guardian seems to exclude her, as in C. *quando mulier officio tutelae fungi possit*, Auth. *matri, et aviae*, there: “alone,” etc., and in the same title, l. 2, § *his illud*. Second, because since the guardianship of the mother and grandmother is a species in itself, and is called an anomalous guardianship, not a appointive one, therefore the grandmother could not be appointed as guardian: because appointive guardianship is of another species than anomalous guardianship. We therefore adhere to the old law, D. *de testamentaria tutela*, l. *iure nostro*. Third, because if the legitimate guardian stands in the way of the petition by the mother, according to the objections of many: therefore all the more does the testamentary guardian stand in the way. It seems to me, however, that the said grandmother is not to be repelled: because since the mother and grandmother are today capable of accepting guardianships, they can undertake guardianship of genus and form: hence, according to the true opinion, the mother and grandmother can today be a testamentary guardian, as noted in the said Auth. *matri, et aviae*. Likewise, she can be a legitimate guardian, as in C. *in quibus causis pignus tutelae contrahatur*, l. *si mater*. Likewise, an appointive guardian: because she is capable of guardianship, because she can be a curator: and a curator is appointive, as noted in the said Auth. *matri*. And therefore I believe that if the testamentary guardian were removed as suspect, the judge could appoint both the mother and the grandmother as guardians. This therefore being presupposed, that she can be an appointive guardian, I say that the testamentary guardian does not exclude her. And when there are several co-guardians testamentary, and one of them is repelled from the guardianship, another can be appointed in his place: and this suspect one is not repelled by the testamentary guardian, who was not in place from the beginning, as in D. *de testamentaria tutela*, l. *si quis sub conditione*, and noted in Inst. *de curat.*, § *interdum*. But it is so here: because he recedes from the guardianship: therefore he is to be substituted in his place. But no one more trustworthy than the grandmother can be sought or constituted, because although it is within the power of the mother to seek, and not to choose this or that one, D. *qui petant tutelam*, l. *qui credendum*, nevertheless it is valid, because the judge followed the petition of the mother, and the judge is deemed to have chosen, while the mother is deemed to have petitioned thus, D. *de procuratoribus*, l. *inuiti*, § *his qui*, in the gloss *matri*. Therefore, she petitioned by reason, as in Auth. *de nuptiis*, § *sui*, Auth. *tutelam*, and the judge decreed by reason. It supports what is noted in l. *si quis sub conditione*, at the end of the great gloss, and noted in C. *quando mulier officio tutelae fungi possit*, Auth. *sacramentum*. As to why the guardianship of these is called anomalous, I answer: because certain special rules are observed therein, it has received a differing name. Likewise, assuming for the present, but not conceding, nor denying, that the legitimate guardian is preferred by order of guardianships to the one sought by the mother in legitimate appointive guardianships: nevertheless that would be by reason of the order given by the mother. But in our case there is no order between the testamentary and the appointive, rather they concur: and to the one having a guardian, this guardian is given here, because the first guardian did not alone have the fullness of the guardianship: because the testator wished the guardianship to be administered by several, as in the said l. *si quis sub conditione*. Therefore, the reason of the fullness of power, which deigns to have a peer, ceases. And the way given by the testator, which was that it should be carried out by several, would be fulfilled, C. *in quibus causis tutela habetur*, l. 1. For the law imitates the testator, insofar as it can, D. *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *pater severinam*, § *conditionem*, C. *de institutione et substitutione*, l. *generaliter*, after the beginning, and in Auth. *de nuptiis*, § *disponat*, D. *de verborum significatione*, l. *verbis legis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether thieves may be punished in the place where they remained for several days and into which they carried the stolen goods from a theft committed in another territory.
body: It is presupposed that certain associates, who were wicked and of ill repute, remained for some days in the lands of the Lord Marquis of Montferrat; and then, departing, they went to commit robbery and plunder in another territory; and after the plunder and certain thefts, albeit small, they returned to the territory of the Lord Marquis; and there they were captured.

† It is asked whether they can be punished there, and briefly? I answer that yes: because it is written, “Where I find you, there I will judge you.” Moreover, crimes are not said to remain unpunished; but if they were released, they would go their own ways and would never be punished. Furthermore, these men can be called vagabonds, as noted in l. 1 and 2, C. de quo loco de crimine agi oporteat. Furthermore, that they be punished is a matter of good example, so that the punishment of one may be a deterrent to many, as in C. de legibus iudiciorum repetundarum, l. 1, § si fecerunt. If they made a plan on the land of the said Marquis, it is certain that they began to commit the crime there; therefore, they ought to be punished there, as in ff. de adulteriis, l. si amicis, according to Bartolus. To the contrary, it is noted that these preparatory acts are merged with that final and ultimate crime, as in ff. ad legem Aquiliam, l. illud, § si, and C. de accusationibus, l. qui de crimine, and there it is noted; hence it suffices that they are condemned or punished in the territory where they committed the theft and robbery. Also, it is nothing to the officials of the said Marquis concerning what was committed outside their territory; because by this their territory was not offended, as in l. extra territorium, ff. de iure iudiciorum, with its subject matter. Furthermore, in crimes, the place where the crime ends is considered, not where it began, as fully noted by Bartolus in de adulteriis, l. quod ait, § si. We also have an example of one who killed a man with a crossbow; because the place where he draws the bow is not considered, if he wounds there, as is usually noted in l. 1, C. de quo loco de crimine agi oporteat. Solution: either the theft committed outside the territory of the said Marquis is carried and brought within the territory; and then it can be punished by the officials of the said Marquis in the territory of the said Marquis, according to the opinion of Master Bartolus, because a new territory means a new dominion, as in ff. de conditionibus furtivis, l. nec legatarius; or it would follow that crimes committed outside the territory can be accepted with impunity, which is false, as in l. C. 1, de his qui latrocinii causa. And although this is not observed in fact, it is true in law. If, however, the goods were not transported to the territory of the said Marquis, neither law nor custom provides that they be punished there as for theft perpetrated to the full penalty of theft, namely hanging; but because they ought not to be able to be released with impunity in the territory of the said Marquis, they would be punished for the planning, if it is true that they planned there, or ordered by arbitrary penalty, since they have not been punished elsewhere. And even if they were punished elsewhere, they can therefore be punished by a furtive blow or a pecuniary penalty. But I advise that this be done after consulting the said Marquis and ascertaining his good pleasure, because it is a question of law. Hence, it is well that a superior be consulted, as in ff. de iudicibus, l. eum quem temere, § si. To the foregoing, because the attempted crime is not punished as severely as the consummated crime, as noted by Cynus in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si quis non dicam. The objection to the foregoing, that it is said that the preliminary acts are merged, is not valid; because it is true where they concern the same territory; but when there are two presidents, each ought to punish the crime perpetrated in his own jurisdiction. Argument from C. de sportula, l. 2, because the offender does injury to each, which ought not to remain unpunished, as in ff. ad legem Aquiliam, l. ita vulneratus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a compromise shall be made between relatives upon receipt of security, whether it is necessary to have sureties or pledges, or whether it suffices to secure by stipulation. And no. 3.
2. The word "security": how it is to be understood or taken in any matter.
body: † On the point which is inquired,

Whether, by the aforementioned words of the statute stating that a compromise shall be made between kinsmen with security received between the parties, it is necessary to secure this with sureties or pledges, or whether security made by solemn stipulation according to the custom of compromises, without adding sureties, suffices? It appears at first that sureties are not found to be necessary.

† The word *securandum* [to be secured] is verified even where no surety or pledge intervenes. C. si cert. pet. l. si; C. de test. l. testium; de non numerata pecunia l. in contractibus § 1; de inofficioso testamento l. si quis § si; C. ad Velleianam l. si uxor; ff. de liberatione legatorum l. si quis; ff. de praetoria stipulatione l. 1; C. ad Trebellianam l. pen.; ff. de poenis l. capitalium § ad statuas; C. de apographis publicis l. 1 lib. 10; C. de exactione tributorum l. nemo; in Auth. de manumis. § sed neque col. 3; in Auth. habita C. ne filius pro patre. If, therefore, the word *securitas* [security] is adapted to a bare caution, then necessarily satisfaction is not required, because when one is bound in general, he is discharged by performing the number of that which is to be provided in that genus, as is fully noted extra de regulis iuris c. cum in obscuris; and l. semper in stipulatione ff. de regulis iuris; and l. legato generali de legatis 1, with similar authorities. But here security must be provided, and it has two species, namely bare and suitable: therefore bare security suffices. Argument to the same effect: ff. de verbis oblig. l. quicquid astringendae; de conditionibus ob causam l. legem in principio; de iudiciis l. in omnibus; de haerede vendito l. 2. This benefits the point, because by the force of speech the word *securitas* is naturally apt also for bare security. Which I prove: because security is either full, or fullest, as is noted ff. de minoribus l. ait praetor § permittitur. Therefore *securitas* is a name as if a genus, and thus is predicated of full and not full; of more suitable and less suitable. Otherwise it would not be a genus, unless it were predicated of at least two things. ff. de adoptione l. 1; si certum petatur l. 2, where it is noted. And because it is so with speeches, obligations of words are understood of bare caution: because whatever is divided, etc., as ff. de verbis oblig. l. quicquid. But another thing is understood regarding the interpretation of law concerning that which is clothed, as in praetorian stipulations: because the praetor has interpreted it thus: and he may, because it belongs to him to interpret, to whom it also belongs to establish. C. de legibus l. si; thus speaks ff. de praetoria stipulatione l. praetoriae; Inst. de satisdatione. But statutes receive this interpretation, which can be called extensive: when it imports more obligation than the significance of the word compels. The laws are common, etc., thus speaks ff. qui satisdare cogantur l. 1; C. de tutoribus et curatoribus qui satisdare non debent l. 1. Furthermore, this is confirmed: because by the force of the vocabulary, to make someone secure, or to remove fear of danger, whether one fears regarding a right acquired, or a right to be acquired, by handing over for execution in due time, or fears regarding the person: for security is the trembling of the mind, or the terrible one introducing adversity. ff. de venditionibus in possessione immissis l. 1 § quotiens; and there by Salic. de causa rei; C. de his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt l. praesenti. Whether, therefore, one removes fear of the transgression of pacts by the solemnity of words and the addition of a penalty, or otherwise, it is not law. ff. de verbis oblig. l. qui seruus; C. de institutione et substitutione l. si mater; de legatis 3 l. fideicommissum § si filio. And thus it seems that the judge has discretion to determine whether it is so, as the word sounds, which can be ascertained from the quality of the persons. For if the person is suspect, and attends to poverty, he would not be well secured who did not have sureties or pledges: and therefore then the good man will arbitrate as he sees expedient in law. Argument: ff. de privilegiis creditorum l. si creditores; C. de manumis. l. si postea; C. de iudiciis l. ubi. But if the person is suitable, possessing suitable immovables, then the good man will not be constrained to give sureties, as argued ff. qui satisdare cogantur l. sciendum in principio; and he will also add a penalty on account of the nature of compromises. ff. de arbitris l. litigatores § quod ait. For words are to be heard according to the quality of the matter. ff. de locato § si uno. It serves this purpose that is noted de iudiciis l. 1 and 2 § quod si dubites; ff. de alienatione iudicio mutata causa facienda l. 3 in fine; si cui plus quam per legem Falcidiam l. nihil § quamuis; qui satisdare cogantur l. 2; de praetoria stipulatione l. sin.

For further clarification, I distinguish, that either we speak of liberatory security: and that draws its execution with it, and is always suitable, as l. 1 § si debitori ff. ut in possessionem legatorum; or of obligatory security: then it matters whether that word, *securitas*, is uttered in a stipulation, and is understood in doubt to be bare, as l. quicquid astringendae ff. de verbis oblig.; C. de verbis silentii lancimus. Or it is uttered by law: and then either by the praetor: and the praetorian law speaks, and what is noted C. de procuratoribus l. 1; or by civil law, or by canon law: and then it refers to an obligation born to be proven, and an instrument must be made or repaired, if perhaps it was previously lost or consumed by age, as C. de fidei instrumentis l. plures apocis; C. de libello causae l. sicut; ff. solutione matrimonii l. 2 ver. nec cogitur. And what is noted in Auth. de haereditate et falcidia in principio col. 1; de administratione tutorum l. chirographis. Or to an obligation to be made more valid: and a surety or pledge is required; because more caution, etc., ff. de re iudicata l. plus cautum; because it is made for addition. Argument: C. de contrahenda emptione l. poena conuenta in ratione sui. And the law does this sometimes on account of suspicion, as l. si creditores praeallegant de privilegiis creditorum; sometimes on account of odious things obtained by unjust law, as C. de precibus imperatoris offerentis l. universi. Or to an obligation to be born or conceived: and then it is understood of stipulation, not of extraneous obligation, as ff. de damno l. 2. Yet I do not exclude the addition of a penalty and the hypothecation of goods, if some reason persuades the judge to require it: and especially when the obligation is not present, but future, as ff. de iudiciis l. in omnibus; solutione matrimonii l. si constante § quo. Or it is uttered by municipal law: and then either according to those who consider the statute to be strictly law in all respects, it is to be understood as bare, just as in stipulation, for statutes are made in the manner of stipulation by the expression of words, preceding interrogation, and following response. Inst. de iure naturali § plebiscitum; ff. de legibus l. de quibus in fine. According to others, who represent that statutes receive interpretation according to what is good and equitable, it will be discretionary according to the quality of the persons: and this pleases me. Argument: ff. de legibus l. non possunt.

† Returning therefore to the question proposed, I say that if the question of liberation is at issue before arbitrators, for example, of a legacy or a promise, a surety is not necessary. Arg. D. de arbitris, l. litigatores, §. interdum. But if the question of obligation is at issue, then the judge has discretion: whose office is very broad. D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, and he will deliberate according to the causes and the persons, as has been said. For diverse causes cannot be limited under a rule: and therefore they are left to the discretion of a good man. D. de usu, l. mora, and D. de testibus, l. tertia, §. tu, D. de legatis tertio, l. si filio, with similar cases. Provided that it would be interpreted from custom: because the law is interpreted, custom must be followed, as in l. si de interpretatione, D. de legibus. And provided that it were established that there was another common usage of speaking, as in l. cum de lanionis, §. asinam, D. de fundo instrato. For common usage of speaking implies the use and mode of understanding. §. quod bene Cassius, D. de legibus 3, and there noted. And sometimes it induces a mode of signifying, whether this usage is contrary to the law, as in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. Tig., and l. ut Alphenus. And sometimes it has more force than the contrary signification, if the common usage is contrary to the law, as in l. 1, in fine, D. de suppleto legato. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Bal. de Peru. V. l. Doct. et c.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:

2. The term "manifest" and how it is to be understood.
3. Whether a confession made by the testator in his will regarding the restitution of usury constitutes proof.
body: How: it is established in the Council of Lyon. Speculator, in his commentary on c. Usurarum voraginem, says thus.

† Those are manifest usurers, concerning whom it is manifest by the evidentia facti [evidence of the fact] that nothing can be concealed by tergiversation, or who have confessed in court, or have been condemned by sentence, on account of usury. cle. c. si. Or say that those are manifest and public practitioners of usury, who openly and commonly lend money in their houses and receive pledges, who in Italy are called praestitores. ar. de ver. sig. l. palam. Moreover, the same Spec. in c. quanquam says thus. One can be called manifest with respect to what is said here, if he confesses this before the priest, who is his judge, and orders restitution to be made in a public instrument, or in a writing sealed with his own seal; or if he confesses before witnesses and orders restitution to be made. arg. C. de non nu. pec. l. generaliter. Or if perhaps this is contained in a book of accounts. ar. 65. dis. c. qui sincera. Or if perhaps public fame works against him: and some arguments appear, because fame alone would not cause them to be judged usurers; nor would it suffice that two or three witnesses proved that he committed usury, unless fame were proved to this effect, so that he might be called a manifest usurer, according to Bar. in l. 1. C. de sa. san. ec. no. de vsuris. c. cum in dioecesi. The same regarding the book of accounts is noted by Arch. in d. c. qui sincera. On fame with supporting evidence, Garsias treats in d. c. vsurarum. And he says that fame with supporting evidence is sufficient: so that by this the bishop may publish him; from which publication he cannot before be called a manifest usurer. And the same, by reference, is held by Lord Fede. de Senis in his consilia, consi. 61. Generally, however, who is called a manifest usurer. The same Fede. discusses in the same work, q. 9, saying thus.

† It is asked how the term *manifestum* is to be understood in the Council of Lyon, c. *Quamquam*, de usura, lib. 6. And it is certain that it can be taken to mean *notorium*, which has the evidence of fact, or is notorious in law: for example, by confession, or by sentence, or by the judge’s publication; or it is clear from clear and undoubted proofs, Extra, de verbis significandis, c. *Cum* and c. *Super quibusdam*. Furthermore, *manifestum* can be said of that whose proof is evident and manifest, de verbis significandis, c. 2, lib. 6. Hence, when account books appear and there is no doubt that they are usurious books, this proof must be called clear and manifest, d. c. *Quamquam*, according to Arch. Confession even on the point of death has the same effect according to the aforementioned Fede. Bart. also, ff. de furtis, l. *Furem*, says that the frequency of acts, by easy and peremptory proof, makes one a manifest usurer. I say that those things which are done in secret, or said, when they come to light become manifest, and therefore, although one lends secretly, and books are written in silence concerning death, when it comes into public, the manifestation of the truth occurs; it is indeed manifest concerning the delict: but by this the mode of committing the delict is not manifest. Therefore, the quality which is signified by the mode *manifestum* is sometimes required as accompanying the delict to aggravate the word *manifestum*; sometimes it is required as accompanying the delict to aggravate the delict, and then it must be inherent in the delict. ff. de conditionibus furtivis, l. *Et ideo*. Sometimes it is required as giving rise to infamy, whose testaments the canon condemns in this species of infamous persons: then it is not necessary for such quality to be present in the act at its inception; but it suffices that it arises afterwards from confession, or similar things. In every kind of infamy, after sentence, nothing is more valid than confession, as noted, ff. de iureiurando, l. *Sed et si possit*, §. *Finis*.

But there is doubt, because the confession was not made in the presence of the opposing party; therefore, it does not constitute clear proof, but only an indication. D. de aedil. edict. l. quæro, § fin. Indeed, even if the party were present, for it seems to me that it yields only an indication. D. de adulteriis, cap. 5. But the contrary is true according to all the doctors: because a confession made in a will does not require the presence of the opposing party, and yet it makes one a manifest usurer. Here it must be considered that either the confession is reduced to a specific effect with respect to a certain person: then presence is required, if we are dealing with an obligation. Or to a general effect, which reflects only upon the confessor, and not upon a specific adjacent party, nor does it require anything else external: for example, to inform the good and grave persons, and to deprive him of the power to make a will. There, the presence of another is not acquired; because the matter does not concern the right of another, but only that of the confessor. And he alone is the entire extreme from which and in which. Arg. D. de negotiis gestis, l. Nesennius. And this is our case. Having therefore considered the aforementioned point and the instruments, I say that the said testator, as a manifest usurer, could not make a valid will, and that the inheritance is his in the case of intestacy, and not of testacy; and that nothing of what he disposed by will, or by a codicillary clause, is valid. And especially because the canon states that where a confession is made concerning usury, or ill-gotten gains, it does not run on the presence of the party, but on good faith, and on the substance of the truth, as in Extr. de sepultura, c. Parochianus. And it supports this. J. q. 6, Cer. quotiens cordis oculus. Since they are made for the most part at the point of death: and it would be most difficult to require the presence of a thousand men perhaps, with whom great usurers exercised their loans. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether usury is due, and when it is to be paid on a girl's dowry: and whether it is lawful.
body: After two years from the day of the girl’s taking, interest is due; because by the lapse of two years irregular delay is incurred. C. de iur. dot. l. fin. §. praeterea. and note it through the gloss and doctors in l. de diuisione. ff. sol. mat. and this unless the claim has been omitted for a long time. For then it is presumed to have been omitted more favorably toward the debtor, and the claim for interest is tacitly remitted. l. cum quidam. §. diuus. ff. de vsu. where there is a notable text.

And usury is lawful in a dowry, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on usury, chapter *Salubriter*. And they are contained more under the name of alimony than of usury, as in the law *Insulam*, section *Usuras*, in the Digest on the dissolution of marriage. But the time is not said to be ten years. And therefore, if the said accessions, alimony, or usury have not been claimed, they are presumed to have been remitted, according to our understanding, and cannot be claimed for the past time. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a mother shall not succeed to an intestate son except in the eighth part, whether it applies to a son who is a ward, or insane, or otherwise incapable of making a will; and whether such a statute is odious. nu. 3.
2. To die intestate is one thing, to die intestabilis is another.
body: By following

† I have elsewhere stated the common opinion of the doctors, and I say that the Todi statute, which provides that a mother shall not succeed to an intestate son except in the eighth part, does not apply to a son who is a ward, or insane, or otherwise incapable of making a will.

† For it is one thing to die intestabilis, another to die intestatus, as is stated in l. 1, ff. de suis et leg. de propria et vera significatione vocabuli, but with a broad interpretation. Bartolus says the contrary by that text, when it says: “Sed et hos quoque etc.” And he says that this is the common usage of speech. I, Baldus, say that this custom of speaking must be proved in court, because it is not presumed. And I say that if in a statute, or between the proper and the improper meaning, the reason for the difference arises, we should never depart from the proper meaning. But here the difference is more pertinent, because an adult can institute his mother; and thus it is probable, and thus it appears that he usually institutes her; and she is rarely excluded. And if a pubescent person does not make a will tacitly, it seems that he wishes the statute to have effect in his disposition or succession, l. 2, C. de iure codicillorum. But in the case of a minor under guardianship, the mother would always be excluded, because he can never make a will, and the condition of the mother would be most wretched, which is most absurd.

† Moreover, the aforementioned statute is odious: for extremes are odious, since it excludes the favor of the transmitting party and of the party to whom transmission occurs; and therefore the odium must be restrained to the strict meaning of the words. Cf. l. cum quidam, C. de libe. et posthu. And I, Baldus, hold whatever Bartolus holds, for "Plato is a friend, etc." And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who says, "de la ne sia Dio" or "al despetto de Dio," is said to blaspheme God.
body: He,

† who says, "de la ne sia Dio" [God forbid] or "al despetto de Dio" [in spite of God], is he said to blaspheme God? And it seems that yes, as in Auth. ut non luxu. contra nat. and c. 2. de maledi. and l. 1. si quis impera. maledi. 25. dist. c. qualis. and in the canonical epistle of the Apostle Jude after the beginning, there, "when Michael the Archangel", etc. I say the contrary from the common usage of speech, and because these are injurious and contumelious words rather than a curse or blasphemy. ff. de haere. institu. l. quoties. §. si quis nomen. according to the understanding of Rum. Therefore, not every insult is a blasphemy or a curse; especially according to the usage of speech in an unhappy homeland in these wicked expressions. And so I, Baldus, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the usufructuary is bound to pay debts and taxes.
body: Usufructuary

Whether he is bound to pay debts and taxes: say that if he is the usufructuary of the universitas, he is bound to pay debts; otherwise, he is not. D. de usufr. l. l. fin. per Bartolus. Whether he is a usufructuary legatee is clear. D. de usufr. leg. l. si quis ibi.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the names of debtors fall into the legacy of the castle, if the instruments in which the names of debtors are contained are found in the castle: and what about the arms that were for the defense of the castle.
body: Whether

† Debts mentioned in a legacy lapse if the instruments containing the names of the debtors are found in the castle: I believe that they do not. And this is expressed in D. 34, 2, *Si uxor*, § *Legauerat*; and more expressly in D. 34, 2, *Si minime*. For, properly speaking, the distinction of perpetuity does not apply to instruments in the manner of a treasure, as in D. 34, 2, *Si chorus*, because a treasure consists in money, not in instruments, D. 41, 1, *Nunquam*, § *Thesaurus*. Hence, in case of doubt, one must adhere to the rights alleged. However, the arms which were in the castle for the defense of the castle seem to have been bequeathed, D. 7, 1, *Generaliter*, § *Uxori*. The other things in the castle will change, as it were, D. 39, 7, *Quaesitum*, § *Si quis eodem*; and D. 28, 5, *Ex facto*, § *Ex consimilibus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If someone establishes a usufruct in his own property for another, and is later deported on account of a crime, does the usufructuary lose the usufruct?
body: Suppose.

†A certain person granted a usufruct in his property. Subsequently, he committed a felony, on account of which he was deported or condemned to the mines. Does the usufructuary lose the usufruct? I answer that he does not. And the reason is that the right which he has does not depend on the grantor’s right. Cf. D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. et si mors; D. de pignoribus, l. si superatus. This appears to be resolved and understood with respect to that right which has a successive dependency. Not because it was perfected at the first instant, as D. de pignoribus, l. vectigal; D. de locato conducto, l. si quis domum, § huic; and l. si fundus. Cf. D. de donationibus, l. post contractum; C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si mors, in principio. You will adapt these laws from both sides. Baldus, ad litteram, de controversiis inventis, c. 1, at the end. And see on this matter Bartolus in l. postulauerit, § iubet lex, D. de adulteriis; and l. si finita, § si de vectigalibus, D. de damno infecto. I, Baldus. OPINION CCCCLXXX. Punctus. Brothers by blood stood together for a long time, etc. Add that this opinion is found above in opinion 452, beginning “duo fratres,” etc.
Point. Two full brothers lived together for a long time, etc. Add that this consilium is [found] above in consilium 452, beginning "duo fratres" [two brothers], etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether descendants of spurii benefit from a favorable and privative statute.
body: Statute

It is observed that in all cases ordinarily ventilated, a tenth must be paid, except in cases that are contested between ascendants and descendants, in which summary procedure is followed without the payment of any tenth. Now the question arises whether spurious descendants are included in this exception of benefits: and it seems that they are included, because where the statute does not distinguish, neither do we. L. demptio, s. de publicia. And because nature is common. L. hos accusare, §. fin., ff. de accusa. And because they are included in particular penalties. C. de his, qui pa. occ., l. 1. And also in the penalty of the Julian law of majesty, as in l. quisquis, C. ad legem Iul. maie. And especially by canon law, by which they are to be supported, as in c. cum haberet, de eo, qui duxit in ma. quam pol. per adul. And because they are truly sons: and natural law is immutable, as in Inst. de iure naturali, §. sed et naturalia, de capi. dimi., l. tutelas. The contrary is true, for as regards the imitation of civil law, spurious persons should not be called descendants. L. per uerba, C. de adul., ff. de rit. nu., l. legis Iuliae, §. nec distinguetur. And thus note Gul. de in ius uo., l. parentes. And it is the ordinary gloss in c. 1, in cle., per quagl. pat. sol. These words, therefore, although they are natural, should nevertheless be understood civilly: and they should not be extended to incongruities by civil law. Let the conclusion therefore be that in privative and favorable privileges, spurious persons are not included.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How the fruits of the property ought to be divided among brothers, and what is to be shared.
body: How

† Fruits of the goods should be divided among brothers, from whom sons remained, and regarding ransom, when two were captured and paid, whether the others are bound: and what concerning dowries paid from common money, and also what concerning an uncle and nephews living together at one bread, and at one wine, and common expense, and performing many labors, and cultivating lands together, and thereby acquiring sheep, pigs, and other animals, how the fruits of the aforementioned labors, and the animals profited therefrom, ought to be divided. First, I say regarding dowries, that dowries paid from common money must be repaid by the other brother, whose daughter was dowered, for one-half, because it is the father’s duty to dower his daughter, as C. de iur. dot. l. si pater. However, it must be considered from which common funds the dowries were paid. For if they were from the price of things sold, it suffices to restore one-half of the price reduced from the said things, as C. de rei vend. l. mater. And the same applies where there is an uncle and nephew in a similar case. Furthermore, regarding the fruits of labors with animals acquired. I answer, one-half is attributed to the oxen, and animals, with which the cultivation is made: and it pertains to the owners of the aforementioned animals: the other half is attributed to the labor, and must be divided per capita among those acquiring. And if any other animals were acquired therefrom, let the division of the animals be in the same manner. But if the fruits are those sought from one’s own possessions, and not from another’s possessions, they must be divided into two parts: because one half must be given to the owners of the possessions, to be divided commonly among them. The other half must be divided among all. Furthermore, regarding what was paid for those who were captured, while standing guard over the sheep, and animals of the house, whether the loss of the aforementioned animals, and the ransoms paid, ought to be common. I say, that yes. ff. pro socio. l. cum duobus. §. damna. and §. sequen. and fina. and l. adeo. §. quod si in alia. Furthermore, an uncle having from his wife 15 florins in dowry, from which, with another certain quantity of common funds, he bought one house. I answer, this house must be divided commonly. First, however, restoring to the said uncle the 15 florins. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a lease made by the rector of a church for a not inconsiderable period, or for a short period, is binding to the prejudice of his successor. Likewise, what if the rector dies in the interim, and in the first year had received the pension for nine years, what shall be done. nu. 2.
body: Whether a lease

† acts performed by the rector of the church for a not inconsiderable time, or if he holds it for a short time to the prejudice of his successor; and there is no doubt that a lease by the rector of the church may be made for a short time, which according to custom is ten years. Although Johannes Andreae does not affirm this in the title *De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis* in the *Clementinae*, nevertheless it is so true that a period from now until ten years will not be considered a long time, as is established throughout the Code, *De praescriptione longi temporis*, and in the Digest, *Qui et a quibus*, law *Fideicommissum*, section *Aristo*.

But let us suppose that this rector dies in the meantime, and that in the first year he had received the pension for nine years; what is to be done? The Archdeacon, in 12 q. 2 c. Alienationes, says that the successor is not bound to stand by the tenant, nor the buyer to the usufructuary, unless this contract had been celebrated for the utility of the church with the authority of the superior. Note this. C. de loc. et cond. l. Emptorem. And it seems rather to be said that, since such a successor is necessary, not voluntary, as is the buyer, he is bound to stand by the tenant. As I say in the case of a woman, who is bound to stand by the tenant of her husband, otherwise her husband, as l. Divortio, ff. de sol. matr. And just as she recovers the pension pro rata temporis of the dissolved marriage, so here the successor recovers from the heirs of the predecessor. Arg. ff. de us. et hab. l. Pe. and l. Defuncta. Innocentius says, extra, de praeb. Vices suas, c. Fin., that either the administrator of the church lets, or the administrator of the prebend. In the first case, if the lease is made in the name of the church, and for a probable cause, the successor is bound to stand by the tenant, lest those contracting with the predecessor be deceived, l. Permissione et authoritate. Arg. l. Iubemus, §. Sane ne omnino, C. de sac. san. ecc. For since he could bind the church by a lawful contract, rightly the successor is bound to stand by it. In the second case, in the administrator of the prebend, he cannot bind the successor. The reason is that a personal obligation does not follow the land, as ff. de loc. l. Emptor, because the prebendary has the status of a usufructuary; therefore also C. de loc. l. Si quis domum. And because he does not contract in the name of the church, for he is not the administrator of the church, nor in the name of the land, for he is not the owner of the land; nor does he have consent, but contracts in the name of his own person; and therefore he does not bind the successor of the thing, or the minister. Arg. C. de dec. l. Prouidendum, lib. 10. What the Archdeacon says about the authority of the superior must be understood in alienation, not in a simple lease for a short time. And this is true, unless fraud has intervened on the part of this lessor, for example, because he promised to renounce the prelature in this lease, as ff. de sol. matr. l. Filiae meae, and de mand. l. Creditor, §. Lucius, in fi., and ff. de manum. test. l. Qui filium. This is stated by the learned Baldus in l. Iubemus, C. de sacrosan. eccle. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a double penalty should be imposed for a single blow from which multiple wounds were inflicted, or not.
body: A. ntiCIIII

† they held, and Lauro de Arezzo followed them, that one penalty should be imposed: because there is one purpose, one act, and one crime. But Bartolus holds that in effect there are multiple crimes: and therefore punishment should be made for multiple offenses, based on the effect, which causes multiple things to be considered as one. L. illud, in the end, ad legem Aquiliam; and one thing to be considered as multiple, as in C. de accusationibus, L. qui de crimine; and it supports this, ff. de iure omnium iudiciorum, L. si familia. And thus Bartolus holds in L. si gemina arbor, ff. de arboribus furtim caesis. But Cynus holds with the ancients, as he states in L. 2, ff. de excusationibus tutorum, in his additions. For Bartolus, the aforementioned Ariston says that the law looks to the damage; hence, whoever causes harm in multiple respects seems to offend in multiple ways. It seems absurd to say that he who inflicts ten wounds with one blow, for example with a comb, should not be punished more than he who inflicts one wound, for example with one tooth of a comb. Such absurdity must always be avoided in laws and statutes. I say that sometimes the law considers the act absolutely; sometimes it considers the act with respect to the manner. In the first case, the controversy of opinions applies. For example, if the statute says absolutely, "if anyone strikes, etc." In the second case, for example, the statute says, "if anyone strikes someone with a blow of a comb, or a fork, or a two-pronged instrument, and blood flows, let him be punished with ten [units]." For if multiple wounds follow from one strike, there is nevertheless one penalty: because the law seems to have considered this, since it disposes regarding the instrument suited for this purpose; because it seems to speak according to the nature of that instrument. As we say similarly in L. 2, ff. si certum petatur. But the question arises in the present case: if someone, it is said, strikes with an empty hand. For the hand has five fingers, like combs or forks. And although each finger causes blood to flow, there is nevertheless one penalty: because this offense consists not only in the blood, but in the manner and the organ. And although there are multiple flows of blood, there is nevertheless only one hand; and thus one offense, and for this reason one penalty. And this is confirmed by the form of the inquisition in the section "semel," which is stated both actively and passively. Also, blood can flow from four parts, and there is nevertheless only one laceration, as when the entire lip is torn, blood flows upward, downward, to the right, and to the left. And therefore the inquisition does not conclude regarding plurality. To this also contributes that word, "from which strike," which is singular in number. Also, the statute seems to have considered that which happens likely and usually according to the nature of that instrument, because the law seems to consider all things that can easily and frequently happen, as in L. 3 and 4, ff. de legibus. Also, one and multiple can be said in many ways: as in ff. de vulnere, sub L. patris, et filii, and many other things can be alleged, but this is the conclusion. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether this substitution, etc., as here in the principal part, is to be considered pupillary or fideicommissary. And number 3.
2. The mother is preferred to the consanguineous brother.
3. The word "succeed" is more appropriate to direct substitution than to oblique substitution.
4. Whether the benefit from a pupillary substitution comes into a fideicommissum made to another.
5. Whether what someone receives from a fideicommissum must be restored on account of the substitution.
body: The point on which the opinion is requested to be given is as follows.

† A certain man named Vanellus, of the Clauelli family, residing in Orto, in his final days, drew up his last and legitimate will. In which, among other things, he used these words, namely: in all his movable and immovable goods, wherever they may be found, present and future, he instituted as his universal heirs John and Nicholas, his sons, and Peter Sentij, his nephew, in equal shares: and if the said John should die without sons or daughters born of legitimate marriage: then he wishes that the said John and Peter succeed [to his share]; and if the said Peter should die at any time without sons or daughters born of the same legitimate marriage, then he wishes that the said John and Nicholas succeed; and if all should die, etc. After this, the said testator died in the year of our Lord 1069, with the said John, Nicholas, and Peter surviving. The said John was then over 30 years of age and had children, and the said Nicholas and Peter were then under 7 years of age. The said John and the father of the said Peter, namely Sentius, were full brothers, related on both sides; and the said Nicholas was the consanguineous brother of the said John, and the affine [step-brother] of the testator through Lady Luminata, the second wife of the said testator. After this, the said Peter Sentij died in pupillary age, without surviving children, with the said John and Nicholas, sons of the said testator, surviving. After this, the said Nicholas died intestate, being over 26 years of age, without sons or daughters surviving him, with the said John, his consanguineous brother, and the said Luminata, his mother, surviving. A question arises concerning the inheritance of the said Nicholas between the aforementioned John and Lady Luminata. It is now asked, what is the law regarding the inheritance of the said Nicholas, and to whom does the intestate inheritance of the aforementioned Nicholas devolve: and what is the share in the inheritance of the said Nicholas.

It must be premised for the sake of clarity that the mother is preferred to the consanguineous brother, as in the Authentica *Defuncto*, Codex, *Ad Tertullianum*, and as noted by Cynus, Codex, *Communia de successionibus*, Authentica *Itaque*. Hence, since Nicholas, who died in adult age, is deceased, his mother, Luminata, succeeds intestate to all the goods of the said Nicholas; nevertheless, she must restore by right of fideicommissum to the said John one-half of the portion of the said Nicholas, as in chapter *Raynaldus* and in chapter *Raynaldus*, *De testamentis*, and chapter *Si patre*, *De testibus*, Book 6, together with similar authorities. Secondly, it must be premised that it may be doubted,

Whether the substitution made to Peter, the testator’s grandson through a predeceased son, considering that Peter died in pupillary age, should be regarded as pupillary or fideicommissary. And it seems that it should be regarded as pupillary because of the word “succeed,” which is more appropriate to direct substitution than to indirect. And because this person was a pupillus and in the power of the substitutor; and because the testator separately substituted to each person, as is proved by the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, law 2, and law *Iam hoc iure*, section *Pe*, and law *Lucius*, in the gloss, Digest, *de verbis significandis*, law *Sciendum*, with *Si*, and *Si ita est*. And if it is thus that it should be regarded as pupillary, then Peter’s share would have come to Nicholas by half through the pupillary substitution, and the other half to John, who are both substitutes.

† And then another question arises, whether that which Nic. profited from the pupillary substitution comes into the fideicommissary substitution made to Nicolaus. For if it does not come in, it remains with the mother. If it does come in, it is owed entirely to Ioann. On this point there are differing opinions, as is clear. D. ad Trebellianum, l. ita tamen, §. qui suspectam. The text indeed states that it does not come into the fideicommissum unless he is compelled to accept. But Bartolus says that that which is taken from the father’s goods by virtue of the pupillary substitution comes into the fideicommissum, if he was first substituted pupillarily before being burdened; otherwise, if afterwards. Nevertheless, even according to him, considering the order of the substitutions, that which is taken from the pupillary substitution would not here come into the fideicommissum, because Nicolaus was first burdened and afterwards substituted. And thus the mother would freely have half of Petri’s portion. But if the substitution made to Petri is considered fideicommissary, which seems to be the case, so that it may be valid at all times in one uniform manner; also so that equality may be preserved among the children; also and by us, by us, by the Ultramontanes in l. quanuis, in the said l. iam hoc iure, then Ioann would have all of Petri’s goods intestate, because he, being related on both sides, is preferred to Nicolaus, who is related on only one side; nevertheless, by virtue of the substitution, he is bound to restore to Nicolaus, if he were alive, by right of fideicommissum, half of the half-portion of Petri. For first, half is deducted for the legitime and the Trebellianic portion. Secondly, the other half would be divided equally. And the same right which Nicolaus would have, the mother would have. But

Here arises the doubt whether that which Nicholas received from the fideicommissum regarding Peter’s share ought to be restored on another ground, namely because John was substituted for Nicholas. And from the order of substitutions it appears that it ought not, as is noted in the Digest, ad Trebellianam, in the law Marcellus, § quidam liberis. Finally, it must be said that one-fourth of Peter’s share pertains to the lady Luminata by right of Nicholas. And three parts out of the four parts of Peter’s portion pertain to the said John: and thus I hold in these difficult points of law. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a witness who says one thing outside of court and another in court ought to be punished for perjury.
body: Although the possessors, going through the Bar., just like blind men, trust themselves more than the gloss and than the truth, nevertheless this is very reprehensible.

† Bartolus states that if a witness said one thing out of court and another in court, he ought to be punished for perjury, even if nothing else is proven. L. eos., D. de falcidia, where it is said to be a case. But the truth is to the contrary. And on this point is the ordinary gloss in C. cum causam, quae inter, Extr. de testibus, in the gloss “haec littera.” For the gloss says that the testimony given by him in court proves what it would not prove at all if he were to be condemned for perjury. And this is clear from the reason: for either we say that he spoke falsely; and this is not established, since he, who said out of court that he did not know, can testify to the truth in court. 1st col., quid sit investitura, C. 1, where there is a unique text in the law. The objection from L. eos. does not hold, because that law speaks of three cases. First, when in one and the same solemn production the witness is self-contradictory. Second, when he is contrary to his own seal. Third, when he is self-contradictory in different productions solemnly made in court; it says nothing there about extrajudicial matters. And I marvel that so illustrious a master of mine erred, and especially in the statement of the case. And the discretion of the judge operates for nothing, because this case is not subject to the penalty for perjury; otherwise it would be proven that he spoke falsely through rebutting witnesses who were present at the act. And thus he cannot in any way be condemned, which note. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The statute provides that no contract shall be made, nor ought to be made, with a person under 25 years of age, unless it is concluded in a public place in the presence of five witnesses. Then the statute adds, and because women are easily deceived, we say the same regarding contracts of women. Now, a certain person contracts with a minor: and he bound himself not in a public place, but in the field of Sempronius: and he swore not to come against the occasion of minority, nor any other occasion. Now it is asked, whether the said contract is null or valid.
body: It must be considered,

It is asked whether no contract with a minor is valid, that is, whether the prohibition is directed at the minor himself, or against the party acting, so that he may not receive; or whether the act itself, and not the actor and the receiver, is prohibited. For when the prohibition is directed at the minor himself, so that he may not do, or may not give, for example, so that he may not contract or alienate: nevertheless, if he swears an oath, because the oath is considered to make him of age, the contract and alienation are valid, as in Auth. sacramenta puberum, and in c. quamuis, de pactis, lib. 6, and extra de iureiurando, c. mulieres. And thus it seems at first sight. But Bartolus, in l. is, cui bonis, ff. de verbis obligatis, says that such an oath is not valid, because such an act is interdicted by a superior, and administration is interdicted to him, and he is similar to a spendthrift due to the interdiction of the superior, as noted by Jacobus de Arena in l. qui habet, ff. ad Trebellianum. It must be said, however, that either the statute reproves the contract and the oath expressly by saying that it is not valid; and then, because by an oath no one can make it so that laws have no place in his contract, as in ff. de legibus, l. si quis inquilinos, §. si, and l. nemo potest, C. de legibus, and l. codicillos, §. ult., C. de codicillis. Or it does not prohibit consent, but alienation, because it follows from it; then the oath is valid, because it adheres to the consent, which is commonly valid by the law of nations, as in the aforementioned Auth. sacramenta puberum. And from these it follows that the minor is prohibited from contracting; because by this he is prohibited from consenting, and the oath is not valid. ff. de pactis, l. 1, §. quotiens, and l. iuris gentium, §. et generaliter. And it supports the aforementioned distinction, what is noted in l. dotis, ff. de militum testamento, by Jacobus de Arena. The Canonists, however, say that the oath must be kept, insofar as it can be kept without the loss of eternal salvation. 22. q. 1, c. iuramenti. It is not a matter of the subtleties of the law. 15. q. 7, c. quotiens cordis oculis. And thus they pass through by a simple path.

When, however, the prohibition is directed at the creditor himself, or the receiver, for example, no one shall contract with a minor. ff. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo, and there Bartolus [says] that the prohibition seeks no right, even if the minor swears an oath; and therefore the minor does not seem to execute in fact what he swears, since it ought not to obtain the effect of law. For it was considered a matter of law, and not of fact; and therefore that oath is rather temerarious than obligatory, whence penance for temerity ought to be imposed; he ought not to be compelled to observe it. For since every obligation requires two extremes, one is founded on the person of the promisor, the other on the person of the stipulator, as in l. 3, ff. de stipulationibus servandis, from which, if the person who can stipulate is lacking, nothing done is valid, as in ff. de verbis obligatis, l. 1, in principio. But against this it is made in extra de iureiurando, c. debitores. For the usurer is prohibited from making a usurious contract; he is also prohibited from receiving, nevertheless, if he swears an oath, the oath is valid, and is to be observed out of reverence for the divine name. And the Lord Bartolus says more in l. omnes populi, that if a statute prohibits on account of presumed calumny, with this reason added in the statute, so that frauds may be avoided, that then the oath is not valid by the law itself. And he says truly, that this prohibition is on account of presumed hatred, and on account of presumed fraud, as noted elegantly in l. si quis sub conditione, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. It necessarily follows that the oath is not valid. We say the same in the Macedonian law. We say the same in a donation between husband and wife. Cynus says in l. 1, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis. Since therefore, having regard to the reason, the statute disposes for the removal of frauds: it follows that the contract of the said minor is not valid. It is not an obstacle that he swore an oath, because it was not done in a public place, but secretly in a field, and it is presumed that what is done secretly is done with fraud, as in l. nemo, C. de summa Trinitate et fide catholica, and there fully by Cynus, and extra ut ecclesia, de beneficiis, c. 1, de ritu nuptiarum, l. finalis, de officiis delegatorum, c. consuluit, and C. de senatu, l. inter. And these are true.

But it is better and more cautious that, on account of the fraud which is presumed and proven, from the form of the statute, a relaxation of the oath or sacrament be requested; and then action be brought, as noted in extra de electione, caput venerabilis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the testator substituted his nearest relatives, and there is a sister and the son of a sister, whether they succeed equally, or the sister alone. And number 2.
2. The word "meos" (my). What it signifies.
body: The case is as follows. A certain Titius died, leaving two daughters, Gaja and Seia, and one son, Sempronius. This Sempronius was instituted as universal heir by his father, the said Titius, with a substitution made by these words, namely: “In all my other movable and immovable goods, present and future, rights, and actions, I institute my son Sempronius as my heir; and if it should happen that the said Sempronius dies in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate children, I substitute my nearest heirs as his heirs, etc.” After the testator’s death, Gaja died, leaving a certain son, Martin. Afterwards, Sempronius died in pupillary age, leaving the aforementioned Seia and Martin, son of the said Gaja.

† It is asked, who comes to the succession of the said Sempronius: for the said Seya says that she comes to the succession by reason of substitution and that she is nearer than the daughter of the said Titius, Martin, the son of Gaea, being excluded. And on the other hand it is said that the said Martin comes equally to the succession with the said Gaea by the Authentica *Post fratres*, from the chapter *Utroque* which is above the law *Consanguinitatis*, C. de legatis haeredibus, where it says, “these sons of brothers, since they are equal from the brothers, etc.” From which text it is expressly gathered that the sons of brothers and brothers are equal as regards succession. This is also gathered in the law *Nomina*, otherwise *Omnia*, §. *Si*, ff. de legatis 2, and there noted by the gloss which begins, *Quandoque*, etc. The truth is sought to be declared on the above matters. Those who are nearer in the case are called. ff. de legatis 2, l. *Cum ita*, §. *In fideicommissis*, and l. *Cum pater*, §. *Libertus*. And this writing of the testator also says, when he says “my nearest”: and if one of the nearer ones died in the meantime, he does not transmit to his heir. ff. de legatis 2, l. *Cum pater*, §. *Haereditatem filius*, and there noted, de legatis 1, l. *Filius*, §. *Divus*, otherwise *Diui*.

† Therefore, it seems that one should say that the sister, and not the daughter of the sister, is called here, because there is no doubt that the sister is truly closer in degree to her brother. Likewise, a daughter is closer in degree to her father than a grandson through another daughter, as is clear in *l. Iurisconsultus*, D. de gradibus. Moreover, the testator said "my nearest relatives," which is understood at the time of the testator's death, not afterwards. *l. si cognatus*, D. de rebus dubiis.

† because that word, "my," restricts the indefinite appellation of the nearest relatives. Hence, if both daughters had died, nevertheless the son of the daughter would not be a substitute, especially after the death of the grandfather conceived. L. Item Praetor, De suis et legitimis heredibus non obstantibus. Glossa, § In fideicommissis, because it has regard to the rights of intestacy, not to the rights of testacy, as is clear from the law which it alleges. And that gloss was to this effect. But against this it is argued, because the son is subrogated in the place of the mother. Inst., De hereditatibus ab intestato, § Cum filius. And because the grandfather seems to have had him in mind. C., De conditionibus insertis, L. 1. And words are to be understood civilly, as is argued from D., De servis, L. Si cui. And the nearer relative is in his share, because in it no one precedes. D., De verborum significatione, L. Proximus. And the grandfather's will is interpreted according to the order established both by our law and by the law of charity. D., De liberis et posthumis, L. Gallus. § Because he referred to the law, it seems that his will is subrogated in place of the legal disposition: therefore also, as in Auth. Defuncto, and in Auth. Cessante, and in the Corpus from which it is taken. And this opinion could sufficiently be defended, if the daughter had predeceased while the father was alive, as in the case at hand it seems to contain on account of the word "my"; because at the time of the testator's death the grandson was neither truly nor interpretatively the nearest relative, either in whole or in part, as stated in the aforementioned law L. Si cognatus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a bill of complaint is rightly formed when, from the facts narrated by the plaintiff, a conclusion is drawn against the defendant.
2. Whether the plaintiff in a possessory action for retention ought to specify the place, time, and circumstances.
3. What effect is produced by the clause placed in the bill of complaint, namely, "in every manner, way, right, and form, etc."
4. The words of the bill of complaint are to be interpreted most broadly.
5. What is the form of proceeding in the interdict for retention.
6. The interdict for retention: for what purpose it was introduced, and for what things it is available.
7. Who ought to prevail in the interdict *uti possidetis*.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case pending between the chapter and the convent of the monks of the Holy Cross of Monte Bagnolo on one part, and Ser Peter Lucae and Lady Margarita Vannis on the other, the following matters have been principally committed to me for discussion. First, concerning the libel, whether it ought to be reformed. For it is vitiated by the ineptitude of the petition, which appears before or after the joinder of issue, as stated in the extrajudicial title *De iudiciis*, chapter *Examinata*; and in the Digest, title *Si mensor falsum modum dixerit*, and title *De emptione et venditione*, chapter *Cum dilecti*. Second, the process must be examined. For the form, by which the order of proceeding in judgment is given, if not observed, renders the process null by the law itself, as stated in the extrajudicial title *De rescriptis*, chapter *Cum dilecta*; title *De restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *Pisanis*; and title *De electione*, chapter *Dudum*. For even in a favorable act, the omission of the mode or form vitiates it, as stated in the Digest, title *De verborum obligationibus*, law *Qui Romae*, section *Flavius Hermes*. Third, consideration arises regarding the middle parts of the causes, such as all kinds of proofs; for if the plaintiff does not prove his case, the defendant is absolved, as stated in the Code, title *De edendo*, law *Qui accusare*; and in the Digest, title *De probationibus*, law *Actor*. What is asserted, return to the first point.

And that the libel is defective, it seems to be proved in several ways, and first as follows: Where a crime is brought forward either criminally or civilly, the circumstances of place and time ought to be stated, as in l. libellorum, C. de accusationibus, and c. tuae, de procuratoribus. But here they are not expressed; therefore, etc. Moreover, where the action is by interdict for retaining possession, the modes of disturbance must be expressed, as in extra de probationibus, c. licet causam, according to Innocentius, which was not done here; hence, etc. The gloss, that this libel does not proceed, seems to be proved thus: Where the action is for retaining possession, the judgment is ordinary, and one ought to proceed ordinarily; but here summary procedure is requested; therefore, the libel does not proceed. But the truth is to the contrary, namely, that notwithstanding the aforesaid, such a libel proceeds. I answer: I prove it thus: That libel is correctly drawn up where, from the facts narrated by the plaintiff, a conclusion against the defendant is inferred; therefore, the greater point is established. And it is proved in l. 2, §. arta, ff. de exceptione doli. The greater point is proved by c. licet, de probationibus, where it properly teaches how to draw up a libel. And by Roffredus in libels, supra, in the matter of interdicts uti possidetis. Nor do the above-mentioned arguments to the contrary regarding the omission of circumstances stand in the way.

† because if the party bringing the action by the interdict of retaining alleges the fraud of the disturber, he is bound to specify the circumstances: for he who alleges the crime of another, which he brings into judgment, must allege the time and place. 3. quaest. 8. cap. libellorum. even if the action is brought civilly, as in the said cap. tuae. Or if he does not allege the fraud of the disturber: and then the rule is different, as noted by Ioan. de Imo. in the said cap. licet. and Barto. ff. uti possidetis. l. licet. Moreover, it is no objection that this is an ordinary judgment, therefore they ask improperly by asking that summary procedure be followed,

† because that general clause follows, “and in every manner, way, right, and form, etc.” This should be interpreted in the manner most advantageous to the plaintiff, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, title *De rerum amotione*, law *Quidam*; and by Johannes Andreae in chapter 1, title *De novo operis nuntio*, in his additions. For regarding the interpretation of the words of the libel, we favor the plaintiff, as noted in the Digest, title *De verbis significandis*, law *Si non potest*. If summary procedure cannot be followed, ordinary procedure shall be followed; and in every manner in which it can be done better according to the plaintiff’s intention, as in law *Si quis intentione ambigua*, Code, title *De iudiciis*. To this point it is highly pertinent what Innocentius notes in the Decretals, title *De ordine cognitionis*, chapter 2, concerning that libel “I ask that justice be done to me”; and in the Speculum, title *De libellorum conceptione*, section *Iam nunc*, under the words “Moreover, such” and the following words. It is also pertinent what Innocentius notes in chapter *Cum ex officio*, Extravagantes, title *De praescriptionibus*; and what is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Mulier*. And if it is said that a genus added to a species is restricted by the enumeration of the species, as in law *Finis*, section *Cui dulcia*, Digest, title *De vino legato*; title *De procuratoribus*, chapter 2, in the Clementines; and by Dyther in chapter *Generi per speciem*, title *De regulis iuris*, Book 6; so that the sense is that procedure shall follow in every manner, way, and form in which it can be done better, provided that it proceeds simply and *de plano*; thus that general clause “in every manner, etc.” placed after the enumeration of species refers to the enumerated species according to the aforementioned authorities. For I say that this does not constitute an obstacle; because this applies where the plaintiff or the one presenting the petition is not granted an Impetration; rather, the interpretation is made entirely against him, as in law *Veteribus*, Digest, title *De pactis*.

† Moreover, the words of the libel ought to be interpreted most broadly, as noted by Innocentius in the cited chapter *Licet causam*, at the end, from which I conclude that the said libel proceeds. The aforementioned point is well supported, because, however the libel may be tolerated, it ought to be admitted, as noted by Innocentius in *De iudicibus*, chapter *Examinata*. And this concludes the first point.

I come to the second point, concerning the mode of procedure. It appears that the response is that the form of the statute was not observed here, for the statute, posited under the rubric “In what manner and order shall one proceed upon the libel, etc.,” requires that the defendant be cited twice, and peremptorily, in case he does not appear; and this is expressly contained in the statute itself. Regarding this third matter to be examined, see absolutely l. 3, in principio, ff. uti possidetis; and what is noted by Roffredus in his libelli in the title Utrubi; and the Speculum in the title De petitione et possessione, § 1, verso “Quid si peto fundum,” A. P.; and absolutely see what Baldus places thereon in the gloss on the law, and on the words “et tu possides,” etc.; otherwise you will not understand it. But these formalities do not appear to have been observed here; therefore, the procedure is null, as in the cited chapter Dilecta and chapter Pisanis. However, I do not believe the contrary objection holds here, for the aforementioned statute has two heads. The first is when the cited defendant does not appear; and then what I have said applies. The other head is when he does appear, in which case the aforementioned form is not observed; because where we have the presence of the person, no other citation is required, which is made only for the purpose of appearing; but then a term of three days is assigned for obtaining a copy of the libel and for putting in opposition; which form exists as having been observed here; therefore, the procedure is valid. It remains, therefore, to come to the third point, namely, to the merits of the case.

† Concerning which it should be known that this interdict was introduced so that prior possessors may not be disturbed in their possession. D. 43.17.1. And this interdict is granted directly for corporeal immovable things, both urban and rural. Nevertheless, it does not lie as a useful action for incorporeal rights, whether real or personal, as is stated in the cited chapter *Licet causam*, Extr. de probat., there, *Emens*.

Secondly, it must be known that in this interdict *uti possidetis*, either one party proves his case better than the other, for example by showing older possession or by producing a greater number of witnesses, and he obtains the judgment; or both parties prove possession equally, and then he obtains the judgment who proves title, thus justifying possession by title, as stated in the cited laws. Now, in our question, considering the statements of the said witnesses and their attestations with respect to both possession and title, the act of the plaintiffs is proved much more strongly by witnesses than that of the defendant. For regarding the possession of the goods of Vanni, which the plaintiffs claim, their act is fully proved, namely that they possessed for a period of twenty years and more, and until the time of their death, specifically by Angelo Vtti and by John Vtti, for a period of fifteen years, it is proved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A special inquisition is brought against a specific person: and concerning a specific crime, it must contain the place and the time; otherwise, it does not conclude as a special one, but whether it proceeds as a general and indefinite one: for example, if from the evidence received regarding it, the place and time become apparent, let condemnation be made.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is as follows: A certain person was investigated for the falsification of false instruments; during his excuse, he denied the contents of the investigation. The point is as follows: the statute says that whoever knowingly writes a false instrument shall lose his hand, which he may recover for twenty-five florins, if he has confessed the offense voluntarily and paid within 25 days. Now, since the proceeding is against a certain notary for the falsification of certain instruments by way of simple investigation, ex mero et puro officio. To the same. In the Name of Christ, Amen. Asked only about the subscription, and since the matter has been fully and subtly consulted by the eminent doctor of both laws, my lord, Lord Marcus, I will briefly conclude.

And as to the first point, that the inquisition does not proceed on account of the place where the maleficium was committed, it seems true according to the *ius commune*, which he consulted, because a special inquisition, which is conducted against a certain person and concerning a certain crime, must contain the place and time; otherwise it does not conclude as a special inquisition, as by the laws cited above. But whether it proceeds as a general or indefinite inquisition, so that if the place and time appear from the proofs received thereupon, condemnation may be made, it seems that it does, as noted by the gloss in the *Institutes*, *De publicis iudiciis*, in the beginning. Others say it does not proceed. Bartolus in the law *Libellorum* and Jacobus Butrigarius in the *Institutes*, *De actionibus*, in the beginning. In favor of the gloss it is argued that the law *Libellorum* speaks of writing, but in inquisitions there is no writing; therefore the law *Libellorum* ceases to apply. But against the gloss, because exceptions which can be raised against an accusation can be raised against an inquisition, as noted by Innocentius in *De officio delegati*, chapter *Venerabili*. And therefore I conclude regarding this that the said inquisition does not proceed, and therefore the said inquisition does not proceed, because it is not proven. Nor does it avail that it was proven in a civil suit, because from acts done in a civil case the judge could be moved to proceed in a criminal case, but not to punish ordinarily, as noted by Guillaume and Cynus in the last law of the *Digest*, *De officio praesidis*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Both Laws: and for the faith of me, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether to be such, or to be held as such, are the same thing: and whether a statute making mention of one has application to the other.
2. The phrase *ipso iure* imports a sentence pronounced.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Having examined the aforementioned petition, the statements made, and the testimonies produced in support thereof, and having reviewed the aforementioned statutes mentioned in the petition, and presupposing the power to enact statutes, as well as the authority to establish one’s own law, which is held by the entire people possessing jurisdiction, and which is called civil law: ff. de iustitia et iure, l. omnes populi; ff. de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis, l. finalis; and de privilegiis creditorum anteriorum, noted in C. de fideiussoribus, l. barsagoram; and in c. ut animarum, de constitutionibus, lib. 6; and de decretis decurionum, l. in facta, lib. 10, together with similar authorities.

It must be considered whether, by virtue of the aforementioned provisions, the said Calderinus can banish and cause to be banished two persons who are either already banished or condemned by the commune of Perugia, or who are banished or condemned solely for some other cause than rebellion; and whether the armed officials of the commune of Perugia and their notaries, who have the power to do so, are bound and ought, upon having legitimate faith in the aforementioned matters, to cease and cancel any sentences and all proceedings issued or made against them or either of them in any manner, form, or for any cause whatsoever. And it seems that he cannot, because it is found that the said Ciancha was a rebel and condemned as a rebel; therefore, according to him, he ought to be treated as such. C. si contra ius, vel utilitatem publicam; l. et si non cognitio. And although the statute wished for him to be held and reputed as a rebel on account of the cavalry raids, invasions, and condemnations made according to him against the Perugian territory, this seems to proceed by virtue of a certain fiction, which does not appear to have a place in statutes. The words of the statute must be taken properly and truly, not improperly and fictitiously. ff. de negotiis gestis, l. 3, § haec verba; ff. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. praetor ait; and noted by Ioan. de Ligna and others in cap. quod circa, de electione, in Clementina.
