But notwithstanding these arguments, I believe the contrary should be said in law. For as Bartolus notes in l. his qui pro emptore, ff. de usucapione, and ff. de adulteriis, l. si maritus, it is equivalent for someone to be such or to be held as such, unless the statute disposes concerning matters of law and those which can be true. Hence, if the statute says that someone is to be held as a citizen, he will be a citizen; because this can be done by the truth of the power of the law; hence it is not a fiction. Since, therefore, the aforementioned statute wishes that anyone who invades the Perugian territory, or in any way makes cavalry raids, or commits any offenses therein, by committing any homicides, thefts, or robberies, plunderings, or rapines, etc., in the said territories, shall immediately by law and by the fact itself be understood to be rebels and traitors to the commune of Perugia, and to be reputed and held as rebels and traitors to the commune of Perugia, as if they were legitimately condemned by the form of the statute and decrees, etc., it follows that the said Ciancha, hardened in evil days, was truly a rebel by virtue of the aforementioned acts committed by him; and the disposition of the statute applies in a true case, not a fictitious one. Moreover, the statute disposes and speaks through a substantive and essential verb, because it says "they are"; hence it induces true rebellion.

And it is a crime of broad interpretation, because it states ipso iure and ipso facto. [See] de rescriptis clericorum, c. 1, in fine; de consanguinitate et affinitate, c. eos qui, in the Decretals; de haereticis, c. vergentis; de privilegiis religiosorum; de poenis, c. cupientes; as well as C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus; § is tabellionibus, de iure fisci, l. eius qui debitorem. And thus, the objection based on § haec verba does not hold, given that if... Moreover, this statute regards public utility: and by the hope of reward, it invites men to pursue and capture the most wicked and criminal men, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, whose feet are swift to shed blood, and who are eager, having fixed their plunder on foreign territories, to invade the territory of the Perusians, whom it is necessary to uproot from the land and extirpate. ff. de officio praesidis, l. congruit; de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. impium; [they] need laws armed with weapons to punish rebels, and arms to the law. de iustini. C. comp. in principio, in the gloss on the word auxilio; and de re militari, l. 3, § miles. Since therefore this statute concerns public utility, it is lawful, and even if the force of law were argued to the contrary, to depart from the strict path of the law and follow the public good, as noted in the gloss in l. 1, C. qui accusare non possunt; 23 q. 4, c. Galizanus; 31 q. 6, c. 1; de poenis, c. aut facta, in fine; and in poenis in the Decretals, c. si quis suadente, § civitas; and according to Innocentius de Constitutionibus in c. 1. For it is introduced on account of many roaming bandits, otherwise it would not be introduced, although strict, as in the Extravagant bona, 8, which begins Rem non novam; as in the Decretals, 1, de iudicibus, and there is room for examples with many roaming bandits. Otherwise, the law says that many things in civil law, against the strict reasoning of debate, for the utility of the republic, i.e., for the public good, are commanded and ordered according to nature, thus it should be, as noted in l. ita vulneratus, § si quis, ff. ad legem Aquiliam. And it supports the aforementioned what my lord noted in the Summa Decretorum, dist. 16, c. multos. Furthermore, since the statute says that they are rebels ipso iure and ipso facto, another sentence does not seem necessary, as noted in l. Imperator, ff. de iure fisci; and in l. commissa, ff. de publicanis. And thus, the objection based on what is noted in d. c. cum secundum, de haereticis, lib. 6, does not hold, because beyond the statute, it wants them to be rebels, as if they had been condemned as rebels: therefore the law effects what the judge would do by his sentence, nor are the officials mere executors for the judge; rather, it seems to want that faith can be made before them regarding injustice, and they have cognition: since the statute says at its end that the said armed officials and their notaries may, are bound, and ought, having legitimate faith regarding the aforementioned, to annul and cancel any sentences, etc. Note that it says, having legitimate faith regarding the aforementioned: and they seem to have some cognition. Hence, they are not mere executors, as noted by the great gloss extra de officio delegati in c. pastoralis, § quia vero; by Bartolus in l. a divo Pio; by my lord in d. l. et si non cognitio. Since therefore, through the said Calderi, what ought to be proven has been proven, I conclude that the said armed officials and notaries ought to carry out the condemnation of the said Andrea Fran., by the rights and reasons aforementioned. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a lawsuit brought against a son for the recovery of possession without the father's consent is valid; and when a son may sue and be sued without the father's consent.
2. The presumption is in favor of the judgment, unless, etc.
3. When a cause is said to be civil or criminal.
4. When an appeal is said to be abandoned, or not.
5. Whether nullity may be alleged after an appeal has been abandoned.
6. When in the petition I declare the judgment null, and if there is any, I appeal: whether the cause of nullity is then said to be incidental.
1. What is the effect, whether nullity is alleged principally or incidentally.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the case pending between Blasius Mattheoli on one part, and Cola and Andrea Petri Iani on the other part, having viewed the acts and proceedings both in the first cause and in the cause of appeal, three matters principally occur to be investigated. And first, because here an interdict of recovery was brought against the filiusfamilias without the interpellation or consent of the father: whether such judgment subsists, or whether it is indeed null. Secondly, whether by the judge of the first cause there was a condemnatory judgment, from which an appeal was taken, and whether the appeal is deserted. Thirdly, whether if the appeal is deserted, it can in any way be said to be null. I come to the first,

† And it appears that such a judgment stands, whether we speak of ancient law or of new law. For the presumption is that the sentence passed against the son was just; therefore, it must be observed. For the sentence. The judge presumes, as in the gloss in *l. Haerennius*, § *Gaya*, D. 47.2, and in *c. Sicut nobis*, in fine, X. 2.28, and the text is in *c. In praesentia*, X. 2.1. That under ancient law the father’s consent is not required for a son suing or fleeing is proved by many laws, especially by *l. Denique*, § *Sed utrum*, D. 4.4; *l. Noxali*, with the following law, D. 9.1; *l. Tam ex contractibus*, D. 49.1; *l. 2*, D. 29.1; *l. 3*, D. 44.7; *l. Filius*, D. 48.5; *l. Inter liberos*, § *Si*, D. 49.15; *l. Post legatum*, § *Si filius*, D. 47.10; *l. Lex Cornelia*, § *Iudicium*, and § *In l. Probari potest* by evident reasons: and first by the argument from equality, for judgments imitate quasi-contracts, as in D. 7.1, *l. Si quis servum*, and also *l. Si quis cum filio*, ibid. But in contracts the son has a legitimate person, except in loan and vow, as noted in Inst. 3.13, in principle, and C. 8.52, *l. Eius*, and *l. Si ex alio*. Therefore, it is proved also in judgment: and here, that if the son is sued on account of a delict, he may stand in judgment without the father, and that the sentence passed against him is valid. For we see this in the case of a slave, because otherwise he is not a suitable person to stand in civil judgment, as C. 4.1, *l. Servus*. Yet in delicts, even if sued by the master, he is not defended, but stands alone in the case, and the case stands well, as D. 4.8, *l. Servus*. The father must consent: and the master must defend the slave in a noxal action, as C. 4.26, *l. 3*. Hence, just as the judgment against a slave without the master stands, as has been said: so it appears that the judgment made with the son without the father stands. For this, see *l. Noxali*. Moreover, judgment is an act prohibiting certain persons; but the son is not regularly required to be prohibited; therefore, etc., as D. 4.4, *l. Nunc vero*, § *Sed quod eis*, and C. 10.10, *l. Statuas*, with the following. And this is according to ancient law. But according to new law, this seems expressly proved; and I argue thus: the father is the legitimate administrator of the son by reason of usufruct, as in Auth. *Excipit*, C. 5.52, and *l. 1*, C. 5.27. Where therefore usufruct is not sought for the father, he is not the legitimate administrator; therefore, his consent is not necessary, so to speak. Either the father has usufruct in the son’s goods, and the son cannot in any way be in judgment, because administration does not belong to him, but to the father, C. 5.52, *l. Cum non solum*, § *Ubi autem*, and § *Filius*, and *l. 1*, C. 5.27. Or usufruct is not sought for the father: then either it is not sought because he does not wish it; and his consent is required as a sign of repudiation, as in § *Necessitatibus*, according to the law of the action, which Bartolus follows. Or usufruct is not sought for the father, because it cannot be sought for him; and then his consent is required, in Auth. *Ut liceat matri*, in principle, according to the said § *Necessitatibus*, and in *l. 3*, D. 13.6, *Si filio*, and D. 50.17, *l. Si*. This opinion is held by some older doctors, such as Jacobus de Al., Ricardus, Malulus, and Jacobus de Belvis. For this opinion, the case seems today under canon law in *c. Si*, X. 2.1, lib. 6, and in the gloss here expressly holds in the aforementioned judgment, i.e., of momentary possession, by *l. Ultima*, C. 4.18, *Qui legitimam personam*. From the foregoing, therefore, it appears that, since in our case usufruct is not sought for the father, because neither for the master by the slave, nor for the father by the son is it sought on account of delict or misdeed, as *l. Quod servus*, D. 10.3, that the aforementioned judgment is null. This is proved first by argument from similarity. For it is lawful to argue from contracts to judgments, as has been proved. But in a donation *causa mortis* the father’s consent is required, as D. 39.6, *l. Si*, § *Si*. Therefore, also in judgment: for a donation *causa mortis* accedes more to contract than to last will, as the gloss notes in *l. 2*, D. 32, in fine. Likewise, argumentation from last wills to judgments is lawful. Moreover, according to the words of Accursius, paternal power is of civil law, as Inst. 1.9, § *Propterea*. According to the gloss, the son under paternal power is not a whole man; therefore, to complete the person of the son, consent or authority of law is required, as the gloss expressly holds in § *Necessitatis*. Moreover, the son is regularly not in judgment with the father; therefore, paternal power regards judgment; therefore, he will not be in judgment with another without his consent. This is clear, etc., by argument from sufficient enumeration of parts, because paternal power consists in seven things, as Inst. 1.9, § 1. But this case is enumerated among the aforementioned: for among other things it is said there that the son cannot be in judgment without the father’s consent; therefore, this also supports the gloss in the said *l. Denique*, § *Necessitatis*, which speaks generally that the father must consent to the son suing or fleeing; therefore, it is to be understood generally and indistinctly, as D. 50.17, *l. Cum pater*, § *Dulcissimus*. Nay, if one looks closely, it seems to me that the case in the said *l. Cum non solum*, joined with § *Necessitatis*, which comes continuously to the beginning of the said law. For in the said *l. Cum non solum* it is said that if an inheritance is left to the son, and the father does not wish him to accept it, and the son wishes to accept it, that then if he is of legitimate age, the son may accept it, and compel suit; and the father in every way must consent to him suing and fleeing; and yet it is certain that in such a case nothing is sought for the father, neither profit nor loss, as is expressed; therefore, Bartolus’s doctrine does not seem true, that where usufruct is not sought for the father, the son by himself has a legitimate person to stand in judgment without the father’s consent. And against this his doctrine is the gloss expressly in the said *l. 3*, § *Si filio*, D. 13.6. For it is certain that in a loan made to the son, or a deposit with him, usufruct is not sought for the father; and yet if the son is sued on loan or deposit, he must be sued with the father authorizing, as the gloss there expressly holds, from which it is not safe to depart in doubt. It is clear, etc., that the father’s consent is not required even in delicts, by *l. Si longius*, § 1, D. 4.8, where it is said that with the father absent, the judgment brought against the son on a noxal action of theft or injury is valid; therefore, it is clear that with the father present it would not be valid without his authority. Argument from the contrary sense, which is very strong in law and is held as law, as *l. Qui testamento*, § *Mulier*, D. 28.5. And the text there speaks by the word “provided that” (*ita tamen*), which has an implicit negative, as in *c. Cum ecclesia Sutrina*, X. 3.18. And properly, and preceding words limit and restrict, *l. Lucius*, § *Quae habeat*, D. 36.1. And see in Speculum on the word “provided that.” And although the text speaks when the son sues, the gloss there says the same if he is sued. For this, D. 3.3, *l. Filius familias*, ver. *Si forte neque pater*. My lord also holds this part in the said § *Si filio*, and in the said *l. Si longius*, where he says that either the father has usufruct, and the exercise belongs to the father by reason of usufruct; or he does not have usufruct, and the authority belongs to the father, because he must authorize the son. The exercise, however, does not belong to the father in his own name, but in the name of the son. For this, D. 4.4, *l. Patri pro filio*, and in Auth. *Apud quos oportet me causam dicere*, in the great gloss. He concludes therefore in the said § *Si filio*, with the gloss, that where usufruct is not sought for the father, at least the son must be authorized on account of the reverence of paternal power. For it is in the father’s interest that the son not misuse his substance by litigating improperly. He holds the same in private crime in § *Necessitatis*, and Cynus in public judgment if it is for a pecuniary penalty. Moreover, if the father’s consent were required solely to denote repudiation of usufruct, and thus in that case, and not to substantiate the judgment: therefore, with respect to ownership, the judgment stands, and in civil case without the father’s consent: which is not true. And the gloss in the said § *Necessitatis* requires the father’s consent to substantiate, so that without it the judgment is not valid. And this part, in doubt, I believe to be the more true opinion, following the paternal one, although here it is not without doubt, where diversity of opinions is found. And therefore in such matters truth should be followed, which the good man holds in his hands: for where great men are in different opinions, adhering to one is not a sin, nor is it counted as such, as noted by Innocentius, X. 1.6, *c. Ne innitaris*. With two friends existing, i.e., two contrary opinions, it is holy to fight for the truth. Now it remains to respond to the more substantial counter-arguments.

And first, to that which is presumed in favor of the sentence: it is true, unless an appeal has been lodged, as stated in the cited chapter *In praesentia*, under the title *De renuntiationibus et probationibus*; and in the chapter *Quam contra*, according to Innocentius. Or, it is not presumed in favor of the sentence with regard to the solemnity of judicial procedure; but it is well presumed with regard to justice and truth, according to the law *Denique* and other laws. Some say that this was different under the old law. But this is not true, because today the son is strong in court, whereas formerly full acquisition was made to the father; and therefore, as to the law *Denique*, section *Sed dicendum*, according to Bartolus, the father there consented to the preceding judgment, and therefore he is deemed to consent in the subsequent one, and there the gloss holds this view. For there the sentence against the son is ordered to be executed; and the executory process is valid, even if the father does not consent to the son; because it suffices that he consented in the principal judgment. Also, because the process of execution is extraordinary; and in extraordinary processes, the father’s consent is not required, as noted in law 1, Code, *Qui admittuntur ad bonorum possessionem*. As to the law *Notatur tam ex contractibus*, it seems to be said that, since it does not appear there whether the father’s consent intervened or not, the consent is understood to have intervened, so that the correction of the laws may be avoided, as in the Authentica *Quas actiones*, under the title *De saecularibus*; and according to the similar laws cited above. And thus the gloss seems to hold in law *Denique*, section 1, *Quod vi aut clam*. Or, it is understood that the father is absent or unable to act, as in law *Si longius*, law *Sed si unicus*, section *Filio*, under the title *Ad inter liberos*, section *Si*, and to the law *Gatam*, section *Filius*. I say that they speak of judges in whom paternal power is not required, as in the Digest, *De his qui sui iuris*, law *Filius*, to the Trebellian Trust, law *Quod attinet*. And the reason is that in such cases the son represents a double person; the person represented is, insofar as he is not subject to paternal bonds. Imola says, and in the cited section *Cessi*, in question 8, that by reason of paternal power. And indeed, it is public, unless the action is personal, but pecuniary. In private matters, expressly Jacobus and Bartolus, and he adds that in public matters it is safer to proceed. Now it remains to respond to that which is new, book 6. I say that there he speaks of beneficial and spiritual causes, which seem to pertain to those matters, hence in these the son is considered sui iuris; and this seems to be proven by the note, according to Innocentius, *De aetatibus et qualitatibus*, chapter *In decretum*, which generally requires the father’s consent, except in beneficial and spiritual matters. Moreover, since in such matters one proceeds extra ordinem, as in the decretal *Dispendiosam*, therefore the father’s consent is not required, as in the cited law 1, Code, *Qui admittuntur ad bonorum possessionem*. But as to the response to the gloss there at the end, which expressly seems to hold that the son has a legitimate person in court for momentary possession, by law *Ultima*, Code, *Qui legitimam personam*, I respond that the said gloss must be understood where the son acts in the first instance; otherwise, if he is sued: lest what has been granted in his favor be turned to his detriment, as in law 1, *Quod favore*. And thus the gloss there holds, according to one opinion, which is commonly approved. Also, the aforementioned statute does not obstruct the foregoing, which provides that a condemnation in a criminal cause shall not be invalidated by a defect; because it is understood, unless the crime is prosecuted criminally, or for a corporal or pecuniary penalty to be applied to the fisc.

† For then that is called a criminal cause: but civilly, as when that which is sought must be applied to the party: then the cause is called civil, as in l. agraria. ff. de termino moto. de priua. delic. l. si. C. de sepul. uiola. l. qui sepulchra. when a civil action prejudices the crime. l. unica. ff. de testi. c. mediatores. li. 6. de procu. c. ne. ut li. non conte. ti. 1. ff. de sepul. uio. l. praetor. and there the gloss is explicit. and Bartolus. For cause is the same as instance, which instance is civil. For as that Roman eloquence Tullius, and otherwise the gloss, your cause is the thing which has in itself a controversy placed in judging with the interposition of certain persons. And this of the first point. As to the second, of the desertion of the appeal,

Whether it is deserted or not, I say that it is deserted on account of the expiration of the peremptory time limits. For in the prosecution of an appeal, great diligence is required; and it is necessary that one be solicitous near the end of the peremptory time limits, because the final delay is harmful and is considered as a desertion. Codex, On the Time of Appeals, Authentics: "Es qui" and "Lit unde." Therefore, protests made to the judge that he ought to expedite the case are more clearly made at the end of the peremptory time limits than at the beginning, as stated in the aforementioned laws. Indeed, the judge is not compelled to render sentence with precipitous haste, when there is still a long postponement of time remaining. Digest, On Judges, Law "Properandum," Section "Huius autem." And note, through Cynus in that law, Section "Et si quidem," in the First Decree. According to Peter of the Order, this matter is touched upon by Innocentius in Chapter "Plene," On Appeals, from the reason given by the Gloss, On Election, Book 6, in the Gloss on "Si appellatur," On Appeals, Chapter "Cum sit Romana." Digest, On Which Causes a Major Case is to be Heard, Law "Sed et si praetorem," Section "Sed nec nos." In the Authentic, On Those Who Enter into an Appeal, Section 1, and there by Jacobus de Belvis, and in the laws cited above. Now, holding the opinion which I have refuted above, namely, that the judgment is null due to the defect of paternal authority.

It must finally be considered whether the cause of nullity is perempted by the abandonment of the appeal. And first, there are two points to be observed here. First, whether the libel proceeds; I say that the sentence is null, and if there is any appeal. The glossa formats the libel in this manner in l. 1, C. quoniam prouocare non est necessarium, and consequently holds that the libel proceeds and is well-formed; otherwise, it would not format it. Doctor Dy says that either the plaintiff appeals, and the libel does not proceed, as if the appeal were then an action, and the plaintiff cannot act by contrary ways; or the defendant appeals, and then the libel proceeds, as if the appeal were then a defense, and the defendant can allege contraries at successive times, or at the same time, and in a successive or conditional manner, according to Dy. Innocentius in c. Dilecto, de appellationibus, seems to hold that the libel proceeds against a definitive sentence, but not against an interlocutory one; the reason is that the nullity of an interlocutory sentence is never devolved to the superior; otherwise in the difference of nullity. But this seems contrary to l. Arbitro, qui satisdare cogitur, and ff. Quibus appellationes non licent, l. Si. In which it is said that the superior proceeds by the way of nullity even in an interlocutory sentence. To the same effect, ff. De appellationibus, l. Si constat, for that nomination is interlocutory. I therefore say that the said libel proceeds, and indistinctly, because although these are contrary, they are connected; and they are ventilated together, and one is the cause for the form of pronouncement in the other. And therefore, what is the cause is said to be incidental, and the incidental is annexed, therefore it comes into the same judgment. C. De iudiciis, l. Quotiens. Moreover, nullity comes tacitly, therefore it cannot be expressly deduced. For these contraries do not stand thus in ventilation, that one excludes the other, but rather includes it. Moreover, the remedies themselves are prepared successively, and therefore they are not like certain others, which are so contrary that, one being elected, the other expires. l. 1, C. Si seruus extero; l. Si, C. De codicillis.

Secondly, the question is whether it should be stated that this is gathered from the above, or whether in this libel I declare the sentence null, and if there is an appeal, whether the cause of nullity is said to be incidental. The gloss in the aforementioned law 1 says yes. To the contrary, why is it deduced in the first place and primarily? And this is held by Jacobus Butrigarius. But in favor of the gloss it is argued that, unless it were incidental, the libel would not proceed, especially as to the plaintiff according to the opinion of Dyonisius.

But what will be the effect, whether it is incidental or not? I answer that, if it is incidental, the appeal being abandoned, these are the consequences: although the cause of nullity is thereby extinguished, nevertheless the instance of nullity raised is extinguished. No. Innocentius, Extra, de appellationibus, caput Saepe; argumentum, Digesta, Si pendente appellatione mors interuenit; lex 3. But if the cause of nullity were co-equal and equally principal, there would be two causes for the appeal, not one, and therefore, one being abandoned, the other instance would still remain. It is therefore necessary that the nullity be litigated anew, separately from the appeal. Digesta, de appellationibus, lex Si expressim, where the case is found. For the abandonment of an appeal made or to be made does not operate more than if the appeal, already made, were deemed not made, and they are equated, as in lex Si, § 1, Codex, de tempore appellationum. But the abandonment of an appeal to be interposed does not prejudice the cause of nullity; therefore, neither does the abandonment of the appeal, yet the office of the judge from whom does not sleep on account of the prosecution of nullity, as noted by Bartolus in lex Si expressim, unless such nullity is proved ipso facto because the contrary is not proved, as in our case in lex 4, § Condemnatum, de re iudicata, according to Bartolus. And thus I hold for the present. Hence, concluding, the appellate judge will pronounce the appeal abandoned; and that by virtue of the same instance one cannot prosecute the nullity, but that it must be litigated anew.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A surety who has undertaken suretyship for any cause is bound for another; and what is comprehended under this general promise.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. Point: A certain John, an executor of the art of exchange, appearing before us, the auditors of the said art, by obligating himself and all his goods, promised and agreed with the said notary, as a public person present, stipulating and receiving on behalf and in the name of the auditors of the said art, and for the university of the said art, and for all whose interest it might be, to obey and comply with the mandates of the present and future auditors in all and each matter pertaining to the art of exchange, and to the exercise or traffic of the said art in any manner; and he submitted himself to the auditors of the said art as to his judges. And thus he promised to exercise the said art well and regularly, and to do so without fraud, and to observe the ordinances of the art, and to answer according to law before the auditors for all those who might demand or require anything on account or occasion of exchange; and to fulfill all and each promise which he might make or promise as a money-lender, or on occasion of exchange. For which, Angelus, by obligating himself, stood as surety and promised the said notary that he would see to it, and ensure with effect, that the said John would fulfill all things promised by him, and that he would pay all creditors to whom he would be bound as a money-lender; and that if he should pay and satisfy, he promised to pay from his own funds up to the quantity of 200 pounds, and he renounced, etc. Finally, the said John raised a bill of exchange after some time had passed. Then the said John, as a money-lender, by obligating himself, etc., promised to keep Martin indemnified, and to extract and bind, at his petition and term, from the fourth part of all and each quantity of florins and money paid and to be paid, promised and to be promised by the said Martin, in the name and on the occasion of the money-lending of meats and things dependent thereon. It is asked: whether, if the said Martin pays any quantity on the occasion of the money-lending of meats, or on this account makes a promise, the said Angelus, the surety, is bound to him. By the form of this ordinance, two things are provided for, which pertain to the art of exchange, and to the exercise or traffic of the said art in any manner, and on account or occasion of exchange. Regarding the aforesaid, he promises to obey the mandates of the auditors; and to answer before them concerning the aforesaid before the said auditors, in whom he consents as in his judges. Secondly, it is provided alternatively, when he promises to fulfill all and each promise which he might make or promise as a money-lender, or on occasion of exchange; and concerning all the aforesaid, he promises to answer before the auditors of exchange; and regarding the observance of these, this John gives a certain Angelus as surety.

† It is therefore doubted, if the said John, as a money-changer, promises to keep Martin indemnified against a certain sum of money paid, to be paid, promised, and to be promised, on account of money-changing, whether the said Angelo, surety of John, is bound, if the said Martin pays any sum of money on account of money-changing of flesh, even though the said John has lifted the bill of exchange, before he kept the said Martin indemnified? It must be premised that, although the said John lifted the bill, he is not thereby released from his own obligation: for lifting the bill is not a mode of extinguishing the said obligation, but the payment of those things which he promises. Inst., Quibus modis obligationes tolluntur, in principio. Secondly, it must be premised that in alternative obligations it suffices that one part be true. D., De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Si haeredi plures; Inst., De hereditatibus instituendis, § Si plures; De verborum obligationibus, l. Si quis and l. Si quis ita; D., De solutionibus, l. Cum quaerebatur; D., De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Cum pupillis; Extr., De rescriptis, c. Inter ceteras. It accords with what is noted in the rule In alternatiuis. Thirdly, it must be premised that this universal name, comprehending and including all things, as in l. Omnes populi, D., De iure et iudiciis; Extr., De electione, c. In Genesi. From the foregoing, I conclude that, from whatever cause the promise was made by John as a money-changer, whether it was made on account of exchange or of matters pertaining to the exercise of the art of exchange, or from any other cause whatsoever, the said surety is bound to it. For the statute only weighs that he promises as a money-changer, and does not limit the cause, but includes every cause. Cf. Qui filii sint legitimi; c. Per venerabilem, Extr., De electione; c. Cum inter universos, Extr., De adoptionibus; l. Si pater, D. And therefore the said Angelo, surety, is bound to the said Martin by virtue of the preservation and indemnity made by John to the said Martin. And so I say and advise, I, Peter of Peru.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The species in which contracts are classified are known from three sources.
2. Whether jurisdiction is said to be prorogated by a promise, and by a promise of response.
3. If someone promised on behalf of another to satisfy all creditors of that person arising from the cause of the art of exchange, what falls under this promise, together with the following three considerations.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. The sequence of facts clearly brings to my knowledge how an obligation is to be considered. For knowledge of the obligation is given from the form of the words employed; for the form of the words is the matter, from which matter the obligation arises.

For they are known from three things, in which the hope of the contract lies: namely, from the form of the words. D. de cond. ob causam; l. si ex parte rerum, D. si cert. pet.; and from the utility. D. de donat.; l. Lucius, D. de coniunctis; l. 1, D. de poenis; and what is noted by the gloss in the aforementioned l. 2, D. si cert. pet. And the species is known, for the contract is known by the action. Therefore, it must be examined regarding the force of this contract, into what obligation we have fallen. And indeed, this Lo. submitted himself to the auditors of the art of exchange, promising to obey their mandates in matters pertaining to the art, and by this, jurisdiction is considered to have been prorogated over them. l. 1, D. de iudic.; which is evident, when it is added,

† as if before their own competent judges. And afterwards it is added that he is to answer according to law in the presence of the auditors. That which is noted supports this: D. de iure omnium iudiciorum, l. si conuenerit; and l. impertinens ad quaesitum. But it must be examined, since he promised to pay all and each of the promises which he would make or promise as a money-changer, in the event in question, which is included in the case under discussion.

† And it seems, in the first place, that [the obligation does not cease] on account of the diversity of causes. For the obligation arising from the cause of exchange is different from that which proceeds from the cause or occasion of money-lending; therefore, etc., by the argument in *l. si de calumnia* and *l. si maritus*, Codex, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*; and *l. his consequenter*, § 1, Digest, *De familia erciscunda*. Moreover, this Angelo is not a surety, as is noted in *l. hi qui*, Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, since he did not become surety for that cause; nor is the suretyship obligation for a different cause than the principal obligation. In support of this also serves the removal of the tablet, since it is an act designating that the exercise of exchange is not to take place: and outside the exercise [of exchange], the surety wished to be bound. Argument in *l. Tutelae*, Digest, *De capitibus diminutis*. Therefore, such an obligation having been removed by a new obligation of the principal thing, the surety does not fall back into it. Digest, *De pactis*, *l. si facit*; *l. si cum heres*, Codex, *De locato et conducto*. For the suretyship obligation, being of strict law, binds with words. *l. blanditus*, Codex, *De fideiussoribus*; and *l. ultima*, § *satis acceptio*, Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*. And those things which are of strict law do not admit extension. *l. quicquid astringendae*, Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*.

To the contrary, this is the truth in my judgment. For in human acts, regard must be had to the words by which one binds oneself. Institutes, *De obligationibus*, in the beginning. And once an obligation is contracted, its resolution cannot be effected by the arrangement of one party, if it was conceived by the arrangement of two. Codex, *De actionibus et obligationibus*, *l. sicut*; Digest, *De communi dividundo*, *l. in commodato*, § *sicut*. This John indeed bound himself to all and each of the promises which he would make or promise as a money-lender; and for this case Angelo acted as surety; and thus in this case the obligation rests upon the words; and through the notary, as a public person whose interest it is, the action is sought. *l. 2*, Digest, *De re publica salva*; and *l. non aliter*; and *l. his verbis*, Digest, *De adoptionibus*, with its authorities. Also, because the acts of agents operate according to their intention, although not beyond it. Digest, *Si certum petatur*, *l. non omnes*; and *l. obligationum substantia*, Digest, *De actionibus et obligationibus*. And it is clear from their intention that he wished to be bound to the promises which he would make as a money-lender; and for this case the surety wished to be bound, and for no other; therefore he is bound by the contract. Noted in *l. ex conventione partium accipiunt*, Digest, *De deposito*, *l. 1*, § *si convenit*.

Nor does it avail if it is said that this is not the cause and occasion of exchange; for I admit it, yet it was not considered solely as such, but he referred himself to any [transaction] as a money-lender; which appears from the form of the words universally pronounced. *l. omnes*, Codex, *Sine censu vel reliquis*; and *l. omnes*, Codex, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, with its authorities. Nor does the removal or lifting of the tablet avail, for by this the obligation would not be resolved. In support, *l. praetor*, § *sed et*, Digest, *De edendo*. And by this it seems to be said that such John is bound, and his surety, since he became surety for this case; and that this Martin ought to be kept indemnified. And concerning this preservation of indemnity, see *l. 2*, *De sententiis*, *Quam sine certa quam proferas*.

And as consulted above, I say and counsel, I, Dionysius, Doctor of Nicholas of Barigianis, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A surety is not bound beyond the amount of the principal debtor: nor can he obligate himself for more.
2. A surety promises in vain that which the principal debtor will do or give; otherwise, if he promises that he himself will do and see to it that the principal gives or does.
3. One who promises on behalf of another to satisfy all creditors of that person arising from a bill of exchange: to what is he bound by this promise? And add the preceding opinion, and the two following ones.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A surety who intervenes for a certain amount is not bound beyond that amount, even if the principal has obligated himself for a greater sum. See Digest 46.1.11 (*Fideiussores*), § 1; and Digest 46.1.1 (*Fideiussores magistratuum*), § *Pro Aurelio*. One who intervenes simply is deemed to intervene for the entire cause. See Digest 19.2.1 (*Quaero*), in the beginning; and Digest 12.3.1 (*Centum Capuae*). One who intervenes for the entire amount owed by the principal debtor is bound for the entire amount, according to the form of his specific obligation; and this is most well-known. See Digest 46.1.12 (*Si ita stipulatus a Sevo*). One who intervenes for a greater amount than the amount owed by the principal debtor is bound for nothing; for the useful is vitiated by the useless, since it is said that he intervenes to a harsher condition, which the laws do not permit, as is read and noted in Digest 46.1.13 (*Graece*), § *Illud*; and noted in Digest 22.1.1 (*Pecunia fenebri*), in the beginning. If one were to intervene for that which cannot be preserved from the principal debtor, he is not bound, provided the principal debtor is solvent; or even if, after the creditor’s delay, he becomes insolvent. See Digest 46.1.14 (*Si fideiussores in id accepti*), in the beginning.

† Having premised the above, it must be known that a surety promises in vain that the principal debtor will give or do something. But if he promises that he himself will do and see to it that the principal debtor gives or does something, he is effectively bound, as is read and noted in the same title, l. sicut suis. Facit. ff. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio ista habere licere. in princ. inst. de inut. stip. §. si quis alium. and ff. de duob. reis. l. nemo est, qui nesciat. Now, with regard to the matter at hand, the said Ang. as surety promised that he would do and see to it that Ioan. fulfills all things promised by him; and thus, with respect to the promise to be made by Ioan., as by a money-lender, or on account of the bill of exchange, the obligation of Ang. was general and in no way restricted; but with respect to the amounts contained in the promises, it was restricted to 200 pounds. Therefore, Ange. is liable for all the aforementioned promises up to the said sum of 200 pounds and not beyond, as appears from the foregoing. Since, therefore, the said promise of conservation of indemnity made by the said Ioan. d. Mar. was made by the said Ioan. as a money-lender, as is stated in the point above, it is evident that the said Ange. is bound to the said Mar. on account of the said promise of conservation of indemnity. It supports this what is said otherwise in l. tanquam. ff. quod cuiusque univers. nomine. l. Item eorum. in princ. with many others.

It does not object that the said promise of conservation does not appear to have been made on account of the bill of exchange; for it suffices that it was made as by a money-lender from whatever cause, as clearly appears from the nature of the alternative. And although Ioan. lifted the bill of exchange before the said promise of conservation, nevertheless such election does not cause him to cease to be a money-lender: he remains a money-lender in habit, although not in act and exercise. It supports this what the doctors say in l. si. C. de haer. vel actione vendita. in that question there formed by the gloss, whether the possessing owner can cede the vindication of the thing. And granted that we purely wished to say that by such lifting he ceases to be a money-lender: nevertheless it would not obstruct the foregoing; for it is altogether different for someone to be a money-lender, or for someone to be bound as a money-lender; one can bind oneself as a money-lender, although one is not a money-lender. It supports this ff. de adulter. l. si maritus. §. 1. ver. quod si quis praesens. and l. praetor. §. 1. de nox. oper. nunc. But the form of the aforementioned intercession does not require of necessity that Ioan. continue as a money-lender, if he wishes that it suffice that he bound himself as a money-lender. And thus I say and counsel, I, Ludouicus de Perusio, Doctor of Laws, and so forth.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because the above-named eminent doctors of the law have fully advised, and for this reason I agree with the aforementioned truest other allegations, namely that the said Ang. is bound and obligated by the force of the aforementioned suretyship up to the amount to which he limited his surety, with respect to that cause in which the said Ioan., as a money-lender, obligated himself to the said Martin. For he who obligates himself as a surety, after the principal has promised many things, appears to have given surety for every cause that can be comprehended under the obligation of the principal; such is this one, about which it is asked, as is clear above through the aforementioned, and has been most widely demonstrated by my masters through laws and reasons. Hence, I say and advise the same, I, Fran., son of Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Civil Law. And I have subscribed to the faith, and affixed my seal.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because the wording of an obligation must be carefully considered, so that it may be seen whether anyone is bound, as is noted in the Digest, *De verbis obligationum*, in the law *Si quis stipulatus fuerit stichum*; and as is noted by Innocentius in the chapter *Ut nobis*, in the Extravagant, *De clericis percipiendis*. And this John bound himself to all obligations which he would make as a money-changer. Similarly, his surety is bound for all things: for all things which are done with a money-changer for the sake of the money-changing business bind his surety, as in the Digest, *De institoria*, in the law *Cuiuscumque*, section *Non tamen ratione*. And if the aforementioned matters come about tacitly, or as a consequence, as in the same title, law 3, with section *Servus*, and the aforementioned law *Cuiuscumque*, section *Si ei*, it is said that those things not accepted, given, and promised from various causes are considered to pertain to the money-changer, provided that they were done for his benefit. Which is noted in the law *Quidam*, section *Nummularios*, and in the law *Argenti*, section *Edi autem*, in the Digest, *De edendo*. Moreover, the words of contracts, and especially stipulations, are to be understood strictly and against the party who proffers them, as is noted in the law *Veteribus*, in the Digest, *De pactionibus*; it is supported by the Extravagant, *De sponsalibus*, chapter *Ex his*; and as is noted by Paulus de Leaza in the prologue to the Clementines; and as is noted by Baldus in the chapter *Ordinarii*, *De officio ordinarii*, Book 6. Therefore, those words, "which he would make, or promise as a money-changer, or on the occasion of exchange," ought to be interpreted against the said John and his surety. It is necessary to state the law and the objection more clearly. It is supported by what is noted by Petrus de Perusio in the Extravagant, *De testamento*, chapter *Officii*. From the foregoing, I conclude that in those matters in which the said John bound himself truly as a money-changer, both he and his surety are bound. And as is written above, I say and counsel, I, Marcus Angelus.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. The point is that the testator instituted all equally: and he substituted to the predeceasing heir, if without children, the survivors; and even after the death of all, he substituted the brothers John, Angelo, Valentine, and Antonio Seraglione Tengarini. In whose inheritance there remained 1,000 gold florins, of which each ought to have 200 gold florins for his part and portion. First, the said Valentine died, being over 14 years of age. Half of the said 200 florins pertains to the above-mentioned Antonio, as a brother related on both sides, and to the said Matheola, their mother, ab intestato; the other half pertains equally and alike to the said other four brothers by virtue of the said substitution of their father’s fideicommissum. Then the above-mentioned Angelo died, being over 14 years of age. Half of his original portion, namely 200 gold florins, pertains to Antonio, his brother related on both sides, and to the said mother; and thus the portion which came to him ab intestato from the death of the said Valentine, which was one-third of 100 gold florins, pertains to the same Antonio and the said Matheola. The other half of the said 200 gold florins pertains to the said John, Angelo, and Antonio, by virtue of the paternal substitution. And also to them pertains the fourth part which accrued to the said Ser Angelo by virtue of the substitution made to the said Valentine, which was 25 florins. Then John died, being over 14 years of age, having made a will, in which he instituted Angelo and Antonio, his brothers, as his heirs in equal portions. Half of his original portion, which portion was 25 gold florins, pertains to the said Angelo and Antonio, heirs instituted by the said will of John. The other half pertains to the said Angelo and Antonio by virtue of the will made by the said Tengarini; and also to them pertains by virtue of the said substitution made by the said Tengarini the said 25 florins which accrued to John from the death of the said Valentine, the said 25 florins which the said Ser Angelo had. And then the value of Tengarini’s inheritance is 100 florins. The portion touching Angelo, his son, from his own portion by virtue of the institution is 200 florins. Also from the will of John, his brother, he has 50 florins. Also by virtue of the substitution made by Tengarini, 400 florins. In total, of the said 1,000 florins, he ought to have 600 florins. There accrue to the heirs of Antonio, sons of the said Tengarini, joining the portion of Tengarini with the mother, from the death of the sons, computing the portion touching her in the person of the brothers, sons of the said lady, and computing the portion touching her from the will of John Tengarini, of that which he could dispose of by will from his own portion, 350 florins. The point is this: a universal fideicommissary for pious causes sued the heir of the person requested to restore the inheritance, that he would restore the inheritance left to him, of which the said heir had been requested to make restitution. Finally, while the said judgment concerning the said restitution was pending, the said universal fideicommissary sued as heir against a certain prior of certain things of the said inheritance. It is opposed against the said plaintiff by the said prior that the said plaintiff was not an heir; because the judgment of restitution was pending regarding the event of the inheritance; and the said inheritance had not been, nor was, restored to him; hence before the said restitution it was said that he was not an heir; and if he was not an heir, he could not be heard as an heir. It is asked, what is the law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An instituted heir, who protests that by any act which he has made or will make in the future, he does not intend to enter upon the inheritance, unless he expressly declares himself heir by subsequently paying the census for the emphyteutic house of the said inheritance, is deemed to have entered upon it. And the following counsel.
2. By what acts an heir is deemed to have entered upon the inheritance. And in number four.
3. Whether a protestation contrary to the act operates anything.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† When an instituted heir makes a protestation that by any act which he has performed or will perform in the future, he does not intend to enter upon the inheritance, unless he expressly enters upon the said inheritance by words, whether afterwards the said heir, by paying the census for the house held in emphyteusis of the said inheritance and asserting himself to be the heir, appears to have entered upon it notwithstanding the preceding protestation; or whether the protestation is valid, and the act of acceptance is vitiated.

It must be said that certain acts pertain solely to the heir and cannot be performed without the right and name of heir. Certain acts are entirely extraneous to the heir, that is, those which do not pertain to him, nor can they pertain to him. Certain acts are indifferent, that is, those which can pertain to the heir and do not pertain to him, that is, those which can be performed by the heir and by an outsider. In the first case, either he performs the act by contracting with another, or by receiving payment; and then he seems to accept the inheritance and to recede from a preceding protestation, as in l. pro haerede, §. si quid tamen, in fine. Otherwise, if he performs the act by himself, not with another, for example, if he were to accept it by his pure will, as in l. qui in aliena, §. Celsus. And thus that §. should be understood according to Bartolus in the said §. si quid tamen, in fine. In the second case, when the act is entirely extraneous, so that it cannot pertain to the heir, then even if he performs that act as heir, and even without a preceding contrary protestation, he does not seem to accept the inheritance, nor is he bound by hereditary burdens, as in the said §. si quid tamen, in principio. For, due to the nature of services, which are not owed to anyone other than the patron, unless they fall into the common form of certain obligations: for, since certainly a son, by claiming those services as heir, does not seem to accept the inheritance, because the nature of the thing stands in the way, as is expressly stated there. In the third case, when the act is performed by the heir, which is indifferent: then either he exercises that act simply, or as heir, or asserting himself to be heir. In the first case, he does not seem to accept the inheritance, and if the protestation does not proceed, since it could be done without the name and right of heir. Or he exercises it with this quality, namely, as heir, or asserting himself to be heir, or as heir: and then he seems to accept the inheritance, especially when exercising it with another. The objection from §. Celsus does not hold, because it speaks only if someone accepts by his pure will by exercising an act of fact, such as possessing hereditary goods, or exercising another act of fact; otherwise, if he exercises both acts simultaneously, namely, of word and of fact, as in our case, for example, when he pays the census and performs an act of fact while asserting himself to be heir. Behold, an act of word. As to this matter, fully noted by Bartolus in l. pacta novissima, C. de pactis. Or, if you wish to speak somewhat more broadly, say as follows.

In the Name of Christ, Amen. Because the matter has been abundantly and profoundly consulted by the aforementioned my lords, most learned doctors of the laws, therefore I briefly dispatch and consider that whenever a protestation is contrary to the act itself, it is then indiscriminately removed by a subsequent contrary act: and thus it depends on the will of many, and even if it has come to the knowledge of the adversary. And so the law speaks with many. §. locatore rei.

† For there the protestation is against the act, because contracts are acts, or matters of counsel, regarding the cause of the insane. He did not protest that he did not wish to be bound, but that he would not accept [the arrangement] with his father, such that he would be liable for the risk; and afterwards he accepted it simply: therefore the protestation is removed, because a subsequent act contrary to it occurred: see the law *pacta nouissima*, C. de pac.; and l. *si mihi*, §. *in legatis*, de leg. 1. Sometimes the protestation is contrary to the effect of the act: because he does not declare that he will not do it, but that he does not wish the act to have effect. And then either the act did not depend solely on the will of the protesting party, but he was bound by necessity to do it: and then the protestation operates for nothing, unless the adversary consents. And thus speaks l. *fi*, §. *item si praedixit*, ff. nautae, caupo, stabu.; l. *fin.* If, however, it depends on the power of the protesting party and of the other, then either he notified the adversary, and removes the effect, as in l. *at si quis*, §. *plerique*, ff. de religiosis; and thus proceeds what is noted by the doctor in the said l. *pacta nouissima*; or he did not notify the adversary, and then it does not avail for a testament. There is also a third case, namely when the act depends on the mere will of the protesting party: and this is our case.

† Concerning which it should be known that certain acts are naturally directed toward acceptance [of an inheritance], because they cannot be performed except by the heir: and then, if he proceeds in favor of a contrary will, or if that act was subsequently performed with another, such as by contracting, or receiving payment, or releasing hereditary debtors, and the like: and then he appears to recede from his protestation, as in l. pro haerede, §. Papin., and there by Bartolus, ff. de acquirenda hereditate; or if he says by his pure will that he accepts: and then he does not appear to recede from the protestation, as in l. qui aliena, §. Celsus, eodem titulo, unless he were to say that he repented of his prior will, as in l. si quis in principio, ff. de testamentis. Or if no protestation preceded: and then he appears to accept, as in Inst. de hereditatibus qualiter et quibus modis differant, §. fin. Certain acts, however, are naturally directed toward another end, and then he does not appear to accept indiscriminately, as in the aforementioned l. pro haerede, §. si quid tamen, at the words “ceterum” and “servos” and “proinde.” Certain acts are indifferent: and this is our case. And then either he proceeds in favor of the will: and then if he performs that act simply, he does not appear to accept, for when an act can be understood in multiple ways, one must adhere to the protestation, Extra de constitutionibus, c. cum M. Ferrariensis; de appellationibus, c. per venerabilem; and noted by the gloss and doctors in l. 1, C. de litis contestatione. Or he acts as heir, or as heir, or asserting himself to be heir: and then the same rule applies as in an act directed toward acceptance: because with that act are joined words inducing acceptance. Since therefore in the case there concurs an act inducing acceptance by words, together with an act of fact exercised with another, acceptance is induced: especially if it was exercised after an interval, notwithstanding a protestation not distinguishing whether the protestation is conceived for the future or not: because by its nature a protestation sounds for the future, as elegantly noted by my lords in the aforementioned l. pacta novissima. What more? As was notably shown above by the first consulting jurists, the said lady, by inhabiting the said house and possessing the hereditary goods, because this act precedes the protestation, to which it is certain that the subsequent protestation extends, appears to have accepted the inheritance, unless she protested to the contrary, as noted by the gloss in l. 1, C. de repudianda hereditate, which did not happen here, because of the protestation. It does not obstruct the foregoing that it is noted in the aforementioned l. pro haerede, §. si quid tamen, because the nature of the thing stands in the way. For on account of the nature of services [operae], which are not owed to anyone other than the patron, unless they fall into the common form of other obligations, as because certainly a son, by claiming them as heir, does not appear to accept, otherwise it would be different, as was shown above. And therefore I conclude, as was concluded above by others, namely that acceptance of the inheritance is induced by an act contrary to the protestation exercised with another, with which is joined the act of words inducing acceptance, as because, asserting himself to be heir, he paid the census.
